Article.Title: Early visual cortex is not functionally necessary for temporal attention: A TMS study
Article.Authors: Lee, H.-H.; Carrasco, M.
Article.Abstract: Temporal attention enhances the selective processing of information at a specific point in time and improves perception. Previous neuroimaging studies investigating its neural mechanisms have either conflated temporal attention with temporal expectation or provided correlational evidence. Thus, whether early visual cortex is functionally necessary for temporal attention remains unknown. Here, we combined psychophysics with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to examine whether V1/V2 are functionally necessary and play a causal role in temporal attention. Observers performed an orientation-discrimination task in which two consecutive stimuli, T1 and T2, were presented in the periphery, preceded by a precue providing either valid or neutral temporal information. Double-pulse TMS was delivered under four conditions: at T1 (T1-TMS), at T2 (T2-TMS), at both T1 and T2 (both-TMS), or not at all (none-TMS), to assess its effects on temporal attention and the efficacy of the stimulation was verified by pupil size analysis. Behavioral results revealed robust temporal attention benefits on d', reaction time, and the Balanced Integration Score (BIS) across all four TMS conditions, indicating that the benefits of temporal attention were unaffected by occipital TMS. Furthermore, pupil dilation was largest in the both-TMS condition, followed by the T1-TMS and T2-TMS conditions, and smallest in the none-TMS condition, providing physiological verification of the stimulation protocol. Together, these findings reveal the first causal evidence that the early visual cortex is not functionally necessary for endogenous temporal attention.

Article.Title: Novel Tau Interaction Partners as Potential Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets in Neurodegenerative Diseases
Article.Authors: Pichlerova, K.; Sinsky, J.; Njemoga, S.; Skrabana, R.; Polak, A.; Kotasek, M.; Majerova, P.; Cente, M.; Matyasova, K.; Hanes, J.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimers disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder leading to cognitive decline and ultimately death. One of the main hallmarks of this disease is the accumulation of pathological tau protein into neurofibrillary tangles. To better understand these pathological mechanisms, it is essential to characterize the tau protein interactome in health and disease. In this study, we performed a yeast two-hybrid screening using a human brain cDNA library, from which we identified 15 novel tau-interacting proteins that bind to full-length human tau, or its fragments: the N-terminus, microtubule-binding domain, or C-terminus. We subsequently validated these novel interactions using in vitro co-immunoprecipitation and colocalization assays with both physiological and pathological tau isoforms. Furthermore, their interactions with the human tau protein were analyzed using surface plasmon resonance. Finally, an in silico interactome analysis of these newly discovered tau-binding partners revealed several additional interactors that can link them to downstream processes critical to neurodegenerative pathways Our findings offer fresh insights into tau biology and highlight novel targets for therapeutic intervention and biomarker development.

Article.Title: Mapping the brain-web morphology to characterise ageing and cognitive impairment
Article.Authors: Kitaura, F.-S.; Carnero-Rosell, A.; Sosa Ysalguez, J. L.; Anido Pereiro, D.; Sinigaglia, F.; Janssen, N.; Maselli, A.; Pereda, E.; Huertas Company, M.
Article.Abstract: Ageing reshapes human brain anatomy across spatial scales, yet its geometrical organisation remains difficult to quantify. Here we introduce SHARP (Spectral Hierarchy Analysis, Reconstruction and Prediction), which transfers hierarchical cosmic-web classification to structural MRI, identifying knots, filaments, sheets and voids at four spectral levels and combining their morphology with higher-order spatial statistics and anatomical measurements. In CamCAN, selected filament- and sheet-associated features show opposing correlations with age and distinct associations with subcortical and ventricular volumes. To quantify their contribution, we compare SHARP with a neural-network baseline combining 36 regional anatomical measurements, total brain volume and sex. Adding cosmologically motivated descriptors reduces the mean absolute error of MRI-only age prediction from 6.04 to 4.71 years (22%) in CamCAN and from 4.57 to 4.07 years (11%) in OASIS-3 under participant-independent validation. Brain-web morphology with only brain volume and sex already achieves 5.12 years in CamCAN. For cognitive-status classification in OASIS-3, SHARP identifies 85% of Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-positive observations at 86% specificity, compared with 78% sensitivity for the anatomical baseline at matched empirical specificity. These results demonstrate that cosmological methods provide complementary geometrical information and measurable gains in characterising brain ageing and cognitive impairment.

Article.Title: Disentanglement of persistent and dynamic neural substrates of working memory
Article.Authors: Abbasi, A.; Nanda, A.; Dang, W.; Singh, B.; Wang, Z.; Constantinidis, C.; Rubinov, M.
Article.Abstract: Competing theories of working memory have alternatively emphasized the importance of persistent and dynamic substrates of this cognitive function. Here, we directly tested these theories by computationally isolating the contributions of persistent and dynamic activity to working memory. We analyzed neuronal population activity recordings in macaques doing match/non-match working memory tasks. We first extracted signatures of persistent and dynamic activity through cue-specific temporal means, temporal principal components, and correlations of activity patterns across task epochs. We then generated synthetic data constrained by these signatures, and decoded cue stimuli from these data, separately from persistent and non-persistent neurons. We found that high decoding performance arose from a nuanced interplay of persistent and dynamic activity. Specifically, we could decode stimuli at empirical or above-chance levels across all tasks only from persistent neurons, but only after constraining correlations of activity patterns across epochs. In this way, we showed distinct roles for persistent and dynamic neuronal activity that help to unify two competing theories of working memory. More broadly, we also advanced computational controlled experiments as a principled framework for adjudicating between competing models of neuronal population activity.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: working memory; persistent activity; neural population activity; stimulus decoding

Article.Title: Testing and training geometrical knowledge in baboons through a conceptual categorization task
Article.Authors: Dighiero-Becht, T.; Ciccione, L.; Sable-Meyer, M.; Fagot, J.; Claidiere, N.; Dehaene, S.
Article.Abstract: Sensitivity to geometric regularity has been proposed as a signature of human cognitive singularity. Baboons can detect an intruder shape among quadrilaterals but, unlike humans, show no advantage for regular shapes such as squares and rectangles, suggesting they are not sensitive to geometric regularity. Here we asked whether, with symbolic training, baboons may show an enhanced attention to geometric features and their compositions. Using a symbolic match-to-sample task with frequent introduction of new generalization stimuli, we trained baboons and human controls to categorize stimuli as representing a given concept (A) or not (not-A) across two non-geometric domains (image category and line color) and three geometric domains (line perpendicularity, parallelism, and length equality). Baboons learned to perform above chance with all categories and generalize them to novel positive and negative exemplars (except for length equality). These findings provide evidence that baboons can extract geometric properties and associate them to arbitrary symbols. Crucially, this explicit geometry training did not result in the emergence of human-like performance in the quadrilateral intruder task: overall performance improved uniformly across shapes, but the geometric regularity effect failed to emerge. Thus, in baboons, recognizing individual geometric properties is insufficient to trigger the compositional perception of shapes that characterizes human cognition.

Article.Title: Projection-specific filtering of delta-theta input by layer 5 neurons in mouse secondary visual cortex
Article.Authors: Takemoto, H.; Ye, Z.; Rancz, E. A.
Article.Abstract: Delta- and theta-band oscillations are thought to coordinate cortical activity and to convey top-down signals, but how the different output neurons of a cortical area transform such rhythmic input is less well understood. Layer 5 contains two projection classes, extratelencephalic (ET) and intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, which carry different information to different targets. Here we asked whether they also differ in how they process slow rhythmic input in the delta-theta range. We combined whole-cell recordings in three stimulus regimes in mouse medial secondary visual cortex (V2M) with local field potential (LFP) recordings in awake mice. With small inputs, IT cells summated strongly and acted as low-pass filters, whereas ET cells resonated at low frequencies, forming moderate-resonance (ET1, about 3 Hz) and high-resonance (ET2, about 5 Hz) subgroups. With large inputs, ET cells amplified depolarisation more than hyperpolarisation, at similar resonance frequencies. When driven to fire by a 4 Hz sinusoid at threshold, cells of all classes fired at a similar phase and kept it nearly constant across cycles. In awake mice, visual stimulation increased deep-layer LFP power across about 1-6 Hz, a band that spans the mean ET1 and ET2 resonance frequencies. Thus, the two output classes of layer 5 in V2M filter slow rhythmic input differently, but once firing, they show no detectable difference in spike timing.

Article.Title: Serotonin Reuptake Inhibition Reduces NMDAR-Associated Reward Liability Without Compromising Rapid Antidepressant Efficacy
Article.Authors: Pan, L.; Wang, G.; Ji, J.; Cai, Y.; Pang, Y.; Chen, Y.; Lu, Q.; Tang, X.; Hu, Z.; Zheng, B.; Xiang, Y.; Hou, Q.; Nie, K.; zhao, j.; Hu, T.; He, Y.; Zhang, Y.; Shen, V.; Zhu, W.; Aisa, H. A.; Tian, G.; Shen, J.
Article.Abstract: Ketamine has changed the treatment landscape for depression by providing rapid antidepressant effects, yet its clinical utility remains limited by psychotomimetic effects and abuse potential. It remains unclear whether rapid antidepressant efficacy can be dissociated from mesolimbic dopamine activation and its associated reward-related effects. Here, we show that the serotonin reuptake inhibitor escitalopram, by enhancing serotonergic signaling, attenuates S-ketamine-induced dopamine (DA) release in the nucleus accumbens (NAc). Inspired by this finding, we designed and evaluated VV147 by incorporating SERT inhibition into NMDAR antagonism to reduce the reward-related liability of NMDAR blockade. Unlike S-ketamine, VV147 did not increase NAc dopamine signaling but retained rapid antidepressant effects in chronic stress models of depression. Together, these findings suggest a potential dissociation between rapid antidepressant efficacy and acute dopamine activation, providing a possible strategy for developing rapid-acting antidepressants with reduced dopamine-related reward effects.

Article.Title: The mouse midbrain periaqueductal gray is organized into target-specific output populations
Article.Authors: Strosche, A.; Tamaki, A.; Mader, J. N.; De Biasi, E. S.; Stempel, A. V.
Article.Abstract: How brains select between behaviours and coordinate their execution is a central question in neuroscience. The vertebrate periaqueductal gray (PAG) controls a remarkable range of instinctive behaviours, from escape and freezing to hunting, vocalization, and micturition. Its columnar organization, the classical framework for mapping these functions, cannot explain how one region controls so many, often mutually exclusive, behaviours. To determine how PAG output is organized, we generated a whole-brain, column- and cell-type-specific synaptic projection atlas of the mouse PAG, showing distinct dorsal and ventral outputs and dense within-PAG connectivity. Retrograde tracing from four motor-related target regions identified segregated PAG populations, biased towards, but not confined to, individual columns. Channelrhodopsin-2-assisted circuit mapping showed that one such population, projecting to the cuneiform nucleus, provides substantial local collaterals, positioned to shape ongoing PAG activity. These findings uncover a modular output architecture that extends the columnar framework, offering a circuit logic for how one brain region produces diverse behaviours.

Article.Title: Transcriptomic and Metabolomic Analysis of the Caudate and Putamen in ADHD
Article.Authors: Patel, R.; Wang, S.; Deshmukh, E.; Fajen, S.; Williams, J.
Article.Abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly heritable, heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder that typically manifests in childhood; however, transcriptomic studies have inadequately accounted for age of onset and subtype, with cohorts largely comprising of adults. To address this gap, we established a stringently phenotyped ADHD cohort (up to 19 years; clinically diagnosed combined and inattentive-type ADHD) and integrated postmortem caudate and putamen bulk RNA-seq, LC-MS metabolomics, MEGENA gene co-expression analysis, and cross-study comparison. We identified 279 up- and 35 downregulated DEGs in the caudate and 110 up- and 89 downregulated DEGs in the putamen. The combined caudate-putamen metabolomic analysis revealed dopamine dysregulation (1.68-fold reduction) and dysregulation of four additional metabolites. Enrichment analysis revealed shared molecular signatures involving immune responses, ATP metabolism and calcium ion-dependent signaling, with region-specific differences in the direction of alteration. Neuronal homeostasis, and protein stress showed suppression in the putamen, along with activation of neurotransmitter reuptake, whereas CSF circulation and ECM organization were activated in the caudate, with suppression in CNS myelination, and signs of ventricular perturbations. MEGENA identified 26 ADHD-associated caudate modules and 33 putamen modules. These modules captured canonical synaptic and neuronal-circuitry pathways alongside cellular differentiation, metabolism, and cell-survival processes. FGD1 emerged as a candidate caudate hub gene among the neuronal modules. Cross-study comparison analysis suggested that molecular alterations in ADHD may be age-dependent. Additionally, assessing levels of 76 potential risk genes identified by a large ADHD GWAS study one ARTN exhibited dysregulated levels in putamen and none in caudate. Together, these findings reveal brain-region-specific molecular dysregulation in ADHD across pathways extending beyond canonical neurotransmission to immune, differentiation, and energy-metabolic processes, along with novel evidence of perturbations in the understudied lateral ventricles.

Article.Title: Ogg1 regulates context-dependent glial states in Alzheimer's disease
Article.Authors: Abentung, A.; Sakshaug, T.; Schnur, P.; Egiazarian, M.; Damiao, C.; Aakre, K.; Obermann, T.; Sousa, M.; Kunath, N.; Bjoras, M.; Scheffler, K.
Article.Abstract: Oxidative DNA damage is an early hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), but whether Ogg1, a key enzyme in oxidative DNA repair, contributes to disease pathogenesis remains unclear. Here, we show that Ogg1 exerts opposing effects under physiological and disease conditions. Ogg1 deficiency impaired memory and induced glial transcriptional alterations under physiological conditions, whereas in APP/PS1 mice it improved memory, reduced amyloid burden and attenuated AD-associated glial remodeling. These effects occurred without changes in global 8-oxo-dG levels and were accompanied by changes in chromatin accessibility and gene expression, supporting a non-canonical role for Ogg1 in transcriptional regulation. Single-nucleus transcriptomics revealed strong transcriptional responses to Ogg1 deficiency across all major glial cell types and showed that Ogg1-dependent glial transcriptional programs are strongly conserved in human AD. These findings identify Ogg1 as a context-dependent regulator of glial cell states and reveal an unexpected role in AD-associated glial remodeling.

Article.Title: Automatic orofacial behaviors remap within cortical substrates for voluntary motor control in freely moving primates
Article.Authors: Ferretti, E.; Ferrara, F.; Ismaiel, E.; Lanzarini, F.; Palagi, E.; Maranesi, M.; Bonini, L.
Article.Abstract: Orofacial behaviors, like yawning and emotional facial expressions, involve phylogenetically conserved subcortical circuits. Yet, their context-dependent modulation in primates suggests overlooked cortical contributions. Here, we wirelessly recorded from 640 ventral motor and premotor sites in two freely moving macaques during spontaneous orofacial actions combining automatic and voluntary components to varying degrees (yawning, threat, bite, drink). We identified coupling between synaptic input (local field potential) and spiking output in 169 spatially distributed sites during yawning, while threat display was sparsely represented. Yawn-related sites exhibited an early beta-band suppression followed by high-gamma power enhancement. Of 401 isolated single neurons, 95 (predominantly putative medium-sized pyramidal cells) encoded yawning, mostly together with voluntary biting and drinking actions. No modulation was found during the observation of yawning by conspecifics. Yawn-related units either switched or maintained their mouth opening/closing tuning across yawning and more voluntary actions, suggesting counteracting and synergistic downstream influences on yawning motor control. In contrast, threat-related units predominantly preserved their opening/closing tuning during biting and drinking. Head-free intracortical microstimulation of sites hosting yawn-related units preferentially evoked localized mouth and face movements, supporting their causal role in orofacial motor control. Finally, projecting neural activity into a low-dimensional manifold showed that voluntarily controlled and largely automatic behaviors engaged distinct population dynamics while preserving the discriminability of individual orofacial displays. These findings reveal that cortical substrates of voluntary motor control can be recruited to shape otherwise automatic orofacial displays.

Article.Title: Visual capture of the head-direction signal in a rat model of Fragile X Syndrome
Article.Authors: Duszkiewicz, A. J.; Rastedt, A. A.; Vadher, A.; Wood, E. R.; Peyrache, A.; Dudchenko, P. A.
Article.Abstract: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is a common inherited monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability (ASD/ID), conditions frequently associated with altered sensory processing and multisensory integration. However, the circuit mechanisms underlying these alterations remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the integration of visual and self-motion information in the head-direction (HD) system in a rat model of FXS (Fmr1-/y rats). Using high-density silicon probes, we recorded neuronal activity in the postsubiculum (PoSub), a cortical hub of the HD system, while adult Fmr1-/y and wild-type (WT) rats experienced repeated rotations of a visual landmark. In WT rats, the HD signal only partially followed landmark rotations, consistent with weighted integration of visual and self-motion information, and visual landmark control progressively weakened across repeated cue conflicts. In contrast, the HD signal in Fmr1-/y rats closely followed landmark rotations and failed to show experience-dependent recalibration. This enhanced visual capture was accompanied by reduced angular head velocity tuning in PoSub neurons, indicating weakened representation of self-motion information. Together, these findings reveal an altered balance between visual and self-motion inputs to the HD system in a rat model of FXS and identify a possible circuit-level mechanism through which sensory integration of vision and self-motion may be disrupted in ASD/ID.

Article.Title: A Common Recognition Architecture Across Memory Scales
Article.Authors: Zhao, C.; Kim, A.; Horwitz, S.; Adekoya, T.; K. Vogel, E.
Article.Abstract: Recognition decisions occur across memory episodes that vary vastly in scale, from compact single-item episodes to extended experiences involving hundreds of items. To test how memory scale shapes the neural mechanisms underlying old/new judgments, we recorded EEG while participants performed a recognition memory task across set sizes ranging from 1 to 128 items (spanning 2 to 256 recognition judgments). Classic electrophysiological signatures of recognition, including frontal and parietal old/new effects, persisted continuously across set sizes. Furthermore, multivariate neural classifiers trained on small memory scales generalized robustly across set sizes. Rather than revealing distinct neural formats, increasing memory scale produced systematic, continuous shifts in the timing and strength of a shared recognition response: signals emerged progressively later and weaker at larger memory scales. Temporal-alignment and cross-correlation analyses demonstrated that responses across scales followed a common waveform trajectory, with timing shifts propagating into motor response preparation. Finally, individual difference analyses revealed that this common recognition format exhibits scale-dependent behavioral relevance, tracking working-memory capacity at smaller scales and long-term memory performance at larger scales. Together, these findings demonstrate that recognition signals share a common neural format across scale while changing dynamically in timing, strength, and behavioral relevance, providing evidence for convergence onto a shared recognition architecture.

Article.Title: Bayesian Modeling of Context-Specific Goal-Directed and Habitual Control in Sequential Decision Making
Article.Authors: Hieke, W.; Schwoebel, S.; Hranova, S.; Pietsch, A.; Kiebel, S. J.; Smolka, M. N.
Article.Abstract: It is an open question how context-specific habits develop alongside goal-directed planning. We examined action sequence repetition, contingency change, and context switching using a three-step optimization task with interleaved planning and habit contexts. During an initial acquisition phase, optimal sequences varied in the planning context but remained constant in the habit context. When contingencies changed, the original habit sequence became suboptimal and another became optimal. Action sequence repetition improved response speed and optimal-choice performance in the habit context relative to the planning context. Following the contingency change, both advantages initially reversed. Optimal-choice performance in the habit context subsequently recovered but did not significantly exceed that in the planning context, while responses remained slower in the habit context. Context switches reduced optimal-choice performance in both directions, with additional slowing when switching from habit to planning. The Bayesian contextual control model captured choice patterns through learned action sequence priors, goal-directed evaluation, and context inference. Allowing a context-stability bias to vary across participants did not improve model performance. These findings suggest that sequence repetition facilitates performance under stable contingencies while impairing adaptation to change.

Article.Title: Pre-synaptic facilitation of corticospinal output improves dexterity and finemotor control after stroke
Article.Authors: Damiani, A.; Macellari, N.; Xu, Z.; Liang, L. T.; Jezerc, C.; Tang, L. W.; Jones, K.; Uribe, M.; Goswami, C.; Hoffmann, K. A.; Simpson, T.; Grigsby, E. M.; Naddeo, I.; Gerszten, P.; Capogrosso, M.; Gonzalez-Martinez, J. A.; Pirondini, E.
Article.Abstract: The corticospinal tract (CST) is a neural pathway that supports skilled use of the arm and hand. Lesions of corticospinal axons result in muscle weakness, deficits of gross motor function, and loss of proximal and distal dexterous control for which effective treatments are still lacking. Here we exploited excitatory connections from motor thalamus to primary motor cortex to potentiate surviving descending signals and restore volitional arm and hand control in three monkeys with corticospinal tract lesion, using deep brain stimulation. Stimulation targeted to thalamocortical projections facilitated upper-limb movements, enabling monkeys with arm and hand paralysis to perform unconstrained 3D reach and fine dexterous tasks. Stimulation improved strength, hand gross motor function, and digits control. Electrophysiology suggested that effects were mediated by and more effective when targeting fibers with monosynaptic connection to the corticospinal motoneurons. Stimulation was delivered in continuous with FDA-clinically approved parameters holding realistic promises of clinical translation.

Article.Title: Human medial frontal neurons represent integrated semantic content and sensory evidence to inform decision-making
Article.Authors: Aquino, T. G.; Riveland, R. G.; Kim, R.; Mamelak, A.; Reed, C.; Pouget, A.; Rutishauser, U.; Rungratsameetaweemana, N.
Article.Abstract: Humans can reconfigure how they act on the world from a single verbal instruction. Central to this capacity is the ability to represent what an instruction specifies and to bring that content to bear on incoming sensory evidence. However, little is known about where in the human brain instruction content is encoded, how it combines with sensory evidence to produce a choice, and how this integration relates to behavior. Here, we characterized single-neuron and population responses recorded in the ventral temporal cortex, medial temporal lobe, medial frontal cortex and ventromedial prefrontal cortex of neurosurgical patients performing a verbal instruction task. On each trial, a written instruction specified which stimulus feature was relevant and whether the correct response was to choose or to reject the stimulus that best matched it, so that the same image pair required opposite responses under different instructions. Only medial frontal populations jointly encoded the instructed task, and the target feature, whereas ventral temporal populations encoded stimulus features along axes that generalized across instruction conditions. Choice representation emerged first in ventromedial prefrontal and then in medial frontal cortex during stimulus presentation, before a motor response could be prepared. Shuffling instruction content selectively degraded prediction of medial frontal population activity, whereas shuffling stimulus identity selectively degraded ventral temporal activity. To ask how these representations could be computed, we trained a vision-language model with separable visual and linguistic streams converging on a recurrent decision module to perform the same task. Its visual embeddings predicted held-out ventral temporal activity and its recurrent activations revealed a task solution space that predicted medial frontal activity, and the strength of this alignment tracked behavioral accuracy. These results identify a cortical hierarchy in which medial frontal circuitry represents the content of verbal goals and acts on a ventral temporal substrate whose representational axes remain stable, and indicate that functional hierarchies discovered in artificial networks can serve as predictive models of human neural circuitry.

Article.Title: First-in-class -PET radiotracers for GPR39: A platform for noninvasive target engagement imaging in vivo
Article.Authors: Bhoopal, B.; Fitzgerald, R. W.; Gollapelli, K.; Miller, M.; Damuka, N.; Baity, C.; Roy, P.; Myburgh, P.; Zhou, D.; Jadiya, P.; Cerevera-Juanes, R.; Solingapuram Sai, K. K.
Article.Abstract: Disrupted zinc homeostasis is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. As a key zinc-sensing receptor, GPR39, a G protein-coupled receptor implicated in neurodegeneration, vascular regulation, and neuropsychiatric disorders, represents an emerging target for molecular imaging. However, the lack of suitable positron emission tomography (PET) radiotracers has limited the in vivo characterization of GPR39. Quantitative assessment of GPR39 in vivo could improve our understanding of its role in physiology and disease and facilitate the development and evaluation of targeted therapeutics. Here, we introduce [18F]GPR39 2.1 as a PET radiotracer for specific imaging of GPR39. [18F]GPR39 2.1 exhibited excellent serum stability with negligible radiometabolite formation. In vitro cell uptake studies demonstrated a 55-70% reduction in tracer uptake following pharmacological blockade. PET imaging showed rapid brain uptake, efficient blood-brain barrier penetration, and gradual washout. Blockade studies in rats demonstrated significant reductions in brain uptake of up to approximately 90% (p<0.0001) across multiple brain regions. GPR39 specificity was further validated in GPR39 knockout mice, which showed 76% (p<0.002) and 90% (p<0.0002) reductions in brain uptake by PET imaging and biodistribution, respectively. Moreover, 5xFAD transgenic mice exhibited significantly lower brain uptake by PET imaging (40%, p<0.0002) and biodistribution (77%, p<0.002), indicating sensitivity of [18F]GPR39 2.1 to disease-associated alterations in GPR39. Biodistribution studies demonstrated favorable pharmacokinetics, while autoradiography further confirmed GPR39-specific binding, consistent with the PET and biodistribution findings. Collectively, these results establish [18F]GPR39 2.1 as a stable, brain-penetrant, and highly specific PET radiotracer for noninvasive imaging of GPR39 in vivo. This work provides a translational framework for investigating GPR39 biology and supports the development of GPR39 as an imaging and therapeutic target in neurological and systemic diseases associated with GPR39 dysregulation.

Article.Title: Midbrain neurons regulate the production of courtship squeaks in female mice
Article.Authors: Zheng, D.-J.; Henderson, R. J.; Ziobro, P.; Zhou, Z.; Tschida, K. A.
Article.Abstract: Animals produce different vocalization types (e.g., contact calls, mating calls) to communicate in different behavioral contexts, but how the brain is organized to enable the production of different vocalization types remains poorly understood. Recent work found that specialized neurons in the midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) regulate the production of ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) in female and male mice, but these PAG-USV neurons are not required for the production of broadband vocalizations (squeaks). To identify PAG neurons that may regulate the production of squeaks, we used an activity-dependent labeling strategy (TRAP2) to identify and manipulate PAG neurons that are active in association with the production of courtship squeaks in female mice. Optogenetic activation of courtship squeak-TRAPed PAG neurons elicits the production of squeaks, while ablation of TRAPed PAG neurons blocks the production of courtship squeaks without altering female non-vocal courtship behaviors. Surprisingly, ablation of courtship squeak-TRAPed PAG neurons did not affect the production of footshock-elicited squeaks. Moreover, non-selective PAG ablation, which blocked the production of courtship squeaks in females and USVs in both sexes, attenuated but did not block the production of footshock-elicited squeaks. Our results identify a population of PAG neurons that critically regulates the production of courtship squeaks in female mice and also suggest that a non-canonical, PAG-independent pathway regulates the production of pain-elicited vocalizations.

Article.Title: Replicable Connectivity and Spectral Alterations of Functional Networks in Major Depression
Article.Authors: Baker, B. T.; Sridhar, M.; Calhoun, V.
Article.Abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is usually characterized in functional MRI through connectivity alone, often in samples too small to resolve its modest effects. Here we applied multi-scale, template-guided independent component analysis to resting-state data from the multi-site MDD-DIRECT cohort and jointly examined the connectivity, spectral content and spatial composition of 105 intrinsic brain networks. Differences between patients and controls were widespread, small and structured: cerebello-subcortical coupling was reduced, subcortical--somatomotor coupling was increased, and spectral power shifted from lower to higher frequencies, most prominently in the thalamus, which also showed the most altered connectivity. Spatial composition differed in every network examined. In a smaller independent cohort, the direction of effect agreed for 95% of significant connections, 78% of significant spectral effects and 77% of the largest spatial-composition effects. Depression therefore alters several distinct properties of intrinsic networks, consistently across cohorts and most prominently in the thalamus.

Article.Title: Quantifying Excitation-Inhibition Harmony and Its Breakdown during Epileptogenesis in a Spiking Neural Network of the Hippocampal CA1
Article.Authors: Kim, S.-Y.; Lim, W.
Article.Abstract: Epileptogenesis is often linked to disruptions in excitation-inhibition (E-I) balance, yet its quantitative characterization remains limited. Understanding and quantifying this E-I balance could enable earlier diagnosis and targeted treatment of epilepsy. We investigate competitive E-I harmony and its breakdown using a biologically grounded spiking neural network model of hippocampal CA1 that incorporates two structural pathological mechanisms: pyramidal cell (PC) axonal sprouting and loss of inhibitory interneurons. As recurrent excitatory connectivity increases via PC axonal sprouting or inhibitory interneuron populations decline through interneuron loss, the network undergoes sequential transitions from a healthy phase (HP) to an interictal pathological phase (IIP) and finally to an ictal pathological phase (IP). At the input level, we introduce the competition degree, Cd (= SE / SI), as the ratio of the strengths of excitatory (SE) to inhibitory (SI) synaptic inputs to PCs, to quantify their competitive E-I harmony. As an input-side indicator, Cd remains near 2.6 in HP, exhibits a discontinuous, abrupt jump to ~ 60 at the HP [->] IIP transition and rises further thereafter. At the output level, the corresponding output-side measure, the population-averaged mean firing rate (MFR) of PCs, < fi(PC) >, also exhibits a discontinuous, abrupt jump from ~ 4 to ~ 200 Hz at the HP [->] IIP transition and rises further thereafter, indicating progressive pathological hyperexcitability. Together, these results establish a cause-and-effect framework linking the input-side indicator Cd (cause) to the output-side measure < fi(PC) > (effect). Accordingly, Cd may serve as a potential quantitative biomarker of competitive E-I harmony and its breakdown, providing a computational causal framework that links structural pathological mechanisms to epileptogenic state transitions and offering potential for translation into diagnostic tools and therapeutic applications.

Article.Title: An anatomical and day-night atlas links cochlear immunity to adjacent bone marrow
Article.Authors: Wang, H.; Yeong, J.; Cai, Y.; Mo, Y.; Tian, Y.; Chen, W.; Zeng, D.; Ning, H.; Xu, Y.; Dai, S.; Liu, X.; He, R.; Liu, H.; Huang, J.; Hao, J.; Ni, Y.; Tian, C.
Article.Abstract: The cochlea lies within marrow-bearing bone. How this neighbouring marrow relates to cochlear immunity and daily physiology remains poorly resolved. We profiled 160,643 cells from mouse cochlea and adjacent temporal-bone marrow at six times of day, with rhythm inference calibrated for one pooled sample per time. Three-dimensional confocal reconstruction mapped vascular connections between marrow and cochlea and localized neutrophils along this interface. Neutrophils also occupied healthy cochlear fluids. Parabiosis findings were consistent with a local marrow contribution to cochlear immunity. Structural cochlear cells maintained synchronized, light-entrained clocks. Cochlear neutrophil programmes aligned with circulating neutrophils and opposed those in marrow, with independent flow cytometry supporting daily changes in immune composition and CXCR4. A shared night-associated heat-shock programme was attenuated after noise in an independent cohort. These anatomical and temporal data provide a reference for testing local marrow supply and the origins of cochlear immune rhythms.

Article.Title: Targeting distinct neuronal populations with AAV vectors reveals neurogenesis-associated anxiolytic effects of JNK inhibition
Article.Authors: Jokela, A.; Tiwari, N.; Flinkman, D.; Abyari, S.; Deshpande, P.; John, J. M.; Coffey, E.
Article.Abstract: c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) regulates stress responses and affective behaviour, but the neural populations mediating these effects remain unclear. Here, we delivered a nucleus-targeted JNK inhibitor to the mouse brain using blood-brain barrier-crossing adeno-associated virus vectors with distinct cellular tropisms. JNK inhibition produced strikingly different behavioural outcomes depending on the neuronal populations targeted. Only AAV-PHP.eB-hSyn1-mediated delivery reproduced the previously reported anxiolytic phenotype, whereas AAV.CAP-B10-hSyn1 increased locomotor activity and depressive-like behaviour and AAV.CAP-B10-mDlx reduced locomotion while enhancing object recognition memory. The anxiolytic response was accompanied by reduced hilar mossy cell abundance and an approximately two-fold increase in doublecortin-positive newborn granule neurons in the dentate gyrus. Notably, this phenotype mirrors our previous findings following selective JNK inhibition in adult hippocampal progenitor cells, implicating the neurogenic niche as a convergent substrate for anxiolytic responses to JNK inhibition. Proteomic analysis of plasma extracellular vesicles revealed widespread alterations in metabolic and inflammatory proteins upon JNK inhibition, despite neuron-restricted transgene expression. Together, these findings demonstrate that the behavioural and systemic consequences of JNK inhibition depend critically on the neural populations targeted and identify hippocampal neurogenesis-associated circuits involving mossy cells as candidate mediators of JNK-dependent anxiety regulation.

Article.Title: Changes in anterior cingulate connectivity associated with response to antidepressant treatment for major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Lam, C. S. T.; Kuhn, M.; Borchers, L. R.; Ren, B.; Woronko, S. E.; Li, M.; Zhang, E. M.; Brennan, B. P.; Vitaliano, G.; Lees, T.; Bogdanov, M.; Daskalakis, N. P.; Ressler, K. J.; Zhukovsky, P.; Pizzagalli, D. A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) involving the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the hippocampal formation has been implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD) and antidepressant response. However, it remains unclear whether connectivity changes in distinct ACC subdivisions and hippocampal formation reflect general antidepressant effects or are specifically associated with clinical improvement. Methods: Forty-one, unmedicated adults with MDD underwent functional MRI before and after 8 weeks of sertraline or bupropion treatment. Seed-based rsFC analyses examined subgenual ACC (sgACC), pregenual ACC (pgACC), dorsal ACC (dACC), and hippocampal formation connectivity. Linear mixed-effects models tested whether connectivity change was associated with treatment response, remission, and dimensional improvement in depressive symptoms. Results: Thirty individuals (73.2%) responded to treatment and 26 (63.4%) achieved remission. Overall, rsFC decreased pre- to post-treatment between (1) dACC and pgACC (but not sgACC and hippocampal formation) and (2) cortical regions primarily involving default mode and frontoparietal networks. When considering treatment response, differences in sgACC and pgACC connectivity with temporal and inferior frontal regions emerged (increased in responders vs. decreased in non-responders). Remission was similarly associated with increased sgACC connectivity with temporal and prefrontal regions, and increased sgACC connectivity with temporal cortical regions related to greater reductions in depressive symptoms. Conclusions: Antidepressant treatment was associated with distinct patterns of ACC connectivity change, with general reductions in dorsal and pregenual connectivity but increases in subgenual and pregenual connectivity associated with favorable clinical outcomes. Findings suggest that changes in sgACC/pgACC connectivity are particularly relevant to antidepressant treatment response. Article.Title: Distinguishing evidence accumulation from choice confidence in neural signatures of perceptual decision making
Article.Authors: Monakhovych, D.; Grogan, J. P.; Kelly, S. P.; O'Connell, R. G.
Article.Abstract: Human electrophysiology research has identified the centro-parietal positivity (CPP) as an apparent neural correlate of sensory evidence accumulation during perceptual decision-making. The CPP has also been shown to closely scale with subjective confidence. Coupled with the fact of its domain-generality and lack of choice selectivity, this observation raises the possibility that the CPP might in fact trace subjective confidence rather than cumulative evidence, two quantities that are closely correlated in most experiments. To disentangle confidence from cumulative evidence, we used predictive cues with 80% validity to manipulate prior expectations of participants during a contrast discrimination task while recording electroencephalography (EEG). At the time of decision termination, confidence is expected to reach a higher level for validly cued versus invalidly cued choices, whereas the opposite would be expected of a cumulative evidence signal due to biased decision starting points. As expected, valid cues led to faster, more accurate and more confident responses compared to invalid and neutral cues. At the neural level, cues produced systematic increases in preparation of the expected action prior to evidence onset as indexed by premotor mu/beta activity, consistent with cue-biased criterion adjustments. The pre-response CPP amplitude was significantly reduced for validly cued choices and the effect remained even when matching for confidence. Together these findings suggest that the CPP is not a direct read-out of subjective confidence, but an evidence accumulation signal that contributes to both decision formation and confidence estimation.

Article.Title: Mapping and longitudinal imaging of potentiated synapses in the mouse hippocampus using SynActive-eGRASP
Article.Authors: Latini, F. C.; Jacob, A.; Mirzapourdelavar, H.; Cattaneo, A.; Attardo, A.; Mainardi, M.
Article.Abstract: Identifying individual synapses that undergo long-term potentiation following learning at specific circuits remains a major challenge in neuroscience. To address this problem, we developed SA-eGRASP, a genetically encoded reporter that combines SynActive (SA) targeting with enhanced GFP Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners (eGRASP). SA drives the expression of the postsynaptic half of eGRASP at potentiated spines via the 5' and 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of the immediate-early gene Arc, thus enabling selective labeling of individual synapses that are both structurally connected and have undergone potentiation through transsynaptic GFP reconstitution. Here, we validated SA-eGRASP and combined it with high-resolution optical imaging to generate a detailed map of hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapses subjected to potentiation following contextual fear conditioning in mice. The high signal-to-noise ratio of SA-eGRASP, allowed us to track individual potentiated dendritic spines over the course of several days, to investigate the long-term dynamics of CA3-CA1 potentiated dendritic spines, and to study the selective potentiation of a subset of spines upon experience. SA-eGRASP paves the way to the investigation of synaptic engrams by enabling longitudinal, circuit-specific investigation of synapses potentiated during learning in mice performing naturalistic behaviors.

Article.Title: Precon_all: A species-agnostic automated pipeline for non-human cortical surface reconstruction
Article.Authors: Benn, R. A.; Xu, T.; Mars, R. B.; Boch, M.; Roumazeilles, L.; Heuer, K.; Toro, R.; Margulies, D. S.; Manzano-Patron, J. P.; Montesinos, P.; Galan-Arriola, C.; Lopez-Martin, G.; Sanchez-Gonzalez, J.; Duff, E. P.; Ibanez, B.
Article.Abstract: Cortical surface reconstruction has transformed the study of brain morphology and cortical geometry in human neuroimaging. Here we present precon_all, an open-source structural imaging pipeline that generalizes reconstruction of the neocortical surface to multiple species. Adopting a modular framework that mirrors FreeSurfer's recon-all in humans, precon_all produces surfaces for non-human species compatible with FreeSurfer and Connectome Workbench. Precon_all reduces the dependencies of surface reconstruction to an image with T1-like contrast and five user-defined masks. This removes the dependence on species-specific atlases and tissue priors, and in turn extends surface reconstruction to species where these resources do not yet exist. The pipeline supports a wide range of imaging conditions, including in-vivo and post-mortem data, and has thus far been used to reconstruct the cortical geometry of primates, carnivores, and ungulates across multiple sites, spanning both highly gyrified and lissencephalic brains. Precon_all can be automated for high-throughput processing, and its template construction module can build surface-based common spaces to enable group-level analysis of cortical morphometry in new species. In short, precon_all is a flexible, modular pipeline that enables the comparative neuroimaging community to study brain evolution through cortical geometry in an ever-growing number of species.

Article.Title: A Neurocompliant Ionic Conductive Hydrogel Orchestrates Glial and Vascular Remodeling to Mitigate Traumatic Brain Injury
Article.Authors: Okoro, P. D.; Jaberi, R.; Blackburn, S.; Patel, D.; Halasah, N.; Mapa, J.; Shih, M.; Botzbach, R.; Tan, J.; Vullev, V. I.; Liu, H.; Santhakumar, V.; Noshadi, I.
Article.Abstract: Developing conductive scaffolds for neural regeneration is often hindered by the cytotoxicity and mechanical mismatch inherent to conventional electronic fillers. Here, we report an ultrasoft ionically conductive hydrogel engineered by grafting choline-based bioionic liquids (BIL) onto fish gelatin (FiBGel). Systematic optimization yields brain-mimetic conductivity (0.25-0.68 S/m), elastic moduli (0.6-0.9 kPa), and physiological water content (72-81%). In 3D culture, the matrix drives spontaneous neurogenesis, achieving ~90% MAP2+ neurons with robust calcium signaling, while concurrently supporting endothelial network formation. We report the first intracerebral administration of a BIL hydrogel, demonstrating remarkable biocompatibility and immunomodulation. In a traumatic brain injury model, a single FiBGel dose halves reactive astrogliosis, enhances cortical revascularization, and limits lesion cavity expansion. Leveraging an FDA-recognized micronutrient, FiBGel offers a translatable strategy that integrates neuromechanics, conductivity, immune modulation, and vascular support within one injectable scaffold for minimally invasive treatment of brain injuries.

Article.Title: One placement, many fields: robust voxel-wise mapping with multichannel TMS
Article.Authors: Numssen, O.; Qiu, R.; Souza, V.; Laine, M.; Matsuda, R. H.; Buchberger, L.; Martin, C. W.; Scherf, N.; Weise, K.; Knoesche, T. R.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the human brain at the individual level is central to understanding its function and a prerequisite for personalized therapy. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can map structure-function relationships at high resolution by regressing trial-wise variation in the TMS-induced electric field (E-field) against a response such as motor evoked potentials (MEPs). This requires distinct E-fields across pulses at different cortical locations, which single-coil TMS (sTMS) achieves by physically repositioning the coil (typically supported by neuronavigation software such as InVesalius Navigator; Souza et al., 2018)--increasingly reliant on robotic guidance and capped by the coil geometry. Multichannel TMS (mTMS) instead steers the E-field electronically via independent currents in several coils, opening a design space of high variability without physical repositioning. We adapt determinant-based sequence optimization from discrete sTMS coil-placement sets to the continuous mTMS current space (D-optimal design), identifying pulse sequences whose induced cortical E-fields are as mutually dissimilar as biophysical constraints allow. We benchmarked optimized mTMS sequences against random baselines and optimized sTMS placements in virtual motor mapping across multiple head models, assessing three mTMS array geometries (5-channel planar, 6- and 12-channel spherical), two figure-of-eight sTMS coils, and varying pulse counts, response noise, and cortical depth. D-optimal mTMS currents substantially outperformed random currents and optimized sTMS at matched pulse counts. The gain was modest without noise but increased significantly with it: at the highest noise level, optimized sTMS failed to converge after 100 pulses (~20-22 mm error), whereas all mTMS arrays reached median errors at or below 6 mm. mTMS also recovered deep targets better than sTMS (up to 35 mm skin-cortex distance, versus 25 mm) and performed uniformly across the region of interest. A coil-space scheme based only on the magnetic vector potential, precomputable once per array without per-subject MRI, captured most of the benefit, matching subject-specific optimization at 100 pulses. mTMS thus makes voxel-wise mapping robust throughout a region of interest without coil repositioning.

Article.Title: Ergodic breakdown of brain dynamics under chronnectome complexity across cognitive states and age
Article.Authors: Kazemivash, B.; Zhu, D.
Article.Abstract: Chronnectome complexity, the extent to which time-varying functional connectivity follows a structured sequence of distinct configurations, contributes to shaping large-scale brain dynamics. However, it remains unclear how this complexity influences the encoding of information that distinguishes resting state and task conditions. In ergodic theory, time averages represent ensemble behavior under ergodicity, which breaks down when dynamics are non-stationary, as when activity moves sequentially between distinct regimes. We hypothesize that this information resides in time-averaged connectivity under lower-complexity conditions but in trajectory geometry under higher-complexity conditions, where brain activity traverses distinct configurations over time, consistent with ergodic breakdown, which we term the \textit{information migration principle}. We formulate this as dynamics-driven multi-class classification and introduce the Brain Dynamics Classifier (BDC), an interpretable data-driven mechanistic model in which a graph neural network embeds dynamic functional connectivity into a latent space and a neural ordinary differential equation learns the vector field governing trajectories through that space. The proposed model derives two complementary representations within a single learned dynamical system, capturing time-averaged connectivity, which is sufficient under ergodic dynamics, and trajectory geometry, which preserves the temporal organization obscured by averaging under non-ergodic dynamics. Our results show high classification accuracy, $97.4\%$ for eight conditions in the Human Connectome Project young adult cohort and $92.2\%$ for four in the aging cohort. To test the information migration principle, we ablated the time-averaged representation and found that trajectory contributions varied with chronnectome complexity, from high for Working Memory to absent for Relational Reasoning, consistent with ergodic breakdown. Including subcortical regions further increased trajectory contributions for affective conditions. In aging, the distinction between higher and lower complexity conditions was preserved, resting-state dynamics became less ergodic with advancing age, and higher fluid intelligence was associated with more ergodic resting-state dynamics.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction is Part of a Novel Mechanism for Chemotherapy-Induced Neuropathic Pain
Article.Authors: Sakas, R.; Abu-Ata, S.; Nakhleh-Francis, Y.; Abd Elkarim, N.; Kotiyal, A.; Politte, H.; Awad-Igbaria, Y.; F. Soustiel, J.; Palzur, E.
Article.Abstract: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is a common, persistent complication of cancer treatment, yet the mechanisms sustaining pain remain unclear. Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in chronic pain, but its role in spinal cord dysfunction after chemotherapy, and whether it can be reversed, is unknown. Paclitaxel also increased susceptibility to mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP)-induction, lowering calcium retention capacity at 3, 8, and 13 days after the last injection. Acute ex-vivo paclitaxel exposure had a similar effect, and cyclosporin A, an mPTP blocker, significantly reversed it. Consistent with a causal role for mitochondrial impairment, hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT), initiated after allodynia developed, improved oxygen consumption and {Psi}m and progressively enhanced mechanical thresholds. Likewise, intrathecal delivery of healthy mitochondria to the spinal cord attenuated established allodynia in paclitaxel-treated rats and reduced mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity in other pain models, sciatic nerve crush and capsaicin. These findings identify persistent spinal mitochondrial dysfunction and increased mPTP susceptibility as features of CIPN and support mitochondrial protection as a therapeutic strategy for CIPN and other pain conditions.

Article.Title: Identifying a neurochemical signature of the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus that predicts individual variability in cue-reward learning
Article.Authors: Flagel, S. B.; Ramos, B. A.; Chakrabarty, S.; Cain, C. N.; Levina, E.; Kennedy, R. T.
Article.Abstract: To investigate neurochemical factors that may confer vulnerability to psychiatric disorders, we used an animal model that captures a transdiagnostically relevant neurobehavioral endophenotype. A subset of rats, sign trackers, also attribute incentive motivational value to the lever cue. Relative to non sign trackers, STs are more impulsive, have attentional deficits, and show greater reinstatement of drug seeking behavior. The paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus is a key neural node implicated in these individual differences. We combined in vivo microdialysis with liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry to quantify 22 neurobiologically relevant small molecules in the PVT before and 24 hours after Pavlovian training. Before training, glucose concentrations in the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus were higher in rats subsequently classified as sign trackers than in non sign trackers and were correlated with the Pavlovian conditioned approach index used to phenotype the rats. Glucose concentrations decreased after training, and the magnitude of change differed between phenotypes. Multivariate regression identified baseline neurochemical profiles in the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus associated with subsequent Pavlovian conditioned approach behavior. These findings identify a candidate PVT neurochemical signature that precedes behavioral phenotyping and may mark the propensity to sign track, providing insight into potential mechanisms underlying vulnerability to psychiatric disorders characterized by maladaptive cue motivated behavior.

Article.Title: Allele-agnostic KCNH1 suppression rescues gain-of-function developmental epileptic encephalopathy
Article.Authors: Chi, W.; Corbett, E. E.; Thompson, C. H.; Simkin, D.; Adil, H.; Hawkins, N. A.; Callow, N. A.; Barse, L.; George, A. L.; Kearney, J. A.; Kiskinis, E.
Article.Abstract: Gain-of-function variants in KCNH1, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv10.1, cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) characterized by seizures, developmental delay and intellectual disability. While pathogenic variants enhance channel activity, loss of KCNH1 is tolerated in humans and mice, suggesting that allele-agnostic gene suppression may represent a viable therapeutic strategy. Neurons carrying the pathogenic KCNH1 variants I494V or G375R exhibited a shared phenotype characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential and abnormalities in neuronal network activity despite largely preserved intrinsic firing properties. ASOs efficiently reduced KCNH1 expression without disrupting network activity in control neurons. In contrast, ASO treatment normalized network dysfunction across both mutant genotypes, demonstrating that distinct KCNH1 gain-of-function variants converge on a reversible disease state. To assess the efficacy of ASOs in vivo, we generated a new Kcnh1-R357Q knock-in mouse model that exhibited profound seizures and early mortality. A single ASO treatment reduced seizure burden significantly and restored survival to near-normal levels. Together, these findings establish KCNH1 suppression as a precision therapeutic strategy for KCNH1-related DEEs and provide a framework for treating gain-of-function epilepsies in which partial gene reduction is clinically tolerated.

Article.Title: Elementary Dynamics of Neural Microcircuits
Article.Authors: Masserini, S.; Kempter, R.
Article.Abstract: In neural circuits with multiple excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) cell types, qualitatively new dynamics arise when one population is silenced by the others, an effect linear theories cannot capture. Using threshold-linear networks, the simplest nonlinear population model, we derive closed-form conditions for multistability, oscillations, and paradoxical responses across microcircuits. In E-I circuits, strengthening E$\rightarrow$I rather than I$\rightarrow$E connections controls runaway excitation without silencing E cells. In a canonical neocortical circuit, two distinct gamma-oscillation mechanisms reproduce optogenetic silencing experiments, reconciling conflicting models. In hippocampal E-I-I circuits, cross-inhibition determines whether transitions between gamma rhythms are gradual, abrupt, or non-oscillatory. Two E populations or assemblies can cooperate, compete, or suppress each other depending on cross- versus self-excitation. Balanced inhibition prevents competition between E-I assemblies, unless I$\rightarrow$I connections are more assembly-specific than I$\rightarrow$E ones, a condition automatically met by somatostatin-positive interneurons, which lack mutual inhibition. Lateral inhibition yields winner-take-all dynamics even without assemblies. These testable conditions link connectivity to dynamics across brain areas.

Article.Title: Allele-selective knockdown of mutant DNAJB6 improves molecular features in a primary mouse myotube model of LGMDD1
Article.Authors: Vohra, A.; Haller, M.; Paing, M. M.; Dam, A. B. L.; Daw, J. A.; Bengoechea, R.; Pittman, S. K.; Wang, T.-Y.; Yuede, C. M.; Miller, T. M.; True, H. L.; Harper, S. Q.; Chou, T.-F.; Weihl, C. C.; Findlay, A. R.
Article.Abstract: Dominant variants in DNAJB6 cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy D1 (LGMDD1), a progressive myopathy associated with disrupted protein homeostasis. Because complete loss of DNAJB6 is embryonic lethal in mice, we evaluated allele-selective knockdown as a strategy to reduce mutant DNAJB6 while preserving wild-type protein. We generated a knock-in mouse carrying an N-terminal 3xFLAG tag on the wild-type Dnajb6 allele, allowing endogenous wild-type and F90I DNAJB6, the murine equivalent of human F89I, to be measured within the same sample. Flag-LGMDD1 mice recapitulated the functional, myopathological, and biochemical features seen in other LGMDD1 models and in human disease. F90I DNAJB6 was more abundant and degraded more slowly than wild-type DNAJB6, and LGMDD1 muscle and primary myotubes showed altered protein handling at baseline and following proteostatic stress. Comparative proteomic analyses identified DNAJA4 as a candidate marker responsive to pathogenic DNAJB6 activity. A two-stage mismatch screen identified a lead candidate siRNA with 264-fold selectivity for F90I DNAJB6. In primary Flag-LGMDD1 myotubes, this siRNA selectively reduced F90I DNAJB6 and shifted several baseline and stress-dependent molecular abnormalities involving p62, HSP70, DNAJA4, and markers associated with unfolded protein response signaling toward control values. These findings establish cellular proof of concept for allele-selective knockdown in LGMDD1.

Article.Title: I err, therefore I am: Neural signature of error-monitoring predicts self-awareness in infants
Article.Authors: Gal, C. G.; Askitis, D.; Begus, K.
Article.Abstract: Self-reflection is central to human cognition and arguably a defining feature of human consciousness, yet the mechanisms enabling our mind to reflect upon itself and to construct a sense of self are unclear. Specifically, whether metacognition implies self-awareness, is independent of it, or emerges because of it, remains a subject of debate, fuelled by reports of metacognitive-like behaviour in preverbal infants and non-human animals. Building on evidence that 12-month-old infants show neural signatures of internal error-monitoring, we follow infants longitudinally from 12 to 18 months, when infants first start exhibiting evidence of a conceptual self-representation. Using a gaze-contingent match-to-sample paradigm with concurrent eye-tracking and EEG, we confirm that infants exhibit a neural signature of internal error-monitoring (error-related negativity, ERN) after making an incorrect decision (saccadic eye-movement) and before receiving visual feedback. Critically, we find that ERN at 12 months developmentally predicts which of the infants will evidence self-representation (mirror self-recognition) six months later. Infants' self-recognition was predicted specifically by internal error-monitoring, and not by external feedback-monitoring (FRN), nor by infants' age or general development. Moreover, we show that only infants who later self-recognised adjusted their behaviour post-error, by slowing their decisions and increasing visual exploration. Thus, internal error-detection, if available, can be utilised for online adjustments in information-seeking and decision-making as early as 12 months of age. These converging neural and behavioural findings support the idea that, rather than presupposing a self, early metacognition may be functionally involved in building conceptual self-awareness in humans.

Article.Title: Variable errors suppress implicit motor adaptation among older adults
Article.Authors: Zhou, Y.; Andrews, I.; Sang, A. F.; Torres, J. M.; Kim, O. A.
Article.Abstract: Age-related changes in motor control networks manifest in a highly task-dependent manner. Although older adults can display enhanced implicit sensorimotor adaptation, this effect is inconsistent across perturbation types (e.g., visuomotor vs. force-field perturbations). Because these perturbations induce different errors to drive learning, their distinct effects on learning suggest that specific properties of the error signal modulate the extent of adaptation among older adults. Here, we investigated whether age-related hyper-adaptation is modulated by error variability. More specifically, we manipulated the consistency of error direction during an error-clamp visuomotor adaptation task in both younger and older adults. While consistent errors elicited enhanced implicit adaptation in older adults relative to younger controls, variable errors did not. These findings reveal that error consistency is a critical prerequisite for age-related enhancements in implicit motor learning. Rather than exhibiting unconstrained hyper-adaptation, older adults maintain an adaptive error-sensitivity mechanism that prevents hyper-recruitment of implicit systems in noisy motor environments.

Article.Title: Comparing apples to oranges from photoreceptors to inferior temporal cortex through neural manifolds
Article.Authors: Xu, Y. G.; Maruya, A.; Conway, B.; Zaidi, Q.
Article.Abstract: In the neural processing of color, cone photoreceptor outputs are combined over successive stages to form inferior temporal cortex (IT) cells with narrower color tuning and more diverse peak preferences. To understand the benefits of these transformations, we explored the capability of photoreceptor, retinal ganglion cell and IT population responses to distinguish between pairs of natural fruits and vegetables, based solely on their color distributions extracted from hyperspectral images. Simulations with realistic Poisson response variability show that linear separations are possible for many more pairs by IT neurons. Shapes of low-dimensional manifolds extracted from neural population responses explain the improvement.

Article.Title: A caudate-centered network for alexithymia derived from patients with brain tumors
Article.Authors: McMahon, J. T.; Healey, M. R.; Sanchez-Gama, Y.; Campanella, F.; Skrap, M.; Ferguson, M. A.
Article.Abstract: Alexithymia is a trait characterized by impaired emotional awareness. Previous accounts examining the neurobiological underpinnings of this trait have centered on a variety of structures, and alexithymia-causing lesions occur in disparate locations. We use lesion network mapping to derive a neural circuit for alexithymia. In a neurosurgical cohort of 45 patients with gliomas (19 female; aged 18-75 years), we compute each lesion's connectivity to the rest of the brain using a normative connectome (n = 1,000) and relate these connectivity maps to preoperative Toronto Alexithymia Scale scores using permutation testing. Lesions associated with higher alexithymia are connected to a common network that includes the bilateral caudate heads (right greater than left) and the anterior cingulate cortex, peaking in the right caudate head (family-wise error-corrected p < 0.05). The network converges with coordinates from an independent meta-analysis of gray matter volume in alexithymia (13 of 14 coordinates positive; p = 0.0004). Of the three subscales, difficulty identifying feelings localized to this network. Within the striatum, the network spans the executive and limbic subdivisions. These findings suggest a caudate-centered circuit, at the interface of affective and executive systems, that unifies disparate lesion locations.

Article.Title: Linking Covariates to State Durations in Dynamic Brain Networks via Hidden Semi-Markov Models
Article.Authors: Shappell, H.; Lindquist, M.
Article.Abstract: Hidden semi-Markov models (HSMMs) provide a flexible framework for studying dynamic functional connectivity because they represent brain activity as transitions between latent network states with explicit dwell time distributions. Although dwell times are often associated with behavioral and demographic variables, these associations are typically assessed only after model fitting using indirect group comparisons, limiting formal covariate modeling and the simultaneous inclusion of multiple predictors. In this work, we extend the HSMM framework by introducing covariate-dependent dwell time distributions through a regression-based formulation, allowing expected state duration to vary with subject-level covariates and enabling direct inference on how these factors relate to state persistence. Model parameters are estimated with an expectation-maximization algorithm, and uncertainty in the dwell-time regression coefficients is quantified using a subject-level nonparametric bootstrap. In simulations, the proposed model accurately recovered covariate effects under both shifted-Poisson and Gamma dwell time specifications, with low bias and variability. We applied the method to resting-state fMRI data from 1,000 UK Biobank participants and found that age and sex were associated with dwell times in a subset of brain states. Together, these results show that modeling dwell-time behavior directly provides a more flexible framework for studying individual differences in brain dynamics, revealing not only which states occur, but also how long individuals remain in them.

Article.Title: Mu opioid receptor expression by nucleus accumbens inhibitory interneurons promotes affiliative social behavior
Article.Authors: Toddes, C.; Swanson, J. L.; Lefevre, E. M.; Retzlaff, C. L.; Cunitz, L. B.; Girdwood, U. C. H.; Zugschwert, L.; Khan, S.; Myhre, E.; Gauthier, E. A.; Fernandez de Velasco, E. M.; Kieffer, B. L.; Rothwell, P. E.
Article.Abstract: Mu opioid receptors in the nucleus accumbens regulate motivated behavior, including pursuit of natural rewards like social interaction as well as sensitivity to exogenous opioids. However, the specific circuit elements where mu opioid receptor expression promotes these motivated behaviors remain unclear. In mice of both sexes, we used a suite of genetic and viral strategies to conditionally delete mu opioid receptor expression from major neuron types in the nucleus accumbens, as well as monosynaptic inputs to this brain region. We pinpointed local inhibitory interneurons as an essential site of mu opioid receptor expression for typical social behavior. Mu opioid receptor deletion from inhibitory interneurons decreased both social interaction and preference, while shifting the ratio between synaptic excitation and inhibition onto medium spiny projection neurons, but did not alter exogenous opioid sensitivity. Conversely, mu opioid receptor deletion from medium spiny neurons altered exogenous opioid sensitivity but not social interaction, revealing a double-dissociation in the behavioral functions of mu opioid receptors expressed by nucleus accumbens projection neurons versus interneurons. Chemogenetic activation of inhibitory interneurons in the nucleus accumbens also decreased social interaction, mimicking the effect of mu opioid receptor deletion from these cells. Our findings suggest that circuit-specific engagement of mu opioid receptors could circumvent the risk of misuse associated with conventional exogenous opioids, with important implications for the pathophysiology and treatment of neuropsychiatric conditions involving social differences.

Article.Title: Electrophysiological Dynamics of Default Network Suppression
Article.Authors: Sun, W.; Libowitz, M. R.; Cowan, R. L.; Tobel, T.; Du, J.; Feldman, D. A.; Davis, T. S.; King, J. B.; Rahimpour, S.; Smith, E. H.; Buckner, R. L.; Shofty, B.
Article.Abstract: Distributed brain networks compete with one another in the service of information processing. One dramatic example is antagonism between networks that support internally directed cognition, often collectively referred to as the default network, and networks that orient to external events and drive action. Here we combined within-individual precision functional neuroimaging and intracranial electrophysiology to investigate network competition at high spatiotemporal resolution. In six patients, robust antagonism between networks was established during a target detection task. Network-assigned electrophysiological recordings displayed concordant responses, including in single-neuron firing rates, and further revealed the temporal dynamics of network competition. Networks involved in salience detection and action planning showed early, transient responses that peaked near the participant response. Default network suppression occurred later, reflected in decreases in high-frequency broadband activity and in single-neuron firing rates in response to targets. Examining subcortical regions revealed rapid activity increases in the thalamus and posterior hippocampus aligned to the participant response. Critically, a late evolving, sustained suppression was observed throughout the hippocampus. These findings suggest that, across cortical and subcortical regions, network competition is temporally layered. Furthermore, the hippocampus can be dissociated along its long axis during competition. Such push-pull antagonism may be fundamental to advanced human cognition, and its disruption may underlie mental illness.

Article.Title: Sensory experience-induced plasticity of somatostatin interneurons occurs through two-pore potassium (K2P) channels
Article.Authors: Bohannon, B. M.; Alonso, N. L.; Walker, M. G.; Wang, M.; Kaimaktchiev, K.; Yang, C.; Feldman, D.
Article.Abstract: GABAergic interneurons (INs) are powerful modulators of plasticity and learning in cortical networks, but plasticity of INs themselves is not well understood. We studied experience-dependent plasticity in somatostatin (SST) INs, which critically regulate dendritic integration, sensory tuning, and plasticity in pyramidal neurons in sensory cortex. Whether SST INs exhibit experience-dependent plasticity, and by what mechanisms, is unknown. We found that 3 days of whisker deprivation strongly downregulated intrinsic excitability of SST INs in L2/3 of somatosensory cortex, by reducing input resistance. Deprivation also increased mEPSCs onto SST INs. The reduction in intrinsic excitability was caused by an increase in leak potassium current through two-pore K+ (K2P) channels, without changes in HCN, KV1, or KV7 currents, which contribute to plasticity in other IN types and brain areas. Immunohistochemistry showed an increase in TRESK, but not other K2P channels, indicating a novel role for K2P channels in experience-dependent plasticity of interneuron excitability.

Article.Title: A cross-frequency architecture links biological and behavioral periodicities
Article.Authors: Criscuolo, A.; Liu, T.; Schwartze, M.; Kotz, S. A.
Article.Abstract: Spontaneous behaviors, e.g., walking and speaking, are thought to rely on an internal sense of time that provides a scaffold for precise temporal coordination. Yet endogenous rates of many behavioral processes often diverge from arbitrarily defined unit of objective time, raising a fundamental question: what temporal reference frame coordinates behavior? Using high temporal resolution multimodal recordings, we show that endogenous body-brain periodicities (including pupil fluctuations, saccadic eye movements, respiration, cardiac activity and neural oscillations) as well as spontaneous behaviors such as tapping, walking, and speaking, form a cross-frequency architecture organized as an arithmetic progression in a natural logarithmic frequency space. Successive rates are spaced by about {varphi} (golden ratio {approx} 1.618 1), while the ratio between rhythm classes are captured by e (e {approx} 2.72 2). The absence of power law scaling and harmonic anchoring to individual heart rates excluded the possibility that the frequency architecture scales to, and depends uniquely on, a single pacemaker. Rather, the irrational scaling suggests each rate to be principally independent and maximally de-coupled from others, yet capable to dynamically engage in cross-frequency interactions. We propose that the body-brain frequency architecture may provide an emergent temporal reference frame to scaffold perception and action.

Article.Title: Sex Differences in Human Subcortical Anatomy are Robust and Replicable in Adulthood, Already Evident Prepubertally, and Aligned with Sex Chromosomal and Gonadal Influences
Article.Authors: Lee, H. M.; Liu, S.; Lalonde, F.; Clasen, L.; Guma, E.; DeCasien, A.; Moraczewski, D.; Thomas, A. G.; Lerch, J. P.; Devenyi, G. A.; Chakravarty, M.; Berman, K. F.; Delaney, A.; Raznahan, A.
Article.Abstract: The existence and mechanistic bases of sex effects on human subcortical anatomy remain unclear. To address these gaps, we combined structural neuroimaging of sex differences in subcortical volume and shape across three independent cohorts (combined N=2,886) with neuroimaging maps of sex chromosomal and endocrine effects from three clinical cohorts (combined N=313, including sex chromosome aneuploidies and isolated gonadotropin-releasing hormone deficiency). We found that human subcortical anatomy shows focal sex differences of moderate-strong effect size during young adulthood (male-biased surface area overlying lateral/ventral putamen and pallidum, nucleus accumbens, ventral posterior complex of thalamus, anterior hippocampus, and medial and central nuclei of amygdala; female-biased surface area overlying caudate head, posterior/dorsal pallidum, mediodorsal, lateral dorsal, lateral geniculate, and medial geniculate nuclei of thalamus, posterior hippocampus, and basolateral and lateral nuclei of amygdala). These regional sex differences show strong within-sample reproducibility at modest sample sizes (N[≥]200) and are replicable in a fully independent mid-adulthood cohort. Strikingly, we find that the topography of adult subcortical sex differences is already established by pre/early puberty (age 9 years), and the same holds for cortical sex differences. Comparison with neuroimaging data from rare disorder cohorts reveals that subcortical sex differences show a statistically significant spatial and directional congruence with the anatomical effects of X-chromosome dosage in the striatum and effects of testicular hormones in the amygdala. Together, these findings provide a reference map for the fine-grained spatial patterning of sex differences in adult subcortical shape, demonstrating its replicability, establishment before pubertal progression, and spatial concordance with potentially causal sex chromosomal and gonadal effects.
