Article.Title: Preemptive SOD1 Silencing via Neonatal Intramuscular AAV Therapy Modifies Disease Trajectory in an ALS Mouse Model
Article.Authors: Gong, X.; Xie, Y.; Wei, H.; Wang, Q.; Wu, J.; Bian, Z.; Wang, W.; Xu, T.
Article.Abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and fatal neurodegenerative disorder with limited therapeutic options. A major challenge for developing effective therapies is the safe and efficient delivery of genetic cargo to the spinal motor neurons that degenerate in the disease. This is particularly pertinent for SOD1-linked familial ALS, where gene silencing approaches are promising but remain constrained by suboptimal delivery. Here, we establish a gene delivery platform that overcomes this barrier by combining the retrograde transport of rAAV2-retro with an artificial miRNA to achieve pan-spinal SOD1 silencing. A single intramuscular injection of rAAV2-retro-miRNA into neonatal SOD1G93A mice achieved widespread transduction of spinal motor neurons, significant reduction of mutant SOD1 protein, and conferred multifaceted therapeutic benefits. Treated mice exhibited delayed disease onset, extended lifespan, preserved motor function, reduced neuroinflammation, and protection of neuromuscular junctions and spinal motor neurons. These findings establish the rAAV2-retro-miRNA platform as a versatile and efficient tool for spinal motor neuron-targeted gene silencing, addressing the delivery challenge and providing a foundation for further development in motor neuron diseases.

Article.Title: High-throughput light-sheet 3D microscopy of whole rodent brain microstructure for integration with MRI
Article.Authors: Hanmer, J. M.; D'Antonio, F.; Assimopoulos, S.; Manzano-Patron, J.-P.; Wood, S. C.; Tachrount, M.; Shen, Q.; Craig, M.; Lai, C.; Hickman, G. J.; Radfar, E.; Chisholm, K. I.; Farr, T. D.; Jasanoff, A.; Hoerder-Suabedissen, A.; Molnar, Z.; Ligneul, C.; Tisca, C.; Jbabdi, S.; Howard, A. F. D.; Miller, K. L.; de Guzman, E.; Lerch, J. P.; Sotiropoulos, S. N.
Article.Abstract: Whole-brain cellular mapping is essential for understanding how differences in cellular architecture shape brain organisation and function. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides whole-brain coverage in humans and animal models but is only indirectly sensitive to cellular features. Integrating MRI with whole-brain microscopy is therefore critical for interpreting existing microstructural MRI measures and developing more specific ones. Here, we present a scalable cross-resolution framework integrating 3D light-sheet microscopy (LSM) of intact rodent brains with diffusion MRI (dMRI). By combining active tissue clearing and immunolabelling with accelerated LSM acquisitions, we achieve multiplexed whole-brain mapping of neuronal and glial populations on timescales comparable to conventional histology and 2D microscopy. This throughput enables LSM and MRI integration at scale, linking macroscopic MRI contrasts to spatially-matched microscopic cellular features within the same tissue. We apply this framework across eight genetically diverse mouse strains to develop predictive models of 3D microscopy-derived cellular features from dMRI contrasts. We demonstrate that data-driven combinations of state-of-the-art multi-shell dMRI measures predict neuronal and astrocytic features better than individual contrasts, across all animals. Our approach enables 3D microscopy to guide the development and interpretation of biologically-specific microstructural MRI measures, with the potential for translation to the living human brain.

Article.Title: Shared experimental materials inflate and reorder cross-participant decoding benchmarks
Article.Authors: Cui, H.; Zhu, Y.; Huang, S.; Xu, T.
Article.Abstract: Decoding mental states from brain activity underpins brain-computer interfaces and cognitive neuroscience. Decoders are judged by how well they generalize to people left out of training, taken as evidence that they capture what transfers between brains. However, most benchmarks present the same experimental materials to every participant, so held-out participants are tested on materials the model has already seen. Here we show, across 15 EEG, fMRI and eye-tracking datasets and 318 matched comparisons, that shared materials inflate cross-participant accuracy by up to 46 percentage points. They also reorder methods, reversing the advantage of foundation models over handcrafted features on the largest emotion EEG benchmark. The inflation tracks cross-participant item identifiability and, in sealed prospective tests, vanished where items could not be identified. Adding training items improved new-material accuracy more reliably than adding participants. These findings call for reporting new-material accuracy alongside conventional scores and for measuring item identifiability first.

Article.Title: Widespread oscillatory suppression in autism persists in the absence of psychotropic medication.
Article.Authors: Amorim, A. K. J.; Alves, G. M.; Pontes, G. C. L.; Dias, L.; Hondermann, B. M. F.; Silva, M. C. C.; Costa, L.; Ceriatte, C.; Pereira, A.; Brasil, L. M. B. F.; Souza, I. C. N.; Machado, C. L. M. V.; Lima, B.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: Investigate the neural oscillatory activity associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings in children and adolescents. Compare the corresponding oscillatory power between ASD patients taking psychotropic medication with a drug-naive group. Methods: ASD diagnosis was done using DSM-IV and CARS (Childhood Autism Rating Scale). EEG recordings employed 22 scalp electrodes (10/20 system). ASD vs. neurotypical groups were matched for sex and age (5 females; average age: ~10 years old). We analyzed the resting state (eyes open) EEG power spectrum during ~2-minute recordings. The multitaper FFT method was used to estimate spectral power for the delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma frequency bands. We pooled together data from several electrodes to compute comprehensive power spectra and assess the oscillatory behavior of macro brain regions. Results: We observed widespread (~4Hz - 20Hz) oscillatory suppression comprising the theta, alpha and beta frequency bands. The most widespread and robust ASD-associated power suppression was in the high theta and alpha bands. Delta and gamma bands showed no significant power change for any of the brain regions studied. Results from a subgroup of patients (N = 9) who never used psychotropics confirmed these findings, indicating that they are not an artifact of medication. Conclusion: Suppression in theta, alpha and beta oscillations may offer insights into the neurophysiological underpinnings of autism and could be used as an accessible and comprehensive tool in ASD diagnosis, regardless of the patients being or not on medication.

Article.Title: Accessing Mesoscale Functional Organization from Standard Functional MRI Leveraging AI-Based Super-Resolution
Article.Authors: Nasr, S.; Li, H. B.; Zemlyanker, D.; Huber, L.; Rosen, M. S.; Iglesias, J. E.
Article.Abstract: Access to the fine-scale functional organization of the human brain is essential for understanding cognition and neurological disorders yet remains beyond the reach of conventional functional MRI (fMRI) because of its limited spatial resolution and contrast-to-noise ratio. To overcome this limitation, we developed f-LENNS (functional Localization Enhancement via Neural-Net-Sharpening), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework that enhances the effective spatial resolution of reconstructed fMRI magnitude images. The model was trained exclusively on high-resolution synthetic MRI data using extensive domain randomization and no adversarial or generative components. This approach enables robust out-of-the-box generalization (without retraining) to experimental datasets obtained with diverse acquisitions, while effectively curbing hallucination. Our experiments show that our publicly available model substantially improves the spatial fidelity of functional activation maps across multiple imaging paradigms and generalizes to a cohort of individuals with atypical brain function caused by amblyopia (lazy eye). F-LENNS consistently outperforms conventional resolution enhancement approaches, including interpolation-based upsampling and sharpening methods. These findings demonstrate that AI-driven super-resolution combined with domain randomization can overcome domain shifts arising from differences in MRI acquisition, enabling scalable, fine-scale functional brain mapping with widely available MRI hardware.

Article.Title: Rab10 and Arhgef7 interact to promote axon extension by linking vesicle supply and exocytosis
Article.Authors: Olocco, F.; Bekker, E.; Ravindran, P.; Pietralla, T.; Puschel, A. W.
Article.Abstract: The formation of functional neural circuits begins with the extension of a single axon by immature neurons. Axon elongation requires an expansion of the plasma membrane that depends on the polarization of vesicle trafficking and exocytosis. It is not completely understood how the increased transport of vesicles into the growing axon is linked to their subsequent insertion into the plasma membrane. An analysis of early stages of neuronal differentiation indicates that an asymmetry in neurite length precedes axon specification and the accumulation of PPVs in the nascent axon. We show that increasing the transport of vesicles in unpolarized neurons is sufficient to promote the extension of additional axons. The link between vesicle transport and exocytosis is mediated by the interaction of Rab10 with Arhgef7. Rab10 stimulates Arhgef7 activity on PPVs as a GEF for Cdc42b to promote axon extension through exocyst-dependent exocytosis, suggesting that their interaction links the increased supply of PPVs to their exocytosis.

Article.Title: Geometric Kinematics of Human Eyes
Article.Authors: Turski, J.
Article.Abstract: In previous studies by the author on binocular vision with the asymmetric eye (AE), which models a healthy human eye with misaligned optical components, the results were primarily presented in the Rodrigues' vector (RV) framework and supported by simulations and 3D visualizations in GeoGebra's dynamic geometry environment. In this paper, the novel geometric kinematics of the human eye, that is, the eye with misaligned optics, and simplified assumptions about the eye rotations (the eye's translational movements are disregarded), are developed within the framework of rigid-body rotations. The originality of the analysis lies in a precise geometric decomposition of a full rotation of the eye's posture into a torsion-free rotation (the geodesic part) and a torsional rotation (the non-geodesic extension of the geodesic part). This decomposition is extended to the corresponding decomposition of the angular velocity. A novel derivation of the eye's angular velocity from the RV formulation of the eye kinematics is proposed.

Article.Title: SPOUT: An open-source hardware and software platform to study decision making while manipulating and recording from neural activity
Article.Authors: van den Boom, B. J. G.; Dash, D.; Rutherford, M.; Girasole, A. E.; Gorelik, P.; Mazor, O.; Sabatini, B. L.
Article.Abstract: Recording and manipulating brain activity during behavior is critical to understanding the underlying mechanisms of decision-making. Linking neural activity to behavior requires behavioral hardware and software tightly integrated with recording and perturbation systems on a shared clock. We built SPOUT (State-machine Platform for Operant Uni/dual-spout Tasks), an open-source, Teensy-driven state-machine platform with a MATLAB interface that runs 10 unique decision-making tasks (with dozens of variations available through user-friendly settings) to study behavior in head-restrained mice. The platform is built on several custom hardware devices: a dual-lick detector, headplate designs for optogenetics and two-photon calcium imaging, a three-axis motorized spout manipulator, and an optogenetics power modulator. The firmware differentiates between one and two lick spout tasks and can be controlled by a user-friendly interface. Task settings can be selected through the interface or by loading predefined settings files. We validated the clock speed and lick detection against an independent, external acquisition system and identified highly precise, sub-millisecond detection of single licks. Using a pseudo-random synchronization pulse generated by SPOUT, we corrected for missing data due to glitches in the acquisition system and clock drift. We showcase the versatility of SPOUT by training mice on an uninstructed lick-left/lick-right task in which the rewarded side switches unexpectedly and found that mice use history-dependent action-outcome associations to guide future behavior. Transiently inhibiting the anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM) during cue presentation induced contralateral deficits, without affecting ipsilateral trials. Finally, two-photon imaging of ALM neurons revealed stronger population responses during contralateral choice licks compared to ipsilateral ones. Together, SPOUT offers an open-source, affordable platform to study decision-making in head-restrained mice while combining neural recordings and manipulations.

Article.Title: Sex differences in astrocytic reactivity and its association with cognitive decline in cognitively unimpaired older adults
Article.Authors: Reichert Plaska, C.; Jacobs, T.; Bruno, D.; Lee, S. H.; Imbimbo, B. P.; Osorio, R.; Benedet, A. L.; Ashton, N. J.; Zetterberg, H.; Pomara, N.; Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,
Article.Abstract: INTRODUCTION: Astrocyte reactivity may contribute to increased Alzheimers disease (AD) risk in women. Although plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) levels have been reported to be higher in women than in men, few studies have examined sex-specific associations with other plasma AD biomarkers and cognition. The Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) was included as a replication cohort. Higher baseline GFAP was also associated with steeper longitudinal decline in global cognition and episodic memory; however, GFAP x sex x time interactions were not significant. In ADNI, higher baseline GFAP was associated with higher p-Tau217 and NfL levels and with steeper longitudinal decline in global cognition and selected executive and semantic measures, without consistent evidence of sex-specific longitudinal effects. DISCUSSION: Plasma GFAP levels were consistently higher in females across two independent cohorts. GFAP was associated with AD-related blood biomarkers and longitudinal cognitive decline, but sex did not consistently modify these associations. These findings support a role for astrocytic reactivity in early AD-related processes while underscoring the need for further replication of sex-specific effects.

Article.Title: Using wearable EEG to examine age trends in sleep macro- and micro-architecture across adolescence
Article.Authors: Lokhandwala, S.; Cooper, R. E.; Hayes, R.; Sathe, S.; Elder, I.; Corcoran, M.; Horta, B.; Fray-Witzer, M.; Keller, L.; Chan, S.; Franzen, P.; Buysse, D.; Hasler, B. P.; Levenson, J. C.; Wallace, M. L.; Clark, D. B.; Blake, R. G.; Soehner, A.; Jalbrzikowski, M.
Article.Abstract: Adolescence is a period of distinct maturational changes in sleep physiology. Age-related trends in sleep physiology have been captured using laboratory-based polysomnography, a method limited by logistical burden and high cost. Typically developing youth (N=100, 9-26 years) completed 3-4 consecutive nights of at-home sleep recording. These findings highlight the promise of wearable EEG devices for characterizing developmental sleep physiology while underscoring the need for further validation across sleep measures and age groups.

Article.Authors: Lippiello, P.; Hoxha, E.; Cristiano, C.; Pascarella, S.; Volpicelli, F.; Speranza, L.; Cuomo, M.; Ferraro, M. G.; Stanley, A.; Rominto, A. M.; Filiz, K. D.; Liguori, F.; Tropea, D.; Di Angelantonio, S.; Chiariotti, L.; Sulzer, D.; Miniaci, M. C.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: Early-life adversity has been associated with cerebellar abnormalities, but the cellular and circuit-level changes involved and their persistence across development remain poorly understood. In parallel, methylation analysis revealed hypermethylation of the glucocorticoid receptor promoter and reduced cerebellar receptor expression, indicating that early-life stress also engages stress-related epigenetic mechanisms in this region. Importantly, these neurobiological changes were associated with motor coordination deficits, altered stress-coping behavior, and impaired social interaction. Discussion: These findings identify the developing cerebellum as a target of early-life adversity and suggest that disrupted cerebellar maturation may contribute to lasting functional consequences. Article.Authors: Kehnemouyi, Y. M.; Coleman, T. P.
Article.Abstract: The vagus nerve plays a central role in gut--brain communication, yet the physiological dynamics associated with cholinergic vagal signaling remain difficult to characterize non-invasively in humans. Food-related sensory cues increased gastric myoelectric activity as well as swallow and heart rate while eliciting frequency-specific changes in cortical oscillations. Strikingly, anticipation was accompanied by opposing changes in physiological coordination: synchronization within cortical and gastric networks decreased, whereas coupling between the brain and stomach increased. These changes largely returned toward baseline following ingestion, suggesting a distinct anticipatory organization of brain--body activity. Moreover, gastric responses were associated with various aspects of subjective appetite, whereas cortical responses were selectively associated with craving. Both gastric and cortical responses independently explained the variation in participants' self-reported craving. Together, these findings reveal that food anticipation reorganizes physiological coordination within and across central and peripheral systems, establishing the cephalic phase as a non-invasive framework for investigating brain--body interactions associated with cholinergic vagal signaling in humans.

Article.Authors: Nakamura, K.; Kosugi, A.; Nakamichi, R.; Kurimoto, R.; Matsushima, T.; Chiba, T.; Ko, M.; Morita, T.; Yoshii, T.; Seki, K.; Asahara, H.

Article.Title: Decomposing the modulation of interactions between neuronal populations
Article.Authors: Celotto, M.; Sooter, J. S.; Ährlund-Richter, S.; Jenks, K. R.; Sur, M.; Panzeri, S.
Article.Abstract: Identifying, through analysis of large-scale neural recordings, subpopulations of neurons interacting across brain areas is key for understanding across-brain communication with cellular resolution. In simulations, MICs reliably recovers the presence and geometry of ground-truth modulation even in the high-dimensional, low-sample regime. Applied to a benchmark macaque dataset, MICs recovers the geometry and functional form of the stimulus modulation of interactions between primary and secondary visual cortices. Applied to simultaneous calcium imaging of prefrontal axons and interneurons in mouse visual cortex, MICs reveals that behavioral state asymmetrically modulates top-down interactions, reconfiguring the prefrontal projection patterns that interact with a stable set of visual interneurons. Article.Title: The neural circuit implementation of distributional reinforcement learning
Article.Authors: Matias, S.; Rullan Buxo, C.; Xu, S.; Campbell, M. G.; Lowet, A. S.; Lu, X.; Wu, Y.; Schalek, R.; Lichtman, J. W.; Watabe-Uchida, M.; Drugowitsch, J.; Uchida, N.

Article.Authors: Hüppe, L.; Reinhard, N.; Karl, A.; Kirsch, V.; Wollny, L.; Palmer, A.; Rieger, D.; Senthilan, P. R.; Helfrich-Förster, C.
Article.Abstract: Organisms are exposed to predictable daily and seasonal environmental oscillations. Biological clocks enable organisms to anticipate these changes and coordinate physiology and behaviour accordingly. While circadian mechanisms are well studied in terrestrial model organisms, little is known about the neuronal organisation of biological clocks in non-model species, especially those inhabiting marine environments. Article.Abstract: The global signal characteristics of scalp-recorded electroencephalography (EEG) are composed of periodic oscillatory rhythms and aperiodic broadband fluctuations that together comprise the neural power spectrum. Microstates are characterized by a small repertoire of topographic voltage configurations that each reflect the momentary functional state of the cortex, and it is their time-domain dynamics that mathematically constitute periodic and aperiodic spectral features. We isolated and removed the spatial projections of distinct microstate configurations from high-density EEG using orthogonal subspace projection applied to both the surface scalp recordings and their modeled cortical generators to computationally test this dependency. Spectral parameterization of the residual power spectral density revealed that removing these spatial projections strongly attenuated alpha and theta rhythms and features of the aperiodic 1/f background. Furthermore, correlational analyses of microstate temporal dynamics demonstrated that the average duration and temporal persistence of microstates strongly correlate with periodic alpha power, theta power, and the aperiodic 1/f background. Our findings suggest that dominant periodic and aperiodic spectral features are more accurately understood as the frequency-domain expressions of the dynamics of EEG microstates.

Article.Authors: Duan, D.; Wang, Y.; Dai, H.; Zhang, R.
Article.Abstract: Balancing the exploitation of known rewards against the exploration of uncertain options is central to adaptive decision making, yet the cognitive limits on strategic exploration are poorly understood. Directed exploration, the deliberate sampling of uncertain options for information, may depend on working memory (WM), but whether WM capacity (WMC) is selectively related to it, and through which processes, is unknown. 52 participants from the upper and lower tails of an operation-span distribution (26 high-WMC, 26 low-WMC) performed an adapted Horizon Task during EEG recording. We combined behavioral strategy classification, hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement learning, stimulus-locked event-related potentials (ERPs), and an exploratory Bayesian mediation analysis. High-WMC participants showed more directed exploration and less exploitation, with no group difference in random exploration. A model in which accumulated sampling history discounts option value best explained choices in both groups, and the discounting parameter {omega} was larger in the high-WMC group. Statistically, {omega} accounted for the association between WMC and directed exploration (indirect effect ab = 0.64, 95% CrI [0.28, 1.05]). Frontocentral P2 amplitude (180 to 280 ms) during directed exploration was larger in the high-WMC group, and the P2 difference between directed exploration and exploitation correlated with behavioral preference for directed exploration (r = .29, p = .040). These findings suggest that individual differences in exploration may reflect not only the willingness to seek information but also the capacity to use what has been sampled. The WMC-related difference lay in information use rather than choice noise and was already visible in early option evaluation.

Article.Title: Brain Network Dynamics from Neuronal Avalanches for Longitudinal Motor-Imagery Decoding
Article.Authors: Mannino, C.; Longhena, A.; Chavez, M.; Corsi, M.-C.
Article.Abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer opportunities for personalized neurorehabilitation, but inter-session variability, repeated calibration, and the need for expert supervision limit their use beyond supervised settings. We propose a longitudinal BCI framework that integrates neuronal avalanches dynamics, reflecting cascades of propagation neural activity, with graph-theory and data-driven region of interest analysis to extract computationally efficient and neuro-physiological interpretable features. Source-reconstructed EEG from 20 BCI-naive participants performing right-hand motor imagery (MI) and rest across four training sessions was represented by a directed weighted connectivity network based on neuronal avalanches. Local, mesoscopic, and global network measures revealed task-related changes predominantly in contralateral sensorimotor regions and distributed reorganisation across training. We modelled here the learning-related evolution of feature distributions across previous sessions and used this trajectory to predict class-conditional distributions in an unseen fourth session, anticipating future brain states before new session calibration. PageRank-based ROI selection achieved an AUC of 73.5 +/- 7.9%, compared with 64.5 +/- 10.6% using all ROIs, while reducing computational time by approximately 39% relative to performance-driven selection. The proposed framework provides interpretable, compact descriptions of avalanche propagation and exploits training-related changes for prospective decoding. Moving spatial selection and model optimization to an initial offline phase may reduce subsequent calibration demands and facilitate more autonomous BCI use.

Article.Title: NeuroDisco: Interfacing neuronal populations - cell by cell, millisecond by millisecond, day by day
Article.Authors: Adler, C. S.; Schwarz, F.; Kerger, H. Z.; Sreekrishnapurath Variyam, H. P.; Ruschmeyer, T. S.; Bode, L. A.; Preuss, F.; Vogel, J.; Priesemann, V.; Schoenekess, M.; Barbery, J.; Diaz-Maue, L.; Wolf, F.; Schottdorf, M.; Neef, A.
Article.Abstract: Neuronal cultures offer comprehensive access to living networks, but their value as functional models is limited by synchronized bursts that drive pathologically strong neuronal depolarization. Theory attributes such bursting to a lack of external input. Here we present NeuroDiscos, compact {micro}LED and OLED projectors that operate inside standard incubators and deliver patterned, long-term optogenetic stimulation, synchronized with submillisecond precision to multi-electrode array recordings. Weak, uncorrelated NeuroDisco stimulation dispersed the bursts but left the population firing rate largely unchanged. In this asynchronous regime, neuronal activity reproducibly follows the weak stimulation, and stimulus-response relations characterize receptive fields and putative functional connections. At hardware costs of {euro}500-1,000, NeuroDiscos offer a scalable route to functional characterization of primary and patient-derived cultures.

Article.Title: Maternal deprivation impairs social recognition by diminishing the number of adult-born granule cells in the dentate gyrus
Article.Authors: Waters, R. C.; Gore, I. R.; Brown, C. J.; Diethorn, E. J.; Skweres-Gilmartin, A. L.; Gould, E.
Article.Abstract: Childhood neglect increases the likelihood of developing neuropsychiatric disease in adulthood. Maternal separation and early weaning (MSEW), a rodent model of maternal deprivation, was used to investigate effects on social recognition, a commonly impaired function in neuropsychiatric disorders in humans. MSEW male, but not female, mice had diminished numbers of adult-born granule cells (abGCs) in the dentate gyrus, as well as a lower density of abGC axons in the CA2 region compared to controls. MSEW males also showed a reduced rate of sharp wave ripples (SWRs) in the CA2 region in response to novel mouse exposure, as well as a reduction in differential SWR rates in response to novel and familiar mouse exposure. Living in an enriched environment restored the number of abGCs in the dentate gyrus of MSEW males to control levels and improved social recognition. Furthermore, chemogenetic activation of 4-6 week old, but not older, abGCs in a double transgenic model improved social recognition and partially restored CA2 SWR patterns in MSEW mice. These findings suggest that MSEW impairs social recognition through diminished adult neurogenesis, which can be restored in adulthood by living in a proneurogenic environment or by increasing the activity of existing abGCs.

Article.Title: Pupil size reflects effort but not motor fatigability during a sustained motor task
Article.Authors: Imhof, J.; Heimhofer, C.; Baechinger, M.; Meissner, S. N.; Ramsey, R.; Wenderoth, N.
Article.Abstract: Pupil size has been shown to reflect physical effort during brief, discrete motor tasks. It remains unknown whether pupil size similarly scales with effort during sustained repetitive movement, or whether it also reflects the accumulation of motor fatigability, a reduction in motor performance during prolonged movements. In our previous work, sustained maximal tapping induced motor slowing, a subtype of motor fatigability, characterized by decreasing movement speed and associated with increased antagonistic muscle coactivation. Next to these behavioural effects, pupil initially dilated and then gradually decreased over time. Whether this temporal change in pupil size is shaped by physical effort alone or also by motor fatigability remains unclear. Here, we combined a repetitive wrist tapping paradigm with force measurement, electromyography, and pupillometry, and paced participants at three different tapping speeds to dissociate physical effort from motor slowing, which has been shown to be speed-dependent. Fatigability-related motor slowing emerged selectively at the fastest speed. Moreover, we showed that antagonistic muscle coactivation increased more steeply at faster speeds, even in the absence of motor slowing, suggesting it may reflect an early change in motor control. While we found clear evidence that pupil size scaled with overall tapping speed, we did not find evidence that the temporal change of the pupil was pacing-dependent. These findings extend the pupil effort relationship to sustained, dynamic motor tasks and suggest that pupil size is a marker of physical effort but not motor fatigability during sustained repetitive movement.

Article.Authors: Moriyasu, D.; Watakabe, A.; Imayoshi, I.; Fujimoto, S.; Saha, B.; Ishida, Y.; Takeshima, H.; Sakamoto, M.; Skibbe, H.; Hata, J.; Oshiro, H.; Okano, H.; Imai, T.

Using FluoCode, we mapped projections from up to 21 cortical areas to subcortical regions in individual mice, revealing fine-scale topographic maps in small subcortical nuclei. Article.Title: PhyMorphS: A Physics-Guided Framework for Mesh-Based Morphological Synthesis of White Matter Microstructures
Article.Authors: Cui, R.; Amirrashedi, M.; Corral-Bolanos, M.; Thiran, J.-P.; Baerentzen, J. A.; Dyrby, T. B.
Article.Abstract: Numerical phantoms provide controlled 3D representations of brain tissue microstructure for developing and evaluating biophysical models of diffusion-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (dMRI). Existing phantom synthesizers employ different geometric primitives and optimization strategies to generate densely packed substrates with diverse axonal morphologies. However, direct deformation of axonal surfaces under mechanical constraints remains less explored. We propose PhyMorphS, a mesh-based framework in which axonal morphology emerges through physics-guided growth and interactions with the local microstructural environment, without constraining cross-sections to predefined symmetric shapes. In PhyMorphS, axons, myelin sheaths, and cell bodies are represented by triangle meshes, while a mass-spring system and collision-resolution scheme guide iterative axonal growth under mechanical and packing constraints. This enables irregular, asymmetric, and non-convex cross-sections, longitudinal diameter variation, and user-defined morphological alterations such as axonal beading and myelin layer decompaction. We evaluate PhyMorphS against large-scale X-ray nano-holotomography segmentations of real 3D axons from four white matter regions with distinct fiber organizations. The synthesized axons reproduce key region-specific morphological characteristics and achieve high packing densities, while the parallelized implementation scales approximately linearly with axon count in the generation voxel. By reproducing the geometric variability observed in real WM tissue, PhyMorphS provides controlled substrates for investigating how realistic morphology influences simulated dMRI signals, testing the geometric assumptions of biophysical microstructure models, and generating diverse paired microstructure-signal datasets for training machine-learning models.

Article.Title: Somatic symptom burden is associated with anger internalization measured as reduced reactive aggression
Article.Authors: Arima, A.; Umeda, S.
Article.Abstract: Difficulties in emotion regulation, including anger suppression, have been linked to more severe somatic symptoms in patients with chronic pain. Because this evidence comes mainly from clinical samples, it remains unclear whether such difficulties precede or follow symptom chronification. We examined whether somatic symptom burden is associated with reduced reactive aggression, as a behavioral marker of anger internalization. Forty-four healthy adults (25 females) completed the Taylor Aggression Paradigm, a competitive reaction-time task in which they selected noise intensity delivered to a fictitious opponent across three provocation conditions (low, moderate, and high). somatic symptom burden was evaluated using the Somatic Symptom Scale-8 (SSS-8) and Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15). Alexithymia was evaluated using the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20). Participants with higher somatic symptom burden selected lower noise intensities overall, with significant differences at low and moderate provocation levels. Difficulty identifying feelings tended to be positively associated with somatic symptom burden, whereas alexithymia was not associated with reactive aggression. These findings suggest that inhibited retaliation, previously reported in chronic pain patients, may already be present in healthy individuals with higher somatic symptom burden, potentially aiding early identification of chronic pain risk. Difficulty distinguishing emotions from bodily sensations may also contribute to somatic symptom expression.

Article.Title: Computational model of developmental self-assembly of a cortical microcircuit
Article.Authors: Abubacar, U.; Harris, C. R.; Bournes, R.; Bauer, R.
Article.Abstract: Cortical microcircuits emerge from local developmental interactions, yet large-scale computational models typically prescribe connectivity rather than explain its formation. Here we use BioDynaMo to simulate the self-assembly of ~70,000 cortical neurons from 1,200 progenitors in 3D physical space through migration, neurite growth and contact-based synapse formation. With one calibrated filling fraction per connection type, the locally formed synapses reproduce experimentally measured connectivity across 64 connection types (mean absolute error 0.0062) without prescribing individual connections. The grown spiking networks sustain stable, inhibition-dominated activity, and the same developmental rules, given different targets, generate both a canonical cortical microcircuit and a visual-cortex variant. Inverting the migration programme produces a reeler-like column whose aberrant connectivity destabilises network activity. Together, these findings provide a mechanistic link between local developmental processes and the emergence of cortical anatomy, connectivity and function.

Article.Title: Beyond Exploration: Heightened Recent Reward Reliance and Midfrontal Sensitivity to Outcome Differences in ADHD
Article.Authors: Naveilhan, C.; Konan, R.; Hayotte, M.; Caci, H.; d'Arripe-Longueville, F.; Ramanoel, S.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive decision-making requires balancing the exploitation of known rewards with the exploration of alternative options, yet how attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) shapes this trade-off remains unclear. Across 450 trials with dynamically changing payoffs, choices were classified against the highest last-observed payoff, and behavioral modeling quantified the influence of reward history on subsequent decisions. Contrary to our predictions, exploration rates, task performance, and neural differentiation between exploration and exploitation did not differ significantly between groups. However, adults with ADHD were more likely to repeat an option after high reward feedback and switch after low rewards, driven primarily by the immediately preceding outcome. At neural level, ADHD participants also showed greater midfrontal sensitivity to unsigned changes between consecutive payoffs, expressed in a feedback-evoked response spanning 280 to 568 ms and carried by slow activity below 2 Hz. Together, these findings dissociate the raw frequency of exploration from the dynamic weighting of recent outcomes in ADHD. Rather than reflecting an indiscriminate drive for novelty, behavior was characterized by heightened recent reward reliance paired with amplified slow-wave midfrontal sensitivity to outcome shifts. Crucially, this profile emerged without compromising overall performance, suggesting that, in this volatile environment, ADHD was associated with an increased weighting of recent outcomes rather than with a performance deficit.

Article.Title: Early visual experience redistributes cFos-tagged neurons toward the cortex while preserving presynaptic spatial stereotypy
Article.Authors: LEsperance, O. J.; Rijsketic, D. R.; Pritchett, N.; Meier, T.; Hunt, E.; Heifets, B. D.; Subramanian, J.
Article.Abstract: The macroscale functional organization of the brain is spatially stereotyped across individuals, but whether this extends to finer spatial scales is not known. Furthermore, how experience shapes this organization across the brain remains unclear. Using serial two-photon tomography and voxel-wise statistics, we mapped brain-wide distributions of cFos-tagged somata or their presynaptic terminals during the first week of visual experience or its deprivation. We found that midbrain and subcortical regions show greater stereotypy for cFos-tagged neurons and their presynaptic terminals compared to cortical regions. This fine-scale spatial stereotypy remained largely preserved despite visual deprivation, which shifted the relative recruitment of cFos-tagged neurons from cortical toward the highly stereotyped midbrain and subcortical regions. Our findings identify heterogeneous, spatially constrained functional organization across the brain that is conserved across subjects yet accommodates experience-dependent reorganization of neuronal recruitment.

Article.Title: Geometry-Conditioned Hyperalignment for Generalizable EEG Decoding Across Datasets and Paradigms
Article.Authors: Hoang, H.; Li, S.; Yamashita, O.; Kawanabe, M.; Kawato, M.
Article.Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) supports promising applications, but daily use remains limited by poor cross-subject and cross-dataset generalisation. That is because EEG recordings made with different electrode montages do not even share an observation space, and each subjects's leadfield projects the same neural sources onto the scalp differently. We present hTSMNet, which combines a novel geometry-conditioned hyperalignment frontend with a Riemannian symmetric positive-definite (SPD) manifold backbone that reduces the residual cross-subject distribution shift. From electrode coordinates alone, the frontend builds a linear map from any montage onto a fixed set of scalp anchors, placing every recording in one shared space. Because this map has no subjectspecific parameters, an unseen subject, dataset, or montage is aligned from its geometry alone, so transfer is zero-shot by construction. On a leave-one-dataset-out left-/right-hand motor-imagery (MI) benchmark across three datasets (172 subjects) and eight comparators, hTSMNet matches the strongest comparator at strict zero-shot, and attains the highest accuracy on every dataset once a few calibration trials for adjusting only final-layer classifier are available. We show that it orients the binary decision the same way in every dataset, so that a single linear rule learned on the source data is already correctly oriented on a held-out one. The same frozen MI-pretrained model also transfers across paradigms: with only a re-fit final-layer classifier, hTSMNet decodes mental workload and steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) well above chance, yet remains at chance on stimulus-locked event-related potentials (ERP). This dissociation follows from the architecture: covariance pooling reads oscillatory band power and is largely insensitive to the phase-locked potentials that ERP tasks depend on. What the representation generalizes is a signal family (band-limited oscillatory activity), not the named task. Geometry-conditioned hyperalignment thus yields an inspectable representation, which is generalizable across datasets and, within the oscillatory regime, across paradigms.

Article.Title: Neural Encoding Geometry of Human Voluntary Visual Selection
Article.Authors: Koevoet, D.; Zinkovic, K.; Van der Stigchel, S.; Strauch, C.
Article.Abstract: Selecting relevant targets from competing alternatives is a core cognitive function. While human visual selection can be tracked with high spatiotemporal precision, it remains unsolved how selected targets and non-selected alternatives are neurally encoded to effectively separate them. Initially, selected and non-selected objects showed equal spatially selective neural activity, yet the selected target was represented more strongly after 300-350 ms. Using cross-decoding, we found that selected and non-selected objects are encoded along a shared sensory axis, whereas selected targets are encoded along an additional spatially selective axis. This encoding geometry effectively separates selected targets from non-selected alternatives in neural space. Our results generalized across selection conditions: we found comparable results in instructed and free-choice selection, as well as in delayed oculomotor and covert visual selection. Together, we demonstrate that the human brain selectively encodes targets, but not distractors, along an additional axis, revealing a neural mechanism through which voluntary selection prioritizes behaviorally relevant information.

Article.Title: A trio of brain networks dynamically orchestrates music recognition
Article.Authors: Grosjean, B. A. P.; Bonetti, L.; Rosso, M.; Ramineni, M.; Blenkmann, A. O.; Endestad, T.; Solbakk, A.-K.; Kim-McManus, O.; Willie, J. T.; Brunner, P.; Dastjerdi, M.; Lin, J. J.; Knight, R. T.; Quiroga-Martinez, D. R.
Article.Abstract: Recognition memory continuously integrates internal representations with sensory information to guide adaptive behavior. Yet most theoretical models conceptualize recognition as the retrieval of an isolated stimulus through a discrete sequence of steps including sensory processing, hippocampal retrieval, and cortical reinstatement. However, in natural settings, perception, memory, and predictions interact continuously within an evolving context to guide adaptive responses. It is unclear how brain networks coordinate the integration of internal and external information during dynamic recognition. During recognition of memorized sequences, sensory activity progressively attenuated, sensory inputs were combined with mnemonic and contextual information, and decision-related activity evolved toward sensorimotor engagement. Novel sequences disrupted this organization by sustaining sensory responses and accelerating decision-related activity. Sensory and integrative networks communicated bidirectionally. Our findings reveal recognition as a distributed, context-dependent, and goal-directed process emerging from the continuous and bidirectional coordination of large-scale brain networks.

Article.Title: Beyond organ age gaps: comparing plasma proteomic metrics of organ biology in relation to brain structure and neurodegenerative disease.
Article.Authors: Zendehdel, R.; An, L.; Chauveau, L.; Oh, H.; Vilkaite, G.; Hristovska, I.; Warrier, V.; Seidlitz, J.; Bethlehem, R. A. I.; Pichet-Binette, A.; Vogel, J.

This can be investigated using biological age measures that are increasingly used to estimate how biological systems deviate from chronological aging. The three metric classes were related but not interchangeable. Global all-protein and all-organ-protein models showed strong age-related proteomic structure. However, organ-specific PC analyses showed that age was often but not always the dominant source of variation in protein signal across organs. Age gap metrics showed the most consistent associations with subsequent ICD-10-based neurodegenerative and vascular diagnoses, whereas all three metric classes showed distinct associations with brain structure and organ-relevant physiological phenotypes. Brain structure analyses revealed heterogeneous organ-brain association patterns across organs, suggesting that proteomic variation relates to brain structure in both a systemic and an organ-specific manner. Similarly, organ metrics provided modest incremental predictive improvement over baseline demographic models, with the largest increase in ROC-AUC observed for Alzheimer's disease when all organ age gap metrics were added jointly (delta ROC-AUC = 0.037). These results link brain related outcomes to proteomic variation across both CNS and non-CNS systems. Our work suggests that proteomic organ metrics capture complementary dimensions of biological variation rather than a single construct of organ aging. Although these measures may provide informative biological and potentially predictive signals, their incremental predictive value in the present analyses was modest.

Article.Title: Mechanism and subunit-dependence of disease-associated lurcher mutation in AMPA-type glutamate receptors
Article.Authors: Edwards, A. J.; Arslan, C.; Wyllie, D. J.; Baranovic, J.
Article.Abstract: AMPA receptors are glutamate-activated neuroreceptors responsible for the majority of fast excitatory neurotransmission in vertebrate brains. Activity-dependent changes in their functional and trafficking properties underpin cognitive processes such as learning and memory formation. In the past 15 years, a number of mutations within AMPA receptor genes have been identified as disease-causing leading to some form of neurodevelopmental delay. Here, we focused on one such mutation called lurcher, resulting from a change of the third Ala in the highly conserved SYTANLAAF motif to Thr. We determined functional consequences of lurcher mutation in homomeric AMPA receptors composed of subunits GluA1 or GluA2. In GluA1 subunit, lurcher mutation has been identified as a hotspot in a large cohort of patients with neurodevelopmental disorders. We confirm previously established lurcher phenotype characterised by slower deactivation and desensitization kinetics as well as more profound block of desensitization compared to the wild-type (WT) homomers. We show that these effects are more pronounced in GluA2 than GluA1 homomers. Lurcher phenotypes are attenuated, but still present, in more physiologically abundant heteromeric AMPA receptors composed of two GluA1 lurcher and two GluA2 WT subunits (GluA1 lc/GluA2 WT). Schild analysis indicates lurcher enhances activity of AMPA receptors by primarily changing the efficiency with which they open their ion channel upon glutamate binding rather than by changing affinity for glutamate. Perampanel, the only widely licensed drug that targets AMPA receptors, is an anti-convulsant that acts as a non-competitive inhibitor. We show it continues to inhibit GluA1 lc/GluA2 WT heteromeric receptors and that its IC50 depends on the auxiliary subunits associated with the heteromers. Specifically, stargazin (TARP {gamma}-2) brings the IC50 for perampanel into the submicromolar range, just like in the WT receptors.

Article.Title: A complete adult Drosophila melanogaster brain tracheolar network
Article.Authors: Cho, H.; Ng, T.; Schoenberg, K.; Huntress, S.; Suh, J.; Manandhar, A.; Lin, S.; Woldetsadik, B. M.; Kang, R. S.; Bui, M.; Zebrowski, L. M.; Reynolds-Cornell, F.; Agbedun, E.; Cruz, Y.; Lewis, C. A.; Bhasiin, K.; Lin, K.; Mooney, C.; Dacks, A. M.; Schlegel, P.; Bock, D. D.; Colodner, K. J.

We observe that synapses are not preferentially positioned near tracheoles, and are instead slightly depleted from a region approximately 15 um around tracheoles, relative to other points along the same neurons. We also quantify the relative proximity of neurotransmitter-specific synapses and cables to tracheoles across neuropils. This detailed anatomical description of the tracheolar network establishes a reference for future studies examining how neuronal patterning, activity, and metabolic demand couple with tracheole development and function.

Article.Title: HMGB1/CXCL12 heterocomplex activates CXCR4 to suppress the ability of Muller glia to become proliferating progenitor-like cells in the chick retina
Article.Authors: Kelly, L.; Taylor, O.; El-Hodiri, H.; Lee, S.; Parekh, E.; Hawthorn, E.; Wright, J.; Guest, M.; Tangemen, A.; Fischer, A.
Article.Abstract: We investigated how High Mobility Group Box 1 (HMGB1) signaling regulates glial reactivity and Muller glia-derived progenitor cell (MGPC) formation in the chick retina. HMGB1 released from stressed cells is known to form a heterocomplex with C-X-C chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12) to activate C-X-C chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4). HMGB1 is broadly expressed in retinal neurons and glia and is rapidly exported from the nuclei of stressed inner retinal neurons after damage, a process blocked by inflachromene. CXCL12 is expressed by amacrine, horizontal, and bipolar cells, whereas CXCR4 is expressed by Muller glia and is rapidly upregulated following damage. CXCR4 agonist or recombinant HMGB1/CXCL12 treatment selectively stimulates mTOR and Jak/Stat signaling in Muller glia in undamaged retinas. Inhibition of CXCR4 signaling, HMGB1 nuclear export, or HMGB1/CXCL12 complex formation potently stimulated MGPC proliferation without affecting neuronal death or microglial activation. In retinas treated with insulin and FGF2, to induce MGPC proliferation independent of injury, HMGB1 remains confined to nuclei, CXCR4 is downregulated, and inhibition of HMGB1 or CXCR4 has no effect. We further demonstrate that microglia are required to maintain CXCR4 expression in Muller glia, and blockade of HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling does not restore MGPC proliferation in microglia-depleted retinas. Article.Title: Pharmaco-genetic evidence of presymptomatic lysosomal dysfunction coupled to detrimental DPR secretion in Drosophila Models of C9orf72-linked ALS/FTD.
Article.Authors: Smeele, P. H.; Ferrari, V.; Spina, G.; Dona', E.; Cauchi, R.; Poletti, A.; Vaccari, T.
Article.Abstract: Hexanucleotide repeat expansions in C9orf72, the most common genetic cause of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), drive neurodegeneration through both loss of gene function and toxic gain-of-function mechanisms, including transcription of repeat RNA and repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation into dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs). Both disease mechanisms have been linked to disruption of the autophagy-lysosome pathway (ALP), though how this contributes to disease progression remains unclear. By expressing toxic C9orf72 repeats in Drosophila melanogaster, we observed presymptomatic lysosome impairment, coupled with largely preserved autophagosome formation. Pharmacological treatment with valproic acid (VPA) partially prevented neurodegenerative and locomotor phenotypes in expressing animals in presence of Mitf, which is required for lysosomal biogenesis. Genetic inhibition of residual lysosomal degradation enhanced neurotoxicity, whereas downregulation of autophagy and secretory autophagy genes suppressed toxicity, uncovering a previously unrecognized contribution of secretion to disease. Consistent with this, in vitro experiments indicated that disabling lysosome function, but not autophagy induction, leads to an increase in neuronal release of autophagy-associated proteins and DPRs, which can be found be uptaken by nearby neurons and glia in vivo. We propose that repeat-driven presymptomatic lysosomal dysfunction, prevented by pharmacologic treatment, promotes secretory autophagy, which, in turn facilitates extracellular release and intercellular propagation of neurotoxic DPRs.

Article.Title: Capturing continuous spectrotemporal pupil--brain coupling with simultaneous wearable EEG/Eye tracking
Article.Authors: Liu, T.; Kotz, S. A.; Schwartze, M.; Criscuolo, A.
Article.Abstract: Spontaneous fluctuations in pupil diameter are closely linked to neural dynamics, yet most evidence for pupil--brain coupling has been obtained in conventional laboratory settings. Using combined lightweight mobile EEG (MUSE) and eye tracking (Tobii Pro Glasses 3) devices, we investigated resting-state pupil--brain coupling and explored interoceptive attention to determine whether the core organizational principles observed with stationary equipment are detectable within and preserved across continuous recording states. Lower EEG frequencies (2-12Hz) preceded pupil dynamics by roughly 764ms, while higher frequencies showed a distinct coupling range. Granger-causality analysis further indicated predominantly EEG-to-pupil directional coupling. Similar observations were made during interoception. Article.Title: Sensory and Motor Building Blocks of an Extra Robotic Digit Representation
Article.Authors: Dowdall, L.; Amoruso, E.; Dominijanni, G.; Molina-Sanchez, M.; Diedrichsen, J.; Clode, D.; Makin, T. R.
Article.Abstract: Supernumerary limbs provide a unique opportunity to ask how the brain represents an entirely novel effector within an existing sensorimotor system. Using fMRI, we compared participants following short-term exposure with participants who had undergone longitudinal Third Thumb training. The device was controlled by the toes but operated alongside the biological fingers, while its sensory consequences were experienced on the hand. Following prolonged experience, greater activity was elicited in the M1 hand area both during Third Thumb control, and in response to its sensory consequences alone. Multivariate analyses showed that the Third Thumb representation became more distinct from its biological toe controller. Pattern component modelling further showed that the representation could be explained by a combination of its constituent motor and sensory patterns, but their relative contributions changed substantially with experience, from toe-dominated following short-term exposure to sensory-dominated following longitudinal training. Article.Title: Whole-Brain MRSI Metabolic Connectomics Reveals Network Disruptions and Altered Gradient Coherence in Psychosis Risk
Article.Authors: Lucchetti, F.; Celereau, E.; Jenni, R.; Petrova, T.; Abrahamyan, L.; Conus, P.; Hagmann, P.; Aleman-Gomez, Y.; Klauser, A.; Klauser, P.
Article.Abstract: Brain network alterations preceding first-episode psychosis often escape connectomic approaches based on conventional neuroimaging, such as diffusion or functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Network-based statistics identified a significant metabolic connectivity subnetwork with higher connectivity in HR than in HC, whereas no corresponding structural or functional connectivity differences were detected. Nodes of this subnetwork had modestly higher structural strength but were not consistently enriched among structural hubs, and no significant regional abnormalities in individual metabolite concentrations were detected. Eigenmode analysis of metabolic connectivity revealed a low-dimensional organization spanning a posterior unimodal-to-transmodal axis and a transmodal-to-limbic axis. Path analysis revealed higher bilateral energy in HR, indicating reduced coherence along a metabolic gradient that parallels the neurodevelopmental sensorimotor-to-association axis. Article.Authors: Pandit, K.; Fouts, C.; Rodwin, S.; Maniatis, S.; Dhingra, K.; Marrakchi, S.; Domovic, D.; Singh, J.; Dumitrascu, B.; Phatnani, H.; Pleska, M.; Vickovic, S.

This early expansion preceded the later decline of non-reactive gray matter and detectable motor-neuron loss. Article.Title: Evidence-based re-identification: Leveraging appearance cues to correct tracking mistakes rather than trying to prevent them
Article.Authors: Coulombe, V.; Leboulleux, Q.; Gosselin, B.; Testard, C.; Labonte, B.
Article.Abstract: Naturalistic behavioral neuroscience experiments, in which groups of animals interact in enriched environments over prolonged periods, require each animal's identity to remain correct throughout the recording. Current multi-animal tracking tools assign identities frame by frame without revisiting past assignment decisions. A single, even sporadic, identity swap is therefore likely to persist until the end of the recording. Consequently, error-free tracking results become progressively less likely as recordings lengthen and cohorts grow. Even state-of-the-art multi-object tracking (MOT) methods that leverage appearance cues do so only to make each assignment more robust. This robustness, however, only delays the inevitable as even the most robust assignment process will eventually make a mistake over prolonged recordings. A mistake that will then persist just as it otherwise would have. Here, we introduce evidence-based re-identification, which uses appearance cues to correct tracking mistakes rather than prevent them. This fundamental shift allows the algorithm to build and progressively enrich appearance representations for each tracked subject. Tracking mistakes are then detected by continuously monitoring the evolution of these representations, triggering a correction whenever two representations drift toward one another in a sustained way. On two distinct, minutes-long benchmarks of mice interacting in enriched environments, motion-only trackers (DeepLabCut, SLEAP, ByteTrack) and the appearance-based BoT-SORT-ReID began accumulating identity errors within seconds, whereas ByteTrack paired with evidence-based re-identification remained reliable, outperforming even ByteTrack paired with the marker-based Tailtag system. This reliability was also positively correlated with the accuracy of the appearance extractor, but only when it was used through evidence-based re-identification. Foundation image encoders (CLIP, MegaDescriptor, DINOv3) showed promising out-of-the-box performance yet still required fine-tuning to be effective. Together, these results show that multi-animal tracking algorithms can remain reliable over prolonged periods only if they can reliably recover from tracking mistakes, and that fine-tuning appearance extractors remains essential to doing so.

Article.Title: Competing routes back to firing shape population hyperexcitability and its selective suppression
Article.Authors: Kamaraj, A. K.; Szuromi, M. P.
Article.Abstract: Whether a neuron will fire again is fundamentally a different question from whether a quiescent neuron will activate. Even within the same neuron, successive spikes can follow distinct post-spike trajectories, with after-depolarization permitting early return to firing and depolarization block prolonging inactivity. Therefore, we propose that hyperexcitability involves changes in the opportunities to fire again across the spike cycle, and not just from quiescence. The firing hazard makes these opportunities measurable: in whole-cell recordings of midbrain dopamine neurons, the subthreshold voltage trough resolves a non-monotone aggregate firing hazard into physiologically distinguishable components. We represent these components as competing return pathways within a population renewal model and show that they lead to heterogeneous firing patterns within a single neuronal population subject to a common drive. An immediate-return pathway provides an early opportunity to fire by skipping some stages of recovery, and promotes population hyperexcitability independent of quiescent activation. Conversely, a sequestration pathway diverts recently active neurons into a prolonged non-recruitable state, representing depolarization block or use-dependent blockade. Pharmacological selectivity of anti-seizure medications such as phenytoin and carbamazepine arises from the redistribution of neurons among return pathways at every renewal, with fast-cycling pathological regimes providing more opportunities for renewal and eventual sequestration.

Article.Authors: Ince, M.; Hübner, C.; Rolfs, M.
Article.Abstract: Saccadic eye movements sweep objects across the retina at high speed, and this motion is routinely omitted from conscious perception. Two Gabor patches each carried a digit, then disappeared and reappeared in place, reappeared displaced, or travelled continuously to their new locations; the intervening interval lasted 300 ms or was matched to the mean or peak speed of a saccade. A target digit then appeared in one patch, and participants identified it. At the long duration, we replicated the Object-Specific Preview Benefit (OSPB): responses were faster when the target had been previewed in that same object than in the other one. At saccadic durations, the OSPB disappeared, and adding a distinguishing surface feature in Experiment 2 did not restore it. The general preview benefit, faster responses to any previewed digit than to a new one, persisted at every duration. Object features therefore survive motion at saccadic speed, but their link to a particular object does not.

Article.Authors: Bohic, M.; Salamone, P. C.; Zuo, W.; Negm, A.; Fulton, S. L.; Du, S.; Jayakumar, S.; Keating, J.; Soubeyre, V.; Gradwell, M. A.; Upadhyay, A.; Shorter, L.; Kim, J.; Inoue, Y. A.; Ye, J.-H.; Peirs, C.; Poulen, G.; Lonjon, N.; Vachiery-Lahaye, F.; Bauchet, L.; Bourinet, E.; Tao, Y.-X.; Olausson, H.; Abdus-Saboor, I.; Bohme, R.; Abraira, V. E. G.

We find that this circuit architecture is conserved in humans, as oxytocin receptors are similarly expressed on spinal excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Article.Authors: Wang, X.; Lyu, B.; Qin, L.; Li, J.; Zhang, Y.; Zalesky, A.; Yang, C.; Chen, Y.; Cao, M.
Article.Abstract: Traveling waves of neural activity are fundamental to cortical function, yet their spatiotemporal dynamics and structural constraints remain less understood in human brain. Article.Authors: Vijayakumar, P.; Cauwenberghs, K.; Garg, M.; Choy, J.; Charara, S.; McKaughan, Q.; Su, C.-Y.
Article.Abstract: Extracellular particles, including non-vesicular extracellular particles (NVEPs) and extracellular vesicles (EVs), are emerging as key contributors to sensory signaling, yet their ultrastructural organization within native tissues remains underexplored. Article.Title: Combined pharmacotherapy suppress ferroptosis and inflammation after neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage
Article.Authors: Zigelstein, M.; Castro Diaz, V.; La Gamma, C.; Hu, F.; Sharma, S. C.; Subbian, S.; Velisek, L.; Veliskova, J.; Sacchidanandam, R.; Vinukonda, G.; LaGamma, E. F.
Article.Abstract: Neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) is a common complication of extremely premature newborns, and results in reduced neurogenesis, white matter injury, cortical atrophy, and subsequent cerebral palsy, learning and memory disabilities. However, the impact of IVH on the hippocampus, an area critical for memory and learning capabilities throughout life, remains relatively unexplored. Using a preterm rabbit pup model that structurally resembles human perinatal brain development, we report, widespread hematoma and iron accumulation in the hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) following IVH. This accumulation is facilitated by the anatomical positioning of the hippocampus within the unidirectional CSF flow pathway and the vulnerability of the immature dentate gyrus vasculature. Sulforaphane (SFN; an activator of nuclear factor erythroid 2 related factor 2 [Nrf2] transcriptional factor and anti-inflammatory pathways) and deferoxamine (DFN; an iron chelator) reduced iron deposition, free hemoglobin, and activated glial cells (sp. astrocytes and microglia), particularly in the DG molecular layer and hilar regions. The attenuated inflammatory responses correlate with decreased ferroptosis-mediated neuronal death, and substantial restoration of the dysregulated gene pathways associated with inflammation, immune activation, and neuronal cell death in the developing hippocampal/DG region. This was associated with a gene profile favoring ferroptotic cell death rather than apoptosis or autophagy pathways. Moreover, we also identified a regional specificity to certain effects as no astrogliosis was observed in hippocampal CA1 to CA4 regions after IVH or when compared with healthy controls. Our study is the first to demonstrate hippocampal hematoma and iron accumulation associated pathologic mechanisms following neonatal IVH. The results provide mechanistic insights into hippocampal injury as well as a therapeutic proof-of-concept for targeting iron toxicity and inflammation in the developing brain to mitigate injury. These results justify extending analyses of injury reversal to long-term postnatal ages and behavior studies to assess therapeutic potential. The study illustrates novel therapeutic interventions that attenuate early mediators of injury that improves recovery of hippocampal/DG formation/maturation and neuroprotection after neonatal IVH. We speculate that these protective effects may prolong donor stem cell survival thus, potentiating benefits of living cellular therapy in the future.

Article.Title: Reprogramming transcription factor networks with a HOX inhibitor to address Huntington's disease biology beyond mutant huntingtin
Article.Authors: Klukinov, M.; Orr, R.; Martin, W. K.; Kori, S.; Yeomans, D. C.; Mamet, J.
Article.Abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by CAG-repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene. Although inherited CAG-repeat length and the underlying somatic instability are key determinants of age at onset, they explain only part of onset variability, suggesting additional disease mechanisms. We applied the Core Coefficient (CC), a transcription-factor (TF) network-decoding technology that quantifies TF functional dominance, to >100 post-mortem neuronal transcriptomes from HD and control brain datasets. Among human TF families, the HOX family is the only family that uniformly exhibits quiescence in controls versus large and significant functional dominance in vulnerable neurons of each HD donor brain we investigated. HOX TFs are already dominant at Vonsattel grade 0 and at inherited CAG-repeat length. The magnitude of HOX CC values correlates with age at onset and increases with disease grade and CAG-Age Product. HOX TFs form a self-sustained pathological unit targeting >4,000 genes implicated in neuronal patterning, identity, stress, signaling, structure, and senescence. In zQ175 mice, abrogation of mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein production only transiently attenuates HOX dominance and does not durably eliminate it. COR-H800, a HOX inhibitor, restored TF-network hierarchy toward wild type, normalizing the functional dominance of transcription factors involved in neuronal differentiation, cell-fate determination, and developmental patterning, and improved disease-relevant phenotypes in R6/2 mice. These findings support the direct selective inhibition of HOX TFs to address the aberrant transcriptional state that can persist despite mHTT lowering or somatic instability-targeted therapeutic interventions.

Article.Title: An LFP-based characterization of population-level heterogeneity during motor preparation & execution
Article.Authors: DePass, M.; Falaki, A.; Quessy, S.; Dancause, N.; Cos, I.
Article.Abstract: The goal of the present work is to characterize mesoscale heterogeneity of population-level neural activity in the motor areas during motor preparation and execution using high-frequency local field potentials (HF-LFPs). Understanding the distribution of neural activity at this scale is necessary since ensembles of neural populations underlie most behaviors. HF-LFPs have emerged as a promising signal for such analysis due to their stability and relationship with cortical population dynamics. Here we analyzed HF-LFPs in non-human primates performing a reach-to-grasp task. We quantified three complementary aspects of heterogeneity: variance, latent dimensionality, and directional coherence. Heterogeneity varied by region and neuromotor state, and was specific to the motor behavior being implemented, even in regions exhibiting high correlation. In addition, more heterogeneous activity tended to better encode neuromotor states. Namely, regions and neuromotor states exhibiting higher variance and dimensionality yielded superior motor decoding performance. Further analyses involving low-dimensional linear projections of the signals revealed rich intra-region interactions between ensembles of populations. The present work helps establish intra-region heterogeneity as a multi-faceted and informative measure of neural activity, even on small spatial scales. It also establishes HF-LFPs as an effective signal for capturing complex intra-region dynamics, making it a suitable candidate for multi-region, systems-level analysis.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: motor execution; latent dimensionality; directional coherence; reach-to-grasp; local field potentials; motor preparation; non-human primates

Article.Title: An application of fNIRS for the prediction of hearing thresholds in sleeping infants: a proof of principle
Article.Authors: Gao, D. X.; Mao, D.; Wunderlich, J.; Esmaelpoor, J.; Balasubramanian, G.; McKay, C.
Article.Abstract: This study applied a two-component-response modelling approach to fNIRS recordings obtained from naturally sleeping infants presented with auditory stimuli at different sound intensities. We investigated whether the relationship between fNIRS response measures and stimulus intensity could be modelled to estimate individual auditory hearing thresholds. In the normal-hearing group, 75% of infants had threshold estimates for the sound /ba/ within the expected normal-hearing range, with an estimated mean equivalent normal loudness (ENL) of 10.72 dB HL (SD 8.64 dB HL). A case study further explored the potential application of this approach in an infant with hearing impairment, highlighting the importance of reliable responses at lower stimulus intensities and appropriate regression model selection. These findings provide preliminary evidence that cortical haemodynamic responses can be quantitatively related to sound intensity for estimating auditory sensitivity.

Article.Title: Hippocampal dorsal and ventral CA2 enable social discrimination after acute social defeat
Article.Authors: Sheng, W.; Boyle, L. M.; Pimpinella, D.; Kassraian, P.; Matthew, P.; Li, H.; Siegelbaum, S. A.
Article.Abstract: Remembering the valence of conspecifics based on past aggressive compared to non-aggressive interactions is important for proper adaptive social behaviors. How a single naturalistic encounter establishes a lasting memory of the valence of the experience remains unclear. Our recent work shows that the CA2 region in ventral hippocampus, unlike dorsal CA2, is not required for social novelty discrimination but does contribute with dorsal CA2 to promote social aggression. How CA2 contributes to valence-associated social memory across the dorsoventral axis remains unresolved. We developed an acute defeat-associated social threat discrimination memory (AD-STDM) paradigm after which a male mouse preferentially interacted with a familiar non-aggressor male compared to a familiar aggressor male 24 h after a single defeat episode. Chemogenetic inhibition of Avpr1b-expressing CA2 neurons in either dorsal or ventral hippocampus during learning impaired subsequent discrimination. Acute defeat also increased cFos expression in ventral CA2 neurons relative to non-aggressive social interaction. Thus, although ventral CA2 is not required for social novelty recognition memory, it is required for social memory of an aversive social experience, with a relatively greater level of neural activation during aversive compared to non-aversive social encounters. In contrast, dorsal CA2 is required for both non-aversive and aversive forms of social memory.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: dorsal hippocampus; chemogenetic inhibition; CA2; AVPR1B; c-fos; social memory; social defeat; ventral hippocampus

Article.Title: A high-throughput all-optical platform for mapping gene perturbations to electrophysiology
Article.Authors: Zhang, J.; Gong, D.; Barrios, A. M.; Itkis, D. G.; Sahni, K.; Fandl, H.; Uenaka, T.; Walton, R. T.; Plutkis, S. E.; Lavis, L.; Blainey, P. C.; Wernig, M.; Nehme, R.; Lee, R. T.; Fraenkel, E.; Farhi, S. L.; Cohen, A. E.
Article.Abstract: Electrical phenotyping remains a bottleneck in linking genes to cellular function. We developed a high-throughput all-optical electrophysiology platform combining an engineered human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) line, wide-field voltage imaging, and automated analysis. The hiPSC line integrates inducible NGN2, CRISPR interference, and degron-gated expression of Voltron2 and CheRiff, enabling neuronal differentiation, targeted gene knockdown, and optical electrophysiology. The microscope records approximately 1,500 spiking glutamatergic neurons at 800 Hz across a 4x4 mm field, with larger fields supporting approximately 3,000 neurons at 660 Hz. Automated analysis extracts single-cell voltage traces and quantifies firing patterns, action-potential waveforms, and subthreshold dynamics. Arrayed knockdown of five sodium- and potassium-channel genes produced distinct electrophysiological phenotypes. The engineered hiPSC line also supported optical electrophysiology recordings from motor neurons, astrocytes, and cardiomyocytes. These results establish a scalable platform for high-throughput electrophysiological phenotyping and functional genomics in hiPSC-derived cells.

Article.Title: Visual object recognition in the fly: the internal representation of a predator drives defensive behaviour
Article.Authors: Denagamage, S.; Foltz, M.; Dalstein, V. M.; Behnia, R.; Card, G. M.; Axel, R.; Cury, K. M.
Article.Abstract: Animals recognize visual objects and respond to them appropriately to survive. This process is thought to unfold in stages: the visual scene is first deconstructed into constituent features, which are then reconstructed into representations of object identity and relayed to motor circuits. Here we define a neural circuit in Drosophila that underlies the visual recognition of a natural predator, the parasitoid wasp, and orchestrates defence. We found that flies exhibit a repertoire of directed defensive actions structured by the wasp's position within the fly's field of view. Expression of these behaviours is driven by visual detection of a conspicuous morphological cue -- the wasp's elongated antennae. A small subset of lobula columnar (LC) visual projection neuron types are required for defence and are activated by constituent visual features of the wasp. Three LC types respond selectively to the wasp's antennae, and relay this information to LC9, which sums antennal- and body-feature signals to form a composite representation of the wasp. Spatial filtering of this representation onto a descending premotor pathway translates the wasp's location in visual space into directed defence. Feature combination followed by spatial filtering may constitute a general mechanism for coupling object identity to context-appropriate action.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: visual object recognition; spatial filtering; Drosophila; defensive behavior; parasitoid wasps; feature combination

Article.Title: Geometric determinants of time series learning and attractor stability in closed-loop circuits
Article.Authors: Barri, A.; Gurnani, H.; Silver, R. A.
Article.Abstract: Skilled volitional behaviours arise from recurrent circuits, which can sustain structured neural activity in the absence of external drive, through internal feedback. But how such autonomous activity is learned and stability maintained in distributed motor circuits is poorly understood. To investigate the relationship between neural representations and learning we compared a cortex-like recurrent neural network (RNN) and a cortico-cerebellar-like circuit with a feed-forward layer (RNN+FFL), both in a closed-loop configuration. RNN+FFL circuits learned periodic target signals that parameter-matched RNNs could not, due to a failure to form attractor states. Decomposing population activity by frequency, rather than variance, separated the task-relevant and task-irrelevant subspaces. Quantifying their geometric arrangement revealed that the feed-forward layer improved learning and stabilised attractor states by increasing the angles within and between these subspaces. Our results show that task-specific representational geometry is a better predictor of periodic time series learning in recurrent circuits than classical global measures such as dimensionality.

Article.Title: Phase-specific stimulation of prefrontal beta oscillations modulates distinct cognitive processes
Article.Authors: Wischnewski, M.; Gueth, M. R.; Alekseichuk, I.; Opitz, A.
Article.Abstract: Oscillatory phase has been proposed to organize neural information processing, but whether endogenous phase can be leveraged to causally shape human cognition remains unclear. Here, we tested whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) delivered at specific phases of endogenous beta oscillations over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates working memory and response inhibition. Participants received EEG phase-controlled, closed-loop rTMS delivered at either the peak or trough of their endogenous beta rhythm, using each participant's dominant beta frequency (20-30 Hz). A conventional 20-Hz rTMS delivered independently of the beta phase served as an active control. Compared to this control and each other, peak-targeted rTMS improved response inhibition, whereas trough-targeted rTMS improved working memory. Both phase-specific behavioral effects were accompanied by corresponding increases in event-related potentials, which were not observed after conventional stimulation. Across participants, behavioral improvements correlated with stimulation-induced electrophysiological changes. Finally, phase-specific rTMS induced distinct DLPFC network expansions that complemented the behavioral effects: peak stimulation enhanced posterior centro-parietal connectivity for inhibitory control, while trough stimulation expanded anterior prefrontal networks for working memory. These findings provide first evidence that opposite phases of endogenous prefrontal beta oscillations coordinate distinct cognitive and neural processes. This establishes prefrontal beta phase as a causal dimension for shaping executive function and as a target for prefrontal rTMS to modulate cognition and non-invasively probe phase-dependent brain function.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: response inhibition; dorsolateral prefrontal cortex; working memory; executive function; event-related potentials; non-invasive brain stimulation
