Article.Title: Postpartum resource scarcity reshapes maternal care, offspring prioritization, and the steroid-sensitive medial preoptic area
Article.Authors: Aspesi, D.; Soriano, V.; Rolle, S.; Mahrous, M. Y.; Brenhouse, H.; Krishnan, K.; Bangasser, D. A.
Article.Abstract: Parental care requires balancing offspring needs with environmental constraints, yet how resource scarcity alters the organization of maternal responses remains poorly understood. Here, we examined maternal behavior, offspring prioritization, and steroid receptor-associated extracellular matrix organization in postpartum rats exposed to limited bedding and nesting (LBN) or control conditions with ample nesting materials. LBN increased pup-directed and reduced self-directed behaviors but also increased behavioral entropy, a measure of behavioral fragmentation, indicating less predictable caregiving sequences. LBN dams preferentially retrieved male pups first, whereas control dams preferentially retrieved females first. LBN also increased the proportion of pup-investigation time directed toward males compared with controls. In offspring on postnatal day 10, corticosterone was elevated in female but not male LBN pups, a pattern that paralleled the maternal male bias. To identify associated neurobiological changes, we assessed steroid receptors and extracellular matrix organization in the medial preoptic area (mPOA), a key region for maternal behavior. LBN increased numbers of estrogen receptor (ER)- and androgen receptor (AR)-immunoreactive cells, reduced perineuronal net (PNN) abundance, and decreased receptor-positive cell enwrapment. Because PNNs constrain structural plasticity, these findings suggest that the postpartum environment alters the organization of steroid receptor-associated extracellular matrix, potentially modulating experience-dependent plasticity in neurosteroid-sensitive circuits. In sum, LBN increases the levels of maternal engagement while reshaping its temporal organization and allocation, accompanied by selective remodeling of steroid-sensitive preoptic architecture. Therefore, maternal adaptation to adversity may be better understood as changes in caregiving allocation strategies rather than a simple gain or loss of maternal care.

Article.Title: Geometric constraints and cognitive inputs jointly shape emergent brain dynamics and topology
Article.Authors: Beyh, A.; Kim, J. Z.; Bajwa, W. U.; Parkes, L.
Article.Abstract: How the brain's physical geometry gives rise to its flexible functional repertoire remains a central question in neuroscience. Here, we approached this question through recurrent neural networks (RNNs). We trained three RNN classes on a cognitive working-memory task, forming a graded hierarchy of spatial constraints: Vanilla RNNs (no spatial constraints), Masked RNNs (projection constraints limiting where information enters and leaves the network), and biophysical RNNs (bioRNNs; projection constraints and spatial embedding of the networks' connectivity using the brain's inter-regional Euclidean geometry). We assessed how well each RNN class predicted empirical fMRI activity without exposing them to it during training. Our results showed that bioRNNs were the only networks to successfully predict empirical brain activity and to organize their dynamics into a spatial pattern that recapitulated the brain's principal hierarchy (the sensorimotor-association axis). Additionally, bioRNNs' ability to predict empirical brain activity emerged along a training trajectory in which the effects of brain geometry were encoded by the network first, then partly traded back as the task was mastered. Importantly, brain-like topological features emerged in bioRNNs as they increased their task proficiency while maintaining their ability to predict brain activity. Taken together, our results indicate that physical geometry and cognitive inputs play distinct, complementary roles: while geometry constrains the space of possible brain dynamics, cognitive inputs determine which dynamics are expressed. Our results also situate topology as the scaffold through which the physically embedded brain reconciles wiring costs and computational demands.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: recurrent neural networks; working memory; brain geometry; projection constraints

Article.Title: Sentence-level neural dynamics in speech motor cortex
Article.Authors: Levi-Aharoni, H.; Jude, J. J.; Haro, S.; Acosta, A. J.; Allcroft, S. B.; Ottenhoff, M. C.; Card, N. S.; Wairagkar, M.; Iacobacci, C.; Pritchard, A. L.; Richards, B.; Brandman, D. M.; Stavisky, S. D.; Au Yong, N.; Pandarinath, C.; Paulk, A. C.; Hadar, P. N.; Li, J.; Williams, Z. M.; Cash, S. S.; Simeral, J. D.; Hochberg, L. R.; Rubin, D. B.
Article.Abstract: Prior recordings from speech motor cortex have revealed phonemic, syllabic, articulatory and speech-sequence representations, while more recent studies indicate that activity may also reflect higher-order features of speech production. However, whether speech motor cortex is sensitive to the linguistic organization of sentences remains unclear. Here we show that single-unit activity in speech motor cortex contains information about sentence-level linguistic structure. In three BrainGate2 participants with implanted microelectrode arrays in the left precentral gyrus, we recorded neural activity during an instructed-delay speech task comprising English sentences, word lists, syntactically structured nonword sentences and nonword lists. Neural activity in areas 6v and 55b contained speech- and language-related components, with stronger stimulus-condition effects in 55b, and stimulus condition was decodable in all three participants. In two larger datasets, semantic categories of English sentences were decodable from neural activity. These findings demonstrate that speech motor cortex encodes information about linguistic structure and semantic content at the level of sentences.

Article.Title: The Computational Grammar of Human Behaviour in a Biological Environment
Article.Authors: Serratos Hernandez, U. D.; Goekay, U.; Kornemann, L.; Hutabarat, Y.; Sen, D.; Bach, D. R.
Article.Abstract: Human behaviour unfolds as an extended stream of spontaneous actions shaped by environmental demands and the agent's goals. The organisation of these actions, situated between setting abstract goals and concrete movement execution, remains poorly characterised. Here, we introduce DynaClade, an unsupervised temporal action segmentation algorithm for human full-body motion capture data, and apply it to freely moving participants navigating ecologically realistic risky foraging environments in virtual reality. DynaClade identifies discrete actions whose kinematic characteristics and spatial distributions correspond to environmental affordances, supporting the validity of the approach. Among these actions, we discovered a hitherto undescribed movement pattern defined by increased body sway without locomotion. Action sequences were highly non-random and showed clear history dependence beyond first-order Markov structure, most of which was explained by a second-order prediction. This higher-order structure was well captured in a hidden Markov model, in which some of the observed actions were associated with more than one latent state. Each of these latent states corresponded to the same action in a distinct action context. These findings suggest that spontaneous human actions are predominantly selected based on the current action and context, rather than following pre-planned or habitually assembled sequences.

Article.Title: Identifying a neurochemical signature of the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus that predicts individual variability in cue-reward learning
Article.Authors: Ramos, B. A.; Chakrabarty, S.; Cain, C. N.; Levina, E.; Kennedy, R. T.; Flagel, S. B.
Article.Abstract: To investigate neurochemical factors that may confer vulnerability to psychiatric disorders, we used an animal model that captures a transdiagnostically relevant neurobehavioral endophenotype. During a Pavlovian conditioned approach paradigm, rats learn the predictive relationship between a lever cue and food reward. A subset of rats, sign trackers, also attribute incentive motivational value to the lever cue. Relative to non sign trackers, STs are more impulsive, have attentional deficits, and show greater reinstatement of drug seeking behavior. The paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus is a key neural node implicated in these individual differences. We combined in vivo microdialysis with liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry to quantify 22 neurobiologically relevant small molecules in the PVT before and 24 hours after Pavlovian training. Before training, glucose concentrations in the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus were higher in rats subsequently classified as sign trackers than in non sign trackers and were correlated with the Pavlovian conditioned approach index used to phenotype the rats. Glucose concentrations decreased after training, and the magnitude of change differed between phenotypes. Multivariate regression identified baseline neurochemical profiles in the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus associated with subsequent Pavlovian conditioned approach behavior. These findings identify a candidate PVT neurochemical signature that precedes behavioral phenotyping and may mark the propensity to sign track, providing insight into potential mechanisms underlying vulnerability to psychiatric disorders characterized by maladaptive cue motivated behavior.

Article.Title: Loss of GluN2A Selectively Impairs Excitatory Synaptic Integration in Hippocampal Somatostatin Interneurons
Article.Authors: Hunter, D. W.; Kaese, H.; Kind, P. C.; Wyllie, D. J.
Article.Abstract: N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) are widely considered key determinants of excitatory synaptic kinetics and activity-dependent plasticity, yet their specific contribution to postsynaptic potentials across distinct hippocampal CA1 cell types remains poorly defined. Null variants in GRIN2A are strongly associated with epilepsy-aphasia spectrum disorders, and GluN2A loss has recently been linked to delayed electrophysiological maturation of parvalbumin interneurons, a process regulated by somatostatin interneuron activity. Here, we used Grin2a haploinsufficient and knockout rats to determine how GluN2A depletion affects excitatory synaptic transmission, integration and firing across CA1 pyramidal neurons, parvalbumin interneurons and somatostatin interneurons. Using whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in acute hippocampal slices, we found that NMDARs made no discernible contribution to shaping Schaffer collateral-evoked EPSP kinetics, temporal summation or spike recruitment in CA1 pyramidal neurons at physiological resting potentials. Hebbian long-term potentiation at pyramidal neuron Schaffer collateral synapses was also preserved. Parvalbumin interneuron EPSP kinetics and synaptically evoked firing were similarly unaffected. By contrast, GluN2A loss selectively prolonged EPSP decay in CA1 somatostatin interneurons, increasing EPSP area, enhancing frequency-dependent temporal summation and elevating action potential output during repetitive and theta-frequency synaptic stimulation. These changes occurred alongside an increase in intrinsic excitability, indicating a cell-type-specific alteration by GluN2A loss. Selective enhancement of somatostatin interneuron recruitment provides a candidate mechanism - upstream of delayed parvalbumin interneuron maturation - and may contribute to hippocampal network dysfunction in GRIN2A-related disorders.

Article.Title: Same Movements, Different Skills: How Context Shapes Learning in Humans and Neural Networks
Article.Authors: Gupta, M. W.; Taylor, J. A.
Article.Abstract: What determines whether experiences are integrated into shared representations or split? Motor skill learning offers a revealing test: when two tasks require an identical sequence of movements, both intuition and theory suggest that practice in one should generalize to the other. Yet we find that changing context can make identical movements different skills. In simple recurrent networks trained on the same sequence across contexts, splitting was greatest when strong contextual inputs coincided with a high initial weight scale; neither alone sufficed. Greater representational separation coincided with separate context-specific learning curves. Humans practicing the same finger sequence while alternating between two performance-irrelevant contexts likewise exhibited context-specific curves, rather than the single continuous trajectory observed when practicing in a single context. State-space modeling favored split learning states in humans and very weakly coupled states in the most context-dependent networks. These findings have broader implications for understanding how learning generalizes across contexts.

Article.Title: The extended default mode network dysconnectivity in schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Zarghami, T. S.
Article.Abstract: The default mode network (DMN) extends beyond cortex into subcortical structures, yet how this extended DMN (eDMN) is causally reorganized in schizophrenia (SZ) remains unclear. Here, resting-state fMRI from 74 healthy controls (HC) and 66 SZ patients was analyzed. Subject-specific eDMNs were identified using spatially-constrained independent component analysis, and effective connectivity among 13 regions was estimated with spectral dynamic causal modeling, with group effects assessed using parametric empirical Bayes. Causal centrality--a dynamics-sensitive and causality-based measure of nodal importance--was computed per region, compared between groups, and correlated with MATRICS cognitive scores in patients. Causal centrality rankings were highly similar across groups ({rho} = 0.87), with both favoring subcortical over cortical regions. Group differences were regionally specific: temporal cortex was more causally central in patients, whereas posterior parietal cortex was more causally central in controls. Most connection-level SZ-HC differences originated from ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, prefrontal cortex, basal forebrain, temporal cortex, and thalamus. In patients, temporal causal centrality correlated negatively with reasoning/problem-solving, and ventrolateral prefrontal causal centrality with processing speed and composite cognition. The eDMN's core causal architecture is preserved in schizophrenia, but temporal influence is enhanced and parietal influence attenuated--alterations that are behaviorally meaningful and consistent with pathological reorganization.

Article.Title: Dissection of neuropsychiatric-relevant behavioral and structural phenotypes utilizing neuron type-specific ablation of the Bassoon gene in mice
Article.Authors: Kreutzmann, J. C.; Angenstein, F.; Fejtova, A.; Stork, O.; Gundelfinger, E. D.; Fendt, M.; Annamneedi, A.
Article.Abstract: Rare pathogenic mutations in the human BSN gene, which encodes the presynaptic cytomatrix protein Bassoon-a key organizer of the neurotransmitter release apparatus have been linked to neuropsychiatric conditions including schizophrenia. Here we began to dissect the potential contribution of Bsn deficiency in distinct populations of mouse (fore)brain neurons on behavioral and anatomical alterations resembling schizophrenia-like phenotypes. To this end, conditional knockout mice lacking Bassoon in subsets of inhibitory synapses (BsnDlx5/6cKO), in forebrain excitatory synapses (BsnEmx1cKO), or at dopaminergic release sites (BsnDATcKO) were generated. The mice were assessed using prepulse inhibition, a paradigm that models sensorimotor gating, which is often impaired in schizophrenia, and a fear/safety learning paradigm. Further, anxiety-related behaviors were evaluated and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed to assess anatomical brain alterations. Our data reveal synapse-specific effects of the Bassoon deficiency. Sensory gating deficits were observed in both BsnDlx5/6cKO and BsnEmx1cKO mice. BsnDlx5/6cKO mice further demonstrated impaired discrimination between conditioned fear and safety-a condition frequently observed in individuals with schizophrenia. By contrast, BsnDATcKO mice displayed enhanced discrimination between conditioned fear and safety. All mouse strains showed elevated anxiety-like behavior in the light/dark box. Structural MRI revealed increased brain volumes in BsnDlx5/6cKO and BsnEmx1cKO mice, with the most pronounced changes in the hippocampus and cortex. Previous studies have shown that BsnDlx5/6cKO mice display autistic-like behaviors, altered hippocampal network activity and epilepsy. Our findings support the notion that deficits in Bsn-mediated functions, particularly in interneurons, may contribute to the etiology of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions.

Article.Title: Identifying molecular instructions to hard-wire a sensory neuron's synaptic connectivity
Article.Authors: dos Santos, J. V.; Yu, R. Y.; Terceros, A.; Pires, P. M.; Rusu, D.; Cvektkovska, V.; Bucio-Mendez, A.; Lin, T.-J.; Emran, F.; Djambazian, H.; Berube, P.; Sladek, R.; Chen, B. E.
Article.Abstract: The neural circuitry underlying innate behaviours must be pre-specified using precise molecular instructions. However, it is not clear what specific molecules are required to generate one neuron's wiring pattern that make it distinct from a neighboring neuron's wiring pattern. Here, we repeatedly sequenced three identified Drosophila sensory neurons that each have a unique and stereotyped hard-wired synaptic connectivity, to determine the cell-surface molecules that distinguish their identities. Repeated sequencing of the same neuron across different animals revealed that the variability of transcription is < 1%. We find that fewer than 100 cell-surface molecules can distinguish a mechanosensory neuron from a chemosensory neuron. Functional characterization of the cell-surface receptors verified their different roles in axonal and synaptic targeting. Finally, we expressed combinations of the different cell-surface receptors to mis-wire the chemosensory neuron and increase its axonal branching.

Article.Title: Impaired Sensory-motor Reconfiguration and Pupil-linked Arousal in Aging
Article.Authors: Ribeiro, M. J.; Calder-Travis, J.; Canario, N.; Castelo-Branco, M.; Donner, T. H.
Article.Abstract: Mounting evidence points to a key role of the brainstem arousal systems in controlling the adaptation of behavior to changing contexts. Both, brainstem arousal systems and cognitive flexibility seem to deteriorate in aging. We hypothesized that these two impairments are related. To test this hypothesis in humans, we compared adaptive behavior and arousal dynamics between older and younger adults (60% women). Arousal dynamics were measured by means of luminance-independent pupil responses. Participants performed a hierarchical decision-making task, which required frequent switches between two stimulus-response mapping rules for reporting a perceptual categorization judgment. These rule switches were hidden, and participants needed to infer them from noisy evidence. Older adults were less accurate than younger adults. This impairment was due to more frequent use of the incorrect rule. Neither the perceptual categorization nor the detection of rule switches differed between age groups. Moments of high probability of rule switches were associated with pupil dilation in both age groups, which was, however, reduced in older people. We propose that impaired cognitive recruitment of pupil-linked arousal in aging might limit the ongoing reconfiguration of the neural pathways that support flexible cognitive behavior.

Article.Title: Input-dependent directionality of interactions between cortical areas
Article.Authors: Mastrogiuseppe, F.; Carmona, J.; Yu, B. M.; Kohn, A.; Machens, C. K.
Article.Abstract: Studying the temporal coordination of activity signals across areas is essential for understanding brain function. Recent studies using cross-covariances show that activity directionality can shift rapidly with behavioral or task demands; yet, the circuit mechanisms underlying these changes remain unclear. Here, we use recurrent network models to investigate how directional interactions emerge and are flexibly reconfigured in multi-area cortical circuits. We show that, for fixed connectivity, directionality is shaped by how common inputs align with recurrent connectivity and the associated internal timescales of activity. In multi-area circuits with locally balanced excitation and inhibition, this reveals a predominant role for inputs to excitatory over inhibitory populations in controlling directionality. These inputs govern the directionality of the latent signals that account for most of the shared activity across areas, predominantly reflecting widespread and coherent activity fluctuations. Our models capture key features of cross-covariances from primate areas V1 and V2 and suggest parsimonious candidate mechanisms for the shift in directionality reported in these areas. This work establishes a mechanistic framework for understanding dynamic changes in temporal coordination across brain areas.

Article.Title: Brain states recur during longitudinal viewing and relate to content across narratives and sensory formats
Article.Authors: Chen, Y.; Ghavami, M.; St-Laurent, M.; Bellec, L.; Ghosh, S. S.
Article.Abstract: Models of brain dynamics propose that brain activity revisits a repertoire of configurations, and that current input influences which configuration is expressed. How broadly this holds across a person's extended experience is unknown. We analyzed 38-57 hours of fMRI per participant in six adults watching the television series Friends. Participant-specific hidden Markov models identified 42-47 active brain states, and independent fits to separate portions of viewing recovered similar states with similar tendencies to recur. States matched across participants' separately fitted models tended to occur at the same moments of the episodes. Among states retained after temporal screening, features from pretrained video, audio, and language networks partly predicted state identity, most strongly from intermediate-to-late layers. Predictions learned from Friends generalized without retraining to new films, and language-based predictions extended to reading and audiobook listening. State usage corresponded across stimuli little beyond what each recording's spectra and covariance reproduced.

Article.Title: RhabdoForge: A Modular, Biophysically-Grounded Rendering Framework for Insect Vision Neuroethology
Article.Authors: Le Moël, F.; Webb, B.
Article.Abstract: Insects solve complex behavioural tasks with remarkable efficiency, using minimal neural hardware tuned to the specific requirements of their ecological niches. To truly understand or replicate these behaviours, it is insufficient to model the brain in isolation: one must account for the dynamic, closed-loop interactions between the environment, the physical organisation of the sensory periphery, and internal biophysical dynamics. To address these issues for visually controlled behaviours, we present RhabdoForge, a modular, hardware-agnostic and high-performance rendering framework specifically designed for insect neuroethology and neuromorphic research. Designed for seamless integration into Python-based workflows, RhabdoForge implements both real-time ray-tracing and stochastic path-tracing using hardware-agnostic GPU pipelines. Crucially, the engine moves beyond the static "ommatidium-as-a-pixel" paradigm by introducing a fully parametrisable model where every layer of the compound eye (from the geometric shape and the topological lattice to the internal rhabdomere blueprint) is a discrete, swappable component. The engine is capable of simulating the high-frequency, sub-ommatidial rhabdomere photomechanical actuation, waveguide optics, intracellular pupil adaptation, and retinal sheet movements, allowing for the investigation of a variety of active sensing phenomena within a real-time closed-loop environment. The framework also includes an automated morphological pipeline that allows transforming 2D anatomical data into faithful 3D sensory models. We demonstrate the engine through two case studies: a closed-loop optic-flow centring response in a virtual tunnel, and a decomposition of the mechanisms that can contribute to spatial hyperacuity (axial and lateral rhabdomere microsaccades, aperture clipping, and the intracellular pupil). By providing a bridge between high-fidelity visual ecology and neuromorphic modelling, RhabdoForge enables researchers to explore how the interplay of sensory optics and neural processing can generate complex behaviour in both biological and artificial agents.

Article.Title: Estimating trial-wise modulation of functional connectivity using event-related fMRI
Article.Authors: Hwang, K.; Stokes, S. E.; Leach, S. C.; Jiang, J.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the neural basis of human cognition requires measuring not only localized brain activity but also how functional interactions between brain regions change in response to different cognitive demands. Event-related fMRI is an efficient design for linking trial-wise behavioral and computational variables to brain activity, but comparable methods for examining their effects on functional connectivity remain limited. Here, we introduce a regression-based beta-series modeling (BSM) framework that leverages single-trial response estimates from event-related fMRI to quantify how task-related variables modulate functional connectivity. By modeling the interaction between regional activity and task-related variables, this framework provides a statistical approach for testing connectivity modulation by both continuous and categorical variables. We evaluated this approach using comprehensive simulations across several experimental conditions and signal qualities. The regression-based BSM approach can sensitively detect ground-truth effects with well-controlled false-positive rates. Compared with generalized psychophysiological interaction, BSM achieved comparable performance across most conditions while demonstrating improved statistical power under lower signal-to-noise conditions. We further validated the approach using empirical event-related fMRI data. Distinct trial-wise cognitive variables selectively modulated functional connectivity during their corresponding trial epochs, demonstrating the temporal specificity and flexibility of the approach. Together, these findings demonstrate that regression-based BSM provides a flexible framework for examining task-modulated functional connectivity in event-related fMRI, with applications ranging from conventional experimental manipulations to continuous computational model-derived variables.

Article.Title: The TRIM32 granule promotes TDP-43 inclusion formation and amyloid aggregation through shuttle condensates
Article.Authors: Meng, F.; He, Z.; Zhou, J.; Zhang, R.; Nauen, D. W.; Troncoso, J. C.; Worley, P. F.; Zhang, W.
Article.Abstract: Aberrant protein aggregation and inclusion formation are hallmarks of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), which share overlapping genetic and pathological features. Similar aggregates are increasingly recognized in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE). However, it remains unclear whether a shared molecular pathway drives this pathological aggregation. Here, we report the formation of stress-responsive cytoplasmic TRIM32 granules, distinct from stress granules. The E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM32, together with the shuttle factor UBQLN2 and the autophagy adaptor p62/SQSTM1, drive condensation of TRIM32 granules that depend on E3 ligase activity and a network of intermolecular interactions. These condensates act as scaffolds that capture client proteins, including TDP-43 and ANXA11, and modulate their mobility. A unique hydrophobic loop within TRIM32's substrate-binding domain mimics low-complexity motifs in ANXA11 and TDP-43, enabling selective retention via competitive binding mediated by the UBQLN2 STI1 domain. Moreover, TRIM32 granules promote amyloid aggregation of TDP-43, an effect that is exacerbated by a pathogenic UBQLN2 mutation. In brains from individuals with diverse neurodegenerative diseases, TRIM32 co-localizes with pathological phospho-TDP-43 (pTDP-43) inclusions, supporting a model that TRIM32-driven granules function as selective proteostasis sorting compartments that broadly contribute to TDP-43 proteinopathy.

Article.Title: Emergent representations of graphical structure in mechanistic neural models of causal judgment
Article.Authors: Triplett, M. A.; Kay, K.
Article.Abstract: Humans have a remarkable ability to judge causal relationships from a limited number of unreliable observations. Past work on causal cognition has largely focused on normative accounts of human behavior, leaving unknown how biologically plausible neural systems can learn causal relationships from observations and update representations of causal structure with additional evidence. Here, we leverage task-optimized recurrent neural networks to discover candidate implementation-level neural mechanisms of causal judgment. We propose a novel cognitive task in which a subject observes stochastic samples from an unknown causal structure (e.g. among variables A, B, and C with unknown causal relationships), and must judge whether a specific causal relationship is present given a query (e.g. "does A cause C?"). We found that, after training, recurrent neural networks perform the task at high accuracy, adopt strategies that incorporate observations from non-queried variables to form judgments, and exhibit neural activity with an emergent geometry reflecting underlying causal structure. We then use dynamical systems analysis to identify a set of low-level neural mechanisms that implement causal judgment and form representations of causal relationships. Together, these findings lay the groundwork for a "bottom-up" approach to causal cognition, providing a potential basis for experimental study in the brain.

Article.Title: Default Feature Representations of the Cognitive Map
Article.Authors: Bazarjani, A.; Piray, P.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive maps allow animals and artificial agents to predict where they are likely to go next, and computational models show how such predictive maps guide planning. Environments, however, rarely stay fixed. When the goal changes, a door closes, or a barrier appears, the predictive map needs to be updated. However, given that predictive maps look far ahead, a local change in the environment potentially influences what is predicted from many other states, including distant ones, even though the agent experiences it only locally. Here, we propose Default Feature Representations (DFR) to address this problem. Our solution separates a predictive map into a fixed set of features shared across environments and an operator that carries the current environment. We show that the operator has a model-based closed form when the structural change is known (DFR-MB), and we present a temporal-difference rule for learning it from sampled transitions (DFR-TD) and prove that it converges to the same solution. Using samples alone, DFR-TD efficiently learns the perturbed map, plans about as well as the model-based solution, and outperforms successor-representation baselines on replanning. The model also reproduces the local remapping of grid cells under environmental change, mirroring the stability of entorhinal grid fields across environments.

Article.Title: Evidence-Gated Plasticity and Context-Dependent Consolidation for Multi-Goal Learning in Spiking Neural Networks
Article.Authors: Neymotin, S. A.; Hazan, H.; Unal, G.; Earl, C.; Anwar, H.; Franaszczuk, P.; Boothe, D.
Article.Abstract: Background / Introduction: Biologically inspired spiking neural networks offer a mechanistic framework for adaptive behavior, yet learning multiple goals remains challenging when synaptic updates for different targets interfere. We investigated whether multi-timescale plasticity and context-dependent consolidation improve interleaved multi-goal learning in a spiking navigation system inspired by entorhinal-hippocampal circuitry. Methods: We introduce evidence-gated plasticity (EGP), in which STDP-based reinforcement learning (STDP/RL) generates transient synaptic proposals and need-weighted behavioral evidence modulates their slower consolidation into durable weights. Global EGP pools these proposals and the corresponding evidence across goals. Target-context EGP extends this framework through goal-specific proposal and evidence stores and additional need-dependent scaling of consolidation. We compared the algorithms across paired spiking networks, tested learned weights with plasticity disabled, and examined upstream representations and consolidation components. Results: Global EGP supported multi-goal learning and durable navigation, while target-context EGP improved reward acquisition across replicated network comparisons and increased target-contact success during extended training. Independent evaluation confirmed that both algorithms retained navigation competence when plasticity was disabled. Additional controls suggested that overall consolidation strength contributes to the target-context reward advantage. In matched short-training experiments, conventional STDP/RL acquired shaped reward more rapidly, whereas EGP networks achieved higher target-contact success with learned synaptic weights held fixed. Conclusions: EGP supports durable multi-goal learning in spiking neural networks, and its target-context extension improves acquisition and conditional target selectivity in this interleaved navigation task. The framework offers a basis for testing context-sensitive, evidence-modulated plasticity in other multi-context learning problems.

Article.Title: Next generation Human Neocortical Neurosolver model with biophysically realistic somatic, dendritic and synaptic dynamics
Article.Authors: Duecker, K.; Soplata, A.; Tolley, N.; Pugliese, S.; Jones, T. A. E.; Kandpal, C.; Waller, D. A.; Daniels, D. S.; Jones, S. R.
Article.Abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca2+) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate how the updated circuitry and new features in the HNN software can be used to disentangle somatic, synaptic, and dendritic contributions to human E-/MEG signatures. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. These enhancements allow extensive model validations based on in vitro and in vivo electrophysiology, voltage and Ca2+ imaging, and provide users with novel insights on the mechanisms underlying E-/MEG signals.

Article.Title: A novel function of neuroligin 3: Beyond sociality, Regulating lifespan in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Kurbaj, J. M.; Ataei, R.; Simon, A. F.
Article.Abstract: Neuroligins are conserved postsynaptic adhesion proteins involved in synaptic function and behaviour. In Drosophila melanogaster, Neuroligin 3 (Nlg3) regulates social behaviour, sleep and synaptic architecture. We now report, through analysis of publicly available transcriptomics data, confirmed with RT-qPCR data, that loss-of-function of the nlg3 gene downregulates the expression of longevity-associated genes foxo, hsp70s, and hsp68. Graded genetic manipulation of the Drosophila melanogaster neuroligin 3 (nlg3) gene indeed modulates both social spacing and lifespan. Specifically, reduced nlg3 expression (via heterozygous deletion, or transposable-element insertion) extends lifespan in both sexes, while overexpression or complete deletion shortens it. In contrast, overexpression or complete loss of nlg3 leads the flies to be further apart (increased social distance, or social space), as does RNAi knockdown, while heterozygous reduction of nlg3 expression either lowers or does not alter the flies social space. This work identifies a previously unrecognized link between a conserved synaptic gene, social behaviour, and organismal longevity.

Article.Title: Sleep promotes neuronal autophagy for intracellular clearance
Article.Authors: Yang, L.; Zhang, X.; Li, J.; Liu, X.; Liu, D.
Article.Abstract: Sleep is essential for brain health, yet how it maintains neuronal homeostasis at the cellular level remains poorly understood. Here, we show that extended wakefulness selectively suppressed neuronal autophagic flux in the cortex of mice, whereas sleep rapidly restored it, accompanied by a shift in autophagic cargo from mitochondrial components to synaptic proteins. Sleep upregulated ATG7 expression in the cortex, involving both lysosomal degradation and a putative noncanonical secretory route. Moreover, low neuronal activity is associated with efficient flux, as Gq-mediated neuronal activation impaired autophagy and promoted intracellular amyloid-beta; accumulation. Notably, closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of lysosomal acidification, exclusively during sleep, reduced amyloid pathology in 5xFAD mice, whereas wake-targeted stimulation worsened pathology. Together, these findings demonstrate that sleep serves as a physiological gatekeeper for cortical neuronal autophagy, and highlight the importance of brain-state timing for enhancing intracellular proteostasis in neurodegenerative disease.

Article.Title: An AAV model of tauopathy targeting the mouse dentate gyrus reveals greater trans-synaptic tau spreading with aggregation-prone tau variants
Article.Authors: Leal, P.; Duwat, C.; Adamski, C.; Gaillard, M.-C.; Auregan, G.; Guillermier, M.; Bernier, S.; Dufour, N.; Petit, F.; Jan, C.; Herard, A.-S.; Fourmy, D.; Kabani, M.; Bonvento, G.; Cambon, K.; Bemelmans, A.-P.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease is characterized by progressive memory and cognitive decline, which is strongly correlated with the anatomical progression of tau pathology. Resulting from the intraneuronal aggregation of misfolded tau protein, tauopathy propagates in an anterograde manner between synaptically connected neurons through a prion-like mechanism. While glial cells, particularly microglia, are implicated in this process, the precise mechanisms underlying tauopathy propagation remain poorly understood. A critical unresolved question is whether aggregated or soluble pathologic tau forms mediate this spread. Here, we show in vivo that tau spreading scales with the aggregation propensity of the tau variant expressed. We developed a mouse model using adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated gene transfer to overexpress distinct tau forms in the dentate gyrus, alongside a reporter gene. This design enabled discrimination between transduced neurons and those secondarily affected by pathology propagation. Leveraging contralateral neuronal projections, we quantified propagation levels. To investigate the role of microglia and of extracellular vesicles, we analyzed microglial morphology in response to different tau forms and measured tau protein levels in extracellular vesicles isolated from injected mouse brains. We first confirmed the presence of vector-derived tau protein in non-transduced neurons, validating our model for studying tau propagation. We then found that aggregation-prone tau variants were associated with a greater number of tau-positive neurons in the contralateral hippocampus than wild-type tau. Additionally, extracellular vesicles from brains injected with aggregated tau contained higher levels of tau protein. Given that insoluble tau aggregates represent the ultimate stage of tauopathy, our findings suggest that propagation occurs at advanced stages of tau pathology, and that extracellular vesicles may contribute to the transfer of pathological tau, although the cellular origin of these vesicles was not determined in this study. Furthermore, our model provides a robust experimental paradigm for exploring therapeutic strategies aimed at inhibiting tauopathy propagation.

Article.Title: Exponential Map Models as an Interpretable Framework for Generating Neural Spatial Representations
Article.Authors: Pettersen, M.; Haug, N.; Bergli, J.; Surowiec, T.; Lepperod, M. E.
Article.Abstract: A foundational challenge in neuroscience and AI is understanding how physical space is mapped into neural representations. While artificial neural networks can learn brain-like spatial representations, their ``black-box'' nature obscures whether these representations reflect general principles or artifacts of specific architectures, objectives or optimization choices, offering no guarantee that solutions for tasks like path integration generalize beyond training data. Here, we use a first-principles framework based on the matrix exponential, in which generator matrices map physical locations to neural population vectors without gradient-based optimization. Within this formalism, navigational properties follow directly from algebraic constraints on the generators: commuting generators enable trajectory-invariant, exact path integration, while skew-symmetry yields equinorm representations with translation-invariant similarities. Preserving the flat Euclidean metric further constrains the generator spectra to balanced wavevector configurations, such as the roots-of-unity constellations that generate periodic grid fields. Similarity preservation further produces localized place-like fields, and extending the generators to a context signal models context-dependent remapping. Beyond its algebraic relation to continuous attractor and oscillatory interference models, the framework natively supports goal-oriented multi-map navigation through hyperdimensional bundling and binding, fits recorded grid and place cell data, extrapolates their rate maps far beyond the fitted region, and makes testable predictions for entorhinal circuits. By grounding spatial representations in exact algebraic conditions, this work offers a transparent alternative to empirical representation learning, revealing the conditions under which a coherent neural map of space arises.

Article.Title: Activity drives local CaMKII synthesis and subcellular localization via autophosphorylation-dependent pathways
Article.Authors: Clements, K. J.; Chen, N.; Gonzalez, K. M. D. L.; Zhang, Y.; Rodal, A. A.; Griffith, L.
Article.Abstract: Strong repeated stimulation of a neuron triggers an increase in local protein synthesis along with a change in localization of proteins, allowing the neuron to rapidly adjust its proteome in response to activity. One of these proteins, calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), is involved in mediating structural and functional changes after activity. While postsynaptic CaMKII translation has been studied, very little is known about presynaptic synthesis, including its mechanisms and the functional consequences. We utilized the Drosophila larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) as a model to study the molecular requirements for activity-dependent synthesis along with the localization of CaMKII protein. Presynaptic-specific tagging of endogenous CaMKII demonstrates that spaced stimulation rapidly increases presynaptic CaMKII through local translation of pre-existing mRNA, independently of somatic factors. This activity-dependent synthesis requires the distal 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of the CaMKII mRNA, which is also necessary for steady-state synaptic accumulation. Additionally, we show that activity-dependent synthesis requires CaMKII T287 autophosphorylation-induced activation of the PI3K/Akt/mTor pathway. While activity-dependent redistribution of CaMKII has been previously identified, very little is known about how local synthesis and translocation may interact to define different pools of protein that may have distinct functions. We demonstrate that CaMKII with a T287D phosphomimetic mutant localizes to the synaptic membrane and pulse-chase experiments show that the localization of newly-synthesized CaMKII differs from pre-existing CaMKII, indicating neuronal activity generates spatially distinct, and likely functionally distinct, CaMKII populations which may underlie long-lasting plasticity.

Article.Title: Simple, static, spiking nonlinearities can account for seemingly complex interactions between visual, motor and cognitive variables in the visual cortex.
Article.Authors: Zajkowski, W. K.; Quinn, K.; Seillier, L.; Bellet, M. E.; Butts, D. A.; Nienborg, H.
Article.Abstract: Neural activity in the visual cortex is driven by the stimulus and modulated by multiple task-related variables, including spatial attention, eye movements, and perceptual decisions. These multiple influences are each typically described as nonlinear interactions such as gain or normalization, raising the question of how these diverse signals can be combined through cellular or circuit mechanisms. Here we address this problem by examining neuronal responses in macaque visual areas V2 and V3 during a visual discrimination task that dissociates spatial attention from motor planning and microsaccadic eye movements. Using a statistical modeling framework, we show that attentional, microsaccade-related, and choice-related influences on neural activity are best explained by a simple additive stimulus-independent input modulation, which manifests as a gain via a spiking nonlinearity. In addition to explaining how interactions between variables might be accomplished mechanistically, this framework also resolves a controversy about the relationship between microsaccades and spatial attention. We find that neither microsaccade direction nor microsaccade-related neural activity accounts for attentional modulation, although these variables are often correlated, leading to apparent interactions. Thus, visual cortex can integrate sensory, motor-related, and cognitive signals through a parsimonious mechanism that preserves stable stimulus representations while supporting flexible, context-dependent modulation.

Article.Title: Comparative Evaluation of Assumption Lean Community Detection Methods for Human Connectome Networks
Article.Authors: Bhattacharya, A.; Chakraborty, N.; Tu, J.; Wang, X.; Dierker, D.; Eck, A.; Elison, J. T.; Lahiri, S.; Eggebrecht, A.; Wheelock, M. D.
Article.Abstract: Community detection on resting-state functional connectivity provides a principled lens on mesoscale organization in functional brain networks. The choice of community count K, lacks a standardized or principled guideline. We conducted a benchmark of three approaches that do not a priori restrict communities to an assortative mesoscale topology: the Weighted Stochastic Block Model, Spectral Clustering, and K-means Clustering. Performance was assessed on synthetic networks with ground truth and on three neuroimaging cohorts which included adult and infant datasets. We compared several strategies for selecting K, including the silhouette index and other approaches commonly used in the literature. These were evaluated alongside a likelihood-based criterion for the weighted stochastic block model that employs bootstrap confidence intervals for differences in log-likelihood between successive values of K. For the synthetic networks, WSBM and Spectral Clustering correctly identified the true number of communities, whereas K-means Clustering did not. In adult datasets, most indices did not yield a unique optimum, whereas the likelihood-based criterion selected K=11, which is consistent with established sensory and association systems. In infants and toddlers, the same procedure supports a larger K around 15 and reveals developmentally distinct mesoscale architecture, including anterior and posterior subdivisions within default mode and frontoparietal systems.

Article.Title: Subthreshold Asynchronous States and Computations in Biophysically Detailed Populations of Neurons
Article.Authors: Nicola, W.; Mahani, A.; Turner, R. W.; Zamponi, G.
Article.Abstract: Spikes are metabolically costly to generate and transmit, and spiking rates should be kept to a minimum for efficient coding. Many invertebrate circuits do not fire spikes or fire spikes at extremely low rates by using graded synaptic transmission as the communication mechanism between neurons. We show that computations and asynchronous states based on excitatory/inhibitory balance can exist without firing any spikes through self-sustaining subthreshold voltage fluctuations powered by graded synaptic transmission in networks of biophysically detailed Hodgkin-Huxley neurons. This novel subthreshold asynchronous state, which we call subthreshold voltage chaos, can be controlled for useful computation and pattern generation, also without firing spikes. Further, we identify candidate ion channels, low-voltage-activated T-Type calcium channels that provide a biophysical mechanism for this type of subthreshold computation. Our work demonstrates a mechanism for computation with graded synaptic release with very few spikes.

Article.Title: Multimodal Reorganization of Gut--Brain Physiology During the Cephalic Phase of Digestion
Article.Authors: Kehnemouyi, Y. M.; Coleman, T. P.
Article.Abstract: The vagus nerve plays a central role in gut--brain communication, yet the physiological dynamics associated with cholinergic vagal signaling remain difficult to characterize non-invasively in humans. The cephalic phase response, which prepares the gastrointestinal system for food ingestion through anticipatory vagal pathways, offers a unique opportunity to investigate these interactions. Here, we used simultaneous recordings of cortical, gastric, cardiac, and swallow physiology in healthy adults to characterize brain--body responses during food anticipation and subsequent ingestion. Food-related sensory cues increased gastric myoelectric activity as well as swallow and heart rate while eliciting frequency-specific changes in cortical oscillations. Strikingly, anticipation was accompanied by opposing changes in physiological coordination: synchronization within cortical and gastric networks decreased, whereas coupling between the brain and stomach increased. These changes largely returned toward baseline following ingestion, suggesting a distinct anticipatory organization of brain--body activity. Moreover, gastric responses were associated with various aspects of subjective appetite, whereas cortical responses were selectively associated with craving. Both gastric and cortical responses independently explained the variation in participants' self-reported craving. Article.Title: Variation in infant subcortical brain development from 6 to 12 months in Down syndrome
Article.Authors: Garic, D.; Ren, M.; Hawks, Z.; Hong, Y.; Lasch, C.; Grzadzinski, R.; Kim, S. H.; Azrak, O.; Elison, J.; Wolff, J.; Pruett, J. R.; McKinstry, R. C.; Estes, A.; Dager, S.; Pandey, J.; Schultz, R.; Evans, A. C.; Shen, M. D.; Styner, M.; Piven, J.; Botteron, K.; Hazlett, H.; Gerig, G.; Marrus, N.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: Down syndrome (DS), arising from Trisomy 21, is the most common genetic condition associated with intellectual disability. While smaller total brain volumes have been consistently observed in DS, no longitudinal neuroimaging studies have examined volumetric brain development in DS during infancy, a period of rapid neural growth when interventions may have the greatest impact. Method: High-resolution T1- and T2-weighted images were acquired during natural sleep in a multisite longitudinal cohort of 44 infants with DS and 39 control infants without DS at ages 6 and 12 months. Neuroimaging data were harmonized to reduce batch effects, and a novel deep-learning, repeated-measures segmentation approach was applied to optimize neuroanatomical segmentations. Total intracranial volume (ICV) and bilateral absolute subcortical volumes (amygdala, caudate, hippocampus, pallidum, putamen, thalamus) were first directly compared in infants with and without DS at 6 and 12 months. Hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) evaluated longitudinal group differences for each structure, accounting for sex, gestational age, and laterality. Subcortical group differences estimated by HLM were also compared to group differences in total ICV. Results: ICV in infants with DS was lower than controls at 6 months (12.6%; p<.001) and 12 months (16.3%; p<.001). Subcortical structures displayed a range of lower volumes (6.9%-13.1%; p's<.003) in infants with DS, although the caudate and putamen were exceptions. Caudate volumes were on average lower in DS but not significantly different from controls, while putamen volumes were on average higher in DS but not significantly different from controls, except for the right putamen, which was significantly larger (5.3%; p=.018) at 6 months. In HLM, ICV and all subcortical structures showed slower growth in DS from 6 to 12 months, except for the amygdala and putamen, which displayed similar growth rates to controls. DS-associated reductions in subcortical volumes were similar in magnitude to ICV, although 12-month caudate and 6- and 12-month putamen volumes were enlarged relative to ICV. Conclusion: Infants with DS exhibited substantially reduced ICV and widespread reductions in subcortical volumes and growth from 6-12 months. Across a range of volumetric differences, findings were most distinct in the basal ganglia, for which volume reductions were attenuated in the caudate, while the putamen was uniquely enlarged with comparable growth to controls. These observations support early regional specificity in the neural impact of Trisomy 21 and underscore the utility of infant neuroimaging to inform biologically based interventions and clinical trial readiness in DS.

Article.Title: PKR drives neuropathology in a mouse model of Leigh syndrome
Article.Authors: Gonzalez-Torres, M.; Bianchi, P.; Blanco-Ramos, M.; Luna-Sanchez, M.; Prada-Dacasa, P.; Puighermanal, E.; Canal, C.; Cutando, L.; Le, S.; Gella, A.; Girona, M.; Sanchez-Benito, L.; Armengol, B.; Appiah, I.; Fernandez-Irigoyen, J.; Alkhatib, M.; Feist, L.; McElroy, G.; Lisowski, P.; del Sol, A.; Santamaria, E.; Prigione, A.; Sanz, E.; Quintana, A.

Here, we uncover a cell-type-specific antiviral program in vulnerable GABAergic neurons of Ndufs4-deficient mice and human brain organoids modeling Leigh syndrome. Despite robust type I interferon responses, genetic ablation of innate immune mediators Ifnar1 or Sting1 fails to ameliorate disease progression. Instead, we identify the double-stranded RNA sensor protein kinase R (PKR) as a critical mediator of mitochondrial neuropathology. PKR associates with mitochondrial RNA, while its genetic deletion or silencing delays neurological decline, attenuates neuroinflammation, and extends survival without restoring mitochondrial respiration. PKR deletion also normalizes JNK signaling without detectable global translational repression, suggesting a noncanonical contribution to disease. Together, our findings reveal PKR-mediated antiviral RNA sensing as a pathogenic mechanism in mitochondrial complex I deficiency and highlight PKR as a candidate target for mitochondrial encephalopathies.

Article.Title: Robust Cable Models for Complex Neuronal Morphologies
Article.Authors: Fox, J. M. R.; Fischer, B. J.; DeBello, W. M.; Pena, J. L.
Article.Abstract: We present a free and open-source, semi-automated, topologically robust pipeline for fitting cable models to 3D surface mesh morphology data of neuronal membranes, particularly suited to structures with complex shapes and topological holes. The motivation for this work is the discovery of morphologically complex neuronal spines on the auditory space-specific neurons of the barn owl, dubbed "toric spines", notable for their high curvature, branching density, and topological holes. Multicompartmental simulation software requires morphology to be represented as cable models, yet existing software tools for fitting cable models to complex 3D surface meshes generally assume acyclic topology, and thus did not work well for toric spines. We present the Mesh and Skeleton Cable Fitting (MASCAF) pipeline and software, which fits a cable model to a closed 3D surface mesh using mean-curvature flow skeletonization, and automatically handles cyclic topology. In this paper, we demonstrate how MASCAF is applied to fit cable models, how loop connections can be reconstructed in multicompartmental simulation software, and how the results can be validated using geometry and simulator-based methods. While non-tree morphologies such as toric spines are neuroanatomically special, our software pipeline provides a cable-model fitting approach for surface mesh data that is topologically robust, deterministic, open-source, and applicable to general morphologies, thereby closing a crucial gap between neuronal imaging and high-resolution simulation.

Article.Title: Age-dependent accumulation of neuromelanin in African mole-rats
Article.Authors: Canales, C.; Ilarduya, M. M.; Chocarro, J.; Rico, A. J.; Gariznabarreta, G.; Lorenzo-Ramos, E.; Hoyo, J.; Carbonell, D.; Sumbera, R.; Okrouhlik, J.; Ruiz-Molina, D.; Lanciego, J. L.
Article.Abstract: Although neuromelanin (NMel) is a dark pigment characteristic of catecholaminergic cell groups in the primate CNS, rodent brains lack pigmentation in ventral mesencephalic cell groups and in the locus coeruleus (LC). Even though these neurons possess the molecular machinery required to produce NMel, it remains unknown why the brains of mice and rats are not pigmented. Accordingly, postmortem brain samples of two species of African mole-rats (Heterocephalus glaber and Fukomys mechowii) were used to evaluate whether these longest-living rodents accumulate NMel. The results revealed time-dependent pigmentation beyond two years of age, with the highest pigmentation levels observed in LC neurons. In conclusion, the physiological pigmentation of catecholaminergic neurons in the brain of African mole-rats appears to result from a slow kinetic process that requires a lifespan long enough to allow detectable NMel accumulation.

Article.Title: Systematic and dynamic task coding in the frontal cortex
Article.Authors: Park, J.; Park, H.-B.; Holmes, C. D.; Snyder, L. H.
Article.Abstract: Behavioral flexibility depends on the capacity to form and utilize task representations. Prior work has shown that baseline activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) can differ between two tasks. Comparing more than two tasks makes it possible to ask whether different neuronal populations share a common form of task encoding, that is, a conserved representational geometry across tasks. We trained two rhesus monkeys to perform 6 cognitive tasks and recorded spiking activity simultaneously from hundreds of neurons in the frontal eye field (FEF) or the dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC), one area per session. During the fixation period, before any task-specific stimulus appeared, the population activity state already reflected the upcoming task, and task identity could be decoded on single trials. Strikingly, the geometry of the 6 task states was conserved across populations recorded in different sessions, across the two areas, and across the two monkeys. Global signals that differ between tasks, such as expected reward, task difficulty, and attention, measured by reward amount, hit rate, and reaction time, did not fully account for this shared geometry. These findings suggest that the frontal cortex systematically adjusts its population state to encode and prepare for the upcoming task.

Article.Title: The thalamic reticular nucleus provides spatially and temporally tuned inhibition to the lateral geniculate nucleus across species
Article.Authors: Miao, Y.; Ciftcioglu, U. M.; Gorin, A. S.; Dakwala, R.; Ahn, S.; Sommer, F. T.; Hirsch, J. A.
Article.Abstract: By proposing a role in spatial attention, Francis Crick piqued interest in the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), a GABAergic structure that receives input from relay cells projecting to cortex and feeds back inhibition in return. Importantly, predictions of Crick's hypothesis extend beyond attention to suggest that TRN provides selective, localized inhibition to relay cells and, thus, influences sensory processing per se. To ask if this latter role for TRN holds across species, we compared previous recordings from cat with a novel dataset from mouse, focusing on vision. We estimated receptive field size and structure of reticular cells in the visual sector of TRN and of relay cells in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN). Cells in both nuclei encoded specific visual features and had receptive fields of comparable size within binocular visual space. Moreover, paired recordings from both structures suggested that TRN is able to promote burst firing in dLGN in addition to modulating spike rate. Thus, TRN is not only important for attentional regulation, but is also able to make fine-tuned contributions to early sensory processing.

Article.Title: Opposing actions of cis- and trans-ligands at a single GPCR link osmotic state to habitat choice
Article.Authors: Tsukasa, Y.; Ohbayashi, T. S.; Kurio, M.; Kohsaka, H.; Maeta, K.; Matsutani, E.; Tsumadori, A.; Li, K.; Matsui, R.; Suzuki, J.; Nose, A.; Uemura, T.; Usui, T.
Article.Abstract: How internal physiological states are translated into altered behavioral responses to the same sensory cue remains poorly understood. Here we show that the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored Ly6/uPAR protein Belly roll (Bero) acts as a cis-ligand for the neuropeptide receptor Allatostatin C receptor 2 (AstC-R2) in Drosophila larvae. Bero--AstC-R2 signaling establishes a phospholipase C{beta}-dependent high-Ca2+ state in abdominal leucokinin-producing (ABLK) neurons that suppresses nociceptive sensory transmission. Desiccation raises hemolymph osmolality, which activates AstC-producing neurons; the secreted AstC peptide then opposes Bero--AstC-R2 signaling, lowers ABLK Ca2+ activity, and unlocks avoidance of dry substrates. As a consequence, dehydrated larvae bias their pupation sites toward humid environments, mitigating desiccation risk during the immobile pupal stage. Thus, a membrane-tethered cis- and a secreted trans-ligand can act in opposition at a single GPCR, providing a non-canonical mechanism by which organismal physiological state is encoded in receptor signaling and converted into an adaptive behavioral choice.

Article.Title: Heterogeneous plasticity rules generate diverse structures in recurrent networks
Article.Authors: Cusseddu, C.; Festa, D.; Miehl, C.; Gjorgjieva, J.
Article.Abstract: How do local changes at individual synapses give rise to structured recurrent connectivity? Experiments have revealed diverse forms of spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) across the brain, making it difficult to predict which circuit structures arise from different rules. We developed an analytical framework mapping excitatory Hebbian, anti-Hebbian, and symmetric STDP rules to directed three-neuron motifs. Individual homogeneous rules generate restricted subsets of motifs, and no single rule produces all motifs. Combining different rules generates motifs inaccessible to individual rules and yields the full motif repertoire. These predictions generalize to larger recurrent networks. The mapping is nevertheless highly non-unique, with distinct rules and parameters producing similar motif distributions, including distributions compatible with experimental connectivity. Thus, circuit structure constrains candidate plasticity rules but does not uniquely identify them. Finally, networks with similar motif distributions can nonetheless differ in their firing rates and pairwise correlations, suggesting that activity may provide an additional constraint on candidate plasticity rules.

Article.Title: Design and Test Novel EEG Electrode Attachments for Type 4 Afro-textured Hairstyles
Article.Authors: Broor, M.; Ogunniyi, K.; Williamson, L.; Liu, C.
Article.Abstract: Black participants remain underrepresented in electroencephalography (EEG) research, partly because current EEG devices work poorly with dense, coily Type 4 Afro-textured hair. Research-grade EEG typically wires electrodes on a cap, and therefore the electrodes often fail to reach the scalp through dense, Afro-textured hair. Protocols that ask Black participants to unbraid or restyle protective hairstyles add burdens that discourage enrollment in research studies. To address this, we designed and tested 3D-printed attachments that fit onto an EEG electrode and anchored it directly in the hair, using the hairstyle itself as the mounting structure. We fabricated three design configurations for natural Afro-textured hair, cornrows/braids, and twists/microlocs. Seventeen healthy adults with Type 4a-4c hair used electrode attachments that matched their hairstyle. During a single visit, EEG was recorded with 16 conventional cap electrodes defined by the international 10-20 system and with 16 electrodes using novel electrode attachments anchored directly to their hair. Participants completed resting and walking trials with each system. Electrode-to-scalp distance and gel volume were measured during setup. Electrode disconnection, impedance, signal quality (i.e. peak alpha power and aperiodic (1/f) component), and comfort level were measured throughout the data collection. Compared with the conventional cap, the novel attachments reduced electrode-to-scalp distance, gel use, and impedance. Twenty percent of the conventional cap electrodes failed to connect to the scalp compared with 0.1% of novel electrodes. Impedance rose across trials for the conventional cap, whereas the novel attachments showed a smaller increase and maintained lower impedance throughout. Signal quality was significantly better using the novel attachments, while comfort level did not differ between systems. In conclusion, hair-anchored electrode attachment may present a feasible alternative to conventional cap-based EEG for people with Type 4 hair, yielding more usable channels and better signal quality, and supporting more inclusive EEG acquisition.

Article.Authors: Calbick, D.; Kim, J. Z.; Sohn, H.; Yildirim, I.
Article.Abstract: Neuroscience aims to uncover the algorithms by which the brain builds and manipulates rich internal representations of objects, agents, and places. Existing reverse-engineering frameworks remain ineffective for identifying these algorithms. Here, we present Dynamical Structure-Preserving Manifolds (dSPMs)---a novel multilevel reverse-engineering framework that programs, without training, recurrent neural networks to enable hypothesis-driven identification of the brain's algorithms that generate symbolic, structure-preserving representations of the world around. We apply dSPM to identify an algorithm for physical scene prediction in the dorsomedial frontal cortex (DMFC) of macaques intercepting a ball on a Pong-like virtual gameboard. dSPM better explained DMFC than alternatives, made predictions confirmed in neural data, and revealed an algorithm of DMFC that we term 'manifold-based simulation': perceived initial conditions rapidly collapse neural activity onto a low-dimensional manifold whose geometry encodes a physics-based representation of the scene, supporting far-out predictions without traditional next-step simulation. dSPM supports effective exploration of the computational foundations of biological intelligence.

Article.Title: Polysemanticity in human hippocampal neurons
Article.Authors: Yan, X.; Li, J.-A.; Franch, M.; Zhu, H.; Cowan, R. L.; Belanger, J.; Chavez, A. G. L.; Chericoni, A.; Ismail, T.; Katlowitz, K.; Kolibius, L.; Mickiewicz, E.; Paulo, D.; Bartoli, E.; Hennig, J. A.; Fraczek, T.; Provenza, N.; Rahimpour, S.; Shofty, B.; Smith, E. H. Article.Abstract: As we perceive language, neurons in the brain represent the meanings of each word we hear. Polysemanticity increases capacity, robustness, and scalability, and facilitates contextualization. These peaks, corresponding to the stimuli that most effectively drive the neurons, are not random; instead, they have overdispersed, isotropic geometry, consistent with interference-minimizing repulsive coding, although they lack grid-like hexagonal structure. Individual neuron responses are strongly modulated by context while population geometry remains stable and generalizable, allowing for pattern separation without sacrificing generalizability. Together, these results indicate that hippocampal neurons represent meaning using a distributed, dense, contextualized, polysemantic code consistent with the demands of superposition.

Article.Title: Predictive stability code: Trial-by-trial conflict expectations tune task representations via proactive and reactive spatio-temporo-spectral dynamics
Article.Authors: Viviani, G.; Visalli, A.; Montefinese, M.; Di Pietro, I.; Vallesi, A.; Ruz, M.; Ambrosini, E.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive stability, or task focus, enables goal-directed behavior through representational dynamics: by prioritizing task-relevant representations over competing task-irrelevant ones. Beyond corrective reactive mechanisms operating after conflict arises, stability can also be engaged predictively through the statistical learning of conflict regularities, either proactively, based on global conflict expectations, or through a predictive reactive mode, guided by item-specific conflict expectations. Yet, the representational mechanisms enabling such predictive adjustments remain underspecified. We addressed this by re-analyzing EEG data from a spatial Stroop task concurrently manipulating list-wide (LWPC) and item-specific (ISPC) proportion congruency. Moving beyond existing analytical approaches, we developed a framework that combines trial-by-trial Bayesian conflict-expectancy modeling with a novel spatio-temporo-spectral searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis, and leveraged directional representational modeling complemented by ridge-regression decoding. We first identified the necessary computational substrate for predictive stability reconfigurations: the spatio-temporo-spectral patterns encoding task (Target, Distractor) and conflict-expectancy (LWPC, ISPC) representations, with the latter already encoded in the pre-stimulus windows. Crucially, conflict expectations modulated Target and Distractor encoding strength with distinct spatio-temporal and spectral dynamics, revealing a functional dissociation. LWPC-induced proactive stability follows a "Target-first" policy, primarily strengthening the Target representation early after stimulus onset via Alpha and lower-Beta patterns, and weakening Distractor encoding only later; conversely, ISPC-induced predictive reactive stability follows a "Distractor-first" policy, rapidly weakening Distractor encoding via response-locked posterior Beta patterns, and strengthening the Target representation only downstream. Our study refines theoretical cognitive control models, incorporating a mechanistic explanation for predictive stability, while also establishing a multidimensional methodological template for investigating the underlying substrates of adaptive behavior and beyond.

Article.Authors: Krogh, S. M.; Pylkkänen, L.
Article.Abstract: In language, not only do sentence meanings depend on how words are structured together, but word meanings also depend on their roles in the structure. Here we used magnetoencephalography to track the neural dynamics of animacy, a fundamental semantic feature that guides conceptual organization. Regardless of how animacy was operationalized (as discrete semantic categories or more abstractly), the same pattern emerged: When word-level animacy conflicted with the structural context, it disappeared from the word's neural representation. Our findings show how compositional processes rapidly reconfigure neural traces of word meanings, allowing phrase-level meanings to even override word-level features.

Article.Authors: Lei, W.; Tian, X.; Dong, C.; Lou, J.; Zhao, X.; Dong, X.; Du, L.; Yang, R.; Hong, Y.; Yu, Y.; Yang, C.; Qian, L.; Liu, S.; Li, A.; Wang, M.; Liu, B.

By relating these cellular maps to cortical imaging features, we demonstrate their utility for investigating cellular contributions to global cortical organization and regional specialization. Together, RIDGE provides a unified framework and spatially continuous cellular reference resource for integrating cellular architecture with human cortical imaging across spatial scales.

However, many neurons within each region project to just one of the subnuclei, suggesting they can be recruited independently. To test this, we combined optogenetics and widefield Ca2+ imaging and showed that stimulating prefrontal cortical projections to the HDB or SI results in distinct large-scale patterns of cortical activity via a cholinergic mechanism. Article.Title: Visual object recognition in the fly: the internal representation of a predator drives defensive behaviour
Article.Authors: Denagamage, S.; Foltz, M.; Dalstein, V. M.; Behnia, R.; Card, G. M.; Axel, R.; Cury, K. M.
Article.Abstract: Animals recognize visual objects and respond to them appropriately to survive. Here we define a neural circuit in Drosophila that underlies the visual recognition of a natural predator, the parasitoid wasp, and orchestrates defence. We found that flies exhibit a repertoire of directed defensive actions structured by the wasp's position within the fly's field of view. Expression of these behaviours is driven by visual detection of a conspicuous morphological cue -- the wasp's elongated antennae. A small subset of lobula columnar (LC) visual projection neuron types are required for defence and are activated by constituent visual features of the wasp. Three LC types respond selectively to the wasp's antennae, and relay this information to LC9, which sums antennal- and body-feature signals to form a composite representation of the wasp. Spatial filtering of this representation onto a descending premotor pathway translates the wasp's location in visual space into directed defence. Feature combination followed by spatial filtering may constitute a general mechanism for coupling object identity to context-appropriate action.

Article.Title: Mice, marmosets and humans use ambiguous local motion to stabilize gaze
Article.Authors: Rosselli, F. B.; Buettner, M.; Bucci, A.; Mitchell, J. F.; Franke, F.
Article.Abstract: Animals need to infer properties of the environment that are only ambiguously encoded by neurons in the sensory periphery. Using stimuli that dissociate local edge motion from global, object motion, we found that responses of NOT neurons were strongly biased towards local motion. This bias propagated to behavior: eye movements followed local motion; in mice, to the point that changing the edge orientation of vertically moving objects produced horizontal eye movements. Marmosets and humans exhibited similar biases, amplified in humans when central vision was masked. Thus, the brain can transform ambiguous sensory signals directly into behavior, without first resolving the ambiguity.

Article.Title: Serotonergic anxiety is a stress intensity-dependent state mediated by dopaminergic signaling
Article.Authors: Varga, Z. K.; Mieghem, J. V.; Jimenez-Fernandez, L.; Ujhelyi, A.; Kermen, F.
Article.Abstract: Despite the central role attributed to serotonin in anxiety, its involvement and therapeutic efficacy are inconsistent, raising the possibility that serotonergic recruitment depends on the stress history from which anxiety emerges. Using larval zebrafish, we combined graded glucocorticoid exposure with chemogenetic DRN manipulation, whole-brain activity mapping, and pharmacology to test whether stress intensity determines serotonergic involvement in anxiety. Increasing stress intensity did not simply increase anxiety severity but generated distinct anxiety phenotypes. Lower glucocorticoid exposure produced context-general anxiety that required the serotonergic DRN, whereas higher exposure produced context-dependent, DRN-independent anxiety. Whole-brain mapping identified a posterior tubercular/hypothalamic dopaminergic region associated with DRN-dependent anxiolysis, while D1, but not D2 receptor antagonism abolished the anxiolytic effect of DRN ablation. Together, our findings identify stress intensity as a determinant of serotonergic recruitment during anxiety, reveal a downstream contribution of D1-dependent dopaminergic signaling, and provide a framework for understanding the mechanistic heterogeneity of anxiety and its variable response to serotonergic treatments.
