Article.Title: Learning Interpretable Switching Dynamics in Shared Neural-Behavioral Latent Space
Article.Authors: Zhang, Y.; Caro, J. O.; Oren, R.; Higley, M. J.; Cardin, J.; Churchland, A.; Saxena, S.
Article.Abstract: Modern recording technologies enable simultaneous measurement of high-dimensional neural activity and rich behavioral variables, creating both an opportunity and a modeling challenge: identifying the shared latent structure that mediates the brain-behavior relationship and the underlying dynamics through which it evolves across behavioral states. Existing approaches focus on different parts of this challenge: shared representation learning methods identify neural-behavioral subspaces but typically do not model dynamical structure, while dynamical models capture temporal variation and discrete state transitions in neural activity, but do not explicitly disentangle shared neural-behavioral structure from modality-specific variability. We introduce Switching Shared Latent Dynamics (SSLD), a unified framework that learns a latent representation shared between neural activity and behavior and endows this shared space with nonlinear switching recurrent dynamics to reflect the hypothesis that behaviorally relevant neural representations exhibit structured dynamical changes across behavioral states. Complementary private latent variables capture modality-specific variability, providing a window into neural activity that does not directly interact with behavior. We evaluate SSLD on a simulated dataset and four diverse experimental datasets spanning species, brain regions, and recording modalities: monkey motor and premotor cortex during reaching, somatosensory cortex during a bump task, widefield calcium imaging across mouse dorsal cortex during (a) self-initiated decision-making and (b) spontaneous movements. Across all four datasets, SSLD accurately reconstructs neural and behavioral signals, recovers discrete states in the dynamics that align with experimentally defined behavioral epochs, and isolates behaviorally-relevant neural information in the shared latent while preserving private neural variability. Ablations confirm that shared representation learning, behavioral supervision, and switching dynamics each contribute to performance. SSLD offers an interpretable approach to modeling shared neural-behavioral dynamics that complements ongoing efforts toward foundation models for neuroscience.

Article.Title: Testing the Vogt-Bailey Index using task-based fMRI across pulse sequence protocols
Article.Authors: Galea, K.; Escudero, A. A.; Attard-Montalto, N.; Vella, N.; Mora Corral, M.; Smith, R. E.; Farrugia, C.; Galdi, P.; Scerri, K.; Butler, L.; Bajada, C. J.
Article.Abstract: Local connectivity analyses in fMRI such as the Vogt-Bailey Index, investigate the prevalence of co-fluctuations in the time-series of adjacent voxels. While there have been in silico assessments of the VB Index, this technique has not yet been assessed systematically. This study has two aims: first, to assess the VB Index using a task paradigm with well established a priori expectations on the brain region predominantly responsible for executing this task to determine whether the VB Index specifically highlights this area. Second, we investigate if, and how, the spatial resolution of the sequence protocols employed, with their inherent effects on the signal-to-noise ratio, affect the resultant VB maps. A cohort of 10 research volunteers underwent fMRI acquisitions utilising a block design finger tapping experiment. Each volunteer was scanned with three sequence protocols, with all parameters equivalent except for the volume of the voxels. Task-associated VB maps derived from statistical comparison of normal VB maps with task-regressed VB maps were compared with those obtained from the conventional General Linear Model approach. Particular emphasis was placed on the identification of the hand portion of the motor homunculus. Across sequence protocols, the VB Index consistently identified elevated local connectivity in, qualitatively, the same portion of the motor cortex as that yielded by the General Linear Model based on the task paradigm. The consistently significant task-associated increases in the VB Index, across sequence protocols, in the cortical region associated with an fMRI task paradigm, provides support for the biological relevance of such local connectivity measures.

Article.Authors: Taylor, S. R.; Olson, C.; Ripoll-Sanchez, L.; Valperga, G.; McWhirter, R.; Barney, S. T.; Atkinson, A.; Goel, S.; Weinreb, A.; Hardin, A.; Rolfson, A.; Pattee, J.; Aguilar, G. Article.Title: A cortically gated sensory reference to the basal ganglia guides vocal reinforcement learning in songbirds
Article.Authors: Agarwal, A.; Scharff, C.; Vallentin, D.
Article.Abstract: Songbirds learn to sing by copying a memorized tutor song. Reinforcement learning models of vocal imitation propose that a dopaminergic signal strengthens the cortico basal ganglia synapses whose activity coincides with similarity to the tutor like song. To do so, the circuit must access a representation of the tutor song. Whether such a reference is available within the songbird basal ganglia nucleus Area X, and how it arrives, is unknown. In juvenile male zebra finches that learn to imitate adult courtship songs, we found that lesions of Area X impaired imitation more severely the earlier they were made. Intracellular recordings from Area X in awake juvenile zebra finches showed that the tutor song evokes precise subthreshold depolarizations that inversely scaled with imitation proficiency throughout song learning. Silencing the upstream nucleus HVC reduced these tutor-evoked responses, whereas disinhibiting HVC enhanced them. An inhibitory gate in HVC thus supplies Area X with the temporally aligned tutor reference that reinforcement driven vocal learning requires. These findings uncover a critical missing link in biological reinforcement learning, revealing how the brain structurally routes sensory templates to the basal ganglia to guide the acquisition of complex motor skills.

Article.Title: Explainable 3D CNNs Yield Progression-Linked Profiles of Saliency in Early Parkinson's Disease Using T1-Weighted MRI
Article.Authors: Moroze, E.; Zikopoulos, B.; Yazdanbakhsh, A.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) affects 1-2% of adults over 65 and is diagnosed by tracking motor symptoms, underscoring the need for earlier detection. T1-weighted MRI (T1w MRI) is inexpensive and widely available but can lack the resolution to detect established markers of PD pathology, such as substantia nigra degeneration. We trained 3D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on five site-stratified folds of 249 T1w MRIs from 141 early PD subjects (<10 years since first symptoms) and 185 from 126 controls. Because every fold was evaluated only on sites absent from its training data, the ensemble accuracy of 67.8% (AUC 0.670) reflects generalization to unseen sites. To interrogate these decisions, we parcellated saliency from a cohort-contrastive GradCAM, which baselines PD-class saliency against controls, and from Integrated Gradients, using the Julich Brain atlas. Both showed saliency in neocortical areas matching later Braak stages (5-6), when pathology reaches the neocortex, and lower subcortical saliency, suggesting limited sensitivity to earlier stages. Saliency was more correlated within functional networks than among random region groupings, and pooled saliency tracked motor symptoms and medication rather than cognitive scores or duration. These findings show explainable 3D CNNs can identify meaningful network and regional signatures of early PD from T1w MRI.

Article.Title: Control of Synchrony by Inhibitory Motifs in Spiking Neural Networks
Article.Authors: Biswas, A.; Kumar, A.
Article.Abstract: The connectivity in biological neuronal networks is known to deviate significantly from the random network (Erdos-Renyi) model. Specifically, di-synaptic motifs like reciprocal, convergent, divergent, and chain are found to be either over-represented or under-represented in certain brain regions. Over-representation of such motifs among excitatory neurons is known to induce synchrony. However, cortical activity is typically asynchronous. Thus, it remains unclear how synchrony induced by excitatory motifs may be reduced to physiological levels. To address this question, we systematically vary the prevalence of these four motifs in an Excitatory-Inhibitory (EI) network. We found that over-representation of chain and convergent motifs in the excitatory population led to increased firing rates and greater synchrony. However, this excess synchrony was quenched when we introduced the same type of motifs among inhibitory neurons. Because of the overabundance of motifs, some inhibitory neurons received fewer recurrent inhibitory inputs. Such weakly coupled neurons were primarily driven by uncorrelated external inputs, and therefore, these neurons exerted stronger inhibition on excitatory neurons and reduced both synchrony and firing rates. Thus, we also provide a new mechanism by which synchrony can be controlled in excitatory-inhibitory networks. We predict that the same kind of di-synaptic motifs should be present in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.

Article.Title: Local consequences of FMRP loss: cell type-specific mRNA and protein profiles of Fmr1-KO synapses
Article.Authors: Desch, K.; Aghabashlou Saisan, S.; tom Dieck, S.; Fuerst, N.; Nassim-Assir, B.; Langer, J. D.; Juengling, M.; Kaulich, E.; Schuman, E. M.
Article.Abstract: Brain function relies on billions of neurons interconnected by synapses with unique molecular composition specialized for cell type, brain region, and their role in circuit dynamics. Pathological synaptic dysfunctions - so-called synaptopathies - underlie many neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), including Fragile X Syndrome (FXS). While synaptic deficits are well documented in FXS, molecular studies have largely relied on bulk brain homogenates or synaptic fractions, which typically represent ''average'' molecular identities, potentially masking synapse type-specific alterations. To provide synapse type resolution, we use fluorescence-activated synaptosome sorting coupled to RNA-sequencing and mass spectrometry to isolate and profile cortical excitatory and inhibitory synapses of hemizygous and heterozygous Fmr1-deficient mice. We found that full or partial FMRP loss leads to cell type- and compartment-specific molecular remodeling (syndive.org), affecting mRNAs and proteins related to synaptic organization and metabolic pathways. Strikingly, only a minority of dysregulated mRNAs/proteins were shared across excitatory and inhibitory synapses - the substantial majority were uniquely regulated at one subtype. Indeed, FMRP loss often resulted in opposing protein changes in each synapse type. Changes in mRNA or protein abundance were also not well coordinated, consistent with substantial post-transcriptional regulation, including changes to the translational and ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation machinery. For example, our data suggest a disturbed, cell type-distinct coordination of protein degradation via CAND1 as one key consequence of FMRP loss. Furthermore, we observed differences in male (Fmr1-/y) and female (Fmr1-/+) transcriptomes, where, for example, FMRP dosage was coupled to reciprocal regulation of the NDD-risk gene Trpc4 in both synapse types.

Article.Title: Oscillatory Entrainment Guides Temporal Prediction in Non-Deterministic Continuous Environments, Independent of Bayesian Sequential Learning
Article.Authors: Hosseini, E.; Breska, A.
Article.Abstract: Predicting future event timing is essential for human interaction with our environment, and has been established in stimulus streams containing deterministic regularities. However, real-world streams often lack such regularities, leaving it unclear whether and how temporal predictions operate. Here we show that oscillatory entrainment, a mechanism identified for deterministic streams, operates in non-deterministic streams containing substantial temporal jitter. Model simulations revealed divergent dynamics and predicted timepoints between the oscillatory mechanism, which tracked local input regularities, and Bayesian learning, an alternative computational mechanism, which encoded global statistics. Across two speeded detection experiments using mechanism-dissociating streams, human performance was facilitated for targets appearing at oscillator-predicted times in streams with intermediate jitter levels, relative to maximal-jitter streams. Importantly, this effect was decoupled from Bayesian-based prediction and non-specific preparation, and could flexibly adapt to stream rate variations. These findings reveal the parallel mechanisms employed by humans when faced with continuous temporal uncertainty.

Article.Title: Channel expression aligns with dendritic conductance load in the reinforcing, not compensatory, direction in cortical GABAergic neurons
Article.Authors: Cirrincione, G.; Grassia, F.
Article.Abstract: Neurons could offset the conductance load imposed by their dendrites through channel expression (compensation), or channel expression could move with that load (reinforcement); which arrangement holds in adult cortex is unknown. Writing rheobase as the product of input conductance and an effective-voltage factor turns the question into a sign test. In mouse cortical GABAergic Patch-seq neurons, after removal of transcriptomic type and covariates, an out-of-fold channel-gene score co-varies positively with residual input conductance (median Spearman {rho} = 0.32 over 20 cross-fitting splits, n = 493) and with a conductance score predicted from dendritic morphology alone ({rho} = 0.23, n = 483). The association is carried mainly by Sst and Pvalb cells and is close to zero in Vip cells. Its slope on the compensation axis is 0.13, against -1 for compensation and 0 for independence, so the finding concerns direction rather than magnitude: it excludes a population-wide compensation rule without implying strong amplification. Reduced NEURON models show that a compensatory correction is biophysically feasible, and the morphology-derived conductance predictor transfers from mouse to human reconstructions ({rho} = 0.27, n = 128).

Article.Title: Closed-loop neurofeedback reshapes preparatory brain states to bias subsequent pain processing
Article.Authors: Zhang, Y.; Qiu, S.; Zheng, Q.; Chen, S.; Li, J.; Li, X.; Jin, R.; Peng, W.
Article.Abstract: Pain perception is shaped not only by nociceptive input but also by neural activity preceding stimulation. Whether these preparatory states can be modified through neurofeedback, and whether such effects depend on feedback authenticity, remains unclear. We used a double-blind, sham-controlled 2 x 2 mixed factorial design, crossing active regulation versus passive observation with real versus sham EEG feedback. Across feedback groups, active training was associated with changes in preparatory EEG activity and reductions in pain intensity and unpleasantness. Compared with sham feedback, authentic EEG-contingent feedback produced greater enhancement of power in the targeted somatosensory cortex, also evident in source estimates of the right postcentral gyrus, and selectively reduced transitions from microstate E to D. Authentic feedback was also associated with greater attenuation of laser-evoked N2 and P2 responses and a larger reduction in pain intensity, but not unpleasantness. Exploratory structural equation modeling identified indirect associations linking feedback authenticity, preparatory and microstate changes, P2 attenuation, and pain-rating changes. Together, these findings provide experimental evidence that preparatory neural activity can be modulated through authentic neurofeedback and that this modulation is accompanied by changes in subsequent nociceptive processing, supporting a state-based account of pain.

Article.Title: New disease models for investigating SynGAP1-related disorder (SRD) caused by a common heterozygous nonsense SYNGAP1 mutation
Article.Authors: von Sivers, J.; Unger, C.; Bauersachs, D.; Kupryianchyk-Schultz, I.; Gupta, T.; Proce, R. O.; Rybak-Wolf, A.; Rademacher, N.; Schmitz, D.; Schuelke, M.; Hoernberg, H.; Kuehn, R.; Shoichet, S. A.
Article.Abstract: Mutations in the SYNGAP1 gene cause SynGAP1-related disorder (SRD), a severe neurodevelopmental disorder marked by intellectual disability, epilepsy, ataxia, autism spectrum disorder, and global developmental delay. We established an integrated disease-modelling pipeline centered on the recurrent SYNGAP1 c.427C>T, p.(Arg143Ter), nonsense mutation, integrating neuronal and organoid models from patient-derived human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and a humanized knock-in mouse line to investigate mutation-specific disease phenotype across complementary experimental systems. In vivo, mice harboring the c.427C>T mutation show a hyperactivity phenotype that corresponds well to phenotypic features seen in patients such as absence of fear, hyperactive behavior and a strong urge to investigate the immediate surroundings. Taken together, our molecular and behavioral data in the humanized mouse are in line with studies on conventional heterozygous SynGAP1 knockout models, underscoring the relevance of these new disease models for further investigations into disease pathology. Moreover, with the three models described here, we present a translational platform that enables the development and evaluation of gene therapies that target disease-causing single nucleotide variations in the SYNGAP1 coding sequence.

Article.Title: A neural circuit for stereopsis in the fly
Article.Authors: Mearns, D. S.; Park, Y.; Shin, I.; Murthy, M.
Article.Abstract: Stereopsis involves combining different views from the two eyes to infer depth, an ability that has intrigued neuroscientists for almost two centuries (Wheatstone, 1838). It enables insects such as the praying mantis to estimate the distance of prey (Nityananda et al., 2018), or primates to fixate objects at different depths (Cumming and Judge, 1986; Rashbass and Westheimer, 1961). While theoretical models for stereopsis have been proposed based on neural activity recordings (Marr and Poggio, 1976; Grossberg, 1983; Ohzawa et al., 1990), we do not have a detailed circuit mechanism for stereopsis founded on neural wiring. Here we achieve this in the fly, Drosophila melanogaster, by analyzing two whole-brain connectomes (Dorkenwald et al., 2024; Berg et al., 2026). Flies have sufficient overlap between the eyes to utilize binocular vision (Kemppainen et al., 2022); however, a circuit that performs stereopsis has not been uncovered in this model system. We show that a cell type that connects the two optic lobes called LC14 (Otsuna and Ito, 2006) forms a recurrent circuit across the brain that is capable of depth estimation. By building a connectome-constrained model, we demonstrate that recurrence is critical for binocular distance tuning in this circuit. Tuning is optimal for the size and distances of social targets (other flies), and we uncover a pathway within the brain specific for binocular vision computations. Silencing LC14 neurons renders this downstream circuitry sensitive to only monocular information and alters distance-dependent courtship behaviors, while activation of LC14 neurons causes flies to slow in response to an illusory object in their binocular visual field. In sum, we predict function from structure, uncovering how the fly brain computes distance from binocular cues, and identify a role for binocular vision in patterning social behavior.

Article.Title: Brain2voice 2.0: High-performance voice synthesis brain-computer interface
Article.Authors: Wairagkar, M.; Srinivasan, A.; Card, N. S.; Singer-Clark, T.; Hou, X.; Iacobacci, C.; Miller, L. M.; Hochberg, L. R.; Brandman, D. M.; Stavisky, S. D.
Article.Abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising solution to speech loss due to neurological injury by decoding intended speech directly from brain activity. While recent BCIs have restored high-accuracy text-based communication, they fail to provide instantaneous voice output essential for the natural flow of conversation. We use self-supervised and adversarial training objectives that enhance acoustic feature quality and improve synthesis intelligibility. At each 10 ms timestep, the model causally outputs continuous and tokenized acoustic features for real-time voice synthesis as well as time-aligned phoneme predictions (raw phoneme error rate: 7%, comparable to the latest brain-to-text models). We evaluated this new approach on our prior intracortical brain-to-voice benchmark dataset (Wairagkar et al. 2025). Naive human listeners transcribed brain2voice 2.0 synthesized voice with a word error rate of 5.24%--an 8x improvement in intelligibility over previous SOTA results (43.75%). Brain2voice 2.0 demonstrates that highly intelligible real-time voice synthesis from neural signals is achievable, for the first time crossing the intelligibility threshold necessary for clinically viable brain-to-voice BCIs for people with paralysis.

Article.Authors: Hanmer, J. M.; D'Antonio, F.; Assimopoulos, S.; Manzano-Patron, J.-P.; Wood, S. C.; Tachrount, M.; Shen, Q.; Craig, M.; Lai, C.; Hickman, G. J.; Radfar, E.; Chisholm, K. I.; Farr, T. We apply this framework across eight genetically diverse mouse strains to develop predictive models of 3D microscopy-derived cellular features from dMRI contrasts. We demonstrate that data-driven combinations of state-of-the-art multi-shell dMRI measures predict neuronal and astrocytic features better than individual contrasts, across all animals. Article.Title: A coronavirus protease activates sensory neurons via TRPA1 to drive sneeze, cough, and pain
Article.Authors: Mali, S. S.; Gong, Z.; Silva, R.; Flamm, A. N.; Cook, C. P.; Shallow, L.; Souza, J.; Arp, C. J.; Mousa, A. A. K.; Cronce, M.; Vo, U.; Vuong, C.; Keasling, J.; Moayedi, Y.; Cox, J. S.; Ramachandran, R.; Stanley, S.; Bautista, D. M.

SARS-CoV-2 infection of the trigeminal ganglia altered transcriptional programs associated with nociception, including upregulation of the TRPA1-CGRP signaling pathway activated by PLpro. Together, these findings reveal a direct mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 triggers pain and airway reflexes and identify PLpro and TRPA1 as potential therapeutic targets for COVID-19.

Article.Title: Reusing pipettes in Patch-seq: a foundation for automated multimodal profiling
Article.Authors: Campagnola, L.; Chase, M.; Trinh, J.; Koch, M.; McCutcheon, A.; Lee, M.; Lee, B.; Dalley, R.; Mann, R.; Cahoon, A.; Braun, T.; Gudsnuk, K.; Best, F.; Sorensen, S.; Jarsky, T.
Article.Abstract: Patch-seq is a technique for single-cell multimodal characterization. It combines whole-cell electrophysiology, single-cell transcriptomics, and morphological reconstruction in single neurons. Patch-seq morphologies are a critical bridge among cell types, genes, physiology, and large-scale connectivity platforms such as EM connectomes and single-cell-resolution projectomes. However, patch-seq experimental complexity and operator dependence limit throughput. Automation could enable scalable Patch-seq but requires procedural adaptations, including detergent-based pipette cleaning, robotic nucleus extraction and collection. The impact of these automations on Patch-seq quality has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we show that each of these modifications preserves or improves key Patch-seq outcomes. Automated nucleus extraction performs comparably to, or better than, expert manual operation, preserving key RNA and morphological metrics. Detergent-cleaned, reused pipettes supported a viable sealing success rate across multiple cleaning cycles and preserved electrophysiological quality and transcriptomic yield without introducing excess contamination. Sonication effectively allows collection of nuclear material without damaging RNA and supports subsequent pipette cleaning and reuse. Enhanced automated sealing and break-in procedures increased throughput regardless of brain region, cell type or species. Together, these results validate the core procedural adaptations required for automated Patch-seq and establish a foundation for high-throughput, standardized multimodal single-cell characterization.

Article.Title: A Mechanistic Account of Dedifferentiation in the Aging Visual System
Article.Authors: Rechardt, A.; Bellucci, G.; Mok, R. M.
Article.Abstract: To uncover the mechanisms of age-related dedifferentiation, we simulated neural degradation in a computational model of the ventral visual stream. Severing connections or adding noise, whether in inferotemporal cortex (IT) or upstream, reduced IT differentiation, indicating that dedifferentiation need not originate locally. Degrading peripheral V1, which preferentially drove place-selective IT neurons, selectively reduced place differentiation, a candidate mechanism for the stronger place dedifferentiation reported in aging.

Article.Title: Development of direction selectivity in the Xenopus tadpole optic tectum and midbrain tegmentum
Article.Authors: Zheng, K.; Mondal, Y.; Roth, B. P.; Udoh, U. G.; Calabrese, R. L.; Pratt, K. G.
Article.Abstract: Detecting motion direction is a fundamental function performed by direction selective (DS) neurons. DS neurons in the optic tectum (superior colliculus in mammals) enable the tracking of moving objects. DS neurons of the accessory optic system support reflexive eye / head movements that stabilize gaze during self-motion. By developmental stage 48 (10 days postfertilization), Xenopus tadpoles display visually guided behaviors that require both types of DS neurons. Our previous work has shown that these two regions are not only functionally distinct but also follow different developmental programs. Here we characterized and compared how direction selectivity develops in both visual processing centers. Using in vivo electrophysiological recordings during moving bar visual stimulation, we measured DS synaptic inputs and spiking outputs in both regions across three key developmental stages of the retinotectal projection. Tegmental neurons were direction selective ab initio, and both input and output tuning remained stable across development. Tectal neurons were observed to receive DS inputs early, and their input selectivity also remained stable across development. However, their spiking output grew substantially more DS at the later developmental stage. This was due at least in part to a naturally occurring decrease in intrinsic excitability which preferentially dampened overall spike rates, but especially in response to the non-preferred direction of motion, thereby increasing direction selectivity. These results reveal distinct developmental trajectories in parallel visual pathways. Tegmental direction selectivity is established early and stays stable, whereas tectal output tuning sharpens during development through a decrease in intrinsic excitability.

Article.Title: Oligodendroglial dysfunction drives parvalbumin interneuron hypomyelination, circuit dysfunction and social deficits in an ASD model
Article.Authors: Villafranca, M.; Ugarte-Arakistain, I.; Sanchez-Camacho, A.; Peiro-Moreno, C.; Robledo, A.; Calovi, S.; Mata, P.; Bayon-Cordero, L.; Fresnedo, O.; Sanchez-Gomez, M. V.; Rueda, Y.; Battefeld, A.; Soria, F. N.; Penagarikano, O.; Rosa, J. M.; Domercq, M.
Article.Abstract: Altered social behaviour in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) has been linked to disruptions in neural circuit development, with emerging evidence implicating abnormal myelination. Yet how myelin development is affected and how this impacts circuit function remain unclear. Here, using the cntnap2-/- mouse model of ASD, we show that oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC) differentiation is transiently impaired during early postnatal development, resulting in delayed myelination in the somatosensory cortex and corpus callosum, altered myelin lipid composition, and impaired sheath wrapping, accompanied by transient microgliosis and increased oligodendrocyte apoptosis. Transcriptomic analysis reveals upregulation of interferon and immune-related pathways alongside downregulation of GABAergic synaptic genes in oligodendrocytes. These alterations converge on disrupted GABAergic interneuron to OPC communication, leading to hypomyelination and impaired maturation of parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons through a non-cell-autonomous mechanism, with selective deficits in PV function, excitation/inhibition balance and gamma oscillations. Early treatment with the promyelinating agents clemastine or pranlukast restores OPC differentiation, myelination, and PV maturation, rescues circuit dysfunction, and ameliorates social deficits and behavioural inflexibility. Our findings establish that transient developmental failure in OPC differentiation drives PV interneuron hypomyelination, linking oligodendroglial dysfunction to circuit-level and behavioural alterations in ASD, and highlight early myelin-targeted interventions as a potential therapeutic strategy.

Article.Title: The adaptor protein DAB2 cell-autonomously links APOE with disease-associated microglia (DAM)/TREM2 state dysregulation associated with Alzheimer's disease
Article.Authors: Salih, D. A.; Barber, M.; Andrews, W. D.; Kubelka, A.; Singer, H.; Gavriouchkina, D.; Blunskyte-Hendley, M.; Becalick, A.; Hao, X.; Birkle, T.; Northeast, R.; Yaman, U.; Magusali, N.; La Penna, S.; Shazad, Z.; Chapman, L.; Siow, R. C.; Aarsland, D.; Pocock, J. M.; Howell, B. W.; Parnavelas, J.; Hardy, J.
Article.Abstract: The neuron-secreted Reelin (RELN) protein and its adaptor DAB1 modify Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk through genetic interaction with APOE4. While RELN and APOE4 exert antagonistic effects on amyloid and Tau pathology in mice, how risk is conferred in the human brain remains unclear. The related adaptor DAB2 endocytoses RELN/APOE receptors and, via LRP8, modulates non-canonical pro-inflammatory signalling in non-neuronal cells. We hypothesised that RELN and APOE signalling directly influence microglial function to modify AD risk. Integrating human brain transcriptomics, a Reln-deficient mouse, and DAB1/DAB2 knock-down in APOE isogenic iPSC-microglia, we found that microglial DAB1/DAB2 pathways were dynamically regulated across the lifespan, with DAB2 dysregulated with increasing amyloid pathology. DAB2 transcriptional networks correlated with disease- and lipid- associated microglial states (DAM/LDAM) linked to networks expressing dementia-risk loci (TREM2, GRN, ACE, SORL1) and associated with endolysosomal and lipid-handling pathways. DAB2- knockdown cell-autonomously shifted microglia away from gene networks enriched in DAM/TREM2 states and towards pro-inflammatory cytokine-responsive states and TNFNF{kappa}B pathways. APOE4/E4 microglia showed elevated APOE and reduced DAB1pY232 under inflammatory stress, and blunted DAB2-knockdown transcriptomic responses, consistent with pathway-level genetic interaction. In vivo, RELN-deficiency reduced microglial ramification and increased CD68. These findings identify DAB2 as a regulator of microglial state transitions and a modifier of dementia-risk networks linking APOE genotype to inflammatory, phagocytic and amyloid-beta clearance pathways relevant to AD.

Article.Title: Peptide-centric proteomics reveals molecular subtypes of sporadic Alzheimer's disease
Article.Authors: Plubell, D. L. L.; Merrihew, G. E. E.; Park, J.; Patterson, K.; Smith, J. D.; Hsu, C.; Wu, C. C.; Keene, C. D.; Montine, T. J.; MacCoss, M. J.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a complex, age-related disease that continues to increase in incidence worldwide. Although some cases are caused by known pathogenic mutations, the majority of cases are sporadic, with uncertain etiology and commonly complicated by comorbid diseases. To better understand the molecular landscape of AD we constructed a unique brain sample set free from neuropathologic comorbidities. This cohort consists of autosomal dominant AD dementia, sporadic AD dementia, cognitively normal individuals with high AD neuropathologic change - a condition called resilient to AD, and cognitively normal cases with no or minimal AD neuropathologic change. Through quantitative mass spectrometry proteomics we obtain measures of peptides mapping to A-beta; and to tau, capturing differences in the histopathologic burden of disease. Correlations of these peptide abundance differences within sporadic AD dementia cases in the superior and medial temporal gyrus indicate the presence of two separate sporadic AD phenotypes. Additional differences are characterized at a peptide level between sporadic AD dementia and autosomal dominant AD dementia in the inferior parietal lobe and caudate nucleus. These findings indicate both shared and distinct molecular features in AD influenced by cause and age of onset of disease.

Article.Title: Hierarchical cortical plasticity in congenital sight impairment
Article.Authors: Maimon-Mor, R. O.; Farahbakhsh, M.; Hedger, N.; Rider, A. T.; Anderson, E.; Rees, G.; Knapen, T.; Michaelides, M.; Dekker, T.
Article.Abstract: A robust learning system balances adaptability to new experiences with stability of its foundational architecture. To investigate how the human brain implements this we combined structural imaging with population receptive field (pRF) and connective field (CF) modelling to study plasticity and stability across hierarchical processing stages in visual cortex. We compared the rod system of individuals born with rod-only photoreceptor inputs (achromatopsia) to the typically developed rod system, allowing us to dissociate impacts of life-long versus transient responses to altered input. Cortical input stages (V1) exhibited high stability, with input-deprived cortex showing no substantial retinotopic remapping and exhibiting structural hallmarks of deprivation. However, downstream cortex (V3) showed plasticity in how it read out these inputs. In achromats, more cortical resources in V3 were dedicated to sampling input from the near-fovea, and V3 neuronal populations aggregated information across smaller areas along the V1 cortical surface. We propose that these hierarchical dynamics reflect a broader principle of brain plasticity, in which later stages adapt to atypical input by altering how they sample earlier stages. This has important implications for emerging sight-rescue therapies, where restored input must be interpreted by a system that has already adjusted to its absence.

Article.Title: Learned attraction replaces innate aversion in the evolution of an olfactory response in Mus musculus
Article.Authors: Conway, P. B.; Wang, Z.; Shettigar, N.; Urrieta, E.; McCrea, I.; Dennis, E.; Ryan, T. J.
Article.Abstract: The evolution of behavior is typically attributed to changes in innate circuitry, but learning can also drive behavioral evolution. Mus musculus evolved to produce trimethylamine (TMA) and behaviorally approach it, unlike the ancestral response retained by other mammals including Mus caroli. Here we demonstrate that this attraction is not innate but learned, depending on developmental TMA exposure. Whole brain immediate-early gene mapping reveals experience-dependent patterns of activation in response to TMA olfaction. Using activity-dependent TRAP2 labelling, we find that TMA-responsive neurons in the anterior olfactory nucleus are necessary and sufficient for attraction, consistent with a memory engram. Meanwhile, Mus caroli innate aversion is dependent on excitatory neurons in the posterior cortical amygdala. These results demonstrate how innate and learned circuitry both contribute to behavioral evolution in mammals.

Article.Title: The temporal dynamics of animacy-related neural representations are robust to controversial training
Article.Authors: Etkin, L. O.; Kömürcü, E. B.; Chen, C.-Y.; Op de Beeck, H.; Costantino, A. I.
Article.Abstract: Animal bias refers to the human tendency to prioritise the neural processing of animate over inanimate stimuli, a phenomenon observed across multiple cognitive domains, such as attention, perception, memory, and language. Lookalikes (also referred to as zoomorphic objects), inanimate objects that visually resemble animals, tend to be interpreted as animate regardless of their inanimate identity. We examined whether this animal bias can be modified through learning to understand how experience and plasticity shape visual object representations. We tested whether feedback-based categorisation training in which lookalikes had to be categorised as inanimate could reduce the animal bias. Thirty healthy participants completed three weekly sessions of animacy categorisation training, followed by an EEG recording session during which they performed an animacy task. Repeated-measures ANOVA on behavioural data revealed that categorisation efficiency, measured as the inverse efficiency score, improved both within and across sessions, but there was no evidence that this improvement was specific to lookalikes. Time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis and representational similarity analysis on EEG data obtained after this training showed a descriptively smaller animal bias relative to the no-training dataset from \citet{Chen2023}, but this reduction was not statistically significant in any analysis. Moreover, a significant animal bias was still present in participants who underwent training. Thus, neural reorganisation related to the animal bias is limited even after several training sessions to overcome this bias.

Article.Title: Functional mapping of synaptotagmin 1 Ca2+ ligands that mediate excitation-secretion coupling in neurons
Article.Authors: Mishra, S.; Mehta, N.; Dominguez, M. J.; Beckett, E. R.; Wozney, M.; Vukovic, A.; Sutton, R. B.; Chapman, E. R.
Article.Abstract: Synaptotagmin (SYT) 1 is a Ca2+ sensor that triggers rapid synaptic vesicle exocytosis, but how it is activated by Ca2+ remains enigmatic. SYT1 contains two Ca2+-sensing motifs, C2A and C2B. Structural studies have proposed that five acidic residues in each C2 domain mediate Ca2+-binding, but their functional relevance remains unclear. Here, we mutated each of the ten putative ligands and conducted side-by-side comparisons of Ca2+-binding activity and evoked glutamate release. Remarkably, all ten putative ligands are crucial for evoked synchronous release, overturning the view that binding of Ca2+ to C2A is dispensable. Importantly, Ca2+ binding to C2B is essential for synchronization. Furthermore, we report that two new human mutations, corresponding to Ca2+ ligands in C2B, are dominant-negative. Finally, four new crystal structures reveal how the choice of neutralizing substitution differentially alters SYT1 structure and, consequently, function.

Article.Title: Dopamine reward prediction error signal encodes effort cost as negative reward value
Article.Authors: Burrell, M.; Pastor-Bernier, A.; Schultz, W.
Article.Abstract: All life must balance the economic problem of allocating scarce energy resources to maximize reward. Economic theory proposes that rational (reward-maximizing) decision makers balance the possible benefits from rewards against the cost of efforts for obtaining the rewards. Here we measured how the reward prediction error signal of monkey dopamine neurons reflects the negative value of effort cost (joystick resistance) and compared it with the dopamine signal for the positive value of reward. The animals repeatedly made binary choices between options varying in reward amount and effort to obtain the reward. Midbrain dopamine neurons signaled the negative value of effort cost both at effort-predicting stimuli (as reduction of reward-predicting excitation) and at experienced effort (as inhibition with more effort than predicted and as excitation with less effort). These effort signals contrasted with the opposite signal reflecting the positive value of reward relative to prediction (reward prediction error; RPE). Thus, dopamine neurons code effort cost as negative value opposite to the positive value of reward. In occurring with both stimuli and outcomes, this dopamine signal complies with the formalism of temporal difference reinforcement learning.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: reward prediction error; effort cost; reinforcement learning; dopaminergic neurons; temporal difference learning; energy allocation

Article.Title: A Dual Effort Choice paradigm reveals pharmacological divergence between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation within the same task environment
Article.Authors: Fachouridou, F.; Xeni, F.; Marangoni, C.; Salisbury, P.; Grayson, E. W.; Robinson, E. S. J.; Jackson, M. G.
Article.Abstract: Motivation loss is a transdiagnostic symptom, prevalent across neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases. Current treatments fail to effectively treat this symptom domain, giving it significant clinical importance. The fields of neuroscience and drug development have primarily focused on extrinsic motivation, whereby an animal must perform an action to receive an external food or water-based reward. However, many of our everyday activities are facilitated by intrinsic motivation, where completing an action is inherently rewarding. By utilising tasks focused only on extrinsic motivation, we may miss critical neurobiological and therapeutic differences between motivation types. Previous work has shown divergence in drug effect between extrinsic and intrinsic motivation tasks across a wide range of clinically-used drugs, indicating translationally-relevant differences across motivation domains that warrant further study. Therefore, the aim of this work was first to develop a task capable of simultaneously quantifying intrinsic and extrinsically motivated behaviour within the same task environment. Secondly, to use this task to further investigate this neurochemical divergence by examining a wide range of clinically-relevant drugs within this new task context. Here, we find that a pharmacological reduction in dopaminergic signalling reduced motivation across both extrinsic and intrinsic options within the new task, though this effect was mechanism dependent. In contrast, acute serotonergic and dopaminergic signalling increase produced a more heterogenous pattern, indicating nuanced mechanistic differences even when presented in the same task environment. Therefore, this task provides a new approach for characterising drug effects on distinct forms of motivated behaviour that may go unnoticed using conventional assays.

Article.Title: Aging limits the reduction of reactive muscle activity to perturbations but spares the retrieval of context-specific patterns with practice
Article.Authors: Liu, S.; Weinstein, A.; Torres-Oviedo, G.
Article.Abstract: Moving smoothly through a changing environment requires immediate reactive responses to maintain balance at an environmental transition, and learned, context-specific responses to efficiently meet the new environmental demands. People use both the reactive and context-specific responses to adapt to new environment and to re-adapt more rapidly on subsequent re-encounters. While re-adaptation slows with older age, the underlying muscular mechanisms are unknown. We hypothesized that practice would reduce reactive recruitment and increase context-specific recruitment and that both changes would be smaller in older adults. To test this, younger and older adults practiced split-belt walking (one belt faster than the other) over three days. We recorded surface electromyography from 10 muscles per leg and used linear regression to decompose each session's activity into a reactive component (template from naive, early exposure) and a context-specific component (template from practiced activity). Mixed-effects models showed that, with practice, older adults decreased reactive recruitment less than younger adults, particularly in distal muscles, with no strong evidence for an age difference in context-specific recruitment. In sum, with practice, aging limits the reduction of reactive responses to a novel walking context but spares the retrieval of context-specific muscle patterns, suggesting that mobility rehabilitation for older adults could target reactive mechanisms.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial dysfunction activates a translational stress response that drives diabetic pain
Article.Authors: Meyer, A. R.; Garcia, G.; Ruhly, S.; Mikesell, A. R.; Shapiro, J. B.; Chase, R.; Campbell, Z. T.
Article.Abstract: Neuropathic pain is common and debilitating among diabetics. The reactive glycolytic metabolite methylglyoxal (MGO) is strongly associated with painful diabetic neuropathy. MGO triggers pain through activation of the integrated stress response (ISR). The underlying molecular mechanisms are unclear. Here, we show that general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) kinase acts as a conserved sensor that bridges glycolytic and mitochondrial dysfunction to pain hypersensitivity. In human sensory neurons derived from dorsal root ganglion (DRG), MGO increased eIF2 phosphorylation and suppressed global translation. These effects were blocked upon inhibition of GCN2. Unbiased ribosome profiling of mouse DRG revealed that MGO triggered repression of mRNAs that encode components of the electron transport chain. Based on this observation, mitochondrial dysfunction was examined as a potential upstream trigger for GCN2 activation. MGO directly glycated mitochondrial complex I and increased the NADH/NAD+ ratio. Correcting this redox imbalance via expression of a mitochondrial-targeted bacterial NADH oxidase (mitoLbNOX) prevented ISR activation by MGO. In a streptozotocin-induced mouse model of diabetic neuropathy, pharmacological GCN2 inhibition or sensory neuron-specific conditional deletion significantly attenuated mechanical allodynia. Calcium imaging revealed that genetic deletion of GCN2 reduced calcium influx in response to an agonist of TRPA1. Finally, expression of mitoLbNOX using adeno-associated viruses (AAV) in DRG sensory neurons in vivo reduced streptozotocin-induced mechanical hypersensitivity. Our findings demonstrate that GCN2 is a central, conserved driver of translational dysregulation downstream of mitochondrial redox stress in diabetic pain. This work highlights the critical role of mitochondrial function and translational control as key drivers of painful diabetic neuropathy.

Article.Title: Single-Session HRV Biofeedback Alters Neural Activity but Not Subjective Anxiety
Article.Authors: Dao, C.; Man, I.; Healy, K.; Estel, K.; Nelli, S. M.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety and stress are among the most prevalent mental health concerns worldwide, yet barriers to effective treatment remain high. Biofeedback-based approaches offer a promising, low-cost complement to traditional interventions. The present study examined whether real-time heart rate variability (HRV) biofeedback enhances the efficacy of paced breathing for reducing state anxiety, and whether self-reported and neural measures of anxiety relief converge. Healthy adults completed a speeded Stroop task for stress induction, followed by a ten-minute paced breathing exercise. Participants were randomly assigned to an HRV biofeedback condition, in which real-time cardiac variability was displayed, or a control condition with the same breathing cue and no physiological feedback. State anxiety was assessed using the Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-S), and neural activity was measured via EEG spectral power across delta, theta, alpha, and beta frequency bands. The Stroop task reliably elevated state anxiety, and paced breathing reduced STAI-S scores equivalently in both groups; HRV biofeedback did not confer additional subjective benefit. In contrast, EEG analyses revealed that the biofeedback group showed increases in delta and bilateral theta power relative to controls, and spatially widespread increases in alpha and beta power. Time-frequency analyses further showed more extensive and sustained spectral modulation in the biofeedback condition. These findings reveal a dissociation between self-reported and neural responses to a brief HRV biofeedback intervention: paced breathing alone was sufficient to reduce acute state anxiety, while HRV biofeedback produced distinct changes in neural oscillatory activity without enhancing self-reported anxiety relief. These results show that subjective anxiety recovery and neural recovery can diverge during acute HRV biofeedback, suggesting that physiological engagement with biofeedback emerges before conscious benefits.

Article.Title: Neural and Experiential Dynamics of High-Ventilation Breathwork Mirror Psychedelic States
Article.Authors: Porter, L. K.; Kaya, E.; Chalise, K.; Klarmann, J.; Goffin, A.; Abd El Hay, M.; Harrter, N.; Rodriguez-de-Santiago, B.; Hindmarsh, J. N.; Jain, N.; Nemri, A.; Breitenstein, B.; Timmermann, C.; Scholvinck, M. L.; Dziobek, I.; Havenith, M. N.
Article.Abstract: High-ventilation breathwork (HVB) is a simple breathing technique that nevertheless frequently triggers experiences resembling psychedelic states. While recent studies have begun to pinpoint physiological and neural changes involved in altered states of consciousness (ASCs) evoked by HVB, the interplay between neural and experiential dynamics throughout an HVB session remains unclear. Here we tracked neural activity (via 64-channel EEG recordings) as well as subjective experience depth and content in 25 experienced HVB practitioners across resting-state recordings interleaved throughout a naturalistic HVB session. We find that neural dynamics evoked by HVB emulate the most robust neural signatures of classical psychedelic states, specifically (1) loosening of temporal structure, including broadband cortical desynchronization, increased signal complexity, and decreased oscillatory power in the Alpha (8 - 13 Hz) range, and (2) reorganization of spatial structure, including a flattening of cortical processing hierarchy. These neural effects directly correlated with participants subjective depth with minute resolution, but were not explained by isolated features of HVB such as music listening or active interoception. Together, these results identify unifying neural features of psychedelic-like ASCs regardless of induction method, demonstrating that cortical states triggered by psychedelics can also be accessed by non-pharmacological routes, and breathwork is a powerful way to do so.

Article.Title: Identifying aligned tensor decompositions across heterogeneous neural datasets
Article.Authors: Kralik, M.; Tinelli, S.; Kozloski, J.; Ponte Costa, R.; Sharott, A.; Peach, R. L.
Article.Abstract: Large-scale neural recordings increasingly span many sessions, brain regions and animals, but differences in neuronal sampling make it difficult to identify and interpret shared patterns. We introduce Neuralign, a tensor- based model that jointly aligns and decomposes recordings into components, each pairing a shared temporal pattern with its expression in individual trials and neurons, without requiring matched neurons, matched trials or behavioural labels. In simulations, pooling recordings improved recovery of shared components; in recurrent networks, Neuralign distinguished related from distinct task solutions. In the macaque motor cortex, label-free components recovered the ring-like organisation of reach directions. Across 93 brain-wide mouse recordings, Neuralign discovered a single component that isolated the response to inhibition of the anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM). A reference learned from correct, uninhibited trials revealed inhibition-related activity outside the choice direction on error trials, most strongly in the ALM and thalamus. Neuralign provides an interpretable framework for studying the shared structure of large neural datasets, linking shared patterns to individual trials and recorded populations.

Article.Title: Excitatory neurons downregulate synaptic proteins before motor onset and glia reduce neuronal support in Huntington disease mice
Article.Authors: Alvarez Pardo, R.; Luo, S.; Rodriguez, P.; Lazaro Sanchez, J.; Albert-Gasco, H.; Olmedo Salinas, C.; Desch, K.; Gubert-Olive, M.; Muncunill, J.; Diaz-Hernandez, M.; Fornasiero, E. F.; Jovanovic, M.; Doron-Mandel, E.; Alvarez-Castelao, B.
Article.Abstract: Background: Huntington's disease burdens protein homeostasis and affects neurons and glia differently across brain regions, but how these two main cell populations respond as the disease progresses remains unresolved. Whole-tissue proteomes mix these cell types and hide how the proteome of each changes. We therefore measured the proteome of each cell type separately at different disease stages. Methods: We metabolically labelled cell-type-specific proteomes in living R6/1 mice and wild-type littermates for 15 days at different disease stages. We examined cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons at 1.5, 3 and 7 months, cerebellar inhibitory neurons at 3 and 7 months, and cortical, striatal and cerebellar glia at 7 months. We combined mass spectrometry with functional enrichment and competitive protein-set tests to understand the differential proteostatic response to mutant huntingtin across disease progression, brain regions and cell types. Differential abundance was tested with a peptide-centric linear mixed model (msqRob, Benjamini-Hochberg q < 0.1), and proteins whose levels varied together in cortical and hippocampal neurons were grouped into modules by weighted correlation network analysis. Results: Hippocampal excitatory neurons showed broader and more coordinated regulation than cortical neurons already before motor onset, whereas the cortical response increased with age and no cortical protein module differed between genotypes before the most severe stage. All three neuronal populations upregulated ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) proteins as the disease advanced. Protein folding changed, with more subunits of the chaperonin CCT/TRiC but fewer J-domain proteins and, in excitatory neurons, fewer HSP70 chaperones. At the most severe stage, glia of the three studied regions regulated mainly different proteins, but all increased UPS proteins and decreased key proteins of neuronal support, among them the main glial glutamate transporter GLT-1. Cholesterol-related proteins decreased in cortical and cerebellar glia, and respiratory-chain proteins in striatal glia. Conclusions: Synaptic proteins decreased early in cortical and hippocampal neurons and were not restored at later ages. A later and broader maintenance response coexisted with their continued and increasing downregulation. In this first cell-type-resolved view of the labelled proteome in a Huntington's disease mouse model, progression appears as a change in the coordination of cellular functions, which whole-tissue measurements would dilute.

Article.Title: State-dependent structure-function coupling reflects dynamic engagement of the brain's structural scaffold
Article.Authors: Pedersen, R.; Sala-Llonch, R.; Persson, J.; Salami, A.
Article.Abstract: Functional brain organization is shaped by the brain's anatomical scaffold, yet how structure-function coupling varies across cognitive states remains unclear. Across 723 adults from two independent cohorts, we examined coupling using diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging. In the primary cohort, coupling was strongest during movie-watching, intermediate during rest, and weakest during working memory, declining further with increasing working-memory load. The movie-rest difference replicated in an independent sample, challenging the primacy of rest for revealing anatomical constraints. State effects were superimposed on a stable unimodal-to-transmodal cortical hierarchy, with movie-watching preferentially enhancing coupling in sensory and language systems. Regions with more stable functional connectivity across states showed stronger coupling. Older age was associated with lower auditory and somatomotor coupling in both cohorts, alongside heterogeneous increases in association cortex. Together, we show that cognitive context shapes structure-function alignment, supporting a framework of complementary structure-constrained and distributed-integrative modes of communication.

Article.Title: Probabilistic mapping of brain connections without random sampling
Article.Authors: Kruper, J.; Cieslak, M.; Rokem, A.
Article.Abstract: For two decades, most tractography has mapped brain connections by sampling millions of pathways probabilistically. Sampling makes results non-deterministic and costly to store. We show that it is unnecessary: modeling tractography as an absorbing Markov chain gives the expected result of infinitely many streamlines. This approach is more reliable than streamline-based tractography across test--retest scans. It readily maps tracts in clinical-grade data and neonates, around tumors and along small pathways. MPAT is available as open-source software at https://github.com/rokemlab/mpat .

Article.Title: Single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas of 5xFAD mouse brain maps cell-type-specific transcriptional disruption and preferential rolipram rescue in VIP interneurons
Article.Authors: Potokiri, A.; Dwamena, A. A.; Wang, H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease is characterized by progressive synaptic dysfunction and inhibitory circuit disruption across multiple brain cell types. Rolipram, a selective phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitor that elevates intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP), activates proteasome, and produces robust procognitive effects in AD mouse models. Still, the cell-type-specific transcriptional mechanisms underlying these effects remain uncharacterized. Methods: We profiled 29,664 nuclei from 5xFAD and wild-type (WT) mouse right hemisphere across four conditions: WT Vehicle, WT Rolipram, 5xFAD Vehicle, and 5xFAD Rolipram (0.03 mg/kg/day, 30-day subcutaneous osmotic pump) using the Parse Biosciences Evercode WT v3 combinatorial barcoding platform. Nuclei were clustered into 16 annotated cell type populations using Seurat v5. Disease and rescue effects were quantified as log fold changes (LFCs) across all clusters, with Gene Ontology enrichment assessed using clusterProfiler and transcription factor activity inferred using decoupleR. Results: Disease-associated transcriptional disruption was highly cell-type-specific in its magnitude. Among inhibitory subtypes, VIP/Reln disinhibitory interneurons (n = 149 nuclei) showed the most coherent transcriptional disruption: 289 candidate genes were lower in 5xFAD, with Gene Ontology enrichment concentrated in synapse organization programs, including regulation of synapse structure or activity (padj = 1.5x10^-14, 44 genes), regulation of synapse organization (padj = 1.9x10^-14, 43 genes), and postsynapse organization (padj = 1.1x10^-13, 38 genes). This pathway-level specificity was not reproduced in PVALB or SST interneurons. Astrocytes showed loss of cell-adhesion programs (cell-substrate adhesion padj = 2.4x10^-4, 10 genes). Rolipram rescue was preferential: VIP interneurons yielded 72 true rescue genes and astrocytes yielded 42, with the remaining 14 clusters showing substantially fewer. The cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase Pde7b was disease-context-specifically lower in 5xFAD VIP interneurons (LFC -0.53) and restored by rolipram (LFC +0.54), with WT expression unchanged. decoupleR CREB1 activity inference identified reduced CREB1 activity in 5xFAD VIP interneurons with partial restoration in 5xFAD Rolipram, supporting a stepwise transcriptional cascade in which amyloid pathology reduces cAMP, which suppresses PKA and CREB1 activity. This in turn reduces Pde7b transcription, and rolipram reverses this cascade by blocking cAMP hydrolysis upstream. Conclusion: This single-nucleus atlas provides the first cell-type-resolved characterization of rolipram's transcriptional effects in the 5xFAD brain. VIP disinhibitory interneurons emerge as the most transcriptionally vulnerable inhibitory subtype and the preferential site of rolipram-associated rescue, with the Pde7b/CREB1 signaling axis nominating a tractable, disease-context-specific pharmacological substrate.

Article.Title: The Xist locus on the X chromosome of males regulates cognition and metabolism despite minimal expression
Article.Authors: Sivakumar, N.; Wang, D.; Dubal, D. B.; Abdulai-Saiku, S.
Article.Abstract: The long non-coding RNA Xist is the master regulator of X chromosome inactivation (XCI) in females, but its functional significance in males, where Xist expression is normally minimal, is unknown. Here we investigated whether the Xist locus influences male physiology and brain function across the lifespan using mice carrying a targeted Xist deletion ({Delta}Xist). Xist deletion produced a small further reduction in the very low, residual Xist signal in aged male hippocampus. Metabolically, Xist deletion lowered fasting blood glucose in old, not young, males, without affecting body weight. In the brain, Xist deletion modestly improved spatial memory at 24 hours in the Morris water maze in young males, with a similar trend at middle age in an interactive place avoidance task, independent of anxiety-like behavior or locomotor activity. This early cognitive benefit did not persist with aging and motor function on the rotarod was unaffected by genotype at any age. Together, these findings indicate that the Xist locus exerts age- and domain-specific effects on male metabolic and cognitive functions despite near-absent baseline Xist expression. These data identify an unexpected role for a canonically female-associated regulatory locus in males and raise the possibility that Xist-associated mechanisms contribute to male brain function and metabolism.

Article.Title: Daily light exposure differences between extreme chronotypes persist after alignment to habitual sleep timing
Article.Authors: Zauner, J.; Spitschan, M.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: Morning and evening chronotypes may receive light at different clock times, thereby providing differently timed signals to the circadian pacemaker. Prior studies have suggested phase-specific exposure patterns that could counter further advances in early types and delays in late types. We examined whether photoperiod modifies these exposure patterns in a way that could reasonably counteract timing extremes. Methods: We analysed near-eye melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (EDI) in 140 participants from an international cohort across seven countries (778 participant-days; 35,949 half-hour observations). We compared four quartiles of midsleep on free days corrected for sleep debt (MSFsc) in clock time and relative to MSFsc using cyclic generalized additive mixed models, accounting for day type, site, photoperiod and individual patterns. In exploratory analyses, we tested moderation of these differences by daylength and used phase-response-curve (PRC) weighting as a conceptual comparison of exposure timing. Results: The modelled extreme evening-type/morning-type exposure ratios averaged 0.16 (95% CI 0.06-0.40) 9.6-11.3 hours before MSFsc (pre-MSFsc) and 14.0 (5.6-34.8) 0.9-4.4 hours after MSFsc (post-MSFsc). The models performed similarly well by ordinary in-sample R2 (0.795 for clock time; 0.794 for MSFsc-relative time). Pattern differences were broadly similar on work and free days, with the pre-MSFsc contrast descriptively attenuated on free days. The post-MSFsc ratio increased by a factor of 2.59 (95% CI 1.06-6.34) between civil photoperiods one hour below and above each site's average photoperiod, with no significant moderation of the pre-MSFsc contrast. Exploratory weighting by the published PRC gave higher advance-weighted point estimates in extreme evening than extreme morning types; the group difference was not statistically significant. Conclusions: Extreme chronotypes differ in daily exposure both in clock time and relative to MSFsc. The established questionnaire-based MSFsc measure showed significant post-MSFsc daylength moderation. The exposure patterns and conceptual PRC comparison suggest a possible pathway linking daylight availability to entrainment in extreme chronotypes.

Article.Title: Direction of oscillatory networks in the human medial temporal lobe reverses across verbal working memory phases
Article.Authors: Choi, D.; Han, H.-B.
Article.Abstract: Working memory (WM) requires neural circuits to change how they interact as information is encoded, maintained and used. Directional oscillatory interactions in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) contribute to memory processing, but how these interactions are spatially organized during verbal WM remains unclear. Here, we analyzed intracranial electroencephalogram and neuronal spiking recorded from the human MTL during a verbal Sternberg task. Theta- and gamma-band activities in MTL showed predominant directionality in the posterior-to-anterior axis during WM encoding, but this direction was reversed to anterior-to-posterior during retrieval. Theta activities reflecting the WM load were more prevalent in left than right MTL, and theta in left MTL coordinated spike timings more strongly. Moreover, interhemispheric interactions showed a predominant left-to-right influence, with posterior-to-anterior interactions enhanced during encoding and anterior-to-posterior interactions enhanced during retrieval. Together, these findings suggest that verbal WM engages a spatially organized MTL network in which the predominant direction of oscillatory interactions changes across task phases.

Article.Title: Impaired cholinergic modulation of striatal spiny projection neurons in repetitive behaviors associated with TSHZ3-linked autism spectrum disorder
Article.Authors: Graniou, J.; Caubit, X.; Fatmi, A.; Ouagazzal, A.-M.; Kerkerian-Le Goff, L.; Fasano, L.; Gubellini, P.
Article.Abstract: Alterations in central cholinergic systems are implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We previously identified TSHZ3 as an ASD-linked gene and provided evidence, from transgenic mouse models, supporting the view that striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs) are key players in the core ASD trait represented by repetitive behaviors (RBs). Indeed, conditional deletion of Tshz3 in cholinergic neurons (Chat-cKO model) results in RBs associated with reduced SCIN firing activity and decreased striatal cholinergic tone. Here we tackled the resulting adaptations in the striatal circuitry underlying RBs in Chat-cKO, focusing on the two populations of striatal projection neurons (SPNs) that express dopamine D1 (D1R) or D2 (D2R) receptor. Using patch-clamp electrophysiological recordings, as well as behavioral, pharmacological and molecular approaches, we show reduced cholinergic transmission through the muscarinic M1 receptor onto SPNs, with no changes in the functionality or expression of this receptor. Notably, we demonstrate a loss of the differential excitability of D1R- vs. D2R-SPNs. Finally, acute in vivo treatment with the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor donepezil significantly alleviates RBs in mutant mice. These findings point to dysfunction of SCINs as a pathological and druggable mechanism underlying RBs in Tshz3-linked ASD, and to altered SPN excitability as a critical contributor in the resulting pathophysiological functioning of the striatum.

Article.Title: Combining non-linear and spectral cardiac variability metrics differentiates rat alcohol drinking with and without challenge
Article.Authors: De Oliveira Sergio, T.; Zareb, A. W.; Frasier, R. M.; Wean, S. E.; Starski, P. A.; Grippo, A.; Hopf, F.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) remains a substantial global challenge, with notable individual and sex differences. Heart rate variability (HRV) offers a potential link into the autonomic system underlying alcohol drinking. While simpler, time-domain HRV metrics have been explored, non-linear indicators could provide unique insights into more complex states like compulsive drinking, intake that persists despite negative consequences. We examined heart rate traces from male and female rats during intake of alcohol-only and alcohol+10mg/L quinine, a putative compulsive drinking model. In particular, we re-analyzed previously published findings, but newly focused on several non-linear HRV metrics: the Poincare ratio (possibly reflecting sympathovagal balance) and MultiScale entropy (MSE, perhaps reflecting unpredictability in broader and narrower time windows), along with the previously unexamined spectral HRV metrics (the parasympathetic indictor high-frequency HRV, HF-HRV%). HRV was assessed for the first ~1100 heart beats (~2.5 minutes), to assess HRV correlates of greater alcohol front-loading while having approximately similar amount of data per session. Lower Poincare ratio and higher HF-HRV% were overall related to higher alcohol consumption. In contrast, compulsive drinking, but not alcohol-only, was associated with lower broader-window HRV entropy, which was more pronounced in males. Drinking- and sex-related patterns were further identified using Principle Component Analysis, Ordinary Least Squares, and Linear Mixed Models. Limitations included perhaps being underpowered to detect significant relationships, especially in females. Thus, our preliminary findings suggest that combining HRV metrics could represent useful biomarkers for consumption levels during front-loading, which distinguished general intake from compulsion.

Article.Title: State-Dependent Stimulation for Seizure Termination in a Morris-Lecar Network: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
Article.Authors: Hazi, V.; Stippinger, M.; Kiss, T.; Somogyvari, Z.
Article.Abstract: The efficacy of neurostimulation for seizure termination depends not only on the stimulus itself but also on the dynamical state of the epileptic network. Here, we develop a dynamical-systems-informed reinforcement-learning framework that learns when to deliver a predefined pulse to terminate seizure-like activity. We simulate a sparsely connected network of 100 extended three-dimensional Morris-Lecar neurons. Bifurcation analysis of the single-neuron model identifies bistable regimes and provides a mechanistic basis for considering transitions between resting and oscillatory activity. The learning agent uses semi-gradient Q-learning with tile coding and receives a two-dimensional time-delay embedding of either the population-averaged membrane potential or a derivative-based proxy for extracellular potential. It learns a state-dependent policy that selects between stimulation and no stimulation, without modifying the pulse waveform. Across 30 independently generated test networks, both learned policies markedly reduced median seizure duration compared with trigger-only and state-independent stimulation controls. The two learned policies performed comparably, indicating that the estimated extracellular potential proxy retained sufficient dynamical information for control in this model. These results provide a proof of concept that combining dynamical-systems-based state reconstruction with online reinforcement learning can identify effective stimulation timing for terminating seizure-like activity.

Article.Title: Non-invasive temporal interference stimulation targeting the hippocampus enhances fast motor memory consolidation
Article.Authors: Pan, X.; Taylor, J.; Violante, I. R.; Grossman, N.; Inman, C.; King, B. R.; Albouy, G.
Article.Abstract: Converging neuroimaging evidence indicates that the hippocampus is involved in motor sequence learning (MSL) and its consolidation at multiple timescales. However, direct evidence for a causal role of the hippocampus in these processes in healthy humans remains scarce, partly due to the inability of conventional non-invasive brain stimulation techniques to reach this deep brain structure. Here, we used temporal interference stimulation (TIS) - a technique enabling non-invasive stimulation targeted toward deep brain regions - to probe the functional role of the hippocampus in MSL and its consolidation. In two separate experiments, sixty-four young healthy adults (36 females) received, in within-subject counterbalanced designs, active (5 Hz envelope) or control (0 Hz envelope) hippocampal-targeted TIS either during active practice of an MSL task (task-TIS experiment, n = 32) or during the short rest periods interleaved with task practice known to support rapid forms of consolidation (rest-TIS experiment, n = 32). Consolidation was assessed at both the micro timescale (i.e., over the short "micro-offline" rest intervals interspersed with task practice) and macro timescale (i.e., over a 24-hour "macro-offline" retention interval). Our results indicate that TIS targeting the hippocampus during inter-practice rest periods - but not during task practice - significantly enhanced micro-offline gains in performance as compared to control stimulation. While this effect did not carry over to the 24-hour retention interval at the group level, participants with greater stimulation-induced micro-offline gains showed larger overnight performance improvements. These findings provide the first direct evidence that experimental interventions targeting the hippocampus modulate offline motor memory consolidation processes.

Article.Title: Selective ultrasonic suppression of pathological brain hyperactivity via an endogenous CAV3-NCX1 axis
Article.Authors: Lee, K.; Lee, J. M.; Kim, H.-J.; Koo, M.; Lee, S.; shin, S.; Youn, W.; Phan, T. T.; Lee, C. J. J.; Park, J.; PARK, J. M.

Prolonged ultra-low-intensity ultrasound stimulation engages NCX1-mediated Ca2+ extrusion in hyperactive neurons and astrocytes, sparing cells with basal activity. NCX1 is both necessary and sufficient for this inhibitory response, and disruption of the CAV3-NCX1 interface abolishes the ultrasound-induced effects. In vivo, targeted ultrasound stimulation suppresses fear-evoked hyperactivity and freezing in an NCX1-dependent manner and attenuates neuropathic pain-associated hyperactivity, allodynia, and hippocampal epileptiform activity. These findings establish a molecular mechanism for state-dependent ultrasound inhibition, providing a basis for a new approach to neuromodulation that selectively targets pathological hyperactivity.

Article.Title: TRACE: Trajectory Reconstruction and Clustering From Sparse Evidence For Disease Subtyping and Staging
Article.Authors: Zhang, Y.; Li, H.; Wang, C.; You, G.; Fan, Y.
Article.Abstract: Chronic progressive diseases often follow heterogeneous courses, with individuals differing in the pattern and timing of biomarker abnormalities. However, observed data are typically sparse and predominantly cross-sectional, with limited follow-up covering only short segments of disease progression. Reconstructing heterogeneous trajectories from such data requires disentangling variation along disease trajectories from subtype heterogeneity while inferring individuals' unknown subtype assignments and disease stages. Existing approaches may confound disease stage with subtype, scale poorly as the number of biomarkers increases, or fail to effectively integrate cross-sectional and longitudinal observations. We propose TRACE: Trajectory Reconstruction And Clustering from Sparse Evidence, a probabilistic framework that jointly reconstructs biomarker trajectories and infers disease subtypes and continuous stages. TRACE combines monotonic neural networks for flexible modeling and data-driven clustering of subtype-specific progression trajectories with temporal regularization derived from longitudinal observations when available. All model components are jointly optimized end to end using stochastic gradient descent, enabling efficient and scalable estimation. We evaluate TRACE on semi-simulated MRI biomarker data with known subtype and stage structures and demonstrate its ability to identify clinically meaningful subtypes and disease stages in real-world neurodegenerative disease datasets.
