Article.Title: Neuronal Aralar/AGC1 deficiency impairs social behavior through dopaminergic and redox dysfunction and is rescued by β-hydroxybutyrate
Article.Authors: Herrada-Soler, E.; Murugarren, N.; Serrano-Lope, M.; Casarejos, M. J.; Palazuelos, J.; Satrustegui, J.; del Arco, A.; Pardo, B.
Article.Abstract: Background: Pathogenic variants in SLC25A12/AGC1 (Aralar) have been linked to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the mechanisms connecting neuronal metabolic dysfunction to altered social behavior remain poorly understood. Aralar is a key component of the malate-aspartate shuttle, supporting neuronal oxidative metabolism and lactate utilization. Here, we investigated the consequences of postnatal neuronal Aralar deletion and the therapeutic potential of {beta}-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). Methods: We generated neuron-specific Aralar knockout mice (Neu Aralar-KO) using CamKII-Cre, producing efficient recombination in cortex, hippocampus, and striatum. Behavioral, transcriptomic, neurochemical, morphometric, histological, and biochemical analyses were performed in adult mice. The effects of systemic BHB administration were assessed using behavioral, metabolic, oxidative stress, and transcriptomic endpoints. Results: Despite a 55-65% reduction of Aralar expression in forebrain regions, Neu Aralar-KO mice displayed normal growth, survival, brain structure, and myelination. Unexpectedly, loss of neuronal Aralar did not impair spatial memory, episodic memory, or reversal learning. In contrast, Neu Aralar-KO mice exhibited hyperactivity and a marked deficit in sociability, revealing an ASD-relevant behavioral phenotype. Morphological analysis showed significant remodeling of striatal dendritic spines without changes in spine density. Transcriptomic profiling identified 433 differentially expressed genes, the vast majority being upregulated, with enrichment of pathways related to neuropeptide signaling, synaptic transmission, membrane excitability, and behavior. Notably, genes involved in dopamine (DA) and glutamate handling, synaptic connectivity, neuromodulatory signaling, and ASD-associated pathways were strongly induced. Neurochemical analyses revealed preserved glutamate and GABA levels but reduced striatal DA content accompanied by an increased DOPAC/DA ratio, indicating enhanced DA degradation. DAergic neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) showed minimal recombination, suggesting that DA dysfunction arises through non-cell-autonomous mechanisms. Consistent with increased DA oxidative catabolism, Neu Aralar-KO striata displayed elevated lipid peroxidation, induction of glutathione-related pathways, upregulation of antioxidant genes, and astrocyte activation. Remarkably, BHB treatment restored sociability, normalized striatal metabolic alterations, reduced oxidative stress, and abolished genotype-dependent neurochemical abnormalities. Transcriptomic analyses further revealed that Aralar deficiency recapitulates a substantial fraction of the fasting/BHB-induced epigenetic transcriptional program. Conclusions: Postnatal neuronal Aralar deficiency uncouples social behavior from cognitive performance and drives ASD-like phenotypes through a mechanism linking neuronal metabolic dysfunction, oxidative stress, glial activation, and impaired DAergic homeostasis. The rescue of behavioral, metabolic, and redox abnormalities by BHB identifies restoration of metabolic homeostasis as a major therapeutic mechanism and highlights metabolic interventions as promising strategies for AGC1 deficiency and ASD-associated disorders involving neuronal metabolic dysfunction.

Article.Title: Neural dynamics track the approach to physical exhaustion
Article.Authors: Avancini, C.; Arco, J. E.; Alameda, C.; Bekinschtein, T. A.; Sanabria, D.; Ciria, L. F.
Article.Abstract: Physical exhaustion has long been described through its cardiorespiratory and metabolic cost, while the neural dynamics of its approach remain largely unexplored. Here we recorded high-density electroencephalography in 28 trained cyclists during a maximal incremental test to characterise how neural dynamics change towards exhaustion. As physiological strain rose, oscillatory power shifted to lower frequencies, neural activity became more regular and predictable, and functional coupling extended to longer timescales. Participant-specific models built on neural dynamics tracked proximity to exhaustion with accuracy comparable to cardiorespiratory measures. Over the final minutes, neural features remained informative while cardiorespiratory measures lost accuracy. Models trained across participants still tracked proximity to exhaustion, but less precisely. The approach to exhaustion thus follows a common neural path, tuned to each individual.

Article.Title: Zdhhc17/Hip14 functions in neurons to control behavior via DHHC-dependent and independent mechanisms
Article.Authors: Cheng, Y.; Santistevan, N. J.; Fink, K.; Jacobson, S.; Mosimann, C.; Burger, A.; Nelson, J. C.
Article.Abstract: To navigate a complex sensory environment, animals filter out inconsequential sensory inputs and habituate to familiar stimuli. By establishing innate response thresholds and modifying them through habituation, animals can focus on key sensory stimuli while ignoring irrelevant ones. Huntingtin-interacting protein 14 (Hip14), also known as zDHHC17, is a palmitoyl acyltransferase (PAT) that regulates both of these sensory filtering processes. Larval zebrafish lacking Hip14 are hypersensitive to acoustic stimuli and cannot regulate their responses to repeated acoustic stimuli via habituation. Prior work demonstrates that Hip14 is expressed throughout the nervous system, but where it functions to control these overlapping sensory functions remains unaddressed. We found that the catalytic (DHHC) domain, despite being a defining feature for PATs including Hip14, is not required for regulating acoustic startle sensitivity, but is sufficient to regulate habituation. We find, furthermore, that Hip14 function in either mechanosensory hair cells or neurons can restore normal startle sensitivity, whereas habituation is regulated exclusively by neuronal expression. Finally, we found that the Hip14 N-terminal ankyrin repeat domains are crucial for its control of behavior. Together, our study establishes that habituation and startle sensitivity are regulated through distinct circuit and molecular mechanisms and establishes a new in vivo catalytic-independent role for Hip14.

Article.Title: A Variational Principle for the Emergence of Neural Geometry Underlying Bayesian-Like Behavior
Article.Authors: Serrano-Fernandez, L.; Parga, N.
Article.Abstract: Neural population geometry constrains how task variables are represented and read out into behavior. We propose a variational principle in which learning balances task accuracy and representational smoothness under stimulus-dependent weighting. This balance links stimulus statistics to the shape of a latent neural coordinate. For magnitude estimation, the principle predicts distortions near the edges of bounded ensembles, global affine contraction for Gaussian ensembles, and warping toward high-probability regions for bimodal ensembles. We test the bounded-uniform case in recurrent neural networks trained to reproduce time intervals. Their learned geometries occupy three regimes as the boundary distortions change from too narrow to resolve, to measurable, to extending across the stimulus range. A shape parameter selected from an empirical neural coordinate predicts the nonlinear component of mean behavior through an affine readout, with only behavioral gain and offset fitted afterward. In this bounded-uniform setting, the variational coordinate and Bayesian least-squares mean response have closely matching shapes after affine normalization. These results suggest a variational account of how stimulus statistics shape neural geometry and yield Bayesian-like behavior.

Article.Abstract: Sensory satellite glial cells actively contribute to inflammatory and neuropathic pain, but their roles in pelvic pain remain unclear. In CPP conditions, sensory SGCs exhibit increased translation of mitochondrial and vesicular genes and suppression of immune genes in both sexes; an anti-inflammatory cytokine profile was detected in female pelvic sensory ganglia. We are the first to characterize SGC translatome in pelvic pain conditions and to report sex differences in SGC translatome. Our data suggested that mitochondrial and vesicular gene translation in sensory SGCs may be important to afferent hypersensitivity.

Article.Title: Amyloidosis and tauopathy progressively disrupt near-critical dynamics in selectively vulnerable circuits
Article.Authors: McGregor, J. N.; Fosque, L. J.; Brunwasser, S. J.; Farris, C.; Higashikubo, B. T.; Berriman-Rozen, Z. D.; Elmore, H.; Kest, K.; Whitesell, J. D.; Harris, J. A.; Shew, W. L.; Holtzman, D. M.; Hengen, K. B.
Article.Abstract: Mechanistically distinct neurodegenerative diseases result in similar cognitive deficits, and pathology is often concentrated in a set of circuits known to be selectively vulnerable. Selective vulnerability is an intrinsic property of a circuit: in APP/PS1 mice, where plaques are global, functional disruptions are confined to circuits within the default mode network. What characterizes the dynamics of vulnerable circuits from those of spared circuits is unknown. We asked whether the distinguishing property is the proximity of population dynamics to criticality, a homeostatic set-point of network activity that determines computational capacity. We recorded single units simultaneously in three selectively vulnerable regions (retrosplenial cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and CA1 hippocampus) and in primary visual cortex of freely behaving young and old APP/PS1 and wild-type mice. Firing rate and spike-time variability differed by genotype inconsistently across regions and ages. In contrast, three measures from criticality theory each revealed deficits that emerged only with age and only in the vulnerable regions. No measure detected a progressive change in V1. Avalanche scaling is not fixed in neural activity, but varies along a scaling line as the network state changes. As a result, the lines generated by each genotype revealed a constitutive effect of the transgene in young animals, which inverted with age in amyloid-bearing animals, but only in vulnerable circuits. If the destabilization of near-critical dynamics directly reflects a circuit's functional capacity, the same signature should identify a mechanistically distinct degenerative disease. In a model of tauopathy (P301S/E4), CA1 dynamics were displaced from the control scaling line with the same age-dependent reversal observed in APP/PS1. Article.Title: Electrophysiology of multisite direct electrical stimulation in the human brain
Article.Authors: Sehgal, D.; Paulk, A. C.; Hadar, P. N.; Peralta, J. D.; Salami, P.; Rolston, J. D.; Richardson, R. M.; Cash, S. S.; Zelmann, R.
Article.Abstract: Human cognition and neurological disorders reflect properties of distributed networks, yet how best to engage these networks therapeutically remains unknown. Multisite stimulation is a principled strategy for engaging brain networks, but a key translational barrier is understanding how a network combines concurrent inputs from multiple nodes. Here, we investigated the electrophysiology of simultaneous multisite direct electrical stimulation in 20 participants implanted with stereo-EEG electrodes. Synchronized dual-site stimulation engaged a larger effective network than single-site stimulation. Linear superposition explained most responses, but distinct nonlinear responses were also observed. Moreover, low-intensity dual-site stimulation matched or exceeded single-site stimulation at higher intensities. These principles extended to three-site stimulation. These findings systematically characterize how responses to simultaneous multisite stimulation interact in the human brain, a foundational step towards principled, network-guided neurostimulation therapies.

Article.Title: Repeated self-administered EEG recordings enable longitudinal measurement of brain activity at home
Article.Authors: van Moorselaar, D.; Kock, R.; Theeuwes, J.
Article.Abstract: Mobile electroencephalography (EEG) offers new opportunities to investigate brain activity outside the laboratory, but the quality and reliability of self-administered recordings remain important concerns. The recordings captured established spectral signatures of physiological state and task demands, including increased alpha activity during eye closure and changes in theta activity associated with cognitive load. Auditory stimulation elicited clear event-related responses, while exploratory multivariate decoding distinguished standard from target tones across recording sessions. For example, split-half reliability of the auditory N1-like response increased from r = .22 with one session to r = .76 with seven sessions per half. By demonstrating the feasibility of repeated self-administered EEG measurements, this study provides a step toward investigating how brain activity varies both between individuals and within individuals over time in everyday environments.

Article.Title: Nucleus reuniens gates selective hippocampal-prefrontal interactions during NREM sleep
Article.Authors: Shao, S.; Ferrero Lopez, J.; Kawano, T.; Bhagvat, C.; Khodagholy, D.; Gelinas, J.
Article.Abstract: Memory consolidation requires functional synchrony between the hippocampus (HC) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). Although ripples were independently detected in all three structures, we found that coupling between HC and mPFC ripples mainly involved co-occurring RE ripples. Article.Title: Inactivation of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase reduces phosphatidylcholine amounts in the brain of infant mice
Article.Authors: Nowak, L. G.; Marie, G.; Balayssac, S.; Delos, O.; Mornet, E.; Gilard, V.; Bertrand-Michel, J.; Fonta, C.
Article.Abstract: Hypophosphatasia is a rare disease caused by dysfunctions of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP). TNAP is expressed in numerous tissues, notably the brain, and patients with hypophosphatasia exhibit neurological symptoms, including epilepsy in the most severe forms of the disease. We used a targeted lipidomic approach, examining four main categories of lipids: fatty acids, neutral lipids, sphingolipids and glycerophospholipids, subdivided into 16 lipid classes and amounting to 296 lipid species. Eleven lipid species showed significantly reduced amounts in the brain of TNAP KO mice. All belonged to the phosphatidylcholine class. As phosphatidylcholines are major constituents of brain cell membranes, our results suggest that hypophosphatasia could be associated with alterations in membrane structure and functions, which could contribute to the neurodevelopmental disorders associated with the disease.

Article.Authors: Sharifi, K. A.; Norat, P.; Jannatifar, N.; Wang, Z.; Vergeres, C.; Padigala, M.; Sluzewski, M. F.; Liu, L.; Zhao, A.; Hoch, M. R.; Le, H.; Jansen, M. A.; Kellogg, R. T.; Kuan, C.-Y.; Miller, G. W.; Tvrdik, P.

At 48 hours, cKO males had 2.2-fold larger infarcts, while cKO females did not differ from controls. Moreover, cKO lesions showed a lower apparent diffusion coefficient, indicating more severe tissue injury. Neither hemispheric swelling nor cerebral arterial anatomy accounted for these differences. Article.Title: Direction-dependent misalignment between joint and muscle spaces predicts different generalization patterns following adaptation to opposing visuomotor rotations
Article.Authors: Creitz, L. K.; Gurgone, S.; Murai, R.; Hagura, N.; Essers, J. M. N.; Ikegami, T.
Article.Abstract: Learned movements are thought to be represented in both extrinsic and intrinsic reference frames. Intrinsic representations are traditionally characterized using joint-based coordinates, although the relationship between muscle activation patterns and joint movements strongly depends on limb configuration. Consequently, movement directions aligned in joint space may not be aligned in muscle space. The implications of this mismatch for motor learning, however, have remained largely unexplored. Experiment 2 confirmed this prediction, revealing a systematic shift between the CW and CCW generalization patterns that was consistent with the prediction based on muscle-pattern similarity. These findings suggest that intrinsic representations of learned movements cannot be fully captured by joint-based coordinates alone and that muscle-based coordinates contribute to the representation and generalization of learned movements. Together, these findings highlight the importance of considering the underlying biomechanics when interpreting motor representations using generalization paradigms.

Article.Title: A Two-Dimensional Grid-Cell Code for Three-Dimensional Navigation in Freely Flying Bats
Article.Authors: Qi, K. K.; Yartsev, M. M.
Article.Abstract: Animals evolved to navigate three-dimensional worlds, a capacity that relies on internal representations of position. In one- and two-dimensional environments, grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex provide a periodic signal for self-location that persists throughout the environment and is thought to arise from toroidal population dynamics. Yet global grid periodicity has not been observed during navigation through three-dimensional volumes, leaving unresolved whether grid cells and the underlying two-dimensional toroidal code can support navigation in three dimensions. Using large-scale wireless recordings in freely flying bats, we found that grid cells retained periodic firing during flight and that co-modular ensembles exhibited toroidal organization across behavioral states. Analyses of flight geometry in the laboratory and the wild showed that bats largely traverse volumetric space along two-dimensional planes of motion. Article.Abstract: Population receptive field (pRF) modelling is a ubiquitous tool in sensory neuroscience for estimating the functional architecture of the human brain. Importantly, the best-fitting HRF differed substantially from canonical HRFs or from those measured independently. HRFs also peaked earlier in higher than early visual cortex, suggesting response nonlinearities. This variability need not only be hemodynamic but could result from neural factors. Article.Title: Neuronal Hyperexcitability and Seizure Susceptibility in a Novel Kcnt1 G269S Mouse Model
Article.Authors: Olguin, S. L.; Rehman, A.; Davis, D.; Berg, S. W.; Patil, M.; Haouchine, O. Y.; Sullivan, P. D. M.; Oswalt, P. S.; Sahagun, E.; Zhang, B. L.; Silverman, J. L.; Bryda, E.; Ben-Shalom, R.

The majority of pathogenic KCNT1 mutations are gain-of-function (GOF), with each exhibiting unique channel biophysical properties, channel dynamics, electrophysiological spiking, and epileptiform characteristics. These diverse neuronal electrical profiles, contribute to a spectrum of epilepsy syndromes ranging from severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathies to focal epilepsies with milder outcomes. Among these, variants at Gly288 are recurrent, reported in 29 of 248 individuals in the largest published cohort to date, and 79% (23/29) of whom presented with severe early-onset epilepsy, yet no in vivo model of this pore-domain variant currently exists. Our multi-disciplinary collaboration generated a novel mouse model (C57BL/6-Kcnt1em1Bryd) that carries the G269S variant of Kcnt1, corresponding to the human G288S variant, located within the coding region of the channel pore. We characterized network excitability of primary cultured cortical neurons from all three genotypes (Kcnt1+/+, Kcnt1+/G269S, and Kcnt1G269S/G269S) on high-density microelectrode arrays, since many KCNT1 mouse models require homozygosity for phenotypic detection. Kcnt1+/G269S neurons exhibited sustained hyperexcitability and hypersynchronous bursting versus Kcnt1+/+ controls, while Kcnt1G269S/G269S neurons showed early excessive bursting followed by a progressive decline in coordinated network activity by 28 days-in-vitro. Therefore, behavioral comparisons were conducted between Kcnt1+/G269S and Kcnt1+/+ mice including developmental milestones, motor and cognitive abilities, respiratory physiology, and seizure susceptibility. Kcnt1+/G269S mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures, poor motor coordination, erratic breathing, and increased apneas, as functional outcome measures. Critically, Kcnt1+/G269S mice were more susceptible to thermal-induced seizures in early life and chemoconvulsant induced seizures in adulthood. In summary, these data: (i) generated and validated a novel mouse model of KCNT1-related epilepsy, (ii) provide strong in vitro evidence of neuronal hyperexcitability, (iii) illustrate behavioral spontaneous seizures, early-life seizures, and adult seizure susceptibility as functional outcome measures, (iv) elucidated alterations in exploratory locomotion and poor motor coordination, (v) identified increased erratic breathing in female and increased apneas in male Kcnt1+/G269S mice and (vi) lay the groundwork for future analysis of neural activity in vivo and modeling circuit level dynamics in vitro, in vivo, and in silico.

Article.Authors: Phogat, R.; Behler, A.; Sonkusare, S.; Pang, J. C.; Koussis, N.; Roberts, J. A.; DeKraker, J.; Dionisio, S.; Shine, J.; Fornito, A.; Robinson, P. A.; Breakspear, M.

The human brain provides a canonical example, with large-scale neural dynamics evolving on distinct anatomical surfaces such as the cortex and hippocampus. These surfaces support characteristic intrinsic dynamics shaped jointly by their geometry and internal feedback architecture. We capture both these influences in our geometry-constrained neural-field theory of cortical and hippocampal dynamics. In the brain, topographically organised reciprocal interactions couple these two systems, giving rise to collective cortico-hippocampal dynamics. Extending our theory to these collective dynamics therefore requires a coupling framework for fields evolving on geometrically distinct surfaces lacking a natural point-to-point correspondence. We achieve this by introducing a geometry-constrained coupling scheme that uses quasi-conformal mapping to place the two surfaces in a shared coordinate system, enabling spatially organised interactions between them. The resulting coupled system exhibits distinct dynamical regimes that capture characteristic signatures of recorded physiological and pathological cortico-hippocampal data. At moderate coupling, topographically linked regions show enhanced coordination while retaining their intrinsic cortical alpha (8-12 Hz) and hippocampal theta (4-8 Hz) rhythms. Stronger coupling, combined with increased hippocampal excitability, produces coherent low-frequency activity that recapitulates key features observed in human and rodent hippocampal seizures. Together, our results establish geometry-constrained coupling as an organising principle by which distinct neural manifolds reshape their intrinsic dynamics and undergo collective state transitions.

Article.Abstract: Across multiple timescales, neural rhythms coordinate cognitive and physiological processes. Here, we recorded infra-slow EEG alongside respiratory, cardiac and skin conductance signals during the perceptual crossing experiment, a social interaction and EEG hyperscanning paradigm. These findings suggest that the gastric rhythm - potentially in unison with other physiological signals - provides a stable, global scaffold for large-scale oscillatory brain organization. Article.Title: Acute FMR1 reduction alters cellular and circuit properties in human cortex
Article.Authors: Singh, A.; Abbaspoor, S.; Chung, L.; Heinrich, M. J.; Stone, S.; Lidov, H.; Maio, B.; Tran, T. P.; Yoon, J.; Teng, J.; Reyes, C. M.; Hammarlund, E.; Xu, X.; Hirsh, R.; Guardado, R.; Buttermore, E.; Rotenberg, A.; Gavornik, J.; Ferguson, B.; Farrell, J. S.; Osterweil, E. K.
Article.Abstract: Transcriptional silencing of FMR1 results in Fragile X syndrome (FXS), the leading inherited cause of intellectual disability (ID) and autism. Although the impact of FMR1 reduction on cortical function has been studied using the Fmr1-/y mouse model, mechanistic insights from the human brain are lacking. Here we show that acute FMR1 reduction in ex vivo human cortical slices induces transcriptomic changes that are concordant with those observed in FXS patient cortex, identifying many targets not altered in the Fmr1-/y mouse model. Consistent with changes in ion channel expression specifically in human tissue, FMR1 reduction drives increased intrinsic excitability of deep-layer pyramidal neurons and network-level population bursts observed with two-photon calcium imaging. Together, these findings define the consequences of FMR1 loss in human cortex and establish an experimental framework for identifying human-specific mechanisms and therapeutic targets relevant to FXS.

Article.Title: Distinct contemplative traditions share a common EEG complexity signature
Article.Authors: Shrimali, P.; Sasidharan, A.; Malipeddi, S.; Ventura, B.; Venugopal, R.; Nair, A. K.; Tewarie, P. K. B.; Nagendra, R. P.; Kutty, B. M.; Northoff, G.
Article.Abstract: Meditation encompasses diverse practices that train attention inward, unlike externally oriented task states. Which brain-activity features are shared across contemplative practices, which accompany long-term training, and which are tradition-specific remains unclear. We leveraged electroencephalography data from 226 participants: advanced meditators of four contemplative traditions and non-meditating controls. We developed a neurodynamic profiling approach spanning 21 features across four feature families: oscillatory, aperiodic, complexity and timescale. Using extensive machine learning, we found that meditation and task states were reliably separable, driven by a large, uniform drop in complexity during meditation. Meditators differed from controls primarily in timescale dynamics. Traditions exhibited distinct signatures in all feature families except complexity, and meditators neurodynamic profiles identified the contemplative tradition they practiced. A classifier trained on three traditions could still detect meditation in the fourth, regardless of which tradition was left out, relying mainly on complexity features. Diverse contemplative techniques therefore converge on a shared neurodynamic signature - reduced complexity during meditation relative to an external task, that generalizes across traditions. This shared signature coexists with tradition-specific profiles in oscillatory, aperiodic, and timescale features.

Article.Title: A general method for bootstrapping dense 3D segmentations from sparse 2D annotations
Article.Authors: Thiyagarajan, V. V.; Sheridan, A.; Harris, K. M.; Manor, U.
Article.Abstract: Volumetric electron microscopy (vEM) provides unparalleled insight into cellular architecture, transforming our understanding of fundamental biological processes. Precise quantification of volumetric bioimaging data requires 3D instance segmentation, but the time and cost of manual ground-truth annotation present a major bottleneck for training accurate machine learning models. Our lightweight two-stage method generates complete 3D instance segmentations from sparse 2D annotations. A 2D network predicts dense boundaries on every section from minimal 2D labels. A 3D network pre- trained on synthetic data infers connectivity between sections. Across the imaging modalities and biological structures tested, our method generates base segmentations with minutes of human effort per volume. Models trained on these 2D [->] 3D pseudo ground-truth segmentations approach the accuracy of fully supervised models while reducing human annotation time by four orders of magnitude. This method does not require dense 3D labeling and thus democratizes scalable volumetric analysis across imaging modalities in basic science and biomedical applications.

Article.Title: Synaptic pruning, myelination and the emergence of psychiatric disorders in late adolescence
Article.Authors: Averbeck, B. B.; Brunel, N.
Article.Abstract: Adolescence is an important developmental period during which there are diverse changes in the brain and behavior. Goal-directed behaviors, including working memory, response inhibition, and reinforcement learning, improve during adolescence. At the same time there is substantial pruning of excitatory connections in prefrontal cortex and ongoing myelination of axons, which likely underlie these improvements in behavior. However, psychiatric disorders also become increasingly prevalent in late adolescence. In this study, we develop computational models that suggest a hypothesis for how ongoing changes in the brain can give rise to the increased prevalence of psychiatric disorders including depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), schizophrenia and substance use disorders (SUDs). We show that both myelination and pruning during adolescence lead to attractor landscapes in which strongly encoded memories, embedded in patterns of synaptic connectivity, come to dominate brain activity. Pruning and myelination lead to large, strong dynamical attractors which, if they are related to aversive emotions, can drive intrusive thoughts and compulsions in OCD, rumination in depression, or if they are related to drug exposure, compulsive drug seeking in SUDs. Thus, we suggest that psychiatric disorders emerge when early experience embeds pathophysiological patterns of synaptic connectivity in neural circuits. The neural changes during adolescent development then cause these memories to inflexibly dominate the neural and behavioral landscape.

Article.Title: Network modularity reveals context and state-dependent reorganization of time-varying functional connectivity in single-cell resolved neural activity recordings
Article.Authors: Moon, S.; Liang, J.; Lee, H. J.; Maalouf, A.; Yu, Z.; Moza, S.; Zhang, Y.; Lu, H.
Article.Abstract: An important goal of neuroscience is to understand how biological neural networks organize activity at multiple scales to enable complex information processing and behavioral output. To address this challenge, large-scale neural activity datasets with increased resolution and wider coverage have become more prevalent across many model systems. However, bridging the gap in scale between changes in pairwise functional connectivity between neurons and changes in brain-wide organization of activity remains a key challenge. In this work, we demonstrate application of modularity-based community detection and network modularity to single-cell resolved recordings, for the first time, as a method to summarize complex changes in time-varying functional connectivity, facilitating comparisons across multiple time windows, recordings, and conditions. We apply these methods to both single-cell resolved multi-cell and whole-brain activity recordings. In the multi-cell recordings, we find that food odor changes functional connectivity between existing network modules in a C. elegans locomotory interneuron network, rather than reorganizing them. In spontaneous whole-brain activity, we identify several key hub neurons and combinations that significantly destabilize module assignments when silenced. Together, these results demonstrate community detection and modularity as a method for detecting context and network state-dependent changes in functional connectivity at the intermediate scale of network modules in single-cell resolved neural activity. Results from these analyses facilitate future investigation of mechanisms that mediate organization of neural activity at intermediate scales.

Article.Title: Reactive and predictive processes during unpredictable driving collisions in virtual reality: an exploratory immersive study with multimodal neurophysiological monitoring
Article.Authors: Cannard, C.; Yesilbas, D.
Article.Abstract: Anticipatory neurophysiological activity before unpredictable emotional events has been reported for decades, but the effects are small, difficult to replicate, and obtained almost exclusively in stripped-down laboratory paradigms. Whether they reflect genuine predictive processes or methodological artifacts remains debated; one rarely tested possibility is that such settings mute it. We examined anticipation in an immersive virtual reality (VR) driving simulation whose collision outcomes were assigned by a quantum random number generator, while EEG, photoplethysmography (PPG), EMG, EOG and inertial (IMU) signals were recorded from a single wireless dry-electrode headset built into the VR display. Sixteen participants passively observed 120 driving sequences ending in a collision or no collision. Length-matched pre- and post-stimulus windows were analysed identically with mass-univariate hierarchical general linear models under permutation cluster correction, plus machine-learning classification across held-out participants. Two post-stimulus clusters differentiated the conditions, the largest peaking at 451.6 ms (d = -1.35), with broadband power modulation robust to baseline modelling, decoded from held-out participants with up to 93.8% accuracy. No time-domain effect or decodable information preceded stimulus onset, but a broadband spectral difference did, surviving preregistered controls for expectation bias (run length), time-on-task build-up and ocular or facial-muscle artifact: directionally consistent in 13 of 15 participants, with pre- and post-stimulus power coupled in all 16. Heart rate differentiated the conditions neither alone nor when added to the classifier. The study was preregistered; the BIDS-format data, analysis code and an open-source EEGLAB plugin are publicly available.

Article.Title: Immersive display systems for simulating natural vision
Article.Authors: Katti, H.; Murphy, A. P.; Helde, M.; Deshpande, H.; Lee, T. J.; Knight, R.; Gregg, C.; Solinas, C.; Cameron, K.; Bandy, D.; Dold, G.; Leopold, D. A.
Article.Abstract: Vision is traditionally studied using simplified stimuli presented briefly near the center of a flat display while subjects maintain visual fixation. This paradigm contrasts sharply with real-world vision, which is immersive, dynamic and strongly influenced by self-initiated actions. Traditional approaches have allowed researchers to systematically study the neural encoding of visual features and the influence of cognitive operations such as attention. However, other methods are needed to study more holistic and first-person perspectives on vision, such as those related to physical space, continuous time, and self-movement. To enable the study of these and other aspects of real-world vision, we developed hemispherical ("dome") display systems for macaque visual neuroscience. For functional MRI experiments, a compact rear-projection dome display fits within the bore of a clinical MRI scanner. For electrophysiological recordings, a larger front-projection dome display is illuminated from above using a spherical mirror. Both setups complete and dynamic stimulation of approximately 180 degrees of the subject's field of view, thus facilitating studies requiring visual immersion. To ensure accurate angular geometry across the hemispherical display, we present unified rendering and calibration software that supports natural fisheye videos, conventional visual stimuli, and virtual 3D environments. The calibration procedure automatically compensates for projector, mirror, and dome distortions through geometric pre-warping, ensuring correct visual-angle representation across the display. Pilot fMRI experiments demonstrate robust activation of peripheral visual cortex during both conventional pattern stimulation and naturalistic self-movement. Together, these dome systems provide a flexible platform for investigating aspects of vision that are difficult to study with conventional displays, including peripheral processing, visual immersion, optic flow, self-motion, and holistic scene perception.

Article.Title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low Trust Speakers
Article.Authors: Hannah, J.; Di Liberto, G. M.
Article.Abstract: Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using non-invasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from twenty young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function (TRF) analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal TRF dynamics.

Article.Title: Precocious maturation and Purkinje cell dysfunction in the mouse Chd8 haploinsufficient cerebellum
Article.Authors: Seban, N.; Merino, E.; D'Ambra, A.; Jung, S. J.; Dunga, J. L.; Lozano, S.; Fenton, E.; Chu, N.; Jackson, K.; Rahbarian, D.; Kopley-Smith, A.; Corea, M.; Cichewicz, K.; Ardekani, C.; Wade, A. A.; Antzoulatos, E. G.; Canales, C. P.; Fioravante, D.; Nord, A. S.
Article.Abstract: The cerebellum plays an emerging, but understudied, role in neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). Mutations in CHD8 cause a monogenic NDD (CHD8-NDD) characterized by autism and other manifestations, and prior work in Chd8 mutant mice reported cerebellar abnormalities, raising the possibility of cerebellar contribution to CHD8-NDD. To characterize the impact of Chd8 haploinsufficiency on cerebellar development and function, we profiled the postnatal day 12 (P12) cerebellum of germline Chd8+/- mice using transcriptomic, morphological, and electrophysiological approaches. Gross cerebellar morphology was unaffected, but single-nucleus RNA sequencing revealed transcriptomic signatures of pathophysiology across cell types, including accelerated maturation of molecular layer interneurons, granule cells, and oligodendrocytes lineages. Purkinje cells (PCs) showed the strongest transcriptomic burden of any cell type and, consistent with this, exhibited altered morphology and electrophysiological properties. Bulk RNA sequencing confirmed that transcriptomic pathology persists into adulthood, indicating lasting impacts on both neuronal and glial gene expression. Together, these results capture cell-type-specific cerebellar perturbations associated with Chd8 haploinsufficiency and support the cerebellum as a relevant locus of pathology in CHD8-NDD.

Article.Title: A cross-species protocol for ultrasound-guided intrauterine injections across gestation
Article.Authors: Ribeiro Gomes, A. R.; Hamel, N.; Mastwal, S.; Ide, D. C.; Wang, K. H.; Leopold, D. A.
Article.Abstract: This step-by-step protocol provides a cross-species, non-surgical approach that enables prenatal gene delivery to the developing nervous system in rats and marmosets. Under transabdominal ultrasound guidance, intracerebroventricular viral injection (FIVI) of recombinant adeno-associated virus vectors into the fetal brain achieves robust and long-term transduction from prenatal stages into adulthood. This approach can be adapted to multiple species and target sites outside nervous system, enabling safe and selective intrauterine manipulation and the generation of diverse experimental models for basic and preclinical research. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Ribeiro Gomes et al (2026).

Article.Title: Physiological robustness of MScanFit to simulated motor unit loss and remodelling
Article.Authors: Ahmed, D.; Almokdad, M.; Jones, K. E.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: MScanFit estimates motor unit number and size from compound muscle action potential (CMAP) scans, but its accuracy may depend on the physiological processes that shape motor unit loss and remodelling. We reproduced the general dynamic remodelling framework used in the original MScanFit simulation and expanded it to test MScanFit robustness across physiologically heterogeneous conditions. Methods: Generative computational models simulated CMAP scans from motor unit pools undergoing progressive loss from 160 to 5 surviving motor units. Twelve remodelling conditions combined denervation pattern (random or selective), reinnervation method (random, distributive, or size-weighted), and neuromuscular resilience (20% or 60%); two additional conditions modelled denervation without collateral reinnervation. MScanFit estimates were compared with the known motor unit numbers and mean motor unit sizes used to generate each scan. Results: MScanFit reproduced the principal behaviour reported in the original simulation and generally tracked progressive motor unit loss across heterogeneous remodelling conditions. However, motor unit number estimation (MUNE) error changed systematically with remodelling physiology. Selective denervation and distributive reinnervation increased error at several intermediate stages of motor unit loss, whereas 60% resilience produced greater error than 20% resilience at every stage after remodelling began. Motor unit size estimates also tracked the underlying increase in mean unit size, but their accuracy was more strongly affected by remodelling, particularly with 60% resilience and advanced motor unit loss. Conclusion: MScanFit motor unit number estimates were broadly robust to substantial motor unit loss and neuromuscular remodelling but were not physiologically invariant. Denervation and collateral reinnervation systematically influenced the magnitude and direction of estimation error, indicating that variation in MScanFit performance can arise from differences in the underlying motor unit population. These findings support MScanFit as a robust measure of motor unit loss across heterogeneous neuromuscular phenotypes and show that some of its estimation variability has a physiological basis.

Article.Title: Dissecting the functional heterogeneity of glutamatergic synapses with high-throughput optical physiology
Article.Authors: Barlow, S. T.; Levy, A. D.; Contreras, M.; Anderson, M. C.; Blanpied, T. A.
Article.Abstract: Fluorescent reporters for neurotransmitter release and Ca2+ signaling are essential tools for quantifying synapse function across neurons and circuits. However, leveraging these reporters requires scalable experimental frameworks. Here, we devised a high-throughput approach to efficiently collect and analyze hundreds of optical recordings of glutamate release activity using iGluSnFR3 at synapses in cultured rat hippocampal neurons. Our approach facilitated deep analysis of single-synapse properties following single action potentials, paired stimuli, or spontaneous release, and together with mean-variance analysis, we mapped synaptic functional diversity across the dendritic arbor. We then developed a novel all-optical assay of pre- and postsynaptic glutamatergic synapse function, deploying iGluSnFR3 along with a red-shifted, postsynaptically targeted Ca2+ sensor to enable direct imaging and analysis of both NMDA receptor and AMPA receptor-mediated synaptic transmission at single dendritic spines. Direct observation of the flow of information at single synapses should speed detailed investigations of synaptic mechanistic heterogeneity.

Article.Title: Primary and Supplementary Motor cortex implement parallel control solutions for rhythmic and discrete arm movements
Article.Authors: Colins Rodriguez, A.; Fuentes-Flores, R.; Humphries, M. D.
Article.Abstract: Arm movements are rhythmic, discrete, or some combination of the two. Conflicting evidence supports each of two possible solutions for how motor cortex controls them: that either it uses the same strategy for controlling rhythmic and discrete movements or different strategies for distinct movement types. Using recurrent neural network modelling and multi-unit recordings during an arm-cycling task, we show that primate motor cortex uses both solutions. Primary motor cortex (M1) dynamics converge to the same limit-cycle when executing both movement types. In contrast, supplementary motor area (SMA) dynamics diverge according to the type of the upcoming movement before reaching a helical spiral. Our results reconcile opposing views on the cortical control of rhythmic and discrete movements by showing that the two solutions are not mutually exclusive but implemented in parallel within motor cortex. Instead, our results challenge us to understand why both solutions are implemented to solve the same problem.

Article.Title: Self-generated cues and learned landmarks support spatial learning in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Chen, Y.; Alfredson, R.; Zuo, X.; Motevalli, D.; Fogleman, S.; Stern, U.; Yang, C.-H.
Article.Abstract: The ability to return to remembered goal locations is essential for animal survival. Although animals are known to use visual landmarks, how well they can exploit non-visual cues for spatial learning remains poorly understood. Here we show that Drosophila can combine learned olfactory cues with self-motion information to return to initially unmarked goals. In feature-poor arenas, flies assign positive value to self-deposited scents near the rewarded goal and combine these cues with self-motion cues to guide their return. This strategy depends on the mushroom body, an olfactory learning center that associates odors with reinforcement1, and PFN neurons, which encode egocentric translational velocity2,3. External olfactory landmarks away from the goal improve performance: flies assign them negative value, again through the mushroom body, and use them as aversive guideposts to constrain search area. Comparisons among wild-caught strains suggest that the capacities to learn in feature-poor arenas and to benefit from external olfactory landmarks are genetically separable. Complementary transcriptomic analyses reveal differences in learning-associated gene expression in feature-poor and landmark-enriched arenas. Our findings reveal that flies can construct and combine complementary spatial information to navigate without prominent visual cues and that the ability to learn in different sensory contexts is under partly distinct genetic control.

Article.Title: Distinct Hippocampal Cellular Pathologies Influence Cognition Across Diagnostic Categories and Distinguish Schizophrenia from Affective Psychosis
Article.Authors: Ruby, E.; Gonen, O.; Walsh-Messinger, J.; Lotan, E.; Tal, A.; Rusinek, H.; Clemente, J. C.; Robinson-Papp, J.; Lafont, E.; Karlsgodt, K. H.; Malaspina, D.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive deficits are core features of psychosis and strong predictors of functional outcome, but are largely refractory to pharmacological treatments. It remains unresolved whether these deficits share cellular mechanisms across the psychosis spectrum (as in transdiagnostic models) or differ across DSM-5 diagnostic boundaries, particularly those separating schizophrenia from affective psychoses. We tested this by examining associations between MATRICS Cognitive Battery scores and whole-hippocampal proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (1H-MRSI) neurometabolite biomarkers of cellular pathologies in 33 participants with psychosis (20 schizophrenia, 13 affective psychosis), 22 with non-psychotic affective disorders, and 25 healthy controls. Metabolite biomarkers included N-acetylaspartate (NAA) for neuronal integrity; myo-inositol (mI) for glia; choline (Cho) for membrane/myelin turnover; and glutamate+glutamine (Glx) for glutamatergic neurotransmission. Metabolite concentrations did not differ between groups but showed group-specific associations with cognition. In healthy controls, lower NAA was associated with poorer overall cognition, working memory, and reasoning (rs=.41, .42, and .43, respectively; p's<.05). Among non-psychotic affective cases, lower mI and higher Cho were associated with worse verbal learning (rs=.50 and -.45, respectively; p's<.05). In psychosis, lower Cho predicted poorer visual learning (rs=.51; p=.002). The clearest between-group divergence involved social cognition, the cognitive domain most predictive of functioning in psychosis: worse performance was associated with lower Glx in schizophrenia (rs=.67; p=.033) but higher Cho and NAA in affective psychosis (rs=-.58 and -.58, respectively; p's<.05). Each metabolite-social cognition association was opposite in direction and differed significantly between these groups (p's<.05), contrary to what transdiagnostic models would predict. These findings suggest distinct hippocampal cellular substrates of social cognitive impairments in schizophrenia and affective psychosis, supporting diagnosis-specific treatment targets and warranting replication in larger samples.

Article.Title: Complex Spatial and Temporal Organization of Functional Brain Networks
Article.Authors: Sassenberg, T. A.; Wilson, S.; DeYoung, C. G.
Article.Abstract: Recent research exploring brain-behavior associations has relied on the language of complex systems to understand how stable behavioral individual differences emerge from brain function. At the same time, advances in neuroimaging have provided greater insight into both the topological and temporal properties of macroscale cortical networks. These new approaches offer a potential avenue for understanding how functional activity in the brain might behave in a manner that aligns with complex-systems interpretations of psychological traits. The present study used resting-state data from the Human Connectome project (N = 994) to explore associations between the spatial and temporal features of functional brain networks. Using an adaptive frequency approach to explore brain function at different timescales together with a family of methods from complex systems theory, we identified patterns of brain state organization reflecting a state-trait continuum, with more stable trait-like dynamics and greater functional coupling between networks in lower frequency oscillations. Additionally, we found evidence of greater coupling across timescales in brain networks associated with higher-order cognition. This research supports interpretations of brain organization as a spatiotemporal hierarchy and provides future avenues for exploring brain-behavior associations from a complex system perspective.

Article.Title: E2F4 gene therapy reverses established synaptic and cognitive deficits and remodels learning-associated signaling in Alzheimer's disease mice
Article.Authors: Sanchez-Puelles, C.; Hernandez-Vivanco, A.; Grieco, A.; Camacho-Olmos, I.; Montero-Calle, A.; Lopez-Sanchez, N.; Fraj-Cebrian, A.; Garrido-Garcia, A.; Cano-Daganzo, V.; Lozano-Urena, A.; Valdes-Lora, L.; Barderas, R.; Perea, G.; Pascual-Leone, A.; Frade, J. M.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) causes progressive synaptic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline, yet strategies capable of reversing established deficits remain limited. Here, we show that neuronal expression of a p38MAPK phosphorylation-resistant human E2F4 variant (hE2F4DN), delivered by adeno-associated virus, restores hippocampal long-term potentiation and memory in homozygous 5xFAD mice after functional impairment is established. Treatment also reduces amyloid-{beta} and phospho-tau pathology and prevents hippocampal neuronal loss. Integrated proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses reveal remodeling of metabolic, redox, neuroimmune, synaptic-vesicle, and GSK3{beta}-associated signaling pathways. Following contextual fear conditioning, hE2F4DN-treated mice exhibit broader learning-associated synaptic proteomic signatures and distinct phosphoregulatory responses involving synaptic machinery. These findings demonstrate that E2F4 gene therapy can reverse established synaptic and cognitive deficits while preserving neuronal integrity and reshaping molecular responses to learning, identifying E2F4 phosphorylation as a potential therapeutic target for advanced AD states.

Article.Title: Primate Saccade Rhythmicity
Article.Authors: Näher, T.; Zhang, Y.; Spadacenta, S.; Pandinelli, M.; Bastian, L.; Thier, P.; Hafed, Z. M.; Fries, P.
Article.Abstract: Rhythmic sampling is a hallmark of many sensory systems across diverse organisms. In primate vision, rapid foveating eye movements repetitively sample the visual environment at a rate of approximately 4 Hz. Yet, the observed inter-saccadic interval distributions might equally well be produced by a non-rhythmic stochastic process as by a - putatively variable- rhythmic generator. This raises the fundamental question whether primate visual sampling differs from the numerous examples of rhythmic sampling strategies exhibited across sensory modalities and species. Here, using experiments in humans, macaques, and a marmoset, as well as statistical approaches adopted from studies of temporal structure in neuronal spiking patterns, we show that primate saccade generation is unambiguously rooted in a rhythmic source. This finding was remarkably consistent across the three primate species despite their significant evolutionary distance. Importantly, we find that saccade rate undergoes smooth, slow fluctuations on the scale of seconds, and accounting for those rate fluctuations was crucial for revealing the true degree of saccade rhythmicity. Thus, exact saccade timing is determined by an interaction between the slow saccade-rate fluctuations and the more temporally-local rhythmic generator. This demonstration of rhythmicity in overt oculomotor sampling behavior provides a link to the fundamentally rhythmic nature of many central perceptual and cognitive processes, and places primate saccadic sampling into the large family of rhythmic active sampling behaviors.

Article.Title: EPHB2 promotes long-range axon extension and its variants cause callosal dysgenesis
Article.Authors: Park, S. S.; Nagy, G. N.; Perez Ferrer, I.; Coca, Y.; Herrera, M.; Kahwaji, C.; Zhang, X. B.; Liu, L.; Kolluru, S.; Neira, M.; Kerdjemil, Y.; Palombo, F.; La Morgia, C.; Caporali, L.; Carelli, V.; Waisfisz, Q.; Elting, M. W.; Houge, G. D.; Gradek, G. A.; Tveitnes, D.; Sheridan, E. G.; Prescott, K.; Redman, M.; Imam, A.; Ostergaard, P.; Anderson, K.; Weaver, D. D.; Schaefer, E.; Laugel, V.; Gan-Or, Z.; Dalva, M. B.; Depienne, C.; Jones, E. Y.; Herrera, E.; Kania, A.
Article.Abstract: The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest fibre tract connecting the cerebral hemispheres, essential for integrating neural activity across large-scale brain networks. Accordingly, abnormal CC development is associated with diverse neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Callosal projection neurons (CPNs) of the cortex form the CC by extending long-range axons to the contralateral hemisphere; however, the mechanisms that sustain axon elongation over such remarkable distances remain poorly understood. Here we show that variants in the human gene EPHB2, which encodes a tyrosine kinase receptor regulating nervous system development and implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, cause CC dysgenesis. We characterise variant- specific effects on EPHB2 signalling and demonstrate that variants identified in individuals with distinct CC morphologies differentially alter CPN axon outgrowth and integration in vivo. We further show that EphB2 has a cell-autonomous, ligand-independent function in promoting CPN axon outgrowth by spatially organising actomyosin at axonal growth cones. These findings reveal a previously unrecognised role for EphB2 in promoting long-range axon extension and provide the first evidence that EPHB2 variants cause CC dysgenesis in humans. More broadly, our study links molecular variation in EPHB2 to individualised abnormalities in brain connectivity and provides a framework for understanding how heterogeneous circuit-level phenotypes arise in neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: Do altered neural responses during self-reflection converge across psychiatric disorders? A systematic review and meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies
Article.Authors: Zhu, S.; Yan, W.-J.; Chuan-Peng, H.
Article.Abstract: Altered neural responses during self-reflection have been reported across psychiatric disorders, but it is unknown whether there exist common brain regions across studies. To fill the gap, we conducted a systematic review and coordinate-based activation likelihood estimation (ALE) meta-analysis of task-based neuroimaging studies. Through systematic literature search and article screening, we identified 36 studies across 8 diagnostic categories, of which 25 studies were eligible for the ALE meta-analysis. Qualitatively, these studies revealed altered neural response among psychiatric disorders in brain regions include cortical midline and lateral association regions. ALE analyses were conducted separately for self-versus other and self-versus control contrasts, the former identified convergence in the right anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and the latter found converged activation in the left middle frontal gyrus (MFG). These findings revealed a broad interest in neural response to self-evaluation but unevenly distributed studies across psychiatric disorders, and the available results only provided weak evidence of spatial convergence for altered neural response across psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Mathematical model for visual cortical development based on molecular mechanisms underlying the generation and elimination of dendritic spines
Article.Authors: Tanaka, S.; Miyashita, M.
Article.Abstract: In the developing brain, neural circuits are elaborated by the activity-dependent rewiring of synaptic connections. The current view of synaptic rewiring in early development is that filopodia spontaneously generated along dendrites transform into spines by establishing contacts with neighboring axonal boutons to form synapses whereas spines of inappropriate synapses are eliminated in an activity-dependent manner. In this theoretical study, we mainly focus on the processes of spine generation, maturation, and elimination to build a mathematical model of synaptic rewiring, incorporating experimental findings on actin polymerization and depolymerization under the activation of Rho-GTPases mediated by the binding of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) to neurotrophin receptors such as tropomyosin kinase receptor B (TrkB) and the low-affinity-nerve growth factor receptor (p75NTR). TrkB receptors are dephosphorylated by chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans (CSPGs) mediated by protein-tyrosine phosphatase {sigma} (PTP{sigma} in an age-dependent manner. The model describes the generation or elimination of dendritic spines of visual cortical neurons under actin polymerization and depolymerization to establish appropriate synaptic contacts on afferent fibers of cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus. The simulations based on the model reproduced not only simple-cell-like receptive fields and orientation-direction maps but also a characteristic profile of the total number of synapses, which shows an early increase and a delayed decrease during the critical period. It is also demonstrated that the formation of direction selectivity is delayed behind the formation of orientation selectivity, which is likely promoted by the pruning of inappropriate synapses.

Article.Title: Biological network topology is a structural prior for data-efficient sparse learning
Article.Authors: Jamal, T.; Celikel, T.
Article.Abstract: Biological networks, from gene co-expression circuits to cortical connectomes and animal societies, share sparse, modular, small-world topologies thought to reflect optimization for efficient infor-mation routing under resource constraints. Whether these structural signatures can act as inductive biases for artificial learning is unknown. We initialized sparse multilayer perceptrons with adjacen-cy matrices inferred by mutual information from molecular, structural, functional, and behavioral networks. We compared them with dense networks and density-matched synthetic graphs on four classification benchmarks. Biologically initialized networks outperformed fully connected baselines, most strongly when training data were scarce: with 100 training examples, a gene co-expression template classified handwritten digits with 65% accuracy, versus 11% for a dense network. Ran-domly sparsified, rewired, degree-preserved, scale-free, and small-world graphs of matched densi-ty did not reproduce this low-data advantage or the low trial-to-trial variance of biological templates. The arrangement of connections, not their number, carries a transferable computational prior.

Article.Title: Elementary Dynamics of Neural Microcircuits
Article.Authors: Masserini, S.; Kempter, R.
Article.Abstract: In neural circuits with multiple excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) cell types, qualitatively new dynamics arise when one population is silenced by the others, an effect linear theories cannot capture. Using threshold-linear networks, the simplest nonlinear population model, we derive closed-form conditions for multistability, oscillations, and paradoxical responses across microcircuits. In E-I circuits, strengthening E$\rightarrow$I rather than I$\rightarrow$E connections controls runaway excitation without silencing E cells. In a canonical neocortical circuit, two distinct gamma-oscillation mechanisms reproduce optogenetic silencing experiments, reconciling conflicting models. In hippocampal E-I-I circuits, cross-inhibition determines whether transitions between gamma rhythms are gradual, abrupt, or non-oscillatory. Two E populations or assemblies can cooperate, compete, or suppress each other depending on cross- versus self-excitation. Balanced inhibition prevents competition between E-I assemblies, unless I$\rightarrow$I connections are more assembly-specific than I$\rightarrow$E ones, a condition automatically met by somatostatin-positive interneurons, which lack mutual inhibition. Lateral inhibition yields winner-take-all dynamics even without assemblies. These testable conditions link connectivity to dynamics across brain areas.

Article.Title: Categorical Bayes Filtering for Computational Phenotyping in Adaptive Learning
Article.Authors: Chen, J.; Piray, P.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive learning depends on inferring the sources of uncertainty in the environment. Simultaneous estimation of two such sources, volatility and stochasticity, is difficult, but critical for adaptive learning. The two require opposite adjustments of the learning rate, yet both inflate the variance of experienced outcomes, and no closed-form solution exists for dissociating them. Particle filters are the standard method for this joint inference, but their likelihood is stochastic and their objective is not differentiable, so fitting requires derivative-free methods that add estimator noise. This is a serious problem for individual-difference analyses, because estimator noise attenuates any correlation between fitted parameters and other measures. Here we introduce the Categorical Bayes Filter (CBF), a deterministic alternative. The CBF keeps the conditional structure of recent particle-filter models, but replaces the stochastic outer layer with a categorical distribution over a quantile grid, parameterized by differentiable Beta quantile functions. Fitting is therefore evidence maximization with an exact, deterministic, and differentiable marginal likelihood. In a large-scale study of a volatility-stochasticity task, the CBF outperformed a state-of-the-art particle filter in predicting trial-by-trial empirical learning rates, its dispersion parameters captured volatility-blind and stochasticity-blind participants, and its trial-by-trial ambiguity predicted response times. Fitted CBF parameters also predicted psychiatric symptoms in the direction previously hypothesized. More broadly, the CBF applies to any particle-filter model with continuous latent parameters, and makes individual-level analyses with such models practical in cognitive modeling and computational psychiatry.

Article.Title: Deep sequencing of 3,367 maize genomes uncovers substantial contribution of rare variants to agronomic traits
Article.Authors: Huang L.; Bian C.; Xin B.; Zhang X.; Lu Q.; Yue Y.; Li Y.; Zeng R.; Liu X.; Fan X.; Wang T.; Wang Y.; Cao J.; Zhang J.; Wu J.; Lin Z.; Zhao J.; Cheng W.; Gao S.; Chen Y.; Lu Y.; Yang J.; Liu W.; Chen Z.; Sun H.
Article.Abstract: Rare variants are highly abundant, yet their genome-wide contributions to agronomic traits remain elusive in plants. Here, we performed deep whole-genome sequencing of 3,367 diverse elite maize inbred lines, uncovering 75.3 million variants, of which 79.2% were rare. Overall, we identified 411 independent association signals for 10 agronomic traits, including 359 attributable to globally rare variants, with rare variants showing effect sizes approximately 2.4 times those of common variants. Frequency-stratified genome-based restricted maximum likelihood (GREML) analyses indicated that rare variants captured a substantial proportion of phenotypic variance for traits under strong adaptive selection, consistent with the allele frequencies of trait-associated variants shifting from common in tropical to rare in temperate maize. Complementing conventional variant-level genome-wide association studies (GWAS), gene-based tests identified an additional 94 candidate gene-trait associations. Our study highlights rare variants as important components of the genetic architecture of complex agronomic traits in maize and provides much-needed resources for future functional studies and breeding.

Article.Title: Fatty acid desaturation controls cellular fate decisions between senescence and ferroptosis
Article.Authors: Kuehnemann C.; Jezak S.; Mogck B.; Kura N.; Tariq R.; Che Y.; Vaittinen M.; Siokas I.; Deshpande S.; Guthrie C.; Tan X.; Aimontche E.; Kahn A.; Reifsnyder P.; Lee G.; Majidipur A.; Kung A.; Wang Q.; Jurk D.; Zheng T.; Greenberg A.; Wang X.; Kitazawa K.; Dolnikowski G.; Cheng Y.
Article.Abstract: When subject to damage or stress, cells develop responses in order to maintain tissue homeostasis. Here, we show that senescent cells increase import and membrane levels of multiple polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), but a specific intermediate PUFA, dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3ω-6), is reduced. Exogenous repletion of DGLA instead results in cell death by ferroptosis. Senescent cells manifest additional features associated with ferroptosis, including labile iron and expression of lipoxygenases as well as low-level membrane peroxidation. Oral DGLA supplementation lowers markers of senescence in aged mice and improves age-related functional outcomes. Finally, obese humans with lowered DGLA desaturation rates have lower markers of adipose tissue senescence. Together, our data implicate shifts in PUFA metabolism as a driver of decisions between senescence and ferroptosis.

Article.Title: Subsistence transition preceded population turnover in the eastern Colombian Andes
Article.Authors: Sirak K.; Delgado M.; Triana Vega A.; Rivas S.; Argüello P.; Boada A.; Rivera-Sandoval J.; Peña G.; Langebaek C.; Ospina J.; Archila S.; Torres Orjuela S.; Mejía Cano M.; Rodríguez Saza F.; Barton A.; Callan K.; Curtis E.; Frost T.; Iliev L.; Kearns A.; Kellogg J.; Lawson A.; Qiu L.; Workman J.; Mah M.
Article.Abstract: The Altiplano Cundiboyacense in the eastern Colombian Andes preserves one of the Americas' most continuous archaeological sequences, recording cultural and demographic change. We generated genome-wide data from 212 individuals spanning over 7,000 years, including early-middle and middle Holocene hunter-gatherers, initial late Holocene groups with mixed economies and the earliest isotopic evidence of maize consumption, and increasingly sedentary Herrera and Muisca populations. Two individuals dating ∼2,800 years before present (BP) retain autochthonous ancestry while showing isotopic signatures consistent with maize consumption, decoupling subsistence change from population replacement. The emergence of Herrera culture ∼2,200 BP coincided with a sharp genetic break by ∼2,000 BP, which reflects migration by people descended from admixture ∼4,000 BP between groups with Chibchan- and Amazonian-Andean-related ancestries. Herrera and Muisca Period individuals show north-south genetic substructure paralleling archaeological differentiation.

Article.Title: Convergent genomic evolution of human gut bacteria along an industrialization gradient
Article.Authors: Rühlemann M.; Ma Y.; Szánthó L.; Waschina S.; Moitinho-Silva L.; Mews L.; Faus-Camarena J.; Jebens H.; Costa J.; Juimo V.; Fezeu A.; Agyei A.; Afihene M.; Asibey S.; Awuku Y.; Duah A.; Nartey Y.; Ibrahim F.; Lim Y.; Tan M.; Onyekwere C.; Rusine J.; Mwikarago I.; Baines J.; Franke A.
Article.Abstract: Whether human-associated environments drive adaptive genome evolution in gut commensal bacteria remains largely unknown. Here, we investigate how genomic adaptation in gut bacteria differs between industrialized and non-industrialized human populations. We generated a collection of isolate genomes spanning diverse host geographies, lifestyles, species, and strains. We first found that, compared with metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), paired isolate genomes recover more functional elements and signals of horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Leveraging isolate genomes from multiple species, we find that strains from industrialized hosts experience an expansion of proteome size and harbor greater pangenome fluidity, driven by recent HGT events. Gene- and variant-level analyses reveal convergent patterns of lifestyle-specific adaptation in functions that are critical for ecological adaptation, such as the stress response, cell-envelope remodeling, and central metabolism. Our results demonstrate that industrialization drives convergent genome evolution in gut bacteria, providing a framework for understanding the mechanisms of microbial adaptation to rapidly changing human environments.

Article.Title: Industrialization drives convergent microbiome and host physiological shifts in the human metaorganism
Article.Authors: Poyet M.; Rühlemann M.; Schaan A.; Ma Y.; Moitinho-Silva L.; Wacker E.; Jebens H.; Patel L.; Nguyen L.; Zimmer A.; Plichta D.; McDonald D.; Stevens C.; Agyei A.; Afihene M.; Asibey S.; Awuku Y.; Badiane A.; Corzett C.; Deme A.; Dominguez-Rodrigo M.; Duah A.; Fezeu A.; Froment A.; Gibbons S.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how industrialization reshapes the human metaorganism requires integrating microbiome ecology with host physiology across globally diverse populations. Here, we generate multivariate data from the Global Microbiome Conservancy cohort, including gut microbiome, immunoglobulin A (IgA) sequencing, host genotyping, diet, lifestyle, and fecal biomarker profiles, to investigate host-microbiome interactions across gradients of industrialization and geography. We show that industrialization is associated with homogenized microbial compositions, reduced microbial diversity, and lower community stability, independent of host confounders. We further show that industrialization is linked to elevated markers of gut stress, increased IgA secretion, and altered patterns of IgA-bacteria interactions. Finally, we show that microbiome-based disease predictors trained on industrialized populations are uninformative in less industrialized cohorts, highlighting limited cross-population transferability. Together, our results reveal coordinated restructuring of the microbial ecosystem and host physiology and emphasize the need for inclusive, globally representative data to improve translational microbiome applications across diverse human populations.

Article.Title: TECR palmitoylation triggers a necrotic cell death program driving acute liver injury
Article.Authors: Ru X.; Li X.; Wu Z.; Ren X.; Zong Y.; Cui Y.; Li Y.; Ding Z.; Wang X.; Zhang Z.
Article.Abstract: Acute liver injury caused by drug toxicity or immune activation remains a major clinical challenge with limited mechanistic understanding and few effective therapies. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized form of regulated cell death driven by palmitoylation of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident enzyme trans-2,3-enoyl-coenzyme A (CoA) reductase (TECR). We show that multi-site palmitoylation of TECR, redundantly catalyzed by the palmitoyl acyltransferases ZDHHC5 and ZDHHC2 and dynamically reversed by the depalmitoylase ABHD10, activates PERK-dependent ER stress signaling to trigger cell death. This cell death pathway is a TECR-dependent, palmitoylation-induced, ER stress-mediated necrotic cell death program (TPNCD). TPNCD contributes to liver injury in mouse models of acetaminophen- and concanavalin A-induced hepatotoxicity and is attenuated by hepatocyte-specific TECR ablation or by pharmacological inhibition of palmitoylation or ER stress signaling. Together, these findings establish TPNCD as a distinct, necrotic cell death pathway underlying acute liver injury and highlight new therapeutic entry points for hepatoprotection.

Article.Title: Reconstructing developmental and disease progression with sample-level embeddings
Article.Authors: Jiang L.; Tan Z.; Grabski I.; Hao Y.; Nakatsuka N.; Sarkar S.; Shenoy A.; Satija R.
Article.Abstract: Single-cell genomics is transformative for characterizing cellular heterogeneity, but many biological questions require comparing samples rather than individual cells. Typical analyses compare "case" and "control" groups, ignoring sample-level variation within them. Here, we present scSLIDE (single-cell sample-level inference using density estimation), a framework that transforms each sample's single-cell data into a compact profile describing where its cells are distributed in high-dimensional space. By comparing these density profiles, scSLIDE calculates embeddings to characterize variation across samples. We implement scSLIDE in version 6 of our Seurat package and apply it to COVID-19 infection, Alzheimer's disease, and zebrafish embryogenesis. scSLIDE reveals patient subgroups, reconstructs disease trajectories, and identifies coordinated cellular programs across samples. We discover separable axes of infection and severity, a trajectory of Alzheimer's progression, and embryonic "pseudostages" that vary across and within time points. Our results demonstrate how case-control analyses collapse rich biological variation into binary labels and how sample-level embedding represents a powerful analytical alternative.

Article.Title: COP1 is a temperature-responsive switch in Arabidopsis
Article.Authors: Zeng W.; Lamelas L.; Scaramozzino D.; Chen Z.; Rappsilber J.; Xue S.; Jaeger K.; Orellana L.; Sampathkumar A.; Wigge P.
Article.Abstract: Temperature is molecular motion, but how living systems sense this is poorly understood. Many responses in plants integrate light and temperature signals, for example, via light receptors and the circadian clock. CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENESIS 1 (COP1) regulates light signaling and is necessary for responding to temperature. We show that COP1 acts as a temperature-dependent switch, becoming activated by a warm temperature-induced conformational change. An intramolecular Val-Pro (VP) motif binds to the active site of COP1 at low temperatures, preventing substrate docking. At warmer temperatures, the VP motif becomes detached, enabling client proteins to bind and be degraded. This discovery explains how plants are able to obtain a precise readout of temperature within a given climate range. Altering the binding of the VP motif is sufficient to adjust the temperature range within which the plant responds. This helps us understand how plants are able to adapt to different climates.

Article.Title: The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through pathways impaired early in Alzheimer’s disease models
Article.Authors: Zhou H.; Maynard J.; Pennacchio A.; Apolonio A.; Liu X.; Yao L.; Negahban M.; Zhang Z.; Ding B.; Oberhauser J.; Wen X.; Yang M.; Huang F.; Chayama Y.; Doddipalli S.; Bernardi M.; Domke L.; Lo I.; Simms J.; Pan A.; Du S.; To N.; Wong P.; Duong D.; Fox E.

This cell-type tropism relies on a BBB-parenchyma receptor hand-off: APOA1 crosses the BBB via SR-B1 and engages astrocytic ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), a key Alzheimer's risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity. These findings recast the BBB as a selective interface that recruits neuroprotective circulatory proteins for brain health.

Article.Authors: Xie Y.; Chang L.; Zhong G.; Rink J.; Báez-Becerra C.; Armand E.; Ding W.; Li K.; Bonne E.; Indralingam H.; Lie A.; Dong K.; Loe T.; Huang B.; Wang Z.; Barcoma A.; Willier J.; Knutson K.; Liu J.; Cho S.; Cao S.; Russo K.; Young C.; Arzavala J.; Sanchez Y.

Article.Authors: Chang L.; Li K.; Xie Y.; Zhong G.; Rink J.; Báez-Becerra C.; Lie A.; Indralingam H.; Loe T.; Dong K.; Gao X.; Wang Z.; Zu S.; Kern J.; Zhao Z.; Boone E.; Flores J.; Monell A.; Olness J.; Barragan C.; Osgood E.; Owens W.; Schenker-Ahmed N.; Zhang W.; Liu D.

This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis-regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. Article.Title: Single-cell, multi-region profiling of the macaque brain across the lifespan
Article.Authors: Yang W.; Watkins K.; DeCasien A.; O’Neill M.; Bohlen M.; O’Day D.; Smith E.; Duran M.; Qiu C.; Meleshko A.; Vo A.; Menke M.; Calderon D.; Sallet J.; Higham J.; Martínez M.; Trapnell C.; Starita L.; Montague M.; Platt M.; Chiou K.; Shendure J.; Snyder-Mackler N.
Article.Abstract: Brain aging is a complex process with profound health and societal consequences. Article.Title: Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities

Article.Title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes
Article.Authors: Fu Y.; Kempynck N.; Ding W.; Turner M.; Garcia A.; Schmitz M.; Close J.; Kapen I.; Hewitt M.; Seeman S.; Long B.; Ding S.; Ho W.; Mahoney J.; Mich J.; Levi B.; Klein A.; Behrens M.; Ecker J.; Aerts S.; Johansen N.; Hodge R.; Lein E.; Bakken T.
Article.Abstract: Astrocytes shape synapses and circuits, yet their diversity within the human basal ganglia remains poorly defined. Integrating single-nucleus transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with spatial transcriptomics, we identify three anatomically organized astrocyte subgroups-striatal gray matter (GM), extra-striatal GM, and white matter (WM)-distinguished by neurotransmitter transporter expression and synapse-associated programs that reflect afferent input.
