Article.Title: Spatial and regulatory organization of cell identity across the primate subcortex
Article.Authors: Dan S.; Turner M.; DeBerardine M.; Caceres L.; Nieto-Caballero V.; Schembri J.; Levandowski K.; Cardenas C.; Wang N.; Li C.; Basu S.; Zheng H.; Liu X.; Höllt T.; Feliciano J.; Zhang Q.; Nakamoto R.; McMillen D.; Martin N.; Cuevas N.; Olsen P.; Nagra J.; Campos J.; VanNess M.; Waters J.

Article.Title: Deploying liquid intelligence in cancer: Finding answers in our blood
Article.Authors: George J.; Wielenga A.; Iyer M.; Chinnaiyan A.
Article.Abstract: Liquid biopsies are one of the few noninvasive procedures for probing disease at the molecular level. They represent a scalable solution to cancer detection and monitoring by capturing tumor-derived signals from circulating biomolecules such as proteins, DNA, RNA, and metabolites. However, these signals are often sparse, heterogeneous, and shaped by genetics, demographics, and comorbidities. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, especially with multimodal foundation models, have proven capable of extracting signals from noisy, high-dimensional data. Pretraining on large cohorts and integrating complementary modalities may improve sensitivity for tumor signals in blood, though significant clinical and infrastructural barriers remain. This review synthesizes advances in liquid biopsy technologies and artificial intelligence and examines how their convergence can enable enhanced cancer monitoring.

Article.Title: Mesoscale molecular architecture of the striatum across cell types and adult aging
Article.Authors: Kraft A.; Lee M.; Gao H.; Mohsin A.; Rayan N.; Lawler A.; Kim G.; Milidantri J.; Vanderburg C.; Balderrama K.; Nadaf N.; Kumar V.; Flowers K.; Finn E.; Shabet M.; Muratoglu E.; Yoo O.; Shakir K.; Nemesh J.; Burger S.; Drouin S.; Catalini O.; Raj M.; Budnik N.; Reese L.
Article.Abstract: The human striatum governs diverse motor, cognitive, and affective behaviors yet lacks the obvious cytoarchitectural boundaries defining functional territories elsewhere in the brain. Using Slide-tags single-nucleus spatial transcriptomics, we profiled 1.1 million cells across 19 postmortem donors to uncover the striatum's spatial organization. These data revealed a consistent subdivision of the striatum into six zones, each defined by molecularly distinct populations of spiny projection neurons (SPNs) and featuring spatially coordinated neuron-astrocyte interaction networks. To determine their structural relevance, we generated a companion mouse spatial atlas that identified four homologous zones that aligned with territories defined by brain-wide afferent projections. Finally, imputing zonal identities onto a 131-donor single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cohort revealed that dorsal zones exhibit the greatest age-related transcriptional change and that the expression differences defining zonation attenuate with age. This resource establishes a conserved mesoscale spatial framework for the mammalian striatum, linking single-cell molecular identity to structural connectomics and aging.

Article.Title: Toward an integrated framework for a human and mammalian brain cell atlas
Article.Authors: Garcia A.; Uematsu A.; Watanabe A.; Watson A.; Monell A.; Ropelewski A.; Nolan A.; Klein A.; Rivera A.; Tolias A.; Bandrowski A.; Bartlett A.; Byrd A.; Kovalsky A.; Mahurkar A.; Kriegstein A.; Awdeh A.; Bhandiwad A.; Macdonald A.; Dichter B.; Ren B.; Huo B.; Lelieveldt B.; Kalmbach B.; Herb B.
Article.Abstract: The NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is developing a standardized, integrated reference framework for classifying and studying brain cell types across human, macaque, marmoset, and mouse. We present a cross-species, multimodal atlas of the basal ganglia, a group of subcortical nuclei central to motor control, adaptive behavior, and neurological disease. Built from large-scale single-cell transcriptomic classification and integrated with epigenomic, spatial genomic, multiomic, and developmental datasets, the atlas provides a curated, data-driven taxonomy with standardized nomenclature, extensive phenotypic characterization, and community-informed annotation. Cell types are mapped into species-specific anatomical reference frameworks and linked across species through structural ontologies. Realizing this resource required coordinated standards for tissue acquisition and processing, harmonized donor metadata, anatomical registration, sequencing pipelines, data infrastructure, visualization, mapping tools, and interoperable metadata. The BICAN basal ganglia atlas demonstrates how pipelines and standards can be implemented, validated, and scaled toward a whole-brain human and mammalian cell-type reference.

Article.Title: Harmonized brain ontology and 3D atlases for human, macaque, and marmoset basal ganglia
Article.Authors: Ding S.; Bhandiwad A.; Rosen B.; Seeman S.; Long B.; Johansen N.; Bayindir U.; Facer B.; Fu Y.; Halimi Y.; Hou Y.; Hu D.; Huang M.; Ikeda T.; Lesnar P.; Liu X.; Luo Z.; Ray P.; Royall J.; Schmitz M.; Uematsu A.; Vezoli J.; Yazdani F.; Bakken T.; Freiwald W.
Article.Abstract: A major goal of the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is to create a suite of foundational reference cell atlases and associated standards for human and nonhuman primate brains. Central to this goal is the creation of cross-species-harmonized cellular taxonomies and structural parcellations with formal ontologies that can be mapped onto 3D reference frameworks, bridging neuroimaging and cellular and histological resolutions. We describe an iterative approach, focused initially on the basal ganglia, to co-create structural and cellular ontologies for human, macaque, and marmoset brains and to map and refine structural parcellations into neuroimaging-based common coordinate frameworks. We create a Harmonized Ontology of Mammalian Brain Anatomy (HOMBA) to meet these needs. These references provide the framework for documenting and mapping all experimental sampling in BICAN, allowing analyses of cellular and molecular variation as a function of topographic position and enabling comparisons of cellular, molecular, and neuroimaging-based functional variation across species.

Article.Title: Sub-second dopamine reinforcement shapes juvenile social play
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Tao X.; Zhong Z.; Zhu F.; Zhang Y.; Wang Y.; Wang M.; Li Y.; Sun L.; Ouyang Y.; Ding Z.; An M.; Zhao Y.; Zhou J.; Zhang R.; Xiong W.; Ji N.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Juvenile social play is critical for neurodevelopment, yet the neural mechanisms organizing moment-to-moment interactions remain elusive. Using social behavior sequencing (Social-seq)-an occlusion-robust 3D pose estimation and unsupervised clustering pipeline-we found that nucleus accumbens (NAc) dopamine was tightly coupled to sub-second social syllables during naturalistic interactions. In wild-type juveniles, males exhibited a sharper dopaminergic contrast between proactive play and forced submission than females did, consistent with sex-divergent play strategies. In Shank3-deficient autism models, this process was fundamentally corrupted: proactive play-evoked dopamine responses were abolished in males and significantly sign-inverted in females, with male-specific enhancements during non-social behaviors, driving social play deficits. A multi-agent reinforcement learning model parameterized by disrupted, play-related dopaminergic reinforcement values recapitulated mutant phenotypes. Closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of ventral tegmental area (VTA)-NAc dopamine projections, time-locked to proactive play, restored reciprocal play in Shank3-deficient rats. Sub-second dopaminergic reinforcement thus orchestrates naturalistic social behavior, providing a behaviorally contingent interventional framework for neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
Article.Authors: Guo X.; Huang J.; Zhao J.; Gan Y.; Liu X.; Chen L.; Song T.; Wu W.; Li Y.; Lin J.; Bao J.; Nie G.; Tang Y.; Chen M.; Xu J.; Dun J.; Wang L.; Huang J.; Mao Y.; Yang X.; Ding Y.; Wang E.; Wan L.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: RNA-derived 2',3'-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes1-3, but how plants perceive them remains unknown. Sucking insects inject digestive enzymes including RNases into the host plant to acquire nutrients. Here we demonstrate that NIB1, a glycine-rich RNA-binding protein in rice, senses 2',3'-cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2',3'-cNMPs; 2',3'-cAMP and 2',3'-cGMP) and adenylyl-(3'→5')-guanosine 2',3'-cyclic phosphate (ApG>p) produced by a salivary T2 ribonuclease of green stink bug during feeding. Binding of the RNase products promotes formation of nuclear condensates containing NIB1, which recruit the core immune regulator Enhanced Disease Susceptibility 1 (EDS1) and activate defence, potentially contributing to the immune signalling of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) proteins that also produce the nuclease products. Exogenous application of 2',3'-cAMP, 2',3'-cGMP or ApG>p elicits NIB1 and EDS1-mediated immune responses. Our findings unveil a conserved pathway in plants, in which glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins perceive the nuclease-generated second messengers to launch defence and point to a potential link between plant TIR nuclease activity and EDS1 signalling.

Article.Title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
Article.Authors: Luo J.; Yang J.; Tien J.; Wang M.; Das S.; Wang X.; Young E.; Tošović J.; Mannan R.; Xiang W.; Jiang X.; Cai J.; Liu Y.; Gu K.; Mahapatra S.; Li S.; Yin Y.; Eyunni S.; Todd A.; Jin S.; Cao X.; Su F.; Miner S.; Sudharshan R.; Rao A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Transcriptional addiction to the androgen receptor (AR) underlies metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer 1 , in which AR maintains oncogenic programs through domain-specific interactions with the acetyltransferases p300 and CBP (collectively p300/CBP) 2 . Here we describe a novel therapeutic modality, domain-alteration chimeras (DALTACs), that rewire endogenous protein complexes by enforcing non-native domain–domain interactions. Our first-in-class AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 induces synthetic proximity between the ligand-binding domain of AR and the bromodomain of p300/CBP, misconfiguring their native interface and locking the complex in a non-productive state. DALTAC-1 triggers a ‘super-inhibitory’ effect, suppressing AR-driven transcription and proliferation more potently than combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition. Mechanistically, DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate engagement, abolishing the histone mark H2B N-terminal acetylation and inducing neomorphic acetylation of AR and coactivators, ultimately collapsing the AR neo-enhanceosome. Chromatin profiling revealed redistribution of AR and p300/CBP towards palindromic androgen response elements, accompanied by disruption of cofactor and transcriptional machinery recruitment at oncogenic AR and ERG neo-enhancers. DALTAC-1 exhibits exquisite lineage selectivity, displaying potent activity in AR–p300/CBP dual-dependent cells and sparing AR-negative cells. In multiple in vivo models, DALTAC-1 induces deep and durable tumour regressions. Together, these findings establish DALTACs as a broadly applicable strategy to rewire disease-defining complexes through domain-topology alteration, expanding induced-proximity therapies, and the precise lineage selectivity of DALTAC-1 supports its translational potential in AR-driven prostate cancer.

Article.Title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*
Article.Authors: Lai S.; Thyagarajan N.; Wong O.; Diakogiannis F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A new epoch for direct visualization of accretion dynamics near the event horizon of a black hole began when the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration synthesized an Earth-sized aperture with millimetre radio interferometry and published the first reconstructed image 1–4 of a black hole shadow at the core of radio galaxy Messier 87 (M87). The image appeared as a ring-like structure, representing the gravitationally lensed and redshifted emission around the central supermassive black hole, M87*, located at the galactic nucleus. However, application of various data analysis and imaging heuristics resulted in divergent representations of M87* fine-scale features 3,5–7 , with some external analyses even challenging the fundamental ring-like morphology of the source 8,9 . Such difficulties arise as a consequence of the inherent sparsity of the very long baseline interferometry measurements, making interferometric image reconstruction an inadequately constrained problem. Moreover, the solution is sensitive to instrument calibration, post-processing algorithms and imaging hyperparameters. Here we apply an independent imaging algorithm that we have developed to the M87* dataset that is free from prescriptive morphological priors and founded on observables immune to instrument calibration errors. We reconstruct the black hole shadow image and unequivocally reproduce a ring-like morphology, with an angular diameter of 42.2 ± 1.5 μas corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of approximately 20° from the approaching jet.

Article.Title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
Article.Authors: Donaldson G.; Lima dos Reis G.; Saad M.; Wichmann C.; Mamede I.; Chen G.; Harrer C.; DelGaudio N.; Zhang D.; Aydin B.; Castro T.; Grivennikov S.; Reis B.; Liu E.; Eisenbarth S.; Birsoy K.; Tavazoie S.; Stadtmueller B.; Victora G.; Mucida D.
Article.Abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4-8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. Article.Authors: Yu M.; Heidari M.; Palacio-Rodriguez K.; Ruan H.; Mingu S.; Chen Y.; Gou X.; Shen P.; Liu S.; Chen S.; Hidayat A.; Bode M.; Sikora M.; Tang A.; Hummer G.; Lemke E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The nuclear pore complex (NPC) regulates molecular traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm 1,2 . Its permeability barrier is formed by intrinsically disordered phenylalanine-glycine-rich nucleoporins (FG-NUPs), whose physical state has long been debated 3–13 . Deciphering how FG-NUPs behave inside living cells is crucial for understanding how NPCs achieve both selective and rapid transport. Experiments and molecular-dynamics simulations further show that importin-β, a principal nuclear transport receptor, and O-linked β- N -acetylglucosamine, a key post-translational modification of FG-NUPs, together stabilize the dynamic FG network. Finely balanced FG–FG and FG–importin-β interactions maintain FG-NUP liquidity and generate a radial organization in which importin-β is enriched near the NPC periphery and extended FG domains remain in the central channel, forming the transport barrier. This organization explains recent MINFLUX observations 14 of rim-biased transport trajectories and is supported here by direct MINFLUX imaging of importin-β in mammalian cells. Article.Title: Bureaucratic incentives shaped effectiveness of the one-child policy in China
Article.Authors: Meng L.; Yang H.; Miller G.; Li H.
Article.Abstract: Empirical research so far largely suggests that population policies around the world do not explain a majority of the global fertility decline1-10. Notably, even China's total fertility rate declined little after implementation of the one-child policy in 1979 and 1980, but fertility then fell sharply by more than one-third during the early 1990s. Here we show that strengthening bureaucratic incentives under China's one vote veto policy, which strictly prohibited career advancement for adherence failure, was instrumental in more effective implementation of the one-child policy, and in its delayed impact on fertility. Using provincial variation in implementation timing, we find that the one vote veto explains nearly half of China's total fertility rate decline during the 1990s, driving fertility below the replacement rate. Increases in use of intrauterine devices (the most prevalent form of modern contraception in China) that were recommended by local officials were particularly salient. Overall, our findings suggest that population policy, when more strictly enforced due to stronger bureaucratic incentives, made a greater contribution to low fertility in China than suggested by past research.

Article.Title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
Article.Authors: Watson C.; Poon G.; MacGregor H.; Fonseca A.; Apostolidou S.; Damaskou A.; Boniface C.; Hackett S.; Gentry-Maharaj A.; Menon U.; Blundell J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers 1,2 . However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples 3 , collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism.

Mechanistically, we identify Panx1 as an NRF2-regulated gene that promotes NLRP3 activity. Moreover, alveolar macrophages from patients with pulmonary fibrosis displayed reduced NRF2 activity. Finally, NRF2 was required for antitumour immunity induced by cancer vaccines consisting of NLRP3 agonistic adjuvants. Article.Authors: Song A.; Wang Y.; Wang G.; Bae M.; Wang Z.; Gao G.; Wu Z.; Lu G.; Meng J.; Yu J.; Park S.; Garcia-Ocaña A.; Fueger P.; Rao L.; Frontini A.; Liu Y.; Jiang L.; Zhu Y.; Wang Q.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity 1–5 . Article.Authors: Pillet M.; Maitner B.; Arakaki M.; Araujo D.; Baker M.; Barrios D.; Boyle B.; Breshears D.; Feng X.; Goettsch B.; Guerrero P.; Hernández-Hernández T.; Majure L.; Meriño B.; Nikolopoulos E.; Puente-Martínez R.; Roehrdanz P.; Serra-Diaz J.; Urban M.; Merow C.; Enquist B.
Article.Abstract: Extreme climatic events are increasing in frequency and intensity with climate change1. Their effects on species' distributions and extinction risk remain poorly understood2-9. With severe drought, restricting dispersal from 100 to 0 km increased the share losing suitable area from 69-72% to 84-85% across SSPs. These declines reduced regional richness, with five bioregions potentially losing over 25% of species. Article.Authors: Xie H.; Dong C.; Li P.; Ge R.; Wilde S.; Liu S.; Liu D.; Wan Y.
Article.Abstract: The scarcity of terrestrial rocks older than 3.9 billion years (Gyr) has hindered our understanding of Earth's early evolution, fuelling persistent debates on how and when the first continental crust formed and plate tectonics started. Article.Authors: Both C.; Chen A.; Gao T.; Mooij N.; Charara M.; Wadhwa J.; Portela C.; Barabási A.
Article.Abstract: Materials, at their essence, are networks defined by homogeneity: uniform bonds, fixed thicknesses and discrete length scales. Governed by only two parameters, scale-rich networks span orders of magnitude in structural features, overcoming previous constraints in metamaterial design. This network-based framework establishes a minimal and universal model for engineering multifunctional materials whose mechanical behaviour emerges directly from scale diversity, and also opens avenues of enquiry for network science itself.

Here we show an all-day-wearable AR glass prototype based on spatially varying, interwoven metasurfaces that provide several grating vectors for multidirectional light control. The resulting dual-layer metasurface-based waveguide (meta-WG) achieves a 30° FoV and an 8 × 8-mm2 two-dimensional (2D) eyebox while maintaining an average luminance efficiency of 1,938 nits lm-1 (up to 4,225 nits lm-1) within a 1.5-mm-thick form factor. The prototype produces bright and stable virtual images under outdoor ambient illumination, demonstrating the compatibility of meta-WGs with practical wearable display requirements. By expanding the degrees of freedom for light routing beyond conventional diffractive WGs, our approach provides a scalable framework for balancing efficiency, viewing range and form factor, bringing high-performance AR glasses closer to practical consumer applications.

Article.Title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
Article.Authors: Polo Rivera C.; Roske J.; Hands E.; Fassetta F.; Sale J.; Yeeles J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase 1,2 . Failure to efficiently restart and/or protect stalled replication forks is a major source of genomic instability 3–6 . Stalled forks can be restarted by a variety of mechanisms, including repriming downstream of the impediment 4 . In human cells, the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL promotes fork progression during replication stress 7–10 , but how its activity is coordinated by the replisome is unresolved. Here, by reconstituting replication fork stalling and restart with purified human proteins, we show that the CMG helicase directs PRIMPOL for efficient replication fork restart. Unexpectedly, the interaction between PRIMPOL and replication protein A 9,11 is not critical for fork restart in this system. We show that PRIMPOL binds directly to CMG, and a cryo-electron microscopy structure illustrates how this targets PRIMPOL specifically for leading-strand priming to minimize the size of post-replicative gaps. Ablating the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction abolishes fork restart in vitro and PRIMPOL-dependent DNA damage tolerance in human cells. Our work establishes PRIMPOL as an integrated component of the human replisome dedicated to leading-strand priming.

Article.Title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
Article.Authors: de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz M.; Desbiez A.; Alves M.; Calabrese J.; Cumerlato A.; Jacoby F.; Grechi N.; Kluyber D.; Lin E.; Milazzotto M.; Soresini G.; Medici E.; Mastromonaco G.; Noonan M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Plastic pollution is a defining feature of the Anthropocene 1 , and microplastics are dispersed by air and water into even remote terrestrial habitats 2–7 , yet the ecological and landscape-level processes that shape microplastic accumulation in terrestrial ecosystems remain poorly understood. Human land-use change is rapidly transforming landscapes worldwide, but the influence of this expanding human footprint on the microplastic burdens in wildlife remains largely unknown. This knowledge gap is particularly pressing in regions that are facing escalating environmental pressures, such as Brazil. Here we pair in vivo microplastic measurements with high-resolution tracking data from lowland tapirs and giant anteaters across Brazil and show that the microplastic burdens carried by free-ranging mammals increase with both the magnitude of their human footprint exposure and their proximity to development and waste management infrastructure. Microplastics were also detected in the blood of individuals occupying seemingly pristine habitats far from development, suggesting that direct exposure to human-modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic microplastic burdens. In a period of accelerating global land-use change, these findings reveal how individual habitat use and anthropogenic land-use change interact to shape wildlife exposure to microplastics and suggest that managing animals’ proximity to development and waste management infrastructure may reduce the microplastic burdens carried by terrestrial wildlife.

Article.Title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts
Article.Authors: Pan A.; Yang S.; Ramos R.; Li X.; Xie J.; Eckel R.; Mingrone G.; Blanch J.; Jiang J.; Liu H.; Chen S.; Geng T.; Wu S.; Ravussin E.; Fernández-Real J.; Rubino F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract In 2025, a Lancet Commission proposed distinguishing clinical obesity, defined by adiposity-related organ dysfunction, from preclinical obesity, defined by excess adiposity with preserved function, and recommended using anthropometric measures beyond body mass index (BMI) to confirm obesity status 1 . Here we report the comparative performance of this framework versus conventional BMI-based classification using prevalence, incidence and mortality data from 844,108 adults across four cohorts in China, the UK, the USA and Spain. Complementing BMI with waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio data showed that BMI alone overestimated obesity in 1.2–3.1% and underestimated it in 5.2–8.6% of participants across cohorts. The combined anthropometric definition increased overall obesity prevalence by 3.3–7.4% relative to BMI-based classification. Clinical obesity accounted for 22.7–31.3% of total obesity, with an overall population prevalence of 5.6–10.9%. A large proportion of individuals (between 77.4% and 91.3%) with preclinical obesity at baseline showed no progression to clinical obesity over 10 years. Increased mortality risk was associated with the combined anthropometric definition of obesity, but not with BMI-only obesity. Clinical obesity was associated with substantially higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.69, 95% confidence interval 1.64–1.73), whereas preclinical obesity conferred only modest risk (1.19, 1.14–1.24). These findings support the global adoption of the Lancet Commission diagnostic framework to improve obesity care and policy.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial protein import defects enhance tumour immunogenicity
Article.Authors: Jackson T.; Palozzi J.; McGann C.; Vitale T.; Choa R.; Nguyen H.; Paulo J.; Latorre-Muro P.; Van Vranken J.; Ravichandran M.; Zhang B.; Yadav M.; Gygi S.; Puigserver P.
Article.Abstract: Tumour cells evade detection and elimination by the immune system through a suite of adaptations1, including the repression of antigen presentation, which is required for the recognition of tumour cells by CD8+ T cells. Mitochondria have emerged as targets for enhancing antitumour immunity; however, the extensive mitochondrial proteome has remained largely unstudied for its ability to modulate immune responses. Here we show that defects in the mitochondrial protein import machinery promote tumour immunogenicity and synergize with immune checkpoint blockade treatment in melanoma models. Mitochondrial protein import perturbation, specifically through depletion of the TIM23 import complex subunit TIMM50, enhances tumour immunogenicity through a pathway involving mitochondrial DNA escape, cGAS-STING pathway activation and interferon-β (IFNβ) secretion. Secreted IFNβ signals through the type I IFN receptor to activate the JAK-STAT pathway, resulting in increased antigen presentation on MHC class I complexes. Mitochondrial DNA escape in Timm50-depleted cells is linked to the formation of mitochondrial-derived vesicles. Depletion of SNX9 and RAB9, involved in mitochondrial-derived vesicle formation2, suppresses mitochondrial DNA-dependent type I IFN production and signalling. By disrupting mitochondrial proteostasis and membrane architecture, defective protein import in Timm50-depleted cells drives the immune phenotype. This study shows that mitochondrial protein import inhibition causes tumour immunogenicity, including sensitization to immune checkpoint blockade, by promoting mitochondrial DNA escape and IFNβ-driven MHC class I antigen presentation.

Article.Title: Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics
Article.Authors: Yang N.; Zhang J.; Lu Y.; Wang Z.; Chang Y.; Zheng F.; Yang Z.; Li L.; Chou A.; Yang Z.; Liu H.; Huang L.; Li C.; Yao C.; Yang P.; Li W.; Meng W.; Li M.; Cheng C.; Ki D.; Chiu Y.; Ang K.; Liang G.; Wan Y.; Ang Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Aggressive scaling in silicon electronics—although essential for improving power, performance, area and cost—faces increasing challenges in further reducing power consumption due to electrostatic and leakage constraints 1,2 . Achieving efficient operation at low supply voltages therefore requires new materials and gate-stack engineering strategies. Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors offer intrinsic advantages because their atomic thickness affords excellent gate control, and their sizable bandgaps suppress off-state current. However, a major obstacle is the imperfect interface between 2D channels and gate dielectrics, which degrades subthreshold swing, hysteresis and bias-temperature instability 3 . Here we demonstrate that a wafer-scale, transferable, single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric can be van der Waals integrated with 2D transition metal dichalcogenides. The obtained pristine 2D-dielectric interface enables subthreshold swing close to the thermal limit, record-low hysteresis and well-matched transfer characteristics for both n- and p-type enhancement-mode field-effect transistors. Building on this, we demonstrate complementary field-effect transistors, whose inverters achieve high voltage gain and large noise margins with subpicowatt static power consumption. These results highlight the promise of 2D semiconductors for ultra-low-power operation.

Article.Title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Tan J.; Neba E.; Morival S.; Frankowski K.; Daval B.; Viola I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource 1 . However, the highly unsteady sea environment subjects turbines to severe hydrodynamic loads, greatly increasing capital and maintenance costs 2,3 . Large-scale state-of-the-art turbines at present rely on complex, expensive active pitch systems to mitigate these fluctuations. Here we present a reliable, passive alternative: flexible rubber blades featuring chordwise trailing-edge deformation. We experimentally demonstrate that these flexible blades achieve an equivalent total energy yield over simulated tidal cycles compared with rigid blades with active pitch control, while mitigating high-frequency fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third. This passive load regulation arises from aeroelastic deformation that flattens blade camber under load, enabling structural robustness without added mechanical complexity. These findings suggest that chordwise-flexible blades can enhance the durability and performance of tidal turbines, offering a promising pathway towards more reliable and cost-effective tidal energy generation.

Article.Title: In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering
Article.Authors: Mizoguchi T.; DeNizio J.; Chadwick A.; Mazzola A.; Brown M.; Mishra S.; Damle M.; Matsumoto Y.; Neang V.; Garrity R.; Mantri M.; Olorife J.; Hsu H.; Peshdary V.; Shabani E.; Ganey J.; Santos R.; Federico A.; Garcia S.; Hao P.; Wu Y.; Glass Z.; Kasiewicz L.; Summers C.; Sanjeev A.
Article.Abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease1. Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model2,3. Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor-encapsulated within a GalNAc-lipid nanoparticle-leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

Article.Title: Opportunistically Detecting Signs of Hypertension on a Consumer Smartwatch
Article.Authors: Di Achille P.; Cai L.; Wu J.; Gao M.; Daryani B.; Wang J.; Khanna U.; Ko H.; Pathak A.; Malhotra M.; Patel S.; Shreibati J.; Juraschek S.; Rudrapatna P.; Thompson M.; Poh M.
Article.Abstract: Hypertension is a silent killer, with over half of affected adults unaware of their condition1,2. This lack of awareness is a major concern, as early intervention is critical for preventing major adverse cardiovascular events3,4. Here we show that applying artificial intelligence (AI) to multimodal waveforms (photoplethysmography and accelerometry) recorded using a widely available consumer smartwatch (AI-PPG-ACC-HTN), without any cuff calibration, can detect hypertension with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed blood pressure (BP) devices in the existing clinical framework. We validated AI-PPG-ACC-HTN in a prospective, multicenter study of 196 diverse participants free from known cardiovascular disease and antihypertensive medication against gold-standard 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring. Over seven days of real-world monitoring, AI-PPG-ACC-HTN detected hypertension with a sensitivity of 65.8% (95% CI, 54.0%-76.3%), specificity of 90.0% (95% CI, 83.2%-94.7%), and positive predictive value (PPV) of 80.6% (95% CI, 68.6%-89.6%). In comparison, initial office BP screening achieved a sensitivity of 55.3% (95% CI, 43.4%-66.7%), specificity of 90.0% (95% CI, 83.2%-94.7%) and PPV of 77.8% (95% CI, 64.4%-88.0%). These results highlight an opportunity for consumer smartwatches to facilitate population-level opportunistic hypertension screening by prompting at-risk individuals toward clinical assessment and confirmatory diagnosis using established cuff-based methodologies, offering an accessible tool to address this major public health challenge.

Article.Title: Hydrogen Derivatives Enable Cost-Effective Carbon Neutrality in China
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Guo X.; Yang X.; Li J.; McElroy M.
Article.Abstract: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change recommended 1.5°C carbon reduction target, requiring powerful enforcement from major economies. China, the largest CO2 emitter, is facing severe difficulties for both variable renewable accommodation and decarbonization of hard-to-abate sectors. Hydrogen, as a critical green energy carrier bridging renewable to end-users, faces significant obstacles in real-world deployment such as costly transportation, storage and fuel-cell adoption. Affordable and coordinated hydrogen deployment plan to accelerate the carbon-neutral transition remains ambiguous. Here, we present cost-effective carbon-neutral transition pathways for entire energy economy of China emphasizing the significant role of hydrogen and derivatives as green energy carriers, considering high-resolution renewable deployments, hourly power system operations in 29 provincial regions, over 46,000 rail/road/marine/pipeline transfer routing of hydrogen derivatives, process-level fuel adoption strategies in all end-use sectors. Results show that incorporating hydrogen and derivatives can reduce the overall transition cost by $ 10.7 trillion compared with renewable and electrification pathways, achieving negative carbon abatement costs ($-6.15/ton), eliminating external oil import expenses, equivalent to over 50% of China trade surplus (2023 level)1, significantly boosting employment and economic growth. Hydrogen derivative based transition pathway offers a vital direction for affordable and secure decarbonization for China and beyond under volatile international energy markets.

Article.Title: Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting
Article.Authors: Darbha S.; Khudorozhkov A.; L. S. Lopes P.; Liu F.; Rrapaj E.; Balewski J.; Hamdan M.; Dolgirev P.; Schuckert A.; Klymko K.; Wang S.; Lukin M.; Camps D.; Kornjača M.
Article.Abstract: The dynamics of isolated quantum systems following a sudden quench has a central role in many areas of material science, high-energy physics and quantum chemistry1-4. Such far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics-which features complex phenomena with implications for thermalization, non-equilibrium phase transitions and Floquet phase engineering5-8-is challenging to study numerically, in particular, in high-dimensional systems9,10. Here we use a programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator11 to systematically explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits. By initializing the system in a product state and performing quenches across a broad parameter space, we discover several stable, qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes. We trace their robustness to Floquet-like prethermal steady states8 that are stabilized over exponentially long emergent timescales by strong dynamical constraints. We further observe sharp peaks in the dynamical response that are quantitatively explained by the structured melting of prethermalization through resonances. In two dimensions, we uncover a prethermally driven, first-order dynamical phase transition linked to the proliferation of Néel-order defects6,12, and probe it quantitatively using a generalized Clausius-Clapeyron test. Together, these results establish a programmable route to high-energy prethermal phase structure: long-lived dynamical phases, their resonant breakdown and a first-order dynamical phase transition that is not inherited from the equilibrium phase boundaries.

Article.Title: Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise
Article.Authors: Kuhlisch C.; Soffer E.; Raina J.; Tadmor G.; Nir-Zadock T.; Barak-Gavish N.; Schleyer G.; Joffe N.; Nussbaum I.; Clerc E.; Stocker R.; Schatz D.; Zeevi D.; Vardi A.
Article.Abstract: Algal bloom demise, often caused by viruses, is a major driver of carbon cycling in the surface ocean1,2. However, although blooms collapse synchronously, fewer than 30% of algal cells are actively infected by viruses3, indicating the involvement of additional mortality agents. Here we quantified tripartite interactions within a synthetic community composed of the abundant coccolithophore Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, bacteria and viruses isolated during a bloom. We found that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-induced algal mortality in G. huxleyi as well as in three other globally widespread microalgae. We quantified this interaction using two new metrics: the synergy index, which measures viral-bacterial interaction strength, and the benefit index, which assesses changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral-bacterial co-infection, with consistently high synergy index and benefit index. We found that during algal blooms, Alteromonas displayed high chemoattraction towards infected cell extracts, accumulated in aggregates derived from bloom demise, and increased in abundance during oceanic bloom collapse. Viral-bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent that controls bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, which influence global carbon cycling4-6.

Article.Title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
Article.Authors: Iravedra-García J.; Guthman E.; Tsin D.; Cherepanova P.; Cuturela L.; Ocasio-Arce E.; Pillow J.; Falkner A.
Article.Abstract: The ability to observe the social behaviour of others and use observed information to bias future action is a fundamental building block of social cognition1-3. Aggression observation activates hypothalamic neurons relevant for aggression control4,5, but whether observation and experience engage common circuit mechanisms that promote a new shared behavioural policy is unclear. Here we develop a strategy to perform large-scale cell-type-specific recordings across subcortical networks for social behaviour generation and learning. We record longitudinally while animals train through direct aggression experience or observation, then probe shared differences in behaviour and neural activity in a novel aggression context. After training, we detect unique signatures of a shared adaptive behavioural strategy that is absent in animals without training. During aggression observation, observed behaviour recruits widespread activation across subcortical networks for behavioural generation and mimics activity evoked by experienced behaviour, and shared neural changes persist into the novel aggression context. Multiregion modelling reveals shared changes to a core aggression network across both experience and observation, including a widespread reduction in inhibition, which we find is necessary for adaptive behavioural change. Together, this demonstrates that experience-like activity during aggression observation can recruit a shared inhibitory plasticity mechanism that biases behaviour toward adaptive proactive behavioural strategies.

Article.Title: Twist-angle-dependent quantum phase diagrams in moiré bilayer MoTe2
Article.Authors: Sun Z.; Xu F.; Li J.; Jiang Y.; Gao J.; Xu C.; Jia T.; Cheng K.; Wang S.; Tian W.; Zhang J.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Jia J.; Jiang S.; Zhang Y.; Zhang Y.; Lei S.; Liu X.; Li T.
Article.Abstract: Two-dimensional semiconducting moiré superlattices provide a highly tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated and topological quantum phases1-5. As a prototypical example, twisted bilayer MoTe2 (tMoTe2) has been shown to host fractional topological phases at zero magnetic field6-20. However, their evolution with twist angle and competition with other correlated quantum states remain largely unexplored. Here we report a systematic transport study of twist-angle-dependent phase diagrams in tMoTe2 across a range of 3.79°-5.76°, revealing an evolution from valley-polarized, fractional topological states to valley-degenerate correlated states and superconductivity. At relatively small twist angles, partially filled Chern bands of tMoTe2 host fractional quantum anomalous Hall states following the Jain sequence, together with signatures of an anomalous composite Fermi liquid at moiré hole filling factor νh = 1/2. Increasing twist angle progressively suppresses fractional topological phases and reconstructs the half-filled Chern band into symmetry-breaking integer Chern insulating states. At νh = 1, we observe a transition from robust integer quantum anomalous Hall insulators at small angles to displacement-field-tuned, topologically trivial correlated insulators at larger angles. At twist angles above approximately 5.6°, superconductivity emerges adjacent to the νh = 1 correlated insulator, with a phase diagram closely resembling that recently reported in twisted bilayer WSe2 (refs. 21-24). Our results indicate a unified twist-angle-driven phase evolution linking fractional topology, symmetry breaking, magnetic order and superconductivity, providing new insight into the emergent quantum phenomena in moiré systems.

Article.Title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
Article.Authors: Kresse I.; Sayegh N.; Munsamy-Govender V.; Na A.; Nitz S.; Ozakman Y.; Bosch B.; Gonzalez Behn-Eschenburg S.; Poulton N.; Reddy A.; Wallach J.; Aguilera Olvera R.; Castro A.; Kim H.; Wong A.; Tornow S.; Bueler S.; Law W.; Glickman M.; Rubinstein J.; Schnappinger D.; DeJesus M.; Rock J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mycobacterium tuberculosis , the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen 1 . Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations 2,3 . Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis . These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions 4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.

Article.Title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs
Article.Authors: Zhou L.; Renauer P.; Tang K.; Li S.; Luo Z.; Feng Y.; Lin S.; Zhang F.; Park D.; Fang S.; Vest G.; Zhao Z.; Dorst W.; Yang L.; Dong C.; Pan X.; Klemm L.; Yi S.; Sahni N.; Peng L.; Müschen M.; Zhou X.; Chen S.
Article.Abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies, but its efficacy remains limited by multiple negative regulatory mechanisms intrinsic to T cells1-4. Here we perform a high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double-knockout (DKO) CRISPR screen, and identify multiple DKO gene pairs that are both effective and synergistic. The top pair, NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO, has multiple favourable immunological features. Whole-transcriptome profiling and in vivo single-cell RNA sequencing reveal that NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO specifically upregulates metabolic pathways in CAR-T cells, which show significantly higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity. NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO CAR-T cells and T cells exhibit exceptionally potent antitumour efficacy and long-term tumour control across different tumour models without compromising safety features. NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO outperforms several benchmark single-gene and dual-gene modifications in T cells and CAR-T cells5-9. These data demonstrate high-throughput in vivo CAR-T DKO screening for rapid discovery of combination targets, and establish NR4A1-SOCS3 as a promising pair of intracellular checkpoints to engineer high-performance CAR-T therapies against cancer.

Article.Title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
Article.Authors: Wang Q.; Chen A.; Liu Y.; Yu X.; Zhang H.; Yu Y.; Chen P.; Zhang Y.; Chan F.; Gao X.; Mao Y.
Article.Abstract: Ribosomal frameshifting, an uncommon translational recoding event, is best known for its regulatory roles in viral gene expression1,2, whereas its physiological relevance in mammals remains poorly understood. Here we show that specific codon pairs trigger efficient -1 frameshifting preferentially in cancer cells. Mechanistically, this recoding arises from ribosomal pausing associated with tRNA and amino acid availability, and is amplified by impaired ribosome quality control and sustained phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6. We found that this codon-pair-specific frameshifting represents an intrinsic state of translational dysregulation, which is prevalent across cancer cells and reshapes protein synthesis. Taking advantage of this frameshifting-permissive state in cancer cells, we engineered a frameshifting-activated synthetic therapeutic circuit (FAST) that conditionally expresses the pyroptotic effector gasdermin D. FAST is activated across diverse cancer cell types, inducing potent and selective pyroptosis, while sparing normal tissues from detectable toxicity. As a proof of concept, systemic AAV9-mediated delivery of FAST in mouse models of colorectal and pancreatic cancer elicited pronounced tumour regression, robust immune activation and synergistic effects with immune checkpoint blockade. Collectively, these findings reveal codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting as a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells and establish translation-coupled gene circuits as a strategy for cancer-selective therapy.

Article.Title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
Article.Authors: Wu M.; Wang Z.; Wang J.; Dong Z.; Yang J.; Li Q.; Huang T.; Zhang C.; Song P.; Zhao L.; Li M.; Zuo X.; Wang F.; Fan C.; Chen H.
Article.Abstract: Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1-4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an 'add-on' architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing various applications in synthetic biology and information storage.

Article.Title: The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning
Article.Authors: Grove J.; Hakimi A.; Li Q.; Zhang J.; Backes H.; Kuzmanovic B.; Choi J.; Ubadiah V.; Qiu L.; Liu Z.; Small D.; Tittgemeyer M.; Knight Z.
Article.Abstract: Animals learn about the external world in part through interoceptive signals1,2. For example, the nutrient content of food is first estimated in the mouth, in the form of flavour, and then it is measured again through slower signals from the gut. How these signals from the mouth and gut are integrated to drive learning is unclear. Here we identify a dopamine (DA) pathway that enables learning about the nutrient content of food. We show that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area are necessary for associating nutrients with flavours, and that post-ingestive nutrients trigger DA release selectively in a small region of the anterior basolateral amygdala (BLA) but not in canonical DA targets in striatum. This nutrient-triggered DA release occurs preferentially in the left BLA in mice, and this same structure is preferentially activated by post-ingestive nutrients in humans. We identify the gut sensors that are responsible for nutrient-triggered DA release; show that they activate BLA-projecting DA neurons defined by expression of cholecystokinin; and demonstrate that stimulation of DA axon terminals in the anterior BLA drives flavour-nutrient learning but not other aspects of feeding behaviour. Two-photon imaging of neurons in the left anterior BLA reveals that they integrate gustatory and post-ingestive cues, and silencing these neurons prevents flavour-nutrient learning. These findings establish a neural basis for how animals learn about the nutrient content of their food.

Article.Abstract: Sub-ångström spatial resolution combined with attosecond temporal resolution enables direct observation of electron motion in matter1. Attosecond hard X-ray pulses generated at X-ray free-electron laser sources provide the requisite spatiotemporal sensitivity, yet their application has been limited by the absence of precise pulse metrology and control. Here, building on a broadband X-ray split-delay line, we establish metrology of attosecond hard X-ray pulses. Field-correlation measurements provide the first time-domain characterization of the pulse coherence time and demonstrate attosecond synchronization between the generated pulse pairs. By exploiting non-sequential two-photon absorption as a nonlinear probe, intensity autocorrelation quantifies the average pulse duration directly in the time domain to be 170 as. The demonstrated experimental tools and techniques enable systematic attosecond time-resolved experiments, including X-ray pump-X-ray probe spectroscopy and diffraction, and open a pathway to probing electronic phenomena with unprecedented spatial-temporal resolution.

Article.Title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
Article.Authors: Andersen R.; Talukdar M.; Sakamoto T.; Exposito-Alonso D.; Song J.; Qian X.; Lee S.; Murugan N.; Delgado R.; Zhao S.; Eichfeld G.; Harms J.; Page D.; Walsh C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD 1–3 . Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge 4 . Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals 5 , and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts 6,7 ; however, the biological basis of this ‘female protective effect’ (FPE) has remained unknown 8,9 . Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST . Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals 10 , emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

Article.Title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
Article.Authors: de Jong G.; Memi F.; Gracia T.; Lazareva O.; Gould O.; Solomou G.; Aivazidis A.; Dave M.; Zhang Q.; Jensen M.; Rifaioglu A.; Barros-Silva J.; Eckert S.; Zhou D.; Wood Y.; Tuck E.; Er S.; Rademaker K.; Petryszak R.; Marshall H.; Roberts K.; Trinh A.; Rai S.; Shaw T.; Oszlanczi A.

This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework.

Article.Title: A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping
Article.Authors: Gao G.; Jiang C.; Wu W.; Kan J.; Guo Y.; Jayakodi M.; An C.; Sun M.; Cheng C.; Feng J.; Wang J.; Liu J.; Li X.; Camara A.; Xu X.; Yang H.; Zeng Y.; Shen H.; Zhou W.; Zhang J.; Stein N.; Mascher M.; Yang P.
Article.Abstract: Adapting crops to intensive cultivation systems under climate change requires varieties that combine yield potential with optimized flowering and maturation1,2. In central and eastern China, barley has long been cultivated in a double-season cropping system, in which early flowering and maturation are critical for escaping presummer terminal heat stress and enabling flexible rotation with summer crops3,4. Here we trace the genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China using 505 representative cultivars and identify a flowering-time module defined by a single amino acid substitution in PHYTOCHROME C in combination with a winter-type VERNALIZATION 1 haplotype that underpins this adaptation. The derived allele accelerates heading and maturity, and its frequency has risen sharply in modern autumn-sown varieties. Using base editing in barley and wheat, we confirm causality and demonstrate that this flowering-time combination module, PhyC-VRN1, is functionally conserved across Triticeae. Our results identify and experimentally validate a breeding-relevant flowering-time module that has been selected during modern breeding to enable intensive crop rotations, as well as demonstrate how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct such adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design.

Article.Title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells
Article.Authors: Mori Y.; Sakata M.; Nakatsu Y.; Hori T.; Ino Y.; Suzuki S.; Nishi M.; Kawase M.; Kakizaki M.; Nagai M.; Fukano K.; Aizaki H.; Hayashi H.; Murayama K.; Kodama E.; Taguwa S.; Okura T.; Takahashi T.; Kamitani W.; Shirato K.; Isogawa M.; Kimura Y.; Kaji H.; Matsuura Y.; Ryo A.

In placental models, nectin-4 is highly expressed on syncytiotrophoblasts and facilitates infection at the maternal-fetal interface, although additional nectin-4-independent pathways contribute to infection of other trophoblast populations. Together, these data establish nectin-4 as a key factor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of RuV and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of rubella and related diseases.

Article.Title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
Article.Authors: Zhu H.; Li R.; Chang A.; Chen H.; Zhang F.; Tang F.; Ye T.; Li X.; Gu Y.; Xiong P.; Zhou S.
Article.Abstract: RNA language models have achieved strong performance across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by hierarchical structure, making structural information important for pre-training. Existing approaches often depend on noisy annotations or task-specific objectives that can limit generalizability. Here we present structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model trained on 21 million RNA sequence-structure pairs by integrating base-pairing interactions into masked language modelling through a pair-matching operation. We also introduce MUSES, a multi-source ensemble of secondary structures designed to mitigate predictor bias, and a dynamic masking ratio that balances structure-guided and nucleotide-level masking. structRFM learns joint sequence and structure representations as sequence-level, nucleotide-level and pairwise features for broad downstream adaptation. It ranks highly in zero-shot homology classification and establishes new benchmarks for secondary-structure prediction. Its tertiary-structure adaptation, Zfold, consistently improves both three-dimensional predictions and their extracted secondary structures, with performance comparable to AlphaFold31 across CASP15-natural, CASP16 and RNA-Puzzles. structRFM also improves performance on function-prediction tasks and generalizes to newly released RNA families and long non-coding RNAs. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight multimodal RNA language models for robust structural and functional inference. The complete 21-million-pair dataset, model weights and source code are openly available to support multimodal RNA foundation-model development.

Article.Authors: Wang M.; Fang S.; Xiao X.; Guo Z.; Shan T.; Han H.; Tang C.; Xiao D.; Wang G.; Liu Z.; Zhao B.; Li S.; Liu M.; Wang Y.; Li J.; Li M.; Chen L.; Du Z.; Yao C.; Du Y.; Liu J.; Stoddart J.; Sessler J.; Li G.; Huang F.
Article.Abstract: Inspired by macroscopic weaving techniques1-4, molecular weaving, which interlaces molecular strands into ordered networks, has emerged as a powerful strategy for designing functional materials with emergent properties5,6. However, so far, molecular weaving has relied mainly on linear building blocks and biaxial structures. Higher-order weaving (≥3 axes) of nonlinear building blocks is expected to produce intriguing architectures and bring new and unforeseen functions to the resulting materials; however, their construction and property investigation remain underexplored. Here we report a two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven polymer network constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into the woven structure through dative B-N polymerization. Article.Title: Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures
Article.Authors: Wang D.; Goumagias A.; Andreu-Sánchez S.; Peng H.; Ruiz-Moreno A.; Zhernakova D.; Krempel T.; Zhang Y.; Wu J.; Kurilshikov A.; Gacesa R.; Temba G.; Kullaya V.; N/A N/A.; N/A N/A.; Xavier R.; de Mast Q.; Joosten L.; Riksen N.; Rutten J.; Netea M.; Sanna S.; Wijmenga C.; Weersma R.; Zhernakova A.

Yet species-level composition alone can obscure extensive within-species genetic diversity and functional variation. This has driven a shift towards strain-resolved, genetic-level analysis of the microbiome, leveraging microbial genetic variation to identify disease-relevant genes and pathways3-6. Here we conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) analysing 12.8 million gut microbial single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) with 244 host health phenotypes and environmental exposures in 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts. For example, we identified an age-associated SNV in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii that affects an amino acid within the protein pocket that binds glutathione. To support future efforts, all study summary statistics are provided in an online catalogue ( https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/ ). Together, these results identify new biological connections between the human host and microbial genetic variants at base pair resolution and provide a resource for hypothesis generation that will aid future understanding of the strain-level functionality of the gut microbiota.

Article.Title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
Article.Authors: Huang C.; Liu S.; Lv W.; Chen C.; Shen S.; Niu R.; Xu Z.; Tu Y.; Shen S.; Wu C.; Liu P.; Gao K.; Yang Y.; Yen H.; Mao X.; Fu E.; Cairney J.; Pang X.; Shi R.; Chen E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Hydrogen-bearing materials are central to low-carbon energy technologies 1 , but hydrogen itself is difficult to detect and localize at the nanoscale 2–6 . This hinders the development of advanced materials with better efficiency. Atom probe tomography (APT) can map hydrogen in three dimensions and at high resolution, yet characterization of dilute, mobile, interstitial hydrogen in metals has remained challenging because of low solubility, the ambiguity owing to hydrogen trapping by structural defects, as well as the artefacts introduced during hydrogen introduction 4–6 . Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, together with face-centred cubic (FCC) multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) containing coherent FCC precipitates, we show that deuterium atoms reproducibly concentrate in hydrogen-affinitive phases in a manner consistent with theoretical predictions. We further resolve differences in deuterium content between phases with distinct local chemistries and crystal structures, consistent with their different calculated hydrogen solution energies. These findings demonstrate that APT can move beyond identifying hydrides and solute-decorated defects to examine hydrogen in solid solution, providing new insights into hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys and informing materials design for hydrogen-related applications.

Article.Title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling
Article.Authors: Garcia-Gonzalez I.; Rocha S.; Oliveira F.; Sanchez-Muñoz M.; Lytvyn M.; Garcia-Cabero A.; Ipe U.; Graupera M.; Mäkinen T.; Benedito R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival 1 . Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells 2,3 . The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported 4,5 . These Vegfr2 -knockout ( Vegfr2 KO ) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs. Vegfr2 KO ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF, Vegfr2 KO ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2 KO ECs. Article.Title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Brand P.; Keller K.; Coleman R.; Eghbali N.; Zylka S.; Prieto-Godino L.; Ruta V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities 1–6 . Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta ’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster , where food odour can promote arousal 7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta . Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.

Article.Title: The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity
Article.Authors: Dhungana S.; Flament N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Great Unconformity marks a globally extensive erosive surface linked to climatic shifts 1 and environmental transitions 2 that preceded the Cambrian explosion of life. The processes proposed to explain the formation of the Great Unconformity include glacial erosion during the Snowball Earth 1,3,4 , rifting and plume activity 5–7 , sea-level fall 8 and mantle-driven dynamic topography 6,9–11 . However, the dynamics of these processes have not been tested. Here we show that continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography 12 due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. Our models predict prolonged continental-scale Neoproterozoic uplift and long-term Phanerozoic subsidence for Laurentia, Baltica and North China. This vertical motion scenario is ideal for the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity, which is a first-order surface expression of deep Earth processes. The predicted prolonged continental uplift throughout Cryogenian times would have resulted in marked erosion due to the action of glaciers 13 . The large area of Laurentia and limited deformation at its margins explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved and documented there. Our models predict cycles of dynamic topography that are broadly reflected in preserved sediment volume across continents 1,14 , and open new avenues for understanding the environments of Cambrian animal diversification.

Article.Title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
Article.Authors: McColl H.; Kroonen G.; Pinotti T.; Barrie W.; Koch J.; Ling J.; Demoule J.; Kristiansen K.; Sikora M.; Willerslev E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age 1–3 . How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested 4 , with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce ) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp ), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp ), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts 5–8 . Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory 9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.

Article.Title: Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
Article.Authors: Fang Z.; Rao Z.; Liu C.; Ding L.; Lv A.; Qin Y.; Xue J.; Hnapovskyi V.; Xu F.; Lukas T.; Lou Z.; Zheng Q.; Zhang H.; Yin Y.; Lu L.; Mo H.; Zhang F.; He Y.; Xu X.; Stolterfoht M.; De Wolf S.; Jiang L.; He B.; Yin J.; Wang K.
Article.Abstract: Perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells on rough textured substrates are at present limited by a critical trade-off in self-assembled monolayer (SAM) design because increasing molecular conjugation enhances conductivity but often leads to unfavourable aggregation that impairs conformal coverage1,2. Here we overcome this challenge using a rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation that incorporates tailored intramolecular distortion to suppress excess π-π stacking without sacrificing charge-transport efficiency. This steric regulation facilitates the formation of a highly ordered, conformal SAM across rough pyramidal textures. By reconciling molecular packing with interfacial coverage, the tailored interface provides optimized energy-level alignment for ultrafast charge extraction, enables improved defect passivation through adaptive conformational adjustment and acts as a robust template for high-quality perovskite film growth. Making use of this interface, the optimized tandem device achieves a notable fill factor (FF) of 85%, yielding a certified stabilized power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 35.1%. Furthermore, the device demonstrates outstanding stability, retaining more than 94% of its initial performance after 1,500 h of ageing under the ISOS-L-1 protocol. Our findings provide a clear molecular engineering route to reconcile conductivity and film uniformity while maximizing the performance of tandem photovoltaics on textured silicon substrates.

Article.Title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
Article.Authors: Ferrer-Chavez R.; Wang J.; Bouman K.; Freeman W.; Pueyo L.; Feng B.; Perrin M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1 au (ref. 1 ) but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light. As well as sophisticated instrumentation 2,3 , effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation 4 . Standard algorithms use reference images for starlight modelling and thus they are limited by inevitable telescope instabilities that change from reference to science observation 5,6 . Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories 7 . Here we present a new physics-based method for starlight subtraction. Our method combines a multistep optimization with a flexible physical model to produce a starlight model, allowing modelling and compensation of instrument instabilities. We use automatic differentiation (autodiff) 8 to optimize millions of model parameters. We demonstrate our method on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam) 9–11 coronagraph instrument. We achieve sensitivity 2–15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51 Eridani b (ref. 12 ) at 4.3 μm. This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success.
