Article.Title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits
Article.Authors: Woo J.; Williamson M.; Choi D.; Akdemir E.; Zlatkov T.; Yu K.; Kwon W.; Maleki E.; Ko Y.; Sanchez K.; Maleki H.; Choi J.; Serin-Harmanci A.; Deneen B.
Article.Abstract: Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes1,2. Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes3; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies4, we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51+ and CD51- astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51+ and CD51- astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51+ astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51+ astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51+ astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain.

Article.Title: Amazon carbon emissions driven by human actions amplified by droughts
Article.Authors: Gatti L.; Cunha C.; Blas J.; Denning A.; Reis M.; Marani L.; Arai E.; Messias C.; Conciani D.; Miller J.; Schumacher V.; Naccarato K.; Marengo J.; Alencar A.; Soler L.; Almeida C.; Domingues L.; Correia C.; Neves R.; Nobre C.; Corrêa S.; Campbell E.; Johnson J.; Berry J.; Sanchez A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Amazon carbon sink is weakening as deforestation 1–5 , rising tree mortality 6–8 and climate change disrupt the climatic conditions that sustain a humid tropical forest 9–11 . Forest loss reduces precipitation, increases temperatures and lengthens the dry season, driving higher carbon emissions 1–4,11,12 . Climate stress is stronger in more deforested regions, rendering forests progressively more flammable 1,9,13 . Large-scale climate events, such as El Niño, further amplify regional climate impacts 9,14–17 . Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO 2 measurements. We determine a carbon balance of 0.32 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 , with fires acting as the dominant source (0.40 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and forest uptake becoming increasingly unable to offset emissions. Furthermore, we investigate key drivers of the carbon emissions of Amazonia and identify three distinct year groups. Group 1 (2011–2014, 2017 and 2018) represents the role of the Amazon in the global carbon balance (0.11 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 ) during wetter years with low human activity, such as deforestation, biomass burning and degradation. Group 2 (2019–2022) represents Amazon carbon emissions (0.43 ± 0.13 PgC yr −1 ) from human activities (mainly deforestation and degradation) during years with low climatic stress. Group 3 (2010, 2015, 2016, 2023 and 2024) has the highest carbon emissions (0.49 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and comprises warm and dry years (high climate stress), such as El Niño and the warming of the Tropical North Atlantic Ocean, associated with biomass burning.

Article.Title: WEE1 opposes APC/CCDH1 activity to promote S phase entry
Article.Authors: Vuillemenot L.; Morales L.; Dragoi C.; Pennycook B.; Harris E.; Lin L.; Weston W.; Brown J.; Graham E.; Moulin L.; Andrew I.; Roumelioti G.; Montoya A.; Game L.; Young G.; Datta K.; Shliaha P.; Novák B.; Yamano H.; Barr A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract WEE1 phosphorylates and inhibits the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases to prevent mitotic entry and establish a G2 DNA damage checkpoint 1–3 . Consequently, WEE1 inhibitors have been developed to be synthetically lethal in TP53- mutated tumours that become reliant on this WEE1-mediated checkpoint, and such inhibitors are undergoing clinical trials. However, WEE1 inhibitors also have efficacy in TP53- wild-type tumours, and many trials have been terminated owing to high levels of toxic side effects, suggesting that WEE1 has unknown functions. Here we show that WEE1 promotes cell cycle re-entry from quiescence (G0) by opposing the activity of the E3 ubiquitin ligase, anaphase-promoting complex–cyclosome bound to CDH1 (APC/C CDH1 ). WEE1 phosphorylates CDH1 ( FZR1 ) at key residues that mediate the interaction between CDH1 and APC/C. Cells with loss of function of WEE1 during G0/G1 have delayed S phase entry, impaired G1/S transition, abnormal S phase accumulation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21 Cip1/Kip1 and a p21-dependent G2 arrest. Reduced expression of APC/C CDH1 or p21 renders cells more sensitive to acute WEE1 inhibition, and both pathways are downregulated in cells with acquired WEE1 inhibitor resistance. These results reveal a mechanism of cell cycle control that has implications for how WEE1 inhibitors should be used in the clinic.

Article.Title: Touch-sensing digital pixel fibre enables interactive garment GUI
Article.Authors: Fu H.; Li Z.; Chaturvedi S.; Zhang X.; Li X.; Li Q.; Khudiyev T.
Article.Abstract: Wearable computing promises to transform human interaction with information, yet conventional graphical user interfaces (GUIs) rely on planar, rigid displays incompatible with textiles, which are composed of one-dimensional fibres. Despite recent progress1,2 in flexible and fibre-based displays, bridging this fundamental dimensional mismatch remains challenging because existing approaches do not naturally provide the digitally addressable, high-throughput, information-rich interfaces required for interactive GUIs. Here we present a digital pixel fibre integrating addressable pixels, a common propagation-axis interconnection for scalable in-fibre circuitry and a coaxial sensing layer for fibre-level touch localization. Microelectronic components and a touch-gated resistive path system form a linear circuit that acts as both an interactive display backbone and a computational bus, while peripheral multimodal fibre sensors and actuators enable physiological, inertial, optical, and acoustic input and output. We integrate these fibres into the forearm portion of a garment sleeve to realize a GUI with a 96 × 54-pixel display, 30-frame-per-second refresh rate and 8-bit colour depth. It supports dynamic graphics, integrated audio-video playback, wireless data exchange and interactive computing functions, while maintaining the flexibility, washability, breathability and mechanical robustness of everyday textiles. By merging display, sensing and computation within a single fibre, this work establishes a scalable platform for intrinsically interactive textiles, opening pathways toward garments that operate as fully integrated computational systems.

Article.Title: Enzyme-embedded polyesters for accelerated biodegradation in the deep sea
Article.Authors: Huang Q.; Iida N.; Isobe N.; Kabe T.; Omura T.; Ilangovan M.; Kimura S.; Seok J.; Nomaki H.; Kasuya K.; Iwata T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The accumulation of persistent plastics in the ocean is causing wide-ranging environmental problems 1–3 . Some commercially available compostable plastics 4–7 , developed to address these issues, degrade efficiently under industrial composting conditions; however, their degradation in marine environments, particularly in the deep sea, remains limited 8–10 . Here we demonstrate that thermally embedding enzymes into compostable polyesters (poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene succinate- co -adipate) (PBSA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(butylene adipate- co -terephthalate) (PBAT)) significantly accelerates their degradation in both coastal and deep-sea environments from water depths of 2–6 m to 5,503 m. Enzyme-embedded polyesters achieved near-complete degradation at a deep-sea depth of 757 m within 5 months. Furthermore, moderate biodegradation of enzyme-embedded polyesters was observed under extreme conditions on deep-sea floors of 5,503 m. In coastal seawater, films embedded with trace amounts (0.1 wt%) of enzyme underwent rapid degradation. The mechanical properties of enzyme-embedded polyesters were similar to those of enzyme-free polyesters. Chemical analysis confirmed the formation of low-molecular-mass degradation products and biochemical oxygen demand measurements supported the mineralization of the enzyme-embedded polyesters. The enzyme-embedding strategy enables enhanced marine degradation of compostable polyesters and represents a potential solution to marine plastic pollution.

Article.Title: Zeolite-catalysed olefin carbonylation based on tuning spatial confinement
Article.Authors: Qi L.; Sheng Y.; Zhang W.; Ni Y.; He L.; Li B.; Wang A.; Zhu W.; Bell A.; Liu Z.
Article.Abstract: Carbonylation is an important process used to produce aldehydes, carboxylic acids and esters1-5 that is usually catalysed by homogeneous metal complexes with ligands and iodide promoters6-12. Koch has reported that protons of mineral acids can also catalyse carbonylation13. Previous studies have demonstrated that Brønsted acidic zeolites can act as a heterogeneous, Koch-type catalyst for carbonylation of alcohols and olefins, but the products in this case are limited to tertiary carboxylic acids14-18. Here we show that targeted use of spatial confinement in a zeolite together with a high CO/olefin ratio can help break this limitation. We report that, with FER zeolite and a CO/olefin ratio of 360, olefin carbonylation can produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products; ethylene carbonylation to propanoic acid (PA) is achieved with 80% selectivity over 100 h and propylene carbonylation to isobutyric acid (IBA) is achieved with 95% selectivity over 750 h. The propylene and ethylene carbonylation selectivities decrease to 61% and 57%, respectively, as the CO/olefin ratio decreases to 24 and 90, respectively. Experiments in combination with theoretical calculations suggest that T2-O5 in eight-membered ring (8-MR) cavities of FER zeolite are the primary active sites for ethylene carbonylation and T3-O1 in ten-membered rings (10-MRs) are the primary active sites for propylene carbonylation. Our findings open new directions for olefin carbonylation and provide critical insights into the prerequisites for developing new zeolite-based carbonylation processes.

Article.Title: Drought and disease trigger novel interactions among top predators
Article.Authors: Sergio F.; Natsukawa H.; Tanferna A.; Chicano J.; Carro F.; Soriguer R.; Hiraldo F.; Blas J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Interactions among species are increasingly recognized as key determinants of climate change impacts on ecosystems 1–5 . However, we know little about how climatic perturbations affect interactions among top vertebrate predators. Here we show that, when an emergent disease caused the decline of shared prey (rabbits), after decades of neutral co-existence a mammalian carnivore (lynx) started to prey heavily on a top predatory raptor (kites). These predation bouts occurred exclusively under drought conditions and when lynx found rabbit remains under the raptor nests, consistent with the removal of a potential competitor. Drought-induced lynx predation depressed lifetime reproductive success and triggered territory abandonment and dispersal by the raptor, suggestive of a new arms race among predators. A reduction in raptor abundance was associated with an increase in an insectivorous bird (a small owl), showing that the new interaction had the potential to reach lower trophic levels. These results underline the importance of diet flexibility and mobility as important mediators of resilience to stressors. In the future, synergistic effects of multiple anthropogenic stressors may reshape the interactions and ecological roles of many apex predators, with potential cascading consequences for whole ecosystems. A key to forecasting the future impact of global change may reside in understanding how behavioural flexibility and interacting keystone species respond to interacting shocks.

Article.Title: The anatomy of a personal health agent
Article.Authors: Heydari A.; Gu K.; Srinivas V.; Yu H.; Paruchuri A.; Zhang Z.; Zhang Y.; He Q.; Palangi H.; Hammerquist N.; Metwally A.; Winslow B.; Kim Y.; Ayush K.; Yang Y.; Narayanswamy G.; Xu M.; Garrison J.; Schmidgall S.; Armento Lee A.; Vafeiadou J.; Graef B.; Galatzer-Levy I.; Schenck E.; Barakat A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Large language models are enabling a new generation of health agents, yet their ability to address the diverse needs of individuals in everyday health settings remains underexplored 1,2 . Here we developed a comprehensive personal health agent that reasons over multimodal data from consumer wellness devices and medical records to provide personalized health support. Through analysis of web search and health forum queries, together with user-centred research involving end users and health experts, we identified four key user journeys: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice, and symptom assessment. These journeys informed three specialist sub-agents: (1) a data science agent that analyses longitudinal wearable and medical data, incorporating population-level statistics to contextualize numerical insights; (2) a health domain expert agent that integrates personal and contextual data with health knowledge to generate personalized insights; and (3) a health coach agent that synthesizes insights, supports multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applies specified psychological strategies and tracks progress. We integrated these capabilities in the personal health agent, an open-source multi-agent framework for dynamic, personalized health interactions. We evaluated the sub-agents and full system across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users. This represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far and provides a concrete foundation for improving access to high-quality personalized health support more broadly.

Article.Title: A single archaeon couples long-chain fatty acid oxidation to methanogenesis
Article.Authors: Yi Y.; Cao Z.; Wu K.; Ding H.; Fu L.; Gao W.; Li L.; Zhou L.; Zhou Z.; Dai L.; Lu Y.; Cheng L.
Article.Abstract: Anaerobic degradation of complex organic compounds to methane and carbon dioxide is common in the deep subsurface biosphere and has long been considered to require syntrophic cooperation, with methanogens confined to the terminal use of simple C1 and C2 substrates. Thermodynamic considerations, multi-omics analyses and microcosm experiments suggest that archaeal lineages are capable of methanogenic degradation of complex substrates1-6. However, experimental validation in pure culture was lacking. Here we report the isolation of a thermophilic archaeon, Methanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75, affiliated with Archaeoglobi, from a Chinese petroleum reservoir. Strain AA-75 not only converts methanol into methane, carbon dioxide and acetate, but also uses saturated fatty acids varying from C7:0 to C18:0 and unsaturated fatty acids including C16:1, C18:1 and C18:2 to produce methane. We term the latter lipotrophic methanogenesis, which integrates β-oxidation of fatty acids with the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway and the canonical methyl-tetrahydromethanopterin:coenzyme M methyltransferase and methyl-coenzyme M reductase complexes, together with an intracellular electron transfer system. A formaldehyde-methanol branch probably functions as an auxiliary route for C1 metabolism during methanogenesis. Methane produced from stearate is moderately 13C-enriched (δ13C-CH4 = -40.0‰ to -36.3‰), distinct from the strong 13C depletion characteristic of canonical methanogenic pathways. These findings demonstrate that methanogens can function as primary degraders of complex organic matter, challenging the classical syntrophic paradigm and calling for refinement of current models of carbon cycling in the deep subsurface biosphere.

Article.Title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms
Article.Authors: Willemsen P.; Mason V.; Zelst V.; van Bergeijk V.; Breteler M.; Muller J.; Dermentzoglou D.; Vouziouris A.; van Veelen T.; Dzimballa S.; Wijnberg K.; Hoitink A.; Buring P.; Paul M.; Antonini A.; Bouma T.; Borsje B.
Article.Abstract: Salt marshes protect coastlines by attenuating wind waves with their elevated marsh platform and above-ground vegetation1. Confidence in the persistence of this service under a changing climate requires knowledge on how extreme storms damage the platform and vegetation; however, a comprehensive, quantified understanding of salt marsh-wave interactions under extreme events is lacking. A unique experiment was conducted by transferring intact salt marsh to one of the world's largest wave flumes, and subsequently exposing it to increasingly higher waves that reach up to 2 m significant wave height. We show that marsh substrates can persist with negligible erosion, despite cumulative wave exposure. By contrast, the vegetation was progressively damaged during continued wave exposure, gradually reducing vegetation-related wave attenuation. Results emphasize that vegetation was most effective in attenuating waves at low-energy marsh coasts (up to 1 m), where attenuation exceeded 10% (up to 50%), whereas attenuation at high-energy marsh coasts (wave height > 1 m) does not exceed 10%. Our global assessment supports the differentiation between low- and high-energetic conditions resulting from the flume experiment. Our results suggest that the marsh platform remains stable under extreme wave events and that substantial wave attenuation by marsh vegetation is limited to low-energy marsh coasts.

Article.Title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
Article.Authors: Lee H.; Doğan C.; Koyuncu S.; Wehrmann M.; Artan M.; Petrovic D.; Loureiro R.; Sahu A.; Schnubel J.; Grobushkin P.; Prymidis D.; Georgomanolis T.; Sokol A.; Yang M.; Hoppe T.; Frezza C.; Vilchez D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species 1–3 , yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear. Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans . Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1. BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan. This BH2–BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing. Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington’s disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.

Article.Title: GRP75-dependent SIMPA mediates inter-organellar quality control
Article.Authors: Yu F.; Jiang L.; Liu H.; Yang S.; Yuan Y.; Jin H.; Liu J.; Liu X.; Dong Y.; Ren D.; Kang J.; Huang Y.; Meng Q.; Bai F.; Li Y.; Li S.; Liu H.; Zhao W.; Xiao J.; Chen Q.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondria are bound by a double membrane and are semiautonomous organelles, rendering them highly vulnerable to global and internal proteostatic stress1. Multiple surveillance mechanisms at proteostatic and inter-organellar levels have evolved to maintain mitochondrial integrity and cellular health2-7. However, the precise mechanisms by which proteostatic damage relays stress signals across organelles and how the quality surveillance machinery coordinates these functions remain unknown. Here we report that under proteostatic stress, damaged mitochondrial proteins are sequestered to form stress-induced mitochondrial protein aggregates (SIMPAs) that activate specific quality control mechanisms in a spatially confined manner without perturbing the mitochondrial network. Quantitative proteomic and correlative light-electron microscopy analysis revealed that SIMPA mediates inter-organellar communication via mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes. Mechanistically, GRP75 coordinates SIMPA biogenesis and focally activates endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response pathways via mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes for the targeted clearance of SIMPAs. Functionally, in both cellular and liver disease models, we found that a GRP75-dependent SIMPA signalling cascade attenuates mitochondrial stress and preserves mitochondrial integrity under proteotoxic stress. Overall, we show that SIMPAs, functioning as protein condensates, serve as a central cross-compartment communication hub for mitochondrial quality control, supporting cellular and organismal fitness.

Article.Title: Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language
Article.Authors: Dai F.; You S.; Zhu Y.; Gao Y.; Fu L.; Zhou X.; Su J.; Wang C.; Fan Y.; Tan Q.; Ma X.; Deng X.; Yu L.; Qian H.; He Y.; Ke Y.; Zhang Z.; Han C.; Chang X.; Zheng L.; Wang S.; Ji Y.; Hao K.; Cao L.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Programming biological function-designing bespoke proteins to perform specified molecular tasks-is a foundational goal of molecular engineering. However, current design models remain fundamentally limited1-3: they typically require either natural proteins as starting points for optimization or manual reformulation of functional goals as geometric and sequence-level constraints to guide candidate generation. Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function. Trained on 1.7 billion synthetically annotated protein-text pairs, Pinal links functional intent to protein sequence and structure. In computational evaluations, generated candidates combined high predicted foldability with functional-description alignment and sequence diversity, providing a basis for prioritizing experimentally testable designs. We applied Pinal to four distinct design tasks-a fluorescent protein, a polyethylene terephthalate hydrolase, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein-and experimentally observed the intended function in each case, including catalytic activity for both designed enzymes. Without iterative experimental optimization, a Pinal-designed H-protein increased product titre by 1.7-fold relative to the corresponding native Escherichia coli H-protein in a multi-enzyme CO2 fixation pathway. These findings support natural language as a high-level interface for candidate generation in protein design, enabling programmable exploration with reduced reliance on manually specified structural or sequence constraints.

Article.Title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts
Article.Authors: Mishra S.; Payal N/A.; Evans D.; Bortey K.; Bootwala H.; Gonzalez-Gutierrez G.; Vázquez R.; Baker D.; Lewis J.
Article.Abstract: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1-5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6-8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

Article.Title: Cortex-wide imaging in naturally behaving mice with 1-gram wireless mesoscopes
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Li A.; Yuan L.; Wang M.; Zhao W.; Wang Z.; Zang B.; Zhou Y.; Yu T.; Gao L.; Wu Y.; Zhu R.; Tian M.; Li K.; Wu J.; Dai P.; Dai Q.
Article.Abstract: Revealing how distributed cortical circuits coordinate behavior in freely moving animals remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience, constrained by limited fields of view, low throughput, and the tethering required by current miniaturized microscopes1-4. Here, we present Airscope, a wireless mesoscope delivering 4 μm lateral resolution across a 6 mm field of view at 12.5 Hz, weighing 1.0 gram. An aspheric-lens design achieves a 2.84× shorter total track length than previous miniaturized microscopes1,2,5,6 while matching the neuron yield of benchtop one-photon mesoscopes; a tailored wireless link supports cable-free calcium imaging from >8,500 neurons per animal (25‑fold increase). Paired with a zero-shot behavior analyzer, Airscope enables cortical imaging across rich behavioral conditions, including room-scale enriched arenas, swimming assays, and multi-organ implantation, with concurrent recording from multiple animals. Using Airscope, we demonstrate versatile applications of untethered cortical imaging across diverse behavioral paradigms. We identify cortical activity patterns across multiple dorsal regions that correlate with behavioral signatures of social dominance, and show dorsal-cortical population activity prospectively decodes competition outcomes across paired animals. We observe reward-location-associated cortical activity patterns during maze exploration, and characterize Granger-causal influence from spinal cord to cortex during fear conditioning, enabled by simultaneous brain-spinal recordings. By uniting large-scale, cellular-resolution recording with unconstrained behavior, Airscope makes naturalistic, multi-animal cortical recording experimentally practical, and provides a broadly accessible technology for systems neuroscience.

Article.Title: Antiferroelectric hafnia down to the 2D limit
Article.Authors: Li X.; Ren G.; Lu H.; Samanta K.; Shah A.; Huang K.; Omprakash P.; Yun Y.; Buragohain P.; Cao H.; Wu Y.; Hachtel J.; Lupini A.; Chi M.; Idrobo J.; Tsymbal E.; Gruverman A.; Mishra R.; Xu X.
Article.Abstract: Antiferroelectricity is a material property characterized by alternating electric dipoles spontaneously ordered in antiparallel directions. Antiferroelectrics are promising for energy storage, solid-state cooling, and memory technologies; however, these materials are scarce, and their scalability remains largely unexplored. In this work, we demonstrated that single-crystalline hafnia, a lead-free complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS)–compatible material, exhibits antiferroelectricity under compressive-strain conditions. We observed antiparallel sublattice polarization and stable double hysteresis in single-crystalline (111)-oriented epitaxial lanthanum (La)–doped hafnia films grown on yttrium-stabilized zirconia and showed that the antipolar orthorhombic phase of hafnia adheres to the Kittel model of antiferroelectricity. Compressive strain strengthens the orthorhombic order in thinner La-doped hafnia films, achieving a very high ordering temperature of 850°C in the two-dimensional limit, highlighting hafnia’s potential for advanced antiferroelectric devices.

Article.Authors: He S.; Thennavan A.; Wei R.; Bai S.; Li J.; Bethell C.; Sei E.; Rao M.; Kumar T.; Tang C.; Marin I.; Montalvan J.; Nagi C.; Lim B.; Krishnamurthy S.; Thompson A.; Navin N.
Article.Abstract: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common preinvasive breast cancer, however our knowledge of the DCIS tumor microenvironment (TME) remains limited. We constructed a comprehensive atlas of the TME in estrogen-receptor positive DCIS using fresh samples collected from normal breast tissues, DCIS and invasive breast cancers. We analyzed 854,911 cells from 159 patients by single cell RNA sequencing and 39 samples by spatial transcriptomics, which identified 9 cell types and 60 cell states. This study delineates early alterations in the DCIS TME, including many changes that persist during invasive progression.

Article.Title: The cryosphere beyond a planetary safe operating space
Article.Authors: Su B.; Rockström J.; Chen D.; Fetzer I.; Feng H.; Hugelius G.; Winkelmann R.; Norström A.; Xiao C.; Hanna E.; Alverson K.; Box J.; Qin D.; Sommerkorn M.; Andreassen L.; Heil P.; Yao T.; Richardson K.; Lade S.; Bai X.; Gupta J.; Stewart-Koster B.; Zheng Z.; Pomeroy J.; Mackintosh A.
Article.Abstract: The cryosphere plays a vital role in regulating planetary dynamics and habitability, yet it remains unclear whether its essential functions remain within a safe operating space (SOS) amid Anthropocene change. Here, we propose a cryosphere SOS and systematically evaluate its contributions to Earth system resilience using the planetary boundaries framework. Multiple lines of evidence indicate an accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity, driven by amplifying feedbacks. Key cryospheric control variables either have left or are committed to departing from Holocene-like conditions. We conclude that the cryosphere has breached its SOS and is on a trajectory that locks in long-term risks for human societies and ecosystems. Safeguarding planetary resilience therefore requires explicit consideration of cryosphere change and its interactions across the Earth system.

Article.Abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Article.Title: Quantitative measurement of viscosity in two-dimensional electron fluids
Article.Authors: Zeng Y.; Guo H.; Ghosh O.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Levitov L.; Dean C.
Article.Abstract: Electron hydrodynamics is an emerging framework that describes dynamics of interacting electron systems as conventional fluids. Although evidence for hydrodynamic-like transport has been reported in a variety of two-dimensional materials, precise quantitative measurement of the core parameter, electron viscosity, remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate that magnetoresistance in Corbino-shaped graphene devices offers a simultaneous ohmmeter and viscosometer capability, allowing us to disentangle the individual ohmic and viscous contributions to transport, even near viscous-ohmic crossover. In both monolayer and bilayer graphene, the effective electron-electron scattering rate scales linearly with temperature, deviating markedly from the T 2 dependence expected in conventional Fermi liquids. Instead, it is consistent with a recently identified tomographic fluid regime, theoretically predicted to be generic for two-dimensional electron systems.

Article.Authors: Betti S.; Chen C.; Xie C.; Worthen K.; Brittain S.; Najita J.; Rebollido I.; Beck T.; Bolin B.; Hines D.; Ingebretsen C.; Lisse C.; Perrin M.; Pueyo L.; Wong I.; Stark C.
Article.Abstract: The star β Pictoris is orbited by a dusty debris disk, within which planet formation is occurring. The outer disk is sufficiently far from the star that volatile molecules are expected to freeze into solid ices. We observed the β Pictoris disk in the near-infrared using the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum shows features due to amorphous water ice (<7% crystallinity) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) ice in both the 12 CO 2 and 13 CO 2 isotopologues. Article.Title: Giant elastoresistance in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene
Article.Authors: Ma X.; Liu Z.; Cai J.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Xu X.; Chu J.; Yankowitz M.
Article.Abstract: Strongly correlated and topological phases in moiré materials are exquisitely sensitive to lattice geometry at both atomic and superlattice length scales. Here, we examined electrical transport in twisted bilayer graphene subjected to continuous uniaxial strain. Near the magic angle (≈1.1°), devices exhibited a pronounced elastoresistance that depended on band filling and temperature, with a gauge factor more than two orders of magnitude larger than that of conventional metals. Article.Title: Atmospheric O <sub>2</sub> reveals a strengthening ocean carbon sink and a stagnant net land sink since 1990
Article.Authors: Morgan E.; Jin Y.; Kozlova E.; Watson A.; Manning A.; Zaehle S.; Tohjima Y.; Lan X.; Keeling R.
Article.Abstract: The global ocean and land biosphere absorb roughly half of fossil fuel carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. The temporal evolution of these sinks remains difficult to quantify owing to data sparsity. Leveraging 30+ years of atmospheric oxygen (O 2 ) and CO 2 observations, we find that the ocean carbon sink increased by 0.63 ± 0.19 petagrams of carbon per year per decade (Pg C year −1 decade −1 ) (a mean of 2.8 ± 0.4 Pg C year −1 ), accounting for 35% of fossil emissions between 1990 and 2019. The net land sink shows no robust trend (with a mean of 1.0 ± 0.5 Pg C year −1 , accounting for 13% of fossil emissions), despite large decadal variability. These results challenge many process-based model simulations of the land and ocean sinks, questioning their ability to accurately predict future climate states.

Article.Title: Limited genomic predictability of complex trait evolution despite genotype-phenotype stability
Article.Authors: Smiley-Rhodes J.; Bitter M.; Berardi S.; Beltz J.; Petrov D.; Schmidt P.
Article.Abstract: Whether genomic data can be used to effectively predict adaptation in natural populations is unknown. Here, we tested the efficacy of genomic prediction of complex trait evolution by monitoring genome-wide allele frequencies and pigmentation variation in genetically diverse populations of Drosophila melanogaster during evolution in both field mesocosms and a controlled, lab-based setting. Article.Abstract: Nitrate pollution is widely perceived as a signature of human inputs. Article.Title: Tracking danger on the peaks
Article.Authors: Jackson M.; Thapa A.
Article.Abstract: The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

Article.Title: Discovering molecular modulators with nanoswitch screening
Article.Authors: Hansen C.; Lipstein M.; Erlandson S.; Schwalbe T.; Bernier S.; Gmeiner P.; Kruse A.; Wong W.
Article.Abstract: Molecules that modulate protein-protein interactions, including through ternary complex formation, have been established as key therapeutics. Yet they can be challenging to discover, as standard screening approaches often lack throughput or fail to directly assay multibody interactions. We addressed this by combining DNA nanoswitch–based selection of nucleotide-encoded libraries with next-generation sequencing to create FIND (Functional Interaction–based Nanoswitch Discovery), which enables ultrahigh-throughput discovery of compounds that induce or increase protein-protein interactions. We demonstrate FIND by discovering nanobodies that stabilize the interaction between angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and the receptor-binding domain of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and by discovering agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor gamma from a DNA-barcoded small-molecule library. By enabling rapid discovery of molecular modulators, FIND could lead to new therapeutics across many conditions.

Article.Title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
Article.Authors: Kunc H.; Schmidt R.
Article.Abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

Article.Title: Quantum gas microscopy of three-flavor Hubbard systems
Article.Authors: Mongkolkiattichai J.; Liu L.; Dasgupta S.; Hazzard K.; Schauss P.
Article.Abstract: Hubbard systems are paradigmatic realizations of strongly correlated many-body systems. Introducing additional species breaks the SU(2) symmetry of the Hubbard model and leads to a wide variety of new exotic quantum phases. Here, we extended quantum gas microscopy to three-flavor Fermi lattice gases in the Hubbard regime. Relying on site- and flavor-resolved detection, we studied the phase diagram of the three-flavor Hubbard model and found signatures of flavor-selective localization and selective pairing at temperatures down to the tunneling energy scale. Our measurements were then compared with numerical linked-cluster expansion calculations. Further increase of phase space density may enable the observation of a distinct pair Mott phase at half filling and shows a path toward the study of color superfluidity and other aspects of quantum chromodynamics.

Article.Title: Tumor metastasis co-opts liver hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression
Article.Authors: Pan Q.; Wang X.; Li Y.; Li N.; Han Y.; Zhang G.; Guo J.; Zhang L.; Cui A.; Gu Y.; Lian Y.; Zhang W.; Lin N.; Xu B.; Jin Z.; Zeng X.; Wang L.; Li Y.; Peng J.; Wang X.; Yu Z.; Wang G.; Lu W.; Qin J.
Article.Abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. However, whether tumors can initiate localized extramedullary hematopoiesis to suppress antitumor immunity remains unclear. In this study, we identify a distinct form of hepatic hematopoiesis driven by liver metastasis–associated hematopoietic stem cells (LM-HSCs). Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1 + ) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8 + T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.

Article.Title: Glacial abrupt transitions in ocean circulation were much slower than ice-core records imply
Article.Authors: Dong X.; Zhang X.; Sun Y.; Kathayat G.; Li Y.; Rasmussen S.; Svensson A.; Buizert C.; Sinha A.; Barker S.; Pérez-Mejías C.; Knorr G.; Chen R.; Zhao K.; Du W.; Zhang H.; Li H.; Columbu A.; Tan L.; Zhang Y.; Ning Y.; Werner M.; Wang Y.; Edwards R.; Cheng H.
Article.Abstract: Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Greenland ice cores suggest warming transitions within only a few decades—or even just over 10 years. Using precisely dated speleothem oxygen-isotope records from the Asian monsoon region, we have shown that the same DO warmings unfolded over more than a century. Isotope modeling revealed that Greenland records primarily capture a rapid atmospheric reorganization triggered by the initial sea-ice retreat in the northeastern North Atlantic, whereas the parallel AMOC recovery and hemispheric thermal adjustment proceeded much more slowly. These findings reveal that natural AMOC transitions evolved more slowly than the rapid North Greenland oxygen-isotope shifts would imply, thereby refining our understanding of “abruptness” during DO events.

Article.Authors: Qi X.; Chen H.; Nie Q.; Niu H.; Ding Y.; Luo X.; Si M.; Wu S.; Xiong X.; Li M.; Dong B.; Ma H.; Guo C.; Wang Y.; Long X.; Zheng J.; Wang K.; Nie S.; Jiang C.; Pang Y.; Qiao J.
Article.Abstract: Excessive androgens serve as a primary driver for many phenotypic features of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Article.Title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease
Article.Authors: Drareni K.; Seale P.
Article.Abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.

Article.Title: Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago
Article.Authors: Caspari G.; Sadykov T.; Fomicheva D.; Blochin J.; Armbruster D.; Happel O.; Ryabogina N.; Boxleitner K.; Spengler R.
Article.Abstract: Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

Article.Title: Seafloor geodesy delineates fast megathrust relocking after the giant 2011 Tohoku earthquake
Article.Authors: Tomita F.; Sun T.; Kido M.; Iinuma T.; Uchida N.; Ohta Y.; Hino R.; He J.; Wang K.
Article.Abstract: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Here we report the delineation of the relocking process after the 2011 magnitude 9 Tohoku earthquake with 14 years of postseismic seafloor geodetic observations. These data, combined with onshore geodetic observations, analyses of repeating earthquakes, and numerical modeling, reveal how the recovery of locking is interrupted by afterslip on the megathrust and accompanied by stress relaxation in the viscoelastic upper mantle. The results indicate that the megathrust has already arrived at a locking state today similar to that before the earthquake despite the ongoing stress relaxation. The acquired knowledge aids understanding of megathrust earthquake cycles at other subduction zones.

Article.Title: Stacked porous NiTi structure with low cost and ultrahigh fatigue life for elastocaloric cooling
Article.Authors: Su C.; Li Y.; Deng Z.; Zhong S.; Hu J.; Li X.; Li Q.; Sun Q.
Article.Abstract: Elastocaloric cooling (eC) uses shape memory alloys (SMAs) as energy-efficient, eco-friendly refrigerants. However, cost-effectively fabricating SMAs into fatigue-resistant, heat transfer–enhanced structures remains a key obstacle to commercialization of the eC technology. We introduce a “stamping and stacking” (S-S) method for producing porous, fatigue-resistant SMA structures. Honeycomb-like chips are stamped from nitinol (NiTi) thin sheets and then stacked into a layered tubular structure to increase heat exchange surface and at the same time avoid buckling and splitting failures encountered in existing SMA structures. The stacked structure endures >10 8 compression cycles and can deliver high specific cooling power of 3850 watts per kilogram. Our S-S method reduces fabrication costs by one order of magnitude compared with existing approaches, enabling mass production of eC refrigerant structures for commercial deployment.

Article.Title: The first 1000 days: Modeling language learning from individual children’s everyday speech
Article.Authors: Raviv H.; Tsyhanov A.; Gousios K.; Altenhof A.; Wang H.; Chen B.; Raviv O.; Rosenwein T.; Lew-Williams C.; Hasenfratz L.; Hasson U.
Article.Abstract: Children learn to understand and speak from the speech around them, yet how that everyday input shapes learning remains unresolved. Large language models show that language is learnable from data, but their scale and training conditions differ sharply from a child’s natural experience. We trained cognitively feasible, child-specific models on longitudinal home recordings from eight children across their first 1000 days of life. Each model learned incrementally from a single child’s ordered speech input without prior linguistic knowledge, developing phoneme-like and word-form representations that tracked each child’s learning pace. These findings show that everyday experience contains sufficient structure for language learning and establish child-specific modeling for testing developmental theories.

Article.Title: Obesity management medications: The way forward
Article.Authors: Blüher M.
Article.Abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.

Article.Title: Denoising the US Census: Succinct block hierarchical regression
Article.Authors: Ghazi B.; Kamath P.; Kumar R.; Manurangsi P.; Sealfon* A.
Article.Abstract: The 2020 United States Census adopted differential privacy to protect individual confidentiality, adding calibrated noise to summary demographic measurements that are then reconciled into population tables. We developed BlueDown, a postprocessing algorithm that combines techniques from linear regression and constrained optimization while exploiting measurement structure for efficiency. On 2020 Census data, BlueDown reduced the error of groupings by race at the county level by 21 to 36% and of all county-level groupings by 9 to 58%; at the tract level, it reduced error of groupings by housing type by 38 to 61%. These gains came at no cost to confidentiality or computational efficiency and would improve the validity of research relying on this definitive dataset and analyses used to guide the distribution of more than $1.5 trillion in annual federal spending.

Article.Title: Expanding global access to GLP-1s: Challenges and opportunities
Article.Authors: Shadlen K.; Wouters O.
Article.Abstract: ore than 1 billion people worldwide are obese, and roughly 500 million have type 2 diabetes.These conditions are major risk factors for dementia, heart disease, and various cancers.Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, commonly referred to as GLP-1s, have transformed the treatment of both obesity and type 2 diabetes.Yet despite their promise, global use of these therapies remains uneven.Access has largely been concentrated in high-income countries, even though low-and middle-income countries account for more than 80% of the world's population and a substantial share of the global burden of obesity and type 2 diabetes.Generic versions of the popular GLP-1 drug semaglutide became available in a number of countries in 2026, offering opportunities to substantially expand access.The likely emergence of newer GLP-1s with moredesirable attributes, however, may produce a segmented global market that gives rise to familiar tensions over access to newer, patentprotected therapies.Clinical trials have shown that GLP-1s, part of a broader category of incretin-based therapies, support weight loss, improve glycemic control, and reduce the risk of heart disease (1).Other potential uses are under investigation, including for cardiovascular disorders, neurodegeneration, liver disease, and addiction.The first GLP-1 receptor agonist to be approved in the US for both diabetes and weight management was liraglutide.An earlier drug in this class, exenatide, was approved for diabetes only.Semaglutide, marketed by Novo Nordisk for both diabetes and weight management, revolutionized obesity therapy and, in doing so, became one of the most commercially successful medicines in history (2).Newer incretinbased therapies target multiple gut hormones to produce greater metabolic effects.Tirzepatide, a dual GLP-1 and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist marketed by Eli Lilly, has overtaken semaglutide in prescription volume for both indications in many markets.These medicines are all polypeptides (i.e., amino acid chains) that mimic the natural GLP-1 hormone.In 2026, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved orforglipron, an oral, nonpeptide small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist, for chronic weight management.

Article.Title: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition
Article.Authors: Börchers S.; Mazzini G.; Zetterberg H.; Clemmensen C.
Article.Abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer’s disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)–based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.

Article.Title: Zero-sum mindsets and economic policy preferences
Article.Authors: Rasul I.
Article.Abstract: When economists talk about inclusive growth or shared prosperity, they have in mind economic policies generating widespread gains across individuals in society.For example, economists since Adam Smith have argued there are potentially large gains to be had for society from fostering trading with others.However, for voters to support such 'win-win' policies partly depends on whether they perceive the world in zero-sum terms, where zero-sum thinking (ZST) is the belief that gains for an individual or group necessarily come at the expense of others.The idea originally stems from work by anthropologist George Foster, based on pre-industrial societies with scarce resources.However, work in psychology and economics has established that zero-sum mindsets are also relevant, perhaps increasingly so, for understanding preferences over economic policies in modern times in advanced economies.This has spurred work to understand the prevalence, nature, and malleability of zero-sum mindsets.

Article.Title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
Article.Authors: Running Horse Collin Y.
Article.Abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.

Article.Abstract: Ultracold atom platforms enable low temperatures and long free evolution times, which are crucial for fundamental physics tests and atom interferometry. Article.Authors: Shamshirgar A.; Portugal G.; Ershadrad S.; Ivanov R.; Dahlqvist M.; Chabanais F.; Chakraborty S.; Traksmaa R.; Jussila T.; Karppinen M.; Hussainova I.; Heintz F.; Persson P.; Rosen J.
Article.Abstract: MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. We used machine learning–assisted database mining to uncover hidden multilayer MXenes. Screening reveals 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized MXene candidates. Guided by these findings, we synthesized seven multilayer MXenes using a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature method that requires no sustained external heating and completes within minutes. We further realized 11 previously unexplored rare earth–based MXenes (M = praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, terbium, holmium, and thulium). Experiments and modeling suggest semiconducting behavior and diverse magnetic states across this family. Together, these results expand the MXene family and demonstrate a data-driven strategy for accelerating materials discovery through sustainable methods.

Article.Title: The delocalized nature of chemical bonding at a catalytic metal surface
Article.Authors: Nitz F.; Hörandl S.; Pätzold J.; Kandratsenka A.; Kitsopoulos T.; Auerbach D.; Wodtke A.; Borodin D.
Article.Abstract: Adsorbate bonding at metal surfaces requires hybridization of localized molecular orbitals with delocalized electronic bands of the metal; hence, the electronic wave function involved in bonding may extend far beyond the adsorption site. We revealed the consequence of this delocalization by determining the distance over which structural variations of the metal surface influence the molecule-metal bond strength. Velocity-resolved kinetics provided adsorption energies for three molecules bound at atomic steps of platinum (Pt), each exhibiting bond-strength changes of up to 0.2 electron volts as the step-step distance varied over 100 angstroms. We observed molecule-specific behavior reflecting the hybridization of molecule-specific orbitals with symmetry-selected orbital bands of the metal that respond differently to structural modifications of the solid. We discuss implications of these observations for adsorption on Pt nanoparticles.

Article.Title: When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
Article.Authors: Thorp H.
Article.Abstract: “Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?

Article.Title: Noncoding transcription controls the developmental dynamics of long-range gene regulation
Article.Authors: Batut P.; Levine M.
Article.Abstract: The genomic regions regulating gene expression are often themselves transcribed into a variety of noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs). However, the regulatory roles of this noncoding transcription remain largely unknown. By using live imaging, we reveal that the sequential transcription of ncRNAs emanating from distinct regulatory elements underlies gene activation in Drosophila embryos. Single-allele covisualization uncovers that optimal gene activation is achieved by only moderate levels of enhancer activity. Disrupting enhancer-associated ncRNAs causes precocious gene activation, providing evidence that ncRNAs control the timing of gene expression in development. We further show that enhancer transcription can regulate long-range interactions within complex regulatory landscapes. We propose that ncRNAs locally modulate regulatory element activity in cis to shape genome organization and orchestrate the temporal control of gene expression in development.

Article.Title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Eckmann P.; Miao J.; Mahon A.; Zou J.
Article.Abstract: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type–specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

Article.Title: Safeguarding global terrestrial vertebrate species from future sea level rise
Article.Authors: Jiang Z.; Xiao H.; Hanson J.; Zeng Y.; Wilcove D.; Schuerch M.; Kirwan M.; Yan Q.; Chen Y.; Ma L.
Article.Abstract: Sea level rise (SLR) threatens terrestrial biodiversity, yet its spatiotemporal and species-specific impacts remain unclear. Integrating relative SLR projections across five shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs) with area of habitat (AOH) maps for 34,120 terrestrial vertebrate species, we project that species exposed to SLR will increase from up to 13,680 in 2050 to 15,324 by 2100, including 57 to 63% of birds, 47 to 52% of mammals, 28 to 36% of reptiles, and 20 to 24% of amphibians. In Southeast Asia, inland inundation areas support high richness. Under SSP5-8.5, species facing >10% habitat inundation surge from 18 in 2050 to 109 by 2100, with reptiles and already threatened species overrepresented. Safeguarding SLR refugia—the noninundated habitats for exposed species—is critical, yet more than 96% lie outside protected areas, which means that early international action is required.

Article.Title: Thermodynamic origin of the phonon Hall effect in a honeycomb antiferromagnet
Article.Authors: Meng Q.; Li X.; Liu J.; Zhao L.; Dong C.; Zhu Z.; Li L.; Behnia K.
Article.Abstract: The underlying mechanism of the thermal Hall effect generated by phonons in a variety of insulators is yet to be identified. Article.Authors: Thinel M.; Huang X.; Chica D.; Turkel S.; Rossi S.; Koay C.; Li H.; Mihalyi-Koch W.; Samanta B.; Holbrook M.; Devarakonda A.; Nashabeh L.; Georgescu A.; Roy X.; Zhu X.; Pasupathy A.; Queiroz R.
Article.Abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are quantum states that remain localized despite lying within a continuum of extended, delocalized states. Whereas optical BICs have been realized in photonic systems, achieving electronic bound states embedded in a metallic background remains an ongoing challenge. Article.Authors: Maity D.; Guha Ray P.; Buchmann P.; Charpin-El Hamri G.; Fussenegger M.
Article.Abstract: Lifestyle-related type 2 diabetes and associated obesity (diabesity) affect >2.5 billion people worldwide and impose nearly $3 trillion in annual health care costs. Article.Title: Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet
Article.Authors: Young N.; Miller G.; Raynolds M.; Bueltmann H.; Lehman S.; Raberg J.; Seward K.; Pendleton S.; Andrews J.; Webber P.; Schaefer J.
Article.Abstract: During interglaciations, the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS), which is the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, retreats to Arctic Canada, where it achieves a minimum configuration. The reexpansion of the LIS following this minimum marks the start of the next glaciation. Here, we show that the last remaining remnant of the most recent LIS, Barnes Ice Cap (Baffin Island, Canada), achieved its minimum interglacial dimensions after ~3.6 thousand years ago, before reexpanding ~2000 years ago, marking the onset of the next glaciation. The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate.

Article.Authors: Schmidbauer P.; Nieder A.
Article.Abstract: Perceptual decision-making is well studied in mammals, but its operation in other vertebrates remains unclear. We show that carrion crows ( Corvus corone ) make deliberate decisions in a classic visual motion discrimination task with unprecedented speed, reporting choices in approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy. Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Kang Y.; Feng F.; Hu T.; Xu R.; Yu H.; He K.; Yang Z.; Wang Z.; Lau C.; Low Z.; Gu Q.; Liu J.; Wang H.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Nanochannels capable of fast and selective mass transport are central to applications in energy, resources, biomedicine, and the environment. Article.Abstract: Two-dimensional moiré materials provide a versatile platform to explore phase transitions in strongly correlated systems. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we imaged the density-driven melting of generalized Wigner crystals (GWCs) and Mott insulators (MIs) in electron-doped, near-60°–twisted molybdenum diselenide bilayers featuring a triangular moiré superlattice. We observed notable electron-hole asymmetry in GWC melting: Hole-doped GWCs yielded interaction-driven disordered states, whereas electron-doped GWCs melted into delocalized liquid-like states. This asymmetry arose from the broken particle-hole symmetry of the moiré superlattice, which produced electron and hole Fermi pockets with different momentum geometries upon GWC condensation. MI states melted without such asymmetry, consistent with the absence of a symmetry-breaking density modulation. This work provides direct visualization of the emergent phases that appear as GWCs undergo quantum melting transitions.

Article.Title: Visualizing symmetry-broken Chern insulators and their quantum melting

Article.Abstract: In the presence of a magnetic field, electronic states of moiré quantum materials develop a Hofstadter spectrum that provides a distinctive setting for studying the interplay between band topology and strong electron-electron interaction. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we studied Hofstadter’s states in bilayer graphene aligned with hexagonal boron nitride and directly visualized the formation of interaction-driven symmetry breaking Chern insulators. Our measurements revealed the formation of phases that double, triple, or quadruple the moiré unit cell at fractional filling of the Hofstadter bands as well as states with complex intra–unit cell wave functions. We visualized two distinct quantum phenomena in different Chern states, including quantum melting driven by the appearance and proliferation of topological defects and a quantum transition co-occurring with phase competition and separation.

Article.Abstract: The power conversion efficiency (PCE) and stability of flexible perovskite solar modules (PSMs) are less than those of their rigid devices because surface hydroxyls desorption on flexible substrates, which disrupts self-assembled monolayer (SAM) anchoring and perovskite crystallization. Article.Title: The many facets of human brain asymmetry
Article.Authors: Wang M.; Kong X.; Luders E.; Fisher S.; Thompson P.; Francks C.
Article.Abstract: Asymmetry on the left-right axis is an organizing principle of the human brain that is important for diverse cognitive and behavioural functions. Advances in neuroimage analysis, genomics and large-scale data collection in the past decade have transformed our understanding of the biological foundations and multivariate nature of brain asymmetry. In this Review, we synthesize evidence across scales - from functional and macro-anatomical asymmetries and their inter-relations to microstructural, cellular and molecular levels. We examine inter-individual variation and atypical forms of brain asymmetry, which reveal that diverse aspects of asymmetry can vary largely independently across individuals rather than constituting a single trait. In this context, we discuss the developmental origins, lifespan trajectories and genetic architecture of hemispheric differences. We also summarize the relevance of brain asymmetry for neurological and psychiatric disorders and evolutionary changes of brain asymmetry that occurred in humans. Through this synthesis, we illustrate how contrasting the left and right hemispheres provides an informative window into the multi-level brain organization that supports cognition and behaviour.

Article.Title: The neuroscience of delirium: a perfect storm for acute brain dysfunction
Article.Authors: Cunningham C.; Kimchi E.
Article.Abstract: Delirium is a frequent and distressing neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by acute disturbances of attention, awareness and cognition. Delirium emerges in response to diverse medical insults, particularly in hospitalized patients. Despite its high prevalence and association with accelerated cognitive decline, dementia and mortality, the neurobiology of delirium remains incompletely understood, and there are no treatments for delirium. Evidence from electrophysiology, neuroimaging, biomarkers and emerging animal models has begun to clarify the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying delirium. Delirium can be conceptualized as the interaction of acute systemic or cerebral stressors with pre-existing vulnerabilities, creating a 'perfect storm' for brain dysfunction. Generalized electroencephalographic slowing and network disintegration are convergent signatures across diverse types of delirium. Disruptions in neuromodulatory systems, energy metabolism and neuroimmune signalling may underlie impairment of large-scale brain function. The mechanisms that drive acute delirium may also contribute to subsequent brain injury and long-term decline, compounding its broad personal and societal impact.

Article.Title: The cortico-basal ganglia–thalamic network: a connectomic framework
Article.Authors: Dong H.; Foster N.; Hintiryan H.
Article.Abstract: Classical anatomical and physiological studies have established the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic (CBGT) system as a set of topographically organized, functionally specialized circuits that link the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia and thalamus while allowing convergence and interaction between information streams. Recent advances in mesoscale and single-neuron connectomics now enable these organizational principles to be resolved at unprecedented spatial and cellular scales. Here we synthesize the findings of recent connectomic studies of the CBGT network to define an emerging structural and network framework. Modern connectomic data reveal how parallel processing and information integration are implemented through a multiscale architecture characterized by modular organization, graded and overlapping boundaries, stage-specific patterns of segregation and convergence, and re-entrant interactions among cortical, basal ganglia, thalamic and brainstem nodes. Molecular, transcriptomic and neuronal morphological datasets further reveal spatial heterogeneity that broadly aligns with this connectivity-defined organization. This structural framework provides a foundation for understanding how CBGT networks preserve functional specialization while enabling cross-domain integration and generates testable hypotheses about the links between circuit architecture and neural computation, behaviour and dysfunction in neurological and psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Network approaches to community detection in nanoscale connectomics
Article.Authors: Wang Q.; Gutierrez G.; Kunin A.; Vogelstein J.; Bassler K.; Josić K.; Betzel R.
Article.Abstract: Although network science has offered insight into the organization and function of nervous systems, much of this work has focused on mesoscale, interareal connectomes. This leaves open the question of whether similar organizational principles apply to nanoscale connectomes, where individual neurons and synapses are the focus. These neuron-level datasets are uniquely complex, necessitating the refinement of existing tools and the development of new ones to handle their distinctive structure. Network science offers a range of approaches for analysing these data. Here, we focus on community detection, a family of methods for identifying subnetworks of functionally related neurons. We suggest that finding such communities could be valuable for several reasons: they could help us understand how modular organization supports adaptability and specialization, serve as a method for dimension reduction, and potentially aid in the discovery of new functional circuits. Article.Title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of cellular heterogeneity in Alzheimer disease
Article.Authors: Emerson N.; Vallejo K.; Rahimzadeh N.; Kwang N.; Swarup V.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is defined neuropathologically by the presence of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, yet these canonical lesions alone cannot account for its clinical, regional and cellular heterogeneity. AD is a multicellular, spatially organized disease shaped by the interactions of neurons, glia and vascular cells within distinct anatomical microenvironments. Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing have made it possible to dissect the transcriptional signatures of individual cell populations in the AD brain, revealing selective neuronal vulnerability, stage-dependent glial remodelling and widespread disruption of cell-cell communication networks, whereas spatial transcriptomics and multiplexed imaging have anchored these molecular changes to their tissue context. Studies of defined populations, such as people with autosomal-dominant AD or Down syndrome-associated AD, and of the oldest-old cohorts help disentangle the molecular changes that are causal drivers from those that are downstream consequences. Across individuals, AD heterogeneity is further shaped by sex and ancestry, underscoring the need for broader representation of these factors in single-cell and spatial studies. These advances are also reshaping translational pipelines through multi-omic benchmarking of animal models and single-cell-based drug-repurposing strategies. Thus, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are redefining our understanding of AD heterogeneity and informing precision approaches to treatment.

Article.Title: The nanotubular network as a new dimension of intercellular communication in the nervous system
Article.Authors: Chang M.; Ryu S.; Kwon H.
Article.Abstract: Communication between cells in the nervous system has long been understood to occur through chemical and electrical synapses, and through the release of signalling molecules and extracellular vesicles across the extracellular space. Intercellular nanotubes (NTs) - thin, membranous tubular bridges that physically connect distant cells - represent a structurally distinct route of communication, enabling the direct, targeted transfer of cellular cargoes between selected cells. Once studied almost exclusively in culture, NTs have now been visualized in situ and in vivo throughout the nervous system, including dendritic NTs between neurons, NTs formed by microglia and astrocytes, interpericyte NTs in the retina and NTs between satellite glia and peripheral sensory neurons. Through these connections, cells exchange mitochondria, proteins and their aggregates, and calcium, supporting three emerging roles: homeostatic rescue of stressed cells, pathological propagation of toxic proteins in neurodegeneration and non-synaptic calcium signalling, respectively. NT networks are dynamic and stress-responsive, suggesting that they provide a plastic infrastructure for resource sharing among neurons and glia. Understanding their function will require establishing a standardized definition, achieving rigorous in situ validation and quantification, and developing specific molecular tools to manipulate NTs.

Article.Title: Interneurons and network activity in the cerebral cortex: a developmental dialogue
Article.Authors: Moissidis M.; Marín O.
Article.Abstract: The mammalian cerebral cortex undergoes profound functional changes during early postnatal development. During this period, neurons generate spontaneous electrical activity long before sensory experience, coordinating into distinct patterns of synchronous activity. Traditionally, neuronal activity has been viewed as instructing interneuron development by modulating transcriptional programmes, morphology and connectivity. However, accumulating evidence in rodents reveals that this relationship is bidirectional: cortical interneurons are not merely passive recipients of activity-dependent signals but also active architects of developing network dynamics. They regulate spontaneous activity transitions from gap-junction-mediated synchronous events to large, synaptically driven bursts, and later to sparse firing characteristic of mature circuits. Critically, different interneuron subtypes mature at distinct timelines and orchestrate transitions in network activity. Activity-dependent mechanisms, in turn, regulate interneuron wiring, programmed cell death, diversification and terminal differentiation. This reciprocal dialogue between interneurons and network activity is essential for establishing functional cortical circuits.
