Article.Title: PANGEA: an integrated cell atlas across diverse biological contexts enables systematic profiling of multicellular responses in human diseases
Article.Authors: Kim S.; Cheong S.; Lee S.; Kim Y.; Xie R.; Koh I.; La J.; Hwa C.; An H.; Park J.; An J.; Wang B.; Park J.
Article.Abstract: Diseases affect multiple cell types within tissues, but the overall landscape of the multicellular responses in human diseases remains largely unexplored. Here we categorize the multicellular responses of human diseases based on a remapped atlas of human cells, PANGEA, incorporating 12.6 million cells acquired from a pipeline that automatically processes raw sequence files from public repositories. We constructed a hierarchical cell classification framework comprising 32 major cell types and 165 cellular subtypes. On the basis of this annotation framework, we explored an extensive atlas of human cells containing 46.5 million cells from 160 diseases across 48 organs and revealed core archetypes of human diseases repeatedly found across organs. We show that this cell atlas could also serve as a reference for unbiased analysis in spatial transcriptomics, revealing spatial features associated with immunotherapy responses. Collectively, our study provides foundational resources for cell ontologies, enabling cross-tissue comparisons of cellular features in human diseases.

Article.Title: Advancing multimodal tools to decode organoid complexity
Article.Authors: Reynolds D.; Morales R.; Vallapureddy P.; Kumar S.; Huynh E.; Messerschmidt C.; Hornet V.; Lim J.; Roh Y.; Lutolf M.; Ko J.
Article.Abstract: Organoids are complex, miniaturized three-dimensional structures that replicate key biological features and functions of human tissues and organs. These characteristics make them powerful model systems for investigating tissue and organ development, homeostasis and regeneration; understanding disease mechanisms; and advancing drug development and personalized medicine. To fully harness their potential, it is essential to develop advanced tools capable of comprehensively profiling their intricate composition. In particular, cutting-edge technologies are needed to accurately characterize their genotypic and phenotypic profiles, including DNA, RNA, proteins and physiological functions. In this Review, we examine molecular and functional profiling methods for organoids, providing an overview of emerging techniques, recent advancements, future technologies, key knowledge gaps and challenges, and a framework for multimodal integration of methods. Additionally, we examine current barriers to progress and explore opportunities to refine organoid profiling methods with the aim of deepening our understanding of organoid biology.

Article.Title: In situ profiling of plasma cell clonality with image-based single-cell transcriptomics
Article.Authors: Yang E.; Aceves-Salvador J.; Castrillon C.; Herrmann U.; Akama-Garren E.; Carroll M.; Moffitt J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Image-based single-cell transcriptomics can identify diverse cell types in intact tissues. However, in adaptive immunity, V(D)J recombination generates unique immune receptors in cells of the same type, leading to important functional variation that is not yet defined by these methods. Here we introduce B cell receptor multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (BCR-MERFISH), which measures plasma cell clonality based on V gene usage in combination with transcriptome profiling. We demonstrate that BCR-MERFISH accurately identifies V gene usage in cell culture and in mice with restricted or native plasma cell diversity. We then use BCR-MERFISH to elucidate the microbiota-dependent changes in plasma cell abundance, clonal diversity, and public clonotype usage in the mouse gut and the non-uniform distribution of plasma cell clones along the mouse ileum. Given that tissue context is an essential modulator of plasma cell dynamics, we anticipate that BCR-MERFISH may offer new insights into a wide range of immunological questions.

Article.Title: Deciphering the gene-centric spatial dynamics across tissue and time with GeneSPOT
Article.Authors: Zou Q.; Wang Z.; Li S.; Lin S.; Han C.; Cui Y.; Li S.; Wang L.; Zhang D.; Zhang W.; Qian B.; Gao R.; Yuan Z.
Article.Abstract: Spatial omics technologies provide unprecedented opportunities to investigate how molecular programs are organized within tissues. However, existing analytical frameworks primarily focus on identifying cellular states and characterizing differentially expressed molecular features across these states. The relational spatial organization of molecular features and its dynamics across biological contexts therefore remain largely unexplored. Here we present Gene SPatial Optimal Transport (GeneSPOT), a gene-centric computational framework for characterizing the spatial relationships among genes and quantifying their reorganization across biological conditions. Although gene-centric in design, GeneSPOT generalizes to other molecular features. Across diverse applications, GeneSPOT resolved tissue structures, integrated paired and unpaired spatial multi-omics data, unveiled the spatial convergence of gene programs during embryonic development and identified aging-associated spatial reorganization among genes whose expression did not change significantly with age. GeneSPOT thus complements conventional cell-centric analysis, providing a framework for deciphering how spatial relationships among molecular features are reorganized across biological conditions and over time.

Article.Title: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC
Article.Authors: Xu C.; Liu S.; Heng Y.; Yang C.; Cao Y.; Gao J.; Wei S.; Jia D.; Liang D.; Ma Y.; Ng S.; Li H.; Zhang X.; Gong Y.; Shen H.; Deng H.; Chen A.; Xu X.; Liao S.; Jiang Q.; Liu B.
Article.Abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies measure multiple molecular layers within intact tissues. Two central challenges are vertical integration, which combines different molecular modalities, and horizontal integration, which aligns cell types across studies. Here we show domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration (DIRAC), a geometric deep learning model that unifies these tasks in a generalized domain adaptation framework. DIRAC learns task-discriminative features that are insensitive to domain shifts caused by batch effects, omic modalities or study sites, enabling a shared embedding space and automated cell-type annotation through label transfer from reference datasets. Across sequencing-based and imaging-based datasets, DIRAC identified a new microvascular proliferation domain in glioblastoma, corrected cortical-layer annotations in severe Alzheimer's disease, resolved subtle structures in mouse embryos and remained robust to missing data and unseen cell types. We generated mouse spleen and thymus Stereo-CITE-seq data and used DIRAC to reveal thymic T cell migration and splenic immune cell interactions. DIRAC is fast and scales to millions of cells.

Article.Title: Automated identification of individual birds by song enables multi-year recapture from passive acoustic monitoring data
Article.Authors: Lapp S.; Lyon R.; Wilson S.; Rhinehart T.; Czarnecki C.; Chronister L.; Fiss C.; Larkin J.; Bayne E.; Kitzes J.
Article.Abstract: Autonomous sensors and machine learning are transforming ecology by enabling large-scale observation of organisms and ecosystems. However, camera traps, audio recorders and other sensors currently produce species-level detections. Tracking individuals continues to require invasive, high-effort capture-mark-recapture. Here we introduce an automated, general approach that identifies individual animals in passive acoustic recordings based on individually distinctive vocalizations. We train a convolutional neural network to extract salient features from audio recordings using a location-prediction task, then apply dimensionality reduction and clustering on features to achieve song-based individual identification. We identify individuals not included in the training data with 96% accuracy. We apply this approach to track 405 male ovenbirds (Seiurus aurocapilla) from 126 locations across 4 years, then model abundance and apparent survival. We provide open-source code to facilitate applications of our approach to other species. Performing automated individual identification on passive acoustic datasets will support the study of population trajectories and inform proactive ecosystem management to prevent biodiversity loss.

Article.Title: abcFISH enables multiplexed, single-molecule visualization of circular RNA spatial heterogeneity
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Jiang B.; Liu K.; Yang L.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the subcellular localization of RNAs is critical for their functions, but visualizing circular RNAs (circRNAs) has been hindered by their sequence overlap with linear counterparts. Here we developed amplicon-based circRNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (abcFISH), which uses an optimized rolling-circle amplification strategy targeting back-splicing junction sites for robust, high specificity, single-molecule circRNA imaging. abcFISH enables quantitative, multiplexed imaging in cells and tissues, allowing us to reveal alternative circularization patterns from the single locus, uncover cell-type-specific circRNA expression linked to combinatorial effects of RNA-binding proteins, map distinct spatial distribution patterns of circRNAs in neurons and brain tissues, and show functional colocalization of circRNA Cdr1as and long noncoding RNA Cyrano. We further applied abcFISH to validate therapeutic double-stranded circRNA aptamers, simultaneously visualizing AAV-delivered double-stranded circRNA aptamers and the resulting reduction in astrocyte infiltration around transduced cells. Collectively, abcFISH provides a robust, user-friendly toolkit for deciphering circRNA localization and function in vivo.

Article.Title: Limitations of de novo peptide sequencing in resolving sequence ambiguity
Article.Authors: van Puyenbroeck S.; Beslic D.; Suomi T.; Holstein T.; Muth T.; Elo L.; Martens L.; Bouwmeester R.; Van Den Bossche T.; Claeys T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract De novo peptide sequencing enables peptide identification from fragmentation spectra without relying on sequence databases. However, incomplete spectra create ambiguity, making unambiguous identification challenging. Recent deep learning advances have produced numerous de novo models that predict sequences and refine peptide-spectrum matches under such conditions. Yet, their relative strengths, weaknesses and ability to handle spectrum ambiguity remain unclear. Here we benchmark eight state-of-the-art models on three publicly available proteomics datasets, comparing performance using established metrics and quantifying inter-model agreement. We assess post-processing approaches, including iterative refinement, rescoring and reranking, for their ability to improve identification accuracy, and perform an error analysis to identify common mispredictions and their causes. Model performance varied, with considerable overlap of correct identifications. Post-processing yielded no or only modest improvements. Most sequencing errors were model-independent and driven by limited fragment ion coverage, a limitation also observed in database searches with large search spaces.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: de novo peptide sequencing; model benchmarking; peptide identification; error analysis; post-processing

Article.Title: Head-mounted camera for reconstructing outdoor behavior in freely flying birds
Article.Authors: Voit K.; Sawinski J.; Klioutchnikov A.; Junker K.; Cheekoti A.; Wallace D.; Stahr P.; Matheson E.; Gill L.; Fischer D.; Kerr J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Capturing the fine details of behavior when animals perform complex tasks, such as prey pursuit and capture, in natural environments is a challenging endeavor. For birds of prey, commonly used tracking approaches, such as lightweight GPS and inertial measurement units, cannot simultaneously track the bird’s position and the fine details of body part motion or moving external objects. Here we designed a head-mounted, tetherless, 4π camera system which, combined with a high-resolution environmental scan, enabled detailed three-dimensional measurement of both head position and orientation in freely flying Harris’s hawks ( Parabuteo unicinctus ) performing aerial pursuit in the wild. This stable head-mounted imaging approach enabled reconstruction of flight trajectories in natural environments, detailed quantification of head motion, optic flow and target position, while the bird tracked and captured airborne targets.

Article.Title: Selective profiling of translationally active tRNAs and their dynamics under stress
Article.Authors: Monti M.; Yilmaz H.; Del Piano A.; Arnoldi M.; Bonomo I.; Llovera L.; Sarabando J.; Ribeiro D.; Soares A.; Clamer M.; Novoa E.
Article.Abstract: During translation, transfer RNAs (tRNAs) deliver specific amino acids to the ribosome in a coordinated manner with the sequence encoded by the messenger RNA. Despite their central role in protein synthesis, their precise contribution to the modulation of translation remains poorly understood, primarily due to lack of methods to characterize tRNA abundances and their modifications from actively translating ribosomes. Here we develop tRIBO-seq, a simple and robust nanopore-based method to selectively capture ribosome-associated native tRNA populations (ribo-tRNAs) from actively translating ribosomes, providing tRNA abundance, modification and fragmentation information from a single experiment. Using tRIBO-seq, we find that ribo-tRNAs, but often not total tRNAs, are significantly altered on stress. Notably, we find that tRNAome alterations strongly vary depending on the stress type; while viral infection and leucine deprivation leads to changes in ribo-tRNA abundances, methionine starvation causes a dramatic loss of methyl-based tRNA modifications. By contrast, we find that arsenite exposure does not alter tRNA abundances nor modification patterns, but rather causes major fragmentation events in selected subsets of ribo-tRNAs. Altogether, tRIBO-seq offers a robust and reproducible approach to map the full tRNA landscape-capturing tRNA abundance, modification and fragmentation patterns-across both total and actively translating tRNA populations, revealing the dynamics of the tRNAome with unprecedented resolution, in a single experiment.

Article.Title: RobPicker: a meta-learning framework for robust identification of macromolecules in cryo-electron tomograms
Article.Authors: Liang Y.; Hosseini R.; Rahmani H.; Singh D.; Zhang R.; Zhang L.; Guo H.; Choe S.; Lee J.; Xu M.; Segal E.; Zou J.; Williamson J.; Villa E.; Grotjahn D.; Xie P.
Article.Abstract: Accurate particle picking of macromolecules of diverse types, shapes and sizes in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is critical for understanding the molecular architecture of biological systems in their native state. Current deep learning methods have shown potential for identifying macromolecules in tomograms; however, they are vulnerable to annotation noise in the training data and to imbalanced distributions of macromolecule species. Here, to address these limitations, we developed RobPicker, a meta-learning framework that effectively mitigates these issues by automatically learning to correct label errors and by placing greater emphasis on smaller and rarer macromolecule species. In evaluations across diverse cryo-ET datasets with noisy labels and imbalanced species distributions, RobPicker substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in identifying small and rare macromolecules. The robustness and efficiency of RobPicker led to improved resolution in 3D density maps of protein structures, enabling high-resolution cellular structural biology analysis.

Article.Title: Nondisruptive 3D profiling of combinations of epigenetic marks in single cells
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Radda J.; Alderman M.; Jin S.; Cheng Y.; Zhang Y.; Liu M.; Xiao A.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: Advances in single-cell sequencing and spatial omics technologies have enhanced our understanding of diverse cellular identities, compositions, architectures and functions. However, the single-cell three-dimensional (3D) organization of the epigenome is still not well understood, due to an absence of spatial single-cell methods that allow high-resolution, locus-specific detection of combinations of epigenetic marks while maintaining 3D genome organization. Here we develop epigenetic proximity hybridization reaction (Epi-PHR), a nondisruptive image-based single-cell spatial epigenetic profiling technology. Epi-PHR detects combinations of epigenetic marks in situ at hundreds of gene targets within single cells while preserving 3D genome organization. Phased Epi-PHR combined with chromatin tracing reveals unexpected associations between epigenetic mark enrichment and chromatin folding of an imprinted gene cluster at the single-chromatin-copy level for the distinct alleles from different parental origins. We expect Epi-PHR will be broadly applicable in research requiring single-cell spatial epigenetic information, advancing our understanding of the combinatorial epigenetic code and its relationship with chromatin organization.

Article.Title: Spatial single-cell mapping of transcriptional differences across genetic backgrounds in mouse brains
Article.Authors: Hemminger Z.; Tam G.; De Ocampo H.; Wang A.; Underwood T.; Xie F.; Zhao Q.; Song D.; Li J.; Dong H.; Wollman R.
Article.Abstract: Genetic variation can alter organ structure and function. Comparative statistical analysis of organs across genetic backgrounds requires spatial, single-cell, atlas-scale data in replicates. Here we introduce atlas-scale transcriptome localization using aggregate signatures (ATLAS), a scalable tissue mapping method that learns transcriptional signatures from single-cell RNA sequencing data, encodes them in situ with tens of thousands of oligonucleotide probes and decodes them to infer cell types and imputed transcriptomes. We validated ATLAS against direct MERFISH measurements of marker genes and through quantitative comparisons to four other technologies. We profiled 40 million cells across more than 400 coronal sections from central brains of five male and five female C57BL/6J mice and five male BTBR T+tf/J mice, an idiopathic autism model. Our analysis revealed more than 40 significant differences in cell-type distributions and identified 16 regional composition changes across male-female and B6-BTBR comparisons. ATLAS thus enables systematic comparative studies, facilitating organ-level structure-function analysis of disease models.

Article.Title: Enhanced cfDNA methylation profiling by detection and correction of jagged ends
Article.Authors: Wang R.; Hamilton E.; Almanza D.; Bonilla R.; Sugio T.; Hui A.; Tian F.; Phillips N.; Liu C.; Yoo C.; Alig S.; Rossi C.; Juul N.; Chen E.; Liu K.; Shen E.; Shi W.; Olsen M.; Kang X.; Nair V.; Wakelee H.; Shrager J.; Shi S.; Desai T.; Esfahani M.
Article.Abstract: Analysis of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation can enable noninvasive disease detection by leveraging tissue-specific epigenetic differences between malignant and nonmalignant cells. However, such analyses can be confounded by the repair of jagged DNA fragment ends during double-stranded sequencing library preparation, which introduces spurious methylation signals into cfDNA molecules. Here we present JEEPERS, a framework to detect and correct jagged-end-induced methylation errors while preserving duplex integrity and native methylation patterns. We showed high fidelity for measuring tumor burden and demonstrated allele-specific methylation differences at recurrent somatic mutations, revealing a link between adjacent CpG methylation and EGFR/TP53 driver and resistance mutations. We further demonstrated enhanced diagnostic performance across liquid biopsy applications, including tumor-type-specific methylation profiles, hemimethylation profiling, epigenetic-clock-based age estimation and cell type deconvolution. By faithfully correcting end-repair errors, JEEPERS provides a versatile framework for integrating mutations and methylation features in cfDNA at high resolution, enabling more precise molecular profiling and disease monitoring.

Article.Title: Advancing morphological profiling with self-supervised learning through comparative insights into representation learning of cellular perturbations
Article.Authors: Abdelmoula W.; Albuquerque T.; Jaensch S.; Pati P.; Van Dyck M.; Allen S.; Zhang L.; Mansi T.; Liao R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Self-supervised learning (SSL) enables scalable, label-free foundation models (FMs) that learn task-agnostic representations directly from images, bypassing cell segmentation and feature engineering inherent to classical morphological profiling. Here we show that top-performing SSL models outperformed CellProfiler in compound-replicate retrieval on the held-out JUMP–Target2 set (302 annotated compounds, P ≤ 0.001). DINO and DINOv2 generalized across diverse perturbations and cell types, outperforming CellProfiler with 31–37% gains in site-averaged mean average precision for mechanism-of-action retrieval on EU-OPENSCREEN Bioactives (2,464 compounds), and consistently surpassing masked-based models across all benchmarks. This study provides a systematic assessment of SSL approaches for advancing morphological profiling and offers pretrained FMs to accelerate drug discovery.

Article.Title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain
Article.Authors: Santra K.; Barber K.; Logiacco F.; Frechou M.; Bellafard A.; Liou J.; Vaziri A.
Article.Abstract: Extending the depth reach of multiphoton microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an 'exponentially hard' problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain; however, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal. Here we demonstrate a three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and nonlinear limits for safe laser exposure while satisfying the spatiotemporal requirements of single-cell resolution calcium (Ca2+) imaging. TrUDI achieves a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photon yield at the same laser power as in previous approaches thereby enabling in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 × 230 µm2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

Article.Title: Aptamer-mediated multivalent endogenous ADAR1 recruitment for highly efficient RNA editing
Article.Authors: Zhu H.; Zhou Y.; Huang R.; Wang Y.; Hu Y.; Wang L.; Jin J.; Ye Q.; Liu X.; Wang Z.; Xie H.; Li J.; Pang D.; Liu S.
Article.Abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing mediated by endogenous ADAR enzymes represents a promising therapeutic strategy because it can correct mutations at the transcript level without inducing permanent changes to the genome. However, existing systems face challenges, particularly the limited editing efficiency, which limits their practical applications. Here we introduce MARRS (multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system)-an efficient and specific RNA editing platform that leverages engineered multivalent RNA aptamers to robustly recruit endogenous ADAR1 enzymes. MARRS also exhibits remarkable versatility across a range of transcript targets while maintaining high specificity with minimal off-target effects. Operating without the need for exogenous enzymes, the MARRS system offers a safe, efficient and programmable platform.

Article.Title: Benchmarking segmentation methods for spatial transcriptomics
Article.Authors: Martínez-de-Morentin X.; Khan S.; Maillo A.; Lehmann R.; Kiani N.; Lagani V.; Gomez-Cabrero D.; Tegner J.
Article.Abstract: Cell segmentation is a critical yet under-standardized step in spatial transcriptomics, directly affecting cell identity assignment, spatial organization and downstream biological interpretation. Despite rapid advances in spatial transcriptomics technologies, systematic evaluations of segmentation methods across platforms and biological contexts remain limited. We introduce biologically informed evaluation metrics that quantify segmentation quality, transcript recovery, cell composition, morphology, expression purity and spatial organization. Article.Title: CauTrigger: deciphering biological system state transitions by hierarchical causal decomposition
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Cai D.; Aihara K.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Biological systems exhibit complex hierarchical regulation, with interactions across multiple layers governing transitions between states. Identifying the causal architecture underlying these state transitions remains challenging because confounding can produce spurious associations in observational data. Here we present CauTrigger, a hierarchical deep latent variable model that integrates do-calculus to identify potential causal triggers and predict perturbation outcomes across multiple regulatory layers. By disentangling causal and spurious latent factors, CauTrigger recursively reconstructs the underlying regulatory hierarchy and enables interpretable reasoning from observational data. Across synthetic and real-world datasets with multilayer regulatory structures, CauTrigger outperforms existing methods in identifying causal triggers and forecasting system-level responses. Applied to single-cell multi-omics and gut microbiome datasets, CauTrigger prioritizes candidate causal triggers and uses in silico perturbations to generate testable hypotheses about biological state transitions and inform potential strategies for state navigation. Together, these results establish CauTrigger as a general-purpose framework for causal discovery in complex biological systems.

OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. Article.Title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism

Article.Title: Gene discovery and pleiotropic architecture of multidimensional pain in a genome-wide association study of >1.2 million individuals
Article.Authors: Toikumo S.; Davis C.; Jinwala Z.; Khan Y.; Jennings M.; Davis L.; Sanchez-Roige S.; Kember R.; Kranzler H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chronic pain is highly prevalent worldwide, yet its genetic architecture remains to be fully elucidated. Here we leveraged data from 1,235,695 European-ancestry individuals across three biobanks. In a meta-analytic genome-wide association study of multidimensional pain (MP), we identified 343 independent loci, 92 of which were new pain associations. Sex-specific meta-analyses revealed 115 independent loci (12 of which were new) among males ( n = 583,066) and 12 loci (2 of which were new) among females ( n = 241,266). Multi-omic gene prioritization analyses highlighted 490 genes associated with MP through their effects on brain-specific and blood-specific regulation. Mendelian randomization analyses showed causal associations between MP and psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders and C-reactive protein levels. MP variants also showed pleiotropic associations with several brain imaging-derived phenotypes. This study expands our knowledge of the genetics of pain and its pathogenesis, highlighting the importance of its pleiotropy with multiple disorders and elucidating its multi-omic pathophysiology.

Article.Title: Information formatting in neuronal populations predicts differential functional contributions to behavior
Article.Authors: Ruff D.; Markman S.; Kim J.; Cohen M.
Article.Abstract: Neurons throughout the brain encode essentially everything, so why have distinct areas? We proposed that areas format different information sources differently, implying their computational role. In a task that required monkeys to combine motion and reward information, both regions encoded both motion and reward, but formatted differently. A recurrent network model trained to reproduce that formatting predicted a distinct effect of stimulating those areas. Consistent with predictions, MT stimulation biased choices whereas dlPFC stimulation produced 'winner-take-all' outcomes. Our findings suggest that a modular structure flexibly reformats information to enable complex behaviors.

Article.Title: Single-neuron encoding of rapidly learned visual information reshapes human perception
Article.Authors: Armendariz M.; Blumberg J.; Singer J.; Aiple F.; Kim J.; Domínguez-Iturza N.; Brandt A.; Reinacher P.; Schulze-Bonhage A.; Kreiman G.
Article.Abstract: Humans can swiftly learn to recognize visual objects after minimal exposure. Integrating new information with existing knowledge requires forming enduring neuronal representations to enable future recognition. Yet, the neuronal mechanisms in the human brain underlying such rapid perceptual changes remain unclear. Here we recorded single-neuron activity in occipital cortex (OC) and medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions as participants rapidly learned to recognize degraded images. Population decoding revealed that OC neurons required additional processing time to resolve the identity of learned images, with delayed neuronal responses in the MTL. These results provide mechanistic constraints for biologically plausible models of visual recognition and few-shot visual learning.

Article.Authors: Lu O.; White K.; Raymond K.; Liu C.; Klein A.; Green N.; Vaillancourt S.; Gallagher A.; Shindy L.; Li A.; Wallquist K.; Li R.; Zou M.; Casey A.; Perez N.; Asim M.; Metanat S.; Logas K.; Chhaya V.; Enos A.; Ho E.; Cameron L.; Pomrenze M.; Tucciarone J.; Sohal V.

Article.Title: Serotonin signaling enhances phagocytosis by brain macrophages through Htr2b and alleviates brain injury after stroke
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Chen Y.; Cheng Y.; Li R.; Chen W.; Li Y.; Fan Q.; Zhou Y.; Huang T.; Xie W.; Guo Y.; Liesz A.; Wan J.; Ginhoux F.; Li P.
Article.Abstract: Brain myeloid cells, including infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) and microglia, play critical roles in ischemic brain injury, clearing debris and shaping neuroinflammation and neurological outcomes. Article.Abstract: Controlling whether an experience is encoded into long-term memory and thus later remembered is a crucial aspect of memory. Article.Title: Circuit mechanisms for disentangled representations and generalization in the hippocampus
Article.Authors: Tang W.; Chang H.; Liu C.; Perez-Hernandez S.; Zheng W.; Park J.; Karaba L.; Oliva A.; Fernandez-Ruiz A.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how the heterogeneous activity patterns of individual neurons give rise to coherent population dynamics and cognition is a central challenge in neuroscience. The temporal and contextual components of these representations are governed by local inhibitory interactions and input-driven cell-assembly dynamics, respectively. Our findings reveal the circuit basis of disentangled hippocampal representations, offering a unifying geometric principle of population coding that supports flexible memory representations and enables rapid generalization of prior knowledge to new situations.

Article.Title: Microglial NUS1 deficiency drives dopaminergic neurodegeneration through intercellular iron dysregulation in Parkinson’s disease models
Article.Authors: Liu L.; Hong Y.; Wang X.; Huang X.; Ma Y.; Wang R.; Sun Q.; Sun H.; Hao Z.; Mu C.; Lu X.; Hu L.; Guo J.; Tang B.; Wang G.; Ren H.

Article.Title: Sustained antidepressant-like effects of psychedelics through 5-HT2AR–β-arrestin signaling
Article.Authors: He L.; Tang L.; Cao D.; Duan W.; Yu J.; Zhang P.; Li H.; Wang Y.; Meng B.; Wang H.; Zhou Y.; Li W.; Li X.; Liu Z.; Zhang L.; Cheng J.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: Psychedelics produce long-lasting antidepressant effects, but their hallucinogenic properties limit clinical use. Using structure-guided design of 5-HT2AR-β-arrestin-biased agonists, we identified β-arrestin signaling as a critical driver of prolonged antidepressant-like effects in mice. Here we show that the slow-dissociation kinetics of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) enable progressive accumulation of 5-HT2AR engagement during repeated low-dose administration, approaching the receptor occupancy achieved by an acute high dose while avoiding its high peak concentration. This kinetic separation sustains β-arrestin signaling while limiting robust Gαq-mediated Ca2+ responses. Consistent with this framework, repeated low-dose LSD and repeated low-dose psilocybin pretreatment followed by a high-dose psychedelic challenge produced sustained antidepressant-like behavioral effects in mice. In parallel, these regimens produced no detectable psychedelic-associated behavioral disruption in mice and cynomolgus macaques. Together, these findings uncover the signaling basis of sustained psychedelic efficacy and provide a rational framework for developing nonhallucinogenic psychedelic therapies for psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Behavioral genomics identifies Creld1 as a cross-modal regulator of somatosensation
Article.Authors: Jiang Y.; Huang W.; Yao H.; Chen Y.; Bi C.; Ye T.; Wang S.; Yin H.; Cui Y.; Xiao B.
Article.Abstract: Somatosensation is mediated by dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, which convert physical and chemical stimuli into electrical signals. However, the full repertoire of molecular components underlying somatosensation remains incompletely identified. Here we developed an efficient postnatal CRISPR-Cas9 knockout platform for interrogating DRG-expressed genes (such as Piezo2, Trpv1 and Scn9a) in mice using AAV9-mediated single-guide RNA delivery. Combining this approach with somatosensory behavioral assays, we performed a targeted screen of 20 genes and identified Creld1 as a cross-model regulator of somatosensation. Either single-guide RNA-mediated postnatal knockout or tamoxifen-induced Cre-mediated deletion of Creld1 in DRG neurons resulted in profound behavioral deficits in touch, temperature, pain and itch, whereas its overexpression enhanced touch and thermal responses. Mechanistically, CRELD1 functions as an auxiliary regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) for controlling DRG neuron excitability. Together, this work establishes a robust postnatal screening platform for behavioral genomics and identifies Creld1 as a master regulator of somatosensory function.

Article.Title: Network geometry shapes the transformation of task representations across the human cortex
Article.Authors: Chakravarthula L.; Ito T.; Tzalavras A.; Cole M.
Article.Abstract: Flexible cognition requires the brain to generalize across tasks while preserving task-specific information. Previous work showed that task representations are compressed in the association cortex and expanded in sensory and motor systems, but the mechanisms underlying these transformations are unclear. Here we test whether the geometry of intrinsic brain connectivity constrains how representations change between cortical regions. We analyzed functional MRI acquired during 16 diverse cognitive tasks together with activity flow modeling, finding that connectivity dimensionality predicts representational changes across the cortex. Low-dimensional connectivity compressed task representations and increased similarities across tasks, whereas high-dimensional connectivity expanded representations and supported conjunctive coding of task features. Activity flow modeling reproduced the observed compression-to-expansion pattern along the sensory-association-motor hierarchy and generated representational geometries that more closely matched targets than sources, consistent with transformation rather than transfer of information. These findings identify network geometry as a systems-level principle that shapes cortical representations and supports flexible cognition.

Article.Title: A corticohypothalamic circuit that mediates maternal awakening to pup cries
Article.Authors: Tang P.; Wu K.; Pan Y.; Yang S.; Cai Z.; Liang Y.; Mai F.; Chen P.; Peng M.; Wang Y.; Chen X.; Song C.; Ji X.; Liang F.
Article.Abstract: Maternal caregiving requires sensory vigilance to ensure offspring survival, particularly during sleep. Infant cries are salient sensory cues that reliably trigger maternal arousal and caregiving responses in both humans and dams, but the underlying neural circuitry remains poorly defined. Here we identify a corticohypothalamic circuit in mice that mediates maternal awakening in response to pup calls. We show that layer 6 (L6) neurons in the temporal association cortex and ectorhinal cortex (TeA/Ect) projecting to the preoptic area (POA) exhibit enhanced responsiveness to pup calls after the transition to motherhood. This enhanced responsiveness is mediated by increased expression of dopamine receptor D1 (Drd1) in TeA/Ect → POA neurons. Additionally, we reveal a pathway from the auditory thalamus to L6 TeA/Ect neurons that transmits pup cues during sleep. Together, these findings identify a dedicated neural circuit that grants infant cries privileged access to arousal systems, likely representing a fundamental adaptation for caregiving across mammals.

Article.Title: SIK3 controls synaptic localization of NMDA receptors by phosphorylating GluN1
Article.Authors: Lu R.; Morishita W.; Han X.; Temkin P.; Malenka R.; Südhof T.
Article.Abstract: Synaptic NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs) are central components of all neural computations. NMDAR levels critically vary between synapses but how the synaptic localization of NMDARs is controlled remains unclear. Here we show that SIK3, a serine-threonine protein kinase, localizes to synapses where it phosphorylates the obligatory NMDAR subunit GluN1 at a single site. This single phosphorylation event controls NMDAR recruitment to synapses. Genetic deletion of SIK3 severely and selectively decreases synaptic GluN1 levels by ~60% without altering AMPA-type glutamate receptor levels or inducing major transcriptional changes. Pharmacological inhibition of SIK3 impairs synaptic NMDAR responses within 45 minutes. Mutating the SIK3-phosphorylation site inhibits GluN1 synaptic recruitment. 'Sleepy', a gain-of-function mutation in SIK3 that increases sleep, selectively enhances synaptic NMDAR levels by increasing GluN1 phosphorylation. Thus, SIK3 phosphorylation of GluN1 provides a key signal for recruiting NMDARs to synapses.

Article.Title: Early lineage divergence segregates sensory and motor-associative identities in the thalamus
Article.Authors: Puche-Aroca L.; Andrés-Bayón B.; Wilson E.; Javed A.; Torregrosa-Mira A.; Rodríguez-Malmierca L.; López-Atalaya J.; López-Bendito G.
Article.Abstract: The thalamus integrates sensory, motor and associative functions through distinct nuclei, yet the developmental principles driving their specification remain unclear. Here we generate a spatiotemporal single-cell multiomic and spatial transcriptomic atlas of the embryonic mouse thalamus, combined with barcoding-based lineage tracing. We identify two major glutamatergic lineages, sensory-related and motor-associative, each governed by different gene regulatory programs and temporal dynamics. These lineages arise from spatially and molecularly distinct progenitor domains, revealing an early segregation of functional identities. Within the sensory lineage, we resolve branching sensory trajectories leading to first-order visual and somatosensory neurons, both emerging from a shared higher-order-like state. Using in silico predictions and in vivo perturbation, we identify Sp9 as a key regulator of visual thalamic fate. Together, our findings define the molecular architecture and developmental trajectories that underpin thalamic modality specification, providing a framework to understand how functional circuits emerge in the mammalian brain.

Article.Title: Dysregulated cholesterol trafficking through ABCA1 drives neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s disease
Article.Authors: Ma F.; Zhao X.; Wang X.; Fang S.; Xu S.; Wang M.; Liu Y.; Wang C.; Wang Q.; Lu M.; Cao L.
Article.Abstract: Although brain cholesterol dysregulation is implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), targeting cholesterol synthesis has shown limited efficacy. Here we identify ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) as a critical regulator of cholesterol homeostasis in PD. We show that ABCA1 expression is elevated in the substantia nigra of postmortem PD brains and in a PD mouse model, with regional analyses revealing preferential alterations in nigral and striatal circuits. Mechanistically, astrocytic ABCA1 drives excessive cholesterol efflux in mice, promoting neuronal cholesterol overload. In neurons, ABCA1 localizes to lysosomes, where it facilitates cholesterol import, leading to cholesterol accumulation, autophagy impairment and α-synuclein pathology. Genetic silencing of Abca1 in either astrocytes or dopaminergic neurons attenuates neurodegeneration and behavioral deficits in vivo. Furthermore, we identify magnesium citrate as an ABCA1 inhibitor and show that it reduces dopaminergic neuronal loss in a PD mouse model. Our findings identify an ABCA1-dependent cholesterol pathway underlying PD pathogenesis and support ABCA1 inhibition as a potential disease-modifying strategy.

Article.Title: An amygdala-mediated simulation-to-decision cascade aligns interbrain dynamics to solve social dilemmas
Article.Authors: Ni J.; Meng F.; Zhang C.; Tan H.; Zeng X.; Yang J.; Li H.; Qi Y.; Yan Y.; Zhang Y.; Zhang K.; Ma Y.
Article.Abstract: Mutual cooperation (MC) requires independent decision-makers to coordinate under uncertainty about each other's intentions. Using simultaneous intracranial electroencephalography from epilepsy-patient dyads playing a real-time iterated prisoner's dilemma, we identified neurocognitive mechanisms that enable interacting brains to align during mutual cooperation. Amygdala interbrain representational alignment (IBRA), similarity in fine-grained neural spectral patterns across partners, emerged selectively during MC and predicted trial-by-trial outcomes. Early θ-suppression-characterized IBRA reflected rapid, history-sensitive alignment, whereas later IBRA, characterized by low-frequency suppression and γ increases, supported coordinated commitment and action. Furthermore, mutual cooperation relied on an amygdala-mediated, simulation-to-decision cascade, operationalized here as a model-based prospective estimate of partner cooperation that guided self-choice. Amygdala low-frequency suppression tracked this prospective estimate of partner cooperation and θ-γ coupling linked this partner estimate to self-decision processes. Conditional cooperators strategically relied on partner tracking, whereas unconditional cooperators leveraged dispositional tolerance of uncertainty to transition into anticipatory neural alignment. These findings reveal the neural interdependency underpinning MC, redefining cooperation not as isolated decision-making but as a dynamic, interbrain, cognitive alignment.

Article.Title: Spatiotemporal remodeling in habenula marks the onset of depression-related phenotypes
Article.Authors: Molina P.; Osypenko D.; Garnica J.; Amossé Q.; Bouteldja F.; Camelot L.; Mondoloni S.; Congiu M.; Kathe C.; Mameli M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chronic stress has lasting adverse consequences that can lead, over time, to depression, yet the optimal timeframe for effective therapies remains unclear. The lateral habenula (LHb) has been implicated in stress-related behavioral repercussions, but the precise timing of its contribution is not understood. Here, using spatial transcriptomics, we generated a spatially resolved molecular atlas of the LHb of male mice, revealing a topographically organized and temporally defined remodeling of gene expression after chronic stress. Longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of individual LHb neurons revealed progressively heightened excitatory responses to aversive stimuli. These neuronal adaptations mirrored both the progression of transcriptional changes and the emergence of depression-related behavioral phenotypes and were reversed by the antidepressant ketamine. Moreover, chemogenetically limiting LHb neuronal activity or administering ketamine at the onset of these changes exerted antidepressant effects. These findings link spatiotemporal signatures of LHb neuronal ensembles and genetic landscape with the onset of stress-induced depression-related states.

Article.Title: Low-order assemblies drive oncogenic RTK fusion signalling without condensation
Article.Authors: Gonzalez-Martinez D.; Mumford T.; Wilde D.; Wissert S.; Gao Y.; Brackhahn E.; Kriwacki R.; Rhoades E.; Bugaj L.
Article.Abstract: Receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) fusions are a large class of oncoproteins found in ~5% of cancers. Key questions remain, however, about how RTK fusions transmit oncogenic signals, including how these largely cytoplasmic proteins activate downstream pathways that originate at the plasma membrane. Fusions are often multimeric and can form mesoscale condensates in cancer cells, and condensation has been implicated as an essential mechanism to enable signal transmission from the cytoplasm. However, whether condensates play a causal role or whether smaller 'diffuse' assemblies are sufficient to transduce signals, has been challenging to establish. Here we apply advanced microscopy, single-cell analysis and synthetic fusions to determine the principles by which multimerization and condensation drive signalling from cytoplasmic RTK fusions. For EML4-ALK, a prominent fusion that forms condensates, we found poor correlation between condensation and signalling and abundant EML4-ALK activity in the diffuse phase. Synthetic RTK fusions showed that cytoplasmic dimers of ALK or RET domains-and even constitutively active monomers-were sufficient to induce strong Ras-Erk signalling despite the absence of condensates, and non-condensing fusions were sufficient to transform cells in vitro and in subcutaneous tumour models. A panel of various other cancer-driving RTK fusions showed that low-order multimerization was widespread across fusions, whereas mesoscale condensation was rare and did not correlate with signalling. Our results suggest that low-order multimerization is sufficient to drive fusion phosphorylation, which is necessary and sufficient to trigger downstream oncogenic signalling.

Article.Title: Mapping mammalian placental formation and implantation transitions with single-cell transcriptomics and live imaging
Article.Authors: Chen D.; Hu W.; Nakagawa S.; Williams B.; Readhead C.; Meglicki M.; Thomson M.; Wold B.; Zernicka-Goetz M.
Article.Abstract: Implantation remains the most inaccessible stage of mammalian development. Consequently, we know remarkably little about how the embryo coordinates the cellular transitions that establish the body plan and initiate placental formation, despite this being the period when most pregnancies are lost. Here we combine single-cell transcriptomics, live imaging and functional experiments to define these transitions at cellular resolution. Our results identify an intermediate state bridging naive and primed pluripotency in the embryonic lineage, trace anterior-posterior axis specification origins in the extraembryonic endoderm, and reveal trophectoderm bifurcation into distinct placental progenitors. Strikingly, we find that the placenta arises from two sources: the classically recognized polar trophectoderm and a previously unrecognized population of mural trophectoderm that migrates from the polar-mural border. Human mural trophectoderm shows similar region-specific behaviour and may include invasive-trophoblast-biased progenitors. These findings open new directions for improving stem-cell-derived embryo models and uncovering the early determinants of pregnancy success.

Article.Title: The optogenetic tool ASAP acutely inhibits autophagy
Article.Authors: Mondal P.; Cyril A.; Mamriev D.; Parham L.; Wierzbicki I.; Shen C.; Doglioni G.; Dufrense S.; Komarla A.; Gonzalez D.; D’Angelo M.; Towers C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Autophagy, a conserved recycling process, manages intracellular quality control to mitigate stress. To determine the rapid effects of autophagy perturbation, we developed an optogenetic tool to rapidly inhibit autophagy, termed ASAP. Our approach leverages light-induced proteolytic cleavage to selectively inhibit autophagy within 5 min of light exposure, providing a precise and dynamic approach to study autophagy regulation. Proteomic profiling with ASAP revealed the most tightly regulated autophagy substrates along with previously unidentified substrates, including nuclear pore complex proteins. Of note, autophagy regulates quality control of cytoplasmic complexes of nucleoporins via specific LC3-interacting regions, sparing nuclear pore complex proteins embedded in the nuclear envelope. Upon rapid autophagy inhibition, incomplete nucleoporin complexes accumulate and instead of undergoing autophagic degradation, cytoplasmic nucleoporin complexes aggregate in processing bodies (P bodies). Using ASAP, we demonstrate rapid and specific inhibition of autophagy, revealing that nuclear pore complex proteins are tightly regulated autophagy substrates.

Article.Title: TMEM192 is a calcineurin-regulated membrane receptor for ubiquitin-independent lysophagy
Article.Authors: Liu X.; Yang Y.; Li W.; Peng K.; Qiu X.; Xu Y.; Zeng S.; Neculai D.; Sun Q.; Zhou T.; Shen H.; Liu W.
Article.Abstract: Lysophagy is a selective form of autophagy responsible for clearing damaged lysosomes. Although existing models predominantly highlight ubiquitin-dependent mechanisms, here we identify the lysosomal membrane protein TMEM192 as a key ubiquitin-independent receptor for lysophagy. We demonstrate that lysophagy persists in cells even when protein ubiquitination is inhibited or autophagy adaptors are deleted. Following lysosomal damage, the efflux of calcium from lysosomes activates calcineurin, leading to the dephosphorylation of TMEM192 at Ser229. This exposes a latent LC3-interacting region and enables direct recruitment of autophagosomes. Depletion of TMEM192 or blockade of its dephosphorylation severely impairs lysophagy, resulting in the accumulation of damaged lysosomes. In a mouse model of acute hyperuricemic nephropathy, deficiency in TMEM192 exacerbates renal tubular injury. Our findings establish a ubiquitin-independent lysophagy pathway, which holds important implications for understanding and intervening lysosomal-related diseases.

Article.Title: Full-length RNA sequencing profiles intracellular and extracellular RNAs in euploid and aneuploid human embryos
Article.Authors: Sugimoto T.; Mariya T.; Kato T.; Hitachi K.; Furusato S.; Maruhashi Y.; Kishigami S.; Kawachiya S.; Sakurai A.; Saito T.; Nishizawa H.; Kurahashi H.
Article.Abstract: Cell-free RNA (cfRNA) in human embryo culture medium may provide molecular information about preimplantation development, but its origin and regulation remain unclear. Here we show, using full-length total RNA sequencing of individual human blastocysts and matched spent media, that extracellular cfRNA profiles differ according to embryonic chromosomal status. Euploid embryos showed relatively stable intracellular and extracellular transcriptomic programmes, whereas aneuploid embryos displayed disrupted transcriptional states with stress-associated signatures, including nonsense-mediated decay and TP53-mediated apoptosis. Analyses of stable non-differentially expressed genes and long non-coding RNA-mRNA co-expression modules linked cfRNA signatures to RNA processing, RNA export, vesicle trafficking, autophagy and RNA degradation pathways. Mouse perturbation experiments further supported a connection between autophagy-lysosome-vesicle pathway activity and embryo-derived cfRNA signatures. These data establish a transcriptomic resource for studying intracellular and extracellular RNA states in human embryos and support cfRNA as a biologically informative readout of embryonic state.

Article.Title: Tau monomers and fibrils escape microglial clearance via distinct cellular mechanisms
Article.Authors: Kulkarni V.; Fredrickson C.; Adrian M.; Town J.; Ho H.; Dutka P.; Shangguan J.; Reid D.; Hayne M.; Kschonsak M.; Ndoja A.; Jeong C.; Hoogenraad C.
Article.Abstract: Tauopathies, such as Alzheimer's disease, are neurodegenerative disorders characterized by the accumulation and propagation of toxic extracellular forms of the microtubule-associated protein tau across brain regions. Microglia, the resident macrophages of the brain, are known for clearing and degrading toxic proteins. However, emerging evidence suggests that microglia also enhance tau spreading. To dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying microglial responses to extracellular tau, we use high-resolution imaging and biochemical approaches to assess the trafficking dynamics of different extracellular tau species in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Here we find that tau monomers are internalized by microglia via cell-surface LRP1 receptors but fail to reach terminally degradative lysosomes; instead, they are persistently recycled back to the extracellular space. In contrast, tau fibrils are not internalized and primarily adhere to the cell surface through an HSPG-dependent mechanism, triggering TLR4-mediated microglial activation and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Heparin or anti-tau treatments dampen tau fibril-mediated microglial activation. In addition, disease-associated variants of the Alzheimer's disease-related protein APOE reduce microglia-tau interactions, further reducing tau uptake. Together, these findings demonstrate that microglia fail to efficiently clear extracellular tau monomers and fibrils through mechanistically distinct cellular processes, emphasizing the need for tailored therapeutic strategies to enhance extracellular tau clearance in neurodegenerative diseases.

Article.Title: Positional replication fork instability drives PARP inhibitor cytotoxicity
Article.Authors: Gupta D.; Ding X.; Zhang L.; Coleman K.; Tang G.; Lee W.; Oyer J.; Kang X.; Ramms D.; Yu Z.; VanArsdale T.; Fenyo D.; Huang T.; Rothenberg E.
Article.Abstract: Although poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) show promise for treating homologous recombination-deficient cancers, the observed PARPi hypersensitivity in additional genetic contexts expands their potential use in precision oncology. Yet, the DNA lesions driving PARPi-induced cytotoxicity remain poorly defined. Here we uncover distinct replication-fork lesions in specific genomic regions as key determinants of PARPi cytotoxicity. Using CRISPR screens, we identify that loss of replication-coupled cohesin acetyltransferase ESCO2 confers PARPi hypersensitivity independently of homologous recombination deficiency. Quantitative single-molecule imaging reveals that ESCO2 loss promotes accumulation of G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures at a subset of replication-associated sites, associated with PARP1 activation and engagement of fork protection factor TIMELESS to mitigate G4-induced stress. Notably, these G4 lesions localize to fragile pericentromeric regions and engage the G4 helicase DDX11. PARP inhibition disrupts this protective G4-processing response by preventing PARP1-dependent engagement of TIMELESS and DDX11, leading to G4 accumulation, DNA damage and chromosomal instability. Together, our findings define the G4-PARP1-TIMELESS-DDX11 axis as a critical safeguard of replication fork stability at hard-to-replicate loci and reveal ESCO2 as a therapeutic target for promoting synthetic lethality in PARPi-treated cancers.

Article.Title: STING-dependent TNF signalling promotes IKKβ-mediated ATG9A phosphorylation and autophagy
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Zhong Y.; Tian X.; Long M.; Lin S.; Wang S.; Hu Z.; Lu G.; Shang Z.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Chemotherapeutic drugs, either alone or in combination with immunotherapy, are routinely used in cancer treatment. However, cancer cells frequently develop resistance to chemotherapy, and the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using head and neck squamous cell carcinoma as a model, we show that chemotherapy activates the cGAS-STING pathway, leading to the induction of TNF. TNF mediates a paracrine signalling pathway in recipient tumour cells, leading to IKKβ activation and ATG9A phosphorylation at serine 654, thereby promoting autophagy. Moreover, IKKβ activation and ATG9A S654 phosphorylation are induced by TNF, nutrient deprivation and mTOR inhibition, suggesting that the IKKβ-ATG9A axis may represent a common regulatory mechanism of autophagy. Analysis of patient samples further reveals that chemotherapy induces autophagy, and elevated phosphorylation of ATG9A at S654 correlates with poor chemotherapy response. Of note, TNF blockade enhances therapeutic efficacy in both chemotherapy alone and chemotherapy combined with immune checkpoint inhibition. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized TNF-IKKβ-ATG9A signalling axis that promotes autophagy and highlight TNF blockade as a promising strategy to overcome chemotherapy resistance.

Article.Title: Reconstructing the emergence of the human chorion via Hippo-mediated trophoblast induction
Article.Authors: Zhang M.; Lim R.; Reis A.; Piszker W.; Boyd W.; Pagon A.; Mahajan A.; Wu L.; Zhao C.; Petropoulos S.; Ronda C.; Simunovic M.

Article.Title: Phase separation of SMARCAL1 orchestrates epigenetic reprogramming and methionine metabolism to foster radioresistance and immunosuppression
Article.Authors: Zheng C.; Cui Q.; Li J.; Chen J.; He L.; Zhang X.; Liu Z.; Chen T.; Lyu Y.; Liang C.; Ma S.; Li M.; Shi X.; Jia Y.; Li Z.; Wang X.; Xu W.; Li B.
Article.Abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation has emerged as a key mechanism governing cellular organization and function, but its role in pathological processes and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely elusive. Here we show that SMARCAL1 forms nuclear condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation to enhance histone H4 lactylation and chromatin accessibility. This SMARCAL1‑driven epigenetic reprogramming not only facilitates the recruitment of DNA repair proteins, leading to radiotherapy resistance, but also regulates methionine adenosyltransferase transcription, thereby promoting the methionine cycle and inducing T cell exhaustion and immune therapy tolerance. Importantly, pharmacological disruption of SMARCAL1 condensates by digoxin sensitizes tumours to both radiotherapy and anti-PD1 therapy in multiple models. These findings highlight the crucial role of condensates centred on SMARCAL1-histone H4 in governing DNA repair and immune microenvironment remodelling, as well as propose an innovative strategy to overcome radioimmunoresistance.

Article.Title: Methylated eEF1A selectively decodes mRNA to shape cancer proteomes
Article.Authors: Liu S.; Cruz-Navarrete F.; Hausmann S.; Szkop K.; Ikram S.; Brady R.; Lu X.; Dong R.; Vu J.; Flores N.; Zahn E.; Thompson J.; Garcia B.; Larsson O.; Topisirovic I.; Blanchard S.; Gozani O.; Mazur P.

Article.Title: Motile vesicles (MoVes) are a cancer cell migration-associated extracellular vesicle population
Article.Authors: Tsering T.; Nadeau A.; Ghasemi M.; Mousovich-Neto F.; Tobias G.; Chen Y.; Kienzle L.; Dickinson K.; Douanne N.; Serganova I.; Zappasodi R.; Matei I.; Lyden D.; Burnier J.
Article.Abstract: Migrating cancer cells release diverse extracellular vesicles (EVs) that carry cargo capable of influencing tumour progression and intercellular communication. Here we identify and characterize a previously undescribed population of large EVs (2-5 μm), termed motile vesicles (MoVes), that are generated during active cancer cell migration and associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Comparative analyses across EV populations show that MoVes display distinct ultrastructural features, molecular composition and sedimentation behaviour. Article.Title: Tubulin acetylation regulates nuclear shape fluctuations and DNA repair
Article.Authors: Wallis S.; Tse W.; Donker L.; Baxter A.; Dave N.; Weber A.; Gillespie E.; Chen B.; Burden J.; Friskes A.; Medema R.; Charras G.; Calado D.; Godinho S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Genome stability depends on the accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). While chromatin-based mechanisms have been well studied, emerging evidence reveals that nuclear mechanics actively shape repair outcomes, although the mechanisms remain unclear. Here we identify microtubule acetylation as a regulator of nuclear mechanics that promotes DSB repair via homologous recombination (HR). DNA damage induces progressive tubulin acetylation, leading to displacement of the perinuclear vimentin cage. Loss of the vimentin cage softens the nucleus and renders the nuclear envelope responsive to microtubule forces, which drives transient nuclear shape fluctuations, localized DSB mobility and repair. Inhibiting tubulin acetylation abolishes these fluctuations, restricts DSB mobility and negatively impacts the homology search during HR, leaving non-homologous end joining intact. Consequently, persistent DSBs coalesce and cluster at the nuclear periphery, triggering cell-cycle arrest and senescence and increasing sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents. Removal of the vimentin cage is sufficient to rescue these effects, with restored nuclear fluctuations and repair efficiency. Thus, we propose that nuclear fluctuations act as a mechanical strategy to accelerate error-free repair. These findings reveal how cytoskeletal forces shape nuclear function and establish nuclear fluctuations as a fundamental principle for maintaining genome stability.

Article.Title: A three-dimensional human co-culture system reveals reciprocal embryo–endometrial adaptation at implantation onset
Article.Authors: Bi Y.; Tu Z.; Zhang X.; Hu J.; Chen C.; Xu Y.; Zheng Y.; Song Y.; Chen Y.; Lin T.; Wang H.; Che X.; Li J.; Huang G.; Gao S.; Wang Y.

Article.Title: Keratin 9 regulates mechanosensitive YAP1 signalling in palmoplantar epidermis
Article.Authors: Steiner S.; Horst E.; Chiu E.; Athaiya M.; Johnson C.; Shen J.; Kerns M.; Kirma J.; McCarthy R.; Shah S.; Sarig O.; Samuelov L.; Sprecher E.; O’Toole E.; Gudjonsson J.; Mehta G.; Iglesias-Bartolome R.; Coulombe P.

K9 loss-of-function variants driving KRT9-pEDD, a palmoplantar epidermal differentiation disorder, result in aberrant YAP1 subcellular partitioning and elevated levels of the stress-induced keratin 16 (KRT16/K16). Krt9 null mice recapitulate these molecular phenotypes as early as postnatal day 3. We further identify dynamic, YAP1-dependent regulation of Krt16/K16, upstream of and necessary for Krt9/K9 expression, during early postnatal development in situ and in response to mechanical compression of keratinocytes ex vivo, highlighting the role of mechanical stress in epidermal specification. Mechanistically, K9 interacts with the YAP1 binding protein 14-3-3σ and sequesters YAP1 in the cytoplasm, inhibiting its transcriptional activity; these functions are disrupted by KRT9-pEDD-causing variants in K9. Finally, we show that genetic or pharmacological inhibition of YAP1 ameliorates palmoplantar keratoderma in Krt9 null mice. Article.Authors: Wang L.; Yang H.; Song J.; Zhao R.; Liu S.; Hou H.; Zhang C.; Tian H.; Gao J.; Chen J.; Chen Z.; Zhao H.; Liu B.; Wu K.
Article.Abstract: Organogenesis marks one of the most dynamic periods of early human embryonic development. Article.Title: On the nature of GABAB receptors and their plasticity in the mammalian brain

Article.Abstract: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian CNS, essential for circuit function and behaviour. Article.Authors: Calafate S.; Mancuso R.
Article.Abstract: Sleep is a fundamental regulator of brain homeostasis, yet how distinct brain cell types contribute to this process remains poorly understood. Microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, actively regulate neuroinflammatory tone, metabolic waste clearance, and synaptic remodeling, thereby contributing to neural circuit maintenance and proteostasis. Delineating the different functions played by microglia during specific brain states, such as sleep, represents an active area of research. In this article, we review a growing literature supporting the notion that sleep dynamically shapes microglial functional outputs. We further suggest that the failure of the sleep-microglia axis may represent an important component of the molecular framework of Alzheimer's disease (AD), contributing to disease progression. Finally, we discuss preclinical and clinical evidence suggesting that sleep-targeting interventions may modulate AD pathology, and highlight the possibility that restoring sleep physiology could recalibrate microglial homeostatic functions and slow disease progression.

Article.Title: The mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome in aging and brain diseases
Article.Authors: Shawky A.; Huang H.; Parikh D.; Morris-Blanco K.
Article.Abstract: The mitochondrial genome is a dynamic regulatory platform that extends far beyond its protein-coding capacity. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) harbors epigenetic modifications and produces diverse noncoding RNAs that influence mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis. Evidence from animal models and human studies indicates that mtDNA methylation, mitochondrial-encoded noncoding RNAs, and cytosolic release of mitochondrial nucleic acids regulate transcription, metabolism, and stress signaling. Furthermore, these mechanisms are altered in aging, neurodegenerative disease, and acute brain injury. In this review, we synthesize emerging insights into how the mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome shape mitochondrial function and serve as regulatory interfaces linking cellular stress and neuronal vulnerability in brain aging and disease.

Article.Title: Resilience and vulnerability in the midbrain dopamine system during aging
Article.Authors: McMurtrie G.; Mabry S.; Glausier J.; Rocha E.; Freyberg Z.
Article.Abstract: The midbrain dopamine system is integral to movement, reward, and motivation, and its dysfunction underlies a range of brain disorders. Age is a primary risk factor for many of these disorders, yet systematic analysis of how the dopamine system changes during healthy aging remains relatively understudied. In this review, we first examine the impact of healthy aging on the dopamine system across sexes and species, including flies, mice, rats, and humans. We next consider the neuroadaptive mechanisms that sustain dopamine neuron function with age. Finally, we contrast the molecular mechanisms of age-related neurodegenerative diseases with those of healthy aging, exploring the possibility that loss of neuroadaptive reserve drives dopamine neurodegeneration. Elucidating these neuroadaptive mechanisms could offer a path toward preserving dopamine neuron function across the lifespan and potentially preventing age-related neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Apolipoprotein E4 and immune dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease: mechanisms and therapeutic implications
Article.Authors: Shi H.; Zhao Y.; Zhu W.; Wang Y.; Bu X.
Article.Abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) functions as an organizer of brain-periphery immune crosstalk, coupling maladaptive microglial states with peripheral immune remodeling to establish a self-reinforcing neuroimmune loop that may accelerate the progression of Alzheimer's disease. In the central nervous system, APOE4 pushes microglia away from homeostatic surveillance toward metabolically stressed, inflammatory, and synaptotoxic phenotypes, thereby weakening pathological protein clearance and promoting neurodegeneration. In the periphery, APOE4 primes innate and adaptive immune cells toward a pro-inflammatory state, creating a reservoir that can communicate with the diseased brain and infiltrate it. In addition, APOE4 erodes the separation between central and peripheral immune compartments, enabling bidirectional immune crosstalk that amplifies neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. In this review, we synthesize evidence for APOE4-driven central and peripheral immune dysregulation; discuss therapeutic opportunities for targeting the APOE4 immune axis; and highlight the need for human-derived, longitudinal, cross-tissue studies to identify causal, stage-specific, and targetable immune nodes for precision intervention.

Article.Title: Tumor innervation in non-central nervous system tumors: origins, mechanisms, and phenotypic plasticity
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Ye Z.; Wang Y.; Tang S.; Chen G.
Article.Abstract: The peripheral nervous system has emerged as an important regulator of solid tumor biology. We synthesize recent advances in cancer neuroscience, focusing on three interconnected themes: the cellular origins of tumor-associated nerves, the molecular mechanisms that govern neural recruitment and remodeling, and the resulting phenotypic plasticity within the tumor microenvironment. Tumor innervation arises through axon extension from pre-existing nerves, recruitment of neural precursors, and neuron-like transdifferentiation of non-neuronal cells. These processes are driven by neurotrophic factors, axon guidance cues, extracellular vesicles, and stress-associated pathways. The functional consequences of innervation are context-dependent, with sympathetic, parasympathetic, and sensory inputs exerting distinct effects across tumor types and stages. We conclude by outlining key challenges and future directions for therapeutic translation.

Article.Title: Evolving perspectives on cardiac innervation: from relay to a complex regulated network
Article.Authors: Habecker B.; Montgomery J.
Article.Abstract: Neural control of the heart adjusts cardiac output to the functional demands of the body in order to maintain homeostasis. Sensory afferents monitor blood pressure, metabolites, and other parameters, sending information to the brainstem that then alters the balance of stimulatory sympathetic and inhibitory parasympathetic transmission to the heart. 'Autonomic imbalance' between sympathetic and parasympathetic efferent transmission in the heart is a characteristic of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases that contributes to pathology. In this review, we discuss recent studies related to the peripheral components of the cardiac control circuit. We summarize data from induced pluripotent stem cells, small and large animal models, and human studies that reveal more complexity in peripheral components of this system than previously understood. We also discuss peripheral neuroplasticity in cardiovascular disease and the potential impact of neuromodulation therapies.

Article.Title: Constructing events across perception, action, and thought
Article.Authors: Kwon D.; Park J.; Shim W.
Article.Abstract: The brain organizes continuous experience into events that structure episodic memory and guide behavior. Traditional accounts have primarily focused on sensory discontinuities and prediction errors that trigger updates of event models. Here, we broaden this view to consider event boundaries arising during goal-directed behavior, spontaneous thought, and memory recall, including transitions generated in the absence of corresponding changes in sensory input. We propose that prediction error and uncertainty provide complementary signals for event model updating: prediction errors signal a violation of current expectations, whereas uncertainty may promote updating when upcoming states become difficult to predict. We further suggest that the hippocampus may serve as a candidate hub linking boundary-related representational changes across perception, action, and thought. Together, this framework offers an integrative account of how the brain detects and generates event structure in continuous experience to support memory and behavior.

Article.Title: Functional brain signatures of successful cognitive aging
Article.Authors: Behrenbruch N.; Fischer L.; Kirschner H.; Harrison T.; Maass A.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive aging trajectories vary markedly. While many older adults experience gradual decline in memory and executive function, some maintain high cognitive performance well into advanced age. Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying this variability carries important implications for early detection of unfavorable aging trajectories and the development of interventions. Here, we review functional brain signatures associated with successful cognitive aging in humans, integrating evidence from functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography within a unified conceptual framework of brain maintenance and compensation. Across both modalities, evidence increasingly links successful cognitive aging to the preservation of youth-like neural dynamics, while the contribution of compensatory neural recruitment remains empirically contested and methodologically difficult to establish.

Article.Title: Assembly of a renal countercurrent system in a beetle
Article.Authors: Beaven R.; Fafinska M.; Dai J.; Halberg K.; Denholm B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Countercurrent exchange describes the crossover of some property between two bodies flowing in opposite direction. Countercurrent circuits, which work more efficiently than concurrent circuits, are common in nature and mimicked in human engineering. An example is the beetle cryptonephridial complex (CNC)—a multi-organ water conservation system which makes key contributions to the water budget in a vast number of species. It is even used by some to harvest water from the atmosphere. The system evolved by a radical reorganisation of insect internal anatomy bringing the renal/Malpighian tubules and rectum into countercurrent configuration, and their isolation in a chamber by an unusual tissue of unknown origin—the perinephric membrane. The CNC is richly supplied with tracheae to meet the high metabolic demands of the system. How the CNC is assembled during development is unknown. Here we characterise CNC development in the model beetle Tribolium castaneum and discover the molecular signals orchestrating its assembly. We find that dynamic crosstalk between the developing precursor cells of the rectum, Malpighian tubules, perinephric membrane, and trachea rely on a single, differentially spliced fibroblast growth factor (FGF) receptor and two FGF pathway ligands. We also map the origin of the perinephric membrane to a previously uncharacterised population of mesodermal cells, providing clues to its evolutionary origin. This work illuminates the developmental processes underpinning the reorganisation of the insect internal body plan to assemble a natural countercurrent system, one which is fundamental to beetle physiology, ecology and evolutionary success.

Article.Title: Rhizospheric pH mediated thermo-signalling coordinates root growth under heat stress
Article.Authors: Lale A.; Bansod A.; Chakraborty S.; Ghafouri E.; Davis J.; Nghiem T.; Sun F.; Gapare B.; Teh W.; Xu X.; Pan L.; Borkar A.; De Veylder L.; Swarup R.; De Smet I.; Bhosale R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Heat stress events pose a major threat to global agriculture due to elevated air and soil temperatures. While plant roots regulate their growth in response to elevated soil temperatures, they appear to rely on thermosensory mechanisms distinct from those used by shoots. Here, we report pH as a key component of a thermo-signaling mechanism that regulates temperature-dependent root responses via ROS-mediated control of cell cycle dynamics in Arabidopsis thaliana . At moderately high temperatures, alkalization of meristematic and transition zones increases superoxide (O₂⁻) levels, promoting cell division and root growth. Conversely, higher temperatures inhibit growth by increasing acidification and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) accumulation in these zones. Elevating external pH buffers this acidification, reduces H₂O₂ levels, and confers heat resistance. Our data support that this pH-mediated heat resistance is also effective under soil conditions. The heat-induced pH shifts are controlled by plasma membrane H⁺-ATPases (PM-H⁺-ATPases), which are under the control of the kinases TOT3 and TOI5. Our findings reveal an interesting pathway for plant adaptation to heat stress, linking pH, ROS and root thermomorphogenesis, with major implications for improving plant resilience in warming climates.

Article.Title: Directly visualizing the energy level structure of quantum dot molecules
Article.Authors: Yoo H.; Janda T.; Nasseraddin C.; Petta J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The orbital, spin and valley degrees of freedom in silicon quantum dots (QDs) support many modes of spin qubit operation. However, it is generally challenging to probe the energy level spectrum over a large parameter space. We demonstrate a spectroscopic technique capable of mapping the energy level structure of a double quantum dot as a function of level detuning, interdot tunnel coupling, and magnetic field. In the one-electron regime, we directly observe the transition from the atom-like energy levels of isolated QDs to molecular-like bonding and anti-bonding states with increasing interdot tunnel coupling. We also resolve the Zeeman splitting of ground and excited valley states in a magnetic field. In the two-electron regime, we gain access to the detuning dependent singlet-triplet splitting. Our work may be extended to a broader class of systems, such as strong spin-orbit materials or proximitized QDs, allowing the direct extraction of various energy gaps.
