Article.Title: Chemogenetic dissection of the H2O2–salicylic acid feedback loop in PTI and ETI evolutionary conservation
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Tang S.; Xia C.; Wang Q.; Wei S.; Guo D.; Yan J.; Zhang K.; Ai G.; Han X.
Article.Abstract: The signaling interplay between hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and salicylic acid (SA) is fundamental to plant stress responses, yet resolving their spatiotemporal dynamics in vivo remains challenging due to spatial ambiguity when using multiple probes. Here, we present RhCy-NI, a single-molecule dual-responsive fluorescent probe featuring orthogonal reaction sites for crosstalk-free detection of H2O2 and SA. The probe exhibits ~25-fold and ~250-fold fluorescence enhancements at 562 and 751 nm, respectively, with detection limits of 96 and 24 nM and high selectivity. Time-course imaging in rice under salt and cadmium stresses reveals that a rapid, transient H2O2 burst precedes SA accumulation. In Nicotiana benthamiana challenged with the Phytophthora infestans elicitin INF1, pharmacological inhibition and SA-deficient genetic backgrounds show that early oxidative signaling is required for SA accumulation, whereas SA sustains a secondary oxidative phase. Genetic analysis reveals that enhanced disease susceptibility 1 (EDS1) primarily supports SA accumulation, whereas helper nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) receptors of the NLR-required-for-cell-death (NRC) family (NRC2/3/4) support both SA accumulation and sustained secondary H2O2 amplification. These findings establish RhCy-NI as a tool for resolving H2O2–SA feedback and implicate components associated with effector-triggered immunity in cell-surface-triggered defense. Interaction between hydrogen peroxide and salicylic acid is important for plant stress responses. Here, the authors develop a dual-responsive fluorescent probe that simultaneously resolves the two signals in living plants.

Article.Title: Photocatalytic radical hydrogenation of unactivated alkenes via an intermolecular hydrogen-atom-transfer relay
Article.Authors: Lan W.; Wei Z.; Wu Z.
Article.Abstract: Despite the ubiquity of alkene reduction in chemical synthesis, developing safe, general, and chemoselective hydrogenation methods that avoid pressurized hydrogen gas or precious metals remains a significant challenge. Herein, we report a redox-neutral photocatalytic radical transfer hydrogenation strategy that addresses these constraints via an intermolecular hydrogen-atom-transfer (HAT) relay. This approach leverages a synergistic diaryl ketone–cobalt–thiol triple catalytic system to utilize naturally abundant γ-terpinene as a sustainable hydrogen donor. Driven by visible light, the reaction proceeds through a HAT cascade to generate a reactive cobalt–hydride species, enabling the efficient hydrogenation of a broad spectrum of unactivated alkenes—ranging from terminal to sterically demanding tetrasubstituted variants—under mild, additive-free conditions. The protocol exhibits excellent chemoselectivity, preserving sensitive functionalities such as aldehydes, epoxides, carboxylic acids, and Lewis basic heterocycles. The practical utility of this protocol is demonstrated through gram-scale synthesis with low catalyst loadings, establishing a versatile and environmentally benign platform for alkene reduction. Cross-electrophile coupling between unactivated alkyl halides and alkynyl halides has long been challenged by reactivity mismatch and poor chemoselectivity. Here the authors report nickel-catalyzed crosselectrophile coupling enabled by a tridentate ligand that controls the sequence of electrophile activation, allowing direct construction of alkynyl–alkyl bonds.

Article.Title: Taming crystallization to achieve superior soft magnetic performance via fine nanocrystallines
Article.Authors: Sun R.; Li X.; Zhou J.; Yan Y.; Di S.; Luan J.; Peng H.; Sun B.; Ke H.; Wang W.; Bai H.
Article.Abstract: The increasing demand for high-efficiency power electronics in emerging technologies such as 5 G and artificial intelligence is limited by the intrinsic trade-off between high saturation magnetic flux density (Bs) and low coercivity (Hc) in soft magnetic materials. Here, we report a rotational magnetic field annealing strategy for Fe-(Co)-Si-B-Cu-Nb and Fe-Co-B-P alloys that enables precise control of crystallization kinetics. The applied rotational magnetic field promotes dynamic structural fluctuations in amorphous precursors, enhancing nucleation while suppressing grain growth. Consequently, fine nanocrystalline structures with grain sizes of 1–5 nm are obtained, achieving a high Bs of 1.94 T and a low Hc of ~0.8 A m−1. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that rotational magnetic fields generate spatially heterogeneous fluctuations, facilitating dense and uniform nucleation. This work provides a pathway for designing fine nanocomposite soft magnetic materials through external-field-controlled crystallization. Researchers demonstrate that rotational magnetic field annealing controls crystallization to produce ultrafine nanocrystals, enabling soft magnetic alloys with both high magnetic flux density and low coercivity for next-generation energy-efficient power electronics.

Article.Title: DPI-score: a deep learning-based metric for assessing protein-protein interfaces in cryoEM derived assemblies
Article.Authors: Bhujel N.; Whyatt N.; Joseph A.; Thomas J.; Elliot L.; Sabapathy T.; Thiyagalingam J.; Malhotra S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Advances in cryoEM have led to a surge in high-resolution structures; however, model building and refinement at resolutions ( > = 3 Å) and in regions with variable local resolution remain challenging, making validation essential. CryoEM derived assemblies often contain extensive protein-protein interfaces, however, most existing validation metrics focus on density fit or overall geometry without directly assessing interface quality. To address this, we present DPI-Score, a deep learning-based metric for assessing protein-protein interfaces in cryoEM derived complexes. The method uses only raw structural coordinates of interface atoms, without requiring engineered features, and achieves 87.53% validation accuracy. DPI-Score was applied to 29,120 interfaces from 6,011 fitted entries with resolutions worse than 3 Å in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank. Here, we show that DPI-Score provides complementary information to existing validation metrics and can identify interface errors in modelled assemblies that are not detected by density-based scores alone.

Article.Title: A subspecialty diagnostic system powered by self-supervised learning for cervical histopathology
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Chen L.; Huang Q.; Guan T.; Deng X.; Shen Z.; Li J.; Chen X.; Hu B.; Lei Z.; Ling X.; Zhu T.; Huang Z.; Yu D.; Zeng F.; Liu Y.; Chen J.; Zhu L.; He Q.; Liu Y.; Shi D.; Liu H.; Hu J.; Gao H.; Song Z.
Article.Abstract: Cervical cancer remains a major malignancy in women, with large-scale human papillomavirus-based screening generating a large volume of biopsies and, for advanced cases, surgical specimens, imposing an overwhelming diagnostic burden that necessitates precise histopathological evaluation. Although deep learning shows promise, general foundation models offer a broader reach but remain limited in capturing subspecialty-specific features and task adaptability. We introduce the Cervical Subspecialty Pathology (CerS-Path) diagnostic system, built upon the subspecialized dataset and developed through two synergistic pretraining stages: self-supervised learning on approximately 190 million tissue patches to build a cervical-specific feature extractor, and multimodal enhancement with 2.5 million image-text pairs, followed by diagnostic functions integration and downstream task enhancement. CerS-Path integrates eight functions—across morphological diagnosis, predictive analytics, and multimodal tasks—to cover the diagnostic workflow from biopsies to resection specimens. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate improved performance in cervical pathology in female patients, where CerS-Path outperforms state-of-the-art foundation models across 26 of 30 diagnostic tasks. Furthermore, in multicenter retrospective and prospective validation across six independent cohorts of women, CerS-Path achieves up to 99% sensitivity for clinically relevant lesion detection with acceptable specificity across sites, highlighting its potential for screening-derived histopathology and suitability for integration into high-volume diagnostic pathways. Foundation models could be promising for cervical cancer screening, but have important limitations for their clinical deployment. Here, the authors introduce the Cervical Subspecialty Pathology (CerS-Path) diagnostic system, a self-supervised learning framework for cervical cancer pathology that outperforms state-of-the-art foundation models across multiple diagnostic tasks.

Article.Title: Kinetic balancing for near-equilibrium growth of defect-suppressed lead bromide perovskite single crystals
Article.Authors: Zhao X.; Li Z.; Zhou T.; Hao Y.; Wang S.; Meng G.; Xu Y.; Fang X.
Article.Abstract: Controlling crystallization pathways for solution-grown lead-bromide perovskites remains a major unresolved challenge. Herein, we present a ligand-regulated crystallization strategy that achieves near-equilibrium growth for lead-bromide perovskite single crystals. Such regulation mitigates kinetic imbalance during crystal growth, thereby suppressing non-equilibrium defect incorporation, improving lattice coherence, and facilitating spatially uniform crystal growth. This strategy is applicable to a representative set of lead-bromide perovskites. Specifically, the resulting CsPbBr3 single crystals exhibit a high resistivity of 5.1 × 1010 Ω·cm and carrier mobility up to 93.95 cm2·V−1·s−1. Reduced electron-phonon coupling weakens optical-phonon scattering and raises the effective thermally activated conduction barrier from 0.43 to 0.71 eV, extending stable bias operation from 40 to 200 V·mm−1. These advances enable sensitive and stable ionizing-radiation detection under both photon-counting and charge-integrating modes. Overall, this work establishes a general kinetic-design principle for defect-suppressed, near-equilibrium crystallization of lead-bromide perovskites, enabling reliable high-field operation for ionizing-radiation detectors. A ligand-regulated crystallization strategy achieves near-equilibrium growth of lead bromide perovskite single crystals, suppressing defects and improving quality. The resulting CsPbBr3 crystals enable stable, sensitive ionizing-radiation detection.

Article.Title: Chirality-locked low-dimensional bound states in the continuum lasers
Article.Authors: Kim H.; Shin C.; Bae S.; Kim K.; Park H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Bound states in the continuum (BICs) support high-quality-factor resonances embedded in extended spectra, and their radiation properties can be tailored through perturbative symmetry breaking and chiral engineering. However, because BICs are intrinsically delocalized states of infinite periodic structures, they typically require large spatial footprints. Achieving localized BIC modes while preserving radiation suppression and topological singularities, and simultaneously enabling chiral responses, remains a challenge. Here, we experimentally realize low-threshold BIC lasers localized at one-dimensional interfaces and zero-dimensional junctions by interfacing domains with identical bulk BIC characteristics but opposite chirality. The resulting interfaces and junctions host spatially localized states that exhibit optical spin–momentum-locked emission governed by the assigned chirality, while retaining intrinsic BIC properties, including narrow far-field divergence and pump-selective lasing localization. In addition, polarization singularities confirm the topological nature of these low-dimensional BICs, particularly the well-defined topological charge of the zero-dimensional junction mode. Coupling two zero-dimensional BICs further gives rise to bonding and antibonding supermodes, enabling non-Hermitian, chirality-locked behaviors. These results establish a route to compact, high-quality-factor photonic states with engineered chirality through dimensional reduction of BICs, without relying on defect confinement or band inversion.

Article.Title: Sensory cortical disinhibition underlies long-term fear memory in humans
Article.Authors: Brown J.; Ma Y.; Wang Y.; Massa J.; Cheng P.; Chen C.; Ding M.; Schmidt N.; Milad M.; Soares J.; Dolan R.; You C.; Li W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract How transient threats turn into persistent, long-term fear memories is a fundamental problem in neuroscience, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Early sensory cortex, traditionally viewed as a passive feature analyzer, is increasingly recognized as an active participant in fear processing. Combining high-definition α-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (HD α-tACS) with simultaneous EEG-fMRI (electroencephalography-functional magnetic resonance imaging) and transformer-based neural decoding, we tracked fear memory development across formation, consolidation, and long-term retention (assessed at 15 min, 24 h, and 7 days after fear conditioning). Spatiotemporal memory traces were identified at all three assessments, beginning at an early sensory stage (40–60 ms post-stimulus) and distributed across visual cortex and limbic regions. Conditioning potentiated occipital α-oscillation desynchronization, a marker of visual cortical disinhibition, which subsequently predicted the strength of long-term memory traces. Critically, targeted α-tACS over early visual cortex induced early visual cortical (V1/V2) inhibition, abolished conditioning-potentiated α desynchronization, and selectively disrupted fear-memory consolidation and retention while leaving initial acquisition intact. These findings establish sensory cortical disinhibition as a necessary mechanism for long-term fear memory in humans and identify early sensory cortex as crucial node for intervention of persistent maladaptive fear.

Article.Title: Molecular profiling of repeated self-sampled blood reveals dynamic immune phenotypes in young adults
Article.Authors: Bendes A.; Björkander S.; Kere M.; Merid S.; Kumar A.; Dahl L.; Pottinger T.; Yu Z.; Gardell A.; Vogt A.; Kim C.; Pan-Hammarström Q.; Bergström A.; Kull I.; Merritt A.; Ekström S.; Lövquist A.; Murrell B.; Roxhed N.; Melén E.; Schwenk J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Although population-based studies of circulating blood proteins have provided profound insight into human biology, transient changes to time-dependent exposures often remain elusive. Here, we perform a longitudinal dried blood spot (DBS) self-sampling study in 808 young adults (aged 24–27, 64% females) from the Swedish Barn [Children], Allergy, Milieu, Stockholm Epidemiology cohort. In total, we collected ~2400 samples from 2020 to 2022. Each sample was profiled for SARS-CoV-2 serological, anti-interferon autoantibodies (AAbs), and 365 inflammation-related proteins. We subsequently linked these samples to registry-confirmed infection and vaccination exposures, physiological traits, genetic variation, and blood counts. We show that data-driven seroclustering captures the response to both infection and vaccination exposures, while stable AAbs against interferon receptors IFNAR1 and IFNGR2 associate with the duration of self-reported COVID-19 symptoms. Genome-wide mapping reveals 664 protein quantitative trait loci (pQTL) across 65 proteins, with cis -pQTLs associated proteins showing greater longitudinal stability. Paired pre- and post-exposure samples indicate temporal changes in protein levels after infection (LAP3) and vaccination (TIMP3). This multi-molecular epidemiological profiling of self-sampled blood captures dynamic immune trajectories and shorter-term variability in a population of young adults.

Article.Title: Global patterns of radial growth-structural heterogeneity relationships in forests
Article.Authors: Yao Y.; Shu S.; Feng J.; Hu H.; Yang W.; Liu R.; Wang X.; Zhang S.
Article.Abstract: Classical theory predicts that environmental improvement intensifies competition and increases forest structural heterogeneity (variation in tree radial size). Whether warmer and wetter conditions drive convergence in stress-dominated regions remains unknown. Using a global tree-ring dataset ( > 900 sites, > 55,000 cores) with mixed-effects and mediation models, and accounting for Taylor’s law, we show that the negative growth–structure correlation is widespread, but its absolute slope increases along the stress gradient and becomes non-significant in low-stress regions (warm low-altitude, South Temperate, and tropics). Climate-to-structure pathways shift from growth-mediated in stress-dominated regions to non-significant in low-stress regions, with mediation strength increasing from temperate to alpine zones. On the Tibetan Plateau, warmer and wetter conditions are associated with homogenization via enhanced radial growth and reduced climate sensitivity. These findings challenge the classical expectation that environmental improvement inevitably increases structural heterogeneity, revealing a shift from stress-driven convergence to decoupling under low stress and providing a unified framework for predicting forest responses to climate change. Climate change can reshape forest size structure. Using tree rings from > 900 sites, the authors found warming and wetter conditions reduce tree-size inequality in high-stress regions but have little effect in low-stress forests.

Article.Title: Enhancer-driven gene regulatory network of human forebrain development provides insights into autism
Article.Authors: Jourdon A.; Mariani J.; Natu A.; Wu F.; Li B.; Capauto D.; Hagy K.; Norton S.; Tomasini L.; Safi A.; Amiri A.; Schreiner J.; Nguyen C.; Nolan N.; Nelson M.; Ramos D.; Ward M.; Szekely A.; McPartland J.; Pelphrey K.; Ventola P.; Chawarska K.; Gersbach C.; Crawford G.; Abyzov A.
Article.Abstract: Cell differentiation is orchestrated by transcription factors binding to enhancers, shaping gene regulatory networks that drive neuronal lineage specification. Deciphering these enhancer-driven networks in human forebrain development is essential for understanding the genetic basis of neurodevelopmental disorders. Through integrative epigenomic and transcriptomic analyses of human forebrain organoids derived from 10 male individuals with autism spectrum disorder and their neurotypical fathers, we construct a comprehensive enhancer-driven gene regulatory network of early neurodevelopment. This network reveals hierarchical regulatory layers upstream of neuronal cell fate genes, experimentally validated via CRISPR interference and loss-of-function analyses. A subnetwork links autism-associated transcriptomic alterations to opposite activities of the transcription factors FOXG1, BHLHE22, EOMES, and NEUROD2, driving increased or decreased excitatory neuron specification in (respectively) macrocephalic or normocephalic individuals with autism. These findings support the association of autism with disruption of enhancer-driven regulatory networks altering neuronal cell fate decisions in the developing fetal brain. The authors construct a gene regulatory network showing the potential role of specific enhancer elements in driving lineage imbalance in autism, explaining why forebrain organoids from autism probands show heterogeneity in the generation of excitatory neurons.

Article.Title: Tuning methanol-CO selectivity in CO2 hydrogenation by Ga coordination engineering in ZnGa2O4
Article.Authors: Fu Z.; Qin H.; Chen Y.; Gao X.; Xue Y.; Zhang H.; Wang T.
Article.Abstract: Structure sensitivity limits the rational control of CO2 hydrogenation over oxide catalysts, yet how cation coordination governs product selectivity in spinel remains unclear. A synthesis-structure-mechanism framework for ZnGa2O4 is established by linking Ga coordination to methanol and CO production. Ammonia-mediated coprecipitation favors octahedrally coordinated Ga, whereas organic-assisted hydrothermal synthesis enriches tetrahedrally coordinated Ga. Catalytic measurements, structural characterization, in-situ spectroscopy and calculations show that Ga coordination is associated with reaction pathway selection, while surface area, crystallinity and oxygen vacancies also influence CO2 conversion. Octahedral Ga-rich surfaces readily form oxygen vacancies and expose Zn-containing sites, promoting the hydrogenation of formate intermediates to methanol. In contrast, tetrahedral Ga-rich surfaces suppress extensive vacancy formation and favor a carboxyl-mediated pathway to CO. This coordination-based framework links synthesis to operando active-site structure and product distribution, providing a general strategy for programming methanol/CO product distributions in Zn-based spinel catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation. Controlling whether carbon dioxide hydrogenation yields methanol or carbon monoxide remains challenging. This study shows that tuning gallium coordination in ZnGa₂O₄ directs distinct reaction pathways and product selectivity.

Article.Title: Glutamine binding and sodium coordination reveal the transport mechanism of y⁺LAT1/CD98hc
Article.Authors: Aparicio D.; González-Subías M.; Gómez-Gejo P.; Gaitán-Peñas H.; Luengo M.; Gelpí J.; Martínez-Molledo M.; Caballe A.; Llorca O.; Guallar V.; Estévez R.; Palacín M.
Article.Abstract: The heteromeric amino acid transporter y⁺LAT1/CD98hc (SLC7A7/SLC3A2) mediates electroneutral exchange of cationic and neutral amino acids, with Na⁺ required for efficient transport of neutral substrates. Loss-of-function mutations cause Lysinuric Protein Intolerance (LPI), and emerging evidence highlights the physiological relevance of L-glutamine uptake in immune and bone cells. Here, we present the cryo-EM structure of human y⁺LAT1/CD98hc at 3.4 Å resolution in an outward-open conformation bound to L-glutamine, revealing a non-canonical substrate-binding pose involving Cys320 in TM8. Combining docking and molecular dynamics simulations, and functional assays, we identify a Na+-binding tetrad (Asn49–Ser131–Gly323–Ser327) that underlies Na⁺-dependent transport of neutral amino acids. By contrast, cationic substrates such as L-arginine occupy the same locus with their positively charged side chain, effectively replacing the role of Na⁺ and enabling Na⁺-independent exchange. Mutagenesis and kinetic analyses support this mechanism and reveal a key role for Glu128 during transitions toward inward-facing conformations, providing structural insight into the transport cycle. Collectively, these findings establish how y⁺LAT1 integrates Na⁺ and substrate recognition to mediate the selective exchange of neutral and cationic amino acids. Here, cryo-EM, functional and computational studies reveal how the lysinuric protein intolerance transporter y⁺LAT1/CD98hc integrates Na⁺ and substrate recognition to mediate selective exchange of neutral and cationic amino acids.

Article.Title: Emergent mesoscale nanoparticle patterns from a non-equilibrium liquid lens
Article.Authors: Palumbo J.; Asthagiri A.; Hanrath T.
Article.Abstract: Colloidal nanoparticles can assemble into richly structured materials, yet the complex morphologies that emerge under non-equilibrium conditions are often viewed as irreproducible artifacts. Here we show that evaporating a lens-shaped colloidal suspension at a fluid–fluid interface produces a robust cascade of nanoparticle film morphologies, ranging from continuous monolayers to perforated films, ribbon networks, and isolated tiles. Using in situ confocal microscopy and ex situ electron microscopy together with coupled cross-scale simulations, we identify the physical principles that govern this sequence. A macroscopic transport model determines the deposition history imposed by evaporation, which drives a nanoscale kinetic Monte Carlo model capturing particle rearrangement and solvent-mediated kinetic arrest. A coarse-grained Cahn–Hilliard–Stokes framework rationalizes the observed mesoscale periodicity as a finite-wavelength instability of the evolving film. By tuning concentration and solvent volatility, we control the system’s trajectory through this dynamic phase space and establish a predictable framework for navigating non-equilibrium nanoparticle assembly. Nanoparticle assembly at fluid interfaces is often viewed as unpredictable and dominated by uncontrolled non-equilibrium effects. Here, the authors show that evaporation-driven nanoparticle assembly reveals predictable morphologies through multiscale modeling, linking transport dynamics and kinetic arrest.

Article.Title: Theoretical frameworks for credit assignment via behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity
Article.Authors: Cone I.; Clopath C.; Costa R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Behavioral Timescale Synaptic Plasticity (BTSP) is a form of plasticity which drives place field formation in hippocampal pyramidal neurons. Unlike traditional learning rules, BTSP learns pre-post correlations on timescales of seconds and rapidly changes single-unit activity in only a few trials. To study how BTSP-like learning can be integrated into network models, we propose a generalized theoretical framework, gBTSP, which we apply to unsupervised and supervised tasks in feedforward and recurrent networks. We show that unsupervised gBTSP learns place field maps in the feedforward case and attractor memories in the recurrent case. For supervised learning, we derive how plateau events can reduce task error, enabling gBTSP to solve trajectory matching and delayed non-match-to-sample tasks. Finally, we find that the speed of credit assignment via gBTSP is limited by network depth or CA3-like recurrence, suggesting that additional mechanisms are necessary to account for BTSP-driven few-shot learning in naturalistic settings.

Article.Title: A Miniaturized Electrostatic Field Sensor Based on MOS Depletion-Layer Capacitance Modulation
Article.Authors: Liu X.; Wu S.; Ye Y.; Jiang X.; Liang F.; Shen X.; Ye W.; Li C.; Zhang B.; Li Q.; He J.; Hu J.
Article.Abstract: Static and low-frequency electric fields are ubiquitous in natural and engineered systems. Space-charge accumulation, migration, and dissipation regulate local field distributions and are central to dielectric characterization, high-voltage insulation assessment, and power electronic device analysis. However, existing measurement approaches remain limited for embedded online electrostatic field monitoring by mechanical structures, grounding requirements, system size, and complex external readout. Here, we report a miniaturized electrostatic field sensor based on MOS depletion-layer capacitance modulation. An external electric field is converted by an induction electrode into an equivalent bias voltage, which modulates the depletion-layer width and total capacitance of a MOS structure and is read out by a bias-tunable MOS capacitance bridge. By engineering the MOS C–V operating window, the depletion response is positioned within a monotonic regime suitable for bipolar electric field measurements. After calibration in a parallel-plate electrode system, the sensor achieves a measurement range of ±1000 kV/m, a resolution of 178 V/m, and a linearity of 0.9999. Monitoring surface-charge evolution on insulating materials and scanning of surface electric fields on power devices demonstrate that this MOS-based sensor enables miniaturized, floating, and low-perturbation electrostatic field measurements at charged interfaces and in device environments. Static and low-frequency electric fields are important in power systems and insulating materials, but compact non-perturbing sensors remain challenging to build. Here, the authors show a miniaturized MOS-capacitance sensor that measures electric fields with high linearity and enables monitoring of surface charge and device electric fields.

Article.Title: Phenotypic variation in Drosophila complex traits is influenced more by genotype and environmental interactions than by mitonuclear coevolutionary history
Article.Authors: Darwin L.; Lemieux F.; Bachtel R.; Blocker J.; Brown C.; Griffin A.; Lerman J.; Maule O.; Raynes Y.; Rand D.
Article.Abstract: The interdependent relationship between mitochondrial and nuclear genomes is a powerful model for understanding how epistasis shapes the architecture and evolution of complex traits. Once considered a neutral marker, mitochondrial DNA variation is now recognized as critical to phenotypic evolution because of its epistatic interactions and history of coevolution with the nuclear genome. A central challenge in evolutionary genetics is to quantify the relative importance of stabilizing and directional selection shaping complex trait distributions within and among species. Both can act on interacting and/or co-evolving genes contributing to quantitative traits, but resolving their relative roles is complicated by the complex architecture of most traits. Here, we use a panel of 90 Drosophila mitonuclear genotypes to quantify the relative contributions of mitochondrial, nuclear, and environmental variation and their interactions to four metabolically demanding complex traits. We sample both within-species and between-species mitochondrial variation and observe stronger interaction effects attributable to within-species variation, consistent with stabilizing selection maintaining mitonuclear function. Additionally, culturing the flies on a mitochondrial Complex I inhibitor, rotenone, reveals significant genotype × environment (G × E and G × G × E) interaction effects, providing insight into how genetic variation can be maintained across changing environments. Complex traits depend on energy produced by proteins encoded in both mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. By mixing and matching Drosophila variants of these genomes, this study finds that recent mtDNA mutations have more impact on traits than divergent mtDNAs revealing the influence of purifying selection.

Article.Title: Field-angle-resolved heat transport in UTe2: determination of nodal positions in the superconducting order parameter
Article.Authors: Hayes I.; Fang E.; Saha S.; Mishra V.; Hirschfeld P.; Paglione J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract One of the recurring hurdles in studying unconventional superconductivity is the challenge of efficiently and conclusively identifying the symmetry of the superconducting order parameter in a new material. Uranium ditelluride (UTe 2 ) exhibits an unprecedented number of superconducting phases, and none of them has had its symmetry conclusively identified so far. Here we report results of an extensive study of the thermal conductivity of UTe 2 in the superconducting state as a function of the angle of an applied magnetic field rotated in the b-c plane. We observe substantial oscillations in the thermal conductivity as a function of field angle, and, utilizing the experimentally determined Fermi surface, we model this phenomenon for all potential gap structures in UTe 2 . This allows us to identify point nodes near the b-axis, implying that the superconducting order parameter most likely belongs to the B 2 u irreducible representation of the crystal point group.

Article.Title: Multi-ancestry genetic analysis reveals 29 novel rheumatoid arthritis loci, effector genes and drug repurposing opportunities
Article.Authors: Kwon A.; Bang S.; Ha E.; Kim Y.; Joo Y.; Kim B.; Lee H.; Bae S.; Kim K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a complex autoimmune disease with a substantial heritable component. We perform multi-ancestry genome-wide association meta-analyses of 351,498 individuals (comprising 39,600 RA cases and 311,898 controls) by integrating published and new datasets. This analysis identifies 29 novel RA susceptibility loci and systematically classifies association signals as population-specific, population-dominant, or population-shared between East Asian and European populations. Bayesian fine-mapping and functional annotation prioritize putative causal variants, highlighting 67 variants with posterior inclusion probability>0.1 in novel loci, including an SLC27A6 missense variant (rs137898880) and a STIM1 3′ UTR variant (rs3750996). Our gene-prioritization framework combining genetic and biological evidence identifies 203 high-confidence effector genes, 16 of which reside in novel loci (e.g., IFI16 , AIM2 , RGS1 , ITPKB , CD80 , RHOH , NFKB1 , SIK3 , and CCND2 ). Colocalization analysis leveraging tissue-specific eQTL datasets provides mechanistic insights by implicating shared causal variants underlying RA association signals. Notably, the transcription factor gene RUNX3 at a novel locus shows evidence of cis -regulation in immune cells, and RUNX3-binding sites are enriched for variants explaining excess RA heritability, suggesting a potential role for RUNX3 as a trans -regulatory mediator of RA risk at distal RA loci. Finally, exploratory gene-drug interaction networks weighted by RA association strength highlight population-informed therapeutic opportunities and drug-repurposing targets driven largely by novel loci.

Article.Title: Single cell RNA sequencing reveals unexpected heterogeneity and identifies AP2XI-6 as a mature bradyzoite specific cell cycle regulator
Article.Authors: Franklin E.; Arriojas Maldonado A.; Lee K.; Hilliard G.; Martorelli Di Genova B.; Ward G.; Zarringhalam K.; Kent R.
Article.Abstract: Toxoplasma gondii prevalence is due, in part, to its ability to persist in hosts while retaining the capacity to transmit and recrudesce. This process, while critical, is poorly understood. Through single cell RNA profiling of in vivo-derived bradyzoites, we show that bradyzoites are heterogeneous and not G1-arrested, as expected from in vitro studies. Instead, they progress through two distinct cell cycles that branch from a single G1 state. One is common amongst tachyzoites and in vitro- and in vivo-derived bradyzoites; the other is newly identified within the population of in vivo-derived bradyzoites. While in G1b, these in vivo-derived bradyzoites express cyst wall proteins predicted to replenish the wall that protects cysts and prevents clearance. We demonstrate that AP2XI-6, a putative AP2-transcription factor expressed by bradyzoites in G1 in vivo, is dispensable for tachyzoite growth and cyst formation in vitro but necessary for encystation or persistence in vivo. We propose that AP2XI-6 is a driver of replication through the newly identified in vivo bradyzoite specific cell cycle and that this is required for cyst maturation or persistence. Authors show mature chronic-stage T. gondii adopt cell-cycle-controlled cyst-wall protein expression and two cell-cycle architectures in vivo. AP2XI-6 is required for the mature architecture; without it, parasites form cysts in vitro but fail in vivo.

Article.Title: Built-in electric field driven MXene/perovskite Schottky heterojunction for photo-electro-thermal energy redistribution in thermochromic smart windows
Article.Authors: Li X.; Lu X.; Wang C.; Li Q.; Fu Y.; Wang W.; Zhang R.; Shi Q.; Li Z.; Feng D.; Liu S.; Zhu Y.; Fan X.; Wu H.; Liu Y.; Tso C.
Article.Abstract: Perovskite-based thermochromic smart windows offer a sustainable solution for energy-efficient building technologies. However, existing strategies to reconcile the transition temperature of thermochromic perovskites with practical application temperatures primarily rely on extrinsic composite engineering, often neglecting the intrinsic multi-energy field conversion and photo-electro-thermal coupling effects of perovskites. Here, we introduce a band structure engineering strategy by constructing a MXene/perovskite Schottky heterojunction, leveraging an interfacial built-in electric field to induce photon energy redistribution. The Fermi level alignment between Ti3C2Tx and MAPbI3-xClx facilitates light-activated band bending, which enhances ultraviolet/visible photon harvesting for charge generation (photoelectric channel), complementing the inherent broadband photothermal effect of MXene (photothermal channel). This dual-energy utilization pathway, integrated within a MXene-enhanced perovskite architecture, significantly enhances the photo-electro-thermal performance. The fabricated multilayer Cl-doped perovskite smart window demonstrates a self-induced room-temperature thermochromic transition with a narrow thermal hysteresis of 5.2 °C and a 55% enhancement in photocurrent density. It also exhibits scalable manufacturability, competitive stability, extensive energy-saving performance, and multi-band communication compatibility. This work establishes a universal design paradigm for thermally responsive materials, and the multi-channel photon energy utilization strategy can be extended to other energy-efficient phase-transition systems, with promising implications for global carbon neutrality efforts. A MXene and chloride-doped perovskite Schottky junction uses a built-in electric field to route ultraviolet and visible light into charge separation and interfacial heating, enabling room-temperature switching with 5.2 degrees Celsius hysteresis, 20.5% solar modulation, and 55% higher photocurrent.

Article.Title: A split RNA-guided Cas9 system for PAM-independent and cis-cleavage-free nucleic acid detection
Article.Authors: Yin W.; Xu H.; Xia X.; Du Y.; Wang X.; He R.; Chen Z.; Qiao J.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: The CRISPR-Cas9 system exhibits limited trans-cleavage activity, restricting its utility for nucleic acid detection. Here, we present a split RNA-guided Cas9 system (SCas9) that overcomes this limitation. By partitioning single-guide RNA into functionally independent scaffold and spacer modules, SCas9 enables amplification-free detection of single-stranded DNA and RNA with picomolar sensitivity within 30 min and single-nucleotide specificity. Incorporation of λ exonuclease permits PAM-independent detection of double-stranded DNA without cis-cleavage activity. Coupling SCas9 with recombinase polymerase amplification or reverse transcription–recombinase polymerase amplification extends detection of double-stranded DNA and long RNA to attomolar sensitivity. We further developed an autocatalytic SCas9 strategy for attomolar microRNA detection. SCas9 demonstrates broad substrate compatibility and was validated in clinical specimens, including human papillomavirus 16 in vaginal secretions and miR-21 in colorectal cancer tissues, highlighting its potential for point-of-care diagnostics. CRISPR-Cas9 lacks collateral cleavage for nucleic acid diagnostics. Here, authors show that splitting the guide RNA into scaffold and spacer converts Cas9 into SCas9, enabling rapid, single-nucleotide-specific DNA/RNA sensing, PAM-independent dsDNA detection, and attomolar clinical assays.

Article.Title: Light-driven oxidative coupling of methane via charge-symmetry-breaking
Article.Authors: Xue F.; Zhang C.; Fu W.; Cheng C.; Yan X.; Liu S.; Liu F.; Peng H.; Li H.; Zhang Q.; Qin Y.; Hu Z.; Huang W.; Pao C.; Chen M.; Liu M.; Huang X.; Xu Y.
Article.Abstract: Light-driven oxidative coupling of methane into C2+ chemicals represents a sustainable route towards carbon-neutral management, yet faces critical challenges including narrow solar spectrum utilization, inefficient charge carrier dynamics, and tricky C − C coupling. Herein, we achieve highly active and selective light-driven methane conversion to C2+ chemicals over multi-interfacial CuO/ZnO heterojunction. Mechanistic investigations reveal that charge redistribution at CuO/ZnO interface creates interfacial sites with unbalanced electronic states, which promote methane dissociation, alleviate coupling energy of methyl intermediates, and suppress electrostatic repulsion, thereby facilitating C − C coupling. Additionally, Z-Scheme charge transfer spatially decouples oxygen reduction on CuO and methane oxidation on ZnO, respectively. Consequently, CuO/ZnO delivers an ethane yield of 30.87 mmol g−1 h−1 with a C2+ selectivity up to 97.8%, an apparent quantum yield of 3.9% at 420 nm and a durability of 124 h. Here, we show that charge symmetry breaking provides a feasible strategy for converting methane to high-value C2+ chemicals. The successful construction of multiple CuO/ZnO interfaces with charge symmetry breaking achieves a high POCM performance with a C2H6 yield of 30.87 mmol g − 1 h − 1 and C2+ selectivity of 97.8% under ambient conditions in flowing reactor.

Article.Title: Boosting reinforcement learning for critical node detection with multi-topology training strategies
Article.Authors: Bhandari K.; Chen P.; Havlin S.; Gao J.
Article.Abstract: Identifying pivotal components in complex networks—such as key intersections in transportation systems, influential actors in social networks, or keystone species in ecosystems—is essential for improving the resilience and mitigating catastrophic failures of these systems. However, existing methods for critical node detection are typically tailored to specific network types and objectives, limiting their generalizability. To overcome this limitation, we propose a machine learning framework that combines reinforcement learning with an attention-based graph neural network. By leveraging multi-topology training, our model learns to adapt and generalize across diverse network structures and objective functions. Experiments on real-world and synthetic networks uncover distinct topological features that are important for identifying critical nodes. Notably, our method applied to personalized gene networks, prioritizes genes that are significantly enriched for cataloged cancer drivers. This work provides a robust critical node detection model with a comprehensive multi-topology training approach, suitable for a broader range of real-world applications. Critical node detection helps identify network elements whose removal most disrupts connectivity. Here, the authors develop a reinforcement-learning approach that trains on diverse graph topologies to improve generalization to both synthetic and real networks.

Article.Title: Agricultural economic responses to ecoclimate teleconnections induced by forest loss
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Zhao L.; Fei C.; McCarl B.; Wang X.; Liu M.; Breshears D.; Feng X.; Baldwin E.; Cheng H.; Derbridge J.; Golding J.; Lien A.; López-Hoffman L.; McLaughlin D.; Swann A.; Soto J.
Article.Abstract: Forest disturbances are increasing globally, altering vegetation in ways that can affect distant agricultural systems through ecoclimate teleconnections. We examine how large-scale U.S. regional forest loss with C3 grass replacement affects agricultural production and markets. We integrate climate simulations, econometric yield models, and an agricultural sector model to trace impacts from vegetation change through climate anomalies to yields, land allocation, prices, and welfare, while isolating vegetation-driven effects from greenhouse-gas forcing. Teleconnection-induced yield responses are spatially heterogeneous. Soybean yields decline, particularly in the Southern Plains, while wheat gains occur there and corn responses are muted. This shifts regional crop mixes and increases total production by 1–3%, lowering crop prices, increasing consumer surplus, and reducing producer surplus, with small positive net agricultural welfare effects. Our study excludes forest-sector impacts and ecosystem-service losses and therefore does not imply that forest loss is beneficial. Forest loss across 14 U.S. regions can affect distant climates. Linking these teleconnections to crop yields and agricultural markets reveals soybean losses, wheat gains, 1–3% higher total production, lower crop prices, and small net gains in agricultural welfare.

Article.Title: Functional diversity of GPCR–Gustducin complexes controls signaling output and suppresses alternative pathways
Article.Authors: Jaime Arce V.; Lettmann M.; Tögl M.; Bonn Garcia S.; Bauer M.; Neukirch M.; Kleinstück O.; Langolf A.; Kaczmarek I.; Hilger D.; Schihada H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Gustducin (G gust ), the G protein mediating taste receptor signaling, is expressed not only in sensory taste cells but throughout the human body alongside numerous non-taste G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). Whether and how these receptors engage G gust , and the functional consequences of such interactions, remain poorly understood. Here, we develop two complementary biosensors that enable direct monitoring of GPCR–G gust interaction and downstream signaling in living cells, allowing pharmacological characterization of G gust activity induced by non-taste GPCRs. We find that several non-taste GPCRs do not activate G gust but instead stabilize the G protein heterotrimer and suppress basal signaling by forming unproductive GPCR–G protein complexes, whereas others induce conventional G gust activation and signal transduction. We further show that these unproductive GPCR–G gust complexes suppress the activation of alternative signaling pathways by sequestering receptors from other G proteins. This mode of interaction functionally partitions GPCRs into activators and inactivators of G gust and represents a mechanism for balancing concurrent signaling pathways within a cell.

Article.Title: Sunflower pollen microgels enable sonication-free dispersion of carbon nanotubes for bio-based conductive inks
Article.Authors: Gao C.; Yang D.; Liang J.; Wang Z.; Zhao M.; Zhao Z.; Deng H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Sustainable, high-performance conductive inks are crucial for next-generation wearable electronics. While biopolymer-based dispersants offer renewable and biocompatible routes for stabilizing carbon nanotube (CNT) inks, a critical paradox persists: utilizing molecular biopolymers typically requires energy-intensive extraction, depends on high-power ultrasonication for debundling, and lacks the rheological strength needed for precision extrusion printing. Here, we present a sonication-free strategy utilizing sunflower pollen microgels in their native, soft granular state. Leveraging the pollen’s amphiphilic, spiky architecture, we achieve CNT debundling through mechanically driven colloidal collisions, while a synergistic alginate corona provides electrostatic stabilization. The resulting pollen–alginate–CNT (PAC) inks exhibit rapid thixotropy and high viscoelasticity, enabling high-fidelity 3D extrusion and screen printing. Uniquely, drying induces a layered self-assembly, where microgels collapse into lamellar architectures to form anisotropic conductive networks. These structural features unlock multifunctional performance, including humidity sensing via interlayer-spacing modulation, direction-dependent strain sensing, and outstanding electromagnetic interference shielding. This work establishes a scalable, energy-efficient particulate-stabilizer framework that overcomes the processing and rheological limitations of conventional bio-based inks, advancing sustainable, adaptive printed electronic systems.

Article.Title: Anion manipulation for breaking through 3.0 V of aluminium–graphite batteries
Article.Authors: Guo K.; Huang Z.; Wang W.; Song W.; Jiao S.
Article.Abstract: Aluminium-graphite batteries offer low cost and intrinsic high safety. However, the voltage window mostly remains limited because conventional chloroaluminate ionic-liquid electrolytes with Lewis-acidic Al2Cl7−([AlCl3–AlCl4]−) anions are intrinsically moisture-sensitive and unstable beyond 2.5 V. To extend the voltage window, a polytetrafluoroethylene/AlF3 framework‑confined, fluorine-rich chloroaluminate ionic-liquid composite quasi-solid-state electrolyte cosolvated with 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl ether is designed for constructing stable aluminium-graphite batteries with a cut-off voltage of 3.0 V. With the presence of AlF3, the Al2Cl7− is regulated through AlF3-associated chloroaluminate interactions, which reduces its activity and suppresses its electrochemical decomposition in the range of 2.5–3.0 V. Meanwhile, the fluorinated ether coordinates with the AlCl3 units in Al2Cl7− and promotes the formation of a fluorine-rich artificial interface on the graphite, essentially improving the electrochemical stability via alleviating electrochemical decomposition of AlCl4− up to 3.0 V. Furthermore, ion transport channels could be well maintained during large mechanical deformation induced by anion-intercalation/deintercalation of graphite interlayer. Therefore, the Al|electrolyte|graphite cells deliver discharge capacity beyond 137 mAh g−1 up to 3.0 V (specific current: 5.0 A g−1) (compared to 64 mAh g−1, charged up to 2.5 V at 5.0 A g−1) along with stable cycles beyond 35,000, demonstrating long-term high-voltage operation in rechargeable aluminium–graphite batteries. Aluminium–graphite batteries are limited by electrolyte decomposition above 2.5 V. Here, authors regulate chloroaluminate anions with a fluorine-rich, framework-confined quasi-solid-state electrolyte, enabling stable 3.0 V operation for Al | |Graphite cells.

Article.Title: Room-temperature continuous-wave lasing-like emission from solution-processed bulk monolayer MoS2 thin films
Article.Authors: Zhou B.; Li H.; Hu B.; Zhou J.; Li C.; Zhou J.; Huang Y.; Duan X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are promising laser-gain media for their direct bandgap and strong excitonic effects. However, existing TMD lasers typically rely on mechanically exfoliated or high-temperature chemical-vapor-deposition-grown materials, with their atomic-scale thickness inherently limiting the available optical gain volume. Here, we report room-temperature continuous-wave lasing-like emission from solution-processed bulk monolayer MoS 2 (BM-MoS 2 ) thin films in whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) cavities. Using solution exfoliation and spray coating under ambient conditions, we produce area- and thickness-scalable BM-MoS 2 films composed of electronically decoupled MoS 2 monolayers separated by organic spacers. This layered architecture preserves the intrinsic monolayer excitonic properties while providing a tunable gain volume beyond that of an isolated monolayer. Integrated with WGM cavities, the thickness-scalable BM-MoS 2 films enable a balance between the quality ( Q ) and optical confinement ( $$\varGamma$$ Γ ) factors. Power-dependent measurements reveal key lasing signatures, including a threshold-like input-output crossover accompanied by linewidth narrowing at a pump power of approximately 1.4 nW, and pump-induced polarization selection. Solution-processable BM-MoS 2 thus offers a scalable gain medium for thin-film laser photonics.

Article.Title: Signatures of a Kondo insulator in a multilayer moiré Superlattice
Article.Authors: Wu Q.; Cui J.; Wu A.; Meng Y.; Chen D.; Wang Y.; Yan L.; Ma L.; Taniguchi T.; Watanabe K.; Lin S.; Shi S.; Cui Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Kondo insulators are paradigmatic strongly correlated materials, traditionally found in f-electron compounds. They originate from the hybridization between itinerant conduction electrons and localized magnetic moments, which opens a gap in the electronic spectrum. Two-dimensional moiré systems provide a new route to flat bands with strong electron correlation, which host localized moments at half filling. Here we report signatures, based on local conductivity measurements using microwave impedance microscopy, of a Kondo insulator in a moiré superlattice of monolayer WS 2 / bilayer WSe 2 , in which one WSe 2 layer carries flat moiré bands and the other dispersive ones. When both layers are partially doped with two holes per moiré unit cell in total, an insulating state appears when the moiré band contains less than one hole. The insulator becomes metallic above a certain threshold magnetic field, evidence for the singlet nature of the Kondo insulator, and the observed behavior is reproduced by a periodic Anderson model. Our results open a route to simulating Kondo physics in tunable moiré systems.

Article.Title: The posterior paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus to nucleus accumbens medial shell circuit mediates an anti-pruritic response
Article.Authors: Zheng J.; Wang Z.; Lin J.; Huang C.; Pan G.; Xu D.; Hu X.; Gao S.
Article.Abstract: Notable differences between histamine-dependent and histamine-independent itch have been extensively researched at peripheral and spinal levels. However, the way in which the brain processes histamine-dependent and histamine-independent itch remains unknown. We discovered that the posterior paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (pPVT)→the nucleus accumbens medial shell (NAcMed) circuit exhibits reverse response patterns to histamine-dependent or histamine-independent itch and serves as a central anti-pruritic role. Mechanistically, histamine-dependent itch activates excitatory inputs from the lateral hypothalamus (LH) to mobilise the anti-pruritic centre, thereby buffering its intensity. In cases of chronic itch, however, there is a decrease in the efficiency of the anti-pruritic circuit’s postsynaptic transmission, thereby promoting itch sensitisation. Our research reveals that histamine-dependent and histamine-independent itch are processed differently in the mouse brain, offering insights into the neural mechanisms underlying chronic itch sensitization. Neural mechanisms underlying itch are not fully understood. Here authors show that the pPVT-NAcMed (posterior paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus to nucleus accumbens medial shell) circuit oppositely responds to histamine-dependent vs -independent itch, with LH inputs buffering the former, but chronic itch reduces postsynaptic efficacy, promoting sensitization and revealing differential processing.

Article.Title: Thermodynamic-guided tailoring of single-atom coordination environments via oxygen chemical potential for efficient C-N coupling
Article.Authors: Gong Q.; Lan H.; Zhao H.; Zhang W.; Li X.; Chen M.; Huang T.; Si J.; Huang H.; Zhao H.; Hu Y.; Yang X.; Wang J.; Yan X.; Chen Z.
Article.Abstract: Systematic and precise regulation of coordination environments in single-atom catalysts (SACs) remains challenging due to thermodynamic constraints and kinetic traps. Herein, we report a thermodynamic-guided strategy to tailor the local coordination of Fe single atoms on CoWO4 support by regulating oxygen chemical potential. Via fine-tuning hydrogen partial pressure during pyrolysis, a series of Fe1Ox SACs is synthesized with well-defined Fe-O coordination numbers ranging from 3 to 6. Combining operando characterizations and density functional theory calculations, Fe1O4 is identified as the optimal configuration for hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) electrosynthesis, which delivers balanced kinetics by moderating free water dissociation for *NH3 generation and strengthening HCHO chemisorption via pronounced Fe 3d-O 2p orbital hybridization near the Fermi level. As a result, the Fe1O4 SAC achieves a HMTA yield of 0.21 mmol h−1 cm−2 with 83.04% Faradaic efficiency at 1.75 V and stability over 200 h in a flow cell. This work establishes a universal thermodynamic approach for precise coordination engineering of single-atom electrocatalysts and provides a general paradigm for kinetically balancing complex multi-intermediate electrocatalytic systems. Precise control of single-atom coordination is hindered by thermodynamic and kinetic constraints. Here, the authors report tuning Fe-O coordination on CoWO4 via oxygen chemical potential control. Optimal Fe1O4 boosts hexamethylenetetramine electrosynthesis with high yield, efficiency and stability.

Article.Title: Post-pandemic immunity debt and environmental decoupling reshape urban influenza transmission
Article.Authors: Xing A.; Ng H.; Lin J.; Ye Q.; Tong H.; Li Y.; Liang J.; Ma Y.; Jiang G.; Li K.
Article.Abstract: Relaxation of COVID-19 non-pharmaceutical interventions was followed by a global resurgence of respiratory infections, yet how accumulated population susceptibility interacts with environmental forcing and human mobility remains unclear. Here we analyse ~1.88 million clinical influenza tests from Macau (2010-2025) alongside meteorology, air quality, digital information-seeking, and independent surveillance and time-resolved viral genomes from Hong Kong, benchmarked against global surveillance data. Counterfactual inference indicates a post-pandemic excess in influenza activity consistent with immunity debt, mirroring global resurgence patterns, and an independently parameterised susceptible–exposed–infectious–recovered–susceptible model reproduces this excess (best-fit debt fraction 42%; approximate Bayesian computation posterior 58%, 95% uncertainty interval 32-77%). Susceptibility rises disproportionately in adults rather than children, whereas vaccination coverage in high-risk groups does not decline, arguing against reduced uptake as the driver. Time-varying models and convergent cross mapping reveal environmental decoupling, whereby high susceptibility weakens meteorological constraints and sustains influenza A transmission, and asymmetric suppression of influenza B. Spatiotemporal and phylogenetic evidence supports travel-linked reintroduction from ports of entry into dense neighbourhoods, and digital information-seeking shifts from lagging to leading clinical burden. These findings indicate a post-pandemic regime shift in influenza dynamics rather than a return to historical baselines, motivating adaptive, multi-source surveillance in high-density cities. Using 1.88 million clinical records from Macau and regional and global surveillance, in this study, the authors show how reduced population immunity and renewed travel reshaped post-pandemic influenza transmission and weakened its usual links with climate.

Article.Title: Epithelium stratifies via nucleation and growth induced by foam-geometric instability
Article.Authors: Fukamachi S.; Datta R.; Wuergezhen D.; Ichikawa T.; Yagasaki R.; Leeaw P.; Arai M.; Teranishi A.; Horiguchi S.; Omachi K.; Sada A.; Imayoshi I.; Kajiwara K.; Hiraiwa T.; Oshima M.; Fukuma T.; Fujiwara H.; Okuda S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Epithelial stratification, the transition from a monolayer to a multilayer structure, occurs across a wide range of phenomena. Recent studies have identified several cell behaviors as triggers, including junctional tension, cell density and geometry, and topological defects. However, how these factors drive stratification throughout the entire epithelium remains poorly understood. Here, we show that epithelial stratification proceeds through a nucleation-and-growth mechanism. Combining cell culture with three-dimensional vertex modeling, we demonstrate that multilayer origins emerge in a dispersed manner and expand across the epithelium through disordered intermediate states. This transition is induced by a mechanical instability inherent in the foam-like geometry of the epithelium. Moreover, the nucleation-growth concept applies to embryonic skin development and intestinal cancer transformation. These findings conceptualize epithelial stratification as a form of structural transition governed by foam mechanics, offering a physical perspective on various epithelial developments.

Article.Title: Sublevel-selective electron spin hyperpolarization of triplet radical pairs in metal–organic frameworks
Article.Authors: Hamachi T.; Huang Y.; Eckvahl H.; Carella A.; Peinkofer K.; Young R.; Krzyaniak M.; Ito T.; Kurashige Y.; Yabuki R.; Wasielewski M.; Yanai N.
Article.Abstract: Molecular spin systems are promising platforms for spin-based technologies because their electronic structures can be synthetically tailored and integrated into higher-order assemblies. Photogenerated radical pairs can exhibit spin hyperpolarization under ambient conditions, yet extending such spin dynamics from isolated molecules to structurally organized materials remains challenging. Here, we report a metal-organic framework that regulates the generation of spin-polarized radical pairs within locally well-defined donor-acceptor arrangements. N,N'-di(4-pyridyl)-1,4,5,8-naphthalenetetracarboxdiimide is introduced into a zinc tetrakis(4-carboxyphenyl)porphyrin-based framework. Dense donor-acceptor packing promotes efficient quenching of the porphyrin singlet excited state and selectively forms strongly coupled triplet radical pairs polarized in the zero-spin projection sublevel. These radical pairs exhibit narrow electron paramagnetic resonance signals and long spin-lattice relaxation times. Their spin-lattice relaxation dynamics persist in various guest solvents and vary with guest identity, demonstrating a route to chemically responsive spin materials based on porous, locally organized donor-acceptor frameworks.

Article.Title: Strain-induced correlated metallic phase in 1T-TaS2
Article.Authors: Suzuki S.; Nakayama K.; Yanagizawa K.; Sugawara K.; Souma S.; Ozawa K.; Takano S.; Takahara R.; Hara T.; Wakabayashi Y.; Takahashi T.; Nojima T.; Ueno K.; Sato T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Layered transition-metal dichalcogenide 1T-TaS 2 has long been considered a prime example of a Mott insulator driven by strong electron correlations. However, this view has been recently challenged by proposals which favor a band insulating state arising from interlayer dimerization. This ongoing debate opens a frontier in 1T-TaS 2 research focusing on stacking order, and raises a fundamental question with broad implications for two-dimensional materials: can electronic phases be engineered by actively tuning interlayer coupling? Here, using micro-focused angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy supported by first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that uniaxial strain drives 1T-TaS 2 from its insulating charge-density-wave phase into a stable metallic phase. This metallic phase, distinct from hydrostatic-pressure-induced or non-equilibrium hidden phases, emerges via a strain-induced rearrangement in the interlayer stacking of the Star-of-David charge order, effectively disrupting interlayer dimerization. Furthermore, the emergent metallic phase exhibits a significant quasiparticle mass renormalization, a hallmark of strong electron correlations, indicating its correlated nature and proximity to a Mott instability. This finding necessitates a re-evaluation of the interplay between structural and strong correlations in 1T-TaS 2 . The present results establish uniaxial strain as a powerful method for tuning the interlayer coupling, opening pathways for exploring quantum phases inaccessible under ambient conditions.

Article.Title: Vagal afferent activation induces a dissociated NREM sleep-like state with wake-related locus coeruleus activity
Article.Authors: Cherrad N.; Foustoukos G.; Fernandez L.; Osorio-Forero A.; Buron J.; Eliasson N.; Emmenegger Y.; Milanese P.; Ferreira Morais J.; Mansuy-Aubert V.; Franken P.; Lüthi A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Parasympathetic nervous system activity, vital for restorative sleep, is influenced by vagal sensory afferents, but how these shape brain-body correlates of sleep remains open. Here we combined vagal sensory neuron (VSN) stimulation in the mouse with EEG/EMG, heart rate, brain-body temperature, noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC) neuron population activity measures and in vitro synaptic physiology to investigate the effects of VSN activation on sleep-wake states. We show that chemogenetic VSN stimulation during the resting phase induced a non-rapid-eye-movement sleep (NREMS)-like state with enriched, but homeostatically regulated, low-frequency (0.75–4 Hz) EEG activity, yet suppressed REMS. Simultaneously, brain-body temperatures dropped while LC activity increased. The gradual recovery towards normal NREMS-REMS-cycles was accelerated by external warming, identifying cooling as key contributing factor. We conclude that VSN activation can promote brain-body correlates as a continuum of normal NREMS while engaging wake-promoting forebrain neuromodulation, revealing a coexistence of classically incompatible sleep- and wake-associated signatures.

Article.Title: Photonic-assisted ingenious agile non-periodic oscillator (PIANO)
Article.Authors: Hao T.; Yang T.; Cen Q.; Wang L.; Xiao S.; Li M.; Wang A.; Li W.; Hao P.; Steve Yao X.; Capmany J.; Zhu N.; Dai Y.; Li M.
Article.Abstract: The development of high-performance frequency-agile microwave signal generators has long been constrained by the inherent limitations of electronic technology. To overcome this challenge, researchers have increasingly turned to photonics, leveraging its high-frequency and broad-bandwidth capabilities. Here, we introduce and demonstrate a Photonic-assisted Ingenious Agile Non-periodic Oscillator (PIANO), which enables high-performance frequency-agile microwave signal generation with flexible frequency agility, ultra-low phase noise, rapid switching speed, and large time-bandwidth product (TBWP). The key innovation of PIANO lies in incorporating a dynamic frequency-shifting module into an optoelectronic oscillator (OEO) cavity, thereby extending the conventional delay-based OEO framework by decoupling frequency-agility behavior from the cavity-delay constraint. During experiments, PIANO successfully generated various flexible frequency-agile waveforms, with a frequency-switching time of 27 ns, phase noise as low as −134 dBc/Hz@10 kHz, and TBWP up to 1,440,000. This work offers a promising approach to high-performance frequency-agile microwave signal generation for applications such as radar and communication systems. The study presents PIANO, a microwave photonic oscillator that generates frequency-agile microwave signals with rapid switching and ultra-low phase noise, while overcoming the cavity-delay constraint of conventional delay-based oscillators.

Article.Title: Selective aromatization of polyolefins by temporal decoupling from cracking
Article.Authors: Xu X.; Ding Y.; Qi G.; Wang R.; Bai L.; Guo C.; Gao R.; Feng G.; Feng Y.; Chen S.; Zhao Z.; Pei C.; Fu D.; Gong J.
Article.Abstract: Cracking of polyolefins is a prerequisite for their selective conversion over microporous zeolites to value-added small molecules such as monocyclic aromatics. However, cracking and aromatization often proceed concurrently, creating an intrinsic accessibility-selectivity conflict that limits aromatic yield and productivity. This paper describes a strategy that temporally decouples polyolefin cracking from selective aromatization in one-pot with tandem catalysts. This strategy delivers an aromatic yield of ca. 60.3 wt% within 0.5 h at 380 °C from postconsumer polyolefins over 40 consecutive cycles, corresponding to an aromatic space-time yield of 11 g gcat−1 h−1, more than twofold higher than reported values of ≤ 5 g gcat−1 h−1. Kinetic and mechanistic studies reveal that self-pillared pentasil zeolite rapidly and processively cracks polyolefins to small olefinic intermediates below 320 °C, enabling temporal decoupling of low-temperature cracking from higher-temperature aromatization through distinct dominant kinetic windows. Process modeling further suggests favorable economic potential and life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions 26% lower than fossil-based aromatics production and 66% lower than incineration. This work establishes temporal decoupling as a reaction-engineering strategy for reconciling polymer accessibility with micropore-controlled selectivity in plastic upcycling. Turning plastic waste into useful chemicals is limited because breaking polymer chains and controlling products need conflicting conditions. This study separates these steps in time, enabling fast, durable aromatic production with lower emissions.

Article.Title: Failure of TSPO-dependent metabolic compensation marks the loss of mitochondrial bioenergetic adaptation in parkin-deficient neurons
Article.Authors: Cho J.; Cho S.; Kim E.; Jo M.; Choe J.; Lee S.; Hyeon D.; Kim T.; Chung C.; Kim M.; Lee Y.; Park H.; Lee W.; Hwang D.; Seo J.; Lee S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neurons require mitochondrial bioenergetic flexibility to withstand chronic mitochondrial quality control failure, yet the compensatory safeguards that preserve mitochondrial functional output during neurodegenerative progression remain unclear. Here, using parkin- deficient fly models, we identify an early mitochondrial metabolic signature characterized by reduced pyruvate and increased glutamate and α-ketoglutarate. Substrate-specific mitochondrial respiration and ATP assays showed impaired pyruvate-supported bioenergetic capacity but preserved glutamate-supported bioenergetic capacity, supporting a transient glutamate-linked compensatory state before neurodegenerative deterioration. We identify neuronal TSPO upregulation as an adaptive compensatory mechanism that sustains glutamate-supported mitochondrial bioenergetic capacity under parkin -deficient conditions. In human iPSC-derived neurons, parkin deficiency was similarly associated with TSPO upregulation, and TSPO modulation altered neuronal vulnerability. TSPO induction was controlled by JNK-Jun/Nrf2 signaling, whose age-associated attenuation compromised compensation and accelerated neurodegeneration. Thus, loss of TSPO-dependent glutamate-linked bioenergetic compensation marks the transition from mitochondrial adaptation to neurodegenerative deterioration under parkin -deficient conditions.

Article.Title: Comparative genomics analysis of luminescent and non-luminescent fireflies reveals mechanisms underlying adult light organs development
Article.Authors: Fu X.; Zhu X.; Wu G.
Article.Abstract: The genetic and developmental basis for the gain and loss of complex traits remains a central question in evolutionary biology. We investigate the loss of the adult light organ (LO) in the diurnal non-luminous firefly Pristolycus diversecostatus as a natural case of lineage-specific gene loss. A high-quality genome assembly of Pri. diversecostatus, combined with comparative multi-omics and functional analyses with its luminous relative Aquatica leii, reveals that LO loss correlates with large-scale gene family contraction and transcriptional rewiring of three core metabolic modules. RNAi experiments in Aqu. leii show that Laccase2 is required for LO integrity and bioluminescence. Key regulators of LO-specific cuticle transparency are identified, and a homeobox centered gene regulatory network is uncovered. This multi-omics study provides a genome-wide perspective on the regulatory modules underlying a complex organ and offers a framework based on regulatory network simplification for understanding the formation and loss of complex traits in evolution. Not all fireflies emit light. Here they perform comparative genomics between luminous and non-luminous fireflies to reveal that light organ loss stems from simplified gene networks. They show that Laccase2 is essential for light organ integrity, offering insights into bioluminescence trait evolution.

Article.Title: Intrinsic neural dynamics reveal a body-part-specific topography in mouse secondary motor cortex
Article.Authors: Xu W.; Yagielski A.; Thibodeaux D.; Carmona L.; Ugorji K.; Shahsavarani S.; Kim S.; Lodgher F.; Zhao H.; Malan E.; Xu L.; Freeman C.; Bisht A.; Swayze K.; Cambareri M.; Li W.; Hillman E.
Article.Abstract: The mammalian sensory cortex (S1) has a well-characterized body part-specific topography. However, most motor cortex atlases to date are only coarsely defined. Here, we demonstrate that optical mapping of neuronal activity in awake mice reveals a distinct, body-part specific organization of mouse secondary motor cortex (M2). This M2 topography was identified by recognizing that intrinsic neuronal fluctuations are selectively synchronized between homologous sub-regions of S1 and M2. These fluctuations were strongest during rest and quenched during movement, and were not prominent in corticospinal neurons (CSNs), indicating that they do not represent motor output. Functional characterization of M2 sub-regions during spontaneous movements confirms body-part specificity, and stronger engagement during multi-effector coordinated actions. Structural connectivity atlas tracings from S1 regions confirm projections to homologous M2 sub-regions. These results reveal an important underlying topography within M2, and demonstrate intrinsic neuronal dynamics as a window into the functional architecture of the motor cortex.

Article.Title: A microfluidic fluorescence lifetime screening platform bridges in vitro and in vivo formats and enables discovery of Amyloid β aggregation inhibitors
Article.Authors: Collins S.; D. van Vliet L.; Gielen F.; Janeček M.; Läubli N.; Valladolid S.; Poudel C.; Fernandez-Villegas A.; Deingruber T.; Fusco G.; De Simone A.; Michel C.; Kaminski C.; Spring D.; Hollfelder F.; Kaminski Schierle G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Inhibiting the aggregation of Amyloid β (1-42) is a promising strategy for the development of disease-modifying Alzheimer’s disease therapeutics. To date, however, no sufficiently efficacious inhibitors have been identified, despite the best efforts of more than 200 advanced drug development campaigns. This failure can be partially attributed to limitations in current in vitro compound screening and in vivo validation assays. Here, we report a high throughput assay platform based on the use of a fluorescence lifetime aggregation sensor that can be applied in vitro and in vivo. This microfluidic “nanoFLIM” assay presents a cost-effective and reliable alternative to conventional early-stage small molecule discovery platforms for cell-free Amyloid β aggregation. The fluorescence lifetime sensor can dynamically monitor peptide aggregation in cellular and Caenorhabditis elegans disease models, providing directly comparable aggregation kinetics, which is not achievable by any other method. The power of this unified platform for accelerating hit-to-lead strategies, lowering attrition rates and expediting in vivo screening, was demonstrated with a pilot screening campaign of 445 compounds, revealing an inhibitor that can inhibit Amyloid β self-assembly both in vitro as well as in cellular and whole organism disease models.

Article.Title: Depth-enhanced molecular imaging with two-photon oblique plane microscopy
Article.Authors: Keomanee-Dizon K.; Clenman Y.; Duran A.; Ryabichko S.; Hansen P.; Borjigin T.; Thornton R.; Toettcher J.; McNamara H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves ~ 300 nm lateral and ~ 650 nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and < 60 nm localization precision in vivo. Compared with two-photon point scanning, the lower illumination NA delivers order-of-magnitude lower peak intensity, enabling > 5 × faster volumetric acquisition (up to 3.25 × 10 6 voxels s −1 ). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by ~ 2 × and restores volumetric resolving power by > 2 × relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

Article.Title: Sex differences in the genetic basis of human recombination within 190,000 parent-child pairs
Article.Authors: Krätschmer I.; Hegemann L.; Pálsson G.; Hofmeister R.; Richmond A.; Hayward C.; Andreassen O.; Jugessur A.; Sønderby I.; Askelund A.; N/A N/A.; Metspalu A.; Milani L.; Esko T.; Mägi R.; Nelis M.; Hudjashov G.; Kutalik Z.; Marioni R.; Hardarson M.; Stefansson Ó.; Jónsson H.; Kharchenko P.; Stefánsson K.; Halldórsson B.
Article.Abstract: Meiotic recombination drives genetic diversity and chromosome segregation, yet the genetic factors governing variation in human recombination rates across studies remain poorly understood. Here, we analyze 112,144 maternal and 78,653 paternal meiosis events across four countries and identify 58 independent genomic regions (24 unique across phenotypes) associated with recombination frequency and location. These include six novel female-specific regions harboring genes linked to ovarian function and a seventh novel region linked to male recombination, with many loci demonstrating sex-dependent effects. The between-sex genetic correlation is 0.374 (0.072 SD). While DNA markers account for 30-40% of individual-level variation in recombination rate, previously known global modulators explain only 37.7% (2.7% SD) of this variation in females and 47.1% (3.8% SD) in males. We create a polygenic predictor that significantly predicts recombination rates in women and men after adjusting for age and birth year. Furthermore, female recombination correlates significantly with reproductive outcomes and aging, after adjusting for study ascertainment. In the largest meta-analysis to date of human meiotic recombination, these findings uncover novel sex-specific loci and clarify the polygenic architecture underlying meiotic variation. A meta-analysis of 190,797 human meioses across four countries maps 24 recombination loci, seven novel and mostly female-specific. Between-sex genetic correlation is 0.37, and a polygenic predictor links female recombination to reproduction and aging.
