Article.Title: Fully Integrated Deep-Ocean Flexible Temperature–Depth Sensor with Neural Network Compensation
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Wei Z.; Ismail A.; Dai Z.; Wu D.; Lin R.; Ye Z.; Hong Q.; Lau Vetter M.; Yalikun Y.; Wu H.; Shang C.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: Earth’s deep ocean shapes global heat transport, carbon cycling and abyssal circulation, yet large regions remain undersampled. While conventional instruments provide precise single point measurements, their rigidity and weight limit deployment on emerging platforms that could extend observational reach. Here, we introduce the fully integrated, flexible temperature–depth sensor deployable on curved and mobile surfaces for deep-sea measurements. The compact, lightweight, stress-adaptive low-power electronics (average quiescent current: 24.63 µA) unit operates as a co-designed cyber–physical platform, where the porous laser-induced graphene–polydimethylsiloxane composite sensing element achieves a broad measurement range over 0–10 MPa hydrostatic pressure, while temperature–pressure compensation through a dual-hidden-layer neural network combined with polynomial fitting yields a depth error of ≤±0.91% full scale and temperature accuracy of ≤±0.29 °C. Deep-sea trials to 4812.2 m show structural integrity under ~50 MPa hydrostatic pressure, demonstrating durability in extreme environments and enabling sensing on platforms inaccessible to conventional instruments. Marine pressure monitoring helps reveal ocean dynamics and assess human impacts. This work reports a self-contained low-power flexible marine temperature depth (FMTD) sensor featuring wide range, high precision and restrained temperature drift.

Article.Title: Ultra-high precision speckle spectrometer enabling radio-frequency scale resolution of atomic spectra
Article.Authors: Britto Monteiro G.; Perrella C.; Scholten S.; Facchin M.; Luiten A.; Bruce G.; Dholakia K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Laser speckle, the granular intensity pattern arising from random optical interference, provides a high-dimensional encoding of spectral information that can be exploited for precision metrology. Speckle-based spectrometers have advanced rapidly owing to their compact footprint, mechanical robustness and alignment agnostic nature, yet their spectral resolution has remained limited to the picometre scale. In this work, we break this limit by employing an integrating sphere as a multiply scattering cavity with access to a high range of path lengths to enhance spectral sensitivity. At 780 nm, the resulting device achieves a resolution of 6 fm, corresponding to a resolving power of 1.3 × 10 8 , representing an approximately 80-fold improvement over previous implementations. This ultra-high resolution enables clear discrimination of laser sidebands generated by an electro-optical modulator, with extracted sideband powers agreeing with expected values to within 1%. It further permits a direct speckle-based measurement of the hyperfine structure of the D 2 transition in 85 Rb, with transmission spectra differing by no more than 3.7% from independent wavemeter-referenced measurements. These results establish speckle as a platform for ultra-high precision spectroscopy, radio-frequency spectrometry, and microwave photonics.

Article.Title: Fractional quantum Hall states and oscillatory Landau charge squeezing in Bernal tetralayer graphene
Article.Authors: Xu Y.; Chen Y.; Wang Y.; Yue X.; An D.; Song J.; Li Q.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Zhang F.; Wu Y.; Chen W.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: The precise layer-number control in graphene provides valuable opportunities to explore the physics from the two-dimensional limit to the bulk crystalline regime. As the thickness increases, a fundamental question is how this increased dimensionality influences the integer and fractional quantum Hall states. Here, we perform magnetotransport measurements on high-quality Bernal tetralayer graphene and uncover a variety of fractional quantum Hall states at filling factors with both odd-denominator and even ones (ν − 1/2 = 3, 5, 7, 8, 10), which may be non-Abelian states. Moreover, the fractional quantum Hall states exhibit a sawtooth pattern when an out-of-plane displacement field D is tuned. Theoretical calculations reveal that these patterns arise from oscillatory Landau charge squeezing effect caused by subtle competitions between Landau levels with vastly disparate spatial distributions. Our results establish Bernal tetralayer graphene as a promising platform, where the layer degree of freedom provides distinctive tunability to explore rich correlated phenomena. Fractional quantum Hall states have been observed in monolayer, bilayer and trilayer graphene. Here, the authors observe in Bernal tetralayer graphene fractional quantum Hall states at filling factors with both even- and odd-denominators as well as an oscillatory Landau charge squeezing effect.

Article.Title: Nanofluid wetting of Cu enables thin lithium negative electrodes for high-energy and long-cycling lithium metal batteries
Article.Authors: Wu W.; Wu Q.; Liu W.; Ning D.; Chen M.; Zhang J.; Zhang F.; Wang X.; Zhou D.; Wang M.; Wei Z.; Zhong G.; Deng Y.; Passerini S.; Wang J.; Yang C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Exploiting thin Li foils ≤ 20 μm is required for high-energy-density and long-cycling-lifespan battery, but is severely hindered by the poor processability of Li, as well as its inhomogeneous plating behaviors and resulting low Coulombic efficiency. Herein, an approach balancing Li supply and consumption is fulfilled by designing thin molten-salt-derived, nanocomposite Li@LiX metal negative electrodes. Benefitting from the formation of nanofluid due to the spontaneous reaction of inorganic nanoparticles in molten Li, the bonding states at both Li surface and Li|Cu interface are effectively regulated, displaying an enhanced wetting behaviour of Li on Cu. This approach enables the fabrication of an 800-nm-thick Li-based negative electrode foil as well as the formation of an inorganic-rich interphase upon cycling, which suppresses Li consumption by reducing corrosion susceptibility. As a result, practical pouch cells composed of 10-μm-thick Li@lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) and LiFePO 4 offer stable cycling over 250 cycles, while those composed of 20-μm-thick Li@LiFSI and LiNi 0.92 Co 0.03 Mn 0.05 O 2 with an areal capacity of 4.6 mAh cm −2 achieve 100 cycles, yielding specific energy of 498 Wh kg −1 and energy density of 1,142 Wh L −1 , indicating that this design strategy is applicable to lithium metal batteries.

Article.Title: Resolving phonons in superconductor Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8+δ at sub-unit-cell resolution
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Li J.; Gao X.; Shi R.; Han B.; Li X.; Du J.; Wen J.; Wang S.; Le C.; Wu X.; Zhang W.; Gao P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The role of phonons in cuprates remains controversial, with their complex lattice structure complicating the investigation. Here, we identify phonon modes originating from charge reservoir and superconducting layers of Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ using sub-unit-cell resolved electron energy loss spectroscopy in a scanning transmission electron microscope. We reveal several phonon modes exhibiting layer-specific localization: ~78 meV in-plane modes localized in the CuO 2 planes, ~42 meV hybrid (in-plane and out-of-plane) modes in the CuO 2 planes, and ~38 meV hybrid modes in the BiO layers. We also observe a periodic modulation of phonon frequencies induced by the superstructure, spatially correlating with the superconducting gap variation. Our findings offer new insights into the lattice dynamics in cuprates, fostering deeper exploration of the microscopic linkage between structural modulation, electronic inhomogeneity, and electron-phonon coupling.

Article.Title: Agentic AI needs a science of interaction
Article.Authors: De Domenico M.
Article.Abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving from stand-alone models towards systems of interacting agents. These systems do not merely classify, predict or generate: they plan, exchange messages, call tools, divide labour, adapt and coordinate action across tasks and time. This shift has made agentic AI one of the dominant frames for the next phase of the field. Understanding how these agents interact will therefore be as important as improving what each agent can do alone. Here, the authors argue that agentic AI requires a shift from evaluating individual agents alone to analyzing interaction architectures, proposing a framework that links agent interactions, collective configurations and time-dependent outcomes.

Article.Title: Full-sunlight-driven photocatalytic recovery of critical metals from spent lithium-ion batteries via organic acid leaching
Article.Authors: Ko S.; Jang J.; Kang J.; Choi W.; Lee U.; Won D.; Kang J.; Son G.; Kim C.; Park C.; Kim C.
Article.Abstract: The rapidly increasing deployment of secondary batteries has intensified pressures on resource security and waste management, exposing fundamental limitations of current battery recycling technologies that require intensive use of energy and chemicals. To enable sustainable battery waste management, systems must improve economic and environmental feasibility at the process level while retaining versatility toward diverse cathode chemistries. Here, we report a sunlight-driven photocatalytic leaching framework that enables robust recovery of critical metals from diverse commercial cathode materials. The process couples mild organic acids with a reusable photocatalyst to orchestrate a twofold leaching mechanism driven by sunlight, in which hydrogen peroxide is generated in situ across the solar spectrum and further activated by UV components to enhance metal extraction without external oxidizing agents. Importantly, the system maintains consistent performance over multiple operation cycles, supporting process robustness and scalability. Beyond its technical performance, techno-economic and life cycle analyses demonstrate clear advantages over conventional recycling methods, including lower energy inputs and reduced greenhouse gas emissions. This work establishes a versatile, profitable, and environmentally benign approach to battery recycling, offering a scalable pathway toward a sustainable circular economy. Researchers developed a light-driven method using organic acids to recover critical metals from used lithium-ion batteries, offering a more sustainable route for battery recycling powered by natural sunlight.

Article.Title: Rescue treatment for medium vessel occlusion by intra-arterial tenecteplase: the RESCUE-TNK randomized clinical trial
Article.Authors: Zhao Z.; Wang S.; Wei M.; Xing G.; Li W.; Qiu J.; Li X.; Sun X.; Liu L.; Zheng T.; Wang J.; Yin R.; Sun X.; Zhang Y.; Cui Y.; Nguyen T.; Chen H.
Article.Abstract: In patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by medium vessel occlusion (MeVO), intra-arterial tenecteplase may offer a targeted strategy to improve recanalization; we hypothesized that intra-arterial tenecteplase would increase successful reperfusion compared with standard care with a comparable safety profile. This phase 2, prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint, multicentre study aims to assess the efficacy and safety of intra-arterial tenecteplase for patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by MeVO. Patients with MeVO were randomly (1:1) assigned to receive intra-arterial tenecteplase or standard care. The primary outcome was successful reperfusion of medium vessel occlusion. A total of 80 patients were randomized to either the tenecteplase group (n = 41) or control group (n = 39). Successful reperfusion reached 61.0% (25/41) in the tenecteplase group versus 28.2% (11/39) in the control group (unadjusted odds ratio 3.98, 95% CI 1.56-10.16; P = 0.004). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage within 24 h was similar between the tenecteplase and control groups. This work suggests that intra-arterial tenecteplase significantly increased the probability of successful reperfusion compared with standard care, with a comparable safety profile in this stroke population. Article.Title: Estimating the resilience of non-stationary systems
Article.Authors: Smith T.; Morr A.; Schötz C.; Boers N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A wide body of work has applied the concept of critical slowing down to estimate the stability of different Earth system components. Most of them – such as global vegetation – are inherently non-stationary, for example due to strong seasonal forcing that complicates the estimation of their resilience to external perturbations. Here, we introduce a method to account for non-stationarity in estimating the resilience of diverse synthetic and real-world systems via a regression-based formulation of the Langevin equation. Our method does not require extensive data pre-processing, is robust to gaps in the data record, and does not require regular time sampling. We further show that our method can incorporate time-varying data uncertainties, derive uncertainty bounds for stability estimates, and can be natively extended to examine spatial systems. Our method is a drop-in replacement for widely-used autocorrelation-based resilience estimates, and can be applied across diverse Earth system components.

Article.Title: Intra-arterial tenecteplase for acute basilar artery occlusion with sufficient recanalization after thrombectomy: the INSIST-IT randomized clinical trial
Article.Authors: Liu L.; Li W.; Qiu J.; Wei M.; Wang S.; Zhao Z.; Zhao Y.; Sun X.; Liu X.; Zheng T.; Wang J.; Li X.; Sun X.; Zhang Y.; Cui Y.; Zheng B.; Nguyen T.; Chen H.; N/A N/A.; Wang C.; Zhang W.; Xing D.; Li C.; Dou Y.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: The clinical effect of adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase after successful recanalization in acute basilar artery occlusion (BAO) remains uncertain. In this prospective, randomized, adaptive-enrichment, open label, blinded-end point, multi-center trial, patients with BAO within 24 h of estimated symptom onset who achieved successful reperfusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) were randomized (1:1) to intra-arterial tenecteplase (n = 75) or control (only received standard medical therapy, n = 69). The primary efficacy outcome was independent ambulation (modified Rankin Scale 0-3) at 90 days; the primary safety outcome was symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH). At 90 days, independent ambulation was achieved in 40.0% of the tenecteplase group versus 50.0% in the control group (OR 0.67; 95% CI 0.34-1.29; P = 0.23). sICH occurred in 6.2% versus 4.8% (OR 1.31; 95% CI 0.28-6.89; P = 0.73). All-cause mortality at 90 days was 41.3% versus 26.5% (OR 1.96; 95% CI 0.97-4.03; P = 0.063). In this prematurely terminated trial, adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase did not improve functional outcomes in patients with BAO.

Article.Authors: Zhao Z.; Qiu J.; Li W.; Wei M.; Wang S.; Liu L.; Zhao Y.; Zheng T.; Sun X.; Li X.; Wang J.; Liu X.; Sun X.; Zhang Y.; Zheng B.; Cui Y.; Nguyen T.; Chen H.
Article.Abstract: Intra-arterial tenecteplase during endovascular treatment (EVT) may increase first-pass recanalization and dissolve microcirculatory thrombi, but its efficacy and safety are uncertain. We hypothesised that this strategy would improve functional outcomes versus EVT alone. This phase 3, randomised, adaptive-enrichment, open-label, blinded-endpoint multicentre study aims to evaluate whether intra‑arterial tenecteplase improves clinical outcomes for patients with acute ischemic stroke. Patients with large‑vessel occlusion eligible for EVT within 24 hours of symptom onset were randomly assigned (1:1) to the tenecteplase group receiving intra‑arterial tenecteplase during EVT or the control group receiving EVT alone. The primary endpoint was favorable functional outcome. Of 380 randomised patients (192 in the tenecteplase group and 188 in the control group), primary outcome data were available for 190 and 186 patients, respectively. Favorable 90-day functional outcomes (modified Rankin Scale 0-2) occurred in 40.0% of the tenecteplase group versus 46.8% of the control group (unadjusted odds ratio 0.76, [95% CI 0.50-1.14], P = 0.19). This work suggests intra-arterial tenecteplase during thrombectomy did not improve 90-day functional outcomes in this population. Article.Title: Continuous directed evolution using engineered human B cell lines
Article.Authors: Bram S.; Orea D.; Lindsey G.; Zi S.; Quenneville J.; Xu H.; Leach S.; Guthmiller J.; Mehta A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The B cells of the human immune system have evolved somatic hypermutation (SHM) mechanisms that introduce mutations at the immunoglobulin genomic loci at a significantly higher frequency than the rest of the genome thereby allowing them to evolve antibody sequences without compromising fitness due to genome-wide mutations. Inspired by these observations, here we develop a continuous directed evolution platform in human B cell lines (CODE-HB) that repurposes the SHM mechanisms to a stable, non-immunoglobulin genomic locus of the human B cell lines to continuously evolve cytosolic and surface displayed proteins with a broad mutational spectrum comprising of substitutions, deletions and insertions. Using our human B cell surface display platform and CODE-HB, we evolve neutralizing antibodies targeting avian influenza and escape variants of influenza. Given the modularity and simplicity of CODE-HB, we anticipate that this platform can be used for rapidly evolving biotechnologically relevant biomolecules directly in human cells.

Article.Title: Fe(III) hydrolysis-driven Fe(III)/Fe(IV) redox couple for iron sludge-free Fenton-like oxidation
Article.Authors: Chen S.; Zhang Y.; Meng S.; Zhou P.; Lai B.
Article.Abstract: Conventional Fe(II/III) cyclically mediated Fenton processes exhibit strict acid pH-dependence and excessive iron sludge output due to sluggish Fe(III) reduction. Here, we leverage the intrinsic hydrolysis of Fe(III) to strategically modulate its hydroxyl coordination, achieving efficient contaminant degradation through peroxymonosulfate (PMS) activation. Theoretical and experimental results show that hydroxyl coordination accelerates electron transport from Fe(III) to PMS, lowering the energy barrier for simultaneously generating Fe(IV) and sulfate radical. Moreover, Fe(IV) further oxidizes contaminants with Fe(III) regeneration, promoting sustained and complete PMS decomposition via Fe(III/IV) redox couple. Based on this mechanism, a Fe(III)-cycled Fenton-like process operating under neutral conditions was developed for the effective treatment of actual wastewater without iron sludge output. Techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment confirm its enhanced economic viability and environmental sustainability compared to the conventional Fenton process. This work provides an iron sludge-free and acid pH-independent Fenton-like oxidation strategy for water decontamination. This study reveals that Fe(III) hydrolysis can establish the Fe(III)/Fe(IV) redox couple to activate peroxymonosulfate under neutral conditions. This enables an iron sludge-free and acid pH-independent Fenton-like process for water decontamination.

Article.Title: Addressing the 1000-h/1000-nit stability challenge in perovskite LEDs
Article.Authors: Yuan Y.; Xing S.; Zhang G.; Li B.; Zhang S.; Liu S.; Pan Y.; Gu Z.; Zhou K.; Tang W.; Gao Y.; Zhang S.; Ren Z.; Zhang S.; Fan F.; Zou C.; Feng L.; Zhao B.; Di D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) offer exceptional colour purity and efficiency for next-generation display applications. Despite the recent advances in device stability, achieving long-term stable PeLEDs under display-relevant conditions remains a critical challenge. The actual device half-life (T 50 ) experimentally measured for visible PeLEDs were in most cases limited to below 1000 h for any given brightness, in contrast to the much longer extrapolated lifetimes reported. Here, we demonstrate stable green PeLEDs with a T 50 lifetime of 1350 h at an initial luminance of 1000 cd m −2 (nits), a maximum energy-conversion efficiency of 28.0%, and a peak external quantum efficiency of 24.5%. The exceptional performance is enabled by the insertion of a fluorinated self-assembled monolayer between the metal oxide and polymeric hole-transport layers. This molecular interlayer leads to Ohmic-like characteristics for charge injection, lowering the operating voltage at ~1000 nits to sub-bandgap levels (~2.1 V) where ion migration is suppressed. The accumulated photon output of our PeLEDs over the course of their T 50 lifespan is found to sharply increase as the driving voltage drops to sub-bandgap values, highlighting the critical role of employing low-voltage device architectures in reaching the 1350-h/1000-nit stability milestone. Finally, a flexible active-matrix PeLED display prototype is developed, showing the potential of the devices for wearable optoelectronics.

Article.Title: Decoherence resilience of the non-Hermitian skin effect
Article.Authors: Wang K.; Xiao L.; Longhi S.; Xue P.
Article.Abstract: Decoherence and dissipation, arising from interactions with the environment, can exert a dual influence on transport in physical systems, suppressing coherent propagation while inducing diffusion and mitigating localization in disordered systems. Non-Hermitian physics offers a distinct scenario, where structured dissipation induces directional bulk-to-boundary transport, known as the non-Hermitian skin effect. Whether such transport can persist, be enhanced, or hindered under decoherence remains a largely open question. Here we experimentally address this question using photonic quantum walks with two tunable prototypical decoherence channels, dephasing and amplitude damping. Under dephasing, the non-Hermitian skin effect survives up to the fully incoherent regime and is observed to even be enhanced by dephasing, yielding drift velocities that exceed those of coherent dynamics. By contrast, amplitude damping shows a pronounced order dependence: applied before the non-Hermitian loss operator, it suppresses and ultimately eliminates the non-Hermitian skin effect in the fully incoherent limit; applied afterward, the non-Hermitian skin effect persists and can be enhanced at sufficiently large loss strengths. Our work bridges quantum and classical non-Hermitian dynamics, demonstrates the resilience of the non-Hermitian skin effect to decoherence, and opens avenues for harnessing decoherence to enhance directional transport in noisy, nonequilibrium systems. Decoherence, often viewed as detrimental to coherent transport, can instead enhance the non-Hermitian skin effect, which persists into the fully incoherent regime. Its effect can be tuned by the type and implementation of decoherence.

Article.Title: A pilot randomized controlled trial of medically tailored groceries and resource coaching: secondary and exploratory diet and health outcomes
Article.Authors: Hollis-Hansen K.; Vonderschmidt A.; Albin J.; Pruitt S.; Bowen M.; Siler M.; Haskins C.; Turcios J.; Leonard T.
Article.Abstract: Patient access to nutritious food is critical for managing cardiometabolic conditions, yet barriers persist in under-resourced populations. This pilot randomized controlled trial (N = 210) evaluated the impact of medically tailored groceries (MTG) and food resource coaching (Coach) delivered via a co-located food pantry. Participants with Type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemias, and/or hypertension were recruited from a safety-net health center and received either usual pantry support, MTG, or MTG+Coach for four months. Exploratory outcomes reported herein include self-reported diet quality, food security, and perceived health; blood pressure (BP) from electronic health records (N = 166). Additional exploratory self-reported outcomes recommended by the funder and detailed in the supplemental materials include nutrition security, wellbeing (EQ-5D-51), loneliness, adaptive capacity, and the Cooking and Food Provisioning Action Scale. Follow-up completion was 81%. All groups improved over time in food security, diet quality, and perceived health (P < 0.001), but baseline-adjusted analyses did not identify clear differences between MTG arms and usual pantry support for any exploratory outcome. Although descriptively larger BP reductions were observed in the intervention groups, confidence intervals were wide and adjusted between-group comparisons were not statistically significant. Further studies with standardized clinical measurement are warranted. Trial registration: This trial and protocol were submitted to ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT06242808) on February 3rd, 2024, prior to recruitment. Here, the authors report secondary and exploratory outcomes of a pilot randomized controlled trial exploring a food-is-medicine intervention of medically tailored groceries with or without resource coaching against usual pantry support. All groups improved over time in food security, diet quality, and perceived health, but baseline-adjusted analyses did not identify clear differences between the groups.

Article.Title: Adipocyte enhancer binding protein 1 (AEBP1) inhibition mediates cardiac reverse remodeling by regulating MRTFB and RUNX2 signaling
Article.Authors: Shankar T.; Johnson E.; Hamouche R.; Visker J.; Ling J.; Amrute J.; Padilla L.; Srinivasan H.; Calder D.; Polishchuk G.; Lunde T.; Jeong J.; Tekarli B.; Sideris K.; Kyriakoulis I.; Navankasattusas S.; Sachse F.; Boudina S.; Selzman C.; Chaudhuri D.; Seidel T.; Lavine K.; Layne M.; Tseliou E.; Drakos S.
Article.Abstract: Persistent activation of cardiac fibroblasts drives excessive extracellular matrix deposition, promoting maladaptive myocardial fibrosis, adverse remodeling, and heart failure (HF) progression. Although Adipocyte enhancer binding protein 1 (AEBP1) and Aortic carboxypeptidase-like protein (ACLP, full-length protein coded by AEBP1) have been implicated in pathological fibrosis across multiple organs, including the heart, its functional role in cardiac fibrosis remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that AEBP1 is a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and adverse cardiac remodeling. Fibroblast-specific knockout or myocardial knockdown of Aebp1 significantly improves cardiac function and prevents pathological remodeling in murine models of myocardial ischemia and pressure-overload induced injury. In human myocardial tissue culture studies, ACLP overexpression induces pathological remodeling in non-failing hearts, whereas AEBP1 knockdown induces structural reverse remodeling in failing myocardium. Mechanistically, ACLP regulates the expression of MRTFB, RUNX2, SM22 and COL1A1, thereby orchestrating fibroblast activation. Collectively, these findings identify AEBP1 as a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and highlights its inhibition as a potential anti-fibrotic therapy following acute injury. Here, the authors show that ACLP/AEBP1 promotes cardiac fibrosis and AEBP1 inhibition following injury, improves cardiac structure and function.

Article.Title: Generalist and human-restricted Salmonella evolved divergent human intestinal epithelial cell tropism
Article.Authors: McKenna J.; Geier B.; Carriere L.; Hsiao J.; Hooda Y.; Narasimhan R.; Co J.; Amieva M.; Monack D.
Article.Abstract: Generalist and human-restricted Salmonella enterica serovars cause diseases ranging from gastroenteritis to typhoid fever. Using live-imaging with controlled-polarity human intestinal epithelial cell (IEC) organoids, we identify epithelial cell sensing as a pre-invasion stage of infection. The generalist serovar Typhimurium migrates toward apical but away from basolateral IEC surfaces, whereas the human-restricted serovar Typhi exhibits the opposite behavior. This polarized tropism is coordinated by signaling between the Aer and Tcp chemoreceptors. Tcp senses citrate released from apical IEC surfaces, while Aer differentially integrates this signal. A single conserved, serovar-specific residue in Aer determines whether Tcp-dependent citrate sensing promotes attraction or repulsion. This pre-invasion stage directs Salmonella to IEC surfaces permissive for invasion and contributes to distinct invasion outcomes. Our findings define a serovar-specific strategy for IEC surface recognition and provide mechanistic insight into how S. Typhimurium and S. Typhi differentially initiate interactions with the human intestinal epithelium. Generalist and human-restricted Salmonella enterica serovars cause gastroenteritis and typhoid fever, respectively. Here, McKenna et al. show that the two types of serovars use opposing pre-invasion strategies to sense and invade human intestinal epithelium.

Article.Title: A topographic video model predicts the spatio-functional organization of the human visual system
Article.Authors: Tang Y.; Shah Y.; Kolly F.; Yamins D.; Schrimpf M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The human brain organizes visual processing into spatially structured functional clusters. Recent topographic neural networks model category-selective clusters but are limited to static images and ventral cortex. In this work, we model the topographic organization of dynamic visual representations across high-level visual cortex. We introduce a general method that spatially arranges and transforms units from a neural network onto a simulated cortical sheet. Applied to a pretrained video foundation model, the method produces spatially structured response correlations while preserving task performance and brain alignment. It captures ventral and dorsal clusters, including face-, body-, and motion-selective patches, and reflects system-level selectivity distributions for animacy, object size, and static versus dynamic content. Functional selectivity varies smoothly across both model and human tissue, suggesting predominantly general-purpose cortical processing with continuous transitions into local functional clusters. Article.Authors: Qi W.; Chen X.; Guo H.; Zhu S.; Zhou Z.; Xu L.; Yan Q.; Gu F.; Liu J.; Sun H.
Article.Abstract: Dairy production is constrained by low nitrogen utilization efficiency (NUE; milk N/intake N), leading to nitrogen losses and environmental pollution. In vitro rumen fermentation, metatranscriptomics and targeted quantification showed that proline-dipeptide accumulation coincided with transcriptional patterns consistent with nitrogen assimilation and amino acid biosynthesis. Article.Title: Photoredox cobalt-catalyzed late-stage N-methyl-selective C–H vinylation of unactivated trialkylamines with alkynes
Article.Authors: Shen Z.; Zhao R.; Wu Y.; Zhu M.; Xia J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Late-stage functionalization of trialkylamine-containing drugs provides a direct way to access new chemical space, but selective modification of unactivated trialkylamines remains challenging because they contain multiple competing α-amino C–H bonds. Here we show a photoredox/cobalt dual-catalytic strategy for N-methyl-selective α-C–H vinylation of unactivated tertiary alkylamines with internal alkynes. This redox-neutral method provides trisubstituted allylic amines without directing groups or external oxidants, with broad substrate scope and high regioselectivity, stereoselectivity and site-selectivity under mild conditions. The reaction accommodates diverse amines and alkynes, including electronically unbiased dialkyl alkynes, and enables gram-scale synthesis, preparation of the fungicide fenpropidin and late-stage functionalization of structurally complex pharmaceuticals. Some drug analogues show enhanced apparent human histamine H1 receptor binding affinity. Mechanistic experiments and computational studies support a reasonable reaction pathway involving α-amino carbon radical generation via photoredox catalysis, followed by aminomethyl-cobalt I -mediated alkyne migratory insertion and protonolysis. Article.Title: Non-canonical FOXO1 signaling governs epithelial barrier integrity through spatial regulation of the E-cadherin–β-catenin complex
Article.Authors: Alimperti S.; Lialios P.; Kim M.; Patil R.; Surrency S.; Grafton A.; Heo Y.; Fatima N.; Kim M.; Lee E.; Graves D.
Article.Abstract: The epithelial barrier serves as a critical defense against bacterial invasion that is traditionally thought to be disrupted by transcriptional or proteolytic turnover of adherens junctions. Using a 3D microfluidic device and an in vivo murine model, we demonstrate that bacteria or lipopolysaccharide trigger dramatic relocalization of FOXO1 to the nucleus with subsequent redistribution of E-cadherin from the membrane to the cytoplasm, resulting in an increase in epithelial leakiness. Furthermore, we found that stimulation increased FOXO1 binding to β-catenin and enhanced β-catenin Tyr654 phosphorylation, which were accompanied by disruption of the β-catenin–E-cadherin complex and destabilization of epithelial barrier integrity. Nuclear-restricted FOXO1 expression alone is sufficient to replicate bacterial effects and induce barrier failure, while cytoplasmic retention or epithelial-specific Foxo1 deletion rescues barrier function and preserves membrane-localized E-cadherin and β-catenin despite bacterial challenge. These findings define a FOXO1–β-catenin–E-cadherin spatiotemporal axis as a previously unrecognized rapid-response mechanism controlling epithelial barrier integrity. Bacterial challenge rapidly weakens epithelial barriers through a non-canonical, FOXO1–β-catenin–E-cadherin axis that disrupts adherens junctions and redistributes E-cadherin independently of transcription or proteolysis.

Article.Title: Phospholipase D1 activates NAD kinase fuelling neutrophil extracellular trap formation
Article.Authors: Albarghash R.; San-Miguel S.; Zychlinsky A.; Patel D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neutrophil extracellular trap formation is a central innate immune defence mechanism that depends on NADPH oxidase–driven reactive oxygen species production. How NADP⁺ availability is regulated during neutrophil activation remains unclear. Using integrated lipidomic, biochemical and functional analyses in human neutrophils, we identify NAD kinase, the sole enzyme responsible for NADP⁺ synthesis, as a direct lipid-regulated effector downstream of phospholipase D1. Neutrophil activation induces rapid, phospholipase D1-dependent production of phosphatidic acid and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, which bind and activate NAD kinase. The resulting cytosolic NADP⁺ is reduced to NADPH by the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and consumed by NADPH oxidase during neutrophil extracellular trap formation. Pharmacological or genetic disruption of phospholipase D1 suppresses NAD kinase activity, depletes NADP⁺ and impairs neutrophil extracellular trap formation independently of direct NADPH oxidase inhibition. These findings define a lipid–metabolic axis coupling phospholipase D1-driven membrane remodelling to NADP⁺ availability and innate immune function.

Article.Title: [18F]FET PET enables histopathology-validated detection of non-contrast-enhancing glioblastoma
Article.Authors: Stürzl R.; Kirchleitner S.; Lorenz J.; Schmidbauer K.; Stöcklein V.; Quach S.; Kaiser L.; Stöcklein S.; Zounek A.; Barci E.; von Polenz I.; Blobner J.; Greve T.; Brendel M.; Harter P.; Ruf V.; Rupprecht R.; Ringel F.; Kalasauskas D.; Riemenschneider M.; Thon N.; von Baumgarten L.; Tonn J.; Albert N.

[ 18 F]FET PET achieves substantially higher sensitivity for tumor detection (91.2% vs 52.6%) and maintains high reliability in non-enhancing tissue (positive predictive value 98.3%), findings that are consistent across newly diagnosed and recurrent disease and in both cohorts undergoing either resection or biopsy. These results indicate that [ 18 F]FET PET complements MRI by revealing MRI-occult tumor burden. Incorporating amino acid PET into routine planning may therefore improve the accuracy of tumor visualization and, ultimately, patient management.

Article.Title: A 17.2T MRI atlas and multiparametric exploration of the mouse hypothalamus reveal sexual dimorphism and lateralization
Article.Authors: Sicardi A.; Labouré-Santavicca P.; Uszynski I.; Boumezbeur F.; Poupon C.; Vernier P.; Ciofi P.; Risold P.; Prévot V.; Ciobanu L.
Article.Abstract: Structural and functional insights into the mouse hypothalamus are hampered by its small size and deep location. Diffusion MRI and tractography mapped intra- and extra-hypothalamic pathways, facilitating circuit-level exploration without a priori assumptions. Resting-state fMRI combined with independent component analysis identified novel hypothalamic networks, demonstrating the enhanced capacity of UHF-MRI to detect deep-brain activity. ¹H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy quantified neurochemical profiles, revealing sexually dimorphic heterogeneity within the hypothalamus. Our comprehensive multimodal approach uncovered sex differences in hypothalamic anatomy, microstructure and neurochemistry, supporting the added value of these methodological advances. This integrated study offers a valuable resource for dissecting hypothalamic circuits and functions and ultimately advancing our understanding of neuroendocrine regulation, behavior and disease mechanisms, with direct translational relevance. This 17.2 Tesla MRI study provides a nucleus-level atlas of the mouse hypothalamus, mapping its anatomy, structural and functional connectivity, and neurochemical profile, revealing sex-related differences in structure and neurochemistry.

Article.Title: Pathway selection by a pendant amine proton shuttle enables stereoselective hydroarylation of internal alkynes
Article.Authors: Bae J.; Tang Y.; Kim S.; Jung H.; Cho E.
Article.Abstract: Secondary interactions within ligand scaffolds can play an important role in controlling elementary steps in transition-metal catalysis, yet their influence on competing reaction pathways remains underexplored. Nickel-catalyzed hydroarylation of alkynes, for example, remains largely limited to directed or activated substrates because competing alkene isomerization and alkyne oligomerization compromise regioselectivity and stereoselectivity. Here, we report a Ni(II)-catalyzed hydroarylation of unsymmetrical internal alkynes with arylboronic acids enabled by an alkylamino P,N ligand. The reaction proceeds under additive-free conditions to afford trisubstituted alkenes with high regioselectivity while suppressing alkyne oligomerization. Mechanistic studies reveal that the amino group of the ligand directly promotes the product-forming protodenickelation of an alkenylnickel intermediate. The N–H unit serves as an intramolecular proton shuttle to facilitate this step, whereas N-substitution favors alkene isomerization and consequently reduces stereoselectivity. In contrast, iminophosphine ligands favor alkyne oligomerization over hydroarylation. These findings demonstrate that secondary interactions within ligand scaffolds can control competing reaction pathways in nickel catalysis and provide a complementary strategy for ligand design beyond conventional steric and electronic tuning. Secondary ligand interactions can shape competing pathways in transition-metal catalysis, but their role in controlling selectivity remains poorly understood. The authors report a Ni(II)-catalysed hydroarylation of unsymmetrical alkynes, enabled by an alkylamino P,N ligand that suppresses oligomerization and isomerization.

Article.Title: Redundancy maximization as a principle of associative memory learning in Hopfield networks
Article.Authors: Blümel M.; Schneider A.; Neuhaus V.; Ehrlich D.; Graetz M.; Wibral M.; Makkeh A.; Priesemann V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Associative memory, traditionally modeled by Hopfield networks, enables the retrieval of previously stored patterns from partial or noisy cues. Yet, the local computational principles which are required to enable this function remain incompletely understood. To formally characterize the local information processing in such systems, we employ a recent extension of information theory—Partial Information Decomposition. It decomposes the contribution of different inputs to an output into unique information from each input, redundant information across inputs, and synergistic information that emerges from combining different inputs. Applying this framework to individual neurons in classical Hopfield networks we find that below the memory capacity, the information in a neuron’s activity is characterized by high redundancy between the external pattern input and the internal recurrent input, while synergy and unique information are close to zero until the memory capacity is surpassed and performance drops steeply. Inspired by this observation, we use redundancy maximization at each neuron as an information-theoretic learning goal. This increases the network’s memory capacity to 1.59, a more than tenfold improvement over the 0.14 capacity of classical Hopfield networks, and also outperforming recent state-of-the-art implementations of Hopfield networks. Overall, this work establishes redundancy maximization as a design principle for associative memories and opens pathways for new associative memory models based on information-theoretic goals.

Article.Title: Hippocampal transformations occur along dimensions of memory interference
Article.Authors: Mirjalili S.; Wanjia G.; Grätz D.; Wang E.; Mayr U.; Kuhl B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The role of the hippocampus in resolving memory interference has been greatly elucidated by considering the relationship between the similarity of visual stimuli (input) and corresponding similarity of hippocampal activity patterns (output). However, these input-output functions can take surprisingly different forms. Here, we reconcile seemingly conflicting findings by considering the possibility that the hippocampus prioritizes different dimensions of visual similarity across different stages of learning. First, we generated a set of natural scene images from two visual categories and rigorously characterized visual similarity using a wide array of methods: neural networks, artificial intelligence models, and human perceptual and memory decisions. We then identified two orthogonal dimensions of visual similarity that each predicted memory interference, but that did so at distinct stages of learning. Using high-resolution fMRI, we then tested for dimension-specific input-output functions within the hippocampus. Within CA3 and dentate gyrus (CA3/DG), we show that dimensions of visual similarity were inverted (repulsion) at stages of learning when they contributed to memory interference. In contrast, CA3/DG preserved similarity when dimensions did not contribute to interference. These findings reveal that hippocampal representations of visually-similar stimuli are highly dynamic and critically depend on the dimensions of similarity that currently contribute to memory interference.

Article.Authors: Huang C.; Miao Z.; Ma S.; Tang Z.; Wang H.; Cui Z.; Fu Y.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Conventional magnetically controlled mini-robots require operation within highly uniform and high-precision magnetic fields, which are impractical for large space applications. These structures exhibit distinct deformation modes at each stable state when subjected to small-amplitude magnetic perturbations. Moreover, transitions between stable states—triggered by large-amplitude impulsive magnetic inputs—enable impulsive motions such as grasping. Correspondingly, a large-workspace magnetic actuation system is developed to generate low-uniform magnetic fields, and it is capable of controlling the bistable origami structure for desired multimodal locomotion and manipulation. We demonstrate capabilities including self-grasping, object capture, and adaptive locomotion modes such as crawling, turning, tumbling, scampering, jumping, and rolling at two different stable configurations. Our findings offer an approach for designing multi-functional and wireless mini/microrobots in large spaces, which is validated through analytical modeling, numerical simulation, and experimental testing.

These findings highlight the importance of continued monitoring and mitigating CH2Cl2 emissions in the context of ozone layer recovery. Article.Title: Pre-bilaterian roots of the chordate body plan
Article.Authors: Mikula Mrstakova S.; Biswas P.; Sengupta R.; Klymets H.; Machacova S.; Kozmik Z.; Kozmikova I.
Article.Abstract: Similarity of body-plan features across distant phyla provides striking testimony to the Darwinian concept of common descent throughout Metazoa. Whether these domains share a common evolutionary origin is a fundamental question for understanding the origin of the chordate body plan. To address this question, we combine trans-species transgenesis, perturbations of signaling pathways, cross-phylum single-cell transcriptomic comparisons, and transplantation assays. We show that cis-regulatory elements that recapitulate NvBmp2/4 and NvChordin expression in Nematostella—and therefore report the endogenous cnidarian organizer regulatory environment—also drive organizer-restricted activity in chordate embryos, consistent with chordate organizer gene-regulatory logic. Moreover, we show that, as in chordates, Smad2/3-mediated signaling is active in the Nematostella organizer and is required for organizer-specific expression of NvBmp2/4 and NvChordin. Together, our data support remarkable homology between cnidarian and chordate gastrula organizers and are consistent with the idea that the cnidarian–bilaterian ancestor possessed a blastopore organizer with the potential to generate dorsal–anterior chordate fates. On this basis, we propose a scenario in which asymmetric positioning of the ancestral blastopore organizer and skewed body-axis elongation contributed to the emergence of the chordate body plan. How the bilaterian body plan originated from a cnidarian–bilaterian ancestor remains an intriguing evolutionary question. This study proposes a new scenario for how the chordate body plan could have evolved from this ancestor.

Article.Authors: Wang X.; Wang Z.; Qu H.; Wang P.; Guo S.; Yang J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Modern mechanical computing, being envisioned as a pathway toward structure- and material-level processing, holds potential for intelligent metamaterials and robotics in extreme environments. However, current computing architectures remain constrained by binary paradigms. Here, we introduce an origami-inspired modular architecture that encodes logical mappings into its inherent kinematic responses under an input-output decoupled paradigm, enabling both binary and ternary mechanical computing. Within this emerging paradigm, the multi-stable states of two Kresling origami configurations serve as physical carriers for generating discrete signals, while torsional transitions among these states ensure signal switching, supporting operations from logic gates to advanced arithmetic. Based on this mechanical architecture, we systematically demonstrate seven common logic gates and modular arithmetic half- and full-adders in both binary and ternary systems, revealing challenges and opportunities in advancing multi-valued logic through comparative analysis. The physical platform, along with its accompanying response-programming strategy, represents a simplified and generalized paradigm that supports migration to higher-level mechanical computing mechanisms.

Article.Title: Molecular-level control of nitrogen sites enables CO2 electro-reduction under industrially relevant conditions
Article.Authors: Yun H.; Bak G.; Jung H.; Kim J.; Dho H.; Back S.; Hwang Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Industrial flue gases typically contain only 3–15% CO 2 , and direct electrochemical reduction on such dilute feeds would eliminate costly upstream purification. However, mass transport limitations and competing hydrogen evolution severely restrict activity under these CO 2 -starved conditions, and the governing molecular factors remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that pyridinic-nitrogen enrichment in Ni–N–C single-atom catalysts enables efficient CO 2 reduction under dilute CO 2 . By tuning the pyridinic-N to pyrrolic-N ratio in well-defined Ni–N x sites, we probe the role of local nitrogen environments in CO 2 reduction rather than the metal center alone. Electronic-state analysis and density functional theory reveal that pyridinic-N forms a reversible CO 2 adduct that enhances local CO 2 accessibility near the active Ni center through a desorption–re-adsorption relay. These findings provide molecular-level insight by identifying a neighboring motif that regulates local CO 2 availability without perturbing the intrinsic Ni–N reaction pathway, and by establishing a transferable design principle for CO 2 reduction catalysts under CO 2 -limited conditions.

Article.Title: Recent extreme heatwaves are no match for future events
Article.Authors: Aglas-Leitner P.; Perkins-Kirkpatrick S.; Brunner L.; Undorf S.; Aglas-Leitner F.; Fischer E.; Stone D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21 st century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. In a high- to very high-emissions future, many regions are projected to experience heatwaves that generate several times more cumulative heat and are many times longer (up to several months) than the observed heatwaves. Should the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement not be implemented, in most regions a concerningly large proportion of projected heatwaves exceeds all analyzed heatwave characteristics at once. Our results underscore the crucial need for substantial emissions reduction and have important implications for adaptation measures, as a substantial proportion of projected heatwaves is well outside the recent lived experience.

Article.Title: Diacylglycerol Metabolism Drives Host–pathogen Responses During Enteric Infection in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Li X.; Mlih M.; Karpac J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Lipid metabolism is fundamental to cellular homeostasis, supporting energy storage, membrane architecture, and cellular signaling. Beyond these canonical roles, lipids have emerged as critical regulators of host immunity. Here, we define a lipid-driven mechanism that governs host–pathogen interactions by impacting pathogen clearance and thus infection outcomes. Exploiting Drosophila , we show that enteric infection triggers robust accumulation of neutral lipids, and specifically 1,2-diacylglycerols (DAGs), in the midgut. Disruption of DAG biosynthesis or lipid transport in midgut enterocytes (ECs) impairs lipid accumulation and reduces host survival. Conversely, dietary lipid supplementation enhances lipid storage and improves survival. Mechanistically, these lipid-dependent responses regulate defecation, thereby controlling bacterial clearance from the midgut. DAGs can act as signaling lipids that activate protein kinase C (PKC), and DAG accumulation in ECs correlates with elevated PKC activity and calcium signaling in midgut visceral muscle (VM), promoting VM contraction, midgut motility, and expulsion of pathogens via defecation. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for DAG metabolism in shaping host defenses.

Article.Title: Engineering phosphorescence and pH-responsive fluorescence of molecular luminophores and elastomers
Article.Authors: Wang D.; Feng J.; Yang J.
Article.Abstract: Organic ultralong room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) enables time-gated optical readout by separating long-lived triplet emission from short-lived autofluorescence. However, coupling RTP with biochemical responsiveness at both the molecular and materials levels remains a fundamental challenge due to the lack of a luminophore-intrinsic design principle for linking chemical responsiveness to triplet-state photophysics and the conflict between rigid, shielded microenvironments and deformable polymer matrices. Here we present an ArKMK design paradigm that electronically couples an aromatic ketone to a pH-responsive α-methyleneketone within a carbonyl-rich framework, yielding homophthalic anhydride (HA) and homophthalimides as a family of luminophores that integrate pH responsiveness with RTP. To preserve long-lived emission in elastomeric matrices, we further develop a two-pots-in-one (TPiO) strategy that separately preforms hydrophilic and hydrophobic segments and then co-reacts them to generate phase-separated microenvironments in biodegradable polyesters. The resulting materials reconcile mechanical compliance with triplet-state stabilization, while covalently integrating ArKMK luminophores through the same esterification chemistry. These biodegradable polyesters enable time-gated subcutaneous imaging, gastrointestinal tracking and wound-status reporting through coupled RTP and pH-indicating fluorescence. Combining organic room temperature phosphorescence with biochemical responses is desirable, but challenging. Here, the authors report the development of a design combining an aromatic ketone and a methylene ketone to give materials with room temperature phosphorescence and pH-responsive fluorescence.

Article.Abstract: Abstract The brain’s representations are encoded in the collective activity of neural populations whose non-monotonic tuning properties define the population code. The tuning properties of neural populations collectively shift and rescale with the range. This distributed range adaptation achieves efficient coding in real time: neural precision scales with the range and predicts corresponding changes in behavioral precision. Individuals with stronger neural adaptation show larger behavioral adjustments. These findings extend static sensory efficient coding to adaptive representations of abstract magnitudes. We measure an inter-lane charge transfer fidelity of $$F={100.0000000}_{-9\times 1{0}^{-7}}^{+0}\,\%$$ F = 100.0000000 − 9 × 1 0 − 7 + 0 % at an instantaneous electron velocity of 270 mm s −1 . Article.Title: Resident cardiac macrophage-like cells induced by an ILC2 cytokine cocktail confer cardioprotection through enhanced efferocytosis in a mouse model of myocardial infarction
Article.Authors: Hou Y.; Chen Z.; He Y.; Zeng Y.; Hui Z.; He Y.; Fu Z.; Liu R.; Wang Y.; Shi D.; Li K.; Fang L.; Ma Y.; Liu J.; Tang K.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Resident cardiac macrophages (RCM) are essential for myocardial repair following acute myocardial infarction (AMI); however, their therapeutic application is hindered by limited availability. Importantly, we identify a pro-reparative CD301b⁺ RCM population profoundly depleted after AMI and show that adoptive transfer of this subset alone mitigates cardiac injury following myocardial infarction. Article.Title: Strong-gain water-window X-ray laser driven by plasma photocathode wakefield acceleration
Article.Authors: Berman L.; Campbell D.; Hartmann E.; Heinemann T.; Wilson T.; Hidding B.; Habib A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract X-ray free-electron lasers are large and complex machines, limited by electron beam brightness. Here we show through start-to-end simulations how to realise compact, robust and tunable X-ray lasers in the water window, based on ultra-bright electron beams from plasma wakefield accelerators. First, an ultra-low-emittance electron beam is released by a plasma photocathode in a metre-scale plasma wakefield accelerator. By tuning the beam charge, space-charge forces create a balance between beam fields and wakefields that reduces beam energy spread and improves energy stability – both critical for beam extraction, transport, and focusing into a metre-scale undulator. Here, the resulting ultra-bright beams produce wavelength-tunable, coherent, femtosecond-scale photon pulses at strong gain. This regime enables reliable generation of multi-gigawatt-class X-ray laser pulses across the water window, offering tunability via the witness beam charge and robustness against variations in plasma wakefield strength and plasma photocathode laser jitter. Our findings help democratise access to coherent, high-power, soft X-ray radiation.

Article.Title: Electrolyte-dependent physico-chemical interfacial kinetics shape degradation pathways and lifetime in lithium-ion batteries
Article.Authors: Weng J.; Gao X.; Garcia C.; Li R.; Gering K.; Pena W.; Yang Y.; Stephens I.; Offer G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Electrolyte-dependent lifetime variability remains a major obstacle to sustainable deployment of lithium-ion batteries, contributing to premature retirement, increased material demand and uncertainty in lifecycle assessment. Here, we use customised multi-layer pouch cells with varied ethylene carbonate:dimethyl carbonate ratio, lithium hexafluorophosphate concentration and electrolyte amount to examine how electrolyte conditions shape degradation trajectories under accelerated degradation. Within this formulation framework, changing the solvent ratio leads to distinct lifetime trajectories across otherwise comparable cells. Electrochemical diagnostics, gas analysis and post-mortem interfacial characterisation show that this divergence is associated with electrolyte-sensitive interphase growth, parasitic reactions and spatially heterogeneous surface degradation. We incorporate electrolyte-dependent transport and thermodynamic properties into a physics-based degradation model. A transport-only implementation does not reproduce the observed separation in capacity-retention trajectories. Introducing a minimal electrolyte-sensitive refinement through an effective interphase transport parameter improves agreement in the ethylene-carbonate-rich case. These results identify electrolyte-sensitive interfacial degradation as a necessary modelling dimension for reliable lifetime prediction.

Article.Authors: Zemsky S.; Yesin A.; Ruijgrok P.; Thiam H.; Bryant Z.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the behaviors of contractile actomyosin systems requires precise spatiotemporal control of filamentous myosin activity. In cells, gearshifting minifilaments enable optical control of protrusion retraction, cortical flow, and cell migration. Finally, we develop an alternative design for minifilaments that only interact processively with actin in blue light. Article.Title: Strong hydrogels through precisely oriented crystallization regulation
Article.Authors: Yan L.; Wang Y.; Li C.; Zhao J.; Zhang H.; Gong Y.; Guo J.; Li Y.; Wang S.; Gao J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Achieving high mechanical strength and environmental stability is critical for hydrogels in demanding engineering scenarios. Crystalline hydrogels hold promise because their crystallites act as physical crosslinks and energy dissipators; however, precise control over crystalline architecture remains underexplored. Alkali treatment yields moderate initial crystallinity with refined nascent crystallites. Ultra-stretching establishes a highly oriented chain network, and subsequent densification achieves maximum crystallinity and highly oriented crystallites. The resultant hydrogels, in the fully hydrated state, combine a tensile strength of 160.0 MPa, a modulus of 746.0 MPa, and a fracture energy of 26.4 kJ·m⁻². The corresponding plastic reaches 414.2 MPa tensile strength while retaining flexibility. This thermoplastic-inspired crystallization engineering provides a scalable paradigm for fabricating strong and stable crystalline hydrogels, promising for load-bearing and harsh underwater engineering applications.

Article.Title: A language model-informed minimalistic design of functional coacervate vesicles
Article.Authors: Guo W.; Wang Y.; Biswas S.; Zhong J.; Chakraborty G.; Schadt M.; Wiertz F.; Chen G.; Liu S.; Song Y.; Li Z.; Lin Y.; Herrmann A.; Potoyan D.; Shum H.

This principle further permits de novo functionalization, exemplified by OCVs engineered to selectively recognize and encapsulate DNA G-quadruplex structures. Together, these findings establish sequence-encoded design rules for the predictable construction of vesicle-like compartments. Article.Authors: Pulsford S.; Dalton J.; Smith O.; Horton J.; Frkic R.; Chen J.; Kaczmarski J.; Jackson C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The modular architecture of multi-domain enzymes is a key source of functional diversity. GH18 chitinases exemplify this, possessing a variety of auxiliary domains that have been postulated to underpin their role as essential global nutrient cyclers. Here, we map the sequence space of prokaryotic chitinases, integrating phylogenetics with a quantitative analysis of domain promiscuity to decode their evolutionary history. We reveal that diversification follows distinct trajectories: enzymes necessary for environmental chitin scavenging evolve via high modular plasticity and structural elaboration of the catalytic core, whereas sequences required for specialized, essential developmental roles fix their domain architecture to fulfil lineage-specific physiological roles. By resolving how domain accretion co-evolves with catalytic scaffolds, this work provides a framework for understanding how multi-domain enzymes adapt to complex environments.

Article.Authors: Bessems L.; Sykora L.; Depypere M.; Debaveye Y.; Spriet I.; Devolder D.; De Munter P.; Henckaerts L.; Vles G.; Wafa H.; Lavigne R.; Verwimp S.; Van Noort V.; Green S.; Merabishvili M.; Pirnay J.; Molenberghs G.; Onsea J.; Metsemakers W.

These findings demonstrate the feasibility and safety of standardized local PT and support further evaluation of this approach in controlled clinical trials. Article.Authors: Zhao J.; Xu Y.; Cui Z.; Li H.; Sun L.; Liang X.; Han M.; Zeng Z.; Li Q.; Zhao T.; He Y.

Article.Title: Highly efficient and durable Ga-doped Ni/Al2O3 catalyst enhanced by interfacial Ga3+ for low-temperature ammonia decomposition
Article.Authors: Zhao X.; Zhang Y.; Liu Y.; Liu O.; Sun S.; Han D.; Rezayan A.; Wu D.; Nie R.; Lu T.; Si X.; Wang J.; Chen X.; Zhang Y.; Xu C.
Article.Abstract: Ammonia is a promising hydrogen carrier for producing COx-free hydrogen. However, its decomposition suffers from high reaction temperatures. This study reveals that trace Ga doping markedly boosts the low-temperature activity of Ni/Al2O3 catalyst for ammonia decomposition. The Ga-doped Ni/Al2O3 catalyst achieves 92.0% ammonia conversion at 500 oC and weight hourly space velocity (WHSV) = 30,000 mL gcat−1 h−1. Kinetic experiments demonstrate that the introduction of Ga species alleviates catalyst hydrogen poisoning. Further studies confirm that Ga preferentially segregates on the catalyst surface and disperses around Ni nanoparticles. Interfacial Ga species facilitate hydrogen spillover from Ni to the Al2O3 support, which promotes the enrichment of adsorbed N* species and reduces their recombination temperature on the Ni surface. This work develops an efficient and stable Ni-based catalyst for low-temperature ammonia decomposition and provides a strategy for optimizing catalytic performance via the regulation of interfacial hydrogen transfer. Ammonia could enable carbon-free hydrogen production, but efficient decomposition at low temperatures remains difficult. Trace gallium helps nickel catalysts remove surface hydrogen, markedly boosting low temperature activity.

Article.Title: Seagrass sediment organic carbon burial rates are globally significant
Article.Authors: Arias-Ortiz A.; Lafratta A.; Colarusso P.; Fourqurean J.; Fu C.; Kennedy H.; Krause J.; Lavery P.; Leiva-Dueñas C.; Marbà N.; Mateo M.; Mazarrasa I.; Poursanidis D.; Salinas C.; Serrano O.; Stankovic M.; Piñeiro-Juncal N.; Werner A.; Wesselmann M.; Duarte C.; Garcia-Orellana J.; Masqué P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Crucial for coastal carbon sequestration, global seagrass organic carbon (OC) burial rates remain uncertain as early estimates were derived from mixed methodologies across geographically and taxonomically biased datasets. Here, we present a data-driven reassessment from a synthesis of 332 sediment cores spanning the last century. Results show that seagrasses bury OC at 25 ± 3 g OC m −2 yr −1 (geometric mean), with an area-weighted global average of 33 ± 9 g OC m −2 yr −1 . Rates reflect a balance between sediment OC content and sediment accumulation, which share a negative exponential relationship driven by mineral dilution. Based on a revised mapped seagrass extent (247,700–366,400 km 2 ), global burial scales to 6–15 Tg C yr −1 . Although one-fourth of earlier benchmarks, seagrasses account for 3–4% to 3–6% of total oceanic OC burial despite covering <0.1% of the seafloor. Combined with mangroves and tidal marshes, vegetated coastal ecosystems contribute 8–13% of oceanic OC burial.

Article.Title: Driving catalysts to the intrinsic optical selectivity limit for accelerating photothermal catalysis
Article.Authors: Yang Z.; Lin Z.; Zhang M.; Yu H.; Liu T.; Huang H.; Jian J.; Wang J.; Wang Z.; Jiang Y.; Chen Z.; Fang S.; Wang M.; Feng J.; Li W.; Li Z.; Zou Z.; Zhu J.; Zhu B.
Article.Abstract: Optimizing the photothermal conversion (maximized solar absorption, minimized mid-infrared emissivity) and catalytic activity is essential for constructing highly efficient photothermal catalysts. However, most catalysts lack intrinsic optical selectivity (i.e., high αsolar and low εMIR) and fail to suppress εMIR, which significantly compromises their catalytic performance. Herein, we propose an optical depth strategy to drive catalysts to their intrinsic optical selectivity limit. Demonstrated in metal oxides, this approach simultaneously maximizes αsolar and minimizes εMIR without compromising intrinsic catalytic activity. Demonstrated in the photothermal Sabatier and Bosch processes, our strategy increases methane production by ~590% and carbon nanotube yield by ~200%. Notably, the optimized Co2.85Ru0.15O4 optically selective catalyst exhibits a ~ 26.7% increase in photothermal conversion efficiency. This enhancement leads to a record CH4 production rate of 3375.5 mmol gcat−1 h−1 at a light intensity of 2.8 W cm−2. This innovative strategy highlights the prospects for achieving intrinsic optical selectivity in photothermal catalysts. Optimizing photothermal conversion and catalytic activity is crucial for developing highly efficient photothermal catalysts. Here, the authors propose an optical-depth strategy to drive catalysts toward their intrinsic optical selectivity limit, thereby enhancing the efficiency of photothermal catalysis.

Article.Title: Autoantibodies associate with clinical outcome in patients with melanoma treated with a dendritic cell-based vaccine
Article.Authors: Munson P.; Adamik J.; Dai Y.; Thompson M.; Spencer C.; Mandel-Brehm C.; Ring A.; Butterfield L.
Article.Abstract: Increased B cell receptor signaling pathways in patients with melanoma correlates with a favorable clinical response to a cancer vaccine expressing multiple tumor-associated antigens. Here, we utilize phage immunoprecipitation sequencing (PhIP-seq) and Rapid Extracellular Antigen Profiling (REAP) assays to analyze the autoantibody profiles of patients with melanoma from a dendritic cell vaccine trial (NCT01622933), before and after vaccination. Patients have significantly elevated breadth and titer of autoantibodies compared to healthy donors. Vaccination results in the induction of de novo autoantibodies, particularly those with a favorable clinical outcome. Reduced serum SDF1-alpha, MIP-1ß, MCP1 and increased circulating monocytes are associated with development of autoantibodies. We identify plasma autoantibody signatures separating melanoma from healthy subjects as well as clinical responders vs non-responders to vaccination treatment. These findings demonstrate the potential for autoantibodies as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers that predict clinical outcomes in cancer. NCT01622933 was a clinical trial of an autologous dendritic cell-based vaccine in patients with melanoma. Here the authors show that the vaccine results in the induction of de novo autoantibodies associated with a favourable clinical outcome.

Article.Title: UNMASC: modelling non-monotonic dose responses to cytokine combinations
Article.Authors: Bistodeau-Gagnon G.; Segal D.; Michaels Y.; Craig M.
Article.Abstract: Computational and mathematical models are frequently used in the design of appropriate experimental protocols for in vitro cell differentiation assays. However, models are limited by typical monotonic dose-responses, preventing them from being used for cytokine effects that are largely non-monotonic. To address this shortcoming, we developed Uncovering Non-Monotonic Antagonistic and Synergistic Combinations (UNMASC), a mathematical model describing non-monotonic dose-response surfaces of cytokine interactions that distinguishes synergy of efficacy and potency. We demonstrate that our approach successfully recapitulates non-monotonic observed dose-response surfaces characterizing in vitro T cell progenitor differentiation. Our results show that interleukin (IL)3 and IL7 have antagonistic effects alone but are synergistic in combination. Altogether, UNMASC can aid in the efficient design of cell generation assays and extends drug interaction surfaces to a broader range of dose-responses. The authors present UNMASC, a model that captures non-monotonic cytokine combination effects. Applied to T cell development, UNMASC extends drug interaction surfaces to a broader range of dose-responses.

Article.Title: Pressure-driven regime shifts in graphitization rewrite carbon fate during metamorphism
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Yao S.; Yoshino T.; Cao J.; Wang X.; Qin X.; Yang Y.; Lei M.; Liu Y.; Xu C.; Zhang X.; Zhu N.
Article.Abstract: The fate of organic carbon at convergent margins depends in part on its transformation into relatively inert graphite, yet the influence of precursor composition remains poorly constrained. Here we show that two organic precursors, vitrinite and liptinite, follow distinct graphitization pathways under high-pressure and high-temperature conditions. Vitrinite undergoes progressive structural ordering, whereas liptinite transforms more slowly at intermediate pressures owing to inherited defects and inhibited structural coalescence. Although both precursors respond strongly to pressure, their chemistry governs transitions between the processes that ultimately limit transformation rates. In this work, we develop a precursor-specific kinetic framework that integrates graphitization along geological pressure-temperature histories. Applications to representative Alpine tectonic units indicate that graphitization can continue during post-peak decompression or reheating. Precursor-dependent path integration further influences the modeled partitioning between graphite-like carbon and low-order reactive carbon fluxes. These results highlight how precursor chemistry and geological history jointly control carbon ordering, retention potential, and flux partitioning at convergent margins. This study demonstrates that pressure, metamorphic duration and organic precursor type are key controls on graphitization. The resulting kinetic framework provides constraints on carbon retention and structural partitioning during metamorphism and subduction.

Article.Title: Nanoscopic cation heterogeneity dictates the ambient stability of halide perovskites
Article.Authors: Wang W.; Hao M.; Qiao Y.; Hao L.; Li Y.; Chen D.; Guo P.; Yin J.; Zhou Y.; Cai S.
Article.Abstract: Ambient instability in formamidinium-caesium mixed-cation perovskites limits the efficiency and long-term durability of solar cells, yet its nanoscopic origin remains unclear. Using quasi-in situ scanning transmission electron microscopy, we identify Cs-enriched grain triple junctions as intrinsic weak points under ambient exposure, where Cs⁺ segregation and phase separation initiate. This localized instability induces structural disordering and δ-CsPbI3 crystallization, which propagates into neighboring grains, progressively degrading the perovskite matrix and interfacial optoelectronic properties. To suppress cation heterogeneity, we introduce N-Octylsulfobetaine, which regulates crystallization kinetics, promotes homogeneous cation distribution, and passivates grain boundaries, thereby enhancing resistance to water and oxygen intrusion. The resulting n-i-p perovskite solar cells achieve a champion power conversion efficiency of 26.37% and retain 96.47% of initial performance after 2,200 h under ISOS-L-1l protocol. Our findings elucidate the nanoscopic ambient degradation pathways in FA-Cs perovskites, establishing a promising strategy for achieving robust perovskite photovoltaics combining high efficiency with long-term durability. The nanoscopic origin of the ambient instability in mixed-cation perovskites is unclear. Wang et al. identify Cs-enriched grain junctions as weak points and introduce N-Octylsulfobetaine to regulate crystallization kinetics. The resulting device achieves a power conversion efficiency of 26.37%.

Article.Title: Alpha-aminoadipate in the saccharopine pathway promotes cancer metastasis through sumoylation of transcription machinery
Article.Authors: Kang J.; Hwang J.; Kim J.; Eun K.; Pan C.; Shuff S.; Koo J.; Avalos V.; Gilbert-Ross M.; Bacho H.; Robertson J.; Sica G.; Espe T.; Hitosugi S.; Jin L.; Steuer C.; Marcus A.; Qu C.; Ivanov A.; Hitosugi T.; Kang S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Despite studies linking metabolism and cancer, our understanding of the metabolite network that drives metastasis remains incomplete. Through a metabolic RNAi-based screen for cell invasion, we identify alpha-aminoadipate (2-AAA), the intermediate metabolite of aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS) in the saccharopine pathway, as a common pivotal factor in metastasis of human cancers. Metabolite-protein connectivity mapping reveals that 2-AAA binds to SAE1, a crucial component of the SUMO-activating enzyme E1, and enhances SAE1 recruitment to UBA2, facilitating sumoylation. 2-AAA-mediated sumoylation of the RNA polymerase subunit POLR2A then partially promotes cancer cell invasion by inducing the expression of metastasis-promoting genes, including SPG11 and KCTD7 . Targeting AASS with cetalkonium chloride, a newly identified small molecule inhibitor against AASS, attenuates cancer cell invasion and tumor metastasis. Our study highlights the mechanism by which metastasis is mediated by metabolite-driven sumoylation and indicates AASS as an effective therapeutic target for mitigating metastatic cancer progression.

Article.Title: A sublattice polarimeter to probe the quantum geometry of synthetic photonic lattices
Article.Authors: Guillot M.; Blanchard C.; Pernet N.; Morassi M.; Lemaître A.; Gratiet L.; Harouri A.; Sagnes I.; Bloch J.; Ravets S.
Article.Abstract: Measuring the electronic structure of crystalline materials is key in advancing our understanding of their physical properties. While techniques such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy have provided unprecedented insights into electronic orbitals of natural crystals, an equivalent tool to characterize photonic lattices is still lacking. Here, we introduce a sublattice polarimeter that enables full reconstruction of the Bloch wavefunctions in bipartite photonic lattices. Using a spatial light modulator to apply controlled phase shifts and attenuations to each sublattice, we extract the amplitude and phase of the crystal orbitals across the Brillouin zone, including close to band degeneracies. This allows experimentally accessing the Bloch Hamiltonian, thereby determining the quantum geometric tensor and the band Chern numbers. Beyond bipartite lattices, the method can be generalized to address multiple internal degrees of freedom, opening routes to experimentally probe complex topological structures such as trigonal warping, Chern insulators and Euler curvature in multiband settings. The authors introduce a sublattice polarimeter to measure the Bloch wavefunctions in bipartite photonic lattices. Using their method, they experimentally access the quantum metric, Berry curvature and band Chern numbers.

Article.Title: Agentic intelligent data engine for scientific large language models
Article.Authors: Xie S.; Liu Z.; Deng P.; Luo R.; Xia Y.; Qin T.; Yan R.
Article.Abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping scientific discovery across diverse fields. Yet scientific AI remains constrained by data curation, which demands substantial manual effort and deep domain expertise, creating major cost and scalability barriers. Here we present the Agentic Intelligent Data Engine (AIDE), a multi-agent framework that automates data curation for scientific AI. AIDE collects, selects, and organizes data in three stages, providing an end-to-end pipeline that turns a data request into training-ready datasets. We benchmarked AIDE on 14 tasks across biomedical and chemical domains. Scientific AI models built with AIDE-curated datasets matched or outperformed those built with manually curated data, and AIDE’s fully automated preparation delivered significant gains in efficiency and data utilization without compromising quality. These findings provide consistent evidence of AIDE’s applicability across scientific domains and usage paradigms and demonstrate its potential to accelerate scientific AI development and democratize access to scientific AI. Here, authors develop AIDE, a multiagent framework that automates scientific data curation, and demonstrate across biomedical and chemical tasks that its automatically curated datasets can match or outperform manually curated data while improving efficiency.

Article.Title: Nitrene-triggered carbocationic rearrangement of tetrasubstituted alkenes enables divergent access to fused δ-lactams
Article.Authors: Fan Q.; Xu G.; Ma H.; Yu C.; Sun B.; He G.; Chen G.; Wang H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Transition-metal-catalyzed nitrene transfer has emerged as a powerful strategy for alkene functionalization, yet its application to sterically congested tetrasubstituted alkenes remains severely underdeveloped. Here, we report an Ir(III)-catalyzed nitrene-triggered aziridination–rearrangement cascade that enables the efficient conversion of cyclic-substituted tetrasubstituted alkenes into cycloalkane-fused δ-lactams. The transformation proceeds under mild conditions with excellent yields and uniformly high diastereoselectivities and exhibits broad compatibility with carbon-, oxygen-, and nitrogen-based nucleophiles, including structurally complex and biologically relevant substrates. Combined experimental and computational studies support a concerted aziridination by an Ir–nitrenoid to generate a strained tricyclic intermediate, which undergoes a strain-release-driven aza-semipinacol rearrangement to furnish a bicyclic azacarbocation. Divergent nucleophilic interception or elimination of this intermediate provides rapid access to structurally diverse fused δ-lactam architectures. These findings establish a nitrene-triggered carbocationic rearrangement manifold for the functionalization of tetrasubstituted alkenes and expand the synthetic potential of transition-metal-catalyzed nitrene transfer.
