Article.Title: A distinct class of conjugative megaplasmids is associated with prophages in distantly related bacterial lineages
Article.Authors: Yuan L.; Qin Y.; West-Roberts J.; Anantharaman K.; Wang H.; Zou Y.; Duan Y.; Camargo A.; Koonin E.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Closely related prophages have been found in phylogenetically distant bacteria in the human gut, despite limited evidence of productive phage infections across broad host ranges. It remains enigmatic how the wide distribution of prophages could emerge. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized association between a distinct group of conjugative megaplasmids and prophage genomes. We describe two related but diverged groups of conjugative megaplasmids (>300 kilobases) in the human gut microbiome, which we named Hodors. Hodors encode conserved replication, partitioning, and type IV secretion systems, along with a complex surface-associated gene module. A subset of Hodors harbors complete, intact prophage genomes, and closely related prophages (≥95% nucleotide identity) were detected across phylogenetically distant lineages within the bacterial phylum Bacillota, including both Bacilli and Clostridia. We detected signatures consistent with extracellular particle formation and transcriptional activity of Hodor-associated prophages. Our findings suggest that conjugative megaplasmids could contribute to the movement of related prophage genomes between distantly related bacteria, potentially explaining the widespread occurrence of closely related prophages in phylogenetically distant gut bacteria and the apparent uncoupling between lysogenic and infective host ranges. Closely related prophages can be found in phylogenetically distant bacteria, despite limited evidence of phage infections across broad host ranges. Here, Yuan et al. identify a group of conjugative megaplasmids associated with prophages across distantly related gut bacteria, suggesting a potential route for prophage dissemination in the human gut microbiome.

Article.Title: Fairness in infectious disease modeling
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Gozzi N.; Perra N.; Tizzoni M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The concept of fairness has been extensively examined within the domains of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence more broadly. It remains, however, largely underexplored in the field of Computational Epidemiology. Considering the substantial influence that epidemic models exert on public health policy, particularly in the context of outbreak preparedness and response, this shortcoming is of great relevance. Here, we propose a mathematical framework, grounded in core principles from Social Epidemiology, for evaluating the fairness of computational epidemic models. We begin by applying our framework to a range of epidemic modeling approaches and simulation scenarios, such as the initial spread of COVID-19 in London, New York, and Santiago de Chile, as well as the 2016 Zika virus outbreak in Colombia, demonstrating its consistent capacity to assess model fairness across diverse disease dynamics. Subsequently, we illustrate how our definition of fairness can be incorporated into the design of immunization strategies as a way to enhance health equity while simultaneously improving the overall effectiveness of such interventions. Overall, our results offer a new systematic methodology for quantifying fairness in computational epidemiology.

Article.Title: Culture-independent strain typing of Clostridioides difficile in fecal samples
Article.Authors: Son S.; Ramaswamy R.; Blanco-Míguez A.; Punčochář M.; Mengoni C.; Burgo V.; Smith R.; Woodson C.; Metcalfe C.; McSpadden E.; Adler E.; Moran A.; Sundararajan A.; Lin H.; Segata N.; Pamer E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Clostridioides difficile ( C. difficile ), the leading cause of healthcare-associated diarrhea, is a spore-forming obligate anaerobe that colonizes the intestinal tract and causes colitis in patients with compromised microbiome-mediated defenses. C. difficile is genomically diverse and is subtyped into ribotypes (RTs) and sequence types (STs) that vary in virulence and epidemic potential. Since secretion of the TcdB exotoxin is common to nearly all disease-associated C. difficile strains, PCR detection of TcdB has become a key clinical test used to diagnose C. difficile infection (CDI). This test and other available clinical laboratory tests, however, do not determine the prevalence of different C. difficile STs, making it impossible to identify transmission events or outbreaks in healthcare settings. Strain typing, because it requires technically demanding and time-consuming anaerobic fecal culturing of C. difficile , is not routinely performed, leaving healthcare epidemiologists unable to distinguish sporadic from epidemic occurrences of CDI. Herein, we optimized the established strain-level profiling tool, MetaPhlAn4 and StrainPhlAn, to distinguish C. difficile strains in the complex fecal microbiomes of hospitalized patients and demonstrate the utility of metagenomic short-read sequencing for culture-independent, rapid epidemiologic surveillance of CDI in healthcare environments.

Article.Title: Microglia-dependent PDGFB regulation of neuronal KCND2 in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus determines propofol anesthesia induction
Article.Authors: Cao B.; Hu J.; Yao H.; Liu Y.; Zhu Z.; Wang H.; Chen P.; Song X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying anesthetic-induced unconsciousness remains a central question in both anesthesia research and neuroscience. However, the role of non-neuronal components in modulating anesthetic sensitivity is poorly understood. In this study, we identify a microglia-dependent platelet-derived growth factor subunit B (PDGFB) signaling pathway that modulates propofol anesthesia sensitivity and contributes to the induction of anesthesia in mice. We demonstrate that PDGFB signaling regulates the potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily D member 2 (KCND2) in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN) in mice, thereby orchestrating the excitability of PVN glutamatergic neurons (PVN Glu ) and the activity of their projections to lateral hypothalamic glutamatergic neurons (LH Glu ). Microglia deprivation induces PDGFB deficiency and downregulates KCND2, resulting in PVN hyperexcitability and hyperactivation of the PVN → LH arousal circuit, which contributes to resistance to anesthesia induction in mice. Our findings identified non-neuronal molecular mechanism that governs anesthetic sensitivity, complementing the classical γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor-centric model and providing insights into the regulation of anesthesia induction.

Article.Title: No-go theorems for sublinear-depth group designs
Article.Authors: West M.; García-Martín D.; Diaz N.; Cerezo M.; Larocca M.
Article.Abstract: Constructing ensembles of circuits which efficiently approximate the Haar measure over various groups is a fundamental problem in quantum information theory, with breakthrough recent results showing that for the unitary group this can be achieved with depths scaling logarithmically in the system size. Here we prove that, for groups G possessing an invariant state G ⊗ k Ψ = Ψ satisfying certain conditions on its entanglement structure, no subset of G consisting of sublinear-depth one-dimensional circuits with constant-locality gates can form an approximate k-design over G. More generally, on a D-dimensional lattice of side-length n, our results imply that such group designs require depths scaling at least as n1/D. Among other examples, we show that there is a constant separation between the maximum depth and gate counts for which no circuit can approximate even the second moment of random matchgate circuits, and those required to implement the matchgate Haar distribution exactly. Finally, we relax the assumption of working with local gates, and prove the impossibility of obtaining approximate designs over G using any circuit comprised of a sublinear number of gates generated by Pauli strings.

Article.Title: HuBMAP Data Portal: a resource for multimodal spatial and single-cell data of healthy human tissues
Article.Authors: Turner M.; Smits T.; Liaw T.; Honick B.; Shirey B.; Choy L.; Akhmetov N.; An S.; Betancur D.; Bordelon D.; Burke K.; Cao-Berg I.; Conroy J.; Csonka C.; Cuda P.; Donahue S.; Fisher S.; Furst D.; Hanna E.; Hardi J.; Kakar T.; Keller M.; Lange D.; Li X.; Ma Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The NIH Human BioMolecular Atlas Program (HuBMAP) Data Portal ( https://portal.hubmapconsortium.org/ ) serves as a comprehensive repository for multimodal, multi-scale spatial and single-cell data from healthy human tissues. As of August 2026, the portal hosts 9,316 public datasets from 26 data types spanning 29 organ classes across 501 donors. Portal infrastructure and user interfaces support data search and discovery, visualization, and analysis directly in web browsers. These capabilities include metadata- and data-driven search, collaborative Workspaces with access to high-performance compute, and interactive Vitessce visualizations across non-spatial, 2D, and 3D spatial datasets. Data-type-specific uniform processing pipelines and rigorous quality control processes ensure comparability of results across laboratories, organs, and donors, while externally processed community-contributed datasets provide complementary perspectives. Here we describe portal functionality, infrastructure, and design, and highlight its role as a platform for large-scale spatial single-cell research across diverse data types, organs, and scales.

Article.Title: Short-depth designs beyond the unitary group
Article.Authors: Grevink L.; Haferkamp J.; Heinrich M.; Helsen J.; Hinsche M.; Schuster T.; Zimborás Z.
Article.Abstract: Random quantum operations are a central tool in quantum information and beyond, having applications ranging from benchmarking and cryptography to many-body physics. While recent advances have shown that shallow-depth circuits can realize approximate unitary designs, which are ensembles that appear to be random to a restricted observer, it remained unclear whether similar constructions extend to other groups that play important roles in quantum computing. We provide a range of results on several groups of broad interest in quantum information science: the Clifford group, the orthogonal group, the unitary symplectic groups, and the matchgate group. For these groups we prove that designs cannot be generated by any circuit ensemble with lightcones that are smaller than the system size. We moreover show that commonly considered circuit ensembles cannot generate designs in sub-linear depth on any circuit architecture. On the other hand, we prove that slightly weaker forms of randomness-including additive-error state designs and anti-concentration-nevertheless emerge at logarithmic depths in many cases. Our results reveal that the onset of randomness in shallow quantum circuits is a widespread yet subtle phenomenon, dependent on the interplay between the group itself and the context of its application.

Article.Title: Reconstructing the single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics of glioblastoma invasion
Article.Authors: Mangukiya H.; Skeppås M.; Lasses Armatowski A.; Uppman I.; Hallin L.; Kruse F.; Nordquist C.; Kundu S.; Berglund M.; Malik A.; Krona C.; Jörnsten R.; Nelander S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma invasion into healthy brain tissue remains a major barrier to effective treatment, but the dynamic single-cell behaviors underlying this process remain difficult to measure across patient models. Here, we introduce GlioTrace, an ex vivo imaging and computational framework for real-time tracking of glioblastoma invasion in patient-derived xenograft brain slices. Combining whole-specimen confocal microscopy with machine learning-based morphology classification and probabilistic modeling of state transitions, GlioTrace reconstructs how tumor cells switch between invasion phenotypes and how these dynamics are shaped by local tissue context and therapy. Across six patient-derived models, GlioTrace reveals that invasion plasticity is patient-specific, spatially organized, and modulated by vascular proximity and microglial interaction. Targeted therapies selectively alter phenotype composition and transition probabilities, whereas standard-of-care treatment enriches a highly motile, transition-connected branching state consistent with a treatment-tolerant invasive phenotype. Thus, GlioTrace makes glioblastoma invasion a measurable dynamic process for comparing patient-specific treatment responses in living brain tissue.

Article.Title: Structural basis for N-glycopeptide preference in an infant-derived Bifidobacterium bifidum PNGaseA
Article.Authors: Bakshani C.; Caulton S.; Taleb V.; Ojuri T.; Coughlan K.; Montesa A.; Pérez-Latorre A.; Merino P.; Kozak R.; Çakaj S.; Bottacini F.; Lovering A.; van Sinderen D.; Hurtado-Guerrero R.; Crouch L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract N-glycans are abundant nutrient sources for human gut bacteria, which deploy peptide: N-glycosidases to release them from glycoproteins. Breast milk is comprised of a high proportion of N-glycosylated bioactive proteins that can be accessed by infant colonic microbes. Here, we biochemically and structurally characterize a PNGaseA-family enzyme from infant-associated Bifidobacterium bifidum LMG13195. This enzyme acts on a broad range of N-glycan structures but shows a marked preference for N-glycans attached to glycopeptides rather than to denatured or native proteins, highlighting a specialized route for N-glycan acquisition in infant-associated Bifidobacterium species. Structures of the apo enzyme, an unliganded E236Q mutant, and a D107N–E236Q complex with a G2-peptide reveal a canonical two-β-sandwich PNGase core plus an additional ten-strand β-sheet cradle and are the first structures of this superfamily. Comparison of these states, combined with molecular dynamics simulations, indicates that glycopeptide binding is coupled to β-sheet cradle-loop movements that close against β-sandwich 1 over the peptide C terminus. The complex defines recognition of the two core GlcNAc residues and the central mannose, reveals that peptide contacts are concentrated around the +2 Thr residue of the NXT sequon, and positions the scissile amide at the active site. These findings, together with mutational and computational analyses, provide a structural basis for N-glycopeptide preference by linking glycopeptide binding to cradle closure and catalysis, thereby expanding the host-glycan nutrient landscape accessible to infant-gut Bifidobacterium species.

Article.Title: Differential methanogenic archaea-induced TLR8-dependent signaling engages gene classes regulated by NF-κB p65 and STAT1/2
Article.Authors: Xu F.; Sieverding J.; Zhou P.; Sah S.; Weinberger V.; Moissl-Eichinger C.; Wohlers I.; Heine H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Archaea are prevalent in the human gut but lack canonical bacterial cell wall-associated immune ligands. Time-resolved RNA-seq of human PBMCs showed that Methanosphaera stadtmanae and Methanobrevibacter smithii induced a shared immune program but with distinct kinetics: M. stadtmanae triggered an earlier and stronger response, whereas M. smithii acted more gradually. Conserved early-upregulated genes separated into Class I genes, preferentially induced by M. stadtmanae , and Class II genes, similarly induced by both. M. stadtmanae showed greater early uptake, while responses to both archaea were broadly TLR8-dependent. ChIP-qPCR linked the stronger Class I gene activation induced by M. stadtmanae to greater NF-κB p65 binding at Class I promoters, whereas STAT1/2 binding at Class II promoters occurred with both stimuli. Dose-response analyses with archaeal RNA inputs supported distinct activation thresholds, with Class II genes at lower input and Class I genes requiring higher input. Together, these findings support an input-tuned TLR8-dependent mechanism shaping differential immune programs towards archaea.

Article.Title: Algal symbiosis adaptively restructures the cnidarian microbiome to enhance holobiont metabolism
Article.Authors: Cui G.; Ngugi D.; Konciute M.; Cheng S.; Liew K.; Mi J.; Al-Babili S.; Aranda M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Microbiomes are integral to the function and resilience of cnidarian holobionts, yet the spatial and functional integration of microbial communities within host tissues remains poorly understood. Here, we show that symbiosis with photosynthetic dinoflagellates induces adaptive, tissue-specific restructuring of the microbiome in the cnidarian model Aiptasia, fundamentally enhancing holobiont nitrogen assimilation and metabolic flexibility. Using laser microdissection, tissue-resolved metatranscriptomics, gnotobiotic hosts, and stable isotope tracing, we reveal that symbiosis profoundly restructures microbial communities across the epidermis and gastrodermis, enriching for taxa and pathways that support nitrogen assimilation in photosynthetically active tissues. Expression of microbial nitrite reductase is strongly upregulated in the symbiotic gastrodermis, and 15 N-tracer experiments demonstrate that bacterial assimilation of nitrite synergizes with algal symbionts to fuel the biosynthesis of essential amino acids. These findings show that symbiosis drives spatially compartmentalized microbiome adaptation within animal tissues, aligning microbial metabolism with host-algal nutrient exchanges to enhance holobiont functioning.

Article.Title: PrinTE: a forward simulation framework for studying the role of transposable elements in genome expansion and contraction
Article.Authors: Benson C.; Chen T.; Thomson S.; Deng C.; Ou S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Genome expansion and contraction are driven by transposable element activity, but the underlying dynamics remain enigmatic due to a lack of historical records tracing these changes. Here, we present PrinTE, a forward-time simulator of whole-genome sequences with customizable transposon dynamics for identifying the evolutionary parameters most consistent with an observed genome. Across simulations spanning four orders of magnitude, PrinTE recovers transposon insertion and deletion rates with less than 6% error. We demonstrate PrinTE on Arabidopsis and the fungal subdivision Pucciniomycotina, including myrtle rust ( Austropuccinia psidii ), which expanded its genome size to 1,018 Mb through transposon amplifications. Our simulations show that recombination-based removal of LTR retrotransposons alone cannot prevent genome obesity, and that preventing their invasion in the first place is more effective. We hypothesize that A. psidii might have experienced a prolonged expansion phase followed by a potent and ongoing period of contraction.

Article.Title: The Genome Atlas of 1,020 Probands and 409 Unaffected Parents Decodes the Clinical Heterogeneity in β-thalassemia
Article.Authors: Ye Y.; Huang Y.; Deng L.; Liu X.; Guo X.; Zhang Q.; Zhao Y.; Xie D.; Long Y.; Li S.; Fang M.; Niu C.; Zhang P.; Qin L.; Zeng J.; Gao Y.; Li Y.; Liao L.; Cai J.; Liu R.; Zhang X.; Zeng L.; Li Y.; Lin B.; Li K.
Article.Abstract: β-thalassemia is an extensively studied monogenic disorder, yet the basis of its striking phenotypic diversity remains unresolved. Here we present the 1000 β-Thalassemia Genomes Project (KbTGP), providing the first comprehensive atlas of 1,429 Chinese genomes (1,020 probands and 409 unaffected parents, 61.63× coverage) linked to 77 clinical traits. We identify 11 independent phenotype-associated loci in probands, and 15 additional loci by integrating 2,746 ethnically matched controls from the NyuWa Project and the 1000 Genomes Project. Functional experiments further highlight non-coding regions at 17p13.3 and the autophagy-related gene PIK3C3 as modulators of thalassemic phenotypes. Loss-of-function structural variants are enriched in hemoglobinopathy-related genes, and structural variants in TF and SLC25A37 are significantly associated with iron metabolism and fetal hemoglobin, respectively. Notably, de novo structural variants and clonal hematopoiesis mutations are enriched in severe cases. These findings collectively establish a phenome-genome resource that delineates the genetic architecture of β-thalassemia, offering candidate targets for precision therapies and laying the groundwork for future research into dissecting the Mendelian disease variability. The authors sequence 1020 Chinese patients with beta thalassemia and 409 unaffected parents to identify genes that modulate the phenotypes. Functional validation in mice and cultured cells confirm the role of autophagy-associated gene PIK3C3.

Article.Title: Complex magnetism in a transition metal nitride
Article.Authors: Werhahn D.; Steinberg S.; Ritter C.; Drötboom F.; Attfield J.; Kloß S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract High-symmetry lattices of transition metal ions such as the body-centred tetragonal (bct) arrangement are model systems for correlated electron physics and frustrated magnetism. Transition metal oxides or halides with the bct K 2 NiF 4 -type structure are extensively studied and have ground states dominated by strong interactions within the square layers, but materials exemplifying other bct ground states are much rarer. Here we show that Ca 2 CoN 2 , from the underexplored class of transition metal nitrides, has one of the complex magnetic ground states predicted for the bct lattice lying close to a spin-liquid instability. Ca 2 CoN 2 has been synthesised at high pressure in a large-volume press, and has a Na 2 HgO 2 -type structure where weakening of intralayer superexchange interactions leads to frustration. Our magnetisation and neutron diffraction experiments reveal an incommensurate spin order below 54 K, consistent with a double- k spin density wave with propagation vectors ( k 00) and (0 k 0) where k = 0.57. This phase lies close to the predicted crossover (at k = 0.64–0.69) to a modulated spin liquid, which could be explored through further chemical tuning. This work demonstrates the potential of transition metal nitrides as magnetic model systems, alongside the much-studied oxides and halides, for exploring complex spin orders and associated quantum phases.

Article.Title: Reply to: Evidence of widespread sequencing errors in global avian influenza study
Article.Authors: Wannigama D.; Amarasiri M.; Phattharapornjaroen P.; Hurst C.; Modchang C.; Besa J.; Miyanaga K.; Cui L.; Fernandez S.; Huang A.; Ounjai P.; Werawatte W.; Rad S. M A.; Vatanaprasan P.; Jay D.; Saethang T.; Luk-in S.; Kanthawee P.; Thuptimdang W.; Tacharoenmuang R.; Cynthia B.; Vitharana S.; Ngamwongsatit N.; Ishikawa H.; Furukawa T.
Article.Abstract: The primary issue arose due to an error during the sequence submission process to GISAID. Following GISAID’s advice for bulk submissions, we used the command-line software “FluCLI” to upload our data. During reformatting of files for submission, an analysis file originally prepared for phylogenetic tree construction and containing both our study sequences and reference sequences was inadvertently uploaded. In addition, sample identifiers were reformatted incorrectly, which led to duplication and mixing of study and reference sequences. Importantly, in our original analyses, we did not find such anomalies. We would like to apologize for the confusion caused by the erroneous sequences. The sequences have been corrected both in GISAID and in GenBank, under the same accession numbers provided in the original manuscript (GISAID: EPI_ISL_19613337 to EPI_ISL_19613573/ EPI_ISL_19812857-EPI_ISL_19812874; GenBank: PV422873-PV423054, PV422241-PV422430, and PV440337-PV440372, now version 2). They must not be used to model, predict, or otherwise infer health or commercial applications. The data are not permitted for use in generative AI modeling, dashboard development, or border-related health prediction systems.

Article.Title: Evidence of widespread sequencing errors in global avian influenza study
Article.Authors: Wille M.; Banyard A.; Bonfante F.; Breed A.; Brown I.; Fusaro A.; Karlsson E.; Lewis N.; Nelson M.; Sims L.; Swayne D.; Uhart M.; Wong F.
Article.Abstract: Wannigama et al. (2025) 1 present a study whereby guano samples from infrequently sampled countries were assessed for the presence of avian influenza viruses. Samples were collected from Africa (Madagascar, Mozambique, Somalia), the Middle East (Yemen), South Asia (Maldives, Sri Lanka), South East Asia (Indonesia, Myanmar, the Philippines) and Oceania (Papua New Guinea). The study aims to address critical gaps in global surveillance and provide important data that could enhance understanding of regional viral diversity and evolution, as well as inform high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) incursion risk assessments. However, the data presented and the conclusions drawn from this study are of high concern to the global influenza community. The viral sequence data on which the study is based contradict long-established understanding of global avian influenza evolution, resulting in conclusions that are incongruent with the global evidence base. The publication of erroneous viral sequences in public databases such as GenBank or GISAID hinders rational interpretation of data in a global context, resulting in misleading conclusions that affect disease risk assessments and policy decisions.

Article.Title: Polymorph-tuned photoinduced red luminescence and room-temperature phosphorescence in macrocyclic molecular crystals
Article.Authors: Hou J.; Fan Z.; Lin H.; Zhang Z.; Zhang C.; Tong F.; Qu D.
Article.Abstract: Despite the increasing demand, fabricating organic functional molecular crystals with highly tunable photoluminescent properties in the same system remains a significant challenge. Here, we demonstrate that photoinduced red emission and room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) can be effectively regulated via crystal-polymorph modulation in a macrocyclic diphenylamine[3]arene (DPA[3]) compound. During crystal growth, kinetic control directs DPA[3] molecules to adopt distinct stacking motifs, resulting in two polymorphs (Type A and Type B) with divergent luminescent properties. Type A crystals exhibit photoinduced red emission extending to 630 nm, while Type B crystals show long-lived green RTP (lifetime >450 ms) after ultraviolet light excitation. Notably, thermal treatment of Type A crystals induces a partial polymorphic evolution toward the Type B crystals. Experimental and calculation analyses reveal that paired DPA[3] molecules in Type A form a columnar packing motif, which may facilitate photoinduced electron transfer to generate charge transfer intermediates for red luminescence. In contrast, Type B crystals feature a more distorted herringbone stacking motif with a tighter molecular stacking structure, enabling stabilizing triplet excitons that support efficient RTP. Our findings present an effective strategy for achieving single-component materials with multiple luminescent functionalities by regulating the aggregate state. Molecular crystals with luminescent properties are desirable, but tuning of properties within one system is challenging. Here, the authors report crystals with photoinduced red emission and room temperature phosphorescence regulated by polymorph modulation.

Article.Title: Techno-economic and environmental assessment of next-generation battery-powered farming robots
Article.Authors: Schlehuber S.; Gutsch M.; Stegemann L.; Hendrickson T.; von Delft S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Decarbonizing agriculture without compromising productivity is a major challenge under rising input costs and labor scarcity. Autonomous battery-powered agricultural robots (ABARs) could help by reducing dependence on conventional machinery and enabling more precise application of inputs, but their system-level economic and environmental performance remains unclear. Here, we integrate total cost of ownership and life cycle assessment to evaluate a small ABAR for cradle-to-farm-gate crop production of strawberries, onions, lettuce, and peanuts under organic and non-organic management. Across modeled scenarios, benchmarked costs range from 76% below to 17% above literature-based reference ranges, while greenhouse-gas emissions fall within or below reported ranges. Variable inputs dominate both outcomes, contributing 72–90% of costs and 72–95% of global-warming impacts, with seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation water as main drivers. These results suggest that ABAR value depends less on the platform than on the ability of autonomous operation to reduce input use and labor demand.

Article.Title: Human subthalamic neurons track speech features and couple with auditory cortex during preparatory listening
Article.Authors: Zhu Y.; Bush A.; Vissani M.; Bullock L.; Richardson R.
Article.Abstract: The basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop is widely implicated in speech production, yet its role during listening remains underexplored. Here, using a listen-and-repeat syllable-triplet task during deep brain stimulation implantation, we show that human subthalamic nucleus (STN) single‑unit activity is modulated during auditory presentation, and that a subset of neurons encodes phonetic (consonant and vowel) and position features prior to overt speech onset. Using intraoperative microelectrode recordings, across 205 units, ~39% of units changed firing rate during listening. Within these, auditory-syllable units carried phonetic and/or position information, primarily in units also modulated during speech. Auditory presentation also elicited beta‑band desynchronization in STN local field potential (LFP) and revealed frequency‑specific spike‑phase coupling (SPC) with cortex: auditory‑specific units coupled predominantly with superior temporal gyrus (STG) in alpha, whereas units modulated during both auditory and speech epochs preferentially coupled with sensorimotor regions in beta. Together, these results indicate that auditory inputs can rapidly modulate human STN activity during a listen-and-repeat task, support a role for the STN in auditory-motor integration, and indicate frequency‑specific routing within human cortical-subcortical loops from listening to subsequent speech production. The authors show that neurons in a deep-brain region involved in movement respond to heard speech, encode syllables, and coordinate with auditory and motor areas, supporting a role in linking listening and speaking.

Article.Title: MELK drives neointimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis via vascular smooth muscle cell phenotypic transition
Article.Authors: Wu J.; Zong J.; Zhao X.; Aili T.; Qiu M.; Yu J.; Zhou Y.; Liu Y.; Hu B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cardiovascular diseases associated with atherosclerosis and post-injury restenosis remain leading global causes of mortality. Despite therapeutic advancements, effective treatments targeting the phenotypic transition of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs)—a pivotal event in neointimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis—are still limited. This study identifies Maternal Embryonic Leucine Zipper Kinase (MELK) as a key regulator of VSMC phenotypic transition in both injury-induced neointimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis. MELK is significantly upregulated in VSMCs in response to pathological stimuli, driven by transcriptional activation through C/EBPβ. Mechanistically, MELK phosphorylates EZH2 at threonine 367, stabilizing it and enhancing H3K27me3 modifications on VSMC contractile genes, thereby promoting VSMC dedifferentiation. SMC-specific knockout of MELK substantially reduces neointimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis in mouse models. Notably, selective MELK inhibitor OTSSP167 significantly diminishes neointimal hyperplasia without impairing re-endothelialization, a critical process for vascular repair. This study highlights the potential of MELK inhibition as an approach to treating restenosis and atherosclerosis.

Article.Title: Anterior cingulate neurons perform parallel processing of fixated and peripheral information to guide information sampling and choice
Article.Authors: Butler J.; Muller T.; Veselic S.; Malalasekera W.; Behrens T.; Hunt L.; Kennerley S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract We use our eyes to evaluate objects around us. Models of economic choice emphasise the impact of sequential fixation on valuation and choice, with prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) encoding values of fixated items. Yet whether these regions also evaluate non-fixated peripheral information to guide choice remains unknown. Here we show that in a decision-making task involving four simultaneously presented cues, rhesus macaques use peripheral information to guide information sampling and choice, and that ACC neurons encode this peripheral information. This served two distinct purposes: subjects were more likely to fixate valuable peripheral cues, and more likely to choose valuable options whose cues were never even fixated. ACC, orbitofrontal cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and ventromedial prefrontal cortex neurons all encoded cue value as they were fixated. ACC was unique, however, in also conducting parallel processing of peripheral cues, including cues never fixated, to guide information sampling and choice.

Article.Title: Rbpj restrains regulatory T cell exhaustion in tumors
Article.Authors: Papadopoulou M.; Karkanis L.; Tharra P.; Mitletton M.; Klinakis A.; Cossarizza A.; Hatzioannou A.; Lavigne M.; Flaherty D.; Tartaro D.; Verginis P.
Article.Abstract: Although regulatory T (Treg) cells are vital for immune homeostasis and prevention of autoimmunity, they also exert an essential role in promoting tumor development. The mechanisms explaining why Treg cells remain functional in the hostile tumor microenvironment, while their effector counterparts become exhausted, remain incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that Treg-cell-specific deletion of Rbpj, the master transcription factor regulating Notch signaling, reduces tumor burden in mice. This is associated with the induction of an exhausted phenotype characterized by marked PD-1 upregulation. PD-1 deletion in Rbpj-deficient Treg cells reverses their exhausted phenotype and restores their tumor-promoting function. Finally, pharmacological inhibition of Rbpj using a novel small molecule promotes Treg cell exhaustion and reduces tumor growth. Collectively, our findings indicate that Notch-Rbpj signaling may act as an immune checkpoint pathway that hinders Treg exhaustion in tumors. The mechanisms explaining how the tumour microenvironment promotes regulatory T cell function, while rendering effector T cells exhausted, are incompletely understood. Here, the authors demonstrate that the transcription factor Rbpj, acts as checkpoint that prevents regulatory T cell exhaustion in tumours

Article.Title: Enhancing salivary gland siRNA activity through transgenic Dicer-2 overexpression restricts arbovirus transmission in Aedes aegypti
Article.Authors: Dong S.; Ciomperlik-Patton J.; Zhao Y.; Dong Y.; Ling B.; Myles K.; Dimopoulos G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The mosquito Aedes aegypti is the primary vector for arboviruses that are pathogenic to humans, including dengue, Zika, and chikungunya viruses. Following a blood meal, arboviruses initially infect the midgut, disseminate systemically to the carcass, and eventually reach the salivary glands for transmission. Here, we investigate tissue-specific small interfering RNA (siRNA) activity and test whether enhancing this pathway can restrict arbovirus infection. Our results show that salivary glands are less refractory to arboviral infection relative to the carcass, with low expression patterns of siRNA pathway genes. Transgenic overexpression of Dicer-2 , a key component of the siRNA pathway, in salivary glands leads to a significant decrease in orthoflavivirus and alphavirus replication. DENV4 small RNA sequencing reveals altered viral RNA processing and increased levels of 21-nt virus-derived siRNAs. Conversely, Dicer-2 overexpression in the fat body, a major carcass tissue, only moderately suppresses dengue and Mayaro virus infection. Notably, simultaneous overexpression of Dicer-2 in both midguts and salivary glands produces the strongest reduction in viral load in saliva, indicating reduced transmission potential. These findings reveal tissue-specific differences in antiviral pathway activity and demonstrate that targeted enhancement of salivary gland antiviral defense can restrict arbovirus transmission.

Article.Title: Building a pre-trained model for single-cell multi-omics analysis beyond highly variable feature selection
Article.Authors: Yuan Z.; Jiao S.; Xiao Y.; Peng J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Single-cell multi-omics technologies enable simultaneous measurement of transcriptomic, epigenomic, and proteomic modalities in individual cells, offering a unique opportunity to dissect cellular identity and regulation. The heterogeneity of multi-omics data, together with the wide range of downstream analytical tasks, underscores the need for a versatile computational framework for integrative analysis. However, current multi-omics analysis approaches typically rely on task-specific training and highly variable feature selection, which can hinder effective knowledge transfer across datasets and discard biologically informative signals. Here, we present scPMMI, a pre-trained multimodal model for integrative analysis of single-cell multi-omics data. By grouping features into patches according to genomic coordinates, scPMMI processes tens of thousands of features per cell with reduced reliance on prior feature selection, thereby preserving more complete biological information. Our results demonstrate that scPMMI learns biologically coherent cell representations by jointly modeling multi-omics data. Through further transfer learning, the model can be readily adapted to achieve superior performance across diverse downstream tasks, including multi-omics integration, cell type annotation, protein abundance prediction, transcriptomic enhancement, and trajectory reconstruction.

Article.Title: Ketogenic diet stimulates tumor cGAS-Sting pathway and attenuates systemic inflammation via Flavonifractor plautii derived uridine
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Deng L.; Xie H.; Shi J.; Qin Q.; Xu C.; Liu C.; Xu Z.; Lin S.; Ruan G.; Li X.; Bu Z.; Wang Y.; Ruan H.; Li X.; Zhang L.; Wang S.; Chen Y.; Li C.; Chen Y.; Luo C.; Wang J.; Wang Z.; Tang M.; Liu T.
Article.Abstract: Cancer progression is frequently accompanied by systemic inflammation and host-wide disturbances, including neuroinflammation-associated cognitive impairment, yet interventions that simultaneously target tumor growth and host dysfunction remain limited. Here we show that a ketogenic diet suppresses tumor growth while improving emotional and cognitive deficits in tumor-bearing mice. The diet elevates circulating and intratumoral uridine and enriches Flavonifractor plautii, a gut bacterium that contributes to host uridine availability. In tumor cells and patient-derived organoids, uridine cooperates with β-hydroxybutyrate to promote cytosolic DNA accumulation and activate cGAS–Sting signaling, consistent with enhanced antitumor immune activity. In parallel, ketogenic diet, uridine supplementation and F. plautii transplantation reduce systemic and hippocampal inflammatory readouts and improve neurobehavioral phenotypes. These findings identify a diet–microbiota–metabolite axis that links ketogenic metabolism to tumor immune signaling and reduced peripheral-to-brain inflammation in preclinical cancer models. Ketogenic diets are reported to regulate cancer progression and therapy response. Here, the authors show that a ketogenic diet boosts microbial uridine, activates tumor immune signaling, slows tumor growth, and dampens brain inflammation in mouse cancer models.

Article.Title: ATP-dependent dimerization of BrxC coordinates BrxBCZ assembly for phage exclusion
Article.Authors: Li S.; Xu T.; Zhang W.; Du S.; Qi L.; Tang Y.; Xie R.; Chen G.; Zhu L.; Sun L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Bacteriophage Exclusion (BREX) systems protect bacterial genomes via sequence-specific DNA methylation while blocking phage replication through a poorly understood “restriction-without-cleavage” mechanism. Here, we present cryo-EM structures and functional characterization of the core BREX machinery from Escherichia coli . We determined the structures of the ATPase BrxC in its monomeric state and two ATPγS-bound dimeric conformations, showing that ATP binding, not hydrolysis, triggers dimerization. The conserved Arg328 couples dimer formation to ATP hydrolysis and is required for both phage restriction and host methylation; the R328A mutant supports assembly but abolishes defense. We further resolved the BrxBCZ ternary complex, revealing BrxB as a central scaffold bridging the BrxC dimer and BrxZ without direct BrxC–BrxZ contact. Biochemical assays show that BrxZ is a dual-function enzyme with alkaline phosphatase and metal-dependent nuclease activities. Thus, ATP drives BrxC assembly and inhibits BrxZ activities. Disruption of the BrxB–BrxC interface or the BrxC ATPase cycle selectively eliminates restriction while preserving methylation, establishing BrxBCZ as a restriction-specific structural core. Collectively, these findings delineate the structural basis for ATP-dependent coordination of BREX, revealing how energy metabolism is integrated into bacterial innate immunity.

Article.Title: Observation of ultra-low thermal conductivity in ultra-thin single-crystalline PbI2 nanosheets
Article.Authors: Zhong J.; Li Z.; Yuan D.; Fu Y.; Gu G.; Gao Z.; Wei J.; Zhu C.; Wei N.; Nie M.; Yin K.; Sun L.
Article.Abstract: Low thermal conductivity materials are key for next-generation thermal management. However, non-destructive characterization of ultra-thin single crystals remains challenging. Here, we report a room-temperature thermal conductivity of 0.24 W/(m·K) in 7.9 nm single-crystalline PbI2 nanosheets, representing an experimentally realized ultra-low value in the ultra-thin single-crystal regime. This observation is enabled by an integrated in‑situ growth‑location‑measurement strategy that couples aqueous‑solution nucleation with gas‑flow‑assisted alignment, enabling the non‑destructive transfer of nanosheets onto a suspended thermal bridge. Combining first‑principles density functional theory calculations and Raman spectroscopy, we trace the suppressed thermal transport in PbI2 to flattened flexural acoustic phonons with markedly low group velocities and short lifetimes. Furthermore, this suppression is exacerbated by thickness-induced vibrational softening, while in-situ irradiation allows for dynamic thermal modulation. This work establishes a robust experimental framework for characterizing ultra-thin single crystals with ultra-low thermal conductivity, bridging theoretical prediction with experimental realization for advanced flexible thermal management applications. The authors report low room-temperature thermal conductivity (0.24 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) in 7.9 nm single-crystalline PbI₂ nanosheets. Non-destructive suspended-device measurements and theory reveal flexural-phonon suppression, while irradiation enables dynamic thermal tuning.

Article.Title: Hierarchical mode of evolution in freshwater SAR11 driven by species dispersal and lake history
Article.Authors: Fernandes C.; Okazaki Y.; Salcher M.
Article.Abstract: Microorganisms dominate aquatic ecosystems, yet the evolutionary forces shaping their population structure especially across fragmented freshwater habitats remain poorly understood. Here, we apply comparative population genomics to the globally distributed freshwater SAR11 genus Fontibacterium, analysing genome-wide single nucleotide variants from three species with contrasting dispersal capacities across 21 lakes on five continents. The geographic scale of genetic differentiation was predictable from species traits, ranging from complete isolation between ancient rift lakes in an African endemic (F. africanum), through regional connectivity limited by continental barriers in a temperate specialist (F. temperatum), to global cohesion in a cosmopolitan species (F. commune), where ecosystem properties, not distance, shaped genetic structure. Geographic distance shaped population differentiation in the dispersal-limited species independently of environmental confounders, while ecosystem age, size, and geological setting were the primary predictors for the cosmopolitan species. Within lakes, ancient African Great Lake populations exhibited elevated pN/pS ratios consistent with relaxed purifying selection, a pattern absent in another ancient, but smaller lake (Lake Biwa), suggesting that ecosystem size and physical structure drive selective dynamics rather than lake age alone. These findings support a hierarchical model in which intrinsic dispersal capacity sets the geographic scale for gene flow, while local ecosystem properties shape within-population evolutionary dynamics. Microbes may be distributed everywhere, but whether they form distinct regional populations is unclear. Across 21 lakes on five continents, this study shows that freshwater SAR11 species’ dispersal ability sets the geographic scale of its evolution, while local lake conditions shape its selection.

Article.Title: Genome-anchored foundation model embeddings improve molecular prediction from histology images
Article.Authors: Jin C.; Zhou F.; Yu Y.; Ma J.; Wang Y.; Xu Y.; Zhou H.; Jiang H.; Luo L.; Mao L.; He Z.; Zhang X.; Zhang J.; Chan R.; Yao H.; Chen H.
Article.Abstract: Precision oncology requires accurate molecular insights, yet obtaining these directly from genomics is costly and time-consuming for broad clinical use. Predicting complex molecular features and patient prognosis directly from routine whole-slide images (WSIs) remains a major challenge for current deep learning methods. Here we introduce PathLUPI, which uses transcriptomic privileged information during training to extract genome-anchored histological embeddings, enabling effective molecular prediction using only WSIs at inference. Crucially, it achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of at least 0.80 across 18 biomarker prediction and molecular subtyping tasks, and a concordance index of at least 0.70 across survival cohorts spanning five major cancer types. Moreover, PathLUPI embeddings reveal distinct cellular morphological signatures associated with specific genotypes, whose spatial fidelity is substantiated in representative high-resolution spatial transcriptomics samples. By effectively encoding molecular context to refine WSI representations, PathLUPI offers a strategy to bridge molecular insights with routine pathology workflows for wider clinical application. Obtaining accurate molecular insights for precision oncology remains costly and time consuming. Here, the authors develop PathLUPI, a deep learning method to enable effective molecular prediction in cancer using only routine whole-slide images, with evaluation across 49 molecular oncology tasks in 20 different cohorts.

Article.Title: Li+-locked domain effect for breaking the temperature stability bottleneck in thermal-detection high-entropy energy storage ceramics
Article.Authors: Zeng X.; Liu Z.; Wang Z.; Cao L.; Sa B.; Wu X.; Luo L.; Zhang S.
Article.Abstract: Conventional brain pacemakers rely on electrochemical batteries, which suffer from leakage, performance degradation, and neurotoxicity, posing serious safety risks. Ceramic-based pulse generators with ultra-fast discharge, high-temperature stability, and self-diagnostic capability offer a promising alternative. However, most dielectric ceramics lose their polarization activity at elevated temperatures. To address this challenge, we introduce a high-entropy composition design that induces a Li-locked domain effect in the ceramic system (1-x)[0.9(Bi0.47Na0.47Yb0.03Tm0.01)TiO3−0.1LiTaO3]−0.06(Ba0.3Sr0.7)(Sn0.5Hf0.5)O3. We demonstrate that Li+-enriched regions lock polar nanodomains, preserving them even at 300 °C. This mechanism yields a recoverable energy density of 11.43 J·cm−3, an efficiency of 84.67%, and excellent temperature stability (Δη/η < 0.3% up to 320 °C). Moreover, Yb3+/Tm3+ co-doping enables anomalous thermal enhancement of photoluminescence and precise temperature monitoring. Remarkably, the experimentally measured temperature sensing deviation is only ±0.23 K. The integration of stable energy storage and optical self-diagnosis provides a new paradigm for ceramic-based brain pacemaker pulse generators with early warning capability, pointing toward a possible solution to the intrinsic safety limitations of conventional battery-powered devices. Dielectric energy-storage ceramics lose polarization at high temperatures, limiting harsh-environment use. Here, the authors show a Li+- locked domain effect in high-entropy BNT-based ceramics, achieving Wrec = 11.43 J cm−3, η = 84.67%, Δη/η < 0.3% up to 320 °C, with self-diagnostic thermometry.

Article.Title: Small-molecule targeting of kinesin-13 KIF2C enhances double-strand break DNA repair and slows down aging
Article.Authors: Macedo J.; da Silva M.; Sousa-Soares C.; Magalhães J.; Ala M.; Ribeiro R.; Barroso-Vilares M.; Galhardo M.; Sousa M.; Silva E.; Seluanov A.; Gorbunova V.; Sampaio P.; Vasques-Nóvoa F.; Nascimento D.; Logarinho E.
Article.Abstract: DNA damage is a central driver of the aging process. We previously found that the kinesin-13 KIF2C, shown to play a role in DNA repair, is repressed in aged cells. Here, we investigate whether increased KIF2C activity can counteract DNA damage and alleviate aging-related phenotypes. Article.Authors: Gao Z.; Han K.; Ling Z.; Zhang H.; Botchwey E.; Liu W.; Hua X.; Nie S.; Jia S.
Article.Abstract: Optical scattering in biological tissues fundamentally limits fluorescence imaging by disrupting spatial and angular information, thereby restricting volumetric visualization. By transforming scattered light into a structured encoding resource, VSM establishes a scalable pathway toward routine three-dimensional fluorescence imaging in complex biological systems. Article.Title: A stem-like CD8+ T cell reservoir resists exhaustion and sustains alloimmunity a decade after transplantation

Article.Title: Layer-by-layer water filling in molecular-scale capillaries monitored by AFM
Article.Authors: Chen M.; Wang J.; Mishchenko A.; Timokhin I.; Ge Q.; Wang F.; Geim A.; Yang Q.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Under ambient humidity, water spontaneously condenses in pores only a few nanometers in size, making nanoscale capillarity central to numerous natural phenomena and technological applications. At these dimensions, water may no longer be treated as a continuous fluid, yet the consequences of molecular discreteness for capillary condensation and filling remain poorly understood. Here we study two-dimensional (2D) nanocapillaries fabricated by van der Waals assembly and, using atomic force microscopy (AFM), monitor their wall deformations during humidity-driven water uptake. We observe two distinct regimes: layer-by-layer filling of flexible capillaries and abrupt filling of more rigid ones. Flexible walls deform in ≈3 Å steps, consistent with the entry of individual molecular layers of water. The different filling regimes are explained by a competition between wall deformation energy and oscillatory wall-water interactions. These results, together with the theoretical framework developed here, show how molecular discreteness can profoundly affect ubiquitous capillary phenomena, with wall rigidity determining whether this discreteness is exposed or hidden within an apparently classical, Kelvin-like response.

Article.Abstract: Abstract Electric-dipole forbidden spectroscopic transitions in atoms form the basis of many advanced implementations of quantum computers, atomic clocks and quantum sensors. Article.Authors: Luo Y.; Zhu H.; Tran T.; Diao T.
Article.Abstract: Alcohols are among the most abundant and structurally diverse chemical feedstocks. Article.Abstract: Abstract Heterojunction engineering is one of the most effective strategies for enhancing charge separation and improving the performance of photo-functional materials. Article.Authors: Hannan Parker A.; Zhang P.; Man K.; Tirot L.; Rolfe S.; Smith L.; Wilkinson S.; Ton J.

Integrated CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq analyses reveal that histone lactylation is positively associated with gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Functional studies ex vivo and in vivo show that elevated histone lactylation delays erythroid differentiation, prolongs the progenitor state, enhances erythroid expansion, and promotes HSC maintenance and post-transplantation reconstitution. Mechanistically, histone lactylation contributes to the upregulation of the transcription factor FLI1, a positive regulator of HSPC maintenance, and genes encoding negative regulators of the cell cycle, thereby slowing cell-cycle progression to preserve HSPCs. Notably, although histone lactylation and acetylation at the same lysine residues show similar chromatin occupancy patterns, lactylation correlates more strongly with chromatin accessibility. Together, these findings support a role for histone lactylation in HSPC maintenance and early erythropoiesis, with potential implications for HSC culture optimization and therapeutic development. Histone lactylation promotes hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell maintenance, delays erythroid differentiation, and enhances erythroid expansion by modulating chromatin accessibility and regulating the expression of FLI1 and cell-cycle genes.

Article.Title: Support for a role of sex chromosome turnover and mitonuclear conflict in reproductive isolation in darters
Article.Authors: Radcliffe W.; Dye M.; Kim D.; Muralidhar P.; Moran R.
Article.Abstract: Identifying the genetic basis of reproductive barriers is essential for understanding the origin and maintenance of biological diversity. While some hybrid incompatibilities evolve as incidental byproducts of divergence, theory predicts that sex chromosomes and cytoplasmic genomes can generate especially strong and repeatable barriers to gene flow through conflict, linkage, and constrained coadaptation. Yet tests of these predictions in natural systems with ongoing hybridization remain limited. Here, we combine whole-genome resequencing and experimental backcrosses in North American darter fishes to show rapid sex chromosome turnover. Across two hybrid zones involving closely related lineages, sex determination maps to different, nonhomologous chromosomes in the hybridizing partners, indicating two independent turnovers. Sex chromosomes show reduced introgression in hybrid zones and transmission distortion in hybrids. We also detect cytoplasmic-background–associated allele-frequency shifts concentrated on sex chromosomes and enriched near nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes, indicating the potential for cytonuclear selection being involved in postzygotic barriers. Finally, parental crosses and comparative genomic patterns support a recessive female-determining mutation underlying one turnover, providing a rare empirical example of a predicted but seldom observed route to sex chromosome evolution. Together, these results implicate dynamic sex chromosomes and their linkage context as recurring features shaping hybrid genomes and reproductive isolation despite gene flow. Identifying the genetic basis of reproductive barriers is essential for understanding the maintenance of biological diversity. This study finds evidence implicating dynamic sex chromosomes and their linkage context shape hybrid genomes and reproductive isolation in the face of gene flow in darters.

Article.Title: A combinatorial genetics approach reveals limits to redundancy within Plasmodium falciparum invasion ligand families
Article.Authors: Silvester E.; Kuroshchenkova A.; Briggs C.; Colombowala A.; Flores V.; Kals E.; Rayner J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract To maintain infection in the human bloodstream, Plasmodium falciparum parasites undergo repeated cycles of invasion of and multiplication inside red blood cells (RBCs). Two protein families, the Erythrocyte binding-like (EBA) and Reticulocyte binding-like (Rh) proteins, are known to play a key role in invasion, mediating early stages of attachment of the P. falciparum merozoite to the host RBC. There is a degree of redundancy within these families, such that disrupting the function of individual EBA/Rh proteins in vitro is not sufficient to prevent invasion. By employing a novel approach to disrupt multiple EBA and Rh genes in combination, we systematically assess functional interdependency across these families for the first time. This analysis, and further characterisation of mutant parasites, reveals that disruption of some pairs of EBA/Rh ligands significantly impacts P. falciparum invasion, whereas others do not. Disruption of PfEBA175 in combination with either PfRh2b or PfRh4 significantly reduces parasite multiplication in vitro, indicating that the remaining EBA/Rh proteins cannot fully compensate for the absence of these three key invasion ligands. PfEBA175, PfRh2b and PfRh4 may therefore represent a critical nexus of the parasite invasion machinery, and combinatorial approaches that target these specific ligands could be a beneficial therapeutic approach.

Article.Title: Hydrogen-bond-mediated quasi-two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks for ultrahigh gold extraction
Article.Authors: Zhu Z.; Wang Y.; Zhou H.; Qi J.; Yang Y.; Zhou Y.; Zeng G.; Xu Q.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are ideal for precious metal recovery due to their high surface areas and tunable binding sites. However, the confinement of binding sites within inner pores often leads to restricted mass transfer, resulting in poor site accessibility and limited extraction capacities. Herein, we report a quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) topology-directed strategy to construct exposed binding sites for highly efficient gold recovery. By incorporating outward-pointing hydroxyl groups, the local conformation of the imine-linked skeleton is effectively locked via inter-chain hydrogen bonding (ICHB), which suppresses molecular torsion and promotes ordered assembly of the 1D chains into a quasi-2D crystalline architecture. This structural rigidification creates unobstructed ion-diffusion pathways and maximizes the exposure of active sites for rapid [AuCl4]− capture and reduction. Remarkably, under mild thermal and vibratory stimulation, gold nanoparticles form in situ and aggregate, yielding a high gold extraction capacity of 5082.32 mg g−1. Theoretical calculations demonstrate that ICHB-induced structural planarization creates a cooperative coordination environment and optimizes the energetic landscape for dechlorination, synergistically promoting guest enrichment and interfacial gold reduction. This work establishes a new blueprint for creating COFs with exposed active sites via inter-chain assembly, offering a scalable approach to maximize site accessibility and electron transfer for selective gold capture. Covalent organic frameworks are ideal for precious metal recovery but the confinement of binding sites within inner pores often leads to restricted mass transfer and limits extraction capacities. Here, the authors report a quasi-2D topology-directed strategy to construct exposed binding sites for highly efficient gold recovery.

Article.Title: Weakened association between sequential phenological events corresponds to interphase extension
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Gao M.; Zhang Y.; Peñuelas J.; Fu Y.; Wu C.; Xia J.; Hong S.; Piao S.
Article.Abstract: The sequential occurrence of leaf unfolding, flowering, fruiting, foliar senescence and other life-cycle events constitutes a full cycle of plant phenology. Temporal shifts in the seasonal timing of these phenophases have been regarded as key evidence of global environmental change. Most previous studies, however, have focused on the timing of individual phenophases. Little is known about the relationships between changes in timing across sequential phenophases. Here, using in-situ phenological records of major European tree species between 1980 and 2017, we show strong positive associations between consecutive phenophases. In particular, the statistical relationship between the timing of consecutive phenophases is comparable to that of temperature for spring phenological events and substantially exceeds the relationship with climatic factors for late-season phenological events. However, the associations themselves have shifted across years, with a significant decrease in the association between the timing of fruit ripening and autumnal coloration, corresponding to the largest extension of interphase duration. Current process-based phenological models largely overlook associations between consecutive phenological events and their interplay with climate change, potentially leading to biased projections of phenological changes and ecosystem adaptation to future climate change. Seasonal events in temperate deciduous trees, from leaf-out to leaf fall, follow a fixed annual sequence. This study shows that the timing of consecutive events is statistically associated in European trees, but that the association between fruiting and leaf coloration has weakened in some species as the interval between these phases has increased.

Article.Title: B7-H4‒directed antibody-drug conjugate AZD8205 (puxitatug samrotecan) in patients with advanced/metastatic solid tumors: the Phase 1/2a (BLUESTAR), first-in-human study
Article.Authors: Meric-Bernstam F.; Naito Y.; Gaillard S.; Shimoi T.; Chung V.; Davis A.; Proia T.; Wang J.; Dubois V.; Rebelatto M.; McFarlane M.; Kulkarni M.; Upadhyay S.; Tian J.; Miller N.; Luheshi N.; Varga A.; Oh D.; Mileshkin L.
Article.Abstract: B7-H4 is a promising antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) target with high expression in several solid tumors and limited expression in normal tissue. B7-H4 negatively regulates T-cell function, and high expression of B7-H4 is associated with disease progression. AZD8205 (puxitatug samrotecan [Puxi-Sam]) is a novel B7-H4–directed ADC with a stable cleavable linker and a bystander-capable topoisomerase-1 (TOP1) inhibitor payload. In this first-in-human study, 47 patients with advanced/metastatic B7-H4−positive endometrial cancer, ovarian cancer, breast cancer or cholangiocarcinoma received intravenous Puxi-Sam at 0.8–3.2 mg/kg every 3 weeks. The primary objectives were to evaluate the safety and tolerability of Puxi-Sam (incidence of adverse events [AE], serious AEs and dose-limiting toxicities), and to determine the maximum tolerated dose and/or recommended phase 2 dose of Puxi-Sam. Secondary objectives included characterizing the pharmacokinetics, assessing the antitumor activity (objective response rate [ORR]), and determining the pharmacodynamics of Puxi-Sam. The most common treatment-related adverse events were nausea (51.1%), neutropenia (48.9%) and anemia (38.3%). At 3.2 mg/kg, dose-limiting neutropenia and thrombocytopenia were observed. In patients treated at ≥1.6 mg/kg (predicted efficacious range), partial responses were observed in ovarian, endometrial and breast cancer (ORR 20.5% [9/44]). Translational data indicated selective localization of the TOP1 inhibitor payload to B7-H4–expressing tumor cells and induction of target-dependent DNA damage. Our findings demonstrate manageable safety and promising efficacy with Puxi-Sam in heavily pretreated patients; further development is ongoing. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05123482. B7-H4 is a promising therapeutic target in solid tumors because of its frequent expression in cancer cells, limited normal tissue distribution, and immunosuppressive functions. In this first-in-human trial, the authors report safety and efficacy outcomes for B7-H4–directed antibody-drug conjugate AZD8205 (puxitatug samrotecan) in patients with heavily pretreated ovarian, endometrial, and breast cancers, and cholangiocarcinoma.

Article.Title: One Health genomic surveillance identifies potential genetic links of antimicrobial-resistant foodborne pathogens across sectors
Article.Authors: Kitamura N.; Shinomiya H.; Kawanishi M.; Konishi N.; Ohya K.; Tomita H.; Asano Y.; Kimura C.; Sekiguchi H.; Ozawa M.; Ishihara K.; Kurushima J.; Tanimoto K.; Nomura T.; Hashimoto Y.; N/A N/A.; Hirai S.; Fukuguchi Y.; Aoki N.; Otsuka Y.; Yamagami T.; Takahashi Y.; Hashimoto Y.; Osanai S.; Iwama T.
Article.Abstract: Foodborne pathogens and antimicrobial resistance are major global health concerns. The integration and analysis of genomic surveillance data across human, animal, and environmental sectors remain a critical challenge in the study of foodborne bacteria. Agona isolates carrying fosA7.2, with pairwise SNP distances of 13–15 SNPs, suggesting that resistant Salmonella strains are shared between human and food sectors. For Campylobacter, we identified closely related human- and food-derived ST-22 isolates carrying a tetracycline resistance gene and a fluoroquinolone resistance-conferring gyrA mutation, with a pairwise SNP distance of 4 SNPs. These findings highlight potential genetic links of antimicrobial-resistant foodborne bacteria between food and humans. In this study, the authors use nationwide genomic data collected across sectors in Japan to identify closely related antimicrobial-resistant Salmonella and Campylobacter isolates in food and humans, highlighting the value of integrated One Health surveillance.

Article.Abstract: Abstract The global impact of the COVID-19 pandemic highlights the need for a deeper understanding of SARS-CoV-2 replication. Together, these findings map SARS-CoV-2 RNA–protein interactions across the viral genome and delineate specific regulatory regions for potential antiviral intervention.

Article.Authors: Yao X.; Zhang W.; Zheng R.; Qin H.; Yu J.; Cong H.
Article.Abstract: Inspired by organisms capable of adaptive morphological regulation, hydrogel actuators with softness and large deformability are attractive for biomedical devices and information encryption, yet remain limited by the lack of hierarchically oriented structures simultaneously enabling rapid actuation and high-order complex deformation. Owing to the periodic asymmetric stresses that amplify deformation and hierarchical porous channels that accelerate water transport, the obtained hydrogel exhibits large three-dimensional deformation with the rapidest recovery speed of 112.5°/s among the reported thermo-responsive hydrogels, facilitating programmable shape morphing by orchestrating localized curvature. Furthermore, a spatial orientation-patterning strategy is developed to precisely regulate the site-specific arrangement of lamellar-cellular structures for diverse cooperative sophisticated deformations at high speed. Importantly, the highly oriented architecture endows the hydrogel with tunable birefringence, enabling a dynamic encryption platform that couples programmable deformation with information encoding. This work provides a flexible structural strategy for preparing hydrogels with biomimetic dynamic information encryption. Article.Abstract: Abstract Drug/proton antiporters of the Major Facilitator Superfamily are key drivers of antimicrobial resistance. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying proton-coupled drug efflux are inherently complex and remain unresolved. Here, we dissect the timing and mechanism of proton coupling in the multidrug transporter LmrP, a prototypical exporter of clinically relevant antibiotics and toxins. By directly tracking chamber opening in the native plasma membrane, we capture functionally relevant conformational transitions within a lipid environment and map them onto the catalytic carboxylates that govern transport. Our results suggest that earlier DEER distance measurements in detergent solution captured a restricted subset of conformational states, which our pH 8.0 data extend and place into a broader framework. Complementary pH 5.0 measurements reveal additional mechanistic features and, together, these datasets define the transport cycle in a membrane-embedded context. Supported by molecular dynamics simulations, the results reveal a coordinated, transport cycle-dependent mechanism in which paired catalytic carboxylates act sequentially in substrate binding, proton relay, gate control, and transporter resetting.

Article.Authors: Dindo M.; Metson J.; Ren W.; Chatzittofi M.; Yagi K.; Bevilacqua A.; Fukuhara E.; Sugita Y.; Golestanian R.; Laurino P.
Article.Abstract: Biomolecular condensates have so far been studied in terms of their structural, compositional, and functional properties. However, condensate enzymatic activity - a key aspect of cellular metabolism - remains unexplored due to the complexity of the system. In this study, using a combination of experimental, computational and theoretical techniques, we have discovered that the non-equilibrium activity which originates from catalytic reactions couples with the environment through various feedback mechanisms across five orders of magnitude of length scales. We observe that condensed enzymes catalyze more rapidly in the presence of crowding proteins and show that the increased enzymatic activity within these droplets stems from the emergence of lower-energy protein conformations induced by the highly crowded environment. Despite the crowding in the environment of the droplet, which might suggest an effective increase in its overall viscosity, we find that it becomes more agile, as evidenced by the observation of enhanced diffusion and macroscopic flow, due to the enzymatic activity. These findings shed light on the dynamic interplay between enzymatic activity, composition and crowding in condensates, and their roles on the mobility and accessibility of various functional units in these environments, expanding our understanding of liquid-liquid phase separation in metabolically active conditions.

Article.Title: Canopy nutrient balance predicts autumn senescence across U.S. forests
Article.Authors: Chen H.; Wei Y.; Townsend P.; Kovach K.; Finley A.; Peñuelas J.; Qiu T.
Article.Abstract: Terrestrial ecosystems are changing rapidly under global nutrient enrichment, yet how canopy nutrients balance shapes the seasonal end of photosynthesis, a critical control on ecosystem carbon cycling, remains unclear. Rising anthropogenic nitrogen inputs are shifting many ecosystems towards relative phosphorus limitation, with uncertain consequences for autumn phenology. Here, we combined airborne imaging spectroscopy with remotely sensed phenology to test whether canopy nutrient ratios predict spatial variations in autumn senescence across National Ecological Observatory Network sites in the United States. Higher canopy N:P is consistently associated with earlier senescence in 20 out of 25 sites, whereas higher N:K has opposite effects in 19 sites after controlling for climate, elevation, dominant species, and canopy structure. Growing-season productivity is generally related to later senescence, but only modestly mediates the direct nutrient-phenology associations. These findings add a phenological dimension to the functional impacts of nutrient imbalance on terrestrial ecosystems and demonstrate that nutrients provide predictive power beyond climate alone. Continued nitrogen deposition is expected to increase relative phosphorus limitation, a shift that could be associated with earlier senescence and shorter growing season. Incorporating canopy nutrients into phenological models may therefore improve forecasts of canopy duration and carbon fluxes under ongoing nutrient enrichment.

Article.Title: Towards the real diamond formation conditions: insights and perspective
Article.Authors: Murri M.; Gilio M.; Nestola F.; Duretz T.; Marone F.
Article.Abstract: Pressure and temperature conditions of diamond formation provide valuable insights for reconstructing paleo-geotherms and the deep carbon cycle. These conditions can be determined by investigating mineral inclusions in diamonds using elastic geobarometry, which can be applied to any mineral inclusion in a diamond. However, it assumes purely elastic host-inclusion behaviour throughout exhumation. In reality, almost all mineral inclusions in diamonds are surrounded by cracks. Here, we combine in situ high-temperature micro-Raman spectroscopy with thermo-elastic modelling to evaluate the pressure-release process in one of the most common diamond inclusions, olivine [(Mg,Fe)2SiO4]. Our results indicate that a diamond can sustain pressures of ~2.5 GPa before undergoing minor fracturing, which induces only partial loss of inclusion pressure rather than a complete reset. The estimated pressure loss can lead to an underestimation of up to 2.5 GPa in the entrapment pressure at 1150 °C, a typical temperature for diamond formation. This study shows that olivine in diamond can undergo partial release of pressure during kimberlite eruptions due to fast adiabatic decompression, leading to cracked olivine inclusions and entrapment pressures underestimated by up to 2.5 GPa at 1150 °C

Article.Title: Liquid-metal physical unclonable functions resistant to both physical and digital cloning
Article.Authors: Lee S.; Kim M.; Kim W.; Heo S.; Ahn Y.; Lee J.; Kwon D.; Oh S.; Yoon S.; Dickey M.; Song Y.; Jeong J.
Article.Abstract: Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) leverage device-specific randomness for hardware security, yet their static, persistently accessible responses allow attackers to collect sufficient data for digital cloning. We present a liquid-metal PUF (LM-PUF) that integrates physical unclonability with material-driven resistance to digital attacks. Randomly mixed, visually indistinguishable LM particles form thermally unique microstructures, ensuring physical unclonability. Digital protection arises from two concealment mechanisms: time-limited accessibility restricts meaningful data collection, while decoy obscuration prevents reliable key identification. At equilibrium, the device remains cryptographically silent, but heating through a transient non-equilibrium window reveals thermal patterns convertible to cryptographic keys. Outside the predefined temperature range, misleading thermal patterns conceal the authentic key among decoys. LM-PUF supports scalable patterning, demonstrated in secure labels and QR codes, highlighting its potential for secure supply chains and physical unclonable authentication. Here, authors report a liquid-metal PUF whose thermal keys appear only briefly during heating and are hidden among decoys, resisting both physical and digital cloning.

Article.Title: Observation of quantized charge accumulation in a quantum anomalous Hall system
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Chen J.; Wang R.; Zhang Y.; Deng Y.; Xie J.; Kou X.; Liu Y.; Liang T.
Article.Abstract: The quantum anomalous Hall effect in magnetically doped topological insulators exhibits a quantized Hall conductance σxy = e2/h arising from the two-dimensional surface states. While conventional transport probes confirm this quantization, they remain insensitive to the field-induced surface charge accumulation as a direct manifestation of σxy. Here, we experimentally validate an out-of-plane capacitive method that directly detects this quantized charge accumulation in a quantum anomalous Hall system. Using Corbino and simple disk devices, we measure charge accumulation proportional to field variation ΔB, with dissipation characterized by longitudinal conductance σxx and frequency f. A quantitative dissipation model extracts the intrinsic quantized charge density η0 = (e2/h)ΔB, which is confirmed through f- and σxx-dependent measurements. Under ultra-low dissipation (σxx ≈ 10−9 S), we directly resolve the fully quantized charge accumulation. This methodology establishes a direct charge-accumulation probe and provides a pathway toward detecting the topological magnetoelectric effect, a condensed matter manifestation of the four-dimensional quantum Hall effect. The quantum anomalous Hall effect in a magnetically doped topological insulator exhibits a quantized Hall conductance. Here, the authors demonstrate an out-of-plane capacitive method that directly measures field-induced quantized charge accumulation originating from the quantized Hall conductance.

Article.Title: Ultrahigh strength aluminum alloy by green laser additive manufacturing
Article.Authors: Liu T.; Cheng X.; Mikula J.; Ng F.; Xiong L.; Zhao Y.; Laskowski R.; Luan J.; Wu X.; Tan C.
Article.Abstract: Infrared laser additive manufacturing of high-strength 7××× aluminum (Al) alloys is hindered by low absorptivity, high cracking-susceptibility, and insufficient precipitation strengthening. Herein, we investigate a new approach to process high-performance AA7075 by integrating green laser directed energy deposition (L-DED) with nano-TiC embedded composite AA7075 powder. The green laser achieves better energy-material coupling, enabling high-quality deposition at a lower laser power than conventional infrared lasers. The green laser also stabilizes the melt pool, reduces thermal gradients and elemental evaporation, and promotes more uniform grains with lower dislocation density. Heat treatment yields an ultra-high density of nano-scale η′ precipitates and GP zones (~2.13×1016 m−2) in the green laser deposited Al alloy, achieving a tensile yield strength of ~600 MPa, which is higher than forged AA7075 and almost all L-DED-processed Al alloys hitherto reported. This work presents an integrated material-process strategy for additive manufacturing of highly reflective, hot-crack-susceptible alloys using short-wavelength lasers. Cracking and poor laser absorption curbed additive manufacturing of high-strength aluminium alloys. Using a TiC/AA7075 composite powder and a green wavelength laser, researchers produced crack-free aluminum alloy with a yield strength of nearly 600 MPa.
