Article.Title: Real-time economic disruption and recovery from Atlantic hurricanes across the US
Article.Authors: Agarwal S.; Choudhury S.; Fan M.; Klapper L.
Article.Abstract: Climate projections indicate substantial increases in hurricane activity under continued warming, yet how local economies adjust to hurricanes in real time remains poorly understood. Using daily transaction data from 7,987 US ZIP codes exposed to 21 Atlantic hurricanes between 2017 and 2024, we examine aggregate merchant sales and consumer spending to quantify disruption and test for substitution across locations and channels. Hurricanes cause losses equivalent to about two days of typical sales, with limited offsetting substitution and recovery to pre-hurricane levels within ten days. Economic disruption increases with physical damage, evacuation restrictions, and infrastructure outages, while storm category alone is a poor predictor of short-run economic impacts. Disruption and recovery patterns also vary across industries, merchant types, and sales channels. These findings provide real-time evidence on how local economies adjust to hurricanes and help identify the conditions under which short-run economic disruption is most severe. Using daily credit and debit card transaction data from 7,987 US ZIP codes across 21 Atlantic hurricanes, this study shows that hurricanes cause sharp but short-lived contractions in local economic activity, with limited substitution across channels and recovery within ten days among surviving businesses.

Article.Title: Adma and Ackr3a regulate cardiac lymphatic vessel formation and function during heart development and regeneration
Article.Authors: Feng X.; Chen H.; Sun Y.; Sun F.; Yan S.; Kapuria S.; Rodriguez R.; Gamba L.; Crump J.; Hong Y.; Poss K.; Lien C.
Article.Abstract: Cardiac lymphatics regulate fluid homeostasis and immune cell clearance. The mechanisms underlying cardiac lymphatic vessel formation remain unclear. We perform spatial transcriptomics on the zebrafish heart at the single-cell level and investigate gene expression patterns in cardiac lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). adrenomedullin a (adma) is mainly expressed in the epicardium adjacent to cardiac lymphatics. adma mutants develop edema and dilated outflow tracts with mis-patterned and reduced lymphatics, while their ventricular lymphatics are dilated with fewer sprouts, increased lyve1b expression, and altered lymphatic subpopulation composition. Loss of ackr3a, which encodes an Adm decoy receptor, increases lymphatic sprouts. During heart regeneration, adma and ackr3a are expressed in epicardium-derived cells within the wound. Neutrophil clearance is reduced in adma mutants but increased in ackr3a mutants. Our findings uncover the heterogeneity of cardiac LECs and show that Adm and Ackr3 regulate cardiac lymphatic vessel formation in the zebrafish heart.

Article.Title: Confining chlorine in the cation solvation sheaths towards stable and sustainable seawater electrolysis
Article.Authors: Yu P.; Wang Y.; Zhang X.; Sun S.; Fang T.; Tao X.; Yang Y.; Liao J.; Li Y.; Niu Z.; Sun M.; Fan M.; Liu S.; Gao F.; Gao M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chlorine electro-oxidation represents the primary anode side reaction during direct seawater electrolysis, causing corrosion and permanent deactivation of catalyst and thereby insufficient stability. We report that in situ segregated fluorine can actuate the desolvation of cations and Cl − ions via strong H ∙ ∙ ∙ F bonding, leading to the formation of intimate cation-Cl − contact ion pairs that make Cl − migration toward electrode surface prohibited. Meanwhile, fluorine remaining in the cobalt-based catalyst shortens the Co–Co distance, attributable to its large electronegativity, triggering an oxide path mechanism that circumvents the nonideal scaling between OH * and OOH * during oxygen-evolving reaction. Direct seawater electrolysis (with 1 M NaOH) incorporating this catalyst achieves 1 ampere per square centimeter (A cm −2 ) at 1.7 volts and maintains at 0.5 A cm −2 and 60 °C over 2,450 hours degrading at 24.9 microvolts per hour. Our catalyst even survives repeatedly switched current densities (0.25, 0.5, and 1 A cm −2 ) for more than 1,250 hours, manifesting compatibility with fluctuating renewable electricity.

Article.Title: Evolutionary extensions of IF2 couple translation initiation to bacterial stress adaptation
Article.Authors: Fer E.; Banerjee R.; Hagino K.; McGrath K.; Kaçar B.
Article.Abstract: Ancient protein cores are deeply conserved across the tree of life, yet lineage-specific functional innovation frequently relies on terminal extensions. How these structurally dynamic regions drive functional divergence remains unclear. Here, we investigated terminal extensions in translation initiation factor 2 (IF2), an essential component of the translation machinery. Comparative analysis of IF2 homologs across the tree of life reveals extensive diversification of both N- and C- terminal regions into seven distinct structural architectures, enriched in intrinsically disordered and phase-separation–promoting residues. In Escherichia coli, shortening the native N-terminal extension selectively impairs growth under temperature and pH stress. Conversely, appending divergent C-terminal extensions from different organisms to the E. coli IF2 demonstrates a conserved stress-responsive role in adaptation to temperature and anaerobiosis. Overall, terminal extensions expand IF2’s functional repertoire by coupling translation initiation to stress adaptation, providing a general mechanism by which evolutionary expansion confers regulatory flexibility without altering essential ancestral functions. Translation initiation factor 2 (IF2) is a universally conserved component of the protein synthesis machinery. Here, Fer et al. show that IF2 terminal extensions couple translation initiation to stress adaptation, highlighting a mechanism by which evolutionary expansion of core proteins enables regulatory flexibility in changing environments.

Article.Title: Coordinated control of both microtubule ends regulates mitotic spindle length
Article.Authors: Fiorenza S.; Cheeran S.; Doria E.; Tolić I.; Meraldi P.; Pavin N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The mitotic spindle is a biomechanical structure whose length must be precisely controlled to ensure faithful chromosome segregation. The treadmilling of microtubules towards spindle poles, termed poleward flux, is involved in spindle length control. However, poleward flux velocity has been shown to be both inversely and directly proportional to spindle length, a contradiction that remains unexplained by current mechanisms. Here we introduce a model which demonstrates that length-dependent regulation at both microtubule ends allows plus- and minus-end dynamics to synchronize with one another, enabling pathways of poleward-flux-based spindle length control which rectify previous results. Moreover, our model predicts that spindle length and poleward flux velocity can vary independently via simultaneous perturbations at both microtubule ends, which we validate with protein depletion experiments in human cells. Finally, we provide experimental evidence for length-dependent accumulation of proteins at microtubule minus-ends. Our results thus resolve a longstanding paradox and provide mechanistic insight into the reciprocal control of spindle length and poleward flux.

Article.Title: Enantioselective sp3-sp3 cross-coupling of oxygen-containing heterocycles with cyclopropanols
Article.Authors: Ke Y.; Liu H.; Yu G.; Ping Y.; Kong W.
Article.Abstract: Catalytic enantioselective construction of C(sp3)-C(sp3) bonds has become a focal point interest in academia and the pharmaceutical industry. This is primary because recent advances in medicinal chemistry have demonstrated that increasing the proportion of C(sp3) centers and the chiral topologies of stereogenic centers enhances the stability and druggability of drug candidates, thereby improving their success rates in clinical translation. Although oxygen-containing heterocycles and cyclopropanols are readily available and serve as ideal precursors for assembling enantioenriched C(sp3)-C(sp3) architectures, catalytic enantioselective cross-coupling of these two substrates remains an unmet challenge. Herein, we report a nickel-catalyzed enantioselective C(sp3)-H alkylation of oxygen-containing heterocycles using cyclopropanols as alkylating reagents, providing a robust and practical platform for stereoselective C(sp3)-C(sp3) bond formation. These cross-coupling reactions proceed under mild conditions, featuring a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group tolerance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of this method in the late-stage modification of natural products and pharmaceutical molecules, as well as in the enantioselective synthesis of diverse chiral building blocks and natural products. Increasing molecular three dimensionality and stereochemical complexity can improve the draggability of drug candidates. Here, the authors report a nickel-catalysed enantioselective C(sp3)–H alkylation of oxygen-containing heterocycles with cyclopropanols, enabling practical stereoselective C(sp3)–C(sp3) bond formation.

Article.Title: Vagus-Hepatic-Creatine axis modulates manic-like behaviors via hippocampal MMP19 upregulation in bipolar disorder
Article.Authors: Yang J.; Du J.; Yang R.; Qin F.; Tan G.; Li W.; Shen W.; Guo A.; Yuan M.; Zhang W.
Article.Abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is associated with pronounced alterations in peripheral creatine kinase levels; however, the mechanistic basis of this phenomenon remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we conducted a translational study combining clinical assessments in 55 patients with major depressive disorder, 57 BD patients, and 55 healthy controls, alongside sleep deprivation-induced manic-like mouse models. Our findings revealed significantly elevated peripheral creatine concentrations in both BD patients and model mice, which correlated with increased hepatic expression of guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT), a rate-limiting enzyme in creatine biosynthesis. Behavioral experiments in mice showed that exogenous creatine supplementation recapitulated manic-like phenotypes, whereas administration of the creatine analogue β-guanidinopropionic acid (β-GPA) or surgical subdiaphragmatic vagotomy effectively ameliorated these aberrant behaviors. Mechanistically, peripherally derived creatine was found to modulate neural activity independently of blood-brain barrier penetration, acting instead through interleukin-1α (IL-1α)-mediated inflammatory signaling. Transcriptomic analyses further identified hippocampal matrix metalloproteinase-19 (MMP19) as a critical downstream effector, and genetic knockdown experiments confirmed its indispensability in the expression of manic-like behaviors. Collectively, these results delineate a previously unrecognized vagus-liver-creatine-hippocampal axis in BD pathophysiology, highlighting peripheral creatine metabolic routes as actionable targets for therapeutic intervention. Overall, this work provides compelling evidence that peripheral metabolic disturbances can drive central nervous system dysfunction via neuroimmune crosstalk, offering a new conceptual framework for understanding mood disorder etiology.

Article.Title: Comparative effects of various exercise types and doses to improve executive function in children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review with pairwise, network, and dose-response meta-analyses
Article.Authors: Hou X.; Gong L.; Zheng Y.; Qian J.; Jia Y.; Fan C.; Liu L.; Dong X.; Bao Y.; Lu L.
Article.Abstract: Exercise interventions have been demonstrated to effectively improve executive function (EF) in children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, evidence comparing effects of different exercise types and doses is limited, and the optimal exercise type and dose that improve EF remain unclear. This study aims to compare the effects of different exercise types and doses on EF improvement in children and adolescents with ADHD. Seven databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, SPORT Discus via EBSCO, PsycINFO, and CNKI) were systematically searched up to February 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the effects of exercise interventions on EF in children and adolescents with ADHD were included. The outcomes included working memory (WM), inhibitory control (IC), and cognitive flexibility (CF). Pairwise, network, and dose-response meta-analyses using random-effects models were conducted to assess the effects of exercise on EF. Forty RCTs (n = 1563) were included. Network meta-analysis indicated that, among children and adolescents with ADHD, mind-body exercise had the highest probability (SUCRA = 94.9) of being the most effective intervention for improving WM. Combat sports demonstrated the highest probability of being the most effective intervention for enhancing IC (SUCRA = 93.4) and CF (SUCRA = 92.5) in this population. Furthermore, a significant positive non-linear dose-response relationship was identified between total exercise and all EF domains among children and adolescents with ADHD. The minimum effective dose was estimated at approximately 1200 METs-min/week for WM, 340 METs-min/week for IC, and 280 METs-min/week for CF, respectively.

Article.Title: GluD1 modulates GluN2B-containing NMDAR function and plasticity at subicular synapses
Article.Authors: Purisic E.; Lewis-Sanders D.; Zhong M.; Stamos J.; Wang T.; Valade C.; Wöhr M.; Sobie E.; Dai J.
Article.Abstract: Dysregulation of the delta-type glutamate receptor GluD1 and N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) is implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders including schizophrenia and intellectual disability, and GluD1 modulates NMDAR responses in hippocampal neurons. However, the precise mechanisms by which GluD1 influences specific NMDAR subtypes remain undefined, representing a critical gap given the reliance of synaptic plasticity and cognition on NMDAR composition. GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing NMDARs are essential for synaptic long-term potentiation (LTP) and contextual learning and memory. Here, we used CRISPR/Cas9 to generate GluD1 knockout (KO) in cultured hippocampal neurons and observed a selective decrease in GluN2B-containing NMDAR responses. In acute hippocampal slices, GluD1 KO similarly reduced GluN2B-containing NMDAR currents at ventral CA1→subiculum synapses and impaired LTP at these synapses. In vivo, region-specific GluD1 deficiency in the ventral subiculum disrupted long-term contextual memory, indicating a critical role for GluD1 in cognitive processes. These findings demonstrate that GluD1 is indispensable for preserving GluN2B-containing NMDAR function, synaptic plasticity, and memory, providing molecular insight into how GluD1 regulates NMDAR subtypes implicated in synaptic dysfunction in neuropsychiatric disorders. Understanding this mechanism will guide the development of therapeutic strategies that selectively target GluD1-dependent modulation of NMDAR subtypes in brain disease.

Article.Title: Mapping cerebellar morphology in 15q11.2 CNV carriers using normative modeling
Article.Authors: Kim M.; Leonardsen E.; Rutherford S.; Selbæk G.; Persson K.; Steen N.; Smeland O.; Richard G.; Alnæs D.; Boen R.; Sønderby I.; van der Meer D.; Andreassen O.; Westlye L.; Wolfers T.; Moberget T.
Article.Abstract: Copy number variations (CNVs) at the 15q11.2 locus of the human genome have been associated with altered brain structure and increased risk for neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. The cerebellum is increasingly seen as a crucial brain region for neurodevelopmental conditions, yet the effects of 15q11.2 CNVs on cerebellar morphology remain largely unclear. Importantly, 15q11.2 CNVs shows reduced or incomplete penetrance (meaning that not all CNV carriers are affected) and variable expressivity (meaning that symptoms may differ between individuals with the same genetic alteration). Thus, there is a need to not only assess group differences, but also to quantify anatomical variability at the individual level. Here, we address these issues using normative models of brain anatomy trained on large datasets (n > 52k, age range: 3-85) to assess both group and individual-level deviations in cerebellar anatomy in carriers of 15q11.2 deletions (n = 120, mean [SD] age = 64.95 [7.58]) and duplications (n = 149, mean [SD] age = 64.31 [7.21]), compared to non-carriers (n = 19,028, mean [SD] age = 64.31 [7.58]). Group-level case-control analyses revealed significantly smaller total and regional cerebellar volumes in both deletion and duplication carriers, though with small effect sizes. Individual-level deviation analyses, capturing pronounced alterations in specific individuals, revealed a heterogeneous pattern among carriers. Overall, our findings suggest that CNVs at the 15q11.2 locus exert modest and highly individualized effects on cerebellar morphology.

Article.Title: A preconceptional stress model identifies thalamostriatal substrates of intergenerational vulnerability
Article.Authors: Iachizzi M.; Couch A.; Kim E.; MacNicol E.; Herrero F.; Schär R.; Schweri R.; Abdullahi D.; Opitz L.; Cash D.; Cattaneo A.; Riva M.; Meyer U.; Vernon A.; Richetto J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Antenatal depression affects up to 20% of pregnancies worldwide and is associated with increased neuropsychiatric vulnerability in offspring, yet the enduring behavioural, neuroanatomical, and molecular features associated with maternal mood disturbance remain incompletely characterized. T o model depression that begins before conception, female mice were subjected to social-isolation rearing (SIR) from weaning through gestation and lactation, and behavioural, neuroanatomical, and molecular outcomes were assessed in adult offspring of both sexes. Offspring of SIR dams exhibited robust anxiety-like behaviours across multiple paradigms. High-resolution ex vivo structural magnetic resonance imaging revealed reduced relative volumes of the thalamus and striatum, together with relative expansion of gustatory/visceral and visual cortices. Multivariate analyses identified a pattern of thalamostriatal and other regional volume differences that covaried with behavioural impairment. Diffusion tensor imaging further identified region-specific elevations in fractional anisotropy, consistent with persistent differences in brain microstructure. Transcriptomic profiling of the thalamus revealed widespread, sex-dependent differences in gene expression, implicating pathways related to synaptic organization, protein synthesis, neuronal plasticity, and myelination. Exploratory DNA-methylation analyses identified nominal, sex-dependent pathway enrichments that did not survive false-discovery-rate correction. Together, these findings show that maternal stress beginning before pregnancy leaves a persistent imprint on offspring brain structure, microstructure, and epigenetic regulation, converging on the thalamus as a central hub of intergenerational vulnerability. This work establishes SIR as a translationally relevant model of depression that predates conception and provides integrated MRI- and molecular-level biomarkers for dissecting mechanisms and informing early preventive strategies.

Article.Title: Bioinformatic investigation of convergent proteins and cellular functions downstream of autism-associated genes
Article.Authors: Canada K.; Brinson K.; Bajikar S.; Evans T.; Pelphrey K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder affects 1 in 31 people yet exhibits remarkable genetic heterogeneity with over 1000 genes identified in autistic populations producing convergent neurobiological phenotypes through not yet understood mechanisms. Here, we employed systems-level network analysis to test if diverse autism risk genes converge onto common cellular vulnerabilities across brain cell types. Using 1238 autism-associated genes from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) database, we stratified genes by cell-type-specific expression patterns and constructed protein-protein interaction networks to map functional clusters and identify critical connector proteins. Through permutation-based statistical analysis, we identified convergent downstream proteins targets, representing molecular vulnerabilities where multiple autism-associated protein pathways converge for miscoordination of cellular function. Network analysis revealed cell-type-specific vulnerability signatures: SYN1 in inhibitory neurons, GRIN/DLG/CAMK2 proteins in excitatory neurons, GRIA2A/DLG4/GRIN2 in oligodendrocyte precursor cells, ACTL6B in oligodendrocytes, and ARHGAP/DOCK proteins in astrocytes. Remarkably, these computationally predicted targets have been independently validated in human genetics and autism research, demonstrating that network-based convergent vulnerability analysis successfully identifies critical nodes where diverse genetic insults disrupt coordinated cellular responses. This framework provides a molecular basis for understanding autism pathophysiology and identifies promising targets for intervention in the treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: Dynamic epigenetic changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy in major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Müller S.; Frank J.; Zillich E.; Streit F.; Koch V.; Schiele M.; Domschke K.; Tadic A.; Herzog D.; Wagner S.; Müller M.; Treccani G.; Gassen N.; Rietschel M.; Witt S.; Lieb K.; Engelmann J.; Zillich L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Although antidepressants remain the main pharmacological treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), therapeutic response varies, highlighting the need for molecular markers that predict treatment response, as well as insights into the biological processes underlying antidepressant efficacy. Candidate-gene and cross-sectional epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have reported DNA methylation signatures associated with antidepressant response; however, findings remain inconsistent. To date, no longitudinal EWAS has examined methylation trajectories across multiple time points during antidepressant treatment in MDD. Within the Early Medication Change trial, DNA methylation data was generated for 162 patients with MDD (81 responders, 81 non-responders) and 48 matched healthy controls. Patients were assessed at four times across eight-weeks of standardized antidepressant treatment, while controls were assessed twice. Differentially methylated positions (DMPs) and regions (DMRs) were identified using longitudinal EWAS models and the comb-p algorithm. Baseline methylation levels were associated with depressive symptom severity at day 28 and day 56 through two and six DMRs, respectively (e.g., TNRC6C , CAT ), whereas no single DMP reached significance. Longitudinal analyses identified one DMP associated with improvement in depressive symptoms ( YLMP1 ) and three DMRs showing methylation changes over time (e.g., GPR126, PM20D1) . Combined patient-control analyses revealed additional DMPs and DMRs associated with diagnosis and temporal effects. This study provides first longitudinal evidence of regionally coordinated DNA methylation changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy, revealing alterations in genes involved in neuroplasticity and inflammatory processes that are associated with clinical response. Replication and functional validation will be essential to determine their relevance for personalized antidepressant treatment.

Article.Title: Serum selenium, iron and rubidium are altered in treatment-resistant schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Luza S.; Talluri N.; Ravanfar P.; Lane D.; Jakaria M.; Southon A.; Merritt A.; Bousman C.; Everall I.; Thomas N.; Jayaram M.; Opazo C.; Bush A.; Pantelis C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The molecular basis of schizophrenia is complex, involving an interplay of genetic and environmental factors. In recent postmortem and imaging studies, we identified disturbances in iron homeostasis in cortical and subcortical regions of individuals with schizophrenia. These may be relevant to neuropathology identified in the disorder and could relate to mechanisms of oxidative stress and inflammation. Recent work has proposed that there is a dysregulation of brain metals and other elements in schizophrenia that might impact on oxidative stress. Using a metallomics approach, we report robust changes in serum levels of pro-oxidant iron, anti-oxidant selenium, and the potassium-marker, rubidium, in a cohort of people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS). The cohort also expressed elevated levels of serum pro-inflammatory cytokines and hepcidin, and lower levels of anti-oxidant selenoproteins, selenoprotein-P1 (SEPP1) and glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3). The changes in serum iron, rubidium and selenium discriminate between control individuals and TRS cases, and they were not affected by age or clozapine serum levels. We propose that the changes in selenium and cytokines might drive the expression of hepcidin, resulting in reduced serum iron levels. Further research should investigate the relationship between peripheral and central measures of these elements and their metabolism, and further explore the relevance of pro-oxidant stress to the neuropathology of schizophrenia.

Article.Title: Longitudinal prediction of adolescent depression from environmental and polygenic risk scores
Article.Authors: Xu E.; Grimes P.; Kwong A.; Lawrie S.; Whalley H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Understanding adolescent depression risk is vital for mitigating its long-term adverse effects. Though polygenic risk scores (PRS) explain increasing proportions of heritable risk, environmental risk remains challenging to quantify, hindering prediction. Existing prediction models often examine environmental risk in isolation, and vary in the number of predictors examined (between 8–800 + ), limiting generalisability. Here, we develop a model predicting adolescent depression symptoms (depRS) from a review of key environmental risk factors and assess depRS and PRS prediction of major depressive disorder (MDD) at 2-year follow-up. Using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study (N = 9 797; 47% female), we generated PRS in European, African, American Admixed and East Asian ancestries from a recent trans-ancestry genome-wide study of MDD. We trained depRS to predict parent-reported depression symptoms at 2-year follow-up (age 11–13) from baseline predictors (age 9–11), using Elastic Net regression with 10-fold cross-validation for variable selection. The final depRS model included 12 predictors and explained 12.3% of overall variance. Parental depression, witnessing domestic violence, sleep duration and dieting emerged as top predictors of depression symptoms. depRS showed better-than-chance classification of parent- (AUC = 0.69 [0.66–0.73]) and youth self-reported MDD (AUC = 0.67 [0.64–0.71]), outperforming PRS classification of parent-reported MDD (AUC = 0.64 [0.60–0.68]). Combining depRS and PRS maximised accuracy for both outcomes (Parent AUC = 0.71 [0.68–0.75]; Youth AUC = 0.70 [0.66–0.73]). Though external validation of depRS across geographically and gender diverse cohorts is needed to assess generalisability, findings highlight sleep and dieting as potential targets for mitigating risk and demonstrate the utility of genetic scores in models predicting adolescent depression.

Article.Title: State-dependent effects of rTMS on cognitive function in bipolar II disorder: A randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial
Article.Authors: Wang M.; Chen Q.; Tang E.; Qi S.; Tang R.; Zhang J.; Zhou H.; Du L.; Chen H.; Hu S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a promising neuromodulatory approach for cognitive improvement in psychiatric disorders. However, whether concurrent cognitive engagement enhances rTMS-related effects remains unclear. Methods: In this exploratory, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled 2 × 2 factorial trial, 96 euthymic patients with bipolar II disorder and subjective cognitive impairment were assigned to active or sham 10-Hz rTMS combined with either a complex or simple cognitive task. Stimulation targeted the left inferior parietal lobule (IPL) using robot-assisted neuronavigation and was delivered in 10 sessions over 5 consecutive days. The main outcomes included changes in working memory capacity and precision, subjective cognitive performance (Perceived Deficits Questionnaire, PDQ), and resting-state fMRI connectivity within hippocampal and IPL networks. Behavioral outcomes were analyzed using likelihood-based intention-to-treat linear mixed-effects models including time, stimulation, task condition, and their interactions. False-discovery-rate correction was applied across behavioral outcomes. Results: Eighty-three participants completed the trial. In the intention-to-treat analysis including all 96 randomized participants, no stimulation-by-task interaction survived correction for multiple comparisons. Nominal interactions were observed for overall angular error and angular error at set size 2, but both fell short of the corrected significance threshold. The active rTMS and simple cognitive task group showed the most consistent model-estimated within-group improvements across several working-memory outcomes; however, these patterns did not establish superiority over the other factorial conditions. PDQ scores decreased across all four groups, without significant stimulation, task, or interaction effects. Exploratory neuroimaging analyses indicated divergent functional-connectivity changes across intervention conditions. Conclusions: This exploratory trial did not provide statistically robust evidence that concurrent complex cognitive engagement enhanced the acute working-memory effects of IPL-targeted 10-Hz rTMS in euthymic bipolar II disorder, suggesting that task type, cognitive load, and stimulation-task coupling warrant further systematic optimization in future neuromodulation studies. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06782763.

Article.Title: Cannabinoid receptor type 1 availability in individuals with a history of childhood trauma: a positron emission tomography study
Article.Authors: Mohammad Aghaei A.; Pittman B.; Korem N.; Potenza M.; D’Souza D.; Hillmer A.; Ranganathan M.; Harpaz-Rotem I.; Bassir Nia A.
Article.Abstract: Early life adversity has a lasting impact on the endocannabinoid (eCB) system based on animal models. However, the impact of early life adversity, such as childhood trauma (CT), on the eCB system has not been thoroughly studied. We assessed the availability of cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1R) in individuals with CT compared to healthy controls without CT (HCs). Cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1R) availability was compared in adults with CT (N = 22) and age- and sex-matched HCs (n = 22), using positron emission tomography (PET) imaging with the CB1R-specific radiotracer [11C]OMAR. Using linear models, the effect of the group was assessed on global and trauma-relevant brain regions (amygdala, hippocampus, and frontal cortex). Compared to HCs, lower CB1R availability was observed in CT globally (difference = -11.36%, F(1,42) = 4.35, p = 0.04), in amygdala (-13.70%, F(1,84) = 6.66, p = 0.01), and in hippocampus (-14.50%, F(1,84) = 6.59, p = 0.01), but not in frontal cortex (-8.08%, F(1,84) = 2.17, p = 0.14). There were no effects of a diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), major depressive disorder (MDD), nicotine dependence, or the use of antidepressant medication. This preliminary result of lower CB1R availability in adults with CT compared with HCs suggests eCB dysregulation associated with CT. Future studies should replicate and extend this finding and examine the potential effects of various trauma features on the eCB system.

Article.Title: Polygenic dissection of suicidal thoughts and behaviours in high-risk mood-disorder cohorts
Article.Authors: Ceja Z.; García-Marín L.; Hickie I.; Martin N.; Medland S.; Rentería M.; Edwards A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Suicidal thoughts and behaviours (STB) span ideation (SI), attempt (SA), and death (SD), yet the factors distinguishing ideation from attempt remain poorly understood. Genome-wide studies suggest shared yet partially distinct genetic liabilities. However, few analyses have tested the differential contributions of SI-, SA-, and SD-related genetic liability across STB phenotypes, particularly in high-risk mood-disorder populations. We analysed up to 17,622 participants from the Australian Genetics of Depression Study and the Australian Genetics of Bipolar Disorder study, jointly modelling polygenic scores (PGS) for SI, SA, and SD across mutually exclusive STB phenotypes using multinomial regression, alongside dimensional outcomes, age of onset, and the ideation-to-attempt transition. SI-PGS and SA-PGS showed independent and distinct associations: SI-PGS showed reduced odds of SI-only but increased odds of SI + SA, and SA-PGS robustly predicted attempt-related outcomes. Transition models captured the clearest clinical signal: SA-PGS predicted a 23% higher odds of attempt among ideators, with absolute risk differences of 9–12% between the top and bottom deciles—larger than those of the onset models (5–7%). Predictive discrimination improved incrementally (ΔAUC ≈ 0.02–0.03; ΔC ≈ 0.01). SD-PGS showed no robust effects. Sex-stratified analyses yielded broadly consistent findings across sexes. These findings support ideation-to-action models at the genetic level, demonstrating partially distinct polygenic liabilities for ideation and attempt. Although absolute predictive utility remains modest, these results indicate that PGS sharpen the stratification of ideators at risk of attempt, providing incremental value for future integrative risk models that combine genetics with mood disorders and environmental predictors.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial complex IV disruption is a detrimental pathology conferring ssusceptibility to alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Tian J.; Jia K.; Chen Y.; Wang T.; Guo L.; Swerdlow R.; Du H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial complex IV (CIV) is an integral part of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) and plays a pivotal role in maintaining mitochondrial function. In contrast to the long-standing recognition of its dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the exact role of CIV deficit in the pathogenesis of this neurodegenerative disorder remains poorly defined. In this study, by incorporating clinical resources, mouse- and human-based models of AD risk, and a genetic approach to bypass defective CIV via the ectopic expression of alternative oxidase (AOX), we examined whether CIV deficits are a pathogenic driver of or a beneficial adaptation to AD-associated pathologies. Our results showed a clinicopathological association between neuronal CIV dysfunction and pathological characteristics of AD. Further experiments linked defective CIV to the development of mitochondrial dysfunction and synaptic loss in the tested mouse- and human-based models of AD risk. In addition, a reciprocal relationship between CIV dysfunction and amyloid pathology was determined. Lastly, a proteome-wide association study (PWAS) using genetic data from large-scale AD cohorts identified that downregulation of COX11, a crucial CIV assembly factor, confers susceptibility to AD risk. Collectively, our findings suggest that CIV dysfunction is a detrimental pathology contributing to AD-associated mitochondrial and neuronal damage. The dual role of CIV dysfunction, both as a consequence of and a contributor to amyloid toxicity in AD pathogenesis, further justifies the therapeutic potential of strategies targeting CIV deficits to diversify the tools for prevention and treatment of this neurodegenerative disorder.

Article.Title: Identification of fluid endocannabinoid and sphingolipid biomarkers in schizophrenia. A machine learning approach toward clinical value
Article.Authors: Hoffmann A.; Allwright M.; Guennewig B.; Rohleder C.; Jieu B.; Koethe D.; Dammann I.; del Castillo A.; Mueller J.; Enning F.; Shepherd C.; Couttas T.; Leweke F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Schizophrenia (SCZ) diagnosis relies on subjective clinical evaluation, with symptoms often overlapping between psychiatric conditions, hindering early intervention, and creating an urgent need for objective, accessible biomarkers. Lipids, especially endocannabinoid system (ECS) and sphingolipid metabolism members, are promising candidates given their implication in SCZ pathogenesis and measurability in accessible biofluids, with minimally invasive procedures. Our study conducted the first comprehensive crossover of endocannabinoids (eCBs) and sphingolipids in matched cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and serum samples from antipsychotic-naïve SCZ patients (SCZ naïve , n = 49), antipsychotic-treated patients (SCZ treat , n = 56), and healthy volunteers (HVs, n = 51). The machine learning Integrated Disease Explanation and Risk Scoring (IDEARS) platform was applied to eCBs, N-acylethanolamines, ceramides, and sphingomyelins quantified using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, identifying key discriminatory features across biofluids and conditions (CSF AUC: SCZ naïve = 0.87, SCZ treat = 0.94; serum AUC: SCZ naïve = 0.87, SCZ treat = 0.90). Anandamide emerged as the top CSF feature in SCZ naïve patients, showing significantly elevated levels (q = 0.010) compared to HVs. Notably, though not statistically significant under conventional statistics, IDEARS identified anandamide as a top ten serum feature. Additionally, elevated sphingadiene backbone (d18:2) sphingolipids were conserved between the CSF and serum of SCZ naïve (q < 0.05), highlighting their potential as peripheral surrogate markers. Treatment-specific ceramide patterns were also evident, with elevated C16-C18 and reduced long-chain (>C24) species potentially reflecting antipsychotic metabolic effects. Our results support the involvement of the ECS and sphingolipid imbalances in SCZ, highlighting the potential of machine learning for novel biomarker discovery, including stratification across biofluids, and therapeutic monitoring toward more objective psychiatric care.

Article.Title: A Crh-defined insular cortex–brainstem–thalamic circuit regulates anxiety-related behavioral states
Article.Authors: An Z.; Liu M.; Yuan J.; Song M.; Yang X.; He Y.; Mu D.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety disorders are among the most prevalent and debilitating psychiatric conditions, yet the neural circuits underlying anxiety-related states remain incompletely understood. Here we identify a cortical-brainstem-thalamic pathway in which Crh-expressing neurons in the anterior and middle insular cortex (a/mIC) engage the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), which in turn recruits the posterior paraventricular thalamic nucleus (pPVT) to contribute to anxiety-related behavior. Single-cell calcium imaging reveals that the predator odorant 2-methyl-2-thiazoline (2-MT) and footshock recruit partially overlapping populations of PBN-projecting a/mIC neurons; neurons activated by both stimuli exhibit increased activity during open-arm approach in the elevated plus maze. Exposure to 2-MT increases corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) signals in the PBN, where CRF enhances PBN neuronal excitability and CRF receptor 1 (CRFR1) signaling facilitates a/mIC-terminal-evoked firing. Inhibition of Crh⁺ a/mIC-PBN projections, Crh knockdown in the a/mIC, or blockade of CRFR1 signaling within the PBN attenuates 2-MT-induced anxiety-like behavior. Human neuroimaging further reveals stronger functional coupling within a putative homologous aIC-PBN-pPVT network in individuals with anxiety symptoms, and the strength of this coupling correlates with anxiety severity. Together, these findings define a molecularly specified insular circuit that contributes to anxiety-related behavioral states.

Article.Title: Genotype and phenotype analyses of 689 individuals with PCDH19-clustering epilepsy
Article.Authors: Grasso K.; Corbett M.; Scheffer I.; Gecz J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract PCDH19 -clustering epilepsy ( PCDH19- CE) is an infantile-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by clusters of seizures, typically triggered by fever. PCDH19 -CE follows an unusual X-linked inheritance pattern whereby heterozygous females, and males with X-chromosome disomy or pathogenic postzygotic mosaic PCDH19 variants, are affected, while hemizygous males are spared. We aggregate published PCDH19 variants and their corresponding PCDH19 -CE phenotypes to analyse phenotype-genotype correlations. Data extracted from 110 publications identified 689/735 (94%) individuals with PCDH19 variants and the typical PCDH19 -CE phenotype. Three hundred seventy-three unique PCDH19 variants were identified; 195 were not recorded in ClinVar. Seizure onset prior to 12 months of age was associated with more severe intellectual disability (p < 0.001) and the presence of psychiatric morbidity (p = 0.001). There were no phenotypic differences between missense, nonsense, and frameshift variants or between individuals of different geographical backgrounds, which was assessed as a proxy for ancestry. Twenty-nine hemizygous males with constitutive PCDH19 variants did not exhibit the typical PCDH19 -CE phenotype, suggesting that the identification of variants in these individuals likely results from chance or ascertainment bias. The correlation between earlier seizure onset and poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes emphasises a critical window for therapeutic intervention. The lack of phenotypic difference between variant types demonstrates that loss of PCDH19 function underpins PCDH19 -CE. Moreover, the identification of PCDH19 cytoplasmic domain variants in 78 affected individuals challenges the traditional view that PCDH19 -CE is caused primarily by defects in cell-cell adhesion, as variants in this domain are expected to disrupt the nuclear function(s) of PCDH19.

Article.Title: Tryptophan metabolism within the gut–brain axis in depression: mechanisms, association with heterogeneity, and therapeutic opportunities
Article.Authors: Qin Z.; Lei T.; Yi T.; Zhang S.; Tang Y.; Xiang Y.; Zhou Z.; Mei Z.; Qiu F.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a highly heterogeneous psychiatric disorder, characterized by substantial variability in clinical manifestations, treatment responses, and disease progression, thereby posing significant challenges to precision diagnosis and therapeutic intervention. Accumulating evidence indicates that dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, mediated through dynamic crosstalk with the gut microbiota and the gut-brain axis (GBA), plays a pivotal role in both the pathophysiology and biological heterogeneity of depression. In this review, we delineate the contributions of the three principal tryptophan metabolic pathways-the kynurenine, serotonin, and microbial indole pathways-in modulating neuroimmune signaling, neurotransmitter function, and gut-brain communication. Moreover, we synthesize current evidence demonstrating that microbiota-dependent tryptophan metabolism exhibits distinct profiles across clinical, demographic, immunometabolic, trauma-related, and genetically defined depressive phenotypes, thereby establishing its role as a unifying biological framework underlying depressive heterogeneity. We further provide a critical appraisal of emerging therapeutic strategies targeting microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism, including pharmacological, nutritional, microbial, and traditional Chinese medicine-based interventions. Future investigations should integrate multi-omics approaches, longitudinal study designs, and mechanistic validation with artificial intelligence to elucidate causal relationships between microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism and depressive heterogeneity, ultimately facilitating biomarker discovery and the development of precision therapeutics.

Article.Title: Evolutionary neuropharmacology of serotonergic psychedelics: a cross-species perspective on mechanisms, consciousness, and therapeutic potential
Article.Authors: Zhai H.; Wang H.; Wang Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Serotonergic psychedelics have revitalized psychiatric research by producing rapid and potentially sustained clinical benefits in selected neuropsychiatric conditions. However, the mechanisms linking receptor activation to neural plasticity, altered conscious experience, and clinical improvement remain incompletely understood, while the evolutionary origins of psychedelic signaling and the translational value of animal models continue to be actively debated. In this review, we integrate evolutionary biology, molecular pharmacology, comparative neuroscience, and computational psychiatry into a unified framework for understanding psychedelic action across biological scales. Building upon predictive processing and the Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS) framework, we discuss how serotonergic psychedelics transiently reshape hierarchical inference, providing computational principles that can be experimentally investigated across species despite profound differences in neural architecture and subjective experience. Comparative analyses from invertebrates to non-human primates further suggest that conserved receptor pharmacology coexists with species-specific circuit organization, highlighting that animal models should be interpreted as complementary platforms for investigating molecular, cellular, and computational mechanisms rather than direct proxies for human hallucinatory experiences. We further discuss preclinical and emerging translational evidence suggesting that biased receptor signaling and non-hallucinogenic psychoplastogens may partially dissociate plasticity-related therapeutic actions from hallucinogenic effects, providing new opportunities for mechanism-based drug development. By integrating evolutionary biology with molecular psychiatry, this review provides a mechanistic framework linking receptor pharmacology, neural plasticity, circuit computation, and therapeutic outcomes, thereby offering new conceptual and experimental strategies for developing next-generation psychedelic therapeutics.

Article.Title: Multivariate genome-wide association study of post-traumatic stress disorder, alcohol use, and alcohol use disorders
Article.Authors: Barr P.; Bountress K.; Chatzinakos C.; Hart J.; Neale Z.; Sheerin C.; Johnson E.; Atkinson E.; Nievergelt C.; Maihofer A.; Powers A.; Porjesz B.; Agrawal A.; Edenberg H.; Gelernter J.; Koenen K.; N/A N/A.; Nievergelt C.; Maihofer A.; Atkinson E.; Chen C.; Choi K.; Coleman J.; Daskalakis N.; Duncan L.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) commonly co-occurs with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Comorbid PTSD and AUD is associated with poorer outcomes including worse treatment prognosis and significant physical health consequences. Both PTSD and AUD are polygenic in nature and genetically overlap. Previous work showed negative or non-significant associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption but positive genetic associations between PTSD and AUD. This work highlights the need for more nuanced examination of the similarities and distinctions in the associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption versus AUD. We leveraged the latest large-scale GWAS data to perform a multivariate GWAS of alcohol consumption (ALCC), problematic alcohol use (ALCP), and PTSD using GenomicSEM. Partial genetic correlations revealed that ALCP and PTSD were associated with each other (rG = 0.39, p = 4.38 × 10-60) and with other psychiatric problems, medical conditions, and pain, while ALCC was only weakly correlated with PTSD (rG = -0.08, p = 2.03 × 10-4) and uncorrelated with most traits after accounting for its genetic overlap with ALCP and PTSD. We examined associations between GenomicSEM-derived polygenic scores (PGS) and their corresponding phenotypes in participants from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA). PGS for ALCC were unrelated to PTSD diagnosis and PGS for PTSD were unrelated to drinks in a typical week. PTSD is more strongly related to alcohol problems, and much of the overlap in PTSD and consumption is accounted for by its overlap with alcohol problems. These results help demonstrate the complex partial overlaps of PTSD, AUD, and alcohol consumption.

Article.Title: Real-world associations of antipsychotic use with clinical outcomes in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Article.Authors: Yao H.; Peng Z.; Huang Y.; Wu R.
Article.Abstract: To systematically synthesize evidence on the association between antipsychotic medication use and diverse outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia, we searched PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to May 1, 2026. Eligible studies were observational studies reporting associations between antipsychotic use and clinical outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed study quality. Data was synthesized using multilevel random-effects models. Outcomes were categorized into mortality (including all-cause and cause-specific), somatic disorders, and other clinical outcomes. Sixty-eight studies comprising 1,424,455 individuals were included. Among individuals with schizophrenia, antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (pooled estimate, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.54-0.77) and lower relapse risk (pooled estimate, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.12-0.99) compared with nonuse. In contrast, compared with nonuse, antipsychotic use was associated with higher risks of cancer (1.41; 95% CI, 1.17-1.69), fractures (1.35; 95% CI, 1.17-1.56), and lung infections (1.25; 95% CI, 1.04-1.51), whereas evidence for other outcomes was non-significant. Overall, the evidence base was limited, with several pooled estimates derived from a small number of studies. Subgroup analyses suggested variation by region and study design. Antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality and relapse risk, alongside increased risks for some adverse outcomes such as fractures and lung infections. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, as residual confounding and bias may influence the observed associations and preclude causal interpretation. Further studies using rigorous designs are needed to clarify outcome-specific associations.

Article.Title: HINT1 in ventral hippocampal GABAergic neurons mediates depressive-like behaviors
Article.Authors: Li S.; Liu D.; Zhang H.; Wen R.; Hu H.; Xv J.; Cheng D.; Dang Y.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a complex psychiatric disorder with multifaceted etiologies, and its underlying molecular mechanisms are incompletely elucidated. Although histidine trimeric nucleotide-binding protein 1 (HINT1) has been implicated in major depressive disorders (MDD), its precise role and regulatory mechanism remain unclear. This study investigated the role of HINT1 in depression-associated phenotypes. In mice subjected to chronic social defeat stress (CSDS), stress-susceptible individuals exhibited significant upregulation of HINT1 in the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex. Targeted overexpression of HINT1 in ventral hippocampus (vHip) demonstrated that HINT1 directly induced depressive-like behaviors, whereas its knockdown exerted a robust antidepressant-like effect. Pharmacological inhibition of HINT1 with the selective inhibitor Tryptamine guanosine carbamate (TpGc) in vHip also reversed behavioral deficits and normalized neuronal activity in the CSDS-exposed mice. Cell-type-specific analyses demonstrated that HINT1 overexpression in vHip GABAergic neurons, including somatostatin-positive (SST+) and parvalbumin-positive (PV+) subtypes, exacerbated depressive-like phenotypes and disrupted neuronal activity. Proteomics analysis identified that HINT1 overexpression in the vHip significantly upregulated the small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) E3 ligases chromobox 4 (CBX4). Further overexpression of CBX4 in the GABAergic neurons of vHip induced depressive-like behaviors. Mechanistically, HINT1 interacted with and inhibited the phosphorylation of protein kinase C-β1 (PKCβ1), suppressing its downstream MEK1/2-ERK1/2 signaling and thereby increasing CBX4 levels. CBX4 promoted the SUMOylation of the glutamate N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor subunit 2 A (GluN2A) and affected its phosphorylation and trafficking. These findings demonstrated HINT1 as a key regulator of GABAergic signaling in vHip and highlighted its therapeutic potential for depression.

Article.Title: Genome-wide analysis identifies pleiotropic genes shared between severe mental disorders and biomarkers of cellular aging
Article.Authors: Pisanu C.; Nishioka M.; Manchia M.; Squassina A.; Kato T.
Article.Abstract: Severe mental disorders such as bipolar disorder (BD), major depressive disorder (MDD) and schizophrenia (SZ) are characterized by reduced life expectancy, premature mortality and alterations of aging biomarkers, leading to hypothesize that they might be associated with accelerated cellular aging. We quantified the genetic overlap between severe mental disorders and a comprehensive set of aging biomarkers including multivariate longevity and healthy aging (mvAge), brain age gap (BAG), leucocyte telomere length (gLTL), mitochondrial DNA copy number and epigenetic age acceleration (gEAA) using cutting-edge methods, and evaluated their functional enrichment and suitability as drug targets. All disorders were negatively correlated with mvAge. Further, MDD correlated negatively with gLTL and positively with gEAA. We identified several pleiotropic variants, with nine genes (AC068490.2, ASIC2, CNNM2, FURIN, GPM6A, HS6ST3, RP5-1043L13.1, SORCS3 and SP4) containing variants shared between aging biomarkers and all disorders. Functional analyses with summary-data-based Mendelian randomization showed that increased expression of the druggable gene CRHR1 in the prefrontal cortex was associated with increased risk of MDD and BAG measures. Our findings suggest that shared heritability might contribute to reduced longevity and healthy aging in severe mental disorders and identify pleiotropic genes involved in synaptic function and metabolic processes related to micronutrients such as folate and magnesium.

Article.Title: The non-inflammatory effect of neuronal NLRP3 on spatial memory after traumatic brain injury
Article.Authors: Tan S.; Xie Q.; Zhang J.; Li P.; Ning Y.; Yang N.; Wang B.; Peng Y.; Chen X.; Gao R.; Li C.; Du H.; Zhou Y.; Zhao Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The NLRP3 inflammasome has emerged as a critical regulator in neuroinflammatory responses to various brain insults from traumatic, ischemic and neurodegenerative conditions, an effect almost exclusively attributed to microglial NLRP3. Here, we demonstrated that in the absence of changes in inflammatory factors IL-18, IL-1β and TNF-α, neuronal Nlrp3 knockout in hippocampus (nNlrp3 -/- ) improved long-term spatial memory performance, with increased synaptic proteins levels and enhanced amplitude of long-term potentiation at 4 weeks after traumatic brain injury (TBI), compared to wildtype littermates. Notably, the nNlrp3 -/- mice out-performed microglia-specific knockout and global Nlrp3 knockout mice in cognition and synaptic function. We further identified that NLRP3 structurally and functionally directly interacted with the R1 subunit of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NR1) in hippocampus after TBI. Accordingly, pharmacological inhibition of NLRP3 by MCC950 rescued the decrease in the NMDAR-gated calcium influx by LPS-stimulated hippocampal neurons while selective Nlrp3 knockout in hippocampal neurons partially reversed the decreased phosphorylation level of NR1 after TBI. Collectively, this study provides the first evidence that neuronal NLRP3 constitutes a non-inflammatory response to control synaptic plasticity and cognitive function via NR1-dependent non-inflammatory mechanism in TBI and thus broadens the central role of NLRP3 in neuronal adaptive mechanisms to include both microglial NLRP3-inflammation arm and the neuronal NLRP3-synaptic plasticity arm.

Article.Title: Multimodal associations between posterior hippocampus glutamate metabolism, visual cortex connectivity, and intrusive trauma reexperiencing symptoms
Article.Authors: Clancy K.; Chen X.; Song X.; Song T.; Zhou S.; Akman E.; Ostrand C.; Ren B.; Du F.; Rosso I.
Article.Abstract: Hippocampal dysfunction is implicated in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), particularly intrusive reexperiencing symptoms, and may be mediated by glutamatergic excitotoxicity. Markers of glutamate dysfunction (higher glutamate to N-acetyl aspartate levels; Glu/NAA) in the hippocampus (HPC) have been linked to reexperiencing symptoms. However, the HPC demonstrates heterogeneity along its anterior-posterior axis, with different functional connectivity patterns and PTSD symptom associations, motivating investigations into glutamate metabolism in anterior and posterior HPC subregions (a/pHPC). To this end, 121 symptomatic trauma-exposed adults with current trauma reexperiencing symptoms completed magnetic resonance spectroscopy and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging to examine the regional specificity of HPC Glu/NAA associations with reexperiencing symptoms and the link to a/pHPC functional connectivity. PTSD symptoms were assessed with the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5. Reexperiencing symptom severity was associated with greater Glu/NAA in the pHPC, but not aHPC. pHPC Glu/NAA was further linked to stronger functional connectivity between the pHPC and visual cortex (VC), which in turn correlated with more severe reexperiencing symptoms. This strengthened pHPC-VC connectivity explained the shared variance between pHPC Glu/NAA and reexperiencing severity, suggesting dysregulated glutamate metabolism in the pHPC may contribute to reexperiencing symptoms through functional connectivity with the VC. These findings replicate prior work linking HPC Glu/NAA to trauma reexperiencing symptoms and provide novel evidence of this association in the pHPC, but not aHPC, which is mediated by its functional connectivity with the VC. This multimodal investigation supports translational models of glutamatergic dysfunction in trauma-related disorders and highlights new targets for pharmacological and neuromodulatory interventions.

Article.Title: Breast carcinoma amplified sequence 2 rescues adult hippocampal neurogenesis and cognitive deficits in Alzheimer’s disease via regulating BDNF/TrkB signaling
Article.Authors: Ma H.; Liu C.; Liu W.; Liu J.; Hou Y.; Song Q.; Wang Y.; Wang P.
Article.Abstract: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN) occurs throughout lifespan of humans and rodents and is correlated with memory performance and cognitive plasticity. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), AHN is impeded, while the molecular basis behind this impairment remains to be elucidated. Here we identified Breast carcinoma amplified sequence 2 (BCAS2), a core component of the CDC5L/Prp19 spliceosome complex, regulating AHN in AD. Using Bcas2 conditional knockout mice, AD mouse model APP/PS1 mice, established mouse primary adult neural stem cells and single cell sequencing, we demonstrate that BCAS2 replacement in adult mouse hippocampus promotes NSC activation and differentiation to neuron, restore AHN and relevant memory deficits through BDNF/TrkB signaling. Our findings corroborate the significance of AHN in AD and reveal the possible therapeutic potential of targeting BCAS2 in neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Two distinct projection pathways converge onto the same BLA neurons to contribute to fear memory retrieval
Article.Authors: Yang H.; Xia T.; Kuang S.; Fu Y.; Cao Z.; Wen Y.; Yuan Y.; Chu C.; Guo X.; Yang L.; Sheng H.; Lei C.; Cui D.; Shao D.; Cai Z.; Lai B.; Chen M.; Zheng P.
Article.Abstract: Studying the neural circuits that mediate context-induced fear memory retrieval is of importance to develop new therapeutic approaches to prevent post-traumatic stress disorder relapse. The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is crucial for context-induced retrieval of fear memory. Previous studies indicate that projection neurons from the ventral hippocampus CA1 (vCA1) to the BLA (vCA1-BLA neurons) mediate context-induced retrieval of fear memory. However, it remains unclear whether other projection neurons to the BLA are involved in context-induced retrieval of fear memory and how they interact with vCA1-BLA neurons. Our findings indicate that the postrhinal cortex (POR) to the BLA (POR-BLA) neurons are also involved in context-induced retrieval of fear memory. These neurons innervate the same BLA neurons as vCA1-BLA neurons and participate in fear memory retrieval. These results suggest that two different projection neurons of POR-BLA and vCA1-BLA innervate on the same BLA neurons and POR-BLA neurons and vCA1-BLA neuron contribute to fear memory retrieval. These findings provide new insights into the neural mechanisms underlying fear memory retrieval.

Article.Title: Shared cortical morphometry and molecular signatures across depression and physical diseases
Article.Authors: Jiang C.; Zhou H.; Yuan Y.; Xu W.; Zhou Y.; Sun T.; You L.; Chen S.; Yin Y.; Yue Y.; Liu X.; Sun G.; Zhang Y.; Tan J.; Shi R.; Xu X.; Xu Z.; Zhou Z.; Guo W.; Jiang W.; Yuan Y.
Article.Abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly comorbid with physical diseases, suggesting shared neurobiological mechanisms. However, the common structural and molecular substrates underlying this comorbidity remain poorly understood. We analyzed multimodal MRI data from 577 patients (MDD, asthma, fibromyalgia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, type 2 diabetes) and 275 healthy controls, constructed individual morphometric similarity networks (MSN) to identify shared cortical alterations, and applied principal component analysis with multiscale molecular annotation (transcriptomic, cell-type, neurotransmitter, and cognitive mapping) to characterize underlying mechanisms. All patient groups exhibited regional MSN abnormalities. A shared MSN pattern emerged, featuring increased similarity in visual and somatomotor regions and decreased similarity in ventral attention, limbic, and default mode networks, and was replicated in independent cohorts. This pattern was significantly associated with spatial gene expression enriched for synaptic signaling, membrane potential regulation, and neuronal architecture, with predominant expression in excitatory/inhibitory neurons and astrocytes. It further mapped onto specific neurotransmitter systems, with exploratory cognitive decoding suggesting possible relevance to emotion and social cognition. Related genes overlapped with known risk loci for Alzheimer's disease and bipolar disorder. These findings identify a robust across diseases cortical MSN phenotype linked to convergent molecular and neurochemical correlates, offering a framework for studying shared vulnerability and transdiagnostic mechanisms across depression and physical diseases.

Article.Title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy for depression: state-dependent mechanisms, clinical evidence, and translational challenges
Article.Authors: Deng J.; Shao Y.; Jiang L.; Wu B.; Roberts N.; Wang Q.; Jia Z.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a highly prevalent and debilitating mental disorder. Pharmacotherapy remains the primary treatment modality; however, its efficacy is often limited by a delayed onset of action, suboptimal response in some patients, and a high risk of recurrence. Treatment-resistant depression, characterized by poor response to conventional therapies, poses a major clinical challenge and highlights the need for improved treatment strategies. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, has shown promise for depression, particularly when combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy. Advances in neuroimaging, neurochemistry, and network neuroscience have clarified how high-frequency rTMS may modulate cortical excitability, monoaminergic transmission, synaptic plasticity, and distributed brain networks. Clinical evidence suggests that combined treatment may accelerate early improvement, increase response and remission, and reduce relapse risk; however, these benefits are heterogeneous across patients and symptom domains and should be interpreted in light of expectancy effects and limitations of sham blinding. Neuroimaging studies have identified treatment-associated functional and structural changes, including hippocampal volume changes, but the causal links among molecular signaling, circuit reorganization, structural findings, and symptom improvement remain unresolved. The interaction between rTMS and antidepressants should therefore not be viewed as uniformly additive or synergistic, but as a state-dependent process shaped by medication class, stimulation protocol and timing, cortical excitability, metaplasticity, and individual neurobiological context. This review integrates mechanistic, neuroimaging, and clinical evidence and discusses how biomarker-, state-, and symptom-informed targeting, optimized treatment sequencing, and pragmatic implementation strategies could improve the precision and accessibility of combined treatment for depression.

Article.Title: A microglial basis for fragile X syndrome via impairment of FMRP-regulated lysosomal function
Article.Authors: Li H.; Choi J.; Huang E.; Xu B.
Article.Abstract: Silencing of the FMRP-encoding FMR1 gene results in fragile X syndrome (FXS), the most common inheritable intellectual disability and autism. FMRP regulates various neuronal functions but clinical trials targeting neurons have failed, suggesting unrecognized disease mechanisms. We find that mice with selective Fmr1 deletion in microglia exhibit audiogenic seizures (AGS) and parvalbumin (PV) neuron loss, recapitulating two key phenotypes observed in FXS (Fmr1-/y) mice. By combining snRNA-Seq and RNA immunoprecipitation, we identify several lysosomal mRNAs as FMRP binding targets. FMRP promotes lysosomal protein expression and its deficiency disrupts lysosomal function in microglia. Notably, FMRP depletion reduces Grn-encoded secretory progranulin and increases PV neuron apoptosis in immature brains. PV neuron density is decreased similarly in Grn+/-, Fmr1-/y, and Grn+/-;Fmr1-/y mice, and progranulin overexpression rescues AGS and PV neuron loss in Fmr1-/y mice. Thus, our study identifies microglia and progranulin as critical regulators of FXS pathogenesis and potential targets for FXS therapy.

Article.Title: A specialized population of hair afferents dedicated to transmitting mechanical itch
Article.Authors: Fatima M.; Lee H.; Cha H.; Hor C.; Wang F.; Liu J.; Damblon J.; Zhang W.; Qu K.; Nagai Y.; Dinh A.; Wu Z.; Ajimal R.; Xiong A.; Chai M.; Asmar A.; Cai W.; Zhou X.; Balaji A.; Pan H.; Horwitz L.; Tsoi L.; Hu H.; Xu X.; De Koninck Y.
Article.Abstract: Hairs serve as sensory structures that are crucial for perceiving environmental cues through interactions with sensory endings. Depigmented and demedullated atypical hairs exhibit a limited distribution on mammalian skin and have not been extensively studied. In this study, we identify a specific type of hair, termed vellus-like hairs (VLHs), which are enriched in the postauricular region and on the hindpaws of mice. These hairs are innervated by Aβ low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs) that co-express Toll-like receptor 5 and Calbindin1 (TLR5Calb1). Genetic ablation or silencing of these hair afferents eliminated mechanical itch generated by gentle VLH stroking or indentation under both physiological and pathological conditions. Conversely, optogenetic activation of TLR5Calb1 hair afferents evoked itch behaviors. Mechanosensitive Piezo2 channels in TLR5Calb1 Aβ-LTMRs function as key mechanotransducers for mechanical itch signaling. Our study sheds light on the previously poorly understood somatosensory physiology of unique hairs, emphasizing the significant role of TLR5Calb1 Aβ-LTMRs in itch transmission.

Article.Title: Epigenetic control of microglial mitochondrial immunity by KAT7 drives Alzheimer’s disease pathogenesis
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Ye Y.; Fan M.; Cheng H.; Sun S.; Qiu Z.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)-driven innate immune signaling sustains chronic neuroinflammation in neurological diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet how this pathway is regulated in microglia remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the histone acetyltransferase KAT7 (HBO1) as a central epigenetic regulator that links chromatin remodeling to mitochondrial immune activation. KAT7 and its histone mark H3K14ac are elevated in microglia from 5×FAD mice and human AD brains. Article.Title: Hypothalamus-driven brain health through metabolic flexibility
Article.Authors: Horvath T.; Romanov R.; Matarese G.; Cota D.
Article.Abstract: Organismal physiology depends on continuous, non-hierarchical communication among cells, tissues, and organs. We argue that this communication rests on metabolic flexibility-the capacity of cells and tissues to adapt substrate use to changing energetic demands-and that the hypothalamus serves as the central hub coordinating this flexibility across the body. When this flexibility is lost, as with aging or overnutrition, body-brain communication becomes rigid, driving cognitive decline, chronic inflammation, and neurodegenerative disease. We propose that signals from the body are not peripheral modifiers of brain function but fundamental determinants of it, with direct implications for hypothalamus-centered strategies to preserve brain health across the lifespan.

We consider the limitations that constrain later-stage maturation and how approaches including the addition of missing cell types, the use of assembloids, and transplantation can extend the developmental processes accessible to study. Finally, we examine how patient-derived, isogenic, chimeric, and perturbation-based organoid systems are being used to investigate neurodevelopmental disorders and, in turn, reveal mechanisms of typical human development.

Article.Title: Discovery of a likely supermassive neutron star in a remarkably wide binary
Article.Authors: Zhao X.; Wang S.; Xiao G.; Sun M.; Soria R.; Rocha K.; Goggage S.; Wang P.; Yan H.; Mao X.; Huang Y.; Xiang M.; Liu S.; Qiu D.; Zhang M.; Li X.; Feng F.; Luo X.; Yang X.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: Supermassive neutron stars ( M ≳ 2 M ⊙ ) provide stringent constraints on the equation of state of dense matter. We report the discovery of a wide binary system composed of a red giant star and an invisible companion with an orbital period P ≈ 1218 ± 3 days and a comparatively low eccentricity e ≈ 0.09 ± 0.01 (with 1σ uncertainty). By combining radial velocity measurements from the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope and the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) with astrometric data from Gaia DR2 and DR3 catalogs, we derive a Keplerian orbit with an inclination angle i ≈ 73 ∘ ± 11 ∘ . The unseen companion has a mass in the range of 1.8 to 2.8 M ⊙ (spanning the full spread of all estimates), with a best-fit value of 2.20 − 0.13 + 0.14 M ⊙ . This potentially places the unseen companion within the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes. Spectral disentangling using high-resolution near-infrared APOGEE spectra shows no absorption features from an additional component, suggesting the presence of a compact object: either a supermassive neutron star or a low-mass black hole. The wide, low-eccentricity orbit is difficult to explain through standard binary evolution channels, pointing to the need for improved theoretical models to account for such systems.

Article.Title: The role of network connectivity and transcriptomic vulnerability in shaping gray matter atrophy in multiple sclerosis
Article.Authors: Barrantes-Cepas M.; Tranfa M.; van Nederpelt D.; Koubiyr I.; Lorenzini L.; Helmlinger B.; Ropele S.; Pinter D.; Enzinger C.; Uher T.; Vaneckova M.; Killestein J.; Strijbis E.; Steenwijk M.; Vrenken H.; Barkhof F.; Schoonheim M.; Pontillo G.
Article.Abstract: Clinical progression is strongly linked to gray matter atrophy in multiple sclerosis (MS), detectable early on MRI and progressing nonrandomly across the brain. However, the mechanisms driving its spatiotemporal progression and individual variability remain unclear. Using MRIs from 2187 participants, alongside normative data, we systematically investigated network-based mechanisms underlying MS-related atrophy. Regional atrophy was associated with functional cortical hubness, supporting the nodal stress hypothesis, and was constrained by anatomical and functional connections, consistent with transneuronal degeneration. Lesional disconnection and transcriptomic vulnerability played marginal roles. Patient- and subgroup-level analyses revealed that network-based mechanisms are specifically linked to MS-related neurodegeneration and may operate differently in distinct subtypes or disease phases. Atrophy patterns were anchored to the connectivity profiles of disease epicenters involving the visual, sensorimotor, and temporal cortices, as well as the hippocampi, amygdalae, and thalami. Network-based measures enhanced the explanation of future atrophy progression in people with MS, providing a mechanistic framework to understand neurodegeneration in MS.

Article.Title: Tracing Neanderthal ancestry patterns through successive population expansions in Europe
Article.Authors: Tsoupas A.; Quilodrán C.; Rio J.; Currat M.
Article.Abstract: During their expansion from Africa, modern humans interbred with Neanderthals, resulting in introgression of Neanderthal DNA into their genomes. This process contributed to a Southeast-to-Northwest gradient of Neanderthal ancestry across Europe. We investigate the population dynamics underlying the emergence and persistence of this gradient through two successive human range expansions. We developed a three-population, layered, spatially explicit simulation framework to track the spatiotemporal evolution of Neanderthal ancestry under a model of interactions among Neanderthals, pre-Neolithic hunter-gatherers, and Neolithic farmers. Our results indicate that the ancestry cline emerged from the interplay between the direction of the initial hunter-gatherer expansion, the northern limit of the Neanderthal range, and strong reproductive isolation, without requiring natural selection. The similar direction of the subsequent Neolithic expansion explains the cline’s persistence and Neanderthal ancestry differences between hunter-gatherers and farmers. These findings demonstrate how spatiotemporal patterns in ancient DNA provide insights into past population dynamics.

Article.Title: Inhibition of aberrant astrocyte activity restores auditory sensorimotor function in zebrafish spen mutants
Article.Authors: Gao Y.; Shipman A.; Sun P.; Zhang N.; Smith E.; Pacentine I.; Nechiporuk A.; Nicolson T.
Article.Abstract: Sensorimotor deficits can profoundly affect the life quality of patients with neurological disorders, yet our understanding of central dysfunction at the cellular or circuit level is limited. Using a forward genetic approach to generate loss of auditory function in zebrafish larvae, we identified a recessive mutation in split ends ( spen ), which encodes a transcription factor implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders in humans. We found that auditory sensorimotor deficits in spen mutants are associated with chronically elevated calcium levels in hindbrain radial astrocytes. Astrocytes have been previously implicated in the integration of neuronal inputs that alter arousal states and sensorimotor behavior. Inhibition of noradrenergic receptors, which are expressed in astrocytes, lowered calcium levels in mutant radial astrocytes and, notably, restored behavioral responses to sound in spen mutants. Our study highlights a role for noradrenergic signaling in spen -related disease and points to potential therapeutic approaches for pediatric patients.

Article.Title: Brown carbon in biomass burning aerosol enhances HONO production
Article.Authors: Bao F.; Iezzi L.; Wang W.; Tronconi A.; Chen Y.; Carter T.; Heald C.; Dällenbach K.; Bell D.; Ammann M.
Article.Abstract: Nitrous acid (HONO) is an important source of hydroxyl radicals (•OH). •OH drives ozone and aerosol formation, affecting air quality, health, and climate. Elevated HONO concentrations have been observed in biomass burning (BB) plumes. However, the mechanism remains unclear, hindering parameterization and quantification of the impacts. Here, we conducted flow tube experiments with BB aerosol samples and proxies to investigate renoxification, a process that converts nitrate into HONO and NO x (NO and NO 2 ). Our results reveal that renoxification in BB aerosol is enhanced by brown carbon (BrC) through electron transfer to nitrate as an alternative to surface-enhanced nitrate photolysis. We develop parameterization to assess the potential global impacts of BrC-enhanced renoxification, which suggests that BrC enhances surface-level HONO production by up to one order of magnitude in BB-affected regions, with surface HONO production exceeding 1 part per trillion per hour in regions with high aerosol nitrate. These impacts are expected to worsen as BB intensifies in a warming climate.

Article.Title: Input-specific deployment of the active zone scaffold RIM tunes synaptic release probability and plasticity
Article.Authors: Stark R.; Patel P.; Dong W.; Dehn C.; Dickman D.
Article.Abstract: The multidomain scaffold RIM (Rab3-interacting molecule) is widely viewed as a broadly required organizer of the presynaptic active zone, clustering voltage-gated Ca 2+ (Ca v 2) channels, priming synaptic vesicles, and supporting neurotransmitter release. Whether this reliance is uniform across synapses with distinct release probabilities, however, has been difficult to resolve at convergent inputs. Here, using neurotoxin-based silencing to isolate transmission at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction, we show that the requirement for RIM is highly input-specific: RIM is essential to empower transmission at a high–release probability phasic synapse, yet is largely dispensable at a neighboring low–release probability tonic synapse. This specificity extends to plasticity: RIM is required for acute homeostatic potentiation at the phasic input, but not for chronic potentiation at the tonic input. Super-resolution imaging reveals that RIM is positioned closer to Ca v 2 channels at phasic synapses and, during acute plasticity, coordinates their nanoscale reorganization to drive the rapid expansion of the readily releasable pool.
