Article.Title: The transcription factors OsIDD and OsSHR jointly regulate ground tissue patterning and differentiation in rice roots
Article.Authors: Peng L.; Chen Z.; Li Z.; Cao S.; Liu J.; Liu R.; Yu J.; Zhang B.; Liang X.; Gao B.; Chen X.; Xia J.
Article.Abstract: Rice roots have a distinctive ground tissue architecture with multiple cortical layers and a single endodermal layer concentrically surrounding the stele. This architecture promotes aerenchyma formation and adaptability to waterlogged environments, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here, we identified the INDETERMINATE DOMAIN (IDD) and SHORTROOT (SHR) families as key regulators of ground tissue development in rice. OsIDD2/3/6/8 govern cortical radial symmetry by coordinating cortical organization and auxin distribution independently of OsSHR1/2/3/4/5. Quadruple knockout of OsIDD2/3/6/8 caused cortical asymmetry without affecting apoplastic barrier integrity or mineral uptake but reduced shoot-directed ion transport. OsIDD8 also controls the number of cortical cell layers and endodermal cells, whereas OsSHR1/2/3/4/5 redundantly promote periclinal divisions of the cortical cells, which require OsIDD8 activity. Moreover, OsIDD and OsSHR members coordinate endodermal differentiation by regulating localization of Casparian strip membrane domain protein OsCASP1 and lignin/suberin deposition. These findings establish a genetic framework underlying the spatial organization and functional differentiation of ground tissue in rice roots.

Article.Title: The ZmJAZ14–ZmMYC2 module regulates anthesis–silking synchrony in maize
Article.Authors: Lu X.; Lv D.; Ma S.; Yan Y.; Li C.; Zhu J.; Miao L.; Li S.; Yang W.; Zhou X.; Chen R.
Article.Abstract: The evolution of traits can increase yield potential but may create physiological constraints. Jasmonic acid (JA) signaling regulates sex determination in male (tassel) and female (ear) inflorescences in maize. Although the formation of ears laid the foundation for high yields, the asynchronous development of the tassel and the ear prolongs the anthesis-silking interval (ASI), threatening reproductive success and reducing yield. Whether JA signaling coordinates ear and tassel development remains unclear. Here, we show that the core JA signaling module, ZmJAZ14-ZmMYC2a/b, orchestrates the expression of SPL29 for reproductive transition, BA1 for female inflorescence initiation, and EXPA5 for silk elongation. Coordination of these physiological processes underpins synchronous growth of the tassel and ears, whereas disruption of ZmMYC2a/b or accumulation of the repressor ZmJAZ14 prolongs ASI. Our work suggests that the repurposing of JA signaling to coordinate ear and tassel development may represent a lineage-specific evolutionary burden in maize. Deciphering the link between gains and unforeseen costs of evolution could further improve yields.

Article.Title: Passive imaging with quantum advantage
Article.Authors: Gong L.; Zhang A.; Dastidar M.; Duplinskii A.; Lvovsky A.
Article.Abstract: Far-field optical imaging inevitably involves low-pass spatial filtering, limiting the resolution. Moreover, conventional imaging suppresses high spatial frequency components close to the cutoff, making them invisible under noise—particularly the shot noise arising from discrete and random nature of quantum light. Here, we propose and implement a method for reducing the effect of this noise by optically preprocessing the incoming light before detection, thereby optimizing the quantum measurement performed on it. Our scheme, termed Fourier domain division (FDD), partitions the Fourier plane into multiple regions for independent detection and subsequent post-processing for image reconstruction. By analyzing the quantum and classical Fisher information, we show that our method is advantageous with respect to direct imaging for high spatial-frequency components. As a result, the number of photons required to achieve a certain signal-to-noise ratio in the Fourier domain is reduced, thus enhancing the overall resolution in the photon-starved regime. We demonstrate our method in microscopy, achieving fivefold improvement of Fisher information on high spatial frequency components. Unlike active super-resolution methods, FDD is passive, making it broadly applicable in microscopy and other imaging scenarios, where active illumination is impractical, including astronomy and remote sensing, in the photon-starved regime. Our work establishes a general strategy for designing quantum optimized superresolution imaging systems, bridging fundamental quantum limits, practical image analysis, and computer vision applications.

Article.Title: Phototropin-mediated blue light signaling orients the asymmetry of Marchantia polymorpha spores
Article.Authors: Roetzer J.; Slovak R.; Wallner E.; Edelbacher N.; Asper B.; Deiber S.; Seitner S.; Colombini M.; Dolan L.
Article.Abstract: Multicellular organisms produced by sexual reproduction develop from single cells, and the asymmetry of these cells can define the orientation of the earliest developmental axes. The haploid multicellular stage of the plant, Marchantia polymorpha, develops from a single cell—the spore—that divides asymmetrically, producing an apical germ cell that generates the plant body and a smaller basal cell that differentiates as an anchoring germ rhizoid cell. We show that the orientation of this asymmetric cell division is controlled by an external environmental cue—blue light—that is perceived by the photoreceptor phototropin. This process requires the NCH1 (NRL PROTEIN FOR CHLOROPLAST MOVEMENT 1) protein for downstream signaling. Together, these findings define core elements of the mechanism by which a directional environmental signal orients cell division, which, in turn, orients the first axis of symmetry.

Article.Title: Electronic hair: Transforming hair into a scalable bioelectronic interface
Article.Authors: Shweta S.; Giompliaki M.; Sohail L.; Cornuéjols R.; Donaldson P.; Abrahamsson T.; KC D.; Ntzouni M.; Cengiz S.; Drakopoulou S.; Donahue M.; Seitanidou M.; Zhao Z.; Simon D.; Berggren M.; Mclntyre S.; Raedt R.; Strakosas X.; Spyropoulos G.
Article.Abstract: In electroencephalography, hair remains a major barrier to electrode-skin contact, limiting signal quality. Here, we introduce electronic hair (eHAIR), a strategy that converts hair into a bioelectronic interface using mixed ionic-electronic conductive polymer dyes. Hair, a keratinized filament anchored within the skin, provides a stable and naturally distributed platform for interfacing. Two complementary approaches based on polythiophene derivatives enable rapid, washable functionalization of hair bundles or semipermanent coating of individual strands. The resulting eHAIR forms conformal, low-impedance interfaces that support electrophysiological recordings with increased signal amplitude and spectral power while preserving the underlying neural dynamics without gels or rigid hardware. Beyond passive sensing, eHAIR-based organic electrochemical transistors enable local signal amplification, with gain defined by hair geometry. By repurposing hair as an active bioelectronic interface, eHAIR establishes a wearable and biointegrated platform that can be implemented from individual hairs to larger hair-covered regions.

Article.Title: Cell adhesion molecule–related proteins signal to promote cytoneme elongation from Sonic Hedgehog–producing cells
Article.Authors: Daly C.; Dillard M.; Hall E.; Lavado A.; Klein J.; Zhai J.; Pruett-Miller S.; Pagala V.; High A.; Carisey A.; Hom C.; Koehler N.; Ogden S.
Article.Abstract: Tissue morphogenesis and postdevelopmental homeostasis rely on efficient information exchange between communicating cells. Cytonemes are actin-based protrusions that contribute to precise information flow by facilitating contact-mediated directional transport of diverse signaling cargoes. How pathway-specific cytonemes are formed is poorly understood, as are the molecular mechanisms promoting actin organization for elongation and stability of the dynamic cellular extensions. We investigated biogenesis of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) cytonemes, revealing functional repurposing of cell adhesion molecule-related proteins Brother of CDON (BOC) and Cell adhesion molecule-related, Down-regulated by Oncogenes (CDON) into recruiters of actin regulators FARP1 and Cdc42 for cytoneme elongation. Loss of BOC and CDON function blunts protrusion-localized Cdc42 activity, reducing cytoneme lengths and occurrence in SHH-expressing cells. Live imaging of developing murine spinal cords reveals that CDON loss in SHH-expressing cells reduces the frequency of neuroepithelial cytonemes and alters neuronal cell fate specification. These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.

Article.Title: Multimodal switches exploiting electromechanical snap-through for versatile robotic information processing
Article.Authors: Fan S.; Guo J.; Jia F.; Sun J.; Liu Y.; Sitti M.
Article.Abstract: It is highly desirable to design and engineer lightweight, low-power-consumption, and rapid physical intelligence (PI) structures that couple with multiple robotic functions. Here, we present a multimodal electromechanical switch (mEMS), consisting of a stretchable droplet-amplified electrostatic zipping structure, a convex bump, and a pair of electrical contacts, that can be used to achieve the widely used mechanical momentary, mechanical latching, and electrically actuated switching modes by simply tuning the applied voltage and using the same structure. We theoretically investigate the snap-through behavior of the elastic zipping membrane, which can be used to endow the mEMS with voltage-dependent memory, and the theoretical considerations are experimentally validated. As a result, we can apply the mEMS array for robotic memory, such as information writing and erasing; robotic communication by reprogrammable information encrypting, decrypting, and display; robotic computation by electrically reprogrammable logic gates; and reprogrammable binary information transferring. The mEMS represents a comprehensive PI structure for next-generation autonomous machines that can better adapt in unstructured and complex real-world environments.

Article.Title: Cocrystals for sequestering and separating large PAHs
Article.Authors: Vasquez-Ríos M.; Campillo-Alvarado G.; Li C.; Samra K.; Höpfl H.; MacGillivray L.
Article.Abstract: Highly adaptive boroxine organic assemblies (BOAs) derived from a boronic acid and a linear alkene function as a first-generation constitutional dynamic library (CDL) to sequester and separate large polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in form of cocrystals. Configurational and conformational isomerism of the organoboroxines in host-guest assemblies is induced by electronic properties, shape and size of the PAHs through a “shrink-wrap” process/mechanism, which reveals a templating role of the PAH during the CDL assembly. The CDL was applied to separate up to three different PAHs. The cocrystals exhibit tunable electronic properties. The CDL afforded a cocrystal wherein alkenes of two different BOAs undergo [2 + 2] photocycloaddition in the same solid.

Article.Title: Dynamic plasmonic imaging of electromechanically driven nano-oscillators for charge-resolved multiplex biosensing
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Liu X.; Wu J.; Ma J.; Cui B.; Ma G.; Ma J.; Liu Q.; Wang D.; Zhang F.
Article.Abstract: Multiplexed profiling of diverse biomarkers is essential for precision diagnostics, but remains challenging for label-free sensors because signals typically scale with analyte mass. Here, we present a dynamic plasmonic imaging platform based on electromechanically driven nano-oscillators for multiplexed, label-free quantification of nucleic acids, proteins, and small molecules within a unified sensing architecture. Size-encoded nanoparticles tethered to a plasmonic surface are electrically actuated to oscillate vertically within the evanescent field and tracked by distance-resolved surface plasmon resonance imaging. Molecular binding alters the effective surface charge of each nano-oscillator, modulating the electrostatic-driven forces and changing oscillation amplitude. This charge-to-motion transduction mechanism reduces dependence on molecular mass and enhances sensitivity for low–molecular weight analytes. This platform simultaneously detects microRNAs, proteins, and small molecules spanning a ∼300-fold molecular weight range within a single field of view. We further demonstrate multiplexed profiling of tumor-associated microRNAs in pretreated supernatants from patient-derived breast cancer cells across 24 clinical samples. Dynamic plasmonic nano-oscillators provide a scalable architecture for multiplex molecular diagnostics.

Article.Title: Neuromelanin-inspired metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks restore neuronal excitability in radiation-induced brain injury
Article.Authors: Deng R.; Li K.; Duan R.; Zhang X.; Gu B.; Mao L.; Cao W.
Article.Abstract: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) affects up to 30% of patients receiving cranial radiotherapy, representing an irreversible complication lacking effective therapies. Research advances are limited by poor blood-brain barrier drug penetration and overreliance on ex vivo pathology, which cannot resolve dynamic neuronal dysfunction. Inspired by neuromelanin, we fabricated metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks (MSMNs), combined with in vivo electrophysiology to investigate and mitigate radiation-triggered neural dysfunction. In 6-gray whole body–irradiated mice, MSMN normalized neuronal excitability and restored medium spiny neuron firing and striatal circuit activity, improving locomotor and anxiety-related behaviors. Besides central functional recovery, MSMN provides systemic radioprotection, ensuring full 30-day survival, protecting radiosensitive organs and facilitating hematopoietic recovery. This work identifies neuronal excitability as an underexplored therapeutic target for RIBI, establishing neuromelanin-mimetic selenomelanin nanonetworks as a bioinspired platform linking molecular radioprotection to circuit-level restoration for radiation-induced neurological injury.

Article.Title: Controllable fabrication of visible-spectrum 3D photonic crystals
Article.Authors: Hu H.; Li D.; Gao H.; Chen F.; Zhang M.; Li Z.; Mao A.; Xiong W.
Article.Abstract: The fabrication of visible-spectrum three-dimensional (3D) photonic crystals (PhCs) remains highly challenging, because existing manufacturing techniques cannot simultaneously achieve high processing precision and sufficient geometric freedom. Here, we propose a suspended pyrolysis-assisted two-photon polymerization (SP-TPP) printing strategy, achieving the controllable fabrication of visible-spectrum 3D PhCs. The resulting 3D diamond PhCs exhibit a remarkable lattice-period standard deviation of only 5.75 nm, approximately 1/45 of that achieved without suspended pyrolysis. Microscopic reflection spectra confirm these PhCs possess uniform optical responses across all spatial positions. By tuning the lattice period and structural duty cycle, the PhCs operating at diverse wavelengths are systematically realized. Moreover, through the demonstration of PhC prototype structures and in situ arrayed fabrication, the SP-TPP printing strategy paves the way for applications in photonic microcavities, 3D optical waveguides, optical splitters, and integrated micro-optical systems.

Article.Title: Boosting stability and charge transfer of conducting polymer poly(benzodifurandione) (PBFDO) through complementary topology
Article.Authors: Geng Y.; Yao B.; Lu Y.; Liu J.; Chen Z.; Zou S.; Yin Z.; Huang X.; Xu J.; Fu J.
Article.Abstract: Poly(benzodifurandione) (PBFDO) is a benchmark n-type conjugated polymer known for its record-high electrical conductivity. Nevertheless, its thermal robustness and charge/ion transport characteristics remain insufficient. To address this issue, we report a hierarchical complementary topology strategy via doping PBFDO with choline chloride (ChCl). At the molecular scale, the cations Ch + selectively intercalate along the out-of-plane direction while simultaneously densifying the in-plane π-π stacking, accompanied by partial removal of H + . At the submicrometer scale, this induces distinct phase separation into high- and low-density stacking domains. As a result, the product PBFDO-ChCl exhibited a synergistic performance boost, with a 2.8-fold enhancement in high-temperature resilience, a 1.6-fold increase in sheet conductance, and a 15.9-fold reduction in ion diffusion resistance. Then, organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) using PBFDO-ChCl as channel material further confirm these performance enhancements. As a whole, this work closes the performance gap between n-type PBFDO and state-of-the-art p-type conjugated polymers, potentially advancing its applications from energy storage to bioelectronics and neuromorphic computing.

Article.Title: Weak adsorption, strong consequences: How trace gases control ice growth and quasi-liquid-layer structure
Article.Authors: Yerby C.; Chen X.; Bertho G.; Zhu C.; Francisco J.; Yang D.
Article.Abstract: Gases in the atmosphere are often treated as passive background species in cold environments, yet their molecular roles at icy interfaces remain poorly understood. Here, we show how hydrophobic and hydrophilic trace gases can actively reorganize the ice interface and regulate freezing through interfacial stabilization. We find these gases can actively modulate both the kinetics and thermodynamics of the water-ice interface. Using molecular simulations, we find that all gases examined retard ice-front propagation relative to pure water to different extents. This slowing arises from weak but preferential adsorption at the water-ice interface, where gases occupy water-dense interfacial layers and locally suppress ice-like ordering. After freezing is complete, gases do not distribute uniformly across the frozen surface, but partition selectively among multiple adsorption regions across the ice–quasi-liquid-layer (QLL)–air interfacial landscape. Relatively hydrophobic gases exhibit a three-region adsorption pattern, whereas relatively hydrophilic gases occupy only two dominant adsorption regions. Despite these differences, both classes preferentially accumulate near the QLL-air boundary and its immediate outer region rather than the ice-QLL interface. There, gases pair with and compensate for dangling surface bonds (through a surface-passivating effect reminiscent of ligand stabilization), reducing the thermodynamic driving force for premelting and thereby thinning the QLL. These results establish a unified molecular picture in which atmospheric gases are active interfacial modulators of both ice growth and ice structure, with implications for freezing, ice-cloud microphysics, and heterogeneous atmospheric chemistry.

Article.Title: Single-cell profiling of the duodenum during chronic human norovirus infection
Article.Authors: Matsushima Y.; Durkee-Shock J.; Alves D.; Nagata B.; Kim S.; Chan E.; Chaimongkol N.; Ishiyama R.; Barton K.; Han A.; Kelly L.; Ogbogu P.; Kumar S.; Xu X.; Briggs K.; Murakami K.; Cohen J.; Keller M.; Sosnovtsev S.; Green K.

Norovirus infection was associated with the up-regulation of MHC class I-related genes and IL15 in duodenal macrophages and late enterocytes, together with increased IFNG expression by CD8 T cells. Macrophages and late enterocytes up-regulated CXCL9 and CXCL10/11 , respectively, consistent with CD8 and CD4 T cell recruitment to the duodenum. Article.Title: Incomplete synaptic vesicle priming functionally disconnects CA1 pyramidal cells
Article.Authors: Holderith N.; Nusser Z.
Article.Abstract: The hippocampal CA1 area is perceived as a nonrecurrent neuronal network, i.e., CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) within the CA1 area innervate mainly γ-aminobutyric acid–releasing interneurons but not each other. Here, we performed an unbiased examination of the functional properties of local CA1PC output synapses using in vitro two-photon glutamate imaging. Fluorescent transients measured with iGluSnFR3 in individual boutons displayed extraordinary heterogeneity in their amplitudes and short-term plasticity patterns upon a complex train of presynaptic action potential firing. Post hoc electron microscopy of the imaged boutons demonstrated that distinct postsynaptic structure-innervating boutons display different functional properties. Approximately 25% of the boutons innervate CA1PC spines, which either release glutamate with very low release probability or completely fail to release. Phorbol 12,13-dibutyrate and elevated calcium (2+) concentration, manipulations that enhance synaptic vesicle priming and fusion, convert these silent into properly functioning synapses. Our results provide evidence that CA1PCs are interconnected with structurally and molecularly intact glutamatergic synapses, but incomplete synaptic vesicle (SV) priming precludes SV release.

Article.Title: A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Chen P.; Zhang S.; Pan D.
Article.Abstract: Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

Article.Title: Structural insights into light harvesting and photosystem II evolution in the basal streptophyte Mesostigma viride
Article.Authors: Bai T.; Mao Z.; Sun D.; Ma F.; Ma B.; Gao Y.; Li Y.; Yang Y.; Tang W.; Hitchcock A.; Johnson M.; Qian P.; Wang Y.; Tian L.
Article.Abstract: The basal streptophyte Mesostigma viride represents a critical evolutionary transition toward land plants, yet the molecular basis of its ancestral light-harvesting strategy remains elusive. Here, we present a 2.25-angstrom resolution cryo-EM structure of the M. viride PSII-LHCII-LHCP supercomplex, revealing a unique C 2 S 2 M p2 L p2 -type architecture. Our structure reveals a nearly complete set of conserved PSII core subunits, indicating that much of the PSII structural framework found in terrestrial plants was established early in the streptophyte lineage. At the periphery, the complex features a specialized antenna module in which two ancestral LHCP monomers flank CP29. These ancestral antenna proteins bind an unusually high number of carotenoids, with seven carotenoids per subunit, and extensively incorporate marine-type keto carotenoids, siphonaxanthin, and siphonein, throughout the complex, thereby broadening absorption in the blue-green region. The canonical LHCII trimer exhibits a distinctive chlorophyll b macrocluster and a 96-femtosecond ultrafast energy transfer component. Together, these findings provide a high-resolution molecular framework for an evolutionary intermediate that combines high-capacity aquatic light harvesting with structural features potentially relevant to photoprotection during the transition toward terrestrial life.

Article.Title: Piezoelectrically actuated magnetic dipole twisting resonators enable miniaturized low-frequency antennas
Article.Authors: Chang J.; Li B.; Gao X.; Song K.; Wang Y.; Jiao J.; Hasanyan D.; Zhang S.; Li F.
Article.Abstract: Miniaturized low-frequency antennas are essential for underwater, underground, and biomedical communications, yet their performance is constrained by the fundamental size-efficiency trade-off, a long-standing physical bottleneck. Here, we introduce a radiation mechanism that circumvents this constraint by replacing the time-varying currents in conventional antennas with the mechanical twisting oscillation of a magnetic dipole. This electromechanical-magnetic transduction enables underwater cross-medium communication over 115 meters with only milliwatt-level power consumption, using 99.9% less power than loop antennas. It also supports implantable wireless devices that achieve a fourfold increase in communication range at identical power consumption, opening a route to long-range, low-power wireless systems capable of operating in some of the most demanding environments.

Article.Abstract: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a pleiotropic cytokine that drives macrophage functions ranging from tissue homeostasis to inflammation, yet how STAT3 specifies these divergent outcomes remains unclear. Article.Title: Integrating biomass production platform and identification approach for stereochemical assignment of super-carbon-chain compounds
Article.Authors: Liu F.; Xu G.; Chen H.; Li D.; Xiao X.; Mándi A.; Wu J.; Zeng K.; Kurtán T.; Shen L.
Article.Abstract: Super-carbon-chain compounds (SCCCs), marine long-carbon-chain polyketides featuring numerous carbon stereocenters, fall into untapped chemical space in between drug-like small molecules and biopolymers. In this work, a modern microalgal biomass production-platform is created for pilot-scale cultivation of marine dinoflagellates to produce over 100 milligrams of minor SCCCs. The modular fragment-based identification (MFBI) approach is successfully employed to establish the relative and absolute configurations of SCCCs. As an example, 157.7 mg of a minor SCCC, named amphidiketol A, featuring a highly-flexible C 76 -linear carbon backbone and thirty-three carbon stereocenters, is obtained from Amphidinium sp. in our platform. Its hybrid architecture contains eleven‌ distinct modular fragments. Its relative and absolute configurations are successfully established by the MFBI approach. Collectively, an undescribed paradigm for stereochemical assignment of SCCCs is presented. Nine senescence-associated protein targets of amphidiketol A in lung cancer A549 cells are identified.

Article.Authors: Cao Y.; Dovgusha O.; Ebrahimi A.; Cruz C.; Bevan S.; Widmer L.; Torabi F.; Kurlovich J.; Rodríguez-Polo I.; Khan S.; Patel M.; Shiels O.; Pradeepa M.; Flynn S.; Günesdogan U.; Schoenfelder S.
Article.Abstract: Enhancers are key gene regulatory elements that ensure the precise spatiotemporal execution of developmental gene expression programs. Article.Authors: Carrara F.; Brumley D.; Hein A.; Cooper T.; Salek M.; Keegstra J.; Levin S.; Stocker R.
Article.Abstract: Chemotaxis, the ability of cells to detect and respond to chemical gradients, allows them to acquire nutrients, seek hosts, or escape toxins. Analyzing single-cell nutrient exposure for tens of thousands of cells revealed that the nutrient exposure and distribution of exposure among bacteria depend strongly on the spatiotemporal characteristics of the patchy landscape. Furthermore, bacterial trajectories revealed a progressive decrease of swimming speed counter-balanced by an increase in chemotactic precision, resulting in stable nutrient exposure over time. Article.Title: The persistent multidomain health effects of the early-life exposome
Article.Authors: Anguita Ruiz A.; Amine I.; Luo C.; Guillien A.; Arteaga M.; Setó-Llorens A.; Stratakis N.; Maitre L.; Güil-Oumrait N.; Ruiz-Rivera M.; Montazeri P.; Urquiza J.; Nieuwenhuijsen M.; Thomsen C.; Småstuen Haug L.; Granum B.; Andrusaityte S.; Grazuleviciene R.; Dedele A.; Yuan W.; Heude B.; McEachan R.; Vafeiadi M.; Chatzi L.; Wright J.
Article.Abstract: The environments experienced early in life can shape health across multiple body systems, yet most research on exposome health effects has focused on isolated exposure windows and health outcomes, limiting understanding of their combined and enduring effects. We identified a set of “master regulator” exposures, such as maternal smoking, indoor air pollution, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, and dietary and urban factors, that influenced multiple health domains, with effects persisting into adolescence. Article.Title: Fault-tolerant quantum computing with high-rate symplectic double codes
Article.Authors: Kanomata N.; Goto H.
Article.Abstract: High-rate and large-distance quantum codes are expected to make fault-tolerant quantum computing more efficient, but most of them lack efficient fault-tolerant encoded-state preparation methods. We propose such fault-tolerant encoders for two symplectic double codes, [[30,6,5]] and [[36,12,5]]. The advantage of these codes is their compactness, namely, their small code block sizes for their high encoding rates and large distance, allowing for early experimental realization of high-rate codes. Detecting crucial errors during encoding with as few auxiliary qubits as possible, our encoders can reduce resource overheads while keeping low logical error rates compared to more naive methods. Numerical simulations with a circuit-level noise model demonstrate the reliability and effectiveness of the proposed methods. We also develop arbitrary-state encoders that enable the injection of arbitrary quantum states into the code spaces. Combined with basic fault-tolerant operations, they support universal quantum computation. We thus demonstrate that efficient and reliable logical state preparation is achievable even for compact and high-rate codes, offering a potential step toward efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing suitable for near-term experiments.

Article.Title: Origins of low density and low accretion rate in classical T Tauri stars
Article.Authors: Liang G.; Wei H.; Yuan D.; Zhong J.; Ma Z.; Ping Y.; Wang L.; Xiong J.; Xie Z.; Ma X.; Cui W.; Zhao G.
Article.Abstract: High-resolution x-ray spectroscopy of classical T Tauri stars (CTTs) reveals a soft x-ray excess, low electron density, and accretion rate inferred from helium-like oxygen (O VII). Accretion shock models have been widely studied via numerical simulations and can reproduce observations with appropriate accretion stream structures. Within the standard accretion shock framework, we propose a distinct physical model involving energy exchange between postshock hot plasma and cold infalling material during reverse shock propagation into the accretion stream. Incorporating charge exchange processes, the electron density derived from the O VII triplet shows excellent agreement with helium-like neon diagnostics and standard accretion shock model predictions. The mass accretion rate inferred from O VII emission also becomes consistent with optical results. Complementing our theoretical work, we conducted a laboratory simulation of CTT accretion shocks supported by hydrodynamic similarity principles. Time-integrated x-ray self-emission and temporal optical shadowgraphy reveal the dynamic formation of two dense clumps, the “core” and “shell,” which morphologically resemble hydrodynamic oscillations driven by heating/cooling instabilities in CTT accretion shocks. The core is a standing shock formed by a preheated low-density plasma flow impinging on a carbon-hydrogen foil, while the shell is shocked aluminum plasma (the reverse shock) arising from interactions between accumulated aluminum plasma and its following flow. High-resolution experimental spectra confirm that charge exchange occurs in the shocked x-ray–emitting region. Our results demonstrate that dynamic interactions between postshock and infalling material, mediated by charge exchange cooling, is the reason for the low O VII density problem in CTTs.

Conversely, ectopic DACH1 expression in the rodent neocortex induced bRG formation and promoted callosal neuron production. Article.Title: Lynx1 suppression reopens the window for effective rehabilitation after stroke in mice
Article.Authors: Nakanishi T.; Itokazu T.; Tsujioka H.; Shibuya N.; Morishita H.; Yamashita T.
Article.Abstract: Rehabilitation is an effective and reliable approach for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, its efficacy decreases during the transition from the subacute to the chronic phase after stroke, posing a major barrier to complete functional recovery. This limited efficacy during the chronic phase is believed to result from declining neural plasticity. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating neural plasticity and its temporal changes after stroke remain unclear. To address this gap, we established a focal ischemic stroke mouse model that allows causal interrogation of the mechanisms responsible for the reduced efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase. Using this model, we identified Lynx1, an endogenous negative allosteric modulator of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, as a negative regulator of post-stroke neural plasticity. Lynx1 expression in layer 5 pyramidal neurons was transiently down-regulated and returned to normal levels in the peri-infarct area. Longitudinal intravital imaging revealed that Lynx1 suppression promoted synaptic clustering with increased dendritic spine turnover in the peri-infarct area, an emerging structural basis for memory formation. As anticipated, Lynx1 suppression improved spontaneous motor recovery and the efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase after stroke. Furthermore, we developed a Lynx1 -targeting antisense oligonucleotide and found that its administration during the chronic phase after stroke enhanced the efficacy of rehabilitation. These findings suggest that dendritic spine dynamics in the peri-infarct area are a key determinant of rehabilitation responsiveness through the regulation of clustered spine formation and that Lynx1 may represent a promising therapeutic target for augmenting dendritic plasticity after stroke.

Article.Authors: Jiang L.; Li R.; Li Y.; Guo D.; Li Y.; Liu J.; Huang L.; Pang D.
Article.Abstract: The anti-Stokes shift, a critical parameter reflecting the conversion of low-energy photons into high-energy photons, has been constrained by energy losses inherent to multi-step energy transfer processes. Furthermore, we have found that the ground-state thermal vibrations of tetracene derivatives can promote the population of electrons to high vibrational states, which facilitated the endothermic triplet energy transfer from the ligand to the annihilator, thereby substantially enlarging the anti-Stokes shift. These findings present a feasible design route toward NIR-II–excitable photon upconversion with large anti-Stokes shifts by precisely tailoring quantum dot–based sensitizers and annihilator units, which promotes the efficient exploitation of low-energy photons in chemistry, materials science, and photonics.

Article.Authors: Liu M.; Xie S.; Yang D.; Gerya T.; Liu L.; Qi R.; Shan X.; Dong X.; Xu X.
Article.Abstract: Age-progressive seamount chains are fundamental archives in revealing the past plate motion and mantle convection. However, for a representative example such as the New England Seamounts chain on the North American Plate, both its plume source and its evolutionary trajectory remain debatable. This long-lasting uncertainty is mainly caused by the absence of quantitative high-resolution constraints on plume dynamics and its interactions with multiple plates. Here, we aim to answer this question using data-assimilation–based numerical simulations. We propose that the New England chain and the Corner Seamounts on the North American Plate, the Great Meteor Seamounts on the African Plate, and the Azores archipelago on the Eurasian Plate were created by a single plume—the Azores plume. This plume experienced two stages of motion through time. Subduction-induced sublithospheric mantle flow exerts a dominant control on the spatiotemporal distribution of volcanoes along the track and the geometry of this track, surpassing the influence of plume-plate interaction. The latter primarily affects the continuity of this trans-plate hotspot system. These findings offer a reinterpretation of hotspot-track formation and new constraints on how mantle flow reorganizes across multiple plates.

Article.Title: Single-nucleus multiomic profiling uncovers epigenetic dysregulation driving hippocampal vulnerability in Alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Tao Q.; Luo T.; Wang P.; Jiang M.; Lai Z.; Jin B.; Liu Y.; He Y.; Wei Y.; Gao Y.; Zhu L.; Du H.; Wang L.; Peng Y.; Hou Y.; Liu S.; Liu L.; Zhang J.; Han L.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) exhibits region- and cell-type–specific vulnerability, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly defined. We performed integrated single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of human hippocampus to resolve gene regulatory architecture in AD. By linking chromatin accessibility to transcription, we identified more than 1000 disease-associated cis-regulatory interactions, highlighting coordinated epigenomic-transcriptomic remodeling. Excitatory cornu ammonis (EX.CA) neurons exhibited disproportionate regulatory disruption, characterized by increased chromatin accessibility coupled to activation of apoptosis-related gene programs, whereas dentate gyrus (EX.DG) neurons remained comparatively resistant. In glial cells, regulatory network inference revealed activation of transcription factor modules centered on SPI1/KLF4 in microglia and STAT3 in astrocytes, defining epigenetic programs that are highly associated with inflammatory and metabolic state transitions. Comparative evaluation with the prefrontal cortex uncovered conserved inflammatory activation alongside region-specific immune regulatory divergence, indicating spatially distinct microglial responses. Furthermore, cross-species integration demonstrated that a substantial fraction of AD-associated regulatory elements are human-specific, with AD-risk variants enriched in microglial cis-regulatory elements at loci including BIN1 and APOE . Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework linking chromatin remodeling to cell-type–specific dysfunction and reveal human-specific regulatory architecture as a crucial factor to AD vulnerability and translational limitation.

Article.Title: Aneuploidy impairs B cell development but accelerates their MYC-driven transformation
Article.Authors: Weiss J.; Petermann P.; Rigato I.; Lohmüller M.; Honold F.; Schapfl M.; Spöck S.; Kinz N.; Tijhuis A.; Wardenaar R.; Losito M.; Foijer F.; Rizotto D.; Schubert M.; Herzog S.; Riley J.; Labi V.; Finotello F.; Villunger A.
Article.Abstract: Chromosomal instability (CIN) is an established driver of aneuploidy and cell death. Here, we investigate the role of apoptosis as a barrier against CIN-driven aneuploidy in B lymphocytes. We found that impairment of their spindle assembly checkpoint via deletion of Mitotic Arrest Deficient 2-Like 1 or mutation of Monopolar Spindle 1 kinase curtails B cell survival. Notably, cell death inhibition by BCL2 was insufficient to cause aneuploidy-driven B cell transformation, while loss of P53 strongly synergized with tumors featuring stochastic aneuploidies. In contrast, high cell death rates rapidly select for specific karyotypes, facilitating aneuploid tumor cell survival in E μ -Myc transgenic mice. Hence, cell death inhibition fails to allow CIN-driven aneuploidies to prevail. In contrast, BCL2-regulated apoptosis selects viable aneuploid tumor karyotypes in the presence of oncogenic MYC, a notion with implications for the clinical use of BCL2-targeting therapies.

Article.Title: High-precision <sup>81</sup> Kr dating overcomes radiocarbon limits in Late Pleistocene groundwater
Article.Authors: Li H.; Yang G.; Bao X.; Jiang W.; Lu Z.; Yang H.; Zhang M.; Zhao L.
Article.Abstract: Groundwater preserves continental hydroclimate signals, but its use as a Late Pleistocene archive is limited by uncertainties in radiocarbon ( 14 C) dating caused by carbon geochemical processes. The noble gas isotope 81 Kr has simpler transport behavior, yet its effective dating limit was traditionally ∼50 thousand years (ka) because of analytical constraints. Here, we extended the 81 Kr dating lower limit to ∼10 ka using high-precision atom trap trace analysis, thus covering the entire Late Pleistocene. We conducted a direct 14 C- 81 Kr comparison in the North China Plain. Within the 10- to 30-ka range, 81 Kr independently validates 14 C ages; beyond this range, it provides reliable ages for older groundwater. The dual-tracer approach reduces model uncertainty in 14 C correction and identifies mixing-affected samples. After screening, groundwater δ 18 O records closely match polar ice-core climate archives. High-precision 81 Kr dating, combined with 14 C, offers a robust age framework for reconstructing Late Pleistocene hydroclimate.

Article.Title: Deep learning–assisted electron microscopy for apparent Z-height mapping of atomically dispersed catalysts
Article.Authors: Han X.; Meng Y.; Cai Q.; Hong Y.; Qiu Z.; Hu W.; Miao S.; Li K.; Zhao J.; Meng F.; Hai X.; Zhang Z.; Lu J.; Zhang J.; Zhao X.
Article.Abstract: Atomically dispersed catalysts (ADCs) offer maximal metal utilization and local atomic/electronic structures, yet resolving their actual atomic configurations using aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-STEM) remains fundamentally constrained by depth ambiguity and complex experimental noise. Existing STEM–machine learning (ML) approaches often rely on ideal simulations or manual annotations, limiting their transferability to realistic ADC images and causing ambiguity between isolated atoms, projected dimers, and small clusters. Here, we develop a physics-informed, domain-adaptive CycleGAN-UNet framework for depth-aware ADC analysis. CycleGAN translates height-labeled simulations into experimental-like images while preserving atomic coordinates and apparent Z-height labels, and a depth-supervised UNet performs simultaneous atom localization and discrete Z-height classification. Support-specific simulations further incorporate support-dependent background contrast, including uniform amorphous carbon (am-C), am-C with local thickness variation, and crystalline supports, thereby improving the applicability of the framework to different ADC imaging conditions. Across diverse metals (Mn, Fe, Cu, Pd, and Pt) and supports (am-C, black phosphorus, and polymeric carbon nitride), the framework achieves high atom detection precision (∼95%) and reliable apparent Z-height classification at ∼2-nanometer binning. By encoding depth-dependent beam broadening features, the framework converts conventional 2D projections into quantitative, apparent Z-height atomic maps. In geminal Pt/PCN catalysts, it resolves the loading-dependent transition from isolated Pt monomers to Pt 2 sites and links these configurations to dehydrogenative aromatization activity. This framework transforms STEM images from projected atom maps into quantitative, depth-aware atomic descriptors for ADC structure–activity analysis.

Article.Title: When and how particles are removed by drops
Article.Authors: Naga A.; Sabath F.; Vollmer D.; Kusumaatmaja H.
Article.Abstract: Particulate contaminants decrease the power output of solar panels and the transparency of windows and are detrimental to microelectronics, where even a single particle can induce a short circuit. Despite substantial research on particle adhesion and self-cleaning, it remains unclear when and how a drop can remove a particle from a surface, thus efficiently cleaning the surface. Here, by combining lattice Boltzmann simulations and confocal microscopy experiments, we show that at least six different scenarios arise from the complex interplay between capillary and friction forces when a drop collides with a particle on a surface. Notably, the capillary force plays a dual role in particle removal: While its tangential component always drives removal, its normal component can also hinder it. We introduce a dimensionless capillary capture parameter that successfully predicts particle removal across a wide range of particle and surface properties. Our results reveal that the design of easy-to-clean surfaces should focus not only on maximizing hydrophobicity but also on minimizing the particle-surface friction.

Article.Title: Increases in Northern Hemisphere winter circulation waviness over 1989 to 2011 driven by decadal oceanic variability
Article.Authors: Ma W.; Wang H.; Lubis S.; Chen G.
Article.Abstract: Large-scale circulation waviness shapes day-to-day weather and extremes. During 1989 to 2011, Northern Hemisphere midlatitudes experienced a pronounced increase in wintertime waviness, coinciding with rapid Arctic warming and more frequent cold-air outbreaks. While Arctic amplification was hypothesized to cause this trend via jet weakening, subsequent studies have failed to support this mechanism, leaving the origin unresolved. Here, using large-ensemble simulations, statistical analyses, and dynamical diagnostics, we demonstrate that variability in sea surface temperature and sea ice accounts for approximately half (48.7 to 63.3%) of the observed increase. A positive phase shift of the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) is the prominent driver, enhancing waviness across northern Eurasia, the northwest Pacific, and the North Atlantic. A concurrent negative Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation shift partially offsets the AMO-driven anomalies in the northwest Pacific. Projections indicate that internal variability will outweigh model differences as the main source of near-term uncertainty. These results refine attribution of recent winter waviness changes and identify an AMO-linked source of predictability for long-term shifts in midlatitude extremes.

Article.Title: Ketogenic diets induce proinflammatory macrophage accumulation through long-chain saturated fatty acids driving cGAS-STING signaling
Article.Authors: Wei S.; Schell J.; Sezaki M.; Baseviciene A.; Qian W.; Chen W.; Trevino R.; Sreenivas P.; Chocron E.; Jiang H.; Dong F.; Chang J.; Nazarullah A.; Huang G.; Munkácsy E.; Horikoshi N.; Gius D.
Article.Abstract: Ketogenic diets (KDs) have demonstrated both pro- and anti-inflammatory effects; however, the mechanisms underlying divergent outcomes on a KD are unclear. In both murine and human macrophage tissue cultures, we demonstrate that long-chain saturated fatty acids (LC-SFAs) promote M1-like polarization, while no effect was observed with medium-chain fatty acids or unsaturated fatty acids. Transcriptomics showed multiple up-regulated proinflammatory pathways, including inflammasome activation and cyclic guanosine 5′-monophosphate–adenosine 5′-monophosphate synthase (cGAS)–stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling. Myeloid-lineage specific Sting knockout mice demonstrated that cGAS-STING is required for the observed proinflammatory effects of a KD. These data suggest that elevated LC-SFA on a KD may induce proinflammatory macrophage accumulation in multiple tissues, a finding with potential clinical implications.

Article.Title: Swarm-inspired magnetic metal-organic framework-based microbots for on-demand moisture manipulation
Article.Authors: Cheng M.; Tuo C.; Liang Y.; Wang X.; Cao M.; Bu X.
Article.Abstract: Hygroscopic metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising candidates for atmospheric water harvesting (AWH) and humidity control. Nevertheless, their practical application is often hindered by the poor manipulability of inherent powder forms and mass transfer limitations caused by the shaping. Drawing inspiration from the “hot defensive ball” aggregation morphology of honeybee swarms, a versatile magnetic shaping strategy hereby was reported to assemble MOF-based microbots, which enhances the formability of MOF powders. The obtained magnetic hygroscopic MOF (mMOF-303) exhibits enhanced water adsorption kinetics and enables efficient regeneration via multimodal heating strategies, including photothermal, electrothermal, and magnetothermal heating. Besides, the magnetic MOF-based microbots can change their aggregation patterns and perform directional motion according to application scenarios, enabling rapid water vapor sorption-desorption rates and precision confined space humidity control. This work provides a universal strategy to impart versatile formability to static MOF powders, paving the way for MOF engineering and advanced moisture management.

Article.Title: Carrier-free Arg-CpG augments antitumor efficacy by triggering specific immune activation
Article.Authors: Li H.; Lin Q.; Xie Y.; He X.; Yang S.; Zhou Y.; Zhao X.; Wang X.; Han Y.; Cao F.; Gan L.; Zhang S.; Liu P.
Article.Abstract: The delivery of nucleic acids using nonviral vectors represents a promising approach for cancer therapy. Nevertheless, nucleic acid–based drugs suffer from poor potency and rapid degradation. Herein, we report a carrier-free nucleic acid delivery system termed Arg-CpG, which is easily constructed through charge-driven assembly of poly( l -arginine) (Arg) and the immune adjuvant unmethylated cytosine-phosphate-guanine oligonucleotide (CpG). This Arg-CpG functions as both a carrier and a therapeutic agent, thereby eliminating the need for a conventional drug delivery vehicle and minimizing potential toxicity. The guanidinium groups of Arg endow Arg-CpG with dual functionalities: enhancing cellular uptake and serving as the nitrogen donor for iNOS-mediated nitric oxide (NO) generation. This NO production further synergizes with CpG to drive macrophage reprogramming toward an antitumor phenotype. Notably, Arg-CpG exhibits cell-type–dependent modulation of autophagy. It disrupts autophagic machinery in 4T1 tumor cells while preserving functional autophagy in RAW264.7 macrophages. This differential activity results in selective killing of tumor cells without compromising the viability or function of normal immune cells. Consequently, Arg-CpG elicits a robust antitumor immune response in vivo. Moreover, the modular design of Arg-CpG enables its straightforward assembly with CpG oligonucleotides and other nucleic acid payloads (e.g., anti-miR oligonucleotides and siRNA), establishing a versatile and promising platform for nucleic acid–based cancer therapy.

Article.Title: All-optical sensing of dermal activity enables an AI-powered wearable ring for continuous stress monitoring
Article.Authors: Hassan M.; Das S.; Addepalli D.; Xiong L.; Islam M.; Rakib A.; Tasnim S.; Yu X.; Rawson E.; Arfan M.; Brun A.; Lucas G.; Becerik-Gerber B.; Frank A.; Khan Y.
Article.Abstract: Electrodermal activity (EDA), a primary stress-sensing signal in today’s wearables, requires skin-electrode contact that drifts and degrades over time, limiting long-term use. Here, we present an artificial intelligence (AI)–powered ring for all-optical sensing of dermal activity (ODA), using light rather than electrodes to track sweat gland activation, thereby enhancing durability and comfort. An optimized dual-wavelength design (960 and 1250 nanometers) captures perspiration dynamics while concurrently recording photoplethysmography. The ODA ring integrates temperature and motion sensors for multimodal monitoring with on-device inference. In correlation studies, ODA and EDA signals showed 86% agreement. In classification tasks, the ODA ring achieved 92.3% binary accuracy versus 77.95% for EDA. In multiclass tasks, ODA outperforms EDA by 100 to 74.58% (short term) and 89.72 to 43.20% (long term). On-device one-dimensional convolutional neural network inference enabled 87.53% autonomous accuracy. This electrode-free modality establishes a scalable, all-optical platform for rings, watches, and patches for accurate, robust, and long-term stress monitoring.

Article.Title: Symmetry as a common origin of hierarchical emergence and abstraction
Article.Authors: Rosas F.
Article.Abstract: Many systems of interest exhibit nested emergent layers with their own rules and regularities, and our knowledge about them seems naturally organized around these levels. How do such hierarchical structures arise, and why should observers track these hierarchies so closely? This paper proposes symmetry as an answer to both questions. By combining principles from information theory, group theory, and statistical mechanics, it is shown that dynamical processes that are equivariant with respect to a symmetry group give rise to multiple emergent macroscopic levels arranged according to the algebraic structure of the symmetry. The same symmetries shape the Bayesian beliefs of an observer with only partial access to the system, yielding a matching hierarchy of “abstract” beliefs that can be updated autonomously at different levels of resolution. These ideas are illustrated in Hopfield networks, where familiar macroscopic quantities emerge from known symmetries, and in Boolean models of gene regulation, where symmetries are instead found from the dynamics. The computational advantages provided by symmetry are showcased in Ehrenfest diffusion and epidemic modeling, where abstract beliefs enable Bayesian inference over exponentially large state spaces. These results identify symmetry as a sufficient mechanism for hierarchical emergence and—at the same time—for the capacity of abstract beliefs to mirror the systems they track, making feasible inferential problems that would otherwise be intractable.

Article.Title: Identification of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB)–β-ribose as a promising biomarker enabling prolonged detection of GHB intake
Article.Authors: Faldborg K.; Hasselstrøm J.; Sørensen L.; Nielsen C.; Møller S.; Poulsen T.; Johannsen M.; Andersen C.; Nielsen K.
Article.Abstract: For several years, forensic toxicologists have sought biomarkers to extend the detection window of gamma-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), a drug suspected to be involved in drug-facilitated sexual assaults yet difficult to detect due to its rapid elimination, endogenous presence, and postsampling formation. In this study, we used samples from 30 participants in a double-blind, controlled trial, randomized to placebo or a single oral dose (50 milligrams per kilogram) of sodium oxybate, a GHB salt. We collected whole blood and urine samples over 5 days and used untargeted metabolomics to search for biomarkers. The most promising feature, previously suggested as a GHB-pentose, was identified as GHB-β-ribose by chemical synthesis and liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Quantification showed elevated levels of GHB-β-ribose for up to 48 in blood and 24 hours in urine after GHB intake compared with endogenous levels in the placebo group and authentic forensic cases. Thus, we present GHB-β-ribose as a very promising biomarker for GHB intake, with the potential to extend the detection window for GHB.

Article.Title: Direct visualization of light’s polarization and spectrum with a compass-like meta-device
Article.Authors: Xiong Y.; Fang S.; Xu H.; Li T.; Ma X.; Zhang H.; Chen Y.; Chen J.; Lei Y.; Chan C.; Xu F.
Article.Abstract: Rapid and accurate identification of the spectropolarimetric characteristics of light is increasingly demanded across modern optical technologies. Existing spectral-polarimetric analysis typically relies on a limited number of filters and polarizers, yielding discrete and often disordered outputs that require extensive calibration and computational reconstruction. Here, we present a compass-like meta-device that enables direct visualization of both spectrum and polarization by spatially locating resonant signatures. Through dual-dimensional geometric engineering in polar coordinates—based on collective resonances analogous to quasi-bound states in the continuum with symmetry-broken meta-atom anisotropy—the compass-like meta-device exhibits dihedral group ( D n ) symmetry and radially conformal scaling of unit-cell geometry, mapping polarization and wavelength onto azimuthal and radial spatial positions, respectively. This design enables continuous characterization of linear-polarization orientation with a mean absolute angular error of 6.2°, together with continuous spectral readout over the 1450–1600 nm range at a visually resolvable spectral resolution of ∼6 nm. Our approach functions as an intuitive, single-shot, and robust spectropolarimeter for on-chip multidimensional optical sensing and imaging.

Article.Title: Battery-free ingestible electronic capsule with programmable high-output soft actuation for active gastrointestinal interventions
Article.Authors: Fang H.; Xie R.; Jiang X.; Zhu J.; He C.; Zhang K.; Tang W.; Wang H.; Zhang W.; Zhu Q.; Cao Q.; Hu J.; Yang H.; Zhang L.; Liao Z.; Han D.
Article.Abstract: Ingestible capsules have garnered considerable attention due to their high gastrointestinal (GI) transitability and minimally invasive nature. However, constrained by pill-sized dimensions (approximately 2 to 4 cubic centimeters), current ingestible capsules face persistent challenges in achieving both controllable high mechanical output and sufficient onboard power delivery, limiting their capacity for effective in vivo therapeutic interventions. Here, we present a wirelessly powered ingestible electronic capsule that integrates programmable soft phase-change actuation within a rigid-soft architecture to enable programmable, high-output mechanical operations. Leveraging bidirectional thermoelectric regulation and guided rigid-soft coupling, the capsule delivers a peak force of 3.8 newtons and a volumetric stroke of ∼250 cubic millimeters within a confined geometry based on the phase-change actuation. To power this actuation, we implemented a compact wireless power transfer system that achieved a maximum load-received power per unit receiver-coil volume of 9.15 watts per cubic centimeter at a 5-centimeter transfer distance under the tested conditions. The structural adaptability of the soft actuator allows modular integration of functional end-effectors, supporting high-output tissue acquisition, site-directed delivery of model liquid or gel payloads, and active biofluid sampling under magnetic navigation. In vivo experiments in beagles demonstrated the feasibility of mechanical interventions in physiological environments. By overcoming the long-standing power and actuation constraints of capsule architecture, this work establishes a physical framework for high-output ingestible robotics and advances the development of minimally invasive robotic platforms for complex GI interventions.

Article.Title: Physics-informed and data-efficient machine learning for storm surge forecasting during typhoons
Article.Authors: Xie H.; Dong C.; Liu Y.; Feng X.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: This study addresses the challenge of accurately forecasting storm surges during tropical cyclones, which is crucial in reducing coastal damages. We develop a physics-informed and data-efficient model, a storm surge neural network (SSNN), that embeds shallow water equations into a machine learning (ML) framework with a specifically designed piecewise loss function to effectively incorporate physical constraints. The SSNN is iteratively trained to make rolling forecast and can produce more accurate forecasts than a standard data-driven model even with a smaller size of training data. The improvement in the performance by the SSNN model is evident, particularly in coastal areas with varying strong winds. This is especially true for forecasts beyond 16 hours, where the data-driven model struggles to provide accurate predictions. Combining physics with ML could offer a promising way to improve storm surge forecasting and support coastal hazard preparedness.

Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Cui Y.; Li F.; Zhou S.; Wu G.; Jing Z.; Wu L.
Article.Abstract: Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

Article.Title: Electrical spin pumping in exchange-coupled molecules
Article.Authors: Greule P.; Huang W.; Au-Yeung K.; Stark M.; Schwenk J.; Sürgers C.; Wernsdorfer W.; Willke P.
Article.Abstract: Electron spins in single molecules are a promising platform for quantum information processing. However, their practical implementation as qubits requires reliable control at the single-entity level, including an efficient state initialization. Here, we demonstrate the remote, all-electrical spin pumping of the electron spin in single molecules: Using electron spin resonance scanning tunneling microscopy, we investigate coupled pairs of S = 1/2 molecules, where one molecule serves as a readout and pumping unit for the neighboring one. We show that the exchange interaction between them enables angular momentum transfer, which allows for the control of the remote spin state via the direction and magnitude of the spin-polarized tunneling current and the exchange coupling strength. These results establish a general, all-electrical approach for remote spin pumping that is transferable to a wider range of spin-based quantum architectures.

Article.Title: Decoding cancer therapy resistance through advanced 3D organoid systems
Article.Authors: Ye R.; Wang J.; Xu W.; Chen Y.; Zhang Z.; Zhang Y.; Qin S.
Article.Abstract: Precision oncology still faces low clinical translation rates. This is largely because two-dimensional (2D) culture systems cannot reproduce tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental stress. Here, we review the applications of 3D cancer models, including scaffold-free spheroids, patient-derived organoids (PDOs) biobanks, and microphysiological systems (MPSs), in drug resistance modeling and personalized therapy. These platforms effectively model metabolic gradients, lineage plasticity, and immunological features within the tumor microenvironment (TME), thereby bridging the genotype-phenotype gap. They also capture physical immune exclusion, T cell exhaustion, and antigen presentation to facilitate the evaluation of immunotherapies. Last, we discuss key translational bottlenecks such as standardization and throughput, proposing the integration of advanced biomanufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI)–driven phenomics, and computational modeling to develop 3D cancer platforms into clinical predictive systems for optimizing precision treatment strategies.

Article.Title: GEX1-mediated semigamy induces both maternal and paternal haploids in cotton
Article.Authors: Li T.; Pan J.; Li Y.; Yao J.; Fang S.; Cao Z.; Zhu S.; Zhang Y.; Chen W.
Article.Abstract: How semigamy generates haploids during double fertilization has remained elusive for more than six decades. Here, we identify Gamete Expressed 1 ( GEX1 ) as the gene underlying semigamy and show that it mediates dual-origin haploid induction in cotton. A naturally occurring mutation in GEX1 disrupts normal nuclear membrane fusion during fertilization, resulting in delayed or incomplete karyogamy. Cytological analyses reveal that delayed karyogamy allows the closely apposed but unfused gametic nuclei to undergo independent mitotic divisions, giving rise to maternal haploids, paternal haploids, and chimeric progeny. CRISPR-Cas9–mediated disruption of GEX1 reproduced the characteristic defects in nuclear fusion and enabled both maternal and paternal haploid induction within a single generation. Together, our findings uncover a genetically tractable mechanism underlying semigamy that links nuclear membrane fusion dynamics to haploid formation and establish a versatile strategy for rapidly generating doubled haploids from both parental genomes to accelerate crop breeding.

Article.Title: ZSCAN4 links a transient reset of repetitive DNA to genome integrity and cellular plasticity
Article.Authors: Lucci V.; Amendola E.; Albano F.; Ruopolo C.; di Paola G.; Bravoco D.; Sabato C.; Cesta G.; Calabrese C.; Falco G.; Mazzone P.
Article.Abstract: ZSCAN4 is transiently expressed in a small subset of embryonic stem cells and early embryos and has traditionally been linked to telomere elongation and genome stability. However, accumulating evidence indicates that ZSCAN4 does not function as a classical stemness factor. ZSCAN4 acts as a temporally restricted regulator of genome plasticity. Recent mechanistic studies indicate that ZSCAN4 preferentially operates at repetitive DNA regions. In particular, at telomeres, it supports maintenance and elongation, whereas, at microsatellite-rich and two-cell (2C)–associated loci, it has been proposed to enable a brief, locally restricted window of chromatin relaxation. This process involves noncanonical mechanisms, such as proteostasis-dependent removal of repressive chromatin complexes, coordinated engagement of genome surveillance pathways, and rapid restoration of chromatin constraint. ZSCAN4 activity is regulated by multilayered regulatory mechanisms acting at the transcriptional, posttranscriptional, and posttranslational levels, ensuring a sharp burst followed by active shutdown. We propose a unifying model in which ZSCAN4 functions as a transient genome reset factor that facilitates cellular plasticity during zygotic genome activation, 2C-like transitions, and cellular reprogramming, while preserving long-term genome integrity. This framework redefines the role of ZSCAN4 beyond stemness maintenance and highlights repetitive DNA as a central regulatory platform during developmental and reprogramming-associated genome transitions.

Article.Title: H3K9 demethylase KDM3A potentiates interferon signaling and macrophage-driven inflammation in atherosclerosis
Article.Authors: Siebeler R.; Chen H.; Kuznetsova T.; Neele A.; van der Velden S.; Gijbels M.; Griffith G.; van Roomen C.; Prange K.; Boshuizen M.; Seijkens T.; Palm K.; Mokry M.; Lutgens E.; Hoeksema M.; de Winther M.

In a mouse model of atherosclerosis, hematopoietic Kdm3a deficiency reduces lesion size, necrotic core formation, and neutrophil recruitment. Mechanistically, Kdm3a -deficient macrophages show impaired chemokine secretion and reduced neutrophil recruitment both in vitro and in vivo. Together, these findings establish KDM3A as an epigenetic regulator that sustains IFN-driven macrophage activation and promotes progression of atherosclerosis, nominating KDM3A as a potential target for selectively modulating IFN-dependent inflammation.

Article.Title: Raising mountains for a habitable Earth
Article.Authors: Smit M.; van Hinsbergen D.; Guilmette C.; Kooijman E.; King A.; Cutts J.; Bleeker W.
Article.Abstract: The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability. Peak-metamorphic pressures recorded by crustal rocks buried in orogens increased between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, indicating that rocks could be buried deeper and that orogens could grow substantially thicker after each of these periods. The two periods of orogenic growth were broadly synchronous with major increases in terrigenous element and nutrient fluxes and changes in biological sulfur metabolism and surface oxygenation. These changes could be explained by enhanced weathering of higher mountains. The findings support the hypothesis that there are first-order mechanistic links between secular geodynamic change and changes in Earth system state and habitability, which shaped the conditions for the evolution of complex life during the past 3 billion years.

Article.Authors: Huang Z.; Li W.; Zhou M.; Huang Z.; Wei Y.; Yin Z.; Yang C.; Ma Z.; Shen M.; Gong Q.; Braunstein Z.; Rao X.; Jiang D.; Zhong J.
Article.Abstract: As a major cause of morbidity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), the prognosis of lupus nephritis (LN) critically depends on early detection and timely intervention. Mechanistically, the ssDNA backbone demonstrated favorable biocompatibility, without exacerbating autoimmune phenotypes or inducing Toll-like receptor-mediated signaling pathways. In conclusion, this study establishes a robust proof-of-concept for pathology-targeted PET/CT imaging of immune complex deposition. By directly visualizing the disease-driving renal autoantibody deposition at the preclinical stage, prior to overt organ damage, this strategy shifts LN diagnosis to non-invasive, mechanism-based molecular visualization.

Article.Authors: Xu C.; Zhang Y.; He Y.; Liang H.; Wang H.; Long Y.; Pan J.; Ye Y.; Li Y.; Jiang Y.; Lu W.; Shen L.; Tu Y.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Restoring immune microenvironment homeostasis is critical for slowing osteoarthritis (OA) progression. By coupling cerium(IV) oxide–mediated catalytic propulsion with mesoporous polydopamine (mPDA)–enabled thermophoretic motion, the system achieves enhanced active transport, in which near-infrared irradiation reinforces directional movement and drives the nanomotor into deep cartilage. These findings establish active-matrix traversal as a strategy for microenvironment-directed therapy in OA and other diffusion-limited inflammatory tissues.

Article.Title: Structural and biochemical insight into allosteric regulation of the human 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase
Article.Authors: Wu R.; Khamrui S.; Dodatko T.; Xiang Y.; Golestanian A.; Pham N.; Kumar K.; Shi Y.; Osman R.; DeVita R.; Houten S.; Lazarus M.

The mutagenesis of this allosteric Cys 414 has marked effects on the enzyme’s conformation and activity despite being more than 12 angstrom from the active site. We find that small changes near the hinge of an enzyme can have large effects on its catalytic properties. Article.Authors: Sayed A.; Chan T.; Bolinger C.; Chauhan P.; Chakiath M.; Poortman C.; Plummer J.; Klocke B.; Nikoopour E.; Wang A.; Dadon T.; Woessner D.; Joo W.; Zinser C.; Semnani R.; Shah R.; Sabzevari H.; Brough D.; Ahmad S.

Article.Title: Upper plate structure controls nearshore subduction mechanics in Cascadia
Article.Authors: Ashraf A.; Hooft E.; Toomey D.
Article.Abstract: Along-strike upper plate heterogeneity is widely observed at subduction margins, but its direct influence on slab geometry and interseismic deformation remains debated. Here, we investigate the effect of continental crustal segmentation on nearshore subduction mechanics at the Cascadia margin. Using a high-resolution, shore-crossing 3D seismic tomography model from central to southern Oregon, we image sharp along-strike contrasts in seismic velocity associated with distinct accreted terranes. We show that the subducting slab is systematically deeper beneath the coherent, higher-velocity Siletz terrane and shallower beneath lower-velocity faulted Siletz and Franciscan terranes. Numerical simulations constrained by the tomographic velocities demonstrate that rheological contrasts, represented by viscoelastic end-member models, generate the magnitude and pattern of coastal uplift, while upper-plate density contrasts reproduce the observed variation in slab depth. These findings demonstrate that inherited upper-plate structure, despite being ignored in geodetic locking models, can exert a first-order influence on nearshore subduction mechanics by controlling the partitioning of interseismic deformation and contributing to along-strike variations in slab geometry.

Article.Authors: Liu X.; Chen W.; Qi X.; Li Q.; Yan Q.
Article.Abstract: Violet phosphorus (VP), the thermodynamically most stable allotrope among crystalline red phosphorus phases, remains challenging to synthesize due to its sluggish growth kinetics. We further proposed a complete evolutionary model for crystalline red phosphorus growth starting from amorphous red phosphorus and proceeding through transition-state molecular clusters to the final VP or fibrous phosphorus products. This model reveals that Te lowers the high kinetic barrier of VP formation by reshaping the transition-state energy landscape, rendering VP both the kinetic and thermodynamic product. This work resolves the long-standing kinetic bottleneck in VP growth and offers mechanistic insight into the polymorphic synthesis of elemental phosphorus crystals.

This protocol exhibits broad substrate scope across diverse styrenes and glycosyl donors, offering a practical and complementary platform for ketonyl C -glycoside synthesis. Mechanistic studies support a pathway merging single-electron reduction of glycosyl donors with a Kornblum-type oxidation under mildly acidic conditions, challenging the conventional view that such oxidations are restricted to basic media. Article.Title: Time-evolved hetero-alkali interphases enable long-life sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Chen M.; Ye M.; Guo X.; Li D.; Wang H.; Zhu H.
Article.Abstract: Sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries (AFSSBs) offer high energy density and improved safety, but their practical implementation is hindered by parasitic reactions between freshly plated lithium (Li) and sulfide solid electrolytes. These reactions continuously consume the limited cathode-derived Li inventory, increase interfacial impedance, and promote nonuniform Li plating and stripping. Here, sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) is incorporated into Li 5.4 PS 4.4 Cl 1.6 (LPSC) to kinetically program interphase evolution. Heat treatment initially generates a NaF/LiF-rich interphase on the LPSC surface. This fluoride-rich region chemically stabilizes the interface and suppresses direct LPSC reduction. During the early cycles, the outermost region progressively evolves into a LiF/Li 3 N-rich layer, while the NaF-containing phase becomes buried beneath the Li-rich surface region, producing a time-evolved compositional gradient. Although NaF provides effective chemical passivation, its poor Li + conductivity can impede interfacial ion transport. The subsequent formation of Li 3 N-rich domains, which exhibit substantially higher Li + conductivity than NaF, provides more favorable transport pathways, homogenizes interfacial Li + flux, and promotes uniform Li plating and stripping. This time-evolved gradient interphase therefore combines early-stage chemical stabilization and Li conservation with improved long-term ion transport kinetics, suppressing impedance growth, localized inactive Li accumulation, and filamentary shorting. Consequently, the AFSSB using the NaFSI-modified LPSC interlayer retains 77.6% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 0.2 C, whereas the cell with bare LPSC retains only 32.1% after 100 cycles. These findings establish temporally programmed gradient interphases as a general strategy for conserving active Li and stabilizing sulfide-based AFSSBs.

Article.Authors: Marras G.; Mikhailenko D.; McCammon C.; Aulbach S.; Lu Y.; Tao R.; Logvinova A.; Zedgenizov D.; Stagno V.
Article.Abstract: Kimberlite-borne eclogite xenoliths ultimately derive from ancient subducted oceanic crust. Some specimens still record the chemical and redox conditions of their igneous protoliths, allowing a view into contemporaneous convecting mantle sources. However, accurate reconstructions are limited because eclogites have been exposed to metasomatism in the subcontinental mantle for billions of years. Here, we investigated garnet and clinopyroxene inclusions, both touching and nontouching pairs, in 19 eclogitic diamonds from the Siberian craton, hence shielded from post-entrapment overprint. The reconstructed bulk composition points to basaltic oceanic crust formed from an Archaean convecting mantle region that was more oxygen-depleted than today, providing compelling evidence of redox heterogeneities in the source rocks of ancient oceanic crust.

Article.Abstract: Much remains unknown about cholera transmission dynamics in Africa. Article.Authors: de Souza M.; Bruce J.; Cros A.; Jury C.; Drury C.; Toonen R.
Article.Abstract: Coral reefs support over a quarter of marine species and nearly a billion people worldwide but are also among the ecosystems most threatened by anthropogenic impacts. There is long-standing debate about whether coral symbioses will be disrupted or respond adaptively under future ocean conditions. Using a factorial 2.5-year future-ocean mesocosm experiment across eight coral species representing the major coral lineages, we tracked symbiont community shifts within replicate fragments from the same individual coral. Some corals exhibited stochastic divergence, whereas others showed deterministic shifts in symbiont community composition. Heat stress generally reduced symbiont diversity and promoted predictable restructuring, consistent with deterministic adaptation to moderate thermal stress but stochastic accumulation of diversity under extreme conditions. We propose that adaptive and stochastic responses represent endpoints along a continuum of host-orchestrated symbiont sorting. This study bridges coral reef ecology with broader host-microbiome theory, offering an integrated perspective on how symbiotic systems may respond to environmental change.
