Article.Title: Acute degradation of Pumilio proteins reveals a biphasic posttranscriptional regulatory hierarchy in embryonic stem cell fate decision
Article.Authors: Huang Y.; Li W.; Richman H.; Liu Y.; Lin H.
Article.Abstract: Posttranscriptional regulation is critical for mammalian embryogenesis yet has been underexplored. We previously showed that RNA-binding Pumilio proteins (Pum1/2) are essential for early mouse embryogenesis and embryonic stem cell (ESC) functions. Here, using acute protein degradation systems combined with time-resolved RNA sequencing and enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation, we delineate a two-phase regulatory hierarchy modulated by Pum1/2 in mouse ESCs. The first phase, occurring within 10 h of Pum1/2 depletion, is predominantly stabilization of over 100 Pum1/2-target mRNAs, while the second phase, occurring in subsequent 66 h, propagates to over 1,000 mRNAs mostly through indirect regulatory effects. Functionally, Pum1/2 depletion delays transition from naïve to formative pluripotency and alters expression trajectories of neuroectoderm and germline genes during early differentiation. Mechanistically, Pum1/2 directly repress mRNAs encoding Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 subunits, including Suz12 , thereby potentially constraining H3K27me3 deposition at neuroectodermal gene loci. These findings establish Pum1/2 as biphasic posttranscriptional regulators of pluripotency and lineage balance.

Article.Title: Host infection selects for sRNA variants that drive bacterial social cheating
Article.Authors: Dubois Q.; Brual T.; Sprenger M.; Utzinger V.; Mercier R.; Cigna J.; Rodrigue A.; Papenfort K.; Attaiech L.; Gueguen E.
Article.Abstract: Single-nucleotide mutations in regulatory small RNAs (sRNAs) represent a largely unexplored route to social cheating during bacterial infection. Here we show that arcZ , encoding a conserved Hfq-dependent sRNA in the plant pathogen Dickeya solani , undergoes recurrent single-nucleotide mutations during potato tuber infection. Five distinct arcZ alleles define a graded series of ArcZ functional impairment in which antifungal and protease activities are progressively reduced while virulence is compromised only in a subset of alleles. All five variants gain a fitness advantage exclusively during coinfection with wild-type arcZ 1 cells. This advantage is strongest when variants are rare and declines as cheater frequency increases, ultimately correlating with reduced total bacterial productivity, the canonical signature of social cheating and a tragedy of the commons. No fitness benefit is detected in vitro . Transcriptomic profiling of five arcZ variants identifies a conserved core of 186 downregulated genes enriched in secreted and diffusible functions. Systematic genetic dissection, supported by quantitative proteomics, establishes BudAB-dependent limitation of tissue acidification as the dominant cooperative public good exploited during infection. Wild-type arcZ 1 cells divert pyruvate flux toward acetoin via the BudAB pathway, maintaining a less acidic tissue environment that sustains disease progression; arcZ variants, which show reduced expression of this pathway, benefit from the less acidic environment maintained by wild-type cells without contributing to it. These results establish pleiotropic regulatory sRNAs as a previously unrecognized class of mutational targets for the emergence of social cheaters during host infection.

Article.Title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals organizational properties of the mouse spinal cord and alterations in neuropathic pain
Article.Authors: Wang Q.; Hu Y.; Zhu Y.; Chelliah G.; Peng J.; Osei-Asante E.; Sobanko M.; Sanchez B.; Ginty D.; Zhou X.; Meltzer S.
Article.Abstract: The spinal cord integrates diverse somatosensory inputs and executes motor outputs through anatomically and functionally distinct circuits. Here, we employed spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the adult mouse spinal cord to gain insights into the organizational logic of the spinal cord. Our results reveal distinct spatial and laminar distributions of neuronal subtypes, including axial level and sex-specific differences. Many neuronal subtypes exhibit lamina-specific somatic proximities, suggesting potential regionally specific connectivity. Additionally, neuronal subtypes within the dorsal horn exhibit a wide range of predicted cell-cell communication motifs, as assessed by the spatial distribution of neuropeptide- and other ligand-receptor pairs. Finally, we identified several neuronal subtypes with altered transcriptomic states and predicted cell–cell communications in a model of neuropathic pain. This spatially resolved cellular and molecular map of the spinal cord will facilitate the decoding of circuit mechanisms underlying somatosensory and motor functions in health and disease.

Article.Title: The highly heat-inducible HspA6 and the thermolabile DnaJB5 are potent regulators of heat shock transcription factor 1 activity
Article.Authors: Koch M.; Huo Y.; Kmiecik S.; Lenz S.; Mayer M.
Article.Abstract: In response to proteotoxic stress the central regulator of the heat shock response (HSR) in mammalian cells, Hsf1, trimerizes, binds DNA, and drives transcription of heat shock genes. We previously showed that Hsc70 (HspA8) assisted by its J-domain protein (JDP) cochaperone DnaJB1 dissociates Hsf1 from DNA by monomerizing the trimeric Hsf1 and thereby attenuates the HSR. Whether this feedback mechanism is specific to the HspA8–DnaJB1 pair or instead reflects a broader, isoform- and JDP-selective Hsp70 network controlling Hsf1 remained unresolved. Here, we demonstrate that of all cytonuclear Hsp70s the highly heat-inducible HspA6 is most efficient in monomerizing Hsf1 in the presence of DnaJB1 and of all cytonuclear class A and class B JDPs, only DnaJB1, DnaJB4, and DnaJB5 assist in Hsf1 monomerization. Whereas cooperation of HspA6 and HspA8 with DnaJB1 and DnaJB4 absolutely depends on Hsp70s’ C-terminal glutamate-glutamate-valine-glutamate (EEVD)-motif, cooperation with DnaJB5 does not. Consistent with these data, overproduction of EEVD-deleted HspA8 and HspA6 down-regulate the HSR in HeLa cells. DnaJB5 knockdown reduces HspA8–Hsf1 interaction under nonstress conditions revealing DnaJB5 as major targeting factor for HspA8 binding to Hsf1. On temperature upshift DnaJB5 partially unfolds and partitions into insoluble cell fractions, suggesting it is a thermosensor that allows for increased Hsf1 activity by reducing HspA8’s ability to monomerize Hsf1. During ongoing heat shock, upregulated HspA6 and HspA8 then limit the HSR presumably targeted by heat-induced DnaJB1. HspA6 knock-down and overproduction in HeLa cells suggest that HspA6 functions in preventing an overshoot of the HSR.

Article.Title: RNA and proteins joined up at the origins of life: Persistence is the point
Article.Authors: Swailem M.; Dill K.
Article.Abstract: What drove nucleic acids (NA) into functional associations with proteins (PR) at the origins of life? We reason from polymer physics and the Central Dogma that the fitness value of cooperating through a division of labor—NA for replication fidelity and PR for functional fitness—is much higher than for either polymer alone. Our model shows a Pareto Front, where NA and PR can bootstrap each other to achieve autocatalytic cooperativity toward biology.

Article.Abstract: The formation of plant cell walls underpins morphogenesis, growth, and development of all plants. Article.Title: Stereodynamical control of a four-atom reaction: HD + OH → D + H <sub>2</sub> O
Article.Authors: Du T.; Liu S.; Huang Z.; Zhang Y.; Wang Y.; Zhang Z.; Xiao C.; Zhang D.; Yang X.
Article.Abstract: To date, studies of differential steric effect in reactive collisions have been limited to atom + molecule systems. How stereodynamics is affected when the other reactant is also a molecule remains an open question. Here, we present a combined high-resolution crossed-beam scattering and full-dimensional quantum dynamical study of the HD ( v = 1, j = 2) + OH → D + H 2 O reaction, in which the HD molecular axis was initially prepared either parallel or perpendicular to the relative velocity using the stimulated Raman pumping scheme. The OH reactant was unpolarized and in its ground vibrational state, with a rotational temperature of ~85 K in the experiment, and was restricted to the ground rovibrational state in the theory. Pronounced stereodynamic effects are observed in both the backward scattering intensity and the product angular distributions. Detailed analysis of scattering wavefunctions reveals that the initial m = ±2 states access a noncoplanar dynamical transition state, distinct from that accessed by m = 0 ( m denotes the projection of j along the direction of relative velocity). The nonzero dihedral angle, a geometric degree of freedom absent in triatomic reactions, leads to reduced reactivity and enhances sideward scattering for the perpendicular configuration, while leaving the product rovibrational state distributions essentially unchanged. In addition, the alignment of the HD rotational angular momentum is preserved in the rotational direction of the product H 2 O.

Article.Title: A trefoil knot mimic and multiple pore states define the mechanism of a split-shell Tc toxin
Article.Authors: Sitsel O.; Bader R.; Ng’ang’a P.; Günther P.; Kerkmann L.; Kroczek L.; Belyy A.; Obergfäll D.; Janning P.; Raunser S.
Article.Abstract: Toxin complex (Tc) toxins are among the largest virulence factors secreted by pathogenic bacteria, operating via a sophisticated injection mechanism that translocates cytotoxic effectors into host cells. While most structural and mechanistic studies have focused on fused-shell Tc toxins such as PTC3 from Photorhabdus luminescens , the structurally distinct split-shell toxins remain poorly understood. Here we report cryoelectron microscopy structures of the split-shell Yersinia entomophaga Tc holotoxin (YenTc) in multiple conformational states at resolutions of 2.6 to 3.7 Å. We show that the chitinase subunit YenChi2 is essential for shell expression and stabilizes the N terminus of the shell subunit YenA1 in the prepore state. Our structures also reveal the first trefoil knot mimic in Tc toxins, which serves the dual function of stabilizing the linker domain and holding the two halves of the split shell together. We further describe three distinct pore states: the conventional pore state, an inverted pore state in which the shell rotates 180° around a hinge in YenA2, and a lollipop pore state induced at alkaline pH in which the YenA1-YenChi2 subcomplex fully dissociates from the channel. Strikingly, all three pore states also manifest in the TcA pentamer of P. luminescens PTC3, indicating that they represent a general but previously undescribed feature of Tc toxin pore formation. Taken together, our results establish a mechanistic framework for split-shell Tc toxins and expose a dynamic, multilevel intoxication pathway that may apply broadly to Tc toxins.

Article.Title: N-terminal integrity governs heptamer assembly and maturation in a mosquito innexin hemichannel
Article.Authors: Kawaguchi S.; Nakano T.; Hirano H.; Watanabe M.; Suzuki S.; Nishikawa K.; Fujiyoshi Y.; Oshima A.
Article.Abstract: Nonchordate gap junction channels are formed by innexins, yet the structures and subunit assembly mechanisms of insect innexins remain unknown. We determined cryoelectron microscopy structures of AGAP001487, an innexin from the malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae , reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs. The wild-type protein forms a rotationally symmetric heptameric hemichannel with an ordered N-terminal ring stabilized by intersubunit hydrogen bonds. Whereas deletion of a single N-terminal residue preserves channel activity, removal of two or more residues markedly impairs function. Consistent with these functional defects, the structure lacking two N-terminal residues exhibits disrupted rotational symmetry, extensive N-terminal disorder, pore collapse, and altered pore–lipid interactions. In addition, two-dimensional class averages revealed a minor population of hexameric particles, consistent with a potential assembly intermediate. Together, these structures support a stepwise assembly pathway in which intersubunit hydrogen bonding stabilizes N-terminal ring formation as a maturation step leading to a fully symmetric heptameric channel. Our findings identify N-terminal integrity as a critical determinant of oligomer maturation and channel function and provide mechanistic insight into how defined oligomeric assemblies are established in large-pore channel families.

Article.Title: Leaf hydraulic and photosynthetic traits mediate forest-scale resource use efficiencies across the continental United States
Article.Authors: Zhao B.; Sack L.; De Deurwaerder H.; Medeiros C.; Vinod N.; Browne M.; Wood J.; Cushman K.; Shevliakova E.; Malyshev S.; Ongjoco A.; Trugman A.; Orwig D.; McKeown C.; Zailaa J.; Johnson D.; Magee L.; McMahon S.; Shue J.; Schafer K.; Burns S.; Blanken P.; Detto M.
Article.Abstract: Temperate forests play a critical role in global carbon cycling and other ecosystem services, yet their resilience to climatic stresses remains uncertain. We combined physiology, community composition, flux data, and modeling to test a functional trait-based approach to predict forest ecosystem processes. For eight U.S. forests spanning broad precipitation and temperature gradients, we scaled up key leaf functional traits—maximum carboxylation velocity of Rubisco ( V c , m a x ), maximum leaf hydraulic conductance ( K l , m a x ), and turgor loss point (that is, wilting point, π t l p ) to predict gross primary productivity, light-use efficiency, standard and intrinsic water-use efficiency (WUE and iWUE), and their sensitivities to soil drought. In multiple regressions, ecosystem processes were strongly associated with community-weighted mean (CWM) trait values: enhanced productivity was linked with high V c , m a x ¯ , K l , m a x ¯ and π t l p ¯ , whereas high WUE and iWUE were linked with low K l , m a x ¯ and high π t l p ¯ . The CWM functional traits also influenced the sensitivity of ecosystem processes to soil moisture. A causal role of functional traits in driving ecosystem processes alongside climate was supported by parameterizing the LM4.1 vegetation model with CWM functional traits. This study highlights the important role of functional traits in determining forest responses to climate-driven water stress at a continental scale.

Article.Title: Intensification of compound wind drought and heatwave events under climate change
Article.Authors: Qu M.; Shen L.; Yang X.; Wan F.; Zhong H.; Wu S.
Article.Abstract: Compound wind drought and heatwave (WDHW) events, defined as the co-occurrence of low wind speeds and high temperatures, pose growing risks to future power system stability. Yet their future evolution and underlying physical drivers remain poorly constrained. Using daily output from 27 downscaled CMIP6 models (~25 km), we identify a widespread intensification of these compound events over global land areas. Across the low- to high-CO 2 scenarios, global event frequency is projected to increase by 100 to 750% by 2100, with event duration lengthening by 80 to 300%. Mechanistically, this intensification is mainly driven by thermodynamic warming and widespread wind stilling, and further amplified regionally by enhanced climate variability and strengthened wind–temperature coupling associated with poleward jet streams. Applying an emergent-constraint framework that links observed historical trends to future projections can reduce intermodel variance by 10 to 40% at both global and regional scales. These results provide a physically grounded assessment of future compound WDHW risks, with direct implications for climate-impact assessment and energy-system planning.

Article.Title: Structural basis of hypervariable region 1 dynamics on HCV envelope glycoproteins in immune evasion
Article.Authors: Hung S.; Koide Y.; Chen F.; Lee Y.; Ueno L.; Giang E.; Wilson I.; Zhu J.; Stanfield R.; Law M.
Article.Abstract: The hypervariable region 1 (HVR1) of the hepatitis C virus E1E2 glycoprotein plays a crucial role in immune evasion through rapid mutation and shielding of conserved neutralizing epitopes. Despite its important role, the structural properties of HVR1 remain poorly understood, particularly how its conformation influences shielding mechanisms and receptor recognition. To date in all published E1E2 or E2 structures, the C-terminal part of HVR1 (394 to 411) remains unresolved. Using neutralizing antibody (nAb) RM1-38, which targets C-terminal HVR1 (residues 399 to 409), we investigated the folding, positioning, flexibility, and shielding function of the RM1-38 epitope, or antigenic site 399 (AS399), on HVR1 by X-ray crystallography and negative-stain electron microscopy (nsEM). The crystal structure of RM1-38 Fab with the HVR1 AS399 peptide, combined with mutagenesis analysis, delineated the molecular basis of its strain-specific recognition and neutralization. nsEM and competition enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay revealed that HVR1 exhibits pronounced conformational flexibility even in the presence of other nAbs bound to E1E2. Virus neutralization assays using a combination of RM1-38 and broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) demonstrated antagonistic effects of RM1-38 with the bnAbs. Furthermore, RM1-38 reduced E1E2 binding to cells expressing the scavenger receptor SR-BI, an HVR1-dependent receptor, but did not affect binding to CD81 tetraspanin. Together, these findings support a model in which HVR1 functions as a dynamic shield, where its conformational plasticity contributes to both receptor engagement and evasion of humoral immunity in persistent infection.

Article.Title: Isotopically heavy carbon in the core
Article.Authors: Moussallam Y.; Grewal D.; Georgeais G.; Lee H.; Rose-Koga E.; Lerner A.; Holman B.; Wallace P.; Gauer Pasqualon N.; Anderson O.; Jackson M.
Article.Abstract: Constraining the origin of Earth’s carbon requires knowing the isotopic composition of the core—a geochemical signature long presumed to be beyond observation for the planet’s largest carbon reservoir. Here, we report high-precision δ 13 C measurements from Hawaiian plume melt inclusions entrapped before significant degassing and sampling distinct mantle sources. Melt inclusions from shield-stage lavas, interpreted to sample the plume’s central axis, inferred to be rooted in the core–mantle boundary thermal boundary layer, converge toward a primary δ 13 C signature of –1 ± 2‰. In contrast, melt inclusions from rejuvenated-stage lavas, derived from entrained mantle at the plume’s periphery, record a normal mantle source signature of –7 ± 2‰. We interpret the uniquely 13 C-rich shield-stage signature as the isotopic fingerprint of carbon exchanged from the core into the mantle. Our results point to 13 C-rich carbonaceous chondrites as the primary source of Earth’s carbon.

Article.Title: Generating interesting scientific ideas using knowledge graphs and LLMs: Evaluations with 100 research group leaders
Article.Authors: Gu X.; Krenn M.
Article.Abstract: The rapid growth of scientific literature makes it increasingly challenging for researchers to identify novel and impactful ideas, especially across disciplines. Modern AI systems offer new opportunities for scientific ideation, but how compelling are AI-generated ideas, and how can their quality be improved? Here, we introduce SCIMUSE , which generates personalized research ideas using a knowledge graph of 58 million papers and a large language model (LLM). A central focus of this work is to understand how interesting these ideas are. Therefore, we conducted a large-scale evaluation in which more than 100 research group leaders—spanning the natural sciences to the humanities—rated over 4,400 personalized ideas according to their level of interest. Overall, expert ratings were modest (mean 2.40 on a 5-point scale, most common rating 1), while 24.9% of ideas were rated 4 or 5. We find that supplying concept pairs selected using the knowledge graph does not improve expert-rated interest over a titles-only GPT baseline. High-citation-predicted pairs even showed a weak tendency (1.94 σ ) toward lower interest than random pairs. Nevertheless, graph features can be used to control properties of ideas, and, using this unique evaluation dataset, we show that idea interest can be predicted with both a supervised neural network based on graph features and a zero-shot ranking approach based on an LLM. Our work provides an AI methodology for generating scientific ideas and a large-scale interdisciplinary expert evaluation, paving the way to study and improve difficult-to-measure metrics such as expert-perceived scientific interestingness.

Article.Title: A replaceable soma enables negative senescence in harvester ants
Article.Authors: Cole B.; Wiernasz D.
Article.Abstract: Most vertebrates and insects undergo senescence: as they age, their rate of mortality increases while reproduction declines. We present data from a 34-y study on 3,285 colonies of known age in the western harvester ant, Pogonomyrmex occidentalis, that show the reverse pattern, negative senescence, in which mortality decreases and reproduction increases with age. Theoretical models have identified indeterminate growth and a lack of reproductive cost to growth as the key traits favoring the evolution of negative senescence. Ant colonies continue to grow throughout their lifetime, leading to older colonies being larger on average. We found no evidence of a tradeoff between colony growth and reproduction: growth and reproduction were positively correlated, a synergism that may favor continued investment in growth. Harvester ants occupy a temporally variable environment that shapes investment in reproduction. At the population level, greater reproduction in 1 y does not lead to higher numbers of new colonies in the following year. Environmental unpredictability decouples reproduction from recruitment and selects for an extended reproductive lifespan, a trait that parallels changes in aging. We discuss the features that harvester ant colonies share with other organisms to identify functionally homologous mechanisms for avoiding senescence, as well as those traits that are specific to highly eusocial species.

Article.Title: Rapid vaterite-mediated shell repair for acid-induced damage in a deep-sea mussel
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Jia Z.; Kiel S.; Liu Y.; Xu C.; Lu Y.; Wang X.; Li N.; Li J.; Zhang S.
Article.Abstract: Mollusks are able to secrete and repair the most diverse and complex calcareous tissues in the animal kingdom, yet the detailed molecular mechanisms of these biomineralization processes, especially for the deep-sea calcifiers, remain to be elucidated. Here, using an in situ experiment, we report a repair mechanism for acid-induced shell damage via biologically mediated vaterite formation in the deep-sea cold-seep mussel Gigantidas haimaensis . Interestingly, the mussels secreted and recrystallized amorphous calcium carbonate into vaterite to seal the acid-induced dissolution porosities within 30 h. Calcium and nucleation substrates were potentially supplied by the mantle, including calcium-binding proteins and hydroxyapatite. Calcium then reacted with readily available carbonate in the extrapallial space, whose precipitation can be promoted by the nucleation substrates. This rapid repair mechanism is likely an advantage in the habitat of these mussels, which are characterized by pulsed acidification events from the seeping fluids. Furthermore, our finding expands our understanding of the diverse biomineralization mechanisms by which mollusks maintain their protective shells.

Article.Title: Millennial-scale variability in Greenland dust provenance during Dansgaard–Oeschger events of the last glacial period
Article.Authors: Ro S.; Han C.; Han Y.; Hur S.; Ro C.; Steffensen J.; Svensson A.; Fischer H.; Burke A.; Lee K.; Lee A.; Hong S.
Article.Abstract: Greenland ice-core records show an approximately 15-fold increase in dust concentration during cold stadial periods compared to warmer interstadial periods in the last glacial period (LGP). While multiple regions including East Asian deserts and the Sahara have been suggested as potential source areas (PSAs) for Greenland dust, millennial-scale variability of their relative contributions associated with Dansgaard–Oeschger climatic fluctuations during the LGP remains poorly constrained. To address this, we investigate high-resolution (~800 y) Pb and Sr isotopic, mineralogical, and geochemical records from the North Greenland Eemian Ice Drilling ice-core samples covering the entire LGP. Comparison with PSAs suggests that East Asian deserts remained the dominant contributors to Greenland dust throughout the LGP, but contributions from the Sahara increased during stadial intervals. This shift likely reflects climate-driven changes in atmospheric circulation patterns responsible for transporting dust to Greenland. Our findings provide insights into the relationship between dust cycle dynamics and abrupt climate changes on millennial timescales during the LGP.

Article.Title: Active and passive crowding pathways drive topological and mechanical divergence in myoblasts
Article.Authors: Huo Y.; Xu H.; Guo K.; Zhao Y.; Doss B.; Zhou Q.; Wang Y.; Ju X.; Han E.; Huang C.; Hsia K.
Article.Abstract: Cell crowding is closely associated with many physiological processes, yet our understanding of crowded tissue organization has been developed largely in polygonal epithelia, leaving intrinsically anisotropic cell collectives comparatively poorly understood. Using C2C12 myoblasts, we investigate this problem by decoupling the final crowded state from the pathway taken to reach it, comparing active crowding, arising from cell proliferation during incubation, with passive crowding, imposed directly through high-density seeding. Unlike polygonal epithelia, crowded myoblast monolayers do not undergo epithelial-like kinetic arrest: cell motion is strongly suppressed, yet local rearrangements persist and packing remains structurally irregular. However, the two crowding pathways generate distinct collective states, differing in nematic order and junctional coupling. By contrasting these states, we reveal a close interplay among cell geometry, intercellular coupling, tissue-scale nematic order, and force transmission. This mechanical coordination ultimately shapes physiological function, preserving sensitivity to topographical cues and promoting efficient, spatially organized myogenic fusion. These findings broaden the physical framework of collective organization in active matter and establish key mechanical principles for in vitro tissue engineering.

Article.Title: History-dependent droplet friction driven by contact-line aging
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Lee Y.; Hayashi K.; Zhang H.; Miyata K.; Liu J.; Hosomi T.; Yanagida T.; Fukuma T.; Mouterde T.; Shiomi J.
Article.Abstract: The motion of liquid droplets on solid surfaces is commonly described by contact-line friction, which is generally assumed to increase monotonically with instantaneous velocity. However, such a velocity-only description cannot explain why static droplet friction can exceed dynamic friction or why contact-line friction can become velocity-weakening. Here, we demonstrate that contact-line friction depends jointly on sliding velocity and contact history. Using self-assembled alkylsilane monolayers as molecularly tunable substrates and ionic liquids as low-volatility model liquids, we observe pronounced history-dependent strengthening of contact-line friction on solid-like monolayers, manifested as time-enhanced static friction and velocity-weakening dynamic friction. Both effects are progressively suppressed as the surface is tuned toward a more liquid-like state with a lower density of pinning defects, either by reducing the monolayer chain length or by increasing temperature. We attribute this behavior to nanoscopic contact-line aging, whereby contact-line segments thermally fluctuate and progressively occupy interfacial defects, leading to a progressive increase in contact-line pinning. An aging-based model quantitatively captures the history-dependent onset friction and the low-velocity friction dynamics in our system, while similar logarithmic strengthening across diverse liquid–substrate systems suggests broader applicability of the constitutive framework. These findings establish the coupled effects of contact history and sliding velocity on contact-line friction, extending dynamic wetting beyond velocity-only descriptions and providing a physical basis for controlling macroscopic droplet transport through nanoscale interfacial design.

Article.Title: Optimal scenario design for climate emulation
Article.Authors: Womack C.; Bouabid S.; Sokolov A.; Salunke P.; Flierl G.; Eastham S.; Selin N.
Article.Abstract: As deep learning for physical systems continues to grow in popularity, efforts to improve generalizability have primarily focused on designing architectures that embed physical constraints. However, for machine-learning surrogate climate models (emulators), we show that the low structural diversity in existing scenarios commonly used to generate training data places a ceiling on predictive skill. Here, we examine whether training datasets themselves can be optimized to improve generalization. We introduce a method to create datasets that produce emulators capable of generalizing to new, structurally different scenarios absent from the training data. We use a differentiable simple climate model (SCM) to calculate the sensitivity of emulator loss to perturbations in the training data, iteratively updating the training data to maximize emulator skill. For an SCM, an emulator trained on one scenario optimized in this fashion outperforms an emulator trained on six standard Scenario Model Intercomparison Project (ScenarioMIP) pathways. We achieve this higher predictive skill despite training on a smaller dataset, finding that our emulator successfully isolates distinct physical behaviors of different climate forcing agents (e.g., greenhouse gases vs. aerosols) without single-forcing runs. We then demonstrate that scenarios optimized using an SCM, when used to drive an intermediate-complexity climate model, produce a training dataset that yields a more skillful emulator than training on ScenarioMIP outputs. Our results suggest that, in the compute-constrained environment of running full-scale climate models, generating a small number of dynamically rich scenarios provides greater marginal value for emulation and characterizing system responses than expanding the suite of traditional emissions pathways.

Article.Authors: Tian W.; Qiu Y.; Wang W.; Xing X.; Feng Y.; Xu C.; Liu L.; Tie L.; Wei Y.; Lu D.

Article.Authors: Seidler L.; Jannasch L.; Westendorff S.; Nieder A.

Article.Title: Belonging to a group with shared ideology leads preschool children to resist revising their beliefs despite disconfirming evidence
Article.Authors: Finiasz Z.; Kushnir T.
Article.Abstract: Shared beliefs can bring people together but may motivate prioritizing group affiliation over facts supported by evidence. Indeed, affiliation with a group whose membership is tied to shared beliefs (i.e., ideology-based groups) has led adults to endorse and maintain false beliefs. We demonstrate that this resistance to revise beliefs that form the basis of group membership has its origins in childhood. In three studies, 4- to 5-y-old children ( N = 192 ) endorse a claim about a novel causal system and subsequently join a group that shares their endorsement. Children randomly assigned to a focal Belief-contingent condition learn that their membership in the group is based on this claim, framed as a shared belief. We contrast this with conditions where group members hold the same shared belief, but this belief is not a condition for group membership (Experiments 1, 2, and 3), and where group members hold to the same claim framed as a “guess” (Experiment 2). After joining a group, children see evidence that their initial endorsement was incorrect and then have an opportunity to revise based on the new information. Only when group membership was contingent on the shared belief did children hold on to (and act on—Experiment 3) their initial incorrect endorsement. These findings suggest that the affiliative power of ideology has developmental roots; even in our earliest years, affiliative motives override truth-seeking and rationality. Thus, our early-emerging motive to identify with groups may underlie later cases of evidence denial and polarization.

Article.Authors: Tomasto-Cagigao E.; Reindel M.; Cuadrado J.; Lund Valle M.; Kassadjikova K.; Harkins K.; Fehren-Schmitz L.
Article.Abstract: Cyclopia, is an extremely rare congenital condition resulting from severe disruption of early brain and facial development and is typically lethal before or shortly after birth. We examined two infants buried together in a Middle Nasca-period cemetery in Jauranga, southern Peru. One infant, JA13A, exhibited a single median orbit and other skeletal features diagnostic of cyclopia, whereas JA13B showed no comparable congenital variations. Ancient DNA revealed an extra copy of chromosome 13 in JA13A, identifying trisomy 13 as the likely cause. The two maternally unrelated individuals were interred together in a ceramic vessel, a mortuary treatment well documented for Nasca children. By integrating skeletal, genomic, and archaeological evidence, this case provides a view of a severe congenital condition and its mortuary treatment in a past society.

Article.Title: Coevolution of social network structure and life history in toothed whales
Article.Authors: Walmsley S.; Ringen E.; Gero S.; Jaeggi A.; Whitehead H.
Article.Abstract: Toothed whales offer a 34 My-long natural experiment for the evolution of complex mammalian societies. However, quantitative comparative analyses of social structure in these species are lacking. Here, we draw on existing social network analyses to compare social structure across toothed whales. We consider published measures of two social network traits across all toothed whales: modularity ( Q ), which captures divisions or “cliques” in a social community, and social differentiation ( S ), which estimates how much whales vary in their relationships—whether they associate equally with others or form special bonds with specific individuals. Combining these with a recently published database of life history traits, we applied phylogenetic multilevel models with the objective of exploring the origins of social network structure. We identified 98 measures of modularity and 89 measures of social differentiation from 23 toothed whale species. Social network structure was more similar among closely related species (showing strong phylogenetic signal), despite substantial intraspecific variability. Toothed whales with longer lifespans and larger bodies tended to form more modular social networks, as did those where males were proportionally larger than females. Similar but weaker patterns were found between life history traits and social differentiation. Results from causal coevolutionary models provide preliminary evidence that social structure has been both a leader and follower of changes in life history. Our findings reveal the correlated evolution of social network structure and life history traits in toothed whales, shedding new light on the origins of social relationships.

Article.Title: Rare recovery of reassortants between contemporary clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 viruses and human influenza A viruses in vitro
Article.Authors: Ankerhold J.; Kessler S.; Petric P.; Jakob C.; Beer M.; Schwemmle M.; Reuther P.; Ciminski K.
Article.Abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) pandemics can arise when animal-derived and human-adapted IAVs exchange genome segments; however, whether contemporary clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 viruses can generate viable reassortants with human IAVs is unclear. Here, we tested the reassortment potential of two clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 viruses with human-adapted H1N1 and H3N2 IAVs using a biosafe reassortment system. Across multiple coinfection conditions, we genotyped 2,698 plaque-purified viral clones and recovered 20 reassortants (0.74%). Polymerase assays identified human IAV subunits, particularly H1N1 PA or H3N2 PB2, that increased H5N1 polymerase activity. Article.Title: Sub-ice thermal gradients strongly influence winter depth use of an iconic cold-water fish
Article.Authors: Shi L.; Wells M.; Ridgway M.; Dunlop E.; McMeans B.; Fisk A.; Blanchfield P.; Cooke S.; Rennie M.; Young J.; Middel T.; Trumpickas J.; Hrenchuk L.; Hlina B.; Guzzo M.
Article.Abstract: In a thermally stratified lake, freshwater fish select habitats that align with their thermal preferences. While most studies of dimictic lakes have focused on habitat selection during summer stratification, less attention has been given to winter when inverse thermal stratification occurs with water temperatures between 0 to 4 °C. Our results show that winter thermal stratifications vary considerably among lakes. Much of the variation in winter depth use by the cold-water predator, Lake Trout ( Salvelinus namaycush ), can be explained by the depth of the 2 °C isotherm. Selection ratios further support preferential use of this thermal boundary after accounting for habitat availability. Larger, shallower, and windier lakes tend to exhibit colder mean temperatures near 0 °C and deeper isotherms, typically within the 1 to 2 °C range. In contrast, deeper or more sheltered lakes maintained warmer temperatures close to 4 °C and a shallower 2 °C isotherm. Using multiyear acoustic telemetry of Lake Trout from 11 different lakes, we found that in warmer lakes with depth-averaged temperatures above 2 °C, Lake Trout used thermal habitat averaging 2.6 ± 0.6 °C, which occurred in relatively shallow depths (0.1 to 11.3 m). In contrast, in the one large, shallow lake studied, where maximum water temperatures were below 2 °C, Lake Trout occupied the deepest waters during winter (16.8 to 26.4 m) and experienced average temperatures of 1.5 ± 0.4 °C. Applying our model to 877,927 Canadian and Alaskan lakes predicted a roughly even split between warm and cold winter conditions; however, 73% of the 66,500 known Lake Trout lakes exhibited warmer winter conditions, where Lake Trout would occupy the upper water column during winter.

Article.Title: A signal convention in natural chimpanzee communication
Article.Authors: Valet A.; Moore R.; Bortolato T.; Kleinhause G. Gedalyahou T.; de Witasse-Thézy A.; Girard-Buttoz C.; Wittig R.; Crockford C.
Article.Abstract: Human language relies on conventional signals that are arbitrary, stable, and socially transmitted. Whether other animals exhibit meaning-based communicative conventions is virtually unknown. Using a quasi-experimental design, we investigated this in chimpanzee unvoiced calls (UCs), such as acoustic raspberries, known to show usage variation. We collected audio and contextual data in 91 chimpanzees (0 to 55 y), across eight wild and captive groups that differed in the presence or absence of adult role models. Communities with role models emitted UCs in one dominant context, which remained stable over years and from first utterances in development (1 to 2 y old). In contrast, groups without role models displayed highly variable, unstable UC usage across contexts and years. This contextual variation could not be explained by age or by a shared emotional valence, and individuals could use different UC forms within the same context, suggesting a decoupling between the signal form and usage. Together, these findings provide evidence that chimpanzee UCs meet key criteria for a signal convention: arbitrary signal–usage mappings, social transmission, and stability within communities. These findings demonstrate that conventionalized communication is not a uniquely human feature but can also emerge through social learning mechanisms in other animals’ natural communication.

Article.Title: Host and anatomical filters prevent microbiome convergence in avian scavengers
Article.Authors: Margalida A.; Castellano-Hinojosa A.; Oliva-Vidal P.; Boutin S.; María Martínez J.; Braun M.; Sauer-Gürth H.; Schulze-Hagen K.; Wink M.
Article.Abstract: How host-associated microbiomes assemble under intense environmental microbial exposure remains a central question in microbial ecology. Vultures represent a unique natural system because these species differ markedly in feeding ecology and carcass use. We characterized bacterial communities across four anatomical niches (facial, buccal, tracheal, and cloacal) in 155 individuals spanning all four European obligate vulture species (subfamily Gypaetinae: Gypaetus barbatus, Neophron percnopterus, and Aegypiinae: Aegypius monachus and Gyps fulvus ) and the facultative scavenger Milvus milvus . Microbiome composition was jointly structured by host species and anatomical niche, with host identity explaining more variation than anatomical compartment and a significant interaction indicating that interspecific differentiation depended on body site. Each niche supported distinct bacterial assemblages and core microbiomes: Cloacal communities were enriched in anaerobic gut-associated taxa, whereas facial and tracheal communities contained more environmental and respiratory-associated bacteria. Host-specific taxonomic signatures persisted within anatomical niches despite recurrent exposure to the same carrion-associated microbial pool. Age further influenced community composition, whereas sex had little detectable effect. The facultative scavenger showed the same broad anatomical compartmentalization observed in obligate scavengers, although taxonomic signatures differed among species. Thus, sustained exposure to a shared, microbially rich resource was insufficient to produce a common scavenger microbiome. Instead, microbiome assembly reflected hierarchical filtering by host identity, anatomical environment, and ontogeny. These findings distinguish microbial exposure from microbial persistence, establishing avian scavengers as a natural model for understanding how host-associated communities remain differentiated, despite recurrent exposure to shared environmental microbial reservoirs across ecological and anatomical scales in vertebrate hosts.

Article.Title: Bayesian knockoff filter for controlling false discovery rate
Article.Authors: Gu J.; Yin G.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: In many scientific fields, researchers are interested in discovering features with substantial effects on the response from a large number of candidate features while controlling the proportion of false discoveries. By incorporating the knockoff procedure in a Bayesian framework, we develop the Bayesian knockoff filter (BKF) for selecting important features. The BKF is built upon a tight upper bound for the posterior probability of the null hypothesis, which is derived under the Bayesian “flip-sign” property implied by our procedure. In contrast to the standard knockoff methods in the frequentist paradigm, we allow the knockoff variables to be generated in every iteration of the Markov chain Monte Carlo procedure, which removes the unwanted variability of the single-knockoff generation (knockoff is typically generated only once before the model fitting). Compared with multi-knockoffs, the BKF is more principled and natural in incorporating side information through prior distributions under a fully Bayesian framework. We further develop an e-value BKF approach to theoretically guarantee the frequentist false discovery rate (FDR) control. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real data demonstrate the advantages of the BKF over existing knockoff methods and Bayesian variable selection approaches, i.e., the BKF possesses comparable power, yields a lower FDR and more stable selection sets.

Article.Title: Predicting key viral mutations from within-host deep sequencing data
Article.Authors: Su S.; Tang Y.; Li Q.; Cao L.; Zhang Y.; Lou J.; Zheng H.; Liu C.; Sun Y.; Li J.; Zhang Z.; Zee B.; Cheung P.; Chen Z.; Chan R.; Wu W.; Yu J.; Yen H.; Gu H.; Man Poon L.; Hui D.; Hiscox J.; Mok C.; Wang M.
Article.Abstract: Rapid SARS-CoV-2 evolution drives continuous epidemic waves, harming vaccine protection and exerting heavy burden to population health. Predicting virus evolution holds the key for current and future medical countermeasures against infectious diseases by allowing well-matching vaccines and timely epidemic response. However, due to its high genetic diversity, fast transmissibility and evolutionary rate, accurate and timely prediction of SARS-CoV-2 evolution remains a challenge. To address this, we developed a computational framework, Beth-2, to predict key mutations of SARS-CoV-2 through analyzing within-host viral genome deep sequencing data. We leveraged the early fitness signals of variants exhibited within-host and their fitness pattern between-host to infer the emerging mutations with fitness potential. In retrospective data validation, 98.6% of the key SARS-CoV-2 mutations on receptor binding domain could be detected by our model with a median lead time of 9 mo before they reached predominance at population level. Among the 26 prospectively predicted mutations, 69% of them exhibited significantly enhanced transmissibility and five showed significant immune escape from plasma of subjects who received COVID-19 mRNA vaccine collected 6 mo after the prediction time. The mutations predicted by Beth-2 that are functionally enhanced include F456L, the defining mutation of multiple current circulating lineages, including KP.3, NB.1.8.1, and XFG. The model captures mutations of high fitness potential under the natural immune environment of host and is applicable to other pathogens. The framework can be implemented along with the existing genome surveillance network and offers an efficient and effective instrument for vaccine preparation and epidemic response.

Article.Title: Methionine restriction inhibits EZH2-mediated GSDMD methylation to promote pyroptosis in prostate cancer
Article.Authors: Liu S.; Ming D.; Xu Y.; Li B.; Shi M.; Xi S.; Cui J.; Yang J.; Xiong X.; He S.; Wang S.; Wang D.; Zhang J.; Weng H.; Zeng X.; Yuan S.
Article.Abstract: EZH2 is frequently overexpressed in solid tumors, yet the clinical efficacy of its inhibitors remains limited, highlighting an urgent need to elucidate their cytotoxic mechanisms. We revealed that EZH2 inhibition triggered GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis in prostate cancer cells. Clinical specimens showed an inverse correlation between EZH2 levels and cleaved GSDMD (GSDMD N-terminal, GSDMD-N) levels, reinforcing its role as a negative regulator of GSDMD activation. Article.Title: Diffusion in a d -dimensional rough potential
Article.Authors: Jeffries J.; Mendoza Reyes E.; Abdeljawad F.; Daw M.; Martinez E.
Article.Abstract: The prediction of diffusion in solids is necessary to understand the microstructure evolution in materials out of equilibrium. Although one can reasonably predict diffusive transport coefficients using atomistic methods, these approaches can be very computationally expensive. In this work, we develop an analytical model for the diffusivity in a noisy solid solution in an arbitrary number of dimensions ( d ) using a mean first passage time analysis. We observe that roughness always decreases the diffusivity, aligning with sluggish diffusion theories in concentrated alloys, finding that an increase in diffusivity induced by alloying elements must be due to a decrease in the average activation energy, not to the noise. These analytical results are then compared with kinetic Monte Carlo simulations, which are in good quantitative agreement with the simulation data for d ≤ 5, and excellent quantitative agreement for d ≤ 3. This generalization to arbitrary dimensions has been elusive to the community since Zwanzig [R. Zwanzig, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 85 , 2029–2030 (1988)] published his seminal work on one-dimensional systems.

Article.Title: Gastruloids reveal alternative morphogenetic routes for body-axis elongation with distinct cytoskeletal dependencies
Article.Authors: Serrano Nájera G.; Delahaye A.; Steventon B.
Article.Abstract: Morphogenesis requires cells to integrate genetic and environmental information to pattern and shape tissues. Recent studies in vivo and in vitro have shown how alterations in environmental cues can induce alternative morphogenetic programs. However, what determines which morphogenetic strategy cells deploy in different environments remains unknown. Using gastruloids, a model for mammalian posterior body-axis elongation where environmental cues can be controlled in vitro, we show that substrate availability determines which force-generation strategy cells employ to build the body axis. In free-floating conditions, gastruloids self-assemble a single posterior body axis, presumably through cell–cell interactions. When plated on laminin, gastruloids acquire a flat morphology, break symmetry multiple times, and produce several independently elongating cell streams with anterior–posterior polarity through collective cell migration. On laminin, formin activity and focal adhesion-mediated traction are required for tissue elongation, yet both are functionally dispensable in free-floating conditions. Transcriptomic analysis shows that formin inhibition blocks elongation on laminin without any detectable transcriptional changes, indicating that these cytoskeletal components play primarily a mechanical role that is only required when cells engage a substrate. Furthermore, laminin biases cells toward posterior migratory fates while preserving similar Hox expression. Together, these results show that mammalian body-axis elongation can proceed through different morphogenetic modes that engage distinct mechanical effectors depending on substrate availability. These findings have implications for understanding how evolution explores morphological diversity and how tissue engineering might achieve desired forms through precise environmental control.

Article.Title: Evolutionary dynamics of collective behavior across the tree of ray-finned fishes
Article.Authors: Love J.; Nayak A.; Grassick A.; Kong L.; Henry E.; Gil M.; Fahimipour A.; Pennell M.; Hein A.
Article.Abstract: Trait evolution and lineage diversification are thought to be driven by selection on the phenotypes of individuals. However, many important phenotypes are only manifested when individuals interact. Collective behavior is one such phenotype. During collective behavior, interactions among individuals lead to emergent group-level phenotypes that can govern individual fitness. Yet, whether collective behaviors exhibit similar patterns of trait evolution to individual traits and whether these group phenotypes have influenced macroevolutionary diversification is unknown. In ray-finned fishes, the most species-rich of all vertebrate classes, many species exhibit striking displays of collective behavior in the form of collective movement. Here, we use state-of-the-art machine learning methods for text and image analysis to quantify collective movement phenotypes for 2,839 Actinopterygian fishes, comprising nearly 10% of all extant species. We find that collective movement is highly evolutionarily stable in some clades and extremely labile in others, exhibiting over 300 evolutionary transitions. Consistent with theoretical predictions, collective movement is associated with more patchy diets and higher predation pressure. Finally, we find that the evolution of collective movement coincides with an increase in net macroevolutionary diversification rate. Our analyses reveal that collective behavior is deeply intertwined with ecological and evolutionary dynamics across a vast phylogenetic scale, unlocking questions about the evolution of collective phenotypes and their role in shaping the diversity of life on Earth.

Article.Title: Coupling of structural preordering and density fluctuation: A unified picture of nucleation in metallic glasses
Article.Authors: Xu T.; Wang X.; Cao Q.; Ding S.; Liu S.; Yang K.; Zhang D.; Yang Y.; Jiang J.
Article.Abstract: Crystallization is ubiquitous in nature and technology, occurring in pharmaceuticals, biomacromolecules, polymers, metallurgy and glass formation. Yet how crystallization proceeds, particularly at its earliest stage, remains elusive. Studies on glass-forming liquids increasingly suggest that crystallization initiates in structurally preordered regions, with density fluctuations playing a secondary role, a view widely generalized from hard-sphere colloids. Here we show, across disordered metallic systems from pure elements and intermetallic compounds to glass-forming alloys, that density fluctuations and structural preordering emerge simultaneously during nucleation. This coupling reflects local atomic rearrangements in which free-volume reduction, denser packing, and bond-orientational order develop together. Our findings provide a physical basis for a unified nucleation framework for disordered materials.

Article.Title: Respiratory phase orchestrates human olfactory cortical dynamics
Article.Authors: Hathaway A.; Coleman T.
Article.Abstract: Olfaction is fundamental to perception, memory, and emotion, yet the neural basis of human odor processing remains poorly understood. We demonstrate that odor-evoked brain activity is organized by respiratory phase—not absolute time—revealing that natural breathing structures olfactory cortical dynamics. Using simultaneous nasal respiration and electroencephalography recordings in 17 participants, we delivered naturalistic odors (peppermint, oregano, and grapefruit) synchronized to individual breathing cycles. Odor presentation elicited respiratory phase-locked event-related spectral perturbations (RPL-ERSPs) in frontal and temporal regions, emerging during the first breath after stimulus onset. The most discriminative neural signatures were theta-band activity during inhalation and alpha-band activity during exhalation, patterns that were obscured in traditional time-locked analyses due to natural variability in breath duration. Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation of RPL-ERSPs achieved reliable odor detection (peppermint: AUC = 0.79; oregano: AUC = 0.67; grapefruit: AUC = 0.62), establishing that phase-locked features generalize across individuals. To connect neural responses to perceptual experience without relying on odor naming-which can be disproportionately impaired in some populations-we quantified odor recognition using free-response descriptions scored with a semantic-similarity approach. Behavioral recognition strength paralleled the neural decoding hierarchy across odors, establishing the perceptual validity of RPL-ERSPs. RPL-ERSPs revealed rapid habituation, with decoding performance declining over repeated presentations, due to selective degradation of the most informative phase-locked features. These findings establish respiratory rhythm as a temporal scaffold for human olfactory cortical processing, positioning RPL-ERSPs as a sensitive, task-free approach for assessing olfactory function. We provide an open-source, respiration-synchronized olfactometer design to enable replication and adoption.

Article.Title: Simply aging
Article.Authors: Gladyshev V.
Article.Abstract: Biological aging is complex and resists any single mechanistic narrative. This article develops a conceptual framework for aging biology through a series of brief statements on central topics in the field, with the goal of discussing aging simply, directly and accessibly. The organizing principle is that aging is a default outcome of living: because biological processes are inherently imperfect, deleterious changes (the deleteriome) accumulate over time and progressively erode functional reserve. The deleteriome provides a unifying framework for molecular damage, regulatory drift, maladaptive remodeling, and system-level failure, without reducing aging to individual genes, pathways, compartments, hallmarks, or pathologies. Evolution does not program aging; it shapes maintenance and renewal systems that oppose this trajectory with limited fidelity and unavoidable trade-offs. Aging begins during development, following an early embryonic phase of rejuvenation. Modern biomarkers make biological age imperfectly but increasingly measurable. Biological age is heterogeneous across cells, organs, and systems, modifiable by interventions and environment, and in some contexts partially reversible or resettable, although aging itself is irreversible. This model links first principles of aging to measurement, intervention, and longer-term strategies, with the goal of clarifying how substantial longevity gains might be achieved, both within and beyond existing species-level constraints.

Article.Title: Mussels possess distinct vanadium and iron storage systems for fabricating metal-reinforced adhesive fibers
Article.Authors: Jee S.; Singh N.; Merino G.; Babych M.; Tappero R.; Harrington M.
Article.Abstract: Mussels fashion a protein-based fibrous adhesive holdfast known as a byssus to tether themselves in marine habitats against crashing waves. The capacity of mussels to anchor securely is dependent on load-bearing protein-metal cross-links mediated by 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) residues coordinated to metal ions, which significantly enhance byssus mechanical properties (e.g., adhesive strength, abrasion resistance, toughness, self-healing capacity). However, the natural metal incorporation process during byssus formation remains poorly understood—a knowledge gap that limits the decades-old field of mussel-inspired materials from fulfilling its potential. Here, we investigate the natural byssus biofabrication system, the mussel foot, focusing specifically on iron and vanadium storage using a multilength scale ensemble of spectroscopic methods. Confocal Raman spectroscopy, synchrotron µ-X-ray fluorescence and µ-X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and scanning transmission electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy studies indicate that these two metals occupy separate coordination environments: vanadium storage is DOPA-based, while iron is stored in ferritin-like structures. Lacking precedence, these findings indicate that mussels evolved a catechol-based metal storage system to specifically acquire and store what is typically considered a trace metal ion in biology, which they employ subsequently to mechanically reinforce protein-based glues and coatings produced by the mussel. Beyond the biological implications, these findings have potential to transform the field of mussel-inspired materials.

Article.Title: Intuitive knowledge of object acoustics enables perceptual separation of physical variables from impact sounds
Article.Authors: Agarwal V.; Traer J.; Schwartz J.; McDermott J.
Article.Abstract: Upon hearing objects collide, humans can estimate physical attributes such as material and mass. Although the physics of sound generation is well established, the inverse problem that listeners solve—of inferring physical parameters from sound—remains poorly understood. Classical accounts posit the use of acoustic cues that correlate with physical variables but do not explain how humans might distinguish multiple concurrent physical causes. To study this problem, we measured impulse responses from hundreds of everyday objects, extracted their resonances, and used statistics of the resonances to build a probabilistic generative model of impact sounds. We then used the model to synthesize and manipulate stimuli for experiments measuring judgments of physical variables. Humans accurately judged object properties from collision sounds. However, when both of the colliding objects varied, performance was impaired if the distribution of object resonances deviated from those measured in real-world objects. The results suggest that humans have internalized the statistical regularities of real-world object acoustics, and use this knowledge to separate the acoustic contributions of the distinct objects in the world that give rise to sounds.

Article.Title: Majorana edge reconstruction and the ν = 5/2 non-Abelian thermal Hall puzzle
Article.Authors: Lotrič T.; Wang T.; Zaletel M.; Simon S.; Parameswaran S.
Article.Abstract: Pioneering thermal transport measurements on two-dimensional electron gases in high magnetic fields have demonstrated that the quantized Hall state at filling factor ν = 5/2 has a thermal Hall conductance κ quantized in half-integer multiples of κ 0 = π 2 k B 2 T / 3 h . Half-integer κ / κ 0 is a signature of neutral Majorana edge modes, in turn linked to the presence of non-Abelian anyon excitations in the bulk. However, the experimentally observed value of κ corresponds to the “PH-Pfaffian” state, in tension with numerical studies which instead favor either the Pfaffian or the AntiPfaffian. A variety of mechanisms have been invoked to explain this discrepancy, but have been either ruled out by further experiments or else involve fine-tuning. Building on density-matrix-renormalization group studies of physically realistic edges and analytic calculations of edge structure, we propose an alternative resolution of this puzzle involving an “edge reconstruction” solely involving the neutral Majorana sector of the theory. Such a Majorana edge reconstruction can “screen” a Pfaffian or AntiPfaffian bulk, so that transport signatures become indistinguishable from those of the PH-Pfaffian. We argue that this physically natural scenario is consistent with experiment.

Article.Title: Dysregulation of mechanosensing signaling in monocytes of patients with systemic sclerosis is associated with skin inflammation
Article.Authors: Chaudhary V.; Du Y.; Mishra B.; Ah Kioon M.; Ahuja P.; Ivashkiv L.; Truchetet M.; Spiera R.; Lakin K.; Gordon J.; Barrat F.
Article.Abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a severe autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by immune dysregulation and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, resulting in substantial organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Fibrosis is driven in part by infiltration of immune cells, including monocytes that become activated within fibrotic tissue. However, how the mechanical properties of fibrotic skin regulate their function remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that increased stiffness activates human monocytes through mechanosensing. Reanalysis of single cell RNA sequencing datasets revealed that skin infiltrating monocytes exhibit heightened inflammatory signatures as compared to circulating counterparts, with further amplification in SSc. Using collagen-coated hydrogels modeling physiological and fibrotic stiffness, we show that increased stiffness enhances CD86 expression, and broadly upregulates inflammatory transcriptional programs in human monocytes. Mechanistically, stiffness-driven activation was associated with chromatin remodeling and epigenetic reprogramming, identifying the transcription factor Specificity Protein 1 (SP1) as a central regulator. CRISPR–Cas9-mediated disruption or pharmacologic inhibition of SP1 significantly attenuated stiffness- induced inflammatory gene expression, whereas we found no evidence for involvement of the canonical YAP/TAZ–TEAD axis, and pharmacological modulation of PIEZO1 neither reproduced nor blocked the response. Further, monocytes from patients with SSc displayed altered transcriptional trajectories and an exaggerated inflammatory response to high stiffness, accompanied by reduced expression of wound healing and antifibrotic programs. Together, these findings identify SP1-dependent mechanosensing as a previously unrecognized pathway controlling human monocyte activation in the skin and provide mechanistic insight into how tissue stiffness sustains inflammation in SSc.

Article.Title: Polarized twin walls in a halide perovskite
Article.Authors: Li W.; Yuan Q.; Johnston M.; Etheridge J.
Article.Abstract: Halide perovskites have emerged as promising materials for next-generation photovoltaics, laser sources, and X-ray detectors. There is intense debate as to whether some photoactive halide perovskites exhibit ferroelectric behavior and whether it might be possible to utilize the bulk photovoltaic effect to enhance the performance of halide perovskite solar cells. Here, using low-dose scanning transmission electron microscopy, we identify ferroelastic twin walls in vapor-deposited CsPbI 3 thin films, parallel to {110} and {112}. Remarkably, despite CsPbI 3 being centrosymmetric and nonpolar, we observe directly that Pb atoms shift at {110} twin walls driving a local ferroelectric-like polarization. These polar twin walls form an intrinsic array of nanoscale interfaces, spaced ~30 to 50 nm apart, embedded within the nonpolar perovskite lattice. In contrast, {112} twin walls do not show a polar displacement of Pb but strongly suppress octahedral tilt and off-center Cs atom displacements, revealing a different untapped structural degree of freedom. These findings reveal previously hidden nanoscale polarization in halide perovskite semiconductors, opening opportunities for enhanced conductivity and photovoltaic behavior through domain wall engineering.

Article.Title: Intermittent gas–liquid rearrangement controls the mixing of gases in porous media
Article.Authors: Jackson S.; Ellman S.; Kalyoncu G.; Borgne T.; Bultreys T.
Article.Abstract: Gas mixing in porous media governs important environmental and industrial applications in which multiple gas components share the available pore space with liquid water, simultaneously undergoing gas mixing and gas–liquid redistribution. Currently, this process is represented by macroscopic models that ignore pore scale dynamics. We demonstrate that this is not generally valid, and can lead to large errors in the mixing rate. We use 4D X-ray imaging to investigate nitrogen injection into a porous sandstone saturated with krypton and water, jointly imaging the gas mixture composition evolution and multiphase flow of gas and water. In contrast to the smooth, continuous representation of the conventional advection–diffusion model, our results show that gas mixing evolves through a sequence of distinct regimes controlled by gas connectivity. Initially, immiscible gas–water displacement generates gas composition variance as the different gases occupy neighboring pores separated by water. As gas connectivity increases, intermittent gas–liquid interfacial rearrangements rapidly connect regions of contrasting gas composition, driving a fast decay in composition variance. Once connectivity stabilizes, mixing is controlled by a confined diffusion process within the quasi-static gas network. At later times, further mixing is driven slowly by multicomponent Ostwald ripening, whereby trapped gas ganglia exchange solutes through the surrounding liquid phase. These findings provide insights into gas mixing in porous media, suggesting concepts for upscaling the role of pore scale multiphase flow in gas mixing in the subsurface.

Article.Title: Atypical phenylalanine ammonia-lyases that enhance phenylpropanoid production in plants
Article.Authors: El-Azaz J.; Takeda-Kimura Y.; Hall D.; Moore B.; Maeda H.

Whereas overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana PAL1 ( AtPAL1 ) in stable Arabidopsis transgenic lines resulted in very low accumulation of AtPAL1 protein and minor metabolic effects, introduction of EgPALnc rendered high content of EgPALnc protein and hyperaccumulation of hydroxycinnamates derivatives. Article.Title: Trust as a hidden driver of epidemic-relevant behavior: Institution- and behavior-specific associations across 20 national survey waves
Article.Authors: Zapf A.; Dewey G.; Ognyanova K.; Baum M.; Hanage W.; Lipsitch M.; Uslu A.; Druckman J.; Perlis R.; Lazer D.; Santillana M.
Article.Abstract: Compartmental models of infectious disease transmission make assumptions about human behaviors. Specifically, they parameterize interactions across population groups, assumed to have distinct epidemiologically relevant behavioral patterns, primarily through contact matrices stratified by demographic variables such as age, gender, or socioeconomic status. Although such demographic characteristics are readily measurable, they may inadequately capture the social and psychological forces that govern protective behaviors. Drawing on 20 waves of a national survey conducted throughout the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, we show that institutional trust—particularly trust in public health agencies, physicians, and hospitals—is a dominant predictor of protective behavior adoption. For mask wearing during periods of strongest pandemic activity, institutional trust explains more behavioral difference across population groups than age, income, education, and partisan affiliation combined. In unadjusted analyses, the difference in protective behavior adoption between individuals with the highest and lowest trust in the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) was four- to six-fold larger than the corresponding differences by age, income, or education, and exceeded the difference between Democratic and Republican respondents. This association was institutionally specific (the relationship attenuates for trust in banks), and behaviorally specific (trust in the CDC is associated with protective behaviors but not visiting a doctor). The latter suggests that trust modifies voluntary compliance with public health recommendations rather than healthcare access or use. These findings identify institutional trust as a candidate stratifying variable for models of behavior-coupled transmission dynamics, and as a measurable target for public health surveillance.

Article.Title: In-group neural alignment serves as a biomarker of social identity
Article.Authors: Zvi Y.; Kerem N.; Aviv E.; Yeshurun Y.
Article.Abstract: In this study, we propose a perspective on neural synchronization. Beyond reflecting shared understanding between individuals, we suggest it serves as a biological marker of social homogeneity. We examined fMRI neural responses of 42 participants (21 religious, 21 secular) watching neutral and religion-relevant video narratives. While explicit measures of emotional response, agreement, and engagement showed no significant differences in within-group variance, religious participants—representing a tighter social structure—exhibited significantly higher in-group neural synchrony across all content types and brain networks. Remarkably, synchrony values predicted religious orientation with an accuracy of up to 92%. We conclude that a community’s homogeneous social structure drives pervasive neural alignment, positioning neural synchrony as a potential signature of group cohesion beyond explicit behavioral measures.

Article.Title: Normalized Raman imaging for studies of tissue physiology of the kidney
Article.Authors: Trim W.; Oh S.; Diakova M.; Petrova K.; Ichimura T.; Takakura A.; Karmakar R.; Nørrelykke S.; Peshkin L.; Bonventre J.; Kirschner M.
Article.Abstract: Conventional histology relies on fixation, embedding, sectioning, and staining methods that distort cellular architecture, extract lipids, and introduce variability, limiting reproducibility. NoRI computationally corrects protein, lipid, and water Raman signals, allowing quantitative biomass measurements while preserving tissue architecture, facilitating analysis by convolutional neural networks (CNN) for quantitative, morphological feature extraction. Applied to mouse kidney, CNN analysis of NoRI images was able to accurately classify tubule types (F1=0.93; harmonic mean of precision and recall against immunofluorescence-defined labels), anatomical regions (F1 = 0.91), and biological sex (F1 = 0.97), revealing greater cytoplasmic lipid (+6.5 to 7.3 mg/mL; P ≤ 0.028) and nuclear protein (+26.3 mg/mL; P ≤ 0.001) in female tubules. Spatial lipid quantification was central for feature classification in AKI (F1 = 0.99). Quantitative NoRI images also significantly outperformed equivalent raw stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) images in distinguishing early time points (24 to 48 h) of ischemia–reperfusion injury [F1 = 0.99 (NoRI) vs. 0.84 (SRS); P < 0.0001], demonstrating the improvement of NoRI over conventional SRS imaging. Article.Title: Dynamic virulence decomposition disentangles host and pathogen contributions over the course of infection
Article.Authors: Franz M.; Bonneaud C.
Article.Abstract: Decomposing virulence into host and pathogen effects is key to understanding how virulence is generated during infection, and how host and pathogen contributions evolve over time. We applied this framework to existing data from house finches ( Haemorhous mexicanus ) experimentally infected with the emerging bacterial pathogen, Mycoplasma gallisepticum , examining two biologically meaningful infection phases: an early phase dominated by innate immune responses and a later phase in which the adaptive immune response is fully activated. Our analyses revealed that virulence components evolved differently across infection phases, with pathogen exploitation, per-parasite-pathogenicity (PPP), and host resistance each exhibiting distinct trajectories. These findings corroborated several known evolutionary patterns, while also revealing the evolution of increased PPP in this system. In contrast, the apparent evolution of host tolerance inferred from aggregated peak measurements was not supported by phase-specific analyses, demonstrating that aggregated and phase-specific measures can provide different mechanistic insights into virulence. By linking conventional virulence decomposition with disease space analysis, our dynamic virulence decomposition framework provides a general approach for quantifying how host and pathogen processes shape virulence over the course of infection.

In contrast, gain-of-function and mixed variants were predominantly associated with DEE. Finally, we demonstrate that allosteric modulators, including peptides NB6 and TRIP8b nano and the small molecule J&J12e, effectively normalize channel function across three of the four classes in vitro. Article.Title: Intrinsically motivated humans and agents in open-world exploration
Article.Authors: Lidayan A.; Du Y.; Kosoy E.; Rufova M.; Abbeel P.; Gopnik A.
Article.Abstract: What drives exploration? Understanding the intrinsic motivation to explore is a long-standing challenge in both cognitive science and AI. In this study, we directly compare adults, children aged 8 to 12 y, and AI agents exploring a complex, open-ended environment called Crafter ( 1 ). We study how three common information-theoretic intrinsic objectives—entropy, information gain, and empowerment—relate to their behavior. We find that all three are positively correlated with human exploration progress for both children and adults, although entropy and empowerment are more strongly related to exploration progress in children than information gain. Furthermore, across agents and humans we observe that entropy initially increases rapidly, then plateaus, while empowerment increases continuously, suggesting that in early exploration they look for novel states, while in advanced exploration they look for states they can control. Finally, we find preliminary evidence that private speech about goals may aid exploration in children. Our data are available at https://github.com/alyd/humans_in_crafter_data .

Article.Title: Lead impairs long-term memory by disrupting mitochondrial redox homeostasis in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Hsu C.; Lu T.; Yang Y.; Chen C.; Chiu Y.; Yang J.; Wu Z.; Cheng W.; Wu J.; Shiu C.; Chuang S.; Feng K.; Lin H.; Yang J.; Chiang A.
Article.Abstract: Lead (Pb) exposure remains a major environmental risk factor for cognitive dysfunction, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying Pb-induced memory impairment are poorly understood. Here, we show that both developmental and adult-onset Pb exposure selectively disrupts protein-synthesis-dependent long-term memory (LTM) in Drosophila melanogaster while sparing other memory forms. Using a mitochondria-targeted redox biosensor (mito-roGFP2-Orp1), we found that Pb elevates mitochondrial oxidative stress and disrupts redox homeostasis in cholinergic neurons and in dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, a critical locus for LTM consolidation. Pb-induced redox imbalance suppresses training-induced de novo protein synthesis in DAL neurons, thereby impairing memory consolidation. Antioxidant treatment with epigallocatechin gallate restores mitochondrial redox balance and rescues LTM by reinstating activity-dependent protein synthesis in DAL neurons. These findings identify mitochondrial redox dysregulation as a key mechanism linking environmental Pb exposure to impaired memory consolidation. Our results further establish a genetically tractable platform for dissecting neurotoxic mechanisms and for evaluating antioxidant-based strategies to mitigate Pb-induced cognitive dysfunction.

Article.Title: A tetravalent bispecific protein enables targeted degradation of VCAM-1 and VEGFR for treatment of choroidal neovascularization
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Du M.; Ge L.; Cao Y.; Jiang J.; Yin X.; Chen G.; Wang Q.
Article.Abstract: Wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a leading cause of irreversible vision loss, is driven by pathological choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Although anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapies remain the clinical standard, their utility is constrained by incomplete responses in nearly 50% of patients and off-target risks—such as geographic atrophy—stemming from non-specific VEGF blockade. Here, we identify a robust correlation between vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) and VEGF/VEGF receptor (VEGFR) expression in aqueous humor from AMD patients and in murine CNV models. Thus, we engineered a tetravalent bispecific protein, RHV, by functionalizing an L-rhamnulose-1-phosphate aldolase scaffold with peptides that selectively bind VCAM-1 and the VEGFR on neovessels. The tetravalent design confers high apparent affinity, enhancing pathological endothelial targeting while sparing healthy retinal vasculature. RHV induces concurrent internalization and lysosomal degradation of both VCAM-1 and VEGFR via a head-to-tail binding mode, leading to sustained inhibition of the VEGF/VEGFR, PI3K/AKT and Apelin/APJ signaling pathways. In murine CNV models, a single intravitreal injection of RHV exhibits superior ocular retention and lesion penetration, achieving therapeutic efficacy comparable to aflibercept [a ligand-trap fusion protein for VEGF-A, VEGF-B and placental growth factor (PIGF)] at one-quarter of the molar dose. This dual-receptor degradation-based strategy represents a targeted and durable approach for treating ocular neovascularization.
