Article.Title: Reduced dosage of phytochrome F engages SELF-PRUNING 6A to confer heat-resilient tuberization in potato
Article.Authors: Jing S.; Li X.; Jiang P.; Chen H.; Li C.; Qin J.; Zhu B.; Zeng Z.; Song B.
Article.Abstract: Natural variation at the earliness locus, or potato CDF1, enabled cultivated potato to overcome strict photoperiodic control of wild andigena landraces and tuberize under long days. Yet long-day conditions (LDs) are often associated with warm temperatures, which strongly suppress tuberization at night. With the rising ambient temperatures due to global warming, uncovering genetic factors that enable tuber formation under elevated temperatures has become a priority for breeding new cultivars with improved heat tolerance. Here we report that heat-resilient tuberization in potato can be unlocked by inactivating the photoreceptor phytochrome F (phyF) and optimized by exploiting its haploinsufficiency. Knockdown of phyF activates the SELF-PRUNING 6A (SP6A) tuberization-inducing signal and facilitates tuber formation under heat-stress conditions. Unexpectedly, loss of function of both SP6A and phyF still leads to early tuberization and heat escape, although it reduces the resilience of phyF mutants. Intriguingly, we show that haplotype-specific phyF editing in the 5' UTR or exonic regions leads to haploinsufficiency phenotypes enabling tuberization under heat-stress conditions, without other phytochrome-related penalties. Our results suggest that derepressing SP6A by a reduction of phyF dosage provides a key to unlock heat-resilient tuberization and highlight haploinsufficiency as a strategy for generating dominant alleles to enable rapid improvement of crops.

Article.Title: A putative structural transition underlies reliable formation of skeletal muscle
Article.Authors: Mendieta-Serrano M.; Hou Y.; Theis S.; Hall T.; Taylor S.; Verd B.; Parton R.; Saunders T.
Article.Abstract: During organ development cells undergo significant morphological and positional changes. Yet by the end of organogenesis, internal organ structure is typically reliably defined. It remains an open question how the internal structure of an organ emerges, particularly in the presence of dynamic boundary constraints. Here, we utilize live imaging and morphological measures of the developing zebrafish to unravel how early muscle organization materializes. We observed that myocytes undergo an ordered chiral twist according to their position within the myotome. Cell movement undergoes a rapid speed reduction once the cells span the myotome segment. Biophysical perturbation reveals cells are mechanically plastic and can adapt to changes in boundaries and environment. Combining these results, we propose that the early myotome may be undergoing a structural transition from a fluid-like to a solid-like state, which resembles a frozen system. Cell shape plasticity combined with structural changes in the material behavior could be a general mechanism for organ morphogenesis in dense tissues.

Article.Title: Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl
Article.Authors: Mayr G.; Šmídová L.; Richter A.; Wedmann S.
Article.Abstract: It is poorly understood when owls (Strigiformes) became nocturnal, which impedes considerations of the evolutionary reasons behind this distinctive behavior.1,2 Here, we report an extraordinary owl skeleton from the middle Eocene of Germany, which preserves remains of an iridescent cockroach as stomach contents-the first identifiable insect remains ever found as the last meal of a fossil bird. Because iridescence is correlated with diurnal habits in cockroaches,3 the fossil provides the strongest evidence to date for diurnality in archaic Strigiformes. Further support for a diurnal ecology comes from the absence of barred flight feathers as well as the lack of frayed leading edges of the primaries; the presence of these features is associated with nocturnality in extant owls.4,5 The humerus is much stouter than in extant owls, indicating that the wings were less adapted to silent flight. Conversely, a slenderer humerus suggests that late Eocene owls had shifted toward a nocturnal ecology. This timeframe rules out previously suggested factors for nocturnality in owls2 and constrains the origin of an ecological hallmark of these birds.

Article.Title: Neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic circuit regulates selective forgetting of olfactory learning
Article.Authors: Onishi Y.; Arai M.; Sato N.; Takamatsu M.; Teo J.; Kitazono T.; Ishihara T.
Article.Abstract: Forgetting is an active and essential process for adapting to constantly changing environments, yet the molecular and circuit mechanisms underlying selective forgetting remain poorly understood. Our previous studies in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans suggested that non-cell-autonomous neurosecretory signals accelerate forgetting of olfactory memory for diacetyl, an attractive odorant, by erasing its memory trace, which can be detected as changes in odor-evoked Ca2+ responses in sensory neurons. However, the identity of the forgetting signal, the circuit through which it acts to erase the sensory memory trace, and the time window in which forgetting occurs have remained elusive. Here, we identify a neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic circuit in C. elegans that drives the selective forgetting of olfactory memory. Our genetic and imaging analyses revealed that the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)-related neuropeptide NLP-47, secreted from AWC neurons, acts on its receptor GNRR-1 in AIZ interneurons. Glutamatergic neurotransmission from AIZ interneurons then erases the sensory memory trace in AWA neurons via GLR-4, an AMPA-type receptor expressed in AWA. Optogenetic silencing of AWC and AIZ showed that this circuit acts during the recovery phase following conditioning, defining a critical temporal window for active forgetting. This neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic pathway selectively promotes forgetting of a specific odorant memory without affecting another formed simultaneously. Together, our findings demonstrate that neuropeptidergic signaling promotes selective forgetting via a glutamatergic circuit, highlighting that active forgetting is regulated within a critical temporal window and with remarkable specificity.

Article.Title: Army ant raids connect terrestrial and aquatic food webs in mangroves
Article.Authors: Domínguez-Castanedo O.; García-Calva L.; Chiappa-Carrara X.
Article.Abstract: Army ant raids by Eciton burchellii parvispinum are iconic spectacles of Neotropical forests, driving ant-following birds and intense predation on leaf-litter arthropods1,2,3,4. However, whether these terrestrial predators influence energy flows across ecosystem boundaries remains unknown. Apart from isolated natural history anecdotes, evidence for such interactions is lacking despite recognition that cross-ecosystem subsidies strongly affect food-web dynamics5,6,7. Here, we report a previously undescribed cross-ecosystem interaction in the mangroves of Yucatán, Mexico, where army ant raids trigger localized feeding aggregations among aquatic vertebrates. Stomach-content analyses of fishes attending raids at four independent Eciton colonies, complemented by observations across six colonies, show that prey escaping army ant predation can become a substantial terrestrial subsidy for resident fishes. This pulse was associated with marked shifts in fish diet and recurrent higher-order predator aggregations, revealing a pathway through which terrestrial predator effects can extend across ecosystem boundaries.

Article.Title: Hypothalamic cell-type differences associated with selection for tameness in the silver fox
Article.Authors: Klein J.; Shepeleva D.; Vladimirova A.; Kharlamova A.; Miller A.; Kukekova A.; Markenscoff-Papadimitriou E.
Article.Abstract: The hypothalamus is a highly heterogeneous brain region that regulates fundamental physiological processes and behaviors, including innate social behaviors such as aggression, mating, and parenting1. Distinct cell types within hypothalamic nuclei have been linked to social behaviors, a principle established most clearly in mice, where manipulation of defined hypothalamic neuronal subtypes can initiate or suppress behaviors including attack, mounting, and parenting1,2,3,4. Whether hypothalamic cell types are modified as a result of selection during the evolution of social behavior remains unknown. Silver foxes (Vulpes vulpes) have been selectively bred for tame or aggressive behaviors and we have studied whether there are differences relating to these behaviors in the cellular makeup of the hypothalamus. We report here that tame foxes have fewer estrogen receptor-expressing neurons in the ventrolateral subdivision of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMHvl) than aggressive foxes, and that this reduction is specific to a neuronal subtype linked to aggressive states in mice5. We have thus identified a candidate hypothalamic neuronal subtype associated with selection on social behavior during animal domestication.

Article.Title: Hippocampal–prefrontal cortical interactions and neural representations of memory
Article.Authors: Morales-Rodriguez D.; Frank L.
Article.Abstract: The ability to store memories and access past experiences when making decisions in the present is fundamental to cognition. The hippocampus is critical for these processes and has been a primary site of investigation in the learning and memory field for the last several decades. However, it is also clear that the hippocampus must work in concert with cortical brain regions to store and recall memories. Findings that demonstrate the necessity of hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) communication in these processes, as well as findings that link the mPFC to memory storage, retrieval, and decision-making, have contributed to this growing area of study. Here, we review our current understanding of three questions related to this communication. What information is represented in the hippocampus and the mPFC? What are the underlying neural activity patterns and brain states that facilitate communication of those representations? What impact do these patterns have on the ability to learn and remember in new and familiar settings? We highlight evidence for bidirectional communication both during and after experience, and we discuss areas of active investigation to further uncover the role of bidirectional hippocampal-cortical interactions in the formation and maintenance of neural representations of memory.

Article.Title: Fungal–bacterial interactions
Article.Authors: Uehling J.; Gohar D.; Johnson H.
Article.Abstract: The study of fungal-bacterial interactions is an emerging field of biology with relevance for environmental health, medicine, and agriculture, among other sectors. The frequent co-occurrence of fungi and bacteria in many habitats has facilitated the evolution of their symbioses. Both groups are key players in host-associated microbiomes and in nutrient cycling, and these roles often intersect in dynamic ways. Interactions between fungi and bacteria can be mutualistic, commensal, or pathogenic, and they can vary in a context-dependent manner. In mutualistic interactions, fungi and bacteria can exchange nutrients, ameliorate each other's stress, enhance growth, enable dispersal, and facilitate novel niche exploration via metabolite exchange. In contrast, antagonistic interactions frequently involve competition for limited nutrients, such as iron, and active chemical warfare with secreted and bioactive compounds. Bacteria associated with fungi can occur inside of fungal cells (endosymbiotic) or on the surface of fungal hyphae (exosymbiotic). Endosymbiotic bacteria can be further differentiated into facultative symbionts, which retain the ability to enter fungal hyphae but also live independently, and obligate endosymbionts, which are always intracellular and not capable of independent life outside of hyphae. Whereas free-living bacteria can be pathogenic or mutualistic, endosymbiotic bacteria are often regarded as commensals or mutualists, although some can exhibit parasitic attributes in some conditions. A combination of molecular genetics, genomics, and microscopy has been used to study free-living bacteria. In addition to these approaches, fluorescence and electron microscopy have been used as the gold standards to study and differentiate endosymbiotic bacteria based on their intracellular location. More recently, researchers have started using systems-biology approaches to study fungal-bacterial interactions including high-throughput -omics assays. These methods produce expansive datasets that are ideally suited to artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches to tackle long-standing questions about the basic biology and evolution of fungal-bacterial interactions. In this primer we give an overview of fungal-bacterial interactions, including their diversity, community structure, and symbiotic evolution. We highlight two research systems in particular: the intracellular endosymbionts of Mucoromycota fungi and the free-living bacteria associated with edible fungi. We focus on these systems because fungi remain understudied relative to other groups, and only a handful of fungal taxa with their bacterial symbionts are backed by large enough data sets to explore these concepts in detail. Our aim here is not to be comprehensive, but instead to use the most well-understood systems to illustrate emerging principles. We then discuss advances in using AI to infer new aspects of microbial biology and provide suggestions for how these technologies could advance research on fungal-bacterial interactions utilizing existing genomic datasets.

Motility changes extend to non-neuronal cells, where they alter focal adhesion dynamics and can be rescued by manipulating soluble tubulin levels. Patient-derived TTC5 disease mutants phenocopy this motility dysregulation, directly linking loss of TTC5 function to neurological deficits seen in patients. Article.Title: Illusory cold desensitizes touch
Article.Authors: Ramirez J.; Vergara J.; Kim B.; Saal H.; Yau J.
Article.Abstract: In Jack London's To Build a Fire, the doomed protagonist notes that "the tremendous cold had already driven the life out of his fingers… dead fingers could neither touch nor clutch." Indeed, our hands are numbed when exposed to cold, a desensitization process traditionally attributed to biophysical and physiological effects on mechanoreceptor and afferent responses.1 Yet perception is not based solely on sensory inputs and often reflects prior beliefs and expectations.2 Accordingly, the mere experience of coldness, given its association with tactile desensitization, conceivably modulates touch independent of physical effects. We dissociated the physical and subjective influences of cooling on touch by leveraging the thermal referral illusion,3,4,5,6,7 in which cooling of the index and ring fingers induces an illusory perception of coldness that is referred to the middle finger, which did not experience local cooling. We found that both veridical and illusory cold elevated tactile detection thresholds. Threshold shifts scaled with subjective ratings of cold intensity, which varied with thermal adaptation. Thermal referral induction did not result in changes to skin temperature, ruling out indirect physical effects on the tested finger. To account for cold effects on touch, we implemented a computational model incorporating both physical and subjective factors by simulating changes in tactile afferent spiking activity8 and modulation of decision computations, respectively. The model reproduced empirical cooling effects on afferent responses9 and recapitulated psychophysical detection patterns. Our results reveal that subjective thermal perception contributes to cold-induced attenuation of touch, highlighting how multimodal experiences and expectations shape somatosensation.

Article.Title: Brain-wide activity imaging with electron microscopy reveals a distributed brain network for processing threatening somatosensory stimuli
Article.Authors: Randel N.; Wang C.; Clayton M.; Wang K.; Pang S.; Xu C.; Champion A.; Hess H.; Cardona A.; Keller P.; Zlatic M.
Article.Abstract: To understand how brains work, neural activity must be overlayed onto synaptic-resolution circuit architecture. Recent advances in light-sheet microscopy (LSM) enable whole-brain, cellular-resolution imaging of activity of all cell bodies; however, most neurons from such datasets cannot be identified. In most organisms, neurons are identifiable based on their projections (and not based on cell body position), which, when densely labeled, cannot be resolved using LSM. Here, we present a novel methodology to overcome this by combining whole-brain activity imaging with subsequent volume electron microscopy imaging of the same brain to visualize neuronal projections and identify neurons with interesting activity. We used this approach to identify brain neurons that process input from multisensory (nociceptive and mechanosensory) Basin interneurons that trigger vigorous escape in Drosophila larvae in response to threatening somatosensory stimuli. After whole-brain imaging of neuronal activity during Basin activation, we imaged the same brain with an enhanced focused ion-beam electron microscope (eFIB-SEM). We registered the functional and anatomical volumes and reconstructed (in the eFIB-SEM volume) the projections of neurons that responded to Basin activation to determine their developmental lineage and identity. This revealed a distributed network for processing threatening somatosensory stimuli that trigger vigorous escape spanning 25 distinct lineages and many distinct brain areas. Our workflow provides a powerful framework for mapping neuronal activity onto structure across an entire brain, yielding novel insights into the distributed central processing of somatosensory stimuli.

Article.Abstract: Anisogamy-the production of male and female gametes of unequal size-and maternal organelle inheritance have evolved repeatedly across diverse eukaryotic lineages despite extensive diversification in sex-determination mechanisms. Yet the genetic and cellular mechanisms underlying gamete dimorphism remain poorly understood. Coenocytic green macroalgae of the order Bryopsidales, which lack complex reproductive organs, provide an attractive system for studying gamete differentiation. However, the absence of genomic resources has prevented the identification of sex-specific chromosomal regions and sex-limited genes in this group. Despite these pronounced phenotypic changes, BrRWP1 knockdown gametes were not fully masculinized and exhibited fertilization defects, indicating that additional factors contribute to sexual differentiation. Article.Title: Serotonin signaling in the central nervous system is required for correct spine morphogenesis in zebrafish
Article.Authors: Messa G.; Wyart C.
Article.Abstract: Although adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) affects over 1% of children and teenagers worldwide, its causes are not fully understood. Our findings indicate that spinal 5HT signaling plays an essential role for proper spine alignment during post-embryonic morphogenesis.

Article.Authors: Kortenbosch H.; Kanellopoulos S.; Timmermanns L.; Reyes Marquez F.; Zwaan B.; Auxier B.; Snelders E.
Article.Abstract: Agricultural intensification relies on chemical fungicides to manage crop disease,1,2 driving the evolution of resistance in plant pathogens.3 Fungicides persist in the environment, allowing activity beyond their intended targets, affecting downstream ecosystems and agricultural practices. The saprophytic and ubiquitous fungus Aspergillus fumigatus is an important human pathogen causing severe invasive fungal disease.4 Selection by agricultural triazoles, or demethylase inhibitors (DMIs), has led to cross-resistance to clinical triazoles, as both target the cyp51A gene.5,6 In the Netherlands,7,8 most triazole resistance arises from two cyp51A haplotypes, TR34 and TR46.9,10 Genomic surveys show that these resistance alleles often co-occur with resistance alleles to non-DMI fungicides, including quinone outside inhibitors (QoIs) and succinate dehydrogenase inhibitors (SDHIs).11 We hypothesize that agricultural environments with non-DMI fungicides can indirectly select for triazole resistance. Using grass mesocosms to compete A. fumigatus isolates, we found that low concentrations of DMI, SDHI, and QoI fungicides, comparable to agricultural residues, independently increased the proportions of triazole-resistant alleles. Resistance alleles for each class are not intrinsically cross-resistant, indicating that their co-occurrences result from linked resistance alleles. Consistent to these findings, environmental samples from heaps with only non-DMI fungicides contained high phenotypic triazole resistance (>20%). This work provides experimental and field evidence that triazole and non-DMI resistance can increase in parallel, consistent with genomic hitchhiking. We thus predict that novel resistance alleles are likely selected in isolates that have already accumulated resistance alleles to other fungicide classes. Therefore, managing selection and spread of environmental triazole resistance will require consideration of all fungicide classes.

Article.Title: Directional evolution of parasitoid strategies and contingent host shifts shape the radiation of Darwin wasps (Ichneumonidae)
Article.Authors: Santos B.; Bossert S.; Kolasa J.; Broad G.; Bennett A.; Fernandes D.; Klopfstein S.; Rousse P.; Wahl D.; Brady S.
Article.Abstract: Evolutionary change is not always reversible: some traits evolve repeatedly in one direction but rarely in the other, forming evolutionary "ratchets" that constrain future trajectories. Parasitoid wasps provide a powerful system to test this idea because their modes of host exploitation range from relatively simple strategies to highly integrated developmental interactions with living hosts. Here, we investigate the evolution of parasitoid strategies and host use across Darwin wasps (Ichneumonidae), the most diverse parasitoid family, using a phylogenomic dataset comprising 697 species and all ichneumonid subfamilies. Our results reveal that the evolution of parasitoid strategies is strikingly asymmetric: transitions from idiobiosis (permanent host paralysis) to koinobiosis (in which hosts continue development after oviposition) and from ectoparasitoidism to endoparasitoidism occurred repeatedly, whereas reversals were virtually absent. In contrast, host associations were dynamic but contingent on parasitoid strategy: moths and butterflies (Lepidoptera) were inferred as the ancestral hosts, but repeated host shifts subsequently occurred across nearly all holometabolous insect orders despite strong phylogenetic conservatism within major lineages. However, this flexibility was strongly asymmetric, with host-taxon shifts occurring predominantly in idiobiont lineages and becoming much rarer after transitions to koinobiosis. These results show that macroevolutionary dynamics can differ sharply among interacting traits, with directional evolutionary ratchets reshaping not only individual trait trajectories but also the ecological options available to diversifying lineages.

Article.Title: The representation of object-concept primitives across the macaque brain
Article.Authors: Loggia S.; Feibes H.; Duffield S.; Kasi K.; Conway B.
Article.Abstract: Object concepts are mental representations that provide information beyond immediate sensory input, but where and how the brain encodes them remains unresolved. During fMRI, the animals were cued with one feature (shapeless color or colorless shape) and rewarded for subsequently identifying the associated feature. Using a new whole-brain searchlight inspired by convolutional networks, we identified regions that carried information about the unshown feature during cue presentation. Additional passive-viewing experiments showed univariate fMRI response biases to the learned associations in extrastriate visual cortex, which may reflect feedback from regions identified by cross-feature decoding. Together, the results provide a blueprint for how the brain encodes object concepts and suggest how concept representations engage perceptual representations through feedback during vision.

Article.Authors: Pereira S.; Meesawat S.; Malaivijitnond S.; Schülke O.; Ostner J.
Article.Abstract: In primate societies, much of what matters is revealed by watching others. By attending to the social interactions of group members, individuals may acquire detailed knowledge about prosocial tendencies, alliance networks, and dominance structure,1,2,3 which can inform strategic decisions such as bond and coalition partner choice.4,5 Although allocation of visual attention is a fundamental cognitive process,6,7 its immediate and long-term behavioral consequences remain unclear, leaving ethological and neuroscientific research on social attention5,8,9 largely disconnected from work linking sociality to fitness.10,11 Bridging these research areas has been challenging in part due to the difficulty of quantifying social attention under natural conditions.9,12,13,14 Using a novel social scene protocol for recording visual attention to spontaneously unfolding interactions of nearby group members in the wild,15 we show across 46 adult male macaques that individual differences in visual attention to others' affiliative interactions was associated with male social bond strength later that year. Increased social bond strength, in turn, predicted a male's dominance success in the following year, and ultimately, enhanced male mating success. Post hoc analyses point to interventions in friendly behavior as a plausible behavioral mechanism connecting individual differences in attention with social bonding. In sum, our findings connect two largely siloed bodies of work by providing a chain of evidence linking individual variation in social monitoring to both its effects on the affiliation network and long-term consequences for key correlates of direct fitness.

Article.Title: Apical extracellular matrix regulates fold morphogenesis in the Drosophila wing disc
Article.Authors: Fuhrmann J.; Schimmenti V.; Cwikla G.; Lee S.; Barrera Velazquez M.; Yuan M.; Wilsch-Bräuninger M.; Jülicher F.; Popović M.; Dye N.
Article.Abstract: Tissue folding is a fundamental process in animal organ development. Here, we study the progression of fold shape and the underlying mechanics in the development of the Drosophila wing disc. We present a 3D segmentation of the apical surface of the wing disc proper from larval stages, when folds grow, to early pupariation, when the tissue unfolds and remodels into a bilayer. We establish morphological metrics to quantify and resolve fold shape, introducing a definition of fold depth and width that can be used to characterize folds on a curved surface. Furthermore, we identify fibrous extracellular matrix on the apical side (aECM) that physically connects the two apposing sides of the folds. By modeling a tissue fold with a lateral vertex model endowed with an adhesive layer representing the aECM, we predict that unfolding in the wing disc is preceded by the removal of aECM. Using genetic perturbations, we confirm that aECM affects fold stability and wing disc mechanics: loss of aECM leads to abnormal fold shape and unfolding dynamics, whereas failure to remove aECM at pupariation inhibits unfolding. Finally, we show that these aECM perturbations in larval stages cause morphological phenotypes in the adult wing. In total, our work establishes a key mechanical role for aECM in wing disc morphogenesis and advances our understanding of how epithelial tissue folds can be mechanically stabilized during development.

Article.Title: Rapid change in coral composition alters the footprint of mass bleaching
Article.Authors: McWilliam M.; Hughes T.; Baird A.; Doll P.; Hennessy G.; James N.; Kingsbury K.; Pertile E.; Pratchett M.
Article.Abstract: The Great Barrier Reef experienced five mass bleaching events in the 8 years from 2016 to 2024.1,2 Each mass bleaching event can transform coral abundance and diversity,3,4,5,6 yet less is known about the long-term consequences of high bleaching frequencies and shortening recovery intervals. Using bleaching and mortality surveys in 2016 and 2024, we show that an unprecedented frequency of disturbances on the Great Barrier Reef has modified the mix of species within coral assemblages, generating a shift in how reefs respond to extreme climate events. Prohibitively high frequencies of climate extremes in far northern regions (3-4 events since 2016) have delayed reef recovery and diminished bleaching and mortality levels in 2024, a pattern consistent with strong selective pressure in the region. Longer recovery intervals in central and northern regions (7-8 years since the last major event) led to rapidly recovering assemblages with increased abundances of fast-growing, heat-sensitive species (e.g., branching and tabular Acropora). These regions showed severe bleaching and mortality in 2024, equaling declines among relatively intact assemblages on southern reefs, where heat stress was up to twice as extreme. The emerging spatial footprint of diminished recovery and shifts to heat-sensitive species reveals an expanding influence of bleaching history and composition on the resilience of the Great Barrier Reef. While reef bleaching thresholds continue to shift,7,8,9 rapid compositional change is creating more volatile dynamics under accumulating climate stress, in some cases favoring the species most susceptible to damage.

Article.Title: Reciprocal constraints couple architectural protein abundance and pericentromeric satellite expansion
Article.Authors: Dudka D.; Beeravolu K.; Ma J.; Lampson M.
Article.Abstract: Long-read sequencing has enabled precise measurements of highly repetitive centromeric satellites and their rapid divergence between species.1,2,3,4,5,6,7 Large satellite arrays emerge from libraries of shorter arrays via stochastic expansions,8,9 but understanding the selective pressures constraining such expansions remains a major challenge. Here, using the mouse "major" satellite as a model, we reveal reciprocal functional constraints between increasing satellite copy number and abundance of a conserved architectural protein in female meiosis. We show that HMGA2 (high mobility group AT-hook 2) is enriched at major satellite, and its expression correlates with major satellite copy number: both are high in Mus musculus compared to the closely related Mus spretus. To test functional constraints, we modulated HMGA2 abundance by depletion or overexpression and used a musculus/spretus hybrid to generate oocytes with intermediate HMGA2 expression and major satellite copy number. We find that HMGA2 depletion disrupts major satellite packaging in major satellite-rich musculus, but not hybrid, oocytes, indicating that increasing copy number requires high HMGA2 expression. Conversely, HMGA2 overexpression disrupts chromosome segregation in major satellite-poor spretus, but not hybrid, oocytes, indicating that high HMGA2 expression requires expanded major satellite arrays. Based on these results, we propose a co-evolution model in which satellite expansion is constrained by architectural protein abundance, whereas protein abundance is constrained reciprocally by satellite array size.

Article.Title: Discrete functional regions of the olfactory bulb represent region-specific molecular feature sets
Article.Authors: Strauch M.; Brunert D.; Böhm E.; Wallhorn L.; Medinaceli Quintela R.; Sireci S.; Merhof D.; Rothermel M.
Article.Abstract: In the mammalian brain, odors are encoded by combinatorial activation of the glomeruli in the olfactory bulb. The topography of the bulb has been described as tunotopic or chemotopic, such that glomeruli with similar odor tuning or similar chemical property tuning are spatially close. However, several aspects of the bulb topography remain debated, in particular whether there are discrete regions of glomeruli with similar odor tuning, as opposed to a continuous tunotopic mapping, and whether commonly used molecular features have predictive power for the odor responses and are mapped to specific regions. Here, we measured glomerular odor responses in the mouse olfactory bulb by calcium imaging and analyzed the map between (1) the functional space of glomerular odor responses, (2) the two-dimensional bulb surface, and (3) the chemical space of molecular features. We found an organization of the bulb surface into discrete functional regions consisting of glomeruli with similar odor tuning and with functional discontinuities at the region boundaries. The glomeruli within the same functional region also had similar temporal response dynamics, independent of response amplitude. The chemical property tuning of the regions could be described by region-specific molecular feature sets with region-specific predictive power for the odor responses. Our results suggest a fragmented tuno- and chemotopic organization of the bulb, where glomeruli within the same functional region are tuned to similar chemical properties and are temporally synchronized, which is potentially beneficial for local signal processing.

Article.Title: Brainstem orexigenic neurons drive long-term energy balance via distributed hypothalamic circuits
Article.Authors: Chen J.; Chen W.; Zhang Y.; Chen Q.; Zhang K.; Xu S.; Zhan C.
Article.Abstract: Energy balance control has long been primarily attributed to hypothalamic neurons, whereas the physiological contribution of brainstem feeding circuits to sustained long-term hyperphagia and weight gain remains poorly defined. Here, we combined viral tracing, optogenetics, chronic chemogenetics, and targeted neuronal ablation to functionally characterize the brainstem neuropeptide Y (NPY) neuronal circuit and define its critical roles in regulating feeding behavior and long-term body weight homeostasis. NPY neurons in the nucleus of solitary tract (NTSNPY) send parallel, partially overlapping excitatory collaterals to the hypothalamus, each independently driving feeding. Their orexigenic effects persist following the ablation of hypothalamic AgRP/NPY neurons. Chronic NTSNPY activation induces persistent hyperphagia and weight gain, whereas single or dual ablation of NTSNPY plus hypothalamic AgRP/NPY failed to disrupt baseline energy homeostasis, revealing redundant brain orexigenic networks. Our data identify NTSNPY neurons as an extra-hypothalamic pro-obesogenic population independent of canonical AgRP circuits, offering a therapeutic target for obesity.

Article.Title: A CONSTANS-like transcriptional co-activator couples ethylene signaling to jasmonate biosynthesis and is targeted by a fungal effector
Article.Authors: Meng Y.; Yuan W.; Li J.; Li L.; Xu L.; Huang L.
Article.Abstract: Ethylene and jasmonate synergistically regulate immunity against necrotrophic pathogens, but how ethylene signaling promotes jasmonate biosynthesis remains unclear. Here, we show that the apple CONSTANS-like (COL) protein MdCOL4 functions as a transcriptional co-activator that couples ethylene signaling to jasmonate biosynthesis during disease resistance. The ethylene-responsive transcription factor MdERF098 directly activates the jasmonate biosynthetic genes MdOPR2 and MdOPR3. MdCOL4 physically associates with MdERF098 and enhances its DNA-binding activity, thereby promoting MdOPR2/3 transcription, jasmonate accumulation, and resistance to apple Valsa canker, a destructive trunk disease caused by Valsa mali, a necrotrophic fungal pathogen. We further identify a fungal effector from V. mali, Vm11039, that translocates into the host nucleus and binds MdCOL4 with higher affinity than MdERF098, competitively disrupting the MdCOL4-MdERF098 complex. This interference attenuates jasmonate biosynthesis and promotes pathogen infection. Together, our findings uncover a transcriptional co-activation mechanism that couples ethylene signaling to jasmonate biosynthesis and establish transcriptional co-activator complexes as vulnerable regulatory hubs targeted by pathogen effectors to suppress hormone-mediated immunity, thereby providing a potential target for engineering resistance against necrotrophic diseases.

Article.Title: Lateral orbitofrontal cortex enables new learning to overwrite previously acquired information
Article.Authors: Mahmoudi M.; Gladding J.; Kendig M.; Castorina A.; Turner K.; Soegyono O.; Bradfield L.
Article.Abstract: Responding that has been reduced through experience can recover over time or following re-exposure to a biologically relevant outcome; these phenomena are known as spontaneous recovery and reinstatement, respectively. First described by Pavlov in 1927,1 these effects are most commonly (but not exclusively2,3,4) documented following extinction5,6 and are thought to contribute to relapse following behavioral treatments for anxiety, addiction, and related disorders.7,8 Therefore, extinction is generally considered to suppress rather than erase prior learning.5,6 In contrast, contingency degradation has been suggested to weaken initial response-outcome learning.9 Although previous studies of recovery following degradation have produced mixed results,10,11,12,13 each of these studies combined degradation with extinction, making it unclear whether degradation itself produces persistent reductions in responding. Here, rats learned two action-outcome contingencies (e.g., left lever, pellets; right lever, sucrose), one of which was subsequently degraded by unsignaled, non-contingent delivery of its outcome. Responding to the degraded action was reduced and did not recover following a 2-week interval or unexpected outcome delivery. This indicates that degradation, unlike extinction, produces persistent changes in behavior. We next examined the role of the lateral orbitofrontal cortex (lOFC), a region implicated in resolving interference between competing contingencies. Chemogenetic inactivation of lOFC impaired acquisition but not retrieval of degradation, consistent with the existence of competition between original and degraded contingencies during learning but not at test. These findings indicate that contingency degradation overwrites initial action-outcome learning and identify a potential framework for developing behavioral interventions that are resistant to relapse.

Article.Title: The “dark magic mushroom” co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin
Article.Authors: Kunik A.; Christopher M.; Lemmond B.; Dentinger B.; Slot J.; Garrett T.; Smith M.
Article.Abstract: The most famous chemicals produced by mushrooms are the psychedelic compound psilocybin from "magic mushrooms" and amatoxins from deadly poisonous mushrooms.1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 These compounds are known to occur in several distantly related groups of fungi but have never been shown to co-occur within a single species. Here, we show that the "dark magic mushroom" Galerina indica produces both psilocybin and amatoxins. Mass spectrometry revealed psilocybin and amatoxins in mushroom tissues, and genomic analyses identified corresponding biosynthetic genes. Phylogenetic analyses suggest that G. indica acquired psilocybin biosynthesis via horizontal gene transfer after amatoxin biosynthesis was already established. These findings reveal how horizontal gene transfer can combine powerful bioactive systems in a single species, potentially altering the ecological roles of both compound classes and the evolutionary fitness of the species.10,11.

Article.Title: Volatile emission dynamics are temporally associated with neighbor-modulated movement in climbing plants
Article.Authors: Bonato B.; Simonetti V.; Avesani S.; Guerra S.; Gjinaj G.; Ravazzolo L.; Dadda M.; Castiello U.
Article.Abstract: Climbing plants use circumnutation, a rhythmic exploratory movement of the shoot apex, to locate supports.1,2,3,4,5 Although neighboring plants can alter this movement before physical contact, the underlying mechanisms remain unknown.6,7,8,9 Here, we combined three-dimensional kinematic tracking and real-time volatilomic profiling in Pisum sativum to investigate the temporal association between volatile emissions and circumnutation. Seven volatile-associated m/z features showed transient increases before peak circumnutation velocity in plants growing with a conspecific, a pattern absent in isolated plants. Neighbor presence also increased apex velocity, acceleration, path length, and explored area. Wavelet coherence analysis revealed stronger temporal coordination between real neighboring pairs than between randomly paired individuals. Neighboring plants additionally exhibited faster shoot growth and increased chlorophyll content in upper leaves. Together, these findings link volatile emission dynamics with exploratory movement and reveal coordinated behavioral and physiological responses to neighboring plants. This work establishes a framework for investigating the temporal organization of plant-plant interactions while highlighting the need for experiments to determine whether volatile cues causally influence movement.

Article.Title: A neural circuit mediating altitude control in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Erickson A.; Omoto J.; Stupski S.; van Breugel F.; Dickinson M.
Article.Abstract: Flight is a remarkably efficient mode of locomotion that is largely responsible for the extraordinary evolutionary radiations of birds, bats, pterosaurs, and insects. Whereas walking animals need only control locomotion on a two-dimensional surface, flight requires active altitude regulation, a process by which the brain transforms self-motion cues into motor patterns that regulate lift. Using an integrative approach combining optogenetics, high-speed videography, two-photon imaging, robotics, and connectomics, we identified a single pair of descending neurons in Drosophila that control altitude. To search for candidate cells, we performed an optogenetic screen of sparse driver lines targeting descending neurons that project to the flight neuropil of the ventral nerve cord and identified one bilaterally paired neuron, DNa10, whose activation elicits changes in wing kinematics consistent with descent. A replay of the kinematics on a dynamically scaled robot confirmed that the wing motion elicited by DNa10 activation generates a reduction in upward force. Optogenetic activation of this neuron causes free-flying animals to descend, whereas ablation or silencing of the cell in tethered flies elicits fictive ascent. Functional imaging reveals that DNa10 is activated by downward visual motion and inhibited by upward motion. These results are consistent with a connectomic analysis showing that DNa10 receives monosynaptic input from large-field visual interneurons sensitive to vertical body motion and provides direct output to three wing motor neurons that regulate the lift. Collectively, these results identify core components of a circuit for altitude control that links the detection of visual motion to the alteration of aerodynamic forces.

Article.Title: Global motion deficits following early visual deprivation reflect impaired attention allocation rather than poor information integration
Article.Authors: Orlov T.; Ben-Zion I.; Zohary E.
Article.Abstract: Previous studies suggested that early visual deprivation results in global motion processing deficits. These deficits were typically attributed to poor integration of local motion signals. We challenge this view by dissociating motion integration from feature-based attentional selection. We tested 34 Ethiopian children who had bilateral congenital cataracts and gained pattern vision only years later. Strikingly, they were no different than their typically developing peers when the task required integration across motion directions, with performance well captured by a population vector-averaging model. Thus, core integration mechanisms remain intact despite prolonged early visual deprivation. In contrast, the same individuals were poorer than controls in the motion-coherence task requiring identification of a dominant motion direction. This dissociation is well explained by adding to the model a physiologically plausible attention-dependent process, which selectively amplifies salient motion signals via top-down feedback. Accordingly, the late sighted were impaired across other attention-demanding tasks. We therefore suggest that early visual deprivation disrupts attentional selection, not motion integration.

Article.Title: Sex- and frequency-dependent acute pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic effects of smoked cannabis: a randomized controlled trial
Article.Authors: Lake S.; Pabon E.; Baglot S.; Eversole A.; Murray C.; Hampilos K.; Fong T.; Middlekauff H.; Haney M.; Evans S.; Tran A.; Torrens A.; Piomelli D.; Cooper Z.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cannabis use is rising among women. Studies suggest females are more sensitive to the intoxicating and misuse-related effects of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). While preclinical studies point to sex-specific development of tolerance, this has not been translated to humans. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 44 participants (22 F) smoked three cannabis strengths (0% [~0 mg] THC, 4% [~20 mg] THC, 10% [~60 mg] THC), provided blood for plasma analysis, and completed subjective mood and drug effects assessments and a self-administration task. Outcomes were analyzed by cannabis strength, sex, and use frequency ( > 4 vs. ≤4 days/week; balanced across sex). Relative to placebo, active cannabis strengths increased subjective effects and plasma THC and metabolites ( p s < 0.05). Exploratory follow-up of interactions (cannabis strength*frequency p < 0.10) showed the frequent-use group exhibiting significant increases from placebo in misuse-related ratings (“Like”, “Take again”) and self-administering more cannabis than the occasional-use group ( p s < 0.05), and this was not modified by sex. Ratings of “High”, Sedation/impairment, Dysphoric arousal, and “Bad effect” were higher at active strengths for occasional-use males relative to sex- and/or frequency-matched counterparts ( p s < 0.05; via exploratory follow-up for “High” and Sedation/impairment). THC and metabolites tended to be highest in frequent-use males. These findings contrast with previous evidence of greater cannabis sensitivity among females and point toward future investigation into sex-dependent exposure thresholds for tolerance development/escalation. Article.Title: Children with developmental language disorder show selective impairments in low-frequency neural tracking of speech
Article.Authors: Keshavarzi M.; Feltham G.; Richards S.; Parvez L.; Goswami U.
Article.Abstract: Neural tracking of slow temporal modulations in speech supports extraction of the prosodic and syllabic structure thought to be critical for language acquisition by Temporal Sampling (TS) theory, yet whether these automatic cortical tracking mechanisms are altered in children with developmental language disorder (DLD) remains unclear. As expected a priori by TS theory, children with DLD showed significantly reduced coherence in the 0.9–2.5 Hz range associated with prosodic information in the story, spanning bilateral auditory and speech-related cortex. The strongest regional group differences were in left supramarginal gyrus ( p < 0.001) and right inferior frontal gyrus ( p = 0.001). In the 2.5–5 Hz range, linked to syllabic-rate modulations in the story, children with DLD showed reduced coherence in right temporal regions (all p < 0.02). Stronger low-frequency speech-brain coherence was associated with better language performance, indicating that individual differences in cortical speech tracking were behaviourally meaningful. No reliable differences were observed at higher modulation rates (5–9 Hz or 12–40 Hz). Exploratory functional connectivity analyses did not reveal network-level group differences that were robust across ROI time-series extraction methods. These findings indicate that atypical low-frequency neural tracking of speech is functionally relevant to language outcomes in DLD.

Article.Title: Life-cycle plasticity enables conditional asexual reproduction in a kelp
Article.Authors: Liesner D.; Luthringer R.; Kandjengo L.; Bolton J.; Rothman M.; Valero M.; Haas F.; Coelho S.
Article.Abstract: Many organisms alternate between distinct life stages and can reproduce either sexually or asexually, yet the mechanisms coordinating these developmental and reproductive transitions remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the molecular basis of life stage identity and reproductive mode in the kelp Laminaria pallida , a multicellular organism with a complex life cycle. By combining gene expression analyses with developmental experiments and natural population-level approaches, we characterize the transcriptional signatures associated with developmental state transitions in both sexual and asexual contexts. We show that asexual reproduction is associated with endoreduplication and reduced fitness, while it is retained but rarely expressed in two natural populations. Moreover, we find that the presence of potential mating partners reduces asexual development, revealing that reproductive mode is adjusted in response to reproductive opportunities. Together, these findings suggest that asexual reproduction functions as a conditional alternative to sex, promoting persistence when sexual reproduction is constrained while preserving the long-term benefits of sexual reproduction when mates are available. More broadly, our results reveal how organisms integrate developmental, environmental, and reproductive cues to balance alternative reproductive strategies across complex life cycles.

Article.Title: Category learning drives cortical attentional gain to diagnostic dimensions of perceptual information
Article.Authors: Luthra S.; Razin R.; Tierney A.; Holt L.; Dick F.
Article.Abstract: Humans and other animals develop remarkable perceptual and cognitive specializations for identifying, differentiating, and acting on classes of ecologically important signals. This expertise is flexible enough to support diverse perceptual judgments: a voice, for example, simultaneously conveys what a talker says, as well as myriad cues about her identity and state. Expert perception across complex signals thus involves discovering and learning regularities that best inform diverse perceptual judgments, as well as weighting this information flexibly as task demands change. Here, we test whether this process may involve attentional gain. We use two prospective auditory category learning tasks to relate a complex, entirely novel soundscape to four classes of ‘alien identity’ and two classes of ‘alien size.’ Identity, but not size, categorization requires discovery and learning of patterned acoustic input situated in one of two simultaneous, non-overlapping frequency bands. This allows us to capitalize on the coarsely segregated, frequency-band-specific channels tiling auditory cortex. We use fMRI to ask whether category-relevant perceptual information present in one frequency band is prioritized relative to simultaneous, uninformative information in the other frequency band. Only among participants expert at alien identity categorization do we observe neural prioritization of the identity-diagnostic frequency band. This prioritization persists even when the diagnostic information becomes irrelevant in the size categorization task. Tellingly, the neural selectivity evoked implicitly in the identity categorization task aligns with that in an independent task, where activation is driven by explicit and sustained selective attention to pure tones in one or the other frequency band. Additionally, the learning trajectories taken to achieve expert-level categorization leave fingerprints on the patterns of neural activity associated with the diagnostic dimension. In all, this indicates that learning categories can drive attentional gain to category-diagnostic input dimensions.

Article.Title: Neural integration of acoustic statistics enables mice to detect acoustic targets in noise
Article.Authors: Alishbayli A.; Przewrocki K.; van Heumen P.; Englitz B.
Article.Abstract: Sound detection amidst noise presents an important challenge in audition. Many naturally occurring sounds (rain, wind) can be described and predicted only statistically, so-called sound textures. Previous research has demonstrated the human ability to leverage this statistical predictability for sound recognition, but the neural mechanisms remain elusive. We trained mice to detect vocalizations embedded in sound textures with different statistical predictability, while recording and optogenetically modulating the neural activity in the auditory cortex. Mice showed improved performance and neural encoding if they could sample the statistics longer per trial. Textures with more exploitable structure, specifically higher cross-frequency correlations improved behavioral performance as well as neural representation of vocalizations. Activating parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons had an asymmetric effect depending on the acoustic context, improving detection and neural encoding of vocalizations for low correlations, and impoverishing them for high cross-frequency correlations. In summary, mice exploit stimulus statistics to improve sound detection in naturalistic background noise, reflected in behavioral performance and neural activity, relying on PV interneurons for temporal integration.

Article.Title: The importance of genes does not predict their mutation rate
Article.Authors: Radrizzani S.; Hurst L.
Article.Abstract: The convention that mutation is a random process has been challenged by suggestions that selection has acted on between-gene variation in the mutation rate, with claims that more important genes are protected from mutation in part, in prokaryotes, by being on the leading strand, while those required for rapid adaptive evolution have higher mutation rates, in part by being on the lagging strand. The original selectionist claims have proven contentious with several replication failures. However, none of the replication attempts fully allow for covariates and many employ data from mismatch repair (MMR) knockout strains. To address these limitations, we consider amassed mutation accumulation data for wild-type Escherichia coli , the focal species for adaptive claims, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae , in a multiple parameter-controlled analysis to predict between-gene variation in mutational density (mutations per base pair). Along with covariates, we consider putative selectively relevant parameters: protein level and essentiality to capture genic “importance”, and, in E. coli , strand with respect to DNA replication. We consider deviation of correlation and partial correlation values from those expected under trinucleotide-controlled simulations. While in E. coli more highly transcribed genes may have slightly lower mutation rates, potentially consistent with a selectionist model, the same is not seen in yeast, and in neither species do genes for more abundant or essential proteins have lower mutation rates. In E. coli there is no difference in mutation rate between genes on different strands, a lack of difference replicated in other prokaryotes. The degree of purifying selection is also not predictive of mutation density. We additionally highlight a strong artefact seen using the standard off-the-shelf statistical approach and note that results from MMR-deficient strains are discordant. We conclude that as trends are nearly uniformly unsupportive, not consistent between species and of miniscule effect size, they present no challenge to convention.

Article.Title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo models
Article.Authors: Pauli T.; von Heyl T.; Rieblinger B.; Schleibinger S.; Liang W.; Schmauser A.; Arullmoli M.; Derrer P.; Eckstein A.; Jagana S.; Gatti Corrêa C.; Flisikowski K.; Flisikowska T.; Schusser B.
Article.Abstract: Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human–animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo . Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro, ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.

Article.Title: The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry sequentially drives invasion and host-parasite interface formation
Article.Authors: Cohen A.; Bergner T.; Guérin A.; Lebrun M.; Laue M.; Klotz C.; Striepen B.
Article.Abstract: The apicomplexan parasite Cryptosporidium is a leading cause of diarrheal disease in young children. Within the intestinal epithelium, Cryptosporidium establishes a unique intracellular niche in the apical brush border of enterocytes. A structurally complex interface between host and parasite acts as a holdfast and enables protein and metabolite transport. How the parasite invades its host cell and builds the interface is poorly understood. Here, we reveal parasite invasion with high temporal and spatial resolution using rigorous molecular markers. We find that sequential discharge of specialized secretory organelles anchors the parasite within the host prior to internalization. The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry persists beyond its initial pre-invasion discharge, acting as a conduit for the secretion of multiple waves of effector proteins. Ultimately, the rhoptry membrane gives rise to the feeder organelle that separates host from parasite cytoplasm. These findings lead us to propose a mechanistic model of Cryptosporidium invasion and intracellular parasitism.

Article.Title: Vertebrate paired fins are specified by an ancient dorso-ventral patterning system
Article.Authors: Dale R.; Berger S.; Alaei S.; Davis M.; Tulenko F.; Currie P.
Article.Abstract: The origin of paired fins was a major event in early vertebrate history that fueled the adaptive radiation of the gnathostome clade. Evidence for the conservation of ancient regulatory systems between paired and median fins supports a model in which appendage-patterning mechanisms first evolved in the midline and were later redeployed to a new embryonic context, the flank. However, while paired fins and limbs are asymmetric along the dorsoventral (DV) axis, the equivalent axis does not exist in median fins, which are symmetric across the midline, raising questions of how DV patterning evolved. Here, we combine genetic tools in zebrafish with comparative expression analyses in representative ray-finned and cartilaginous fishes to show that a subset of limb DV patterning genes are expressed during median fin development. Using genetic lineage tracing of the canonical limb dorsalizing factor lmx1bb , we further demonstrate that, although lmx1bb -derived cells occupy distinct spatial domains across fin types, a subset of this lineage is fated to differentiate into fin ray osteoblasts in both paired and median fins. To test the potential conservation of regulatory modules across fin types, we generated a series of deletion mutants for two known lmx1b mouse limb enhancers, LARM1 and LARM2, that we show are partially conserved upstream of zebrafish lmx1bb . These experiments revealed that LARM function is essential for dorsoventral patterning of the paired pectoral and pelvic fins of zebrafish but is dispensable for formation of the unpaired dorsal and anal fins. Collectively, these data support the conservation of an ancient LARM -Lmx1b dorsal determination system in the paired fins of osteichthyans, challenge models proposing simple co-option of a pre-existing median fin gene regulatory network and suggest that the acquisition of this regulatory module may have been a key early step in the evolution of the paired fin DV patterning axis.

Article.Title: Sperm phospholipase C signaling via PLCζ1 and PLCδ4 is essential for Ca2+ oscillations and fertility in mice
Article.Authors: Gupta N.; Zhang L.; Akizawa H.; Gervasi M.; Tourzani D.; Visconti P.; Romarowski A.; Buffone M.; Cui W.; Fissore R.
Article.Abstract: Fertilization-induced calcium (Ca 2+ ) oscillations are essential for egg activation and embryonic development in mammals. The sperm-specific phospholipase C isoform, PLCζ1, is the primary trigger of these oscillations. Functional and clinical studies have linked mutations or reduced expression of PLCζ1 to male infertility. However, whether PLCζ1 alone accounts for Ca 2+ release at fertilization in all mammals remains uncertain. Male mice lacking Plcζ1 exhibit subfertility and reduced litter sizes; their sperm induce delayed, low-frequency Ca 2+ oscillations, indicating a compensatory mechanism. Notably, mouse sperm express high levels of PLCδ4, essential for completing the acrosome reaction (AR). In Plcζ1 -null sperm, PLCδ4 is upregulated and retained post-AR. These observations suggest a secondary functional role for PLCδ4. Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, we generated Plcδ4 knockout (KO) mice. Plcδ4 -null sperm trigger attenuated, delayed Ca 2+ oscillations and significantly reduced fertilization rates, indicating that PLCδ4 contributes to but does not independently drive Ca 2+ signaling. We therefore generated a Double Knockout (DKO) mouse line lacking both sperm-enriched PLCs. DKO males were sterile, with sperm failing to induce Ca 2+ oscillations, and the isolated residual Ca 2+ rise was insufficient to activate eggs. These findings reveal that PLCζ1, the primary oscillator, and PLCδ4, a compensatory factor, work cooperatively within a complex, multi-component PLC system that ensures robust fertilization. This work reveals molecular specialization among mammals in initiating the fertilization Ca 2+ signals. It has implications for understanding male infertility, improving assisted reproductive technologies, and developing contraceptive strategies.

Article.Title: Phylogenetic evidence that migratory behavior increases ungulate extinction rates
Article.Authors: Abraham J.; O’Brien K.; Upham N.; Jesmer B.; Bibi F.; Faith J.
Article.Abstract: Widespread instances of migratory collapse have been documented within the past several decades, indicating that migration may be a fragile strategy in the Anthropocene. Yet the fragility of migration as a strategy for navigating seasonally variable resource availability may extend deeper into evolutionary time. We used phylogenetic imputation to infer the migratory habits of 51 ungulate species that went extinct during the late Quaternary and evaluated whether migration enhances extinction rates on macroevolutionary timescales. We found that ~80% (41 of 51) of recently extinct species were migratory, whereas only 46% (95 of 207) of extant ungulates are migratory. Furthermore, Hidden State Speciation and Extinction modeling indicated that migratory species likely experienced higher speciation and extinction rates compared to nonmigratory species, resulting in elevated lineage turnover for migratory ungulates, though diversification parameter estimates depended strongly upon whether extinct species were included in analyses. The extinctions of these ungulates led to negligible declines in global ungulate functional richness (0.8%) but more substantial declines (2.7%) across Africa. Altogether, our findings indicate that migration has complex macroevolutionary consequences, enhancing both speciation and extinction rates, which may render migration an evolutionarily fragile strategy, particularly as increasingly widespread and intensive anthropogenic activity cause gradients of resource availability to become severed ( e.g ., via human infrastructure) and more unpredictable ( e.g ., via climate change).

Article.Title: Can the exposome help solve the alcohol and cancer mystery?
Article.Authors: Vasiliou V.; Stem A.; Thompson D.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol consumption is a preventable driver of many cancers, yet a central biological question remains unresolved: by what mechanisms does ethanol promote malignancy? We propose that alcohol in the context of the exposome (i.e., the network of chemical, biological, and social determinants that interact with ethanol across the life span) provides a unifying framework for understanding alcohol-related carcinogenesis. Viewed through the lens of the exposome, alcohol is not only as a direct carcinogen but also as a systemic amplifier of environmental risk acting across multiple levels of biological organization, from molecular damage to whole-body physiology. This reframing has important implications for mechanistic research, precision prevention, and public-health policy.

Article.Title: Two parallel lateral hypothalamic GABAergic projections differentially modulate pain and anxiety in mice
Article.Authors: Sun Y.; Peng Y.; Zhang X.; Yin C.; Xiao C.; Chen J.; Zhou C.
Article.Abstract: The lateral hypothalamus (LH) is fundamentally involved in motivated behaviors, yet the precise functional segregation of its GABAergic projections in modulating pain and its affective dimensions remains poorly understood. Here, using male and female mice, we revealed that LH GABAergic neurons sent parallel projections to two pivotal pain and affect processing centers: the lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPB) and the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT). In vivo fiber photometry revealed that LH GABAergic terminals in both the PVT and LPB are robustly activated by noxious, aversive, and rewarding stimuli, indicating their roles in encoding salient and affective information. Critically, we uncovered a remarkable functional segregation of these LH GABAergic pathways. Optogenetic activation of the LH-PVT projection exerted anxiogenic effects without altering pain sensitivity in both naïve and neuropathic pain mice; whereas optogenetic inhibition of this pathway exerted significant analgesic and anxiolytic effects specifically in neuropathic pain, highlighting a context-dependent modulation of pain and affect. In contrast, optogenetic activation of the LH-LPB projection induced contralateral pronociception without impacting affective behaviors, conversely, inhibition of this pathway significantly elevated contralateral pain thresholds in both physiological and neuropathic pain conditions. We also demonstrated that stimulation of the LH-LPB projection acted via a disinhibitory mechanism involving local LPB GABAergic interneurons to enhance activity of LPB glutamatergic neurons. Collectively, our findings delineate two parallel and functionally segregated LH GABAergic output pathways that differentially control distinct aspects of pain experience, thereby offering novel circuit-specific targets for the treatment of chronic pain and its debilitating emotional comorbidities.

Article.Title: Saccadic suppression enhances saliency of ecologically relevant stimuli in the zebrafish optic tectum
Article.Authors: Soto G.; Thomas C.; Funk L.; Hladnik T.; Dehmelt F.; Hafed Z.; Arrenberg A.
Article.Abstract: Saccadic suppression, a reduction in visual sensitivity around the time of rapid eye movements, is well-documented in primate psychophysics, but its mechanisms and functions remain debated. Saccadic suppression thus contributes to more than just compensation for rapid saccade-induced image shifts. We first established a behavioral correlate of saccadic suppression in larval zebrafish escape behavior. Then, using electrophysiology, we show that retinal ganglion cells jumpstart saccadic suppression in a spatial frequency-dependent manner. Calcium imaging, combined with 360° visual stimulation and behavioral tracking, revealed that motor signals enhance peri-saccadic suppression strength in the optic tectum, where suppression lasts for more than 3,000 ms. Notably, saccadic suppression is much weaker and more short-lived for stimuli related to hunting or escape behavior than for behaviorally less relevant global flashes. This unequal attenuation effectively increases the salience of the ecologically relevant stimuli in the optic tectum after saccades. Our results demonstrate that saccadic suppression integrates visual and motor signals to optimize sensory processing within neural constraints, and they provide insights into evolutionarily conserved visual strategies.

Article.Title: Infant presence and mother-infant conflict predict fetal loss in wild mandrills
Article.Authors: Smit N.; Roura-Torres B.; Delaunay A.; Baniel A.; Huchard E.; Charpentier M.
Article.Abstract: Female fitness depends on reproductive pace and offspring survival, both of which are determined by the ability to balance resource allocation between current and future reproduction. Using 11 years of data on 356 pregnancies (52 of which resulted in fetal loss) from 117 wild female mandrills, we show that females who conceive while still caring for a young infant experience a greater probability of fetal loss as well as increased mother-infant behavioral conflict in the form of maternal rejection. In addition, females whose infants throw more tantrums show a greater probability of fetal loss, consistent with observations from other species where living offspring can interfere in parental reproduction. Finally, females who lose a fetus show greater subsequent reproductive success (produce more surviving infants and show shorter inter-birth intervals) than females who give birth but their infants die soon after birth. These findings suggest that fetal loss may represent an adaptive physiological response to the energetic constraints imposed by overlapping gestation and maternal care, potentially limiting the fitness costs associated with short inter-birth intervals and concurrent investment in multiple dependent offspring.

Article.Authors: Bierenbroodspot M.; Kunz C.; Goldbecker E.; Lorenz M.; Irisarri I.; Pröschold T.; Darienko T.; de Vries J.
Article.Abstract: Discerning the nature of the last common ancestor of land plants (embryophytes) and algae allows to retrace the adaptations that ushered in the conquest of land by plants. Albeit initially coming as a surprise due to their plain body plans, all major phylogenomic efforts have concluded that the Zygnematophyceae are the algal sisters to land plants. The Zygnematophyceae are the streptophyte algal class with the greatest species richness and while we now have ample genome information on a few select members of zygnematophytes, our understanding of the genomic divergence as well as genetic potential for key traits is limited by a lack of phylodiverse data that accounts for this diversity and integrates it into a phylogenomic framework. We here sequenced 43 new transcriptome datasets for the Zygnematophyceae and built a phylogenomic tree based on a total of 104 zygnematophyceaen transcriptomes and 2243 loci. We recover a deep genetic structure for the Zygnematophyceae: Despite the deep split between Spirogyrales and their unicellular sister group Desmidiales, most Spirogyrales emerged after pronounced genetic divergence, accommodating the attainment of multicellularity and divergent traits such as unique cell and plastid division. Overall, our data capture signatures of massive ancient radiations that could only be revealed thanks to a phylodiverse sampling. Recognizing the deep genetic divergences and a vast evolutionary history of the Zygnematophyceae are key to illuminate the nature of the algal progenitors of land plants.

Article.Title: A split nozzle and two-protein chain-like fibers define the tail architecture of Pseudomonas aeruginosa podophage A1002
Article.Authors: Pang H.; Chen Y.; Peng Z.; Xiao H.; Chen W.; Li X.; Chen P.; Zheng J.; Liu H.
Article.Abstract: Phage therapy offers unique advantages against antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Based on density maps combined with AlphaFold3 predictions, we identified 11 structural protein components from the head to the tail. Notably, the A1002 nozzle employs a distinct assembly strategy, featuring the unique nozzle-rope protein and nozzle-base protein, which may have evolved through modular evolution and horizontal gene transfer. Furthermore, the nozzle-rope protein provides 11 adsorption sites for fiber dimers, and these dimers are assembled from two proteins, giving rise to two types of dimers: dimers 1–7 correspond to fiber I (gp40), and dimers 8–11 correspond to fiber II (gp41). The nozzle-rope protein and these dimers combine to form a chain-like fiber. The tail tube comprises a double-layered, elongated tube structure that functions to simultaneously increase tail length and provide docking sites for six chain-like fibers. Article.Authors: Raccah O.; Agarwal A.; Zhu Y.; Turk-Browne N.
Article.Abstract: The hippocampus receives convergent input from multiple sensory systems, yet in humans it has been studied almost exclusively through vision. Here we examine how the hippocampus contributes to sensory processing beyond the visual modality and to the multisensory integration of visual information with these other modalities. Whereas univariate analyses detected only visual responses across hippocampal subregions, with no activation for auditory stimuli and no benefit of congruent stimuli, multivariate analyses revealed robust representations of both auditory and visual scenes. The posterior hippocampus showed enhanced pattern similarity for congruent stimuli relative to unisensory stimuli, especially in the left hemisphere, demonstrating multisensory facilitation. The anterior hippocampus showed crossmodal decoding between auditory and visual versions of the same clip, driven by the right hemisphere, suggesting a more abstract representation. Article.Title: An open-source eye-tracking system adaptable to diverse terrestrial vertebrates reveals state-dependent visual acquisition in lizards
Article.Authors: Leberstein N.; Remenick T.; Becker M.; Shein-Idelson M.
Article.Abstract: Gaze shifts are fundamental to visual exploration and processing, yet empirical knowledge is largely confined to a small number of model species, limiting our understanding of general principles of visual acquisition across animals. Here, we introduce a versatile, low-cost, and open-source framework design for eye-tracking in small, freely moving animals. Leveraging photogrammetry, 3D modeling, and 3D-printing, we produce headmounts adaptable to diverse head-eye geometries, as we demonstrate for lizards, turtles, and mice. Detailed recordings in Pogona vitticeps, a laterally eyed ectotherm with a high-acuity retina, reveal a rich oculomotor repertoire with kinematics closely resembling the saccadic main sequence in primates. We found both movement-coupled large binocular saccades, which exhibited a strong axial bias as well as small, isotropic, and monocular saccades suggesting a capacity for visual exploration of local details. Visual acquisition strategies were strongly tied to behavioral states with periods of active sampling (3–5 Hz saccades) separated by periods of ocular stillness lasting many seconds and suggesting a visual acquisition strategy distinct from those commonly described in endothermic model species. Furthermore, active states were correlated with pupil constriction in contrast to mammals and similarly to birds. Our results demonstrate the utility of our experimental approach for understanding visual acquisition across terrestrial vertebrates. Such a multi-perspective view on natural visual acquisition across species will be essential for developing a generalized understanding of vision, its ecological functions, and its evolutionary trajectory.

Article.Title: LEM-3/ANKLE1 nuclease prevents the formation of abnormal syncytium to safeguard neuronal differentiation
Article.Authors: Deng S.; Zheng C.
Article.Abstract: In animal development, cells exit the cell cycle after a final round of cell division to differentiate into specialized cell types. However, the impact of failed cytokinesis on the fate specification of postmitotic cells, especially neurons, remains poorly understood. We analyzed the Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking the midbody-tethered endonuclease LEM-3/ANKLE1, which resolves chromatin bridges during cytokinesis. Using genetic analysis, fluorescence microscopy, and RNA visualization, we found that unresolved DNA bridges lead to the formation of stable intercellular bridges, creating binucleate syncytia between touch receptor neurons and sister cells, which allows thorough cytoplasmic mixing despite independent nuclear transcription. In some cases, the cytoplasmic linkage between sister cells also led to the suppression of neuronal fates and prevention of apoptotic fates. Thus, LEM-3 prevents syncytium formation to ensure proper cellular differentiation.

Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Kragel P.
Article.Abstract: Human emotional experiences vary widely in everyday life, yet they are systematically organized within a continuous affective space defined by valence and arousal. The grid-like signal reflected a metric organization of emotion concepts independent of overt behavior, whereas distance-related signals in vmPFC predicted trial-by-trial affective judgements. Together, these findings suggest that emotion knowledge is structured by a grid-like coordinate system in the human brain that can support predictive inference and flexible decision-making.

Article.Title: CFL1-dependency of discrete cell behaviours driving mouse spinal zippering
Article.Authors: Marshall A.; Krstevski A.; Crosswell H.; Shah R.; Maniou E.; Greene N.; Copp A.; Galea G.
Article.Abstract: Epithelial fusion is critical for formation of many embryonic tissues.
