Key zipper-advancing behaviours are: (i) constriction of supracellular actomyosin cables; (ii) extension of filopodial/lamellipodial protrusions at periodic intervals; (iii) constriction of leading-edge cell borders bringing together protrusions which establish ‘pioneering’ contacts across the midline; (iv) cell-cell and ( v) cell-ECM adhesion remodelling; (vi) zipper advancement through cell partner exchange. In wild-type embryos, CFL1 is enriched at the leading edge of surface ectoderm cells adjacent to the zippering point, and localised within some protrusions. Conditional Cfl1 deletion in the surface ectoderm produces denser F-actin stress fibres, makes filopodial protrusions excessively stable, diminishes their exploratory movements which may establish nascent contacts, and impairs junctional constriction of cells at the point of fusion. Zippering speed is reduced ~30% in conditional Cfl1 -deleted embryos and ~30% develop spina bifida. Article.Title: Resistance mutation supply modulates the benefit of CRISPR immunity against virulent phages in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Article.Authors: Wright R.; Lovell S.; Richmond A.; Harrison C.; Ashworth E.; Kadioglu A.; Fothergill J.; Friman V.; Westra E.; Brockhurst M.

Article.Title: Transient feedforward communication between somatosensory and premotor cortex supports goal-directed behavior
Article.Authors: Ranjbar-Slamloo Y.; Kamigaki T.
Article.Abstract: Goal-directed behavior requires sensory information to be transformed into motor commands, yet the precise temporal structure of communication between sensory and motor cortices during this process remains poorly understood. Article.Title: Full-length genomes evolve in parallel in a long-term evolution experiment with phage φX174
Article.Authors: Bons E.; Chabas H.; MacDonald H.; Escalera Ledermann A.; Ösze S.; Dunstan J.; Ochsner N.; Angst D.; Bonhoeffer S.; Regoes R.
Article.Abstract: The study of evolution in organisms with high mutation rates requires detailed data on the genomic composition of the population. Here we report on an innovative use of high-throughput sequencing technology combined with rapid experimental evolution that allowed us to follow the genetic diversification of four independent bacteriophage populations for 412 generations in extraordinary detail. One of our goals was to assess phylodynamic methods that use genetic information to infer key parameters of the population history. Because phylodynamic methods assume neutral evolution, we did not actively impose any selection pressures in our evolution experiment (in addition to those inherent in the bacterial cell environment). Tracing over 80′000 bacteriophage genomes, representing 884 distinct genotypes, we find that the patterns of viral diversification result in largely non-congruent genotype distributions, but also document multiple instances of parallel evolution. We further show that the observed extent of parallel evolution biases phylodynamic analysis of migration rates, and wrongly estimates significant migration between the independent evolution lines. Our approach is applicable to many other viruses and paves the way to advanced population genetic investigations that aim to shed light on phenomena that relate to genetic linkage across the genome.

Article.Title: Viral disease outcomes are indistinguishable between experimentally infected bats and rodents
Article.Authors: Farrell M.; Tucker S.; Mollentze N.; Streicker D.
Article.Abstract: A common explanation for bats being a conspicuous source of zoonotic viruses is their purported ability to coexist with viruses without suffering overt disease. Widespread acceptance of the idea that bats have unusual antiviral traits has catalyzed the discovery of unique features of bat immune systems which may have translational value as broad-spectrum antivirals, particularly if they evolved as a byproduct of bats’ unique life history rather than through conventional co-evolutionary processes. Surprisingly, whether bats compared to other host groups suffer less disease from co-evolved viruses or from viruses generally has not been formally assessed. Here, synthesizing 86 years of experimental infections, involving 54 viruses, 85 host species, and over 5,600 animals, we document disease in bats following inoculation by taxonomically diverse viruses, including ones that are relatively benign in humans. The occurrence of overt disease, the likelihood of mortality, and the severity of disease in bats were indistinguishable from those experienced by rodents, another group associated with many zoonotic viruses. These patterns were consistent when considering only bat-associated viruses inoculated into bats and rodent-associated viruses inoculated into rodents and among inoculations which lacked shared co-evolutionary history. Instead, disease outcomes following infection were shaped by experimental design, viral host range, and evolutionary context. Unexceptional disease in bats from novel or co-evolved infections suggests that order-level host life history traits such as flight have inconsistent consequences for antiviral immunity and highlights the need to evaluate the functional properties of putatively unique features of bat immunity in vivo. While these results do not exclude the possibility of developing broader-acting or more potent antivirals from bat immune systems or diminish the potential value of mechanistic insights into bat immunity, they suggest that bat immune systems were shaped by conventional co-evolutionary processes rather than through unique circumstances that endow exceptional antiviral defenses.

Article.Title: Pollinator abundance shapes sexual selection in an angiosperm
Article.Authors: Barbot E.; Dufaÿ M.; Janicke T.; Lapeyre B.; Orcel D.; Rousset F.; Tonnabel J.
Article.Abstract: Sexual selection is a central force in evolutionary biology that has been shown to shape phenotypes and population dynamics in animals. While this selective force is increasingly recognized in flowering plants, theory predicts that anisogamy generates sex differences in the fitness benefits of acquiring additional mates—a pattern well supported in animals but with limited tests in plants. Plant studies rely solely on genetic parentage analyses to estimate mate numbers, thereby conflating performance in accessing mates with success in gamete fertilization. Pollinators add an ecological layer, as their behavior and abundance can influence competition for access to mates and their gametes. Here, we disentangle consecutive episodes of sexual selection in the hermaphroditic plant Brassica rapa by combining direct observations of Bombus terrestris movements with genetic paternity analyses in experimental populations, thus providing independent estimates of the observational number of mates acquired and realized fertilization success. Our approach identifies pollen competition for ovules as the primary arena for sexual selection in B. rapa . Competition for access to mates constitutes a secondary force and was found to be stronger in the male compared to the female sex function, as predicted by classic theory. Experimentally reduced pollinator abundance modulated the balance between pre- and post-pollination sexual selection, increasing the opportunity for selection on mate acquisition. Ignoring pollinator movements led to biased estimates of pre-pollination sexual selection. Our findings demonstrate that sexual selection in plants unfolds across multiple, sequential episodes shaped by ecological context.

Article.Title: Tolerance measured at one developmental stage mispredicts climate resilience in an animal with a complex life cycle
Article.Authors: Song H.; Shi T.; Yang M.; Liu X.; Li Z.; Shi P.; Wu Y.; Allam B.; Jeffs A.; Skelton B.; Zhang T.
Article.Abstract: Forecasts of whether marine species can evolve fast enough to survive climate change rely largely on single-stage tolerance assays, tacitly assuming that tolerance measured at one developmental stage reflects adaptive capacity across the organism’s life cycle. Acidification therefore does not merely depress performance—it reorganizes the genetic architecture into a cross-stage conflict. Under ramping RCP 8.5 forcing this conflict geometry dictates the direction—not merely the magnitude—of adaptation: only balanced multi-stage selection preserves family diversity, whereas single-stage selection systematically erodes the opposite axis. In complex life cycles, resilience is a geometric property of ontogeny that forecasts cannot compress into a single-stage without inverting the sign of the answer.

Article.Authors: Skeels A.; Rogger J.; Cardillo M.; Farnsworth A.; Lunt D.; Karger D.

These findings suggest biodiversity tracks the ecological limits set by shifting biomes, leaving sparse legacy of past dynamics. Our results highlight the importance of integrating multiple paleoclimate reconstructions when assessing the historical drivers of biodiversity.

Consistent with predictions, we found both behavioral and neural numerical distance effects. Activation vectors in intraparietal, inferior temporal, prefrontal, hippocampal, and parahippocampal cortices formed a two-dimensional semantic space organized by numerical magnitude and domain (fractions versus integers). Gaussian fits revealed a topographic map of numerical preferences in the anterior inferior parietal cortex, common to both domains. Our results suggest that, when educated adults engage in an explicit magnitude comparison task, their brain can construct an ordered representation that integrates fractions and integers, with a topographic organization in the anterior IPS/IPL.

Article.Title: Host–virus interactions dominate fitness and conceal additive genetic variation
Article.Authors: Belyi A.; Du Y.; Wilson A.; Longdon B.; Jiggins F.
Article.Abstract: Host–parasite coevolution is expected to generate strong selection for resistance and infectivity that has the potential to erode genetic variation. Despite this, natural populations often retain extensive genetic variation in these traits. Genotype-by-genotype interactions on fitness can generate negative frequency-dependent selection, which helps maintain this variation by preventing any host or pathogen genotype from retaining a permanent advantage. Because these interactions place genetic variance in the interaction term rather than in additive differences among hosts or pathogens, that variance is masked from directional selection and can remain ‘cryptic’. Here we combine coevolutionary modelling with large‑scale experimental infection assays to quantify how host-pathogen interactions structure fitness variance in a vertically transmitted virus system, Drosophila melanogaster and sigma virus. Simulations show that coevolution typically erodes additive genetic variance in host and pathogen fitness, concentrating variance in host-virus interaction terms. Consistent with these predictions, experiments spanning 90 host-virus genotype combinations reveal that transmission, viral load, and virulence are overwhelmingly governed by host-virus genetic interactions rather than host or virus main effects. As a result, neither host resistance alleles nor viral genotypes confer consistently higher fitness across genetic backgrounds. Interactions tend to be sex‑specific, further limiting heritable fitness variation. Our results demonstrate that coevolution can substantially mask heritable genetic variation from directional selection by rendering fitness context-dependent. This extensive cryptic genetic variation may be revealed either when ecological or evolutionary conditions shift, or when the process of coevolution itself alters the direction of selection. This demonstrates the need to account for genotype-specific interactions when forecasting evolutionary responses.

Article.Title: A macrophage-targeted TIMD4 Peptide-Nanoparticle attenuates colitis symptoms and monocyte recruitment in a mouse model
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Wang Y.; Yu R.; Liu K.; Zheng D.; Wang B.; Chang Y.; Liu B.; Yue X.; Wu Z.; Li C.; Liang X.; Ma C.; Liu G.; Li J.; Xu L.; Gao L.
Article.Abstract: Macrophages play a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain-containing molecule 4 (TIMD4) is involved in the regulation of tissue-resident macrophages. In this study, we found that Timd4 deficiency aggravated DSS-induced colitis, accompanied by increased infiltration of monocytes into the colonic tissues. Mechanistically, in vitro studies revealed that TIMD4 stabilized the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex via its intracellular domain, thereby activating the AMPK pathway and suppressing NF-κB-dependent chemokine production in macrophages. Treatment with T4 (365–378) -NPs reduced P65 phosphorylation and attenuated DSS-induced colitis in mice. Treatment with either T4 (365–378) -NPs or the CCR2 antagonist attenuated DSS-induced colitis, and no statistically significant differences in the assessed outcomes were detected between the two groups. Administration of T4 (365–378) -NPs before DSS exposure also attenuated subsequent colitis. Furthermore, combining the T4 (365–378) ‑NPs with anti-α4β7 or anti-TNF-α antibodies produced greater improvements than either monotherapy in the DSS-induced colitis model. Article.Title: Non-adaptive evolutionary forces predominantly shape nucleotide composition near human transcription start sites
Article.Authors: Qiu Y.; Hebraud E.; Pouyet F.; Palazzo A.
Article.Abstract: In the human genome, mutation rates vary along genes, yet how their fine-scale structure contributes to gene evolution has remained largely unexplored. Here, we map inherited mutations at single-nucleotide resolution and uncover a striking hypermutation peak at transcription start sites (TSSs) of human protein-coding genes. This pattern is observed both in population polymorphisms and in de novo mutations from parent-offspring trios, and is dependent on transcriptional activity in testes. We also find similar hypermutation peaks at TSSs used to produce long noncoding RNAs and at intergenic RNA Polymerase II pause sites. In addition, we identify distinct mutational signatures at exon-intron boundaries and in introns. By comparing the current nucleotide content to predicted equilibrium levels, inferred from mutation and fixation rates, and by analyzing derived ancestral frequency spectrums, we detect signals that are compatible with a low level of ongoing background GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC) throughout the region and ancestral elevated gBGC activity that is centered right downstream from the TSS. Using a forward-in-time simulation algorithm, we show that the current nucleotide composition surrounding the TSS of protein-coding genes is best explained by local mutation biases coupled to ongoing and ancestral patterns of gene conversions. Our simulations allow us to infer several features of these gBGC events. Overall, these findings indicate that the nucleotide composition around TSSs is largely shaped by non-adaptive forces, particularly mutation bias and gBGC.

Article.Title: Oxidative signaling thresholds shape vulnerability in the central and peripheral nervous systems
Article.Authors: Wakatsuki S.; Araki T.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegeneration is frequently associated with oxidative stress, yet the mechanisms that convert reactive oxygen species (ROS) into irreversible degenerative signals remain incompletely understood. This Essay proposes that neuronal vulnerability is shaped by multilayered signaling thresholds comprising ROS production, antioxidant and thiol buffering, redox-sensitive signal detection, molecular gating, and commitment to degeneration, survival, or repair. This framework may help explain selective neuronal vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases and identify intervention points downstream of global ROS suppression.

Article.Abstract: Escherichia coli is highly sensitive to acid and osmotic stress but adapts by modulating the expression of stress-responsive genes. Nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) play key roles in DNA organization and sensing environmental changes. H-NS may alter local chromatin structure to modulate the expression of such genes in response to environmental stress. The H-NS homolog suppressor of td phenotype A (StpA) co-regulates several target genes, but its role is poorly defined. Article.Abstract: Neuronal activity causes topoisomerase IIβ (TOP2B) to form DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) within the promoters of early response genes (ERGs), such as Fos and Npas4. Article.Authors: Li S.; Hong Y.; Deng S.; Wu X.; Jia Z.; Liu Y.; Liu Y.; Wu G.; Chen Y.; Wu A.; Gao X.; Chen Z.

Article.Abstract: Lenvatinib is a first-line therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Li F.; Gao M.; Ma J.; Wang S.; Xiao B.; Zhong B.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic enzymes are increasingly recognized for "moonlighting" functions beyond their primary metabolic roles. Article.Abstract: AKT hyperactivation is a hallmark of many human cancers and contributes to poor clinical outcomes, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Article.Abstract: Probiotic efficacy in inflammatory bowel disease varies widely between individuals, and the sources of that variability remain poorly understood. Article.Abstract: The RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK pathway has been extensively studied for its roles in physiology and disease, yet a systems-level view of its interplay with the broader cellular context is lacking, limiting insight into paralog-specific roles, mutation-driven rewiring, and cross-pathway integration. Article.Authors: Wu D.; Liu C.; Wang H.; Chi C.; Wang Y.; Zhang W.; Wang X.; Jiang D.
Article.Abstract: Amphetamine-type stimulants (ATSs) disrupt the brain monoaminergic system and strongly stimulate motivation, movement, and addiction. Here, we report the cryo-EM structures of human VMAT2 in complex with four ATSs (AMPH, METH, MDMA, and MDA) and the inhibitor lobeline, revealing the molecular mechanisms underlying ATS recognition and modulation. This study provides important mechanistic insights into VMAT2 modulation by amphetamines and lobeline.

Article.Title: Embryonic reprogramming drives anaplastic transformation in thyroid carcinoma
Article.Authors: Kawaura R.; Unome A.; Tomita H.; Ishihara H.; Kuroki M.; Komura S.; Kato K.; Takashima S.; Nishio N.; Shigeyama M.; Hirata T.; Ishii R.; Kimura S.; Tsunekawa S.; Akiyama H.; Hara A.; Yamada Y.; Ogawa T.; Shibata H.
Article.Abstract: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is a highly aggressive malignancy that often arises through anaplastic transformation of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). Although genetic drivers such as BRAF and TP53 mutations are implicated, the mechanisms underlying this transition remain poorly understood. Guided by parallels with induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming, we develop an in vivo reprogramming mouse model. Forced expression of Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc (OSKM) induces anaplastic transformation of Braf-mutant thyroid epithelium even without Trp53 mutation, yielding an ATC-like phenotype that shares molecular and histological features with human ATC. A conventional Braf/Trp53-mutant model shows similar features. Article.Title: SIR2-mediated filament assembly activates the NLR-like protein Avs5 for bacterial antiviral defense
Article.Authors: Wang C.; Xie J.; Shen Z.; Ehrmann J.; Yu C.; Fang M.; Wu H.; Fu T.
Article.Abstract: Like mammalian nucleotide-binding and oligomerization domain receptors (NLRs), bacterial NLR-like proteins mediate antiviral defense. Whereas canonical inflammasome NLRs use NBD oligomerization to nucleate effector-domain filaments, Avs5 forms SIR2-mediated filaments that couple receptor assembly to NADase activation. In the resting state, ATP-bound Avs5 is monomeric and subsequently forms a SIR2-mediated dimer that likely represents an intermediate in a stepwise activation pathway. Upon activation, ATP-dependent conformational remodeling of the NBD promotes conversion of these dimers into active filaments. Structure-guided mutagenesis, biochemical assays, and functional analyses show that filament assembly is required for efficient NAD+ hydrolysis and antiphage defense. Article.Title: Role of Leu and Val synthesis in sensing mitochondrial nutrient and energy availability
Article.Authors: Phan J.; Gay L.; Dokládal L.; De Virgilio C.; Salcedo L.; Tha S.; Wandvik C.; Babst M.
Article.Abstract: How cells integrate nutrient availability to coordinate metabolism and growth remains poorly understood. Here, we identify branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) synthesis as a metabolic sensing system linking mitochondrial activity to translational and transcriptional control. Yeast limits Leu and Val import and instead relies on their synthesis, allowing BCAA production to reflect mitochondrial anabolic capacity. Reduced Val synthesis activates Gcn2, whereas reduced Leu synthesis inhibits TORC1, together decreasing translation efficiency and restricting growth. This response lowers levels of the transcriptional repressor Mig1, suppressing the Warburg/Crabtree effect and promoting alternative carbon source utilization. Remarkably, pharmacological inhibition of Leu/Val synthesis induces this metabolic reprogramming even in nutrient-rich medium, indicating that mitochondrial BCAA synthesis can partially override other nutrient-sensing pathways. Thus, BCAA synthesis couples mitochondrial anabolic capacity to Gcn2 and TORC1 activity and, through translational control of transcription factor abundance, shapes cellular metabolism.

Article.Title: Single-cell multi-omics reveals archetypal regulatory programs shared across T cell subsets
Article.Authors: Walker S.; van der Veeken J.; Rudensky A.; Pritykin Y.
Article.Abstract: T cells differentiate into functionally distinct subsets in response to pathogens, yet essential immune functions such as self-renewal, expansion, cytokine production, and cytotoxicity are common to multiple subsets and therefore must be programmed via shared regulatory mechanisms. To uncover these "archetypal" epigenomic programs, we integrated a single-cell multiomic (scATAC+RNA-seq) dataset of CD4 and CD8 T cells responding to acute and chronic viral infection with a comprehensive bulk ATAC-seq compendium. Our analysis reveals a modular architecture governing T cell identity, implicating distinct transcription factors in reusing regulatory programs across subsets and lineages. Notably, translationally important progenitor CD8 T cells, critical for sustained immunity and present in both acute and chronic infection, exhibit a composite regulatory state, combining a CD8 exhaustion program with a follicular helper CD4 T cell program. In sum, this resource and generalizable computational framework will aid the mechanistic dissection of adaptive immunity and immunotherapy design.

Article.Title: CCN1-mediated stress signaling underlies intrinsic cardiomyocyte dysfunction in spinal muscular atrophy
Article.Authors: Zeng W.; Liu W.; Caudal A.; Liu L.; Kong X.; Zhu W.; Kim H.; Lee A.; Alamana C.; Melesio J.; Cao X.; Howell K.; Chen K.; Pang P.; Day J.; Wu J.
Article.Abstract: Cardiac involvement in spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is increasingly recognized, but its cellular basis remains poorly defined. Together, these findings identify a CCN1-mediated mechanism underlying SMA cardiac dysfunction and support combination strategies integrating SMN-dependent and independent therapies.

Article.Authors: Striepen J.; Culibrk L.; Dananberg A.; Rozowsky J.; Petljak M.; Maciejowski J.
Article.Abstract: APOBEC3 cytosine deaminases are major sources of cancer mutations. Article.Title: The compositional encoding of hand-eye coordinated movements for single neurons in the posterior parietal cortex
Article.Authors: Mynhier N.; Gamez J.; Moorse K.; Pejsa K.; Bari A.; Murray R.; Andersen R.

Article.Authors: Chen X.; Dong C.; Wang Y.; Yun T.; Wang L.; Chen R.; Shen Y.; Tang C.; Xie Y.; Zeng K.; Yang Y.; Han Z.; Bu J.; Li S.; Zhou A.

Article.Title: Molecular insights into the activation mechanism of the slow anion channel AtSLAH3
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Zhao B.; Pan D.; He F.; Wang S.; Liu J.; Peng M.; Sun H.; Zhou X.; Liu L.; Yao X.; Gao S.
Article.Abstract: The plant slow anion channel SLAH3 regulates essential physiological processes, including stomatal closure and stress responses, yet the structural mechanism underlying its activation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the activation mechanism of SLAH3 by determining cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the wild-type (WT) channel and gain-of-function mutants identified through a targeted mutagenesis screen of pore-lining residues. Notably, the L400A mutant was captured in a dilated, open-like conformation, in contrast to the auto-inhibited WT channel. Structural comparisons revealed concerted rearrangements of the pore-lining transmembrane helices and intracellular regulatory elements. The observations point to an activation model in which displacement of the intracellular auto-inhibitory module relieves pore occlusion, triggering conformational changes that propagate from the intracellular loop to pore-lining segments, ultimately widening the entrance for anion transport. Therefore, our study provides a structural framework for understanding SLAH3 regulation and advances our understanding of nitrate signaling and stress adaptation in plants.

Article.Title: A stress-adapted fiber state promotes clonal expansion of deleted mitochondrial DNA
Article.Authors: Perez-Rodriguez D.; Dalla Rosa I.; Magoulopoulou A.; Ricciardi S.; Davidson S.; Lasalandra R.; Kabiljo R.; Moylett A.; Hill T.; Wan T.; Jones A.; Moss C.; Zierz C.; Salazar M.; Desai R.; Huang S.; Pommier Y.; Hofer M.; Pitceathly R.; Reijns M.; Poulton J.; Proukakis C.; Simons J.; Nilsson M.; Taylor R.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) depletion and multiple deletions frequently coexist in mitochondrial disease, neurodegeneration, and aging, yet how the two relate and why deletions accumulate focally remain unresolved. Here, longitudinal bulk and in situ analyses of Mpv17-/- murine muscle reveal that a compensatory rise in mitochondrial transcripts per mtDNA initially offsets severe, uniform mtDNA depletion, preserving the respiratory chain. However, this response carries a delayed cost: by six months transcripts decline, mtDNA deletions emerge, and respiratory-deficient fibers appear. Paradoxically, fibers harboring deletions accumulate supra-physiological amounts of mtDNA, despite prior depletion. This expansion is invariably accompanied by elevated Hsp60, and the same holds in human mitochondrial myopathy. We propose that depletion reprograms mitochondrial DNA and RNA metabolism, inadvertently promoting deletion formation and creating an Hsp60-high fiber state permissive for clonal expansion. Therefore, depletion and multiple deletions can be sequential phases of a common degenerative process, relevant also to aging and neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Acute respiratory distress syndrome FXR/Sptlc2 signaling promotes alveolar macrophage mitophagy and limits lung inflammation
Article.Authors: Yan M.; Liu Y.; Deng M.; Pi D.; Zhu J.; Yu Q.; Huang C.; Ran Q.; Li W.; Zhou K.; Peng W.; Duan X.; Tang J.; Yang G.; Tan J.; Hu Z.
Article.Abstract: Alveolar macrophages (AMs) undergo functional reprogramming that critically regulates lung inflammation. Although mitophagy is essential for mitochondrial quality control, its role in macrophage functional reprogramming during acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains unclear. Here, we identify the nuclear receptor Nr1h4 (FXR) as a transcriptional regulator of mitophagy in AMs. FXR activation transcriptionally upregulates serine palmitoyltransferase long chain base subunit 2 (Sptlc2), thereby enhancing mitophagy and promoting an anti-inflammatory macrophage phenotype under inflammatory conditions. The FXR/Sptlc2 axis reduces oxidative stress and inflammatory mediator production while increasing anti-inflammatory markers. Conversely, FXR deficiency impairs mitophagy, exacerbates pulmonary inflammation, and aggravates lung injury in vivo. These findings establish the FXR/Sptlc2 axis as a regulator of mitochondrial quality control and macrophage functional reprogramming and identify it as a potential therapeutic target in ARDS.

Article.Title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes
Article.Authors: Setti A.; Stufera Mecarelli L.; Santini T.; D’Angelo A.; Padovano V.; Vitiello E.; Castagnetti F.; Martone J.; Mariani D.; Bozzoni I.
Article.Abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

Article.Title: Locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons have diverse activity patterns across species and biological context
Article.Authors: Kelberman M.; Rodberg E.; Munn B.; Arabzadeh E.; Bair-Marshall C.; Berridge C.; Berrocoso E.; Breton-Provencher V.; Chandler D.; Che A.; Davy O.; Devilbiss D.; Downs A.; Drummond G.; Dvorkin R.; Fazlali Z.; Froemke R.; Glennon E.; Gold J.; Ito H.; Jiang X.; Johansen J.; Kaye A.; Kim J.; Kuo C.
Article.Abstract: The locus coeruleus (LC) brainstem cell group is evolutionarily conserved across vertebrates and influences both mind (cognition) and body (cardiorespiratory, metabolic, and immune functions) via two-putatively distinct-spontaneous activity patterns. Yet, the degree to which spontaneous LC firing rates and patterns are homogeneous across species has never been assessed due to inherently limited sample sizes. To remedy this, we pooled cross-species data from 20 laboratories to show that firing rates differ across species and are modulated by sex, age, and type of in vitro or in vivo preparation. Contrary to the prevailing dual-mode firing pattern schema, we observed patterns spread across a low-dimensional manifold, with subregions enriched for specific biological factors and neurodegenerative disease models. Our findings show considerable diversity in an ancestral vertebrate neuromodulatory system.

Article.Title: CSE1L enrichment in pediatric and young adult acute myeloid leukemia reveals a ribosomal export dependency
Article.Authors: Egan G.; Kumar A.; Voisin V.; Hurren R.; Chegini A.; Ling D.; Thomas G.; Yan Y.; Feng Y.; Duong N.; Khan D.; Sarathy C.; Jitkova Y.; Bansal S.; Zeng A.; Hoff F.; Kornblau S.; Dick J.; Hitzler J.; Schimmer A.
Article.Abstract: Proteins shuttle between the nucleus and cytoplasm through the nuclear pore and via nuclear transport receptors, termed importins and exportins. Although genetic alterations involving nucleoporins are enriched in pediatric, adolescent, and young adult (AYA) acute myeloid leukemia (AML), nucleocytoplasmic transport has not been extensively studied in this disease. We discover that genes encoding nucleocytoplasmic transport pathway components (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes [KEGG]: hsa03013) are enriched in AML cells from younger patients (≤40 years). Within this pathway, CSE1L is the highest expressed exportin in pediatric/AYA AML and shows minimal expression in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). CSE1L depletion reduces leukemic cell growth, proliferation, and clonogenic capacity, targeting leukemia stem cells while sparing normal HSCs. Mechanistically, we identify a novel Ran-GTP-dependent role for CSE1L in regulating pre-60S ribosomal subunit export in AML. Collectively, these data identify nucleocytoplasmic transport and ribosomal subunit export as enriched dependencies in pediatric/AYA AML and establish CSE1L-mediated export as a leukemic vulnerability.

Article.Title: Antibody 3CF5 neutralizes historical and emerging H5Nx influenza viruses by targeting a conserved non-receptor-binding hemagglutinin epitope
Article.Authors: Liang H.; Niu C.; Cheng Y.; Liew K.; Qu L.; Zheng Z.; Yang W.; Wang Q.; Wei L.; Liu B.; Hu F.; Xing C.; Chen J.; Pan W.; Li P.; Tan Y.; Xiong X.; Chen L.; Niu X.
Article.Abstract: Avian influenza viruses of the H5Nx subtype pose persistent pandemic threats. Here, we immunized rhesus macaques with an H5N6 vaccine and obtained 30 H5-reactive monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). Three IgG mAbs, 3CF5, 3BG3, and 3BE7, demonstrated potent neutralizing activity against multiple H5Nx viruses and conferred protection in a lethal mouse challenge model. Notably, 3CF5 exhibited broad neutralization against H5Nx viruses spanning 1997-2024, including contemporary clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 strains associated with an ongoing outbreak in dairy cattle. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) analysis revealed that 3CF5 targets a conserved non-receptor-binding epitope on the hemagglutinin (HA) head, spanning the vestigial esterase domain and an adjacent lateral surface. 3CF5 mediates neutralization primarily through inhibiting membrane fusion and also possesses antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Furthermore, isotype conversion of 3CF5-IgG to mucosal secretory IgA1 (sIgA1) enhanced neutralization potency against H5N1 viruses up to 128-fold, highlighting the advantage of sIgA1 as a nasally administered prophylactic agent.

Article.Title: Influenza virus antagonizes self-sensing by RIG-I to enhance viral replication
Article.Authors: Ledwith M.; Nipper T.; Davis K.; Uresin D.; Zhang Z.; Kleer M.; Khaperskyy D.; McCormick C.; Komarova A.; Mehle A.
Article.Abstract: Innate immune sensors must finely distinguish pathogens from the host to mount a response only during infection. RIG-I is a cytoplasmic sensor that triggers a broad antiviral response in response to sensing foreign RNAs. Here, we show that RIG-I not only binds viral RNAs but is activated by host RNAs. These are primarily non-coding RNAs transcribed by RNA polymerase III. They are benign under normal conditions but become immunogenic during influenza virus infection, where they signal via RIG-I to suppress viral replication. These RNAs are also bound by influenza virus nucleoprotein (NP), which normally functions to encapsidate the viral genome. NP interacts with RIG-I via an RNA bridge and antagonizes sensing of self-RNAs to counter innate immune responses. Overall, we demonstrate that self-sensing is strategically deployed by the cell to amplify the antiviral response and reveal a newly identified viral countermeasure that disrupts RIG-I activation by host RNAs.

Article.Title: Transcriptional and functional profiling reveals a dynamic continuum of beta-cell activation states
Article.Authors: Volov-Ohayon A.; Ben-Arush Y.; Davidovich I.; Hamburg A.; Steinberg B.; Ernan B.; Noiman N.; Elinav E.; Reizel Y.; Helman A.
Article.Abstract: A central question is whether beta-cells respond uniformly to glucose. Using phospho-S6 as an activation marker, this study shows that beta-cells are recruited sequentially as glucose concentrations increase. Recruitment is spatially organized, with high-threshold cells predominantly located in the islet core. Transcriptomic profiling indicates functional heterogeneity among beta-cells. A low-threshold subset is characterized by enhanced stress resilience necessary for sustained secretion. An intermediate subset, enriched for calcium-signaling and vesicle-excitatory genes, modulates postprandial glucose excursions. The high-threshold subset specializes in high-capacity protein synthesis and insulin secretion to manage glucose peaks. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals that these functional subsets form a continuous spectrum rather than discrete subpopulations. This division of labor is adaptable; under high-fat diet-induced metabolic demand, islets undergo remodeling with a global reduction in activation thresholds and a shift toward high-capacity profiles. Collectively, these findings identify a beta-cell hierarchy that balances metabolic resilience with secretory demand to maintain glucose homeostasis.

Article.Title: MHC II-expressing bone marrow megakaryocytes are noncanonical antigen-presenting cells and activate CD4+ T cells ex vivo
Article.Authors: Camacho V.; Wang K.; Hanč P.; Carminita E.; Becker I.; Lee D.; Bassal M.; Falchetti M.; Maggi J.; Barrachina M.; von Andrian U.; Carrascal M.; Gautam D.; Weng C.; Sankaran V.; Italiano J.; Machlus K.
Article.Abstract: While professional antigen-presenting cells drive adaptive immunity, atypical cell types can fulfill this role in the bone marrow. Megakaryocytes (MKs) are canonically recognized for platelet production, but recent studies indicate functional heterogeneity and immune potential. We found that ∼20% of bone marrow MKs express major histocompatibility complex (MHC) II and co-stimulatory receptors CD80, CD86, CD40, and CD83. These MKs process and present antigen to activate T cells ex vivo in an MHC II-dependent manner. MK/T cell interactions induced TGF-β1 secretion and promoted induced regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation. Toll-like receptor (TLR) stimulation of MKs elicited modest Th1-associated responses, including IFN-γ and TNF-α production, without robust Th17 differentiation. Immunopeptidomics confirmed peptide occupancy of MK MHC II in vivo. Using MK-targeted MHC II deletion, we observed altered TLR responses and reduced bone marrow TGF-β1. Together, these findings identify MHC II+ MKs as noncanonical antigen-presenting cells with potential roles in regulating CD4+ T cell responses within the bone marrow niche.

Article.Title: Machine learning-assisted Repli-Histo labeling reveals distinct transcription-dependent constraints on chromatin motion in living cells
Article.Authors: Minami K.; Nakazato K.; Shimizu K.; Tamura S.; Kimura H.; Ashwin S.; Maeshima K.
Article.Abstract: Genomic DNA is wrapped around core histones to form nucleosomes, which are organized in cells from euchromatin to heterochromatin with distinct genome functions. Although transcription is known to shape chromatin behavior in live cells, it remains unclear how different transcription systems act across chromatin classes and nuclear subcompartments. We develop machine learning-assisted Repli-Histo labeling to classify euchromatin and heterochromatin classes (classes IA, IB, II, and III) and combine it with single-nucleosome imaging in living human cells. Nucleosome motion is progressively constrained from euchromatin to heterochromatin. RNA polymerase II inhibition by THZ1, DRB, or α-amanitin increases nucleosome motion in euchromatic classes IA and IB and in heterochromatin around nucleoli, but not at the nuclear periphery. In contrast, RNA polymerase I inhibition by CX-5461 selectively increases nucleosome motion in Class III heterochromatin around nucleoli. Our study reveals that Pol II and Pol I transcription shape chromatin behavior in distinct chromatin classes and nuclear subcompartments.

Article.Title: Conserved disordered regions and ubiquitin-binding motifs within HUWE1 contribute to substrate targeting plasticity
Article.Authors: Ge X.; Jiang F.; De La Fuente C.; Rajkhowa T.; Chen C.; Viswanathan R.; Husain A.; Bennett E.
Article.Abstract: E3 ligases confer substrate specificity within ubiquitin-dependent pathways. However, the pleiotropic HECT-type E3 ligase HUWE1 targets a biochemically and structurally diverse set of substrates through mechanisms that remain largely unknown. We develop a combinatorial cell-based system integrating global proteomics, proximity labeling, and reporter assays to systematically interrogate HUWE1 sequence features that enable substrate targeting. We define a robust HUWE1 activity signature consisting of putative substrates that accumulate upon HUWE1 impairment across multiple cell lines. By re-expressing a panel of HUWE1 deletion mutants, we find that both the largest intrinsically disordered region and the conserved ubiquitin-binding motifs contribute to substrate targeting. Structural modeling and domain analysis further suggest that HUWE1 achieves targeting plasticity through multivalent interactions, engaging both disordered and structured regions within its substrates. Together, our findings establish a framework for understanding how large, modular E3 ligases exploit intrinsic disorder and multivalency to shape their substrate repertoires.

Article.Title: A hyper-IgM2 AID mutation limits IgH break formation but preserves affinity maturation
Article.Authors: Belcheva K.; Chowdhury P.; Kuan V.; Alread W.; Baasan D.; Lue J.; Downs-Canner S.; Frock R.; Yewdell W.; Chaudhuri J.
Article.Abstract: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) drives antibody diversification through class switch recombination (CSR) and somatic hypermutation (SHM). Humans with an AID mutation deleting the last nine amino acids (AIDR190X) develop hyper-IgM syndrome with defective CSR but variable SHM, suggesting that the C terminus plays a marked role in CSR. To model this putative separation-of-function mutation, we generated an AicdaR190X knock-in mouse. These mice show a severe CSR defect and a moderately reduced but ongoing SHM. Mechanistically, the severe CSR defect correlates with defective recombination of double-strand breaks in immunoglobulin switch regions. Strikingly, fusion of AIDR190X to a catalytically inactive AID restores CSR, indicating that the C terminus mediates a non-catalytic function for recombination. This mouse model of the human R190X mutation demonstrates that the AID C terminus is indispensable for CSR and also contributes to efficient SHM, providing insight into the mechanistic basis of hyper-IgM immunodeficiency.

Article.Title: Rheb in central amygdala somatostatin neurons regulates chronic itch and anxiety-like behaviors
Article.Authors: Qi Z.; Tian C.; Jin X.; Pan Q.; Zhang S.; Hu J.; Xie J.
Article.Abstract: Chronic itch represents a significant clinical challenge that substantially impairs patients' quality of life, yet its underlying neural circuit and molecular mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that somatostatin-expressing (SST) neurons in the central amygdala (CeA) are activated and functionally required in a mouse model of diphenylcyclopropenone (DCP)-induced chronic itch. Transcriptomic profiling further revealed upregulation of Ras homolog enriched in brain (Rheb) within DCP-TRAPed CeA SST neurons. Notably, Rheb knockdown suppressed the hyperexcitability of CeA SST neurons and alleviated chronic itch-related scratching and anxiety-like behaviors in DCP-treated mice. Conversely, Rheb overexpression promoted scratching and anxiety-like behaviors in naive mice. Collectively, these findings delineate a Rheb-regulated CeA SST neuronal mechanism that contributes to chronic itch-related scratching and anxiety-like behaviors, highlighting a potential molecular target for therapeutic intervention in chronic itch.

Article.Title: Clusterin, through exercise-mediated liver-heart crosstalk, promotes heart regeneration after myocardial infarction
Article.Authors: Wang W.; Wang F.; He Y.; Zhang Y.; Li C.; Chen X.; Xia X.; Liu Y.; Zhou L.; Hu Z.; Li Z.; Wang J.; Li L.; Zeng C.; Wu G.
Article.Abstract: Loss of cardiomyocytes drives cardiac remodeling and ultimately leads to heart failure, highlighting the need to promote cardiac regeneration. Exercise has been known to enhance cardiac repair and stimulate cardiomyocyte proliferation; however, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we demonstrated that exercise-induced exerkine clusterin mediates the pro-regenerative effects of running plasma on cardiac repair and cardiomyocyte proliferation following myocardial infarction (MI). Cardiac-specific Clu knockout attenuated, whereas clusterin overexpression enhanced, post-MI cardiac regeneration. Recombinant clusterin administration promoted heart regeneration in adult mice after MI. Mechanistically, clusterin activated NF-κB via proteasome-dependent IκBα degradation through direct binding with IκBα. Furthermore, the liver was identified as the major source of exercise-induced circulating clusterin; hepatocyte-specific Clu knockdown abolished the stimulatory effect of exercise plasma on cardiac regeneration. This study reveals a liver-heart crosstalk mechanism by which exercise-induced clusterin promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation, positioning clusterin as a potential therapeutic target for post-MI heart failure.

Article.Title: Pot1a maintains mesenchymal stem cell niche function to support hematopoietic stem cells
Article.Authors: Esaki Y.; Hosokawa K.; Yao H.; Adachi S.; Baba Y.; Arai F.
Article.Abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) maintain their function through interactions with niche cells in the bone marrow. We previously demonstrated that protection of telomeres 1a (Pot1a), a shelterin component, maintains HSCs and neuron-glial antigen 2-expressing (NG2+) mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) by suppressing DNA damage response (DDR) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. However, the role of Pot1a in leptin receptor-expressing (LepR+) MSCs, a primary HSC niche component, remains unclear. LepR-specific Pot1a knockout mice showed decreased LepR+ MSC numbers, increased DDR and ROS production, reduced HSC quiescence, and impaired long-term hematopoietic reconstitution. In contrast, cell-permeable Pot1a enhanced the hematopoietic-supporting function of LepR+ MSCs. Pot1a deficiency reduced pleiotrophin (Ptn) expression, whereas Pot1a overexpression increased its expression. These findings suggest that Pot1a preserves LepR+ MSC function by limiting stress-associated changes, maintaining MSC numbers, and regulating hematopoietic-supportive factor expression, including PTN.

Article.Title: A competitive PDLIM1-USP14 axis destabilizes ACTN4 to disturb the invasive homeostasis of trophoblast in preeclampsia
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Zhang X.; Chen R.; Xiang Y.; Gong E.; Tong H.; Sun X.; Yin H.; Qi H.
Article.Abstract: Preeclampsia (PE) is characterized by insufficient extravillous trophoblast (EVT) invasion, but the cytoskeletal mechanisms restraining EVT motility remain unclear. TMT-based placental proteomics identified the cytoskeletal adaptor PDLIM1 as markedly upregulated in PE. In primary trophoblasts and cell lines, PDLIM1 depletion remodeled the actin cytoskeleton and enhanced migration and invasion, whereas trophoblast-restricted Pdlim1 overexpression impaired trophoblast invasion and placental development in mice. Mechanistically, PDLIM1 bounds the rod domain of α-actinin-4 (ACTN4) and competitively displaced USP14, limiting ACTN4 deubiquitination and shifting ACTN4 toward RNF38-associated K48-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. Importantly, placenta-targeted chondroitin sulfate A-binding nanoparticles delivering Pdlim1 short hairpin RNA (shRNA) alleviated PE-like maternal and fetal phenotypes in mice. Recent studies have shown that non-cognate arbitrium peptides can interact with heterologous receptors, providing evidence of inter-phage crosstalk. Article.Title: eHLAstic reveals an extended canonical and non-canonical HLA-E immunopeptidome in human cancers
Article.Authors: Liao H.; Quastel M.; Shepherd C.; Nicastri A.; Kok L.; van Hateren A.; Palmer S.; Yang Q.; Dzhoneva A.; Peeters B.; Marrer-Berger E.; van Heesch S.; Gillespie G.; Ternette N.
Article.Abstract: HLA-E is a non-classical MHC class I molecule with restricted polymorphism, offering a putative path to broadly applicable off-the-shelf therapies. Using eHLAstic and orthogonal biochemical validation, we report 30 previously unrecognized canonical and non-canonical HLA-E-associated peptides, including six cancer-restricted ligands detected in acute lymphoblastic and myeloid leukemia but not healthy blood or bone marrow cells. Most identified ligands were shared across individuals with diverse HLA backgrounds and were detected across hematological and solid cancers. All but one non-canonical ligands were detected exclusively in cancer-associated samples and not in healthy tissues. Article.Title: Clearing perivascular light chain-derived amyloid to counteract aging-associated decline in liver regeneration
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Yang Y.; He G.; Ren Y.; Wang Y.; Zheng Q.; Li J.; Qing J.
Article.Abstract: Aging impairs organ regeneration, with insufficient angiogenesis as a key contributor. Here, we show that the endothelial immunoproteasome subunit PSMB8 is upregulated in aged mouse livers after partial hepatectomy. Endothelial PSMB8 deletion or PR-957 inhibition promotes angiogenesis and rescues liver regeneration. diGly proteomics identifies TAZ (transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif) as a ubiquitin-dependent immunoproteasome substrate, and TAZ activation restores aged liver regeneration. Aging triggers the infiltration of CD38+IGLC1+ IgM B cells and aberrant perivascular light chain-derived amyloid deposition in the liver. Recombinant light chain-derived amyloid fibrils directly induce PSMB8 expression in vitro. Anselamimab-mediated light chain-derived amyloid clearance mitigates immunoproteasome overactivation and restores regeneration. Single-cell RNA sequencing confirms that anselamimab reverses aging-induced endothelial marker loss and inflammatory gene upregulation. Our findings establish a pathway linking perivascular light chain-derived amyloid deposition to regenerative decline via endothelial immunoproteasome activation, suggesting amyloid clearance as a promising therapeutic strategy for aging-associated decline in liver regeneration.

Article.Title: 5-Azacytidine incorporation into mRNAs disrupts translation and induces ribosome collisions
Article.Authors: Roberson A.; Marks J.; Pitts R.; Tamilselvam B.; Britt G.; Grieb B.; Tansey W.; Meydan S.
Article.Abstract: 5-Azacytidine (5-AzaC) is a cytidine analog chemotherapeutic widely used to treat myeloid malignancies. Although its activity is primarily attributed to DNA hypomethylation, the majority of 5-AzaC is incorporated into RNA, where its functional consequences are less understood. Here, we show that 5-AzaC treatment of cells leads to inhibition of protein synthesis. Ribo-seq, Disome-seq, and RNA-seq in treated cells exhibit a time-dependent C-to-G conversion in mRNAs. These conversion events are enriched within footprint positions corresponding to the A-site of monosomes or stalled leading ribosomes in a disome complex. Footprints are accumulated at sites with C-rich codons in the A-site, with particular emphasis on the second codon position. Consistent with disome-mediated signaling, 5-AzaC activates ZAK- and GCN2-dependent stress responses. Furthermore, loss of the ribosome-associated quality control factor, ZNF598, sensitizes cells to 5-AzaC. These findings suggest that translation disruption represents an additional layer of 5-AzaC's mechanism of action, alongside its known DNA-mediated effects.

Article.Title: Hyperosmotic stress induces rewiring of 3D chromatin interactions
Article.Authors: Flores J.; Perreault A.; Drum Z.; Xu C.; Alonso D.; Rashid T.; Burgess J.; Fox G.; Petros G.; Wu Y.; Quiroga-Barber I.; Kim H.; Sahasrabudhe I.; Lee Y.; Black E.; Li Y.; Demmerle J.; Strahl B.; Dowen J.; Wang G.; Cai D.; Phanstiel D.

Genes at these anchors show delayed activation following loop formation, consistent with loops acting upstream of transcription. Together, hyperosmotic stress triggers rapid, reversible, CTCF-independent chromatin reorganization that correlates with transcriptional adaptation.

Article.Authors: Masaki T.; Watanabe M.; Mandai M.; Kihara M.; Abe T.; Kageyama R.
Article.Abstract: Müller glia (MG) in the adult mammalian retina have long been recognized as a potential endogenous source for the regeneration of lost retinal neurons. Article.Title: Temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte reprogramming
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Chen C.; Wan Y.; Dang B.; Liu X.; Gao Q.; Zhang J.; Cheng S.
Article.Abstract: Epidemiological evidence linking asthma to lung cancer risk remains contradictory, presenting asthma as either a risk factor or a protective condition. We hypothesize that this heterogeneity stems from the temporal dynamics of inflammatory response and host genetic background. Using ovalbumin (OVA)-induced asthma models, we identify a temporal shift in immune effectors driving post-asthmatic tumorigenesis. During acute airway inflammation, eosinophil infiltration accelerates tumor growth across mouse strains. Following resolution, however, tumorigenic outcomes in recovery diverge along genetic lines. Prior asthma reshapes chromatin landscapes of bone marrow myeloid progenitors, establishing innate immune memory that differentially programs monocytes across strains. In C57BL/6 mice, trained monocytes adopt oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), acquiring a suppressive, tissue-remodeling phenotype that promotes tumor progression. Conversely, BALB/c-trained monocytes utilize glycolysis to maintain a pro-phagocytic state, enabling tumor clearance. These findings delineate a biphasic mechanism wherein temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte metabolic reprogramming.

Article.Authors: Mummey H.; Corban S.; Lucero J.; Melton R.; Pittigher M.; Johnston V.; Deutsch G.; D’Antonio-Chronowska A.; Wang A.; Hull-Meichle R.; Gaulton K.

Article.Authors: Zhang L.; Qian S.; Zhong X.

Article.Title: Theta-based organization of information in the frontal cortex
Article.Authors: Broschard M.; Brincat S.; Loonis R.; Miller E.
Article.Abstract: Theta (4-10 Hz) oscillations seem to coordinate activity across long-range distances. It is less clear how theta coordinates activity more locally within frontal subareas. We examined activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC), and frontal eye fields (FEFs) as non-human primates categorized dot patterns. We characterized how theta coordinates activity within frontal cortex. First, theta phase selectively couples to behaviorally relevant information in spiking. Second, theta influences move in a posterior direction during choices (i.e., dlPFC/vlPFC to FEF) and after correct outcomes (i.e., dlPFC to FEF), but not after errors. Instead, anterior-direction (i.e., FEF to vlPFC) theta influences are stronger after errors. Third, theta participates in behaviorally associated nested cross-frequency interactions. Theta couples to beta (15-30 Hz) oscillations during choices and after errors, whereas beta couples to gamma (40-90 Hz) oscillations after correct outcomes. Our results position theta as a critical mechanism that flexibly and dynamically coordinates activity in frontal cortex.

Article.Title: A shared multi-feature population code for sensory reliability across mouse visual cortex
Article.Authors: Edwards E.; Lipton M.; Sereno A.; Dadarlat M.
Article.Abstract: Successful behavior depends on evaluating both what is present in the environment and how reliable that information is. These coherence-dependent response patterns are not fully accounted for by stimulus-based normalization models; rather, they track the distribution of motion energy across directions, while remaining relatively invariant to total motion energy. This multi-feature code is expressed at the single-neuron and population levels and is consistent across visual areas, suggesting a shared encoding scheme rather than area-specific computations. Together, these findings support a common population code for stimulus reliability across visual cortices.

Article.Abstract: Tolerogenic dendritic cells (TolDCs) contribute to immune tolerance and have demonstrated therapeutic potential in early clinical studies of autoimmune diseases. Article.Title: Cell-type specific and nanoscale control of hippocampal presynaptic homeostatic plasticity
Article.Authors: Chipman P.; Fetter R.; Cohill-Milanick W.; Ragozzino F.; Davis G.
Article.Abstract: The lifelong continuity of neuronal function rests upon the perdurance of neurons, synapses and neural circuits that are sustained, in part, by homeostatic signaling. Currently, the implementation of homeostatic signaling within complex brain circuitry remains poorly defined. Article.Title: Lineage-specific metabolic transcription across environmental gradients in geothermal microbial communities
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Xie Q.; Qu Y.; Tang Q.; Cai C.; Chen L.; Hua Z.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how environmental heterogeneity shapes microbial metabolism remains a central challenge. Here, we integrated genome-resolved metagenomics and metatranscriptomics with co-expression network analysis to examine metabolic transcription across geothermal environments. These findings reveal how microbial functional programs and their lineage associations reflect environmental heterogeneity across geothermal habitats.

Article.Authors: Jiang M.; Zhou M.; Tang D.; Li J.; Hao X.; Li R.; Jiang Y.; Cheng S.; Lv J.; Li L.; Yu C.; Wu T.; Chen W.; Wang C.
Article.Abstract: Most genome-wide association studies (GWASs) and polygenic score (PGS) models for lung function are based on European-ancestry individuals. Here, we performed GWASs in 17,738 Chinese individuals from the Dongfeng-Tongji (DFTJ) and Wuhan-Zhuhai (WHZH) cohorts, followed by meta-analysis with lung function GWASs from the China Kadoorie Biobank (sample size, n = 100,285), the Taiwan Biobank (n = 62,901), and European-ancestry studies (n = 400,102). Multi-ancestry fine-mapping pinpoints four novel candidate causal variants: one insertion (rs56381615, LINC02270) and three SNPs (rs6941411, PTK7; rs13315867, EPHA3; and rs2713769, ABI3BP). Cross-ancestry genetic correlations are high (0.682-0.811) but significantly lower than 1 (p < 0.005). Transcriptome-wide association analysis across 16 tissues identifies 1,374 genes, including PTK7, CUL7, and EPHA3 as leading novel candidates. Finally, we develop multi-ancestry PGS models that outperform existing models. Overall, this study quantifies cross-ancestry genetic correlation, prioritizes candidate genes, and enhances PGS prediction accuracy of lung function traits in East Asian populations.

Article.Title: Uncoupling hypersensitive cell death response and disease resistance activated by effector-triggered immunity
Article.Authors: Chhillar H.; Schoonbeek H.; Ngou B.; Jones J.; Ding P.
Article.Abstract: Effector-triggered immunity (ETI) is frequently accompanied by the hypersensitive response (HR), a localized form of programmed cell death considered closely associated with disease resistance. However, the mechanistic relationship between HR and effective immunity remains incompletely understood. We show that the Arabidopsis cbp60g sard1 double mutant exhibits exaggerated ETI-associated HR while retaining partial resistance to bacterial pathogens, providing a genetically tractable system uncoupling disease resistance from cell death without visible pleiotropic defects. Transcriptome profiling reveals that CBP60g and SARD1 coordinate positive and negative immune regulatory programs, including activation of the Nudix hydrolase NUDT7, a downstream target that partially restrains HR. The incomplete restoration of the mutant phenotype by NUDT7 overexpression suggests that additional CBP60g/SARD1-dependent negative regulators buffer excessive cell death. Our findings demonstrate that hypersensitive cell death is genetically separable from effective disease resistance and reveal how CBP60g/SARD1 coordinates transcriptional networks to balance immunity with protection against self-inflicted damage.

Article.Title: Programming intestinal immune tolerance: The pivotal role of gut microbial metabolites
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Xu W.; Yong L.; Wang Q.
Article.Abstract: Intestinal immune tolerance enables the host to coexist with commensal microorganisms and dietary antigens while retaining effective defense against pathogens. The review describes mechanisms underlying the development and maintenance of immune tolerance and how the intestinal barrier and local immune system cooperate to maintain immune homeostasis. Particular attention is given to microbial metabolites, and we summarize mechanisms by which they act as key signals between the gut microbiota and the host, regulating barrier function and immune cell responses. We highlight the dynamic, context-dependent nature of metabolite-mediated immune regulation, influenced by local exposure and host factors including age, genetic background, and inflammatory or infectious conditions. Additional metabolites and regulatory pathways are discussed to broaden understanding of microbe-host interactions. Microbial metabolites may serve as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets for inflammatory bowel disease and other immune-related disorders. However, broad clinical application requires further human validation and more precise intervention strategies.

Article.Title: Longitudinal dynamics of gut microbiota maturation and its modulators from infancy through childhood
Article.Authors: Peng S.; Stokholm J.; Thorsen J.; Jiang J.; Trivedi U.; Li X.; Sørensen S.
Article.Abstract: Early-life gut microbiota development is closely linked to long-term health. We characterize gut microbiota in 695 Copenhagen Prospective Studies on Asthma in Childhood 2010 (COPSAC2010) children using 16S rRNA gene sequencing of 2,689 fecal samples collected from 1 week to 6 years of age. Gut microbiota development is rapid during the first four years and gradually slows over the subsequent two years. A random forest model predicts microbial age from community composition and defines gut age-centered high- and low-maturity states. High-maturity microbiota exhibits greater alpha diversity, lower beta-dispersion, and maturity-associated network structures, reflecting enhanced community stability. We identify putative taxa with transient, persistent, or enduring associations with maturation. Pets, housing conditions, and maternal antibiotic use at birth show transient associations with maturation, whereas sibling presence and birth season show more sustained associations. 1-year microbiota composition predicts 4-year microbial maturity with modest but non-random performance. Our findings link early-life bacterial colonization and exposures to microbiota development and ecological stability.

Article.Title: A SIRT6-OVOL2 axis governs excitatory neuron resilience to chronic stress
Article.Authors: Zhou P.; Li X.; Sun H.; Li Q.; Tang Y.; Chang H.
Article.Abstract: Current antidepressants primarily target monoaminergic and glutamatergic systems, but insufficiently protect against stress-induced neuronal dysfunction, highlighting the need for mechanism-based therapies. Here, we propose SIRT6 as a determinant of stress resilience. Excitatory neuron-specific SIRT6 overexpression attenuates chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced anhedonia, despair, anxiety-like phenotypes, and circadian disruption, whereas astrocytic or inhibitory neuronal overexpression provides no comparable effect. Conversely, excitatory neuron-specific SIRT6 deletion induces depression-like behaviors and disrupts circadian locomotor activity under basal conditions. Hippocampal single-nucleus transcriptomics identifies a stress-sensitive excitatory neuronal subtype depleted following CUMS but restored by SIRT6 overexpression. Regulatory network analysis positions OVOL2 as a central transcription factor governing stress-associated transcriptional alterations. SIRT6 directly interacts with OVOL2 and modulates its stability, thereby driving transcription of downstream targets, including Nrg1. The SIRT6 allosteric agonist MDL-800 recapitulates these findings, eliciting antidepressant-like effects. These findings elucidate SIRT6's role in promoting stress resilience and support SIRT6-targeting strategies for treating depression.

Article.Title: FBXO45-mediated K63 ubiquitination of HYOU1 sustains UPR signaling and promotes chemoresistance in gastric cancer
Article.Authors: Pan G.; Xu Q.; Hu X.; Ding G.; Chen X.; Zhang Y.; Shen H.; Duan Z.; Gong J.; Qin J.
Article.Abstract: The unfolded protein response (UPR), an evolutionarily conserved protective mechanism, promotes tumor progression and acquired drug resistance, yet how UPR dynamics drive resistance through post-translational regulation remains unclear. Article.Title: Retrosplenial cortex exhibits parallel directional codes and contributes to medial entorhinal spatial coding in 3D curved-surface navigation
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Yuan X.; Zhang X.; Wang Z.; Zeng Z.; Wang Y.; Yang Y.; Wen S.; Wang X.; Xu Q.; Tian J.; Miao C.
Article.Abstract: Spatial coding is well studied in 2D, but directional and positional coding across 3D curved surfaces remains unclear. Two-photon calcium imaging in freely moving mice in a cylindrical arena indicates two directional representations in the retrosplenial cortex (RSC). In one, preferred directions shift systematically around the sidewall yet remain coherent with top-platform tuning; this organization persists in darkness with reduced precision. In the other, preferred directions remain stable across sidewall positions and are largely preserved in darkness. Medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) contains fewer, less stable direction-tuned neurons than RSC but shows more precise positional coding. MEC-projecting RSC neurons carry more precise directional and positional information than the RSC population. RSC inhibition selectively degrades MEC sidewall positional precision and cross-cylinder angular alignment in darkness. These findings indicate parallel RSC directional representations and suggest intact RSC activity contributes to stable MEC positional coding during 3D curved-surface navigation, particularly with limited visual support.

Article.Title: Toward a complete diploid chicken genome
Article.Authors: Fan S.; Liu J.; Kang N.; Li D.; Li Z.; Xu N.; Xu L.
Article.Abstract: The repetitive and heterochromatic parts of microchromosomes and dot chromosomes have impeded the creation of a complete, haplotype-resolved chicken genome. To overcome these challenges, we employed a trio-sequencing approach, utilizing long reads from a female chick, supplemented by parental long-read data for accurate haplotype phasing. This strategy generated nearly complete, haplotype-resolved paternal and maternal assemblies, with 14 residual gaps. Telomeric sequences remain missing from two paternal and four maternal chromosomes, suggesting a still incomplete assembly. The dot chromosomes exhibit low nucleotide diversity but a high density of structural variants between haplotypes. We found that the centromere sizes and relative positions of centromere cores sometimes differ between the two haplotype genomes. These findings suggest that comparative genomics must incorporate high-resolution analyses of these dynamic and complex regions to fully understand avian genome evolution and genetic complexity.

Article.Title: ZnuB as a targetable vulnerability to combat colistin resistance
Article.Authors: Cai J.; Liu W.; Zhang H.; Luo J.; Xu T.; Wang Z.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: Plasmid-mediated dissemination of mcr genes has severely compromised colistin efficacy, necessitating adjuvants that restore its antibacterial potency. Despite their essential roles in bacterial survival and virulence, metal ion acquisition systems remain underexplored as therapeutic vulnerabilities. Here, we identify the zinc-uptake gene znuB as a key determinant of colistin sensitivity. znuB deficiency enhances both the bacteriostatic and bactericidal activities of colistin. Mechanistically, znuB deletion upregulates leuO, driving ompS1- and dsbI-mediated membrane damage and oxidative stress upon colistin exposure. Concurrently, znuB loss elevates diacylglycerol levels, inhibiting MCR activity and potentiating colistin efficacy. Furthermore, we identify farrerol and ajmaline as potential inhibitors of both ZnuB and MCR proteins that effectively enhance colistin activity. In murine infection models, combination therapy improves survival and reduces bacterial burdens. Together, these findings demonstrate that targeting zinc homeostasis represents an effective strategy for reversing colistin resistance and combating multidrug-resistant bacterial infections.

Article.Title: Escape at an immunodominant SARS-CoV-2 spike epitope is not compensated by variant-specific CD8 T cells in HLA-A⁎24:02+ individuals
Article.Authors: Li H.; Aritsu Y.; Nakama T.; Wall A.; Jin Y.; Goto Y.; Tajima Y.; Yamada K.; Nagasaki Y.; Minami R.; Nakata H.; Tomita Y.; Sakagami T.; Kitamatsu M.; Hamana H.; Kishi H.; Nakagawa S.; Ueno T.; Sewell A.; Motozono C.
Article.Abstract: The antiviral CD8 T cell response is critical for controlling viral infections, including SARS-CoV-2. Spike mutations can mediate escape from pre-existing T cell immunity but it remains unclear whether such variants induce variant-specific CD8 T cells. Here, we investigate the HLA-A⁎24:02-restricted immunodominant NF9/A24 epitope (S448-456) and its prevalent L452R variant (NF9-5R) in Omicron BA.5 convalescents. NF9-5R-specific CD8 T cells are not detected ex vivo or after short-term in vitro stimulation of PBMCs, despite robust responses to other epitopes. In HLA-A24 transgenic mice, NF9 is markedly more immunogenic than NF9-5R, with rare cross-reactive responses. However, in vitro priming of NF9-5R-reactive CD8 T cells enables identification of a cross-reactive TCR (12E) recognizing both peptides and cells expressing spike L452R. Although the NF9-5R peptide can thus be presented and recognized, escape at an immunodominant epitope is not compensated by variant-specific CD8 T cells in vivo, creating functional "blind spots" relevant to vaccine strategies.

Article.Title: RNA-binding protein Rbfox2 establishes lipid gene programs through hierarchical control of transcription factors in the embryonic heart
Article.Authors: Verma S.; Hasan Chowdhury M.; Raghav Y.; Bluemn T.; Harris B.; Mueller C.; DeLancey R.; Zadrozny K.; Bushra S.; Hendrix E.; Viet A.; Sheynkman G.; Saucerman J.; Lincoln J.; Levental K.; Levental I.; Platig J.; Kuyumcu-Martinez M.
Article.Abstract: The role of RNA-binding proteins in metabolic gene regulation is unclear. Here, we uncover a hierarchical circuit where RNA-binding protein RBFOX2 establishes lipid gene programs and lipidome in embryonic hearts by governing transcription factors (TFs) using multi-transcriptomic and lipidomics approaches. We identified TF and lipid genes as RBFOX2 targets in the embryonic heart. TF SOX4 is a key target of RBFOX2 that drives lipid gene programs. RBFOX2 binds human SOX4 3' UTR and regulates its mRNA stability. SOX4 in turn initiates a lipid gene program by binding promoters of lipid enzymes/regulators. Restoration of SOX4 level, rescues lipid gene expression defects upon RBFOX2 loss. Strikingly, Rbfox2 loss in embryonic hearts modulates cardiac lipidome and leads to accumulation of lipid droplets. We reveal an RNA-mediated mechanism that establishes lipidome identity in the developing heart and may provide unique metabolic nodes vulnerable for pharmaceutic intervention of congenital heart disease in the future.

Article.Title: NANOG and OCT4 dosage shapes non-monotonic gene expression responses during stem cell differentiation
Article.Authors: Yan J.; Cho H.; Luo R.; Zhao J.; Beer M.; Li W.; Huangfu D.
Article.Abstract: Precise regulation of transcription factor (TF) expression is critical for maintaining cell identity, but studies on how graded expression levels affect cellular phenotypes are limited. To address this gap, we employed human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) as a dynamic model to study gene dosage effects and systematically titrated key TFs NANOG and OCT4 expression using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi). We then profiled transcriptomic changes in hESCs under self-renewal and definitive endoderm (DE) differentiation conditions using single-cell RNA-seq. Quantitative modeling of these Perturb-seq datasets uncovered distinct response patterns for different types of genes, including a striking non-monotonic up-regulation of on-target lineage genes during DE differentiation. This behavior extended to the ESC-to-neuroectoderm transition, suggesting non-monotonic responses of lineage genes to pluripotency regulator dosage are a recurring feature of lineage transitions. Together, these findings underscore the importance of characterizing TF function across a gradient of expression levels.

Article.Title: Comamonas aquatica diet inhibits TIR-1/SARM1-induced axon degeneration by providing vitamin B12
Article.Authors: O’Connor L.; Kang W.; Vo P.; Spinelli J.; Alkema M.; Byrne A.
Article.Abstract: Emerging evidence suggests the microbiome critically influences the onset and progression of neurodegenerative diseases; however, the identity of neuroprotective bacteria and the molecular mechanisms that respond within the host remain largely unknown. Here, we leverage Caenorhabditis elegans' well-characterized nervous system and ability to eat uni-bacterial diets to determine how metabolites and neuroprotective molecules from single species of bacteria suppress degeneration of motor neurons. We find that Comamonas aquatica significantly protects against degeneration induced by overexpressing a key regulator of axon degeneration, TIR-1/SARM1. Genetic analyses and metabolomics reveal Comamonas protects against neurodegeneration by providing sufficient vitamin B12 to activate METR-1/MTR methionine synthase in the intestine, which then lowers toxic levels of homocysteine in TIR-1-expressing animals. Defining a molecular pathway between Comamonas and neurodegeneration adds significantly to our understanding of gut-brain interactions and, given the prominent role of homocysteine in neurodegenerative disorders, reveals how such a bacterium could protect against disease.

Article.Title: Fumarate reprograms the ubiquitinated proteome to confer ferroptosis resistance in clear cell renal cell carcinoma
Article.Authors: Fan S.; Li J.; Gao Y.; Ma Y.; Sun C.; Tian Z.; Du Y.; Wang J.; Li H.; Yu M.; Xu Y.; Lv L.
Article.Abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is characterized by aberrant lipid accumulation and intrinsic ferroptosis sensitivity, yet how ccRCC escapes this vulnerability remains poorly understood. Here, we report that fumarate hydratase (FH) deficiency drives fumarate accumulation, which induces extensive remodeling of the ubiquitinated proteome and confers increased resistance to ferroptosis in ccRCC. Mechanistically, fumarate-mediated C706 succination of ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 1 (UBA1) significantly impairs its interaction with ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme E2 G2 (UBE2G2), concomitant with a global reduction of ubiquitination. Specifically, diminished ubiquitination increases the protein levels of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) and elevates solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11) expression, thereby inhibiting ferroptosis. Importantly, a designed cell-penetrating peptide attenuates fumarate-induced UBA1 succination, suppresses ATF4-SLC7A11 axis, and enhances ferroptosis sensitivity of ccRCC. Collectively, these findings reveal that FH deficiency drives ubiquitinome dysregulation and suppresses ferroptosis, thereby linking ubiquitinated proteome reprogramming to tumor progression and suggesting potential therapeutic targets and strategies for treating ccRCC.

Article.Title: Adipose NNAT functions as a molecular rheostat to promote or inhibit lipolysis and insulin resistance depending on the dietary context
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Ko C.; An S.; Choi K.; Hobson B.; Chaudhari A.; Bers D.; Yoon J.
Article.Abstract: Insulin and the catecholamines control key metabolic pathways and often act in opposition. Using male mice, we examined the role of the adrenergically regulated ER protein NNAT in adipocytes and found dichotomous effects on systemic insulin sensitivity, dependent on the diet consumed. On a standard diet, inducible, adipocyte-specific deletion of NNAT results in insulin resistance and adipose tissue loss via lipolysis. We identify alterations in Ca2+ handling and activation of ER stress as principal drivers. On a high-fat diet, adipose NNAT deletion ameliorates ER stress and reduces lipolysis by opposing a decline in ER Ca2+ levels. These mice are protected from diet-induced insulin resistance and exhibit increased energy expenditure. NNAT loss also stimulates adiponectin secretion. We conclude that NNAT regulates adipocyte ER stress, systemic insulin signaling, and intertissue communication in a context-dependent manner. For diet-induced obesity and metabolic dysfunction, disrupting the interaction between adipose NNAT and SERCA carries therapeutic potential.

Article.Title: The neuropathic chameleon: we are hot on the scent
Article.Authors: Kersebaum D.; Forstenpointner J.; Sachau J.; Hüllemann P.; Baron R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A common chronic pain condition, neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory or neural tissue and is characterized by a combination of negative (eg, numbness) and positive (eg, burning pain) sensory symptoms that significantly affect the quality of life. Common comorbidities such as depression and sleep disruption contribute to a substantial disease burden, which is further exacerbated by the apparent lack of effective therapeutic options. Current treatment options frequently achieve only partial, insufficient pain relief or may be completely ineffective in a considerable number of patients. The development of new drugs has thus far achieved moderate success, with many clinical trials failing to meet their primary endpoints; thus, a substantial unmet clinical need persists. One reason for this therapeutic deadlock is the considerable heterogeneity of neuropathic pain, driven by diverse pathophysiological mechanisms that vary between patients regardless of the underlying disease etiology. Accordingly, reclassification efforts follow a mechanism-based approach that reflects pathophysiological pain generators rather than disease etiology. Although diagnosis remains anchored in lesion- or disease-based criteria and structured clinical assessment, treatment development increasingly benefits from mechanism-informed phenotyping. A priori stratification based on individual mechanisms may help identify treatment responders, but implementation requires surrogate markers, as no biomarkers for pain mechanisms currently exist. In this article, we discuss candidate predictive markers and surrogate markers, focusing on sensory symptoms and signs assessed through patient-reported outcome measures and sensory testing, and their integration into future clinical trials.
