Article.Title: CytoLight Labeling as a Practical Extracellular Vesicle Analysis Platform for Quantitation, Phenotyping and Tracking Across In-Vitro and In-Vivo Models
Article.Authors: Rosen I.; Itzhaki E.; Gover-Proaktor A.; Shapira S.; Partouche S.; Qassim L.; Grinshpan-Langman S.; Qasim A.; Erez D.; John F.; Porat Z.; Moskovits N.; Zemel R.; Zur T.; Raanani P.; Offen D.; Granot G.; Samara A.
Article.Abstract: Reliable fluorescent labeling of extracellular vesicles (EVs) requires efficient discrimination of bona fide EVs from non-vesicular noise while avoiding dye-associated artifacts. Conventional dyes commonly introduce limitations including aggregation, membrane intercalation, fluorescence transfer and variable performance across EV preparations, distorting EV quantification, phenotyping, uptake analysis and biodistribution tracking. We evaluated CytoLight Rapid Red, a commercially available luminal dye developed for live-cell imaging, as an artifact-minimizing strategy for EV labeling, surface-marker phenotyping, uptake analysis and in vivo tracking, benchmarking its performance against PKH26, carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE) and ExoBrite across multiple analytical platforms. CytoLight generated stable, EV-associated fluorescence with no detectable aggregation or measurable change in EV size or scatter characteristics under the conditions tested. By fluorescence-mode nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and nano-flow cytometry, CytoLight yielded robust and reproducible staining across EV preparations, while CFSE showed a bimodal distribution consistent with esterase-dependent activation, and PKH26 generated particles of unidentified origin. Gating on CytoLight-positive events increased tetraspanin-positive frequencies 1.97–2.42-fold in HEK293FT-derived EVs and 1.25–1.43-fold in natural killer cell-derived EVs. In uptake assays, CytoLight yielded EV-associated signals exceeding labeled phosphate-buffered saline and protein-matched EV-depleted serum controls. In vivo, CytoLight-labeled EVs produced significantly higher organ-level fluorescence accumulation than controls, consistent with commonly reported EV-biodistribution patterns. Our findings support the feasibility of CytoLight as a practical, aggregation-resistant strategy for EV-labeling and as a positive-selection gate for fluorescence-based EV analysis. CytoLight enabled reliable particle quantification, surface-marker phenotyping, EV-associated uptake analysis and in vivo fluorescence biodistribution studies across multiple analytical platforms, offering a practical, scalable alternative to established EV dyes for standardized and reproducible EV research.

Article.Title: Evolutionary and Functional Roles of LysMs in Fungal Resistance and PGPR-Mediated Drought Tolerance in Barley
Article.Authors: Wang R.; Cheng J.; Wu J.; Deng F.; Zeng F.; Qin Y.; Chen Z.; Zhao C.; Zhu X.; Chen G.
Article.Abstract: Lysin motif (LysM) receptors perceive microbial glycans to mediate immunity and mutualism in plants. However, the regulatory mechanisms and functional divergence of LysM family members in barley under biotic and abiotic environmental cues remain largely elusive. Here, we systematically characterized the 15-member HvLysM family in barley (Hordeum vulgare). Synteny and evolutionary analyses indicated that the family expanded predominantly via segmental duplications and evolved under strong purifying selection. Transcriptomic profiling of spikes and leaves under fungal infections revealed that HvLysM3, HvLysM10, and HvLysM13 were broadly induced by both Fusarium graminearum and Bipolaris sorokiniana, whereas HvLysM7 and HvLysM8 displayed pathogen-specific divergence. Under drought stress and inoculation with novel plant-growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) strains (Aeromonas media and Leclercia aquatilis), HvLysM genes exhibited distinct organ- and genotype-dependent expression. Specifically, HvLysM3 was induced in the roots of both tolerant (XZ141) and sensitive (XZ147) genotypes under drought stress combined with PGPR treatment, HvLysM9–HvLysM12 showed contrasting root responses between two barley genotypes, and HvLysM7/HvLysM8 were co-activated by combined drought and PGPR in XZ141 roots. RT-qPCR experiments validated the strain-specific remodeling of HvLysMs transcription. Furthermore, subcellular localization assays demonstrated the plasma membrane targeting of HvLysM2 and HvLysM3 and the extracellular localization of HvLysM8. Collectively, this study identifies that HvLysM3 is a promising candidate gene for future functional validation, providing important genetic targets for enhancing barley resilience.

Article.Title: A Proposed Sulfur-Redox Adaptive Reserve in Type 2 Diabetes and Obesity: From Metabolic Perturbation to Endothelial and Tissue Responses—A Critical Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework
Article.Authors: Munteanu C.; Bembea V.; Manolaki Y.; Onose G.; Turnea M.; Rotariu M.; Blendea C.
Article.Abstract: Type 2 diabetes and obesity are associated with metabolic stress and heterogeneous endothelial and tissue dysfunction. Baseline measurements of analytically specified sulfur species, thiol–disulfide couples, and operational sulfide pools provide limited information about dynamic pathway turnover or the capacity to respond to metabolic demand. This critical narrative review evaluated human and experimental evidence, published in the last twenty years, linking sulfur metabolism, redox regulation and functional responses, and developed a conceptual framework for sulfur-redox adaptive reserve. Human studies report divergent assay-defined circulating sulfide signals, impaired erythrocyte glutathione synthesis, and weight loss accompanied by lower measured sulfide fractions and sulfur metabolites. Experimental findings support sulfur-sensitive regulation of mitochondrial, endothelial, and tissue function, but do not establish a uniform direction of benefit or clinical mediation. We therefore propose sulfur-redox adaptive reserve as the context-dependent, challenge-evoked capacity of endogenous sulfide generation, mitochondrial sulfide oxidation, persulfide turnover, thiol replenishment, and linked redox systems to support preservation or recovery of independently measured endothelial and tissue function during and after a defined metabolic perturbation. Unlike metabolic flexibility, redox homeostasis, or mitochondrial reserve capacity considered separately, the construct requires coordinated sulfur-network responses to a specified perturbation and linkage to independently measured functional outcomes. Its evaluation requires serial analyte-specific measurements, characterization of the achieved internal metabolic response—such as post-challenge glucose, insulin, and triglyceride trajectories or relative exercise intensity—and an independent functional endpoint. Repeated challenge studies must establish reproducibility, incremental information beyond baseline measures, and mechanistic specificity. The framework generates testable hypotheses, but its prognostic value, mechanistic specificity and clinical utility remain to be established.

Article.Title: Elucidating the Molecular and Functional Effects of Tropomyosin Mutations Associated with Left Ventricular Non-Compaction
Article.Authors: Slushchev A.; Kochurova A.; Antonets J.; Mikhaylova V.; Roman S.; Kleymenov S.; Yampolskaya D.; Koubassova N.; Kopylova G.; Ryabkova N.; Katrukha I.; Bershitsky S.; Tsaturyan A.; Matyushenko A.; Levitsky D.; Shchepkin D.
Article.Abstract: Genetic forms of left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) have been linked to variants in numerous genes, including those encoding sarcomeric proteins, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the structural and functional effects of three LVNC-associated variants, L113V, D159N, and R160H, in the TPM1 gene, which encodes α-tropomyosin (Tpm), a major tropomyosin isoform in the heart. Using recombinant proteins, we characterized these variants by differential scanning calorimetry, co-sedimentation with filamentous actin, viscometry, light scattering, in vitro motility assays, and molecular dynamics simulations. All three variants impaired actin–myosin interactions in vitro using both atrial and ventricular myosin. L113V markedly reduced motility of F-actin–Tpm filaments, possibly due to increased Tpm flexibility. The D159N and R160H variants decreased Ca2+ sensitivity and/or maximum sliding velocity of reconstituted thin filaments over both atrial and ventricular myosin, presumably by altering Tpm interactions with actin and troponin I. Thus, the L113V, D159N, and R160H variants alter the structural and functional properties of Tpm in ways that may contribute to LVNC development.

Article.Title: Integrated Multilevel Experimental Assessment of Heart Support Oil Phytocompounds Across Molecular Motor Proteins, β2-Adrenergic Signalling, Mitochondrial Stress, and Cardiomyocyte Contractile Function
Article.Authors: Dunjic M.; Turini S.; Novakovic T.; Sulovic L.; Jing Z.; Nejkovic L.; Dunjic M.; Dunjic K.
Article.Abstract: Heart Support Oil (HSO) is a multicomponent botanical formulation derived from Juglans regia, Lycium barbarum, Citrus × paradisi, and Origanum vulgare. This study addressed two related but analytically distinct questions: whether selected analytically detectable HSO phytocompounds show direct target-engagement signals at molecular motor proteins and the β2-adrenergic receptor (β2-AR), and whether the complete standardised formulation modifies oxidative- and adrenergic-stress phenotypes in cardiomyocyte models. Selected constituents were examined by target-specific biophysical/biochemical assays, whereas complete HSO was evaluated in human induced-pluripotent-stem-cell-derived cardiomyocytes and AC16 cells using membrane-injury, oxidative-stress, mitochondrial, calcium-transient, electrophysiological, contractile, qRT-PCR, and immunoblot endpoints. HSO produced concentration-dependent improvements under the tested stress conditions. At 20 µg/mL, CellTiter-Glo signal reached 91.0 ± 1.4% of control, reactive oxygen species decreased to 1.29 ± 0.04-fold, and mitochondrial membrane potential and cellular ATP recovered to 89.8 ± 1.6% and 87.3 ± 1.3% of control, respectively. HSO also moderated isoproterenol-associated abnormalities in cAMP signalling, beat rate, calcium handling, and contractility and shifted stress-, inflammatory-, apoptotic-, and antioxidant-response markers toward control values. Direct target assays demonstrated measurable binding and enzymatic changes for selected constituents, but these molecular observations were not interpreted as proving that the same targets caused the formulation-level cardiomyocyte phenotype. The findings support further independently replicated, pharmacokinetic, mechanistic loss-of-function, and in vivo studies; they do not establish a unique causal mechanism or clinical efficacy.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction Is Induced by Cardiac Pressure Overload
Article.Authors: Correa F.; Bautista-Pérez R.; Santamaría J.; Gonzalez-Pacheco H.; Franco M.
Article.Abstract: Pressure overload induced by ascending transaortic constriction was examined to evaluate cytoprotection with cytidine-5´-diphosphatecoline (CDP-choline) targeting oxidative stress and mitochondrial function. Male Wistar rats pre-treated with citicoline or a vehicle showed a decrease in mean arterial pressure (56.16 ± 10.08 vs. 60.55 ± 8.70 mmHg, respectively) with ascending transaortic constriction (AAC). After 60 min of hypotension, arterial blood gases, hepatic, renal, and inflammatory markers were measured together with oxidative stress, oxygen consumption, and the activity of the respiratory chain. Pressure-overloaded animals developed a marked elevation in blood lactate with a fall in pH values and a significant increase in urea nitrogen, creatinine, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH); no changes were seen in hepatic transaminases, interleukins IL-1β, IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα), whereas IL-10 increased. In contrast, under a 60.55 ± 8.70 mmHg fall in blood pressure, preconditioning induced a moderate lactate elevation with a minor decrease in pH compared to the group without preconditioning. Urea nitrogen, creatinine, and LDH were elevated, whereas aspartate aminotransferase (AST)increased only in the pre-treated group; IL-1β, IL-6, and TNFα did not change, and IL-10 increased. Oxidative stress in the heart, liver, and kidney mitochondria was related to dysregulation of oxidative phosphorylation, associated with a loss of complex III and complex IV activity. Thus, CDP-choline attenuated the heart damage caused by pressure overload by reducing oxidative stress and maintaining mitochondrial function.

Article.Title: Conditioned Medium from miR-29a-3p-Overexpressing Mesenchymal Stem Cells Attenuates TGF-β1-Induced Transcriptomic Dysregulation in Renal Proximal Tubular Epithelial Cells
Article.Authors: Lee M.; Lee H.; Jang Y.; Seo D.; Suh N.
Article.Abstract: Proximal tubule (PT) injury drives renal fibrogenesis, necessitating targeted therapeutic strategies. Here, we explored whether conditioned medium (CM) from human adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) overexpressing miR-29a-3p could attenuate transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1)-induced injury in human renal proximal tubular epithelial cells (RPTECs). MSCs were transfected with a miR-29a-3p mimic or control, and the resulting CM was applied to RPTECs during sustained TGF-β1 exposure. Cellular responses were evaluated using bulk RNA-sequencing, mitochondrial membrane potential assays, and immunofluorescence. Furthermore, a 12-gene, three-axis score was constructed to quantify injury and recovery. miR-29a-3p MSC-CM effectively reduced profibrotic activation and induced a broad reversal of approximately half of the TGF-β1-induced transcriptional shifts. Notably, this CM reactivated suppressed metabolic pathways, such as oxidative phosphorylation, attenuated epithelial–mesenchymal transition and cadherin remodeling, and restored mitochondrial membrane potential. Additionally, the 12-gene, three-axis score quantified a 47.6% recovery in vitro and successfully captured progressive adaptive and failed-repair PT injury states in human kidney single-cell/nucleus datasets, including an independent validation cohort. In conclusion, miR-29a-3p MSC-CM drives a selective but robust transcriptional and functional recovery in injured RPTECs. The novel 12-gene, three-axis score provides a quantifiable, cross-dataset metric for evaluating PT injury states.

Article.Title: Positive Allosteric Modulation of mGluR5 by VU0409551 Attenuates Clinical Severity, Anxiety-like Behavior, and Persistent Neuroinflammation in Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis
Article.Authors: Goulart M.; Fahel J.; Cardozo P.; Fantin J.; Maciel E.; Oliveira J.; Silva E.; Rezende-Ribeiro J.; Silva N.; Santos L.; Mello T.; Gorshkov V.; Kjeldsen F.; Verano-Braga T.; Vieira L.; Ribeiro F.
Article.Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune, inflammatory, demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and disability. Current disease-modifying therapies primarily target peripheral immune cells and show limited efficacy in halting relapse-independent long-term progression and the resulting neurodegeneration. The type 5 metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR5) has emerged as a promising therapeutic target due to its role in regulating neuroinflammation and cell survival. This study evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of VU0409551, a selective mGluR5 positive allosteric modulator (PAM), in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) mouse model, the most widely studied animal model of MS. Daily treatment with VU0409551 (10 mg/kg, intraperitoneally) significantly attenuated clinical disease severity and prevented characteristic body weight loss. Proteomic analyses revealed that VU0409551 treatment attenuated molecular signatures associated with immune responses. During remission, VU0409551 ameliorated EAE-associated anxiety-like behavior and attenuated persistent cortical neuroinflammatory alterations, including astrogliosis, microglial accumulation, and increased TNF expression. Notably, treatment also reduced signatures associated with astrocyte and oligodendrocyte reactivity, including C3, C4b, Serpina3n, and H2-D1. These findings demonstrate that VU0409551 exerts robust therapeutic effects, positioning it as a promising and novel disease-modifying candidate for MS.

Article.Title: ATP-Binding Cassette Transporter Expression and Methylation Profiles as Potential Biomarkers in Glioma
Article.Authors: Pilotto Heming C.; Meireles Y.; Moura-Neto V.; Aran V.
Article.Abstract: Gliomas are malignant central nervous system tumors characterized by poor prognosis and therapy failure. Adenosine triphosphate-binding cassette (ABC) transporters mediate multidrug resistance via chemotherapeutic efflux, yet their roles as biomarkers across glioma subtypes remain unclear. We analyzed adult diffuse glioma mRNA expression (n = 693; n = 325) and DNA methylation (n = 159) datasets from the Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas in silico, stratifying samples according to the 2021 World Health Organization molecular criteria. ABC transporter profiles, patient-matched methylation–expression correlations (n = 26 overlapping patients; 78 paired gene–sample observations), and prognostic values were evaluated using non-parametric tests with false discovery rate (FDR) correction, Kaplan–Meier curves, and multivariable Cox proportional-hazards regression analyses. Transporter expression and methylation varied significantly by histology and grade. ABCC1 expression increased with malignancy, predicting worse overall survival in univariable analysis (p < 0.0001). Meanwhile, strongly correlated ABCB1 and ABCG2 expressions (Spearman’s ρ = 0.80 in grade 4 tumors) were higher in lower-grade gliomas. Progressive hypomethylation occurred with increasing grade, with significant differential methylation in ABCB1 (FDR p < 0.0001) and ABCG2 (FDR p < 0.0001). In patient-matched integrative analyses, only ABCC1 exhibited a significant inverse association between methylation and expression (Spearman’s ρ = −0.58, p = 0.0019). Baseline clinical multivariable Cox regression (n = 139) suggested that higher ABCB1 and ABCG2 methylation (HR = 0.11, p = 0.03; HR = 0.12, p = 0.04 per 1.0-unit β increase, corresponding to HR = 0.80 and 0.81 per 0.1-unit β increase) may act as protective factors independent of age and grade (though attenuated upon IDH adjustment), whereas higher grade and ABCG2 expression (n = 542; HR = 1.03, p = 0.001) emerged as independent risk factors. Specific ABC transporter profiles could serve as candidate prognostic biomarkers in glioma, warranting external and translational validation.

Article.Title: FP7 and FP12, Two Synthetic Toll-like Receptor Antagonists, Do Not Cause Adverse Effects in Mice
Article.Authors: Alqallaf J.; Alqallaf A.; Parnell A.; Alonso V.; Al-sady M.; Michael N.; Romerio A.; Shaik M.; Leake D.; Pirianov G.; Peri F.; Patel K.; Vaiyapuri S.
Article.Abstract: Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) is a pattern-recognition receptor that detects lipopolysaccharides (LPSs) from Gram-negative bacteria, triggering innate immune and inflammatory responses. Research into TLR4 antagonists and agonists is crucial for developing novel therapies to modulate immune responses in infectious, inflammatory, and autoimmune diseases. Accordingly, some authors of this study developed synthetic TLR4 antagonists, including FP7 and FP12, and demonstrated their efficacy in inhibiting TLR4-mediated effects. This study specifically assesses the safety profile of these two novel TLR4 antagonists in mice following intraperitoneal administration. Clinical signs, body weights, and biochemical and haematological parameters in mice were assessed over four weeks after intraperitoneal administration of these molecules. No mortality or adverse effects were observed after administration of FP molecules. Key circulating biomarkers were also unaffected by these molecules. Preliminary LC–MS analysis detected both compounds in mouse plasma one hour after administration. Overall, this study demonstrates that FP7 and FP12 were well tolerated in mice, with no significant toxicological effects at the tested dose. These findings are an initial step toward further preclinical and clinical development of these molecules.

Article.Title: Impaired Mitochondrial Quality Control in Vitiligo: An Emerging Mechanistic Hypothesis and Perspective on Therapeutic Innovation
Article.Authors: Banda-Lesole R.; Kgosiemang-Xaba I.; Makhafola T.
Article.Abstract: Vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune pigmentary disorder characterized by selective melanocyte loss. While oxidative stress and immune dysregulation are well-established contributors, the upstream mechanisms that initiate melanocyte vulnerability remain incompletely understood. In this narrative review, we propose impaired mitochondrial quality control (MQC) as an emerging mechanistic hypothesis that may link key pathogenic events in vitiligo. MQC, encompassing mitophagy, mitochondrial dynamics, and biogenesis, is essential for maintaining melanocyte bioenergetics, redox homeostasis, and survival under ultraviolet (UV) and environmental stress. We summarize current evidence suggesting that abnormalities in PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, dysregulated fission/fusion dynamics, and impaired PGC-1α/NRF1-driven biogenesis are associated with the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria in vitiligo melanocytes. These mitochondrial perturbations may contribute to metabolic adaptation, augmented reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, cytosolic mtDNA release, and downstream innate and adaptive immune activation reported in vitiligo, subsequently driving the characteristic features of vitiligo lesions. However, whether MQC abnormalities represent a primary pathogenic driver, a secondary consequence of chronic oxidative stress, or a bidirectional relationship remains to be established. Thus, we critically discuss the perspective that phytochemicals may act as potential modulators of MQC. Unlike general antioxidants, specific plant-derived compounds such as quercetin, sulforaphane, epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), and ginkgolides have been reported in preclinical models to modulate mitophagy, rebalance mitochondrial dynamics, and promote biogenesis, thereby targeting mitochondrial homeostasis rather than only its downstream consequences. By repositioning impaired MQC as an attractive, yet to be validated, hypothesis that may offer new insight into vitiligo pathogenesis, this review provides a framework for future investigation and highlights phytochemical-mediated restoration of mitochondrial homeostasis as a potential therapeutic avenue that warrants further experimental validation.

Article.Title: Insights into Multiple Myeloma: Immune Microenvironment, Disease Mechanisms, and Therapeutic Innovations
Article.Authors: Miyama T.; Mihara K.
Article.Abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) remains a hematologic malignancy characterized by progressive immune dysfunction and the emergence of therapeutic resistance despite substantial recent advances in treatment. The transition from monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) to symptomatic MM is associated with coordinated immune dysfunction across innate and adaptive immune compartments. Single-cell and spatial profiling technologies reveal that immune abnormalities emerge at precursor stages and intensify during progression, including T-cell exhaustion, expansion of regulatory T cells, natural killer cell dysfunction, and impaired antigen presentation by dendritic cells. The cancer immunoediting framework, encompassing elimination, equilibrium, and escape phases, provides a unifying paradigm for understanding tumor-immune coevolution in MM. Disease complexity is further compounded by pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity. Multi-region sequencing studies demonstrate anatomically distinct clonal architectures and immune microenvironments within individual patients, contributing to variable therapeutic responses and facilitating immune escape. Current immunotherapies, including immunomodulatory drugs, proteasome inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies, and bispecific antibodies, have transformed the therapeutic landscape of MM. Nevertheless, durable disease control remains limited by convergent resistance mechanisms, including antigen modulation, T-cell dysfunction, and persistent microenvironmental immunosuppression. A comprehensive understanding of the immune-mediated resistance mechanisms, extending beyond tumor-intrinsic genetic alterations, is essential for the rational design of next-generation therapies. Accumulating evidence suggests that immune dysfunction is closely associated with disease evolution and treatment resistance in MM and may represent a potentially targetable contributor to these processes.

Article.Title: The Discovery of Benzothiophene Derivatives as LasB Inhibitors Against Pseudomonas aeruginosa Infections
Article.Authors: Zhao S.; Lian D.; Chen Q.; Dai S.; Sun P.; Zhang W.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a clinically prevalent multidrug-resistant pathogen that poses a major therapeutic challenge. Targeting the crucial virulence factor elastase LasB has emerged as a promising strategy with which to reduce pathogenicity without imposing strong selective pressure for resistance. Here, we synthesized 19 benzoheterocyclic compounds through virtual screening and identified the benzothiophene derivative C5 as a potent LasB inhibitor (52.99 ± 0.87%). Further studies showed that C5 inhibited lasB expression in a concentration-dependent manner (IC50 = 5.80 ± 2.55 μM), thereby significantly inhibiting elastase production in Pseudomonas aeruginosa reference strain PAO1, the hypervirulent strain PA14, and the clinically resistant strains PA921 and PA929. Notably, the combination of C5 with tobramycin and ciprofloxacin significantly suppressed the development of antibiotic resistance, indicating its potential for antibacterial synergistic activity with these antibiotics. Furthermore, C5 inhibited bacterial swarming without significant cytotoxicity, demonstrating a favorable safety profile and potent activity. In summary, these results suggest that targeting LasB offers a potential strategy for treating Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections, and compound C5 has the potential to be developed as a candidate for LasB inhibitors.

Article.Title: The Molecular Potassium Code: Extracellular K+ Sensing, Allosteric Ion Selectivity, KCC2 Thermodynamics, and the Dynamic Control of Neural Inhibition
Article.Authors: Dumitrescu D.; Dumitru A.; Fulina M.; Dobrin N.; Tulin A.; Șerban M.; Covache-Busuioc R.; Toader C.; Rădoi M.
Article.Abstract: Neuronal excitability can be controlled by the level of potassium (K+) outside a neuron through both its effects on the cell membrane’s electrical properties and its influence on ion transport across the membrane. Recent studies have also shown that certain ligand-gated ion-channel receptors can be modulated by the levels of K+ outside the neuron. Therefore, understanding how each mechanism contributes to the generation of inhibitory signals requires the ability to differentiate between them. This study represents a review that integrates evidence using various methods, including electrophysiology, structural studies, thermodynamics, and optical measurements, to propose a framework called the molecular potassium code that explains how neurons respond to varying levels of K+ in their environment. The framework describes three ways that neurons interact with changing levels of K+: how these changes shift their K+ equilibrium potential and membrane voltage; how they alter the thermodynamic driving force for KCC2-mediated cotransport of K+ and Cl−; and how receptor-dependent modulation occurs at specific receptors when documented. Changes in activation, desensitization, pharmacological sensitivity, and permeation characteristics have been measured in Drosophila DmAlka channels; however, the atomic details of K+ recognition by these channels remain unclear. Human GlyRα2 variants engineered or edited to allow for assessment of K+-associated responses under elevated K+ conditions did not provide sufficient evidence for physiological recruitment of these receptors in mammals. Additionally, the presence and function of astrocytes, as well as geometric factors such as size, shape, and orientation, affect local concentrations of K+. Therefore, the framework described here provides multiple approaches that scientists can use to measure and interpret different mechanisms contributing to the generation of inhibitory signals in the nervous system.

Article.Title: Comparative Analysis of Macrophage Infiltration in Different Types of Nevi and Normal Skin: The Role of CD163+ and CD68+ Cell Populations
Article.Authors: Demyashkin G.; Filippov A.; Sazonova M.; Piskunov A.; Kazhuro D.; Holdeenko V.; Mironova D.; Chernyshev H.; Tsomartova E.; Petrosyan L.; Mingazov A.
Article.Abstract: Melanocytic nevi are common benign skin neoplasms, but the quantitative characteristics of CD68+ and CD163+ immunopositive cells within their microenvironment remain incompletely understood. The present study aimed to compare the density and distribution of CD68+ and CD163+ cells, as well as the CD68+/CD163+ cell density ratio, in benign nevi (BN), dysplastic nevi (DN), halo nevi (HN) with and without histological regression, and normal skin. This retrospective study included 141 patients: 79 with BN, 24 with DN, 12 with HN without regression, 9 with HN with regression, and 17 normal skin controls. Immunohistochemical staining for CD68 and CD163 was evaluated using digital morphometric analysis with QuPath software. DN exhibited the highest median density of CD163+ cells (659.60 cells/mm2), whereas HN without regression showed the lowest densities of both CD68+ and CD163+ cells (109.34 and 93.55 cells/mm2, respectively). In contrast, HN with regression exhibited the highest CD68+ cell density (1343.62 cells/mm2) and CD68+/CD163+ cell density ratio (3.345), both significantly exceeding those in HN without regression (p < 0.001). Normal skin specimens showed lower densities of both markers compared with BN (p < 0.001). Article.Title: Nrf2 Inhibits CXCL2-Dependent Neutrophil Recruitment to Alleviate Airway Inflammation and Epithelial Barrier Injury in House Dust Mite-Induced Murine Asthma

Article.Abstract: Neutrophilic asthma represents a severe, often corticosteroid-insensitive asthma subtype with an unmet clinical need for new therapeutic targets. We combined HDM-induced murine asthma models, dual-luciferase reporter assays and ChIP-qPCR to characterize the transcriptional regulation of CXCL2. Endothelial and mural responses were shared more strongly, whereas immune responses diverged. B/plasma-cell expansion was the only abundance change credible in both diseases. Periodontitis showed classical-monocyte influx and a lower share of C1Q+ macrophages. TREM2+ lipid-associated macrophages rose from leukoplakia to carcinoma, but their gain over tumour-adjacent tissue appeared in only one of two cohorts. Article.Title: Changes in Serum Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor Concentrations Following Tuberculosis Preventive Therapy in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes
Article.Authors: Cheng Y.; Sheu M.; Li Y.; Wu J.; Liu S.; Huang W.; Lee I.
Article.Abstract: Latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) is prevalent among patients with type 2 diabetes, and aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) has been reported to be associated with LTBI. Patients with type 2 diabetes were enrolled for LTBI screening, and serum AhR levels were measured for those with a positive QuantiFERON-TB result. The patients received TPT, according to clinical practice: either weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid for 3 months (3HP) or daily isoniazid for 9 months (9H). Serum AhR levels were measured during a follow-up assessment at 36 weeks after enrollment in the patients who underwent continuous TPT for >3 months. Serum AhR levels significantly decreased after TPT in the 3HP (45.4 [24.8, 55.44] to 13.4 [6.4, 23.8] pg/mL, p < 0.001) and 9H groups (43.4 [27.2, 60.8] to 14.6 [7.3, 21.3] pg/mL, p < 0.001). However, there was no statistically significant difference in the reduction in serum AhR levels between the 3HP and 9H groups (p = 0.286). In conclusion, serum AhR levels significantly decreased following TPT with the 3HP or 9H regimens.

Article.Title: Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals That lpl-a Deletion Reshapes Muscle Lipid Metabolism in Zebrafish: From Storage Limitation to Oxidative Bottleneck
Article.Authors: Liu T.; Xiao H.; Lu C.; Sun Z.; Zhang K.; Kuang Y.; Zheng X.
Article.Abstract: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) regulates tissue lipid partitioning, but its role in fish muscle lipid metabolism remains unclear. Here, a homozygous lpl-a knockout zebrafish line (lpl-a−/−) was constructed using CRISPR/Cas9 and fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 8 weeks. Muscle physiology, biochemistry, transcriptomics, and metabolomics were analyzed in female zebrafish. Muscle lpl-a expression and LPL content were significantly lower in knockout (KO) than wild-type (WT) fish. After HFD, WT fish showed significantly higher body weight, muscle TG and T-CHO contents, and abdominal fat than WT_LF, whereas KO_HF fish had significantly lower body weight than WT_HF, with muscle TG and T-CHO comparable to KO_LF. Multi-omics revealed reduced G3P and downregulated glycogen synthesis genes, consistent with storage limitation; upregulated acsl5 and downregulated acot15/acot17, consistent with enhanced fatty acid (FA) mobilization toward β-oxidation; downregulated ppara and pgc-1α, accumulated long-chain acylcarnitines, and decreased TCA intermediates, consistent with an oxidative bottleneck; and elevated AMP, increased AMPK protein content, accumulated DAG, increased PKC protein content, decreased SOD activity, and upregulated TLR/NF-κB inflammatory genes, consistent with energy stress and inflammation. Thus, lpl-a deletion reshapes muscle lipid metabolism from a storage-dominant mode toward storage limitation, oxidative mobilization, oxidative bottleneck, and energy stress with inflammation, and is associated with reduced HFD-induced lipid accumulation. lpl-a is a key node determining lipid storage versus oxidation, offering a potential target for improving fish muscle quality.

Article.Title: Form and Function in Flux: Molecular Ensembles from Structure to Therapy
Article.Authors: Patarca R.; Haseltine W.
Article.Abstract: Molecular structure, revealed by crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, imaging, and prediction, remains foundational to biology and drug design, yet function also depends on how structures flex, adapt, and interact. Proteins and RNA populate alternative conformations and binding states, while chromatin, membranes, glycans, metabolites, water, ions, and biominerals vary in composition and organization. This narrative review treats form and function as interdependent properties of molecular ensembles: structure constrains which states are accessible, whereas regulatory inputs, partners, and cellular environments determine which states are occupied, exchanged, and used. Without assuming a shared physical mechanism, we compare these systems and propose a cross-class evidence map that links each claimed state variable to its regulatory input, matched measurement, causal test, and organismal or clinical outcome. Examples from cancer, neurodegeneration, infection, and metabolic disease show how specific states become dysregulated, and why restored binding, assembly, or imaging readouts need not indicate functional recovery. Therapies are compared by primary mode of action—direct state modulation, target-abundance reduction, or genetic and RNA-level correction—with clinical successes, failures, and safety limits reported separately. The synthesis identifies where measurement methods must advance to resolve interrelated ensembles in native contexts and to determine when targeting them yields meaningful patient benefit.

Article.Title: Post-Treatment Molecular Biomarker Reassessment in Advanced Endometrial Cancer: An Evidence-Aware Framework for Precision Therapy
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Fei F.; Kong L.; Ye M.; Jin X.
Article.Abstract: Molecular classification has transformed treatment selection in endometrial cancer (EC), but most biomarkers are defined at diagnosis and may not represent the biological state of tumors after therapeutic exposure. In advanced, recurrent, or metastatic EC, treatment can reshape target expression, hormone dependence, immune context, signaling pathways, and DNA damage response (DDR), raising an important clinical question: which treatment-relevant features should be reassessed after progression, and how should the results inform subsequent therapy? This review synthesizes evidence across immune, endocrine, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) and pathway-directed, DDR-directed, and platinum–taxane treatment contexts. We focus on biomarkers that can be evaluated through repeat tissue biopsy, circulating tumor DNA, functional assays, and clinical treatment history, and distinguish biological plausibility from clinical actionability. The evidence is uneven. HER2 evolution and clinical measures of platinum sensitivity have comparatively direct EC-specific human support, whereas hormone receptor dynamics, estrogen receptor 1 (ESR1) evolution, and selected immune features remain clinically emerging, and pathway-rebound and functional DNA repair readouts are largely investigational. We therefore propose an evidence-aware framework for post-treatment biomarker reassessment that prioritizes whether the biological rationale for a previous therapy remains valid, has been weakened, or has been replaced by an alternative dependency. Prospective longitudinal studies are needed to determine when reassessment improves treatment selection and patient outcomes.

Article.Title: Lipotoxic Palmitate Hyperpolarises Mitochondria and Converts Nuclear 5mC to 5hmC: 8-Oxo-dG, 5mC and 5hmC Read on the Same Native DNA Molecules of Human Adipose-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells
Article.Authors: Gospodinova A.; Velichkov A.; Dimitrov N.; Todorova K.; Hayrabedyan S.
Article.Abstract: Lipotoxic stress from saturated fatty acids compromises the mitochondria of human adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (hAdMSCs) and, with them, their regenerative capacity. We exposed hAdMSCs to sodium palmitate at 250 and 500 µM for 24 h and combined live-cell confocal imaging with long-read nanopore sequencing of native DNA, reading 8-oxo-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-oxo-dG), 5-methylcytosine (5mC) and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) directly from the raw signal of the same molecules. Surprisingly, palmitate hyperpolarised mitochondria at both concentrations instead of depolarising them; the lower, obesity-range concentration fragmented the mitochondrial network over 24 h, and both raised mitophagy-associated and lysosomal puncta without preventing a concentration-dependent rise in senescence-associated β-galactosidase positivity. Mitochondrial DNA copy number fell to 56% of untreated, while the remaining mitochondrial genomes tended to carry more 8-oxo-dG (27%) and nuclear 8-oxo-dG tended to be lower (20%), neither contrast reaching significance at this depth. Nuclear CpG methylation fell from 29.87% to 26.84%, uniformly across the genome; the loss of 5mC was matched by an equal gain of 5hmC, consistent with oxidation of the methyl group rather than its loss. Methylation was depressed beside oxidised guanines in untreated cells, and less so under palmitate. In a thirteen-gene adipokine panel, promoter demethylation reached transcript and secreted protein only for IL6. Ribosomal DNA retained its methylation and was neither less oxidised nor exempt from conversion, its 5hmC rising with the genome. Palmitate thus remodels two genomes under one metabolic condition; in the adipose progenitor, lipotoxic stress pairs mitochondrial depletion with a rewritten nuclear methylome, a route by which obesity may compromise the fate and regenerative capacity of the progenitor pool.

Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Chen H.; Xing Y.; Huang M.; Li M.; Hu Y.; Zhao J.; Zhang C.; Shi C.

Although monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) has been implicated in prostate cancer progression, its role in CRPC drug resistance and immune suppression remains underexplored. Furthermore, MAOA-associated YAP1 signaling regulates tumor-cell PD-L1 expression and may contribute to immune evasion. In preclinical models, the combination of ENZ, MAOA inhibition, and PD-1 blockade exhibited enhanced antitumor efficacy compared with the other ENZ-containing treatment regimens. Article.Title: Application GenOA (Gene Optimiser Assistant) Is an Easy Way to Create Genes for a Particular Expression Level
Article.Authors: Zaytsev K.; Plekhanova N.; Makarova A.; Bogatyreva N.; Fedorov A.
Article.Abstract: Accurate expression prediction and rational gene design for specific expression levels are central challenges in synthetic biology and recombinant protein production. Here, we present GenOA, a software toolbox with a graphical user interface that predicts protein expression levels in Escherichia coli from the gene coding sequences with a correlation coefficient of 0.7, and conversely designs novel coding sequences that achieve a user-specified expression level while preserving the encoded amino acid sequence. This tool accepts either nucleotide or amino acid sequences as an input and enables users to specify target expression levels along with additional constraints, including GC content, codon usage irregularity, and the position of the sequence within the E. coli genome subspace. By integrating accurate expression prediction with sequence optimisation under multiple user-defined constraints, GenOA provides a versatile platform for the design of genetic constructs tuned for specific expression levels.

Article.Authors: Nangoli S.; Lee M.
Article.Abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide despite major therapeutic advances, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Although a subset of patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) experiences durable long-term responses, currently available predictive biomarkers, including programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) expression, have limited ability to reliably distinguish responders from non-responders. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have emerged as powerful approaches for extracting clinically meaningful patterns from complex, high-dimensional datasets spanning pathology, liquid biopsy, imaging, and integrated multimodal data. This narrative review examines current applications of AI in NSCLC immunotherapy across these complementary data modalities and evaluates the evidence supporting their clinical translation. Particular attention is given to the methodological limitations of existing studies and to the emerging shift from single-modality biomarkers toward dynamic and multimodal prediction. Although AI-based approaches show potential to complement established biomarkers, limitations in validation, generalizability, and prospective evidence currently restrict their clinical implementation.

Article.Authors: Shi X.; Wang M.; Zhou X.; Diao Y.; Fu Y.; Li G.; Ma C.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: The growing prevalence of high-fat diets and sedentary lifestyles has contributed to a marked rise in metabolic disorders and a concomitant increase in cardiovascular disease (CVD). High-fat diet-induced lipotoxicity is a key pathological driver that exacerbates myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury. Carnosic acid (CA), a natural bioactive compound, shows promise for cardiovascular protection through anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. Differential metabolites clustered primarily in energy metabolism pathways, consistent with lipotoxicity-driven metabolic derangements that worsen myocardial I/R injury. High-fat perfusion amplified the ischemic accumulation of free fatty acids and succinate in mouse myocardium, thereby aggravating I/R injury. Carnosic acid treatment markedly reversed the lipotoxicity-exacerbated cardiac I/R damage. Mechanistically, CA potentially binds to subunits adjacent to the Q site of mitochondrial complex I, decreasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production from reverse electron transport (RET). The Sirtuin 1 (Sirt1) inhibitor selisistat (EX527) abolished CA’s protective effect, indicating that CA also modulated the Sirt1-UPRmt pathway to preserve mitochondrial homeostasis and mitigate myocardial injury.

Article.Title: Composition-Dependent Structure and Electrochemical Performance of MXene/Polypyrrole/ZnO Ternary Nanocomposites for Supercapacitor Electrodes

M-3P-1Z exhibited uniformly distributed ZnO nanorods and the lowest charge-transfer resistance (0.4713 Ω), achieving the highest CV-derived specific capacitance of 888.01 F g−1 at 1 mV s−1. In contrast, M-1P-0.5Z, featuring ZnO nanorods with an aspect ratio of 10.1, achieved the highest GCD-derived specific capacitance of 1548.75 F g−1 at 0.1 A g−1 and a maximum estimated energy density of 161.2 Wh kg−1 at 160 W kg−1. Furthermore, its specific capacitance increased from 56.3 to 306.25 F g−1 after 1000 cycles at 5 A g−1, indicating progressive electrochemical activation. These findings highlight the importance of balancing ZnO morphology, accessible charge-storage sites, and MXene/PPy conductive networks, providing a composition-guided strategy for developing ternary nanocomposite electrodes with improved electrochemical energy storage performance.

Article.Authors: Roumiantseva M.; Saksaganskaia A.; Muntyan V.; Kozlova A.; Gorbunova M.; Vladimirova M.

Striking interspecies differences emerged: S. meliloti acts as the main recipient of phage material, accumulating less ameliorated prophages (mean ΔGC = −2.62%) with a broader spectrum of integration sites, whereas S. medicae maintains a more closed, vertically inherited pool characterized by higher synteny and greater GC amelioration (ΔGC = −1.12%). Furthermore, two types of prophage-to-prophage exchange were identified: recent modular-cassette transfers and ancient recombination events. These findings provide a basis for assessing the risk of stress-inducible prophages in inoculant strains.

Article.Authors: Alekseeva A.; Sentyabreva A.; Arutyunyan I.; Gerasimov A.; Melnikova E.; Soboleva A.; Shpakova K.; Skribitsky V.; Finogenova Y.; Kosyreva A.
Article.Abstract: Adult type diffuse gliomas are malignant neoplasms with a high mortality rate and low therapeutic efficacy. The lack of relevant models hinders the search for and development of new therapeutic and diagnostic methods. The rat glioma tissue strain 10-17-2 was obtained through chemical induction. Through in vitro cultivation, cell and spheroid models were obtained for it, reproducing the features of glioma when implanted intracranially in rats. The study involved a comparative analysis of the morphological and molecular-genetic characteristics of the tissue, cell, and spheroid models of Astrid-17 (10-17-2) rat glioma to identify relevant models for human gliomas. This paper presents a morphological characterization of the models, an assessment of the level of mRNA expression of the Cdkn2a, Trp53, S100b, Pten, Vegfa, Pdgfra, Sox2, Abcb1b, and Mgmt genes, and an assessment of the level of expression of the p53, ATRX, PDGFRA, and MGMT proteins. A significant increase in the expression of Sox2 and Vegfa was observed in all models, along with an increase in Pdgfra, Mgmt, Abcb1b, and Tp53 in the tissue model; a decrease in the expression of Tp53, Abcb1b, and Mgmt was noted in the spheroid model. At the same time, an increase in the expression of the p53 and ATRX proteins was observed in all three models. All models were visualized using MRI and PET-CT. It is shown that the tissue model has the most pronounced morphological similarity, while the spheroid model exhibits moderate morphological similarity to high-grade human gliomas. The molecular profile is individual for each model; however, based on the combination of markers, the spheroid model is the most relevant to human glioma compared to the tissue and cell models.

Article.Title: Proposed Grammatical Rules for the Redox Code
Article.Authors: Andrés C.; de la Lastra J.; Munguira E.; Juan C.; Lebeña E.
Article.Abstract: Oxidative stress biology has long worked within a framework in which reactive species cause damage and antioxidants supply the remedy. Large antioxidant trials have returned null or harmful results, and systemic redox biomarkers such as malondialdehyde and 8-oxo-dG show only modest diagnostic performance. We propose that both disappointments become more tractable once redox signalling is treated as a local, competitive and compartmentalised information system rather than a global balance, formalised here as the system G = {Σ, M, R, E, L, C, T, Φ}, where G denotes the grammar of the redox code and the eight symbols name its element classes. Reactive signallers (Σ) write post-translational marks (M) that editors (E) reverse or repair, effectors (L) read, and compartments (C) and temporality (T) contextualise, with disease outputs (Φ) completing the architecture. Its predictive core is five operative rules, R.S1 to R.S5, stated in terms of kinetic dominance rather than absolute concentrations, each giving a condition under which one modification should prevail on a contested residue. Three worked applications develop PKG1α Tyr247 nitration in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, DJ-1 Cys106 overoxidation in Parkinson’s disease and ApoA-I modification in sepsis, each as a testable hypothesis. G asks which mark dominates, whether it is reversible and what it does functionally, so that intervention is directed at the right level. G is proposed as a complement to quantitative redox modelling and not as a replacement for it, since it generates testable hypotheses where kinetic parameters are incomplete and does not attempt quantitative simulation.

Article.Title: Activity of Protective Blends Comprised of Cinnamon, Clove, Rosemary, Eucalyptus and Lemon Essential Oils Against Clinical Escherichia coli Strains Isolated from Poultry
Article.Authors: Zych S.; Adaszyńska-Skwirzyńska M.; Dzięcioł M.; Konieczka P.; Kozłowski K.; Witkowska D.; Szewczuk M.
Article.Abstract: Poultry colibacillosis is a common bacterial disease caused by pathogenic strains of Escherichia coli. The growing drug resistance of these strains is driving the search for new phytobiotics that are effective against this bacterium. A medieval recipe, the “Thieves” protective blend, shows promising results in this regard. This blend contains essential oils (EOs) from cinnamon bark (cinnamaldehyde chemotype), clove buds (eugenol chemotype), rosemary and eucalyptus (both eucalyptol chemotype) and lemon (limonene). The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) method was used to determine the activity of a total of 12 selected EOs (5 single EOs and 7 protective blends) against fifty clinical isolates of E. coli and the reference strain ATCC 25922. The detailed chemical composition of all EOs and their blends was determined using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). Cinnamon bark EO showed the strongest activity (mean MIC = 0.14% v/v), followed by two mixtures containing 50% and 20% of this EO (mean MICs of 0.22% and 0.25% v/v, respectively). The second most active EO was clove bud EO (mean MIC = 0.28% v/v) and the related blend (mean MIC 0.27% v/v). Rosemary, eucalyptus, and lemon EOs appear to have low activity against E. coli (MIC > 4% v/v). However, typical MIC values for their mixtures ranged from 0.34 to 0.5% v/v, indicating a possible synergy between the individual components of the “Thieves” blend. If additional synergistic effects with antibiotics can be identified in the future, it will be possible to use this type of protective blend in the adjunctive treatment of colibacillosis in poultry.

Article.Title: NAA-Param: Automated De Novo Parameterization of Non-Canonical Amino Acids for Molecular Dynamics Studies
Article.Authors: Carotenuto G.; Menconero E.; Botta L.; Saladino R.; Bottoni P.; Castrignanò T.
Article.Abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are key determinants of protein function and play an increasingly central role in rational drug design. These modifications involve the presence of non-canonical amino acid residues (nAA) within the affected proteins. Force fields typically used in molecular dynamics studies contain parameters for the 20 canonical amino acids; the lack of specific parameters for the nAAs makes it impossible to apply standard molecular dynamics (MD) protocols to proteins with PTMs, as these protocols often fail to generate accurate topologies for proteins featuring such modifications. In this work, we present a robust computational framework designed to parameterize the force fields required to perform MD simulations on proteins with PTMs. We introduce NAA-Param, a tool that derives high-quality, specific force field parameters for nAA on demand. The system automatically replicates the original protocol used to calculate parameters for the Amber99sb-ildn force field, a widely used force field in MD. Output files for the nAA are generated in a GROMACS-compatible format; furthermore, NAA-Param can be executed on HPC platforms.

Article.Title: Research Advances on Gut–Brain Axis in Parkinson’s Disease Pathogenesis and Prodromal Prediction
Article.Authors: Huang L.; Du W.; Zhai J.; Zhu W.; Wu J.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a common chronic progressive neurodegenerative disorder. Traditionally, it has been considered to be a disorder confined to dopaminergic neuronal injury in the substantia nigra of the central nervous system. However, increasing evidence from epidemiology, clinical imaging, and molecular biology suggests that the pathological process of PD may begin in the gut, with the gut–brain axis participating in disease initiation and progression. This review systematically summarizes the structural and physiological regulatory mechanisms of the gut–brain axis, focusing in particular on the aggregation of α-synuclein in the gut and its prion-like propagation, features of gut microbiota dysbiosis, leaky gut and systemic inflammatory cascades, and vagus nerve–related transmission mechanisms. Centering on prodromal PD, we discuss in depth early biomarkers based on this framework and propose a multi-dimensional combinatorial strategy integrating gut microbiota, barrier-related molecules and prodromal clinical phenotypes, to provide new perspectives for the prodromal prediction of PD.

Article.Title: Diagnostic Yield and Variant Spectrum in 375 Patients with Segmental Overgrowth and Vascular Malformations: Implications for Panel Design and Molecular Testing Strategies
Article.Authors: Bychkova E.; Semenova N.; Sagoyan G.; Alimov S.; Zhigulin A.; Somsikov G.; Khagurov R.; Guseva D.; Volodin I.; Kutsev S.; Strelnikov V.
Article.Abstract: Segmental overgrowth and vascular malformations comprise a group of diseases caused by postzygotic variants in genes that regulate cell growth, proliferation, and angiogenesis. The best-characterized group is the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS), which includes syndromes sharing variants in the PIK3CA gene. Beyond PIK3CA, the genes involved fall into two mechanistically distinct groups, with gain-of-function (GNAQ, GNA11, TEK, AKT1, AKT3, MTOR, PIK3R1) and loss-of-function (RASA1, GLMN, PTEN) causative variants. What remains poorly established is how effectively a molecular diagnosis is actually achieved in routine practice, and how this depends on the referral clinical diagnosis. By targeted panel deep sequencing in patients with segmental overgrowth and/or a vascular malformation, we have identified at least one pathogenic / likely pathogenic (P/LP) genetic variant in 266 of the 375 successfully tested patients, giving an overall diagnostic yield of 70.9%. The yield was 63.5% in patients with isolated overgrowth (94 of 148), 75.0% in patients with an isolated vascular malformation (111 of 148) and 77.2% in patients with a combined or syndromic phenotype (61 of 79). The 277 P/LP variants identified were distributed across 17 genes; PIK3CA accounted for 141 variants (50.9%), GNAQ for 44 (15.9%), TEK for 31 (11.2%), RASA1 for 15 (5.4%) and GNA11 for 11 (4.0%); these five genes together accounted for 87.4% of the variants. The spectrum was highly concentrated: the ten most frequent variants accounted for 57.0% of the P/LP variants, with GNAQ variant p.Arg183Gln (15.2%) and PIK3CA hotspot variants p.Glu542Lys (8.7%), p.Glu545Lys (6.9%), and p.His1047Arg (7.6%). In several genes, variants were restricted to specific regions: in GNAQ and GNA11 to two codons, 183 and 209 (98.2% of all findings), and in TEK to the 3′-terminus. Considered together with the referral diagnosis, the distribution of variants, their allele fractions and their mechanisms of pathogenicity suggest molecular testing strategies.

Article.Title: Circulating CD39+ Regulatory T Cells from Patients with Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma: Exploratory Assessment of Neuroprotective and Regenerative Activity in Pooled Preparations
Article.Authors: Ye C.; Jiang Q.; Cai B.; Jiang B.; Xie L.
Article.Abstract: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by retinal ganglion cell (RGC) loss and irreversible visual impairment. Functional experiments using pooled donor-derived preparations showed that CD39+ Treg-conditioned medium and adoptively transferred CD39+ Tregs exerted a degree of protective activity. In vivo, both healthy control- and POAG-derived preparations exhibited neuroprotective effects; healthy control-derived conditioned medium yielded a higher RGC density than POAG-derived medium, and short-distance axon regeneration was numerically greater following treatment with healthy control-derived preparations. Together, these proof-of-concept findings highlight the potential neuroprotective and regenerative properties of CD39+ Treg-derived preparations and support further investigation of their involvement in retinal neurodegeneration.

Article.Authors: Yi X.; Zhu Y.; Zhao Y.
Article.Abstract: Urticaria is a common and heterogeneous inflammatory skin disorder with a complex pathogenesis, and effective treatment options remain limited for some patients. This study employed an integrative multi-omics framework combining Mendelian randomization (MR), summary-data-based MR (SMR), Bayesian colocalization, and mediation analysis to identify candidate genes and inflammatory mediators associated with urticaria susceptibility. Furthermore, C4A expression was significantly downregulated in lesional skin from patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), and a consistent reduction was observed in ear skin from mice subjected to IgE/DNP-induced passive cutaneous anaphylaxis. Collectively, these findings support potential associations of C4A and CCL19 with urticaria risk and provide preliminary statistical evidence for a possible mediating role of CCL19 in the association between genetically predicted C4A expression and urticaria risk. Article.Title: Dendritic Cells Undergo Cytoskeletal, Adhesive, and Inflammatory Remodeling During Productive Infection with Vaccinia Virus Western Reserve
Article.Authors: Biernacka Z.; Markowska M.; Wróblewski M.; Niedzielska A.; Zawadzka K.; Koper M.; Gregorczyk-Zboroch K.; Lasocka I.; Gieryńska M.; Struzik J.; Mielcarska M.; Wierzbicki M.; Toka F.; Szulc-Dąbrowska L.
Article.Abstract: Dendritic cells (DCs) are professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) that regulate key aspects of innate and adaptive immunity. Their functions rely on dynamic cytoskeletal remodeling and specialized adhesive structures, including podosomes and focal adhesions (FAs), which coordinate cell–matrix interactions, antigen sampling, and migration to lymphoid organs, where DCs initiate T-cell responses. Non-pathogenic or attenuated vaccinia virus (VACV) strains can modulate DC functions despite undergoing abortive infection in these cells. However, the capacity of VACV Western Reserve (VACV-WR), a pathogenic and highly mouse-adapted strain with pronounced virulence in murine models, to productively infect DCs and its effects on their cytoskeletal organization, adhesive properties, and immune functions remain poorly characterized. Consequently, podosome-dependent extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation was abolished in infected cells. Despite pronounced morphological and adhesive remodeling, VACV-WR infection did not significantly alter mean BMDC migration distance or speed in the two-dimensional assay, although time-lapse analysis revealed a significantly increased proportion of stationary cells. These findings indicate that VACV-WR induces the coordinated cytoskeletal, adhesive, and immunological reprogramming of BMDCs, with functional consequences for ECM remodeling but not basal motility.

Article.Title: Genotypic and Phenotypic Spectrum of Pediatric β-Thalassaemia: Insights from a 30-Year Single-Center Experience
Article.Authors: Adramerina A.; Goulas I.; Tritou M.; Gkimprixis C.; Malontziki L.; Aidinidou L.; Teli A.; Theodoridou S.; Vrettou C.; Traeger-Synodinos J.; Economou M.

All 36 patients carrying homozygous β0/β0 or β+/β+ variants, or compound heterozygous β0/β+ mutations were transfusion-dependent, whereas the remaining TDT patients carried β0 or β+ and silent β-globin variants or α-globin gene triplication. Four genotypes found in 16 patients were associated with both transfusion-dependent and non-transfusion-dependent phenotypes. Notably, two pairs of related patients carrying the same genotype exhibited discordant clinical phenotypes. The clinical heterogeneity of β-thalassaemia is further highlighted by the discordant phenotypes observed among patients carrying the same genotype, underscoring the need to identify additional factors that influence clinical expression. Characterization of these factors is important, not only for more accurate genetic counseling and prognostic assessment, but also for individualization of treatment strategies and appropriate selection of candidates for emerging therapeutic approaches.

Article.Title: Cell-Penetrating TLR Inhibitor Peptide Ameliorates Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis and Promotes Efferocytosis in Microglia and Macrophages

By day 7, five measures remained FDR-significant, all decreasing: H4, H3/H4 and the three four-marker-positive populations. At day 28, no paired comparison remained FDR-significant; however, H3/H4 showed a significant overall temporal change across the six complete serial trajectories (q = 0.0334). Exploratory day-28 trajectories showed concordant decreases in all three four-marker-positive populations in patients achieving complete remission, with opposite changes in residual disease; however, the response-stratified comparisons were not statistically significant. Article.Title: Life After Catalytic Death: Pseudopeptidases as Key Regulators in Health and Disease
Article.Authors: Dunaevsky Y.; Tereshchenkova V.; Zhiganov N.; Zamyatnin A.; Elpidina E.
Article.Abstract: In recent years, researchers have increasingly focused on a special class of proteins—pseudopeptidases—that have lost their catalytic activity while retaining the ability to bind targets with high specificity. The evolutionary transition from an active enzyme to a pseudopeptidase is often driven by point mutations in the active site that “switch off” hydrolysis, paradoxically increasing affinity for substrates or regulatory partners. This process of “functional exaptation” allows the cell to create complex regulatory networks by repurposing existing domains rather than synthesizing new structures. This review analyzes the mechanisms underlying the emergence of pseudopeptidases across all major peptidase families and their roles in signaling cascades as molecular scaffolds, allosteric modulators, or competitive inhibitors. Particular attention is paid to their contribution to pathophysiology: the loss of proteolytic function does not render these proteins “silent”; on the contrary, their dysfunction is critical in the development of cancer, as well as neurodegenerative and inflammatory diseases. The shift from catalytic inertness to active regulation opens new horizons in understanding the molecular mechanisms of pathologies, positioning pseudopeptidases as promising targets for therapeutic intervention.

Article.Title: Oxyresveratrol and Related Stilbenes in Retinal Diseases: Current Preclinical Evidence, Mechanistic Rationale, and Research Priorities
Article.Authors: Kang B.; Lee D.; Vitiello L.; Lim S.
Article.Abstract: Oxyresveratrol is a naturally occurring stilbene known for its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic activities. However, its relevance to retinal disease requires careful distinction between direct ocular findings and evidence obtained with related compounds or non-ocular models. This narrative review critically examines direct retinal evidence for oxyresveratrol, comparative retinal studies of resveratrol, and non-ocular findings for mulberrosides and oxyresveratrol-containing botanical preparations. The literature search used PubMed and Google Scholar, supplemented with reference-list screening. The direct oxyresveratrol evidence discussed here includes pretreatment studies in hydrogen peroxide- or sodium iodate-exposed ARPE-19 cells and a sodium iodate-induced mouse retinal injury model. Reported improvements in cellular viability and retinal structure support further investigations of RPE oxidative injury, but methodological limitations and the predominantly preventive treatment designs preclude conclusions regarding efficacy in human age-related macular degeneration or other retinal diseases. The reported NRF2-silencing experiments did not establish that NRF2 activation was required for protection. Effects on retinal mitochondrial function, SIRT1/SIRT3 signaling, pathological angiogenesis, and adipose–retina interactions remain hypotheses requiring direct validation. Findings for resveratrol, mulberrosides, or phytochemical combinations should not be treated as interchangeable evidence of oxyresveratrol efficacy. Priorities include independent replication, post-injury treatment studies, quantitative ocular exposure assessment, and evaluation of safety and disease-specific functional outcomes. Oxyresveratrol therefore warrants further preclinical evaluation, while its translational relevance remains to be established.

Article.Title: Dietary Protein or Amino Acid Supplementation and Its Impact on Sarcopenia and Frailty: A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Mercado Nieves F.; Lopez I.; Fulzele S.; McGee-Lawrence M.; Johnson M.; Hamrick M.; Bollag W.; Isales C.
Article.Abstract: Nutrition and physical activity are crucial determinants of age-related frailty, an increasingly common condition that can coexist with sarcopenia. Since protein and amino acid supplements are relatively cheap and accessible, determining the usefulness of this intervention in treating frailty/sarcopenia would be valuable. Several clinical trials have examined the effects of protein and amino acid supplementation on frailty and sarcopenia, and results suggest that adequate dietary protein intake/supplementation can improve muscle mass, strength, and function in older adults. An English literature search was conducted using the PubMed (NLM) database from June 2002 to June 2024, and 458 studies were identified. Of these, 410 were excluded after review of their titles, abstracts and the population studied or identification as duplicate references. The remaining 48 studies investigated a variety of protein or essential amino acid (EAA) supplements in a range of settings. Reported positive results were mostly in combination with exercise, specifically resistance training. However, any overall positive effect remains unclear. More high-quality studies are needed to better understand protein/amino acid supplementation’s role in preventing or treating frailty. Amino acid supplementation may be a more practical approach to increasing dietary protein content for older adults, but beneficial effects may require that it be accompanied by exercise.

Article.Title: Ion Homeostasis Disturbances and Their Cellular Consequences in Metabolic Syndrome
Article.Authors: Topcu A.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is increasingly understood as a network disorder in which disturbances across multiple cellular systems converge to promote metabolic and cardiovascular dysfunction. Although ion homeostasis is essential for cellular function, researchers have often considered its contribution to MetS separately for individual ions or within specific disease contexts. In this narrative review, we propose an integrated framework in which disturbances in calcium (Ca2+), magnesium (Mg2+), sodium (Na+), potassium (K+), zinc (Zn2+), and iron (Fe) homeostasis are viewed as interconnected components of metabolic dysfunction rather than isolated abnormalities. We examine how altered ion gradients, transport processes, buffering mechanisms, and intracellular compartmentalization interact with mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum function, redox balance, inflammatory signaling, and metabolic pathways. Particular attention is given to the crosstalk between ion-dependent processes and insulin–AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)–mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling, as well as to their links with mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and regulated cell death pathways. We further distinguish interactions between ionic systems that have been directly demonstrated from links inferred only through shared downstream effectors, specify the level at which ion status was assessed, and separate ionic effects on insulin secretion from those on insulin action. Rather than providing a descriptive catalog of ion abnormalities, this review synthesizes the available evidence into a systems-level model of ion–metabolism interactions in MetS and identifies major unresolved mechanistic questions. This framework highlights the interconnected ion–metabolism network as a relevant feature of metabolic dysregulation in MetS and provides a basis for future studies integrating ionomics with metabolic, molecular, and spatially resolved approaches.

Article.Title: Genetics of the Leading Causes of Death in Human Aging
Article.Authors: Martignoni A.; Cai W.; Calderon V.; Aguinaldo C.; Park K.; Murakami S.
Article.Abstract: The relationship between age-related genetic factors and health conditions is crucial in aging research, particularly with respect to the leading global causes of mortality identified by the World Health Organization (WHO). To investigate the direct impact of these genes, we conducted a disease association analysis that compared 307 age-related genes with multiple control gene sets. Our results showed that the age-related gene set was significantly enriched with 113 disease categories compared to the controls, achieving a stringent false discovery rate (FDR) of less than 1 × 10−5. Interestingly, the disease ontology categories did not align directly with the WHO’s primary causes, leading us to reclassify them using the ICD-11 framework. Our analysis revealed that age-related genes are enriched among leading causes of death, particularly those affecting the cardiovascular system, brain, and lungs. We identified 15 recurring genes, including TNF, AKT1, IL6, and CDKN2A, with no evident publication bias, except for TP53, which may have a modest effect. These genes are associated with cancer, inflammatory diseases, and metabolic disorders, highlighting protein–protein networks in nitric oxide regulation and insulin signaling. This study provides a comprehensive analysis and reclassification of the genetic factors linked to human aging and health outcomes, generating key hypotheses in human aging.

Article.Title: Molasses-Assisted Green Combustion Synthesis of LaFeO3 Perovskites: Structural and Interfacial Insights for the Simultaneous Electrochemical Determination of Acetaminophen and 4-Aminoantipyrine
Article.Authors: Alfonso-Gonzalez J.; Paredes-Cuarán A.; Toro-Corrales V.; Renteria-Moreno L.; Hernández-Herrera C.; Morales-Morales J.
Article.Abstract: Sugarcane molasses-assisted combustion was employed to synthesize two LaFeO3 perovskite formulations (ELF-4 and ELF-6). X-ray diffraction and Rietveld refinement supported the formation of the orthorhombic Pnma structure, while vibrational spectroscopy and electron microscopy revealed formulation-associated differences in surface-related features and aggregate morphology. Cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy demonstrated distinct interfacial responses without establishing a generalized enhancement in electron-transfer kinetics following LaFeO3 modification. At pH 3.5, ELF-4-modified screen-printed carbon electrodes (ELF-4/SPCE) exhibited distinguishable oxidation signals for acetaminophen (AC) and 4-aminoantipyrine (4-AAP). Differential pulse voltammetry of equimolar mixtures provided concentration-dependent responses over 20–180 µM, with sensitivities of 0.0969 µA µM−1 for AC (R2 = 0.997) and 0.0192 µA µM−1 for 4-AAP (R2 = 0.927). Cross-concentration experiments revealed asymmetric analyte interactions, indicating that peak discrimination does not necessarily ensure independent quantitative responses. Exploratory measurements in diluted and fortified campus garden fountain and tap water samples yielded distinguishable signals, although joint standard additions did not establish reliable individual quantification. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of molasses-derived LaFeO3 as an electrochemical sensing modifier while identifying limitations that must be addressed for accurate simultaneous analysis.

Article.Title: The Chemistry of Ash Dieback: Fungal Metabolites, Host Defence and Endophytes
Article.Authors: Pawłowicz T.
Article.Abstract: Ash dieback combines fungal chemical activity with tissue-specific host defence and interactions with associated microorganisms. This structured narrative review integrates the constituents of Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, ash tissues and fungal associates, and reanalyses public leaf metabolomics data at the genotype level. The fungal repertoire includes furanosteroids, glycosides, a tetramic acid, volatile lactones and extracellular carbohydrates. Fraxetin shows recurring associations with lower-susceptibility bark and has experimentally demonstrated antifungal activity; recent evidence of pathogen-mediated depletion adds a dynamic dimension to host chemistry. Secoiridoid associations depend on candidate identity and sampling context, with the strongest support for several matched candidates concentrated in the Danish panel. Reanalysis of 13 European ash genotypes detected no susceptibility-category association in the primary 54-feature leaf profile (R2=0.047, p=0.915); alternative prevalence filters gave consistent results, with feature-dependent precision. Mature-tree phenolics varied with site and year, while crown-damage coefficients remained near zero in the selected endpoints. Phomopsidin, PF1140, CJ-17,572 and mycorrhizin A inhibited the pathogen in compound assays, and plant observations distinguished antagonism from host compatibility. The synthesis identifies tissue, chemical state and environmental context as essential coordinates of ash chemical phenotyping, connecting molecular evidence with the interpretation of forest disease and host survival.

Article.Title: Lipid Droplet Remodeling at the Glia–Neuron Interface: Metabolic Sinks, Flux Traps, and Therapeutic Pitfalls in Neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Fu M.; Su Y.; Hu G.; Luo X.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by progressive neurological decline, metabolic dysfunction, and chronic neuroinflammatory changes. Dysregulated lipid handling has emerged as an important component of these processes, but the functional significance of lipid droplets (LDs) remains strongly context-dependent. Here, we review LD biogenesis, turnover, and cell type-specific functions in the central nervous system (CNS) and critically evaluate evidence linking LD remodeling to neurodegeneration. Transient LD formation can buffer excess or oxidation-prone lipids and support metabolic adaptation, whereas persistent lipid retention in the setting of impaired lysosomal, mitochondrial, or lipid-export capacity is associated with cellular dysfunction. We compare human tissue data, genetic evidence, LD-specific perturbations, pharmacological studies, and experimental models across Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and Huntington’s disease (HD). Particular attention is given to microglial lipid-associated states, neuron–glia lipid transfer, monogenic disorders of lipid handling, and apparently opposing outcomes of LD manipulation in different disease contexts. Rather than treating LD accumulation as a universal pathogenic mechanism, we propose LD remodeling as a candidate metabolic–inflammatory convergence state whose functional consequences depend on cell type, lipid composition, turnover capacity, and disease stage. Translational strategies should therefore prioritize direct measurements of LD flux, demonstration of CNS target engagement, and biomarker-guided patient and disease-stage selection. We further define experimental findings that would support or falsify the proposed convergence model.
