Article.Title: The Need for Variant-Specific Splicing Assessment in Developing Antisense Oligonucleotide Therapies for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: Lessons from the DMD c.4675−2A>G Variant
Article.Authors: Sunami A.; Horiguchi T.; Takeuchi A.; Ishikawa Y.; Kataoka N.; Komai K.; Nishio H.; Matsuo M.
Article.Abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by pathogenic variants in the DMD gene. Splice-site variants can generate aberrant transcripts whose consequences cannot always be predicted by the classical reading-frame rule. Here, we characterized the c.4675−2A>G variant at the exon 34 splice acceptor site for the development of an exon-skipping therapy. A minigene analysis demonstrated that c.4675−2A>G activated a cryptic splice acceptor within exon 34 rather than inducing skipping of the entire exon, resulting in deletion of the first 7 nucleotides, a frameshift, and a premature termination codon. To restore the reading frame by promoting skipping of the entire exon 34, we used antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting distinct splice-regulatory regions. Among the ASO treatments tested, including individual ASOs and ASO combinations, A1&E4&D1 produced the highest exon exclusion and consistently promoted exon 34 skipping across the examined −2A mutant genotypes. A1&E4&D1 consists of ASOs A1, E4, and D1. A1 targeted the cryptic 3′ splice acceptor region, E4 targeted a predicted exonic splicing enhancer region, and D1 targeted the 5′ splice donor region. These findings illustrate a stepwise, variant-directed strategy in which characterization of aberrant splicing guides the design of a tailor-made ASO intervention.

Article.Title: A Raman Spectroscopic Case Study of Ceramide- and Sulfur-Enriched Microdomains in Human Alzheimer’s Brain: Localized Molecular Signatures Resembling Bacterial Outer Membrane Vesicles
Article.Authors: Pezzotti G.; Murakami A.; Ikegami S.; Son A.; Matsuo Y.; Zavan B.; Franceschini D.; Koutsikos K.; Rigon L.; Pinton P.; Kawada-Matsuo M.; Komatsuzawa H.; Yakushiji Y.
Article.Abstract: We report a high-resolution Raman microspectroscopic case study comparing post-mortem human brain tissue from one Alzheimer’s disease subject and one neurologically healthy subject. Low-wavenumber Raman imaging revealed discrete, micron-sized protuberant microdomains present exclusively in the Alzheimer’s tissue, exhibiting intense ceramide-associated bands and characteristic oxysulfur vibrational features. These localized structures showed spectral similarity to previously reported spectra of outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) from Porphyromonas gingivalis. However, genomic analysis of bulk tissue from the same specimen detected no bacterial DNA. This discrepancy likely reflects differing spatial resolutions between the two methods, as Raman spectroscopy probes micron-scale domains while genomic assays average signals across much larger tissue volumes. Although this single-case study cannot confirm bacterial OMV presence or a causal link to Alzheimer’s disease, it identifies an unusual molecular microenvironment warranting further investigation through spatially correlated spectroscopic, genomic, and histopathological analyses. Beyond these localized structures, Raman spectroscopy also revealed biochemical signatures consistent with Alzheimer’s-associated lipid remodeling, including decreased cholesterol relative to oxysulfur compounds, reduced cholesteryl ester relative to total cholesterol, and altered phospholipid composition marked by phosphatidylserine depletion and elevated phosphatidylinositol signals. These findings demonstrate the Raman microspectroscopy’s capability to detect localized biochemical heterogeneity in diseased brain tissue.

Article.Authors: Hirata A.; Choque P.; Silva R.; Ferreira M.; De Angelis K.; Giannocco G.; Dellê H.; Camacho C.
Article.Abstract: Extra-olfactory receptors (ORs) are expressed in multiple tissues and implicated in cardiovascular regulation and placental biology. Methods: Pregnant Wistar rats were assigned to control, gestational hypothyroid, and levothyroxine (LT4)-treated hypothyroid groups. The circulating ORs correlate with placental Or10j5 in the hypothyroidism group and with kidney Or10j5 in LT4-treated animals. Conclusions: Gestational thyroid dysfunction modified OR expression in the kidney and placenta. LT4 alters placental transcriptional profiles, suggesting hormone sensitivity of extra-olfactory receptor transcripts. The small sample size and ANN-imputed TSH warrant cautious interpretation.

Article.Title: High-Altitude Exposure Is Associated with Sustained Inflammation and Hyperinsulinemia in Healthy Individuals: An Investigative Study on Human Expedition
Article.Authors: Sentinelli F.; Verratti V.; Lucarelli A.; Iacobini C.; Tienforti D.; Moretto C.; Cavallo M.; Bondi D.; Barbonetti A.; Baroni M.
Article.Abstract: This study aimed to investigate the integrated in vivo impact of progressive high altitude on metabolic, inflammatory, and vascular adaptation pathways and to assess their modulation by biological sex and anthropometric profile. A Himalayan expedition was conducted with fifteen volunteers (nine men, six women; age 43 ± 15 years; body mass index (BMI) of 24.2 ± 3.70 kg/m2). Participants received acetazolamide (250 mg/day). Blood samples were collected before (50 m above sea level), during (1400 m and 5000 m), and after the Himalayan trip (return to 1400 m). Serum concentrations of Adipocyte Complement-Related Protein of 30 kDa (Adiponectin/Acrp30), C-Reactive Protein (CRP), Plasminogen Activator Inhibitor-1 (Serpin E1/PAI-1), Monocyte Chemoattractant Protein-1/chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 2 (MCP-1/CCL2), basic Fibroblast Growth Factor (bFGF), Insulin, Leptin, Macrophage Migration Inhibitory Factor (MIF) and Tumor Necrosis Factor alpha (TNF-α) were measured. Progressive exposure to high altitude induced significant activation of inflammatory pathways, documented by progressively increased serum levels, compared to baseline, of CRP, MCP-1, PAI-1, and TNF-α (all p < 0.05). Insulin increased significantly at maximum altitude (p = 0.032), with persistence during descent (p = 0.042). bFGF showed a biphasic trend. Leptin, adiponectin, and MIF changes did not reach statistical significance. A mixed repeated-measures ANOVA confirmed a significant main effect of altitude on insulin concentration (p = 0.005), on CRP (p = 0.009), on MCP-1 (p = 0.004), and on TNF-α levels (p < 0.001). However, no significant interaction of sex and BMI (Body Mass Index) with altitude was observed. Elevated CRP, MCP-1, PAI-1, and TNF-α persisted during descent, suggesting delayed resolution of the high-altitude-induced inflammatory response. These results show that progressive high altitude induces systemic inflammation and hyperinsulinemia, which persist during descent, providing new insights into the relationship between altitude-induced inflammatory pathways and insulin dynamics.

Article.Authors: Sánchez-Padilla A.; Escorcia-Barrera A.; Tafoya-Olvera M.; Valencia-Cruz A.; García-Meza J.; Alarcón-Sánchez B.; Idelfonso-García O.; Márquez-Quiroga L.; Torres-Mena J.; Fuentes-Hernández S.; Valderrama-Cervantes L.; Herrera-López E.; Aguirre-Maldonado I.; Martínez-Magaña J.; Resendis-Antonio O.; Muciño-Olmos E.; Aparicio-Bautista D.; Basurto-Islas G.; Román-González S.; Gutiérrez-Nava M.; Mendoza-Vargas A.; Jiménez-García M.; Pacheco-Rivera R.; Gutiérrez-Reyes G.; Pérez-Hernández J.

The expression of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1a (Cdkn1a) gene, commonly known as P21, was the most dysregulated, and its total (CDN1A/P21) and phosphorylated protein level was increased from early to late stages. P21 was also increased and released into the bloodstream of ALD and MASLD models, both based on multiple hepatotoxins linked to HCC development, as well as in the bloodstream of ALD patients. In conclusion, P21 is altered from early stages of liver diseases leading to HCC, which betrays the onset of liver cancer before developing malignant traits; thus, P21 offers a critical therapeutic window for timely detection of high-risk patients.

Article.Title: Immune Checkpoint-Related Gene Prognostic Signature Characterizes the Immunosuppressive Microenvironment and Predicts Immunotherapy Response in Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma
Article.Authors: Dai L.; Zheng L.; Yuan H.; Li J.; Pang J.; Yue F.
Article.Abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) shows heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). We aimed to develop an immune checkpoint-related gene (ICRG) signature for risk stratification, tumor microenvironment characterization, and immunotherapy prediction. LIPA overexpression suppressed proliferation, migration, and invasion in CAKI-1 and CAKI-2 renal carcinoma cells. This ICRG signature serves as a potential prognostic biomarker and may aid in predicting immunotherapy response. Furthermore, LIPA showed tumor-suppressive potential, providing a rationale for future personalized treatment strategies.

Article.Title: Advances and Application Potential of Functional and Stimuli-Responsive Hydrogels in Diabetic Bone Repair
Article.Authors: Jin Y.; Wang J.; Hu W.; Zhao H.
Article.Abstract: Impaired bone healing in diabetes continues to present a major challenge in orthopedic and regenerative medicine. The compromised osseous regeneration typically stems from a complex pathological cascade—namely, persistent local hyperglycemia, excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), impaired neurovascular coupling, sustained low-grade inflammation, altered insulin signaling, and the deleterious deposition of advanced glycation end products. Together, these systemic and microenvironmental anomalies impede endogenous repair, potentially culminating in delayed union or frank non-union. To overcome these limitations, functional and stimuli-responsive (smart) hydrogel networks have emerged as a versatile therapeutic platform. These matrices provide sustained local delivery, while selected responsive chemistries couple release or degradation to glucose, ROS, proteases, pH, or externally applied light. Temperature-dependent gelation, antioxidant activity, and electrical conductivity are distinguished from pathological-signal-triggered release. In this review, we summarize current progress in the rational design and implementation of functional and stimuli-responsive hydrogels for diabetic bone repair. We evaluate their biological mechanisms together with responsive chemistry, tested trigger levels, release and degradation kinetics, mechanical properties, and the relevance of each experimental model, concluding with prospective strategies to guide subsequent biomaterial innovation and clinical translation in this domain.

Article.Title: G Protein-Coupled Receptors Across Diverse Astrocyte Functions and Cellular Crosstalk
Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Lin Y.; Mah S.; Tang L.; Xu J.
Article.Abstract: Astrocytes are the most abundant and functionally versatile glial cells in the central nervous system, where they maintain homeostasis, regulate metabolic function, and communicate extensively with neurons, microglia and other CNS cell types. To mediate these interactions, astrocytes use G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) to receive diverse extracellular signals, such as neurotransmitters, secreted signals and inflammatory factors. GPCRs translate extracellular signals into intracellular signaling cascades in astrocytes and are essential for intercellular communication. Despite decades of investigation, however, astrocytic GPCR signaling remains difficult to explain within a unified framework, as receptor activation does not necessarily produce predictable outcomes based on receptor identity or G-protein signaling alone. To address this gap, we critically examine representative studies of canonical and noncanonical GPCR signaling and astrocyte-centered cellular crosstalk, considering astrocyte state and the cellular position of receptors within communication pathways. We compare receptor-specific manipulations, functional outcomes, and methodological limitations to distinguish experimentally supported causal relationships from unresolved interpretations. This evidence-oriented approach identifies testable questions and experimental priorities for investigating astrocytic GPCR signaling in physiology and disease.

Article.Title: Comprehensive Search for Channels in African Swine Fever Virus
Article.Authors: Yadav M.; Arkin I.
Article.Abstract: African swine fever virus (ASFV) is arguably the most critical threat to global food security. With a mortality rate approaching 100%, it threatens pork production, a cornerstone of human nutrition that accounts for more than 35% of all meat consumed worldwide. ASFV is also one of the most structurally complex and largest pathogenic viruses, harboring a genome of 170–190 kbp. Consequently, to better understand this pathogen, we exhaustively screened the genome of the HK_NT_202103 strain for encoded ion channels using three complementary bacteria-based assays. Out of 196 genes screened, 24 candidates exhibited transmembrane potential, and their successful expression and integration were verified using maltose-binding protein fusions and Western blotting. Fourteen of these candidates scored positively across all three assays, confirming their status as potential viroporins. This functionally redundant set of 14 viroporins enables the virus to modulate host potassium levels and proton flux across membranes. Beyond identifying general channels, we mapped specific proton-selective pores. By applying kinetic modeling and ternary clustering, we moved beyond qualitative screening to categorize these viroporins into distinct functional zones based on their specific ion-movement dynamics. Genomic comparisons across eleven diverse global genotypes revealed that these key channels have remained virtually unchanged for over a century. The combination of structural stability and functional critical mass establishes these channels as premier vulnerabilities for therapeutic exploitation. Ultimately, this study provides the first validated functional atlas of ASFV ion channels, offering a detailed roadmap for designing broad-spectrum antivirals targeting the viral metabolic core.

Article.Title: Identification of Hypoxia- and Circadian Rhythm-Related Prognostic Genes in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Through Integrative Transcriptomic and Single-Cell Analysis
Article.Authors: Zu X.; Sun G.
Article.Abstract: Hypoxia perturbs circadian rhythm gene expression in hepatocellular carcinoma, yet prognostic genes associated with both processes remain insufficiently characterized. Data from the liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) cohort in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were analyzed. Candidate genes were identified by intersecting differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with 27 hypoxia- and circadian rhythm-related genes and were further refined using univariate Cox regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression; a random survival forest (RSF) risk model was then constructed and validated. Independent prognostic and functional enrichment analyses, immune infiltration profiling, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and immunohistochemistry (IHC) were subsequently performed. Four prognostic genes (ADM, PFKFB3, SERPINE1, and RORA) were identified through integrative computational analysis. The RSF model stratified LIHC patients into the high-risk group (HRG) and the low-risk group (LRG), which had significantly different survival outcomes, and the risk score and tumor stage were combined in a nomogram. The four genes were co-enriched in four pathways; eight immune cell types, including natural killer T (NKT) cells, differed between the risk groups. scRNA-seq identified stem-like/hypoxic malignant cells whose differentiation trajectory showed distinct expression dynamics of the four genes. IHC confirmed significantly higher ADM and PFKFB3 protein expression in LIHC tissues, whereas protein-level evidence for SERPINE1 and RORA was inconclusive. These findings support further prognostic evaluation of LIHC and investigation of the links among hypoxia, metabolic reprogramming, and stemness.

Article.Title: Monogenic Diseases: A View Through the Landscape–Attractor Framework
Article.Authors: Damante G.; Faletra F.
Article.Abstract: Monogenic diseases are traditionally interpreted through a linear causal model linking pathogenic variants to molecular dysfunction and clinical phenotypes. However, this model does not fully explain incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, and heterogeneous disease progression. This review aims to explore the applicability of the landscape–attractor framework, originally developed in evolutionary and developmental biology and subsequently extended to gene regulatory networks, to the interpretation of monogenic diseases. We propose that pathogenic variants act as persistent perturbations of interconnected molecular networks, modifying the stability and accessibility of physiological and pathological states. Within this framework, phenotypic variability emerges from interactions between the causal variant and genetic modifiers, epigenetic regulation, environmental influences, stochastic processes, and compensatory mechanisms. We further extend this perspective across molecular, cellular, tissue, and organismal levels, introducing the concept of functional fitness to describe disease-related physiological performance. Finally, we discuss how therapeutic interventions may redirect biological systems toward more favorable functional states without necessarily correcting the underlying genetic defect. This framework offers a complementary systems-level perspective on genotype–phenotype relationships and suggests experimentally testable hypotheses for understanding and modifying disease expression.

Article.Title: Expression and Membranous Localization of CD44 Define Distinct Cellular and Spatial Phenotypes Associated with Glioma Aggressiveness
Article.Authors: Jaunecker C.; Kerschbaumer L.; Quinot V.; Freund J.; Mager L.; Machreich S.; Pacher L.; Bruckner K.; Marosits L.; Robl B.; Lang A.; Gabler-Pamer L.; Kirchhofer D.; Pirker C.; Rössler K.; Berghoff A.; Kiesel B.; Widhalm G.; Roetzer-Pejrimovsky T.; Berger W.; Lötsch D.
Article.Abstract: Adult-type diffuse gliomas comprise, amongst others, biologically distinct isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant (IDH-MUT) astrocytomas and IDH-wildtype (IDH-WT) glioblastoma (GB). Although IDH-MUT astrocytomas generally have a more favorable prognosis, they frequently recur and progress. Despite extensive molecular characterization, key drivers of glioma progression remain elusive. CD44, a hyaluronic acid receptor, has been implicated in glioma invasion and progression. We investigated CD44 expression, localization, and spatial organization across IDH-WT GB and IDH-MUT astrocytomas and their association with tumor progression and cellular states. CD44 expression and localization were assessed in IDH-WT (n = 15) and IDH-MUT (n = 17) diffuse gliomas across WHO grades by immunohistochemistry (IHC). Multiplex IHC combined with AI-assisted digital pathology (HALO) evaluated associations between CD44, GFAP-positive astrocytic, and NeuN/RBFOX3-positive neuronal regions. Findings were validated using independent snRNA-seq data. IDH-WT GB exhibited significantly higher CD44 expression with prominent membranous localization. Lower-grade IDH-MUT astrocytomas showed reduced, diffuse staining, whereas higher-grade tumors acquired a membranous CD44 localization, resembling IDH-WT GB. CD44 was strongly associated with GFAP-positive astrocytic regions and inversely correlated with NeuN/RBFOX3-positive neuronal areas in IDH-MUT tumors. AI-assisted spatial analyses confirmed distinct CD44-positive astrocytic and NeuN-positive neuronal niches, supported by snRNA-seq demonstrating positive CD44-GFAP correlations. This association was strongest in astrocytic (AC-like) metaprograms of WHO grade 2, while in higher-grade tumors it was more pronounced in mesenchymal (MES-like) states. CD44 exhibits IDH- and grade-dependent spatial patterns marking glioma progression and astrocytic/mesenchymal tumor states. Membranous CD44 acquisition accompanies progression to higher grades in IDH-MUT astrocytomas, suggesting CD44 as a marker of glioma aggressiveness.

Article.Title: Comparative Analysis of Chloroplast Genomes and New Insights into the Phylogenetic Relationships of Lycoris
Article.Authors: Mao L.; Cao X.; Dong Q.; Hu W.; Tian D.; Zou Q.
Article.Abstract: The genus Lycoris, comprising approximately 25 species, has high medicinal and ornamental value. However, frequent interspecific hybridization and polyploidization have complicated species delimitation and germplasm identification. Complete chloroplast genomes are widely used for phylogenetic reconstruction and species identification. In this study, we sequenced and assembled the complete chloroplast genomes of L. haywardii, L. guangxiensis, L. chunxiaoensis, L. wulingensis, L. tsinlingensis, L. sp., L. caldwellii, and L. hubeiensis. The genome sizes ranged from 158,461 bp in L. wulingensis to 158,772 bp in L. guangxiensis. A total of 132 gene copies were annotated in each chloroplast genome, comprising 86 protein-coding, 38 tRNA and eight rRNA gene copies (78, 30 and four unique sequences, respectively, i.e., 112 unique genes). All eight genomes exhibited the typical quadripartite structure, with conserved genome organization and gene content. Size variation was mainly attributable to expansion and contraction at the IR/SC boundaries. Phylogenetic analysis of extant Lycoris species resolved four major clades, each containing one or two representative and widely recognized native species. Divergence-time estimation dated the crown of the sampled Lycoris plastid lineages to the late Miocene (6.65 Mya, 95% HPD 5.73–7.67 Mya), with the two deepest splits within the genus at 6.06 and 4.08 Mya and most terminal plastid divergences occurring during the Pleistocene (0.02–1.47 Mya). This pattern is consistent with previous studies suggesting that most Lycoris species are evolutionarily young and originated through hybridization and polyploidization. Among the newly sequenced taxa, the unidentified wild species (L. sp.) from Shaanxi Province is morphologically nearly identical to L. shaanxiensis, differing mainly in flower color, and plastome phylogenies place it in the same clade as L. shaanxiensis and its allies. The taxon may therefore represent a color variant derived from L. shaanxiensis, but this hypothesis cannot be tested with plastome data alone: recent divergence, shared maternal ancestry, chloroplast introgression, hybrid origin and intraspecific variation remain equally plausible, and nuclear or genome-wide markers with population-level sampling are needed to resolve its status.

Article.Title: Proteomic Landscapes of Aging and Disease: Multi-Omics Integration, Machine Learning, and Translational Opportunities
Article.Authors: Jin X.; Duan X.; Ma J.; Wang Z.; Chen W.; Xu H.; Yang F.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Aging is accompanied by progressive changes in molecular, cellular, and systemic homeostasis. At the protein level, these changes involve altered proteostasis, post-translational regulation, and protein interaction networks, but their direction and functional significance vary by tissue, age, and disease context. Mass spectrometry, affinity-based assays, spatial proteomics, and emerging single-cell methods now support complementary views of proteins across tissues, biofluids, and cell populations. Integrating proteomics with genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, and metabolomic data can identify regulatory relationships that are not resolved by a single molecular layer; such integration prioritizes mechanisms but does not by itself establish causality. Machine-learning methods support spectral prediction, multi-omics integration, and prediction from high-dimensional protein profiles, although their performance depends on study design, calibration, and independent validation. This narrative review synthesizes protein alterations associated with aging and major age-related diseases, describes what multi-omics and computational methods add, compares emerging measurement technologies, and evaluates biomarker and therapeutic opportunities. Chronological-age prediction, estimation of biological aging, and prediction of clinical outcomes are treated as distinct objectives. Current evidence supports discovery and candidate prioritization; prospective clinical utility and causal therapeutic benefit remain to be established.

Article.Title: From Setpoints to System Dynamics: Integrating Light, CO2 and Fertigation in Controlled-Environment Agriculture
Article.Authors: Phaugat A.; Malhotra G.; Jost R.; Brewer P.; Johnson K.
Article.Abstract: Controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) allows growers to regulate temperature, humidity, light, nutrients and root-zone parameters with high precision. However, precision alone does not guarantee improved performance when each control variable is interpreted in isolation, because plants respond to these inputs as an integrated system. Light controls both photosynthetic activity and photomorphogenic signalling. CO2 changes carbon assimilation, stomatal behaviour, water use and source-sink relations. Fertigation variables such as individual macro- and microelement concentrations, electrical conductivity (EC), pH, and nutrient solution flow rate determine nutrient availability, plant development, osmotic status, oxygen delivery and root-zone signalling. In plants, these inputs converge on shared physiological and molecular processes, including carbon–nitrogen balance, transpiration-driven nutrient delivery, nitrate and phosphate uptake, H+-ATPase activity, hormone signalling, root architecture, and sink development. This narrative review proposes a qualitative, conceptual systems-dynamics framework; it does not present a calibrated simulation or validated control model. The central proposition is that plant growth, yield and fruit quality emerge from feedback loops among carbon capture, nutrient acquisition, hydraulic function and developmental sink strength. In crops such as cucumber, tomato, lettuce, strawberry, pepper and basil, the same environmental input can improve one trait whilst weakening another, depending on developmental stage, cultivar, sink demand, and root-zone conditions. A system-dynamics framework is therefore essential for designing production strategies that synchronise light settings, CO2 schedules and fertigation regimes with plant physiological stages. For compact cucurbits and other commercial CEA crops, this approach can help optimise productivity per unit volume whilst maintaining nutrient status, water-use efficiency and fruit quality. These insights also apply to CEA for long-term space, Moon and Mars missions.

Article.Title: Candidate Vacuolar Lipases and Vacuolar Processing Enzymes Associated with Late Autophagic Degradation in Carbon-Starved Lupin (Lupinus spp.) Embryonic Axes
Article.Authors: Wleklik K.; Janicki M.; Nuc K.; Pietrowska-Borek M.; Bernard A.; Moreno I.; Klein M.; Karachitos A.; Nowaczyk G.; Paluch-Lubawa E.; Stefaniak S.; Ludwików A.; Borek S.
Article.Abstract: The degradation of autophagic bodies in the plant vacuole is required to complete autophagic flux, yet the hydrolases involved in membrane breakdown and cargo processing remain incompletely defined. Vacuole-targeted XP_019420123.1 failed to restore Ape1 maturation or AtAtg8a-GFP processing in Saccharomyces cerevisiae atg15Δ cells, indicating that the construct did not functionally substitute for Atg15 under the conditions tested. By contrast, partial inhibition of VPE-like activity with Ac-YVAD-cmk increased the number of intravacuolar autophagic-body-like structures while phagophores and autophagosomes remained detectable. Transcriptomic and RT-qPCR analyses further revealed gene-specific responses of VPE/legumain transcripts to carbon status and pharmacological treatments. Collectively, the results support an association between VPE-like proteolytic activity and efficient late intravacuolar degradation during carbon starvation. Article.Abstract: Porcine deltacoronavirus (PDCoV) is an important enteric pathogen of piglets, yet the host factors that restrict its infection remain poorly understood. Functional analyses showed that TTC7A overexpression (approximately 3-fold higher protein levels) suppressed PDCoV infection, whereas RNA interference-mediated knockdown enhanced infection by approximately 30% relative to the control, demonstrating that endogenous TTC7A restricts PDCoV infection. Co-immunoprecipitation assays further revealed an association between TTC7A and the C-terminal domain of the PDCoV spike protein. Structure-guided analysis identified candidate residues at the interaction interface, and site-directed mutagenesis of these residues impaired the TTC7A-spike interaction (a decrease of approximately 46%), supporting their contribution to this association. Together, these findings identify TTC7A as a host restriction factor for PDCoV and characterize its interaction with the viral spike protein. This study expands our understanding of host-mediated restriction of PDCoV and provides a basis for determining how TTC7A-spike association contributes to its antiviral activity.

Article.Authors: Ramsamooj A.; Yin T.; Osumanu T.; Lucas G.; Imeidopf G.; Akbar S.; Ahmed D.; Nainan S.; Vajinapelly S.; Krishna F.; Vaccaro J.; R. Ghorayeb S.; Currie E.; Merna N.

Analytical electric-field modeling was used to estimate local graft-region exposure and guide selection of biologically tolerated stimulation conditions. A 24 h live/dead screen identified 0 to 70 V/m as a biologically tolerated range using a study-defined 90% viability screening criterion; normalized viability fell below this threshold at 80 and 90 V/m, with a sharp decrease to 51% at 100 V/m. Within this range, electrical stimulation, flow conditioning, and combined electric-perfusion conditioning each produced measurable endothelial organization by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and CellProfiler-based morphology analysis. Endothelialization and flow conditioning also reduced 0.45 µm bead penetration into the middle graft layer, supporting bead permeability as an early barrier-associated readout. Plant grafts conditioned in vitro with electrical stimulation and flow were subsequently evaluated in a pilot abdominal aorta interposition study in male Sprague-Dawley rats. The pilot study supported surgical feasibility and enabled descriptive Doppler ultrasound assessment of graft-region flow and functional patency at the 3-month endpoint. Article.Title: Bone-Directed Drug Delivery: From Mineral and Matrix Recognition to Cellular Regulation
Article.Authors: Kim R.; Jeong D.
Article.Abstract: Bone-targeted drug delivery aims to increase drug exposure at diseased skeletal sites while reducing unnecessary exposure in non-skeletal tissues. Bone provides two complementary targets—the mineralized extracellular matrix and the cells regulating bone remodeling. Structural targeting uses the calcium- and phosphate-rich hydroxyapatite surfaces or collagen-rich extracellular matrix as binding sites for therapeutic cargos and delivery carriers. Cellular targeting aims to regulate osteoclasts, osteoblast-lineage cells, osteocytes, and key remodeling pathways, including receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand (RANKL)/RANK/osteoprotegerin, Wnt/sclerostin, bone morphogenetic protein, and parathyroid hormone 1 receptor signaling. Targeting ligands and delivery platforms, including bisphosphonates, acidic oligopeptides, tetracyclines, collagen-hybridizing peptides, calcium phosphate materials, nanoparticles, aptamers, nucleic acid vectors, and extracellular vesicles, have been developed to enhance skeletal localization, prolong retention, improve cellular uptake, and control cargo release. Clinical experience with anti-RANKL antibodies, sclerostin antibodies, and parathyroid hormone receptor agonists further demonstrates the therapeutic value of regulating bone-remodeling pathways. Successful translation requires more than skeletal accumulation and should establish microanatomical localization, target-cell engagement, cargo release, therapeutic efficacy, and long-term safety. Integrating structural and cellular targeting may enable more precise treatment of osteoporosis, fracture repair, bone infection, and skeletal malignancies.

Cdk5 is expressed in all the cells, while its main protein activator p35, a non-cyclin regulatory subunit, is expressed predominantly in neurons. Nonetheless, p35 expression has been detected in pancreatic β-cells, podocytes, and lymphocytes, which suggests non-neuronal roles for Cdk5/p35 activity. Due to its potentially important role in tissue development and homeostasis, we wanted to track Cdk5 activity in mice by following the expression of its key activator p35. Thereby, we knocked in the Cre recombinase under the p35 promoter and bred the resulting p35-KI-Cre mice to the lacZ reporter strain. β-gal staining was seen not only in neuronal tissues, but also in several non-neuronal tissues. The staining in non-neuronal tissues further illustrates that Cdk5/p35 activity has broader functions beyond regulating neural processes. Notably, we identified novel p35-lineage cells within the salivary gland embryonic epithelial end buds and in the adult acinar cells. The p35-KI-Cre mice thereby provide a valuable tool to determine in which cell types Cdk5/p35 kinase is active.

Exploratory analyses revealed no significant COL1A2 or COL11A1 mRNA disparities between infection-associated (n = 6) and other sPTB cases (n = 7). These findings identify distinct associations between placental collagen-related measurements and clinical pregnancy outcomes. Article.Title: Development and Characterization of Chitosan and Alginate Films Containing Kraft and Organosolv Lignin Nanoparticles for Active Food Packaging
Article.Authors: Jakubska J.; Abdullah N/A.; Pakieła W.; Gołombek K.; Warski T.; Hawełek Ł.; Zabłocka-Godlewska E.; Krukiewicz K.; Dudek G.
Article.Abstract: This study examines the effects of kraft and organosolv lignin nanoparticles on chitosan- and sodium alginate-based films designed for active food packaging. Glycerol-plasticized films containing chestnut extract and different nanolignin concentrations were evaluated for their properties and activities. All films decreased light transmission and exhibited antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, with kraft-containing formulations showing the strongest overall inhibition. All formulations underwent hydrolytic mass loss in phosphate-buffered saline. These findings demonstrate that the matrix, nanolignin type, and concentration can be selected to tailor film properties for specific food-packaging applications.

Article.Title: Exercise in Multiple Sclerosis: Mechanisms, Clinical Benefits, Potential Disease-Modifying Effects, and Practical Recommendations
Article.Authors: Gklinos P.; Christodoulou G.; Konstantinidou E.; Spyropoulos D.; Evangelopoulos M.; Mitsikostas D.
Article.Abstract: The role of exercise in the management of multiple sclerosis (MS) has undergone a remarkable shift. Exercise was once discouraged due to concerns over symptom worsening; this view has since been overturned, and exercise is now recognized as an important component of contemporary MS care. It is increasingly recognized as a safe and effective non-pharmacological, symptomatic intervention improving quality of life, and several disabling symptoms including fatigue, pain, muscle weakness, spasticity, poor balance and cognitive complaints. Beyond its established role in symptomatic management, this review examines the potential role of exercise as a disease-modifying intervention in MS. Mechanistic evidence regarding peripheral immunomodulation, blood–brain barrier integrity, microglial activation, neurotrophic signaling and neuroplasticity is examined, alongside data from clinical trials and meta-analyses on clinical, imaging and biochemical outcomes, suggesting potential effects on disease biology and progression. Finally, based on the available literature and existing published frameworks we provide updated practical recommendations for individualized exercise prescription according to disability level, baseline fitness, individual preferences, and available resources. Together, these recommendations aim to contribute to the integration of exercise into routine MS care, while emerging evidence for its disease-modifying potential provides an important direction for future research.

Article.Title: Simultaneous Serum Profiling of Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, Hypoxia, and Angiogenesis Markers in Lung Cancer: Associations with Clinical Features and Survival
Article.Authors: Serilmez M.; Sen S.; Özkan B.; Tilgen Yasasever C.; Karaman Ş.; Güler E.; Oğuz Soydinç H.
Article.Abstract: Lung cancer pathogenesis involves interconnected pathways, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and hypoxia-induced angiogenesis. This exploratory pilot study aimed to profile serum biomarkers related to these axes in individuals with lung cancer and healthy controls and to evaluate their interrelationships, clinicopathological associations and prognostic relevance. Archived serum samples from 74 individuals with lung cancer and 30 healthy never-smoking controls were analyzed for total oxidant status (TOS), total antioxidant status (TAS), oxidative stress index (OSI), 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), ischemia-modified albumin (IMA), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), hypoxia-inducible factor 1-α (HIF-1α), and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A). Individuals with lung cancer had higher TOS, OSI, 8-OHdG, IMA, IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, HIF-1α and VEGF-A and lower TAS levels than controls (all p < 0.001). Because samples from the two groups were assayed on separate plates, these differences may partly reflect analytical batch effects and were not interpreted as diagnostic accuracy. Within the lung cancer group, oxidative stress indices showed weak correlations with IL-1β and HIF-1α that did not remain significant after correction for multiple testing. In multivariable Cox regression, ECOG performance status (HR 3.62), stage (HR 5.16) and distant metastasis (HR 3.18) were independently associated with overall survival. Higher VEGF-A levels were associated with longer survival (univariable HR 0.36, p = 0.015; HR 0.39, p = 0.048 after adjustment for histology, stage and ECOG), but this association was partly explained by histological subtype, was not significant in non-small cell lung cancer and did not survive correction for multiple testing; none of the other biomarkers was associated with survival. These findings indicate concurrent alterations of oxidative stress, inflammatory and hypoxia/angiogenesis markers in lung cancer and warrant validation in larger prospective cohorts with clinically relevant controls and all samples assayed together.

Article.Title: Single-Molecule DNA–Protein Experiments Using Magnetic Tweezers
Article.Authors: Bhandari R.; Gaire S.; Pegg I.; Sarkar A.
Article.Abstract: Magnetic tweezers (MT) have become an important single-molecule manipulation tool, with several advantages over alternative methods such as optical tweezers and atomic force microscopy. MT are easy to operate, cost-effective, and can apply forces ranging from sub-piconewton (~0.1 pN) to hundreds of piconewtons. Furthermore, they offer exceptional spatial and temporal resolution. These features position MT as a versatile and powerful tool to study many biomolecular processes at the single-molecule level. MT have played an important role in advancing our understanding of DNA–protein interactions, making significant contributions across molecular biology, enzymology, and chromatin dynamics. In this review, we start by describing the principal MT geometries along with force calibration methods and then pivot to a discussion of MT-based studies of DNA mechanics, chromatin organization, nucleosomes, nucleoid-associated proteins, topoisomerases, helicases, and polymerases. We aim to provide the research community with an integrated overview of MT-based approaches to studying DNA–protein interactions, highlighting both foundational work and recent innovations that continue to shape the field of single-molecule biophysics.

Article.Title: Rapid HRM-Based Genotyping of Markers Associated with Yield and Fusarium Resistance in Maize
Article.Authors: Olejnik P.; Narożna D.; Jamruszka T.; Lenort M.; Tomkowiak A.; Bocianowski J.; Jarzyniak K.
Article.Abstract: The growing availability of molecular markers identified through next-generation sequencing platforms has accelerated marker-assisted breeding in maize, but their practical implementation still depends on rapid, reliable, and cost-effective genotyping methods. In this study, we evaluated the suitability of high-resolution melting analysis coupled with polymerase chain reaction (HRM-PCR) for genotyping of six DArTseq-derived markers associated with grain yield and resistance to Fusarium ear rot in maize. Genomic DNA was isolated using a modified Edwards extraction method and used directly in HRM-PCR without additional purification. HRM-PCR assays were developed and tested using 30 maize genotypes with previously validated marker status, enabling efficient discrimination of favorable and unfavorable allelic variants. All six loci were successfully differentiated by HRM-PCR analysis, and Sanger sequencing demonstrated consistency between the observed melting profiles and underlying sequence polymorphisms. These results demonstrate the potential of HRM-PCR as a platform for converting DArTseq-derived markers into practical genotyping assays. The developed protocols provide a framework for the identification of genotypes carrying favorable marker variants associated with grain yield and Fusarium resistance and may support the implementation of these markers in maize breeding programs.

Article.Title: Hybrid Protein Combining Blo t 5 and Der p 2 Allergens from House Dust Mite Shows Allergenic Activity and Diagnostic Potential
Article.Authors: Durango L.; Donado K.; Puerta L.; Regino R.; Marrugo V.; Benedetti I.; Fernado Cantillo J.; Todorovic N.; Reina R.; Mercado D.; Zakzuk J.; Keller W.; Acevedo N.; Fernández-Caldas E.; Caraballo L.
Article.Abstract: Der p 2 and Blo t 5 are main allergens from house dust mites and play central roles in IgE-mediated hypersensitivity. Hybrid allergen molecules represent a promising strategy for component-resolved diagnostics. This study aimed to characterize a recombinant hybrid molecule composed of full-length Der p 2 and Blo t 5 (BP-2) and to evaluate its allergenic activity. Allergenicity and IgE-binding activity of BP-2 were assessed in asthma patients. Immunogenicity was examined in BALB/c mice sensitized and challenged with BP-2, followed by quantification of specific immunoglobulins, histopathological evaluation of airway inflammation and goblet cell hyperplasia, and assessment of airway hyperresponsiveness via methacholine challenge. BP-2 exhibited strong IgE reactivity in asthma patients and effectively discriminated between asthma patients and healthy controls (AUC = 0.806, 95% CI: 0.764–0.844). Cross-inhibition assays demonstrated that BP-2 retains functional epitopes shared with Blo t 5, Der p 2, and allergen extracts. In the murine model, the humoral and cellular immune responses induced by BP-2 suggest a profile with a predominant role of the T2 component characterized by IL-4 and IL-17A production and specific antibody generation. BP-2 is a biologically active hybrid allergen capable of detecting dual sensitization to Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus and Blomia tropicalis, supporting its potential application in component-resolved diagnostics for mite allergy.

Article.Title: N1-Methyladenosine Regulates EIF5A mRNA Stability and Translation to Promote HIV-1 Infection
Article.Authors: Tao L.; Cui F.; Wang X.; Chen Z.
Article.Abstract: N1-methyladenosine (m1A) is a reversible RNA modification that participates in diverse physiological and pathological processes, including viral infection. Objective: To investigate the regulatory role of m1A in host dependency factors required for human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection. Methods: MeRIP-Seq, m1A RIP-qPCR, and SELECT were employed to identify and validate m1A modification sites on EIF5A mRNA. Site-directed mutagenesis, polysome profiling, and chemical inhibition were used to dissect the regulatory mechanism. Moreover, functional assays, including qRT-PCR and Western blot analysis, were conducted to evaluate the role of m1A-mediated regulation of EIF5A in viral infection. We found that m1A promoted HIV-1 infection by upregulating the expression of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 5A (EIF5A). Mechanistically, YTHDF1 bound to m1A-methylated EIF5A mRNA and positively regulated both its stability and translation. We identified A205 within the coding sequence of EIF5A as a key m1A site, its mutation reduced EIF5A expression, mRNA stability, translation, and YTHDF1 binding. Finally, inhibition of m1A methylation decreased EIF5A mRNA stability and translation, and suppressed HIV-1 infection. Collectively, these findings reveal that m1A-mediated regulation of EIF5A promotes HIV-1 infection and suggest that targeting m1A methylation could be a potential antiviral strategy.

Article.Title: Therapy-Related Oral Toxicity Drug Targets: A Data Mining Analysis of Oral Bacteria Interaction with Human Molecular Networks
Article.Authors: Beckman M.; Yobo R.; Mougeot F.; Mougeot J.
Article.Abstract: Cancer therapy-induced oral mucositis (CTOM) is a common side effect of cancer therapy. Our objective was to identify associations between bacteria and human molecular networks, including drug targets from therapy-related oral toxicities. ClinicalTrials.gov database was used to identify drugs tested for oral mucositis/stomatitis. Gene targets were retrieved from the Drug Gene Interaction database (DGIdbv5.0.13). Secondly, associations between human genes and bacterial species linked with oral mucositis were identified using the MSEAv0.0.2 program. Further, publicly available data from an oral mucositis 3D tissue model were used for differential gene expression (DGE) analysis of everolimus-treated cells targeting the IL6/MTOR pathway. Genes common to all analyses were examined using STRINGv12.0. Of 33 oral mucositis/stomatitis trials, we identified 38 drugs with 89 direct and 438 indirect gene targets. MSEAv0.0.2 identified 548 significant associations (Fisher’s exact test; padj < 0.05) involving 35 bacterial genera. DGE analysis identified 3664 significant genes in everolimus-treated cells (empirical Bayes moderated t-test; padj < 0.05). While two genes (i.e., CFTR and PTGS2) were common between the MSEA and DGE analyses and were direct drug targets identified in clinical trials, twenty-eight genes were in common when including indirect potential drug targets. When the two genes were combined with the twenty-eight genes, sixty-six significant Reactome pathways were identified (hypergeometric FDR-p < 0.05), potentially linked to inflammation and compensatory wound healing in oral mucositis.

Article.Title: Current and Emerging Acute Therapeutic Strategies for Ischaemic and Haemorrhagic Stroke
Article.Authors: Hashemi Y.; Cuboni G.; Azhan T.; Deidda G.
Article.Abstract: Stroke is a serious medical condition that occurs when the blood supply to the brain is disrupted. There are two main types: ischaemic stroke, caused by a blocked artery, and haemorrhagic stroke, caused by bleeding within or around the brain. This review outlines the pathophysiology and subtypes of both stroke types, discusses current diagnostic approaches, and focuses on established treatments as well as emerging therapeutic strategies. Current treatment for ischaemic stroke includes thrombolytic drugs to dissolve blood clots and mechanical thrombectomy to remove the occlusion. Management of haemorrhagic stroke focuses on controlling the bleeding, reducing intracranial pressure, and preventing secondary brain injury, often requiring neurosurgical intervention. Advanced imaging techniques play a crucial role in distinguishing between stroke types and their subtypes, as accurate diagnosis is essential because inappropriate treatment can have devastating consequences. We also discuss promising emerging therapies, including novel thrombolytic agents, stem cell-based approaches, and neuroprotective drugs aimed at limiting brain injury and improving functional recovery. Finally, we review ongoing clinical trials evaluating the safety and efficacy of these innovative treatments and discuss their potential to improve future stroke management.

Article.Title: Elementary Steps of the Hydroxide-Catalyzed Double Aldol Condensation of Furfural with Cyclopentanone: A DFT and DLPNO-CCSD(T) Study
Article.Authors: Lgaz H.; El-khlifi A.; Lee H.; Abualrejal M.; Rahaman M.; Aldalbahi A.
Article.Abstract: Furfural and cyclopentanone, both obtained from lignocellulosic biomass, undergo a two-stage aldol condensation that gives first a C10 and then a C15 adduct, the carbon skeletons of jet-fuel-range cycloalkanes. In this computational study, both stages were modeled with hydroxide in water, the system of the available kinetic study. Geometries, frequencies, and reaction paths were obtained at the ωB97X-D3/def2-TZVP level in SMD water, and energies were refined at the ωB97X-D3/ma-def2-TZVP and DLPNO-CCSD(T)/ma-def2-TZVP levels, the latter as an independent check. Each stage consists of α-deprotonation, C–C coupling, deprotonation of the ketol, and loss of hydroxide, which was solvated by two explicit water molecules. At both levels, the loss of hydroxide is the highest step of both stages, and the deprotonation of the ketol lies 1.3–1.9 kcal mol−1 below it, the order found experimentally for related aldol condensations. The highest transition states of the two stages are equally high within the accuracy of the methods, consistent with the nearly equal measured activation energies. The calculated rate ratios of the two stages, 0.9 and 15, bracket the measured value of 4.5. In homogeneous aqueous solution, the product distribution is therefore set mainly by the furfural supply and the conversion.

Article.Title: Drebrin Links Actin Organization to MRTFA–SRF Signaling During Skeletal Myogenesis
Article.Authors: Ngo T.; Giang T.; Kim H.; Oh J.; Lee W.
Article.Abstract: Drebrin is an F-actin side-binding protein previously implicated in myoblast differentiation, but the signaling mechanisms linking drebrin-dependent actin organization to myogenic state transitions remain unclear. Here, we combined transcriptomic prioritization with C2C12 loss-of-function analyses. Drebrin knockdown reduced phalloidin fluorescence and increased DNase I-Alexa Fluor 488 median fluorescence intensity, shifting actin-associated readouts toward a more monomeric state. This was accompanied by increased cytoplasmic MRTFA, reduced nuclear MRTFA and SRF, lower CArG-dependent SMYD1 reporter activity, and decreased expression of SRF-responsive genes. Drebrin knockdown also altered YAP1 abundance and phosphorylation, reduced EdU incorporation and cell-cycle protein expression, increased G0/G1 accumulation, and resulted in approximately 25% fewer cells at 72 h. During differentiation, drebrin knockdown attenuated MyoD, MyoG, and sarcomeric myosin heavy chain (MyHC) expression and impaired myotube formation. Public skeletal-muscle datasets associated DBN1 preferentially with a myogenic transcriptional program, although DBN1/Dbn1 regulation varied across aging and muscle-wasting contexts. These findings support a working model in which drebrin-dependent actin organization contributes to MRTFA–SRF transcriptional competence during myogenic progression. These findings provide a basis for testing the proposed mechanism and for investigating whether drebrin contributes to muscle atrophy in appropriate experimental models.

Article.Title: Ultrastructural Organization and Immunohistochemical Analysis of Bcl-2, Caspase 3, and NeuroN Localization in the Spinal Cord of Juvenile Chum Salmon Oncorhynchus keta in Intact Growth and After Traumatic Injury
Article.Authors: Pushchina E.; Litvinov N.; Vekhova E.
Article.Abstract: The localization of the proapoptotic (caspase 3) and the antiapoptotic B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2) factors in the spinal cord of 2-year-old juvenile chum salmon Oncorhynchus keta, as well as the neuron-specific marker NeuroN, was studied using IHC labeling. Scanning electron microscopy was used to obtain three-dimensional, highly detailed images of the surface structure of the primary motor neurons (MT1) and secondary motor neurons (MT2) of the ventral spinal cord column (VSCC), as well as nerve endings and interneuronal connections in the VSCC. The spatial organization of VSCC neurons, astrocytes, and the surface characteristics of membranes and cell connections in the spinal cord were examined. The localization of apoptotic markers and NeuroN was studied in intact juveniles and three days after traumatic spinal cord injury. The results showed that the pro-apoptotic factor caspase 3 (cas3) in the spinal cord of intact animals had a rather limited localization in the perikarya of primary and secondary motor neurons of the VSCC. Cas3 immunolocalization in the spinal cord of juvenile chum salmon was represented in astrocytes located within the VSCC, as well as among the fibers of the white matter. SEM revealed the morphological features of perineuronal astrocytes of the VSCC. Cas3+ microvascular sites were identified in the spinal cord, and their reactivity increased markedly after traumatic injury. Cas3 synthesis increased in the synaptic projections of VSCC neurons, as well as in blood vessels after traumatic injury. Along with various types of neurons, cas3 was expressed after injury in fibers and small adult neural stem and progenitor cells (aNSPCs) located in the dorsal horn and submarginal regions. The antiapoptotic factor Bcl-2 in intact juvenile chum salmon is relatively widespread in the perikarya of VSCC neurons, white matter interneurons, and dorsal horn cells located in the submarginal zone. In the post-traumatic period, Bcl-2 expression increased significantly both in VSCC neurons and in cells and fibers of the dorsal horn. Along with proapoptotic and antiapoptotic factors, the number of undifferentiated NeuroN-producing cells in the spinal cord of juvenile chum salmon increased dramatically in the post-traumatic period, indicating an active neurogenic post-traumatic process. Thus, in intact animals, proapoptotic and antiapoptotic factors are synthesized during growth; the balance between them determines the successful elimination of cells that have not established connections during ontogenetic growth and regulates programmed cell death. An increase in the number of intensely immunolabeled cells with an undifferentiated phenotype in the post-traumatic period indicates an intensive regenerative process, consistent with the results obtained in other models.

Article.Title: LRRC8/VRAC Channels Beyond Volume Regulation: Molecular Mechanisms, Physiological Functions, and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Abd El-Aziz T.; Sah R.
Article.Abstract: Volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs) drive regulatory volume decrease and maintain cellular homeostasis in nearly all vertebrate cells. The identification of leucine-rich repeat-containing 8 (LRRC8) proteins as the molecular components of VRAC transformed the field by showing that these channels are heteromers composed of the essential LRRC8A subunit together with one or more LRRC8B-E subunits. Advances in structural biology, electrophysiology, and molecular studies have since improved our understanding of LRRC8 channel assembly, regulation, and function. LRRC8 complexes operate through two distinct functional modalities. The first is substrate permeation through the channel pore: beyond chloride transport, LRRC8 channels mediate the movement of organic osmolytes, amino acids, ATP, glutamate, cyclic dinucleotides, and platinum-based anticancer drugs, with permeability determined by subunit composition. The second is pore-independent signal transduction, in which LRRC8A also acts as a signaling scaffold through its cytoplasmic leucine-rich repeat domain (LRRD), which binds partners such as GRB2 and caveolin-1. Because deleting the protein removes both modalities at once and many reported phenotypes cannot yet be attributed to either alone. Altered LRRC8 channel activity has been linked to cancer, ischemic brain injury, epilepsy, diabetes, inflammatory diseases, and inherited disorders caused by both loss and gain of LRRC8 function. This review discusses recent advances in the molecular architecture, regulatory mechanisms, transport properties, and pore-independent signaling functions of LRRC8 channels. It also examines their physiological and pathophysiological roles across the nervous, cardiovascular, immune, metabolic, renal, epidermal, and reproductive systems, highlighting the strength of the supporting evidence. Finally, the review addresses recent progress in pharmacological targeting, with particular emphasis on the off-target effects of current inhibitors and the lack of subunit-selective modulators. Understanding how LRRC8 channels sense cell volume, assemble into native channel complexes, act through the pore or through the LRRD, and can be selectively targeted will be critical for translating recent discoveries into future therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Endophytic Microbial Community of Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) Seeds: Association Between Grain Quality Parameters and Functional Potential
Article.Authors: Solovyova K.; Tarasova D.; Pronovich N.; Kuryntseva P.
Article.Abstract: Endophytic microbial communities of wheat seeds are a potential source of microorganisms that stimulate plant growth and participate in biocontrol, and they are also a potential indicator of the phytosanitary condition of grain. Using amplicon sequencing of 16S rRNA genes and the ITS region, we characterized the endophytic community of 11 wheat seed samples, which were divided, based on agronomic and phytopathological assessment, into a reduced-quality group (n = 4) and a comparison group (n = 7). The functional potential of the bacterial component was predicted using Tax4Fun2. PERMANOVA revealed a statistically significant but moderate difference in bacterial composition between groups (R2 = 0.186–0.197; p = 0.014–0.046), whereas a difference in fungal community composition was not supported. At the same time, the Mantel test showed a significant correlation between fungal community composition and the grain quality gradient (r = 0.665; p_adj = 0.004), which persisted after exclusion of the dominant genus Blumeria, the causal agent of cereal powdery mildew. Differential analysis with ANCOM-BC2 revealed a significant decrease in the representation of 58 predicted bacterial KEGG orthologs (KOs) (of 5248 tested) in reduced-quality grain, including bacterial genes for exopolysaccharide biosynthesis and secretion systems, whereas the assessment based on the PGP/biocontrol gene set revealed no such depletion. The preliminary results suggest that the fungal component of the seed endophytic community is more closely associated with grain quality than the bacterial component. Given the small sample size, these results are exploratory; the predicted functional differences and the potential use of seed endophytes for plant growth promotion and biocontrol are hypotheses that require experimental validation.

Differences in susceptibility between the two species suggest that structural and species-specific factors may influence the activity of these compounds. Overall, these findings identify chemical structures with in vitro activity against parasitic nematodes and provide a basis for further investigation of their anthelmintic potential.

Article.Authors: Zhu A.; Gao L.; Jin Q.; Liao H.; Xiong C.
Article.Abstract: Conjunctival melanoma (CM), a rare malignant tumor of the ocular surface, is characterized by high invasiveness and a poor prognosis. Despite aggressive local control measures such as complete surgical resection combined with cryotherapy, patients still face a high risk of local recurrence (60%) and distant metastasis (20–30%). This article provides a narrative review of the pathogenesis and targeted therapies for CM, focusing on its core molecular mechanisms, with particular attention to therapeutic strategies targeting key driver genes and pathways. It also summarizes the clinical evidence and latest breakthroughs in immunotherapy and emerging treatment strategies. By integrating evidence from basic research and clinical translation, this review provides a theoretical basis for optimizing the diagnostic and therapeutic pathways for CM.

Article.Title: From Vesicle Cargo to Cargo Selection in Obesity-Associated Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS)
Article.Authors: Machairiotis N.; Voros C.; Christodoulaki C.; Panagopoulou R.; Arvanitakis S.; Araka A.; Daskalaki M.; Papapanagiotou A.; Chatzinikolaou F.; Daskalakis G.; Panagopoulos P.
Article.Abstract: In polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), recently renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), extracellular vesicle (EV) microRNA (miRNA) profiles differ from those of comparison groups, but those groups vary across studies. Lean healthy women, women with obesity and no PCOS and lean women with PCOS do not answer the same question, and lean healthy controls confound the syndrome with adiposity. Most work treats these miRNAs as biomarkers and leaves the prior question open: how an miRNA is selected for export. Selection is not passive. Sumoylated hnRNPA2B1 recognises GGAG motifs, YBX1 sorts miR-223 and other small non-coding RNAs, SYNCRIP binds an extra-seed motif and sorting sequences differ by cell type. Obesity alters the inputs to that step: adipose tissue is a major source of circulating exosomal miRNAs, its vesicles alter insulin sensitivity at a distance and gastric bypass changes their content. In the ovary, body mass index associates with EV-linked miRNAs in follicular fluid, and PCOS follicular exosomes carry miRNAs acting on granulosa cell apoptosis, senescence and glycolysis. Those effects are the readout of a loading step that, to our knowledge, has not been quantified in adipose tissue, serum, or follicular fluid of women with obesity-associated PCOS. Future work should measure hnRNPA2B1, YBX1 and SYNCRIP alongside EV miRNA profiles, with comparison groups that separate adiposity from diagnosis. Paired bariatric surgery samples offer one suitable design.

Article.Title: Genetic Polymorphisms of Oxidative Stress Regulatory Genes and Their Association with Coronary Artery Disease Risk
Article.Authors: Ciekot K.; Nowak T.; Niemiec P.; Mizia-Stec K.
Article.Abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Its development results from a complex interaction between environmental risk factors and genetic susceptibility. Evidence indicates that oxidative stress, defined as a state in which free radical production exceeds antioxidant defenses, plays an important role in atherogenesis by promoting endothelial dysfunction, lipid oxidation, vascular inflammation and plaque instability. This review summarizes current knowledge on polymorphisms of the most important genes involved in reactive oxygen species generation and antioxidant defense. Several variants have been associated with CAD, hypertension, carotid atherosclerosis and other cardiovascular phenotypes, although the direction and strength of associations often differ across populations. In many cases, functional effects include altered enzyme activity, changes in promoter activity, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability or impaired antioxidant capacity. The evidence is heterogeneous: many candidate-gene studies are small, differ in ancestry, phenotype definitions and genetic models and are affected by limited replication and publication bias. Among the variants discussed, NOS3 rs3918226 and GPX1 rs1050450, rs1800668 and rs3811699 showed genome-wide significant associations with CAD in a large-scale genome-wide association study. The variants reviewed have no established role in CAD risk stratification and their added value beyond established clinical risk factors and validated genome-wide CAD polygenic risk scores has not been tested.

Article.Title: AP2V-2 Is Required for Tachyzoite Proliferation in Toxoplasma gondii
Article.Authors: Zhong X.; Jiang Y.; Hu D.; Song X.
Article.Abstract: Toxoplasma gondii undergoes multiple developmental transitions during its complex life cycle, which are controlled by coordinated transcriptional and epigenetic regulation. The MORC/HDAC3/ApiAP2 complex has been implicated in the repression of merozoite- and sexual-stage genes in tachyzoites. AP2V-2 (TGGT1_285895) was previously identified as a component associated with this regulatory network, but its biological function remains poorly understood. Here, we characterized AP2V-2 using conditional protein depletion combined with phenotypic, transcriptomic, and genome-wide occupancy analyses. AP2V-2 localized to the parasite nucleus and was detected throughout the tachyzoite cell cycle. Conditional depletion of AP2V-2 markedly impaired plaque formation and intracellular replication but had little effect on parasite invasion. The replication defect was reversible after removal of indole-3-acetic acid. RNA sequencing identified 211 differentially expressed genes after AP2V-2 depletion. Of these, 79.6% overlapped with genes dysregulated after MORC depletion, with particularly strong overlap among upregulated genes. In contrast, CUT&Tag identified only 45 AP2V-2-associated peaks, most of which were located in intergenic regions. Although a subset of enteroepithelial-stage genes was upregulated after AP2V-2 depletion, AP2V-2 did not occupy their promoter regions, typical merozoite markers were not induced, and no endopolygeny-like division was observed. These findings indicate that AP2V-2 is required for normal tachyzoite replication but differs functionally from the ApiAP2 factors that directly control merozoite developmental programs.

Article.Title: Computational Identification and Prioritization of Novel Tankyrase 1 and 2 Inhibitor Candidates Through Structure-Based Design, ADMET Profiling, and Long-Timescale Molecular Dynamics
Article.Authors: Saurith-Coronell O.; Sierra-Hernandez O.; Vargas-Echeverria C.; Rodríguez-Macías J.; Silva-Fernández C.; Cortés Gómez E.; Alcázar J.; Mora J.; Matíz-García S.; Agüero-Chapin G.; Castillo-Mendieta K.; Márquez Brazón E.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains one of the most aggressive breast cancer subtypes and is frequently associated with aberrant activation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Because tankyrase 1 and 2 (TNKS1/2) promote Wnt pathway activation through the regulation of AXIN stability, these enzymes represent attractive therapeutic targets for the development of novel anticancer agents. In this study, an integrated structure-based computational workflow was employed to identify new TNKS1/2 inhibitors. A library comprising known tankyrase inhibitors, structurally related analogues, and 1096 rationally designed compounds was evaluated through molecular docking, ADMET profiling, molecular dynamics simulations, and MM-PBSA binding free-energy calculations. The docking protocol was validated through redocking experiments, yielding RMSD values of 1.42 Å and 1.18 Å for TNKS1 and TNKS2, respectively. Affinity- and pharmacokinetic-based filtering identified three TNKS1 candidates and sixteen TNKS2 candidates, of which fifteen were selected for 300 ns MD simulations. For TNKS1, Output-37 and Output-44 demonstrated stable binding and favorable MM-PBSA free energies (−33.12 and −32.38 kcal/mol, respectively), comparable to the reference inhibitor OM-153. For TNKS2, Output-1036 emerged as a promising candidate, exhibiting a binding free energy of −44.62 kcal/mol, surpassing the co-crystallized ligand and being comparable to the reference inhibitor OM-153, while Output-1015 and Output-997 also displayed favorable energetic and conformational profiles. Interaction analyses revealed the conservation of key catalytic pocket recognition hotspots and stable interaction networks throughout the simulations. Collectively, these results identify Output-1036 as a promising TNKS2 inhibitor candidate and Output-37 and Output-44 as potential TNKS1-targeting scaffolds. However, further in vitro and in vivo studies are required to validate their biological activity and confirm their ability to modulate Wnt/β-catenin signaling in triple-negative breast cancer.

Article.Title: Aquaporins, Colonic Water Transport, and Functional Constipation
Article.Authors: Zheng K.; Li R.; Ma W.; Sun D.
Article.Abstract: Functional constipation (FC) is a common disorder of gut–brain interaction whose clinical signature, hard, infrequent stools, points to disturbed colonic water handling. Aquaporins (AQPs) provide the transcellular route for transepithelial water movement in the colon, and evidence links AQP dysregulation to FC and slow-transit constipation (STC). This narrative review synthesizes human tissue studies, animal models, and in vitro experiments on colonic AQPs in constipation. Limited human tissue studies report segment-specific changes in AQP abundance. AQP3 is upregulated in the ascending colon, whereas AQP9 is downregulated in the descending colon. AQP4 is elevated in STC and correlates with stool consistency and colonic transit time. AQP8 is upregulated and undergoes osmotic-stress-driven translocation to the apical (luminal) membrane. A broader mucosal survey additionally found reduced AQP1, AQP7, AQP10, and AQP11 in FC. Experimental models add mechanistic insight but reveal no conserved direction of AQP change. Because AQPs conduct water passively down osmotic gradients, channel abundance cannot be equated with channel-mediated water flux. Regulatory pathways, including macrophage-derived prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), cytokines, microbial metabolites, and enteric neurotransmitters, converge on the AQP network, with AQP3 as a recurrent node. The available evidence supports an association between AQP dysregulation and the constipated phenotype without establishing causality. Functional readouts of transepithelial water movement in patients are needed before AQP modulation can be translated into therapy.

Article.Title: Baseline Galectin-3 in Patients with Breast Cancer Scheduled for Anthracycline Therapy: Associations with Cardiac Biomarkers, Left Ventricular Function, and HFA-ICOS Risk Stratification
Article.Authors: Borowiec A.; Ozdowska P.; Zebrowska A.; Rosinska M.; Makowka A.; Puton B.; Pogoda K.; Nowecki Z.; Maurea N.; Kotowicz B.
Article.Abstract: The clinical role of galectin-3 (Gal-3) as a biomarker in cardio-oncology remains uncertain. This study evaluated baseline Gal-3 concentrations and their associations with established cardiac biomarkers, left ventricular systolic function, and HFA-ICOS cardiovascular risk categories in patients with breast cancer before anthracycline-based chemotherapy. This cross-sectional baseline analysis included 103 patients enrolled in the EMPACT trial. Gal-3 concentrations were evaluated in relation to high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT), N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), HFA-ICOS risk categories, and clinical characteristics. Associations were assessed using Pearson correlation analyses and median regression. Mean baseline Gal-3 concentration was 6.3 ± 2.7 ng/mL. Gal-3 was positively correlated with hs-cTnT (r = 0.384, p < 0.001) and NT-proBNP (r = 0.278, p = 0.006), but not significantly correlated with LVEF or GLS. Gal-3 concentrations did not differ significantly across HFA-ICOS risk categories (p = 0.237). Patients aged ≥65 years had higher Gal-3 concentrations than younger patients (7.1 ± 2.8 vs. 5.7 ± 2.5 ng/mL, p = 0.003). In multivariable median regression, age was the only variable significantly associated with Gal-3 among the covariates included in the model (β = 0.82 ng/mL per 10-year increase, 95% CI 0.21–1.43, p = 0.009). Associations with hs-cTnT and NT-proBNP were no longer statistically significant after adjustment. In patients with breast cancer before anthracycline therapy, baseline Gal-3 concentrations were associated with age after multivariable adjustment, whereas associations with established cardiac biomarkers were attenuated. No significant associations were observed with LVEF or GLS, and Gal-3 concentrations did not differ significantly across HFA-ICOS risk categories in unadjusted analyses.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification and Characterization of the D-Type Cyclin Gene Family Suggests Its Potential Involvement in Zigzag Stem Formation in Tea Plant (Camellia sinensis)
Article.Authors: Gao H.; Li S.; Duan J.; Chen Y.; Lei Y.; Ding D.; Xie N.; Tian N.; Yu J.
Article.Abstract: Zigzag-shaped stems are a distinctive architectural trait in tea plants (Camellia sinensis), but their underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. D-type cyclins (CYCDs) regulate cell-cycle progression and proliferation, yet their roles in tea plant architecture remain unexplored. Here, we compared the zigzag-stemmed cultivar Lianyuanqiqu with the upright-stemmed cultivar Zhuyeqi using phenotypic, anatomical, lignin, and transcriptomic analyses and characterized the CsCYCD gene family genome-wide. Lianyuanqiqu exhibited locally shortened first internodes, curled leaves, and altered tissue organization, whereas lignin content did not differ significantly between cultivars. Transcriptome analysis identified 4786 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), significantly enriched in plant hormone signal transduction. Genome-wide analysis identified 22 CsCYCD genes belonging to six subgroups, with conserved gene structures and promoter cis-regulatory elements associated with hormone responses, growth, and cell cycle regulation. Expression profiling revealed that most differentially expressed CsCYCD genes, particularly members of the CsCYCD3 subgroup, were downregulated in zigzag stems, whereas CsCYCD1;2 was significantly upregulated. These findings provide the first genome-wide characterization of the CsCYCD gene family in tea plants and suggest its potential involvement in zigzag stem formation, offering insights into the molecular regulation of tea plant architecture.

Article.Title: Extracellular Vesicles in Pregnancy: From Maternal–Fetal Communication to Environmental Perturbation
Article.Authors: Affranchi F.; Aloi N.; Cosentini I.; Smeraldi G.; Colombo P.; Drago G.; Ruggieri S.; Longo V.
Article.Abstract: Pregnancy is a uniquely sensitive moment during which environmental exposures may have profound and long-lasting consequences for maternal health, placental function, and fetal development. A successful pregnancy depends on continuous molecular communication among maternal, placental, and fetal compartments. The disruption of these processes by environmental stressors may increase the risk of pregnancy complications, impaired neurodevelopment, and susceptibility to non-communicable diseases later in life. Pregnant women are exposed to dynamic mixtures of chemical, physical, occupational, behavioral, and social stressors from the air, diet, drinking water, consumer products, and residential or workplace environments. The pregnancy exposome framework integrates these external exposures with internal biological responses, including oxidative stress, inflammation, metabolic dysregulation, epigenetic alterations, and changes in circulating biomolecules. However, the mechanisms through which exposure-related signals are transmitted across the maternal–placental–fetal unit remain incompletely understood. Extracellular vesicles may be a key component of this communication network as they transfer protected molecular cargoes, including proteins, lipids, metabolites, and regulatory nucleic acids. Understanding how environmental exposures modify extracellular vesicle biogenesis, composition, and function may reveal mechanisms linking the pregnancy exposome to placental dysfunction, adverse pregnancy outcomes, fetal programming, and early biomarkers of biological effects. This review examines the role of extracellular vesicles in physiological maternal–fetal communication and critically summarizes current human and experimental evidence on how environmental exposures may affect EV characteristics and function during pregnancy, with particular attention to their potential involvement in placental dysfunction and adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Article.Title: Bile Acid Stress Disrupts Homeostasis and Placental Functional Programs in Human First-Trimester Trophoblast Organoids
Article.Authors: Zhang S.; Li L.; Zheng S.; Xu Q.; Qian Z.; Su J.; Wu W.
Article.Abstract: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) is characterized by elevated maternal bile acids (BAs), yet their effects on human trophoblast organization and transcriptional responses remain incompletely understood. Here, we used human first-trimester trophoblast organoids (TOs) to characterize cellular and transcriptional responses to a defined six-component BA mixture (50–150 μM). BA exposure disrupted organoid architecture and intercellular organization, with attenuated proliferation-associated features and more prominent SDC1 staining. These changes were accompanied by increased DNA fragmentation and cleaved caspase-3 staining and by reduced ATP-dependent viability, supporting an apoptotic component of BA-associated trophoblast injury. Bulk RNA sequencing after exposure to 150 μM BA for 96 h identified 413 differentially expressed genes, of which 364 were downregulated and 49 were upregulated. Downregulated transcripts were primarily associated with placental endocrine and secretory processes, epithelial organization, cell adhesion, and transport, whereas a smaller subset of lipid-handling genes was upregulated. RT-qPCR confirmed concordant upregulation of PLIN2 and ABCG1 in two independent donor-derived TO lines. Collectively, these findings show that BA mixture exposure is associated with structural injury and altered transcriptional profiles in human TOs, thereby providing insight into trophoblast responses to BA stress.
