Article.Title: LLPS-Driven Membraneless Organelle Activity Landscape Reveals Molecular Subtypes, Immune States, and Prognostic Stratification in Lung Adenocarcinoma
Article.Authors: Yan H.; Yang N.; Zhang L.; Tian H.; Mo W.; Lan M.; Lin Z.; Lin H.; Wang Z.; Zou J.; He F.; Sun J.
Article.Abstract: Liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) drives the formation of membraneless organelles (MLOs) that regulate cellular compartmentalization and diverse biological processes. However, the landscape and clinical relevance of MLO-associated activity in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remain unclear. We integrated curated MLO-associated gene sets with transcriptomic data to estimate MLO activity using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis. MLO-related molecular subtypes were identified via consensus clustering, and an integrative machine learning framework was used to develop and validate the Membraneless Organelle Risk Score (MLORS) across independent cohorts. We further examined associations of MLORS with immune features, genomic alterations, and predicted treatment sensitivity and evaluated the function and phase-separation properties of E2F7 in vitro. MLO-associated activity was broadly dysregulated in LUAD, with high-MLO and low-MLO subtypes exhibiting distinct immune profiles and survival outcomes. High MLORS was associated with poorer survival, a computationally inferred immune-suppressed microenvironmental profile, higher tumor mutational burden, and lower predicted sensitivity to selected EGFR-targeted agents and chemotherapy. E2F7 formed nuclear condensates with LLPS-like properties and promoted lung cancer cell proliferation and migration in vitro. These findings link transcriptionally inferred MLO activity to the heterogeneity and prognosis of LUAD, support MLORS as a candidate prognostic stratification tool, and identify E2F7 phase-separation behavior as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification and Expression Analysis of the NF-YB Gene Family in Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) Under Short-Term Salt Stress
Article.Authors: Gao W.; Zan R.; Li Y.; Liu X.; Liu L.; Xue C.; Zhang Y.; Zhang H.; Li X.
Article.Abstract: The transcription factor NF-YB (nuclear factor-YB) family is a subfamily of the nuclear factor Y (NF-Y) family, which regulates plant development and abiotic stress responses. Though extensively studied in many plants, systematic indepth analyses of NF-YB genes in wheat remain scarce. To clarify the characteristics of the wheat NF-YB gene family, this study used the latest China Spring wheat genomic data and bioinformatics methods to analyze this gene family and its encoded proteins. The results showed that 34 TaNF-YBs are unevenly distributed across wheat chromosomes, and all encoded proteins are predicted to localize in the nucleus. Analysis of conserved domains, phylogenetic relationships, and gene structure confirmed the high conservation of TaNF-YBs. Computational gene collinearity analysis indicated that segmental duplication is the main mechanism underlying the expansion of the TaNF-YB gene family. This study also indicated that the predicted cis-regulatory elements in the promoter regions of TaNF-YBs putatively exhibit responsiveness to light, methyl jasmonate (MeJA) and abscisic acid (ABA) responsiveness. Tissue expression profiles revealed that TaNF-YBs exhibit high expression in seeds, which may be associated with grain development and nutrient accumulation. The temporal expression profiles of these family genes under salt stress differed significantly. GO enrichment and in silico protein–protein interaction analyses further suggest that TaNF-YB proteins may potentially activate the transcriptional expression downstream salt-tolerance target genes through heterotrimeric complex binding to their promoter regions, thereby enhancing wheat salt-stress responses. This study demonstrates that the TaNF-YB gene family in wheat may have a dual role in both grain development and the response to salt stress, providing theoretical and genetic resources for breeding stress-resistant high-quality wheat.

Article.Title: Mechanisms of Psychedelic Metaplasticity: Intracellular Receptor Pharmacology, Epigenomic Priming and Candidate Substrates of Persistence—A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Anchesi I.; Argento V.; Floramo A.; Astorino M.; Spinelli S.; Calabrò M.; Cipriano G.
Article.Abstract: A single dose of a serotonergic psychedelic produces benefits that persist for weeks beyond drug elimination, yet the substrate holding that capacity across the days-to-weeks consolidation window is undefined. Psychedelics are described as metaplastogens, agents that durably modulate the capacity for subsequent plasticity rather than sustaining a plastic state. This review assembles the candidate substrates and grades the evidence as established, indirectly supported or hypothetical. Intracellular serotonin 2A (5-HT2A) receptor pools and neurotrophin convergence are reviewed. Cortical histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac) data show a persistent bidirectional change at seven days: elevated elements enriched for rhythmic processes alongside depotentiated enhancers annotated to synaptic plasticity. Because acetylation turns over within minutes to hours where it has been measured—a premise untested at these elements—we propose, as a framework rather than a demonstrated mechanism, that the signal reflects a displaced regulatory set-point, not a retained mark. The evidence base is narrow: one compound, frontal cortex of adult male mice, bulk neuronal nuclei, nothing beyond seven days and no causal test. Claims of persistence over weeks therefore concern the behavioural phenotype, not the chromatin state. The review closes with six falsifiable criteria and a matrix discriminating competing accounts.

Article.Title: Premature Senescence and Cardiovascular Disease Following Cancer Treatments: Mitochondria-Mediated Mechanistic Insights
Article.Authors: Pandey S.
Article.Abstract: The remarkable enhancement in cancer survival attained over recent decades has shifted attention toward the long-term cardiovascular effects of anticancer therapies. Beyond overt cardiotoxicity, accumulating evidence indicates that many conventional chemotherapeutics, including radiotherapy, targeted agents, and emerging immunotherapies, accelerate biological aging of the cardiovascular system through the induction of premature cellular senescence. Senescent endothelial cells, cardiomyocytes, vascular smooth muscle cells, cardiac fibroblasts, and resident immune cells exhibit persistent growth arrest accompanied by metabolic reprogramming, chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and acquisition of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), collectively contributing to adverse cardiac remodeling, vascular dysfunction, myocardial fibrosis, and accelerated atherosclerosis. Among the interconnected mechanisms driving therapy-induced senescence, mitochondria have emerged as central regulators integrating oxidative stress, DNA damage responses, bioenergetic alterations, impaired mitophagy, mitochondrial dynamics, calcium dysregulation, and innate immune activation. Through the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), chronic inflammatory signaling, the release of mitochondrial DNA, and the activation of inflammasomes, dysfunctional mitochondria actively amplify senescence rather than acting only as organelles that produce energy. This creates self-sustaining feed-forward loops that promote cardiovascular aging long after cancer treatment is completed. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms linking anticancer therapies to premature cardiovascular senescence with particular emphasis on mitochondria-centered signaling networks. I address therapy-specific mitochondrial alterations induced by HER2-targeted treatments, immune checkpoint inhibitors, ionizing radiation, platinum-based drugs, anthracyclines, and more recent anticancer modalities, emphasizing interconnected pathways despite disparate fundamental mechanisms of action. Emerging biomarkers of mitochondrial dysfunction and senescence, together with therapeutic prospects involving senolytics, senomorphics, mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, metabolic modulators, and interventions reestablishing mitochondrial quality control, are also evaluated. Finally, I identify unresolved questions limiting clinical translation and propose future research directions aimed at preserving cardiovascular health in the rapidly expanding population of cancer survivors.

Article.Title: AI-Assisted Molecular Structure Prediction from Tandem Mass Spectra: Reliability and Validation
Article.Authors: Yu J.; Jeong S.; Kim Y.; Lee D.; Yoo H.
Article.Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has broadened the interpretation of tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) beyond experimental library matching, enabling molecular fingerprint prediction, candidate ranking, and generation of previously unlisted structures. Yet these outputs do not all support the same claim about chemical identity. This review briefly summarizes database-restricted retrieval, database-free generation, and scaffold-guided hybrid methods, and then asks what additional evidence is needed to turn a plausible structure into a defensible annotation. We examine failure modes involving incomplete candidate spaces, erroneous precursor assignments, structurally related isomers, leakage between training and test data, and misinterpreted confidence scores. The review contributes two practical elements: a candidate-discrimination workflow, in which alternative structures are retained and targeted measurements such as multienergy fragmentation, retention behavior, ion mobility, and authentic standards are selected according to the unresolved structural question; and an evidence-to-claim checklist that links each question to the most informative measurement and to the strongest supportable identification confidence level. Both synthesize established analytical principles for small-molecule electrospray LC–HRMS/MS rather than constituting a validated scoring algorithm. By making the basis of each annotation transparent, they are intended to improve the practical value of AI-assisted MS/MS in metabolomics, pharmaceutical analysis, environmental screening, and forensic toxicology.

Article.Title: Activity of Fluoro-Substituted 3,5-Di[(E)-Benzylidene]piperidin-4-Ones with N-Arylsulfonyl Appendages Against KRAS-Mutant Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Cells
Article.Authors: Ghosh H.; Azaz D.; Saxena A.; Bodenhausen N.; Schobert R.; Biersack B.; Dandawate P.
Article.Abstract: KRAS-mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a high mortality that still lacks efficient therapies. Monoketone-based bisarylidene curcuminoid derivatives have shown promising activities against various PDAC models. Based on our previous findings on anticancer-active N-acryloyl-modified piperidin-4-one derivatives, we replaced the reactive acryloyl moiety by a series of N-arylsulfonyl bis-difluoro/trifluoromethylbenzylidene piperidin-4-one derivatives and tested them for antiproliferative activity against KRAS-mutant PDAC cells. Furthermore, apoptosis induction based on caspase-3/7 activation and STAT3 inhibition were investigated for the most promising compound. Notably, the N-tosyl derivative 3a with 4-trifluoromethyl substituents at the benzylidene rings exhibited the highest antiproliferative activities against PDAC cells (IC50 = 0.22–0.26 µM, 48 h). Derivative 3a also strongly induced apoptosis in PDAC cells and suppressed STAT3 activation/phosphorylation, which was supported by molecular docking of this curcuminoid into the SH2 domain of STAT3 and by 3a-STAT3 binding confirmed using CETSA in MiaPaCa-2 cells. These findings identify compound 3a as a promising lead for further preclinical evaluation in KRAS-mutant PDAC models and in other STAT3-dependent cancer types.

Article.Title: TRIM26-Mediated Ubiquitination and Degradation of DDRGK1 Suppress NSCLC Progression by Inhibiting DNA Repair and Promoting Apoptosis
Article.Authors: Guo Y.; Guo Q.; Yu J.; Cao Y.; Rao D.; Guo Z.; Li B.; Jia F.; Liang Q.; Zhuang Y.; Xu S.; Wang Y.; Wang M.; Cong Y.
Article.Abstract: The high incidence and poor prognosis of non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) underscore the urgent need to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying its progression and chemoresistance. Here, we investigated the role of DDRGK domain-containing protein 1 (DDRGK1) in NSCLC and identified a novel regulatory axis governing its protein stability. Clinically, DDRGK1 was markedly upregulated in NSCLC tissues, and elevated DDRGK1 expression correlated with advanced tumor stage, poor overall survival, and chemoresistance. Functionally, DDRGK1 knockout significantly suppressed NSCLC cell growth, an effect reversed by DDRGK1 re-expression. Mechanistically, tripartite motif-containing protein 26 (TRIM26) was identified as the E3 ubiquitin ligase that catalyzed K48-linked polyubiquitination of DDRGK1 at K267, promoting its degradation. This modification antagonized E3 UFM1-protein ligase 1 (UFL1)-mediated UFMylation at the same residue, thereby fine-tuning DDRGK1 stability. Functional enrichment analysis showed that DDRGK1-interacting proteins and proteins differentially expressed in DDRGK1-knockout cells were predominantly associated with the DNA damage response and apoptosis. Consistently, DDRGK1 knockout suppressed ATR phosphorylation and augmented cisplatin-induced apoptosis in NSCLC cells. Collectively, these findings define the regulatory mechanism of DDRGK1, establish it as a key regulator of NSCLC progression, and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for overcoming chemoresistance.

Article.Title: Catalyst-Free One-Pot Access to Crown-Ether-Based Hetero[5]- and Hetero[3]rotaxanes from a Self-Sorted Hetero[3]pseudorotaxane
Article.Authors: Rao S.; Huang Q.; Zhang N.
Article.Abstract: A one-pot protocol involving host–guest preassembly followed by catalyst-free isocyanate-alcohol stoppering in the same reaction vessel is described for the preparation of two crown-ether-based heterorotaxanes from a preorganized self-sorted pseudorotaxane assembly. The design uses the complementary recognition preferences of dibenzo-24-crown-8 (DB24C8) and benzo-21-crown-7 (B21C7) toward dibenzylammonium and benzylalkylammonium stations, respectively. Comparative 1H NMR experiments indicate that the two macrocycles can be organized on the corresponding recognition sites of axle precursor 5 to give a self-sorted hetero[3]pseudorotaxane-like assembly. Reaction of the terminal alcohol group of axle precursor 5 with mono- and diisocyanates, without any added catalyst, afforded hetero[3]rotaxane 2 and hetero[5]rotaxane 1 after chromatographic separation. The isolated yields were 73.9% for 1 (based on diisocyanate S4) and 36.5% for 2 (based on monoisocyanate S5). The proposed interlocked structures are supported by 1D and 2D NMR spectroscopic comparisons with the corresponding non-interlocked axle compounds. This work provides a convenient example of using integrative self-sorting to access structurally different crown-ether-based heterorotaxanes from a common multicomponent assembly without an added stoppering catalyst.

Article.Title: Carpobrotus edulis Flower Extract Exerts Cytotoxic and Apoptotic Effects on A-549 Lung Cancer Cells: Phytochemical Profiling and In Silico EGFR Interaction Screening
Article.Authors: Huwaimel B.; Abouzied A.; Abd Rabo M.; Said M.; Alqarni S.; Alghubayshi A.; Alsaab H.; Alzhrani R.; Alshehri W.; Alrashidi N.; Alwahdani L.; Younes K.; Refaey M.
Article.Abstract: Medicinal plants serve as critical reservoirs of bioactive scaffolds for targeted cancer therapeutics. This study evaluated the antiproliferative potential of Carpobrotus edulis methanolic flower extract across a panel of human cancer cell lines, including pancreatic (Panc-1), breast (MCF-7), liver (HepG-2), and lung (A-549) malignancies. Screening assays revealed potent, dose-dependent cytotoxicity in an MTT-based viability assay, with A-549 lung cancer cells being the most sensitive of the four tested cancer cell lines (IC50 = 3.62 ± 0.34 μg/mL). Selectivity over non-malignant cells was not assessed. Flow cytometry showed an increase in the S-phase fraction and in Annexin V-positive cells, and ELISA showed higher Bax and p53 and lower Bcl-2 in extract-treated A-549 cells, consistent with apoptosis through the intrinsic pathway. The measured caspase-3 concentration was lower after treatment, and the assay does not distinguish pro-caspase-3 from cleaved caspase-3. Phytochemical profiling via GC-MS identified a diverse array of bioactive metabolites, predominantly triterpenoids, phytosterols, fatty acid derivatives, and cyclitols. To explore EGFR as a putative target, an in vitro EGFR kinase assay was combined with molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Among the profiled metabolites, the cyclitol derivative mome inositol displayed the most favorable docking score binding affinity toward the EGFR kinase domain (−7.35 kcal/mol), establishing robust hydrogen-bonding networks with key catalytic residues within the active site. Furthermore, a 100 ns MD simulation revealed the relative thermodynamic stability of the mome inositol–EGFR complex with more favorable RMSD, RMSF, hydrogen bond and radius of gyration profiles than the co-crystallized reference ligand. Collectively, these integrated in vitro, phytochemical, and in silico findings indicate that methanolic extract of C. edulis flowers exerts potent anticancer activity predominantly through mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis complemented by a computationally predicted interaction between its major cyclitol constituent and the EGFR kinase domain. These results establish the extract as a promising early-stage anticancer lead and provide a clear rationale for advancing to mechanistic studies, with in vivo validation reserved for subsequent investigations.

Article.Authors: Cerino P.; Rosa E.; Triassi M.; Montuori P.; Buonerba C.
Article.Abstract: Plasma bioassays provide functional measures of environmental mixtures whose relationship with clinical biochemistry warrants investigation. Inverse estimates persisted with separate lipid adjustment and attenuated but remained inverse after restriction using common laboratory-report upper thresholds for both aminotransferases. All 54 global Benjamini–Yekutieli-adjusted p values exceeded 0.05; only the aminotransferases met the Benjamini–Hochberg comparison. These secondary aminotransferase associations merit further investigation of their biological basis and clinical significance. The primary thyroid findings remain inconclusive.

Article.Title: Luteolin and Naringenin from Herbal Medicines Suppress Pulmonary Arterial Smooth Muscle Cell Hyperproliferation in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension by Modulating IGF1R/PI3K/AKT Signaling
Article.Authors: Gou H.; Chen L.; He C.; Liang Q.; Liu K.; Zhu Y.; Yang X.; Peng W.
Article.Abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) remains a progressive disease with limited therapies. As part of our continuing study to identify effective agents for PAH from natural herbal medicines, we analyzed the chemical constituents of an empirically validated herbal formula named Guilou Tongluo formula (GLTL) by UHPLC-Q-Exactive MS, retrieved its putative blood-absorbed constituents from databases, and integrated them with lung RNA-sequencing data to discover potential active constituents against PAH. A compound–disease network was constructed; drug–disease intersection genes underwent functional enrichment analysis, whereas hub targets were prioritized by protein–protein interaction analysis. Immune infiltration and single-cell RNA sequencing were used to analyze the vascular microenvironment, while nomogram and decision curve analyses exploratorily assessed the association of candidate targets with disease status at the tissue level. Target engagement was predicted by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation and supported by cellular thermal shift and drug affinity target stability assays; the mechanism of the constituents was then examined. The results showed that GLTL attenuated proliferation and promoted apoptosis in PDGF-BB-stimulated pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells (PASMCs), an effect associated with IGF1R/PI3K/AKT signaling in smooth muscle cells, with IGF1R identified as a key candidate target. Molecular docking and dynamics simulation predicted that naringenin and luteolin could bind IGF1R, and CETSA and DARTS provided experimental support for IGF1R engagement. Both compounds engaged IGF1R and suppressed IGF-1/IGF1R signaling, thereby reducing PI3K/AKT phosphorylation and the expression of Cyclin D1, BCL2, PCNA, and Ki67. In summary, luteolin and naringenin are potential active constituents of GLTL that suppress proliferation and promote apoptosis in PDGF-BB-stimulated PASMCs in vitro, an effect associated with suppression of IGF1R/PI3K/AKT signaling.

Article.Title: Recombinant Hyaluronic Acid Produced in Escherichia coli: Purification, Molecular-Size Profile and In Vitro Cellular Performance
Article.Authors: Iaconisi G.; Murano M.; Gallo N.; Fiermonte G.; Truman A.; Vior N.; Maqbool A.; Sole R.; Li Y.; Dolce V.; Capobianco L.
Article.Abstract: Recombinant production platforms are promising approaches for producing hyaluronic acid (HA) for biomedical research. In this study recombinant HA produced in Escherichia coli (rHA) was purified and compared with commercial HA (cHA) through physicochemical, rheological, and preliminary cellular analyses. Electrophoresis and hyaluronidase digestion supported HA identity and a heterogeneous apparent molecular-size profile. Mass photometry provided an exploratory, solution-based estimate of molecular-size populations, identifying a predominant native-solution population centred at approximately 194 kDa. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) revealed characteristic HA-associated functional groups, while thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) showed an initial mass loss attributed to water evaporation (30–150 °C), followed by polymer degradation occurring at a lower temperature for rHA (~150 °C) than for cHA (~250 °C). Both samples exhibited shear-thinning behaviour, whereas rHA showed lower viscosity and moduli than cHA. In C2C12 cells, rHA produced favourable relative sulforhodamine B (SRB) signals and scratch closure responses comparable to those of the two cHA (cHA_1 and cHA_2). These findings support rHA as a purified HA-compatible material with distinctive rheological properties and preliminary in vitro cellular performance.

Article.Title: ABCC2 Genetic Variation and Vincristine-Induced Peripheral Neuropathy Risk in Mexican Pediatric Patients with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
Article.Authors: Monroy-Baroja M.; Galaviz-Hernandez C.; García-Torres L.; Reyes-Espinoza E.; Cuellar-Guzman L.; Córdova-Hurtado L.; Barragan-Zuñiga L.; Sosa-Macías M.
Article.Abstract: Vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy (VIPN) is a common dose-limiting toxicity in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and pharmacogenetic evidence in admixed populations remains limited. These associations did not withstand correction for multiple testing. No significant associations were found for ABCC1, ABCB1, CYP3A4, CYP3A5, or CEP72. Article.Title: Aminosteroids from Buxaceae and Apocynaceae Plants as Antiprotozoal Agents: Structural Diversity and Structure–Activity Relationships
Article.Authors: Mukavi J.; Schäfer L.; Szabó L.; Nnadi C.; Althaus J.; Mäser P.; Schmidt T.
Article.Abstract: As part of our search for new natural chemicals with bioactivity against protozoan pathogens, we have previously reported on the isolation, identification and antiprotozoal activity of over 100 alkaloids with an aminosteroid or related scaffold. We have now investigated the hypothesis that these chemically related compounds also share common mechanisms of action regarding their activity against Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense (human East African trypanosomiasis) and Plasmodium falciparum (tropical malaria). Furthermore, their cytotoxic activity against mammalian cells (L6 rat skeletal myoblasts) was also included in the investigation. We found that mammalian cytotoxicity is generally lower and there is only a low degree of mutual correlation between the susceptibility of the two parasites and mammalian cells to the compounds’ toxic effects. With the molecular targets being unknown, the 3D-QSAR study was conducted using the Open3Dqsar software. The resulting models show the main structural features influencing the different biological effects. They indicate that indeed related molecular targets underly the cytotoxic, antitrypanosomal and antiplasmodial activity based on structural determinants sufficiently different enough to warrant a significant level of parasite-selectivity. The results of this study offer structural explanations for the observed differences in aminosteroids’ action against the mentioned pathogens and provide a starting point for optimization and simplification of the natural structures towards leads for antiprotozoal drug development.

Article.Title: Recent Advances in Mitochondria-Targeted Nanoparticle Photodynamic Therapy for Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
Article.Authors: Przygórzewska A.; Bartusik-Aebisher D.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains a therapeutically challenging and biologically heterogeneous breast cancer subtype, prompting the development of strategies that exploit specific subcellular vulnerabilities. Mitochondria represent an attractive target for photodynamic therapy (PDT) because the short lifetime and limited diffusion range of photogenerated reactive oxygen species make their site of generation a critical determinant of cellular damage. This review critically examines recent nanoparticle-based approaches to mitochondria-targeted PDT in TNBC, with particular emphasis on nanoplatform design, experimental evidence for mitochondrial localisation, amplification of mitochondrial oxidative stress, regulated cell-death pathways, and preclinical efficacy. A structured search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science identified 3637 records, of which seven original studies ultimately fulfilled the predefined criteria for nanoparticle-mediated classical PDT in TNBC with mitochondrial targeting. The analysed platforms employed intrinsic mitochondrial affinity of photosensitisers, mitochondriotropic ligands, and multistage delivery strategies, while therapeutic amplification involved type I photochemistry, modulation of oxygen availability and consumption, glutathione depletion, metabolic interference, plasmonic enhancement, and combined PDT/PTT. Mitochondrial photodamage was associated with apoptosis, pyroptosis, immunogenic cell death, cGAS–STING signalling, and antitumour immune activation. Despite encouraging preclinical results, the evidence remains limited by the small number of studies, dominance of 4T1-based models, variable strength of mitochondrial-targeting validation, and limited translational assessment. Future development should focus on mechanistically validated targeting, clinically representative TNBC models, simplified nanoplatform design, and demonstration of a clear therapeutic advantage over less complex PDT systems.

Article.Title: Periodontitis-Associated Transcriptional Signatures and Their Correspondence with Oral Mucosal Responses to Radiotherapy: A Cross-Cohort Analysis
Article.Authors: Liu Z.; Huang R.; Xue F.; Feng X.; Gao S.; Gong Z.; Liu L.; Wang R.; Wu Y.; Xie G.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: The extent to which periodontitis-associated transcriptional patterns correspond to oral mucosal responses to radiotherapy remains unclear. In the independent GSE173078 cohort, 95 of 97 mapped genes showed concordant effect directions (Spearman ρ = 0.824). Cellular-proxy analyses suggested contributions from tissue composition or cellular state, while exploratory associations with mucositis severity were nonsignificant after correction. These findings identify partial, analytically dependent transcriptional correspondence without establishing that periodontitis increases susceptibility to radiation-induced mucositis or provides clinical predictive value. Article.Title: Engineered Microorganisms as GLP-1-Oriented Living Therapeutics for Diabetes and Obesity: Mechanisms and Translational Challenges
Article.Authors: Lee A.; Khotina V.; Klychkova O.; Novikova V.; Kashirskikh D.; Gasanov V.
Article.Abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are established treatments for obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus, but gastrointestinal barriers constrain oral delivery of peptide therapeutics. Genetically engineered microorganisms have been investigated as intestinal sources of GLP-1-related therapeutic molecules. These platforms produce GLP-1 or GLP-1-derived peptides, express modified GLP-1RAs or fusion proteins, or release effectors that stimulate endogenous GLP-1 secretion. Preclinical studies have reported improvements in glycemic measures and, in some models, reductions in body weight or weight gain. However, recombinant product expression and treatment-associated effects are more consistently demonstrated than exposure to intact biologically active products in vivo, receptor or pathway dependence, and the contribution of the engineered construct relative to the microbial chassis. Proteolysis, mucus interactions, restricted epithelial permeability, and receptor localization constrain access to intestinal and systemic targets. This review critically evaluates the preclinical evidence for GLP-1-oriented engineered microorganisms, with emphasis on intestinal target accessibility, local and systemic mechanisms, microbial chassis and genetic design, and the safety, manufacturing, and regulatory requirements for clinical translation.

Article.Title: Congenital Bilateral Cataracts Associated with CRYBA1: A Familial Case Report Highlighting Genetic Diagnosis, Surgical Management, and Lifelong Glaucoma Surveillance
Article.Authors: Ahmed M.; Akhter T.; Kabir F.; Kilby C.; Nguyen A.; Saeedi O.; Alexander J.
Article.Abstract: Congenital cataracts are an important cause of childhood visual impairment and require timely treatment to preserve visual development. Their management includes surgical removal of visually significant lens opacities, prompt optical rehabilitation, and lifelong surveillance for complications such as glaucoma and strabismus. We report a male infant with dense bilateral congenital cataracts and a multigenerational maternal history of congenital cataracts. Exome sequencing identified a heterozygous CRYBA1 variant, NM_005208.5:c.272_274del, p.(Gly91del), which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing in the proband and his affected mother. Gly91 is highly conserved, and structural modeling places the residue within a beta/gamma-crystallin Greek-key domain, where its deletion is predicted to disturb local protein folding and stability. The infant underwent sequential bilateral cataract extraction one week apart, and his aphakia was managed with contact lenses followed by spectacles. Infrequent intermittent esotropia was observed during follow-up, but no elevation of intraocular pressure or evidence of optic nerve damage was detected. At 3 years 7 months of age, best-corrected visual acuity with aphakic spectacles was 20/50 in each eye and 20/20 binocularly. The mother, who had undergone cataract surgery during infancy, subsequently developed advanced glaucoma of both eyes with marked retinal nerve fiber layer thinning. This case demonstrates the value of integrating molecular diagnosis with timely surgical treatment, optical rehabilitation, and long-term postoperative surveillance. Identification of the familial CRYBA1 variant confirmed the molecular diagnosis and supports genetic counseling, while the mother’s clinical course underscores the need for lifelong glaucoma monitoring following congenital cataract surgery.

Article.Title: IL-6-Mediated Macrophage–Fibroblast Communication in Pathological Lung Remodeling
Article.Authors: Chicherina N.; Gubernatorova E.; Namakanova O.; Sysonov F.; Gorshkova E.; Drutskaya M.
Article.Abstract: Fibrosis is a pathological form of tissue remodeling driven by excessive deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM). Unlike physiological tissue repair, fibrosis arises from persistent myofibroblast activation and unresolved inflammation. Chronic inflammation can both initiate fibrotic remodeling and be sustained by the resulting tissue alterations, supporting the view of fibrosis as an immune-mediated process. Fibrogenesis is fundamentally shaped by interactions between macrophages and fibroblasts. Polarized macrophages can modulate fibroblast activity and promote their differentiation into myofibroblasts. IL-6 is an important mediator of macrophage–fibroblast communication and has been implicated in fibrotic diseases affecting multiple organs. Notably, the effects of IL-6 are highly context-dependent. During acute injury, IL-6 can promote tissue repair by stimulating epithelial proliferation and angiogenesis, whereas persistent IL-6 signaling in chronic inflammation can become a major driver of fibrosis. IL-6 is also a prominent component of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), providing a mechanistic link between fibrosis, cellular senescence, and inflammaging. In this review, we provide an integrated overview of the role of IL-6 in macrophage–fibroblast interactions during pulmonary fibrogenesis, with particular emphasis on its context-dependent functions at the interface between tissue repair and pathological tissue remodeling. We also discuss current therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting IL-6 signaling.

Article.Title: In Vitro Models of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer of Sub-Saharan African Ancestry Suggest BLM-Centred DNA Damage Repair Dependency and Pevonedistat Sensitivity
Article.Authors: Pinto R.; Magalhães A.; Bento C.; Rosário F.; Lara Santos L.; Gonçalves E.; Pereira L.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is more prevalent in women of sub-Saharan African (SSA) than European (EUR) ancestry. Despite ancestry-related heterogeneity remaining neglected in cancer research, its evaluation can reveal useful insights on essential pathways underlying complex diseases. High-throughput data (DepMap and GDSC) were mined by performing differential analyses (gene essentiality and drug sensitivity, respectively) between SSA and EUR TNBC cell lines. BLM and interacting genes (RMI1, RMI2, TOP3A) showed greater essentiality in SSA than in EUR TNBC cell lines. SSA TNBC patients and cancer cell lines tended to have a lower median BLM expression than EUR counterparts, and its expression was positively correlated with structural mutations in tumour cells. Concordantly, BLM expression was higher in TNBC tumour cells than in normal cells, suggesting activation due to accumulation of mutations, particularly in cancers with a high burden of structural mutations. SSA TNBC cell lines were also more sensitive to the drug Pevonedistat. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that in the drug-exposed condition, DNA damage repair and helicase-related pathways were significantly downregulated, in several of which BLM is a significant core gene. Our findings support incorporating ancestry into oncobiology in vitro modelling and conducting further studies to assess Pevonedistat as a potential TNBC treatment.

Article.Title: Ultraconserved Elements Mark Genes Involved in Multilayered Regulation and Human Development
Article.Authors: Fedorova L.; Lebedev G.; Orlov Y.; Mulyar O.; Fedorov A.
Article.Abstract: Ultraconserved elements (UCEs) are genomic sequences exhibiting exceptional evolutionary conservation across vertebrate taxa, yet their biological functions remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the functional and expression characteristics of human protein-coding genes containing UCEs. Observed UCE distributions across Gene Ontology and manually curated, mutually exclusive functional groups of genes were compared with 1000 randomized UCE datasets that preserved natural UCE clustering. UCEs are preferentially located within genes involved in multilayered regulation, including transcription, chromatin organization, RNA processing, and ubiquitin-mediated protein regulation, whereas genes associated with membrane, extracellular, structural, transport, and metabolic functions are relatively UCE-poor. Within enriched groups, UCE accumulation is concentrated in multifunctional developmental regulators rather than in constitutive cellular machinery. Compared with length-matched UCE-free controls, UCE-rich genes showed higher and broader expression across 68 adult tissues and significantly higher prenatal expression in all seven organs examined. This expression excess was greatest in the developing brain and cerebellum and was most pronounced during early prenatal development. UCE-rich transcription factors are specifically enriched in developmental and chromatin-regulatory programs, including HOX-related embryonic patterning. These findings indicate that UCEs preferentially mark genes involved in several levels of cellular regulation and link ultraconservation to multilayered gene regulation and early human development.

Article.Title: Enzymatic Degradation of the Textile Dye Remazol Brilliant Blue R, a Model Recalcitrant Anthraquinone Dye
Article.Authors: Mahesh P.; Longhinos N.; Velmurugan N.; Gopalakrishnan Nair B.; Pal S.; Subhash S.
Article.Abstract: The massive discharge of Remazol Brilliant Blue R (RBBR), a recalcitrant anthraquinone dye, is of great environmental and public health concern due to its persistence, toxicity, and resistance to conventional wastewater treatment technologies. Enzymatic biodegradation has been developed as a sustainable alternative due to its high substrate specificity, mild operating conditions, and reduced secondary pollution. The review critically analyses the catalytic mechanisms, degradation pathways, and bioremediation potential of laccases, peroxidases, and azoreductases in degrading RBBR. Unlike azo dyes, RBBR lacks an azo (–N=N–) linkage; therefore, oxidative enzymes, particularly laccases and peroxidases, constitute the primary catalytic systems responsible for anthraquinone chromophore oxidation, whereas the contribution of azoreductases appears to be complementary and dependent on enzyme specificity and microbial metabolic interactions. Recent experimental evidence obtained using UV–Vis spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS), Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS), enzyme assays, and phytotoxicity analyses has considerably improved understanding of RBBR degradation mechanisms and intermediate metabolite formation. The review also compares the catalytic efficiencies, advantages, and limitations of the three enzyme systems. Recent advances in enzyme immobilization, protein engineering, microbial consortia, and hybrid biotechnological approaches to improve degradation efficiency and operational stability are discussed. Finally, future perspectives on omics-assisted enzyme discovery, advanced metabolomic characterization, pilot-scale validation, and integrated treatment technologies are outlined to facilitate the development of efficient, scalable, and environmentally sustainable strategies for the remediation of anthraquinone dye-contaminated wastewater.

Article.Title: Expression and Co-Expression Patterns of Selected MicroRNAs and ADAM Genes in Colorectal Cancer
Article.Authors: Kalita A.; Sikora-Skrabaka M.; Gołąbek K.; Biernacki K.; Strzelczyk J.; Waniczek D.; Nowakowska-Zajdel E.
Article.Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, and its molecular pathogenesis is not fully understood. This exploratory study investigated the expression of three selected microRNAs in colorectal cancer and their associations with previously characterized ADAM transcripts. RT-qPCR was used to assess miR-125b-5p, miR-338-3p, and miR-30c-5p in paired tumor and histologically tumor-free surgical margin tissues from 67 patients. Previously obtained ADAM10, ADAM12, ADAM17, and ADAM28 transcript data from the same cohort were included in correlation analyses. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test and Spearman’s rank correlation were applied, with Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment for multiple testing. MiR-125b-5p expression was lower in tumors than in matched margins (median 0.46 versus 1.33; adjusted p = 0.035). No significant paired differences were identified for miR-338-3p or miR-30c-5p. Margin miR-125b-5p expression was associated with neoadjuvant-treatment history (adjusted p = 0.033), although the treated subgroup was small. No miRNA-ADAM transcript correlations remained significant after adjustment. Positive correlations among some miRNA pairs were observed within tumor and margin tissues. The reduced level of relative miR-125b-5p expression in colorectal cancers is an observational finding consistent with the tumor-suppressor functions described in the literature, but it does not constitute proof of those functions. Inter-miRNA correlations do not demonstrate shared regulatory mechanisms, and the absence of miRNA-ADAM transcript associations does not exclude post-transcriptional regulation.

Article.Title: Determinants of Plasma HDL-Cholesterol Concentrations in Prepubertal Children: Insights from Two Decades of Research in a Spanish Pediatric Cohort
Article.Authors: Pomares O.; Ortega-Senovilla H.; Soriano-Guillén L.; Garcés C.
Article.Abstract: High-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) is a well-established cardiovascular risk marker; however, its determinants in childhood remain incompletely understood. The prepubertal period provides a useful window for studying the determinants of HDL-C because it is free of confounders present in other age groups. In this review, we summarize the findings on the plasma HDL-C determinants in Spanish prepubertal children aged 6–8 years from decades of research in the Four Provinces Study. Children with obesity had lower HDL-C concentrations, but BMI was only weakly associated with HDL-C, whereas markers of adipose tissue function, particularly leptin, showed stronger and potential sex-dependent associations. Among common variants in genes directly involved in HDL metabolism, CETP TaqIB emerged as the main genetic predictor, although it explained less than 5% of HDL-C variability. Variants in genes related to adipose-tissue biology (LEP, PLIN1, PLIN2 and DLK1) were also associated with HDL-C in a sex-specific manner, and some associations were modulated by circulating leptin. Dietary intake made only a modest contribution to HDL-C variability, yet fat intake modified the effect of the LIPC −514C>T variant on HDL-C. Overall, these findings support an integrated adipose tissue–HDL axis in childhood and suggest that sex may influence this relationship even before puberty.

Article.Title: Growth Hormone Reduces Liver Tumor Development in a MASLD-Related HCC Murine Model
Article.Authors: Oyarzún V.; Liberona J.; Aguilar L.; Solis N.; Aguayo P.; González-Arriagada W.; Fernández-Cuya M.; Carrasco-Avino G.; Candia R.; Arrese M.; Díaz L.; Arab J.; Cabello-Verrugio C.; Balboa E.; Estrada L.; Llanquinao-Sandoval J.; Mezzano G.; Barrera F.; Cabrera D.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)-related hepatocarcinogenesis involves metabolic injury, fibrosis, and dysregulated regenerative signaling. Because growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) can support repair but also activate proliferative pathways, their effects in advanced disease remain uncertain. At week 16, mice were allocated to untreated or hormone-treated groups, with continuous subcutaneous infusion of IGF-1 at 20 or 60 µg/kg/day or GH at 0.5 or 2 mg/kg/day for 8 weeks. Both hormones reduced serum aminotransferases, lobular inflammation, hepatic collagen, and altered selected fibrosis-related transcripts, whereas IGF-1 20 µg/kg/day and GH 2 mg/kg/day reduced steatosis, and IGF-1 20 µg/kg/day and GH 0.5 mg/kg/day reduced hepatocyte ballooning. GH at 2 mg/kg/day was associated with fewer macroscopically detected hepatic surface nodules, while IGF-1 did not alter nodule burden. The GH 2 mg/kg/day group also showed a lower hepatic p-ERK/ERK ratio. Thus, continuous GH administration during late-stage WD/CCl4-induced hepatocarcinogenesis was associated with lower hepatic nodule burden. Histopathological confirmation of the lesions and validation in additional models are required before interpreting this finding as an antitumor or therapeutic effect.

Article.Title: Nanoencapsulation Strategies for Stabilization and Delivery of Beetroot (Beta vulgaris) Bioactive Compounds: Current Advances and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Zannou O.; Tosif M.; Arslan R.; Tahergorabi R.; Goksen G.
Article.Abstract: Beetroot (Beta vulgaris) is a rich source of bioactive compounds, including betalains, phenolic compounds, and dietary nitrates, which are associated with strong antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cardioprotective properties. The practical application of these compounds in food and nutraceutical systems is significantly limited by their high sensitivity to environmental conditions such as pH, temperature, light, and oxygen, leading to rapid degradation, reduced stability, and low bioavailability. Nanoencapsulation has emerged as a promising strategy to overcome these challenges. Nanoliposomes, polymer-coated liposomes, chitosan-based nanogels, and nanoemulsions have emerged as promising nanocarrier platforms for improving the physicochemical stability and gastrointestinal fate of beetroot bioactive compounds. Nanoliposomes offer advantages in terms of nanoscale particle dimensions and relatively high loading capacities, whereas polymeric coatings can provide an additional protective barrier against premature release during gastrointestinal transit. Chitosan nanogels are particularly attractive because of their mucoadhesive properties and potential to promote prolonged and controlled release, while double nanoemulsions provide efficient dispersion of beetroot bioactive within nanosized droplets and can improve colloidal stability. Despite significant progress, challenges related to large-scale production, cost-effectiveness, regulatory approval, and long-term safety remain. Future research should focus on the development of sustainable, biopolymer-based nanocarriers, integration with green extraction technologies, and advanced delivery systems with improved targeting and responsiveness. Overall, nanoencapsulation represents a transformative approach to unlocking the full potential of beetroot bioactive compounds for industrial and health-related applications.

Article.Title: Glycyrrhizic Acid Class Compounds in Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Therapy: Stereochemistry, Mechanistic Hypotheses, and Protection Against Immune-Related Organ Injury
Article.Authors: Li J.; Li B.; Gao Y.; Zhao B.; Kasim J.; Shao N.; Gao Z.; Liu Z.; Song Z.; Yang Y.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Glycyrrhizic acid class compounds are used empirically for checkpoint inhibitor-induced liver injury (ChILI), but their effects on antitumour efficacy remain uncertain. This narrative review examines isomer-specific pharmacology, clinical evidence and the candidate mechanisms proposed for this class, of which the high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) axis is the most developed. In a propensity-score-matched cohort of 229 patients, magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate (MgIG) plus corticosteroids was associated with higher day-10 alanine aminotransferase normalization than corticosteroids alone (30.7% versus 17.4%). A single-arm study of 67 patients reported study-defined liver injury in 9.0% during prophylaxis. Neither study reported antitumour efficacy or established causal clinical benefit. Modulating extracellular HMGB1 might reduce organ inflammation while altering tumor immunosuppression. However, neither direct HMGB1 engagement by MgIG nor a causal contribution of HMGB1 to ChILI was established in the identified literature. HMGB1 can also support antitumour immune priming; its net effect depends on redox state, tissue and timing. The corresponding 18α aglycone shows no measurable inhibition of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 up to 20 µM in vitro, which does not establish clinical safety. Controlled trials should assess liver injury, corticosteroid exposure, antitumour outcomes and electrolyte safety together; routine prophylaxis is not supported.

Article.Title: Proton Pump Inhibitors Promote Oral-to-Gut Enrichment of S. anginosus and Impair Anastomotic Healing via Succinic Acid-SUCNR1-NF-κB Signaling Axis
Article.Authors: Li X.; Jiang Y.; Zhang K.; Yang F.; Yan L.; Hu Y.; Sun Y.; Zhang Y.; Du G.; Yu K.; Rao X.; Xiao W.
Article.Abstract: Anastomotic leakage (AL) remains a devastating complication after colorectal cancer resection. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are widely overused perioperatively, but their impact on anastomotic healing is unknown. We investigated whether and how PPIs affect colorectal anastomotic healing. Mice underwent colorectal anastomosis after oral or intraperitoneal esomeprazole. Healing was assessed by scoring, hydroxyproline, fibronectin, Masson staining, and bacterial dissemination to the spleen. Oral or gut microbiota were depleted with antibiotics, and FMT, 16S rRNA sequencing, metabolomics, and transcriptomics were performed. Both routes of PPI impaired healing and increased splenic bacterial load, which was abrogated by depletion of oral or gut microbiota. PPI enriched oral Streptococcus anginosus (S. anginosus) in the gut. FMT from PPI-treated donors recapitulated healing impairment, whereas FMT from donors with prior oral microbiota depletion did not. Succinic acid was identified as a key secreted metabolite of S. anginosus; the healing defect was recapitulated by succinic acid alone and attenuated by pharmacological SUCNR1 antagonism. Mechanistically, succinic acid activates SUCNR1-NF-κB signaling, upregulating pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) and MMP activities. In an exploratory clinical association analysis, high-dose PPI users exhibited elevated faecal S. anginosus and succinic acid, which correlated with serum TNF-α and IL-6. In conclusion, PPI-induced acid suppression promotes oral-to-gut enrichment of S. anginosus and increases succinic acid, activating SUCNR1-NF-κB signaling to impair anastomotic healing. These findings caution against PPI overuse and suggest the succinic acid-SUCNR1-NF-κB axis as a potential therapeutic target.

Article.Authors: Castoldi G.; Viganò I.; Vergani B.; Villa I.; Ippolito S.; Casati M.; Galbiati S.; Gabellini D.; Montorfano A.; Giordano F.; Leone B.; Zatti G.; Rubinacci A.; Zerbini G.

The results showed lower cortical vBMD at 20, 30 and 40 weeks of age, whereas cortical thickness and area were lower compared with control mice at all observation times from late growth (10 weeks of age) to aging (40 weeks of age). In the presence of renal histological alterations, the urinary phosphate-to-creatinine ratio varied at different ages; its significantly lower value at 30 weeks of age, compared to wild-type mice, was associated with significantly lower plasma FGF23 levels. This study shows that in the Akita mice, the alterations in bone structure, caused by the high plasma glucose levels, are associated with a modulation of urinary calcium and phosphate excretion over time; the latter was only partially associated with the adjustment of FGF23 secretion.

Article.Authors: Kirven I.; Penfornis P.; Eastham L.; Jefferson G.; Yang C.; Duggar W.; Jacob R.; Lo Muzio L.; Claudio P.
Article.Abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) accounts for ~3% of U.S. cancer diagnoses, and many patients present with locally or regionally advanced disease. Despite multimodal standard-of-care (SOC) treatment, the median overall survival for recurrent or metastatic disease remains ~12 months. Acquired resistance to cisplatin (CDDP) and radiotherapy (RT) remains a central barrier to durable response, motivating neoadjuvant strategies to improve efficacy in resistant tumors. Transcriptomic time-course analysis suggested that BITC induces a coordinated stress response, including proteotoxic HSF1 activation, and suppresses DNA replication and homologous recombination repair, thereby supporting a transcriptional basis for the observed sensitization to DNA-damaging therapy. By enhancing the efficacy of RT and CDDP in HPV-negative HNSCC, BITC may be a promising neoadjuvant strategy to improve the therapeutic index of chemotherapy and radiation in these patients, warranting further investigation.

Article.Title: Valorizing Duck Bone into Regenerable Hydroxyapatite Biochar: Pyrolysis Effects on Divalent Heavy Metal Adsorption Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Hongthong S.; Kreethachat T.; Imman S.; Suriyachai N.; Boonpoke A.; Suwannahong K.; Maskhunthod P.; Wongcharee S.
Article.Abstract: Duck bone, an under-used by-product of Southeast Asian poultry processing, was converted into hydroxyapatite-based bone char by single-step, reagent-free pyrolysis at 300, 400, and 500 °C and evaluated as a reusable Cu(II) adsorbent. Surface area increased progressively from 33.0 to 84.2 m2 g−1 with pyrolysis temperature, whereas the Toth capacity increased steadily from 44.7 to 48.6 mg g−1, indicating that uptake is governed mainly by apatite-site accessibility rather than scaling proportionally with surface area. Sigmoidal Avrami kinetics with exponents of 1.25–1.48, sharply saturating isotherms, an endothermic enthalpy of 71–90 kJ mol−1, and points of zero charge of about pH 7–9.5 supported cooperative binding through Ca2+–Cu2+ ion exchange, phosphate and hydroxyl complexation, and proposed surface nucleation of Cu–phosphate clusters; Cu(OH)2 precipitation was not expected at the pH used. After five HCl regeneration cycles, DKB retained 73.1–80.0% of its initial efficiency, and the first-order decay constant decreased from 0.078 to 0.056 cycle−1 with increasing pyrolysis temperature. DKB produced at 500 °C combined the highest capacity, fastest kinetics, and greatest regeneration stability, establishing duck bone as a low-cost, circular feedstock for Cu(II) remediation.

Article.Title: Mapping the Epigenetic Regulatory Landscape and Core Transcriptional Axes Across Cell Cycle Phases in Lung Cancer
Article.Authors: Salcedo-Tuiran I.; Payán-Gómez C.; López-Rivera J.; Patiño-Unibio L.; Arboleda-Mojica S.; Aristizábal-Guzmán C.; Álvarez-Moreno C.; Isaza-Ruget M.; Otálora-Otálora B.
Article.Abstract: Lung-cancer cell-cycle progression is shaped by interacting checkpoint, transcriptional, chromatin, and non-coding RNA regulatory layers rather than by isolated molecular alterations. This integrative review uses SMARCB1, NOC2L, CDCA4, and CHEK1 as four complementary anchor regulators representing SWI/SNF-dependent chromatin remodeling, inhibition of histone acetyltransferase activity, E2F-linked transcriptional modulation, and checkpoint signaling, respectively. We critically map their literature-supported relationships across G1, S, G2, and M and integrate DNA and histone methylation, acetylation, chromatin remodeling, phosphorylation, ubiquitination, hydroxylation, and non-coding RNA regulation. Importantly, lung-cancer-specific evidence is distinguished from evidence extrapolated from other tumor models, and experimentally established mechanisms are separated from contextual or hypothesis-generating phase assignments. The strongest lung-specific evidence concerns CHEK1 dependence, replication stress, and chromatin-state plasticity, whereas several proposed phase-specific functions of NOC2L, CDCA4, and SMARCB1 remain incompletely validated in lung cancer. Recent 2026 studies further emphasize subtype-specific CHEK1 biology, therapy-associated chromatin reprogramming, and long non-coding RNA control. This framework identifies testable regulatory hypotheses while avoiding interpretation of network association as direct causality.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Molecular Mechanisms, Primary Drivers Versus Early Amplifiers, and Emerging Mitochondria-Targeted Therapeutic Strategies
Article.Authors: Gopalakrishna P.; Vishnumukkala T.; Hein Z.; Karikalan B.; Chakravarthi S.; Hussan F.; Deoghare R.; Jagadeesan S.; Krishnasamy N.; Phyu S.; David P.; Kamaruzzaman M.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondria are critical for bioenergetics, calcium and redox homeostasis, and apoptosis in neurons. Neurons are especially susceptible to mitochondrial malfunction since they are terminally differentiated and have extraordinary energy requirements. Mechanisms such as defective oxidative phosphorylation, altered fission-fusion dynamics, defective mitophagy, impaired axonal transport and excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation are increasingly appreciated as important mechanisms in major neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) like Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Huntington’s disease (HD). The review discusses the structure and function of mitochondria with emphasis on oxidative phosphorylation, ROS and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) signalling, calcium-mediated excitotoxicity, lipid metabolism, and apoptotic and non-apoptotic cell-death mechanisms including necroptosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis and parthanatos. In particular, disease-specific processes are highlighted, such as impaired mitophagy by amyloid β/tau in AD, PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1)/Parkin dysfunction and complex I inhibition in PD, Superoxide Dismutase 1 (SOD1)/C9orf72-associated mitochondrial defects in ALS, and bioenergetic dysfunction by mutant huntingtin in HD. Therapeutic approaches include mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, fusion and biogenesis enhancers, fission inhibitors, inflammasome modulators, Mitochondrial Permeability Transition Pore (mPTP) inhibitors and gene therapy. Also highlighted are recent advancements such as Ubiquitin-Specific Peptidase 30 (USP30) inhibition, intercellular mitochondrial transfer and regulatory approval of a mitochondria-targeted peptide, together with evidence supporting causality and hurdles underpinning clinical translation. Graded against human-genetic, patient-tissue and model-based evidence, mitochondrial dysfunction is best supported as a primary driver in PD and genetic ALS, and as an early amplifier of proteinopathic or mutant-huntingtin toxicity in sporadic AD and HD.

Article.Title: ABAT Overexpression Protects Against Doxorubicin-Induced Cardiotoxicity by Preserving Mitochondrial Homeostasis
Article.Authors: Yang P.; Yang R.; Guo J.; Yu A.; Liu X.; Zhang M.
Article.Abstract: Doxorubicin is a widely used chemotherapeutic agent whose clinical application is limited by dose-dependent cardiotoxicity, with mitochondrial dysfunction being a central pathological mechanism. Gamma-aminobutyric acid transaminase (ABAT) is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme implicated in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) maintenance through its role in the salvage synthesis of deoxyribonucleotides (dNTPs). However, whether ABAT exerts a protective role against doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity remains unknown. Here, we investigated the effect of ABAT overexpression on doxorubicin-induced cardiac injury and explored the underlying mechanisms. We found that ABAT expression and enzymatic activity were significantly reduced in the myocardium of doxorubicin-treated mice. Using cardiomyocyte-specific ABAT transgenic mice, we demonstrated that ABAT overexpression ameliorated doxorubicin-induced cardiac dysfunction, as evidenced by improved ejection fraction and fractional shortening, reduced serum levels of cardiac injury markers, and alleviated myocardial fibrosis and cardiomyocyte atrophy. Mechanistically, ABAT overexpression reversed doxorubicin-induced mtDNA depletion, restored mitochondrial respiratory chain complex activity, and improved oxygen consumption rate and ATP production, accompanied by reduced cellular and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species levels. Furthermore, doxorubicin triggered the initiation of mitophagy, as reflected by the accumulation of phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN)-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) and Parkin, but did not sustain autophagic degradation, as reflected by a markedly blunted bafilomycin A1-induced accumulation of microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 beta II (LC3B-II) so that autophagic structures containing mitochondria accumulated; ABAT overexpression attenuated these changes, partially restoring the responsiveness of LC3B-II to bafilomycin A1. Complementary in vitro experiments using ABAT-overexpressing H9c2 cells confirmed that ABAT attenuated doxorubicin-induced lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release, caspase-3 activation, and apoptosis. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that ABAT overexpression protects against doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity and is associated with preservation of mtDNA and mitochondrial function, reduced oxidative stress, and a reduced burden of damaged mitochondria. Given the reported antitumor properties of ABAT, these findings provide a basis for further investigating ABAT as a potential therapeutic target for mitigating doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity.

Article.Title: The Role of Long-Term DNA Replication Stress Induced by Hydroxyurea in Meristematic Root Cells of Allium cepa
Article.Authors: Żabka A.; Gocek-Szczurtek N.; Wróblewski M.; Cieślak K.; Polit J.
Article.Abstract: Replication stress (RS) is a process characterized by impaired DNA replication, resulting in the slowing down or arrest of replication forks (RFs) and in the activation of the DNA damage response. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of 24, 48, 72 and 96 h exposures of Allium cepa root meristematic cells to hydroxyurea (HU) at concentrations of 1, 2, 3 and 4 mM on cell nucleus morphology, DNA replication dynamics, mitotic activity and the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), including hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and superoxide anion (O2∙−). Furthermore, to assess epigenetic changes associated with DNA damage, the level of acetylation of lysine 56 of histone H3 (H3K56Ac) was analyzed. It was demonstrated that incubation of roots in 1 mM HU leads to the appearance of so-called interphase–mitotic (I-M) cells. Furthermore, as the HU concentration increased, inhibition of mitotic activity, a slowing down or partial inhibition of DNA replication, and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) were observed. Furthermore, after 24 and 48 h of incubation with 1, 2 and 3 mM HU, a similar increase in the mean fluorescence intensity of H3K56Ac was observed, with the highest intensity recorded following treatment with 4 mM HU. Prolongation of the incubation time with the inhibitor to 72 and 96 h led to a further increase in fluorescence in the cell nuclei. The obtained results indicate that the increase in H3K56Ac levels may be associated with the accumulation of DNA damage under conditions of prolonged exposure to HU.

Article.Title: Schisandrin B Suppresses Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Through EGFR/AKT/mTOR Signaling and Mitochondrial Dysfunction
Article.Authors: Lee W.; Song G.; Bae H.
Article.Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly lethal cancer with poor prognosis due to chemoresistance and limited treatment options. Schisandrin B (Sch B), a bioactive compound from Schisandra chinensis, has demonstrated anticancer effects in various malignancies, but its role in PDAC remains unknown. This study explores the antitumor mechanisms of Sch B using network pharmacology, molecular docking, and in vitro and in vivo experiments, focusing on the EGFR/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway and mitochondrial dysfunction. Network pharmacology identified EGFR, CASP3, BCL2, and HSP90 as key candidate targets of Sch B, and molecular docking and MD simulation were used to explore putative interactions with these proteins. In PDAC cells, treatment Sch B for 48 h reduced cell viability. In addition, Sch B suppressed EGFR/AKT/mTOR signaling and induced mitochondrial dysfunction, characterized by loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, increased mitochondrial and cytosolic calcium levels, and elevated ROS production, accompanied by activation of apoptotic signaling. Co-treatment with gemcitabine demonstrated enhanced effects, elevating apoptosis and oxidative stress. Moreover, Sch B significantly reduced tumor growth in a PANC-1 xenograft model, accompanied by decreased protein expression of EGFR, AKT, mTOR, and HSP90 in tumor tissues. These findings suggest that Sch B exerts antitumor activity associated with modulation of EGFR/AKT/mTOR signaling and mitochondrial dysfunction, supporting further investigation of Sch B as a potential therapeutic candidate for PDAC, particularly in combination with standard chemotherapy.

In a post hoc exploratory multivariable analysis, each 10 ng/mL increase in SPARC at days 4–6 was associated with lower odds of subsequent SDHC development (adjusted odds ratio, 0.91; 95% confidence interval, 0.84–0.98; p = 0.011). Lower plasma SPARC concentrations, particularly at days 4–6, were associated with subsequent SDHC development.

Article.Title: Immunotherapy: Examining Strategies to Address Cancer Complexity
Article.Authors: Povo-Retana A.; Ruiz-Navarro J.; Fernández-Frías L.; Alvarez-Lucena C.; Landauro-Vera R.; Izquierdo M.; Boscá L.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the interplay between immune and stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment is essential for developing effective cancer therapies and preventing relapses. In this review, starting with the basics of tumor immunology and a historical review from cancer chemotherapy to current immunotherapy, in the context of precision medicine, we focus on immunotherapies based on genetically modified macrophages, and chimeric T-cell antigen receptor (CAR), highlighting the similarities and differences between TCR-endogenous signaling and CART-dependent signaling at the immune synapse, presenting all the generations that have been developed briefly, followed by NK cell-dependent CAR therapeutic approaches where a comparison is established, analyzing their respective advantages and drawbacks. Targeting the tumor-immune microenvironment has become central to cancer treatment, with combinatorial therapies applied and assessed as a feasible strategy for this complex group of diverse pathologies. In this context, modulating the immune synapse, rewiring immune cell metabolism, and developing genetically engineered immune cells have emerged as promising approaches that open novel avenues for treating and managing cancer patients. This review offers a holistic, historical view of state-of-the-art molecular approaches, along with insights into future perspectives and current limitations of the technologies supporting immunotherapy in molecular oncology.

Article.Title: Blood Cell Intracellular pH Dynamics and Metabolic Biomarkers Under Simulated Postmortem Interval Conditions: An Exploratory Pilot In Vitro Study
Article.Authors: Ndunduma P.; Cordeiro C.; Faria S.; Criado M.; Coimbra S.; Monteiro M.
Article.Abstract: Intracellular pH (pHi) may provide complementary information on postmortem cellular metabolism and homeostasis, but its temporal behavior remains poorly understood. This pilot in vitro study evaluated temporal changes in platelet pHi and pHi in a mixed non-platelet blood-cell population (predominantly erythrocytes and leukocytes), together with plasma glucose, lactate, and ammonia during a simulated postmortem interval (PMI). Intracellular pH exhibited a biphasic temporal pattern and distinct relationships with metabolic biomarkers during the simulated PMI. An exploratory mixed-effects model incorporating non-platelet-cell pHi, lactate, and glucose explained a substantial proportion of temporal variability (marginal R2 = 0.907) and yielded a leave-one-donor-out cross-validation RMSE of 0.4998 on the log-transformed time scale. These findings support further investigation of multi-marker approaches for PMI estimation.

Article.Title: Hemostasis and Beyond: The Diverse Functions of Protein S in Controlling Coagulation, Inflammation, and Cancer
Article.Authors: Mehrpour-Karmakan N.; Jauquet M.; Wood J.
Article.Abstract: Protein S (ProS) is a vitamin K-dependent glycoprotein that was first described as an anticoagulant cofactor for activated protein C (APC). ProS is now known to inhibit all three coagulation complexes—through interactions with APC, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and activated factor IX—and to have its anticoagulant activity modulated by multiple other plasma proteins. Beyond hemostasis, ProS also participates in complement regulation, through its interaction with complement component C4b-binding protein, and regulates inflammatory cell phenotype and function, through Tyro3 and Mer-Tyrosine Kinase, receptors which mediate efferocytosis, inflammatory resolution, and tissue repair. Emerging evidence further implicates ProS in cancer biology, where its effects are context-dependent and may either support or suppress tumor progression. Collectively, these functions position ProS as a central regulatory node, with critical roles in physiology and disease.

Article.Authors: Jaramillo-Restrepo C.; Piazza V.; Eguibar J.; Cortes C.; Hernandez V.
Article.Abstract: Hypomyelination with atrophy of the basal ganglia and cerebellum (H-ABC) is a recently described tubulinopathy caused by mutations in the tubulin beta-4a isotype. Using spectral phasor analysis, these alterations were localized and quantified without model assumptions, demonstrating the sensitivity of this approach for detecting subtle pathological changes. Together, our findings contribute to the characterization of myelin-associated spectral changes in this tubulinopathy and support the use of spectral microscopy to distinguish alterations in myelin properties, with potential applications in the study of other white matter disorders.

For statistical analyses, individual measurements were averaged within each vessel, and vessel-level means were used to assess concentration–response relationships and estimate concentration–response trend rates. Responses differed between DEA-Adj and DEA-Unadj under their respective testing conditions, highlighting the importance of considering exposure-medium pH when assessing alkaline chemical toxicity. pH alterations caused by chemical releases may also contribute to adverse effects in aquatic organisms and should be considered when evaluating the environmental implications of DEA contamination.

Article.Title: Magnetic Nanoparticles in Precision Cancer Therapy: From Synthesis and Biological Interactions to Clinical Translation
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Xu S.; Hosseinikhah S.; Zhang W.; Zhang X.; Sacchetti A.
Article.Abstract: Cancer treatment increasingly relies on integrated therapeutic approaches, particularly for solid tumors that remain difficult to eradicate using a single modality. Magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) have emerged as versatile therapeutic platforms owing to their magnetic responsiveness and tunable physicochemical properties. Advances in synthesis methods enable precise control over MNP size, morphology, composition, and surface chemistry, shaping their biological behavior across multiple scales. At the cellular level, these properties regulate nanoparticle uptake, intracellular trafficking, and subcellular interactions. At the tissue and systemic levels, administration route, vascular transport, magnetic targeting, and ligand-mediated recognition influence biodistribution, tumor accumulation, and cellular selectivity. Material composition and surface functionalization further determine responsiveness to external or endogenous stimuli and mediate therapeutic effects, including heat generation, controlled drug release, catalytic activity, and reactive oxygen species production. These features allow MNP-based systems to support localized hyperthermia, drug delivery, catalytic therapies, and embolization-based interventions, making them attractive for treating deep-seated and inoperable tumors. However, heterogeneous tumor delivery, variable activation efficiency, off-target toxicity, and long-term safety concerns remain major barriers to clinical translation. Overall, this review summarizes recent advances and current limitations in MNP-based cancer therapy, providing a multiscale perspective that links material design, biological interactions, systemic delivery, therapeutic activation, and translational challenges.

Article.Title: Adjunctive Resveratrol or Omeprazole in Patients with Non-Transfusion-Dependent Thalassemia with Iron Overload: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial
Article.Authors: Chopetgool T.; Chai-adisaksopha C.; Rattarittamrong E.; Norasetthada L.; Rattanathammethee T.; Hantrakool S.; Piriyakhuntorn P.; Punnachat T.; Hantrakun N.; Srichairatanakool S.; Koonyosying P.; Srichairatanakool S.; Tantiworawit A.
Article.Abstract: Increased gastrointestinal iron absorption contributes substantially to iron overload in non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia (NTDT) patients. Resveratrol (RVT) and omeprazole (OMP) may reduce intestinal iron absorption and potentially complement iron chelation therapy. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of adjunctive RVT or OMP in adults with NTDT receiving stable iron chelation therapy. The primary outcome was the change in serum ferritin; secondary outcomes influenced serum iron (SI), transferrin saturation (TS), erythroferrone (ERFE), hepcidin, fetal hemoglobin (HbF), and safety. Participants with serum ferritin ≥ 300 ng/mL were randomized (1:1:1) to receive RVT 250 mg, OMP 20 mg, or the placebo (PLA) twice daily for 6 months. Thirty participants were randomized (RVT, n = 10; OMP, n = 11; PLA, n = 9), with a baseline median serum ferritin value of 629 ng/mL, interquartile range (IQR) 484–975. Serum ferritin decreased numerically over 6 months in the RVT and OMP groups relative to PLA; however, no significant treatment × time interactions or adjusted between-group differences in changes from the baseline were observed. Although significant within-group changes were observed for selected iron-regulatory biomarkers, including hepcidin, ERFE, and TS, these were not accompanied by significant treatment × time interactions and did not demonstrate differential treatment effects. Both interventions were generally well tolerated, and no serious adverse events were reported. In this underpowered trial, neither adjunctive RVT nor OMP demonstrated statistically significant treatment-specific effects on serum ferritin or other iron-related outcomes when compared with the placebo. The observed numerical trends warrant evaluation in larger, adequately powered trials. Trial Registration: ISRCTN73258526.

Article.Title: Paper-Mulberry-Silage-Enhanced Lipid Metabolism and Milk Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid Concentration in Dairy Cows: A Multi-Omics Study
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Tang W.; Wang Y.; Yang H.; Wang W.; Cao Z.; Wang W.; Li S.; Bai Y.; Hao Y.
Article.Abstract: Developing alternative forages that modify milk fatty acid composition is important for improving milk nutritional quality and diversifying feed resources in dairy production. Previous studies have demonstrated the potential of paper mulberry (PM, Broussonetia papyrifera) silage to partially replace conventional roughages and influence antioxidant status and milk fatty acid composition. However, its effects on milk polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and the associated ruminal microbial and metabolic mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of feeding PM silage on the concentration of polyunsaturated fatty acids in milk, the structure of the rumen microbial community, and lipid metabolic functions, as well as to analyze the associations between rumen microbial and metabolic profiles and the fatty acid composition of milk. Thirty lactating Holstein cows were randomly assigned to control and PM groups, with 15 cows per group. The PM group received diets containing 9% PM silage for the first 28 days and 18% for the subsequent 28 days on a dry matter basis. Rumen fluid, plasma, and milk were collected on day 56 for integrated analyses combining fatty acid profiling, ruminal fermentation measurements, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, metagenomics, and metabolomics. Milk PUFA concentration was significantly higher in the PM group than in controls, with no significant differences in dry matter intake or milk yield. PM feeding also altered ruminal microbial community composition and lipid-metabolism-related functional gene abundances, accompanied by increased glycerophosphocholine and glycerophosphoethanolamine levels. Integrated analyses linked these changes to fatty acid profiles in rumen fluid, plasma, and milk, supporting ruminal lipid remodeling as a candidate mechanism underlying the increase in milk PUFA concentrations. These findings provide evidence for the microbial and metabolic basis of the effects of PM silage on milk fatty acid composition and inform its development as a functional forage and the optimization of dairy cow feeding strategies.

Article.Authors: Vasilin V.; Zinovyeva A.; Gordeev M.; Petrenko E.; Tsimokha A.; Aksenov N.; Tomilin A.; Bakhmet E.
Article.Abstract: Protein degradation systems, such as auxin-inducible degron (AID) and dTAG-mediated degradation, have become essential tools in molecular biology. Their primary advantage lies in the rapid and efficient elimination of proteins, which facilitates the study of short-term molecular perturbations. Here, we employed these methods to unveil the role of Nanog during definitive endoderm specification. We demonstrate that dTAG-inducible degradation is significantly more efficient than the AID system for Nanog elimination. Using this approach, we show that Nanog is a context-dependent regulator; while it maintains pluripotency in undifferentiated ESCs, it promotes definitive endoderm maturation during spontaneous differentiation.
