Article.Title: The Molecular Mechanisms of Cold Tolerance in Brassica napus
Article.Authors: Luo W.; Zhou Y.; Shen J.; Xu L.; Du X.; Sheng F.; Geng R.; Cai G.
Article.Abstract: Brassica napus is a crucial oilseed crop in China, meeting approximately 55% of the country’s demand for vegetable oils. However, throughout its growth cycle, it frequently encounters low-temperature stress. As a key environmental factor constraining the stability of Brassica napus L. yield and quality, cold damage makes research into the cold tolerance mechanisms of Brassica napus L. highly significant for the breeding of cold-tolerant varieties. This paper focuses on the issue of low-temperature stress in Brassica napus L., synthesizing recent relevant research findings. It first clarifies the phenotypic effects of low-temperature stress on Brassica napus L. at different growth stages. Concurrently, low temperatures disrupt the integrity of the Brassica napus cell membrane and inhibit photosynthesis, in response, plants can mitigate oxidative damage by activating antioxidant enzyme systems, such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT). Based on the above, the current research progress in mining cold-tolerant germplasm resources in China and identifying cold tolerance genes in Brassica napus L. is further summarized as follows. This paper provides a theoretical reference for an in-depth analysis of the cold tolerance mechanisms in Brassica napus L. and for accelerating the breeding of cold-tolerant varieties. Future efforts should focus on the functional validation of key genes within cold tolerance pathways and the application of multi-gene pyramiding breeding technologies to break through the bottleneck in controlling cold damage in Brassica napus L.

Article.Title: Comparative Study on Coffee and Spent Coffee Grounds of Arabica and Robusta Varieties of Ugandan Origin: Bioactive Properties of Extracts as Circular Resources
Article.Authors: Dinu M.; Dumitru A.; Brezoiu A.; Isopencu G.; Iancu P.
Article.Abstract: Coffee consumption is increasing yearly, and so is the quantity of spent coffee grounds, a by-product that still contains bioactive compounds. The goal of this work is to evaluate the lipid fractions (LFs) and polyphenolic fractions (PFs) from roasted coffee grounds (RCG; two varieties of Ugandan origin: Arabica and Robusta) and from the corresponding spent coffee grounds (SCG) extracted with solvents of opposite polarities. A qualitative and quantitative analysis of the extracts was performed using GC-FID, 1H-NMR, Folin–Ciocalteu, HPLC-PDA, DPPH and antibacterial activity methods. A high-quality LF, coffee oil (91.82 g triacylglycerides/100 g LF, 49.85 mol% saturated fatty acids and 50.15 mol% unsaturated fatty acid chains, 8.98 mg GAE/g LF, 20.91% DPPH inhibition), with high extraction yield (10.34 g/100 g SCG), can be recovered from SCG of the Ugandan Arabica variety. In addition, SCG of both Ugandan Arabica and Robusta varieties are promising resources for the recovery of high-quality PF (12.30 and 7.85 mg GAE/g PF, 0.684 and 0.837 mg/g PF chlorogenic acids, 85.17% and 73.95% DPPH inhibition) with good extraction yields (9.35 and 5.63 g/100 g SCG) and with antimicrobial activities that remain after the coffee brewing step. These results highlight SCG of Ugandan origin as a promising resource of bioactive compounds for further valorization.

Article.Title: Antimicrobial Resistance and Infectious Complications in Cancer Immunotherapy: CAR-T Cells, Bispecific Antibodies and Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors
Article.Authors: Lasagna A.; Andreoni M.; Silvestris N.; Pedrazzoli P.
Article.Abstract: Cancer immunotherapies, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), have improved outcomes across hematologic and solid malignancies. Infection risk remains heterogeneous and depends on treatment platform, target antigen, lymphodepletion, immune reconstitution, concomitant immunosuppression, and supportive care. This narrative review synthesizes clinical trials, observational studies, and guidance identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, reference screening, and a targeted literature update through October 2026. It focuses on infection incidence, microbiological spectrum, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), multidrug-resistant (MDR) colonization and infection, antimicrobial exposure, prevention, and stewardship. Severe infections can be frequent with BCMA-directed BsAbs: the MagnetisMM-3 study reported grade 3–4 infections in 39.8% of elranatamab-treated patients, while a pooled global teclistamab cohort reported grade 3–4 infections in 55.3%; these estimates are study-specific and are influenced in part by COVID-19. Direct AMR evidence is concentrated in CAR-T and broader cellular-therapy cohorts, while comparable data for BsAbs and ICIs remain limited. Associations between broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, microbiome disruption, and CAR-T outcomes are clinically important but remain vulnerable to confounding. Prevention should integrate immune status, prior microbiology, antimicrobial exposure, and local resistance patterns rather than infer resistance risk from treatment platform alone. Prospective studies using harmonized outcomes are needed to improve individualized infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship.

Article.Title: Tryptophan and Its Selected Metabolites Modulate Melanoma-Cell Biology: A Preliminary In Vitro Study
Article.Authors: Michalak-Stoma A.; Walczak K.; Kowal M.; Sawa-Wejksza K.; Chojnacki M.; Lemieszek M.; Stoma F.; Krasowska D.
Article.Abstract: Tryptophan (TRP) and its metabolites are involved in numerous physiological and pathological processes within the skin. They may influence melanoma biology, but their role remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated the effects of TRP, anthranilic acid (AA), and cinnabarinic acid (CBA) in melanoma cells in vitro and their potential interaction with the B-Raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase (BRAF) inhibitor vemurafenib. A375, G361, and SK-MEL-3 melanoma cell lines and a THP-1-derived macrophage model were used. Cell proliferation and metabolic activity were assessed using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay, migration using a scratch assay, and cell-cycle distribution by flow cytometry. Western blotting was used to analyze selected signaling proteins. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and nitric oxide (NO) production were evaluated. Bioinformatic analyses investigated associations between BRAF and genes related to tryptophan metabolism and the kynurenine pathway. All compounds showed dose-dependent antiproliferative effects, with prolonged exposure increasing efficacy. TRP and AA increased G0/G1 cell-cycle arrest, whereas CBA increased the G2/M population. TRP also reduced A375 cell migration. All three compounds enhanced the antiproliferative effect of vemurafenib, with CBA showing the strongest effect (approximately 20%). Western blot analysis indicated modulation of p21 expression and ERK1/2 phosphorylation, suggesting implications for cell cycle and stress signaling pathways. Moreover, conditioned medium from A375 cells exposed to tested compounds affected cell viability, ROS, and NO production in THP-1-derived macrophages. TRP and its metabolites may be considered potential supportive agents for melanoma BRAF-targeted therapy. However, further in vivo studies are needed to clarify their therapeutic value and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms.

Article.Title: CASK Positively Regulates Keratinocyte Proliferation and Modulates the EGFR-ERK-p21 Signaling Axis
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Huang D.; Cheong K.; Cheng C.; Chang H.; Lin W.
Article.Abstract: CASK is a multidomain scaffold protein with diverse cellular functions, but its role in keratinocytes remains unclear. RNA sequencing revealed that CASK depletion attenuates proliferation-associated transcriptional programs. Consistent with this, CASK silencing increased p53 and p21 expression while reducing cyclin B and phosphorylated Rb levels, with elevated p53 and p21 mRNA in shCASK cells. Mechanistically, CASK silencing enhanced serum-induced activation of EGFR and downstream ERK signaling, which were accompanied by increased expression of the EGFR ligands amphiregulin, TGF-α, and epiregulin, indicating augmented autocrine/paracrine EGFR signaling. Pharmacological inhibition studies demonstrated that activation of the EGFR–ERK signaling pathway is essential for p21 upregulation upon CASK silencing. Promoter reporter analyses further revealed that CASK deficiency enhances p21 transcription. Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized role of CASK in regulating keratinocyte growth and cell-cycle progression. CASK promotes keratinocyte proliferation by restraining autocrine/paracrine EGFR–ERK signaling and suppressing p21 expression, thereby contributing to epidermal homeostasis and growth control.

Bioinformatics linked high M2-TAM infiltration with poor HCC prognosis. In vivo, SH retarded tumor growth, decreased intratumoral M2-TAM infiltration, and reduced Ki-67 levels. Collectively, SH remodels the TIME to restrain HCC progression, and these effects are associated with inhibition of M2-TAM polarization and attenuation of LIF/PI3K/Akt signaling, revealing a novel immunotherapeutic mechanism and supporting SH as a promising natural agent for HCC immunotherapy.

Article.Title: Erythrocyte Membrane β-Adrenoreactivity as a Systemic Adrenergic Phenotype Associated with Ventricular Tachyarrhythmia in Heart Failure Patients Undergoing Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy
Article.Authors: Atabekov T.; Muslimova E.; Rebrova T.; Afanasiev S.; Batalov R.; Popov S.
Article.Abstract: Chronic hyperactivity of the sympathetic nervous system and remodeling of β-adrenergic receptors represent core pathophysiological mechanisms in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and in the emergence of ventricular arrhythmias. Nevertheless, clinically applicable functional indicators of this axis are still limited. We investigated whether erythrocyte membrane β-adrenoreactivity (EMA), an indirect functional membrane index derived from β-adrenergic antagonist-modulated hypo-osmotic hemolysis, correlates with a ventricular tachyarrhythmia (VTA) phenotype following cardiac resynchronization therapy with defibrillation capability (CRT-D). In a single-center observational cohort, 99 HFrEF patients underwent CRT-D implantation. A total of 70 patients with complete baseline and 12-month data formed the complete-case analysis (NCT03667989: n = 14; NCT05769036: n = 36; non-registry enrollment under the same institutional protocol: n = 20). Patients were categorized by the prespecified database variable “VTA preCRT and 12 m. post-CRT” into VTA-positive (n = 38) and VTA-negative (n = 32) groups. Baseline EMA was higher in VTA-positive patients (31.4% [22.8; 48.3]) than in VTA-negative patients (22.0% [15.8; 33.4]; p = 0.012). In multivariate logistic regression with stepwise selection, two variables were independently associated with the VTA-positive phenotype: EMA (odds ratio [OR] = 1.0446 per 1%; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.0092–1.0812; p = 0.013) and left ventricular end-systolic dimension (LVESD) (OR = 1.1023 per 1 mm; 95% CI 1.0102–1.2029; p = 0.029). The model was statistically significant (likelihood-ratio χ2 = 12.567; p = 0.0019) and well calibrated (Hosmer–Lemeshow χ2 = 9.70; p = 0.286), with good discrimination (AUC = 0.748; 95% CI 0.629–0.844). However, explanatory power was modest (Nagelkerke R2 = 0.220), indicating that most variance in the VTA phenotype remains unexplained by EMA and LVESD. At a cut-off of 0.5, sensitivity was 73.68%, specificity 71.87%, and overall accuracy 72.86%. Internal validation with 2000 bootstrap iterations confirmed robustness (optimism-corrected AUC = 0.727; 95% CI 0.612–0.835). EMA remained significant after adjustment for LVESD, supporting its role as an independent marker of the VTA-positive phenotype. The model outperformed all univariate models in terms of AUC, R2, and overall accuracy. EMA may therefore be associated with a systemic adrenergic membrane phenotype and an arrhythmic substrate. These findings require mechanistic validation and external replication before any clinical application. All reported cut-offs are exploratory and derived from a single center, and the analysis is based on a complete-case cohort with acknowledged potential for attrition bias.

Article.Title: Platelet miRNA-Based Signature as a Potential Non-Invasive Tool for Discriminating Patients with Secondary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis from Healthy Individuals
Article.Authors: Dziedzic A.; Karbownik M.; Arabski M.; Miller E.; Michlewska S.; Saluk J.
Article.Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) lacks minimally invasive biomarkers that reliably reflect disease-associated pathophysiological alterations, particularly during the progressive stage of the disease. Because blood platelets contribute to thrombo-inflammatory signalling and are the major vascular carriers of regulatory miRNA, we investigated whether platelet miRNA alterations are associated with platelet hyperreactivity in MS and whether these changes originate during thrombopoiesis by examining megakaryocytes. We analyzed platelets and megakaryocytes from MS patients and healthy controls by transmission electron microscopy, flow cytometry, ELISA, miRNA profiling based on microarrays, and Real-Time PCR validation. Logistic regression and bioinformatic analyses were used to evaluate the potential and biological relevance. MS platelets exhibited a hyperreactive phenotype, characterized by enhanced degranulation, microparticle release, P-selectin expression, and collagen-induced aggregation. GPVI levels were significantly elevated in platelets but remained unchanged in megakaryocytes. MiRNA profiling revealed widespread downregulation in platelets, while megakaryocytes showed selective upregulation of miR-223-3p. Following microarray screening, PCR validation of 10 selected miRNAs revealed widespread downregulation in platelets, while only miR-223-3p was significantly upregulated in megakaryocytes from MS patients. A two-miRNA model (let-7a-5p and miR-146a-5p) showed good internal discrimination (AUC = 0.89; sensitivity 89%; specificity 85%), but lower external performance (C-index = 0.66; sensitivity 50%; specificity 73%). MS is associated with a distinct platelet miRNA signature linked to acquired platelet hyperreactivity and vesiculation. Platelet-derived let-7a-5p and miR-146a-5p represent potential non-invasive biomarker candidates, although their diagnostic utility requires further validation in larger independent cohorts.

Article.Title: Biomarkers of Immune Injury in Cardiometabolic Disorders
Article.Authors: Zhou L.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Cardiometabolic disorders are accompanied by persistent immune activation that links metabolic stress to vascular and organ injury. Conventional inflammatory measures capture part of this process, but they provide limited information about tissue origin, biological mechanism and disease trajectory. This narrative review examines emerging biomarkers across genetic and epigenetic regulation, metabolic and oxidative stress, gut microbial exposure, innate immune activation, adaptive immune remodeling and circulating inflammatory responses. It integrates mechanistic studies with clinical observations to consider how these signals may inform the assessment of cardiometabolic immune injury. Particular attention is given to the distinction between inherited susceptibility and acquired responses, circulating associations and tissue mechanisms, and potentially injurious versus compensatory immune activity. The evidence supports substantial biological connectivity among these domains, while the strength of clinical validation varies widely. Most candidate markers and proposed combinations require standardized measurement, longitudinal assessment and external validation before biomarker-guided prevention can be justified. We propose a mechanism-informed framework for organizing candidate immune-metabolic phenotypes, recognizing reciprocal interactions rather than a universal temporal sequence. Future studies should determine whether these biomarkers improve prediction and clinical decisions beyond established risk factors and whether changes in biomarker profiles correspond to meaningful treatment benefits.

Article.Title: DNA Glycosylases in Noncancer Diseases: Oxidative Lesion Recognition, Repair Intermediates, and Tissue Responses
Article.Authors: Kang S.; Ko Y.; Cho S.; Jang S.
Article.Abstract: Oxidative DNA damage in noncancer tissues can perturb transcription, compromise telomere integrity, and impair mitochondrial function. DNA glycosylases initiate base excision repair (BER), but their biological consequences also depend on lesion recognition, chromatin residence, catalytic processing, and the persistence or resolution of abasic sites and strand breaks. This review integrates structural and kinetic evidence with experimental models of inflammation, telomeric senescence, cardiometabolic disease, neurodegeneration, and neural injury. Promoter-associated 8-oxoguanine DNA glycosylase 1 (OGG1) can either promote inflammatory transcription or restrict antiviral interferon expression in a locus-dependent manner. At oxidatively damaged telomeres in human fibroblasts, OGG1 and mutY DNA glycosylase (MUTYH) drive acute senescence through repair intermediates, whereas during repeated injury, OGG1 supports telomere maintenance and MUTYH-dependent arrest limits chromosome instability. Mitochondria-directed OGG1 expression improves metabolic outcomes in OGG1-deficient mice exposed to a high-fat diet. By contrast, vascular and neural phenotypes associated with Nei-like DNA glycosylase 3 (NEIL3) remain difficult to attribute to a defined initiating lesion. These findings emphasize distinguishing enzyme occupancy, catalytic processing, and completed repair. Therapeutic studies should define the relevant cell, substrate, compartment, and exposure period and assess tissue function directly alongside unresolved lesions and chromosome stability.

Article.Title: One Disorder, Two Brains: Challenges in Modeling Epilepsy and Associated Movement Disorders in Mice
Article.Authors: Travin D.; Anisimova P.; Bogovarova K.; Kustova A.; Tarabykin V.
Article.Abstract: Modeling epileptic syndromes co-occurring with movement disorders in mice often fails to fully recapitulate human phenotypes due to distinct gene-specific and anatomical mechanisms. This review categorizes these translational barriers into three primary groups. First, ortholog heterotopia and heterochrony drive spatiotemporal shifts in gene expression, causing orthologs to activate at disparate developmental stages or within different cell populations across species. Second, molecular redundancy and compensation obscure phenotypes through the upregulation of alternative proteins in response to target protein suppression, the activation of modifier genes, or neural network rewiring. Third, structural variations in striatal anatomy fundamentally alter corticostriatal loop functioning. Characterizing these divergent mechanisms is essential for improving the predictive validity of preclinical models and advancing targeted therapies.

Article.Title: Cultivar-Dependent Variation in Silicon Accumulation and Phytolith Formation Revealed by Comparative Proteomic Analysis in Rice
Article.Authors: Prakongkaew R.; Pongprayoon W.
Article.Abstract: Silicon is a key determinant of growth, productivity, and stress adaptation in rice (Oryza sativa L.). Silicon accumulation and its deposition as phytoliths contribute to plant performance and environmental resilience. However, although the physiological functions of silicon and the mechanisms governing its uptake and transport have been extensively studied, the proteomic basis underlying cultivar-dependent variation in silicon accumulation and phytolith formation remains poorly understood. In this study, silicon concentration, phytolith content, and proteomic profiles were compared in roots and shoots of three rice cultivars, Chai Nat 1 (CNT), Khao Dawk Mali 105 (KDML105), and RD51, at the flowering stage. RD51 exhibited the highest silicon concentration and phytolith accumulation in shoots, whereas CNT accumulated the highest silicon concentration in roots. Proteomic analysis identified 4086 and 4115 protein groups in roots and shoots, respectively, revealing cultivar-specific differences in protein abundance. Principal component analysis and differential abundance analysis demonstrated the greatest proteomic divergence between CNT and RD51, particularly in shoots. Functional enrichment analysis indicated that KDML105 was enriched in transport- and sulfur metabolism-related processes, whereas RD51 showed enrichment of mitochondrial respiration, energy production, and associated metabolic pathways. Protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis further revealed functional associations between silicon transporter proteins and proteins involved in transport, signaling, and respiratory metabolism. Collectively, these findings provide novel insights into the proteomic mechanisms underlying silicon accumulation and phytolith formation in rice. The superior silicon accumulation and phytolith production observed in RD51 highlight its potential as a valuable genetic resource for enhancing phytolith production, improving silicon-use efficiency, and strengthening climate resilience in rice.

Article.Title: Resistance Gene Pyramiding in Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.): From Marker-Assisted Selection to Functional Validation
Article.Authors: Kwiatek M.; Bobrowska R.; Noweiska A.; Spychała J.; Mikołajczyk S.; Tomkowiak A.
Article.Abstract: Gene pyramiding is widely used in wheat breeding to improve disease resistance; however, combining multiple resistance alleles does not necessarily provide stronger protection or long-term durability. Molecular markers, gene cloning and genome editing have greatly facilitated the tracking and pyramiding of resistance alleles. These approaches define the allelic composition of a line rather than the level of resistance it will express. This review examines why the effectiveness of resistance gene combinations remains difficult to predict despite advances in molecular tools. Evidence from leaf rust, stripe rust, stem rust, powdery mildew, eyespot and Fusarium head blight shows that the observed effects of combined resistance loci depend on the genetic background, gene interactions and environmental conditions, as well as on the methods used to assess disease development. We discuss how genetic characterization, expression analysis, functional assays and multi-environment phenotyping can provide complementary evidence for evaluating resistance gene combinations and how pathogen evolution and deployment strategies affect their durability. As genome editing expands the possibilities for combining resistance alleles, understanding their functional compatibility and their performance across genetic backgrounds remains essential for developing effective and durable resistance in wheat. The central conclusion of this review is that no marker profile, and no edited allele, is by itself evidence that a cultivar will be resistant in the field. Markers and gene editing shorten the route to a combination, but the resistance of that combination still must be validated phenotypically in the target backgrounds and environments.

Article.Title: Differential Modulation of the Ileal Bile Acid Transporter ASBT by Fatty Acids
Article.Authors: Malhotra P.; Farooqui Z.; Ticho A.; Comiskey S.; Qazi A.; Calzadilla N.; Suarez R.; Gill R.; Alrefai W.
Article.Abstract: The ileal ASBT bile acid transporter is a critical mediator of bile acid and cholesterol homeostasis and is modulated by fatty acids via S-acylation. We investigated mechanisms underlying differential regulation of ASBT by saturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids. Using a prenylation mimetic with a CAAX box at the C-terminus of ASBT, we showed that transport activity in transfected HEK293 cells increased significantly, suggesting that direct attachment of a saturated fatty acid stimulates ASBT function. Furthermore, siRNA-mediated attenuation of DHHC21 acyltransferase expression reduced ASBT S-acylation and its function, demonstrating DHHC21 as a positive regulator of ASBT function. Conversely, treatment with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFAs), like eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), reduced ASBT function in HEK293 cells. Supplementation of fish oil, as a source of n-3 PUFAs, to a high-fat, high-cholesterol diet fed to C57BL6/J mice protected them against diet-induced hepatic steatosis, along with reduced bile acid absorption consistent with the inhibition of ASBT. This was supported by increased fecal bile acids, decreased ileal bile acid-stimulated gene expression, and increased hepatic bile acid synthesis-related gene expression. Metabolic labeling with alkyne-EPA in HEK293 cells showed, for the first time, direct binding of this n-3 PUFA to ASBT. Unlike palmitate modification, EPA binding was highly resistant to hydroxylamine retrieval, indicating a mechanism distinct from S-acylation. Our data unraveled a novel role for DHHC21 in regulating ASBT and provided evidence for distinct mechanisms by which saturated palmitate and polyunsaturated EPA fatty acids bind ASBT. The direct effect on ASBT and inhibition of bile acid absorption may partly contribute to the protective effects of n-3 PUFAs on the liver.

Article.Title: Dual Targeting of Alcohol Use Disorder and Alcohol–Associated Liver Disease: Emerging Molecular Targets Along the Gut–Liver–Brain Axis
Article.Authors: Ryu T.; Chung B.; Yang K.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol–associated liver disease (ALD) is the hepatic end of alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet only abstinence and transplantation modify it, and recent liver-only programmes in alcohol–associated hepatitis have not delivered. This review asks whether the receptors, ligands and transporters setting drinking behaviour and alcohol-related liver injury are largely one set along the gut–liver–brain axis, so one molecule could lower both. Where resolved, it is cell-specific: hepatic glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor sits, in non-alcohol models, on sinusoidal endothelial and CD8+ T cells, not hepatocytes, and ethanol induces hepatocyte fibroblast growth factor 21, whose analogue acts on β-Klotho+ amygdala neurons. Organised by target, not organ, each candidate is appraised separately on both sides, negatives, terminations and non-replications counting alike. Of sixteen targets spanning incretin, hepatokine, glutamatergic and microbial or neuroimmune families, three are supported on both sides in the desired direction but only in separate experiments, three point in opposite directions, and ten have had no manipulation read out on both; for none were both organs read out in one experiment. Dual targeting changes what trials must measure: only one of 64 registered trials makes both endpoints primary, so objectively measured intake and a liver endpoint must be co-primary.

Article.Title: Mesenchymal Stem/Stromal Cell-Derived Extracellular Vesicles for Immunomodulation in Osteoarthritis
Article.Authors: Ley M.; Philippon M.; Labib R.; Fuentes-Chandia M.; Liu C.; Best T.; Somoza R.; Kouroupis D.
Article.Abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous disorder affecting multiple joint tissues, in which structural degeneration may be accompanied by varying degrees of synovial inflammation and immune–stromal dysregulation. Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) have demonstrated immunomodulatory and tissue-protective properties, increasingly linked to paracrine signaling. Comparative studies suggest that extracellular vesicles (EVs) make an important, but not exclusive, contribution to MSC paracrine activity, with soluble secretome components providing potentially complementary effects. Drawing on literature identified primarily through PubMed and Scopus and clinical trial records from ClinicalTrials.gov (updated through September 2026), this narrative review examines the immunomodulatory role of MSC-derived EVs (MSC-EVs) in OA, with emphasis on their interactions with the joint immune microenvironment and their contribution to tissue protection. Across experimental OA models, MSC-EVs have been reported to reduce synovitis, cartilage degeneration, subchondral bone alterations, and pain-related outcomes, although responses vary with MSC source, EV composition, engineering strategies, disease context, and treatment regimen. Mechanistically, the most consistent evidence supports modulation of macrophage-associated inflammatory responses, whereas effects on adaptive immune populations remain less established and are largely derived from non-OA models. Clinical evidence remains limited and currently provides mainly preliminary information on feasibility and short-term tolerability, with insufficient evidence to establish therapeutic efficacy. Overall, MSC-EVs represent a potential cell-free immunomodulatory approach for OA, but standardized manufacturing, product characterization, dosing, and rigorously controlled clinical trials are required to define their therapeutic value.

Article.Title: Intrinsic Inflammatory Signaling in Life and Death of Podocytes
Article.Authors: Bobkov D.; Konopleva S.; Osin D.; Demidov O.; Mihailovskaya V.
Article.Abstract: Podocytes are terminally differentiated components of the glomerular filtration barrier whose structural integrity depends on coordinated signaling between the slit diaphragm, actin cytoskeleton, mitochondria, and stress-response machinery. Evidence from cultured podocytes, experimental kidney disease, human tissue, and selected podocyte-specific genetic models indicates that podocytes can execute intrinsic inflammatory responses and, in defined settings, contribute to local inflammatory amplification. This review examines how NF-κB, p38 MAPK, JAK–STAT, cGAS–STING, NLRP3 inflammasome, and Rho-family GTPase signaling interact with cytoskeletal remodeling, mitochondrial dysfunction, senescence, regulated cell death, and podocyte detachment. Particular attention is given to the distinction between podocyte-specific evidence and findings obtained from whole-kidney analyses, global genetic models, or pharmacological interventions. The available evidence supports a context-dependent network in which inflammatory signaling may support adaptation but, when sustained or dysregulated, can contribute to barrier dysfunction and irreversible podocyte loss. We also assess therapeutic strategies targeting inflammatory sensors, kinases, inflammasome components, cytoskeletal regulators, and metabolic stress pathways. Most remain preclinical, emphasizing the need for podocyte-targeted delivery, rigorous cell-specific validation, and human translational studies.

Article.Authors: Figura M.; Zając W.; Otto-Ślusarczyk D.; Milanowski Ł.; Nowak J.; Antoniak A.; Kopczyński M.; Sadowski K.; Hołubiuk Ł.; Walęcik-Kot W.; Szlufik S.; Biliński J.; Struga M.; Koziorowski D.

Article.Title: Pantethine and Neurodegeneration: A Coenzyme A-Centered Framework Linking Metabolism, Neuroinflammation, and Mitochondrial Dysfunction
Article.Authors: Simili O.; Carvalho G.; Simões R.; Detregiachi C.; Pereira E.; Catharin V.; Silva G.; Miola V.; Bishayee A.; Valenti V.; Vécsei L.; Tanaka M.; Barbalho S.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a growing global health burden associated with aging and characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, metabolic failure, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, and chronic neuroinflammation. Among the metabolic pathways implicated in these disorders, coenzyme A (CoA)-linked biology has emerged as a potentially important but still underexplored contributor to neuronal resilience and vulnerability. Pantethine, a disulfide derivative of pantetheine and a CoA-related metabolic precursor, has attracted attention because of its reported effects on cellular metabolism, redox balance, and inflammatory signaling. However, its relevance across neurodegenerative diseases remains unevenly defined, with direct support strongest in pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) and more limited evidence in common disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD). This narrative review critically examines the mechanistic and translational evidence linking pantethine to neurodegeneration. PKAN represents the most logical disease context for pantethine investigation because impaired CoA biosynthesis is proximal to disease pathogenesis, although pantethine remains investigational and its clinical efficacy has not been established. By contrast, proposed applications in AD and PD remain highly theoretical and hypothesis-generating. Nevertheless, research on pantethine and related CoA-restoring strategies may identify new intervention targets across neurodegenerative diseases and other disorders characterized by impaired cellular bioenergetics, including selected neuropsychiatric disorders. These possibilities require biomarker-informed, disease-specific studies that establish active-species exposure, target engagement, and clinically meaningful effects.

The conventional polymerase chain reaction (PCR) method is reliable for molecular detection of vanA but requires thermal cycling and, in conventional formats, post-amplification analysis. In this study, we developed and evaluated a closed-tube colorimetric loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay using hydroxy naphthol blue (LAMP-HNB) for visual detection of vanA. A total of 130 Enterococcus isolates were tested, comprising 100 previously characterized in our published LAMP–lateral flow dipstick (LAMP-LFD) study (52 vanA-positive and 48 vanA-negative) and an additional 30 (13 vanA-positive and 17 vanA-negative), yielding 65 PCR-positive and 65 PCR-negative isolates overall. Reaction conditions were optimized sequentially, and the final LAMP-HNB protocol took place at 63 °C for 45 min with 4.0 mM MgSO4 and 5 μM HNB. The visual endpoint was confirmed by 2% agarose gel electrophoresis. LAMP-HNB correctly classified all 65 PCR-positive and all 65 PCR-negative isolates, yielding 100% sensitivity (65/65; exact 95% CI: 94.48–100%), 100% specificity (65/65; 95% CI: 94.48–100%), and 100% overall agreement (130/130; 95% CI: 97.20–100%). The limit of detection was 8.67 × 103 genome copies/µL (28.52 pg/µL) for LAMP-HNB compared with 8.67 × 104 genome copies/µL (285.2 pg/µL) for conventional PCR, representing a 10-fold lower DNA concentration endpoint under the experimental conditions employed. In the 100-isolate overlapping cohort, LAMP-HNB, the previously reported LAMP-LFD platform, and PCR were concordant. With its 45 min requirement for amplification after DNA preparation, the HNB format provides a rapid, closed-tube visual endpoint without a labeled probe, lateral flow strip, running buffer, or post-amplification hybridization step. These findings support LAMP-HNB as a promising molecular screening approach for vanA-positive enterococci, while larger, fully independent multicenter validation remains necessary before routine implementation.

Article.Title: Engineered Factor VIII: A Comprehensive Review of Molecular Biology, Design Strategies, and AAV-Mediated Gene Therapy
Article.Authors: Khairetdinova A.; Artemyev V.; Astakhova E.; Ambaryan S.; Pilagov M.; Maznina A.; Lobanova V.; Feoktistova S.; Mityaeva O.; Volchkov P.
Article.Abstract: Coagulation factor VIII (FVIII) is a key therapeutic protein for hemophilia A, an inherited bleeding disorder caused by FVIII deficiency or dysfunction. The development and production of FVIII-based therapeutics remains challenging due to the intrinsic complexity of FVIII biosynthesis, folding, secretion, and functional stability. Advances in the understanding of the FVIII life cycle, as well as studies of its natural homologs, have created opportunities to develop improved FVIII variants. In parallel, therapeutic strategies to restore FVIII activity have evolved from replacement therapy with exogenous FVIII to gene-based delivery of a functional F8 copy. Among these approaches, AAV-mediated gene therapy has emerged as a clinically viable platform with a generally favorable safety profile, prompting the development of multiple therapeutic candidates for hemophilia A. This review summarizes established and current knowledge of FVIII structure, biosynthesis, and immunology in the context of developing effective and clinically applicable AAV-mediated therapies for hemophilia A. Particular attention is given to engineered FVIII variants and the latest clinical findings in AAV gene therapy, as well as to long-term efficacy and safety.

Article.Title: Topological Data Analysis Identifies Copy Number Variation Subtypes of Bulls Associated with Fertility
Article.Authors: Bakoev S.; Ermilov A.; Sidorenko D.; Bakoev F.; Kostyunina O.; Altukhova N.; Nemkovskiy G.; Belyakov V.
Article.Abstract: Bull fertility is a polygenic trait of significant economic importance in dairy and beef cattle, controlled by multiple genetic variants, including copy number variations (CNVs). Conventional single-variant association analyses primarily evaluate marginal effects of individual loci, whereas CNV co-occurrence patterns require complementary approaches. This study applied topological data analysis (TDA) to identify groups of bulls based on genome-wide CNVR profiles and to assess their association with insemination success rate. A total of 88 bulls were included, and the presence/absence of 406 consensus CNVR was determined for each animal. TDA was performed using the Mapper algorithm with a two-dimensional UMAP projection as the lens and DBSCAN for clustering, followed by community detection using the Leiden method. Bootstrap resampling (100 iterations) was used to assess the stability of the identified communities, and their association with fertility was tested using ANOVA and permutation testing (n = 1000). TDA with bootstrap consensus identified five bull communities ranging from 10 to 30 individuals each. The identified subtypes differed in mean insemination success rates, ranging from 48.3% to 72.5%. These differences were assessed using ANOVA and permutation testing. Gene annotation of the loci distinguishing these communities using Ensembl release 110 for the ARS-UCD1.2 assembly revealed genes potentially involved in embryonic development, cellular signaling, and immune response (e.g., IGF2, INS, NOTCH1, PAEP, TRAF2). TDA provides a framework for identifying groups of bulls with distinct combinations of CNVRs and evaluating their potential association with fertility. Due to the sample size (n = 88) and unadjusted phenotypes, the findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating. The discovered candidate genomic regions require mandatory validation and independent replication in larger cohorts before being considered for implementation in breeding programs.

Article.Title: The Role of Hypoxia-Inducible Factors (HIFs) in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Radiation Resistance
Article.Authors: Caputo C.; Dingley R.; Al-Jumaili Y.; Mageau E.; Tharmalingam S.; Tai T.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype lacking estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2 expression. Although ionizing radiation (IR) is widely used to treat TNBC, tumour radioresistance remains a major therapeutic barrier. Tumour hypoxia contributes to resistance by limiting IR-induced reactive oxygen species generation and activating pathways that promote tumour survival, progression, and aggressiveness. Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) are oxygen-sensitive transcription factors that regulate many of these pathways; however, the mechanisms underlying HIF-mediated radioresistance in TNBC remain incompletely characterized. This review examines the role of HIF signalling in TNBC radiation resistance and emerging strategies for overcoming hypoxia-mediated radioresistance. PubMed and Web of Science were searched for studies investigating HIFs, TNBC, and radiation response. Relevant studies were screened against the eligibility criteria and analyzed for mechanistic findings and therapeutic interventions targeting HIF-associated pathways. The literature indicates that HIF activation promotes radioresistance through multiple mechanisms, including altered ferroptosis and pH regulation. Proposed countermeasures include pharmacologic inhibition of HIF signalling, nanotechnology-based delivery systems, and alternative radiation-based modalities, including photodynamic and radiodynamic therapies. Collectively, these findings identify HIF signalling as a central mediator of TNBC radioresistance and a promising therapeutic target for improving radiotherapy outcomes.

Article.Title: Association Between Ambient PM2.5 Exposure and Leukocyte Telomere Length Among Rural Adults: Cross-Sectional Study in Northern Thailand
Article.Authors: Kohsuwan K.; Hongjaisee S.; Somsunun K.; Promkam N.; Santijitpakdee T.; Prapamontol T.
Article.Abstract: Ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure has been associated with oxidative stress, inflammation, and biological aging; however, evidence regarding its relationship with leukocyte telomere length (LTL) remains inconsistent, particularly in rural Southeast Asian populations. This study aimed to investigate the association between ambient PM2.5 exposure and LTL across multiple exposure windows and examine whether oxidative stress and systemic inflammation were associated with PM2.5 exposure and LTL. This cross-sectional study included 179 adults from rural communities in Northern Thailand affected by biomass-burning pollution. Cumulative average ambient PM2.5 exposure was estimated for lag 0–7, 0–14, 0–30, 0–60, and 0–90 days, corresponding to 8, 15, 31, 61, and 91 days, respectively, including the blood-collection date (day 0). Relative LTL was quantified using quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Serum 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), the Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index (SII), and the Systemic Inflammation Response Index (SIRI) were also assessed. Analyses included covariate-adjusted linear regression, exploratory wild cluster bootstrap inference, and sensitivity analyses. All p-values were unadjusted for multiple comparisons. Median relative LTL was 0.81 T/S units (Q1–Q3: 0.72–0.89). Adjusted models showed positive associations between PM2.5 and LTL at 0–30-, 0–60-, and 0–90-day windows, but not at 0–7- and 0–14-day windows. Per window-specific IQR increase in PM2.5 (8.13, 7.25, and 6.25 µg/m3, respectively), relative LTL was higher by 0.050 T/S units (95% CI: 0.012–0.089; nominal p = 0.011), 0.079 T/S units (95% CI: 0.035–0.123; nominal p < 0.001), and 0.094 T/S units (95% CI: 0.041–0.147; nominal p < 0.001). The reported confidence intervals and conventional p-values did not account for site–date clustering. In exploratory wild cluster bootstrap analyses using eight site-date groups, none of the five associations reached nominal significance (p = 0.247–0.787). The 0–30-day PM2.5 model explained an additional 3.8% of the variance in LTL (ΔR2 = 0.038; p = 0.011), while 8-OHdG contributed a further 2.4% (ΔR2 = 0.024; p = 0.041); SII and SIRI did not significantly improve model fit (p = 0.499 and 0.603, respectively). Sensitivity analyses showed positive longer-window associations with substantially varying magnitudes, whereas inverse shorter-window associations emerged in the NTAQHI-only analysis. Higher estimated ambient PM2.5 exposure was positively associated with higher measured LTL across the 0–30-, 0–60-, and 0–90-day windows in conventional adjusted models. However, sensitivity to sample composition and nonsignificant wild cluster bootstrap findings limit confidence in the robustness of these associations. Adding serum 8-OHdG, SII, or SIRI produced modest changes in model fit and did not establish mediation by oxidative stress or systemic inflammation. These exploratory findings should not be interpreted as evidence of within-person telomere change or a causal or protective effect of PM2.5.

Article.Title: A Complex Molecular Profile in Melanoma: Intratumoral Heterogeneity and Therapeutic Implications
Article.Authors: Tan Y.; Berardi G.; Guo T.; Seth A.; Olszanski A.; Wu H.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Complex molecular alterations in cancers influence tumor biology, therapeutic response, and resistance. We report a case of cutaneous melanoma demonstrating extensive intratumoral heterogeneity with important clinical implications. A 77-year-old man with stage IIA cutaneous melanoma developed an isolated nodal recurrence one year after resection. Comprehensive next-generation sequencing of the metastatic lesion revealed an uncommon genomic profile consisting of a class 3 BRAF Y472V mutation, two NF1 loss-of-function mutations, and two concurrent KIT mutations: a dominant, potentially targetable K642E mutation and a low-frequency D816V mutation associated with resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors. The tumor exhibited a high tumor mutational burden and microsatellite stability. The patient received neoadjuvant nivolumab plus relatlimab followed by surgical resection, achieving complete pathologic response. Repeat sequencing of the resected specimen demonstrated complete molecular clearance of all previously detected variants. This case illustrates the value of comprehensive genomic profiling in revealing biologically complex melanoma with coexisting driver and resistance-associated alterations. The presence of a treatment-naïve KIT resistance mutation suggests preexisting subclonal heterogeneity that may influence future targeted therapy, while high tumor mutational burden and NF1 loss may have contributed to the excellent response to immune checkpoint blockade.

Article.Title: The Lactate–Mitokine Axis in Exercise Adaptation: Linking Glycolytic and Mitochondrial Stress Signaling
Article.Authors: Tero-Vescan A.; Ștefănescu R.; Ősz B.; Buț M.; Pușcaș A.; Slevin M.
Article.Abstract: Exercise induces coordinated metabolic and mitochondrial stress responses that extend beyond ATP production to regulate cellular and systemic adaptation. Lactate, traditionally viewed as a glycolytic product, is now recognized as an oxidative substrate, interorgan carbon shuttle, and signaling metabolite, whereas mitochondrial stress promotes adaptive signaling and the release of mitokines and mitochondrial-derived peptides. This narrative review proposes the lactate–mitokine axis as a conceptual framework integrating these two exercise-responsive systems, while distinguishing experimentally established mechanisms from potential interactions that remain to be functionally validated. Repeated exercise promotes mitochondrial remodeling and increases oxidative capacity, which in turn reshapes the lactate response to subsequent exercise, as reflected by lower post-exercise lactate concentrations and enhanced lactate clearance after training. Conversely, increased lactate flux may influence mitochondrial adaptation through metabolic, redox, and receptor-dependent signaling, supporting a potentially bidirectional relationship between lactate handling and mitochondrial remodeling. The relative contribution of these interconnected responses appears exercise modality-dependent, with high-intensity, prolonged endurance, and resistance exercise generating distinct combinations of glycolytic and mitochondrial stress. Although lactate metabolism and mitochondrial stress signaling share several regulatory pathways, direct causal interactions between lactate signaling and mitokine expression or secretion during exercise remain insufficiently established. Thus, the proposed lactate–mitokine axis should be regarded as a hypothesis-generating framework requiring further experimental validation.

Article.Title: Therapeutic Advances in Mycobacterium avium Complex Pulmonary Disease: Current Treatments and Emerging Host-Directed Approaches
Article.Authors: Khachatourian N.; Takhmazian R.; Venketaraman V.
Article.Abstract: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is the leading cause of non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) pulmonary disease, with increasing incidence among aging and immunocompromised populations. Despite guideline-recommended multidrug therapy consisting of a macrolide, ethambutol, and a rifamycin, treatment remains prolonged and complicated by incomplete culture conversion, adverse effects, recurrence, and antimicrobial resistance. Intracellular persistence, biofilm formation, and intrinsic resistance mechanisms further challenge disease management. This review summarizes MAC pathogenesis, host immune responses, current treatments, and emerging therapeutic strategies. Promising approaches include novel antimicrobial agents, optimized multidrug regimens, drug repurposing, inhaled delivery systems, and host-directed therapies. Particular emphasis is placed on glutathione (GSH), an intracellular antioxidant with immunomodulatory properties, as a potential adjunctive therapy. Experimental studies suggest that GSH and its precursor N-acetylcysteine may influence oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and antimycobacterial activity. However, MAC-specific evidence remains primarily in vitro, and clinical efficacy in MAC pulmonary disease has not been established. Findings from related mycobacterial infections provide mechanistic insights but cannot be directly extrapolated to MAC pulmonary disease. Further preclinical and clinical studies are needed to determine whether GSH-based interventions can safely complement conventional antimicrobial therapy and improve treatment outcomes.

Article.Authors: Valentelyte D.; Lukosevicius R.; Steponaitiene R.; Salteniene V.; Morkunas E.; Balion Z.; Baldauskaite G.; Zemgulyte G.; Butaite G.; Kulokiene U.; Gedgaudiene G.; Kupcinskas J.; Inciuraite R.; Skieceviciene J.

No significant associations with the evaluated clinicopathological features or overall survival were detected. Article.Title: PTBP1: A Key Hub and a Potential Therapeutic Target in High-Grade Glioma
Article.Authors: Li C.; Hao S.
Article.Abstract: High-grade gliomas (HGGs) are lethal primary brain tumors with poor prognosis despite multimodal therapy. Polypyrimidine tract-binding protein 1 (PTBP1) is an RNA-binding protein that regulates alternative splicing, mRNA stability, and translation. In HGGs, PTBP1 is overexpressed and correlates with tumor grade, IDH mutation status, and patient survival, supporting it as a candidate prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target. Structurally, PTBP1 contains four RNA recognition motifs connected by flexible linkers, conferring conformational plasticity for diverse RNA interactions. In glioma cells, upstream regulators—including non-coding RNAs and post-translational modifications—dysregulate PTBP1, converting it from a physiological regulator into a predominantly oncogenic driver. Multiple lines of evidence suggest that PTBP1 drives malignancy through three interconnected mechanisms: oncogenic splicing switching, stabilization of oncogenic mRNAs, and IRES-dependent translation. Although no selective, direct small-molecule inhibitor of PTBP1 has yet been clinically validated, repurposed compounds (e.g., venetoclax) and indirect modulators have shown preliminary antitumor activity in preclinical models. However, direct target engagement, in vivo efficacy, and blood–brain barrier penetration remain insufficiently established. This review summarizes PTBP1’s structure, upstream networks, downstream mechanisms, and therapeutic potential, highlighting the need for further validation of PTBP1-centered strategies prior to clinical translation.

Article.Title: The Deubiquitinating Enzyme UCHL1 Promotes Radiotherapy Resistance in Glioma by Stabilizing Keratin 18
Article.Authors: Wang H.; Zheng R.; Liu Q.; Ding X.; Zhao Y.; Xu J.; Tang R.; Chen L.; Chen X.; Shi H.; Zhang H.; Wang W.

Agona, S. Corvallis, S. Toulon, S. Virchow. Article.Title: Mapping the MicroRNA Landscape of Arsenic Exposure: A Bibliometric and Evidence-Synthesis Analysis of Directional Consistency and Regulatory Themes
Article.Authors: Öztan G.; Kesin M.; İşsever T.; İşsever H.
Article.Abstract: Arsenic exposure has been associated with altered microRNA (miRNA) expression in human and experimental settings, yet the structure of this literature and the consistency of reported expression directions remain insufficiently characterized. This study combined a three-database bibliometric analysis with an audit of published directional evidence. Searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science on 27 August 2026 identified 1396 records, yielding 752 unique records and a 248-publication bibliometric corpus. Author-keyword analyses highlighted arsenic, microRNA regulation, carcinogenesis, and epigenetic themes, with miR-21 the most frequent individual miRNA keyword. A historical biological inventory contained 319 coded study–miRNA observations from 109 publications; its significance-conditioned selection prevents interpretation as a completed, unbiased evidence synthesis. Although legacy miR-21 directional concordance was 26/27, these codes do not establish independent biological reproducibility. Source-level adjudication of 11 of 137 previously unresolved records identified 10 exclusions and one eligible publication awaiting extraction; 126 records remain unresolved. Re-extraction of a human urinary-miRNA study recovered 18 signed arsenic-association estimates across three miRNAs, one of which (miR-423) was absent from the legacy inventory altogether. All were nonsignificant, but positive and negative estimates occurred across adjustment models, demonstrating that nonsignificance does not imply absence of effect. Aggregating the legacy miR-21 codes into senior-author units reduced the concordance to 8/9 (p = 0.039), and under a modest assumption of upward-reporting asymmetry (p0 = 0.65) the signal was no longer significant (p = 0.121). Mechanism-frequency ranking, aggregated false-discovery-rate control and mature-arm assignment are not supported by the available source data and are therefore not reported. The bibliometric mapping and source audit clarify research themes and reporting limitations, but definitive directional-consistency and biomarker-prioritization conclusions require completed source-level screening, significance-independent extraction, and verification of study independence.

Article.Title: Beyond Efficacy: Preclinical Validation and Translational Readiness of Recent Multimodal Photodynamic Nanoplatforms for Glioblastoma
Article.Authors: Woźnicki P.; Aebisher D.
Article.Abstract: Multimodal photodynamic therapy (PDT)-based nanoplatforms are increasingly being developed for glioblastoma (GBM) to improve photosensitizer delivery, overcome tumor hypoxia, and combine PDT with complementary therapeutic mechanisms. However, promising antitumor activity does not necessarily translate into adequate preclinical validation or clinical readiness. This review critically evaluates recent studies published between January 2025 and August 2026, identified through PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science. Of 3617 records screened, 35 studies met the broader eligibility criteria for nanoparticle-mediated PDT in GBM, including 19 studies incorporating in vivo evaluation. Particular attention was given to the biological relevance of experimental models, survival assessment, biodistribution, pharmacokinetics, clearance, systemic and neurological safety, and platform-specific translational limitations. Orthotopic models were used in 16 of 19 in vivo studies, whereas immunocompetent and immunodeficient hosts were represented almost equally. Nevertheless, clinically challenging settings such as post-resection disease, acquired temozolomide resistance and recurrence after standard therapy were rarely reproduced. Quantitative pharmacokinetic and elimination data were limited, and fluorescence or elemental measurements frequently reflected individual platform components rather than intact nanostructures. Safety assessments were predominantly short-term and often focused on body weight, routine blood parameters and organ histology. Overall, the current evidence demonstrates substantial therapeutic innovation but also reveals a persistent gap between antitumor efficacy and translational validation. Future studies should prioritize clinically representative models, quantitative absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME) characterization, long-term and neurological safety assessment, and comparisons with current standard-of-care treatment.

Article.Title: Genotype-Associated Molecular Phenotypes Across Brain and Gut Compartments in Male 5xFAD Mice: Shared Latent Structure and the Limits of Individual-Level Inference
Article.Authors: Sahin B.; Eken Y.; Sahin F.; Karaman T.; Sezerman O.; Ozer S.; Kaya Z.; Karagözlü M.; Serdar M.; Serteser M.; Baykal A.
Article.Abstract: Whether gut and brain molecular states covary within individual animals, rather than merely co-occurring at the group level, has rarely been tested in Alzheimer’s disease models. We profiled the hippocampus, cortex, cerebellum, intestine and feces of 18 male 5xFAD (5 familial AD mutations) (B6SJL background) mice and wild-type littermates at 3, 6 and 9 months by label-free proteomics, and feces additionally by shotgun metagenomics. The hippocampal proteome reproduced the amyloid-associated signature (App, Apoe, Hexb, Clu, Gfap), and protein-set analysis showed elevated microglial, lysosomal, astrocytic and endoplasmic reticulum chaperone proteins in the hippocampus and cortex, with no detectable difference in synaptic or mitochondrial sets. Fecal Shannon diversity was reduced, and the bile-acid-modifying genera Romboutsia and Turicibacter were nearly absent in all 5xFAD animals from 3 months (cage nested within genotype). Multi-omics factor analysis recovered a genotype-associated factor shared across brain and gut views (exact permutation p = 0.00125) that explained at most 6.3% of variance in any view and was preprocessing-dependent. After removal of group structure, correlation burden did not exceed a within-cell permutation null, and neither did same-animal positive controls. The 5xFAD genotype thus alters every compartment examined, and a modest latent structure links them; because the design excludes only strong or dense individual-level coupling, the null result bounds design resolution rather than showing that gut and brain are uncoupled.

Article.Title: Tiny Carriers, Big Impact: How Tannerella forsythia Extracellular Vesicles Drive Oral Diseases, and Beyond
Article.Authors: Shen Z.; Xu G.; Li Y.; Liu H.; Chen Z.; Chen S.; Han Q.; Wang Z.; He H.
Article.Abstract: Periodontitis influences systemic health through mechanisms that extend far beyond the periodontal pocket, yet the vehicles that mediate this dissemination remain incompletely defined. Within the “red complex” of periodontitis, Tannerella forsythia (Tf) has long been overshadowed by Porphyromonas gingivalis and Treponema denticola, and its extracellular vesicles (EVs) have been correspondingly neglected. This review synthesizes a decade of evidence to reposition Tf EVs as a distinct nanoscale virulence-delivery platform. Their biogenesis couples outer-membrane budding to the type IX secretion system (T9SS), and the crystalline surface layer (S-layer) appears to be actively reprogrammed—rather than passively shed—to accommodate vesicle curvature, a mechanism so far supported by compositional evidence. Their cargo is selectively enriched in T9SS substrates, TonB-dependent receptor/SusD-like nutrient-acquisition proteins, and extensively O-glycosylated virulence factors. Mechanistically, as demonstrated directly at the vesicle level in cellular models, Tf EVs engage Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2), autonomously prime and activate the inflammasome, and drive IL-12-dependent Th1 polarization. These properties define a “purely pro-inflammatory” immunological identity that distinguishes Tf EVs from those of P. gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum. Signature cargo, including BspA, miropin, and PepO, suggests potential links between Tf EVs and cardiovascular, articular, and pulmonary diseases; however, these systemic associations are currently inferred mainly from whole-cell, isolated-virulence-factor, or epidemiological evidence, rather than from direct Tf EV-level experiments, and are therefore presented here as testable hypotheses. We critically appraise isolation and standardization practices, delineate priority gaps such as unverified vesicle subtypes and unexplored small RNA cargo, and propose a four-step roadmap from subtype isolation to clinical cohorts. Tf EVs warrant recognition as an independent research object and a candidate druggable target for periodontitis, whereas their contribution to its systemic comorbidities awaits direct causal validation at the EV level.

Article.Title: Distinct Transcriptional Responses to 17β-Estradiol in Human Meniscal Fibrochondrocytes from a Female and a Male Donor
Article.Authors: Yu Y.; Vergis J.; Eby H.; Markho M.; Kopacz J.; Cartwright K.; Hershey M.; Liu J.; McCullumsmith R.
Article.Abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) affects women more often than men, and estrogen has been implicated in joint homeostasis, yet its effects on meniscal fibrochondrocytes (MFCs) remain poorly defined. Cells from each donor were treated in triplicate with pulsed 17β-estradiol (E2, 240 µM for 1 h every 24 h over 72 h) or vehicle control. In the male donor’s cells, E2 upregulated chromatin remodeling and developmental signaling pathways, with NOTCH1 among the leading-edge genes, and downregulated antigen presentation pathways and mitochondrial genes. At the gene level, some changes were shared by both donors, including lower TIMP1. Because each sex was represented by one donor, these differences cannot be attributed to sex with confidence. The findings are hypothesis-generating and identify candidate pathways for validation in larger, sex-balanced cohorts.

Article.Title: Biomarkers for Cancer Immunotherapy: Advances, Challenges, and Clinical Applications
Article.Authors: Ahmed A.; Haq F.
Article.Abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has revolutionized oncology by harnessing the immune system to recognize and eliminate malignant cells. Despite remarkable clinical successes, a substantial proportion of patients fail to respond or develop resistance, highlighting the urgent need for reliable biomarkers to guide patient selection, predict therapeutic outcomes, and monitor treatment responses. This review addresses both the emerging and established biomarkers for cancer immunotherapy. These include molecular, cellular, and systemic biomarkers within tumor tissues, blood, and the tumor microenvironment. The principal ones include immune checkpoint-related biomarkers (e.g., programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression), tumor mutational burden, microsatellite instability, neoantigen profiling, circulating tumor DNA, and immune cell signatures. We grade each biomarker by analytical validity, clinical validity, clinical utility and regulatory readiness; place it in one of four evidence tiers; and outline the steps needed to bring candidate markers into the clinic. Recent developments in multi-omics technologies, artificial intelligence, and single-cell analysis are accelerating biomarker discovery, providing a clearer understanding of tumor–immune interactions. Furthermore, the integration of dynamic biomarkers is critical for optimally refining therapeutic strategies for real-time monitoring and detection of resistance mechanisms. This review aims to provide a worldwide overview of present achievements, challenges, and future opportunities in biomarker research and ultimately enable the development of more personalized and effective strategies for immunotherapy of cancer.

Article.Title: Comparison of Sonidegib and Vismodegib Efficiency in Drug-Sensitive and Resistant Ovarian Cancer Cell Lines—2D and 3D Model Study
Article.Authors: Stasiak P.; Sopel J.; Płóciennik A.; Świerczewska M.; Korbecki J.; Januchowski R.
Article.Abstract: Ovarian cancer is a leading cause of mortality among gynecological malignancies. Despite the initial effectiveness of chemotherapy, multidrug resistance (MDR), driven by ABC transporters such as P-glycoprotein, limits treatment success by reducing intracellular paclitaxel (PAC) accumulation. Abnormalities in the Cancer Stem Cells signaling pathway Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) play a role in drug resistance development and ovarian cancer progression. We evaluated two Shh pathway inhibitors, Sonidegib (LDE225) and Vismodegib (VIS), in the W1 drug-sensitive ovarian cancer cell line and PAC-resistant sublines, using the 2D monolayer model, as well as the 3D spheroid model, to better simulate conditions of the tumor microenvironment. qPCR analysis showed similar levels of Shh pathway gene expression in 2D and 3D cell culture conditions. PAC-resistant cell lines were 3- to 6-fold more sensitive to both LDE225 and VIS than the PAC-sensitive cell line. LDE225 showed a 6- to 10-fold lower IC50 than Vismodegib, indicating higher potency. Both agents inhibited proliferation and colony formation in a concentration-dependent manner. Differences in IC50 between 2D and 3D dense spheroids formed by the W1 cell line were small, suggesting that high spheroid density does not reduce the activity of LDE225 and VIS against cancer cells. In conclusion, both inhibitors present pleotropic effects against ovarian cancer cells, especially drug-resistant ones, and can be considered as a new treatment opportunity in this cancer. Nevertheless, further investigation of Hedgehog pathway inhibition in more advanced models is required to assess the potential of clinical application for these compounds.

Article.Authors: Acuña M.; Carrasco S.
Article.Abstract: The N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) gene contributes to drug metabolism, yet its pharmacogenetic variation in admixed populations remains incompletely characterized. The inferred poor metabolizer proportion was 57.5% in the lowest and 26.4% in the highest ancestry quartile. Excluding four individuals with indeterminate expanded coding-variant assignments yielded a similar association (n = 343; OR = 0.80; 95% CI, 0.67–0.95; p = 0.0097). These observational associations support further genotype-based investigation but do not establish causality or replace individual NAT2 genotyping.

Article.Title: Conductive Hydrogels for Invasive Neural Interfaces: From Materials Engineering to Neural Signal Interfacing and Neurorehabilitation
Article.Authors: Chen W.; Chen X.; Shen L.; Deng J.; Wang Y.; Ran Y.; Wang Y.; Xie Y.
Article.Abstract: In invasive neural interfaces, mechanical mismatch between traditional rigid electrodes and brain tissue often leads to inflammation and signal attenuation. Conductive hydrogels have emerged as ideal alternative materials due to their tissue-matching modulus, hybrid conductive networks, and wet adhesion properties. In this paper, we provide a narrative review of research progress on conductive hydrogels in invasive neural interfaces: we elucidate electronic, ionic, and hybrid conduction mechanisms; critically compare strategies for modulus matching and interfacial adhesion (such as catechol chemistry and covalent anchoring); and summarize their applications in neural signal recording, electrical/optical modulation, and rehabilitation for spinal cord injury and stroke. Finally, we discuss current challenges regarding long-term stability, wireless integration, and intelligent closed-loop systems and outline future directions involving AI-driven design combined with 3D biomanufacturing.

Article.Title: When Can a Computed Pt(II) Substitution Rate Be Trusted? A DFT Framework with Four Reliability Diagnostics Applied to Cisplatin
Article.Authors: Spiegel M.; Mączyński M.
Article.Abstract: This study presents a DFT protocol for the substitution kinetics of Pt(II) complexes, applied to cisplatin as a case study. We aim to demonstrate that a computed barrier that agrees with experiment does not, by itself, validate the kinetic model, and that further diagnostics are required to assess the reliability of the results. M06-2X/x2c-TZVPall calculations with implicit solvation, explicit treatment of one coordinating water molecule and a set of physical corrections were used to study the aquation, thiolation (with a capped cysteine-thiolate model) and guanine substitution (by 9-methylguanine) pathways. The calculated precomplex-to-transition-state barrier for the first aquation is 2.0 kcal⋅mol−1 below the Eyring barrier inferred from experiment; with the symmetry factor σ = 2 applied, the calculated observed rate constant is 56-fold higher than the experimental value. The formal low-concentration second-order coefficient for thiolation exceeds the reported glutathione rate coefficient by 1.5–1.8 log units, whereas omission of the physical corrections shifts the calculated rate predictions by about 5–8 log units. A direct selectivity descriptor (Sdirect) is introduced and shown to be governed by the precomplex term rather than by the activation step, making it vulnerable to precomplex overstabilization by the implicit solvent. Four diagnostics are proposed that should accompany any computed rate constant or selectivity: the sign of the precomplex free energy, the magnitude of Kpre, the proximity to the diffusion limit, and the decomposition of selectivity into precomplex and activation contributions. These provide a systematic basis for assessing the reliability of computed predictions.

Anti-PD-1 immunotherapy was administered successfully in three patients with multiple or advanced skin tumors.

Article.Title: HSF/HSP Networks and Environmental Memory: From Molecular Persistence to a Recovery-Associated State
Article.Authors: De Caroli M.; Perrotta C.; Rampino P.
Article.Abstract: Plants encounter environmental stresses in sequences of exposure, recovery, and subsequent challenge. Persistent molecular changes alone do not establish how previous exposure influences later responsiveness. Sustained protection may contribute to memory, whereas unresolved physiological disturbance can complicate its interpretation. The heat shock factor/heat shock protein (HSF/HSP) system links transcriptional regulation with protein folding, quality control, and recovery, providing a framework for examining these distinctions. We assess evidence for HSF/HSP-dependent environmental memory through its temporal organisation. Recurrent heat provides the strongest causal evidence, implicating HSF activity, transcriptional and chromatin regulation, chaperone persistence, and protein turnover in distinct aspects of thermomemory. Broader stress histories reveal altered subsequent responses, but causal HSF/HSP involvement remains less clearly resolved. We define experimental criteria for characterising recovery, demonstrating history-dependent functional responses, and identifying when candidate processes contribute causally. We then propose a recovery-associated state as a heuristic working model, rather than a demonstrated discrete cellular entity, to examine how previous exposure changes the configuration of regulatory and proteostatic processes during recovery. Persistent protective components, altered relationships among processes, or consequences outlasting the initiating molecular change may shape the later response. This framework guides experiments across stress sequences and species while distinguishing established thermomemory mechanisms from hypotheses about broader environmental memory.

Article.Title: Human Organoids in Radiation Research: Modeling Tissue Injury, Regeneration and Therapeutic Response
Article.Authors: Hao X.; Li Z.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: Radiation therapy is a cornerstone in the treatment of abdominal, pelvic, thoracic, head and neck and central nervous system malignancies. However, irradiation inevitably damages adjacent normal tissues, leading to radiation-induced enteritis, lung injury, cardiac injury, salivary gland dysfunction and brain injury, which compromise both quality of life and treatment outcomes. Traditional two-dimensional cell cultures and animal models have significant limitations in mimicking human tissue radiation responses: the former lacks three-dimensional architecture and cell–cell interactions, while the latter exhibits species-specific differences. In recent years, three-dimensional organoid technology has rapidly emerged as a powerful platform in radiation biology and radiation oncology. In particular, organoids derived from patient tissues or induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) offer key advantages, including self-organization capacity and near-physiological tissue structure and function, which have greatly advanced in-depth research in the radiation field. This review comprehensively summarizes applications of human organoids in radiation injury and regeneration research across the brain, heart, lung, esophagus, salivary gland, intestine, muscle, thyroid, hematopoietic system, and tumors. Animal-derived and organotypic models are included only as comparative or supporting mechanistic evidence and are explicitly identified as such. We focus on advances in modeling radiation injury, elucidating regenerative mechanisms, screening radioprotective and radiosensitizing agents and predicting patient responses to chemoradiation. Current limitations and future directions are discussed collectively at the end.

Article.Title: Single-Cell RNA Sequencing of Human Lamina Cribrosa Fibroblasts in Glaucoma
Article.Authors: Normile C.; Irnaten M.; Cappa O.; Zhernovkov V.; O’Callaghan J.; Moran B.; Culligan E.; Feris S.; Curry S.; Clark A.; Simpson D.; O’Brien C.
Article.Abstract: The molecular mechanisms that underlie the extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling of the human lamina cribrosa (LC) in glaucoma remain obscure. This is the first study to characterise human glaucomatous LC cells using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). Our aim is to characterise transcriptional changes in human LC cells from glaucomatous and normal eyes and identify signalling pathways contributing to optic nerve head remodelling. scRNA-seq was performed on LC cells from glaucomatous and normal donor eyes. Differential gene expression was analysed using Seurat. Cell identity was assessed using SingleR and GTEx reference datasets. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), and transcription factor (TF) motif enrichment was evaluated using i-cisTarget. Validation was performed using quantitative PCR, Western blotting, immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence. LC cells were treated with ISRIB and 4-PBA. Analysis of 6131 LC cells using shared nearest-neighbour clustering and UMAP visualisation identified four broad transcriptional groups, which were used for subsequent transcriptional characterisation. Cell type mapping identified a fibroblast/mesenchymal cell origin. Glaucomatous LC fibroblasts demonstrated a pro-fibrotic transcriptional profile, with overexpression of multiple pro-fibrotic genes, master TF regulons involved in cell fate decisions, and TF motifs including SRF, as well as key integrated stress response (ISR) genes such as ATF4, ATF3 and CREB3L1. Enriched pathways included E2F, G2M, the Hallmark EMT gene set and MYC, while the p53 pathway was downregulated. Pharmacologic treatment with ISRIB or 4-PBA reduced expression of stress-response and ECM genes, while ISRIB attenuated the increased cellular metabolic activity observed in glaucomatous LC cells. Bioinformatic analysis of scRNA-seq of human glaucoma LC cells identified increased expression of myofibroblast genes, an EMT-associated/profibrotic transcriptional programme, and cell cycle signalling pathways, TF regulatory elements and stress response genes.

Article.Title: Effects of BL Exposure on Circadian Rhythms and Rhythm-Related Disorders
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Pei X.; Ge C.; Chen J.; Xu J.; Wu J.; Lu H.; Xu L.; Weng H.; Chen X.; Deng L.; Xu H.
Article.Abstract: Circadian rhythms represent a core physiological mechanism sustaining human physiological homeostasis and normal bodily function. Environmental light serves as a primary exogenous zeitgeber for circadian regulation. Among visible light spectral components, BL (BL) exerts a critical modulatory influence on the circadian system, with dual implications for physiological regulation and clinical intervention: excessive or inappropriately timed exposure may lead to circadian disruption, whereas appropriately timed BL interventions show potential to improve circadian alignment in selected populations. Accumulated evidence indicates that circadian disruption is associated with sleep disorders, mood disturbances, neurodegenerative disorders, as well as metabolic and immune dysfunction, and may have bidirectional relationships with disease progression. Nevertheless, most existing studies concentrate on circadian modulation by broad-spectrum light. Few efforts have synthesized the molecular mechanisms, potential disease-related pathways, and targeted intervention frameworks of BL-associated circadian disruption, and the translational potential of BL’s bidirectional effects remains under-summarized, forming a prominent research gap. To fill this gap, this narrative review centers on the “BL-circadian rhythm-disease” regulatory axis. It outlines biological pathways in which circadian disruption may be implicated in multiple neurodegenerative disorders, highlights the circadian-modulating properties of BL, describes evidence linking inappropriate BL exposure to circadian disruption and disease onset or progression, and compiles clinical findings on BL-based interventions and their potential benefits for circadian function and selected disease-related symptoms. However, much of the evidence derives from observational studies and animal experiments, and a causal pathway linking BL exposure to disease through circadian disruption has not been definitively established. This review discusses the potential adverse and beneficial effects of BL in circadian disruption-related pathologies, addresses current research limitations, and offers theoretical references and fresh insights for mechanistic investigations, clinical research, and translational development of BL-targeted interventions.
