Article.Title: Drug Design Studio (DDS) 4.0: A Nano-Pharmaceutical Platform for Modelling of Drug–Drug Complexation and Drug–Nanocarrier Encapsulation and Interactions
Article.Authors: Soliman M.
Article.Abstract: Once a candidate molecule has been designed, its therapeutic value in practice is often decided not by its intrinsic potency but by whether it can be formulated—dissolved, stabilised and delivered. Modern pharmaceutics addresses this with nanoscale carriers (cyclodextrins, dendrimers, polymeric nanoparticles, micelles, liposomes and carbon nanomaterials, etc.) and with carrier-free solid-form engineering such as pharmaceutical cocrystals. Predicting, before the bench, whether a given drug will associate with a chosen carrier, in what geometry, and through which specific interactions is therefore of central practical importance, yet it remains fragmented, and expertise-intensive: the researcher must generate three-dimensional conformers, place the guest into a host cavity or onto its surface, minimise the assembly with a molecular-mechanics force field that correctly retains inter-molecular terms, and most importantly analyse the different interaction forces and estimate the binding affinities and solvent effects—each step in a different tool and none accessible to a typical formulation scientist. Here, we present the Nano Bio-Pharmaceutical Modelling module of Drug Design Studio (DDS), an integrated platform that models both drug–nanocarrier and carrier-free drug–drug complexes in one interface. From a SMILES string and a built-in carrier library, DDS generates conformers, runs a deterministic, geometry-aware global search (regime-adaptive random-restart and basin-hopping Monte-Carlo-minimization), and reports an interaction energy decomposed into van der Waals, electrostatic and non-polar terms under a gas-phase or implicit-water model, with hydrogen-bond, hydrophobic and π-stacking profiles, 2D/3D interaction maps, and selectable stoichiometry and thoroughness tiers. We validate the module at two levels over twenty-nine complexes spanning four association regimes. First, mode reproduction: this recovers the experimentally established association geometry across all four regimes—cyclodextrin inclusion, dendrimer-surface complexation, carbon-nanomaterial adsorption and carrier-free drug–drug cocrystals. Second, quantitative agreement: across twelve α-, β- and γ-cyclodextrin inclusion complexes, the predicted implicit-water interaction energy correlates with the experimental binding free energy at Pearson r = 0.85 (p < 0.001; Spearman ρ = 0.73), rising from r = 0.73 in the gas phase—evidence that the implicit-solvent treatment captures the dominant energetic determinants of aqueous binding and tracks the experimental thermodynamic trend (a correlation and correct ranking). The Nano module shares one application and compute engine with the docking, covalent/non-covalent virtual-screening, network-pharmacology and QSAR modules of earlier DDS releases. DDS is publicly and freely accessible software for academic use.

Article.Title: Molecular Science of Eicosapentaenoic Acid (EPA) Omega-3 Fatty Acid Using Nannochloropsis oceanica as a Model Organism
Article.Authors: Stephens E.; Thomas-Hall S.; Galea V.; Heimann K.
Article.Abstract: The EPA-rich marine microalga Nannochloropsis oceanica provides insight into EPA biosynthesis via the characterized Δ6-desaturase pathway, positioning this microalga for both experimental research and sustainable production solutions for non-fish oil-derived EPA oils. This review constructs a comprehensive molecular-to-clinical framework demonstrating how the chemical structure of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) determines its biological activities, i.e., the specific positioning of the Δ17 double bond governs competitive enzymatic metabolism with arachidonic acid (ARA), yielding attenuated 3-series and 5-series eicosanoids while uniquely enabling E-series resolvin biosynthesis. Metabolic pathway modulation (AMPK, NF-κB, and SREBP-1c) translate biochemical events into transcriptional reprogramming. Sustained alterations in gene expression, membrane composition, and inflammatory mediator profiles manifest as clinical benefits across cardiovascular disease, metabolic disorders, inflammatory conditions, and psychiatric illnesses. The pleiotropic nature of EPA effectssimultaneously anti-inflammatory, TAG-lowering, anti-arrhythmic, insulin-sensitizing, and pro-resolving — arises not from independent mechanisms but from coordinated, multi-level integration. The ARA:EPA ratio emerges as the unifying quantitative biomarker, integrating dietary intake, competitive membrane incorporation, eicosanoid biosynthetic balance, and tissue-level inflammatory tone into a single metric predictive of disease risk and therapeutic response. Lowering this ratio through EPA supplementation represents a systems-level intervention: simultaneously reducing pro-inflammatory mediator production, enhancing resolution capacity, improving metabolic flexibility, and stabilizing cellular energetics.

Article.Title: Natural Products for Rheumatoid Arthritis Therapy: Research Progress and Translational Perspectives
Article.Authors: Zhou Q.; Song Z.; Xu B.; Zhang C.; Xing X.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovial inflammation, progressive joint destruction, and substantial systemic complications. Although current pharmacological therapies have improved disease control, important unmet needs for RA remission remain owing to the incomplete response, loss of efficacy, long-term safety concerns, limited capacity for tissue repair, and barriers related to accessibility and adherence. Against this background, natural products have emerged as an important area of interest in RA therapy research because many of them can modulate multiple components of the pathogenic network, including immune dysregulation, synovial inflammation, oxidative stress, and structural damage. Therefore, this review provides an updated overview of natural products for RA treatment, with emphasis on their therapeutic effects, mechanistic basis, and translational potential as well as key challenges. In particular, we discuss the natural-product research in RA therapy along an evolving continuum, from traditionally used complex natural products, such as herbal medicines and venom-based preparations, to structurally defined bioactive compounds, including flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and polysaccharides. The review further summarizes the principal pharmacological actions of these agents, their advantages and limitations in anti-RA intervention, and current strategies to enhance their development, including formulation optimization, delivery systems, and mechanism-guided translational approaches.

Article.Title: Heat-Killed Ligilactobacillus salivarius FFIG56 Modulates Innate Immune Response in Bovine Mammary Epithelial Cells
Article.Authors: Fukuyama K.; Albarracin L.; Arellano-Arriagada L.; Gong W.; Nishiyama K.; Uemoto Y.; Haga S.; Shirakawa H.; Aso H.; Villena J.; Kitazawa H.
Article.Abstract: Immunomodulatory lactic acid bacteria (immunobiotics) have been proposed to prevent bovine mastitis through the enhancement of host immune responses. Furthermore, accumulating evidence suggests that non-viable immunobiotics (postimmunobiotics) can be as effective as viable bacteria in modulating immunity in the bovine host. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the immunomodulatory effects of heat-inactivated lactic acid bacteria in bovine mammary epithelial cells remain incompletely understood. In the present study, we evaluated the effects of heat-killed Ligilactobacillus salivarius FFIG56 (hk-FFIG56) on the Toll-like receptor (TLR)-4-mediated innate immune response in bovine mammary epithelial cells (BMECs) in vitro. BMECs were pre-stimulated with hk-FFIG56 and subsequently challenged with Escherichia coli-derived lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Transcriptomic analyses revealed that, compared with cells stimulated with LPS alone, hk-FFIG56-pretreated BMECs exhibited 743 upregulated and 881 downregulated genes, indicating substantial changes in the LPS-induced transcriptional response. Among the inflammatory mediators evaluated, hk-FFIG56 pretreatment significantly reduced LPS-induced interleukin-6 (IL-6) and interleukin-8 (IL-8) expression at 12 h, as well as CCL2 expression at 6 and 12 h, compared with cells challenged with LPS alone at the corresponding time points. Differential regulation of the negative regulators of TLR signaling, IRAK-M, Tollip, and Mitogen-activated protein kinase phosphatase 1 (MKP-1), was also detected in BMECs pretreated with hk-FFIG56. In addition, hk-FFIG56 pretreatment prevented LPS-induced reduction in IκBα protein levels, whereas no significant changes were detected in the p-ERK/ERK ratio at the evaluated time points. Furthermore, hk-FFIG56 pretreatment attenuated the LPS-induced reduction in CSN3 (κ-casein) mRNA expression in BMECs. Overall, these results suggest that hk-FFIG56 modulates LPS-induced inflammatory responses and CSN3 mRNA expression in BMECs, supporting its potential as a postimmunobiotic candidate for further investigation in the context of bovine mastitis prevention.

Article.Title: Metadata-Driven Project-Level Analysis and Noise Modeling for Amplicon Sequencing Data Using CRISPResso2
Article.Authors: Volodina O.; Smirnikhina S.
Article.Abstract: Here we present a lightweight workflow designed to improve the robustness and scalability of high-throughput amplicon sequencing analysis while leveraging CRISPResso2. To handle large batch processing without sensitive runtime interruptions, our pipeline processes samples sequentially, allowing the analysis to resume from the last successfully completed sample if an error occurs. The workflow implements a fallback mechanism for failed runs, automated extraction and separate processing of control samples, and a background noise model derived from control libraries within defined editing windows. Validation using spike-in datasets across Cas9, base editing, and prime editing demonstrated that our noise-adjusted estimates deviated from the ground truth by only 0.1–0.6%, whereas native CRISPResso2 caused a 1.5–3.7% overestimation. Unlike existing tools such as CRISPECTOR, which focus primarily on CRISPR-Cas9, our approach supports multiple editing modalities and enables project-level organization of large datasets. Input complexity is reduced through configurable flags and modular metadata tables, minimizing manual parameter entry. Together, these features provide a flexible, fault-tolerant, and highly accurate framework for analyzing large genome editing datasets.

Article.Abstract: Small supernumerary marker chromosomes (sSMCs) are additional chromosomal elements smaller than or equal to chromosome 20, with a prevalence of ~0.044% in the population. Their clinical impact ranges from asymptomatic carriage to severe congenital, neurodevelopmental, and other disorders. Accurate diagnosis and interpretation remain challenging due to their small physical size, frequent tissue-specific mosaicism, and variable expression of similar gene content across different genetic backgrounds, which is well known for numerous clinically significant gene variants. This review synthesizes current knowledge on sSMC biology, diagnostics, and clinical management, highlighting the paradigm shift from classical cytogenetics to high-resolution genomic and cytogenomic approaches, including long-read genome sequencing combined with telomere-to-telomere chromosome assemblies. We present an updated sSMC classification based on sSMC DNA content and structural organization, discuss molecular mechanisms of sSMC biogenesis, and critically evaluate the diagnostic utility of microarray comparative genomic hybridization, whole-genome sequencing, and chromosome microdissection-based approaches. We also discuss breakpoint positions in sSMC formation, sSMC localization in nuclear spatial compartments, and tissue distribution patterns as factors with possible influence on the sSMC manifestation. Some of these properties might be used as criteria for assessing the pathogenic potential of sSMCs, while others require further investigation. Furthermore, we refine pathogenicity assessment frameworks by incorporating sSMC content and morphology. By integrating cutting-edge molecular cytogenetics with standardized interpretive guidelines, this narrative review provides a useful framework for precise sSMC characterization, which is essential for genetic counseling and targeted clinical management.

Article.Title: Integration of Transcriptomic and Metabolomic Profiling as a Source of Insight into Key Candidate Genes and Metabolic Pathways Associated with Maize Resistance to Fusarium spp.
Article.Authors: Lenort M.; Tomkowiak A.; Bocianowski J.; Stuper-Szablewska K.; Kosiada T.; Jarzyniak K.; Bobrowska R.; Wolko Ł.; Gawrysiak P.; Padiasek W.
Article.Abstract: Fusarium spp. infections substantially reduce maize productivity, making the identification of molecular and metabolic mechanisms underlying host resistance important for breeding. This study aimed to characterize the maize response to Fusarium infection by integrating pathogen colonization, the expression of 17 candidate genes, and metabolite profiles. Five maize genotypes differing in resistance were inoculated with a mixture of Fusarium spores and analyzed at 0, 6, 12, 24, and 48 h post-inoculation. Six Fusarium species were identified, with F. poae and F. culmorum predominating in susceptible genotypes. Colonization exceeded 70% in susceptible samples, whereas resistant genotypes generally showed 0–2% colonization. Gene expression patterns were strongly genotype- and time-dependent, with 24 h post-inoculation representing a major point of transcriptional activation. Several genes were strongly induced in the susceptible genotype, whereas selected genes, including Putrescine hydroxycinnamoyltransferase (LOC103649226), showed constitutive or induced expression associated with resistant genotypes. Resistant lines, particularly SMH 57524 and SMH 57624, showed higher concentrations of selected phenolic acids and luteolin glycosides and higher peroxidase, polyphenol oxidase, and catalase activities. Regression analyses revealed significant associations between candidate gene expression and the accumulation of selected metabolites, including ferulic, diferulic, p-coumaric, and caffeic acids, as well as lutein, with both positive and negative relationships being detected. These findings indicate that maize resistance to Fusarium is associated with coordinated transcriptional, metabolic, and redox responses and identify gene–metabolite relationships relevant to the molecular characterization of resistance.

Article.Title: DNA Repair Pathways as Determinants of PARP Inhibitor Resistance and Therapeutic Targets in Cancer
Article.Authors: Lavudi K.; Renjith M.; Pithana Sai Venkata Vijay C.; Kokkanti R.; Pandey P.; Ponneganti S.
Article.Abstract: Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) have transformed the treatment landscape for homologous recombination-deficient (HRD) cancers, particularly those harboring BRCA1/2 mutations, including breast, ovarian, prostate, and pancreatic cancers, by exploiting the synthetic lethality induced by HR deficiency (HRD) and utilizing HRD status as a predictive biomarker. Nevertheless, intrinsic as well as acquired resistance limits their long-term effectiveness. Resistance often develops as a result of several complex mechanisms including the restoration of homologous recombination (HR), stabilization of the replication fork, enhanced drug efflux, loss of PARP1 expression, epigenetic modifications, and changes in the DNA damage response signaling. BRCA1/2-mutant cells, deficient in HR, become reliant on alternative repair pathways like classical non-homologous end joining (c-NHEJ) and microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ). Emerging evidence indicates the importance of replication-induced gaps in single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and alternative pathways of DNA repair in defining PARPi sensitivity and resistance. This review aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the established and emerging molecular mechanisms of PARPi resistance, and compensatory DNA repair pathways such as MMEJ. In addition to highlighting resistance pathways, the review also discusses strategies focusing on targeting repair mechanisms and replication stress signaling by using novel drugs targeting DNA polymerase theta (POLQ). It subsequently discusses preclinical advancements and ongoing clinical trials. Through linking the molecular determinants of resistance to the translational status and limitations of the latest therapies, this review offers a comparative framework for understanding resistance mechanisms and strategies to restore PARPi sensitivity in cancers with HRD.

Article.Title: Biphasic Modulation of Absence Seizures by Lisuride in GAERS: Dissecting the Role of 5-HT2A Receptors
Article.Authors: Venzi M.; Crunelli V.; Di Giovanni G.
Article.Abstract: Serotonergic signalling modulates absence seizures, and activation of 5-HT2A receptors with TCB-2 suppresses spike-and-wave discharges in Genetic Absence Epilepsy Rats from Strasbourg (GAERS). We investigated the effects of lisuride, a serotonergic and dopaminergic ligand with low 5-HT2A receptor signalling efficacy, and examined the contribution of these receptors. Spontaneous seizures were recorded in freely moving male GAERS following systemic administration of lisuride (0.1 or 0.5 mg/kg), with or without pretreatment with the 5-HT2A receptor antagonist MDL11,939. Low-dose lisuride produced a modest pro-absence effect, whereas the higher dose produced a biphasic response: early seizure suppression followed by increased seizure activity. MDL11,939 did not abolish the early suppression, but the late increase observed with lisuride alone was not observed following pretreatment. These findings suggest that the early and late responses involve different mechanisms, with 5-HT2A receptors potentially contributing to the later phase. Lisuride’s effects differ from those reported for the potent 5-HT2A receptor TCB-2, consistent with its broader receptor profile. Further work is needed to determine the contribution of its other targets, including dopaminergic receptors.

Article.Title: Natural Bitter Compounds, Intestinal TAS2Rs, and GLP-1 Secretion: Mechanistic Evidence and Translational Challenges
Article.Authors: Lao W.; Liu X.; Zhou J.; Zhu F.; Li J.; Xu W.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: Bitter taste receptors (TAS2Rs) are expressed beyond the oral cavity, and those in the intestine have been implicated in metabolic regulation. Selected natural bitter compounds (NBCs) increase glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) release in experimental enteroendocrine models, but predicted ligand binding, functional receptor activation, and receptor-dependent hormone secretion do not provide equivalent evidence. Intestinal TAS2Rs may thus provide a route to endogenous GLP-1 modulation distinct from receptor agonist therapy. Unlike broader reviews of extraoral chemosensing, this review maps these distinct endpoints for individual NBC-TAS2R pairs and separates measured GLP-1 release from changes in proglucagon expression. We define a receptor-supported enteroendocrine core and distinguish it from indirect evidence and testable hypotheses concerning microbiota-associated, immune–endocrine, and gut–brain interfaces. Receptor-directed perturbation supports selected compound-specific secretory responses, whereas the three proposed interfaces lack complete NBC-TAS2R-GLP-1 causal chains. We critically compare human-derived cell lines, animal models, primary tissues, and organoids, and summarize the experimental concentrations and GLP-1 assay endpoints where reported. Finally, we identify priorities for receptor-selective validation, measurement of intestinal target-site exposure, and prospective human studies. This evidence map clarifies what is experimentally supported and what must be demonstrated before intestinal TAS2Rs can be considered reliable targets for endogenous GLP-1 modulation.

Article.Title: Age-Related and Region-Specific Morphological and Molecular Alterations of Astrocytes and Microglia Following Chronic Oxidative Stress in Male Wistar Rats
Article.Authors: Sentyabreva A.; Gerasimov A.; Melnikova E.; Kharisova C.; Aliper G.; Kosyreva A.
Article.Abstract: Aging is associated with chronic pro-inflammatory background and increased risk of susceptibility to oxidative stress and neurodegenerative processes. However, age-dependent morphological and molecular changes in glial cells under chronic oxidative stress remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to investigate age- and region-specific alterations in astrocytes and microglia in the hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex (EntC) of adult (4–6 months) and old (22–24 months) male Wistar rats following chronic AlCl3 administration (100 mg/kg/day for 60 days). Spatial learning and memory were assessed using the Morris water maze. GFAP+ astrocytes and Iba1+ microglia were evaluated by immunohistochemistry and morphometry. Hippocampal 4-HNE and pTau (Ser404) were assessed by ELISA and Western blotting, respectively. Hippocampal expression of Tnf, Tgfb, Mmp9, Bdnf, Ntrk2, and Gpx4 was evaluated by RT-qPCR, while serum MMP-9 and HSP-70 concentrations were measured by ELISA. Aging was associated with increased glial cell size in both brain regions, elevated hippocampal Tnf expression, decreased Tgfb and Ntrk2 expression, and increased serum MMP-9 and HSP-70 serum concentrations. In adult rats, AlCl3 exposure was accompanied by changes in astrocytic morphology and increased Iba1+ cell density in the EntC, whereas molecular compensatory mechanisms remained preserved in the hippocampus. Only old AlCl3-treated rats demonstrated reduced success in locating the former platform position in the Morris water maze and significantly elevated hippocampal 4-HNE levels, consistent with increased lipid peroxidation. Although hippocampal pTau (Ser404) immunoreactivity showed an age-related increase, no statistically significant effect of AlCl3 exposure or age + AlCl3 was detected. In this group, AlCl3 exposure was associated with increased Iba1+ cell density in both regions, hypertrophic astrocytic morphology in the hippocampus, and reduced astrocytic area with fragmented processes in the EntC. These changes coincided with decreased hippocampal Bdnf and Gpx4 expression, as well as co-existence of reduced serum MMP-9 and HSP-70 concentrations. Overall, these findings demonstrate that aging influences region-specific glial morphological alterations and associated molecular responses to chronic AlCl3-induced oxidative stress. This model demonstrated a translational approach to provide insights regarding mechanisms of age-related neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Engineering Lipid Nanoparticles Beyond ApoE-Mediated Liver Tropism: Design Strategies for Extrahepatic and Organ-Selective Delivery
Article.Authors: Rachamala H.; Medigovic G.; Atla S.; Angom R.
Article.Abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have evolved into a significant delivery technology for nucleic acid therapies, including messenger RNA (mRNA), small interfering RNA (siRNA), and genome editing tools. Although LNPs have demonstrated therapeutic success, they display strong tropism to the liver when systemically delivered, thus restricting their use for targeted delivery to extrahepatic organs. The major factor responsible for the liver targeting of LNPs is the binding of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) to the nanoparticle surface, which enables their recognition by lipoprotein receptors and uptake by liver cells. However, increasing evidence suggests that the tropism of LNPs can be altered by controlling lipid composition, physical and chemical properties, and acquired biological properties. This review discusses the mechanisms responsible for the liver tropism of LNPs as well as recent trends in modulating LNP tropism to extrahepatic organs. How ionizable lipids, helper lipids and sterols, PEG-lipids, LNP properties, and interaction with the protein corona can impact the organ tropism of LNPs as well as approaches for active and endogenous targeting of LNPs for organ- and cell-specific delivery are discussed. The challenges associated with organ- and cell-selective delivery of nucleic acids, such as delivery to functionally specific cell populations, endosomal release, species-specific translation, safety, repeated dosing, and clinical translation, are also described.

Article.Title: Comparative Analysis of Conformational Dynamics and Nucleotide Binding in miniGαi1 and Full-Length Gαi1
Article.Authors: Duan L.; Chung K.
Article.Abstract: Mini G proteins (miniG proteins) are engineered Gα constructs lacking the α-helical domain (AHD) and are widely used to stabilize active G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) conformations for structural and biochemical studies. However, the intrinsic conformational and nucleotide-binding properties of miniG proteins remain incompletely understood relative to their full-length counterparts. Here, we compared miniGαi1 and full-length Gαi1 using fluorescence-based nucleotide-binding assays and hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS). BODIPY–FL–GTP assays showed that miniGαi1 interacted with GTP more rapidly and produced higher fluorescence intensity than full-length Gαi1. Unlike full-length Gαi1, miniGαi1 did not exhibit fluorescence decay following nucleotide binding, suggesting impaired or absent GTP hydrolysis activity. HDX-MS analysis demonstrated globally higher deuterium uptake in miniGαi1, particularly in regions associated with nucleotide binding and GPCR interaction. These results indicate that miniGαi1 adopts a more solvent-accessible and conformationally dynamic state than GDP-bound full-length Gαi1. Together, our findings provide biochemical and structural insight into the intrinsic properties of miniG proteins.

Article.Title: Kynureninase Is a Prognostic Biomarker of Poor Survival and Gemcitabine Resistance in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
Article.Authors: Mercanoglu B.; Schraps N.; Giannou A.; Zhang S.; Papazoglou E.; Schroeder C.; Hong Z.; Kwiatkowski M.; Schlüter H.; Uzunoglu F.; Grotelüschen R.; Melling N.; Bockhorn M.; Hackert T.; Wolters-Eisfeld G.; Güngör C.
Article.Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies, largely due to intrinsic or acquired resistance to systemic therapy. In addition to dysregulated glucose metabolism, emerging evidence implicates amino acid metabolism as a key determinant of tumor growth and treatment adaptation. To identify biomarkers associated with chemoresistance, we performed SILAC-based mass spectrometry secretome profiling of gemcitabine-resistant and chemosensitive PDAC cell models, followed by qRT-PCR and immunoblot validation. Functional relevance was assessed by stable shRNA-mediated KYNU knockdown, proliferation assays, and Transwell migration assays. Clinical significance was evaluated by immunohistochemical analysis of KYNU expression in a PDAC tissue microarray (n = 368) and correlation with overall survival. Transcriptomic and pathway enrichment analyses were used to characterize resistance-associated programs. Kynureninase (KYNU), a tryptophan-catabolic enzyme, was upregulated and preferentially secreted by gemcitabine-resistant cells and induced by gemcitabine, interferon-γ, and hypoxia. KYNU knockdown significantly reduced proliferation without affecting migration. Resistant cells displayed higher KYNU expression and a broader therapy-adapted cellular state. In patient samples, high KYNU expression was associated with significantly shorter overall survival (p = 0.0198). These findings identify KYNU as a marker of a therapy-adapted PDAC phenotype and support its potential as a prognostic and treatment-response biomarker.

Article.Title: Upstream ORFs as Regulators of Viral Replication
Article.Authors: Agapkina Y.; Mashkovskaia A.; Shekhtman S.; Korolev S.; Kikhai T.; Anisenko A.; Gottikh M.
Article.Abstract: Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are widespread regulatory elements located in the 5′-untranslated regions of eukaryotic and viral mRNAs. Once considered rare exceptions to the canonical scanning model, uORFs are now recognized as actively translated features present in approximately half of human transcripts, frequently initiating at non-canonical start codons. In eukaryotes, uORFs fine-tune protein synthesis in response to cellular stress by modulating ribosome reinitiation, as exemplified by the stress-dependent regulation of ATF4 and GCN4. In viral genomes, uORFs serve as compact, evolutionarily conserved modules that optimize protein stoichiometry, coordinate expression with the host cell state, and support persistent infection across diverse viral families through cis-regulation of translation. Beyond this, uORF-encoded peptides (uPeptides) can possess independent biological activities, influencing virulence, tissue tropism, and immune modulation. In this review, we systematize the available data on the dual functionality of uORFs as cis-regulatory elements of translation and as sources of bioactive uPeptides in viruses. Deciphering the full spectrum of uORF-mediated mechanisms may reveal novel layers of viral replication control and uncover potential targets for antiviral development, although, as discussed here, the available evidence for such applications is still largely limited to proof-of-principle mutagenesis.

Article.Title: Identifying a Shared Metabolomic Signature in Mother–Newborn Dyads With and Without Gestational Diabetes: Implications for Early Metabolic Programming
Article.Authors: Omaña-Guzmán I.; López-Alvarenga J.; Palacios-González B.; Jaramillo-Pimentel F.; Lanz-Pérez L.; Alvarado-González A.; Díaz-Olivares C.; Carranco-Martínez J.; Vela-Amieva M.; Ibarra-González I.; Garibay-Nieto N.
Article.Abstract: Pregnancy is a critical window for metabolic programming, during which adverse intrauterine exposures may influence long-term health. GDM alters the intrauterine environment, but its role in early metabolic programming remains poorly understood. Thus, the objective of this study was to identify the shared metabolomic signature in mother–newborn dyads and to assess whether GDM modifies this signature. For this purpose, we conducted a cross-sectional study including mother–newborn dyads recruited at the General Hospital of Mexico. Blood samples were collected from dyads. Sparse partial least squares (sPLS) analysis was used to identify shared metabolomic signatures within mother–newborn dyads. Two shared metabolomic signatures were identified. The first, characterized by arginine, methionine, acetylcarnitine, and free carnitine, showed a strong maternal–newborn correlation. Although this core signature was preserved in both groups, valine and alanine contributed exclusively to the GDM-exposed dyads. In conclusion, a shared metabolomic signature related to fetal development and energy metabolism was conserved regardless of GDM status, although GDM partially modified this signature. These findings provide insights into metabolic processes potentially involved in early metabolic programming.

Article.Title: AlvaQSAR: A Web-Based Platform for Molecular Prediction of Environmental and Toxicological Endpoints Aligned with OECD Principles
Article.Authors: Mauri A.; Bertola M.
Article.Abstract: AlvaQSAR is a web platform for quantitative structure-activity/property relationship (QSAR/QSPR) prediction designed to support rapid molecular screening together with the transparency needed for scientific and regulatory use. The platform combines browser-based molecular input, endpoint selection, prediction, applicability-domain evaluation, and downloadable reporting within a compact workflow, while relying on the Alvascience software ecosystem for molecular standardization, descriptor calculation, and model execution. In version 1.2, the platform provides access to nine models covering environmental fate, bioaccumulation, aquatic toxicity, and human toxicity endpoints, and complements predictions with supporting information such as molecular properties, model documentation, prediction report, and QSAR Model Reporting Format (QMRF) files to address key OECD-oriented expectations on defined endpoints, unambiguous algorithms, validation, and applicability-domain assessment. It aims to facilitate practical use of QSAR models for early screening, communication, and regulatory assessment.

Article.Title: Changing Course: Semaphorins and Plexins as Novel Therapeutic Opportunities and Key Regulators of Pancreatic Cancer Microenvironment
Article.Authors: Bertalmio N.; Marino F.; Brundu S.; Rustichelli S.; Giraudo E.
Article.Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest solid tumors, and despite recent advances in surgical and systemic therapies, outcomes remain poor, rooted as much in the genetic mutations that initiate the disease as in a fibrotic, poorly vascularized microenvironment marked by scarce immune infiltration and a dense network of nerve fibers. Semaphorins, together with their receptors plexins and co-receptors neuropilins, have emerged as pivotal orchestrators of this microenvironment, shaping crosstalk between malignant cells, fibroblasts, macrophages, the endothelium, and peripheral neurons. This review examines how individual semaphorin family members drive, or in select contexts restrain, stromal activation, immune exclusion, pathological angiogenesis and neural remodeling. Building on this mechanistic framework, we explore the clinical relevance that semaphorin-mediated signaling holds for PDAC, from its potential as a prognostic and predictive biomarker to its growing promise as a therapeutic target, positioning this axis as a compelling frontier for improving outcomes in a disease that has long resisted meaningful therapeutic advances.

Article.Title: Electrospun Poly(lactide-co-glycolide-co-ε-caprolactone) as a Bioresorbable Platform for Docetaxel-Degradation, Drug Delivery Study and Anticancer Activity
Article.Authors: Jaworska J.; Orchel A.; Kaps A.; Jaworska-Kik M.; Stojko M.; Musiał-Kulik M.; Kaczmarczyk B.; Pastusiak M.; Kasperczyk J.
Article.Abstract: Drug delivery systems are constantly being developed or modified to meet various requirements, but most of all, they are designed to provide controlled, sustained, and targeted drug delivery. A popular technique of the last few years involves the encapsulation of drugs into polymeric nanofibers with the use of electrospinning. The parameters of the process strongly influence not only the morphology of the fibers but the properties of the whole electrospun system, including the drug release profile. In this study, poly(lactide-co-glycolide-co-ε-caprolactone) and docetaxel were used for the electrospinning process in combination with different kinds of solvents to obtain implantable drug delivery systems. By contrast, the courses of degradation were similar, except during the last period. Drug-loaded electrospun systems exerted a strong cytotoxic effect on DU-145 and PC-3 prostate cancer cell lines. The flexibility of the system, arising from its fibrous structure, and the anticancer activity observed in vitro provide a basis for further in vivo studies, assessing its suitability as an implantable platform for local drug delivery at the site of tumor growth.

Article.Title: Molecular and Functional Characterization of Kv1.3 Channels in Rat Articular Cartilage and Primary Chondrocytes: Regulation During Culture and Pro-Inflammatory Stimulation
Article.Authors: Ponce A.; Hinojosa L.; Roldán M.; Shoshani L.
Article.Abstract: We examined Kv1.3 expression and function in articular cartilage and primary chondrocytes from male Wistar rats using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), Western blotting, immunofluorescence, and whole-cell patch-clamp recordings. Molecular assays supported Kcna3 transcript and Kv1.3 protein expression. PAP-1 and ShK-186 revealed blocker-sensitive outward currents, depolarized freshly isolated chondrocytes, and increased input resistance. During primary culture, total and PAP-1-sensitive conductance densities decreased, without a statistically significant change in the relative PAP-1-sensitive contribution. In unadjusted paired analyses, IL-1α and IL-1β increased PAP-1-sensitive conductance; IL-1β also reduced total conductance and increased the relative contribution. The relative increase with IL-1α was sensitive to the statistical approach. No statistically significant conductance changes were detected after LPS exposure. Blocker effects varied by cytokine and endpoint: PAP-1 reduced propidium iodide (PI) positivity following IL-1α exposure, whereas both blockers attenuated IL-1β-associated changes in metabolic activity, PI positivity, and cell density in paired analyses; the ShK-186 metabolic effect was sensitive to the statistical approach. These findings support a functional contribution of Kv1.3-sensitive conductance to chondrocyte electrical properties and responses to inflammatory stress.

Article.Title: Oral Microbiome–Host Epigenetic Interactions in Oral Carcinogenesis: A Molecular Perspective
Article.Authors: Unlu O.; Demirci M.
Article.Abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma is still found late, and the tumor microenvironment is complicated enough that treatment often fails even when the diagnosis is timely. While genetic mutations partially account for this pathogenesis, they do not fully explain tumor behavior. Attention has therefore shifted to the microbial community around the tumor, which appears to contribute to malignancy less through the genome than through the host epigenome. This review is about the mechanism rather than about cataloging which species are present. We follow what Porphyromonas gingivalis, Fusobacterium nucleatum and Candida albicans do to DNA methylation, histone modification and non-coding RNA expression in host cells. While chronic inflammation plays a well-established role, bacterial and fungal metabolites also reach chromatin directly, and the resulting changes silence tumor suppressors and release oncogenic signaling in epithelium and stroma alike. We then ask what this means for tumor heterogeneity, for immune escape, and for progression, and we close with the two clinical questions that follow: whether salivary microbial and methylation signatures are usable for early detection, and whether epigenetic drugs can be aimed at the microbial component of the oral tumor microenvironment. In conclusion, the oral microbiome–epigenome axis acts as a crucial driver of tumor progression and microenvironmental immunosuppression. While translating these mechanistic insights into clinical practice necessitates rigorous in vivo validation, integrating microbiota-directed interventions with epigenetic therapies represents a highly promising frontier for the early detection and comprehensive management of OSCC.

Article.Title: Trichuris ovis: Prevalence, Molecular Advances, Immunopathogenesis, and Diagnosis of a Neglected Ruminant Whipworm
Article.Authors: Ilić T.; Milosavljević A.; Stevanović O.; Jovanović N.
Article.Abstract: Trichuris ovis is a widespread whipworm of the cecum and colon of domestic ruminants, transmitted through resistant eggs that persist on pastures for years. Although most infections are subclinical, heavy infections in young animals cause typhlitis and colitis. This narrative review summarizes current knowledge on T. ovis, emphasizing molecular systematics, immunopathogenesis, and diagnosis. Complete mitochondrial genomes have confirmed T. ovis as distinct from T. discolor and T. skrjabini, but discordance between ribosomal and mitochondrial markers leaves its relationship with T. globulosa unresolved and suggests cryptic lineages. Reported prevalence ranges from below 1% to over 70% and depends on the diagnostic method, as coprological examination cannot distinguish Trichuris species. Immunological knowledge derives mainly from the T. muris model, in which T helper 2 (Th2) responses mediate worm expulsion and excretory–secretory proteins modulate host immunity, whereas data for ruminants remain scarce. Flotation solutions of higher specific gravity improve egg detection, and combined nuclear and mitochondrial markers are required for reliable species identification. Control should rely on integrated parasite management that prioritizes reducing environmental contamination. Remaining gaps include anthelmintic efficacy and resistance in T. ovis and molecular data from underrepresented regions, including the Balkans.

Article.Title: Molecular Dynamics Reveals Structural Consequences of Schizophrenia-Associated SLC6A1 Variants
Article.Authors: Abashkin D.; Abdurazakov A.; Marilovtseva E.; Semina E.; Chaika Y.; Golimbet V.
Article.Abstract: The SLC6A1 gene encodes the GAT-1 transporter, which mediates the reuptake of GABA in the central nervous system (CNS). Missense variants in this gene are associated with the development of neuropsychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia. Although in vitro assays demonstrate a loss of transport activity, they do not elucidate how specific amino acid substitutions disrupt local interactions within the protein. To delineate the structural consequences of these mutations, we analyzed the inward-open apo-state of human GAT-1 (PDB: 7Y7V) using microsecond-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. This study compares the wild-type transporter with mutant forms, including the schizophrenia-associated variants R211C and A305T, alongside the A346S variant selected via deep learning-based pathogenicity predictors. The results demonstrate that these mutations do not globally destabilize the protein structure; rather, they induce specific rearrangements within local contact networks. The R211C substitution abolishes a hydrogen bond at the interface of extracellular loop 2 (EL2) and transmembrane helix 4 (TM4). A305T alters the TM1–TM6 interface adjacent to the sodium ion-binding site, and A346S strengthens TM1/TM6–EL4 interactions. The identified structural shifts suggest how pathogenic mutations remodel the GAT-1 interaction network and alter its conformational dynamics. These findings provide a foundation for subsequent molecular docking aimed at drug repurposing and for comprehensive MD modeling of the complete GAT-1 transport cycle.

Article.Title: Kombucha Fermentation Remodels the Phytochemical Composition of Gooseberry Juices and Reveals a Divergence Between Phenolic Abundance and HepG2 Cell Growth Inhibition
Article.Authors: Chandran A.; Klein G.; Kawa-Rygielska J.; Rywińska A.; Szumny A.; Zhang J.; Zhang H.; Boycott C.; Stefanska B.; Kolniak-Ostek J.
Article.Abstract: Kombucha fermentation can modify the phytochemical composition and biological properties of fruit-based beverages, although these changes may differ depending on the fermentation substrate. This study investigated the effects of 10-day kombucha fermentation using a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast (SCOBY) on red and white gooseberry (Ribes uva-crispa) juices supplemented with sucrose or buckwheat honey. Red gooseberry beverages were characterized by a greater contribution of esters to their volatile profiles, while alcohols predominated among the identified volatile compounds in white gooseberry beverages. Red gooseberry formulations generally exhibited higher phenolic concentrations and antioxidant capacity, with the honey-supplemented variant showing particularly high values. However, phenolic-enriched extracts isolated from fermented white gooseberry beverages inhibited HepG2 cell growth more strongly than extracts from red gooseberry beverages. White gooseberry extracts also altered the expression of selected genes associated with metabolism and cancer-related signaling. Sensory evaluation indicated the highest overall acceptance for sucrose-supplemented red gooseberry juice. These findings demonstrate that the effects of kombucha fermentation depend on gooseberry juice type and carbon source, and that phenolic abundance and antioxidant capacity do not necessarily predict cellular growth-inhibitory effects or sensory acceptance.

Article.Title: Cocoa Pulp Juice as a Fermentation Substrate for Potential Probiotic Lacticaseibacillus paracasei WU2502: Genomic Characterization, Metabolite Profiling, and Antimicrobial Activity Against Foodborne Pathogens
Article.Authors: Mitsuwan W.; Sornsenee P.; Saki M.; Romyasamit C.
Article.Abstract: Cocoa pulp juice is an underutilized by-product generated during cocoa bean fermentation that is rich in fermentable sugars and phytochemicals but remains largely unexplored as a substrate for microbial fermentation. This study aimed to evaluate cocoa pulp juice as a sustainable fermentation substrate for the potential probiotic Lacticaseibacillus paracasei WU2502 using whole-genome sequencing (WGS), carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) analysis, untargeted LC–QTOF-MS-based metabolite profiling, and antimicrobial evaluation. L. paracasei WU2502 showed substantial growth in cocoa pulp juice, reaching a maximum viable count of 10.70 log CFU/mL in 25% juice and >11 log CFU/mL in 50% and 100% juice, while the pH decreased from approximately 3.9–4.0 at Day 0 to 3.1–3.2 during fermentation. Fermented cocoa pulp juice showed antibacterial activity against Bacillus cereus, Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and Escherichia coli O157:H7 with MIC and MBC values of 12.5–25% (v/v). In a preliminary qualitative assessment, neutralization reduced the observed inhibitory activity, whereas Proteinase K treatment produced little apparent change, suggesting a possible pH-dependent contribution to the antimicrobial activity. WGS resulted in a 3.02 Mb draft genome with a GC content of 46.27%, 3114 coding sequences and genes relevant to glucose metabolism, acid tolerance, oxidative stress response and antimicrobial activity. No acquired antimicrobial resistance genes or virulence-associated factors were detected. CAZyme analysis revealed glycoside hydrolases and glycosyltransferases that may be involved in carbohydrate metabolic pathways and adaptation to plant-derived substrates. LC–MS/MS analysis of unfermented cocoa pulp juice provided baseline chemical characterization of the starting substrate, with representative putative annotations including sucrose, maltotriose, myo-inositol, citric acid, pyroglutamic acid, and choline. These findings support the feasibility of cocoa pulp juice as a fermentation substrate for L. paracasei WU2502 and provide a basis for further evaluation of this strain and fermented matrix for potential food applications.

Article.Title: Global Analysis of Public Cheese Microbiomes Reveals Widespread Bacterial Taxa and Geographic Community Structure
Article.Authors: Sadurski J.; Staniszewski A.; Muyanlı E.; Yılmaz R.; Waśko A.
Article.Abstract: Cheese microbiomes remain difficult to compare globally because public sequencing datasets are fragmented and methodologically heterogeneous. However, public datasets were strongly geographically imbalanced, with European BioProjects dominating the available collection. Together, these results establish a reproducible framework and comparative baseline for investigating cheese microbiome diversity, geographic structure and cross-study patterns across globally distributed public sequencing datasets.

Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Hu W.

Article.Title: Low-Level Light Therapy for Dry Eye Disease in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Randomized, Double-Masked, Sham-Controlled Trial
Article.Authors: Timofte-Zorila M.; Pînzariu A.; Pavel-Tanasa M.; Giannaccare G.; Istrate S.; Vlas N.; Alecu D.; Rotaru T.; Tanasa R.; Lixi F.; Troisi M.; Preda C.; Branisteanu D.
Article.Abstract: Dry eye disease (DED) affects the majority of patients with thyroid eye disease (TED) and frequently persists despite maximal conservative therapy. In this prospective, randomized, double-masked, sham-controlled trial, eyes of patients with TED-associated DED that remained symptomatic despite intensive preservative-free lubrication, bedtime ophthalmic ointment and daily periocular hygiene were allocated 2:1 to periocular LLLT (630 nm LED mask, 15 min per session, applied over closed eyelids) or to sham treatment (identical procedure with light emission reduced to <30% of therapeutic output). Background ocular surface therapy was maintained unchanged in both arms. Assessments were performed at baseline (T0), weekly during treatment (T1–T3) and at one month (T4) and two months (T5) after the last session. The primary outcome was the Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI); secondary outcomes were non-invasive break-up time (NIBUT), fluorescein break-up time (FBUT), Schirmer I test, tear osmolarity, upper- and lower-eyelid meibography, corneal fluorescein staining and lipid-layer grade. The primary OSDI assessment was the change from baseline to T3, the end-of-treatment visit. Additional follow-up assessments were performed at T4 and T5. Forty-six eyes of 46 patients were analyzed (30 LLLT, 16 sham); baseline disease was active in 14/30 (46.7%) and 6/16 (37.5%) eyes, respectively. At T3, adjusted OSDI was lower with LLLT than with sham (between-group difference −7.49 points; 95% CI −11.66 to −3.32; p < 0.001). The difference persisted at T4 and T5 (−11.97 and −16.86 points, respectively; both Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Tear osmolarity was lower with LLLT at T4 (−10.91 mOsm/L; 95% CI −18.96 to −2.87; p = 0.009) and T5 (−13.81 mOsm/L; 95% CI −22.55 to −5.06; p = 0.004). No multiplicity-adjusted between-group differences were demonstrated for NIBUT, FBUT, Schirmer I test or meibography. The adjusted probability of corneal staining was numerically lower with LLLT (T4: 15.7% vs. 34.7%; risk difference −19.0 percentage points; p = 0.100). In exploratory analyses, the treatment-by-visit-by-activity interaction was significant (p = 0.0159), with OSDI differences of −21.45 and −25.90 points in active disease versus −5.50 and −10.09 points in inactive disease at T4 and T5. CAS and OSDI were positively correlated at baseline (Spearman ρ = 0.547; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and at T5 (Spearman ρ = 0.428; Holm-adjusted p = 0.003). No treatment-related adverse events occurred. In conclusion, in TED-associated DED refractory to maximal conservative therapy, LLLT produced a significant and progressively increasing reduction in symptom burden together with an objective reduction in tear hyperosmolarity. Effects on break-up time, aqueous secretion, gland morphology, and lipid layer grade were not demonstrable within two months. The pattern and pace of response differ from those observed with the same technology after cataract surgery and are consistent with a chronic, systemically driven disease in which the ocular surface insult is continuously renewed.

Article.Title: From Proteostasis Collapse to Endothelial Failure: Mechanistic Pathways Linking Heat Stress, Regulated Cell Death, and Coagulopathy
Article.Authors: Dervišević E.; Ajanović T.; Čamdžić N.; Salerno M.; Pomara C.; Esposito M.; Chisari M.; Zorlak A.; Selak N.; Hodžić E.; Sessa F.
Article.Abstract: This review proposes an integrative mechanistic model that brings together apoptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, necroptosis, and necrosis within the broader context of heat-induced proteostasis disruption. Rather than depicting a strictly sequential or fully validated causal pathway, the model provides a conceptual framework through which interactions among cellular stress responses, endothelial dysfunction, heatstroke-induced coagulopathy (HIC), and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) may be understood. Under extreme heat stress, widespread protein unfolding and chaperone saturation activate the unfolded protein response, disrupt endoplasmic (ER) calcium homeostasis, and couple through Ca2+-mediated injury to mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. These processes are reciprocally amplifying: reactive oxygen species (ROS) from failing mitochondria deepen proteostatic damage and potentiate necroptotic and ferroptotic signaling, while inflammation-driven immune activation further increases ROS production, closing a self-reinforcing cycle. The resulting engagement of multiple RCD pathways, apoptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, and necroptosis, each with qualitatively distinct DAMP signatures, promotes inflammasome activation and a cytokine storm that destabilizes the endothelial glycocalyx, impairs barrier integrity, and triggers a pro-coagulant shift underlying HIC. We further examine biomarker candidates reflecting these mechanisms, evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies, ranging from HSP modulation and antioxidant therapy to endothelial-protective agents, mitophagy regulators, and nanomedicine, and outline the future role of multi-omics, machine learning, and regenerative approaches. By bringing together molecular, cellular, vascular, and systemic processes into a single cohesive model, this review proposes a conceptual foundation to guide diagnostic refinement, therapeutic innovation, and forensic interpretation in severe heat-related injury.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Characterization and Multidimensional Transcriptome Profiling of the SABATH Methyltransferase Gene Family in Sunflower (Helianthus annuus L.)
Article.Authors: Gao X.; Wang K.; Li M.; Li D.; Liu X.; Zheng J.; Liu S.; Geng J.; Guo B.; Han Y.; Zhang H.; Zhao C.
Article.Abstract: Plant SABATH methyltransferases contribute to volatile formation, hormone homeostasis and stress responses, but their family-wide organization in sunflower remains poorly characterized. Using the HanXRQr2.0-SUNRISE reference genome, we identified 33 high-confidence HaSABATH genes and integrated phylogenetic, duplication, synteny, promoter and protein-structure analyses with expression profiles from 200 public RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) libraries representing 87 distinct conditions. Twelve genes belonged to the salicylic acid/jasmonic acid methyltransferase-related Clade I, 19 to the benzoic acid/salicylic acid methyltransferase-related Clade II, and two to other lineages. Tandem, proximal, dispersed and whole-genome/segmental duplication contributed to the family, with overlapping tandem and segmental evidence for HaSABATH4 and HaSABATH15. Eleven reliable nonsynonymous-to-synonymous substitution ratios were below one. Most predicted proteins showed high model confidence. Across the sampled conditions, Clade I members generally showed higher expression levels and broader expression, while many Clade II members were weakly expressed or condition-biased. HaSABATH4 and HaSABATH6 were prioritized for follow-up under combined saline–alkali stress. This integrated analysis links evolutionary context to expression divergence and provides candidates for targeted biochemical and genetic studies.

Article.Title: The Role of Collagen in Coronary Artery Disease
Article.Authors: Yang Z.; Xie X.; Shi Y.; Chen Y.; Chen G.; Sun Y.; Xu R.
Article.Abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, imposing a substantial burden on patients and healthcare systems. Its development and progression are driven not only by lipid accumulation and inflammation but also by extracellular matrix remodeling. Collagen is a core component of the cardiovascular extracellular matrix. Its subtype composition, maturation, cross-linking, synthesis and degradation collectively shape the structural and functional properties of vascular and myocardial tissues. Here, we review collagen biology and use expression profiles from GTEx v11 and Heart Cell Atlas v2 to illustrate tissue- and cell type-specific patterns. These profiles illustrate the expression patterns and major cellular sources of the collagen gene family in the coronary artery and left ventricle. We also evaluate evidence linking collagen-related genetic variation to CAD susceptibility. By connecting genetic variation with protein processing and tissue architecture, this review delineates the potential roles of collagen in plaque stability, coronary thrombosis and post-infarction myocardial remodeling. This framework provides a basis for developing biomarkers of collagen remodeling and mechanism-guided therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Progression of Chronic UVB-Induced Skin Damage During Long-Term Topical Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Treatment in Mice
Article.Authors: Phadungsaksawasdi P.; Harnsiriwattana K.; Chukanchitipat K.; Hunsajarupan N.; Pisutpunya A.
Article.Abstract: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), a precursor of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), is widely investigated as a potential anti-aging intervention. However, its long-term efficacy and safety, particularly in topical formulations applied to chronically photodamaged skin, remain unclear. This study evaluated whether topical 5% NMN modifies the progression of chronic UVB-induced skin damage in mice. Female C57BL/6NJcl mice were assigned to four groups: non-irradiated control, UVB alone, UVB plus vehicle cream, and UVB plus 5% NMN cream. UVB was delivered to shaved dorsal skin three times weekly at 120 mJ/cm2, and cream was applied after each irradiation through week 25. UVB-exposed groups developed progressive skin damage, with the UVB plus NMN group showing a nonsignificant trend toward greater clinical severity at week 25 (p = 0.08). Histological analysis showed significant increases in epidermal thickness and dysplasia from week 12 to the late endpoint only in the UVB plus NMN group. These changes were accompanied by marked induction of Krt6, Krt16, and S100a8, whereas Krt1 showed no significant change. In contrast, no increase in Parp1 and Sirt1 was observed at the transcriptional level in the NMN group. Parp1 and Sirt1 were significantly upregulated in the UVB alone and UVB plus vehicle groups but not in UVB plus NMN-treated skin. Overall, these findings indicate that long-term topical NMN did not protect chronically UVB-exposed mouse skin and may have contributed to the worsening of photodamage.

Article.Title: Advanced Cellular Models for Drug Testing and Discovery to Target Cardiac Fibrosis Progression
Article.Authors: Icolaro F.; Chimenti I.; Cozzolino C.; Bordin A.; Pontecorvi V.; Frati G.; De Falco E.; Floris E.; Picchio V.; Pagano F.
Article.Abstract: Cardiac fibrosis is a complex and dynamic pathological process, central for cardiac repair, characterised by continuous cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions. Three-dimensional (3D) models are gaining increasing relevance, compared with traditional two-dimensional (2D) cellular setups, due to their ability to recapitulate key features of the fibrotic microenvironment at different levels of complexity, including cellular heterogeneity, spatial organisation and tissue mechanical properties. These systems have enabled a deeper investigation of fibrosis mechanobiology and the mechanosensitive pathways involved in disease progression, contributing to the identification of potential therapeutic targets for cardiac repair. Increasing biological complexity can reveal therapeutic responses that remain undetected in conventional models; however, the predictive value of 3D systems has so far been confirmed in vivo only for a limited number of platforms and compounds. The role of 3D models is therefore expanding beyond disease modelling towards platforms for the screening and evaluation of antifibrotic strategies, pointing to increasingly functional cardiac reparative strategies. Here, we distinguish model complexity, biological fidelity and demonstrated predictive value, compare current platforms according to their validation level and limitations, and discuss the benchmarks and standards required for their routine use in antifibrotic drug discovery. From this perspective, the development of systems that are not necessarily more sophisticated, but progressively more informative and predictive, may help bridge the gap between conventional 2D in vitro models and animal studies, ultimately improving the translational relevance of preclinical evaluation.

Article.Title: Abuse of Anabolic-Androgenic Steroids: Molecular and Organ Dysfunctions—A Critical Narrative Review for Forensic Interpretation
Article.Authors: Morena D.; Marchesini D.; Manta A.; Caruso A.; Santori V.; Crusco P.; Sirello R.; Umani Ronchi F.; Scopetti M.; Fineschi V.
Article.Abstract: Anabolic-androgenic steroids (AAS) comprise testosterone and synthetic androgenic compounds that differ substantially in pharmacokinetics, receptor activity, route of administration, hepatic metabolism, and clinical risk. From a forensic perspective, the central problem is not simply to catalogue adverse effects but to determine how verified exposure, chronology, co-use of other substances, clinical and electrocardiographic findings, pathological alterations, and toxicological results should be integrated when evaluating an individual death. This critical narrative review therefore distinguishes therapeutic testosterone replacement from non-medical and supraphysiological AAS exposure and examines the evidence connecting exposure to endocrine, cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, musculoskeletal, neuropsychiatric, and immunological findings. Human prospective and observational data support associations between androgen abuse and endocrine suppression, erythrocytosis, adverse lipid changes, increased blood pressure, and left-ventricular structural or functional alterations, with recovery of selected measured parameters reported in the studied cohorts. Electrocardiographic studies also report prolonged repolarization indices and impaired heart-rate recovery in AAS-using bodybuilders; however, these intermediate markers do not by themselves establish an individual risk of fatal ventricular arrhythmia. Forensic autopsy series describe myocardial hypertrophy, fibrosis, coronary disease, and other lesions in AAS-associated deaths, but these findings are not specific and require correlation with toxicology, clinical history, circumstances, and alternative causes. The detailed immunological literature is predominantly mechanistic, in vitro, or experimental and currently provides limited direct forensic evidence in human AAS users. Similarly, Raman spectroscopy is best regarded as a developing adjunct for forensic trace or analytical applications rather than a validated method for confirming AAS accumulation or cause of death in post-mortem tissue. We propose a structured forensic framework in which exposure is first verified, the temporal and pharmacological context is reconstructed, findings are assessed for specificity and plausibility, co-exposures and competing causes are examined, and the final opinion explicitly communicates the degree of certainty and the limitations of the evidence.

Article.Title: Not All EVs Are Equal: Functional Heterogeneity of Extracellular Vesicles in Neuroregenerative Therapies
Article.Authors: Chodkowska-Michalowska M.; Hawryluk O.; Lakomy S.; Slysz A.; Sarnowska A.
Article.Abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly being investigated as cell-free therapies for neurological diseases. However, their clinical application remains limited by biological and functional heterogeneity. EVs should therefore not be considered as a single, uniform therapeutic product defined only by their cell of origin, size, or conventional vesicle classification. EV composition and activity are influenced by extrinsic factors, including donor and tissue source, culture conditions, and isolation procedures, as well as by intrinsic mechanisms of vesicle biogenesis and selective cargo loading. Some vesicles may have beneficial therapeutic effects, whereas others may show little biological activity or act on unintended cellular targets. For this reason, EVs may be better classified according to biological function rather than only physical properties or cellular origin. A functionality-based classification could improve potency assessment, dose selection, reproducibility, and the development of consistent EV-based products. EV properties can be modulated by selecting appropriate parental cells, modifying culture conditions, or using genetic or metabolic engineering to alter EV production and cargo. Single-vesicle approaches can reveal differences between EV subpopulations and identify those responsible for specific biological effects. Overall, understanding EV heterogeneity may provide a rational basis for developing reproducible and disease-specific EV therapies for neurological and neurodegenerative disorders.

Article.Title: IL-18 and NFE2L2/NRF2 in Adult ADHD: An Inflammation–Redox Framework for Salivary Biomarker Research
Article.Authors: Hurjui I.; Serban I.; Hurjui L.; Jipu R.; Hurjui I.; Tanase D.; Tarniceriu C.; Balcos C.; Dobrin I.; Dobrin R.
Article.Abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder, and increasing evidence suggests that inflammatory and oxidative processes may contribute to its biological complexity. Despite these observations, no molecular biomarker has yet been established for clinical diagnosis. In this narrative review, we examine interleukin-18 (IL-18) and the NFE2L2/NRF2 antioxidant pathway as two potentially complementary components of the inflammation–redox landscape in adult ADHD, with particular attention to their possible assessment in saliva. For this purpose, we conducted a focused search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, bringing together evidence from human ADHD studies, mechanistic and experimental research, and studies investigating the feasibility of salivary biomarkers. IL-18 is closely associated with inflammasome-mediated inflammatory signaling, whereas NFE2L2 encodes NRF2, a major regulator of antioxidant and cytoprotective responses. The evidence for these two targets in adult ADHD is not equally developed. Direct human data on IL-18 remain limited, while more recent studies have identified alterations in NRF2-related antioxidant defenses in adults with ADHD. Both IL-18 and NRF2 can be measured in human saliva, although the available evidence comes from clinical populations other than ADHD. Their detection in saliva therefore demonstrates analytical feasibility but does not establish their validity as ADHD biomarkers. At present, neither marker has been validated in the saliva of adults with ADHD. Studying them together may nevertheless provide a useful way to explore the relationship between inflammatory activity and antioxidant regulation. Future studies will require standardized saliva collection, careful assessment of oral health, and characterization of systemic inflammatory and metabolic conditions, medication use, and smoking. Initial studies should also include paired saliva and blood samples to determine how salivary measurements relate to circulating levels and whether they capture biologically meaningful variation in adult ADHD.

Article.Title: Chemical Mechanisms of Cerebral Ischemia–Reperfusion Injury and Neuroprotection in the Thrombectomy Era
Article.Authors: Panos L.; Chakif D.
Article.Abstract: Mechanical thrombectomy has significantly improved outcomes for patients with large-vessel occlusion stroke. However, restoring the artery does not always re-establish full microvascular blood flow, tissue rescue, or a good neurological outcome. Ischemia–reperfusion injury varies over time, with distinct biochemical mechanisms dominating during ischemia, early reperfusion, and the subsequent hours. During ischemia, factors like adenosine triphosphate (ATP) depletion, ionic imbalance, calcium overload, mitochondrial dysfunction, acidosis, and metabolic changes such as succinate build-up render brain tissue highly vulnerable. When blood flow resumes, oxygen delivery to this stressed tissue can induce rapid mitochondrial redox shifts, electron leakage, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species formation, iron-dependent radical generation, and lipid peroxidation. Damage may then persist for hours through ongoing mitochondrial dysfunction, phospholipid hydroperoxide accumulation, reactive aldehydes, ferroptosis, blood–brain barrier breakdown, microvascular issues, and inflammation. Much of the mechanistic evidence supporting these processes derives from experimental studies, and their relevance to clinical outcomes after thrombectomy requires further validation. This narrative review tracks these chemical changes across the main phases of cerebral ischemia–reperfusion injury and connects them to modern thrombectomy practices. It also explores how the timing of each process may inform neuroprotective strategies, drug delivery methods, patient selection via imaging, and future clinical trial approaches.

Article.Title: Oral 25-Hydroxycholesterol Suppresses 4T1 Tumour Growth in an Immune-Context-Associated Manner
Article.Authors: Liang S.; Xu J.; Wang Z.; Liu Y.; Xu Y.; Yao C.; Zhu Z.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype with limited targeted-treatment options. 25-Hydroxycholesterol (25-HC) is an oxysterol involved in metabolic and immune regulation, but its antitumour effects remain context dependent. We examined whether oral 25-HC suppresses 4T1 tumour growth in immunocompetent BALB/c mice and whether host immune status modifies the response. Mice bearing 4T1 tumours received oral vehicle or 25-HC (1 or 10 mg/kg) daily for 14 days (n = 6 per group). 25-HC reduced endpoint tumour volume from 1510.6 ± 235.4 mm3 (vehicle) to 1147.2 ± 243.1 and 866.7 ± 206.6 mm3 (adjusted p = 0.027 and 0.0004); the 10 mg/kg dose also reduced tumour weight and Ki-67 positivity, increased CD8-positive T-cell infiltration and the granzyme B (GZMB)-positive fraction, reduced M2-like macrophages and raised the M1/M2 ratio. Tumour-tissue adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signalling was altered, with p-AMPK/AMPK increased to 1.23- and 1.57-fold of control and p-STAT6/STAT6 decreased to 0.81- and 0.46-fold. Serum 25-HC increased with dose, while intratumoral 25-HC was lowest at 10 mg/kg; no dose-associated reduction was observed in BALB/c nude mice. Oral 25-HC thus suppressed 4T1 tumour growth with immune-context-associated features; however, the treatment-by-host interaction did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.06), and immune-context association of the response remains suggestive rather than established. The reciprocal serum–tumour pattern, a descriptive observation from a single time point whose cause remains unclear, generates a testable hypothesis of immune-cell-associated 25-HC handling.

Article.Title: Single-Cell Transcriptomic Analysis Identifies a Translation/RBP-Related Fibroblast Signature for Drug Repurposing in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
Article.Authors: Qiao Y.; Cui C.; Han Y.; Tang X.; Yang Z.; Ge C.
Article.Abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is characterized by persistent fibroblast activation and excessive extracellular matrix deposition. However, transcriptional heterogeneity associated with translation- and RNA-binding protein (RBP)-related processes within IPF fibroblasts remains incompletely characterized. Here, we analyzed two independent human IPF single-cell RNA-sequencing cohorts to identify fibroblast states that differed in Translation/RBP-related transcriptional programs while sharing high fibrotic output. Donor-paired pseudobulk analysis in GSE136831 identified a transcriptional signature distinguishing these states, and genes showing consistent directional changes in the independent GSE135893 cohort were retained to derive a cross-cohort signature. Reverse-connectivity analysis across CLUE, L1000CDS2, and iLINCS was then used to prioritize compounds predicted to transcriptionally oppose this signature. Candidate compounds were subsequently evaluated in transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1)-stimulated human fetal lung fibroblasts (HFL-1), with cell viability, α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), and collagen I used for initial phenotypic assessment. PP-1, PK-11195, dabrafenib, GSK-1059615, and dasatinib reduced both profibrotic markers within the tested concentration ranges, identifying them as candidates for further investigation. Together, these findings define a cross-cohort Translation/RBP-related fibroblast signature in IPF and support its use as a transcriptome-guided strategy for prioritizing compounds with antifibrotic phenotypic activity.

Article.Title: Biosilica from Agricultural Residues for Hazardous Contaminant Removal and Soil Remediation: Synthesis Routes, Structure–Property Relationships, and Environmental Relevance
Article.Authors: Latini V.; Wawrzyńczak A.; Feliczak-Guzik A.
Article.Abstract: The conversion of agricultural residues into functional silica materials offers opportunities to combine waste valorization with environmental remediation. This review critically examines biosilica production from rice husk and straw, corn, sugarcane, wheat, and selected fruit and potato wastes, focusing on sol–gel processing, hydrothermal synthesis, and acid leaching. To address feedstock heterogeneity, reported silicon and silica contents are distinguished according to their analytical basis, including biomass and ash fractions. Synthesis routes are compared using available quantitative indicators, including silica yield, purity, specific surface area, and processing conditions, while accounting for differences in reporting practices and incomplete datasets. Particular attention is given to the relationships between precursor composition, synthesis parameters, surface chemistry, and contaminant-removal performance. The analysis highlights the importance of accessible surface sites, functional groups, and contaminant speciation, demonstrating that specific surface area alone cannot predict adsorption efficiency. Although biosilica shows potential for water treatment and soil remediation, practical implementation remains constrained by feedstock variability, limited testing under realistic conditions, regeneration challenges, and uncertainties regarding long-term safety. The review identifies key research priorities for developing reproducible, economically viable, and environmentally sustainable biosilica technologies.

Article.Title: Alterations in the Expression of Tight and Adherens Junction Proteins in the Hen Oviduct Following Tamoxifen Treatment
Article.Authors: Frydrych K.; Wolak D.; Hrabia A.
Article.Abstract: Intercellular junctions are essential for maintaining epithelial integrity, barrier function, and tissue remodeling in the female reproductive system. However, their role in the avian oviduct is poorly understood. The aim of this study was to examine the effect of tamoxifen (TMX; an estrogen receptor blocker in birds) treatment on the histoarchitecture and the abundance of transcripts and proteins, as well as the immunolocalization of key tight junction proteins (occludin, claudin 1, and ZO1) and adherens junction proteins (E-cadherin and β-catenin) in the oviduct of hens. Tissue samples were collected from all oviductal segments (i.e., the infundibulum, magnum, isthmus, shell gland, and vagina) on day 8 of the experiment, from control (laying; n = 6) hens and hens treated (6 mg/kg body weight) daily with TMX (non-laying; n = 6). Following TMX treatment for 7 consecutive days, a pause in laying and partial oviductal regression was accompanied by segment-dependent alterations in mRNA transcript abundances (examined by qRT-PCR) and/or protein abundances (determined by Western blot) of the examined junctional molecules. Furthermore, TMX treatment altered the patterns of immunofluorescent staining within the oviductal wall, concomitant with the disorganization of the luminal epithelium and tubular glands. Our results suggest that the expression and localization of tight and adherens junction proteins in the hen oviduct depend strongly on estrogen signaling. Moreover, this study provides novel insights into the regulation of these proteins, indicating their potential involvement in the molecular mechanisms that orchestrate epithelial remodeling and functioning in the hen oviduct, which may affect poultry production.

Article.Title: Vitamin K3 (Menadione) Targets TBK1 to Enhance the Efficacy of Pirfenidone in a Mouse Model of Bleomycin-Induced Pulmonary Fibrosis
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Cao J.; Zhou Y.; Cao X.; Deng S.; Li Y.; Li C.; Tang S.; Chen P.
Article.Abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive and irreversible interstitial lung disease. Current antifibrotic drugs, exemplified by pirfenidone (PFD), only slow disease progression with limited efficacy and adverse effects, underscoring the need for novel therapeutic strategies. By integrating single-cell transcriptomics with the Drug2Cell algorithm, we performed drug prioritization at single-cell resolution and identified menadione (vitamin K3, VK3), a synthetic naphthoquinone and the minimal core of naturally occurring vitamin K, as a candidate preferentially active in alveolar epithelial cells. In bleomycin (BLM)-stimulated A549 cells and a mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis, therapeutic co-administration of low-dose VK3 and PFD reduced vimentin expression by 44.8% and collagen deposition by 50.3%, and decreased fibroblast abundance by 36.7%, thereby attenuating histopathological damage and restoring BLM-disrupted alveolar epithelial homeostasis. Experiments with VK3 alone further demonstrated that its antifibrotic activity is independent of conversion to vitamin K2. Mechanistically, thermal proteome profiling identified TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) as the principal candidate target; molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations predicted a stable binding mode, independently confirmed by biolayer interferometry and differential scanning fluorimetry, demonstrating direct binding of VK3 to TBK1 with nanomolar affinity. TBK1 knockdown suppressed BLM-induced fibrotic responses, establishing TBK1 as a positive regulator of pulmonary fibrosis. In vitro signaling analysis revealed that VK3 plus PFD inhibits phosphorylation of TBK1 and STAT3, whereas PFD alone reduces phosphorylation of JAK1 and STAT3, suggesting that both agents converge on STAT3 through distinct upstream nodes. Although VK3 exhibits dose-dependent cytotoxicity precluding direct clinical use as monotherapy, its validated high-affinity target TBK1 and privileged naphthoquinone scaffold lay a rational foundation for lead optimization toward safer anti-IPF agents, and its ability to enhance PFD efficacy supports further development as an adjunct to existing antifibrotic therapy.
