Article.Title: Noncoding RNAs in Nuclear Condensates and RNA Processing in Skeletal Muscle
Article.Authors: Ngo T.; Lee W.
Article.Abstract: Spatial organization in the nucleus is an active layer of RNA regulation in skeletal muscle, yet localization is often interpreted more strongly than the evidence permits. This critical review compares physiological nuclear RNA compartments with pathological repeat-RNA assemblies using a graded evidence framework. NEAT1-associated paraspeckles provide the clearest muscle-linked example of an RNA-marked nuclear body, although isoform-specific architectural causality remains untested in muscle. MALAT1 regulates speckle-associated splicing-factor and chromatin states but is dispensable for gross speckle formation, and muscle studies report opposing differentiation phenotypes. Nucleolar FRG2 transcripts in facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy connect spatial RNA organization to rDNA transcription and translational capacity. Expanded DMPK CUG and CNBP CCUG RNAs in myotonic dystrophy sequester processing factors and drive spliceopathy, although calibrated imaging in patient-derived DM1 myotubes indicates that most apparent foci are individual retained transcripts rather than bulk condensates. The framework distinguishes spatial association, molecular participation, functional necessity, in vivo relevance, and therapeutic target engagement. It also maps interventions to toxic-RNA abundance, RNA–protein binding, repeat-locus transcription, downstream splicing, or compartment state. Together, this evidence-based synthesis identifies which nuclear RNA mechanisms are established in muscle, which remain extrapolated from non-muscle systems, and which experiments are required before therapeutic modulation can be interpreted mechanistically.

Article.Title: ENO1 Is More Abundant than ENO2 on the Surface of Metastatic and Neuroendocrine Prostate Cancer Cells and Upregulated in High-Risk Prostate Tumors
Article.Authors: Santiago K.; Durán A.; Nyirendah L.; Soliz J.; Morcos A.; Makamure A.; Manrique N.; Escobar-Acuña K.; Whitley K.; Roy S.; Wall N.; Das B.; Almaguel F.; Casiano C.
Article.Abstract: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) remains lethal, and lineage plasticity drives a subset of tumors to neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC), most often treatment-emergent (t-NEPC). Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA), the target of radioligand therapies for advanced prostate cancer (PCa), is heterogeneously expressed across metastatic sites but lost during neuroendocrine differentiation, excluding many patients from these therapies. The glycolytic enzyme Enolase 1 (ENO1) is a promising alternative target because it localizes to the surface of human tumors and promotes cancer growth and metastasis. However, it remains understudied in advanced PCa compared with ENO2 (neuron-specific enolase), a canonical neuroendocrine marker. ENO1 silencing reduced cell proliferation and clonogenic growth even when triggering ENO2 upregulation. This was associated with S-phase accumulation, elevated phospho histone p-H2A.X, and increased apoptosis. Significantly higher transcript expression of ENO1 than ENO2 was observed in clinical prostate tumors, including high-Gleason and neuroendocrine tumors, concomitant with elevated expression of their transcriptional regulator MYC. Article.Title: Widely Targeted Lipidomics of Nasal Fluid Across Upper-Airway Inflammation: Phenotype-Associated Remodeling in Allergic Rhinitis and Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Han J.; Wang X.; Wang W.; Wang L.; Zha Y.; Lv W.; Zhu Z.
Article.Abstract: Allergic rhinitis (AR) and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) share overlapping inflammatory mechanisms while retaining distinct disease biology. Although lipid metabolism is increasingly implicated in airway inflammation, the nasal fluid lipidomic landscape across AR and CRSwNP and its relationship to local eosinophilic inflammation and clinical burden remain incompletely understood. We performed widely targeted liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) lipidomics on nasal fluid from 73 participants, including 22 controls, 23 patients with AR, and 28 patients with CRSwNP. Group differences were evaluated using multivariate analysis and models adjusted for age, sex, and smoking status, followed by trajectory clustering and residual-correlation network analysis. Within CRSwNP, adjusted models were used to assess lipid associations with tissue eosinophilia, the 22-item Sinonasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22), overall visual analog scale (VAS), and Lund–Mackay computed tomography score. Lipid subclass patterns were examined by ranked enrichment and focused subclass score analyses. AR was characterized mainly by higher relative abundances of TG species, whereas CRSwNP showed broader increases involving triacylglycerol species, plasmalogen phosphatidylethanolamines, and lysophospholipids. Exploratory clustering of 147 lipids showing nominally significant differences (p < 0.05) in at least one covariate-adjusted pairwise group comparison yielded four modules with differing biochemical compositions, although the partition was sensitive to the input lipid set. Among these, the diacylglycerol–lysophosphatidic acid-related module displayed strong internal network connectivity, suggesting coordinated variation within the identified module. Within CRSwNP, ranked analysis of lipid associations with tissue eosinophilia showed negative enrichment of plasmalogen phosphatidylethanolamine, sphingomyelin, and ether-linked lysophosphatidylcholine, and positive enrichment of glycerolipid and acylcarnitine subclasses. Clinical burden showed only partial overlap with this pattern: plasmalogen phosphatidylethanolamine was inversely associated with both tissue eosinophilia and patient-reported symptom burden, whereas conventional lysophosphatidylcholine showed stronger positive associations with symptomatic and radiographic burden. These findings suggest distinct and coordinated nasal fluid lipidomic features associated with the upper-airway inflammatory phenotype, local eosinophilic inflammation, and clinical disease burden.

Article.Title: Rapid FAK Phosphorylation and Progressive Tight-Junction Protein Alterations Under Hyperosmotic Stress in Corneal Epithelial Cells
Article.Authors: Zhou Y.; Ma C.; Gao Y.; Wang Y.; Zhang Z.; Shi M.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: Dry eye disease (DED) is characterized by tear hyperosmolality and ocular surface injury, but the contribution of focal adhesion kinase (FAK)-related signaling to tight junction (TJ) protein alterations remains unclear. TJ protein abundance and junctional continuity decreased progressively with increasing osmolarity and exposure duration. PF-562271, a dual FAK/Pyk2 inhibitor, produced a concentration-dependent reduction in FAK Tyr397 phosphorylation and, at 2.5 μM, also reduced Pyk2 Tyr402 phosphorylation while partially preserving ZO-1, claudin-1, and occludin abundance. FAK knockdown independently attenuated TJ protein loss and partially preserved ZO-1 junctional continuity under 500 mOsm/L hyperosmotic stress. These findings support a time-dependent contribution of FAK-related signaling to hyperosmotic stress-induced TJ protein remodeling.

Article.Authors: Perez-Penco M.; Scott T.; Engdal E.; Picon Jara C.; González G.; Barfod L.; Rohrberg K.; Bagger F.; Neukirch L.; Andersson A.; Holst P.

This immunization was able to elicit significant protection against tumor challenge and additive benefit with anti-PD-L1 in therapeutic treatment, establishing proof-of-concept for ERV-targeted immunotherapy in a murine surrogate system rather than direct evidence of HERV-K-targeted efficacy. Our findings suggest an important role of HERV-K in NSCLC immunobiology and that adaptive immunity targeting HERV-K should be explored in the treatment of NSCLC patients.

Article.Title: Various Aspects of Antimicrobial Properties of Populus Propolis
Article.Authors: Okińczyc P.; Widelski J.; Szperlik J.; Sroka Z.
Article.Abstract: Propolis is a bee product which is composed of plant resins and bee glue. In temperate climatic zones, the main sources of resins are buds of different species of the Populus genus. Propolis is known to have multiple medicinal properties, especially antimicrobial (including antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains), anti-inflammatory, and wound treatment properties. Due to growing antibiotic resistance, new antibacterial agents and therapies solutions are still needed. For this reason, this article summarizes the results of research related to the antibacterial activity of Populus genus propolis. We discuss the main types of Populus genus propolis (aspen, aspen–poplar and poplar), propolis’s general effect against different bacterial strains, the classes of antibacterial agents, the mechanism of antibacterial action of propolis, and interactions of propolis with antibiotics. Our analysis of the literature reveals that Populus propolis is a valuable antibacterial agent. However, its activity varies due to the instability of its composition. Therefore, before it can be designated for medicinal use biological and phytochemical standardization is required. Clinical data reveal the efficiency of propolis preparations in mild external infectious diseases in oral cavity and wound treatment. These data are limited only to poplar propolis. Similar efficiency may be possible using aspen and aspen–poplar propolis, but there is no direct clinical data to support this assertion. Combined therapy using propolis with antibiotics remained controversial due to the lack of sufficient clinical data and unclear data from in vitro research. Administering Populus propolis preparations to treat internal bacterial diseases requires further clinical research and should not be a standard therapy at this moment.

Article.Title: Antidepressant-like Activity of a Triple Combination of Venlafaxine, Codeine and Nor-Binaltorphimine in the Mouse Tail Suspension Test
Article.Authors: Lungu C.; Muntean C.; Păunescu H.; Marin R.; Lungu F.; Costescu M.; Ghiță C.; Fulga I.; Coman O.
Article.Abstract: About one-third of patients with major depressive disorder do not remit on conventional monoaminergic antidepressants. Venlafaxine (VEN) is a classic antidepressant that inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake. Venlafaxine does not bind opioid receptors, yet its antidepressant-like action requires intact µ-opioid signalling. The dynorphin/κ-opioid axis exerts an opposing, dysphoria-promoting influence. A possible question is whether combining serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition, µ-opioid receptor activation by codeine (COD) and sustained κ-opioid receptor blockade produces an antidepressant-like effect larger than that of the components given alone. Male NMRI mice were tested in the forced swim test (FST) (one experiment) and in the tail suspension test (TST) (three experiments) using a parallel-design (n = 10 to 17 per group; 277 animals), as follows: VEN 10 to 40 mg/kg in both tests—FST and TST; COD 10 to 40 mg/kg added to VEN 20 mg/kg in TST; and nor-binaltorphimine (norBNI) 10 mg/kg, given 24 h before, combined with VEN 20 mg/kg and COD 20 mg/kg and compared with norBNI alone, COD alone and norBNI + VEN, with amitriptyline (AMI) 20 mg/kg as the positive control in the TST. The three agents and two reference ligands were also docked into eight experimental human structures of the monoamine transporters and of the μ, κ and δ opioid receptors. VEN did not reduce FST immobility at any dose but produced a dose-dependent reduction in the TST, reaching −66.2% at 40 mg/kg. COD did not potentiate VEN 20 mg/kg at any of three COD doses. The triple combination, in the TST, reduced immobility by 65.7% relative to saline (Dunnett p = 0.013), an effect of similar magnitude to AMI with no significant difference detected between them, whereas norBNI alone, COD alone and norBNI + VEN did not reach significance. The design was underpowered for intermediate effects (the calculated n should be about 36 per group, unapproved because of ethical considerations). The triple combination was not significantly more effective than norBNI + VEN (p = 0.375), so the contribution of codeine remains undetermined. Docking reproduced the experimental pose of all eight co-crystallised ligands and was consistent with VEN occupying the transporter S1 site, COD the μ-opioid pocket and norBNI the κ receptor. A triple serotonin-adrenergic and opioid combination produced an antidepressant-like effect that none of the single treatments tested in the same cohort reached, but the fixed-dose design does not establish cooperativity between all three mechanisms. The docking results are consistent with, but do not prove, engagement of three separate sites.

Article.Title: Folate Receptor Alpha (FRα/FOLR1) in Cancer: Diagnostic, Prognostic or Predictive Biomarker? A Critical Review of Its Clinical Utility
Article.Authors: Kapczuk P.; Marcinowska Z.; Kołodziejczak M.; Szubert D.
Article.Abstract: Folate receptor alpha (FRα) plays a key role in folate homeostasis. Folate is involved, among other processes, in nucleotide biosynthesis, and the marked difference between FRα expression in certain cancers and under physiological conditions gives this receptor potential as a cancer biomarker. However, the current state of knowledge points to a specific role for this marker and defines its potential place in cancer diagnosis and treatment. This review aims to critically evaluate the available evidence regarding the clinical utility of FRα. Analysis of the literature indicates that despite differences in expression, the sensitivity and specificity of FRα are insufficient for its use as a standalone diagnostic marker. In contrast, its potential as a prognostic marker is strongly dependent on cancer type. The strongest evidence of clinical utility concerns membranous FRα protein expression assessed by a validated immunohistochemical companion diagnostic assay for selecting patients with platinum-resistant ovarian cancer for mirvetuximab soravtansine treatment. In contrast, the predictive relevance of FRα for other targeted therapeutic strategies remains under investigation. Overall, FRα should be regarded as a clinically actionable biomarker in a defined therapeutic setting and as a promising, but not universally validated, diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive candidate in other oncological applications.

Article.Title: Microbial Siderophores for Sustainable Agriculture: Stress Tolerance, Biocontrol, Mechanism, and Omics Integration
Article.Authors: Akhtar N.; Ahlawat Y.; Singh A.; Wani A.; Panda S.; Kumar A.; Patel L.; Stevanato P.; Celletti S.
Article.Abstract: Microbial siderophores play an important role in improving plant tolerance to abiotic and biotic stresses. Beyond iron acquisition, they support plant health by regulating oxidative stress, chelating toxic metals, and mediating beneficial plant–microbe interactions. This review highlights the role of siderophore-producing microbes in mitigating salinity, drought, alkaline stress, and metal toxicity, as well as in the improvement of nutrient solubilization and uptake. It also delineates environmental and physiological factors affecting siderophore production. The review additionally explores how the microbial interactions within soil consortia moderate siderophore biosynthesis and bio-control activity. Advances in multi-omics and genome editing approaches are discussed for identifying important genes and pathways associated with siderophore-mediated stress tolerance. The mechanisms behind siderophore-mediated stress tolerance are discussed, mainly their involvement in pathogen suppression through iron competition and activation of induced systemic resistance. Furthermore, it addresses the commercialization challenges and integration of siderophore applications into precision agriculture, aligning their agricultural and environmental benefits with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

Article.Title: The Seminal Microenvironment as a Potentially Tractable Interface Between Metabolic Disease and Sperm Damage
Article.Authors: Yao Y.; Zhang X.; Li L.; Fei C.; Zhang Y.; Huang S.; Zong Y.; Zhu L.; Cao Y.; Li T.; Shao M.; Zheng Y.
Article.Abstract: Male reproductive disorders are increasingly linked to metabolic diseases, but mechanistic research remains predominantly focused on the testis. The seminal microenvironment, shaped by epididymal and accessory-gland secretions, contains metabolites, lipids, ions, cytokines, extracellular vesicles, and microbial products, and may act as a metabolically responsive post-testicular interface that continues to influence sperm after spermatogenesis. Obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and chronic inflammation can remodel this environment by disrupting secretory activity, redox homeostasis, immune signaling, and microbial ecology. These changes may converge on oxidative and inflammatory pathways, promoting membrane lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired motility and capacitation, oxidative DNA base lesions, DNA fragmentation, and potentially epigenetic alterations. Mouse studies separately report obesity-associated epididymal vesicle remodeling and RNA-dependent changes in embryonic gene expression. In this Review, we examine the regulation and metabolic remodeling of the seminal microenvironment, how these changes may translate systemic metabolic stress into sperm injury, and emerging interventions including metabolic correction, antioxidant strategies, and microbiome-targeted approaches. Overall, current evidence remains largely observational and cross-sectional, with additional technical limitations in low-biomass seminal microbiome studies. Longitudinal and mechanistic studies are therefore needed to determine whether the seminal microenvironment is a causal mediator of metabolic infertility and a clinically tractable target for mechanism-guided preconception care.

Article.Title: PCSK9 in the Immunometabolism of Type 2 Diabetes
Article.Authors: Villari P.; Labate A.
Article.Abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibition reduces cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes, while experimental studies implicate PCSK9 in immune activation, platelet function and organ-specific metabolism. Whether these mechanisms contribute clinically beyond atherogenic lipoprotein lowering remains uncertain. This critical narrative review integrates an original corpus of 108 appraised publications, with targeted additions during revision. It evaluates whether findings from different compartments and experimental perturbations can be transferred to particular treatments and clinical outcomes. Mechanistic evidence implicates receptor trafficking, intracellular cholesterol, mitochondrial stress and inflammatory signalling. Effects vary by cell type and compartment: local PCSK9 promotes injury in some models but preserves pancreatic, glomerular or cardiac function in others. Global knockout, tissue-specific deletion, extracellular antibodies and hepatic silencing are therefore distinct exposures. Human biomarker and imaging studies provide translational signals but generally cannot isolate direct effects from concomitant lipoprotein changes. Randomised antibody trials establish cardiovascular efficacy and an overall reassuring glycaemic profile, without demonstrating clinically meaningful glucose lowering. PCSK9 has broader immunometabolic functions, but the available evidence does not quantify an additional clinical benefit independent of atherogenic lipoprotein lowering. Tissue-specific mechanisms and causal mediation require further investigation.

Article.Title: Colon Effects of 7-Day Whole-Body Inhalation Exposure of Fischer 344 Rats to Emissions from First- and Second-Generation Biodiesel Fuels with and Without a Particle Filter
Article.Authors: Wilczak J.; Dziendzikowska K.; Gromadzka-Ostrowska J.; Oczkowski M.; Sapierzyński R.; Czerwińska M.; Lankoff A.
Article.Abstract: Biodiesel is projected to reduce greenhouse gas and particulate matter emissions relative to petrodiesel, but biodiesel engine emissions (DEEs) contain higher levels of nitrogen oxides, nano-sized particles, and specific oxygenated volatile organic compounds and aromatics that may increase health risks. Most research on DEE health effects has focused on respiratory, cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and reproductive outcomes, leaving a considerable knowledge gap regarding gastrointestinal effects. We therefore examined and compared the colon effects of DEE produced by combustion of first-generation B7 biofuel (7% v/v fatty acid methyl esters, FAMEs) or second-generation SHB20 biofuel (7% v/v FAME plus 13% v/v hydrotreated vegetable oils, HVOs), with or without a diesel particle filter (DPF). Male Fischer 344 rats were exposed to DEE for 7 consecutive days (6 h/day; seven exposure sessions, 42 h in total) in whole-body inhalation chambers, at measured particulate matter concentrations of 2.19 and 2.13 mg/m3 without DPF and 0.17 and 0.19 mg/m3 with DPF for B7 and SHB20, respectively. Whole-body DEE exposure induced lipid peroxidation, oxidative-stress-associated and redox-related changes, mobilisation of the antioxidant defence system, and an inflammatory-associated response in colon tissue. These colon effects were blend-specific and only partly and endpoint-dependently mitigated by DPF use, with SHB20 DEE without DPF producing the most pronounced responses.

Article.Title: Extracellular Vesicle-Mediated Angiogenesis in Peripheral Artery Disease: Context-Dependent Effects in Ischemic Limbs and Atherosclerotic Plaques
Article.Authors: Tamaru Y.; Yoshioka Y.; Kikuchi S.; Ochiya T.
Article.Abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is most commonly caused by atherosclerotic arterial stenosis or occlusion, which reduces downstream tissue perfusion and causes tissue ischemia. In response to ischemia, reparative angiogenesis is activated and may support tissue perfusion recovery and skeletal muscle protection. In contrast, neovascularization within atherosclerotic plaques may promote intraplaque hemorrhage and plaque destabilization. Thus, angiogenesis has dual roles in PAD-related ischemia and atherosclerotic plaques. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membrane-bound particles that carry various cargo, including proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and metabolites. Through the transfer of bioactive cargo and surface-mediated signaling, EVs can modify recipient-cell functions and thereby influence angiogenic signaling. Investigation of EV-mediated communication may therefore help elucidate the mechanisms underlying angiogenic regulation in vascular disease. In addition, disease-promoting EVs may be therapeutically targeted, whereas engineered EVs may be developed as therapeutic agents or delivery platforms. Recent studies have shown that EVs regulate angiogenic responses in preclinical murine hindlimb ischemia models. However, these effects in ischemic limbs and the potential involvement of EVs in atherosclerotic plaque neovascularization have rarely been reviewed in an integrated manner. This narrative review discusses these contrasting angiogenic processes from a context-dependent perspective. Understanding this context dependency may help develop EV-based strategies that promote functional vascular repair in ischemic tissues while suppressing or normalizing pathological neovascularization in atherosclerotic plaques.

Article.Title: Does Thymoma Plus Hypogammaglobulinemia Define Good Syndrome? A 30-Year Longitudinal Study of a Single Patient with Persistent B-Cell Preservation
Article.Authors: Iguasnia Portilla D.; Castillo Castillo I.; Franco Figueroa V.; Fernández Cabrera H.; Romero Chala S.; Sobieschi I.; Cordero H.; Fernández Pereira L.
Article.Abstract: Good syndrome is commonly diagnosed when thymoma and hypogammaglobulinemia coexist, although universally accepted diagnostic criteria are lacking. Profound B-cell lymphopenia is one of its most consistent immunological features. We describe a woman followed for 30 years in our unit whose severe antibody deficiency preceded thymoma detection by 14 years. Circulating B cells were preserved before thymectomy and throughout 16 years of subsequent follow-up, with maintained class-switched memory B cells despite persistent antibody deficiency. Her clinical course was favorable under immunoglobulin replacement, without documented major opportunistic infections. T-cell differentiation abnormalities were present despite preserved absolute counts. These findings suggest that patients currently classified as Good syndrome may represent a more heterogeneous group than traditionally assumed. Although preserved B cells do not exclude Good syndrome under existing definitions, the present observation should be considered hypothesis-generating and supports further studies evaluating potential biological heterogeneity among patients diagnosed with Good syndrome. This case highlights the need for consensus diagnostic criteria that consider the temporal relationship between both conditions, B-cell numbers, and the accompanying immune abnormalities, rather than relying on the coexistence of thymoma and hypogammaglobulinemia alone.

Article.Title: Molecular and Translational Anti-Inflammatory Strategies After Abdominal and Liver Surgery: From Immunonutrition to Cell-Based Therapies
Article.Authors: Pietrzyk B.; Pierzchała W.; Mikolajczyk J.; Lis P.; Heliasz A.; Kaczmarczyk B.
Article.Abstract: Postoperative inflammation influences recovery after abdominal and liver surgery. This narrative review critically synthesizes clinical and translational evidence on inflammation-modulating strategies using a structured search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library for publications from 2015 to 2025. Case reports, pediatric studies, and publications lacking clinical or translational relevance were excluded. Immunonutrition and early enteral nutrition are the most established approaches, with benefits for postoperative recovery and infectious complications. Perioperative corticosteroids in liver resection and short-course antibiotics following adequate source control offer procedure- and indication-specific benefits. Emerging interventions, including microbiota modulation, N-acetylcysteine, activation of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2/heme oxygenase-1 signaling, and cell-based therapies, show biological promise but lack sufficient high-quality clinical evidence for routine implementation. Established strategies should be integrated into Enhanced Recovery After Surgery pathways according to patient risk and surgical context. Personalized management requires prospective validation of emerging therapies and candidate biomarkers, including interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, and heme oxygenase-1, with standardized assays and sampling schedules.

Article.Title: Arecoline Induces Testicular Injury and Impairs Spermatogenesis in Rats Through Notch Signaling-Mediated Oxidative Stress
Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Li W.; Ge P.; Lv M.; Sun Y.; Chen Q.; Zhang J.; Sun R.; Zhou D.; Liu M.
Article.Abstract: Millions of people chew areca nut to boost work efficiency and relieve stress. Areca nut contains arecoline, which adversely affects reproductive function, although the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Herein, we evaluated arecoline-mediated reproductive toxicity using Sprague–Dawley (SD) rat models and an in vitro GC-1 cell model. Rescue experiments showed that the Notch activator valproic acid, used to enhance Notch signaling, alleviated arecoline-induced toxicity, whereas Notch inhibitor FLI-06 worsened cell injury. Article.Title: Mitochondrial ROS and Mitophagy in Intervertebral Disc Degeneration: Mechanistic Interplay and Links to Regulated Cell Death
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Cao K.; Cheng H.; Fang Z.
Article.Abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) develops through interacting mechanical, matrix, nutritional, inflammatory and age-related processes. Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and mitophagy participate in some of these contexts, but current evidence does not place mitophagy failure at the start of every degenerative trajectory. Most mechanistic studies have been performed in nucleus pulposus (NP) cells. In these models, mechanical overload, inflammatory mediators and oxidant stress can depolarize mitochondria, disturb fission–fusion balance and increase mtROS. Mitophagy can limit injury when damaged cargo is selected and delivered through a competent lysosomal pathway; accumulation of pathway markers during blocked flux, or mitochondrial clearance that is not matched by renewal, need not be protective. The most extensive mechanistic literature concerns apoptosis and senescence. Evidence linking mitochondrial quality control to pyroptosis and ferroptosis is growing but remains model-dependent, whereas direct evidence for necroptosis is comparatively sparse. We use a capacity-matching framework to organize these findings around damage burden, cargo selection, lysosomal completion and mitochondrial renewal within the regional metabolic constraints of the disc. This is an interpretive framework rather than a newly identified pathway. Its purpose is to define testable conditions under which mitophagy is likely to be protective, insufficient or maladaptive, while preserving the distinction between NP-derived evidence and the more limited evidence from annulus fibrosus and cartilage endplate cells.

Article.Title: Oxysterols Are Not Functionally Equivalent: Cell-Type- and Territory-Specific Responses in Human Models of Atherosclerosis
Article.Authors: Truffin D.; Marchand F.; Chatelais M.
Article.Abstract: This study aimed to compare the biological activities of major oxysterols, including 7-ketocholesterol (7KC), 7α-hydroxycholesterol (7α-HC), 7β-hydroxycholesterol (7β-HC), and 27-hydroxycholesterol (27HC), as well as oxidized LDL (oxLDL), in complementary human models representative of the atherosclerotic microenvironment: monocyte-derived macrophages (MΦs), vascular endothelial cells (v-ECs), and vascular smooth muscle cells (v-SMCs) isolated from the carotid artery and abdominal aorta. Cellular responses were strongly dependent on both cell type and vascular territory. Among the oxysterols tested, 7KC exerted the strongest biological effects, markedly reducing cell viability, increasing oxidative stress and apoptosis, promoting endothelial dysfunction, and profoundly altering lipid homeostasis pathways. Spectral Nile Red analysis further revealed distinct patterns of neutral-lipid- and phospholipid-associated fluorescence, indicating oxysterol-specific remodeling of intracellular lipid compartments. In vascular smooth muscle cells, 7KC was associated with increased CD36 expression and reduced ABCA1/ABCG1-mediated cholesterol efflux, whereas macrophages responded predominantly through SREBP1- and NR1H4-associated metabolic reprogramming rather than enhanced lipid uptake. In contrast, oxLDL was the strongest inducer of neutral lipid accumulation and classical foam-cell formation in macrophages. Although 27HC increased intracellular 7KC levels, it induced comparatively limited effects on viability, oxidative stress, and macrophage functions. Moreover, oxLDL promoted a distinct macrophage activation state and altered polarization trajectories depending on the timing of exposure. These findings demonstrate that major oxysterols exert distinct and complementary biological effects across vascular and immune cell populations, highlighting their differential contribution to atherosclerotic plaque development and progression, and support the development of therapeutic approaches targeting multiple oxysterol species rather than a single oxidized cholesterol derivative.

Article.Authors: Yin G.; Chen Z.; Feng G.; Lu J.; Jiao C.; Zhu Z.; Liu L.; Xu C.

Article.Title: Host Ubiquitin-Specific Proteases Regulate All Stages of Herpesvirus Infection
Article.Authors: Maarouf M.; Peterson C.; Mohni K.
Article.Abstract: Herpesviruses are a large group of double-stranded-DNA viruses that replicate their genomes in the nucleus, forming large replication compartments during lytic infection. Herpesviruses are known to modulate host DNA replication and DNA damage-repair proteins to promote their replication. Ubiquitination is a cellular process that can alter protein stability, localization, and availability, including that of multiple proteins involved in genome maintenance. Ubiquitin-specific proteases (USPs) are a class of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) that counter this process by removing ubiquitin chains, thus acting as another level of regulation. Proteins from each of the three herpesvirus subfamilies (alpha-, beta-, and gammaherpesviruses) have been reported to interact with at least one host USP, and USP7 in particular is reported as a target in representatives of all three subfamilies. In this review, we give an up-to-date summary of herpesviruses–USPs interactions, with special emphasis on DNA replication, and how these interactions could shape infection outcomes. We also examine published proteomic datasets for herpesvirus-driven host-proteome modulation and offer a framework for future directions to prioritize potentially important, understudied USPs. Lastly, we visit herpesvirus-encoded DUBs and highlight their roles in viral replication by remodeling ubiquitin signaling, discussing viral DUBs and virus–USP interfaces as proposed antiviral targets.

Article.Authors: Zhao T.; Hoffman M.; Wu G.; Belzil V.

Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Zhou Y.
Article.Abstract: Holliday junctions, four-way DNA crossovers central to DNA origami and key intermediates of homologous recombination, must be accurately modeled for rational DNA-nanodevice design, yet their solution conformational ensemble remains incompletely characterized. In every force field, the junction explores a broad, nearly flat inter-arm-angle landscape, with <1 kcal/mol variation across inter-arm angles of 2–90°: the open state is favored by 0.45–0.63 kcal/mol, the crystallographic-like inter-arm angle occurs in 2–5% of frames, and the crossover remains coaxially stacked whether open or compact. A Mg2+ ion occupies the crossover pocket in 92–94% of frames, specifically bridging the A- and C-strand phosphates (Li–Merz CM Mg2+ set). Stacking-isomer exchange between the A/C-continuous and crystallographic B/D isomers proceeds at ~0.5 ns−1 in this minimal short-arm construct, independent of force field, with A/C-continuous favored ~2:1. parmbsc1 yields a more open junction than OL21 and OL24, which reproduce the crystallographic inter-arm angle of 39–43°; the sugar-pucker shift targeted in OL24 is also visible at the junction. These results establish a force-field-robust baseline for simulation-guided design of crossover-containing nanostructures.

The RyR2R4496C mutation enhanced RyR2 sensitivity to caffeine, resulting in larger increases in intracellular [Ca2+]i and arterial contractions in older mice. Article.Title: Synergistic Anti-Zika Activity of Repurposed Statin and Clofibrate Combinations: Evidence from Oleic Acid-Mediated Metabolic Complementation
Article.Authors: Lee C.; Park S.; Lee G.; Moon H.; Choi J.; Lee J.; Martinez-Sobrido L.; Almazán F.; Ryu E.; Baek Y.; Park J.
Article.Abstract: Zika virus (ZIKV) substantially relies on host lipid metabolism, presenting a prime target for host-directed antivirals. Top lipid-lowering candidates were validated using a reporter virus (rZIKV-Venus) and an authentic wild-type (WT) ZIKV in Vero E6 cells—a model deliberately selected for its interferon deficiency to isolate pure metabolic responses. Dose–response screening of 67 prioritized compounds identified atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, and clofibrate as potent ZIKV inhibitors. Relative LD intensity strongly correlated with viral intensity in both models (Pearson r = 0.951 and 0.956, respectively; both p < 0.0001). Article.Title: A Tailored Sequencing Approach for Identifying SARS-CoV-2 Variants in Challenging Samples from Mink
Article.Authors: Giza A.; Iwan E.; Bomba A.; Orłowska A.; Smreczak M.; Pietruk M.; Chudzik A.; Olejnik M.; Domańska-Blicharz K.
Article.Abstract: High-throughput sequencing (HTS) is an essential tool for genomic surveillance of infectious agents, including SARS-CoV-2 in farmed mink. The custom hybrid-capture approach was selected because of its superior coverage uniformity, the lowest number of ambiguous bases (N), adjustability to low RNA levels and degraded material, and streamlined laboratory workflow. To further evaluate its applicability, it was applied to 35 clinical samples collected as part of routine genomic surveillance. This method generated sequencing data with high mapping rates (median 95%), depth of coverage (median 13,238×), breadth of coverage (median 100%), and mean mapq (median 60). These findings demonstrate that the custom hybrid-capture approach is a useful tool for genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 in mink-origin samples.

Article.Title: Computational Discovery of Plant-Derived Peptides with Therapeutic Potential: A Scoping Review
Article.Authors: Maphumulo S.; Mpofana N.; Ojewole E.
Article.Abstract: Computational methods are increasingly applied to the discovery of plant-derived peptides, but the extent, composition and reporting practice of this literature have not been mapped. Following PRISMA-ScR and Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect and PubMed were searched for records published between 2021 and 2026. Of 5062 unique records, 593 were screened at title and abstract, 88 full texts were assessed, 80 sources met all five eligibility criteria and 79 were charted. Overall, 49 (62.0%) were primary studies, 12 (15.2%) described a tool or database and 18 (22.8%) were narrative reviews. Antimicrobial peptides were the commonest class (33, 41.8%), followed by antioxidant (21, 26.6%) and ACE-inhibitory peptides (18, 22.8%). Only 11 sources (13.9%) trained and evaluated a model of their own, whereas 23 (29.1%) combined prediction with molecular docking. Of 61 empirical sources, 14 (23.0%) reported at least one quantitative prediction-task performance figure and 13 (21.3%) benchmarked a named comparator; the metrics used were not mutually comparable. Moreover, 18 of 62 applicable sources (29.0%) confirmed their own prediction experimentally; 70 (88.6%) named a plant source, most often Arabidopsis thaliana; and 8 (10.1%) linked their material to documented traditional medicine. No source applied machine learning to African plant peptides, an absence within the literature sampled rather than proof that none exists.

Article.Title: Real-Time Automated Fluorescence Imaging Assay for Quantifying GFP-Expressing Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis
Article.Authors: Badia-Bringué G.; Prado-López A.; Alonso-Hearn M.
Article.Abstract: Measurement of Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP) load within macrophages using a mycobacterial growth inhibition assay (MGIA) is an accurate indicator of host immune control of MAP infection. Real-time fluorescent microscopy allows the continuous analysis of infected cells and the quantification of fluorescence intensity, which directly correlates with concentration of fluorescent bacteria. The objective of this study was to develop an automated and real-time live-cell imaging assay using the IncuCyte SX1® platform for quantifying green fluorescence protein (GFP)-expressing MAP (MAP-GFP) within infected macrophages. The fluorescence of serially diluted free MAP-GFP was quantified using the IncuCyte SX1® demonstrating that the fluorescence signal of 3 × 107 CFU was significantly different from lowest MAP concentrations. Significant differences between uninfected and infected BOMAC cells (MOI; 1:10) in DMEM-F12, DMEM-F12 supplemented with fetal bovine serum (FBS), and RPMI-1640 supplemented with FBS were observed, indicating the suitability of these culture media for measuring MAP-GFP-host cell interaction in the IncuCyte SX1®. For the optimization of the MOI and cell density, bovine monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) and the BOMAC cells were seeded at different cell densities and infected with MAP-GFP at different MOIs. After 2 h of infection, the supernatant was removed, the cells were washed three times with HBSS, and fresh RPMI-1640 supplemented with FBS was added to the cells. Then, the fluorescence was quantified in the IncuCyte SX1® at different times p.i. Our results demonstrated that MAP phagocytosis is pathogen number- and cell density-dependent. Overall, the results showed that infection of 1 × 106 cells at an MOI of 1:10 maintained a stable fluorescence signal of approximately 400 to 500 GCU ⋅ μm2/image across 2 h to 4 days p.i. In addition, good correlations between MAP-GFP (logCFUs) estimated in the BACTEC MGIT™ 960 system and fluorescence intensity measured in the IncuCyte SX1® were observed for free MAP-GFP bacilli and from MAP-GFP within infected BOMAC cells, r = 0.79 and r = 0.78, respectively. In conclusion, real-time fluorescent microscopy enables continuous monitoring of MAP-GFP within infected macrophages.

Article.Title: Preliminary Evaluation of the Anticancer Activity of a PGK1 Small Molecule Inhibitor in Ishikawa Endometrial Cancer
Article.Authors: Cao H.; Xue S.; Xue M.; Li F.; Feng L.; Zheng W.; Ding H.; Zhang T.
Article.Abstract: To investigate the roles of a phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) small-molecule inhibitor in Ishikawa endometrial cancer. Moreover, NG52 significantly reduced the migration ability of the Ishikawa cell line in a dose-dependent manner. Flow cytometry (FCM) demonstrated that NG52 affected the survival of endometrial carcinoma cells by arresting the cell cycle at the G1 phase and inducing apoptosis in a dose-dependent manner. Western blot analysis also revealed that the apoptosis-inducing effects of NG52 were accompanied by a reduction in PGK1 expression after 48 h and 72 h of NG52 treatment. Moreover, NG52 partially suppressed tumor growth in a human Ishikawa xenograft model, and transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) showed an increasing trend of NG52-treated tumor tissue apoptosis, with a decreasing trend in PGK1 expression in the treatment group. NG52, a PGK1 small molecule inhibitor, can serve as a structural basis for developing potential anti-endometrial carcinoma agents. The findings are limited to the preliminary preclinical activity of NG52, and further mechanistic, pharmacologic, efficacy, and safety studies are warranted before improved PGK1 inhibitors can proceed to clinical translation.

Article.Title: Evaluation of Dihydropyridine Derivatives as Aldose Reductase Inhibitors: Enzymatic Screening, Molecular Docking and Ex Vivo Assessment of a Selected Compound in a Lens Model
Article.Authors: Alonso-Hurtado K.; Méndez-Pérez T.; Hernández-Gallegos Z.; Cajero-Juárez M.; Navarro-Santos P.; Virgen-Ortíz J.; Martínez-Pacheco M.
Article.Abstract: Aldose reductase (AR) is a key enzyme in the polyol pathway and has been widely implicated in the development of diabetic complications, including cataract formation. Molecular docking using the AR–NADP complex identified favorable binding poses and interactions with residues involved in ligand recognition and stabilization, although no direct correlation was observed between predicted docking scores and experimental inhibitory potency. A representative compound (DHP3, IC50 = 1.11 ± 0.07 µM) was elected for ex vivo evaluation in a rabbit lens model under hyperglycemic conditions. Treatment reduced glucose-induced lens opacity by 89.1%, estimated by image-based analysis, and decreased sorbitol accumulation by 57.48% relative to hyperglycemic control, indicating modulation of the polyol pathway at the tissue level. In contrast, no significant changes were detected in calcium content. These findings support the potential of DHP derivatives as a scaffold for aldose reductase inhibition and highlight their ability to attenuate early alterations associated with hyperglycemia in lens tissue. Further studies are required to expand biological validation and optimize their inhibitory profile.

Article.Title: Ovariectomy Exacerbates Chronic Constriction Injury-Induced Neuropathic Pain Through Dysregulation of Spinal Estrogen Receptor Balance in Rats
Article.Authors: Chan Y.; Lin S.; Huang C.; Zheng T.; Wang Y.; Tsai Y.
Article.Abstract: Estrogen depletion after menopause has been associated with altered pain sensitivity; however, the spinal mechanisms linking estrogen deficiency to neuropathic pain remain incompletely understood. This study investigated whether ovariectomy (OVX)-induced estrogen depletion exacerbates chronic constriction injury (CCI)-induced neuropathic pain and whether this effect is associated with changes in spinal estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) and estrogen receptor beta (ERβ) expression. Female Sprague Dawley rats underwent OVX or sham surgery, followed 5 weeks later by median nerve CCI or sham CCI. Mechanical withdrawal thresholds and thermal withdrawal latencies were evaluated using von Frey filaments and the plantar test, respectively. ERα and ERβ expression in the spinal dorsal horn was assessed via immunofluorescence staining and Western blotting. Selective ERα and ERβ agonists were administered intrathecally to examine their effects on OVX/CCI-induced pain behaviors. Rats in the OVX/CCI group exhibited more pronounced pain behaviors than those in the Sham/CCI group, indicating that OVX exacerbated CCI-induced neuropathic pain. In the spinal dorsal horn, ERα expression was increased in the OVX/Sham, Sham/CCI, and OVX/CCI groups, with the greatest increase observed in the OVX/CCI group. In contrast, ERβ expression was decreased in the Sham/CCI and OVX/CCI groups, with no significant difference between these groups. Intrathecal administration of an ERα agonist further aggravated mechanical allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia in OVX/CCI rats, whereas an ERβ agonist attenuated these pain behaviors. These findings suggest that OVX-induced estrogen depletion exacerbates CCI-induced neuropathic pain, potentially through a shift toward ERα-dominant signaling relative to ERβ in the spinal dorsal horn. Selective modulation of ERα and ERβ may therefore represent a potential therapeutic approach for chronic pain exacerbated by estrogen depletion.

Article.Title: Vitamin K2 and Cardiovascular Calcification: Mechanistic Foundations, Conflicting Clinical Evidence, and Unresolved Questions
Article.Authors: Kothari C.; Chowdhary R.; Babazade S.; Egoavil A.; Abuirmaileh W.; Kapadia S.; Wimalawansa S.
Article.Abstract: Cardiovascular calcification is an active, complex process involving osteogenic transformation, inflammation, extracellular vesicle release, and impaired mineral buffering. These changes result from mineral imbalance and reduced levels of calcification inhibitors. Vitamin K supports the γ-carboxylation of matrix Gla protein (MGP) and other mineralization inhibitors, though some calcification defenses do not depend on vitamin K. Vitamin K deficiency and warfarin therapy increase circulating dephosphorylated-uncarboxylated MGP (dp-ucMGP), which is linked to greater vascular calcification. Preclinical studies demonstrate that disruption of the vitamin K-MGP axis promotes calcification. Supplementation with vitamin K1 or K2 can reduce, prevent, or partially reverse mineralization in certain animal models. In contrast, evidence from human studies is less consistent. Observational studies have identified an association between menaquinone (vitamin K2) intake and cardiovascular outcomes, but causality has not been established. Most randomized trials have shown neutral results for aortic-valve and chronic kidney disease-associated calcification, while the VitaK-CAC and DANCODE studies reported slower progression of coronary artery calcium in selected populations with moderate or severe baseline coronary calcification. These discrepancies may be due to differences in calcification phenotypes, disease stage, vitamin K forms, dosing regimens, vitamin D status, renal function, and response to vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin. Coronary intimal, valvular, and arterial medial calcification should be regarded as phenotypically distinct entities. This review evaluates the mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical evidence linking vitamin K2 to cardiovascular calcification and highlights population groups that warrant further clinical investigation. Large, adequately powered, and phenotype-specific clinical trials are needed to determine whether appropriately dosed vitamin K2 is a safe and cost-effective intervention for slowing valvular and vascular calcification.

Article.Title: Conserved Hepatospora eriocheir Sequences in Chinese Mitten Crabs from Poland, Germany and Belgium: A Comparative Molecular Study
Article.Authors: Stachnik M.; Normant-Saremba M.; Ewers C.; Keirsebelik H.; Schoelynck J.
Article.Abstract: Hepatospora eriocheir is an obligate intracellular microsporidian associated with the Chinese mitten crab, Eriocheir sinensis, an important aquaculture species in Asia and an invasive species in Europe. Both parasite gene fragments were identical across four host mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) haplotypes; the Eriocheir japonica-associated haplotype was detected only in Belgian crabs in this sample. The study provides the first specimen-linked, sequence-confirmed molecular characterisation of infections in the sampled German and Belgian crab populations, together with new Polish infections from 2022 and a comparative two-locus reference dataset. The repeated Baltic detection, combined with shared Polish–German host COI haplotypes and existing evidence of North Sea–Baltic connectivity, is consistent with the arrival of infected migrating crabs, although the parasite’s precise source remains unresolved.

Risk-of-bias assessments classified 123 results as High and 36 as Some concerns; none was Low overall. Selected formulations and procedure-assisted regimens showed benefits for particular outcomes, whereas other comparisons were null or discordant. Retrospective result selection, heterogeneous interventions and outcomes, four access-unresolved reports, and the absence of a prospective protocol constrain confidence. Clinical claims should remain specific to the product, protocol, indication, comparator, and outcome investigated.

Article.Abstract: Cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) and TEMPO-oxidized cellulose nanofibrils (TOCNFs) are hydrated, high-aspect-ratio biomaterials with tunable physicochemical properties, whereas human-derived extracellular matrix (ECM) hydrogels provide matrix-associated biochemical cues. In this study, CNF- and TOCNF-based hybrid scaffolds incorporating human ECM hydrogel components were developed and evaluated in vitro as platforms relevant to cutaneous wound repair. Hybrid formulations gelled at physiological temperature and exhibited formulation-dependent shear-thinning behavior, elastic properties, protein release/leaching profiles, and porous fibrillar microstructures. Selected formulations supported cell-associated metabolic activity of human dermal fibroblasts and adipose-derived stromal/stem cells under two-dimensional and three-dimensional culture conditions. Additional exploratory studies demonstrated qualitative compatibility with adipogenic culture and condition-dependent changes in wound-gap width. In the absence of in vivo validation and confirmatory biological assays, these findings are interpreted as proof-of-concept rather than evidence of wound-healing efficacy. Overall, the results demonstrate the feasibility of combining CNF or TOCNF structural networks with human-derived ECM hydrogels to generate hybrid scaffolds with wound-relevant material properties and preliminary cytocompatibility, supporting further mechanistic and preclinical evaluation.

Article.Title: Pyrrolocytosine as a Fluorescent Sensor of RNA–Small Molecule Interactions
Article.Authors: Coulson T.; Valdez G.; Widom J.
Article.Abstract: Fluorescent base analogues have proven to be valuable probes of RNA structure. Pyrrolocytosine (pC), an analogue of cytosine, exhibits highly environment-sensitive fluorescence within RNA and is strongly quenched in hydrogen-bonded contexts. In this work, we incorporated pC into the aptamer domain of the B. subtilis guanine riboswitch to determine if this quenching mechanism could allow for sensing of RNA–small molecule interactions. We utilized complementary fluorescence spectroscopy methods to understand the functional impacts and ligand sensitivity of pC substitutions distal to and within the binding pocket. We found that pC substitution within a static structural region exhibits the expected ligand-independent fluorescence properties. When placed in the ligand binding pocket, pC exhibits a moderately decreased affinity for the ligands guanine (G) and hypoxanthine (Hx) while maintaining high specificity for G. We found that pC behaves as a turn-off sensor, with distinct changes in fluorescence upon G or Hx binding. These differences are dependent on the number of hydrogen bonds formed with pC and are resolvable in both time-dependent and steady-state fluorescence measurements. Our results show that pC can be used to study RNA–small molecule interactions and can discriminate between similar ligands even when they have identical binding modes.

Article.Title: A Decision-Centric Benchmark of Enrichment and Potency Ranking in CNN-Rescored Molecular Docking
Article.Authors: Lai Y.; Huang H.
Article.Abstract: Virtual screening answers two different questions with one number: enrichment, separating actives from background molecules, and potency ranking, ordering actives by measured activity. We benchmarked both for the same score on the same compounds across five CNS binding sites (SERT, GABAA benzodiazepine site, 5-HT1A, σ1, and NMDA MK-801 pore), docking ChEMBL actives, inactives, and property-matched decoys with Uni-Dock and GNINA under a held-out normalisation/evaluation split, plus an experimentally characterised negative probe excluded from all fitting. Ranking, evaluated among pChEMBL ≥ 7 actives, was negligible for every target (median Spearman ρ = 0.020) and was not recovered by data-quality filtering, multivariate null models, scaffold-aware resampling, strict assay–site matching with rebuilt decoys, or stricter curation. Enrichment proved strongly benchmark-dependent: an apparent ΔAUC gain of +0.153 against molecular weight-matched decoys decreased to ≤0.05 once the decoys were matched to seven descriptors, and the residue was not robust to compound resampling. A classifier using no structural information separated the same actives from the same decoys at ROC-AUC 0.959–0.993, and cognate ligand redocking reproduced the crystallographic pose as the top-ranked solution for one of five targets. Benchmark enrichment should not be equated with protein-specific recognition; the benchmark, the poses, and the ranking require separate validation.

Article.Title: Beyond Mesothelioma: From Diagnostic Biomarker to Therapeutic Opportunity—The Emerging Role of MTAP in Cancer
Article.Authors: Diluvio A.; Lucà S.; Iavarone L.; Masola V.; Fiorelli A.; Morgillo F.; D’Abbronzo G.; Franco R.
Article.Abstract: Methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP) loss is an emerging biomarker in several human malignancies, mainly due to its frequent co-deletion with CDKN2A on chromosome 9p21. Beyond its diagnostic value, MTAP deficiency has important biological consequences, including metabolic reprogramming, immune microenvironment modulation, and increased dependency on PRMT5-related pathways. This review summarizes the current evidence on MTAP alterations across different tumor types. The role of MTAP immunohistochemistry as a practical surrogate for CDKN2A homozygous deletion is discussed, together with its advantages and interpretative limitations. In addition, the potential predictive relevance of MTAP loss for immunotherapy, antifolate-based treatments, and novel PRMT5-targeted strategies is explored. Overall, MTAP assessment represents a promising tool in modern diagnostic pathology and precision oncology, bridging morphology, molecular alterations, and therapeutic decision-making.

Article.Title: From Oxyntomodulin to Retatrutide: A Translational Review of Metabolic Polyagonism
Article.Authors: Saldívar-Cerón H.; Maldonado-Trejo D.; Chavez-Castañeda Q.; Mercado-Guzmán A.; León-Barrita A.; López-García I.; Hernández-Solís A.; Ramírez-Mendoza A.; Terrazas-Delgado D.; Castañeda-Ramírez A.; Quiñones-Lara E.; Jay-Jímenez B.; Pozo-Molina G.; León-Cabrera S.
Article.Abstract: Oxyntomodulin (OXM), an endogenous proglucagon-derived peptide with dual glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) and glucagon receptor (GCGR) agonism, provides a physiological precedent for contemporary multi-receptor pharmacology. Recognition that GCGR signaling regulates not only hepatic glucose production but also amino acid turnover, lipid metabolism, substrate oxidation, and energy expenditure prompted the development of engineered GLP-1R/GCGR co-agonists, including cotadutide, mazdutide, survodutide, and pemvidutide. Retatrutide extends this strategy by integrating GIPR, GLP-1R, and GCGR agonism within a single long-acting peptide and has produced substantial improvements in body weight, glycemic control, and cardiometabolic parameters in phase 2 and phase 3 trials. This review examines the evolutionary and structural relationships of the proglucagon–Class B1 GPCR system, OXM biosynthesis and receptor pharmacology, the mechanistic rationale for therapeutic GCGR agonism, and the molecular and clinical development of dual and triple agonists. We further address receptor balance, the GIPR agonism–antagonism paradox, receptor-specific causal attribution, and the unresolved limitations of translating molecular pharmacology into durable clinical benefit. Finally, we propose an Activity–Exposure–Context framework for interpreting polyagonist pharmacology and discuss prospective enteroinsular phenotyping using standardized mixed-meal testing as a testable strategy to investigate interindividual variability in therapeutic response.

Article.Title: ssDNA Wrapping of Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes and the Role of Sequence Periodicity: A Critical Review
Article.Authors: Al Nissafi L.; Emjeida M.; Venkatesan R.; Vetcher A.
Article.Abstract: Noncovalent hybrids of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are central to chiral sorting and near-infrared biosensing, yet no quantitative rule connects the periodicity of a natural sequence to the geometry of a given nanotube. Earlier reviews treat the sequence as a tool for sorting or sensing; this critical review asks what the published evidence up to 2026 establishes about periodicity. We compare base–wall affinities from calculation, calorimetry and force spectroscopy; the periods reported by cryo-electron microscopy, scanning tunnelling microscopy, atomic force microscopy (AFM) and X-ray scattering in solution; the recognition sequences used for single-chirality sorting; and the few studies of genomic DNA. The experimental order of base affinities depends on the method and on whether the surface is flat or curved. Helical pitches of 1.6–3.3 nm, spacings of 8.6–14.3 nm between strands in solution and the AFM period of about 14 nm are different quantities. Recognition depends on sequence pattern, length, chiral angle and handedness in addition to diameter. To our knowledge, base spacing at fixed composition has been varied only in covalently cross-linked hybrids; for noncovalent wrapping, this test is still missing. We outline the next experiments and the reporting standards and open data they require.

Article.Title: Hormone-Mediated Signaling of Reactive Oxygen Species Under Abiotic Stress
Article.Authors: Fedoreyeva L.; Bursakov S.; Molchanova T.; Muratova O.; Zakharova E.
Article.Abstract: Abiotic stresses trigger the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in various subcellular compartments of plant cells, where they perform a dual function: acting as cytotoxic agents during acute stress and as highly specific signaling modulators under mild or chronic stress. However, the fundamental question of how the cell distinguishes between toxic and signaling ROS pools—and how phytohormones coordinate this distinction—remains unresolved. This review re-examines the molecular logic of the hormone-redox interface, focusing on the post-translational modifications of NADPH oxidases (RBOHs) and antioxidant enzymes as a key mechanism for the rapid tuning of signals. Moving beyond traditional linear cascade models, we propose the concept of a “dynamic hormonal code,” in which abscisic acid acts as the primary initiator of apoplastic ROS bursts via SnRK2-dependent phosphorylation, while salicylates and jasmonates modulate the duration and amplitude of these bursts, thereby determining the outcome—ranging from programmed cell death to systemic resistance. Known mechanisms of the hormonal code have been established (e.g., ABA → SnRK2 → RBOH; SA/JA antagonism mediated by NPR1; and the redox relay involving PRXIIB/GPX3 → ABI2). This review goes beyond simple hormone combinatorics by proposing a conceptual framework: the hormonal code encodes ROS signals through parameters of time, amplitude, and cellular compartment. Particular attention is paid to recent discoveries regarding the roles of auxin and brassinosteroids in reconfiguring chloroplast redox homeostasis during flooding and heat shock. Generalizing these data, we propose an integrated model of spatiotemporal regulation that explains how feedback loops involving ROS, Ca2+ waves, and hormone receptors facilitate systemic acclimation. Thus, targeting key crosstalk nodes—specifically SnRK2 and TOR kinase complexes—offers new strategies for engineering stress-resilient crops in the face of climate change.

Article.Title: Exercise Modalities, Training Dose, and Circulating Myostatin and Follistatin in Adults: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Qiao C.; Yang C.; Guo S.; Yang S.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Exercise-associated changes in circulating myostatin (MSTN) and follistatin (FST) across training modalities remain uncertain. Seven bibliographic databases were searched for controlled exercise interventions lasting at least four weeks in adults (PROSPERO CRD420261492548). Multilevel random-effects models used study-clustered CR2 inference. Renewed retrieval enabled assessment of 203 of 220 reports. The review included 79 reports from 78 study families; 39 studies contributed primary effects. Exercise was associated with lower MSTN (57 effects; 33 studies; Hedges’ g = 1.25, 95% CI 0.68–1.82) and higher FST (42 effects; 23 studies; g = 1.58, 95% CI 0.92–2.23). Heterogeneity remained high and reference-model prediction intervals crossed zero. Excluding extreme effects attenuated the pooled magnitudes. Graph-exclusion and leave-one-study-out analyses retained positive average-effect intervals. Exploratory modality and dose analyses did not establish superiority or an optimal prescription. GRADE certainty was low for both outcomes. Exercise may alter circulating MSTN and FST, but assay differences, retrieval restrictions and heterogeneous protocols limit interpretation. These findings do not establish a confirmed intracellular mechanism or validated clinical surrogate endpoint.

Article.Title: 2B9-Fc Ameliorates Immune Thrombocytopenia by Suppressing STAT1-Mediated M1 Macrophage Polarization and Expanding Regulatory T Cells
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Xing S.; Shen X.; Zhu W.; Ge M.; Xiao H.; Yu K.; Yu Z.
Article.Abstract: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune bleeding disorder in which enhanced platelet destruction and impaired platelet production coexist, and a substantial proportion of patients remain refractory to available therapies. Here, we evaluated 2B9-Fc, a thrombopoietin (TPO) mimetic peptide engineered from a cyclic peptide with high affinity for both human and mouse c-MPL, in passive (anti-CD41 monoclonal antibody R300) and active (guinea pig anti-mouse platelet serum, GP-APS) immunization male C57BL/6J and humanized c-MPL receptor transgenic mouse models of ITP. 2B9-Fc (500 μg/kg, subcutaneously) significantly elevated peripheral platelet counts in both models (p < 0.01), without affecting WBC, RBC, or hemoglobin, and alleviated skin purpura and bleeding scores in the active model. In addition, 2B9-Fc treatment was associated with a reduced splenic M1/M2 macrophage ratio, increased regulatory T cells (Tregs), downregulated IL-6 and iNOS while upregulating TGF-β1 and Foxp3, and suppressed STAT1 phosphorylation. In humanized c-MPL receptor transgenic (MT) mice, 2B9-Fc promoted CD41+ megakaryocyte generation in vitro and sustained platelet recovery in vivo through day 14. These results indicate that 2B9-Fc ameliorates ITP and is associated with promotion of megakaryocyte maturation and restoration of immune tolerance, likely involving inhibition of STAT1-mediated M1 polarization and Treg expansion, supporting its potential for clinical translation.

Article.Title: Raffinose in Brassica Crops: Integrating Plant Stress Physiology, Food Quality, Nutrition and Precision Breeding
Article.Authors: Czernicka M.; Czernicka M.
Article.Abstract: Raffinose-family oligosaccharides (RFOs) have nutritional and physiological significance that cannot be inferred from concentration alone. In Brassica, interpretation of their food value and definition of breeding targets require consideration of edible organ, environmental history, analytical resolution, and intended use. This critical review integrates evidence on RFO composition, plant physiology, food quality, and nutrition with an evidence-weighted assessment of conventional breeding, genetic transformation, and new genomic techniques. Direct Brassica experiments are distinguished from evidence derived from soybean and Arabidopsis and from prospective applications. Direct studies demonstrate that RFO metabolism in Brassica is manipulable, but they do not support a universal strategy for improving vegetable or meal quality. Genome-editing studies in soybean further show that reductions in total RFOs may coexist with increased raffinose and that lower RFO concentrations do not themselves demonstrate nutritional benefit. Tissue-specific regulation may offer a route to balance seed composition with stress responses, although genotype-dependent regeneration remains an important constraint. A three-tier framework is therefore proposed in which raffinose is interpreted as a stress-responsive metabolite, a potential food-quality indicator, and a context-dependent nutritional component. Compound-specific phenotyping, functional validation, and product-relevant physiological testing should precede deployment of low-RFO or stress-responsive Brassica material.

Article.Title: Functional Characterization of Glycosyltransferases from Saussurea involucrata Involved in Rutin Biosynthesis
Article.Authors: Yi P.; Huang B.; Zhan R.; Ma D.
Article.Abstract: Saussurea involucrata is a medicinal plant rich in flavonoids, but the glycosyltransferases (GTs) responsible for flavonoid glycosylation in this species remain largely uncharacterized. Here, five GT genes (SiUGT03, SiUGT09, SiUGT60, SiRhaT68-1, and SiRhaT68-2) were identified. Four of the five proteins (SiUGT03, SiUGT09, SiUGT60, and SiRhaT68-1) possessed an intact PSPG-box, and phylogenetic analysis placed SiUGT03 in the 3GT clade and SiRhaT68-1 in the 1,6GT clade. Recombinant proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli as soluble maltose-binding protein (MBP) fusions and purified. In vitro enzymatic assays showed that SiUGT03 catalyzed the 3-O-glucosylation of quercetin to isoquercetin (quercetin-3-O-glucoside), whereas SiRhaT68-1 catalyzed the 1,6-rhamnosylation of isoquercetin to rutin. Among the substrates tested, SiUGT03 was active only toward the flavonols quercetin and kaempferol, while SiRhaT68-1 was active toward isoquercetin and one of the four tested flavone 7-O-glucosides, diosmetin-7-O-glucoside. These results, obtained from separate in vitro assays, demonstrated that the two enzymes catalyze two consecutive terminal glycosylation steps of rutin biosynthesis and represent promising candidates for further exploration of rutin biosynthesis in S. involucrata.

Article.Authors: Dan Y.; Shelef O.; Buzhor M.; Shimon L.; Satchi-Fainaro R.; Shabat D.; Adler-Abramovich L.

Article.Abstract: Liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) is widely recognized as a fundamental mechanism underlying the formation of membraneless organelles, which are critical for maintaining spatiotemporal precision in cellular function. Dysregulation of LLPS has become increasingly recognized as a key driver underlying the development of multiple human diseases, thereby establishing this process as a rapidly growing focus in biomedical research. In this review, we examine the contributions of LLPS to cellular pathophysiology. We start by outlining the fundamental biophysical and molecular principles that govern LLPS formation. We further explore how aberrant phase transitions contribute to disease mechanisms across different organ systems. Building on this mechanistic framework, we assess current and potential therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting LLPS for clinical intervention. Overall, this review aims to synthesize current understanding of LLPS in disease etiology and to highlight its potential as a novel target for future therapeutic development.

Article.Title: The Impact of Intratumoral Bacterial Response to Vaccine Therapy in Cancer Treatment
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Sun Z.; Qi H.; Zhao D.; Xing X.; Jiang J.; Gao T.
Article.Abstract: Therapeutic Human papillomavirus (HPVs) vaccines are designed to enhance the immunogenicity of HPV and promote the elimination of tumor cells effectively. We analyzed RNA sequencing data from tumor tissues of C57BL/6N female mice treated with a DNA vaccine incorporating HPV16 E6/E7 antigens fused with the chemokine CCL11. Microbial community data were acquired using the PathSeq bioinformatics pipeline. Alpha diversity was estimated using the Shannon index and the number of observed taxonomic features, while beta diversity was assessed via principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) based on Bray–Curtis distance. Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) analysis was performed to identify differentially abundant microbial taxa. Immune cell infiltration was characterized using the xCell deconvolution method. The analysis revealed significant divergence in both the alpha- and beta-diversity metrics of intratumoral microbiota, associated with treatment responsiveness. Vaccinated groups exhibited enriched abundances of the phyla Proteobacteria, together with a concomitant reduction in Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, and were associated with a positive response to cancer immunotherapy. Additionally, intratumoral microbiome composition and diversity correlated with the increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells, natural killer T (NKT) cells, and myeloid cells. This study identifies intratumoral microbiota remodeling as a key feature of therapeutic HPV vaccine response. The observed coordination between bacterial signatures and immune cell infiltration is associative and raises the hypothesis that intratumoral bacteria may modulate, rather than drive, antitumor immunity. These findings support the development of intratumoral microbiota profiling and highlight the potential for microbiota-targeted strategies to enhance cancer immunotherapy efficacy.

Article.Title: Thylakoid Nanoarchitecture and Photosystem II Energy Partitioning in Response to Treatment with Huminatrin Concentrate “Boron”
Article.Authors: Bukhanov E.; Gaevsky N.; Poznakhareva O.; Tikhomirov A.; Ushakova S.; Shabanov V.
Article.Abstract: Photosynthetic acclimation involves coordinated changes in the structural organization and functional activity of the photosynthetic apparatus. However, the structural basis underlying enhanced photosynthetic activity following biostimulant treatment under non-stress conditions remains insufficiently understood. In the present study, we investigated the effects of exogenous application of the humic-boron fertilizer Huminatrin Concentrate “Boron” on the structural and functional organization of the photosynthetic apparatus in spring rapeseed (Brassica napus L.) cv. Siberian. These changes occurred without evidence of pronounced PSII photoinhibition, indicating that the observed changes in PSII photochemistry were not a response to experimentally induced stress. Structural and functional changes were accompanied by increases in plant and leaf biomass. Taken together, these findings indicate that leaf biostimulation is associated with coordinated remodeling of thylakoid architecture and PSII excitation-energy partitioning under the experimental conditions studied.

Article.Title: Selective PAC1 Receptor Antagonist, PA-810-04 Attenuates Oxaliplatin-Induced Hyperexcitability and Coordinated Firing in Cultured Dorsal Root Ganglion Neurons
Article.Authors: Arima T.; Takahama K.; Suetsugu K.; Kobae Y.; Iwai H.; Takasaki I.; Kurihara T.; Terazono H.
Article.Abstract: Oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy (OIPN) is a major dose-limiting adverse effect of chemotherapy, and dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons are its principal targets. Although pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP)/PAC1 receptor signaling has been implicated in neuropathic pain, its contribution to the oxaliplatin-induced hyperexcitability of primary sensory neurons remains unknown. We used a dual-axis multi-electrode array (MEA) platform quantifying the total spike count (TSC) and synchronous spike ratio (SSR), indices of overall activity and coordinated firing. Short-term oxaliplatin exposure produced concentration-dependent increases in TSC and SSR in cultured DRG neurons, which were significantly attenuated by the selective PAC1 receptor antagonist, PA-810-04. Similarly, conditioned medium from oxaliplatin-treated satellite glial cell (SGC)-enriched cultures increased TSC and SSR in naïve DRG neurons, and these effects were suppressed by PA-810-04. Exogenous PACAP alone increased TSC concentration-dependently, with only a modest effect on SSR, as a positive control. These findings identify a PA-810-04-sensitive component of early oxaliplatin-induced hyperexcitability in primary sensory neurons, while the proposed neuron–glia mechanism remains hypothetical. They also provide a quantitative in vitro approach for investigating neuron–glia interactions in early OIPN and evaluating PAC1-targeted candidates.

Article.Title: Immunometabolic Memory in Obesity: Nutritional Drivers, Persistence, and Reversibility
Article.Authors: Reytor-González C.; Zambrano-Villacres R.; Andrade Mejia N.; Duran-Agüero S.; Simancas-Racines D.
Article.Abstract: Obesity reshapes immune function across adipose tissue, circulation, and hematopoietic compartments. Weight reduction improves cardiometabolic health, yet emerging evidence indicates that prior obesity can leave persistent cellular, transcriptional, and epigenetic changes. Whether nutrition can reverse this biological imprint remains uncertain. We conducted a critical narrative review informed by structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and Epistemonikos, complemented by backward and forward citation tracking. We prioritized mechanistic human studies, controlled dietary interventions, longitudinal weight-loss studies, and experiments that tested persistence after stimulus withdrawal or response to re-exposure. Evidence was interpreted according to biological compartment and study design rather than pooled statistically. Obesogenic exposures can alter innate immune metabolism, inflammasome signaling, hematopoiesis, and chromatin states. Animal studies provide the strongest evidence that these changes can persist after weight normalization and amplify responses during weight regain. Human studies show incomplete normalization of adipose immune states, persistent adipocyte programs, and durable methylation changes in T lymphocytes after weight loss. Dietary interventions can lower inflammatory tone and modify immune metabolism, microbial metabolites, and lipid mediator pathways, but no dietary pattern has been shown to erase established obesity-associated immune memory in humans. An evidence map built on a core set of 47 studies showed that experimental work dominates the induction, persistence and re-challenge domains, whereas human evidence clusters in post-weight-loss remodelling and dietary modulation; human re-challenge data were absent and no study provided a direct test of reversal in humans. Obesity-associated immunometabolic memory appears to be distributed across hematopoietic, immune, adipose, stromal, and microbial compartments. Nutrition can modulate mechanisms implicated in this persistence, but human evidence of reversal is lacking, and whether pharmacologically induced weight loss leaves a comparable imprint has not been tested. Mechanistic trials should separate energy deficit, diet composition, adiposity change, and weight-loss modality and include a weight-stable follow-up and functional re-challenge where feasible.

Article.Title: A Comparative Analysis of Microglial and Astrocyte Transplantation in an Amyloid-Induced Rat for Alzheimer’s Disease
Article.Authors: Curecheriu L.; Iliescu B.; Stanciu G.; Mazarianu I.; Szilagyi A.; Gogu M.; Ciorpac M.; Balmus I.; Tutu P.; Horodincu L.; Daraban Bocaneti F.; Hritcu O.; Pasca A.; Tamba B.; Turliuc M.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is recognized as a neuroglial disorder in which dysregulated glial responses contribute to cognitive decline. We investigated whether intrahippocampal transplantation of primary glial cells modifies cognitive trajectories in an amyloid-induced rat model of AD. Sprague–Dawley rats received bilateral hippocampal injections of pre-aggregated Aβ1–42, followed by transplantation of primary astrocytes (AA) or microglia (AM). Memory was assessed using the Y-maze and novel object recognition (NOR) tests. Body weight and serum IL-6 and TNF-α were monitored for adverse effects, and GFAP, S100, Iba1 and TREM2 immunolabeling was quantified with QuPath. Mixed-effects models showed significant session and group x session effects on Y–maze spatial novelty recognition. Both treated groups improved compared with AD animals, with a stronger late effect in the AM group and a significant group × session × sex interaction. In the NOR test, both treated groups outperformed AD animals at the final session, without differences between them. GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) immunoreactivity was reduced in the AM group but remained elevated in the AA group, while TREM2 increased after microglial and decreased after astrocyte transplantation. No adverse effects were detected in the monitored parameters. Intrahippocampal glial transplantation, particularly with microglia, may influence cognitive trajectories in established amyloid pathology.
