Article.Title: Cerium Dioxide-Based Scavenging of Environmentally Persistent Free Radicals in Fine Particulate Matter: A Prospective Review
Article.Authors: Liu Q.; Yang Z.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: Environmental persistent free radicals (EPFRs) are a class of long-lived, redox-active species that persist on fine particulate matter (PM2.5) surfaces for days to months. Upon inhalation, EPFRs catalyze the generation of hydroxyl radicals through Fenton-like cycling, driving oxidative stress and inflammation at the site of deposition. Current air filtration technology focuses almost exclusively on physical interception of particulate matter, leaving the surface-bound radical activity of captured PM entirely unaddressed. This review advances a testable hypothesis rather than reporting a validated outcome: that cerium dioxide (CeO2)-based materials, whose Ce3+/Ce4+ redox cycling is well-established as a broad-spectrum antioxidant mechanism in biomedical contexts, can be functionally migrated to air filtration to chemically quench EPFRs on captured PM2.5. We first summarize the formation and health impacts of EPFRs, then introduce the mechanistic basis of CeO2 radical scavenging, emphasizing its self-regenerating valence cycling. We then examine the existing but functionally distinct use of CeO2 in air pollution control, including its role as an oxygen storage component in three-way catalysis and as an additive in filter media, and argue that these high-temperature oxidation applications do not constitute a functional precedent for ambient-temperature radical scavenging. The central gap is that no study has systematically tested whether CeO2 can chemically quench EPFRs on PM2.5 surfaces under filtration conditions. We articulate the key experimental questions that must be resolved—direct EPFR quenching versus ROS interception, the effects of humidity, airflow, and contact time, and the long-term fate of CeO2 under realistic filtration conditions—and argue that the demonstrated gaseous ROS scavenging of CeO2 in cigarette smoke, together with its self-recovery capability, provides sufficient mechanistic justification to pursue this direction experimentally.

Article.Title: Linear Combination Properties of Spectral Phasors Allow Thermodynamic Analysis of Reversible Denaturation of Multidomain and Membrane Proteins
Article.Authors: Recoulat Angelini A.; Malacrida L.; González Flecha F.
Article.Abstract: Denaturation of small globular proteins is often described as a reversible two-state transition between native and denatured conformations. Conversely, multidomain and membrane proteins frequently populate several partially folded intermediate states during denaturation. Traditional thermodynamic analysis of fluorescence intensity often fails to reliably identify these intermediate states. Alternatively, spectral phasors provide an effective model-free way to monitor these complex conformational changes by resolving overlapping fluorescence signals with small differences in the position or shape of the spectra. Nevertheless, converting phasor trajectories into quantitative thermodynamic information remains challenging when quantum yields do not remain constant during a given process, thus limiting their application to protein stability studies. In this work, we introduce a thermodynamic framework for quantifying protein stability from phasor trajectories. We validate this formalism using simulated spectral data generated from two- and three-state transitions, including changes in fluorescence quantum yields, successfully recovering the thermodynamic parameters used to generate the simulations. Additionally, we applied this approach to analyze published data on urea-induced unfolding of E. coli Outer Membrane Protein A. Phasor analysis identified a two-state transition, and the thermodynamic parameters agreed well with those obtained from total fluorescence intensity, supporting the validity of the proposed approach. Finally, applying this framework to the SDS-induced denaturation of Archaeoglobus fulgidus Cu(I)-transport ATPase enabled a complete thermodynamic characterization of the three transitions identified by phasor analysis of intrinsic fluorescence, which could not be resolved using fluorescence intensity alone. This formalism establishes fluorescence spectral phasors as a powerful quantitative approach for protein stability analysis.

Article.Title: Hijacking the Message: Insights from Targeting mRNA Export and Translation in AML
Article.Authors: Borden K.; Guzman M.
Article.Abstract: Cancer cells hijack RNA metabolism, including splicing, polyadenylation, nuclear export and translation, to change both the amount and the form of the proteins they produce. This creates therapeutic vulnerabilities beyond the mutations and translocations that have guided drug development in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where outcomes remain poor. Using AML as a paradigm, this review focuses on two nodes of RNA metabolism: the eukaryotic translation initiation factor eIF4E, a cap-chaperone that escorts mRNAs through processing, export and translation, and CRM1/XPO1, the major nuclear exporter of proteins and select RNAs that partners with eIF4E for specific mRNA export activity. We describe the RNA biology dysregulated in patients, the mechanisms of the inhibitors that target these pathways, and their pre-clinical and clinical data across AML and other malignancies. Indeed, early-stage clinical trials in AML and other malignancies show promise, including the use of CRM1/XPO1 inhibitors (selinexor, eltanexor) and eIF4E inhibitors (including ribavirin and tomivosertib). We discuss how selecting patients by eIF4E status, confirming on-target activity, and designing rational combinations could improve next-generation therapies.

Article.Title: Stable Strontium Distribution and Effects on Plants
Article.Authors: Seregin I.; Kozhevnikova A.
Article.Abstract: Strontium (Sr) is a wide-spread alkaline earth metal that is similar to calcium (Ca) in its chemical properties, although it does not play the physiological role inherent to the latter. At low doses, Sr can stimulate plant growth and development. However, at elevated levels in the environment, it has a negative effect on many processes occurring in plant cells, leading to growth inhibition and reduced productivity. The majority of studies have been focused on the effects of radioactive Sr isotopes which produce additional toxic effects due to ionizing radiation, but the effects of stable Sr have not received enough attention. The current scoping review summarizes the data on the uptake mechanisms and transport pathways of stable Sr and examines the characteristic patterns of its distribution in plant tissues and organs. Available data on the effects of stable Sr on enzyme activity, mineral nutrition, photosynthesis, plant growth, and morphogenesis are analyzed. Understanding the transport pathways of Sr, as well as the factors determining its dual effects on plant growth and development, underlies the development of approaches used in biofortification and phytoremediation technologies. The review may be useful for researchers working on plant mineral nutrition, metal stress, and phytoremediation.

Article.Title: Metabolomic Profiling Reveals Heat-Responsive Metabolic Markers in Honey Bee Workers Under Contrasting Diets
Article.Authors: Jang H.; Kim H.; Frunze O.; Kwon H.; Kim B.; Jung J.
Article.Abstract: Acute heat exposure challenges honey bee (Apis mellifera) workers, yet the associated small-molecule response and its relationship to nutritional status remain incompletely resolved. Workers were conditioned for 7 days on bee bread plus sucrose (B+S) or sucrose alone (S), maintained at 37 °C or exposed to 45 °C for 3 h, and thorax–abdomen metabolites were profiled by untargeted Ultra-performance liquid chromatography-quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC-QTOF/MS). Three independent cages were used per diet × temperature group, with 15 workers per cage pooled to generate one cage-level biological replicate (n = 3 per group). Putative metabolite annotation used accurate-mass (10 ppm) and isotope-pattern matching against METLIN and the Agilent Personal Compound Database and Library (PCDL), followed by manual curation, without tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) o or authentic-standard confirmation. After statistical filtering and biological curation, 149 heat-responsive metabolite annotations were retained under B+S and 123 under S. Targeted re-extraction of proteinogenic amino acids from the same raw files recovered 16 common peaks across all samples. Fifteen increased at 45 °C in both diets, whereas proline decreased; 14 of 16 showed a larger fold change under B+S. Phenylalanine-related metabolism showed the strongest convergence across targeted amino-acid analysis, untargeted phenylpyruvate detection, and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment. Lipid-class responses also differed descriptively between diets, with a bias toward decreased free fatty acyls under B+S and decreased phospholipids under S. These findings define coordinated metabolic markers of acute heat exposure in worker bees and show that, within the targeted amino-acid dataset, response magnitudes were generally larger under B+S while retaining the same overall direction.

Article.Title: PSY Inhibits Colorectal Cancer Growth and Exhibits an In Vitro Synergistic Interaction with 5-Fluorouracil
Article.Authors: Han S.; Kim H.; Choi H.; Oh M.; Lee M.; Lee J.; Ha I.; Ahn K.; Lee S.
Article.Abstract: PSY is a three-herb formula comprising Patriniae Radix, Mori Cortex Radicis, and Coix Seed that was previously shown to inhibit STAT3 signaling in colorectal cancer (CRC) cells. Here, we investigated molecular and metabolic responses to PSY, its antitumor activity in an HCT116 xenograft model, and its interactions with chemotherapy in vitro. Representative chemical markers were qualitatively verified by UPLC-ESI-QTOF MS/MS. Exploratory RNA sequencing with two biological replicates per group highlighted stress-associated and metabolic processes for further investigation. PSY increased BiP, phosphorylated eIF2α, ATF4, and CHOP levels, intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, and mitochondrial membrane depolarization, while reducing the phosphorylation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR- and ERK-associated proteins. PSY increased the p-AMPK/AMPK ratio and decreased the p-ACC/ACC ratio. PSY reduced several lipid-biosynthetic transcripts and decreased the relative abundance of selected fatty acids in xenograft tumors. Oral administration of PSY suppressed HCT116 xenograft growth without significant body-weight loss. Combination-index (CI) analysis indicated CI-defined in vitro synergistic interactions with 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) at multiple concentration pairs, with interaction patterns varying across HCT116, HT-29, and SW480 cells. Direct cell counting supported the combination response in HCT116 and SW480 cells. The combination increased apoptosis and reduced STAT3 and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation relative to single treatments. These findings characterize concurrent, partly discordant signaling and metabolic responses to PSY and support further preclinical evaluation of its in vitro interaction with 5-FU.

Article.Title: Hearing Loss Caused by Chronic Kidney Disease: Evidence of Cochlear Metabolic Disturbances
Article.Authors: Zheng S.; Liu H.; Bai Y.; Ni G.
Article.Abstract: Hearing loss affects over 1.5 billion people worldwide. Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at an increased risk of sensorineural hearing impairment, although the mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Using an adenine-induced mouse model, we evaluated auditory function, cochlear pathology, and metabolism. The mice exhibited significant hearing loss, marked atrophy of the stria vascularis in the middle and basal turns of the cochlea, and pronounced oxidative stress. Metabolomic profiling identified substantial disruptions in cochlear amino acid and lipid metabolism, with concordant metabolic abnormalities in the serum and kidneys. Notably, the uremic toxin, p-cresyl sulfate, was significantly elevated in the cochlea. Overall, CKD induced metabolic disturbances and disrupted tight junction integrity, which may facilitate cochlear accumulation of uremic toxins, trigger oxidative stress, and contribute to hearing loss. These findings provide novel insights into CKD-associated hearing loss and identify potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

Article.Title: Genetic Susceptibility, Neurodevelopmental Abnormalities, and Neuroimmune Interactions Across Major Psychiatric Disorders
Article.Authors: Lu Z.; Gao Y.; Liu B.; Wu Y.; Li T.; Wang Q.; Qi H.; Ma X.; Yue W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Major psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and autism spectrum disorder, share overlapping genetic, neurodevelopmental, and neuroimmune underpinnings that challenge traditional diagnostic boundaries. This review synthesizes evidence across three interconnected domains: convergent genetic risk affecting synaptic and immune pathways, neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities shaped by early-life insults, and neuroimmune crosstalk involving blood–brain barrier dysfunction, sustained inflammation, and complement-mediated pathology. We propose a multidimensional developmental–immune framework in which genetic liability, environmental exposure timing, and peripheral immune status jointly shape transdiagnostic trajectories. This framework reframes psychiatric disorders as dynamic interactions among stable trait-like susceptibilities and fluctuating biological states, offering a roadmap for biomarker-driven stratification and early immune-targeted interventions.

Article.Title: Transcriptional and Epigenetic Regulation of Atoh1 and Its Therapeutic Applications for Hair Cell Regeneration in the Inner Ear
Article.Authors: Wang M.; Wan J.; Gong C.; Chai R.; Li X.; Bi Z.
Article.Abstract: This review centers on the transcription factor Atoh1 (Atonal homolog 1, also known as Math1) and its pivotal regulatory role in the development and regeneration of inner ear hair cells (HCs). It systematically elucidates the activation mechanisms of Atoh1, its integrated upstream and downstream regulatory networks, and the involvement of key signaling pathways. Additionally, the review comparatively analyzes the differences in regenerative capacity between cochlear and vestibular HCs and provides a comprehensive evaluation of the research progress and existing challenges associated with various Atoh1-targeted intervention strategies. By constructing a systematic theoretical framework, this review aims to offer a solid foundation for deciphering the molecular mechanisms underlying HC regeneration, optimizing clinical therapeutic strategies, and advancing the translational application of research in this field.

Article.Title: GABAergic Neurons in the Dorsal Raphe Nucleus Modulate Emotion Discrimination in Mice
Article.Authors: Li R.; Guo J.; Wang Y.; Xu J.; Fang S.; Huang Z.; Wang Y.; Liu R.; Wang C.; Shan Q.; Qin X.; Chen P.; Zhou J.
Article.Abstract: Accurate recognition of the emotional states of others is essential for social adaptation. The dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) contains a substantial population of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic neurons that are implicated in various social and affective behaviors; however, their role in social emotion discrimination remains unclear. In this study, we used a mouse behavioral paradigm that distinguishes conspecifics under negative (restraint stress) or positive (relief from food/water deprivation) affective states, combined with in vivo calcium recordings and chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations, to investigate the function of DRN GABAergic neurons in this process. Observer mice preferentially investigated conspecifics in both negative and positive affective states compared with naive conspecifics. This preferential investigation was accompanied by increased c-Fos expression in DRN GABAergic neurons and rapid calcium transients, specifically at the onset of sniffing bouts directed toward affectively altered, but not naive, conspecifics. Chemogenetic or optogenetic inhibition of GABAergic neurons in the DRN abolished the preferential investigation of affectively altered conspecifics. In contrast, neither chemogenetic nor optogenetic activation of these neurons disrupted the emotion discrimination performance. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that DRN GABAergic neurons are necessary for discriminating conspecifics in both negative and positive affective states and suggest their critical role in valence-independent social-emotional decision-making.

Article.Title: Age and Neuroimmune Diseases
Article.Authors: Yu Z.; Huang X.; Zhang H.; Shi F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract With the aging population accelerating, age has become a core factor influencing the clinical phenotypes, treatment responses, and prognoses of neuroimmune diseases (NDs), including those affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS). This cross-disease review summarizes the shared and specific age-related characteristics of NDs, focusing on the pathological basis of immunosenescence and neurodegeneration underlying age-related ND progression. We extract the clinical manifestations, immune and neural mechanisms of elderly ND patients, and evaluate the challenges and individualized adjustment principles of therapeutic strategies for this population. We explore the age-related immune dysregulation features between NDs and other systemic autoimmune diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), type 1 diabetes (T1D)). This review aims to construct a cross-disease framework for the precision management of NDs in the aging era, identify research gaps and future directions, and emphasize age-adapted intervention strategies for optimizing the prognosis of elderly ND patients.

Article.Title: Thrombospondin 2 Promotes Neuropathic Pain by Mediating Nav1.7 Membrane Anchoring in Mouse Primary Sensory Neurons
Article.Authors: Wei J.; Wang Y.; Zhao Z.; Chen H.; Chang S.; Yang Q.; Wang H.; Liu X.; Zhou X.; Li X.; Zhang J.; Liang L.
Article.Abstract: Thrombospondin 2 (TSP2), a member of the thrombospondin family of extracellular matrix proteins, mediates critical cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions. However, its potential roles in neuropathic pain remain unclear. We demonstrate that TSP2 is specifically expressed in isolectin B4-negative dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. Following lumbar 4 (L4) spinal nerve ligation (SNL), TSP2 expression was upregulated in both injured (L4) and uninjured (L3) DRGs. Notably, siRNA-mediated TSP2 knockdown attenuated SNL-induced pain hypersensitivity during the development phase, but not during the maintenance phase, of neuropathic pain. Conversely, neuron-specific TSP2 overexpression in the DRG alone was sufficient to produce enhanced nociceptive behavior. Mechanistically, SNL enhanced the interaction between TSP2 and Nav1.7, promoting Nav1.7 membrane anchoring in the L3 and L4 DRGs and thereby increasing DRG neuronal excitability. These findings establish TSP2 as a novel Nav1.7-interacting protein and a potential therapeutic target for preventing chronic neuropathic pain.

Article.Title: Neural Stem Cell Therapies for Central Nervous System Regeneration: Advances, Challenges, and Integrative Technologies
Article.Authors: Marei H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neural stem cells (NSCs) are promising candidates for central nervous system (CNS) regeneration because they self-renew and differentiate into neural lineages. Advances in genome engineering, extracellular vesicles (EVs), biomaterials, organoids, single-cell technologies, and precision medicine have expanded approaches for characterizing, engineering, delivering, and evaluating NSC-based therapies for neurological disorders. CRISPR/Cas9 and related platforms may enable more precise modification of NSC function, while NSC-derived EVs offer potential cell-free strategies. Engineered hydrogels and three-dimensional scaffolds may improve cell survival, engraftment, migration, and integration. Organoids and single-cell omics provide increasingly detailed models of cellular heterogeneity and lineage specification. However, clinical translation remains limited by immune compatibility, tumorigenic risk, manufacturing standardization, graft survival and integration, and regulatory requirements. Rigorous preclinical validation, standardized manufacturing, appropriately designed clinical trials, long-term safety monitoring, and harmonized regulatory frameworks are required before routine clinical application.

Article.Title: Systematic Microcircuit Reconfigurations Underlie Early Experience-induced Visual Cortical Plasticity
Article.Authors: Yao L.; Shang Z.; Ji Z.; Meng M.; Wang F.; Gu X.; He M.; Wu S.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Experience-dependent reorganization of neuronal connections during the postnatal critical period is essential for the functional maturation of the developing primary visual cortex (V1). However, the systematic reconfigurations across microcircuit synapses underlying experience-dependent plasticity are poorly defined. Using paired whole-cell recordings from excitatory pyramidal cells and three other major classes of interneurons (INs) within layers 2/3 and 4 in the developing mouse V1 monocular region, we found that monocular deprivation (MD) for one day in juvenile mice transiently reconfigures local excitatory synapses onto inhibitory INs that specifically express parvalbumin (PV) or vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). In contrast, prolonged MD predominantly strengthens inhibitory synaptic transmission from somatostatin (SST)-expressing INs to PV-INs and VIP-INs across both layers. A physiologically based microcircuit model further recapitulated MD-induced activity changes in visual responses across layer 2/3 neurons in vivo. We provide a detailed microcircuit framework that contributes to the experience-dependent regulation of visual function.

Article.Title: Transcranial Evoked Potentials are Minimally Influenced by Afferent Feedback From Peripheral Muscle Contraction
Article.Authors: Marco M.; Andrea G.; Andrea F.; Carlo P.; Giorgio L.; Rocchi L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) investigates cortical reactivity, yet the contribution of sensory feedback from muscle twitches to the recorded signals remains debated. We combined M1 TMS-EEG with electromyography, accelerometry, and peripheral electrical stimulation to dissociate central and peripheral contributions. We compared EEG responses across trials yielding large versus small motor outputs, while peripheral stimulation isolated pure afferent components. Bayesian analysis revealed that larger motor outputs covaried with distinct EEG morphologies uniformly across all time windows—including those too early for peripheral feedback—indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in baseline motor cortex excitability drive both responses. Conversely, isolated muscle contraction produced delayed (> 65 ms), markedly smaller EEG responses with distinct spatiotemporal profiles. We conclude that sensory feedback from muscle twitches contributes minimally to TMS-evoked EEG responses, which instead primarily reflect the baseline excitability state of the stimulated cortex.

Article.Title: Distinct Contributions and Sensorimotor Encoding of PV and FoxP2 Neurons in the External Globus Pallidus during Perceptual Decision-making
Article.Authors: Pu X.; Ren J.; Xie T.; Zou K.; Xu J.; Li Y.; Liu D.; Yao H.
Article.Abstract: The external globus pallidus (GPe), the central nucleus of the basal ganglia, comprises diverse cell types, including parvalbumin (PV) and forkhead box protein P2 (FoxP2) neurons. Their roles in movement regulation and sensory processing are well established; however, their contribution to perceptual decision-making remains unclear. Using a Go/No-Go visual task in mice, we found that optogenetic activation of either population impaired performance, whereas PV inhibition, but not FoxP2 inhibition, disrupted behavioral accuracy. Electrophysiological recordings showed that PV and FoxP2 neurons differentially encoded visual stimuli, licking movements, and trial outcomes. FoxP2 inhibition produced minimal changes in the spontaneous firing of substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) neurons. PV inhibition altered spontaneous SNr firing and, together with PV activation, altered task-evoked SNr activity, reducing the preference for reward-predicting stimuli in one subpopulation and unrewarded outcomes in another. These findings reveal the distinct roles of GPe PV and FoxP2 neurons in shaping perceptual decisions and modulating basal ganglia output.

Article.Title: Neuroplastin Suppresses Seizures by Downregulating Endophilin A1 to Promote Internalization of GluA1-AMPA Receptors: Therapeutic Implications of Arbutin
Article.Authors: Li S.; Chen M.; Zheng S.; Wei X.; Sun L.; Wei L.; Lu Y.; Ma M.; Wu Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Status epilepticus (SE) is a critical neurological disorder characterized by an imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission. α-Amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission, whereas internalization of GluA1-containing AMPARs regulates neuronal excitability. Although neuroplastin (Np) modulates neuronal excitability, its role in GluA1-AMPAR internalization in epilepsy remains unclear. Using single-cell transcriptomics, virtual knockout, in vitro and in vivo epilepsy models, patch-clamp, biochemistry, and behavioral tests, we identified Endophilin A1 (EndoA1) as a key target through which Np regulates GluA1 internalization. In epilepsy models, EndoA1 was upregulated, surface GluA1 levels increased, and receptor internalization was reduced. EndoA1 knockdown decreased the amplitude and frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs), promoted GluA1 internalization, prolonged seizure latency, and shortened seizure duration. Np overexpression reduced EndoA1 expression, facilitated GluA1 internalization, and suppressed hyperexcitability, whereas EndoA1 knockdown rescued the Np knockdown-induced phenotype. Network pharmacology and molecular docking studies identified arbutin as an EndoA1-targeting compound that reduced hyperexcitability, mEPSC amplitude, and surface GluA1 in a concentration-dependent manner. These findings establish the Np–EndoA1–GluA1 axis as a key epileptic pathway, whereby Np negatively regulates EndoA1 to promote GluA1-AMPAR internalization and suppress excitability. Arbutin, which targets EndoA1, exerts anti-epileptic effects by modulating excitatory transmission.

Article.Title: Spatiotemporal Resolution for Neurodegenerative Diseases: Linking Proteinopathy, Cellular Vulnerability, and Disease Trajectories
Article.Authors: Dong M.; Wang C.; Chen Z.; Ding S.; Peng L.; Jiang H.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by selective and progressive degeneration of specific neuronal populations, often accompanied by glial dysfunction. Despite extensive investigation, proposed pathogenic models remain insufficient to fully explain selective vulnerability and stereotyped spatiotemporal patterns of neurodegeneration across diseases. Spatial omics technologies preserve anatomical context and enable interrogation of cell-type composition, molecular heterogeneity, and intercellular interactions within neural systems. In this review, we synthesize current concepts and technological advances in spatial omics and discuss how these approaches are reshaping our understanding of NDs. Spatial omics provides an integrative framework for linking pathological protein aggregation with selective cellular vulnerability, microenvironment-dependent interactions, and disease progression across molecular, cellular, and anatomical scales. We highlight emerging insights into pathology-associated gene modules, neuron-glia interactions, and mechanisms underlying regional vulnerability. Finally, we discuss multimodal data integration and future directions for translating spatially resolved molecular maps into mechanistic understanding.

Article.Title: Theta-Band Temporal Interference Stimulation Modulates Food Reward Prediction Error Encoding in Individuals with Elevated Food Addiction Symptoms
Article.Authors: Wen Y.; Wang M.; Dong X.; Gola M.; Liu Q.; Tu Y.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Prediction error (PE) signals support feedback evaluation and adaptive updating, and are closely linked to medial frontal theta dynamics, particularly within dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC)-centered networks. However, evidence linking these oscillatory mechanisms to the modulation of PE encoding remains limited. Here, we tested whether theta-band modulation of a dACC-centered medial frontal network altered trial-level PE encoding during food-reward processing. In a single-blind, sham-controlled pre-post design, individuals with elevated food addiction symptoms performed a food incentive-delay task while undergoing electroencephalographic recordings combined with theta-band temporal interference stimulation. Single-trial analyses revealed that feedback-related negativity (FRN) amplitudes varied as a function of both behavioral and model-derived prediction errors. Critically, theta-band modulation altered FRN-PE coupling, with the effect most pronounced for unfavorable outcomes, whereas anticipatory activity remained unchanged. These findings support the hypothesis that theta-band modulation can alter feedback-related PE encoding within this population and task context.

Article.Title: 2-AG as a potential biomarker for predicting response to short-term fluoxetine treatment in a mouse model of depression
Article.Authors: Rodríguez-López A.; Ibrahim E.; Gorgievski V.; Martin M.; Robledo P.; Maldonado R.; Tzavara E.; Álvarez-Pérez B.
Article.Abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a complex psychiatric condition with significant individual and social impact and marked variability in treatment response. Identifying biomarkers that predict antidepressant efficacy remains a major challenge, and metabolomic approaches offer a powerful tool to uncover biochemical changes associated with depression and treatment outcome. The prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus are key brain regions involved in the pathophysiology of MDD and antidepressant response. Fluoxetine, one of the most commonly prescribed antidepressants, influences not only serotonergic signaling but also the endocannabinoid system. Accordingly, evaluating endocannabinoid levels might provide critical insight into their contribution and the effect of fluoxetine. To identify biomarkers associated with early antidepressant response, male mice were exposed for 5 weeks to the chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) protocol, with fluoxetine treatment administered during the final week. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry analyses of hippocampal and prefrontal cortex samples revealed that behavioral improvement following short-term fluoxetine treatment was accompanied by increased hippocampal 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), along with reduced GABA and glutamate levels in the prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that increased 2-AG levels may predict early response to fluoxetine.

Article.Title: Emerging roles of the DLK1-DIO3 imprinted domain in neurodevelopment and complex neurological and psychiatric disorders
Article.Authors: Escamilla S.; Kuang R.; Figueroa C.; Krishnan N.; Hernández A.; Salas-Lucia F.
Article.Abstract: The DLK1-DIO3 genomic domain comprises a cluster of imprinted genes regulated by epigenetic mechanisms that precisely regulate their expression dosage, often in a timely and tissue-specific manner. This is particularly significant during brain development, as transcripts from the DLK1-DIO3 domain are involved in the physiology of most neural cell types, regulating fundamental processes such as neural precursor cell proliferation, neuronal and glial lineage specification, and subsequent functional maturation, as well as the establishment of neural and neuroendocrine circuits. Thus, disruption of the DLK1-DIO3 epigenome, induced not only by genetic alterations but also by neurodevelopmental exposure to environmental factors and maternal disease, may produce abnormal transcript expression within the domain, leading to broader dysregulation of brain gene expression programs during fetal and early development, ultimately influencing brain function and neurological and neuroendocrine phenotypes later in life. Here, we reviewed genetic, epigenetic, environmental, neurobiological, and behavioral studies linking dysregulation of genes within the DLK1-DIO3 imprinted domain to neurological and psychiatric outcomes, including autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, anxiety and depression, epilepsy, neurodegenerative disorders, susceptibility to drug abuse, maladaptive brain inflammatory response, and psychomotor alterations. Additional outcomes include neuroendocrine disorders and associated behavioral alterations. This narrative review covers the increasing observations in humans associating molecular signatures in this domain with neurological and psychiatric conditions, as well as studies in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neural cells and in rodents that provide compelling mechanistic insights about the neurodevelopmental processes affected, which could help interpret the unresolved etiology of these disorders, including increased prevalence, missing heritability, and phenotypical heterogeneity.

Article.Title: Cellular senescence changes and their association with brain structure in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Okada N.; Seitz-Holland J.; Ikegame T.; Omileke F.; Kiyota M.; Shoji E.; Mori S.; Morita S.; Koshiyama D.; Satomura Y.; Koike S.; Jinde S.; Yagishita S.; Kamiya K.; Abe O.; Shenton M.; Kubicki M.; Kasai K.
Article.Abstract: Individuals with schizophrenia (SZ) and major depressive disorder (MDD) may experience accelerated biological aging, potentially linked to cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). While the SASP index, a composite biomarker-based measure, has been reported to be elevated in MDD, its status in SZ and its relationship with brain structure remain unclear. This study investigated whether the SASP index is elevated in SZ and MDD, and examined its associations with brain-predicted age difference (brain-PAD) and regional brain morphology across SZ, MDD, and healthy controls (HCs). A total of 119 subjects (29 individuals with SZ, 40 individuals with MDD, and 50 HCs) underwent both peripheral blood collection and magnetic resonance imaging scanning. First, across all subjects, the effects of diagnostic groups on SASP indices were assessed. Second, associations between age-adjusted SASP indices and brain-PAD were examined within each diagnostic group. Third, exploratory analyses tested associations between SASP indices and subcortical volumes as well as cortical thickness and surface area in each diagnostic group. We found a significant main effect of diagnostic group on SASP indices and significantly elevated SASP indices in both SZ and MDD. Although no significant associations were observed between SASP indices and brain-PAD in any diagnostic group, negative associations were identified in SZ between SASP indices and the surface area of the left transverse temporal gyrus and the right inferior frontal gyrus pars triangularis, regions that play pivotal roles in auditory and language processing alterations observed in SZ. These findings suggest that SASP-related processes may contribute to the neural underpinnings of SZ through localized, rather than global, alterations in brain structure.

Article.Title: Reduced attenuation of neural activation during fear extinction learning in patients with anxiety disorders: a delayed fear extinction fMRI study
Article.Authors: Qian Z.; Yang Y.; Richter J.; Domschke K.; Koelkebeck K.; Deckert J.; Herrmann M.; Plag J.; Ströhle A.; Wittchen H.; Pittig A.; Hamm A.; Arolt V.; Dannlowski U.; Schneider S.; Margraf J.; Rief W.; Lueken U.; Kircher T.; Ridderbusch I.; Straube B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Clarifying the patterns of neural activation during fear extinction in anxiety disorders (ADs) is essential for advancing our understanding of inhibitory learning. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly characterized in large, heterogeneous cohorts of patients. Utilizing a delayed fear extinction fMRI paradigm, this study examined neural responses in 280 patients with ADs — comprising panic disorder, agoraphobia, panic disorder with agoraphobia, social anxiety disorder, and multiple specific phobias — compared to 103 healthy controls (HC). The attenuation of neural activation to conditioned fear (CS+) and safety (CS−) stimuli from early versus late extinction was compared between groups. Subjective ratings of US-expectancy, arousal, and valence were also collected. In a whole-brain voxelwise analysis, patients showed significantly reduced attenuation of neural activation across both CS+ and CS− relative to HC from early compared to late phases of extinction learning. This pattern was observed in a broad network, encompassing the insular cortex (IC) and bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), among other regions. No interaction between group and stimulus type was observed. Region-of-interest analysis of the left anterior insular cortex confirmed that reduced attenuation in this region represents a robust neural signature of altered extinction learning in ADs. Furthermore, patients reported persistently higher fear expectancy and arousal than HC, consistent with sustained alterations in threat-related processing following extinction training. Together, these findings highlight altered extinction-related neural attenuation as a transdiagnostic feature of ADs, offering novel insights into the neural mechanisms underlying fear extinction.

Article.Title: Effects of chronic oxytocin administration on white matter microstructure in autistic adults: a pilot pharmaco-neuroimaging DTI study
Article.Authors: Heemels R.; Deferm W.; Boets B.; Alaerts K.
Article.Abstract: Intranasal oxytocin is a promising therapeutic approach for social and stress-regulatory difficulties in autism spectrum disorder. However, there is limited understanding regarding whether chronic administration regimes can induce neuroplastic changes at the brain’s anatomical level and how such microstructural changes might underlie clinical-behavioral effects. This placebo-controlled pilot assessed the effects of a four-week oxytocin regimen (24 IU daily) on white matter microstructure in 27 young adult men with autism. Diffusion tensor imaging was performed at baseline, post-treatment, and after four-week and one-year retention periods. Tractography focused on fractional anisotropy (FA) in amygdala-centered tracts associated with socio-emotional processing: the bilateral Inferior Longitudinal Fasciculus (ILF), Inferior Fronto-Occipital Fasciculus (IFOF), and Uncinate Fasciculus (UF). Following four weeks of oxytocin administration, a spatially selective impact of intranasal oxytocin administration was demonstrated, indicating bilateral improvements in UF integrity and a hemispherically lateralized pattern of changes for the ILF and IFOF tracts, with FA increases predominantly emerging in the right hemisphere, while reductions were evident in left-sided segments. Especially for bilateral UF and right IFOF, the observed changes were clinically relevant, correlating with enhanced social responsiveness and reduced feelings of avoidant attachment. In conclusion, exploratory findings from this pilot neuroimaging trial suggest that a four-week oxytocin regimen may induce long-lasting neuroplastic changes in white-matter tracts relevant to behavioral improvements in adult men with autism. These hypothesis-generating findings may inform future confirmatory trials. Further investigation of the neuroplastic changes associated with oxytocin’s clinical and behavioral effects may help refine oxytocin-based interventions, not only for autism but also for other neuropsychiatric conditions in which oxytocin is being explored as a potential therapeutic option.

Article.Title: Control of whole-body glucose metabolism by central lactate in the presence of antipsychotics
Article.Authors: Pereira S.; d’Orchymont F.; Tong J.; Au E.; Singh R.; Wu S.; Beroncal E.; Choi J.; Li D.; Humber B.; Chaudhry T.; Alijaniaram M.; Agarwal S.; Vernon A.; Giacca A.; Andreazza A.; Vasdev N.; Hahn M.
Article.Abstract: The brain-liver axis is important in maintaining whole-body glucose homeostasis. Antipsychotics are used to treat schizophrenia, but one of their side-effects is disruption of metabolism. We previously reported that the antipsychotics olanzapine and haloperidol block the ability of central glucose to stimulate whole-body glucose metabolism and suppress glucose production by the liver (EGP, endogenous glucose production). Both effects by central glucose require the conversion of glucose to lactate centrally. In the current study, we therefore examined whether antipsychotics affect the ability of central lactate to stimulate whole-body glucose metabolism and suppress EGP. Using our previous model of central (third ventricle to target the hypothalamus) infusion, acute subcutaneous administration of antipsychotics, and the pancreatic euglycemic clamp in rats, we found that olanzapine completely inhibited the ability of central lactate to stimulate whole-body glucose metabolism and partially blocked central lactate-induced suppression of EGP. Since activation of the hypothalamus-liver axis of glycemic control requires central glucose and lactate to be metabolized, relevant pathways were also investigated. The adverse effects of olanzapine on central lactate sensing were not associated with decreased levels of citrate, a tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate, in the hypothalamus or robust alterations in hypothalamic mitochondrial complex I activity assessed with the positron emission tomography tracer [ 18 F]BCPP-EF. In summary, olanzapine impairs the ability of central lactate to control whole-body glucose metabolism and partially inhibits suppression of EGP by central lactate.

Article.Title: Impaired outcome-based decision-making in human cocaine addiction
Article.Authors: Lim T.; Cardinal R.; Mak E.; Ersche K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Despite rising global rates for cocaine addiction, treatments options are limited. Psychological treatments remain the standard option but have only modest effectiveness. One major barrier to treatment success is that patients often make disadvantageous decisions that go against recovery, highlighting the need for strategies to support decision-making. Converging evidence indicates that decision-making deficits in cocaine addiction are driven by impaired processing of outcomes and risks. We investigated how patients with cocaine addiction use explicit outcomes and risk information to guide decision-making. One-hundred-and-five patients with moderate-to-severe cocaine use disorder (CUD) and 80 healthy control volunteers completed a decision-making task in which reward, loss, and probability information were provided explicitly. A subset of participants underwent diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the orbitofronto-striatal white matter tracts that underpin decision-making. We used generalized linear mixed-effects models to determine how rewards, losses, and probability influence decisions, and combined probabilistic tractography with principal component analysis to characterize the white matter tracts. We found that patients incorporated explicit probability information into their decisions to the same degree as control participants but showed reduced integration of outcomes. Notably, patients were less likely to integrate losses into their decisions than rewards. Although orbitofronto-striatal white matter tracts did not differ between groups, individual variability predicted the extent to which reward and loss information guided decisions, irrespective of diagnosis. Overall, these findings reveal fundamental challenges in using outcomes, particularly negative ones, to guide decision-making in patients with CUD, emphasizing the need for additional support to promote adaptive choices during recovery.

Article.Title: Temporal imprecision of the self in drug-free psychosis: Abnormal infraslow phase dynamics and brain complexity
Article.Authors: Chen I.; Ao Y.; Catal Y.; Liu C.; Hwang T.; Lin Y.; Hsieh M.; Chien Y.; Hwu H.; Lechner S.; Liu C.; Northoff G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Self-disturbance is a core feature of schizophrenia (SCZ) and may emerge during the prodromal phase. Temporal imprecision has recently been proposed as a core neural mechanism in schizophrenia, primarily demonstrated in faster EEG frequency ranges. Whether such imprecision extends to infraslow brain dynamics in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and relates to self-disturbance in early psychosis remains unknown. Here, we examined resting-state fMRI data from drug-free early psychosis patients (EP drug-free, n = 31, scanned before and after medication) and 31 healthy controls (HC). Brain dynamics were quantified using sample entropy (SampEn) and instantaneous peak frequency (PF) in regions associated with different layers of self-processing (interoceptive, exteroceptive, and mental). Compared to controls, EP drug-free showed higher SampEn and slower mean PF with greater variability than HC, particularly in the regions of the exteroceptive self. Moreover, EP drug-free exhibited a decoupling between SampEn and PF, whereas HC showed strong correlations. Both SampEn and PF significantly contributed to diagnostic classification, and increased SampEn was associated with greater severity of negative, disorganized, and anxiety/depression symptoms. Together, these findings indicate abnormal infraslow brain dynamics in early psychosis, characterized by increased neural complexity and disrupted temporal organization. This temporal imprecision, particularly within the exteroceptive self, may represent a key mechanism linking altered brain dynamics to self-disturbance and psychopathology in early psychosis.

Article.Title: Treating diagnostic frameworks as information systems: normative implications and opportunities
Article.Authors: Millroth P.
Article.Abstract: The DSM-5 and ICD-11 are not just clinical manuals; they are information architectures. Every time a clinician applies diagnostic criteria, every time a researcher aggregates symptoms into a diagnostic variable, and every time a committee drafts a revision, they operate on the same basic object: a coded system for transmitting information about mental states. Yet no one has applied information theory [ 1 ] to evaluate the architecture of diagnostic systems themselves. Existing applications of information-theoretic thinking in psychiatry — model-selection criteria such as AIC and BIC — assess how well statistical models fit covariance data; they say nothing about the efficiency of the diagnostic code itself. This Viewpoint argues that information theory (henceforth, IT) — the elsewhere highly influential mathematical framework developed by Shannon to characterize the capacity and efficiency of communication systems [ 1 ] — provides what is currently missing: a principled, quantitative basis for designing, evaluating, and reforming diagnostic frameworks and the instruments that operationalize them. The case for this reframing is not merely theoretical. Diagnostic quality, the product of validity and reliability in the DSM-5 and ICD-11 is, by available estimates, remarkably poor -essentially entailing that the majority of variability stems from measurement error or other irrelevant factors [ 2 , 3 ].
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: ICD-11; DSM-5; information theory; information architecture; psychiatric diagnosis; measurement error

Article.Title: A precision health approach to medication management in neurodevelopmental conditions: a model development and validation study using four international cohorts
Article.Authors: Vandewouw M.; Niroomand K.; Bokadia H.; Lenz S.; Rapley J.; Arias A.; Crosbie J.; Trinari E.; Kelley E.; Nicolson R.; Schachar R.; Arnold P.; Iaboni A.; Lerch J.; Penner M.; Baribeau D.; Anagnostou E.; Kushki A.
Article.Abstract: Psychotropic medications are commonly prescribed to children with neurodevelopmental conditions, but responses vary widely, prescribing is largely off-label, and the expertise required is concentrated in specialized programs. We developed artificial intelligence models to predict prescribing patterns of stimulants, anti-depressants, and anti-psychotics. Feasibility was established in research cohorts by predicting cross-sectional medication use from the Child Behaviour Checklist, with training and internal testing in the Province of Ontario Neurodevelopmental network ( N = 598) and external testing in the Healthy Brain Network ( N = 1764) and Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development ( N = 2396) studies. Clinical evaluation used electronic medical records (EMRs) from the Psychopharmacology Program ( N = 312) at Holland Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital to predict the medication class prescribed at a follow-up visit (~3 months later). In all cohorts, the modelled outcome was the clinician’s prescribing decision, which reflects clinician judgement, family preference, tolerability, and access to care in addition to expected effectiveness, and does not directly measure treatment response or clinical benefit. In the research cohorts, internal testing achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (median [IQR]) of 0.75 [0.73,0.80] for stimulants, 0.83 [0.78,0.87] for anti-depressants, and 0.79 [0.72,0.86] for anti-psychotics, and external testing confirmed generalizability. In the EMR cohort, values were 0.84 [0.81,0.88] for stimulants, 0.82 [0.77,0.87] for anti-depressants, and 0.87 [0.83,0.91] for anti-psychotics. Findings demonstrate that AI can accurately learn expert prescribing patterns and predict medication prescribing decisions, supporting the potential of data-driven tools to guide personalized medication management for neurodevelopmental conditions.

Article.Title: Counteracting the overestimation of effect size in mass-univariate brain-wide association studies using cross-validation
Article.Authors: Goltermann J.; Winter N.; Gruber M.; Fisch L.; Richter M.; Grotegerd D.; Dohm K.; Meinert S.; Leehr E.; Böhnlein J.; Kraus A.; Thiel K.; Winter A.; Flinkenflügel K.; Leenings R.; Barkhau C.; Ernsting J.; Berger K.; Minnerup H.; Straube B.; Alexander N.; Jamalabadi H.; Stein F.; Brosch K.; Wroblewski A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Background Brain-wide association effects are commonly overestimated in psychiatric neuroimaging research, leading to low replicability and generalizability of findings, and ultimately to poor translation to clinical utility. Cross-validation is currently not standardly used in univariate neuroimaging analyses but could pose a potential counteracting measure for this problem. Methods We systematically evaluated the benefit of a cross-validation procedure to expose inflated effect size estimates in mass-univariate voxel-based analysis, using body mass index (BMI) as an example predictor for gray matter. A total of n = 3401 MRI scans from a psychiatric cohort were used to investigate the impact of applying cross-validation on effect size estimates across a range of sample sizes and across different localizations with a range of underlying pooled effect sizes. Results BMI was negatively associated with gray matter density with a maximum underlying effect size of R ² p = 0.036 (in the full sample of n = 3401). However, without cross-validation, effects were substantially overestimated in small samples, with effect sizes ranging up to R ² p = 0.535. Even with an underlying null-effect, effect size estimates up to R ² p = 0.429 were reached in samples with n = 25. Applying cross-validation revealed that these inflated effects in small samples did not generalize to novel data. A minimum sample size of n = 100 was required for largest brain-wide effects to start generalizing, while samples with n = 400 were needed for smaller effects to generalize. This ‘point of initial generalizability’ was not reached for underlying null effects, even with the maximum available sample of n = 3401. Conclusions Results suggest that cross-validation is an effective measure to expose overestimated effects in small samples and thus could help to counteract low replicability and generalizability in brain-wide mass-univariate association studies. Open-source code is provided for practical implementation.

Article.Title: Temporal cortical gray matter volume relates to symptom improvement during cognitive behavioral therapy for depression
Article.Authors: Schöniger K.; Kamrla R.; König P.; Zwiky E.; Küttner A.; Scheiwe G.; Andreev J.; Hamann J.; Brückner A.; Pletsch S.; Wittig E.; Selle J.; Gussew A.; Deistung A.; Tüscher O.; Wohlgemuth W.; Redlich R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a first-line treatment for depression, yet treatment responses vary considerably. Understanding neurobiological factors associated with symptom improvement may help elucidate mechanisms underlying therapeutic change. This study investigated whether baseline cortical gray matter volume (GMV) is associated with reductions in depressive symptom severity during CBT. Therefore, n = 52 patients with unipolar affective disorders and at least mild depressive symptoms (according to BDI-II) and n = 42 healthy controls underwent clinical assessments and structural MRI at baseline; depressive symptom severity was reassessed after six months of outpatient CBT. Multiple regression analyses examined associations between pre-treatment cortical GMV and reductions in depressive symptoms under false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Additional models included anxiety, perceived stress, and childhood trauma as predictors. Compared to controls, patients exhibited significantly higher depressive symptom severity at baseline and greater symptom reduction over time (all p < 0.001). Within patients, baseline GMV of the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG) was significantly associated with symptom reduction (baseline–follow-up; β = 0.55, p FDR = 0.033). Right MTG volume accounted for additional variance in symptom reduction beyond established clinical variables (Δ R ² = 0.15). Group differences in GMV did not remain significant following FDR correction. These findings suggest that temporal gyrus GMV is associated with symptom improvement following CBT in unipolar depression, extending the focus beyond traditionally emphasized limbic regions. Preserved temporal morphology may support cognitive and emotional processes engaged during CBT, underscoring the relevance of temporal cortical structure for understanding the neurobiological correlates of psychotherapy response.

Article.Title: Non-suicidal self-injury in adolescents and young adults: an expert review
Article.Authors: Kaess M.; Reichl C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is highly prevalent among community and clinical adolescent populations and is associated with substantial psychiatric comorbidity, psychosocial impairment, and elevated suicide risk. This review synthesizes key findings on the development and maintenance of adolescent NSSI and discusses the clinical implications of this transdiagnostic behavioural phenomenon. It examines the prevalence and developmental course of NSSI, environmental and biological risk factors, proximal mechanisms, its conceptualization as an independent diagnosis versus a transdiagnostic risk marker, and current treatment approaches including their limitations. Current evidence indicates that adolescent NSSI emerges from interacting environmental risk factors (e.g. adversity and interpersonal stress) and neurobiological mechanisms related to emotional dysregulation, stress responsivity, and altered pain processing. While NSSI prospectively predicts suicidal behaviour, associations with other psychiatric disorders remain probabilistic and diagnostically non-specific. Overall, findings support conceptualizing NSSI as a transdiagnostic risk marker and behavioural phenotype linked to emotion dysregulation rather than as a distinct diagnostic entity. Adolescent NSSI reflects a dynamic biopsychosocial process involving emotional, neurobiological, and interpersonal mechanisms. Early detection and accessible intervention are essential to reduce chronicity, relapse, and the escalation of suicidal behaviour. Future research should prioritize mechanism-informed and personalized treatment approaches, improved identification of at-risk adolescents, and integration of developmental, neurobiological, and digital methodologies to advance prevention and intervention.

Article.Title: Integrative neuroimaging-transcriptomic analysis of neurodevelopment in adolescent-onset mental health problems
Article.Authors: Hou J.; van Wingen G.; van de Mortel L.; Smit D.; Liu S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mental health problems often emerge in childhood and adolescence, yet the neurodevelopmental and molecular processes underlying their onset remain poorly understood. Using longitudinal data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, we examined structural and functional brain cortical changes in youth who developed ADHD, conduct, anxiety, depressive, oppositional defiant, or somatic problems over a two year follow up period compared to healthy controls in five neuroimaging modalities (including structural MRI, resting-state fMRI, and task-based fMRI). We applied partial least squares (PLS) regression to link spatial patterns of neurodevelopmental changes to cortical gene expression profiles derived from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA). Pathway enrichment was assessed using spin-permutation-derived gene rankings. Significant neurodevelopmental alterations were observed in the ADHD and conduct groups only. PLS analysis further revealed significant spatial associations between their neurodevelopmental changes and gene expression distributions (Spearman rₛ >0.64). In ADHD, pathway enrichment highlighted mitochondrial respiration, oxidative phosphorylation, aerobic electron transport, ATP synthesis, and mitochondrial organization, with additional negative-end enrichment for synaptic protein interaction pathways. In conduct problems, all significant pathways were enriched among genes whose cortical expression patterns were inversely aligned with the conduct-problem imaging phenotype and involved translational machinery, ribosomal function, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial translation, protein targeting to mitochondria, and broader RNA/protein regulatory processes. These findings reveal distinct cortical transcriptomic patterns associated with adolescent-onset ADHD and conduct problems, with mitochondrial energy metabolism emerging as a prominent molecular correlate of ADHD-related cortical development and a distinct inverse transcriptional pattern characterizing conduct-related development. Together, our findings suggest that these externalizing problems are associated with neurodevelopmental alterations embedded within distinct cortical molecular contexts.

Article.Title: TCF7L2 functionally relevant genetic variation with clinical implications in bipolar disorder with impaired glucose metabolism
Article.Authors: Miola A.; Winham S.; De Filippis D.; Gardea Resendez M.; Romo-Nava F.; Bond D.; Singh B.; Veldic M.; Ozerdem A.; Pendegraft R.; Pazdernik V.; Ercis M.; Sanchez-Ruiz J.; Prieto M.; McElroy S.; Biernacka J.; Frye M.; Cuellar-Barboza A.
Article.Abstract: Impaired glucose metabolism (IGM) and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) are common in bipolar disorder (BD). Genome-wide association studies have identified variation (rs7903146) in the gene encoding transcription factor 7-like 2 ( TCF7L2 ) as a well-established risk factor for T2DM in the general population and variation (rs12772424) showing a significant association with BD when accounting for BMI. Evaluating T2DM- and BD-associated TCF7L2 SNPs within bipolar IGM groups, along with their clinical correlates, could provide translational insights for future clinical practice. IGM was operationalized as evidence of prediabetes (fasting glucose of 100-125 mg/dL or glycated hemoglobin of 5.7%-6.4%) or T2DM. We compared sociodemographic, genetic, clinical characteristics, and course of illness measures between BD groups with and without IGM, then within BD subgroups (prediabetes, T2DM, and no IGM). Out of 850 BD patients included (mean age 49, SD = 13, 57% female, 8% non-White) 280 (33%) individuals had IGM. Compared to BD patients without IGM, those with IGM were older (p < 0.001), more likely to be non-White (p = 0.005), and obese (p < 0.001). The minor allele for the rs7903146 SNP (T2DM-associated SNP) was significantly greater in the IGM group compared to the group without IGM (11% vs. 5%, p = 0.009). There was no significant association between rs12772424 SNP (BD-associated SNP) with bipolar course of illness measures. Further investigation examining the complex interactions between functional genetic variants, molecular markers, environmental influence, and clinical phenotypes in BD is needed to better understand the mechanistic underpinnings to the high rate of T2DM bipolar comorbidity and identify early targets for treatment of both disorders.

Article.Title: Electroacupuncture alleviates chronic pain and comorbid depression through Gut-Metabolite-Brain axis remodeling to restore mPFC Glu/GABA balance
Article.Authors: Li S.; Huang J.; Lin D.; Luo D.; Fu W.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The comorbidity of chronic pain and depression is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder involving dysregulated microbiota–gut–brain communication. Although electroacupuncture (EA) has demonstrated therapeutic efficacy for both pain and depression, the mechanisms linking peripheral microbial-metabolic remodeling to central neurotransmitter regulation remain incompletely understood. Here, we employed an integrated multi-omics approach in a spared nerve injury (SNI) rat model to investigate the gut–metabolite–brain mechanisms underlying EA’s efficacy. EA significantly alleviated mechanical hypersensitivity and depressive-like behaviors while restoring mPFC Glu/GABA balance, accompanied by normalization of the glutamate transporter EAAT2 and the GABA-synthesizing enzyme GAD67. Metagenomic analysis showed that EA remodeled the gut microbial ecosystem by increasing microbial diversity, suppressing opportunistic pathobionts, including Bacillus cereus, Alistipes onderdonkii , while enriching SCFA-associated genera, including Butyricimonas and Romboutsia . These alterations were accompanied by coordinated remodeling of amino acid and butanoate metabolism. Correlation network analysis identified Pipecolic acid as a central metabolic node linking gut microbial alterations with mPFC GABAergic neurotransmission and behavioral recovery. Although individual bacterial genera did not significantly mediate its restoration, causal mediation analysis demonstrated that the Pipecolic acid–GABA axis significantly mediated improvements in both mechanical allodynia and anhedonia, supporting Pipecolic acid as a functional metabolic hub linking peripheral metabolic remodeling to central GABAergic regulation. Collectively, these findings identify peripheral metabolic remodeling as a key mechanistic interface through which EA coordinates gut microbial ecology and central neurochemical homeostasis, providing a systems-level framework for understanding the therapeutic mechanisms of acupuncture in pain–depression comorbidity.

Article.Title: Large-scale EEG reveals shared and distinct neural oscillatory features across major psychiatric disorders
Article.Authors: Rao S.; Xie J.; Niu M.; Pan Y.; Li Y.; Yu H.; Xie J.; Zhang Y.; Zhao S.; Pan G.; Guo W.; Li T.; Jiang H.
Article.Abstract: Major psychiatric disorders are leading contributors to global disability, yet robust biomarkers to inform diagnosis and treatment remain elusive. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a scalable, noninvasive approach to capture neural dysfunction, but prior findings have been inconsistent due to small, single-disorder cohorts. Here, we report a large-scale, two-site comparative study of resting-state EEG in schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder (BD), and major depressive disorder (MDD) compared with healthy controls (HC). Across 9751 participants’ EEG recordings, standardized preprocessing and feature generation yielded spectral power and functional connectivity (FC) measures tested with both statistical and machine-learning approaches. We identified convergent transdiagnostic alterations—reduced alpha power and increased gamma-band FC, implicating shared disruptions in inhibitory control and large-scale network coordination. Additional spectral differences included more pronounced delta-theta elevation in SCZ and a graded delta-theta continuum (SCZ > BD > MDD), suggesting a dimensional progression of neural dysregulation. Machine-learning models robustly distinguished individuals with psychiatric diagnoses from healthy controls within sites, but cross-site generalization and inter-disorder discrimination remained limited, underscoring challenges of heterogeneity. These findings identify reproducible EEG features that capture both shared and disorder-distinct neural alterations, advancing efforts towards early detection and individualized treatment in major psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Episodic memory-associated weighted atrophy network mapping in mild cognitive impairment and subjective cognitive decline: a multi-center study
Article.Authors: Huang A.; Jiang K.; Chi L.; Qiao M.; Yang X.; Wu H.; Chen S.; Fan J.; Wang H.; Chen Y.; Tong Z.; Lin X.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: This study localizes episodic memory-associated impaired networks in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and subjective cognitive decline (SCD) using a weighted key atrophy network mapping method, and investigates whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) can modulate them. Replicability was assessed across three independent cohorts involving 1312 subjects. First, single-subject key atrophy maps were constructed by comparing cortical thickness with cognitively normal groups and retaining regions showing significant thickness-memory correlations. Second, these maps served as seeds for functional connectivity analysis in a large normative connectome, generating atrophy networks weighted by atrophy extent. Third, group-level comparisons identified impaired networks in MCI and SCD, and methodological reliability was further validated against a memory network derived from patients with focal brain lesions. Finally, the impaired networks were experimentally modulated via a 4-week rTMS intervention (25 MCI, 13 SCD). Despite substantial individual-level heterogeneity, atrophied regions in most MCI patients were functionally connected to a common episodic memory-associated impaired network. This phenomenon was not significant in SCD patients. Both lesion-memory network mapping and cross-dataset validation confirmed consistency across cohorts. Critically, rTMS can modulate the impaired network in MCI patients, primarily reflected by enhanced functional connectivity within this network. In conclusion, this study developed a robust weighted key atrophy network mapping method, localizing common episodic memory-associated impaired networks in MCI/SCD. Modulation of this impaired network may serve as a potential therapeutic strategy to delay MCI progression.

Article.Title: Serum B-cell activating factor and delayed memory in first-episode drug-naïve schizophrenia: a case-control study
Article.Authors: Yang Q.; Jin T.; Jin S.; Jiang F.; Qiu J.; Yang X.; Wang P.; Yan Q.; Tian Q.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive impairment in schizophrenia has been linked to immune dysregulation, but the role of humoral immune regulators remains unclear. We examined serum B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and A proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) in 90 first-episode drug-naïve schizophrenia (FES) patients and 90 matched healthy controls (HCs). Cognitive performance was assessed using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS), and symptom severity was assessed using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). Serum BAFF and APRIL were measured using Luminex technology. After adjustment for age, sex, education, BMI, and smoking status, serum BAFF and APRIL levels were significantly lower in FES patients than in HCs (BAFF: F = 131.935, P < 0.001; APRIL: F = 59.772, P < 0.001). In the hypothesis-driven primary analytic model focusing on RBANS delayed memory, the Group × BAFF interaction was significant ( F (1,171) = 13.524, P < 0.001), with a positive BAFF slope in HCs ( B = 0.015, P = 0.017) but a negative slope in FES patients ( B = -0.022). This interaction remained robust in sensitivity analyses. Exploratory analyses suggested a nominal Group × BAFF interaction for RBANS total score ( F = 5.866, P = 0.016, FDR-adjusted q = 0.082), which was interpreted cautiously. No analogous Group × APRIL interaction was observed, and BAFF/APRIL levels were not significantly associated with PANSS symptom dimensions. These cross-sectional findings identify peripheral BAFF as a hypothesis-generating correlate of delayed memory in early untreated schizophrenia, but do not establish temporality, causality, or central immune-cognitive mechanisms.

Article.Title: Aerobic exercise prevents neuroinflammation and ameliorates depressive-like behaviors via suppression of HMGB1/NF-κB pathway-mediated reactive microglial states in mice exposed to chronic mild stress
Article.Authors: Jiang L.; Zhang C.; Yang D.; Liu S.; Liao R.; Xu E.; Yu Y.; Liu L.
Article.Abstract: Aerobic exercise is shown to have a positive effect on depressive-like symptoms; however, the associated mechanisms have not yet been fully elucidated. The role of neuroinflammation in the pathogenesis of depression is well-documented. High mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), a late mediator of inflammation, can promote the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines in various inflammation-related diseases. This study aimed to investigate the antidepressant effects of aerobic exercise by regulating hippocampal neuroinflammation via the HMGB1/NF-κB pathway-mediated microglial reactivity state. We assessed the depressive-like behaviors of the mice through behavioral tests. It was found that aerobic exercise significantly alleviated chronic mild stress (CMS)-induced depressive-like behaviors in mice. Furthermore, aerobic exercise reduced the total number of microglia and altered microglial morphology and reactive states in the hippocampus, accompanied by down-regulation of pro-inflammatory markers. These effects were observed to be regulated by HMGB1. We found a significant nuclear-to-cytoplasmic translocation of HMGB1 in the hippocampus, in the absence of apoptotic alterations (pyknotic nuclei, karyorrhexis, karyolysis), indicating an active release in the brain after CMS stimulation. Interestingly, aerobic exercise could reverse these alterations by inhibiting the HMGB1/NF-κB pathway. These findings not only enhance the understanding of the processes driving neuroinflammation in the hippocampi of mice exposed to CMS, but also highlight the potential of aerobic exercise as an anti-depression therapeutic strategy.

Article.Title: Neurobehavioral changes in fear generalization in clinical high risk for psychosis
Article.Authors: Clauss J.; Babadi B.; Tuominen L.; Deng W.; Leathem L.; Holt D.
Article.Abstract: Changes in basic associative learning processes have been identified in several psychiatric conditions. However, it remains unknown whether these findings result from ongoing psychopathology or represent an underlying transdiagnostic risk factor for multiple clinical states. In this study, 72 participants with subclinical psychopathology, 23 of whom met criteria for the Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis syndrome (CHR+) and 49 who did not meet these criteria (CHR-), completed a fear conditioning and generalization paradigm while functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data were collected. During this procedure, participants were presented with face stimuli that were either paired (CS+) or not paired (CS-) with a mild electrical shock, as well as eight face “morphs” (stages between the CS+ and CS-) tailored to each participant’s perceptual discrimination ability. Following the scan session, participants rated the likelihood that each stimulus had been previously followed by a shock. Fear generalization-related neural responses (in a subset of the sample, 16 CHR+ and 40 CHR- participants) and the memory ratings were then examined using both categorical and individual-level psychometric modeling approaches. Expected patterns of fear generalization-related responses were observed in the anterior insula and superior frontal gyrus and in the memory ratings. The psychometric modeling analysis revealed a significantly greater threshold in responses of the left anterior insula, representing a wider fear generalization curve, in the CHR+, compared to the CHR-, group. Moreover, across the whole sample, symptoms of anxiety were associated with a wider fear generalization gradient. These findings suggest that specific features of a basic associative memory process, fear generalization, may be linked to CHR status and transdiagnostic risk for psychiatric illness.

Article.Title: Association between tirzepatide use and risk of suicidal ideation among individuals with obesity and major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Liu T.; Chu C.; Liu C.; Wu J.; Tsai Y.; Chang H.; Lai C.
Article.Abstract: Obesity and major depressive disorder (MDD) frequently co-occur and confer mutually reinforcing risks, including elevated suicidality. Tirzepatide has demonstrated substantial metabolic benefits, yet its psychiatric safety in high-risk populations with MDD remains uncertain. This study aimed to compare suicidal ideation outcomes among adults with comorbid obesity and MDD initiating tirzepatide versus non–GLP-1RA anti-obesity medications. This retrospective, propensity score–matched cohort study used deidentified electronic health record data from the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults (≥18 years) with diagnosed obesity and MDD who initiated tirzepatide or non–GLP-1RA anti-obesity medications were included. The primary outcome was suicidal ideation. Secondary outcomes included anxiety disorders, insomnia disorders, all-cause mortality, and emergency department or inpatient encounters. Among 24,103 matched pairs, tirzepatide use was associated with lower risk of suicidal ideation (HR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.42–0.93), anxiety disorders (HR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.81–0.86), insomnia disorders (HR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.86–0.98), all-cause mortality (HR, 0.38; 95% CI, 0.25–0.58), and emergency department visits or hospitalizations (HR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.89–0.99). Risk reduction was generally consistent across prespecified subgroups. Control outcome analyses supported the internal validity of the findings. In conclusion, this study provides real-world evidence that tirzepatide initiation was associated with a lower recorded risk of suicidal ideation, as well as reduced anxiety, insomnia, all-cause mortality, emergency department visits, and hospitalizations, among adults with comorbid obesity and MDD. This observational association should not be interpreted as evidence of a direct antisuicidal effect. These findings support the potential for tirzepatide to serve as a metabolically favorable treatment option associated with a lower risk of suicidal ideation in this vulnerable, high-risk population.

Article.Title: Altered GABAB receptor sensitivity in heavy drinkers indexed using a TMS-based biomarker: a randomized controlled experimental medicine trial
Article.Authors: Montemitro C.; Donahue D.; Costumati A.; Maruottolo F.; Terezza S.; Sjoberg C.; Perini I.; Roman M.; Kugelberg F.; Heilig M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Metabotropic γ-aminobutyric acid type B receptors (GABA B Rs) are implicated in alcohol use disorder (AUD) and represent a promising therapeutic target. However, robust biomarkers of GABA B Rs target engagement and sensitivity in humans are lacking. We examined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)–derived cortical inhibition and growth hormone (GH) release as measures of GABA B R function, and whether heavy alcohol use is associated with altered responses to pharmacological GABA B R activation. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 31 healthy volunteers (16 heavy drinkers, 15 light drinkers) received baclofen 30 mg, baclofen 60 mg, or placebo across three sessions. Long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI), short-interval intracortical inhibition, and intracortical facilitation were assessed with paired-pulse TMS at baseline and ~60 min post-dose. Baclofen blood concentrations and plasma GH levels were measured. Baclofen produced dose-dependent increases in GH release, confirming neuroendocrine GABA B R engagement. The LICI response to baclofen differed between groups: In light drinkers, baclofen at 30 mg potentiated LICI, and a similar potentiation was seen at 60 mg, indicating that a plateau may have been reached. In contrast, in heavy drinkers, a potentiation of LICI similar to that in light drinkers was seen at 30 mg baclofen, but was absent at the 60 mg dose despite comparable pharmacokinetics, suggesting altered GABA B R function. Effects were selective for GABA B R–mediated inhibition, with no consistent modulation of short-interval intracortical inhibition or corticospinal excitability. Acute baclofen administration reveals altered GABA B R sensitivity in heavy drinkers, with preserved responses at lower doses but reduced response under stronger agonist stimulation. LICI and GH release provide complementary biomarkers of central and peripheral GABA B Rs engagement and may support translational development of mechanism-based treatments for AUD.
