Article.Title: Prelimbic cortex CRHR1 regulates Parkinson’s disease-related anxiety through a PrLGlu-avBNSTGABA-VTADA pathway
Article.Authors: Gao S.; Yang J.; Bai Y.; Song M.; Guo Y.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety is a common non-motor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD). Due to the unclear mechanism, treatment becomes challenging and significantly impacts the quality of life of patients. Although corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor 1 (CRHR1) is abundantly expressed in the prelimbic cortex (PrL) and have been implicated in PD and anxiety, the role and mechanism of PrL CRHR1 in PD-related anxiety remain unclear. By combining neuropharmacological, chemogenetic, neuroanatomical, and molecular approaches, the present study were performed to investigate the role of PrL CRHR1 in PD-related anxiety and to explore its neural pathways. In this study, unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine lesions of the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) in male Sprague-Dawley rats induced anxiety-like behaviors and decreased CRHR1 expression in the PrL compared to sham rats. In sham and the lesioned rats, pharmacological blockade of PrL CRHR1 induced anxiety-like behaviors, whereas its activation produced anxiolytic-like effects, with both effects attenuated in the lesioned rats. CRHR1 blockade was accompanied by increased c-Fos expression in the anterior ventral bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (avBNST), while selective knockdown of CRHR1 in avBNST-projecting PrLGlu neurons similarly enhanced anxiety-like behaviors. Activation of the PrL-avBNSTGABA-ventral tegmental area (VTA) pathway or the avBNST-VTADA pathway induced anxiety-like behaviors, whereas inhibition of either pathway produced anxiolytic-like effects. Together, these findings suggest that PrL CRHR1 regulates PD-related anxiety, at least in part through the PrLGlu-avBNSTGABA-VTADA pathway, thereby providing new insights into the neural mechanisms underlying PD-related anxiety.

Article.Title: α7 nicotinic receptors in the ventral tegmental area gate the acute ethanol effects on aversive memory formation.
Article.Authors: Urrea F.; Medina J.; Pastor V.
Article.Abstract: Acute ethanol intoxication is classically associated with impairments in memory formation, yet the circuit and receptor mechanisms through which it modulates aversive memory formation remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of a single post-training injection of different binge-like doses of ethanol on memory formation using an inhibitory avoidance task in young adult male rats. An intermediate dose of ethanol (1.5 g/kg) induced the expected memory impairment, whereas a higher dose (2.5 g/kg) produced a long-lasting enhancement of aversive memory formation that persisted for at least 21 days. Both effects depended on α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (α7nAChRs) within the ventral tegmental area (VTA). Intra-VTA antagonism of α7nAChRs with methyllycaconitine prevented ethanol-induced memory enhancement, while intra-VTA positive allosteric modulation of α7nAChRs with PNU-120596 prevented the memory impairment produced by the lower dose. In addition, pharmacological activation of prefrontal cortical D1 dopaminergic receptors restored ethanol-induced memory enhancement following intra-VTA α7nAChR antagonism, suggesting that prefrontal cortical D1 receptor signaling is involved in the enhancement pathway. Together, these findings identify VTA α7nAChRs as key regulators of the dose-dependent effects of acute ethanol on aversive memory formation, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how acute alcohol exposure can produce opposing mnemonic outcomes.

Article.Title: Activation of GLP-1 receptors in the middle part of the paraventricular nucleus of thalamus suppresses alcohol-related responses
Article.Authors: Aranäs C.; Witley S.; Zhang Q.; Edvardsson C.; Jerlhag E.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) remains a major public health challenge, and identifying the brain circuits through which pharmacological interventions act is central to developing more effective treatments. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists suppress alcohol-related behaviors in rodents and reduce alcohol consumption in clinical populations with AUD, yet the neuroanatomical substrates mediating these effects remain only partly mapped. One candidate region implicated in addiction is the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT), particularly its middle part (mid-PVT), which modulates mesolimbic dopamine signaling, has been implicated in addiction-related processes including alcohol use, and expresses GLP-1R. Whether activation of GLP-1R in the mid-PVT influences alcohol-related responses had not been examined, and that was the aim of the present study. Here, we found that local GLP-1R antagonism in the mid-PVT with exendin-3(9-39) (Ex9) attenuated the suppressive effect of systemically administered GLP-1R agonist exendin-4 (Ex4) on alcohol-induced locomotor stimulation, implicating this region in the central actions of GLP-1R agonists. Intra-mid-PVT Ex4 also attenuated alcohol-induced locomotor stimulation and accumbal dopamine release in male mice, without altering the expression of alcohol-induced conditioned place preference. We further showed that Ex4 into the mid-PVT reduced alcohol intake in male and female rats, although a higher dose was required in females. In a separate cohort of alcohol-consuming, treatment-naive rats, Glp1r mRNA in the PVT did not differ between the sexes. Together, these findings indicate that GLP-1R in the mid-PVT contributes to alcohol-related responses, extending the neuroanatomical map of circuits through which GLP-1R agonists may suppress alcohol intake.

Article.Title: HDAC6 Inhibition Promotes Peripheral Nerve Development and Regeneration via Neurofilament Acetylation
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Zhang X.; Wu Y.; Luo K.; Shen M.; Ji Y.; Ding F.; Zhang Q.
Article.Abstract: Peripheral nerve injury remains challenging due to limited neuronal regeneration. Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) regulates microtubule dynamics, but its role in peripheral nervous system (PNS) development and repair is incompletely understood. This study investigates the expression, function, and mechanism of HDAC6 in PNS maturation and regeneration. HDAC6 was abundantly expressed in dorsal root ganglia and sciatic nerves. During postnatal development (P1-P28), HDAC6 expression progressively declined, inversely correlating with increased α-tubulin K40 and global acetylation. Pharmacological HDAC6 inhibition with Tubastatin A (Tub A) or suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA) accelerated nerve maturation, evidenced by enhanced conduction velocity, myelination, and cytoskeletal integrity. In a sciatic nerve crush model, HDAC6 inhibition promoted functional recovery, axonal regeneration, and remyelination. In vitro, HDAC6 inhibition or siRNA knockdown enhanced neurite outgrowth and growth cone expansion in both motor and sensory neurons. Mechanistically, acetylome identified neurofilament light chain (NEFL) as a novel HDAC6 substrate. Among several hypoacetylated lysine residues post-injury, K316 showed the greatest decrease. Direct HDAC6-NEFL interaction was confirmed by molecular docking and co-immunoprecipitation. Expression of an acetylation-mimetic NEFL (K316Q) mutant promoted neurite outgrowth and growth cone maturation compared with wild-type or acetylation-deficient (K316R) mutants. Collectively, HDAC6 acts as a key negative regulator of PNS development and regeneration, and NEFL K316 acetylation serves as a critical molecular switch for axonal growth. Targeting HDAC6 represents a promising strategy for peripheral nerve repair.

Article.Title: Exercise and insulin independently stimulate galactose uptake into human skeletal muscle
Article.Authors: Luong T.; Pedersen M.; Thorup C.; Mejren A.; Johansen R.; Vendelbo M.; Sørensen M.; Wallis G.; Rowlands D.; Gormsen L.; Søndergaard E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Carbohydrate choice affects glycaemic responses during and after exercise, particularly for individuals with impaired glucose regulation. Galactose causes smaller glycaemic excursions than glucose but is thought to require hepatic conversion to glucose via the Leloir pathway before peripheral use. Whether galactose is directly taken up by skeletal muscle, and whether this is regulated by exercise and insulin remains unclear. In this randomised, controlled crossover trial, eight healthy men (age 68 ± 4 years; body mass index 24.7 ± 2.1 kg/m 2 ) completed two 4 h study days, with and without a hyperinsulinaemic–euglycaemic clamp (1.0 mU/kg/min). Galactose turnover was assessed using a primed‐constant galactose infusion. Participants performed one‐legged, high‐intensity knee‐extension exercise at maximal capacity, with the contralateral leg as a non‐exercised control. Skeletal muscle galactose uptake was quantified by dynamic [ 1 8 F]FDGal positron emission tomography (PET), and arteriovenous (AV) exchange across the leg was determined from femoral blood samples combined with [ 1 5 O]H 2 O PET‐measured leg perfusion. Exercise and insulin markedly increased galactose uptake (exercise effect: P < 0.001; insulin effect: P < 0.001; interaction: P = 0.0769). PET analysis showed that exercise primarily increased tracer influx (K1), while insulin increased intracellular trapping (k3) and modestly reduced efflux (k2). Plasma galactose concentrations were low (0.2 ± 0.1 mmol/L) and galactose AV exchange across the leg did not differ across conditions. Human skeletal muscle can directly take up galactose, and this is stimulated by exercise and insulin. This challenges the assumption that hepatic conversion is required before peripheral utilisation. Future studies should determine whether galactose is incorporated into skeletal muscle glycogen to a physiologically relevant extent. image Key points Galactose causes smaller spikes in blood sugar than glucose, and it has long been assumed that the body must first convert galactose into glucose in the liver before peripheral use. Using positron emission tomography imaging with the galactose analogue 2‐[ 1 8 F]fluoro‐2‐deoxygalactose in combination with a one‐legged knee‐extension ergometer, we demonstrated that human skeletal muscle can directly take up galactose. Both exercise and insulin markedly increased skeletal muscle galactose uptake, with an additive effect when combined. Exercise primarily increased galactose uptake by enhancing muscle blood flow, whereas insulin exerted its effect by promoting phosphorylation and intracellular trapping. Further studies are required to determine whether galactose is incorporated into skeletal muscle glycogen to a physiologically meaningful extent.

Article.Title: Loud acoustic stimulation reveals an online reticulospinal contribution to long‐latency reflexes in humans
Article.Authors: Sugino H.; Nozaki D.; Ushiyama J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The long‐latency reflex (LLR), the fastest feedback response that recruits supraspinal pathways, is an important model for understanding how descending motor pathways shape rapid corrective responses in humans. While the corticospinal tract's contribution to the LLR has been well established, that of the reticulospinal tract, the other major descending motor pathway, remains purely speculative. To address this online contribution to the LLR, we used loud acoustic stimulation (LAS), which can strongly engage brainstem circuits including the pontomedullary reticular formation. By delivering LAS at nine timings (0–80 ms in 10 ms steps) relative to perturbation onset, we tested whether LAS selectively facilitates the LLR but not the short‐latency reflex (SLR), and whether the facilitated epoch shifts systematically with LAS timing. In 12 healthy participants, elbow extension perturbations evoked stretch reflexes in the biceps brachii muscle. LAS produced significant supralinear facilitation in the LLR but not in the SLR. Moreover, when LAS was delivered 40 ms or later after perturbation onset, the facilitated epoch shifted progressively later as LAS was delayed, beginning at an approximately constant delay of 30–40 ms after LAS onset. This constant delay suggests that the facilitation at these timings arose from the same LAS‐evoked descending input acting on the ongoing LLR. Together with the lack of significant SLR facilitation, this temporal pattern is consistent with an online reticulospinal contribution to the human LLR, alongside the established corticospinal contribution. This approach provides a new, non‐invasive means to investigate the physiological role of the reticulospinal tract in human motor control. image Key points The long‐latency reflex is a rapid muscle response to sudden stretch. Unlike faster spinal reflexes, it is shaped by commands descending from the brain and adjusts to the task. Though the corticospinal tract is known to shape this reflex, whether the reticulospinal tract also contributes to the reflex has not been tested in humans. We stretched the arm and, at various delays, played a loud sound that engages the brainstem origin of the reticulospinal tract. The sound significantly enhanced the long‐latency reflex, whereas no significant enhancement was detected in the faster spinal reflex. When the sound came 40 ms or more after the stretch, the enhancement followed the sound at a stable delay, suggesting that sound‐evoked descending signals interacted with the ongoing reflex response. These findings are consistent with a real‐time contribution of the reticulospinal tract to the human long‐latency reflex and provide a non‐invasive way to study this pathway.

Article.Title: Increased inspiratory work exacerbates skin hypoperfusion and attenuates the pressor response during high‐intensity exercise in the heat
Article.Authors: Koike J.; Fujii N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract During exercise in the heat, skin vasodilatation occurs as heat loss response. Increased respiratory muscle work by inspiratory loading during high‐intensity exercise causes vasoconstriction in active skeletal muscles without altering arterial blood pressure. We hypothesized that, during high‐intensity exercise in the heat, inspiratory loading would induce skin vasoconstriction and thus reduce skin blood flow to maintain the pressor response associated with high‐intensity exercise. Fifteen healthy young men cycled in the heat (35°C, 50% relative humidity), consisting of 14 min at 50% peak oxygen uptake () followed by 3 min at 90% . A 1 min inspiratory loading was applied 10 min into exercise at 50% and 1 min into exercise at 90% . The protocol without inspiratory loading was performed on a separate day as the control. Upper back skin blood flow was measured using a laser‐Doppler flowmeter. Arterial blood pressure was measured using finger photoplethysmography, and skin vascular conductance was calculated as skin blood flow/mean arterial pressure. Skin blood flow decreased, whereas mean arterial pressure increased gradually during exercise at 90% , and these responses were greater and smaller, in the inspiratory load than control ( P < 0.003). Skin vascular conductance did not differ between conditions at 90% . At 50% , the inspiratory loading slightly reduced mean arterial pressure but did not modulate skin blood flow or skin vascular conductance. We show that increased respiratory muscle work augments the reduction in skin blood flow, whereas it attenuates the pressor response during high‐intensity exercise in the heat, without modulating skin vasoconstriction. image Key points Skin vasodilatation plays a pivotal role in heat loss during exercise in the heat. Breathing, and thus respiratory muscle work, can be augmented by hyperthermia, ageing and lung or cardiovascular disease. However, whether increased respiratory muscle work influences skin vasodilatation during exercise in the heat remains unknown. Inspiratory loading, which increased the work of breathing, was applied during exercise at 50% and at 90% in the heat. We showed that an inspiratory load reduced skin blood flow and attenuated the increase in mean arterial pressure during exercise at 90% without influencing skin vascular conductance. However, these effects associated with inspiratory loading were not clearly observed during exercise at 50% . Our findings suggest that increased inspiratory muscle work may reduce heat loss associated with increases in skin blood flow and blunted pressor response during high‐intensity exercise in the heat.

Article.Title: Acute intermittent carotid body stimulations induce long‐term facilitation of respiratory–cardiovascular coupling in rats
Article.Authors: Linossier A.; Gestreau C.; Menuet C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Hypertension, the leading modifiable risk factor for global mortality, is driven in >50% of cases by neurogenic mechanisms linked to heightened sympathetic nerve activity (SNA). A hallmark of neurogenic hypertension is the exacerbation of respiratory‐modulated SNA (RespSNA) and resulting blood pressure Traube–Hering (TH) waves, which emerges during the prehypertensive period and contributes to disease development. Carotid bodies (CBs), the peripheral chemoreceptors involved in the hypoxic response, are hyperactive in hypertensive patients and animal models. Their chronic intermittent stimulation, as seen in obstructive sleep apnoea, promotes hypertension characterised by exacerbated RespSNA and TH waves. Yet, their causal role in initiating these changes remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether acute intermittent CB stimulations could directly enhance RespSNA, TH waves and blood pressure from a physiological baseline, using the in situ working heart–brainstem preparation in rats. Four brief CB stimulations with sodium cyanide, mimicking acute intermittent hypoxia, were sufficient to induce a prolonged (>20 min) increase in both inspiratory and late expiratory RespSNA bursts, TH waves and perfusion pressure, with these effects being prevented by carotid sinus denervation. These changes were accompanied by a reconfiguration of central respiratory and cardiovascular control, including elevated respiratory heart rate variability and enhanced respiratory drive targeting upper airway and abdominal muscles. Our findings demonstrate that acute intermittent CB activation triggers sustained RespSNA and elevation of TH waves, supporting its potential role in development of hypertension. Our data also suggest that CBs play a key role in initiating this respiratory–cardiovascular plasticity and that central mechanisms might contribute to its long‐term maintenance. image Key points Carotid body (CB) overactivity is implicated in sympathetic excitation and development of hypertension, but its direct role in initiating respiratory–cardiovascular dysfunction remains unresolved. We tested whether brief, repeated CB stimulations could trigger lasting changes in breathing and blood pressure control from a physiological baseline. In rats, only four stimulations induced a persistent increase in respiratory‐modulated sympathetic activity, elevating blood pressure fluctuations (Traube–Hering waves) and mean blood pressure. These effects, prevented by carotid sinus denervation, were linked to enhanced respiratory–cardiovascular coupling and altered upper airway and abdominal motor control. Our findings reveal that short‐term CB activation can induce long‐term facilitation of respiratory–cardiovascular coupling, relevant to both physiological adaptations and hypertension pathogenesis.

Article.Title: Intracellular α <sub>1A</sub> ‐adrenergic receptor regulation of cAMP production by an inside‐out mitogen‐activated protein kinase signalling pathway in cardiac myocytes
Article.Authors: Fiore C.; Rudokas M.; Masuda R.; Khamsopha B.; Sherpa R.; Chouhan N.; Moshal K.; Agarwal S.; Harvey R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Sympathetic stimulation produces beneficial changes in cardiac function through β‐adrenergic receptor (βAR) production of cAMP and subsequent alteration of electrical and mechanical activity. Long‐term activation of cAMP production also contributes to cardiac remodelling and detrimental changes associated with heart failure. However, sympathetic responses are mediated by the endogenous neurotransmitter norepinephrine (NE), which is also a potent α 1 ‐adrenergic receptor (α 1 AR) agonist, and α 1 AR activation can produce significant effects on the heart as well. What is less clear is how α 1 ‐ and β‐adrenergic responses interact with one another. Previous studies have demonstrated that α 1 AR activation can inhibit β‐adrenergic regulation of the electrical and mechanical activity of cardiac myocytes, although the signalling mechanisms involved were not previously known. In the present study, we used fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)–based biosensors in adult rat ventricular myocytes to demonstrate that this cross‐talk effect involves the inhibition of cAMP production by intracellular α 1A ‐adrenergic receptors (α 1A ARs) acting on βARs found on the plasma membrane. Furthermore, we established that this inside‐out signalling mechanism involves a mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway that uncouples βARs from downstream signalling in a G protein‐coupled receptor kinase (GRK)/arrestin‐dependent manner. These results reveal a novel, non‐canonical signalling mechanism contributing to α 1 AR responses in the heart, and that this effect limits βAR production of cAMP by NE. This mechanism may contribute to the cardioprotective effect previously ascribed to α 1A AR activation. These findings also clearly demonstrate the importance of considering the contributions of α 1 and βARs together when studying the influence of the sympathetic nervous system on the heart. image Key points Acute sympathetic stimulation produces beneficial changes in cardiac function through the release of norepinephrine (NE), activation of β‐adrenergic receptors (βARs) and subsequent production of cAMP. However, long‐term sympathetic stimulation of the same signalling pathway contributes to the development of heart failure and cardiac arrhythmias. NE also activates α 1 ‐adrenergic receptors (α 1 ARs), which have been linked to a cardioprotective effect involving a mechanism not well defined. The present study demonstrates that the activation of intracellular α 1A ‐adrenergic receptors (α 1A ARs) reduces cAMP production by βARs found on the cell surface. This ‘inside‐out’ signalling mechanism acts through a mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway to enhance β‐arrestin‐mediated uncoupling of βARs from downstream signalling. By limiting excessive cAMP production, α 1A AR signalling may help protect the heart during prolonged sympathetic stimulation, highlighting the importance of considering the effects of α 1 ‐ and βAR signalling together when studying sympathetic responses in the heart.

Article.Title: Heat acclimation does not alleviate the reduction in exogenous glucose oxidation that occurs when exercising in hot conditions
Article.Authors: Podlogar T.; Gifford R.; Thomas J.; Civil R.; Malik S.; Lucas R.; Young A.; Pasiakos S.; Margolis L.; Wallis G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Exogenous glucose oxidation (CHOexo) is suppressed during endurance exercise performed in hot conditions, although the underlying mechanisms and effects of heat acclimation are unknown. The present study investigated whether heat acclimation alleviates the heat‐induced suppression of CHOexo and the underlying physiological mechanisms. Seventeen endurance‐trained adults (10 males and seven females) completed 90 min cycling trials at 45% W max with glucose ingestion (90 g·h −1 ) under temperate [20°C; 20% relative humidity (RH); COOL] and hot (40°C; 20% RH; HOT) conditions, and again in the heat (40°C; 20% RH; POST) following a heat acclimation protocol (9 days of isothermic exercise‐heat acclimation across a 10 day period). Dual stable isotope tracers ([U 13 C 6 ] glucose ingestion, [6,6‐ 2 H 2 ]glucose‐infusion), indirect calorimetry and muscle biopsies were used to assess CHOexo, glucose kinetics and muscle glycogen utilisation during exercise. CHOexo (mean [95% confidence limits]) was reduced by ∼27% in HOT compared to COOL (0.37 [0.31, 0.43] g·min −1 vs . 0.51 [0.45, 0.57] g·min −1 ; P < 0.001) and, despite clear thermoregulatory adaptation following heat acclimation, remained suppressed in POST (0.38 [0.31, 0.44] g·min −1 ; P < 0.01 vs . COOL). Rates of plasma glucose appearance, disappearance and exogenous glucose appearance were unaffected by environmental condition or heat acclimation. Glucose metabolic clearance rates and plasma glucose oxidation were reduced in HOT and POST compared to COOL ( P < 0.05). A decreased capacity for plasma glucose disposal and utilisation rather than limitations in splanchnic glucose appearance underpin the reduced exogenous glucose oxidation observed during exercise in the heat, and this is not alleviated by heat acclimation. image Key points Exogenous glucose oxidation is suppressed during endurance‐exercise performed in hot conditions, although the underlying mechanisms and effects of heat acclimation are unknown. A decreased capacity for plasma glucose disposal and utilisation rather than limitations in splanchnic glucose appearance appear to underpin the reduced exogenous glucose oxidation observed during exercise in the heat. Heat acclimation does not alleviate the reduction in exogenous glucose oxidation that occurs when exercising in hot conditions.

Article.Title: Cerebrovascular mechanisms of stroke severity in offspring from pre‐eclamptic pregnancy
Article.Authors: Savage‐Hunt R.; Tremble S.; Brigl J.; Cipolla M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Offspring from pre‐eclamptic pregnancies face elevated ischaemic stroke risk throughout life, yet the mechanisms linking adverse intrauterine exposure to adult cerebrovascular vulnerability remain unknown. Distal leptomeningeal anastomoses (LMAs), which develop during late gestation are key determinants of stroke severity and represent a plausible target of prenatal programming. Here, we show that experimental preeclampsia (ePE) in rats establishes a persistent cerebrovascular structural and transcriptional phenotype in adult offspring. Following transient middle cerebral artery occlusion, ePE‐exposed males exhibited increased infarct volume, oedema, enhanced perfusion deficit and smaller LMA diameters relative to normal pregnant offspring, and 83% had microvascular stasis after stroke. Female offspring were protected from stroke‐induced brain injury despite sharing a similar transcriptional landscape. RNA sequencing and DNA methylation profiling revealed differentially expressed genes and discrete differentially methylated regions enriched for vascular development and VEGF‐Notch signalling in ePE offspring. These findings support the possibility of a developmental origin of cerebrovascular stroke risk, implicating gestational programming of cerebrovascular gene expression as a sex modulated determinant of adult stroke outcome and a potential target for early intervention. image Key points Offspring born from pre‐eclamptic pregnancies have a greater lifetime risk and death from ischaemic stroke, but why this occurs is unknown. Pial collaterals form during the late gestational period and are a key determinant of stroke severity. Using a rat model, we showed that compared to normal pregnancy, male offspring from pre‐eclamptic pregnancies had smaller diameter pial collaterals which was associated with decreased collateral recruitment during ischaemic stroke and worsened stroke outcome. RNA analysis revealed altered expression of genes related to blood vessel development and function in adult offspring. These findings suggest that preeclampsia leads to lasting changes in cerebrovascular structure and gene expression which is associated with increased stroke severity in male offspring suggesting a potential window for early intervention.

Article.Title: German wine and respiration: Remarks on the discovery, properties and significance of the Bötzinger complex
Article.Authors: Lipski J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Bötzinger complex (BötC) comprises a distinct bilateral group of interneurons that are active during the expiratory phase of the respiratory cycle, located in the rostral medulla ventral to the compact formation of the nucleus ambiguus. It was named after the bottles of wine served at the conference dinner of an international meeting held in Germany in 1980, where the first electrophysiological data describing these neurons were presented. In cats, BötC neurons predominantly exhibit an augmenting (E‐Aug) firing pattern, whereas in rats E‐Aug and E‐Dec (decrementing expiratory) patterns are observed. Both subtypes issue axons that often extensively arborise on both sides of the medulla, forming inhibitory glycinergic and/or GABAergic synapses with inspiratory neurons of the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups. Additionally, E‐Aug neurons project to the spinal cord and inhibit phrenic motoneurons. These properties contrast with those of another group of bulbospinal expiratory neurons in the caudal medulla, which do not issue medullary axon collaterals and are excitatory. BötC neurons regulate the interval during which inspiratory neurons remain silent and contribute to synchronisation of respiratory activity across both sides of the lower brainstem. Recent in vivo , reduced‐preparation and in silico studies indicate that they also contribute to respiratory rhythmogenesis through mutual inhibitory synaptic interactions with the pre‐Bötzinger complex. This review provides the history of the discovery and naming of the BötC and a detailed discussion of the properties of BötC neurons, including their location, morphology, afferent and efferent axonal projections, synaptic connectivity and functional role. image

Article.Title: Multiparametric cardiomyocyte profiling with single‐LED excitation reveals subtype‐specific electromechanical coupling in LQTS in vitro
Article.Authors: Khudiakov A.; Alberio C.; Dragani D.; Giannetti F.; Bertasini A.; Mura M.; Gnecchi M.; Moretti A.; Crotti L.; Schwartz P.; Sala L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cardiac excitation–contraction coupling (ECC) is an essential and tightly regulated process that links action potentials to intracellular calcium release and mechanical contraction. At the whole‐heart level, ECC is captured by integrative evaluation of electrical and mechanical components of the cardiac cycle through parameters termed electromechanical delay (EMD) and electromechanical window (EMW). Alterations in the EMD or EMW reflect impaired electromechanical coupling and have been associated with increased arrhythmic risk across multiple cardiac diseases. However, it is currently unclear whether and how equivalent metrics can be derived and interpreted in vitro or meaningfully applied to patient‐specific human disease models. Here, we implement ECC profiling in vitro using a single‐LED optical imaging system that enables simultaneous measurements of membrane voltage, intracellular calcium and contractility. This approach allows quantification of individual transients and their temporal relationships. To investigate distinct perturbations of ECC, we applied this platform to human‐induced pluripotent stem cell‐derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC‐CMs) representing three mechanistically distinct ECC perturbations: a repolarization defect (LQT2, KCNH2 p.A561V), a calmodulin‐associated calcium‐handling defect (CALM‐LQTS, CALM1 p.F142L) and pharmacological contractile uncoupling by myosin ATPase inhibition (blebbistatin). Cellular analogues of the clinical EMD and EMW were robustly quantifiable and provided mechanistically informative ECC signatures that were not entirely captured by conventional metrics focused on asynchronous individual transient analysis. Pharmacological targeting of the main cardiac ion currents further validated these findings and confirmed the robustness of the ECC quantification. This novel technique provides a basis for more sensitive assessment of disease phenotypes, arrhythmogenic risk and pharmacological effects in human cellular models, supporting the development of new approach methodologies. image Key points A single‐LED optical platform enables fully synchronized, simultaneous measurement of voltage, calcium and contraction in human‐induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)‐derived cardiomyocytes (CMs) at a high spatial and temporal resolution. In vitro analogues of the clinical electromechanical delay and electromechanical window can be robustly quantified in hiPSC‐CM monolayers and behave consistently with their in vivo counterparts under genetic and pharmacological perturbations. Despite comparable APD80 prolongation, LQT2 and CALM‐LQTS hiPSC‐CMs display divergent electromechanical signatures, demonstrating that integrative ECC metrics resolve mechanistic differences not captured by conventional single‐transient analyses. Pharmacological recapitulation of the disease phenotypes further confirmed these observations. In vitro ECC profiling offers a sensitive approach for distinguishing mechanistic perturbations of cardiac function and improving the characterization of arrhythmogenic risk.

Article.Title: Epitope‐dependent acute inhibition and potentiation of N ‐methyl‐ d ‐aspartate receptors by GluN1 autoantibodies
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Heckmann J.; Zettner M.; Hasegawa K.; Abdulla T.; Gao S.; Steinke S.; Hust M.; Prüss H.; Furukawa H.; Geis C.; Heckmann M.; Yu‐Strzelczyk J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Transfer of autoantibodies targeting ionotropic N ‐methyl‐ d ‐aspartate (NMDA) receptors from patients with autoimmune encephalitis to mice induces characteristic disease signs. The long‐term effects of pathogenic antibodies include immunoglobulin G (IgG)‐induced cross‐linking and receptor internalization. We investigated the direct and immediate impact of two specific pathogenic patient‐derived monoclonal autoantibodies (IgG #003‐102 and #007‐168) on NMDA receptor (NMDAR) function. We performed cell‐attached recordings from cells transfected with the GluN1‐3a and GluN2A subunits of NMDARs. IgG #003‐102 binds to the R2 lobe of the amino‐terminal domain (ATD) of the glycine‐binding GluN1 subunit. It significantly reduced the number of simultaneous NMDAR openings compared to controls at both low and high concentrations of glutamate and glycine. Closer examination revealed that IgG #003‐102 rapidly reduced the number of open receptors and shortened receptor‐opening bursts. However, antigen‐binding fragments of IgG #003‐102 did not reduce receptor openings. By contrast, IgG #007‐168, which binds to the top of the R1 lobe of the GluN1‐ATD, potentiated the NMDAR response. In conclusion, patient‐derived IgG #003‐102 inhibits NMDARs within seconds, before receptor internalization, and the full IgG is required for this acute inhibitory effect. This suggests that monovalent IgG #003‐102 constructs could be a new treatment strategy to shield a pathogenic epitope on NMDARs. image Key points N ‐methyl‐ d ‐aspartate (NMDA) receptors (NMDARs) are ionotropic glutamate receptors central to brain development and function. Anti‐NMDAR encephalitis is the most common cause of non‐viral autoimmune brain inflammation and is characterized by psychosis, dyskinesias, autonomic dysfunction and seizures. Symptoms are considered to result from autoantibodies that internalize surface NMDARs on neurons. Using patch clamp recordings, we tested the acute effects of two monoclonal anti‐GluN1 autoantibodies and the Fab fragment of one of them on NMDARs. The autoantibody (IgG #003‐102), which binds to the R2 lobe of the GluN1‐amino‐terminal domain (ATD), inhibits receptors within seconds. The entire IgG is required for this inhibition. By contrast, IgG #007‐168, which binds to the top of the R1 lobe of the GluN1‐ATD, potentiates receptor responses. By capitalizing on the null phenotype of a Fab from IgG #003‐102, we propose monovalent constructs as a potential new treatment strategy to prevent pathogenic antibodies from causing receptor dysfunction.

Article.Title: Semilunar nucleus neurons are highly excitable and potentiated by group I mGluRs to drive descending excitation to the mouse MNTB
Article.Authors: Wang H.; Wang X.; Alquraish D.; Wang Y.; Sumser A.; Lao C.; Markkula O.; Cai L.; Kopp‐Scheinpflug C.; Lu Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) neurons receive one of the largest synapses in the mammalian brain, the calyx of Held; however, multiple studies reported additional non‐calyceal excitatory inputs of largely unresolved origin to MNTB neurons. Most recently, the semilunar nucleus (SLN) was identified as a potential source of such non‐calyceal input in the rat. To elucidate the function of this novel pathway, we investigated the connectivity and physiology of the mouse SLN, with particular focus on neuromodulation by group I metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs). Viral tracing not only confirmed the SLN–MNTB pathway in mice, but also revealed that MNTB‐projecting SLN neurons received their input from the ipsilateral auditory cortex. Physiological characterization of SLN neurons using whole‐cell patch‐clamp recordings showed that SLN neurons, unlike most other auditory brainstem neurons, were intrinsically highly excitable. Electrical stimulation of the fibre tracts located dorsal to the SLN, evoked small, slow AMPA receptor‐mediated EPSCs in SLN neurons that readily summated temporally. Immunolabeling revealed a heterogeneous expression of mGluR1 and mGluR5 across SLN neurons. A subpopulation of SLN neurons exhibited spontaneous action potential firing at resting membrane potential. Pharmacological activation of group I mGluRs further increased spontaneous firing of SLN neurons. Probing for functional connectivity between SLN and the ipsilateral MNTB, fibre tracts dorsal and lateral to the MNTB were stimulated, eliciting primarily non‐calyceal AMPA receptor‐mediated EPSCs in MNTB neurons. These findings suggest that SLN output may provide a glutamatergic tonic drive to MNTB neurons, potentially modulating their temporal processing. image Key points MNTB receives a descending input from the ipsilateral auditory cortex via SLN. SLN neurons are highly excitable during development and into maturation, with a subset exhibiting spontaneous firing at resting membrane potential. Descending glutamatergic input to SLN is small and slow, and shows consistent temporal summation. Group I mGluRs further enhance spontaneous firing of SLN neurons and both mGluR1 and mGluR5 are expressed in the SLN. Descending ipsilateral projections to MNTB neurons primarily drive glutamatergic, non‐calyceal inputs.

Article.Title: Leg glucose uptake and substrate utilisation during time trial exercise: Effects of acute hypobaric hypoxia and biological sex
Article.Authors: Hansen A.; Martin‐Rincon M.; Rud B.; Egebjerg J.; Wüstner D.; Ørtenblad N.; Boushel R.; Holmberg H.; Calbet J.; Hallén J.; Nielsen J.; Skattebo Ø.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Hypoxia reduces exercise performance, yet it remains unclear how biological sex and altitude influence substrate utilisation during prolonged maximal exercise. Twenty‐two trained cyclists and triathletes (10 females) completed 30 min time trials (TTs) at low altitude (normoxia; ∼400 m) and moderate altitude (hypoxia; ∼2800 m in a hypobaric chamber) in counterbalanced order. Whole‐body metabolism was estimated from indirect calorimetry, whereas leg glucose uptake and substrate utilisation were derived from arterial and femoral venous blood samples and leg blood flow (thermodilution). Muscle biopsies were obtained from vastus lateralis to measure glycogen utilisation. Across altitudes, females displayed a higher fractional utilisation of during the TTs. TT performance was decreased in hypoxia, and the proportional decrease was smaller in females (−14%) than in males (−18%). Whole‐body substrate utilisation was similar between sexes in normoxia. However, males showed a large decrease in carbohydrate oxidation in hypoxia, whereas females displayed only a modest decrease. Males and females had similar leg metabolic responses to hypoxia: estimated glycogen oxidation decreased, with no change in absolute fat or blood glucose oxidation. However, across altitudes, females showed greater carbohydrate contributions, originating primarily from blood glucose rather than muscle glycogen. Estimates of fat contribution were uncertain but suggested a lower contribution in females than in males. In conclusion, females exercised at a higher relative intensity and derived relatively more energy from blood glucose. Males and females had similar leg metabolic responses to hypoxia, with the lower power output and metabolic rate in hypoxic TTs primarily regulated by reduced estimated glycogen oxidation. image Key points Substrate utilisation during exercise is affected by altitude, sex, training status, food intake and relative intensity. Whether sex‐ and altitude‐related differences in substrate utilisation persist during an ecologically valid maximal time trial in the fed state in trained males and females is unknown. Acute hypobaric hypoxia (∼2800 m) decreased 30 min time trial performance compared to normoxia (∼400 m) in both sexes, with a larger decrement in males. Females completed the time trials at a higher relative intensity than males in normoxia and hypoxia. Hypoxia reduced total metabolic rate primarily by decreasing estimated muscle glycogen oxidation, with no change in fat or blood glucose oxidation. The resulting changes in substrate partitioning were similar between sexes. Across altitudes, females derived relatively more energy from blood glucose despite similar muscle glycogen utilisation between sexes, whereas uncertain estimates suggested a lower contribution of fat in females than in males.

Article.Title: Adenosine‐driven P38 mitogen‐activated protein kinase and protein kinase A signalling constrains 5HT <scp>2a</scp> receptor‐induced phrenic motor facilitation
Article.Authors: Burrowes K.; Mitchell G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Episodic activation of spinal serotonin receptors elicits phrenic motor facilitation (pMF), a form of respiratory motor plasticity. Although 5‐HT 2 and 5‐HT 7 receptors elicit pMF, they do so via distinct cellular mechanisms known as the Q (5‐HT 2A/B ) and S (5‐HT 7 ) pathways. These pathways interact via mutual crosstalk inhibition; thus, concurrent activation of both serotonin receptor subtypes diminishes/abolishes pMF. Although episodic spinal adenosine 2A (A 2a ) receptor activation also elicits pMF via the S pathway, it remains unclear whether 5‐HT 2 and A 2a receptors interact via similar mechanisms. Although some molecules mediating crosstalk inhibition between 5‐HT 2 and 5‐HT 7 receptors have been identified, little is known concerning 5‐HT 2 and A 2a receptor interactions. Thus, we tested the hypotheses that: (1) concurrent 5‐HT 2 and A 2a receptor activation diminishes pMF via mutual crosstalk inhibition, and (2) A 2a receptors inhibit 5‐HT 2a ‐induced pMF via mechanisms that require p38 mitogen‐activated protein kinase (MAPK) and/or protein kinase A (PKA) enzymatic activity. Selective 5‐HT 2a and A 2a receptor agonists were delivered intrathecally at C4 (3, 6 µL injections, 5 min intervals) in urethane‐anaesthetized, ventilated, vagotomized and paralysed Sprague Dawley rats. Spinal 5‐HT 2a (73 ± 12%) or A 2a (90 ± 17%) receptor activation increased integrated phrenic burst amplitude (i.e. pMF). Concurrent receptor activation abolished pMF (15 ± 7.7%), demonstrating crosstalk inhibition. Spinal p38 MAP kinase or protein kinase A inhibition restored pMF, implicating both kinases as key mediators of crosstalk inhibition. Although the functional significance of these complex interactions is not yet fully understood, greater mechanistic understanding will accelerate progress towards optimizing the therapeutic efficacy of acute intermittent hypoxia‐induced respiratory motor plasticity. image Key points Concurrent 5‐HT 2a (Q pathway) and A 2a (S pathway) receptor activation cancels phrenic motor facilitation via mutual crosstalk inhibition. Spinal p38 MAPK or protein kinase A inhibition restores phrenic motor facilitation with concurrent Q and S pathway activation, demonstrating a key role for these kinases in crosstalk inhibition.

Article.Title: Distinct neural input strategies to motor units in the soleus and medial gastrocnemius during quiet standing
Article.Authors: Arakawa H.; Kaneko N.; Hakariya N.; Yokoyama H.; Nakazawa K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Standing posture control depends on the soleus (SOL) and medial gastrocnemius (MG), which serve distinct functional roles. Identifying neural mechanisms remains challenging because invasive techniques sample few motor units (MUs). High‐density surface electromyography (HDsEMG) enables MU analysis and estimation of common inputs to motoneurons. Leveraging this approach, and by comparing standing with an isometric voluntary contraction performed at an EMG level matched to standing, we aimed to elucidate standing‐specific common synaptic inputs underlying the distinct MU behaviors of the SOL and MG. We recorded HDsEMG and electroencephalographic signals from 20 males during standing and isometric contractions. EMG signals were decomposed into MU activity, with common inputs estimated through intramuscular and corticomuscular coherence (IMC and CMC). IMC was used as an index of common inputs to motoneurons, whereas CMC was used as an index of corticomuscular connectivity. During standing, the MG exhibited higher alpha‐ and beta‐band IMC than the SOL. Compared with isometric contraction, CMC decreased during standing in the delta‐, alpha‐ nd beta‐bands in both muscles, whereas beta‐band IMC remained unchanged only in the MG. These findings suggest that MG motoneurons receive more common synaptic input during standing than SOL motoneurons. Although CMC decreased similarly in both muscles, MG maintained higher IMC, suggesting a relatively greater role of non‐cortical common input in the MG. This pattern could reflect differences in the functional roles of the MG and SOL in postural control, with MG contributing to force adjustments that counteract body sway and SOL contributing to stable tonic force production. image Key points Using high‐density surface electromyography, we examined motor unit activity and neural inputs to medial gastrocnemius and soleus during standing. The medial gastrocnemius shows greater common synaptic input than the soleus, potentially associated with its role in phasic ankle plantarflexion torque generation to correct postural sway. The soleus exhibits lower motor unit synchrony, potentially associated with its role in generating stable and continuous ankle plantarflexion torque for body weight support. Corticomuscular coherence was lower during standing than during isometric voluntary contraction in both muscles, suggesting that functional corticomuscular coupling was similarly reduced in the medial gastrocnemius and soleus during standing. This study suggests differences in common synaptic input to soleus and medial gastrocnemius motoneurons, potentially associated with their distinct functional roles during standing.

Article.Title: Knockdown of mitotically associated long non‐coding RNA dysregulates endothelial functions, transcriptome and proteome
Article.Authors: Zhang S.; Zhou C.; Zheng J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Preeclampsia (PE) is a hypertensive disorder during pregnancy, which is characterized by a wide spectrum of endothelial dysfunction. However, the mechanisms underlying PE‐associated endothelial dysfunction remain poorly understood. Our previous RNA‐sequencing analysis showed that PE down‐regulated mitotically‐associated long non‐coding RNA (MANCR) in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). Herein, we tested the hypothesis that knockdown of MANCR dysregulates endothelial functions via disrupting the transcriptome and proteome using HUVECs as a cell model. Reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT‐qPCR) was conducted to confirm the down‐regulation of MANCR in PE‐HUVECs. MANCR was knocked down in HUVECs from normotensive pregnancy using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), followed by functional assays, RNA‐sequencing and proteomics. RT‐qPCR revealed that PE decreased MANCR in male and female HUVECs. Compared with scrambled ASOs, MANCR ASOs reduced MANCR by 71% and 74% in male and female HUVECs, respectively. Functionally, MANCR ASOs blocked fibroblast growth factor‐2 (FGF2)‐ and vascular endothelial growth factor‐A (VEGFA)‐stimulated cell proliferation, whereas they did not affect cell chemotaxis and tube formation in responses to FGF2 and VEGFA. MANCR ASOs dysregulated the expression of 37 and 39 genes as well as 97 and 15 proteins in male and female cells, respectively. Bioinformatics analysis predicted that MANCR‐regulated genes and proteins in male and female HUVECs were differently associated with diseases and biological functions, many of which are relevant to cell mitosis and hypertension. Thus, down‐regulation of MANCR impairs endothelial functions and causes sex‐specific disruption of transcriptome and proteome, possibly partially contributing to PE‐associated fetal endothelial dysfunction. image Key points Preeclampsia causes widespread endothelial dysfunction, but the roles of long non‐coding RNAs in endothelial cells remain poorly understood. Mitotically associated long non‐coding RNA (MANCR) is down‐regulated in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) obtained from preeclampsia. We provide the first evidence that down‐regulation of MANCR blocks endothelial cell proliferation stimulated by fibroblast growth factor 2 and vascular endothelial growth factor A. We also demonstrate that down‐regulation of MANCR disrupts transcriptome and proteome as well as pathways associated with cell division, cardiovascular disease‐related processes and immune responses. These findings identify MANCR as a previously unrecognized regulator of endothelial cell function.

Article.Title: Acute mechanical stretch enhances β‐adrenergic–protein kinase A signalling and increases susceptibility to ventricular arrhythmias
Article.Authors: Wang H.; Lai E.; Hua Z.; Liu C.; Sherstnev I.; Fu J.; Ng F.; Gorelik J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mechanical stretch can increase ventricular arrhythmia susceptibility during sympathetic activation, but the mechanisms linking stretch to altered β‐adrenergic receptor (βAR) signalling, Ca 2 + handling and electrical instability remain unclear. We tested whether left ventricular (LV) stretch alters Cav3‐associated membrane organisation and enhances βAR–protein kinase A (PKA)‐dependent arrhythmogenic signalling. Langendorff‐perfused male rat hearts were studied using a fluid‐filled LV balloon, with sham hearts fitted with an unstretched balloon. Optical mapping during S1–S2 programmed stimulation showed that LV stretch had limited effects at baseline but altered the response to βAR stimulation, increasing ventricular arrhythmia severity, prolonging APD50, reducing local conduction velocity and steepening APD80 restitution. H89 markedly reduced βAR stimulation‐induced arrhythmia severity in stretched hearts, whereas KN93 did not provide comparable protection. LV stretch also increased cardiomyocyte length and altered Cav3 organisation at wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)‐defined membrane regions. In isolated LV cardiomyocytes, hypoosmotic membrane deformation did not alter basal caffeine‐induced Ca 2 + release but enhanced isoprenaline‐induced irregular activity and Ca 2 + ‐transient amplitude, both of which were attenuated by PKA inhibition. Hypoosmotic membrane deformation also amplified isoprenaline‐evoked PKA activity and increased RyR2 Ser2030 phosphorylation. These findings indicate that LV mechanical stretch alters the ventricular βAR response in association with altered Cav3‐associated membrane organisation and enhanced βAR–PKA‐dependent Ca 2 + instability. image Key points Left ventricular (LV) balloon stretch has limited baseline electrophysiological effects but increases arrhythmia severity, slows conduction and steepens APD80 restitution during β‐adrenergic stimulation. LV balloon stretch is associated with cardiomyocyte elongation and altered Cav3 enrichment at wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)‐defined membrane regions. Hypoosmotic membrane deformation enhances isoprenaline‐induced irregular activity and Ca 2 + ‐transient amplitude without increasing basal caffeine‐induced Ca 2 + release. PKA inhibition reduces stretch‐enhanced irregular activity in isolated ventricular myocytes and β‐adrenergic receptor (βAR)‐induced arrhythmia severity in stretched hearts. Hypoosmotic membrane deformation enhances isoprenaline‐evoked PKA activity and increases RyR2 Ser2030 phosphorylation.

Article.Title: Neonatal stress is associated with region‐specific changes in mitochondrial respiration and sex‐dependent respiratory instability in adulthood
Article.Authors: Vallejo Puerta A.; Sanchez L.; Aliaga‐Raduan F.; Iturri‐Soliz P.; Kinkead R.; Bairam A.; Schneider Gasser E.; Soliz J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Early‐life stress is increasingly recognized as a critical determinant of brain development, yet its long‐term impact on the neural control of breathing remains poorly defined. Here we show that neonatal maternal separation (NMS, P3–P12) induces long‐term alterations in respiratory stability and mitochondrial function within respiratory circuits. In adulthood, NMS altered respiratory stability, with significant treatment × sex interactions for total and postsigh apnoeas; post hoc comparisons showed increased frequencies of these apnoeic events in males. Sigh frequency also showed a significant main effect of treatment. Region‐specific high‐resolution respirometry showed that NMS was associated with reduced mitochondrial respiration in the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH) and increased mitochondrial respiration in the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) and ventral respiratory column (VRC), without significant treatment × sex interactions. Normalization to cytochrome c oxidase (COX) activity largely eliminated these differences, suggesting that changes in absolute respiration are consistent with a contribution of differences in mitochondrial content rather than major alterations in respiratory capacity relative to mitochondrial abundance. In the pre‐Bötzinger complex, absolute mitochondrial respiration was preserved, whereas oxygen consumption rate (OCR)/COX ratios revealed treatment‐dependent alterations in mitochondrial respiratory flux relative to mitochondrial content. NMS also altered the expression of selected genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, mitophagy, fusion and fission in the NTS and VRC, with significant main effects of treatment and sex but no treatment × sex interactions. Oxidative and inflammatory markers were largely preserved, although selective effects of sex and treatment were detected. Together, these findings demonstrate that neonatal stress produces persistent, region‐specific remodelling of mitochondrial and molecular pathways within respiratory circuits, accompanied by sex‐dependent vulnerability to respiratory instability. image Key points Early‐life stress induces a persistent, sex‐dependent disruption of respiratory control, increasing apnoeas in adult males, whereas females remain comparatively resistant. This phenotype is associated with region‐specific remodelling of mitochondrial function along the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH)–brainstem axis, characterized by reduced hypothalamic respiration and increased brainstem mitochondrial respiration after neonatal stress. Neonatal stress alters transcriptional pathways involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, mitophagy and dynamics within respiratory brainstem regions, revealing persistent molecular remodelling associated with early‐life adversity.

Article.Title: Combined time‐restricted feeding and resistance training enhance tirzepatide‐induced improvements in adiposity and whole‐body insulin sensitivity in female mice
Article.Authors: Macêdo A.; da Conceição de Mattis L.; de Lima R.; Barbosa L.; Pinotti C.; Brisque G.; Dias L.; Pitoli B.; Avelino A.; Antonio G.; Muñoz V.; Antunes G.; Figueiredo L.; Cintra D.; da Silva A.; Ropelle E.; Pauli J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Tirzepatide is a dual agonist of glucose‐dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon‐like peptide‐1 (GLP‐1) receptors with potent effects on body weight regulation, glucose homeostasis and metabolic health. However, its interaction with dietary and exercise interventions as well as its impact on obesity and hepatic metabolic pathways, particularly in females, remain unclear. Here, we tested whether tirzepatide, alone or combined with time‐restricted feeding (TRF) or resistance training, modulates energy balance, strength performance, adipose tissue remodelling, insulin sensitivity and hepatic lipid accumulation in female mice. Female Swiss mice after 10 weeks of obesity induction were treated with tirzepatide, TRF or resistance training for 8 weeks. Tirzepatide was administered subcutaneously using a dose‐escalation protocol. TRF consisted of a 12 h feeding window, and resistance training was performed as stair climbing on alternating days. Body weight, caloric intake and feed efficiency were monitored longitudinally. Glucose homeostasis was assessed by intraperitoneal glucose and insulin tolerance tests. Adipose depots, skeletal muscle and liver mass were quantified, and hepatic lipid accumulation was evaluated by histology and RT‐qPCR of lipogenic metabolism genes. Tirzepatide reduced body weight gain and feed efficiency, consistent with a negative energy balance. When combined with TRF and resistance training, tirzepatide accelerated weight loss, and the addition of resistance training further enhanced this effect, bringing body weight close to control levels. These effects were associated with reduced adipose mass and adipocyte hypertrophy, indicating improved adipose tissue remodelling. Resistance training improved strength performance and increased skeletal muscle mass. Tirzepatide combined with TRF, with or without resistance training, improved glucose tolerance in female mice. All interventions reduced hepatic lipid accumulation. Collectively, tirzepatide, particularly in combination with TRF and resistance training, exerts enhanced metabolic benefits on obesity, insulin sensitivity and metabolic regulation in female mice. image Key points Tirzepatide combined with time‐restricted feeding and resistance training produced greater reductions in body weight and adiposity in obese female mice. Combined interventions improved whole‐body insulin sensitivity more effectively than isolated strategies. Resistance training preserved skeletal muscle mass during tirzepatide‐induced weight loss. All interventions similarly reduced hepatic lipid accumulation and lipogenic gene expression. Tirzepatide‐based therapies enhanced systemic metabolic health without additional hepatic benefits from combined interventions.

Article.Title: Electrophysiological properties of mesodiencephalic junction neurons projecting to the inferior olive
Article.Authors: Voerman S.; Wang X.; Wang X.; Bosman L.; Broersen R.; De Zeeuw C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The neocortex has the largest volume, whereas the cerebellum houses the most neurons of the mammalian brain, underscoring paramount functions for interactions between them. Neocortical projections to the cerebellum involve both the mossy fibre and climbing fibre systems; mossy fibres find their origin predominantly in the pons, whereas the climbing fibres are relayed via subnuclei of the inferior olive (IO) that receive cortical input via the mesodiencephalic junction (MDJ). Given that climbing fibres regulate cerebellar plasticity in a timing‐dependent manner, the MDJ–IO pathway probably contributes to both sensorimotor and cognitive learning. However, the physiological properties of IO‐projecting MDJ neurons remain largely unknown. Here, we made targeted whole‐cell recordings in brain slices of the mouse MDJ, separating IO‐ from non‐IO‐projecting neurons following retrograde tracing. We show that IO‐projecting neurons are, unlike non‐IO‐projecting neurons, highly spontaneously active and capable of high‐frequency bursts of ≤350 Hz during current injections. Optogenetic stimulation shows that excitatory neocortical inputs to IO‐projecting MDJ neurons can be integrated directly with excitatory inputs from the cerebellar nuclei. Moreover, unlike non‐IO‐projecting neurons, IO‐projecting MDJ neurons depolarize and repolarize quickly, and hyperpolarizing inputs consistently trigger rebound action potentials upon stimulus offset. This hyperpolarization is probably induced predominantly by inhibitory inputs from the ventral tegmental area and periaqueductal grey, which provide prominent bilateral inputs to MDJ neurons, as revealed by viral tracing in Gad2‐Cre mice. Our results highlight how neocortical inputs to the MDJ can be transformed into diverse IO firing patterns and thereby contribute to the required specifics of cerebellar learning. image Key points The mesodiencephalic junction is an important brainstem region connecting the cerebral cortex with the cerebellum through its projection to the inferior olive, the sole source of the climbing fibres that drive cerebellar learning. We find that mesodiencephalic junction neurons projecting to the inferior olive represent a population of physiologically distinct neurons, capable of high firing frequencies and rebound activity following hyperpolarization. We reveal that mesodiencephalic junction neurons receive prominent excitatory inputs from neocortex and cerebellar nuclei, whereas their main inhibitory inputs are derived from the ventral tegmental area and periaqueductal grey. These findings shed light on how the activity of neurons in the mesodiencephalic junction can be regulated and how these neurons might influence activity in the inferior olive, and thereby cerebellar learning.

Article.Title: Conservation of a synaptic blueprint across the animal kingdom
Article.Authors: Houcek A.; Kavalali E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chemical synapses are fundamental computational units of the nervous system that enable rapid and precise information transfer through the nanoscale organization of presynaptic and postsynaptic components. Despite hundreds of millions of years of animal evolution and extraordinary diversity in nervous system architectures, the core physiological principles of chemical synaptic transmission remain remarkably conserved. Studies across Drosophila melanogaster , zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans , frogs and mammals reveal recurring principles governing active‐zone organization, synaptic vesicle exocytosis, calcium signalling and postsynaptic specialization. Here, we examine the evolution of chemical synapses across the animal kingdom, focusing on the relationship between molecular diversification, nanoscale organization and functional conservation. We propose that the evolutionary stability of synapses reflects, in part, a stringent biophysical constraint imposed by the requirements for rapid chemical communication. We further consider how these conserved synaptic operations are assembled into neural circuits of dramatically different complexities, as well as the ctenophore nervous system as a critical test case for distinguishing molecular conservation from architectural and functional convergence. Across species, the emerging picture is that evolution has adhered to conserving the geometry and organizational principles of chemical synapses more stringently than a precise molecular composition. Synapses thus represent stable yet adaptable information‐processing architectures in which conserved nanoscale constraints coexist with molecular flexibility and extensive diversification of neural circuits. image

Article.Title: Postnatal development of inhibition associated with entorhinal cortex input to the CA1 hippocampus
Article.Authors: Vazetdinova A.; Khalilov I.; Gainutdinov A.; Vinokurova D.; Shipkov D.; Kurmashova E.; Nasretdinov A.; Valeeva G.; Khazipov R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract During early development, temporoammonic (TA) input from the entorhinal cortex provides major excitatory drive to the CA1 hippocampus, yet whether this excitation is balanced by feedforward inhibition remains unclear. Using whole‐cell recordings from CA1 pyramidal cells (PCs) in intact hippocampi, we found that TA stimulation reliably evoked monosynaptic excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) from birth, whereas inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) were frequently absent or severely delayed during the first postnatal week. The delay between evoked EPSCs and IPSCs shortened with age, narrowing the temporal integration window. Similar dynamics occurred during early sharp waves in vivo , where IPSC bursts followed EPSC bursts by tens of milliseconds, with this delay decreasing over development. Using paired recordings from fast‐spiking interneurons (FS‐INs) and PCs, we identified two mechanisms underlying delayed feedforward inhibition during the first postnatal week: (i) low FS‐IN→PC connectivity, and (ii) a weak monosynaptic entorhinal cortex (EC) drive to FS‐INs. By the end of the second week, EC inputs to FS‐INs surpassed those to PCs. Together, these findings reveal that feedforward inhibition in the EC–CA1 circuit is delayed, creating a broad temporal window for synaptic integration during the neonatal period. We propose that this extended window supports global bursting, with progressive inhibition maturation contributing to the switch toward sparse coding. image Key points Feedforward inhibition upon entorhinal input is developmentally delayed, creating a broad temporal integration window in the neonatal CA1 hippocampus. Weak entorhinal drive to CA1 fast‐spiking interneurons is the primary cause of delayed feedforward inhibition in neonates. Delayed inhibition is a consistent feature of CA1 early sharp waves in vivo . Maturation of feedforward inhibition may drive the switch from global ‘bursting’ to sparse coding.

Article.Title: TRPM8 and TRPM2 ion channels determine sex differences in thermal preference in mice
Article.Authors: Vilar B.; McNaughton P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Several ion channels belonging to the large TRP family are activated either by increases or decreases in temperature, but it is unclear which of these potential thermosensors actually determine the sensation of temperature in the non‐noxious thermal range, from approximately 20°C to approximately 40°C. Here we show that below 33°C, male cool preference is determined by TRPM8, whereas warm preference is mainly influenced by TRPM2. Female thermal preference is shifted to warmer temperatures by around 4°C when compared to males, consistent with warm shifts in the female activation ranges of both TRPM8 and TRPM2. Removal of testosterone causes a shift in male thermal preference towards female preference; conversely, female thermal preference is shifted towards male by injection of testosterone. Removing or injecting female hormones had no effect on thermal preference. We conclude that TRPM8 and TRPM2 are the main thermal detectors in the non‐noxious range, and that testosterone is an important determinant of the difference in preference between males and females. image Key points In many mammals, including humans, females show a preference for warmer temperatures than males. Deletion of the trpm2 gene, coding for the warmth sensor TRPM2 in male mice shifted preference to warmer temperatures, showing that TRPM2 repels males from warm temperatures. Deletion or block of the cool sensor trpm8 in both males and females shifted preference to cooler temperatures, showing that TRPM8 repels mice from cooler temperatures. Deletion or block of trpv1 had no effect on non‐noxious thermal preference. The results can be explained by a warm shift in females of activation ranges of both TRPM8 and TRPM2 when compared to males. Reducing testosterone in males caused a shift towards the female warm preference. Administering testosterone to females caused a shift towards the male cool preference. Female sex hormones had no effect. We conclude that TRPM8 and TRPM2 determine non‐noxious thermal preference. Testosterone is an important determinant of the differences in thermal preference between males and females.

Article.Title: Bacteroidota‐derived glycine lipids differentially regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation during Western diet feeding in male Ldlr −/− mice
Article.Authors: Kim S.; Noh S.; Ji M.; Vence T.; Gao L.; Otoko O.; Nichols F.; Blesso C.; Kwon O.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Western diet (WD) is associated with skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism, redox imbalance and inflammation. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiome‐derived metabolites contribute to host metabolic regulation, yet the role of Bacteroidota‐derived glycine lipids in skeletal muscle remains unknown. This study tested whether two structurally related bacterial glycine lipids, lipid 654 (L654) and lipid 1256 (L1256), regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial remodelling in WD‐fed Ldlr −/− mice. Male Ldlr −/− mice were fed a normal chow or WD and administered L654, L1256 or vehicle control for 8 weeks. Skeletal muscle glycine lipid accumulation, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial biogenesis markers, mitophagy‐associated signalling, inflammatory and antioxidant proteins and muscle fibre cross‐sectional area were assessed. L1256, but not L654, accumulated in skeletal muscle. Functionally, L1256 selectively enhanced fatty acid‐supported mitochondrial respiration and increased respiratory control ratio. L1256 also increased peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator 1‐alpha (PGC‐1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and electron transport chain complexes IV and V, suggesting enhanced oxidative mitochondrial remodelling. In parallel, L1256 altered markers associated with mitochondrial quality control signalling, increased nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), suppressed nuclear factor kappa‐light‐chain‐enhancer of activated B cells (NF‐κB) signalling and preserved muscle fibre cross‐sectional area. L654 upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis transcripts without altering protein abundance. These findings identify L1256 as a microbiome‐derived lipid retained within skeletal muscle that enhanced oxidative metabolism and preserved mitochondrial quality signalling under metabolic stress. The data suggest that tissue retention of bacterial lipids may be an important determinant of skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation. image Key points Western diet contributes to skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism and chronic inflammation. Microbiome‐derived glycine lipids are bioactive molecules from Bacteroidota species, but their effects on skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism remain poorly understood. Bacteroidota‐derived glycine lipids produce distinct skeletal muscle responses in Western diet‐fed Ldlr − / − mice, where lipid 1256 accumulated in skeletal muscle and enhanced fatty acid‐supported respiration, whereas lipid 654 primarily induced transcriptional responses without detectable tissue accumulation. Lipid 1256 increased peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator 1‐alpha (PGC‐1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and complexes IV and V of the electron transport chain together with restoration of Parkin, nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) while reducing nuclear factor kappa‐light‐chain‐enhancer of activated B cells (NF‐κB) and interleukin 6 (IL‐6) expression and preserving skeletal muscle cross‐sectional area. These findings suggest that gut microbiome‐derived glycine lipids are regulators of skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism, and that tissue retention of bacterial lipids influences mitochondrial oxidative remodelling during metabolic stress.

Article.Title: Breathing‐evoked potentials in humans during wakefulness and sleep
Article.Authors: Grassion L.; Andrillon T.; Niérat M.; Wattiez N.; Patout M.; Njlagni Voutsa J.; Oudiette D.; Arnulf I.; Gonzalez‐Bermejo J.; Similowski T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Breathing modulates cortical activities and cognitive functions, but the neurophysiological basis of the brain–breathing relationship is incompletely understood. We aimed to determine whether breathing at rest evokes scalp EEG‐detectable potentials (as inspiratory occlusions do in the respiratory‐related evoked potential model), whether these signatures persist during sleep and whether they are linked to sleep‐organizing processes. We examined recordings from 729 participants in the Cleveland Family Study to identify cortical activity time‐locked to inspiration during wakefulness and sleep, with a median of 7871 respiratory cycles analysed per participant. Breathing‐related cortical responses were assessed in the time and frequency domains. Quiet breathing evoked a reproducible sequence of cortical potentials during wakefulness, including a pre‐inspiratory component ∼300 ms before inspiration and several post‐inspiratory peaks ≤3 s after. These responses persisted during non‐rapid eye movement stages 2 and 3 (N2 and N3) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, in which they showed simplified morphology resembling K‐complexes and co‐occurred with increased spindle‐range activity. The pattern was present irrespective of body mass index and was qualitatively unchanged in the 203 participants free of sleep‐disordered breathing, arguing against obesity or sleep apnoea as its origin. Scalp EEG can detect breathing‐evoked potentials during quiet breathing in awake humans. These potentials persist during sleep with a morphology that resembles cortical activities previously associated with sleep stabilization. Further studies are needed to determine the physiological and clinical significance of these observations in health and disease. image Key points Spontaneous breathing at rest evokes reproducible breathing‐related cortical potentials detectable with scalp EEG. These potentials persist during sleep. They are associated with time‐locked modulation of cortical oscillatory activity.

Article.Title: Making sense of touch: Spatial tactile cues promote efficient visuo‐somatosensory integration and restore motor accuracy under sensory conflict
Article.Authors: Vlachou M.; Lafaverges E.; Mouchnino L.; Blouin J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Effective interaction with complex environments relies on the integration of somatosensory and visual signals into coherent spatial representations of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, as during goal‐directed hand movements under mirror‐reversed visual feedback, motor performance deteriorates. Despite this conflict, the visual mapping between the hand and the environment remains preserved, and visual information typically facilitates motor performance, whereas tactile feedback impairs it. Here, we tested whether providing tactile input with explicit spatial structure renders visuo‐somatosensory integration functionally relevant and stabilizes motor behaviour under sensory conflict. Healthy adults performed a mirror‐tracing task, tracing a shape's contour with the index finger while tactile feedback conveyed either motion‐related cues alone or additional discrete spatial landmarks aligned with the outline. Spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness relative to motion‐related tactile input, indicating more effective online motor control. EEG source analyses further revealed that, when spatial tactile cues were present, somatosensory activity increased and functional connectivity was largely restricted to sensorimotor areas. In contrast, when tactile cues did not convey spatial information, sensory conflict was associated with widespread reductions in cortical activity, including in somatosensory and parietal areas, and with a diffuse functional connectivity pattern consistent with elevated sensorimotor uncertainty. Together, these findings indicate that providing spatial structure to tactile input can mitigate the detrimental effects of visuo‐somatosensory conflict on motor performance and support more efficient integration of visual and somatosensory information during action. image Key points Accurate movements depend on combining visual and somatosensory information to estimate the position of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, motor performance usually deteriorates and tactile feedback can become disruptive. We tested whether tactile feedback becomes useful for movement control when it provides explicit spatial landmarks, rather than only motion‐related information from finger–surface contact. During a tracing task under visuo‐somatosensory conflict, spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness compared with when touch conveyed motion cues alone. Spatial tactile cues were associated with increased somatosensory cortical activity and a more spatially restricted pattern of functional coupling within sensorimotor networks, whereas their absence was associated with reduced somatosensory and parietal activity and a more distributed connectivity profile. Spatial structure in touch promotes multisensory integration, helping stabilize motor control under sensory conflict and highlighting how tactile cue design may improve sensorimotor function.
