Article.Title: Macaque Area LIP Reflects Confidence-Dependent Changes in Decision Policy
Article.Authors: Tu M.; Vivar-Lazo M.; Fetsch C.
Article.Abstract: The process of forming a decision gives rise to an estimate of its quality or likelihood of success. This graded sense of confidence is important for guiding subsequent decisions, but a neural mechanism linking subjective confidence to formation of the next decision has not been identified. We trained two male rhesus macaques to report a perceptual choice and simultaneous confidence judgment in a reaction-time (RT) motion discrimination task. Monkeys were more likely to repeat a rewarded choice when they reported low confidence on the previous trial, and showed greater changes in RT after a surprising outcome (low-confidence correct or high-confidence error). Neural activity in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) encoded the previous trial's choice and confidence more strongly after a low-confidence correct trial, and the strength of history encoding was correlated with a trial-by-trial estimate of choice bias. Ramping dynamics of the decoded decision variable also depended systematically on the conjunction of confidence and reward on the previous trial, in a manner that reflected individual differences between animals. The findings suggest that LIP not only reflects the formation of the current decision but could participate in confidence-guided learning via adjustments of the subsequent decision process. Significance statement Decision confidence is of primary interest in the study of metacognition, yet it also plays a key role in learning, serving as a graded prediction of accuracy that modulates the response to feedback. Reanalyzing data from nonhuman primates performing a reaction-time (RT) motion discrimination task with explicit confidence reports, we found that adjustments of choice bias and RT were gated by the animal’s self-reported confidence on the previous trial. The interaction of confidence and outcome (reward or punishment) was reflected in the activity of parietal (LIP) neurons on the subsequent trial, in ways largely consistent with the behavioral effects. The results and accompanying computational model suggest plausible functional links between the neuronal substrates of perceptual decision making and reinforcement learning.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: lateral intraparietal area; choice bias; perceptual decision making; decision confidence; motion discrimination; rhesus monkeys; metacognition; reinforcement learning; individual differences; reaction time

Article.Title: PTPRO restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors through TrkB dephosphorylation
Article.Authors: Li J.; Yasumura M.; Iguchi T.; Taniguchi M.; Oka Y.; Tsai C.; Sato M.
Article.Abstract: The structural complexity of axon collateral terminal arbors shapes synaptic connectivity. In corticospinal projections, individual axon collaterals exhibit distinct patterns of terminal arborization, ranging from sparse local branches to dense, highly complex arbors in target regions such as the pontine nuclei. How this complexity is controlled remains poorly understood. Here, using corticopontine projections in male and female mice, we show that protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) selectively restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors in the pontine nuclei without affecting collateral number. This function requires the intracellular phosphatase domain of PTPRO but not its extracellular region. We demonstrate that PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), and that the excessive terminal arborization caused by acute PTPRO loss is rescued by TrkB depletion or phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibition. Together, these findings reveal that PTPRO-mediated TrkB dephosphorylation acts as a molecular brake on corticopontine terminal arbor elaboration. Significance Statement How individual axons regulate terminal branching within target regions is a fundamental question in neural circuit development. This study identifies protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO), a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase that negatively regulates signaling through tyrosine phosphorylation, as a selective regulator of higher-order branching in corticopontine terminal arbors. PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a neurotrophin receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes neuronal growth and branching, thereby restricting terminal arbor complexity without affecting collateral number from the main axon. Given that terminal arbor architecture determines the synaptic territory of each cortical input, PTPRO-dependent constraint on arbor elaboration may represent a general principle by which projection-specific arbor complexity is established across long-range circuits in the central nervous system.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: PTPRO; corticopontine projections; pontine nuclei; PI3K inhibition; protein tyrosine phosphatase; synaptic connectivity

Article.Title: State-Dependent Modulation of Corticospinal and Cortical Responses by Closed-Loop Paired-pulse TMS
Article.Authors: Choi D.; Güth M.; Ma M.; Harmon M.; Wischnewski M.; Park J.; Blenker A.; Lee S.; Opitz A.
Article.Abstract: Brain oscillations shape cortical excitability in a phase-dependent manner. Cortical excitability reflects the net output of intracortical circuits, including inhibitory and facilitatory pathways. However, whether the phase of ongoing brain rhythms differentially modulates inhibitory and facilitatory responses remains unknown. Paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (ppTMS) can selectively engage these circuits, providing a unique tool to dissociate their contributions. We combined real-time EEG-guided closed-loop TMS with single- and paired-pulse TMS in 24 healthy adults (13 female) to probe how sensorimotor mu (8–13 Hz) and beta (14–30 Hz) oscillatory phase shapes responses associated with intracortical inhibitory and facilitatory processes. Single-pulse TMS (spTMS), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) were delivered at four phases (peak, falling, trough, rising). Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) and TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs) were recorded to assess corticospinal and cortical responses, respectively. We found that MEP amplitude was phase-dependent across all three stimulation types, with spTMS-evoked and ICF-conditioned MEPs showing the largest amplitudes at the rising phase, whereas SICI-conditioned MEPs were largest at the peak phase of the mu oscillation. TEP P60-N100 amplitude was modulated by oscillatory phase across all stimulation types, with maximal responses at the trough phase. SICI showed opposing phase patterns between the two measures, revealing a dissociation between cortical and corticospinal responses. MEP and TEP preferred phases were correlated across participants only in the ICF condition. These findings extend phase-dependent spTMS effects to paired-pulse stimulation and show that ongoing mu phase differentially shapes responses to SICI and ICF across cortical and corticospinal levels. Significance Statement Ongoing brain oscillations are known to shape cortical excitability across their phase cycle. However, whether this effect differentially influences inhibitory and facilitatory responses has remained unresolved. Here, using closed-loop EEG-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation in healthy adults, we probed how SICI- and ICF-conditioned responses vary across different phases of the sensorimotor mu and beta rhythms. We show that corticospinal and cortical responses to inhibitory and facilitatory paired-pulse protocols exhibit distinct phase-dependent patterns in the sensorimotor mu rhythm. These findings extend phase-dependent stimulation effects beyond single-pulse TMS and reveal that the relationship between cortical state and stimulation response differs across paired-pulse protocols.

Article.Title: Area MT carries acceleration information in a quickly and directly decodable representation
Article.Authors: Chen P.; Huk A.
Article.Abstract: We sought to better understand the neural representation of visual motion acceleration. A straightforward estimation of acceleration would involve calculating the rate of change of velocity, which itself would be calculated from change in position over time. As it is well-established that neurons in area MT encode velocity, the brain could thus indirectly estimate acceleration by calculating the change in MT’s velocity representations. An alternative mechanism, however, could operate more rapidly and directly. In this case, the brain could exploit interactions between MT’s standard motion encoding and idiosyncratic temporal dynamics of neural responses. Such direct decoding would thus exploit nonlinearities usually ignored in studies of MT coding. We tested between these two theories by measuring from ensembles of MT neurons while two male awake fixating macaques viewed linearly accelerating motion stimuli. Direct decoding of acceleration from MT was possible on faster time scales, and could be done with higher fidelity, than indirect decoding. Distinct motion acceleration information could thus be efficiently read out from rich and heterogeneous MT ensemble responses, regardless of the mechanisms that give rise to various forms of motion tuning that it exhibits. A similar analysis of activity in the medial superior temporal area (MST) did not suggest that this later stage of motion processing has a more refined acceleration representation. Together, these results suggest that the brain may opportunistically exploit nonlinear idiosyncrasies of neural responses to efficiently extract behaviorally relevant information on fast time scales, instead of performing explicit calculation of certain variables. Significance Statement This study aims to understand if linear acceleration information of visual motion is extracted and represented in primate visual motion areas MT and MST. By combining large-scale multi-area neuronal recordings, population-level analyses, and a rich set of moving stimuli, we show that linear acceleration can be decoded from MT activity. Specifically, our results demonstrate that (1) motion acceleration is encoded in MT, and can be directly and quickly decoded from MT ensemble activity, and (2) area MST, despite being a later stage of motion processing, does not refine acceleration representations. These findings call for revisiting how brain areas might efficiently extract behaviorally relevant information from the environment and highlight the importance of temporal dynamics in visual motion processing.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: temporal dynamics of neural activity; area MT; macaque visual cortex

Article.Title: Punishment Enhances Reward Learning through Striatal Prediction Errors
Article.Authors: Blades R.
Article.Abstract: A gazelle cautiously approaches a watering hole, eyeing its surroundings for predators. It is driven by two simultaneous needs: to drink water and to avoid danger. Its survival depends on balancing these opposing forces: approach motivation, which drives reward seeking, and avoidance motivation, which drives evasion of punishment. Reinforcement learning is the process by which animals learn to make decisions through trial and error using rewards and punishments as feedback. Over time, animals learn to select actions that maximize rewards and minimize punishments. Behaviors followed by rewarding outcomes become more likely to be repeated due to approach motivation, whereas behaviors followed by negative outcomes become less likely to occur through avoidance motivation. These dynamics play out continually in day-to-day life as all animals, including humans, learn from these trade-offs. Although rewards and punishments frequently co-occur in real-world environments, little research has investigated how receiving a mix of rewards and punishments influences learning processes. Reinforcement learning paradigms often study them separately, creating siloed research domains that mirror the classic “carrot and stick” metaphor in which rewards and punishments are treated as independent tools for shaping behavior. However, behavioral evidence suggests that they are not discrete learning processes; for example, conditioned suppression studies show that cues signaling a potential punishment can disrupt approach behavior directed toward rewards (Allcoat et al., 2015). This finding demonstrates that reward and punishment systems dynamically interact rather than operate in isolation. One possibility is that experiences of reward and punishment influence each other, because reinforcement learning shares a neural substrate: dopamine. Dopaminergic neurons calculate prediction errors: the difference between what was expected and what actually occurred. Better-than-expected outcomes produce positive prediction errors through increased firing of dopaminergic neurons, whereas worse-than-expected outcomes produce negative prediction errors through reduced dopamine release. Article.Title: Learning from Error Predictions Rather Than Prediction Errors: A Perspective on Self-Supervised Learning in the Brain
Article.Authors: Meirhaeghe N.
Article.Abstract: Humans learn by doing and observing but also by imagining the result of simulated actions in their mind. When learning from executed or observed actions, traditional theories posit that behavior improves by minimizing the difference between (1) the perceived outcome derived from sensory feedback and (2) the desired outcome (performance error) or the outcome predicted by an internal model (prediction error, PE). Supporting these theories, decades of electrophysiological studies have documented the role of the dopaminergic system and cerebellum in generating activity patterns compatible with the hypothesized error signals. In comparison, our understanding of the neural basis underlying the ability to learn from simulated actions is far more limited. Here, I argue that this form of self-supervised learning is best described in terms of a quantity known as the predicted performance error (PPE), theorized more than 30 years ago and yet largely overlooked ever since. Complementary to PEs, PPEs reflect error predictions between predicted and desired outcomes. Unlike PEs, however, PPEs exist even in the absence of sensory feedback and can in principle serve to evaluate actions without executing them, based on an efference copy of the underlying motor plan. I review evidence supporting the computation of PPEs in the brain and propose a network implementation based on a corticobasal ganglia loop interacting at multiple timescales with prefrontal, parietal, and hippocampal areas. I then connect PPEs to recent discoveries on motor planning and formulate novel predictions linking PPEs to various high-level brain functions such as metacognition, problem-solving, and deception.

Article.Title: Object detection through dynamic motor-sensory convergence in freely moving rats
Article.Authors: Nelinger G.; Saraf-Sinik I.; Ahissar E.
Article.Abstract: To detect objects in natural environments, animals must coordinate movement and sensation. This process unfolds dynamically, as perceivers actively shape sensory input through ongoing motor actions in a closed loop. In this study, we use precise tracking of behavioral kinematics to investigate the initial phase of object interaction, asking: what motor-sensory strategies support object detection during natural approach? Using high-speed videography and advanced tracking tools, we tracked whisker and head dynamics as male rats approached and contacted objects. We found that whisker-object interactions converged toward a distinct ratio between changes in whisker angle and curvature, denoted $\alpha ^\ast $ . In a motor-sensory phase plane this ratio appears as a line, reflecting a regime in which small motor adjustments produce large curvature changes during contact. This motor-sensory ratio cannot stabilize during free-air whisking and thus can serve as a signature for object presence. Rats gradually converged toward this object-dependent mechanical signature across contacts, and proximity to $\alpha ^\ast $ predicted subsequent head movements and the termination of object approach. Convergence to $\alpha ^\ast $ was invariant to object shape and texture and to whisker’s length. Moreover, touch-induced pumps both signaled and reinforced convergence. The results suggest that rats use successful convergence to this object-dependent motor-sensory contingency as a signature of object presence. Object detection thus emerges as a closed-loop dynamical process in which action, mechanics, and sensation jointly shape perceptual inference. Significance Statement How does a rat know it is touching an object with its moving whiskers? We trained freely moving rats to discriminate objects while tracking whisker kinematics at high resolution. We found that the detection phase involved whisker-object interactions that converged toward a distinct ratio between changes in whisker angle and curvature. This ratio can arise mechanically only when whiskers contact an external object, making its attainment a reliable indication of object presence. During object approach, rats steered their exploratory movements to seek this motor-sensory contingency, marking the transition to focused exploration or disengagement. These findings reveal a dynamical, closed-loop mechanism for object detection in freely moving rats.

Article.Title: Neurocognitive characteristics of perceptual feedback processing differ in autism
Article.Authors: Zuk N.; Slobodskoy-Plusnin J.; Weiss Y.; Sampath V.; Düsterwald K.; Akrami A.; Ahissar M.
Article.Abstract: Autistic individuals often show reduced adaptation to changing environmental demands, but the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this difference remain unclear. We asked whether it may be explained by reduced sensitivity to external feedback and changes in task difficulty. Autistic and non-autistic adults of either sex, matched for cognitive ability, performed a pitch discrimination task in which their response was immediately followed by feedback. Accuracy was similar between the two groups, yet autistic participants exhibited a markedly reduced feedback-related negativity (FRN), an event-related EEG potential differentiating explicit negative versus positive feedback. They also showed weaker modulation of feedback-evoked EEG responses by perceptual difficulty. Lastly, they showed reduced trial-by-trial behavioral updating of perceptual bias following recent correct and easy trials. These effects were replicated in a follow-up experiment conducted 1–2 years later. When combined they classified autistic and non-autistic participants with about 80% accuracy. Together, our findings indicate that multiple processes for evaluating perceptual decisions and adjusting subsequent behavior differ in autism and likely contribute to slow updating in changing contexts. Significance Statement Autism is associated with reduced adaptation to changing environments in both behavior and neural signals, but the underlying neurocognitive mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that autistic individuals exhibit a reduced feedback-related negativity (FRN), an EEG component that is present when receiving negative instead of positive feedback. They also show weaker neural modulation by perceptual difficulty and reduced trial-by-trial behavioral updating of perceptual bias following recent correct and easy trials. These effects were replicated in a follow-up study. When combined, they classified autistic and non-autistic participants with high accuracy. These findings suggest that reduced flexibility in autism is associated with reduced processing of external feedback and task difficulty.

Article.Title: One-shot learning of paired association navigation with biologically plausible schemas
Article.Authors: Kumar M.; Tan C.; Libedinsky C.; Yen S.; Tan A.
Article.Abstract: After learning a multiple paired-association (MPA) navigation task, rodents can rapidly learn new cue–location associations after a single exposure, a phenomenon proposed to be facilitated by cognitive schemas. However, it remains unclear what schemas support this behavior and how they could be implemented in biological neural circuits. Here, we identify a set of schemas sufficient for gradual then one-shot paired-association navigation, and implement them in a fully neural agent using biologically plausible plasticity rules. The agent gradually acquires a low-dimensional spatial metric representation using a path-integration based temporal-difference error, enabling self-localization across different environments. It also contains a memory network that forms one-shot associations between sensory cues and goal locations, implemented using reward-modulated exploratory Hebbian (EH) plasticity. A third network performs vector subtraction between the agent’s current and goal location to compute goal-directed actions. Supplementing these schemas with an actor–critic enables one-shot navigation past obstacles. Lastly, learning a working-memory gating mechanism using the temporal-difference error enables one-shot learning even with brief cue and distractor presentation. The model reproduces key behavioral features of rodent learning in the MPA task and generates testable predictions about the neural mechanisms underlying schema-based one-shot learning. Significance Statement Schema-dependent learning is exemplified by better recall of a lecture when one already has a schema for understanding. A rodent navigation task showing a shift from slow to rapid learning has been proposed to reflect such schema use, yet how schemas are neurally implemented and enable faster learning is poorly understood. We clarify this gap in this computational study by describing several schemas and implement them as neural networks with biologically plausible learning rules. Composing them into an agent reproduces schema-dependent rodent learning behavior. Because schemas also shape self beliefs, clarifying their neural basis has implications for psychopathology. At the same time, understanding how biological schemas support rapid learning may inform advances in machine learning.

Article.Title: Emotional Content Enhances Attentional Tracking of Conversations through Context-Sensitive Modulation of AuditoryLanguage Networks
Article.Authors: Heikkinen P.; Lepist S.; Wikman P.; Koskinen E.; Perkyl A.; Ravaja N.; Harjunen V.
Article.Abstract: Engagement in conversation often requires continuous monitoring of relevant speech in a continuously evolving auditory environment. Emotional salience of semantic content may influence this process, but its role in attentional tracking of continuous speech remains unclear. We address this question using an audiovisual cocktail-party paradigm combined with source-localized magnetoencephalography and encodingdecoding analyses. Participants (18 females, 14 males) selectively attended to one dialogue while ignoring a concurrent distractor dialogue, with both emotional salience and semantic coherence of the conversations manipulated independently. Decoding analyses revealed that negatively valenced, high-arousal, and socially relevant semantic content strengthened neural speech tracking, but only for attended dialogues. This effect depended on semantic structure, emerging earlier in semantically coherent than incoherent dialogues. Encoding analyses further showed latency- and region-specific effects across temporal, parietal, and frontal cortical regions. Emotional salience and coherence jointly modulated midlatency (100250 ms) responses, whereas late-latency (270450 ms) responses were driven primarily by emotional salience. These findings demonstrate that emotional meaning enhances neural prioritization of attended speech and semantic coherence shapes the temporal dynamics of this enhancement. Together, these results indicate context-sensitive emotional modulation of auditorylanguage processing during selective listening of continuous speech.

Article.Title: Aperiodic EEG activity is a domain-specific marker of attentional aging in neurotypical adults
Article.Authors: Cazares C.; Rigby A.; Kang L.; Getzmann S.; Arnau S.; Wascher E.; Voytek B.
Article.Abstract: Aperiodic neural activity has been reliably shown to be reduced among older adults, and these reductions are associated with age-related cognitive decline. These results suggest that aperiodic activity, as measured by the spectral exponent, might be a viable electrophysiological biomarker for cognitive aging. However, this has not been tested longitudinally, within participants, during normal aging. Here, we used a longitudinal cohort of either sex to test whether changes in aperiodic activity between two sessions, approximately 5 years apart, track behavioral change across two domains: sustained attention (Psychomotor Vigilance Test) and executive function (modified Simon task). We found that aperiodic activity declined within individuals after the interval, independent of age at baseline. This within-person change tracked concurrent changes in reaction times during sustained attention but was not associated with changes in any Simon task measure. Within a resampling framework, the aperiodic-PVT association was stable across cohort resamples and independently fitted partitions, though it was not confirmed in a small, frozen held-out set. These findings suggest the longitudinal decline in aperiodic activity tracks attentional processing speed rather than executive function, supporting its potential as a domain-specific biomarker of attentional aging in neurotypical populations. Significance Statement Aperiodic (non-oscillatory) neural activity, indexed by the aperiodic exponent, is known to decline in older adults, but whether this happens within individuals over just a few years, and in step with cognitive change, remains unclear. Here we leveraged scalp EEG and cognitive-behavioral data from 276 neurotypical adults, tested twice approximately five years apart, and found that the aperiodic exponent declines within individuals over this interval, independent of age at baseline. This decline tracked concurrent slowing on a sustained attention task, but not change on an executive function task, and only in EEG recorded before, not after, cognitive testing. Based on this dissociation, we propose that aperiodic exponent decline indexes attentional processing speed rather than general cognitive decline in neurotypical aging.

Article.Title: Early life stress leads to detectable aberrant spread of neuron avalanches in the prefrontal-amygdala network in males but not females
Article.Authors: Kharybina Z.; Palva J.; Palva S.; Lauri S.; Hartung H.; Taira T.
Article.Abstract: Development of the brain networks is highly vulnerable to stressful events. Early life stress (ELS) has been linked to multifaceted cognitive and emotional deficits in adulthood. Despite a growing body of evidence showing ELS-induced structural and functional changes in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), a circuit crucial for emotional processing, our knowledge of the resulting changes in the network dynamics is incomplete. Here, we investigate how maternal separation (MS) affects prefrontal-amygdala network in terms of neuronal avalanches, spatiotemporal clusters of activity, using simultaneous multielectrode recordings in the medial PFC (mPFC) and the BLA of urethane-anaesthetized juvenile (postnatal day (p) 14 – p15) and young adult (p50 – p 60) rats. Firstly, we show that MS leads to an intensified spread of activity within both regions as reflected in the higher mean branching ratios of the avalanches. Next, we demonstrate that most of the avalanches occur locally in one region, however, a small percentage of avalanches have clusters of activity in both regions simultaneously. We show that in MS animals prefrontal clusters followed by activity in the amygdala tend to be larger compared to controls and each event in the mPFC is followed by smaller number of events in the BLA, pointing towards impaired spread of activity from the mPFC to the BLA. Interestingly, avalanche spread from the BLA to the mPFC remains unaffected by MS. Abovementioned effects manifest only in adulthood and, intriguingly, only in males highlighting prolonged developmental and sex-dependent nature of ELS outcome. Significance statement Brain criticality describes the brain’s ability to maintain a balanced state in which neural activity spreads efficiently without becoming too weak or overly chaotic. This balance can be measured through neuronal avalanches, bursts of cascading activity across interconnected neurons. Here, we show that early life stress (ELS) — adverse experiences during early brain development — disrupts the development of avalanche patterns in the connection between the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), brain regions involved in emotion and stress regulation. These effects were detected in males but not females. Our findings improve understanding of how stable brain activity develops in emotional brain networks and suggest that early life stress is an important factor influencing this critical balance.

Article.Title: Probing the neural geometry of conscious object perception in time
Article.Authors: Hachisuka A.; Baumgarten T.; Spector D.; Koenig L.; He B.
Article.Abstract: Conscious object recognition is a critical brain function, key to making sense of the plethora of visual inputs and guiding adaptive behavior. Yet, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious object recognition remains unclear. Existing proposals alternatively suggest that conscious object recognition proceeds in a “coarse-to-fine” sequence or a “fine-to-coarse” sequence. Here, we recorded high-density EEG while participants of both sexes performed a threshold-level object recognition task under different viewing conditions. Both superordinate and basic-level category information emerged early in neural activity, followed by a late superordinate category representation in an abstract format that is disentangled from low-level object features. Strikingly, in the early period, while basic-level category information positively correlated with perceptual awareness, superordinate category information negatively predicted perceptual awareness. By contrast, both superordinate and basic-level category information positively correlated with objective categorization accuracy in the early period. In the late period, both levels of category information positively correlated with awareness. These results suggest that neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate category level. Significance statement Despite significant interests, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious perception remains unclear. Here, we investigated the unfolding of neural events in time that support perceptual awareness of visual objects. Using a threshold-level object perception task involving three image conditions (normal, low-pass filtered, masked) and high-density EEG, we reveal that basic and superordinate category information both emerge early in the neural activity (at ∼100 ms), but only the basic-level category representation positively contributes to awareness. By contrast, the early superordinate category representation negatively correlates with perceptual awareness. At ∼300 ms, an abstract superordinate category representation emerges, which also positively correlates with perceptual awareness. Therefore, category-level neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate level.

Article.Title: The Roles and Uses of Extracellular Vesicles in Neuroimmunologic Diseases
Article.Authors: Kammeyer R.; Coughlan C.
Article.Abstract: Neuroimmunology is a field of neurology focused on the diagnosis and treatment of diseases where the immune system causes inflammation or injury to the nervous system. This includes diseases such as multiple sclerosis, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, autoimmune encephalitis, autoimmune ataxia, stiff person syndrome spectrum disorder, and neuro-rheumatologic diseases such as neuropsychiatric lupus. Over the past couple decades, there have been significant advancements in the diagnostic methods for several neuroimmunologic diseases. Despite these achievements, major needs remain for additional methods to facilitate earlier diagnosis, monitor disease activity and treatment, and elucidate disease mechanisms to aid in the development of novel or tailored treatment strategies. Currently, there is often a trade-off between the invasiveness of neurodiagnostic testing and the level of detail that can be obtained from the test without causing an iatrogenic injury. Here, we discuss the potential of extracellular vesicles (EVs), especially CNS-derived EVs obtained from peripheral blood, as a promising avenue for advancing research and clinical care in neuroimmunology. This article provides a review of the key clinical features and approaches to care for the most common neuroimmunologic diseases. We identify gaps that remain in our current understanding of these conditions. We then highlight how ongoing research in the EV field may address these existing gaps. Finally, we examine the challenges that must be overcome before EV analysis can be more widely adopted in both research and clinical care in this field.

Article.Title: Fast Corrective Responses in Redundant Motor Control Are Shaped by Intrinsic Constraints of Movement Patterns
Article.Authors: Kobayashi T.; Nozaki D.
Article.Abstract: In real-world motor tasks, body movements unfold in a high-dimensional space, whereas task errors are defined in a lower-dimensional space. How such low-dimensional errors propagate across redundant motor degrees of freedom to generate rapid corrective responses remains poorly understood. To address this question, we developed a redundant bimanual task in which human participants (males and females) manipulated a virtual stick with both hands to move its tip to a visual target. By shifting the tip position (task-relevant perturbation) or rotating the stick with the tip position fixed (task-irrelevant perturbation), we separated task-space errors from redundant-dimension errors. Participants rapidly corrected both types of perturbations using highly stereotyped movement patterns. Corrections to task-relevant errors consistently involved coordinated changes across redundant dimensions, and even perturbations that did not affect task success elicited systematic corrective responses. Together, these results demonstrate that fast corrective responses in redundant motor control are shaped by intrinsic coordination constraints that govern how visual errors propagate through the motor system.

Article.Title: Prefrontal Ensembles Represent Freezing of Conspecifics
Article.Authors: Miranda B.; Torossian A.; Reis F.; Patel N.; Liu X.; Walker E.; Leeds H.; Hilgert E.; Gudipati R.; Adhikari A.
Article.Abstract: Social buffering is a process in which the presence of other members of the same species (conspecifics) decreases stress reactions during threat exposure. In parallel, prior reports showed that groups of individuals display synchronous actions in nonthreatening situations. However, it is unknown if individuals also synchronize actions when facing threats. Prior studies showed social buffering of freezing in pairs of subjects. We now expand these findings and show social buffering of freezing during exposure to a predator and a shock grid in mice of both sexes in a larger group of four conspecifics. Furthermore, mice also displayed synchronized freezing. The presence of freezing synchrony suggests the existence of a neural representation of conspecific freezing. We reasoned that this encoding might be in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), as this region has been implicated in social behaviors and freezing. Strikingly, mPFC neural activity represented the average level of freezing across conspecifics. mPFC ensembles displayed differential encoding of self and conspecific freezing, and during predator exposure the mPFC encoded the number of conspecifics freezing and conspecific freezing bout duration. These data show, for the first time, neural representation of conspecific freezing and suggest that the mPFC may coordinate behavioral responses to threat across conspecifics.

Article.Title: Insulin regulates activity-dependent mitochondrial depolarization and calcium dynamics in dentate granule cells
Article.Authors: Ferrán B.; Rose H.; Gray J.; Redwine T.; Pham S.; Rubin O.; Rice H.; Sonntag W.; Díaz-García C.
Article.Abstract: Systemic insulin resistance is associated with reduced hippocampal energy metabolism and cognitive impairment both in humans and animal models. However, whether insulin rapidly regulates neuronal metabolic stability during activity remains unclear. Here, we examined insulin signaling and queried the corresponding mitochondrial responses in dentate granule cells (DGCs) of adult female mice. This layer of excitatory neurons within the hippocampus plays an essential role in learning and memory. Insulin robustly increased Akt phosphorylation in dentate gyrus tissue when insulin degradation was inhibited, and this response was attenuated by genetic deletion of the insulin receptor in DGCs, consistent with cell-autonomous signaling. We found that insulin did not alter mitochondrial membrane potential at rest, but significantly limited activity-evoked mitochondrial depolarization induced by neuronal stimulation. However, this change had no measurable impact on cytosolic ATP availability and was instead associated with Ca 2+ dynamics. Removing Ca 2+ ions from the extracellular solution, or disrupting mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake, prevented insulin modulation of the mitochondrial membrane potential. Furthermore, insulin limited cytosolic Ca 2+ accumulation through an insulin receptor-dependent mechanism that persisted despite Akt inhibition. Insulin also accelerated the clearance of mitochondrial Ca 2+ transients in active neurons, which occurred without changes in either neuronal excitability or pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphorylation. Together, these findings identify endogenous insulin degradation as a key regulator of hippocampal insulin signaling, and reveal a previously unrecognized interaction between insulin and Ca 2+ signaling in stimulated DGCs. This work also establishes a direct link between central insulin signaling and the maintenance of mitochondrial electrochemical homeostasis in the adult brain. Significance Statement Insulin signaling is known to influence synaptic plasticity, yet its direct effects on neuronal metabolism remain poorly defined. Here, we show that endogenous insulin degradation limits insulin signaling in adult hippocampal tissue. This finding suggests that inhibitors of the insulin degrading enzyme may hold the potential to improve the efficacy of insulin-based interventions aimed at improving learning and memory. Acute insulin signaling does not modify neuronal excitability, or cytosolic ATP availability. Instead, it stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces calcium accumulation in active dentate granule cells. By identifying an insulin-dependent mechanism that regulates the electrochemical homeostasis of mitochondria in active neurons, this work provides insight into how brain insulin resistance may contribute to cognitive dysfunction in aging and neurometabolic disorders.

Article.Title: Wide dynamic range of contrast-encoding in neural responses in macaque V1
Article.Authors: Yoshida H.; Chen Y.; Geisler W.; Seidemann E.
Article.Abstract: The dynamic range of contrast-encoding in the early visual system has been investigated at both single-neuron and population levels in animals using oriented stimuli such as gratings and Gabor patches. However, contrast-encoding of unoriented stimuli such as Gaussians has been less explored, even though such stimuli can evoke a large population response. In studies that employ Gaussians, contrast response functions (CRFs) of neurons and neural populations in primary visual cortex are typically characterized across a limited range of Weber contrasts up to 100%, which may not adequately reflect the statistics of contrast in natural scenes. Indeed, our preliminary analysis shows that locations with center-surround contrasts far exceeding the level comparable to a Gaussian stimulus of 100% Weber contrast are ubiquitous in natural scenes. Thus, our current understanding of contrast encoding remains incomplete in the context of natural environments. Here, we measured spiking activities of individual neurons using electrophysiology and population responses using widefield calcium imaging in V1 of fixating male macaques ( Macaca mulatta ) while Gaussian stimuli were presented over a wide range of Weber contrasts, up to 900%. Both the average spiking response and the average population response continued to increase robustly above 100% Weber contrast. Only a small minority of neurons saturated below 100% Weber contrast. These results demonstrate that the dynamic range of contrast-encoding in V1 is broader than previously assumed and aligns more closely with the statistics of contrast in natural scenes. Significance Statement The dynamic range of contrast-encoding in V1 has typically been characterized using only a limited range of contrasts, often excluding the high contrasts commonly found in natural scenes. We measured contrast response functions of individual neurons and neural populations in V1 across a much wider range of contrasts. We found that the responses of the majority of neurons, as well as the overall population, increased robustly up to extremely high contrasts. These findings suggest that the dynamic range of contrast encoding in V1 extends well beyond the commonly tested range.

Article.Title: A pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts hippocampal synapse maturation and homeostasis
Article.Authors: Xu J.; Wang Y.; Nomura T.; Van H.; Zhu Y.; Castillon C.; Chiesa M.; Marshall J.; Armstrong J.; Zhu Y.; Savas J.; Contractor A.
Article.Abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are critical for activity-dependent synapse maturation and circuit development. De novo missense mutations in AMPAR subunits are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet how these variants disrupt neuronal function remains unclear. Here, we examine a recurrent pathogenic mutation in the GluA1 subunit (GRIA1 p.A636T) that alters AMPAR function and is associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using GluA1 A636T knock-in mice of either sex, we identify impairments in hippocampal-dependent learning and working memory. Quantitative proteomics combined with bulk RNA-seq revealed age-dependent molecular remodeling in mutant hippocampus. Synaptic protein alterations were present in juvenile and adult mice, whereas a pronounced upregulation of mitochondrial and glial-associated proteins emerged more strongly in adulthood. Transcriptomic analyses showed partial concordance and highlighted divergence between RNA and protein regulation. Consistent with these molecular changes, there were increases in markers of oxidative stress in juvenile and adult mutant animals, whereas altered mitochondria morphology emerged selectively in adult mutants. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrated reduced basal excitatory transmission, persistence of silent synapses in adulthood and exaggerated activity-dependent synaptic potentiation, which were associated with reduced spine size consistent with impaired synapse maturation. Together, these findings indicate that a pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts developmental synapse maturation with secondary metabolic adaptations emerging over time. Significance Statement Mutations in genes encoding AMPA-type glutamate receptors are increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism and intellectual disability. However, how these mutations disrupt brain function and development remains poorly understood. Using a mouse model carrying a recurrent disease-associated mutation in the GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit, we show that the presence of this mutant subunit protein impairs the normal maturation of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus. Mutant mice retain immature “silent” synapses into adulthood, exhibit abnormal synaptic plasticity, reduced spine size, and deficits in learning and memory. Molecular analyses reveal age-dependent remodeling of synaptic and mitochondrial proteins, suggesting that metabolic changes arise secondary to disrupted synapse development. These findings clarify how pathogenic AMPA receptor variants alter brain function over time.

Article.Title: Representation of emotional expressions across the face and voice brain networks
Article.Authors: Mattioni S.; Falagiarda F.; Arya T.; Gau R.; Rezk M.; Battal C.; Van Audenhaege A.; Collignon O.
Article.Abstract: Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is fundamental to successful social interaction, yet how the brain represents emotional information across sensory systems remains unclear. Here, we systematically mapped the contribution of individually-defined face- and voice-selective cortical regions in 24 human participants of either sex to unimodal and crossmodal emotion expressions. Using multivariate pattern classification, we show that emotional expressions are robustly decodable from the dominant sensory modality across all individually defined face- and voice-selective areas, and that these representations cannot be accounted for by low- and mid-level stimulus properties alone. Strikingly, emotional information from the non-dominant modality—vocal expressions within face networks and facial expressions within voice networks—was also represented throughout the network, with the exception of the occipital face areas. Crossmodal decoding further revealed a shared neural code for facial and vocal emotions in the temporal voice areas, posterior superior temporal sulcus, and precentral gyrus, indicating that these regions contain emotion representations that generalize across sensory modalities. Furthermore, in most face- and voice-selective regions, audiovisual emotional expressions could be distinguished from representations elicited by the dominant unimodal modality, indicating that bimodal signals are not simply represented as their strongest sensory component. Together, these findings reveal that emotion representations are distributed broadly across face- and voice-selective regions and identify temporo-frontal regions as key sites supporting modality-independent emotion representations. Significance statement Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is essential for everyday social interaction, yet the brain mechanisms that integrate these signals remain poorly understood. Using functional MRI (fMRI) and advanced pattern analyses, we show that emotional expressions are represented widely across both face- and voice-selective brain regions-even when conveyed through a non-preferred sensory modality. Strikingly, specific temporo-frontal regions encode facial and vocal emotions using a partially shared, modality-independent neural code. We further demonstrate that seeing and hearing emotions together reshapes how emotional information is organized in the brain, revealing a graded transition from sensory-specific to multisensory representations. These findings challenge strictly segregated models of emotion processing and provide a more integrated account of how the brain supports social understanding.

Article.Title: Late Integration of Prior Expectations during Precision-Weighted Perceptual Decisions
Article.Authors: Gastrell T.; Rangelov D.; Mattingley J.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive perceptual decision-making relies on the ability to combine sensory evidence with prior expectations in a precision-weighted manner. Although Bayesian inference provides a clear normative account of how such integration should occur, the neural mechanisms through which the brain represents and combines priors and likelihoods remain poorly understood. Across two preregistered experiments, we investigated how the precision of learned priors and sensory likelihoods influence visual motion judgments and associated neural activity patterns during a random-dot motion estimation task. Neurotypical adult participants ( N = 80, 58 female) reported directions of visual motion stimuli, with motion coherence varying randomly across trials. Prior expectations over the continuous motion direction space were manipulated block-wise by implicitly varying the probabilities with which different motion directions were presented. Consistent with precision-weighted inference, response accuracy improved as motion coherence increased with robust response biases toward the expected motion direction. Neural activity measured using electroencephalography (EEG) revealed reliable effects of prior expectation on the univariate central parietal positivity (CPP), consistent with reduced accumulation of sensory evidence under informative priors. Multivariate analysis using inverted-encoding models revealed robust effects of prior precision on stimulus-specific neural representations, but only late, during response planning stages. Together, these findings suggest that priors learned over a continuous space do not modulate the encoding of sensory evidence and are instead integrated later in the decision process.

Article.Title: Specific regulation of transsynaptic nanoalignment and postsynaptic assembly by a novel NCAM family synaptic adhesion molecule
Article.Authors: Van der Linden Costello P.; Wennerberg M.; Rydbom J.; Gratz S.; Terry J.; Fennema L.; O’Connor-Giles K.; Broihier H.
Article.Abstract: Synapse formation underlies the organization of neurons into functional circuits and requires precise alignment and coordinated maturation of pre- and postsynaptic compartments. Many synaptogenic adhesion molecules have been identified that drive target recognition and sustained adhesion between appropriate synaptic partners. Yet the degree to which individual molecules serve distinct functions in synapse formation and maturation remains poorly understood. In particular, how exquisite nanoalignment of pre- and postsynaptic specializations flows from micron-scale adhesive interactions between synaptic partners remains a key unanswered question. Here we shed new light on this question by establishing a specialized set of synaptic functions for Epithelial limiter of Fasciclin II function (Elff ), an NCAM family member with previously unknown roles in the nervous system. Our structural and functional studies at the glutamatergic Drosophila NMJ of both sexes indicate that Elff is required for postsynaptic function and maturation as well as transsynaptic alignment; however, it is not required for presynaptic function, bouton formation, or developmental expansion of the NMJ. NMJs in elff null mutants display reduced glutamate receptor clusters beginning at the embryonic stage when NMJ synapses first form. Using super-resolution STED microscopy, we demonstrate that these poorly defined postsynaptic specializations are frequently out of register with presynaptic release sites. Surprisingly, the striking defects in elff nulls occur in the context of both normal active zone number and developmental expansion of the NMJ. These findings suggest an unexpected degree of specialization among transsynaptic adhesion complexes and demonstrate that Elff-mediated signaling is critical for transsynaptic nanoarchitecture of glutamatergic synapses. Significance Statement This work reveals a surprisingly selective role for a novel NCAM family member called Elff in coordinating postsynaptic assembly and precise transsynaptic nanoalignment without altering NMJ formation, expansion or presynaptic active zone number. This separation of phenotypes is new and provides crucial insight into molecular specialization of adhesion complexes during synaptogenesis. Because NCAM family member dysfunction linked to multiple neurological disorders, most notably schizophrenia, illuminating the molecular mechanisms by which they orchestrate synaptic organization and function is an important goal.

Article.Title: Mechanistic advances in exercise intervention for anxiety and depression via regulation of mitochondrial function
Article.Authors: Yang R.; Tang X.; Shi Y.; Sun J.; Yin Q.; Long Q.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety and depressive disorders are the most prevalent psychiatric conditions worldwide, characterized by complex pathophysiological mechanisms involving neuroplasticity, inflammatory responses, and disturbances in energy metabolism. Mitochondrial dysfunction has been proposed as one contributor, but causal evidence in patients remains limited. Exercise is an evidence-based adjunctive option for reducing depressive and anxiety symptoms, although effect estimates vary. In this narrative review, we comprehensively summarize the current understanding of how exercise may modulate mitochondrial function, including biogenesis, dynamics and energy metabolism, and how these changes could regulate neurotransmitter systems, reduce neuroinflammation, and promote neurogenesis. By integrating findings from both preclinical and clinical studies, we assess the strength of the proposed relationship, outline requirements for causal testing, and discuss the limits of clinical translation. Furthermore, we discuss existing challenges and propose future research directions to optimize exercise-based therapeutic strategies targeting mitochondrial pathways for the prevention and treatment of anxiety and depressive disorders.

Article.Title: Cellular senescence in ageing and neurodegenerative disorders: Molecular mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies
Article.Authors: Verma A.; Goyal A.; Agrawal N.; Yadav H.
Article.Abstract: Cellular senescence has been increasingly associated with neurodegenerative disorders, potentially linking ageing-related cellular impairment with mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and disrupted intercellular signalling. The present study aims to explore the increasing relevance of cellular senescence among key cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, neural progenitor cells, microglia and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells across neurodegenerative ailments such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and multiple sclerosis. This review discusses the findings of pre-clinical and clinical studies which suggest that senescence-associated features may contribute to neurodegeneration. Further, it provides an overview of the biomarkers used in the identification of senescence in the CNS. Also, the review examines senotherapeutic treatment approaches, highlighting their actions on different CNS cell types and the growing clinical evidence. It also points out the challenges in translating these approaches to clinical application, such as targeting specific cell types and the lack of suitable biomarkers. Collectively, present findings suggest that senescence-associated alterations may contribute to neurodegeneration, although their effects appear to vary across cell types and diseases.

Article.Title: Serum metabolic characteristics and potential biomarkers of first-episode schizophrenia: An exploratory machine learning-based metabolomics study
Article.Authors: Peng X.; Liu B.; Meng W.; Huang J.; Zhang Q.; Chen L.; Li K.; Tong H.; Zhang X.; Zhang J.; Rao W.
Article.Abstract: Metabolomics studies in first-episode schizophrenia (FES) remain limited and heterogeneous. This study aimed to characterize the serum metabolomic profile of FES, identify metabolic biomarkers, and develop machine learning-based predictive models. In this exploratory study, serum metabolomic profiles were compared among healthy controls (HCs; n = 10), untreated FES patients (n = 10), and the same patients after second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) treatment. Candidate biomarkers were evaluated using six machine learning algorithms. Bayesian network analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) were further applied to explore the network relationships. Cross-dataset integrative analysis was additionally performed using an external public dataset comprising patients with schizophrenia (n = 30) and HCs (n = 30). Disease-associated candidate biomarkers included PG(16:0/18:1), PC(20:4/15:0), PC(22:5/15:0), PG(18:1/18:1), and PE(16:0/16:0), whereas treatment-associated biomarkers included PG(16:0/18:1), PC(20:4/15:0), PC(22:5/15:0), Chol-S, DG(20:4/22:4), and PTNK. All selected candidate biomarkers achieved Area Under the Curve (AUC) values above 0.9, with performance varying across algorithms. In the Bayesian networks, disease served as a direct parent node of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score and all biomarkers, whereas treatment shared direct edges with the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) score and all biomarkers except Chol-S, which was indirectly connected via PTNK. WGCNA identified metabolite modules significantly associated with disease status (r = -0.88, p < 0.01) and treatment (r = 0.75, p < 0.01). Cross-dataset analysis identified phenylpyruvic acid, SM(d18:1/22:1(13Z)), and 2-octenoylcarnitine as shared differential metabolites with modest-to-moderate discrimination. These exploratory findings reveal potential serum metabolic signatures of FES and provide a basis for the development of objective biomarkers for diagnosis and SGAs treatment monitoring, warranting validation in larger independent cohorts.

Article.Title: Development and cross-tissue validation of a machine learning-based methylation profile score for the cortisol response to stress
Article.Authors: Balfour D.; Mittinty M.; Nguyen D.; Cohen-Woods S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPA axis) dysregulation is a risk factor for poor mental and physical health. Animal studies indicate that DNA methylation may regulate the HPA axis, although studies in humans have produced mixed results. A data-driven, machine learning approach may provide new insight. Methods: Using a novel machine learning pipeline, we developed a methylation profile score (MPS) to predict the salivary cortisol response (AUCi) to the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) from whole blood Illumina Infinium HumanMethylation 450K BeadChip data (N = 84, mean age = 34, 49% female). Results: The MPS was associated with the cortisol response in an independent, cross-tissue cohort (N = 53, mean age = 20, 51% female), both before (β = 0.33, 95% CI [0.09, 0.54]) and after a social stressor (β = 0.3, 95% CI [0.09, 0.47]). The effect remained statistically significant after adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, and smoking, but it became non-significant at the pre-stress (but not post-stress) time point after additional adjustment for cell proportion estimates (pre: β = 0.16, 95% CI [-0.1, 0.47]; post: β = 0.26, 95% CI [0.004, 0.49]). Conclusions: We developed a DNA methylation-based score that was associated with the cortisol response to stress in a separate, cross-tissue cohort. The predictive signal may depend, at least in part, on differences in cell composition associated with the phenotype. The methods used in this paper can be adapted and expanded upon in future research developing and testing novel epigenetic scores for complex, stress-related phenotypes.

Article.Title: Characteristic of anterior cingulate cortex connectivity at subregional level in major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Shao H.; Zhou Z.; Huang X.; Zhang L.; Hu X.; Gao Y.; Li H.; Kuang W.; Gong Q.; Huang X.
Article.Abstract: Background: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) exhibits substantial role underlying the pathophysiology of major depressive disorder (MDD), yet its exact connectivity alteration and the relationship with clinical symptoms remain unclarified. We aimed to systematically investigate ACC subregional functional connectivity alterations with a relatively large sample of MDD and their longitudinal changes associated with clinical state. Methods: From the Huaxi Depression Imaging Cohort Study, we recruited 141 MDD patients and 138 matched healthy controls (HC) with complete clinical information and resting-state functional MRI data, and calculated functional connectivity (FC) of five ACC subregions (subgenual, perigenual, rostral, dorsal, and caudal ACC). A subset of patients who completed follow-up clinical assessments and MRI scanning was further classified into remitted and non-remitted subgroups. ACC subregional FC was compared between MDD and HC, and for longitudinal changes in remitted and non-remitted patients separately. Exploratory correlations between FC alterations and symptom profiles were also assessed. Results: Compared with HCs, MDD patients demonstrated widespread hyperconnectivity between most ACC subregions and regions within frontoparietal network (FPN) and default mode network (DMN) at baseline. At follow-up, remitted patients showed reduced connectivity between perigenual ACC (pgACC) and dorsolateral/ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC/vlPFC), with connectivity approaching HC levels. Non-remitted patients, however, exhibited no significant changes. Conclusions: Our findings delineate specific dysconnectivity patterns of ACC at the subregional level in MDD and suggest the pgACC-dlPFC/vlPFC connectivity may represent a candidate neuroimaging correlate of remission.

Article.Title: Activation of the prelimbic–infralimbic circuitry alleviates dysfunction in conditioned fear processing following traumatic stress in rats
Article.Authors: Crestani C.; Ragonesi L.; Dunn T.; Glorius A.; Omena-Giatti L.; Chambers J.; Packard B.; Oliveira L.; Herman J.
Article.Abstract: Preclinical studies show that traumatic stress, such as single prolonged stress (SPS), leads to hypofunction of the infralimbic (IL) cortex, although the underlying circuit mechanisms remain unclear. Within the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), pyramidal neurons in the prelimbic (PL) cortex project to the IL, forming a microcircuit that is critically involved in fear extinction. Here, we tested whether activation of this PL → IL pathway is sufficient to reverse SPS-evoked deficits in fear memory processing. As a complementary measure, we also assessed the effects of SPS and PL → IL circuit activation on corticosterone responses to acute stress. Using an intersectional chemogenetic approach, we selectively activated IL-projecting PL neurons. Ten days after SPS exposure, animals underwent auditory fear conditioning, extinction, and reinstatement. Corticosterone response to an acute footshock was measured following these procedures. SPS increased freezing during extinction, consistent with impaired fear extinction. Notably, activation of the PL → IL circuit abolished this deficit, reduced cued fear retrieval in SPS-exposed animals, and attenuated fear reinstatement-the latter effect occurring regardless of stress history. SPS also blunted corticosterone responses to footshock; however, this endocrine effect was not reversed by PL → IL activation. Nevertheless, circuit activation reduced corticosterone response to footshock in control animals. Overall, these findings indicate that selective activation of IL-projecting PL neurons rescues trauma-induced impairments in fear extinction, likely by restoring disrupted mPFC circuitry. This effect appears specific to fear-related processes and does not extend to trauma-induced alterations in hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis reactivity.

Article.Title: Caloric restriction and intermittent fasting initiated during lactation alter maternal behaviour and amygdalar redox status in dams
Article.Authors: Veloso N.; Dayrell R.; Roque L.; Duarte S.; Santos M.; dos Reis Advíncola V.; da Silva A.; Pinto N.; Mosienko V.; Rocha-Gomes A.; Riul T.
Article.Abstract: The lactational period requires substantial metabolic and behavioural adaptations, and more than 70% of mothers report weight concerns and attempt weight loss by four months postpartum. Nevertheless, how distinct restrictive paradigms initiated during lactation alter maternal behaviour, and the extent to which associated neurochemical changes relate to these behaviours, remains poorly understood. In the current study, we modeled restrictive diets in lactating rats to evaluate caregiving behaviour and its relationship to amygdalar redox status. Intermittent fasting (IF) and caloric restriction (CR) were administered to lactating Wistar dams from postpartum day 0 to day 28, and impaired maternal care, evidenced by delayed pup retrieval and decreased nursing frequency relative to ad libitum-fed controls. Both diets reduced body and adipose tissue weight, and energy efficiency. IF and CR increased impulsivity-like phenotype: CR doubled open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze; IF and CR increased center-zone exploration in the open field by three- and two-fold, respectively; IF doubled time spent in the light chamber of the light-dark box. A composite behavioural score showed impairment in dams in both IF and CR groups. At the neurochemical level, both diets reduced amygdalar superoxide dismutase activity, which correlated negatively with the composite behavioural score. Both restrictive diets produced an underweight phenotype with weakened dam-pup interactions and an impulsivity-like response. These behavioural changes co-occurred with amygdalar redox imbalance, which correlated with the severity of the behavioural score. Overall, the study refines understanding of the nutritional and behavioural consequences of dietary restriction initiated during lactation and identifies disrupted redox homeostasis as a candidate mechanism.

Article.Title: Beyond diagnostic categories: A narrative review of transdiagnostic mechanisms in neurodevelopmental disorders
Article.Authors: Carone M.; Premoli M.; Shamshiri A.; Bonini S.
Article.Abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) represent a heterogeneous class of early-onset conditions marked by impairments in cognition, reduced social function, hyperactivity and repetitive-stereotyped behaviour. Traditionally classified as discrete clinical entities, NDDs such as autism spectrum disorders (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disability (ID) are now increasingly understood as overlapping, multifactorial conditions shaped by converging genetic, epigenetic, immune, and environmental influences. This review synthesizes current evidence challenging categorical diagnostic boundaries and instead proposes a transdiagnostic and mechanistic framework that integrates shared disruptions in neural circuits, excitatory/inhibitory balance, synaptic architecture, and immune-metabolic signalling. We explore how genes and environment interact during early development, how epigenetics influences long-term outcomes, and how these insights are driving a shift toward precision medicine guided by biomarkers and patient-derived models. Emerging therapies include neuromodulation, immune and microbiota-based interventions, and gene editing, supported by insights from animal and iPSC models. A time-sensitive and biologically grounded approach is needed, moving beyond symptom-based classifications to allow for earlier diagnosis, personalized treatment, and the development of innovative interventions. This paradigm shift aligns with precision approaches already transforming other biomedical domains and holds the potential to more effectively address the complex and lifelong challenges posed by NDDs.

Article.Title: Initial antipsychotic prescription and all-cause mortality after claims-recorded dementia diagnosis in schizophrenia: A nationwide propensity-matched cohort study
Article.Authors: Jung S.; Hong M.; Lee D.; Bae Y.; You S.; Kim M.; Shin W.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: To examine the association between an antipsychotic drug (APD) prescription recorded during the first 90 days after a claims-recorded dementia diagnosis and all-cause mortality in patients with schizophrenia. Secondary analyses compared APD generation and study-defined metabolic and QT-prolongation risk groups. Methods: In this retrospective, nationwide, propensity-matched cohort study using Korean National Health Insurance Service data (2002-2022), the primary analysis included 28,506 patients with schizophrenia who received a qualifying claims-recorded dementia diagnosis (14,253 matched pairs). APD exposure was defined by prescriptions recorded during the first 90 days after the index diagnosis. Separate propensity-matched secondary cohorts compared first- and second-generation antipsychotics (FGAs and SGAs) and SGA metabolic- and QT-prolongation-risk groups. All-cause mortality was analyzed using Cox proportional-hazards models. Results: In the primary matched cohort, mortality did not differ significantly between patients with an APD prescription during the initial 90-day window and those without a recorded prescription during that window (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.976, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.939-1.015; p = 0.2228). Mortality also did not differ significantly between SGA and FGA users (aHR 1.018, 95% CI 0.946-1.095; p = 0.6291). In secondary analyses, mortality was significantly higher in the higher-metabolic-risk SGA group than in the lower-risk group (aHR 1.238, 95% CI 1.105-1.388; p = 0.0002) and in the higher-QT-prolongation-risk SGA group than in the lower-risk group (aHR 1.109, 95% CI 1.019-1.207; p = 0.0164). Conclusions: Among patients with schizophrenia who survived the 90-day classification window, an APD prescription recorded during the first 90 days after a claims-recorded dementia diagnosis was not significantly associated with adjusted all-cause mortality compared with no recorded prescription during that window. Secondary analyses showed higher mortality in the study-defined higher-metabolic- and higher-QT-risk SGA groups than in their lower-risk comparators. These observational associations do not establish comparative treatment safety or imply sustained use or non-use beyond the initial 90-day window.

Article.Title: Structural changes in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex following a randomized clinical trial of virtual reality–based cognitive remediation in mood and schizophrenia spectrum disorders
Article.Authors: Macoveanu J.; Olde T.; Jespersen A.; Lumbye A.; Vinberg M.; Glenthøj L.; Nordentoft M.; Sankar A.; Knudsen G.; Miskowiak K.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: Cognitive impairments are common in patients with mood disorders (MD) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD) and impair quality of life. Developing pro-cognitive treatments is hindered by limited understanding of the biology underlying cognitive impairment and improvement. This structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study examined the neural correlates of cognitive improvement following a Virtual-Reality-based Cognitive Remediation Therapy (VR-CRT) intervention. Methods: Patients underwent eight VR-CRT or VR-control treatment sessions during a four-week period. The study population included data from a transdiagnostic subsample of 41 symptomatically stable, cognitively impaired patients with MD or SSD (VR-CRT: n = 22; VR-control: n = 19) with baseline structural MRI data of which 33 (VR-CRT: 20; VR-control: n = 13) also underwent MRI at treatment completion. Neuropsychological assessment was completed both pre- and post-treatment and additionally at three-month post-treatment follow-up. Results: Gray matter volume in the VR-CRT group increased over time in the right caudal middle frontal gyrus (MFG) compared to VR-control. Secondary hypothesis-driven analysis showed a similar increase in right caudal MFG thickness for VR-CRT patients. These structural changes were not associated with treatment-related cognitive improvement. However, greater left rostral MFG thickness at baseline was associated with more cognitive improvement over time in the VR-CRT group. Conclusion: This study demonstrates treatment-related structural changes in the right caudal MFG and suggests that baseline left rostral MFG thickness may represent a candidate marker of cognitive improvement within the VR-CRT group. These findings support further investigation of MFG structure as a marker of brain response and cognitive treatment outcome. This trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06038955, and is completed.

Article.Title: Differential structural profiles of the hippocampus and thalamus and their cognitive relevance in unilateral mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
Article.Authors: Qin X.; Peng J.; Yao C.; Wang Y.; Zhao S.; Li G.; Bao S.; Li S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Cognitive dysfunction is common in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE), yet how much the hippocampus and the thalamus each contribute remains unclear. We compared fine-grained hippocampal and thalamic structure and their cognitive relevance in unilateral MTLE. Methods: We studied 71 patients with unilateral MTLE (39 with hippocampal sclerosis [HS], 32 without) and 17 controls. FreeSurfer-derived cortical, hippocampal-subfield, and thalamic-nucleus volumes were compared using permutation-based general linear models. In patients, 19 cognitive measures were related to volume using covariate-adjusted partial correlations under seizure-referenced (ipsilateral/contralateral) and anatomical left/right codings. Nested additive models tested the incremental cognitive contributions of hippocampal and thalamic volume. Results: Relative to controls, patients showed widespread thalamic atrophy (34 of 44 nuclei in the full cohort, 32 of 44 in each subgroup), whereas hippocampal subfield atrophy was largely confined to HS and no cortical region survived correction. All 48 corrected volume-cognition associations involved hippocampal subfields; none involved thalamic nuclei. Additive models showed that ipsilateral hippocampal volume explained 7.4%-14.6% of cognitive variance alone and explained an additional 6.8%-18.9% of cognitive variance beyond thalamic volume, whereas global thalamic volume did not add significant corrected incremental variance. Preserving anatomical hemisphere linked verbal comprehension and naming to left hippocampal subfields and working memory predominantly to right subfields. Conclusions: Hippocampal and thalamic abnormalities showed distinct structural and cognitive profiles in unilateral MTLE. Thalamic atrophy was widespread, whereas hippocampal volume was more closely related to cognition and showed additional variation by HS status and anatomical hemisphere.

Article.Title: Agouti-related peptide, cocaine- and amphetamine-regulated transcript, asprosin, progranulin, and leptin in young children with autism spectrum disorder and their associations with eating behaviors and clinical characteristics
Article.Authors: Ağır H.; Coşkun F.; Akça Ö.; Kılınç İ.; Akkuş A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with a multifactorial etiology. Appetite- and energy homeostasis-related molecules have emerged as potential contributors to its pathophysiology. This study investigated serum agouti-related peptide (AgRP), cocaine- and amphetamine-regulated transcript (CART), asprosin, progranulin, and leptin levels in young children with ASD and their associations with eating behaviors and clinical characteristics. Methods: This case-control study included 70 children with ASD and 68 age- and sex-matched typically developing controls aged 18-72 months. Serum concentrations were measured using ELISA. Eating behaviors were assessed using the Children's Eating Behavior Questionnaire (CEBQ), while ASD-related symptoms were evaluated using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) and Autism Behavior Checklist (AuBC). Results: Children with ASD had higher serum AgRP, CART, and leptin levels and lower progranulin levels than controls, whereas asprosin levels did not differ significantly. These differences remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI percentile. Children with ASD showed lower satiety responsiveness, slowness in eating, and emotional undereating scores. Exploratory correlation analyses indicated that, within the ASD group, AgRP was positively associated with CEBQ- food fussiness, and leptin was positively associated with CEBQ- emotional overeating. Higher AgRP and asprosin levels were associated with lower AuBC- sensorial stimulus scores, while asprosin was also associated with lower AuBC- personal and social development scores. Conclusions: Young children with ASD exhibit alterations in appetite- and energy homeostasis-related molecules. These findings may reflect alterations in neuroendocrine pathways associated with ASD and its accompanying eating difficulties.

Article.Title: Neurochemical signatures of morphometric network reorganization in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Links to cognition and behavior
Article.Authors: Niu X.; Zhang S.; Cheng B.; Xu K.; Zhang X.; Song Y.; Fu H.; Xu R.; Xu T.; Wan J.; Zhou Z.; Zhang H.; Yang C.; Ren Y.; Hu Q.; Wang X.; Cai X.; Guo Y.; Xu H.
Article.Abstract: Objective: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is associated with neurocognitive behavior problems and regional morphometric abnormalities, yet large-scale brain network reorganization and its molecular correlations remain unclear. Here, we explored whether remodeling of the individual-level morphological similarity network (MSN) in DMD aligns with specific neurotransmitter systems and associates with cognitive, behavioral, and motor performance. Methods: We studied 111 boys with DMD and 80 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs). Individual MSNs were derived from T1-weighted MRI. Global and nodal graph-theoretical metrics were compared between groups, and network-based statistics (NBS) were used to identify altered subnetworks. Spatial correlations linked altered MSN maps to normative PET/SPECT neurotransmitter maps, and Spearman correlations related MSN alterations and neurochemical indices to clinical measures. Results: The global small-world organization of MSNs was preserved. However, boys with DMD showed increased degree centrality (DC) in the bilateral hippocampus and left cerebellar lobule 3, and decreased DC in the right cerebellar lobule 7b. NBS identified a cerebellar-frontotemporal-subcortical morphological circuit characterized by reduced morphological similarity. MSN alterations showed significant spatial associations with dopaminergic, serotonergic, GABAergic, glutamatergic, cholinergic, and endocannabinoid systems, and the strength of these associations and network disruption were associated with poorer cognitive, motor, and behavioral performance. Conclusions: Children with DMD exhibit MSN remodeling centered on a cerebellar-frontotemporal-subcortical morphological circuit that is neurochemically coupled to specific neurotransmitter systems and linked to cognitive, behavioral, and motor deficits. This study elucidates potential neurochemical mechanisms underlying neurobehavioral abnormalities in DMD and may provide biological insights to inform the development of neuromodulation-based therapeutic strategies.
