Article.Title: Altered white matter functional activity and connectivity in pretreatment breast cancer: Exploratory associations with affective symptoms
Article.Authors: Wu S.; Zhang Z.; Chen N.; Cheng S.; Xu W.; Xu Z.; Jia X.; Wei F.; Cheng Y.; Mao G.
Article.Abstract: Objective: Resting-state fMRI studies in breast cancer have predominantly focused on gray matter, with limited attention to white matter functional organization. This study investigated white matter functional activity and connectivity before treatment and their associations with anxiety and depressive symptoms. Methods: Female patients with breast cancer (BC) were recruited from Zhejiang Provincial Tongde Hospital from November 2023 to December 2025. Amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF) and fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (fALFF) were used to compare local white matter functional activity between the BC and healthy control (HC) groups. Seed-based functional connectivity (FC) analysis was then performed to investigate whole-brain white matter FC alterations. Correlations between clinical scale scores and rs-fMRI indices were analyzed. Results: Compared with HCs, patients with BC showed altered ALFF/fALFF in the anterior and posterior corona radiata, internal capsule, posterior thalamic radiation, body of the corpus callosum, pontine crossing tract, left superior cerebellar peduncle, and left superior longitudinal fasciculus. Seed-based analysis revealed decreased FC within the bilateral anterior corona radiata and between the body of the corpus callosum and right anterior corona radiata, and increased FC between the left superior cerebellar peduncle and left posterior thalamic radiation. Higher ALFF in the body of the corpus callosum and reduced FC between this region and the right anterior corona radiata were associated with higher Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores at an uncorrected threshold. Neither association survived FDR correction. Conclusion: Patients with BC showed altered white matter functional activity and connectivity before cancer-related treatment, suggesting that pretreatment brain functional alterations may also involve white matter functional organization. The relationship between these white matter changes and anxiety or depressive symptoms remains exploratory.

Article.Title: Fetal brain volumes in complete vascular ring: A cross-sectional MRI study
Article.Authors: Ren J.; Chen C.; Zhu M.; Zhang X.; Li Y.; Dong S.
Article.Abstract: Background: The association between complete vascular ring (CVR) and prenatal brain development remains poorly characterized. Objective: To compare global and regional fetal brain volumes between fetuses with CVR and controls, accounting for gestational age (GA), fetal sex, and estimated fetal weight. Methods: In this retrospective single-center study, 70 prenatally diagnosed CVR fetuses and 200 GA-matched controls with normal brain anatomy (22-37 weeks) underwent 1.5-T fetal MRI. Motion-corrected three-dimensional brain reconstructions were generated by slice-to-volume registration, and 19 regions were automatically segmented using a deep-learning pipeline. Linear regression included continuous GA, group, their interaction, fetal sex, and estimated fetal weight. Regional-to-intracranial volume ratios and sensitivity analyses incorporating maternal body mass index were evaluated. Multiple comparisons were controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Results: At the 28-week reference age, adjusted supratentorial brain, cortical gray matter, white matter, thalamic, lentiform nucleus, brainstem, and lateral ventricular volumes were smaller in the CVR group (all false-discovery-rate-adjusted P < 0.05). Intracranial volume did not differ significantly. Thalamic, lentiform nucleus, brainstem, and lateral ventricular proportions were also smaller. No group-by-GA interaction survived correction in the primary model. Conclusions: CVR was associated with differences in selected fetal brain volumes, including regional differences relative to intracranial volume. Larger longitudinal studies with postnatal follow-up are needed.

Article.Title: Lung-brain-axis-mediated mechanisms of sepsis-associated encephalopathy secondary to lower respiratory tract infection: A narrative review
Article.Authors: Cheng X.; hen Qi G.; Zhao S.
Article.Abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) represent one of the most frequent causes of sepsis. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE), a serious complication of sepsis, markedly increases patient mortality and the risk of long-term cognitive impairment. The emerging concept of the lung-brain axis offers a novel framework for understanding the pathogenesis of SAE. Unlike general reviews covering all-cause sepsis-associated encephalopathy, this review specifically focuses on SAE secondary to LRTI, and discriminates its unique epidemiological, clinical and mechanistic signatures from SAE triggered by abdominal, urinary or bloodstream infection. This review systematically summarizes the epidemiological characteristics of SAE induced by LRTIs, the anatomical and immunological basis of lung-brain interactions, and key pathological mechanisms including neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, neurotransmitter imbalance, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Additionally, it highlights advances in biomarker research and clinical management strategies. By integrating evidence from molecular‑biology and neuroimaging studies, this article describes how pulmonary infections drive brain dysfunction via neural, immune, and endocrine pathways. These findings provide a theoretical foundation to support early diagnosis and targeted therapeutic interventions.

Article.Title: Apelin-13 exerts neuroprotection through activation of APJ/mTORC2 axis in microglia after intracerebral hemorrhage in mice
Article.Authors: Fan H.; Sun H.; Hu Z.; Lin W.; Chen Y.; Yao Y.; Zhang A.; Ren R.; Wu Q.
Article.Abstract: Background: Apelin-13, a bioactive peptide that acts via the APJ receptor, exhibits potent anti-oxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-inflammatory properties. However, its role in intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) remains poorly understood. In this study, we aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of Apelin-13 and the underlying mechanisms in a mouse model of ICH. Methods: A mouse model of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) was established and randomly allocated to receive either recombinant Apelin-13 (rApelin-13) or phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). To investigate the role of the APJ/mammalian target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) axis in Apelin-13-mediated neuroprotection, the APJ antagonist ML221 and the mTORC2 inhibitor JR-AB2-Activation of mTORC2 and ERK signaling was examined, and M2-like microglial biom011 were administered. To further elucidate the underlying mechanism, microglia-specific knockdown of Rictor was achieved via intracerebroventricular injection of an adeno-associated virus (AAV) carrying CD68-promoter-driven shRictor. Assessments included brain water content, short-term neurobehavioral tests, Western blot analysis, quantitative RT-PCR, and histological staining. Results: Following ICH induction, the expression of Apelin-13 was upregulated and primarily secreted from neurons. Exogenous administration of rApelin-13 significantly attenuated neuronal apoptosis and improved short-term neurological function in mice after ICH in a dose-dependent manner. Furthermore, rApelin-13 enhanced M2-like polarization of microglia in the post-ICH brain. Notably, the neuroprotective effects of rApelin-13 were abolished by inhibition of mTORC2.

Article.Title: Epidural spinal cord stimulation promotes the expansion of endogenous neural stem cells and neuroprotection via the PI3K/AKT/ mTOR pathway after spinal cord injury in rats
Article.Authors: Li G.; Shen F.; Li J.; Fan Z.; He S.
Article.Abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) often leads to severe motor and sensory dysfunction, yet no effective treatment currently exists. Epidural spinal cord stimulation (ESCS) is a treatment for chronic neuropathic pain in the trunk and extremities, and exerts a significant effect on the recovery of motor function, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. The present study aimed to investigate the effects of ESCS on the endogenous neural stem cells (eNSCs) proliferation and neuroprotection as well as the underlying mechanisms following SCI in rats. In the present study, results showed that ESCS improved hindlimb motor function and markedly increased the numbers of surviving ventral horn neurons of the spinal cord at 7 and 28 days after SCI. ESCS significantly reduced the apoptosis of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord on day 28 post-SCI. Moreover, ESCS remarkably increased the expressions of NSCs markers nestin and sox2, as well as the proportion of nestin/sox2/DAPI-double positive cells (eNSCs) at 7 days after SCI. Notably, ESCS induced only a negligible number of Sox2/NeuN/DAPI double-positive cells at 28 days after SCI. LY294002, a selective inhibitor of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) markedly decreased the ratios of eNSCs and surviving ventral horn neurons after ESCS treatment. Finally, ESCS increased the protein levels of phosphorylated-protein kinase B (p-Akt) and phosphorylated-mammalian target of rapamycin (p-mTOR) at 7 days after SCI, and LY294002 significantly attenuated the effects of ESCS on p-Akt and p-mTOR. This report suggests that ESCS treatment after SCI enhances the expansion of eNSCs and neuroprotection via the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway.

Article.Title: Functional connectivity and white matter microstructural alterations of thalamic subregions in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Article.Authors: Yang K.; Wang Y.; Zhang Y.; Li M.; Yun Y.; Xing J.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Objective: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) is a common peripheral vestibular disorder. Although the thalamus serves as a key node in vestibular pathways, its role in the central regulation of BPPV remains unclear. This study aimed to explore the functional and structural alterations of thalamus in patients with BPPV. Methods: The study recruited 52 BPPV patients and 52 age- and gender-matched healthy volunteers. Seed-based analysis was used to explore functional connectivity (FC) alterations between thalamic subregions and the whole brain in patient group. Probabilistic fiber tracking was then employed to analyze white matter structural differences in brain regions with functional alterations. Additionally, correlation analysis was conducted to investigate the relationship between abnormal imaging metrics and clinical scales. Results: Compared to controls, patients with BPPV exhibited increased FC and higher fractional anisotropy (FA) values of some thalamic subregions to certain cerebral cortices. As a confirmatory finding, decreased FC but increased structural connectivity was displayed between the rostral temporal thalamus and cerebellum in BPPV. Furthermore, the FA value of the rostral temporal thalamus-cerebellar tract showed a correlation with the score of the impact of event scale. The mediation analysis showed emotional distress mediated the relationship between vertigo and FA of the rostral temporal thalamus-cerebellar tract. Conclusions: In BPPV, the thalamic subregions and certain cerebral cortices exhibit synergistic functional and structural enhancement, whereas a distinct dissociation pattern is observed in the cerebellum. This differentiated reorganization may characterize the neural process in the early stage of BPPV.

Article.Title: Interpretable machine learning model based on radiomic features of hippocampal subfields for classifying zoster-associated pain
Article.Authors: Wen X.; Peng R.; Wang M.; Yu M.; Liu S.; Zhang D.; Ren C.; Chen G.
Article.Abstract: Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), the most common complication of herpes zoster (HZ), is difficult to prevent due to limited understanding of the mechanisms underlying the transition from acute to chronic pain and the lack of objective neuroimaging biomarkers for individualized risk stratification. In this study, we aimed to develop interpretable machine learning models based on hippocampal subfield radiomics to classify zoster-associated pain (ZAP) patients and identify neuroimaging biomarkers reflecting microstructural alterations in hippocampus associated with ZAP. High-resolution 3D T1-weighted MR images were obtained from 28 PHN patients, 25 Hz patients, and 21 healthy controls (HCs). We extracted radiomic features of ten hippocampal subfields and used five machine learning classification algorithms to identify the most contributive subfield and robust model for classifying ZAP patients. Furthermore, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was used to interpret the optimal model. In distinguishing ZAP patients from HCs, the SVM_Linear model based on the left subiculum radiomics achieved the highest performance with an AUC of 0.739, whereas the Logistic_L1 model based on the right CA4-DG and left SR-SL-SM radiomics showed the best performance with an AUC of 0.799 in distinguishing PHN patients from HZ patients. SHAP analysis revealed that SmallAreaEmphasis from the right CA4-DG subfield was the dominant feature for identifying PHN patients, followed by ClusterShade from the left SR-SL-SM subfield. Furthermore, both features showed strong associations with disease duration. These results suggest that hippocampal subfield radiomics can effectively stratify ZAP phases. Specifically, right CA4-DG radiomic features may serve as effective neuroimaging biomarkers associated with disease chronicity and have the potential for early risk stratification and intervention of ZAP.

Article.Title: Efficacy of eugenol against N, N′-Dimethyl-4,4′-bipyridinium dichloride (paraquat)-induced NA⁺/K⁺/CA²⁺ dysregulation and behavioral deficits in rat models
Article.Authors: Uchewa O.; Ibegbu A.; Chukwu V.; Igwe E.; Alobu E.; Cookey-Gam T.; Okoronkwo S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Ion level disruption causes mitochondrial aberration and alters cytochrome c activity. Purpose: To evaluate the efficacy of eugenol in Na+/K+/Ca2 + Cytochrome C dysregulation and behavioral deficits in Wistar rats. Methods: Forty male Wistar rats were acclimatised for two weeks and assigned to five groups of 8 rats. Group A received feed and normal saline. Groups B, C, D, and E received 10 mg/kg paraquat (PQ), and then C, D, and E received eugenol at graded doses of 200, 400, and 600 mg/kg. PQ was administered for 28 days at 1-day intervals, before the rats were treated with eugenol for 14 days via the oral route. Social interaction and depression-like behaviours were studied using a sociability chamber and a tail suspension box. Results: In Group B, interstitial Na+/K+ increased, while Ca2 + significantly decreased. In the treated groups, Na+/K+ and Ca2 + levels decreased and increased significantly, respectively. Cytochrome C, Caspase cleavage, and Full-length cytokeratin-18 were significantly increased in the untreated Group B and were reduced by eugenol (p < 0.05). In the PQ-untreated Group, social interaction and immobility were impaired, but eugenol attenuated these behavioral deficits. Dopamine levels and gamma-glutamyl transferase activities were lowered and increased in Group B, respectively, while eugenol increased and reduced them (p < 0.05). Microscopically, paraquat caused a significant loss of dopaminergic neurons, formation of Lewy bodies, and Pyknosis in the substantia nigra. Conclusions: Overall, eugenol shows valuable therapeutic potential against pesticide-induced neurotoxicity and associated ion dysregulation.

Article.Title: Epipharyngeal sensory stimulation is associated with changes in brainstem-cortical functional connectivity and circulating proteomic profiles
Article.Authors: Sakatani H.; Ueda R.; Tha K.; Murakami K.; Kitagawa M.; Kubota S.; Kono M.; Murakami M.; Hotomi M.
Article.Abstract: Neurostimulation has emerged as a potential approach for modulating autonomic and neuroimmune function. Because epipharyngeal mucosa receives sensory innervation from cranial afferents, mechanical stimulation of this region may engage neural pathways. Epipharyngeal abrasive therapy (EAT) involves mechanical and chemical stimulation of the epipharyngeal mucosa and is used clinically for chronic epipharyngitis; however, its central and systemic effects remain poorly understood. This study aimed to investigate whether epipharyngeal stimulation using EAT is associated with changes in brainstem functional connectivity and circulating proteomic profiles in healthy adults. Participants underwent five EAT sessions at 7-day intervals (Protocol A), with restingstate functional MRI performed before, immediately after, and four weeks after the first session. A subset also underwent a control protocol without EAT (Protocol B). Wholebrainstem seed-to-voxel functional connectivity was analyzed. Paired plasma samples collected before and after the first EAT session were analyzed using the SomaScan 11 K assay. Longitudinal analysis identified altered connectivity between the brainstem and subcallosal/medial frontal region, primarily immediately after EAT. A controlled withinsubject analysis identified an EAT-specific increase in connectivity between the brainstem and right temporal pole, extending into the inferior temporal gyrus. Proteomic analysis identified 13 proteins meeting exploratory screening criteria and significant pathway-level enrichment involving RNA metabolism, translation, and extracellular matrix organization. Mechanical and chemical stimulation of the epipharynx was associated with changes in brainstem-cortical functional connectivity and circulating proteomic signatures. These findings suggest that sensory stimulation of the epipharynx may engage cranial sensory afferent-brainstem pathways and contribute to coordinated central neural and peripheral molecular responses.

Article.Title: Neutrophil extracellular traps in ischemic stroke: Thrombolysis resistance, no-reflow, and hemorrhagic transformation
Article.Authors: Zhang S.; Cui Y.; Zhou X.; Wang D.; Cao Y.; Zhao H.; Sun Z.; Li Q.; Yin H.
Article.Abstract: Recanalization is central to acute ischemic stroke treatment. However, reopening an occluded artery does not always restore microvascular perfusion, and hemorrhagic transformation (HT) can occur regardless of recanalization success. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) may help explain these discordant outcomes because they act within occlusive thrombi, the downstream microcirculation, and the neurovascular interface. This review examines the roles of NETs in thrombolysis resistance, no-reflow, and hemorrhagic injury. Within thrombi, NET-associated chromatin reinforces clot architecture and limits fibrinolysis. Intravascular NETs may impede downstream microvascular flow after recanalization, while NET-related inflammatory signaling may aggravate blood-brain barrier disruption and HT. These findings implicate NETs in impaired recanalization, incomplete tissue reperfusion, and hemorrhagic injury and support their evaluation as an adjunctive target during reperfusion therapy.

Article.Title: S-equol mitigates anxiety-like behaviors associated with acute hyperuricemia by restoring neuronal excitability in the medial prefrontal cortex
Article.Authors: Sun Y.; Duan X.; Shi Y.; You W.; Tang Z.; Gao Y.; Lu H.; Wu X.
Article.Abstract: Hyperuricemia (HUA) is a prevalent metabolic disorder closely linked to neuropsychiatric symptoms, including emotional disturbances. However, the neural mechanisms underlying this association remain largely unexplored. We established a mouse model of acute HUA by administering potassium oxonate (PO) and hypoxanthine (HX) intraperitoneally to investigate its effects on emotional behaviors and neural activity in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). The HUA mice exhibited typical hyperuricemia and renal morphological abnormalities, along with increased anxiety-like behaviors, but showed no alterations in mechanical/thermal pain sensitivity or depressive-like behaviors. Immunofluorescence c-Fos mapping revealed extensive activation in emotion-related brain regions, such as the mPFC, paraventricular thalamus (PVT), anterior insular cortex (aIC), lateral hypothalamus (LH), and basolateral amygdala (BLA). Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings demonstrated that HUA was associated with reduced intrinsic excitability of mPFC layer V/VI pyramidal neurons, indicated by a lower firing rate, higher rheobase, and decreased membrane input resistance. Additionally, it was associated with alterations in the excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) synaptic balance, including changes the frequency of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs). Notably, the reduction in mPFC neuronal excitability was comparable between sexes, although female HUA mice displayed less pronounced synaptic alterations in response to HUA. S-equol, a selective estrogen receptor beta ligand, ameliorated anxiety-like behaviors associated with HUA. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that S-equol appeared to restore the intrinsic excitability of mPFC pyramidal neurons in both sexes, although it did not significantly alter E/I synaptic balance. However, its behavioral effects exhibited sex-dependent differences: S-equol significantly ameliorated anxiety-like behaviors in both sexes, with the specific behavioral domains affected varying between males and females. The results suggest that HUA may be linked to anxiety-like behaviors, potentially involving reduced excitability of mPFC pyramidal neurons. Furthermore, S-equol may exert anxiolytic effects in association with restored neuronal excitability, independently of detectable changes in E/I synaptic balance. Together, this study offers new insights into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying HUA-related emotional disorders and identifies sex-specific potential therapeutic targets.

Article.Title: The PVN astrocyte–excitatory neuron functional axis mediates chronic stress-induced depressive-like behaviors
Article.Authors: Lv Y.; zheng T.; Chen J.; Lu B.; Chen Z.
Article.Abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a common psychiatric disorder, and accumulating evidence suggests that astrocytes play an important role in the regulation of emotional behaviors. However, the mechanisms by which astrocytes in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN) contribute to chronic stress-induced depression remain unclear. In this study, a chronic restraint stress (CRS) mouse model was established, and depressive-like behaviors were assessed using the sucrose preference test, open field test, tail suspension test, and forced swim test. Immunofluorescence staining, chemogenetic manipulation, fiber photometry, transcriptomic analysis, and quantitative real-time PCR were employed to investigate the role of PVN astrocytes and their interactions with excitatory neurons. CRS induced robust depressive-like behaviors and was accompanied by reactive astrocyte activation in the PVN, as evidenced by increased GFAP expression and morphological remodeling. Fiber photometry recordings revealed enhanced astrocytic calcium activity under both basal and stress-related behavioral conditions following CRS exposure. Chemogenetic activation of PVN astrocytes induced depressive-like behaviors in naïve mice, whereas inhibition of astrocytic activity alleviated depressive-like behaviors in CRS mice. Moreover, CRS increased c-Fos expression and calcium activity in CaMKIIα-positive excitatory neurons within the PVN. Bidirectional modulation of astrocyte activity correspondingly altered excitatory neuronal activity, indicating a functional coupling between these cell populations. Transcriptomic screening combined with qPCR validation further identified upregulated expression of the stress-responsive genes Timp4 and Manf in the PVN following CRS. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PVN astrocytes are critical regulators of chronic stress-induced depressive-like behaviors and suggest that the PVN astrocyte-excitatory neuron functional axis represents a potential therapeutic target for depression.

Article.Title: High-fidelity and network-based spatio-temporal mathematical models of Alzheimer’s disease progression and their comparison with PET-SUVR imaging data
Article.Authors: Caon B.; Corti M.; Bonizzoni F.; Antonietti P.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease is the most common neurodegenerative disorder. Its pathological development is connected with the misfolding and accumulation of two toxic proteins: amyloid-β and tau proteins. Mathematical models provide a valuable quantitative tool for monitoring disease progression. In this work, we proposed and compare a novel framework where the spatio-temporal dynamics of amyloid-β and tau proteins is modeled based on employing either three-dimensional patient-specific geometries or through reduced network-based models defined on the brain connectome. More specifically, a high-fidelity biophysical model is proposed on three-dimensional brain geometries reconstructed from magnetic resonance imaging, whereas a network-based reduced formulation is defined on the brain connectome. For both approaches, a suitable numerical discretization is proposed. A sensitivity analysis is presented to quantify the influence of model parameters on protein concentration patterns as well as compare the quality of the predictions. For both approaches, the results are compared with group-level PET-SUVR clinical data using [18F]AZD4694 for amyloid-β and [18F]MK6240 for tau protein. The results indicate that the three-dimensional model provides the most accurate and biologically consistent description of the disease progression, but remains computationally demanding. On the other hand, the reduced graph-based model is cheaper, but it is not always able to achieve reliable results.

Article.Title: Sex-specific classification models for cognitive function in cerebral small vessel disease based on MRE and machine learning
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Kang Y.; Yang M.; Zhu X.; Zhang J.; Huang Y.; Yuan J.; Tan W.
Article.Abstract: Background: Early identification of cognitive impairment is crucial for preventing dementia progression. Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), combined with traditional imaging markers, provides a novel dimension for cognitive assessment in cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD). Objective: To develop machine learning-based classification models for cognitive function in CSVD patients by integrating MRE brain mechanical parameters, white matter hyperintensity burden, and clinical indicators, and to analyze sex differences in model performance. Methods: 100 CSVD subjects underwent MRI scanning including FLAIR for white matter hyperintensities, T1WI for hippocampal atrophy assessment, and MRE for measuring brain mechanical properties across 12 regions. Data were split 8:2 (train:test, stratified); within the training set only, candidate features were ranked by Spearman correlation with MoCA score and a final 13-feature subset was selected by Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE). Subjects were stratified by sex (all-sex: n = 100; male: n = 42; female: n = 58), and 10 machine learning models were compared for each group using 5-fold cross-validation (cvAUC), with SHAP analysis used to interpret feature importance. Results: A 13-feature subset was identified, predominantly MRE stiffness parameters. Naive Bayes performed best in the overall cohort (cvAUC=0.704, 95% CI 0.652-0.756), Extra Trees in males (cvAUC=0.828, 95% CI 0.635-1.000), and XGBoost in females (cvAUC=0.617, 95% CI 0.370-0.863). The female subgroup's confidence interval spanned chance-level discrimination. Using the same feature set, classification accuracy was numerically higher in males than in females. SHAP analysis showed atrophy and white matter hyperintensity burden markers dominated in males, whereas right angular gyrus stiffness and other MRE parameters dominated in the overall cohort and in females. Conclusion: Using an identical feature set and modeling pipeline, machine learning models integrating MRE showed markedly different performance between sexes, indicating that a single sex-agnostic model does not generalize equally to men and women. This performance gap, together with divergent SHAP patterns, underscores the need for sex-stratified modeling in MRE-based cognitive screening for CSVD.

Article.Title: Multidimensional EEG feature fusion and interpretable machine learning for identifying cognitive impairment in depression
Article.Authors: Zhou B.; Wang X.; Wang T.; Shi J.; Huang B.; Zhang Y.; Li G.; Cao X.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive impairment is a clinically important dimension of depression that remains insufficiently assessed using objective measures. Existing assessments largely rely on scale-based screening, whereas EEG-based computational studies are often limited by the use of single-feature representations, window-level data leakage, class imbalance, and limited interpretability. In this study, we developed an interpretable subject-level machine learning framework based on resting-state EEG to identify cognitive impairment in patients with depression and investigate potential electrophysiological markers. A total of 142 patients with depression were categorized as having depression without cognitive impairment (D-NCI) or depression with cognitive impairment (D-CI) based on their Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores. Using 16-channel resting-state EEG recordings, phase lag index, relative power, and fuzzy entropy features were extracted across five frequency bands to characterize functional connectivity, spectral activity, and signal complexity. Five-fold stratified cross-validation at the subject level, ensemble undersampling, and a two-stage SHAP-based feature selection strategy implemented within the training procedure were used to reduce the risk of data leakage, mitigate class imbalance, and improve interpretability. The final model achieved an accuracy of 80.39 ± 7.91%, sensitivity of 83.29 ± 8.30%, specificity of 73.89 ± 15.75%, F1-score of 85.67 ± 5.91%, and AUC of 83.74 ± 9.63%. The retained features were mainly distributed in the beta1 and beta2 bands and reflected alterations in interregional phase synchronization, local oscillatory activity, and signal complexity. These findings support the feasibility of an interpretable EEG-based framework with subject-level data partitioning to assist in identifying cognitive impairment in depression.

Article.Title: NF-κB as a context-dependent inflammatory regulator of glial programs in epilepsy
Article.Authors: Meng J.; Luo W.; He C.; Luo H.; He Y.; Chen C.; Zhang N.; Yu M.; Yu L.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognized as an important contributor to epileptogenesis and seizure recurrence, with microglia and astrocytes serving as major regulators of the inflammatory microenvironment. Among the pathways implicated in glia-mediated inflammation, nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) occupies a central position by integrating danger signals, metabolic stress, and activity-dependent inputs into inflammatory transcriptional responses. However, current evidence indicates that NF-κB should not be viewed as a uniformly pro-inflammatory pathway or as a single therapeutic switch. Rather, its effects vary according to cell type, upstream signaling context, activation dynamics, and disease stage. In this review, we synthesize evidence on NF-κB-associated signaling in epilepsy across damage-sensing, amplification, metabolic stress, purinergic, and ncRNA-associated modules. We distinguish relatively well-supported pro-inflammatory and neurotoxic inflammatory outputs from more provisional interpretations regarding repair-compatible glial responses. We also evaluate therapeutic strategies that directly or indirectly target NF-κB-related signaling and discuss the limitations of inferring causal NF-κB involvement from multi-target compounds or downstream inflammatory markers. Collectively, this review presents NF-κB as a context-dependent regulator of glia-associated inflammatory outputs in epilepsy and proposes module-specific modulation as a working framework for organizing current evidence and guiding future experimental validation.

Article.Title: Age-related patterns in local spontaneous activity measured by fNIRS: Greater unpredictability in infancy, local reorganization in childhood
Article.Authors: Li K.
Article.Abstract: The maturation of the brain is typically described at the whole-brain scale, whereas age-related changes in spontaneous activity within local brain regions have received comparatively little attention. Resting-state regional dynamics (RSRD) are defined as the temporal variability characteristics of activity within a single brain region under the resting state, and can stably reflect the intrinsic properties of spontaneous brain activity. The present study explored age-related changes across two age periods: infants (1-8 months of age) recorded during natural sleep and children (4-15 years of age) recorded during wakeful rest, corresponding to distinct developmental stages of rapid postnatal structural and functional brain development. The results suggested markedly different age-related feature patterns between the two groups: during infancy the predominant change was an increase in unpredictability, with RSRD activity becoming increasingly complex, whereas during childhood the dominant feature was a systematic reorganization of local waveform patterns. Age-related RSRD changes in the prefrontal cortex suggested a linear trend in infancy and a mixed linear-nonlinear trend in childhood, with inter-regional differences in the magnitude of feature changes. Vascular maturation-related indices suggested an association with RSRD feature changes during infancy, but not during childhood, suggesting that vascular factors may play a relatively more prominent role in early developmental stages. External data and exploratory internal cross-validation provided preliminary support for the age-related nature of these features, although further validation in larger, independent cohorts is needed.

Article.Title: Reduced BNIP1 impairs autophagosome-lysosome fusion in hippocampal neurons and contributes to Alzheimer's disease pathology
Article.Authors: Li C.; Zhang M.; Xia H.; Zhi X.; Wang N.; Guo J.; Wang K.; Wang L.; Wang X.; Zhang W.
Article.Abstract: BNIP1 (BCL2‑interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N‑ethylmaleimide‑sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that BNIP1 is a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP‑overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells, screened key interacting proteins of BNIP1 via mass spectrometry, and further performed gain‑ and loss‑of‑function assays using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNA (siRNA) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that, in these experimental models, reduced BNIP1 expression contributes to AD‑related pathological alterations by impairing autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b‑mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. This study suggests that reduced BNIP1 expression is involved in AD‑related pathological alterations.NIP1 (BCL2-interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, which renders BNIP1 a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP-overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells. Mass-spectrometry analysis was performed to screen key interacting proteins of BNIP1. Gain- and loss-of-function experiments were further conducted using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that decreased BNIP1 may act as an important contributing factor mediating AD-associated autophagosome-lysosome fusion defects in these experimental models. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b-mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates aberrant autophagosome-lysosome fusion. This study suggests that BNIP1 serves as a potentially key regulatory protein for mechanistic research into Alzheimer's disease.

Article.Title: Plasma cytokines associated with anxiety comorbidity in adult epilepsy
Article.Authors: Wang K.; Li L.; Yang Y.; Li Z.; Zheng Y.; Liu Y.; Wang T.; Jin L.; Luo Y.; Shan Y.; Zhao G.
Article.Abstract: Background: Anxiety comorbidity in epilepsy may reflect altered immune-brain communication, but the peripheral cytokine profile associated with this phenotype remains insufficiently characterized. We examined plasma cytokine alterations in adult epilepsy and explored whether immune-clinical modelling could identify a stable comorbidity-related signature. Methods: We retrospectively enrolled 124 adults with epilepsy, including 35 with anxiety comorbidity and 89 without. Plasma concentrations of 12 cytokines (IFN-α, IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12p70, and IL-17A) and routine hematological parameters were evaluated. Cytokines were measured using a multiplex bead-based flow fluorescent immunoassay. Group comparisons, univariable logistic regression, LASSO regression with bootstrap stability selection, and multivariable logistic regression were performed. Model performance was assessed as an exploratory integrative framework. Results: Patients with anxiety comorbidity had significantly lower plasma IFN-α levels than those without anxiety comorbidity (P = 0.001). In the final four-variable model, lower IFN-α (adjusted OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.05-0.67; P = 0.009) and lower mean corpuscular hemoglobin (adjusted OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65-0.94; P = 0.009) were independently associated with anxiety comorbidity. IL-4 showed a positive association, whereas IL-17A showed an inverse association. The model showed moderate discrimination and acceptable calibration. Conclusions: Anxiety comorbidity in adult epilepsy is associated with peripheral cytokine alterations, particularly reduced plasma IFN-α. These findings suggest type I interferon-related immune dysregulation within a broader peripheral immune-network imbalance. Prospective validation and mechanistic studies are warranted.

Article.Title: Beyond classification accuracy: Building trustworthy artificial intelligence for clinical electroencephalography
Article.Authors: Hu S.; Huang Y.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) remains important in clinical neuroscience because it records brain activity as a time-resolved physiological process. It offers millisecond temporal resolution, can be used at the bedside and supports prolonged monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded EEG analysis through automated pattern recognition, representation learning, large-scale screening and decision support in epilepsy, sleep medicine, cognitive disorders, psychiatric conditions, intensive care, disorders of consciousness and anaesthesia monitoring. High classification accuracy in a research dataset, however, is not clinical readiness. EEG signals are shaped by physiological state, artefacts, acquisition systems, preprocessing choices and clinical context. Labels may come from expert annotations, diagnostic categories, behavioural scales, treatment responses or long-term outcomes, and these sources do not always define the same biological target. This review argues that EEG-AI translation should be judged by the strength of its evidence, not by technical performance alone. We examine why EEG is valuable yet hard to standardize, how EEG features can serve as candidate biomarkers, and why translational maturity differs across clinical scenarios. We then discuss the evidence gaps behind high-performing models, focusing on target validity, data leakage, confounding, external validation and clinically aligned metrics. Finally, we argue for clinical understandability rather than model interpretability alone, and for human-machine workflows rather than isolated classifiers. Future EEG-AI systems should be assessed by whether their outputs are biologically plausible, externally generalizable, understandable to clinicians and safe in real-world care.

Article.Title: Alterations in brain magnetic susceptibility in children with growth hormone deficiency: A quantitative susceptibility mapping study
Article.Authors: Lin L.; Cheng Y.; Gao X.; Huang S.; Deng C.; Qiu H.; Yang Z.; Qian L.; Chen Q.; Su S.
Article.Abstract: Objectives: Brain magnetic susceptibility in children with growth hormone deficiency (GHD) has not been well characterized. This study investigated regional magnetic susceptibility differences between children with GHD and typically developing (TD) children using quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM). Methods: Forty children with GHD and 40 typically developing (TD) children were recruited in this prospective study. QSM images were reconstructed using the MEDI toolbox, and regional susceptibility values were extracted using the Automated Anatomical Labeling atlas. Group differences in regional QSM values were assessed using analysis of covariance. The associations between significantly altered QSM values and clinical variables were evaluated using Spearman correlation. Results: Compared with TD children, children with GHD showed significantly higher QSM values in left amygdala (mean difference = 4.088 ppb, 95% CI [0.421, 7.755], Cohen's d = 0.50, PFDR = 0.028), bilateral putamen (left: mean difference = 2.285 ppb, 95% CI [0.210, 4.360], Cohen's d = 0.49, PFDR = 0.028; right: mean difference = 2.039 ppb, 95% CI [-0.093, 4.171], Cohen's d = 0.43, PFDR = 0.043), and left pallidum (mean difference = 4.440 ppb, 95% CI [0.956, 7.924], Cohen's d = 0.57, PFDR = 0.030), and significantly lower QSM values in the bilateral mid-cingulate cortex (left: mean difference = -0.806 ppb, 95% CI [-1.577, -0.035], Cohen's d = -0.47, PFDR = 0.040; right: mean difference = -0.781 ppb, 95% CI [-1.538, -0.023], Cohen's d = -0.46, PFDR = 0.045) and right lingual gyrus (mean difference = -1.829 ppb, 95% CI [-2.743, -0.915], Cohen's d = -0.89, PFDR < 0.001). In the GHD group, QSM values in left putamen (r = -0.356, P uncorrected = 0.024, PFDR = 0.104) and left amygdala (r = -0.364, P uncorrected = 0.021, PFDR = 0.104) were negatively correlated with serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), whereas QSM values in the right mid-cingulate cortex were positively correlated with IGF-1 (r = 0.414, P uncorrected = 0.008, PFDR = 0.104). Total scores of Achenbach's child behavior checklist were negatively correlated with IGF-1 (r = -0.391, P uncorrected = 0.019, PFDR = 0.131) and GH peak levels (r = -0.365, P uncorrected = 0.029, PFDR = 0.131). However, these IGF-1-QSM associations did not remain statistically significant after adjustment for age and BMI. Conclusions: These preliminary findings indicate regional alterations in brain magnetic susceptibility in pediatric GHD; however, the observed IGF-1-QSM associations require confirmation in larger, adequately adjusted longitudinal studies. (Prospectively registered trials: number: ChiCTR2100048109; date: 2021-07).

Article.Title: Crocin attenuates dopaminergic neuronal injury in 6-OHDA-induced PD rats: Associations with mitochondrial protection and p38/p53 signaling
Article.Authors: Cui H.; Li H.; Wang Y.; Han Y.; Tan J.; Li J.; Li X.; Zhang J.; Wang T.; Du W.; Wang Y.; Tan Y.; Zhao Q.
Article.Abstract: Background: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the degeneration of dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc). Crocin (CRO) has been reported to possess antioxidant and neuroprotective properties. However, whether its neuroprotective effects are associated with preserved mitochondrial integrity and alterations in p38/p53 signaling remains unclear. Methods: A unilateral rat model of PD was established by stereotaxic injection of 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) into the right striatum. Rats were randomly assigned to four groups: control, 6-OHDA, 6-OHDA+CRO (30 mg/kg), and 6-OHDA+levodopa (L-DOPA; 50 mg/kg). Motor function was evaluated using the beam balance, rotarod, and cylinder tests. Nissl staining was performed to quantify neurons in the SNc, while tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) immunohistochemistry was used to assess DA neurons in the SNc and DA fibers in the striatum. Mitochondrial ultrastructure was examined using transmission electron microscopy(TEM), and mitochondrial function was assessed by measuring ATP content and mitochondrial complex I activity in substantia nigra (SN) tissue. Oxidative stress markers were measured in serum and tissues from the SN and striatum using commercial assay kits. Protein levels of TH, p53, total and phosphorylated p38, Bax, Bcl-2, and caspase-3 were determined by Western blotting. Results: CRO treatment significantly ameliorated 6-OHDA-induced motor deficits (p < 0.01, p < 0.001, p < 0.0001) and attenuated reductions in TH-positive neuron counts in the SNc (p < 0.01) and striatal TH optical density (p < 0.01). TEM revealed that CRO alleviated mitochondrial ultrastructural damage and increased the mitochondrial aspect ratio (p < 0.001). These improvements were accompanied by increased ATP content (p < 0.01) and mitochondrial complex I activity (p < 0.05) in SN tissue. Furthermore, CRO increased CAT activity and GSH levels while reducing MDA levels in serum, SN, and striatum (p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 0.001), while SOD activity increased significantly in both brain regions (p < 0.0001). Western blot analysis showed that CRO increased TH protein expression (p < 0.01), reduced the p-p38/p38 (p < 0.05) and Bax/Bcl-2 (p < 0.05) ratios, and decreased p53 (p < 0.05) and caspase-3 (p < 0.01) protein levels compared with the 6-OHDA group. Conclusions: CRO attenuated motor deficits and nigrostriatal DA damage in a 6-OHDA-induced rat model of PD. These neuroprotective effects were associated with reduced oxidative stress, preserved mitochondrial morphology and function, and decreased p38 phosphorylation and p53 expression. These findings support further investigation of CRO as a potential neuroprotective compound for PD.

Article.Title: Neuroprotective effects of calcitriol after experimental ischemic stroke induction via modulation of glutamate excitotoxicity, MMP-9 activity, and oxidative stress
Article.Authors: Rahmatipour S.; Bayat R.; Rezvani Z.; Vahidinia Z.; Tameh A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Ischemic stroke triggers detrimental cascades, including glutamate excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. This study evaluated the neuroprotective potential of calcitriol during the acute phase of stroke, focusing on inflammatory damage and modulation of glutamate transporters. Methods: Male Wistar rats underwent 1-h middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) and were assigned to Sham, tMCAO + Vehicle, and tMCAO + Calcitriol groups. Calcitriol (1 μg/kg) was administered at 30 min, 24 h, and 48 h post-stroke. After 72 h, behavioral outcomes, infarct volume, and histological alterations in cortical region were assessed utilizing Nissl staining. Cortical mRNA expression of glutamate-aspartate transporter (GLAST), glutamate transporter-1 (GLT-1), and excitatory amino acid transporter 3 (EAAT3) was evaluated via RT-PCR. Serum Matrix Metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) activity was measured using gelatin zymography, and oxidative stress biomarkers malondialdehyde (MDA), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and nitric oxide (NO) were quantified in the penumbra. Molecular docking simulations explored calcitriol-MMP-9 binding affinity. Results: Calcitriol significantly reduced infarct volume, improved neurobehavioral scores, and mitigated morphological neuronal damage. It elevated TAC while suppressing MDA and NO levels. In line with docking simulations predicting a moderate binding affinity of -6.5 kcal/mol, a marked decrease in serum MMP-9 enzymatic activity was observed. Furthermore, calcitriol treatment significantly reduced GLAST, GLT-1, and EAAT3 cortical gene expression compared to the untreated ischemia group. Conclusion: Calcitriol administration attenuates acute ischemic brain injury. This neuroprotective effect is associated with parallel downregulations of glutamate transporter gene expression, suppression of penumbral oxidative stress, and reduced serum MMP-9 enzymatic activity.

Article.Title: Sirt1 modulates p53‑acetylation‑dependent Yy2‑Elf‑1‑associated NLRP3‑relevant signaling in CUMS‑evoked aggravated Alzheimer’s disease‑related phenotypes
Article.Authors: Chai F.; Shan Q.; Hu Y.; Liu L.; Zou J.; Xia G.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Depressive disorder (DD) is recognized as an important comorbidity of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is associated with aggravated cognitive impairment and neuroinflammatory responses; however, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unknown. This study investigated the role of the Sirtuin 1 (Sirt1)/p53 acetylation/Yin-Yang 2 (Yy2)/E74-like ETS transcription factor 1 (Elf-1)/NLR family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) axis in DD-associated AD phenotypes and evaluated the effects of resveratrol intervention. Bioinformatics analysis, CoIP-MS, ChIP-seq, and dual-luciferase assays were applied to identify and validate the regulatory relationships among these molecules. APP/PS1 double-transgenic mice subjected to chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) and LPS-stimulated BV2 microglia were used as in vivo and in vitro models. Behavioral tests demonstrated that CUMS-induced depressive-like stress aggravated cognitive deficits and depression- and anxiety-related behavioral abnormalities in AD mice. Sirt1 expression was decreased, whereas acetylated p53 (ac-p53), Yy2, Elf-1, and NLRP3 levels were elevated in the hippocampus of DD + AD mice and activated BV2 microglia, accompanied by enhanced inflammatory and oxidative stress responses. Resveratrol treatment reduced p53 acetylation, suppressed the Yy2/Elf-1/NLRP3 pathway, alleviated inflammatory and oxidative stress responses, and improved behavioral deficits. Yy2 overexpression partially reversed the effects of resveratrol treatment. Collectively, our findings suggest that reduced Sirt1 expression promotes p53 acetylation and activates the Yy2/Elf‑1‑associated NLRP3‑relevant axis (the regulatory link between Elf‑1 and NLRP3 requires further experimental validation), contributing to neuroinflammatory responses and behavioural deficits in CUMS‑aggravated AD‑related phenotypes. Resveratrol treatment partially restored Sirt1‑related signalling and ameliorated these pathological manifestations, although further studies are required to determine its therapeutic potential and exclude Sirt1‑independent effects.

Article.Title: CD55-targeted modulation of C3-mediated microglia polarization improves perioperative neurocognitive disorders in male mice
Article.Authors: Tian Q.; Zhang H.; Zhang X.; Huang H.; Sun R.; Cui S.; Shao J.; Song L.; Qie X.
Article.Abstract: Background: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) are common postoperative complications driven by neuroinflammation and an imbalance in microglial M1/M2 polarization. Complement component 3 (C3) is elevated in PND, while CD55 inhibits C3 activation. Whether CD55 regulates PND via C3 remains unclear. Methods: A PND mouse model and an lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced BV2 model were established. Lentivirus-mediated CD55/C3 overexpression was performed. Cognitive function, neuronal injury, inflammation, microglial polarization, and CD55/C3 expression were assessed using behavioral tests, HE staining, ELISA, immunofluorescence, RT-qPCR, and WB. Results: PND mice exhibited cognitive impairment, hippocampal neuronal damage, elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and C3, and reduced CD55 expression. Overexpression of CD55 improved cognitive function, alleviated damage and inflammation, and suppressed C3. It also restored the balance of M1/M2 markers in BV2 cells. Overexpression of C3 reversed the protective effects of CD55 both in vitro and in vivo. Conclusion: CD55 alleviates PND by regulating complement C3, which may be related to promoting the polarization of microglia toward the M2 phenotype. We have preliminarily identified a potential regulatory target for PND.

Article.Title: Oxytocin receptor activation enhances SK channel-mediated afterhyperpolarization in MPOA neurons of maternally experienced mice
Article.Authors: Ma G.; Yang X.; Huang Q.; Li J.; Mao H.; Xue Q.; Hu E.; Wu S.; Qi C.; Wang W.
Article.Abstract: Maternal experience induces significant behavioral changes; however, the underlying cellular mechanisms within the medial preoptic area (MPOA), a central hub for regulating maternal behavior, remain poorly understood. Here, we combined behavioral assays (e.g., pup retrieval, crouching, nesting, and grooming) with in vitro whole-cell patch-clamp recordings to examine how maternal experience alters the intrinsic excitability of MPOA neurons and to identify the underlying mechanisms. Adult female mice were divided into three groups: virgin females, dams (experienced dams), and co-housed virgins (virgins co-housed with a dam and her pups for five days). Maternal behavior and the intrinsic properties of MPOA neurons were assessed in all three groups. We first compared virgin females with experienced dams, and then tested whether the maternal experience-dependent changes in MPOA neurons were reproduced in co-housed virgins by social co-housing. Our results revealed that MPOA neurons from both dams and co-housed virgins exhibited reduced excitability and increased afterhyperpolarization (AHP) amplitude. This enhancement was mediated by small-conductance calcium-activated potassium (SK) channels, as it was abolished by the SK channel blocker apamin. Furthermore, direct application of an oxytocin receptor agonist to MPOA neurons from virgin females induced similar functional changes, replicating the physiological profile observed in dams. Notably, this oxytocin-induced enhancement of SK channel activity was observed in glutamatergic, but not GABAergic, MPOA neurons, indicating that the effect is not uniform across cell types. These findings suggest that oxytocin modulates SK channel activity to reduce the excitability of a subpopulation of MPOA neurons. Because this effect was prominent in VGLUT2-positive neurons, it may facilitate maternal behavior by reducing the activity of neurons that restrain maternal behavior, a candidate mechanism by which hormonal and experiential signals converge on MPOA excitability.

Article.Title: Glutamatergic dysfunction in major depressive disorder: From receptor and glial abnormalities to circuit pathology and mechanism-based therapeutic strategies
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Chen Q.; Long Y.; Huang S.; Li C.; Zhu D.; Ben X.
Article.Abstract: Major depressive disorder is a heterogeneous psychiatric disorder that cannot be fully explained by classical monoamine-deficiency models. Increasing evidence indicates that glutamatergic dysfunction provides a central framework for linking molecular, glial, synaptic, and circuit-level abnormalities in depression. This narrative review focuses on glutamatergic dysregulation as the organizing mechanism of major depressive disorder. We summarize core abnormalities involving context-dependent N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor dysfunction, impaired α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor-mediated synaptic plasticity, altered metabotropic glutamate receptor signaling, and disrupted astrocytic excitatory amino acid transporter 2-mediated glutamate clearance. These changes converge on excitation-inhibition imbalance, leading to unstable cortical-limbic activity and contributing to emotional dysregulation, anhedonia, cognitive impairment, and impaired stress adaptation. We further discuss upstream mechanisms that regulate glutamatergic dysfunction, including brain-derived neurotrophic factor/mammalian target of rapamycin signaling, neuroinflammation, epigenetic regulation, and microbiota-gut-brain axis-related peripheral crosstalk. At the circuit level, we emphasize abnormalities in the prefrontal cortex-amygdala, amygdala-nucleus accumbens, prefrontal cortex-hippocampus, and lateral habenula pathways. We also consider how monoaminergic and opioid systems modulate glutamate-dependent synaptic and reward-circuit plasticity. Finally, we review therapeutic implications, including ketamine and related N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor modulators, α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor facilitation, astrocyte-targeted strategies, anti-inflammatory interventions, circuit-based neuromodulation, and biomarker-guided patient stratification. By centering diverse pathological findings around glutamatergic dysfunction, this review provides a focused mechanistic framework for understanding major depressive disorder and developing precision, mechanism-based treatments.

Article.Title: Characterizing white matter and structural brain network alterations in children with growth hormone deficiency using diffusion tensor imaging
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Tan H.; Lin D.; Zhang G.; Li K.; Wang J.; Zheng H.; Wang H.; Zheng W.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: To characterize white matter microstructure and structural brain network topology in children with growth hormone deficiency (GHD) using diffusion tensor imaging and explore their associations with clinical indicators. Methods: A total of 77 short-stature children (GHD = 50, idiopathic short stature [ISS] = 27) and 40 healthy controls (HC) underwent 3D-T1WI and DTI. Nineteen participants were excluded due to poor data quality (10 in the GHD group, 4 in the ISS group, and 5 in the HC group), yielding a final analytical cohort of 40 children with GHD, 23 with ISS, and 35 healthy controls. Tract-Based Spatial Statistics and graph-theoretical analysis were applied to characterize white matter microstructure and network topological properties. Clinical metrics including bone age and pituitary volume were collected. Results: Children with GHD showed reduced fractional anisotropy together with elevated mean and radial diffusivity relative to controls. Children with ISS showed elevated mean and radial diffusivity without a reduction in fractional anisotropy, and their diffusivity elevations exceeded those observed in the GHD group. Graph-theoretical analysis revealed that the GHD group had significantly higher global efficiency and lower characteristic path length than the HC group, as well as lower clustering coefficient than the ISS group. Rich-club findings were contingent on both the method used to define core nodes and the connection retention thresholds applied to backbone networks. Nodal analysis identified significantly higher betweenness centrality of the left insula in ISS compared with both the GHD and HC groups. Significant associations were observed between white matter microstructural properties, network connectivity, and clinical variables, including age, bone age, and bone age delay. Conclusion: Children with GHD exhibit altered white matter microstructure and global organization of the structural brain network, which differed from the pattern observed in ISS, and these imaging measures were associated with age, bone age, and bone age delay; given the cross-sectional design, causal inference remains unwarranted.

Article.Title: A single post-stress dose of caffeine preserves threat-safety discrimination but not fear extinction in rats exposed to single prolonged stress
Article.Authors: Lin C.; Chen C.; Chen Y.; Cheng Y.; Chen H.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by impaired fear extinction and fear overgeneralization, yet no early pharmacological intervention has been established. Because the pathophysiology of PTSD develops over a modifiable period after trauma, we tested whether a single moderate dose of caffeine (30mg/kg) administered immediately after single prolonged stress (SPS) protects fear regulation and its underlying neurochemistry in male rats. The abilities of threat-safety discrimination and fear extinction were assessed using a Pavlovian discriminative fear conditioning paradigm, and tissue levels of serotonin (5-HT), dopamine (DA), norepinephrine (NE), and neuropeptide Y (NPY) were quantified in the hippocampus, medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and amygdala. The results demonstrated that caffeine produced a behavioral dissociation: it restored threat-safety discrimination but did not rescue the extinction retention deficits. This selectivity was mirrored neurochemically. Caffeine restored SPS-induced reductions in hippocampal 5-HT and DA and in mPFC NPY, but did not restore hippocampal NE or mPFC monoamines, and no changes were detected in the amygdala. These findings suggest that a single post-stress dose of caffeine acts through region-specific neurochemical pathways rather than providing global protection. Therefore, caffeine emerges as a promising and accessible candidate for early post-stress intervention targeting fear overgeneralization.

Article.Title: XBP-1-mediated suppression of EAAT2 drives glutamate dyshomeostasis and neuronal injury in CORT-induced depression
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Wang S.; Ling Y.; Li L.; Dong M.; Feng S.; Xu H.; Zhang X.; Gu L.; Ma R.; Chen M.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a prevalent psychiatric disorder characterized by significant social and individual burden. Hippocampal calcium overload and glutamate excitotoxicity are key pathological features, with excitatory amino acid transporter 2 (EAAT2) playing a pivotal role in glutamate clearance. Emerging evidence implicates endoplasmic reticulum stress and its downstream mediator X-box binding protein 1 (XBP-1) in neuronal dysfunction; however, their interaction in depression remains unclear. Here, a corticosterone (CORT)-induced mouse model of depression and a primary hippocampal neuron model were employed to investigate the relationship between XBP-1 and EAAT2. Depressive-like behaviors, neuronal injury, and synaptic and mitochondrial alterations were assessed using behavioral assays, histological and ultrastructural analyses, and functional recordings. CORT exposure was associated with increased hippocampal XBP-1s expression, reduced EAAT2 expression, and elevated glutamate content in hippocampal tissue homogenates. In CORT-treated primary hippocampal neurons, XBP-1 knockdown restored EAAT2 expression and reduced extracellular glutamate accumulation and oxidative stress. In mice, Toyocamycin treatment partially improved depressive-like behaviors and attenuated hippocampal neuronal injury, accompanied by reduced XBP-1s and increased EAAT2 protein levels. These findings support a functional relationship between XBP-1 signaling and EAAT2 expression in the experimental models studied. Whether EAAT2 mediates the protective effects of XBP-1 suppression remains to be established.

Article.Title: Recent advances on the role of microRNAs in Alzheimer's Disease: Unraveling Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential
Article.Authors: Ardjmand A.; Khoshnam S.; Zarjani A.; Arjmand A.; Forutan G.; Vastegani S.
Article.Abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are now recognized as key regulators of the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and offer promising opportunities for early detection and treatment. Some miRNAs are responsible for controlling and modulating neuroinflammatory responses, while others directly affect the process of amyloid beta (Aβ) production. Their relative stability in biological fluids supports their potential use in diagnostic panels; however, their diagnostic performance requires further validation before clinical application. From a therapeutic perspective, miRNA antagonists and mimetics have been shown in preclinical studies to reduce amyloid pathology, ameliorate cognitive impairment, and stimulate neurogenesis in animal models of AD. In this review article, we summarize the evidence on the diverse and multifaceted functions of miRNAs in key aspects of AD pathology, including Aβ synthesis via BACE1 and APP regulation, tau aggregation and phosphorylation, APOE4 signaling cascades, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and synaptic plasticity. By linking mechanistic understanding of miRNAs with potential translational applications, miRNA-based strategies may offer promising opportunities for improving the early diagnosis and treatment of AD. However, further preclinical validation and rigorous clinical studies are needed to establish their safety, efficacy, and clinical utility.

Article.Title: Dexmedetomidine Suppresses Cholinergic Neurons in the Basal Forebrain through Distinct Pre- and Postsynaptic Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Wu S.; Li J.; Li Y.; Liu M.
Article.Abstract: Dexmedetomidine (Dex) is a selective α2-adrenoceptor (α2-AR) agonist commonly used for clinical sedation. The cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain (BF) are key components of the ascending arousal systems, playing an essential role in regulating the sleep-wake cycle. However, the precise mechanism by which Dex modulates the activity of these neurons remains poorly understood. To investigate the effects of Dex on identified BF cholinergic neurons, we performed whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in acute mouse brain slices. Intrinsic membrane properties and synaptic responses were assessed before and after Dex administration. Pharmacological agents were applied to identify receptor and ion channel contributions. We found that Dex significantly reduced the excitability of BF cholinergic neurons. This inhibitory effect was mediated through postsynaptic activation of G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels and concurrent inhibition of low-threshold T-type Ca2+ currents without altering their gating kinetics. Additionally, Dex facilitated presynaptic GABAergic transmission onto cholinergic neurons, further contributing to their inhibition. All observed effects were dependent on α2-AR activation. In vivo fiber photometry further confirmed that Dex dynamically depresses BF cholinergic activity in real time, closely aligning with behavioral sedation. These findings elucidate cellular and ion channel mechanisms of Dex on BF cholinergic neurons, offering valuable mechanistic clues regarding its neuropharmacological actions on sleep-wake and arousal-related circuits.

Article.Title: Ketamine Attenuates TNF-α-Induced Blood-Brain Barrier Damage and Neuroinflammation in Association with NF-κB Pathway
Article.Authors: Wang Q.; Qiu M.; Gou X.; Saadoon B.; Hao X.; Jin Z.; Chen Y.; Zhang Y.; Liu K.; Liu W.; Qin S.; Bin Deng N/A.
Article.Abstract: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome is a complex clinical syndrome driven by dysregulated inflammatory cascades, and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) acts as a core upstream mediator in its pathogenesis. In this study, we established a mouse model of acute TNF-α-induced systemic inflammatory brain injury via a single tail vein injection of TNF-α. Ketamine (KET) (20mg/kg) was administered intraperitoneally 20min prior to the insult, and phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA), a protein kinase C activator that can indirectly trigger nuclear factor-κB p65 (NF-κB) pathway activation, was applied in vivo for pharmacological validation. In vivo, behavioral performance, neuronal histopathological damage, blood-brain barrier (BBB) structural and functional integrity, and microglial activation were evaluated; in vitro, inflammatory responses were assessed in TNF-α-stimulated BV2 microglia. KET pretreatment significantly alleviated TNF-α-induced behavioral deficits, mitigated neuronal damage and preserved Nissl body integrity, maintained the continuity of tight junction proteins in cerebrovascular endothelium, reduced BBB permeability, and suppressed microglial overactivation and pro-inflammatory mediator expression. Mechanistically, KET inhibited NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation in both cerebrovascular endothelium and microglia and downregulated endothelial matrix metalloproteinase-9; these effects were partially reversed by PMA co-treatment. Collectively, prophylactic KET administration exerts BBB-protective and anti-neuroinflammatory effects in association with NF-κB pathway inhibition, providing preclinical evidence for the prevention of inflammatory brain injury in the context of systemic TNF-α elevation.

Article.Title: EEG Microstate Alterations and Their Association with Cognitive Performance in Late-Onset Epilepsy of Unknown Etiology: Comparison with Alzheimer’s Disease
Article.Authors: Huang J.; Wan H.; Jiang W.; Chen Y.; Jiang B.; Bi M.; Wang Z.; Zheng K.; Shao X.
Article.Abstract: Background: Cognitive impairment is common in late-onset epilepsy of unknown etiology (LOEU), but its electrophysiological correlates and relationship to Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain unclear. We compared resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) microstate dynamics among LOEU, AD, and cognitively normal (CN) groups and examined their associations with cognitive performance. Methods: Eyes-closed 32-channel resting-state EEG recordings were analyzed from 60 patients with LOEU, 65 with AD, and 60 CN participants. Four canonical microstate classes (A-D) were identified. Group differences in microstate parameters were tested with false discovery rate correction. Associations with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores were examined using multivariable interaction models adjusted for age, sex, education, and cerebral small vessel disease burden. Results: Microstate B duration was longer in LOEU and AD than in CN (Holm-adjusted p=0.011 and 0.016), whereas microstate C occurrence was lower in both patient groups (p=0.001 and 0.018). Microstate D duration was longer in LOEU than in CN and AD (both p=0.038). For microstate A duration, the group interaction survived false discovery rate correction for MMSE (q=0.0255) but not MoCA (q=0.122). In LOEU, longer microstate A duration was associated with lower MoCA and MMSE scores. Pairwise slope comparisons were more negative in LOEU than in CN for both outcomes, whereas LOEU-AD slope differences were not significant. Conclusions: LOEU showed altered resting-state EEG microstate dynamics that partly overlapped with those observed in AD, alongside a group difference in microstate D duration. Microstate A duration was associated with cognitive performance in LOEU, although this association did not significantly differ from that observed in AD. These findings support further investigation of EEG microstates as electrophysiological correlates of cognitive dysfunction in LOEU while also highlighting overlap with AD.

Article.Title: Enhanced functional connectivity in right precuneus after high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in Parkinson’s disease patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain
Article.Authors: Chen L.; Zhuang S.; Luo Y.; Liu M.; Chen J.; Wang E.; Chen Y.; Mao C.; Liu C.
Article.Abstract: Objective: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) can relieve chronic musculoskeletal pain (MSP) in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Methods: In this double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 43 PD patients with MSP were randomly assigned to received 10 sessions of neuronavigated 10-Hz rTMS (n=22) or sham stimulation (n=21) over the bilateral primary motor cortex (M1). Clinical assessments were performed at baseline (T0), after the tenth session (T1), and at 1-month (T2) and 3-month (T3) follow-up; functional MRI (fMRI) was acquired at T0 and T1. Results: In the rTMS group, compared to T0, King's Parkinson's Disease Pain Scale (KPPS) and Visual Analog Scale scores decreased significantly at T1, T2, and T3 (p < 0.05). MDS-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) III, Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA), Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD), and Parkinson's Disease Sleep Scale (PDSS) scores were significantly lower at T1 and T2 than at T0 (p < 0.05), but not at T3 (p > 0.05). No significant correlations were found between KPPS and MDS-UPDRS III, HAMA, HAMD, or PDSS scores (p > 0.05) alterations in the rTMS group. fMRI revealed that patients exhibited decreased amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations in the left cuneus and enhanced functional connectivity between the left cuneus and the right precuneus after rTMS treatment. The sham group showed no significant changes in clinical scores or fMRI. Conclusions: High-frequency rTMS over bilateral M1 was associated with improvement of MSP in PD, accompanied by reduced local neural activity in the left cuneus and enhanced connectivity between the left cuneus and the right precuneus. These findings are preliminary and hypothesis generating.

Article.Title: The probability of self-related stimuli modulates heartbeat-evoked potentials
Article.Authors: Huang Y.; Xie M.; Bao H.; Liu Y.; Huang J.; Qin P.; Han J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Interoception, the cortical processing of visceral signals, has been proposed as a foundation of self-processing. Heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEPs) provide a measure of interoceptive processing and have been linked to self-processing, but whether HEP modulations reflect self-specificity rather than familiarity and depend on probabilistic context remains unclear. We recorded EEG and ECG during passive listening to subject’s own names (SON), familiar names (FN), and unfamiliar name (UN) under equal- and biased-probability conditions. In the equal-probability condition, HEP amplitudes were more positive for SON than for FN and UN over centro-parietal-occipital sites at 164–242 and 258–296 ms after the R peak, whereas FN and UN did not differ. This self-specific pattern was not detected under biased probabilities. Within-name comparisons revealed probability-related HEP effects for SON and UN with distinct spatiotemporal characteristics, indicating that stimulus probability did not produce a uniform effect across name types. The late positive potential showed a comparable probability-dependent self-specific pattern, and SON-evoked LPP amplitudes positively covaried with HEP amplitudes during SON perception across conditions. These findings indicate that self-specific HEP modulations depend on probabilistic context and is associated with relatively late external self-related processing, highlighting a context-sensitive relationship between interoceptive and external self-related processing.

Article.Title: Mirroring emotional faces: Functional connectivity of the Mirror Neuron System in young children and adults
Article.Authors: Ferragina F.; Safar K.; Broeders E.; Rhodes N.; Taylor M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Mirror Neuron System (MNS) underlies important neurocognitive functions, such as imitation learning, social cognition and empathy, and may facilitate the recognition of emotional expressions via motor simulation. However, its development remains poorly understood. This study investigated functional connectivity maturation of MNS-related areas between early childhood and adulthood during an emotional faces task. Using the innovative magnetoencephalography approach of optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs), we assessed whole-brain connectivity with 8 bilateral regions of interest (ROIs), representing the MNS, in 57 typically developing children aged 3-to-5 years and 27 adults. We applied both classical network-based statistic (NBS) and its more recent approach incorporating machine learning, NBS-Predict. We observed networks of increased connectivity after face presentation in both adults and children in broadband, as well as in the alpha and beta bands; only adults recruited a theta band network. The networks included connections between MNS ROIs and key limbic, prefrontal, parietal and occipital areas. Notably, adults exhibited a network of increased connectivity in broadband and theta band, with a trend towards right-lateralisation compared to children. Results were validated with NBS-Predict, with a comparable subnetwork exhibiting predictive features for classification between children and adults. Our findings suggest that the network involving MNS ROIs during observation of facial expressions evolves between early childhood and adulthood, consistent with right-hemisphere specialisation in emotional processing.

Article.Title: Smiling Muscle Stimulation Alters Neural Processing During Emotional Face Comparison
Article.Authors: Baker J.; Lisi M.; Elsenaar A.; Mehu M.; Korb S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Within embodied and predictive-processing frameworks, emotional face perception is informed by bodily states, such as proprioceptive facial feedback. In line with this, our earlier work showed that activation of smiling muscles with facial neuromuscular electrical stimulation (fNMES) can induce a happiness bias in emotional face perception, and reduce visual face processing demands. Here, we extended this research to examine whether the same facial muscle stimulation biases the emotional representation of a face when it serves as a perceptual template (prime) for comparison with a following target face. In a delayed matching-to-sample task, 53 participants judged which of two sequentially presented faces appeared happier (or more female, in a control sex task). On half of trials, fNMES was applied bilaterally to the zygomaticus major during encoding of the prime face. Performance was held constant using an adaptive staircase. fNMES altered comparison judgments only when emotion was task-relevant, flattening the relation between emotion difference and choice. Across tasks, fNMES reduced N170 amplitudes and increased Early Posterior Negativity (EPN) differences between happy and sad faces. The prime EPN predicted choice only when emotion was task-relevant, whereas fNMES modulated emotion effects on the target N170 only in the control task. Facial feedback may thus increase the perceptual salience of emotion-relevant information, with task-dependent consequences for decisions.
