Article.Title: Deep learning identification of SST teleconnections driving early-winter North Atlantic climate
Article.Authors: Galván Fraile V.; Polo I.; Martín-Rey M.; Rodríguez-Fonseca B.; Alonso Balmaseda M.
Article.Abstract: Seasonal predictability over the North Atlantic-European (NAE) sector is strongly modulated by the background climate state, particularly in early winter. In this season, different El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) teleconnections have been reported before and after the 1990s. However, these studies rely on linear analysis, and the reasons for this lack of stationarity and its implications for seasonal forecasting have not yet been fully assessed. Here, we evaluate the non-stationarity of early-winter ENSO teleconnections over the NAE using a non-linear framework, the Neural Network forecast application (NN4CAST). The NN4CAST model predicts November-December mean sea-level pressure anomalies from October sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies. The neural network achieves skill comparable to the ECMWF seasonal forecasting system (SEAS5), and even exceeds it in certain regions like the NAE, despite relying only on October SST predictors. The model skilfully predicts the dominant NAE atmospheric variability modes, with a predictability that is strongly period-dependent. In particular, significant skill is found over the North Atlantic Oscillation centres of action during 1970–1995, especially for the Iceland region, whereas for the East Atlantic pattern, the improvement comes in recent decades (1996–2019). This teleconnection shift is mainly associated with Pacific SST anomalies, with recent decades marked by an intensified Southeast Asian Rossby wave source and a southward displacement of the North Atlantic jet stream. Our results demonstrate that explainable artificial intelligence can identify state-dependent SST precursors of NAE predictability, bridging data-driven and mechanistic understanding of climate teleconnections.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: ENSO teleconnections; East Atlantic pattern; North Atlantic Oscillation; Rossby wave source; sea level pressure anomalies; seasonal predictability; North Atlantic jet stream; explainable AI; non-stationarity; sea surface temperature anomalies

Article.Title: A lightweight graph neural network with decoupled static and dynamic representations for temporal link prediction in social networks
Article.Authors: Han L.; Li M.; Hsieh M.; Li K.; Pop F.; Li K.
Article.Abstract: Temporal Link Prediction (TLP) is a key task in social network research, aiming to predict future network links based on the relative behaviors of previous network changes. The various interaction patterns and nonlinear characteristics of the dynamic network pose challenges for the design of accurate general prediction algorithms. With the development of deep learning technology, graph neural networks (GNNs) have been widely applied to solve graph-related problems and have achieved significant results. However, solving the TLP problem based on GNNs usually involves complex memory update mechanisms, multi-layer iterative message passing paradigms, and reliance on negative sampling strategies, all of which contribute to the overall model’s complexity. To reduce model complexity while maintaining high accuracy, this paper proposes a lightweight temporal aggregation graph neural network model (LAGNN) that uses only a single layer to solve the TLP problem. This model decouples the static identity representation of nodes from their dynamic interaction context, simplifying the message passing mechanism and training objective while preserving the accuracy of temporal link predictions and significantly improving efficiency. The core of LAGNN lies in decoupling representation modeling: static embeddings capture inherent node identities, and a temporal attention module aggregates historical neighbor information to generate context‑aware dynamic node representations. During training, LAGNN optimizes an objective function that maximizes the similarity between positive samples, thereby avoiding the inherent instability and bias of negative sampling strategies. At inference time, the model uses the static embeddings of all candidate nodes and only needs to compute the dynamic representation of the source node. Experimental results on temporal link prediction tasks using four public dynamic social network datasets demonstrate that, despite using only a single‑layer architecture, LAGNN achieves predictive accuracy comparable to or even surpassing state-of-the-art multi-layer methods while also validating its efficiency and stability advantages.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Advanced Graph Neural Networks; Physics and Astronomy > Statistical and Nonlinear Physics > Complex Network Analysis Techniques; Computer Science > Information Systems > Recommender Systems and Techniques

Article.Title: Green and sustainable synthesis of pyrazolyl-coumarin via lemon juice catalysis under solvent-free mechanochemistry conditions
Article.Authors: Abdel-Aziem A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract In this study, a green and efficient synthetic strategy has been developed for the preparation of pyrazolyl–coumarin derivatives using lemon juice as a natural, biodegradable acid catalyst under aqueous conditions. Initially, pyrazolyl-coumarins 4 and 5 were synthesized by condensation of 3-(2-oxo-2 H-chromen-3-yl)-1-phenyl-1 H -pyrazole-4-carbaldehyde ( 1 ) with benzyl or methyl hydrazinecarbodithioates ( 2 , 3 ) in freshly squeezed lemon juice (Citrus limon) as a dual natural acid catalyst and aqueous reaction medium under boiling conditions for 10 min. Subsequently, the target pyrazolyl-coumarin-linked thiadiazoles 7a–d were obtained through a solvent-free mechanochemical grinding reaction of intermediates 4 and/ or 5 with hydrazonoyl halides 6a-d in the presence of three drops of triethylamine (TEA) within only 5 min. This green approach reduces the reaction time, eliminates the need for hazardous organic solvents and affords products high yields. Lemon juice contains natural citric acid which acts as an efficient, biodegradable catalyst that facilitates the condensation reaction.
Article.TopicFields: Chemistry > Organic Chemistry > Multicomponent Synthesis of Heterocycles; Chemistry > Organic Chemistry > Heterocyclic Compound Synthesis and Bioactivity; Chemistry > Organic Chemistry > Synthesis of heterocyclic compounds

Article.Title: Genotoxic stress responses in wild-type and Nijmegen Breakage Syndrome hiPSC and NPC models of early development
Article.Authors: de Amorim V.; Lofrano A.; Szepanowski L.; Wruck W.; Graffmann N.; Adjaye J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Benzo[a]pyrene diol epoxide (BPDE), a metabolite of Benzo[a]pyrene, is a byproduct of incomplete combustion of organic matter. The accumulation of BPDE-DNA bulky adducts can lead to mutations caused by DNA base-pair substitutions. Although the effects of BPDE on somatic cells have been described, its harmful effects on early human development have not been studied. Here, we investigated the effect of BPDE on human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and their differentiated neural progenitor cells (NPCs) as a model of early embryonic development. Furthermore, we compared hiPSCs and NPCs derived from patient suffering from Nijmegen Breakage Syndrome (NBS), which is a chromosomal instability disorder characterized by defective DNA repair and increased risk of malignancies. Transcriptome and selected protein analysis indicated that hiPSCs compared to NPCs are more sensitive to BPDE exposure. The affected biological processes included p53-mediated DNA damage response, DNA repair by lesion bypass, cell cycle checkpoints and extrinsic apoptosis. In addition, NBS-derived cells exhibited a reduced apoptotic response and a distinct p53 response compared their healthy counterparts. Overall, this iPSC-based model provides insights into the cellular responses to BPDE during early human development in both healthy individuals and NBS patients.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: benzo[a]pyrene diol epoxide; neural progenitor cells; Nijmegen breakage syndrome; human induced pluripotent stem cells; cell cycle checkpoints; benzo[a]pyrene; embryotoxicity; apoptosis; early human development; 3Rs; DNA adducts; DNA repair

Article.Title: Patient-level and duplicate-image data leakage inflate reported accuracy in OASIS and KAAD MRI benchmarks
Article.Authors: Santhoshkumar V.; Lanitha B.
Article.Abstract: Deep learning studies of Alzheimer’s disease classification often use two Kaggle-hosted MRI datasets: OASIS, and a widely used Kaggle Alzheimer’s MRI export sometimes falsely referred to as ADNI, here termed the Kaggle-Augmented Alzheimer’s Dataset (KAAD) to reflect its documented Kaggle provenance (Methods). Both are split into training and test sets at the image level without accounting for image provenance, creating an opportunity for identity leakage. In OASIS, patient identifiers recoverable from filenames show that 100% of test images share a patient with the training set under naive random splitting, across all 86,437 images. In KAAD, whose filenames are anonymized, exact-hash and validated perceptual-hash analyses estimate that roughly one-fifth of images are near-duplicates of another image in the set. Using three classifiers of increasing capacity, removing this leakage lowers mean test accuracy from 100.0% to about 46% for OASIS (p < = 0.00005) and from 68.0% to 58.9–62.8% for KAAD ( p = 0.0028-0.09); the OASIS collapse was essentially unchanged by a five-fold capacity increase, indicating it is not an artifact of an under-capacity baseline. A cross-dataset test across five seeds shows a classifier trained on OASIS performs at chance level on KAAD (25.0%) despite perfect training accuracy. These findings, consistent with prior reports, indicate that much published accuracy on these benchmarks reflects identity memorization rather than transferable diagnostic signal. Leakage-free, patient- and duplicate-aware split manifests are released for both datasets.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Psychiatry and Mental health > Dementia and Cognitive Impairment Research; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Machine Learning and Data Classification; Health Professions > Health Information Management > Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare

Article.Title: Discrimination of ranges of closely related RNA targets using CRISPR-based detection assay developed using machine learning-based optimization
Article.Authors: Leski T.; Dean S.; Johnson Z.; Green C.; Díaz S.; Stenger D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Early detection and identification of pathogen strains are crucial for mitigating infectious disease threats, including those posed by closely related zoonotic variants. A key limitation of current molecular detection approaches is their narrow focus on individual targets, which can delay recognition of outbreaks caused by closely related but non-identical pathogens. Here we report a two-channel CRISPR/Cas13a detection assay capable of discriminating between SARS-CoV-2 and a panel of twelve closely related zoonotic sarbecoviruses using a compact duplex assay format. Guide RNA sets with tunable specificity were designed using a two-stage machine learning pipeline: initial candidate filtering with a pre-existing RuleFit model, followed by retraining on 382 sarbecovirus-specific in vitro data points to refine the mismatch threshold from 4 to 6 mismatches for target exclusion. The optimized assay achieved proof-of-concept three-way classification of synthetic RNA targets into: (1) SARS-CoV-2, (2) the closest known near-neighbor BANAL-236, and (3) remaining zoonotic near-neighbors, with a limit of detection of 15–150 fM for synthetic RNA targets. This approach provides a practical framework for surveillance-oriented detection that identifies not only a specific pathogen but also its closest relatives, provided that system-specific validation and model retraining are included for new target systems.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: SARS-CoV-2; mismatch tolerance
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Infectious Diseases > SARS-CoV-2 detection and testing; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > CRISPR and Genetic Engineering; Engineering > Biomedical Engineering > Biosensors and Analytical Detection

Article.Title: A randomized controlled trial of resistance training combined with breathing retraining on cardiometabolic and pulmonary outcomesin overweight young women
Article.Authors: Cai H.; Zhao Y.; Huang T.; Liu J.; Chen S.
Article.Abstract: Physical inactivity and overweight are major public health issues among young Chinese women. This study explored the effects of resistance training combined with breathing retraining on body lipid profile, pulmonary function, circulatory parameters and aerobic capacity in overweight young women. Twenty-eight female participants were assigned to resistance training group (RT) and resistance training plus breathing retraining group (RT + B), undertaking 8-week supervised exercise (3 sessions/week, 60 min/session). After intervention, both groups exhibited significantly reduced triglyceride (TG), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-c), systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), central aortic systolic blood pressure (cSBP), second peak systolic blood pressure (SBP2) and radial augmentation index (rAI), as well as increased vital capacity (VC), forced vital capacity (FVC), maximal voluntary ventilation (MVV), forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1), peak expiratory flow (PEF) and peak oxygen uptake (VO 2 peak) ( p < 0.05). Compared with RT group, RT + B group showed further improvements in anaerobic threshold (AT), peak oxygen pulse, VC, MVV, SBP2 and cSBP ( p < 0.05). These results demonstrate that resistance training combined with breathing retraining is more effective than resistance training alone in enhancing pulmonary function, circulatory function and aerobic capacity in overweight young women.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Physiology (medical) > Cardiovascular and exercise physiology; Medicine > Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health > Physical Activity and Health; Medicine > Orthopedics and Sports Medicine > Sports Performance and Training

Article.Title: Geological substrate and multi-factor controls on RUSLE-estimated water erosion in the Kuye River Basin over 25 years
Article.Authors: Li X.; Zhu Y.; Kang C.; Xi J.; Zhao H.; Xu D.; Yin Z.; Han C.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Quantifying the spatiotemporal dynamics of soil erosion and clarifying its associated driving factors are essential prerequisites for developing targeted soil and water conservation strategies. This study focused on the Kuye River Basin, a primary coarse sediment source in the middle Yellow River. The RUSLE model was used to estimate the soil erosion modulus from 2000 to 2024, and the spatiotemporal evolution and geological differentiation of erosion were analyzed. An interpretable XGBoost-SHAP machine learning framework was constructed, incorporating climatic, topographic, vegetation, anthropogenic, and geological substrate factors, to quantitatively disentangle the contributions of each factor to the RUSLE-estimated erosion spatial pattern. Seven groups of controlled experiments were designed to examine the structural overlap between RUSLE internal factors and model independent variables. The results show that: (1) The overall soil erosion intensity exhibited an improving trend, but the spatial pattern remained stable with a pronounced lithological gradient. Aeolian loess, argillaceous rock, and clastic rock interbedded with argillaceous rock units were identified as persistent high erosion risk zones. (2) Geological substrate was the background factor most closely related to the spatial differentiation of erosion. The spatial distribution of single-factor sensitivity showed that high-sensitivity areas of the K factor coincided with argillaceous rock and aeolian sand, high-sensitivity areas of the LS factor were consistent with steep-slope zones in the loess hilly-gully region, and high-sensitivity areas of the C factor overlapped with low-vegetation-cover areas in the middle and lower reaches. The spatial superposition of these three factors is closely associated with the persistently high erosion risk in the high-risk units. The basin-wide erosion rebound in 2020 under extreme rainfall highlights the sensitivity of soft substrates to extreme climate. (3) Within the RUSLE framework, NDVI and slope, corresponding to the C and LS factors, contributed most to the spatial pattern of erosion modulus. However, controlled experiments indicated that this result partly arises from the mathematical structural relationship of the RUSLE equation, and the model performance primarily reflects its capacity to reconstruct RUSLE outputs under random holdout validation rather than cross-regional predictive transferability. External environmental variables (PET, Distance to roads, Distance to water, Aspect, Soil thickness, and Lithology) showed limited independent explanatory power for RUSLE outputs (M5 R 2 = – 0.011). Therefore, the SHAP results should be interpreted as the “covariate importance of the RUSLE-estimated erosion pattern” rather than the “causal mechanisms of actual erosion processes.” It is recommended that geological unit differentiation be incorporated as a core consideration in future soil and water conservation planning, and that a precision governance system based on zoning of rock-soil erosion resistance be established. Future studies should integrate independent observational data (e.g., check dam sedimentation, 137 Cs tracing, and sediment discharge at hydrological stations) to distinguish RUSLE structural associations from actual erosion drivers.
Article.TopicFields: Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Soil Science > Soil erosion and sediment transport; Environmental Science > Water Science and Technology > Environmental and Agricultural Sciences; Earth and Planetary Sciences > Earth-Surface Processes > Hydrology and Sediment Transport Processes

Article.Title: Preselected voltage vector strategy integrated with virtual flux-based predictive direct power control for AC/DC rectifier
Article.Authors: Nguyen-Minh H.; Nguyen-Minh T.; Hoang M.; Ta D.
Article.Abstract: Aiming at reducing aging mismatch between phase leg of AC/DC rectifier and increasing lifetime of the leg with the highest aging state, a preselected voltage vector strategy integrated with model predictive virtual-flux-based direct power control is proposed in this paper. Starting from the principle of discontinuous pulse-width modulation technique, the preselected voltage vector strategy determines the clamping regions in the leg with the highest aging state and corresponding voltage vectors that maintain the current status of power switches. Thus, it leads to a reduction of switching loss, resulting in decreased thermal stress and an increase in lifetime of AC/DC rectifier. Different from other approaches, the proposed per-phase technique focuses on relieving the thermal stress of the leg with the highest aging state instead of both three-phase legs to achieve minimum switching loss and thermal stress in the leg. The proposed approach can guarantee the performance of line current harmonic distortion under harmonically distorted supply voltage due to the use of virtual flux vector. Additionally, the proposed technique does not require any extra hardware and is straightforward to implement in practical applications. In this study, besides the proposed technique, conventional model predictive direct power control and conventional model predictive virtual-flux-based direct power control methods are implemented in both simulations and experiments. The obtained performance from three control schemes is evaluated and compared to validate the accuracy and effectiveness of proposed method.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Multilevel Inverters and Converters; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Power Quality and Harmonics; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Advanced DC-DC Converters

Article.Title: Data-driven LQ-optimal path tracking with prescribed-performance certificates for autonomous vehicles
Article.Authors: Lu M.; Sun Y.; Wu M.
Article.Abstract: This paper addresses lateral path tracking for an autonomous vehicle whose state-space matrices are unknown. The infinite-horizon linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal steering gain is learned from a single batch of measured state and steering data by off-policy policy iteration, which needs neither the system matrices, nor state derivatives, nor a function-approximation network; each iteration is a linear least-squares problem built from three reusable data integrals, and the iteration coincides with Kleinman’s model-based iteration under a rank condition that we prove in the symmetric quadratic basis. Because the deployed controller is a fixed linear gain, we do not claim that a barrier transformation enforces the tracking bounds. Instead we derive a prescribed-performance certificate : an explicit sufficient per-channel exponential upper bound obtained from the modal decomposition of the closed loop, together with sufficient conditions relating the funnel parameters to the closed-loop decay margin and to the (unmatched) road-curvature disturbance, and a companion bound on the steering angle. Simulations on a 30 km/h S-turn and an 80 km/h lane change show that the learned gain is within 2–6% of the Riccati gain and within \(3\times 10^{-6}\) (relative) of its nominal LQ cost, and that all errors remain inside the certified funnels. We also report the limits of the approach: the certificate is nominal and covers 200/200 and 198/200 trials of a Monte-Carlo study with \(\pm 20\%\) speed and \(\pm 30\%\) cornering-stiffness variation; the learner is markedly more sensitive to measurement noise than identification followed by a Riccati solve; and large initial errors saturate the steering actuator, which requires retuning at the price of a wider certified funnel.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Automotive Engineering > Vehicle Dynamics and Control Systems; Engineering > Control and Systems Engineering > Adaptive Dynamic Programming Control; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Reinforcement Learning in Robotics

Article.Title: Evaluation of machine learning representations for trace asbestos detection in recycled gypsum using wide-angle X-ray scattering
Article.Authors: Wilhelm M.; Lotter F.; Scherdel C.; Förster H.; Welscher J.; Zeh A.; Schmitt J.; Engelmann B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Asbestos contamination blocks gypsum recycling from demolition waste. Regulatory thresholds near 0.1 wt% lie well below the $$\sim $$ 1 wt% limit of conventional X-ray powder diffraction. We evaluate machine-learning detection of trace chrysotile (0.001–9 wt%) in recycled gypsum from wide-angle X-ray scattering, comparing six feature representations under one Extra-Trees estimator on 1532 spectra from 373 samples, with group-aware splits and 18 seeds. Internally the representations are indistinguishable, so we report the minimum detectable difference (0.030–0.062) rather than a ranking. The untransformed spectrum is the strongest internal detector (AUC $$0.9993 \pm 0.0007$$ , zero false negatives at 9.4% false positives), yet misses all 16 measurements of a commercial fibre-cement board absent from training, which an unsupervised linear projection detects in full. Dimensionality reduction, not internal accuracy, determines whether a decision rule transfers to a new matrix. We therefore select on cross-matrix transfer, reporting a PCA model restricted to the diagnostic chrysotile reflections (accuracy $$0.9450 \pm 0.0187$$ ). A retained production sample independently assayed at 0.0201 wt%, one fifth of the regulatory threshold, and used in no selection step is identified as asbestos-bearing. Quantification remains semi-quantitative (log-MAE 0.62) and does not transfer across matrices, so the framework suits on-line screening in industrial recycling.
Article.TopicFields: Chemistry > Analytical Chemistry > Spectroscopy and Chemometric Analyses; Materials Science > Materials Chemistry > Machine Learning in Materials Science; Materials Science > Materials Chemistry > X-ray Diffraction in Crystallography

Article.Title: Rectal compliance and nitrergic and purinergic inhibitory neurotransmission in rectal smooth muscle in mouse
Article.Authors: Lee J.; Sung T.; Corrigan R.; Kim H.; Koh S.; Ryoo S.
Article.Abstract: Rectal compliance for fecal storage is a distinct characteristic, separate from colonic propulsive movements. This study aims to explore the electromechanical properties of rectal compliance in murine rectal smooth muscle and to investigate the contributions of intrinsic inhibitory neurotransmission and interstitial cells. Male C57BL/6 mice were used to record rectal compliance in vivo and ex vivo. Interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC) and platelet-derived growth factor receptor α-positive (PDGFRα⁺) cells were evenly distributed within the circular muscle (CM) layer of the murine rectum. Enteric neurons expressing nNOS were closely apposed. The relative expression of c-kit mRNA was significantly lower, but PDGFRα and nNOS expression were higher in the rectum. The amplitude of inhibitory junction potentials significantly decreased following administration of L-NNA or apamin, while spontaneous Ca²⁺ transients in ICC-CM increased. Rectal smooth muscle contractions during electric field stimulation, segmental contractions and spontaneous Ca²⁺ transients were also significantly enhanced after L-NNA or apamin. Spatiotemporal mapping revealed artificial pellet presented longer transit time in the rectum than colon. Rectal compliance was significantly reduced after L-NNA or apamin. Enteric inhibitory neurotransmission mediated by nitric oxide or purines was associated with rectal compliance and involved ICC and PDGFRα⁺ cells, which regulate rectal smooth muscle activity.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Gastroenterology > Gastrointestinal motility and disorders; Medicine > Surgery > Congenital gastrointestinal and neural anomalies; Medicine > Urology > Urinary Bladder and Prostate Research

Article.Title: Environmental short-term risk assessment in 66,651 cases of urgent hospital admissions among patients with IBD in Poland
Article.Authors: Wieczorek J.; Bochenek B.; Goryński P.; Jankowski M.; Mahadea D.; Kotecki P.; Eder P.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) incidence is rising worldwide, yet evidence on short-term associations between environmental exposures and urgent IBD hospitalisations remains limited in population-based evidence, particularly in Poland, a country at the stage of emergence. A nationwide time-stratified case-crossover, including the cohort of 66,651 cases of urgent hospital admissions among patients with Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis recorded as either a primary or comorbid diagnosis, was conducted in Poland between 2012 and 2019. A two-stage analytical framework was applied; exploratory nationwide screening evaluated 49 environmental exposures at lags 0–10, followed by targeted urban follow-up analyses; pooled multi-city, and Warsaw-specific levels. Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) per interquartile-range (IQR) increase, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple testing. At multicity stage the same-day NO 2 and NOₓ showed the strongest associations (NO 2 : OR 1.081, 95% CI 1.050–1.113; NOₓ: OR 1.056, 95% CI 1.030–1.082; both BH-adjusted p < 0.001 in multicity analysis). Solar radiation at lag 3 showed the strongest association among meteorological factors. Joint exposure to high NO 2 and high solar radiation at lag 3, or high NO 2 and temperatures > 20 °C at lag 0, was associated with 17% and 9% higher odds of urgent IBD hospital admission of patients aged 19–60, respectively. Associations were most consistent among group of working-age adults aged 19–60 years, urban residents, and patients with ulcerative colitis. Overall, the findings indicate short-term associations between ambient air pollution, particularly nitrogen oxides, meteorological conditions, and urgent IBD hospitalisations in Poland, while the observed joint exposure patterns warrant further investigation.
Article.TopicFields: Environmental Science > Health, Toxicology and Mutagenesis > Air Quality and Health Impacts; Environmental Science > Health, Toxicology and Mutagenesis > Health, Environment, Cognitive Aging; Environmental Science > Health, Toxicology and Mutagenesis > Climate Change and Health Impacts

Article.Title: Multi-objective integrated performance prediction and active balancing control for grid-connected multi-energy microgrids with hydrogen storage and SOFCs
Article.Authors: Yang H.; Yi B.; Liu X.; Ren D.; Peng M.; Luo L.; Zhang P.; Deng Z.; Jin Z.
Article.Abstract: Grid-connected multi-energy microgrids face two interrelated challenges: the volatility of wind and photovoltaic generation, load demand, and electricity prices renders dispatch inputs uncertain, while the limited flexibility of conventional electrical storage and controllable units makes it difficult to simultaneously achieve economic operation, smooth output adjustment, and low network loss. To address these challenges, this study proposes a multi-objective integrated forecasting and active-balancing control framework. First, an LSTM-BPNN hybrid model jointly predicts wind power, photovoltaic power, load demand, and day-ahead electricity prices at a 30 min resolution. The model provides 48-step day-ahead forecasts and four-step intraday forecasts. Second, a rolling optimization controller targets operating cost, controllable-source output adjustment, network loss, and day-ahead schedule deviation, and employs MOEA/D to solve the constrained optimization problem. In the case study, the LSTM-BPNN model achieves superior forecasting accuracy in terms of MAE, RMSE, and other metrics compared with standalone LSTM, BPNN, and GRU models. At the dispatch level, compared with NSGA-II, MOEA/D increases HV by approximately 4.7% and decreases SP by 29.2%, demonstrating its superiority in solving the multi-objective dispatch problem. Removing the SOFC, HST, and hydrogen market increases daily operating cost, controllable-source output adjustment, and day-ahead deviation by approximately 11.02%, 4.45%, and 13.73%, respectively. Under the representative summer and winter scenarios, the system maintains stable operation, with the SOFC playing a key role in compensating for renewable generation shortfalls and load fluctuations, thereby supporting the economic efficiency and operational stability of the system under varying external operating conditions.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Control and Systems Engineering > Microgrid Control and Optimization; Energy > Energy Engineering and Power Technology > Hybrid Renewable Energy Systems; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Integrated Energy Systems Optimization

Article.Title: Heterogeneous knowledge distillation via architecture-aware reinforcement learning
Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Fan H.; Zeng Q.
Article.Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from a large teacher network to a compact student network. A central challenge in heterogeneous multi-teacher KD is balancing supervision from teachers with fundamentally different architectures—convolutional neural networks (CNNs), vision transformers (ViTs), and MLP-Mixers—whose features occupy incompatible representation spaces. Most existing methods either assume homogeneous teachers or use uniform weighting, without jointly addressing architecture-adaptive alignment and dynamic teacher weighting. We propose Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation via Architecture-Aware Reinforcement Learning (HARKD), a framework that combines three components: (1) architecture-adaptive projectors that map heterogeneous features into compatible alignment spaces; (2) a heterogeneity-aware state representation that captures teacher performance, architectural compatibility, and branch-level alignment quality; and (3) reinforcement-learning-based optimization that dynamically weights teacher contributions across multiple student exits. The learned policy assigns depth-dependent teacher weights as the student evolves during training. Experiments on ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet show that HARKD consistently outperforms the evaluated multi-teacher KD baselines.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition > Advanced Neural Network Applications; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Domain Adaptation and Few-Shot Learning; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Machine Learning and Data Classification

Article.Title: Integrated genomic, biochemical, and molecular dynamics analyses identify Chromohalobacter sp. D23 as a promising quorum-quenching probiotic for sustainable aquaculture
Article.Authors: Ghosh D.; Alam S.; Mukhopadhyay S.
Article.Abstract: Quorum sensing-driven biofilm formation is a key contributor to the persistence and multidrug resistance (MDR) of pathogenic bacteria, presenting a major challenge in combating infectious diseases. Probiotic quorum-quenching (QQ) bacteria represent a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics by suppressing quorum sensing-dependent virulence in MDR pathogens and simultaneously enhancing fish growth, immunity, and overall health. In this study, the probiotic and QQ attributes of Chromohalobacter sp. D23 were comprehensively investigated. The strain exhibited robust tolerance to gastrointestinal stress conditions, surviving bile salt (1.2%), phenol (0.75%), and acidic environments (pH 2.0–4.0). Additionally, it displayed pronounced antioxidant activity (> 69%), high auto-aggregation (72.0 ± 2.42%), and co-aggregation (> 73%) with fish pathogens, suggesting a high potential for gut colonization and pathogen exclusion. Genome mining also revealed presence of putative proteins involved in resistance to bile, phenol, acid, osmotic pressure along with adhesion and aggregation facilitating host gut colonization. Virtual screening of strain D23 also enabled to predict potential enzymes/proteins for biosynthesis of vitamins and amino acids. In spite of presence of very few antibiotic resistance genes, overall genome-wide analysis of the draft genome of strain D23 detected no putative virulence genes, plasmid, or transposable element-associated genes, suggesting a favorable safety profile. Whole-cell assay showed complete breakdown of synthetic N-acyl homoserine lactones (N-AHLs) as revealed by biosensor-based assay. Strain D23 also degraded natural N-AHLs of Aeromonas hydrophila within 12 h. Co-culture experiment revealed potent anti-biofilm activity against A. hydrophila ( p ≤ 0.0001). Genome mining identified putative metallo-beta lactamase enzyme (lactonase_D23) having conserved ‘ 66 HXHXDH 71 ’ motif. Molecular docking revealed moderate binding affinities of lactonase_D23 towards both C4-Homoserine lactone (C4-HSL) and C6-HSL, however, molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated that the C4-HSL–lactonase_D23 complex exhibited greater conformational stability, indicating highly persistent protein–ligand interaction. Later, in silico mutant enzymes exhibited higher binding affinity than wild-type lactonase_D23 to C4-HSL. This pioneer, integrated study suggests potentiality of strain D23 as safe, beneficial, autochthonous QQ probiotic candidate in aquaculture to improve overall fish health.

Article.Title: Integrating single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing to identify biomarkers associated with phagocytic regulatory factors in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
Article.Authors: Chao L.; Song B.; Xu H.; Cai Z.; Yan X.; Cao J.
Article.Abstract: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) is a progressive pulmonary vascular disorder marked by organized thrombotic material and persistent pulmonary hypertension. However, the contribution of phagocytosis-regulating factors to CTEPH remains insufficiently defined. An in-house bulk RNA-sequencing cohort (eight patients with CTEPH and eight with CTEPD) and a public single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset were jointly analyzed. Cellular subpopulations were delineated from the single-cell data, and high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA) was used to obtain module genes in the pivotal cell type. Candidate genes were defined by overlapping these module genes with differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Three machine learning methods, together with receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, were then used to select diagnostic biomarkers, which were incorporated into a nomogram for performance assessment. The biomarkers were further characterized via functional enrichment, immune infiltration analysis, drug prediction, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, cell‑cell communication inference, pseudotime reconstruction, and virtual knockout analysis. Reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) was used for expression validation in an independent cohort. Among the cell populations resolved by scRNA-seq, mononuclear phagocytes (MPs) showed high activity of the phagocytosis-related gene set in this dataset. Overlap between DEGs and MP‑associated module genes yielded 12 candidates. Further screening retained FOS and CD163 as candidate diagnostic biomarkers, both of which were downregulated in CTEPH. In the training cohort, the two-gene nomogram showed preliminary discrimination. FOS and CD163 shared enrichment in platelet activation and neutrophil degranulation pathways, while CD163 was positively correlated with B cells. Compound CID:71,703,489 was predicted computationally to bind both biomarkers, and the simulated CD163 complex was more stable than the FOS complex. CTEPH samples also showed higher inferred ANXA1-FPR1 communication between MPs and neutrophils. Expression of both biomarkers varied along the inferred MP transcriptional-state trajectory, and virtual deletion of either gene perturbed pathways related to phagocytosis and migration. These findings are computational inferences and require experimental validation. Their reduced expression in the analyzed CTEPH samples was further supported by RT-qPCR. FOS and CD163 emerged as candidate diagnostic biomarkers for CTEPH in the training cohort. Their reduced expression may be associated with changes in MP communication and functional state, as suggested by computational analyses; experimental and cell-type-specific validation is warranted.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Pulmonary and Respiratory Medicine > Pulmonary Hypertension Research and Treatments; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics; Medicine > Internal Medicine > Venous Thromboembolism Diagnosis and Management

Article.Title: Spontaneous emergence of action decisions and slow ramping in a deep brain-constrained model of frontotemporal areas
Article.Authors: Griffin N.; Schurger A.; Garagnani M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Humans are capable of voluntarily initiating actions that are spontaneous—not triggered by any sensory event in the immediate context. In such cases, how does the brain make a decision that the time to act has come? To investigate this question, we used a 6-area brain-constrained neural-network model to account for the neurophysiological and anatomical features of relevant areas of the cortex. To replicate the experimental settings under which volitional non stimulus-triggered button-presses are performed, we analysed the network activity in the absence of any “sensory” input: we observed spontaneous ignitions of previously-learned “perception–action” circuits (linking “visual” information to corresponding “hand/finger movement”) caused by the accumulation of noise within them, which we took as model correlates of self-generated decisions to act. The time to first spontaneous circuit ignition was then used to build a simulated waiting-time histogram. We found that, for select values of the parameters, the network autonomously “decided” to act (or to wait) in a way that accurately reflected participant behaviour under such conditions. Additionally, we found that when the model’s macroscopic behaviour matched that of participants, its microscopic activity prior to a spontaneous ignition event also reproduced the pre-movement slow ramping neural signal (the readiness potential, or RP) experimentally recorded using electroencephalography. Reproducing both behavioural and brain indices of spontaneous voluntary movements, the present brain-constrained architecture offers a neuro-mechanistic explanation of the emergence of endogenous action decisions in the human brain in the form of memory traces’ spontaneous ignitions. Our results also speak to the ongoing debate over the interpretation of the RP, suggesting that, rather than reflecting motor preparation (a decision outcome), the emerging RP is pre-decisional, with overt movement being the result of a distributed perception–action circuit spontaneous ignition.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: frontotemporal cortex; noise accumulation; motor preparation; readiness potential

Article.Title: Restoring myelination in rat sciatic nerve using BM-MSCs and conditioned media
Article.Authors: Mohanty A.; Saijyothi A.; Uppin M.; Vemuganti G.
Article.Abstract: Damaged peripheral nerves post-injury cause loss of the outer protective covering (demyelination) on the nerves, resulting in loss of proper functioning. This becomes challenging due to its progressive nature, limited satisfactory treatment, high morbidity, delayed diagnosis and prognosis. Exploring novel methods of treatment, such as cell-based regeneration using stem cells, seems promising. In this study, we have attempted to use stem cell therapy using cells (BM-MSCs) and the conditioned media (CM) to restore nerve damage and myelination in the surgically induced rat injury model. Male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats ( N = 30) were divided into four groups: Control (Group I), nerve injury group (DEM-Group II), self-recovery (Group III), treatment group (Group IV) subdivided into 2 groups using cells (BM-MSC Group IVa) and the conditioned media (CM Group IVb), with n = 6 animals/condition. Injury in the sciatic nerve was surgically induced by partial Sciatic nerve Ligation (PSNL). Post-injury, the nerve revealed fibre loss, thinning of the myelin sheath (demyelination) and axonal shrinkage as compared to the control, validated by histopathology and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Treatment with BM-MSCs and CM reversed the nerve damage. The nerve looked structurally better, with increased myelin thickness, axonal radius and healthier cells in comparison with the injured nerve. Together, our data show that both BM-MSCs and CM provide evidence of structural and histological remyelination; however, cell-based therapy was better than CM. This study provides preclinical evidence for treating nerve injuries and enhancing nerve regeneration in future.

Article.Title: Two lead-leg knee flexion-extension patterns and their associations with elbow loading in collegiate baseball pitchers
Article.Authors: Cheng K.; Liao P.; Giordano K.; Wasserberger K.; Yang H.; Oliver G.
Article.Abstract: Lead-leg mechanics may influence baseball pitching performance and elbow loading, but discrete event analyses may overlook time-varying movement strategies. This study used a data-driven full-trajectory approach to identify lead-leg knee flexion–extension patterns and examine their associations with ball velocity and peak elbow varus torque (pEVT) in 224 NCAA Division I pitchers. In-game markerless motion-capture data from each pitcher’s 10 fastest recorded fastballs were used to characterize lead-leg mechanics under a high velocity fastball condition and were time-normalized from stride foot contact to ball release, with maximum shoulder external rotation aligned at 80% of the cycle. Functional principal component analysis followed by competitive clustering identified two stable K-means profiles (Cluster 1, n = 131; Cluster 2, n = 93). Cluster 2 showed a modestly higher observed ball velocity than Cluster 1 (mean difference, 0.68 mph [0.30 m/s]; p = 0.032), but this difference was attenuated after adjustment for fastball subtype (0.27 mph [0.12 m/s]; p = 0.454). pEVT did not differ between clusters ( p = 0.755). Cluster-specific statistical parametric mapping revealed no velocity related temporal associations, whereas in Cluster 2, greater knee extension was associated with higher pEVT from 27.6 to 71.3% of the pitching cycle ( p = 0.012). This association persisted after adjustment for ball velocity and body height but was no longer significant after adjustment for body mass or normalization of pEVT to body size. Moreover, the direct cluster-by-pEVT interaction was not significant. These findings identify two lead-leg knee flexion–extension patterns and an exploratory between-pitcher association between knee mechanics and absolute pEVT that cannot be considered independent of body size.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Biomedical Engineering > Sports Dynamics and Biomechanics; Medicine > Surgery > Shoulder Injury and Treatment; Medicine > Orthopedics and Sports Medicine > Elbow and Forearm Trauma Treatment

Article.Title: Deep learning–based detection of stress urinary incontinence in transperineal ultrasound video examinations
Article.Authors: Vuskov R.; Ignatova N.; Truhn D.; Najjari L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is a common bladder dysfunction in women, and transperineal ultrasound (TPUS) enables dynamic assessment of the bladder neck, urethra, and pelvic floor. We developed and compared two deep-learning approaches for automated SUI detection from complete midsagittal TPUS videos with adequate urethral visualization and without manual frame or region-of-interest selection. In this retrospective single-center study, 803 TPUS recordings from unique patients were analyzed. Two video-classification pipelines were evaluated: an ultrasound-pretrained frame-wise encoder with transformer-based temporal aggregation (USCL + TF) and a video-native foundation model (V-JEPA2). For each architecture, we tested a standard input configuration and two anatomically guided variants based on automated segmentation: one restricting the input to an automatically defined region of interest and one augmenting the input with segmentation masks. Both model families showed good discriminative performance. Across 50 repeated paired splits, USCL + TF achieved mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values from 0.84 to 0.88, whereas V-JEPA2 achieved AUC values from 0.89 to 0.90. In paired analyses accounting for overlapping splits and seven comparisons, V-JEPA2 had a higher AUC than USCL + TF in the basic configuration. The other matched architecture comparisons and the comparisons of anatomy-guided with basic inputs were not statistically significant after multiplicity correction. These findings show that deep learning can classify SUI from full TPUS video examinations with good performance and without manual frame selection, supporting further validation of automated TPUS analysis as a decision-support tool.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Urology > Pelvic floor disorders treatments; Health Professions > Health Information Management > Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare; Medicine > Health Informatics > Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

Article.Title: Coupled seismic-seepage modelling of a bridge abutment slope and its stabilisation using geotextile gabion mattresses
Article.Authors: Najar I.; Ahmadi R.; Alkahtani M.; Mourad R.
Article.Abstract: The sequential occurrence of earthquakes and rainfall presents a profound and often underestimated threat to slope stability, particularly in tropical regions. This study addresses this critical gap through a sophisticated coupled numerical analysis of a bridge abutment slope in Sarawak, Malaysia, evaluating a novel stabilisation strategy against this combined threat. Using an advanced sequential modelling framework in GeoStudio, this study integrates dynamic seismic analysis, QUAKE/W with subsequent transient seepage simulation, SEEP/W to replicate the multi-hazard condition. Results from this study demonstrate that the synergistic effect of seismic shaking and post-earthquake rainfall infiltration drives the slope to a critical state reducing the factor of safety to 0.94 due to mechanisms of tensile cracking and pore-pressure amplification. This study shows that the application of a geotextile-reinforced gabion mattress effectively restores slope stability, increasing the factor of safety to a stable value 2.2. This study provides a critical validation of a cost-effective reinforcement technique and establishes an essential coupled modelling framework, offering a robust scientific basis for enhancing the resilience of infrastructure in seismically active and rainfall-prone regions globally.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Civil and Structural Engineering > Geotechnical Engineering and Analysis; Engineering > Civil and Structural Engineering > Geotechnical Engineering and Soil Stabilization; Engineering > Civil and Structural Engineering > Geotechnical Engineering and Underground Structures

Article.Title: Identity-based adaptor signature scheme and its application in cross-chain transactions
Article.Authors: Yi L.; Yasin S.; Ninggal M.; Asmawi A.
Article.Abstract: With the rapid proliferation of blockchain-based applications and mobile devices, ensuring secure and efficient digital signatures in resource-constrained environments has become increasingly important. Traditional public key infrastructure (PKI)-based signatures suffer from certificate management overhead and are not well-suited for decentralized systems. Identity-based cryptography offers a promising alternative by eliminating certificates, while adaptor signatures enable conditional execution and atomic transactions in blockchain systems. In this paper, we propose a novel identity-based adaptor signature (IBAS) scheme tailored for blockchain-enabled mobile environments. The proposed scheme integrates identity-based cryptography with adaptor signatures to support conditional signing and witness extractability, which are essential for applications such as atomic swaps and payment channels. Our construction leverages bilinear pairings and adopts a lightweight design to reduce computational overhead on resource-constrained devices. We formally define the security of the proposed scheme and prove that it achieves existential unforgeability under adaptive chosen message attacks (aEUF-CMA) in the random oracle model. In addition, we establish the witness extractability property, ensuring that the secret witness can be efficiently extracted from a valid pre-signature and its corresponding final signature. We implement the proposed scheme and evaluate its performance on mobile devices under different network conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that the scheme achieves efficient signature generation and verification, making it suitable for practical deployment in blockchain-based mobile applications.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Computer Networks and Communications > Cryptography and Data Security; Computer Science > Information Systems > Blockchain Technology Applications and Security; Computer Science > Computer Networks and Communications > Advanced Authentication Protocols Security

Article.Title: Monitoring the status of potentially toxic and essential metals in the nails of Pakistani patients with diabetes mellitus and pancreatitis using multivariate analysis
Article.Authors: Qayyum M.; Naeem R.; Shafique M.; Mahmood M.
Article.Abstract: Imbalances of certain metals disrupt endocrine system cause metabolic disorder result in the development of pancreatic diseases such as diabetes mellitus and pancreatitis. The aim of present study was to analyze and compare the levels of toxic (Cd, Pb, Sr, Ni, Li), and essential (Mg, Ca, Mn, K, Cu, Fe, Na, Zn, Co, Cr) metals in nail samples of diabetes mellitus patients ( n = 109), pancreatitis patients ( n = 107) and controls ( n = 109). The metal concentrations were measured by atomic absorption spectrometry after nail samples were digested with HNO 3 –HClO 4 mixture. The validity/accuracy was checked by using certified reference material NIST-SRM 8414 and overall recoveries of all metals were examined in the range of 97–103% of certified values. For multiple comparisons, Bonferroni correction was applied. Mann–Whitney U test was also used to assess the differences between groups to compare non-normally distributed continuous variables. In addition, logistic regression analysis was conducted to examine the adjusted odds ratios (adj. OR) of developing diabetes mellitus and pancreatitis diseases. Adjusted odds ratios (adj.OR) of elemental exposure showed significant positive associations with increased risk of diabetes mellitus: Cd (adj. OR = 2.244), Cr (adj.OR = 1.277) and Na (adj.OR = 1.047). Similarly, significantly high levels of Cr (adj.OR = 1.312) and Cu (adj.OR = 1.728) were associated with increased risk of pancreatic disease. The average metal values varied significantly among the acute and chronic pancreatitis patients. Principal component and cluster analyses were employed to identify patterns/distinguish of metals between patients groups and controls. In diabetic patients, mean/median concentrations of Cd and Na were significantly elevated ( p < 0.05) than the controls. Significant higher average/median levels ( p < 0.05) of Cu, Ni and Cr were found in pancreatitis patients compared to controls. Spearman correlation pattern revealed altered inter-metal relationships and associated with increased risk of disease. The multivariate apportionments of the metal levels were significantly divergent among the donors groups. Overall, exposure to metal mixtures was related with an increased risk of pancreatic diseases.
Article.TopicFields: Environmental Science > Health, Toxicology and Mutagenesis > Heavy Metal Exposure and Toxicity; Nursing > Nutrition and Dietetics > Trace Elements in Health; Environmental Science > Pollution > Heavy metals in environment

Article.Title: A swap-adversarial framework for domain generalization in pre- and post-stimulation Parkinsonian state classification
Article.Authors: Jin S.; Choi H.; Kim G.; Yang S.; Park S.; Kim J.
Article.Abstract: We propose a novel swap-adversarial framework that mitigates high inter-subject variability and the high-dimensional low-sample-size problem in electrocorticography (ECoG) data. It achieves robust domain generalization across ECoG and electroencephalography (EEG)-based brain-computer interface datasets. Our framework integrates (1) robust preprocessing, (2) inter-subject balanced channel swap (ISBCS) for cross-subject augmentation, and (3) domain-adversarial learning (DAL) to suppress subject-specific bias. The ISBCS method is a bio-inspired channel swapping strategy that exchanges only spatially corresponding channels across subjects, guided by a motor-cortex brain map, to mitigate inter-subject distribution differences. The DAL strategy encourages the model to learn task-relevant shared features. In addition, we introduce a new ECoG dataset, the first reproducible benchmark for classifying neural states before and after electrical stimulation, constructed from long-term ECoG recordings of 6-hydroxydopamine-induced PD rat models. We validate the effectiveness of this framework through cross-subject and cross-cohort evaluations on ECoG data and cross-dataset evaluations on public EEG data. Our results show that the proposed framework exhibits the best and robust generalization performance both for our newly constructed ECoG and public EEG datasets.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: domain generalization; domain adversarial learning; electrocorticography; Parkinson's disease; interindividual variability; brain-computer interface; cross-dataset generalization
Article.TopicFields: Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > EEG and Brain-Computer Interfaces; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Domain Adaptation and Few-Shot Learning; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Emotion and Mood Recognition

Article.Title: Heuriskryptes framework for identifying covert channels in neural architectures
Article.Authors: Sethi S.; Ahmed S.; Sakshi N/A.; Batra N.; Noonia A.; Kumar A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract This paper introduces Heuriskryptes, a detection framework designed to identify AI-driven steganographic attacks within deep neural networks. The framework addresses the emerging threat of covert channels established within a model’s parameter pool. The evaluated attack vector, termed Stego-GCP, uses an orthogonal embedding to modify model weights with high stealth to leak data. To detect these channels, a specialized agent utilizes a Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture that treats the raw parameter space as an image, providing a self-attention-based mechanism that demonstrates consistent cross-architecture generalizability for efficient model auditing. The framework has been validated using a PooledCNN architecture on the Apple Disease and CIFAR-10 datasets. Results indicate that the carrier model retains a classification accuracy of 99.97%. Furthermore, the Heuriskryptes detector demonstrated high sensitivity, achieving 93.51% overall accuracy and maintaining a 90% detection rate specifically on the most challenging ambiguous, low-payload density scenarios ( $$\alpha < 0.002$$ ). This demonstrates highly competitive performance compared to evaluated frequency-domain anomaly detection baselines. Heuriskryptes serves as a reliable detection framework for verifying model integrity in collaborative and commercial AI environments. By focusing on the structural mathematical properties of the weight spectrum rather than activation-trigger patterns, this research provides a reliable defense against the unauthorized use of neural architectures as covert communication channels.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning; Computer Science > Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition > Advanced Steganography and Watermarking Techniques; Computer Science > Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition > Digital Media Forensic Detection

Article.Title: Care seeking during obstetric emergencies in rural Somalia through the three delays model
Article.Authors: Jayte M.; Hakizimana T.; Karshe A.; Abdi F.; Isse S.; Ismail M.; Jeyte I.; Aden A.
Article.Abstract: Maternal mortality remains critically high in fragile settings such as Somalia, where access to timely obstetric care is shaped by complex social and structural factors. While the Three Delays model is widely used to explain barriers to care, limited evidence explores how these delays are negotiated within households during emergencies. This qualitative study was conducted in rural districts of Jowhar (Middle Shabelle) and Burhakaba (Lower Shabelle), Somalia. In-depth interviews were conducted with 32 participants, including women who experienced obstetric emergencies, husbands, and traditional birth attendants (TBAs). Data were collected using semi-structured guides and analyzed thematically using a hybrid inductive-deductive approach informed by the Three Delays framework. Care-seeking during obstetric emergencies emerged as a socially negotiated process rather than an individual decision. Women’s recognition of danger signs was frequently insufficient to prompt action due to male-dominated decision-making and financial control. Economic hardship and transport constraints further delayed access to care, while perceptions of poor-quality or disrespectful facility services influenced the urgency of referral. Delays were not sequential but interdependent, with anticipated facility conditions shaping earlier decision-making processes. Traditional birth attendants played a dual role as trusted advisors and constrained referral agents. Obstetric emergencies in rural Somalia are shaped by intersecting gender, economic, and health system factors that operate in non-linear ways. Interventions that focus solely on awareness or service availability are unlikely to be effective. Reducing maternal mortality in fragile settings requires integrated strategies that address household power dynamics, financial barriers, referral systems, and trust in facility-based care.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Pediatrics, Perinatology and Child Health > Global Maternal and Child Health; Medicine > Pediatrics, Perinatology and Child Health > Maternal and fetal healthcare; Medicine > Obstetrics and Gynecology > Maternal and Perinatal Health Interventions

Article.Title: Data readiness and cross database transportability of creatinine based acute kidney injury prediction in intensive care
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Wang S.; Chan G.; Yin L.
Article.Abstract: Clinical deployment of acute kidney injury (AKI) AI models depends on whether labels, predictors, missingness, and calibration remain stable across electronic health record (EHR) systems. To develop an AI-ready data passport and transportability stress-test framework for creatinine-based AKI prediction using MIMIC-IV v3.1 and eICU-CRD v2.0. We performed a retrospective secondary analysis of adult ICU stays. Predictions were generated at approximately 24 h after ICU admission using information observed during the first 24 h; this was not an admission-time prediction protocol. The primary outcome was a post-24-hour day-7 serum-creatinine-based operational endpoint, requiring first-24-hour creatinine and post-24-hour follow-up creatinine through day 7. Predictors included age, sex, first-24-hour renal and electrolyte laboratories, missingness indicators, and first-24-hour creatinine count. The endpoint was not intended to represent full KDIGO staging or incident AKI at ICU admission. We assessed endpoint computability and laboratory coverage, then trained L2-regularized logistic regression models in each database and externally validated them bidirectionally. Evaluation emphasized discrimination, Brier score, calibration, and measurement-density failure modes. The feasibility audit included 94,458 MIMIC-IV and 200,234 eICU adult ICU stays. First-24-hour creatinine coverage was 96.8% and 84.6%, respectively; the primary post-24-hour day-7 endpoint was computable in 89.2% and 65.6%. The modeling cohorts included 84,237 stays from 58,782 MIMIC-IV patients and 131,429 stays from 102,013 eICU patients, with primary endpoint event rates of 26.9% and 18.5%. Internal AUROC was 0.732 in MIMIC-IV and 0.723 in eICU. External AUROC was 0.703 for MIMIC-IV to eICU and 0.722 for eICU to MIMIC-IV, with confidence intervals reported in the main table. Calibration shifted directionally: MIMIC-IV to eICU overpredicted risk, whereas eICU to MIMIC-IV underpredicted higher-risk strata. Prediction of a post-24-hour day-7 creatinine-rise operational endpoint was feasible across MIMIC-IV and eICU, but endpoint computability, laboratory coverage, measurement density, and calibration shift differed substantially. The endpoint was not full KDIGO staging or proof of incident AKI at ICU entry, and the retrospective results do not establish clinical deployment readiness. Renal-risk AI should include an EHR data passport and calibration-focused algorithmovigilance before transport or deployment claims.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: acute kidney injury prediction; eICU-CRD; MIMIC-IV; intensive care unit; serum creatinine
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury Research; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Machine Learning in Healthcare; Health Professions > Health Information Management > Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare

Article.Title: Evaluating the reliability and quality of preeclampsia educational content on short-video platforms: a cross-sectional content analysis
Article.Authors: You S.; Ye H.; Dong Z.; Rao J.; Zhang H.
Article.Abstract: Preeclampsia (PE) is a serious pregnancy-specific complication with a global incidence of 2%–8%, and is a major contributor to adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Short video platforms have emerged as important channels for the public to access health information. However, studies evaluating the quality of PE-related content on these platforms remain scarce. This study aims to assess the perceived general information quality and reliability of short videos pertaining to PE on Douyin and Bilibili, and to analyze the impacts of platform characteristics and uploader background on content quality. Employing a cross-sectional design, we searched both platforms using the keyword “preeclampsia”. Following screening, a total of 164 videos (89 from Douyin, 75 from Bilibili) were included. Video quality was evaluated using the Global Quality Scale (GQS), the modified DISCERN (mDISCERN) instrument, and the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) benchmark criteria. The findings revealed that the unadjusted distribution of scores for GQS, mDISCERN, and JAMA varied by platform. Following adjustment for uploader category and video length, with correction for multiple comparisons, only the GQS instrument retained a significant association (Douyin vs. Bilibili: aOR = 3.917, 95% CI 1.753–8.752; adjust P -value = 0.003), while mDISCERN (adjust P -value = 0.479) and JAMA (adjust P -value = 0.053) showed no significant differences. Videos uploaded by healthcare professionals with the relevant specialty constituted 64.02% of the total sample, and these videos scored significantly higher on the mDISCERN and GQS instruments than did videos from other uploader categories; however, no significant difference was observed for the JAMA scores compared with healthcare professionals outside the relevant specialty (adjust P -value = 0.149). The video content predominantly focuses on clinical manifestations (31.10%), treatment (21.95%), and prevention (20.12%), while topics such as etiology and epidemiology accounted for less than 10% of the content. Correlation analyses stratified by platform did not reveal any consistent and statistically robust associations between engagement metrics and quality scores. The overall quality of PE-related educational content on short video platforms is below average. It is recommended that platforms strengthen the verification of credentials for science-popularization video uploaders and establish evidence-based content standards, while actively encouraging professionals to participate in health science communication. Enhancing public understanding of PE may, to some extent, improve the level of public health literacy.
Article.TopicFields: Social Sciences > Health > Social Media in Health Education; Health Professions > General Health Professions > Health Literacy and Information Accessibility; Nursing > Research and Theory > Health Education and Validation

Article.Title: Bayesian morphometric analysis of Recurring Esthetic Dental (RED) and Golden Proportions in the maxillary anterior dentition using AutoCAD software
Article.Authors: Anees R.; Chaudhary M.; Fatima S.; Mir A.; Ahtasham H.; Ashraf J.
Article.Abstract: The purpose of this study was to characterize Recurring Esthetic Dental (RED) and Golden Proportions in a sample of young Pakistani adults using Bayesian statistical analysis. Specifically, the objectives were to estimate RED ratios and their uncertainty, compare these ratios with Ward’s proposed range, estimate the prevalence of the Golden Proportion, and assess sexual dimorphism in esthetic parameters. The study involved a descriptive cross-sectional research design and was carried out on 28 young adult Pakistani respondents (13 males and 15 females; age 18–30 years) with naturally matched dentitions. Standardized frontal smile photographs were acquired and calibrated using an L-shaped scale. Mesiodistal widths and cervico-incisal heights of maxillary central incisors (CI), lateral incisors (LI), and canines (Ca) were measured digitally using AutoCAD linear dimension tool. RED ratios (LI/CI, Ca/LI) and Golden Proportion conformity (ratios within 0.618 ± 10%) were calculated. Bayesian logistic regression models were used to estimate population parameters. Informative priors based on the existing morphometric literature were used to strongly address the small sample size. The Bayesian posterior mean for the LI/CI RED ratio was 0.69 (95% Credible Interval [CrI]: 0.65–0.72), with a probability of 1.00 (100%) falling within the classic 0.60–0.80 RED range. Conversely, the Ca/LI ratio mean was 0.81 (95% CrI: 0.77–0.87), exceeding the standard RED limit. The Golden Proportion was observed in 50% (95% CrI: 33–68%) of LI/CI pairs but only 17% (95% CrI: 6–32%) of Ca/LI pairs. While females in this specific cohort exhibited larger absolute central incisor widths than males (mean difference + 1.46 mm), the esthetic ratios showed no statistically significant sexual diversity. The Golden Proportion was not consistently observed, while RED relationships varied across the anterior dentition. Esthetic proportions were similar between genders despite differences in absolute tooth dimensions. These findings support the flexible rather than rigid application of esthetic proportions in clinical smile design.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: golden ratio; maxillary anterior teeth; dental aesthetics; sexual dimorphism

Article.Title: Valorisation of Bos-indicus excreta biowaste into nanocellulose-reinforced PVA composite films for sustainable seed coating
Article.Authors: Singh P.; Verma S.; Singhal B.; Goyal R.; Kumar Shukla S.; Pathania A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Agro-livestock nano-composite film enhance bio-degradable polymeric property and seed coating technology. Nanocellulose derived from bovine excreta (BNC) offer a promising strategy for sustainable crop production and storage. In this study the optimized film was evaluated for dip seed coating i.e. mung bean (Vigna radiata). Nanocellulose-polyvinyl alcohol coated seeds showed significantly enhanced germination and seedling growth at 5% NC-PVA composite. After 6 days, root and shoot lengths reached 10.20 cm and 13.60 cm, respectively, compared with 6.95 and 9.85 cm for the H₂O control. The improved performance was attributed to the moisture-retaining and gas-permeable nanocellulose network which is suitable for storage application in packaging. In this study novelty lie in, nanocellulose extracted from Bos-indicus excreta through alkaline treatment and sulfuric acid hydrolysis with less percentage of NaOH as reported earlier. NC incorporation in different percentage into polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) to fabricate biodegradable bio-nanocomposite films. Structural analyses ensured the successful elimination of hemicellulose and lignin components along with formation of cellulose I nanocrystals with nanoscale diameter 15.95 nm through TEM morphology. Among the prepared formulations (1–7 wt% nanocellulose), the 5 wt% NC-PVA film exhibited the optimum properties, including a crystallinity index of 79.14%, tensile strength of 31.76 MPa, and improved thermal stability attributed to strong nanocellulose-PVA interfacial hydrogen bonding through (251.4 °C to 362.8 °C). This study demonstrates an effective waste-valorisation approach for producing biodegradable seed-coating materials that improve germination efficiency and extended the period of storage of seed, support sustainable agricultural practices and reduction in white pollution.

Article.Title: Energy-aware event-triggered nonsingular terminal sliding mode control for PMSM-driven electric vehicles
Article.Authors: Javanbakht H.; Bayat F.; Khodabandeh M.; Bartoszewicz A.
Article.Abstract: The ongoing transition toward electrified transportation necessitates robust, efficient, and computationally economical powertrain control systems. This paper presents a novel adaptive energy-based dynamic event-triggered nonsingular terminal sliding mode control (AET-NTSMC) framework for permanent magnet synchronous motor (PMSM)-driven electric vehicles (EVs). A nonsingular terminal sliding surface is designed to ensure finite-time convergence of the speed tracking error without singularity issues, while an Extended State Observer (ESO) with a road-slope decoupling mechanism estimates and compensates for lumped uncertainties and disturbances. In addition, an energy-based hybrid dynamic event-triggering mechanism is developed to reduce unnecessary control updates while preserving tracking performance. Lyapunov analysis establishes finite-time closed-loop stability and excludes Zeno behavior. MATLAB/Simulink simulations, including validation using the EV Powertrain Blockset, demonstrate that the proposed AET-NTSMC achieves a speed-tracking RMSE of 1.14 m/s, compared with 2.13 m/s for PI control and 1.39 m/s for standard ET-NTSMC. Moreover, the torque variance is reduced to 0.51, compared with 1.14 for PI control and 0.70 for standard ET-NTSMC. The proposed method also reduces control signal transmissions by 99.71%, requiring only 295 updates over 30 s compared with continuous transmission. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in improving tracking accuracy, torque smoothness, and communication efficiency.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Control and Systems Engineering > Adaptive Control of Nonlinear Systems; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Sensorless Control of Electric Motors; Engineering > Automotive Engineering > Vehicle Dynamics and Control Systems

Article.Title: Automated quantification of the meiotic spindle-polar body angle and its association with embryo euploidy
Article.Authors: Kratochvílová I.; Teplá O.; Jirsová S.; Moosová M.; Baručić D.; Kybic J.; Komrskova K.; Mašata J.
Article.Abstract: Non-invasive assessment of embryo euploidy from oocyte-derived parameters remains a major challenge in assisted reproduction. Oocyte meiotic competence is closely associated with embryo ploidy. Our proof-of-concept study establishes a methodology for identifying a laboratory-specific meiotic spindle-polar body (MS-PB) angle range in which embryo euploidy is more frequent than outside this range. MS-PB angles were automatically quantified from polarized light microscopy photographs and videos using a U-Net-based deep learning model. Oocytes clinically classified as metaphase II (MII) were recorded ~ 40 h after trigger administration. The final analysis included 81 oocytes with an evaluable MS-PB angle and an available PGT-A result from the corresponding embryo. Embryos derived from oocytes within the exploratory laboratory-specific MS-PB angle range (8-32°) exhibited significantly higher euploidy rates than those outside this interval (72.2% vs. 31.1%; p = 0.000236). Patient-clustered binary logistic regression showed 5.76-fold higher odds of euploidy within this range (OR = 5.76, 95% CI 2.03-16.31; p = 0.00098). Exploratory ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.725, further supporting the association between the MS-PB angle and embryo ploidy. Our findings demonstrate the potential of automated MS-PB angle measurement to provide information on corresponding embryo ploidy.
