Article.Title: Aerodynamic stability enhancement and nonlinear flutter control in piezoelectric integrated bolted multi-plate assemblies under dynamic flow conditions
Article.Authors: Safarpour M.; Foong L.; Yaylacı M.; Bayram M.
Article.Abstract: The current research work focuses on studying the aerodynamic stability and active nonlinear flutter control of a bolted joint multi-panel assembly (BJMP). This structure type, due to its nonlinear aeroelastic properties combined with joint friction and the dynamics of flow, represents a great difficulty for the safety of such a structure. In order to suppress the flutter phenomenon, piezoelectric sensors and actuators are attached to this structure and are shunted with a negative-capacitance piezoelectric shunt damping circuit (NC-PSDC). The complete theory of the BJMP system is formulated, where the contribution of elastic and motional energies of each rim part is included in order to find energy functionals for a hybrid multi-panel assembly using Hamilton’s variational principle. The final eigenvalue problem gives complex eigenvalues; the emergence of flutter is marked by any pair of eigenvalues having positive real parts, thus giving the critical flutter aerodynamic pressure (CFAP) and non-dimensional CFAP (NCFAP). In cases where the critical flutter regime has been exceeded, the non-linear phenomenon is accounted for through a time-stepping approach that involves the combination of Newton’s iteration technique and the Newmark integration technique. The study shows that the NC-PSDC improves aerodynamic stability through a combined mechanism: the shunt modifies the effective electromechanical stiffness of the coupled panel–circuit system, while the resistive branch of the circuit dissipates vibrational energy. The net effect is a substantial reduction of nonlinear flutter oscillations, provided the negative-capacitance ratio is selected below its optimal limit.

Article.Title: Integrating hippopotamus optimization algorithm into machine learning frameworks for predicting suspended sediment concentrations
Article.Authors: Nasrabadi M.; Mehri Y.; Sabbar A.; Nahvinia M.; Omid M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The vertical distribution of sediment concentration is a fundamental component of sediment transport hydraulics, directly impacting the estimation of sediment loads in riverine and channel systems. Therefore, accurate characterization of this distribution remains a critical challenge in hydraulic engineering. To address this, advanced intelligent modeling techniques offer a robust pathway for reliable prediction. This study evaluates the performance of six distinct modeling approaches—ORELM, ORELM-HOA, GPR, GPR-HOA, GMDH-ANFIS, and GMDH-ANFIS-HOA—to predict the relative sediment concentration distribution (C/C a ​). Results indicated that the integration of meta-heuristic optimization significantly enhances the predictive precision of the GMDH-ANFIS, ORELM, and GPR frameworks. Comparative analysis reveals that the GMDH-ANFIS-HOA model achieved the highest predictive accuracy, yielding an RMSE of 0.0434 and R 2 of 0.9747 during the training phase, and an RMSE of 0.0424 and R 2 of 0.9727 during the testing phase. The GPR-HOA model followed as the second-best performer. Furthermore, sensitivity analysis identified the relative depth (y/D) as the most dominant factor influencing model accuracy. These findings demonstrate that the optimized GMDH-ANFIS-HOA model provides a reliable and efficient computational tool for engineers and hydrologists, facilitating improved design and management of irrigation canals, river engineering projects, and sediment-related environmental assessments.

Article.Title: Development of a human respiratory tract effector cell-mediated antiviral assay using blood and airway immune cells from individuals previously hospitalised with COVID-19
Article.Authors: Tomasicchio M.; Semple L.; Londt R.; Esmail A.; Lucas L.; Oelofse S.; Pooran A.; Jaumdally S.; Moore P.; Dheda K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Serum antibody–based neutralisation assays correlate with protective immunity to SARS-CoV-2, but cell-mediated in vitro cytotoxicity assays are lacking. Data on virus-specific respiratory tract immune responses in humans remain limited. Fifteen healthy participants who had previously been hospitalised with severe COVID-19 pneumonia were recruited. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), and nasal lavage (NL) cells were phenotyped by flow cytometry. Cells were stimulated with SARS-CoV-2 S1 receptor-binding domain and nucleocapsid antigens using 15-mer peptide pools or recombinant proteins. Compartment-specific effector cell-mediated cytotoxicity of SARS-CoV-2 Delta pseudovirus by antigen-stimulated effector cells was assessed using a luciferase assay. Cytokine expression was measured by Luminex. Distinct immune profiles were observed across compartments. Macrophages and dendritic cells predominated in BAL, B cells in NL, and T cells and natural killer cells in PBMCs. BAL cells expressed significantly higher IL-1β, while PBMCs showed higher TNF-α, IL-2 and IL-6 expression. Responses did not differ between peptide and protein antigens. Antigen-stimulated PBMC, BAL, and NL cells demonstrated significantly greater pseudovirus cytotoxicity than unstimulated controls ( p < 0.05). This proof-of-concept study establishes a functional human T-cell–mediated SARS-CoV-2 cytotoxic assay in blood and alveolar compartments, providing a platform to study antiviral mucosal immunity relevant to future pandemics.

Article.Title: Waves of control: An ER(S)P study to explore the neural dynamics of proactive and reactive stability
Article.Authors: Viviani G.; Visalli A.; Montefinese M.; Di Pietro I.; Ruz M.; Vallesi A.; Ambrosini E.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive stability, the ability to maintain task focus while facing distractions, is a core component of cognitive control. According to the Dual Mechanisms of Control model, stability can be implemented proactively, through anticipatory goal maintenance, or reactively, through transient, conflict-triggered adjustments. However, their neural dynamics remain debated, mainly due to the limited temporal resolution of fMRI and to EEG designs that fail to disentangle different forms of stability. Here, we recorded EEG while 40 participants performed a spatial Stroop task to dissociate predictive proactive stability, induced by list-wide proportion congruency (LWPC), and predictive reactive stability, induced by item-specific proportion congruency (ISPC). Moreover, using response-locked analyses, we exploratively probed the late, corrective form of reactive stability engaged after conflict detection. Using a state-of-the-art analytical approach combining trial-level Bayesian estimates of the manipulated variables with multilevel modeling, we isolated these predictive mechanisms from low-level confounds like contingency. The analyses of event-related potentials and time-frequency activity revealed neural signatures of proactive stability, including anticipatory pre-stimulus modulations and a systematic reduction of post-stimulus conflict-related activity. In contrast, no reliable neural evidence for predictive reactive stability was observed once contingency was controlled. Importantly, response-locked analyses revealed distinct late neural markers compatible with a corrective reactive stability mechanism engaged to resolve conflict when predictive mechanisms failed. Together, these findings provide clear electrophysiological evidence for predictive proactive stability neural mechanisms, while failing to reveal those of ISPC-dependent predictive reactive stability. Moreover, exploratory analyses provided insights into late corrective reactive stability neural mechanisms, engaged when predictive mechanisms failed.

Article.Title: The effects of foreign accent syndrome on bilingual speech production: Multilevel evidence from a controlled-case study
Article.Authors: Contreras-Ruston F.; Navarra J.; Elvira-García W.; Sierpowska J.; Rico-Pons I.; Paipa A.; Peñaloza C.
Article.Abstract: Foreign Accent Syndrome (FAS) is a rare motor speech disorder with altered speech patterns perceived as a foreign accent. The effects of FAS on the first (L1) and second-acquired (L2) languages in bilinguals have not been examined in depth and knowledge about its neural correlates is limited. Additionally, possible disruptions in auditory-motor feedback processes supporting speech monitoring and voice adaptation are rarely assessed. This study reports on P1, an L1 Catalan- L2 Spanish bilingual with FAS. We sought to characterize FAS in her two languages using a multilevel approach combining perceptual, phonetic, neuropsychological, sensorimotor adaptation to auditory feedback and structural neuroimaging analyses. Results showed that P1's L1 and L2 speech production were perceived as foreign by native bilingual listeners. Phonetic analyses revealed segmental and suprasegmental disturbances in both languages resulting from focal left motor cortex damage. Voice adaptation to auditory noise revealed an abnormal pattern, with differences between L1 and L2, suggesting altered auditory-motor integration. Notably, P1's speech rate, fluency and eloquence were more affected in her L1, suggesting decreased automaticity in this language. She also presented domain-general executive control deficits and increased L1 to L2 switching, as she found L2 production easier. These findings suggest differential effects of FAS on the L1 and L2 speech production of P1, with increased L1-L2 switching as a potential compensatory strategy to decrease executive control burden in L1 production and facilitate more fluent communication. Our findings highlight a potential role for disrupted auditory-motor speech and voice integration in the manifestation of bilingual FAS.

Article.Title: Assessing brain-behaviour coupling in non-invasive brain stimulation: Insights from reliable change indices and Monte Carlo simulations
Article.Authors: Fujiyama H.; Wansbrough K.; Lebihan B.; Tan J.; Levin O.; Mathersul D.; Tang A.
Article.Abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NiBS) studies frequently report exploratory brain-behaviour correlations following the application of NiBS. However, these analyses are typically underpowered and rely on ratio-based change scores with known statistical limitations. We addressed these limitations by pooling individual data from three independent studies (N = 69) and combining empirical analysis with a Monte Carlo simulation framework. All studies applied 20 Hz transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) targeting the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) and right inferior frontal gyrus (rIFG) during a stop signal task. Changes in preSMA-rIFG EEG imaginary coherency (ImCoh) and stop-signal reaction time (SSRT) were quantified using reliable change indices (RCI), z-standardised within studies for pooled mixed-effects regression. We found no meaningful association between tACS-induced ImCoh change and SSRT change (r = .013, marginal R2 = .004), with project-wise correlations being small, non-significant, and directionally inconsistent. While sensitivity analysis using ratio-based change scores converged on the same null result (r = .014), the simulation framework revealed that ratio-based scores show near-complete failure to recover true brain-behaviour associations across all plausible effect sizes. Conversely, RCI-based scores preserved directional accuracy and provided well-calibrated Type I error control, despite moderate attenuation under realistic noise conditions. These results highlight the severe statistical limits of detecting individual-level brain-behaviour coupling following 20 Hz tACS. Rather than ruling out a true biological association, our findings demonstrate that standard sample sizes and typical measurement noise create substantial 'blindness' to realistic effect sizes, underscoring a broader need for more reliable metrics and adequately powered designs in NiBS research.

Article.Title: Imaginal neglect as a disorder of mental scene construction
Article.Authors: Bartolomeo P.; Rode G.
Article.Abstract: Imaginal (representational) neglect-typically revealed by contralesional omissions when patients describe familiar places from long-term memory-provides a test case for theories of mental scene construction. Unlike propositional recall of place-related facts, imaginal tasks require that semantic knowledge be "spatialized" into a viewpoint-dependent scene that can be actively sampled. We review converging evidence from classic behavioral dissociations (viewpoint inversion; preserved semantic knowledge with impaired spatialized retrieval), oculomotor measures during imagery, sensory interventions (caloric vestibular stimulation; prismatic adaptation), and lesion/disconnection findings. Reconsidering the long-standing opposition between a primary "representational scotoma" and a pure attentional/exploratory bias, we argue that this dichotomy may not correspond to how scenes are actually built: construction and exploration are tightly coupled processes, partly implemented through attentional/oculomotor control. Building on convergent lesion, meta-analytic and neuroimaging evidence that a left-lateralized image-generation system (including the Fusiform Imagery Node) supports the generation of visual content, we propose as a working hypothesis that balanced, viewpoint-dependent spatial organization depends on right-hemisphere attentional control and inter-hemispheric integration, plausibly involving posterior callosal pathways. We specify construction and exploration as sets of operations, relate the framework to accounts of conscious access, and set out empirical tests of its network-level claims.

Article.Title: From affect to rules: A conceptual model of compensation in prodromal behavioral frontotemporal degeneration
Article.Authors: Bertoux M.
Article.Abstract: Behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) is typically described in terms of progressive loss of social and behavioral control. However, the earliest stages of the disease may also involve active, developed forms of compensation that remain largely invisible to standard assessment. These strategies are rarely characterized, yet they may offer a unique entry point into the mechanisms by which social functioning is temporarily preserved despite emerging degeneration. Here, I report a longitudinal single-case study of a young C9orf72 repeat-expansion carrier followed from the prodromal stage to established moderate bvFTD. Based on more than a dozen hours of semi-structured interviews initiated at symptom emergence, thematic analysis identified five compensatory subthemes. Together, these strategies suggested a coherent shift in the architecture of behavioral control that remain largely invisible to standard medical or neuropsychological assessment. As implicit, flexible, and internally sustained regulation became less reliable, functioning appeared to rely on control processes that were more explicit, environmentally distributed, routine-based, and effortful. These observations can be organized around three broader principles: explicitation, externalization, and stabilization. The case suggests that early preservation in bvFTD may reflect not only residual capacities, but also an active and fragile reorganization of social and behavioral control. By foregrounding the patient's own compensatory work, this study provides a hypothesis-generating conceptual framework for understanding how everyday functioning may be maintained during the prodromal-to-dementia transition, and highlights qualitative longitudinal single-case designs and participatory research as a powerful tool for identifying hidden forms of adaptation in neurodegenerative disease and refine theoretical models of social behavior.

Article.Title: Valence and expectation effects shape event-related potentials to probabilistic social-evaluative feedback from putative peers
Article.Authors: Schindler S.; Hohls R.; Schlossmacher I.; Moeck R.; Straube T.
Article.Abstract: In everyday life, we receive social evaluative feedback from specific interaction partners that shapes our expectations about future feedback. It has been proposed that feedback processing and expectations are biased toward positive social feedback. However, the neuronal processes underlying biased social feedback processing remain unclear. In the current Event-Related Potentials (ERPs) study, we exposed participants to seemingly real social evaluations from three senders, each providing dichotomous positive or negative feedback on trait adjectives. In reality, feedback contingencies were manipulated with different ratios of positive versus negative feedback (rare 20 vs 80; equal 50 vs 50; frequent 80 vs 20 per cent of all trials). Participants' expectation ratings followed the general feedback ratios, though they indicated higher expectations for positive feedback. A lower probability of feedback increased all investigated ERP components, except the P1. Furthermore, positive versus negative feedback led to relatively more positive amplitudes in the Feedback-Related Negativity (FRN) and Late Positive Potential (LPP) time windows. Interactions between valence and probability were found for exploratory analyses of the Early Posterior Negativity (EPN) and theory-driven analyses of the P3, with specifically increased amplitudes for rare negative feedback compared to rare positive feedback. The results suggest that, even though negative feedback elicited higher prediction-error-related effects in ERPs associated with general surprise responses (P3) and perceptual attentional enhancement (EPN), the LPP, which is related to elaborate processing, integration, and updating, exhibited larger amplitudes for positive feedback, possibly reflecting biased processing of positive feedback. This may be fundamental for maintaining a positively biased self-view.

Article.Title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of interoceptive conceptual processing in the human brain
Article.Authors: Amoruso L.; Birba A.; Moguilner S.; Castillo E.; Kleineschay T.; Ibañez A.; García A.
Article.Abstract: Embodied accounts of meaning describe conceptual knowledge as grounded in bodily experience. Yet, neurophysiological research has privileged exteroceptive domains (concepts associated with visual, auditory, motor or otherwise body-external phenomena), overlooking the spatio-temporal dynamics of interoceptive domains (concepts evoking physiological, visceral and other internal states). This magnetoencephalography (MEG) study combined time-frequency and representational similarity analyses (RSA) with descriptive source reconstruction and cardiac-derived autonomic measures to characterize the spatiotemporal dynamics of interoceptive meaning. Participants (n = 16) performed a lexical decision task involving verbs varying in interoceptive strength. Relative to low-interoceptive verbs (e.g., texting), high-interoceptive verbs (e.g., inhaling) elicited greater low-beta power (15-21 Hz) between 96 and 176 msec over right temporal sensors. Source estimates indicated plausible contributions from right medial temporal, ventral occipito-temporal regions, and sensorimotor cortices. Stronger beta responses to high-interoceptive verbs were associated with lower short-term cardiac variability, indicating covariation between interoceptive semantic processing and concurrent autonomic regulation. Temporal-resolved RSA further showed that interoceptive strength explained unique variance in neural representational structure beyond emotional and lexical dimensions, with this effect extending from 190 to 600 msec. Together, these findings identify interoceptive strength as a distinct dimension of conceptual organization and suggest that accessing interoceptive meaning recruits neural dynamics linked to the processing and regulation of internal bodily states.

Article.Title: Reduced magnocellular-biased visual responses are associated with working memory and linguistic difficulties in Chinese developmental dyslexia: A hypothesized visual-cognitive cascade
Article.Authors: Wong C.; Liu D.; Chan H.; Leung T.
Article.Abstract: Developmental dyslexia (DD) affects 5-10% of children worldwide. Although phonological theories predominate, they may not fully explain reading difficulties in orthographically dense scripts such as Chinese. We investigated whether Chinese children with DD exhibit differences in early visual cortical responses and how these differences relate to reading-related skills. Steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs) were recorded from 50 children with DD and 50 typically developing controls aged 7-11 years using gratings that preferentially bias magnocellular or parvocellular processing. Global motion perception, visuospatial attention, verbal working memory, and linguistic skills were also assessed. Children with DD showed reduced ssVEP amplitudes to low-spatial-frequency stimuli (partial η2 = .43, p < .001), whereas responses to high-spatial-frequency stimuli were preserved. Among the domains examined, the visual-processing model provided the strongest within-sample discrimination between groups (Nagelkerke R2 = .68), with low-spatial-frequency ssVEP amplitude as its only significant visual predictor. Exploratory cross-sectional mediation analyses identified significant indirect associations between ssVEP amplitude and linguistic skills through verbal working memory. For phonological awareness, the indirect association was significant, whereas the corresponding direct association was not; for morphological awareness, both associations remained significant. Visuospatial-attention differences were limited to retrospective selection from working memory rather than initial attentional orienting. For most measures, age-related associations did not differ detectably between groups. These findings are compatible with a hypothesized visual-cognitive cascade involving early visual cortical processing, working memory, and reading-related difficulties. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal or causal relationships; longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to test the proposed model.

Article.Title: Language assessment during awake brain surgery: Challenges in multilingual and underrepresented language contexts
Article.Authors: Rami Y.; El Ouardi L.; Ruis C.
Article.Abstract: Awake surgery for brain tumors in language areas relies on intraoperative language assessment to maximize tumor resection while preserving essential language functions. However, most language assessment tools used in this context were developed in Western, monolingual populations, limiting their validity in multilingual and underrepresented language settings. This position paper examines the challenges of intraoperative language assessment in such contexts, with a focus on Morocco as a representative case of multilingualism and diglossia. We argue that current assessment practices might be constrained by, among others, linguistic diversity, educational and literacy disparities, stimulus limitations, interpreter-mediated testing, and structural gaps in research. The paper proposes several recommendations, including moving beyond direct translation toward principled adaptation of assessment tools, developing culturally and linguistically validated stimuli, improving standardization and reporting of multilingual practices, strengthening multidisciplinary collaboration, and expanding preoperative linguistic profiling. Addressing these challenges is essential for improving the validity and equity of intraoperative language mapping in multilingual and underrepresented language contexts and for ensuring accurate preservation of language function in diverse clinical populations.

Article.Title: Multi-modal lesion mapping of expressive aprosodia
Article.Authors: Peters J.; Boes A.; Griffis J.; Bruss J.; Tranel D.; Kliemann D.
Article.Abstract: Affective prosody facilitates the communication of emotions by modulating paralinguistic features of speech (e.g., pitch and rhythm). Patients with brain injuries may exhibit impaired expression of affective prosody, referred to as expressive aprosodia, adversely impacting social interactions and quality of life. Despite many previous lesion studies, relatively few studies have investigated neural correlates of expressive aprosodia using a combination of lesion location, as well as associated structural and functional network mapping, within a large patient sample. There is especially a need to advance our understanding of the neurobiology associated with expressive aprosodia in the chronic phase (i.e., >3 months after lesion onset) given the practical importance of long-term outcomes in regard to social functioning and quality of life. The present study therefore aimed to characterize how expressive aprosodia relates to lesion location and disruption of associated structural and functional brain networks in a large sample of participants with chronic focal brain lesions (N = 673). Using a clinical expert evaluation of prosody and multi-modal lesion mapping, the results showed that expressive aprosodia was most strongly associated with i) lesions affecting right-lateralized fronto-insular-striatal regions, ii) prominent disconnection of right-lateralized cortico-subcortical pathways, and iii) damage to regions exhibiting functional connectivity with subcortical (basal ganglia, thalamus) and cortical ventral attention/salience networks. Overall, these findings are consistent with a previously proposed dorsal stream for expressive aprosodia and provide further insights into the neural architecture whose damage is associated with chronic expressive aprosodia.

Article.Title: Distribution and age-interactions of cortical thickness associated with specific classes of medication used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder: Results from the international ENIGMA consortium
Article.Authors: Ivanov I.; Dzinalija N.; Abe Y.; Alonso P.; Ameis S.; Arnold P.; Baker J.; Balachander S.; Banaj N.; Bargalló N.; Batistuzzo M.; Benedetti F.; Beucke J.; Bollettini I.; Brennan B.; Buitelaar J.; Calvo R.; Cheng Y.; Ching C.; Cho K.; Dallaspezia S.; Denys D.; Diniz J.; Ely B.; Ferreira S.
Article.Abstract: MRI studies have revealed structural brain abnormalities in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Less is known about how age and medication influence them. We analyzed cortical thickness (CT) data from the ENIGMA-OCD Consortium, the world's largest OCD MRI database (46 datasets from 35 centers). Subjects comprised 2057 healthy controls, 1167 unmedicated individuals with OCD, and 1073 individuals with OCD taking one or more psychiatric medications at time of scan. Using a harmonized FreeSurfer protocol, each MRI was parcellated into 68 cortical regions. Linear mixed models controlling for site and symptom severity mapped associations of OCD diagnosis and medication-any psychiatric medication and the medication classes serotonin-reuptake inhibitors (SRIs), tricyclics, antipsychotics, and benzodiazepines-on CT and their interaction with age in each region. Findings surviving FDR-correction included: 1) Unmedicated OCD participants showed thicker cortex and/or lesser CT decrease with age than controls in precentral, inferior parietal, superior parietal, and superior temporal regions (p < .001-.002); 2) In several regions, OCD participants taking any medication had thinner cortex than unmedicated; negative associations of age with CT were similar to controls (p < .001-.005). 3) Findings for SRIs resembled those in for any psychiatric medication. 4) CT was lower in participants taking benzodiazepines than in unmedicated participants in 30 regions (p < .001-.014). No associations of CT involving tricyclics or antipsychotics survived FDR-correction. Commonly prescribed OCD drugs may influence CT in ways that vary with cortical region and medication class. Potential mechanisms are discussed.

Article.Title: Highly superior autobiographical memory (HSAM) in a 16-year-old male: Investigating involuntary autobiographical memory with questionnaire and laboratory methods
Article.Authors: Barzykowski K.; Santangelo V.; Kvavilashvili L.; Moulin C.
Article.Abstract: Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory (HSAM) is characterized by an exceptional ability to recall personal past events with remarkable accuracy and detail. While the mechanisms underlying this ability have begun to be elucidated, research so far has largely focused mainly on voluntary retrieval processes. The present study aimed to investigate autobiographical memory functioning in a single HSAM case (KCL), with a particular focus on involuntary autobiographical memories (IAMs). We combined standardized HSAM screening procedures with a multi-method assessment of autobiographical memory, implemented remotely under continuous researcher supervision. General autobiographical functioning was assessed using the Autobiographical Recollection Test and the Survey of Autobiographical Memory. Additional measures captured general memory functioning, mind-wandering, metacognitive and phenomenological characteristics, cognitive control, and affective and personality variables. IAMs were assessed using both self-report (Involuntary Autobiographical Memory Inventory) and a laboratory vigilance task with incidental cue-words and probe-caught thought sampling. KCL met established HSAM criteria and exhibited a markedly elevated frequency of IAMs relative to a comparison group, both in self-report and laboratory measures. Crucially, this increase did not reflect a general rise in spontaneous cognition, as overall task-unrelated thought frequency remained comparable, but rather a selective bias toward autobiographical content. At the same time, KCL did not differ from the general population in overall phenomenological experience of remembering, although he reported elevated autobiographical memory ability alongside increased confidence in memory accuracy. The results highlight the central role of involuntary remembering and point to altered cue sensitivity and lowered retrieval thresholds as key mechanisms underlying exceptional autobiographical memory.

Article.Title: Clarifying the scope and boundaries of the motor simulation theory: A constructive perspective for motor imagery research
Article.Authors: Guillot A.; Lebon F.; Vogt S.; Zentgraf K.; Stinear C.; Di Rienzo F.
Article.Abstract: Motor imagery has attracted renewed interest in recent years, along with renewed debate about the Motor Simulation Theory, which posits activation of motor-related neural systems to internally simulate action without execution. While recent work has clarified some empirical limits of imagery, particularly in feedback-based learning, other critiques misinterpret the theory's core assumptions. This paper distinguishes between empirically grounded challenges that refine the Motor Simulation Theory, such as those involving executive processes and partial motor activation, and conceptual misunderstandings that mischaracterize the theory. Claims that the theory predicts exact timing equivalence or complete neural overlap with action execution, or supports sensorimotor adaptation overlook the functional equivalence principle at its foundation. We also argue that alternative, behaviorally focused theories often neglect robust neurophysiological evidence underpinning the Motor Simulation Theory. We advocate for an integrated perspective that maintains its predictive value while accommodating valid critiques, aiming to clarify its boundaries and relevance for imagery research.

Article.Title: The role of extra-striate areas in conscious motor behavior: A registered report with fast-optical imaging
Article.Authors: Colombari E.; Parisi G.; Mele S.; Mazzi C.; Savazzi S.
Article.Abstract: Disclosing the brain areas responsible for the emergence of visual awareness and their timing of activation represents one of the major challenges in consciousness research. In particular, isolating the neural processes strictly related to consciousness from concurrent neural dynamics, either related to prerequisites or post-perceptual processing, has long engaged consciousness research. In this framework, the present study aims at unraveling the spatio-temporal dynamics underlying conscious vision by adopting a distinctive experimental design in which both awareness and motor response are manipulated, allowing the segregation of neural activity strictly related to awareness from response-related mechanisms. The study included 32 participants. We employed a GO/NOGO detection task, in which participants responded or withheld responding according to the experimental condition. Critically, during the performance of the task, participants' brain activity was recorded by means of Event-Related Optical Signal (EROS) technique, which provides accurate information about brain functions both from the temporal and spatial point of view within the covered regions, simultaneously. The combination of this experimental design with EROS recording enabled us to pinpoint the neural correlates underlying conscious vision and to disentangle them from processes related to the response. Extra-striate areas, specifically the Lateral Occipital Complex (LOC), showed greater awareness-related activity independently of motor response. Our findings support the view that LOC plays a key role as a proper correlate of visual awareness, rather than post-perceptual or response-related processes. They also show that awareness modulates motor activity only when a response is executed, clarifying how conscious perception influences downstream motor processing.

Article.Title: Dystextia due to impairment in spatial operation on a smartphone: A case report
Article.Authors: Hayakawa H.; Hatakeyama M.; Otsuki M.; Takahashi T.; Tsuboguchi S.; Ishiguro T.; Ishihara T.; Onodera O.
Article.Abstract: Smartphone texting has become indispensable in modern life. Although dystextia (texting disability) has been reported, dystextia without aphasia or other cognitive impairment remains rare, and its pathophysiology is not fully understood. In Japanese text entry, the consonant is selected first on the screen, and the vowel is then determined by slide direction. Thus, accurate text input likely requires a sequence of processes, including segmentation of morae into consonants and vowels, followed by the spatial operation corresponding to each. Here, we report a patient with dystextia associated with impaired key-position and slide-direction processing. A 57-year-old right-handed Japanese woman developed difficulty with texting. Standard neuropsychological testing showed no aphasia, agraphia, or other cognitive impairment except for apraxia of speech and mild attention/executive dysfunction. Accordingly, dystextia was diagnosed. In addition, the patient had difficulty identifying keys corresponding to consonants and the slide direction corresponding to vowels. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a subcortical infarction in the left cerebral hemisphere. Single-photon emission tomography showed hypoperfusion, including in the left dorsolateral frontal lobe. The left frontal lobe is thought to contribute to spatial operations on digital devices. Therefore, diaschisis of the left dorsolateral frontal lobe secondary to the subcortical lesion may be associated with impairment of key-position and flick-direction processing, which may have contributed to dystextia in this patient.

Article.Title: Beyond dual hubs: Task and aging shape taxonomic and thematic semantic relationships in the human brain
Article.Authors: Kuhnke P.; Martin S.; Chapman C.; Hartwigsen G.
Article.Abstract: Semantic knowledge about concepts and their relationships is central to human cognition. Taxonomic relationships link concepts belonging to the same category (e.g. dog and bear), while thematic relationships connect concepts co-occurring in the same events (e.g. dog and leash). The dual-hub theory proposes that taxonomic relations preferentially engage the anterior temporal lobe (ATL), whereas thematic relations preferentially involve the temporo-parietal cortex (TPC). However, it remains unclear whether taxonomic and thematic representations depend on the concurrent task and how they change with aging. The present fMRI study addressed these gaps by jointly investigating the effects of semantic relationship, task, and age on semantic processing. 41 young and 34 older adults performed taxonomic and thematic judgments on picture pairs that were taxonomically related, thematically related, or unrelated. Our results do not support the dual-hub theory: Both TPC and ATL preferentially responded to thematic over taxonomic relationships. Moreover, their activity was task-dependent. Semantic control regions flexibly responded to task-relevant semantic relations, while inhibiting task-irrelevant relations. Finally, aging was associated with a decline in domain-general and domain-specific semantic control, more bilateral ATL engagement, as well as behavioral and neural shifts from taxonomic towards thematic processing. Increased thematic activity was associated with higher accuracy but slower responses. These findings support accounts of age-related neural dedifferentiation and semanticization: Older adults require increased cognitive resources to maintain accuracy at a high level, but this comes at the cost of efficiency.

Article.Title: Beyond “more synchrony”: Frequency- and phase-specific effects of fronto-parietal theta tACS in enhancing episodic memory
Article.Authors: Aktürk T.; Sack A.
Article.Abstract: Theta oscillations support episodic memory and long-range communication between prefrontal and parietal regions. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) offers a way to test how theta dynamics influence memory. In our previous work, stimulation 1 Hz below the individual theta frequency (ITF-1) improved episodic memory, and this improvement was correlated with changes in fronto-parietal connectivity. Here, we tested whether dual-site fronto-parietal theta tACS produces frequency- and phase-specific aftereffects on episodic memory and theta-network dynamics. Neurotypical adults (N = 42) were assigned to ITF-1 or ITF+1 groups, with ITF estimated from pre-tACS resting-state EEG. Participants completed three counterbalanced sessions of dual-site tACS over left prefrontal and posterior-parietal locations: in-phase, anti-phase, and sham. Pre- and post-stimulation assessments included episodic memory measures, namely free recall and temporal order judgment (TOJ) with confidence ratings, as well as EEG recordings. TOJ accuracy showed a significant Session × Group interaction, driven by greater improvement in ITF-1 than ITF+1 following anti-phase stimulation. In ITF-1, confidence-accuracy discrimination (metacognitive separation) decreased after in-phase relative to anti-phase and sham. Resting-state, but not event-related, theta connectivity showed an anti-phase-specific divergence in fronto-parietal coupling, increasing in ITF-1 and decreasing in ITF+1. Within ITF-1 anti-phase, larger increases in resting-state fronto-parietal connectivity were associated with greater TOJ gains. These findings indicate phase-, frequency, and state-specific modulation of episodic memory and fronto-parietal theta networks by tACS. While the behavioral advantage of lower-frequency stimulation aligned with our hypothesis, the selective benefit of anti-phase stimulation suggests a more flexible, task-dependent reconfiguration of long-range connectivity rather than a uniform increase in synchrony.

Article.Title: Grounding meaning in social and emotional experience: Challenges and opportunities
Article.Authors: Solana P.
Article.Abstract: Within the broader debate on how the mind and brain represent meaning, multiple representation theories have positioned social and emotional experience, along with their underlying neural systems, as key sources for concept grounding. In this article, I review the current evidence for this proposal and discuss several conceptual and methodological challenges, including the limited capacity of behavioral evidence to support this view, the difficulties associated with interpreting neuroimaging findings, the need for stronger causal evidence, and the importance of adopting open science practices. I argue that these limitations converge on a common concern: in their current form, many findings taken to support multiple representation theories of socio-affective grounding do not provide sufficiently diagnostic evidence to empirically adjudicate between them and competing accounts of semantic representation. In response, I outline a set of methodological recommendations and underexplored ideas that may help refine the theoretical framework, generate more decisive tests, and guide future research.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: causal evidence; open science; neuroimaging interpretation; semantic representation

Article.Title: Resting-state and picture-naming EEG reveal aberrant connectomes and outcome-associated dysfunctomes in Cantonese post-stroke aphasia: A multi-frequency exploratory analysis
Article.Authors: Cheung C.; Kong A.
Article.Abstract: Post-stroke aphasia (PSA) is increasingly understood as a network disorder, yet its electrophysiological connectome has been characterized almost exclusively in stress-timed Indo-European languages, and rarely with phase-locking connectivity sampled across multiple frequency bands and recording states in the same cohort. We acquired 61-channel resting-state and overt picture-naming EEG in 31 chronic Cantonese-speaking individuals with aphasia and 14 demographically matched neurologically healthy controls, computed surface-Laplacian-transformed phase-locking-value connectivity in six canonical frequency bands (delta, theta, alpha, low-beta, high-beta, low-gamma), and used Network-based Statistic to identify within-group aberrant naming engagement subnetworks, between-group aberrant subnetwork, and outcome-associated dysfunctomes (subnetworks associated with seven clinical outcomes). Best-supported band × state dysfunctomes were identified through cross-band Akaike model comparison. Results showed that HC and PWA relied on qualitatively different oscillatory subnetworks to shift from rest into naming, with PWA displacing engagement into right-hemisphere and domain-general frontal regions and failing to disengage central alpha. Between-group contrasts highlighted slow-wave-dominant hyperconnective subnetworks in the canonical left temporal regions, reflecting passive cortical dysfunction. Outcome-associated dysfunctomes identified resting-state alpha as the best-fitting candidate for overall aphasia severity, spontaneous speech fluency and informativeness, overall naming, and confrontation naming, and resting-state low-beta as the best-fitting candidate for auditory comprehension. Together, the disrupted naming-engagement subnetworks and peri-lesional slow-wave aberrant connectomes offer mechanistic markers of aphasia-related network reorganization, while the resting-state alpha and low-beta dysfunctomes provide candidate targets to guide outcome-specific precision neuromodulation for PSA.

Article.Title: The cross-modal spread of attention is highly automatic
Article.Authors: Zhao S.; Ma F.; Zhou Y.; Xie J.; Zhou C.; Feng W.
Article.Abstract: Attention can spread across sensory modalities so that when attention is directed to the visual component of a multisensory object, its task-irrelevant auditory component will also be bestowed with enhanced processing, which operates in either a stimulus-driven or representation-driven manner contingent on whether the visual component is attended based on object category. To date, the visual-to-auditory attentional spreading has been widely hypothesized as an involuntary, automatic process, but this core hypothesis has yet to be tested. In particular, the supraliminal auditory components employed in prior studies might have received some sort of voluntary attention after being consciously detected, which impeded the examination of this hypothesis. The present event-related potential (ERP) study examined it in male and female humans (N = 30) by rendering bimodal objects' auditory components sub-threshold (and hence free from being actively attended) in an object-selective visual recognition task wherein ERP correlates of the representation-driven and stimulus-driven attentional spreading could be dissociated. Our ERP data showed reliable stimulus-driven (200-400 msec post-stimulus) and representation-driven (300-400 msec) attentional spreading to the sub-threshold auditory components, and the estimated neural generators of both included regions of the auditory cortex. Meanwhile, multivariate pattern analysis showed that the object categories could be decoded from ERPs to the inaudible sounds, confirming neural processing of these sounds in the absence of awareness. Collectively, these findings offer strong evidence that the visual-to-auditory attentional spreading is highly automatic, which paves the way for elucidating the psychophysiological mechanisms underlying cross-modal attentional spreading.

Article.Title: Neural signatures of harm aversion predict later willingness to exert effort for others' rewards
Article.Authors: Contreras-Huerta L.; Yu H.; Prosser A.; Lockwood P.; Rojas-Thomas F.; Crockett M.; Apps M.
Article.Abstract: Prosocial behaviours, central to human social life, are actions that benefit others. Two key domains are harm aversion, where individuals forgo personal gains to prevent harming others, and prosocial effort, which involves exerting effort to benefit others. Although previous studies suggest a relationship between these behaviours, it remains unclear whether neural responses in one domain can predict prosocial motivation in another. Here, we tested whether neural sensitivity to morally salient information in harm aversion could predict prosocial effort later. Participants (n = 66) completed two tasks: a harm aversion task during fMRI, in which they traded off monetary profit against delivering electric shocks to another person; and, one week later, a prosocial effort task outside the scanner, in which they decided whether rewards for others were worth the required physical effort. We focused on three regions implicated in cost-benefit decision-making and social cognition: the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), anterior insula (AI), and temporoparietal junction (TPJ). Behaviourally, greater harm aversion was associated with increased prosocial effort. Neurally, AI responses to others' harm predicted sensitivity to others' rewards in the effort task, consistent with a role in representing others' outcomes across positive and negative valences. By contrast, TPJ responses to profit from harming others predicted decreased sensitivity to others' rewards, suggesting a role in context-dependent valuation that may constrain prosocial behaviour. These findings reveal that neural responses to morally salient information in one context correlate with prosocial motivation in another, suggesting mechanisms that bridge moral sensitivity and effortful prosociality.

Article.Title: Who owns what? Comprehension of gender information in German possessive pronouns and determiners in aphasia
Article.Authors: Urbanczik G.; Lampe L.; Hanne S.; Arslan S.; Nickels L.
Article.Abstract: Cross-linguistic studies have demonstrated that people with (agrammatic) aphasia often exhibit difficulties in pronoun comprehension, but the role of gender marking has been largely overlooked and prior research has concentrated on only certain pronoun types. This study focused on gender cues in an understudied pronoun type, possessives, in German. German possessive determiners (e.g., seinmasc-efemGabelfem 'his fork') and possessive pronouns (e.g., ihrfem-efem 'hers') comprise two distinct gender cues, with a stem and a suffix providing information about who (possessor) is possessing what (possessee object), respectively. Twelve individuals with a variety of post-stroke aphasia classifications and 31 language-unimpaired controls completed a phrase-picture matching task with parallel eye-tracking requiring identification of the object that was congruent with the possessive form for possessor and possessee gender from an array of four. The off-line accuracy data revealed that the control group performed at ceiling, whereas all participants with aphasia showed difficulty identifying the correct possessee objects. Moreover, a subgroup of participants with aphasia also exhibited impairments in possessor identification. These distinct processing patterns were supported by the on-line eye fixation data. However, the two patterns were not associated with the type of aphasia. We place these findings in the context of previous research on pronoun processing and theoretical accounts of deficits in syntactic comprehension in aphasia. Moreover, we propose possible underlying processing impairments, including differences in the processing of grammatical and semantic gender, and implications for both clinical practice and research.

Article.Title: Salient affective scenes compete with concurrent visual responses in the absence of task demands
Article.Authors: Mirifar A.; Ayomen E.; Engle H.; Gilbert F.; Melville G.; Hammes E.; Lee A.; Mathews C.; Keil A.
Article.Abstract: Visual attention systems of the human brain resolve competition between concurrent inputs by prioritizing information that is relevant to an observer's goals, motives, and biological states. Research shows that concurrent distractors-especially emotionally salient stimuli-reduce task performance and visual responses to task cues. In many naturalistic viewing situations however, there are multiple competing cues with no obvious demarcation between task and distractor. The present study examined whether viewing two overlapping task-irrelevant stimulus streams produces emotion-dependent competition in visual cortex. Steady-state visual evoked potential (ssVEP) frequency tagging independently quantified visuocortical activity elicited by a picture (6.7 Hz) stream that overlapped with a central fixation-cross flickering at 15 Hz. We replicated established interference effects within the picture stream, showing that rapidly changing emotionally salient (pleasant and unpleasant) pictures elicited a strong reduction in the 6.7 Hz ssVEP envelope relative to neutral pictures. The 15 Hz ssVEP to the flickering fixation cross paralleled these findings, being more attenuated when competing with emotional, compared to neutral pictures. Change-point analyses indicated that competition latency varied with picture saliency, occurring earlier for pleasant and unpleasant than for neutral streams. Together, the present study suggests that visuocortical mass activity displays emotion-modulated competition effects in the absence of task demands.

Article.Title: Neural correlates of phi and reverse-phi motion aftereffects: Temporal dynamics of ON–OFF pathway interactions
Article.Authors: Akyuz S.; Kafaligonul H.; Pavan A.
Article.Abstract: Sensory processing is dynamically shaped by neural adaptation, allowing the brain to adjust to recent sensory input. Phi and reverse-phi motion provide a framework for probing adaptive processes and ON-OFF pathway interactions in visual motion processing. We recorded 64-channel EEG while 30 participants completed a rapid motion-adaptation paradigm. Participants adapted to contrast-preserving phi motion or contrast-reversing reverse-phi motion for a short (188 msec) or long (752 msec) duration and then judged the direction of an ambiguous counterphase-flickering test grating. Behaviourally, adaptation duration primarily determined perceptual bias: short adaptation produced a modest same-direction, priming-like bias, whereas long adaptation produced an opposite-direction motion aftereffect. Test-locked event-related potentials (ERPs) revealed a robust Duration × Adaptation Type interaction over early posterior scalp regions (128-160 msec), primarily expressed in the N1 range. This interaction reflected greater differentiation between phi and reverse-phi adaptation after long than short adaptation. Exploratory whole-scalp topographic analyses indicated that the interaction involved changes in scalp-response configuration rather than uniform amplitude modulation. Adapter-locked analyses further showed that phi and reverse-phi motion elicited distinguishable ERP responses during the initial adaptation period and separable multivariate EEG patterns from approximately 50 msec after adapter onset, indicating early neural divergence between the two motion types. Together, these findings provide electrophysiological evidence that rapid adaptation to phi and reverse-phi motion leaves distinct neural traces that differentially influence subsequent processing of an ambiguous motion stimulus, advancing our understanding of rapid sensory adaptation and ON-OFF pathway interactions in human motion perception.

Article.Title: What counts as an error in nonword reading? A methods study of acquired phonological dyslexia
Article.Authors: Tree J.; Zakharchenko V.; Jones A.; Jones B.
Article.Abstract: Acquired phonological dyslexia (PD) is typically characterised by impaired nonword reading, but defining what constitutes a nonword reading "error" is challenging due to variability in how even healthy readers pronounce nonwords. This study examined different methods for classifying such errors using data from younger adults (n = 41), older adults (n = 25), and a case series of individuals with suspected acquired PD (n = 6). Three scoring approaches were compared: (1) a mode-response accuracy method, which matches responses to the most common pronunciation; (2) an average response-overlap method, which assesses similarity to the full distribution of control responses; and (3) a singularly distinct response count, which identifies responses not produced by any other participant. Results showed that older adults exhibited greater variability than younger adults across all measures, suggesting that age significantly affects nonword reading performance. This highlights an important methodological issue: using younger normative data to assess older individuals may overestimate impairment. In the patient group, all three scoring methods broadly agreed in ranking severity across cases. However, the singularly distinct response metric provided clearer separation between patients and controls and captured a wider range of impairment severity. It also revealed that unique responses are relatively common even among typical readers, an underexplored finding. Overall, the study supports the importance of age-appropriate norms and more nuanced, response-level scoring methods in assessing acquired PD, with singularly distinct responses offering a potentially sensitive marker of disruption.

Article.Title: Decoding the time course of intonation planning
Article.Authors: Erden H.; Chen Y.; Meyer A.; van der Burght C.
Article.Abstract: The temporal relationship between sentence-level intonation planning and word-level phonological encoding remains poorly understood. Prosody-first accounts predict that an abstract intonation frame is established before lexical information is retrieved, whereas prosody-last accounts predict that intonation is encoded after lexical information. The present study used EEG combined with time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to investigate when intonation planning occurs relative to other levels of linguistic encoding during spoken word production. Thirty native Dutch speakers named pictures of simple nouns using two different intonation contours, as either questions or exclamations. The target words were disyllabic Dutch nouns that varied in animacy, lexical stress, and manner and place of articulation of the first phoneme. Intonation became decodable after animacy and around the same time as place of articulation. Exploratory analyses revealed that intonation decoding emerged earlier for words with word-final than word-initial stress, suggesting that the temporal profile of intonation planning is shaped by the word's stress pattern. On a methodological level, these findings demonstrate that intonation planning is neurally decodable in an overt production context using EEG. The implications for theories of language production are that sentence-level and word-level prosody closely interact and evolve together during planning rather than being encoded independently.

Article.Title: How right dorsomedial lesions lead to neglect: A functional network-level framework
Article.Authors: Grande E.; Baldassarre A.; Committeri G.; Bartolo A.; Esposito V.; Ciavarro M.
Article.Abstract: Spatial neglect-a disorder characterized by impaired exploration of contralesional space-has only recently been reported following lesions to dorsomedial regions of the right hemisphere. Consequently, the mechanisms underlying the occurrence of neglect in this context remain largely unexplored. Here, we investigated whether alterations in functional connectivity could account for this phenomenon by longitudinally assessing resting-state fMRI in a patient before and after tumor resection. A 71-year-old male underwent resection of an oligodendroglioma involving the right superior frontal gyrus and cingulum. Neuropsychological assessment and resting-state fMRI were acquired before and after surgery. Peripersonal and personal neglect were assessed with two different cancellation tests and the Comb and Razor Test (CRT). System Segregation (SyS), i.e., the balance of within and between network functional connectivity, was computed at both whole-brain and network-specific levels and compared with 20 age-matched healthy controls using Crawford's modified t-test. While no sign of neglect was observed preoperatively, the patient exhibited both peripersonal and personal neglect after surgery. Compared to controls, postoperative data revealed a significant reduction in whole-brain SyS (p < .001). At the network level, the ventral attention network (VAN) showed preserved segregation preoperatively but a marked postoperative decrease (p < .001). These findings show, for the first time, that the clinical manifestation of neglect after right dorsomedial regions may be explained by lesion-induced alterations in large-scale functional connectivity. In particular, reduced VAN segregation may reflect impaired functional differentiation underlying deficits in spatial attention, thereby shedding light on the mechanisms underlying dorsomedial lesions neglect presentation.

Article.Title: Language prediction in multimodal contexts: The contribution of iconic gestures to anticipatory sentence comprehension
Article.Authors: Hintz F.; Emmendorfer A.; Strauß A.; Khoe Y.; Moonen L.; Holler J.
Article.Abstract: Evidence shows listeners predict upcoming words, and iconic gestures in face-to-face dialogue often precede their spoken referents. A recent framework proposes that early-onset gestures can pre-activate the meaning of upcoming nouns. This pre-registered EEG study tested this proposal. 81 Dutch adults watched videos of an actress producing discourses ending with a target noun. The noun was either predictable or not from the discourse. Each noun was paired with an iconic gesture whose stroke began either 520 msec (earlier) or 130 msec (later) before the noun. Discourse predictability produced the hypothesized post-target N400 reduction for predictable versus non-predictable items (H1). In the pre-target window, earlier gestures in non-predictable discourses elicited more negative amplitudes than in predictable discourses (H2a), suggesting that earlier gestures modulated neural responses when predictability was low. No comparable interaction was found for the opposite contrast (early-predictable vs late-predictable & late-non-predictable; H2c). In the post-target window, earlier gestures yielded a modest N400-like positivity relative to late gestures (H2e), but the interaction between gesture timing and discourse predictability (H2f) was not supported. A follow-up indicated that, in non-predictable discourses, later gestures produced a larger N400 than earlier gestures. Thus, the data confirm H1 and support H2a (and partially H2e), while H2c and H2f were not supported, suggesting that when speakers produce monologic discourses, earlier iconic gestures can aid anticipatory processing when linguistic predictions are weak, but their effect is limited and context-dependent. Together with the exploratory follow-up, the findings highlight a nuanced role of the influence of gesture timing on comprehension.
Article.Keywords: Gesture-speech integration; Iconic co-speech gestures; Language comprehension; Multimodal communication; Prediction

Article.Title: Distinct neural representations across discrete and continuous non-symbolic ratios
Article.Authors: Lagacé-Cusiac R.; Grahn J.; Ansari D.
Article.Abstract: Relative magnitudes, such as ratios and proportions, are crucial to everyday life. According to the ratio processing system (RPS) theory, ratios across different formats share a common neural code. Prior neuroimaging studies have shown that ratios across different visual formats are processed by overlapping brain areas and produce similar distance effects. However, this evidence supporting the RPS theory does not necessarily imply common representations. The aim of this study was to probe the key prediction of the RPS theory by investigating the neural representation of individual ratios depicted in discrete and continuous magnitudes using multivariate fMRI analyses. Twenty participants completed a delayed ratio comparison task on discrete (sets of dots) and continuous (line lengths) magnitudes while in the MRI scanner. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA), we examined the similarity between ratio representations across high-level variations, such as format (length and numerosity), and low-level variations, such as variations in line orientation and dot size, throughout the brain. Results showed little support for a shared ratio representation across discrete and continuous magnitudes. Instead, ratios in numerosity and length seemed to be encoded in qualitatively distinct ways. Altogether, results suggest that ratios are not represented in a format-independent way in the brain, thus challenging the RPS theory.

Article.Title: What does it take to grasp a tool? A fine-grained multiple-case analysis of hand-tool and tool-object interaction errors in apraxia
Article.Authors: Baumard J.; Teodoro-Oliveira M.; Guezouli L.; Guzzo N.; Galaverna O.
Article.Abstract: Apraxia of tool use is a neuropsychological syndrome characterized by difficulties in selecting or using familiar tools that cannot be better explained by primary motor, sensory, attentional, or language deficits. The neuropsychological literature indicates that tool use is a complex, multifaceted ability relying on heterogeneous cognitive processes and neural substrates. Patients may commit errors at different stages of the grasp-to-use sequence, including hand-tool interaction errors (e.g., holding tools upside-down), tool-object association errors (i.e., incorrect matching of the functional parts of tools and objects), and tool-object interaction errors (i.e., inappropriate mechanical actions), resulting in reduced performance efficiency. However, the cognitive origins of these distinct error types remain unclear, making their interpretation challenging for both researchers and clinicians. We report the case of D.B., a 69-year-old right-handed woman who sustained multiple strokes. D.B. demonstrated flawless tool selection and subnormal tool-object associations, but clearly abnormal hand-tool and tool-object interactions, in the context of impaired technical reasoning and preserved semantic tool knowledge and planning skills. This profile is discussed in light of previously reported cases of apraxia and optic ataxia. This analysis suggests that tool selection and tool-object association errors may stem from deficits in semantic tool knowledge, whereas hand-tool and tool-object interaction errors are more plausibly explained by deficits in technical reasoning. Motor imagery may also represent a contributing factor and warrants further investigation.

Article.Title: Integrative EEG/fMRI evidence for a multi-scale network underlying self-face and personal-object recognition
Article.Authors: Kotlewska I.; Panek B.; Bielski K.; Asanowicz D.
Article.Abstract: The sense of ownership of our faces and possessions shapes our visual perception. While the neural basis of self-face recognition has been well-studied, the neural basis of recognizing personally owned objects remains poorly understood. The main aim of this study was to investigate brain activity underlying self-face and personal object recognition, with a particular focus on the extent to which the ownership processing can be characterized as either domain-general and/or stimulus-specific. We first review the relevant literature and then report findings from two experiments - one using EEG and the other fMRI - in which the same 30 participants categorized images of faces and objects as either "mine" or "others". EEG results revealed ownership-related visuo-midfrontal activity, reflected in event-related potentials (visual P1 and N170, and midfrontal N150 and SMN), frequency-specific inter-source phase coherence (in theta band), and brain-wide time-frequency power dynamics (in alpha, beta, and theta bands). fMRI results identified ownership-related activity in four right hemisphere regions: the inferior temporal gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, inferior frontal gyrus, and superior parietal lobule; each of which formed distinct ownership-related subnetworks. The findings support "a hybrid model" in which stimulus-specific visual pathways (e.g., face-sensitive regions) interact with domain-general frontal activity encoding self-relevance. This integrative evidence clarifies how a dynamic, multi-scale network underlying ownership perception is constructed across time, frequency, and brain space.

Article.Title: Stage-specific contributions of dorsal and ventral premotor cortices to the acquisition of arbitrary visuomotor associations
Article.Authors: Turrini S.; Amadori A.; Arcara G.; di Pellegrino G.; Avenanti A.
Article.Abstract: The acquisition and consolidation of arbitrary visuomotor mappings (AVMMs) engage premotor regions, yet the distinct contributions of the dorsal (PMd) and ventral (PMv) premotor cortices remain unclear. Here, we applied continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) immediately before AVMM learning to transiently disrupt PMd, PMv, or an occipital control site (V1) in 19 healthy young adults, using a within-subjects design. Participants learned arbitrary stimulus-response associations through trial-and-error feedback and completed a 24-h delayed recall test. Trial-by-trial accuracy and response times were modeled using state-space and Rescorla-Wagner frameworks to quantify learning dynamics, prediction errors, and stabilization across days. Disruption of both PMd and PMv slowed early acquisition of AVMMs to a comparable extent relative to V1. However, only PMd disruption additionally impaired next-day recall, rendering recall performance dependent on sleep quality and decoupled from learning-day performance, whereas recall following PMv disruption remained comparable to the control condition. These findings indicate that PMd, but not PMv, contributes to the stabilization of newly learned visuomotor associations, providing causal, stage-specific evidence for a functional dissociation within the human premotor cortex: PMd and PMv support early rule formation and exploratory learning, whereas only PMd contributes to subsequent stabilization of newly learned visuomotor associations. Furthermore, they emphasize the modulatory influence of sleep on memory retention when consolidation processes are compromised, advancing mechanistic models of premotor contributions to associative sensorimotor learning.

Article.Title: Multidimensional semantic activation in children’s discourse reading is associated with their reading ability
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Zhou W.; Wang X.; Huang L.; Wang S.; Lin N.
Article.Abstract: Around fourth grade, children transition from learning-to-read to reading-to-learn, yet how their multidimensional semantic representation during discourse reading differs from that of adults and relates to reading ability remains unclear. This study investigated multidimensional semantic activation in 42 fourth-to sixth-grade children (mean age 10.3 years) and 44 adults (mean age 25.1 years) during story reading using fMRI. Children were stratified by reading ability using inverse efficiency scores from comprehension questions. Semantic activation across six dimensions (visual, motor, social, emotional, spatial, temporal) was modeled using the Six Semantic Dimension Database. Results showed that high-reading-ability children exhibited significantly stronger temporal but weaker social semantic activation compared to adults, whereas low-reading-ability children showed adult-like patterns. Brain-behavior association analyses revealed that multidimensional semantic activation patterns were linked to reading performance in children (explaining 25.0% of variance), whereas no such relationship was evident in adults. Additionally, high-reading-ability children demonstrated enhanced activation in cognitive control networks relative to both low-ability peers and adults. These findings suggest that high-reading-ability children may strategically modulate multidimensional semantic processing through cognitive control to compensate for limited reading experience, highlighting the flexible, strategy-dependent nature of multidimensional semantic representation during developmental reading.

Article.Title: Inner speech and the architecture of social cognition: A commentary on Silvanto (2026)
Article.Authors: Geva S.; Lœvenbruck H.
Article.Abstract: This commentary builds on Silvanto's (2026) argument that congenital aphantasia should be recognised as a form of cognitive diversity rather than a pathology, with rehabilitation targeting underlying causes of imagery loss rather than the restoration of mental imagery. Silvanto further highlights the association between visual imagery loss and emotional dysregulation. While we support this move away from pathologising aphantasia, we highlight a critical gap in the literature: the underappreciated role of inner speech in social-emotional cognition. We argue that sensory imagery (and aphantasia) should be recognized as a multifaceted process, with dissociations observed across modalities. Furthermore, we propose that inner speech, whether condensed or expanded (accompanied by auditory verbal imagery), serves as a computationally efficient, resource-light alternative to sensory imagery, supporting cognition without the need for detailed sensorimotor simulation. This perspective reframes aphantasia as cognitive diversity and highlights the need for greater empirical and theoretical focus on inner speech.

Article.Title: Differentiating non-fluent and logopenic primary progressive aphasia via automated acoustic speech analysis
Article.Authors: Antonicelli G.; Morin B.; Bogley R.; Newbury R.; Ezzes Z.; Ramkrishnan S.; Miller Z.; Mandelli M.; Tee B.; García A.; Gorno-Tempini M.; Vonk J.
Article.Abstract: In primary progressive aphasia, differential diagnosis between non-fluent (nfvPPA) and logopenic (lvPPA) variants can be clinically challenging. Although linguistic features from connected speech may aid in PPA subtype classification, they depend on labor-intensive transcriptions. In contrast, acoustic features are extracted directly from the audio signal and have shown potential in capturing variant-specific patterns, but their diagnostic relevance is not well understood. In this study, we analyzed connected speech recordings from 242 individuals (40 healthy controls, 91 lvPPA, 111 nfvPPA) performing a ∼2-min picture description task. We extracted 103 acoustic features from each recording and reduced them to 9, which we finally grouped into four domain scores representing speech rate and voice quality. Domain scores were tested as predictors in classification models to detect PPA and distinguish between PPA variants. Voxel-based morphometry was used to investigate brain-behavior relationships. Classification models combining the four domain scores and MMSE yielded 88% balanced-sample accuracy for PPA-versus-controls and 73% accuracy for lvPPA-versus-nfvPPA. Pitch and speech rate were the most discriminative markers. Voxel-based morphometry associated speech rate with the frontal speech production network, pitch with the middle frontal and inferior frontal gyrus, perturbation with the insula, and spectrum with the basal ganglia and the thalamus. We showed that acoustic analysis of brief speech samples has the potential to aid the diagnostic process and contribute to more nuanced phenotyping. With further validation, such measures could be integrated into clinical workflows as low-burden, objective tools to support differential diagnosis and track disease progression in PPA.

Article.Title: Set-size effects for complex objects in developmental prosopagnosia: Visual search for faces, words and cars
Article.Authors: Kim H.; Albonico A.; Hemström J.; Djouab S.; Romero-Ayala G.; Corrow S.; Barton J.
Article.Abstract: Whether developmental prosopagnosia is specific to faces is an ongoing controversy. One difficulty that may contribute to discrepant results is differences in tests used to assess face and object processing. Here, we devised a search test to measure the efficiency of processing for faces, cars, and words. We had 14 subjects with developmental prosopagnosia and 26 controls perform three search tests. For face-search, subjects saw an array ranging from three to seven faces and had to answer whether all depicted the same person or if one was a different person. Similar tests were constructed for cars and words. The main variables were response time and the set-size effect, which refers to the additional time required for every additional stimulus in the array. At the group level, the prosopagnosic subjects were impaired in face search but no different from controls on car or word search. However, at a single-subject level, only 20% had evidence of a putative classical dissociation to support claims that their recognition disorder is face-specific, while 30% had abnormally prolonged car-search times, and 50% had indeterminate results. The results align with a meta-analysis that concluded there was heterogeneity in object recognition in developmental prosopagnosia.

Article.Title: When rhythm guides speech production: Insights from Parkinson's disease and spinocerebellar ataxia
Article.Authors: Fumel J.; Mairano P.; Ott L.; Contreras Roa L.; Devos D.; Moreau C.; Basirat A.
Article.Abstract: Rhythmic auditory exposure modulates subsequent speech processing, yet its effect on speech production remains poorly understood. People with Parkinson's disease (PD) or spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) suffer from dysarthria, for which there is no treatment. Using a rhythmic priming approach, we investigated whether brief rhythmic primes modulate speech production and facilitate it in people with PD and SCA considered here as clinical models of basal ganglia dysfunction and cerebellar dysfunction, respectively. Fifty-eight native French speakers (20 controls, 24 people with PD, 14 people with SCA) read sentences following a regular prime, an irregular prime, or silence. We measured accuracy and the temporal features of speech production including speech initiation time, speech rate, and rhythmic metrics. Bayesian mixed-effects models were used for the statistical analyses of these outputs. Accuracy showed no effect of rhythmic priming. Regular primes consistently shortened speech initiation time in all populations, but the benefit of regular primes was smaller in people with PD than in controls. In People with SCA, speech rate decreased after regular primes. The impact of rhythmic priming on rhythmic metrics was limited. Together, these results indicate that perception-to-production rhythmic priming mainly affects global, rather than fine-grained, timing control of speech during speech production. They also shed light on the implications of the basal ganglia and cerebellum in the modulation of speech by rhythm. They also provide insights for speech production models, which currently lack an explicit mechanism for external rhythmic inputs. Clinically, they help inform rhythm-based speech and language therapy methods.

Article.Title: Two reading routes, two white matter tracts: Evidence from dyslexia following brain tumors
Article.Authors: Kahana Levy N.; Friedmann N.; Singer N.; Gurevitch G.; Arzi M.; Bergman L.; Azolai L.; Yogev R.; Dunetz G.; Richetta C.; Shahar T.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive models propose that reading aloud relies on two routes, a lexical route for familiar word recognition and a sublexical route for graphene-to-phoneme conversion. Selective disruption of these routes results in surface or phonological dyslexia, respectively. Although the dual route model is well supported behaviorally, its white matter substrates remain incompletely characterized. This study examined the anatomical correlates of acquired lexical and sublexical reading impairments in patients with high-grade glioma in the dominant hemisphere. Thirty-seven patients underwent diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and a comprehensive reading battery. Reading aloud of regular and irregular words, and pseudowords was used to classify patients as having intact reading, surface dyslexia or phonological dyslexia, based on normative criteria. Six language-related white matter tracts were reconstructed individually for each patient using subject-specific tractography. Each tract was then systematically segmented along its longitudinal axis, allowing diffusion parameters to be extracted from anatomically defined subsegments. Lesion-tract overlap measures were computed to quantify focal tract involvement. Fourteen patients exhibited impaired sublexical reading, 12 impaired lexical reading, and 11 intact reading. Deficits in the sublexical route were more frequent among patients with arcuate fasciculus lesion overlap, and sublexical error rates correlated with global tract integrity. Deficits in the lexical route were associated with the posterior temporal segment of the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, where surface dyslexia errors correlated with reduced fractional anisotropy. In contrast, uncinate fasciculus involvement was more frequent among patients with intact reading, indicating it does not contribute critically to either reading route. These findings provide a fine-grained structure-function mapping of the dual route reading model onto white matter pathways.
