Article.Title: Mean position of hits in unilateral spatial neglect: An empirical validation
Article.Authors: De Luca M.; Ciurli M.; Matano A.; Nardo D.
Article.Abstract: Numerical indices used to detect and quantify neglect in cancellation tests have traditionally relied on omissions count, which may be misleading, as the derived laterality indices (LIs) do not capture the spatial continuum of responses. More recent approaches (e.g., Mean Position of Hits, MPH) quantify neglect based on the spatial position of hits. The MPH approach relies on a theoretically-founded statistical model, which returns a neglect index and a diagnostic label without the need for a control sample and cut-offs. However, such an approach has not yet been empirically validated in patients. Here, we applied the MPH to three common cancellation tests (Letters, Stars, and Lines) in a consecutive sample of right-brain-damaged stroke patients (n = 173) and determined its diagnostic sensitivity and specificity, and its ability to quantify neglect severity against an independent reference standard that combines conventional neuropsychological tests (excluding the three cancellation tests) and a structured clinical observation. Sensitivity and specificity of the MPH were 88.6% and 84.1% for Letters, 87.1% and 95.3% for Stars, 65.2% and 97.7% for Lines. We also compared the MPH diagnostic accuracy with that of two alternative procedures based on a classical cut-off approach (MPH with cut-offs and LIs). Such alternative procedures yielded comparable diagnostic accuracy. Regression analyses showed that the MPH index corresponded more closely to clinical ratings of neglect severity than LIs. Overall, our results show that the MPH is a valid and user-friendly approach for both clinical assessment and research applications, which allows comparisons across time, settings, and cancellation tests.

Article.Title: Effects of mind-wandering on cognitive and neural processes: Identifying specific impairments in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
Article.Authors: Horáková G.; Weibel S.; Tissot U.; Pham B.; Costache M.; Bonnefond A.
Article.Abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by symptoms of inattention and/or impulsivity/hyperactivity. Although not a core symptom, excessive mind-wandering (MW) is commonly associated with the disorder and may contribute to symptoms as well as performance deficits observed in these patients. The main aim of the present study is to better characterize MW and its impact on performance measures as well as on neural activity in adults with ADHD. Twenty-eight medication-naïve ADHD patients and 28 healthy controls-matched on sex, age, and level of education-completed a prolonged Go/No-Go sustained attention task including thought-probes to detect episodes of MW. Analysis of EEG data focused on P100, P3b, and CRN event-related potentials reflecting early visual, attention allocation, and performance monitoring processes, respectively. MW, particularly spontaneous MW, was more frequent in patients and linked to a more severe ADHD symptomatology. A differentiated negative impact of MW on performance was noted in both groups: variability of reaction times in patients and accuracy in controls were affected. While the same perceptual (P100) and attentional (P3b) impairments were evidenced in both groups during MW, the impairment of the performance monitoring (CRN) process was exclusively highlighted in ADHD patients (as revealed by a significant state × group interaction). Taken together, these results extend the understanding of the cognitive and neural processes associated with increased MW in patients and suggest performance monitoring as a potential key mechanism underlying specific MW-related impairments in ADHD.

Article.Title: The grounding of abstract concepts in the sensory-motor, mentalizing and social interaction brain systems: A multiple representation framework
Article.Authors: Kiefer M.; Trumpp N.
Article.Abstract: For decades, theorizing in the cognitive sciences was dominated by the assumption that abstract concepts, lacking directly perceivable referents, can only be represented and processed through amodal or verbal linguistic representations. More recently, refined hybrid grounded cognition theories have successfully been applied to account for abstract concepts within a multiple representation framework. According to this perspective, the meaning of abstract concepts is constituted by representations distributed across various experiential modal brain systems, including sensory, motor, emotional, mentalizing, and social interaction networks. Representations in these modal systems are complemented by representations in language-related and amodal hub regions, depending on the specific semantic content of the concept. In this article, we first outline a multiple representation framework within a hybrid grounded cognition approach and then review neuroscientific evidence concerning the neural substrate of abstract concepts related to sensory-motor features, mental states and social constellations. These findings indicate that modal sensory-motor, mentalizing, and social interaction brain systems contribute to the processing of particular types of abstract concepts, alongside representations in amodal semantic hub regions and language areas. Moreover, this body of research demonstrates that different modal neural circuits are engaged as a function of a concept's specific semantic content, thereby highlighting the heterogeneity of abstract concepts. Future research should address outstanding questions, including the precise functional contributions of distinct neural circuits to the representation of abstract concepts and the evaluation of predicted patterns of impairment in neurological and psychiatric patient populations.

Article.Title: Temporal dynamics of central and peripheral processes in novel word acquisition: Evidence from co-registration of EEG and kinematics in natural handwriting
Article.Authors: Fu Y.; Enrique Jan Cordón D.; Bermúdez-Margaretto B.; Wang H.; Domínguez A.
Article.Abstract: Current models of handwriting production posit a hierarchy of cognitive subprocesses through which linguistic information cascades from central lexical encoding to peripheral motor execution. Yet it remains unclear how such cascaded coordination supports the formation of new memory traces for novel words. Here, we combined simultaneous electroencephalography and handwriting kinematics in native Spanish speakers (n = 63) to track word learning dynamics across repeated handwritten production. Event-related potentials (ERPs) time-locked to stimulus onset and kinematics-related potentials (KRPs) evoked by the motor execution of the critical letter revealed temporal coordination between central and peripheral learning effects as a function of repeated exposure, with exposure-driven modulation in the 173-309 msec after stimulus onset within a centro-frontal cluster and a comparable effect in the 133-286 msec post pen-down window over posterior sites. While orthographic encoding approached an asymptote after four exposures, motor refinement followed a more protracted trajectory across all encounters, indicating that the central and peripheral processes do not cascade to the same extent. The ongoing neural-kinematic coupling further revealed a parallel unfolding of motor planning and orthographic processing. Critically, the magnitude of exposure-induced neural modulation during learning predicted the strength of subsequent lexical competition in a masked priming lexical decision task after overnight consolidation. These findings substantiate the automatic nature of neural memory-trace formation coupled with cognitive and motor dynamics. The motor system continuously operates on partially specified linguistic information, establishing word-level orthographic representations before refining the letter-level graphomotor details on which lexical competition depends.

Article.Title: Longitudinal inference of hippocampal volume and morphometric hippocampal-cortical covariance in psychosis
Article.Authors: Totzek J.; Heckers S.; Palaniyappan L.; Young A.; Shah J.; Joober R.; Malla A.; Chakravarty M.; Lavigne K.; Lepage M.
Article.Abstract: Schizophrenia and related psychoses are characterized by reductions in hippocampal volume and morphometric hippocampal-cortical covariance. No study to date has inferred the temporal relationship between deviations in subfield and adjacent white matter volume and connectivity across psychosis. To explore this relationship, we sampled cross-sectional neuroimaging data from 174 patients and 120 non-clinical controls from two studies on first- and multi-episode psychosis. We applied Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn), a machine learning algorithm combining clustering and disease progression modeling, to eight measures of hippocampal volume and morphometric hippocampal-cortical covariance (subfields and white matter regions per hemisphere) combined. We then performed in-depth SuStaIn analyses for 18 volumes (five subfields and four white matter regions per hemisphere) and 18 connectivity measures (graph-theory-based participation coefficient) separately. Some patients and controls showed no deviations (no increase or decrease) from control means in volume and covariance. For individuals who did show deviations, we inferred data-driven stages from deviations in volume toward covariance. In-depth SuStaIn analyses inferred three distinct volume patterns (intact volume, subfield-dominant, whiter matter-dominant) followed by one of four possible connectivity patterns (intact connectivity, whiter matter-dominant, subfield-dominant, subiculum-dominant). These subtypes showed significant differences in age, patient-control ratio and associations between data-driven stages and memory. In previous work, altered hippocampal volume and morphometric covariance distinctively precede cognitive and clinical symptoms of psychosis. While not all patients were assigned a staging pattern for hippocampal volume or connectivity, our findings might thus contribute to elucidating distinct hippocampal patterns underlying heterogeneous manifestations of psychosis for a subgroup of patients.

Article.Title: Post-stroke aphasia assessment in Arabic-speaking populations: A critical review of validated tools, structural barriers, and the diglossic validity problem
Article.Authors: Elleuch D.
Article.Abstract: Arabic is spoken by more than 400 million people across a region experiencing a substantial increase in stroke burden. Yet, no comprehensively validated aphasia assessment battery exists that provides dialect-stratified norms across major Arabic-speaking communities. This critical narrative review evaluates Arabic aphasia assessment against explicit psychometric and linguistic criteria, identifying peer-reviewed instruments and synthesizing the methodological progress they represent, alongside two structural questions that are only partially resolved by existing instruments. The first is the diglossic register question: Modern Standard Arabic functions as a learned register whose distance from each speaker's vernacular varies with education, and how this distance contributes to assessment score variance has not been quantified in within-subject clinical samples. The second is the nonconcatenative morphology question: Arabic root-and-pattern morphological operations, not specifically assessed by current aphasia batteries, leave possible morphology-specific vulnerability insufficiently tested. Recent dialect-specific instruments, including the Moroccan Arabic Bedside WAB-R, the Cairene Egyptian Arabic WAB-R, the Egyptian Arabic Comprehensive Aphasia Test, the Short Aphasia Test for Gulf Arabic, and the Arabic Discourse Assessment Tool, represent substantive progress and a necessary foundation. Building on it requires dialect-specific psycholinguistic databases, measurement-equivalence reporting as a publication standard, education- and literacy-stratified normative collection, and a within-subject crossover study quantifying the register-distance effect. Improving Arabic aphasia assessment is essential: lesion-symptom mapping in Arabic-speaking populations depends on instruments validated for the linguistic profile they assess.

Article.Title: Instructing to ignore a color does not promote its suppression but its facilitation in human early visual cortex
Article.Authors: Jänig J.; Gundlach C.; Forschack N.; Müller M.
Article.Abstract: Attentional shifts during feature-based color selection trigger a bi-phasic activation sequence in early visual cortex: rapid facilitation of the to-be-attended followed by delayed suppression of to-be-ignored color(s). Does this sequence reflect a priority bias induced by instructions "to attend" to a certain task-relevant color instead of instructions "to ignore" task-irrelevant colors? In two EEG recording sessions, we instructed 20 participants either "to attend" to two colors (explicit instruction) or "to ignore" one color (implicit instruction) out of three differently colored and flickering random-dot kinematograms (RDKs) that elicited distinct steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs), a neural marker of early visual stimulus processing. Additionally, we tracked the time course of behavioral responses as a function of explicit or implicit cueing, with a behavioral study (N = 20). SSVEP amplitudes replicated the typical pattern of early amplification and delayed suppression under explicit instruction. The implicit instruction did not invert this sequence but paradoxically resulted in rapid facilitation of the cued - but to-be-ignored - color right after cue onset, that was followed by suppression of both task-relevant colors. Behavior followed this paradoxical selection process, causing significantly slower responses for the task-relevant colors compared to the explicit instruction. Clearly, the color cue triggered rapid stimulus-driven facilitation of the RDKs in the cue color(s) that caused subsequent suppression of the other color(s), regardless of their task relevance. This shows that the amplification-suppression pattern is not biased by an instructional prioritization but rather an inherent, possibly hard-wired temporal sequence during attentional shifts in feature-based attention.

Article.Title: The case against the ‘S’: Is functional neurological disorder(s) one condition or many?
Article.Authors: Palmer D.; Edwards M.; Mattingley J.
Article.Abstract: Functional neurological disorder (FND) is one of the most common, but least researched, conditions in neurology. It can cause a broad range of sensory, motor, and constitutional symptoms, with the underlying mechanism of symptom-generation proposed to be an abnormality of perceptual inference. Debate exists as to whether the clinical entity referred to as FND is truly a single disorder or is in fact multiple entities which have been erroneously amalgamated into the same condition. We sought to provide empirical evidence on this question by treating it as a problem of model comparison. We formulated statistical models equivalent to: (1) FND being a single entity with variation in phenotype, represented by latent trait models, and (2) FND being multiple discrete entities, represented by latent class models. We fitted these models to data on the symptoms experienced by 697 people with FND from the FND Research Connect database (www.fnd-research.org) and used Bayesian model comparison to compare their likelihoods. All but one of the latent trait models, representing FND as a single entity with heterogeneous phenotype, fit the data better than all the latent class models. Furthermore, secondary analysis of the latent class models showed results compatible with the models discretising continuous variation rather than capturing true discrete categories. Our results are most compatible with the hypothesis that the symptom structure of FND is the result of a single pathophysiological process, either as a single entity, or a common pathway preceded by multiple causative processes where the common pathway is solely responsible for the phenotype.

Article.Title: Me in action: Distinct processing levels shape the relationship between sense of agency and sense of ownership
Article.Authors: Mariano M.; Stanco G.; Negrone C.; Massaro F.; Sterlicchio A.; Gabbiadini A.; Salvato G.; Zapparoli L.
Article.Abstract: Competing neurocognitive models offer different accounts of how the sense of agency (the experience of controlling one's actions) and the sense of ownership (the experience that one's body belongs to oneself) relate within bodily self-awareness. The additive model proposes that agency entails ownership, the independence model treats the two experiences as functionally distinct, and the interactive model suggests reciprocal influences between them. However, empirical tests comparing these predictions within a single coherent experimental paradigm remain limited. Here, we developed an immersive virtual reality paradigm to orthogonally manipulate agency- and ownership-related cues within a goal-directed action task. Fifty-six participants pressed a (virtual) button to switch on a lightbulb. Agency was manipulated by comparing voluntary self-generated and externally induced passive movements and action-outcome delays, whereas ownership was manipulated through the anatomical plausibility of the avatar's hands. Direct and indirect agency and ownership indices were collected. Direct explicit judgements revealed both domain-specific and reciprocal influences: agency was modulated by action-related cues and by anatomical plausibility, whereas ownership was modulated by anatomical plausibility and by action-related cues, consistent with an interactive account. Indirect measures showed a distinct pattern: intentional binding was influenced by action-outcome contingency and was not affected by ownership manipulations, whereas proprioceptive drift varied as a function of anatomical plausibility. We propose a hierarchical two-stage account that integrates previous cognitive models across distinct processing levels, in which agency and ownership arise from partly independent sensorimotor processes at an implicit level but dynamically interact at the level of metacognitive, explicit self-attribution.

Article.Title: Brain structure–function coupling – relationship with language lateralisation
Article.Authors: Andrulyte I.; Zago L.; Jobard G.; Lemaitre H.; Taylor P.; Rheault F.; Joliot M.; Petit L.; Keller S.
Article.Abstract: Language is one of the most extensively studied lateralised cognitive functions in the human brain, predominantly relying on the left hemisphere in most individuals. However, the mechanisms by which a stable white matter architecture underpins individual language functions remain unclear. Previous studies have employed structural connectivity (SC) and functional connectivity (FC) coupling for individual fingerprinting and task decoding, suggesting that variability in brain entropy may serve as a distinguishing characteristic for language lateralisation. We examined a large cohort of healthy adults (n = 285) to investigate SC-FC coupling and identify markers distinguishing different language laterality groups. Functional connectivity was measured using resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) time-series data, whereas structural connectivity was determined using probabilistic fiber tractography. SC-FC coupling was investigated using the SENSAAS language atlas and defined as the Pearson correlation between the non-zero elements of the regional structural and functional connectivity profiles. Group differences were assessed using the PALM toolbox in the FSL. Our findings revealed that increased SC-FC coupling in the left precentral sulcus was associated with typical language lateralisation, while increased coupling in the right middle temporal gyrus and left anterior insula was observed in individuals with atypical language lateralisation (pFDR <.05). Non-lateralised individuals exhibited increased coupling in the left anterior insula compared to lateralised (pFDR<.05). SC-FC coupling offers a promising framework to uncover functional and anatomical differences among individuals with varying language lateralisation. This regional specificity indicates that typical, atypical, and non-lateralised profiles rely on different structural-functional alignments, likely reflecting the recruitment of alternative pathways for language processing.

Article.Title: Progression of language profiles in primary progressive aphasia: A bicentric longitudinal study
Article.Authors: Mahut Dubos A.; Maso S.; Siguier P.; Denève A.; Trogneux L.; Geraudie A.; Carpentier C.; Forestier N.; Delrutte S.; Manteaux A.; Bertoux M.; Jucla M.; Pariente J.; Danet L.; Lebouvier T.; Tran T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Primary progressive aphasias (PPA) are syndromes characterised by a progressive loss of language functions. To date, four main variants have been identified: semantic (svPPA), non-fluent/agrammatic (nfvPPA), logopenic (lvPPA) and Primary Progressive Apraxia of Speech (PPAoS). Currently, little is known about their clinical course, especially in French-speaking populations, though such data could aid prognosis and guide therapy. Objective: To characterise longitudinal changes in the language profiles in PPA using the GRÉMOTS, a French language assessment tool specifically developed for neurodegenerative disorders. Methods: We retrospectively included PPA patients, as well as patients with typical amnesic Alzheimer's disease (AD) and behavioural variant frontotemporal degeneration (bvFTD), from the Lille and Toulouse Memory Centres, who underwent longitudinal assessment ≥6 months with the GRÉMOTS. We performed between-groups comparisons and within-group paired analyses of GRÉMOTS subscores. Results: Eighty-two patients were included: 20 svPPA, 9 lvPPA, 12 nfvPPA, 9 PPAoS, 20 AD and 12 bvFTD. svPPA patients showed a predominant decline in lexico-semantic domains. nfvPPA patients deteriorated mainly in phonetics and syntactic production. Apraxia remained the prominent symptom in PPAoS patients, although mild agrammatical aphasia emerged at follow-up. lvPPA patients exhibited a significant decline in lexical oral comprehension alongside their core impairments. Language impairments remained modest in AD and bvFTD. Conclusion: Our results highlighted a progression of core language impairments across PPA variants, with lvPPA additionally showing significant decline beyond its defining criteria. These results support the development of tailored speech-language interventions that anticipate the evolving needs of PPA patients in French-speaking settings.

Article.Title: Data-driven cognitive clusters in persistent developmental dyslexia
Article.Authors: Pinheiro-Chagas P.; Kersey M.; Bahar N.; Inkelis S.; Mauer E.; Siebert J.; Vonk J.; Bogley R.; Carpenter E.; Martin-Moreno D.; De Leon J.; Tee B.; Mandelli M.; Pereira C.; Miller Z.; Gorno-Tempini M.
Article.Abstract: Developmental dyslexia is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent reading difficulties despite adequate intelligence and educational opportunities. The cognitive underpinnings of dyslexia remain incompletely understood. Although multiple causal pathways have been proposed, there is a gap in studies that can reliably identify dyslexia subtypes based on comprehensive evaluations that go beyond measures of reading and phonology. We employed one of the largest detailed samples of children with developmental dyslexia resistant to intervention, consisting of 147 extensively phenotyped school-age children aged 7-14 years who were recruited from specialized schools for students with learning differences. We implemented data-driven analyses leveraging a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment to delineate cognitive subdomains and characterize the heterogeneity in the sample. Hierarchical clustering of 24 cognitive measures aided in constructing a framework to subsequently interpret emerging clusters. Five clusters emerged, predominantly associated with: Word Retrieval, Phonological Awareness and Phonological Loop, Visuospatial Functioning, Oral Processing Speed and Executive Function, and finally, Written Processing Speed and Executive Function. Subsequent latent profile analysis identified two distinct dyslexia profiles; one characterized by marked difficulties in processing speed and executive functioning, and another displaying difficulties primarily in verbal short-term memory and word retrieval relative to the other profile. Importantly, both profiles exhibited comparable severity of persistent single word decoding and reading comprehension difficulties despite their divergent cognitive profiles. Together, these findings show that phenotypically similar reading impairments can arise from distinct underlying cognitive factors, emphasizing the role of comprehensive neuropsychological evaluation in developing tailored interventions for affected children.

Article.Title: Screening for post-stroke cognitive impairment: The effect of diagnostic criteria on prevalence and false positive rates
Article.Authors: Webb S.; Huygelier H.; Demeyere N.; Gillebert C.
Article.Abstract: Accurately determining prevalence of post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is essential for research, yet methodological choices vary extensively across studies. This study theoretically and statistically compared four statistical approaches to PSCI classification using a cognitive screen in 1,951 stroke patients and 407 healthy controls. We contrasted (1) the common "at least one positive test" method using 5th centile cut-offs per subtest (uncorrected), (2) a Bonferroni-adjusted variant controlling for multiple comparisons, (3) a total-score summing subtest scores, and (4) a non-parametric Multivariate Normative Comparison (MNC) approach. False-positive rates (i.e., classifying healthy controls as impaired) (FPRs), PSCI prevalence and discrimination of stroke patients and healthy controls were contrasted between methods. PSCI identification using uncorrected 5th centile cut-offs per test resulted in impairment identification in 22% of healthy controls (99% CI [18-27]), while Bonferroni, total-score, and MNC methods maintained a rate of 5% identification of impairment. Corresponding PSCI prevalence estimates in stroke patients were 82%, 63%, 38%, and 55%, respectively. Contrary to predictions, the Bonferroni-adjusted method produced the greatest discrimination between stroke and control groups while ensuring family-wise error control. These findings demonstrate that uncorrected screening criteria can substantially inflate PSCI classifications in healthy controls even for ceiling-bounded screening tests, and that simple correction methods can achieve robust statistical control without loss of interpretability. Bonferroni-adjusted centile cut-offs are recommended for research studies in which PSCI is identified across multiple tests, as they maximize diagnostic specificity and maintain conceptual transparency compared to more complex multivariate approaches.

Article.Title: The functional and neural mechanisms underlying the processing of different action sequences in grasping
Article.Authors: Kämpfer J.; Yu L.; Vogel L.; Schack T.
Article.Abstract: Goal-directed grasping actions are often planned with respect to their intended final states, as reflected in the end-state comfort effect (ESC) where individuals adopt initially uncomfortable grasp postures to ensure a comfortable final posture. The present study investigates the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying the processing of action sequences in grasping using event-related potentials (ERPs) within a priming paradigm. Participants were presented with prime images showing initial grasp postures (overhand or underhand grip) followed by target images representing final grasp postures (thumb-up or thumb-down) that together depicted either possible or impossible action sequences. Participants responded to the color of the upper part of the bar in the target image, while grasp postures were task-irrelevant. The results reveal that responses to target images representing an uncomfortable final grasp (thumb-down) following an underhand grip in the prime were slower and elicited a stronger P300 amplitude compared to responses to comfortable final grasp targets (thumb-up). This effect was observed only when the prime-target sequence represented a physically possible action. These results suggest that perceiving an initial underhand grip leads to the anticipation of a functional final action state. Deviations from this expected outcome result in greater cognitive processing effort, as reflected by increased P300 amplitudes. This suggests that action representations in grasping are anticipatory in nature and incorporate information about likely future action outcomes. The findings are consistent with ideo-motor theories, highlighting the role of anticipated action effects in action processing, and provide novel insights into the cognitive and neural underpinnings of action representation.

Article.Title: Neural processing of natural speech by adults with and without dyslexia: Evidence for atypical temporal sampling of speech information in the delta and theta EEG bands
Article.Authors: Keshavarzi M.; Moore B.; Goswami U.
Article.Abstract: Neural oscillations in the delta (.5-4 Hz) and theta (4-8 Hz) bands play a key role in tracking the temporal structure of speech. According to Temporal Sampling (TS) theory, dyslexia arises from atypical oscillatory sampling of the speech signal in these bands during infancy and childhood, which is particularly disruptive regarding phonological encoding. However, studies of adults with dyslexia have rarely examined both delta and theta oscillatory sampling under naturalistic listening conditions. Using EEG, here we focused on delta and theta band cortical tracking of continuous natural speech by adults with and without dyslexia, applying a decoding analysis previously used with dyslexic children. Forty-eight English-speaking adults (24 dyslexic, 24 control) listened to a 16-min continuous spoken narrative while EEG was recorded. Neural tracking of the speech envelope was quantified using backward decoding models, implemented using the multivariate Temporal Response Function (mTRF) toolbox. Decoding analyses were applied at two levels: a between-group analysis evaluating group-level differences in neural representation patterns, and a within-participant analysis assessing individual decoding accuracy. Cerebro-acoustic coherence was also computed to provide a complementary measure of low-frequency neural-speech synchronisation. Additional complementary analyses examined band power, cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling (PAC), and cross-frequency phase-phase coupling (PPC). Dyslexic adults exhibited less accurate delta- and theta-band decoding in the between-group analysis and reduced theta-band decoding accuracy in the within-participant analysis, alongside reduced theta-band coherence and increased delta-band power, particularly over the right temporal region. No group differences were found for PAC or PPC.

Article.Title: The riddle of anosognosia: A second look at overconfidence in unawareness of hemiparesis with two riddle tasks
Article.Authors: Bahr E.; Mühlig M.; Ritter T.; Saur D.; Klingbeil J.
Article.Abstract: Anosognosia, a lack of awareness of a neurological deficit, is a multi-component disorder involving coexisting neurological and cognitive impairments. Patients with anosognosia for hemiparesis fail to use new information about their bodily self to update beliefs. Overconfidence in situations of uncertainty and a failure to adjust beliefs in a verbal riddle task have been identified in a previous case series. This prospective study extends these findings using the same verbal riddle task and an additional non-verbal picture riddle task in 41 stroke patients and 22 age-matched controls. Each riddle contains five clues leading to a target word or picture. After each clue, participants provide a guess and a confidence rating. All riddles are designed to create an initial situation of uncertainty. The picture riddle is simpler and less dependent on language and memory capacities. In our cohort, 14 out of 41 patients were unaware of their paresis. Contrary to prior work, we found the riddle paradigm to be unsuitable for measuring belief-updating. Regarding overconfidence, the level of confidence for the first two clues differed significantly between patients with anosognosia and controls, but not between patients with and without deficit awareness in the word riddle. In the picture riddle, patients with anosognosia had significantly higher confidence levels than the other subgroups. To conclude, overconfidence was most common in patients with anosognosia but was not exclusive to them.

Article.Title: The Visual Imagery Visually Anchored Scale (VIVAS) reveals dissociable perceptual dimensions and category-specific structure
Article.Authors: Sigurdardottir H.; Árnason D.; Mäekalle M.; Vésteinsdóttir V.; Ásgeirsson Á.
Article.Abstract: Visual imagery varies widely across individuals, from aphantasia (no imagery) to hyperphantasia (highly vivid imagery), yet most measurement tools rely on verbal self-report with limited external anchoring. We introduce the Visual Imagery Visually Anchored Scale (VIVAS), which asks people to reconstruct their mental images of objects from six categories (animals, buildings, faces, food, manmade objects, novel objects) along three dimensions (opacity, sharpness, color saturation) using visually presented anchors. VIVAS was administered to a probability-based panel randomly selected from the National Registry of Iceland (N = 205). VIVAS dimensions were highly related but not interchangeable: individual differences in color imagery reliably dissociated from those of opacity and sharpness, suggesting that imagery partly separates into structural clarity and chromaticity. Imagery also differed systematically across categories. Novel objects elicited the weakest imagery on all three dimensions, which highlights a central role for familiarity in shaping imagery strength. Food items showed selectively enhanced color imagery, consistent with the functional importance of color for evaluating edibility and with the overlap between food- and color-selective regions in visual cortex. VIVAS total scores did not differ by gender, age, education, or device type, supporting robustness for online administration. VIVAS correlated moderately with the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ), well below the ceiling set by each instrument's reliability, and individual-level dissociations were striking: some participants scoring in the bottom 10% on one measure fell in the top quartile on the other. Verbal and visually anchored measures therefore appear to capture complementary, and sometimes divergent, facets of imagery.

Article.Title: Minimal social context decouples affective response modalities
Article.Authors: Judson R.; Davies J.; Briscoe J.; Cuve H.
Article.Abstract: Emotions often occur within social interactions where affective cues are partly accessible or inferable by others. This raises theorethical questions regarding how and to what degree social context modulates subjective, physiological and behavioural affective responses, as well as their coherence, which remain points of tension in emotion research. To investigate this, we measured subjective affective ratings, autonomic sympathetic and parasympathetic activity, and facial behaviour while participants completed an emotion-induction task. In the social-context condition (but not control), participants believed that their video feed was accessible to a potential future interaction partner. Results show that even such "minimal social context" selectively and differentially modulated affective response modalities, characterised by both intensification of autonomic responses and dampening of overt facial and subjective affect. Multivariate dimensionality analysis further identified a cross-modal affective dimension. Notably, social context reduced participants' coupling with this shared affective response structure, indicating weaker cross-modal coherence. These findings suggest that emotional responding relies on a flexible, rather than rigid, configuration of affective features, likely recruited to meet the socioemotional demands of a given context. This has important implications for understanding the structure and function of emotion, as well as typical and atypical socioemotional responding.

Article.Title: EEG signatures for tactile object individuation on a finger tip
Article.Authors: Lou C.; Lei Y.; Noppeney U.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Object individuation (OI), i.e., segmenting sensory signals into individual objects based on spatial or temporal cues, has been studied predominantly in vision but remained largely unexplored in touch. Using EEG we studied the neural activity associated with OI in touch. In two experiments, participants (Experiment 1: n=28; Experiment 2: n=27) were presented with one to eight pins on their index fingertip. In Experiment 1, they enumerated the number of pins, a task relying on OI. In Experiment 2, they detected a brief temporal flicker in the tactile stimulus, a task that did not involve OI. Multivariate analyses showed that neural activity around 860 msec post-stimulus encoded the number of pins, but only during enumeration. Moreover, for Experiment 1, we observed that the amplitudes of two ERP indices, the late contralateral negativity (N1000cc) and the tactile contralateral delay activity (tCDA), increased with the number of enumerated items, peaking at three objects. Time-frequency analysis revealed greater oscillatory power in the alpha-band for small numerosities (1-3 items), corresponding to the range typically associated with tactile subitizing, relative to larger numerosities (4-6 items), suggesting an attentional control mechanism that aids in separating tactile objects from the background while reducing interference from irrelevant sensory information during capacity-limited OI processing. Importantly, these neural effects were not observed in Experiment 2. Collectively, our results provide evidence that tactile object individuation is capacity-limited and is associated with distinct N1000cc, tCDA, and alpha-band activity.

Article.Title: Quantifying the impact of age-related hearing loss on neural signatures of target selection and distractor suppression
Article.Authors: Solmssen N.; Stockar F.; Alavash M.; Popov T.; Wöstmann M.; Obleser J.; Preisig B.
Article.Abstract: Listeners with hearing loss (HL) often report difficulties in separating relevant target sound from irrelevant distraction. These difficulties in auditory selective attention might be caused by inefficient neural mechanisms underlying target selection and distractor suppression. In this registered report, we tested whether neural and behavioural signatures of target selection and distractor suppression were selectively impaired in 30 older listeners with HL, compared to 32 older listeners with normal hearing (NH) and 33 young NH listeners. For this purpose, we used an auditory pitch discrimination task that allowed to dissociate changes in neural alpha activity (∼8-12Hz) and microsaccade direction in response to target selection and distractor suppression due to spatial separation. Our results show that neural signatures of spatial attention may be relatively preserved in individuals with mild-to-moderate hearing loss. Specifically, we found no conclusive evidence that hearing loss affects either target-related or distractor-related alpha lateralization. In contrast, distractor-related, but not target-related, alpha lateralization diminished with age. Furthermore, we found no conclusive evidence that single-trial alpha lateralization predicts listening accuracy or confidence. We found that attentional modulation of microsaccade rate occurred independently of directional bias and alpha lateralization. Microsaccade rate, but not microsaccade direction, was significantly increased during lateral distractor suppression compared to target selection, and we observed no oculomotor pattern mirroring neural alpha lateralization. Collectively, these findings suggest that aging more strongly affects the neural signature of distractor suppression than that of target selection.

Article.Title: Gaze guides language comprehension in adults in a simulated social environment
Article.Authors: Zappa A.; Osokina P.; Fargier R.; Cerda-Company X.; Panisello S.; Anderssen N.; Zambrana I.; Rodriguez-Fornells A.; Slater M.
Article.Abstract: Multimodal cues are crucial for real-life language comprehension. While gaze-following is a well-established mechanism in early language acquisition, its role in adult language comprehension - especially under challenging conditions - remains relatively unexplored. Here, we used a novel immersive and embodied virtual reality (VR) paradigm to examine whether referential gaze facilitates comprehension of unfamiliar spoken words in a noisy environment. Participants interacted with virtual agents whose gaze behavior varied in referential informativeness. Explicit feedback ensured that gaze-guided comprehension outcomes could be disentangled from informational content. Behavioral and eye-tracking data showed that participants identified spoken input more accurately when the teacher’s gaze reliably signaled the intended referent, and when they actively followed it. This facilitative effect of gaze emerged early and persisted across tasks. These findings highlight the enduring role of social gaze mechanisms in adult language comprehension, particularly in ambiguous or noisy contexts. They have important implications for a multimodal and situated language processing perspective, showing that gaze-following plays a meaningful role in real-world comprehension.

Article.Title: Active movement drives recovery of spatial hearing
Article.Authors: Camponogara I.
Article.Abstract: : Auditory localization can be restored following the disruption of binaural cues through brief motor training consisting of moving a handheld sound source. Whether restoration is driven by continuous motor-related kinesthetic signals generated during active movement, by proprioceptive-auditory coupling, or by auditory motion experience alone is still a matter of debate. Here, we addressed this question by comparing auditory localization performance before and after one of four brief (10 minutes) training protocols: dynamic active (actively moved a handheld sound source); dynamic passive (sound source was moved externally); static auditory (listening to sounds presented at discrete positions); or static audio-proprioceptive (holding a stationary sound source at discrete positions without constant movement). Results indicate that continuous active movement of a sound source enables the highest auditory restoration, with passive auditory motion exposure and static proprioceptive-auditory pairing both proving less effective than active movement. A second experiment investigated whether direct haptic information from hand contact with the speaker is relevant to auditory restoration by controlling the sound position through hand hovering over the speaker. Auditory restoration in this condition did not credibly differ from either active touching or passive listening. Together, these results identify continuous movement as the primary driver of limb-based auditory spatial restoration.

Article.Title: Beyond the Microbial Hypothesis: Shared Genetic, Osteoimmune and Vascular Mechanisms in the Oral–Brain Axis Linking Periodontitis and Alzheimer's Disease
Article.Authors: Kabbashi S.; Ahmed M.; Chetty M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Periodontitis, a chronic inflammatory disease of the tooth‐supporting tissues, is increasingly linked to Alzheimer's disease ( AD ), yet mechanistic accounts of this ‘oral–brain axis’ have been dominated by microbial translocation and the gingipain hypothesis. This review argues that the convergence between periodontitis and AD extends well beyond microbes, integrating shared genetic, osteoimmune and vascular‐inflammatory mechanisms that are rarely considered together. Genetic susceptibility reaches beyond APOE ε4 to the osteoprotegerin (OPG) axis, with APOE ε4 linking the two conditions through impaired amyloid‐β clearance, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and altered lipid handling. The OPG/RANK/RANKL system emerges as a bone–brain (osteoimmune) interface, in which OPG shows a dual‐role paradox, reduced locally in periodontal bone loss yet elevated systematically in AD , while soluble RANKL displays neuroprotective properties. Because OPG acts as a decoy receptor for RANKL, we hypothesise that elevated OPG in AD limits RANKL‐dependent microglial amyloid‐β clearance. Endothelial dysfunction, reflected in circulating endocan, provides a shared vascular readout that is raised in both diseases and responsive to periodontal therapy. We propose that these genetic, microbial and vascular inputs converge on microglial priming and trained immunity, a unifying immunological node through which chronic peripheral inflammation may act during the decades‐long preclinical phase of AD . Current evidence nonetheless remains predominantly associative, causality is unproven and mechanistic data rely heavily on animal models. The oral–brain axis is therefore best regarded as a promising yet still unproven framework in which osteoimmune and vascular pathways, and candidate biomarkers such as endocan, represent underexplored targets for future longitudinal and interventional research.

Article.Title: Cortical Adaptation to Muscle Fatigue Does Not Alter Early Proprioceptive Processing in Primary Sensorimotor Cortex
Article.Authors: Chen J.; Mujunen T.; Li F.; Nikander R.; Piitulainen H.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Muscle fatigue potentially interferes with proprioceptive afference from peripheral “movement sensors”—the proprioceptors, which may hinder crucial sensorimotor integration and thus movement performance. However, little is known about how muscle fatigue affects cortical processing of proprioceptive afference. Twenty‐four healthy volunteers (30.7 ± 6.5 years) participated in the experiment, which included magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings during 2‐Hz passive ankle‐joint rotations, and fatigue tasks comprised of isometric ankle plantarflexion. Corticokinematic coherence (CKC) between linear foot acceleration and MEG signals was examined before (PRE) and ~3 min after (POST) the fatigue tasks to compare the cortical proprioceptive processing. CKC peaked in the gradiometer pairs above the foot region of the primary sensorimotor (SM1) cortex in each participant. CKC strength did not show significant difference between PRE and POST at 2 Hz (0.30 ± 0.12 vs. 0.30 ± 0.14, p = 0.981) or its first harmonic at 4 Hz (0.38 ± 0.14 vs. 0.37 ± 0.13, p = 0.724). However, 4‐Hz MEG power was ~30% lower in POST than in PRE. Surprisingly, fatigue‐induced increase of alpha and beta power was observed bilaterally in SM1 hand regions during the ankle movements. Our results indicate that the early processing of proprioceptive afference from the ankle joint was negligibly affected by muscle fatigue or the effect recovered rapidly. The fatigue elevated alpha and beta power while diminishing neuronal activity at the 4‐Hz harmonic frequency, which may reflect a compensatory mechanism for asynchronous proprioceptive afference by enhancing cortical inhibitory control.

Article.Title: Mitochondria‐Associated Membranes as a Convergent Hub of Brain Aging: From Neurodegeneration to Cerebral Ischemia
Article.Authors: Li M.; Xu D.; Li Y.; Zhao Q.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Brain aging is the principal risk factor for both neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) and cerebral ischemic disorders, yet the subcellular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely defined. Mitochondria‐associated membranes (MAMs)—specialized contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria—sit at the intersection of two well‐established hallmarks of aging, mitochondrial dysfunction, and loss of proteostasis, making them an attractive mechanistic node for understanding age‐related brain decline. In this review, we propose a MAM‐centered framework that unifies neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathology under the broader paradigm of brain aging. We first summarize the molecular architecture of MAMs and their core functions in neuronal Ca 2+ transfer, mitochondrial dynamics, lipid metabolism, inflammasome assembly, and autophagic quality control, together with emerging evidence from non‐neuronal brain cells. We then examine how MAM dysfunction intersects with five hallmarks of aging—mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of proteostasis, disabled macroautophagy, chronic inflammation (inflammaging), and altered intercellular communication—drawing on evidence from physiological aging and cellular senescence models. Next, we discuss disease‐specific roles of MAMs in cerebral ischemia and in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease. A central theme emerges: Rather than a unidirectional decline of MAMs, brain aging is associated with a loss of MAM homeostasis, in which both insufficient and excessive ER–mitochondria coupling can be pathological and the shared deficit is the failure to maintain contact‐site function within an optimal range. Finally, we consider age‐relevant therapeutic and biomarker strategies targeting MAMs and their potential translation into geriatric neurology. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate MAM biology across physiological brain aging, cerebral ischemia, and the four major NDDs within a single homeostatic framework, offering a unified perspective on the mechanisms of age‐related brain decline.

Article.Title: Traditional Chinese Medicine Targeting the Ischemic Cascade in Ischemic Stroke: Multitarget Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential
Article.Authors: Song Y.; Yang M.; Wang S.; Chen Y.; Dong P.; Han H.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Ischemic stroke (IS) remains a major cause of mortality and long‐term disability worldwide. Increasing evidence indicates that injury progression after cerebral ischemia is closely associated with dysfunction of the neurovascular unit (NVU). Following ischemia, a series of interconnected pathological events, including metabolic failure, excitotoxicity, calcium dysregulation, oxidative injury, inflammation and cell death, contribute to progressive neuronal and vascular damage. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has been increasingly investigated as a source of multicomponent interventions for IS. Experimental studies indicate that bioactive compounds, extracts and classical formulas may influence multiple components of the ischemic cascade, including energy metabolism, glutamate excitotoxicity, Ca 2+ homeostasis, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation and regulated cell death. These effects have been associated with pathways including AMPK/SIRT1, PI3K/Akt, Nrf2/HO‐1, NF‐κB and NLRP3. However, modulation of multiple pathways does not necessarily establish pharmacological synergy or superiority over single‐target interventions. This review summarizes TCM interventions targeting the ischemic cascade, with a primary focus on studies published between 2015 and 2025. Particular attention is given to the strength of mechanistic evidence, treatment timing, experimental models, pharmacologically active constituents, safety and clinical translation. By critically evaluating both mechanistic findings and current limitations, this review provides a framework for assessing the evidence and translational potential of TCM‐derived neuroprotective strategies in IS.

Article.Title: Cognitive Cerebellum Structure and Functional Connectivity in Relation to Executive Functions in Obsessive‐Compulsive Disorder
Article.Authors: Rosales Mondragón C.; Barbosa Luna M.; Ricardo Garcell J.; Alcauter Solórzano S.; Salvador Cruz J.; Corona Márquez B.; López Lazo L.; Pasaye E.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Obsessive‐compulsive disorder (OCD) has been primarily linked to abnormalities within the cortico–striato–thalamo–cortical circuit; however, recent evidence suggests that the posterior cerebellum may contribute to the executive dysfunction observed in the disorder. In 56 adults (28 OCD, 28 controls), we assessed executive functions using the BANFE‐2 battery and integrated structural MRI (T1) and resting‐state fMRI. Although the Global Executive Index did not differ significantly between groups, patients with OCD showed significantly lower scores in the inhibitory control/decision‐making domain relative to controls. We quantified cortical thickness and volume (% intracranial volume) in Crus I/II and lobule VI using CERES and examined resting‐state functional connectivity (seed‐to‐voxel) in CONN, adjusting for age, sex, medication, and depression. Compared with controls, patients with OCD showed reduced bilateral cortical thickness in Crus I/II and lobule VI (false discovery rate‐corrected q < 0.05; β_OCD − Control = −0.27 to −0.59; ηp 2 = 0.34–0.55), with no significant volumetric differences after correction for multiple comparisons. Functional connectivity results revealed a mixed pattern, including focal hyperconnectivity (e.g., left Crus I with primary auditory cortex; left Crus II with occipital cortex) and widespread intracerebellar hypoconnectivity. In addition, significant Group × executive‐function interactions ( p ‐family‐wise error < 0.05) emerged mainly for bilateral Crus I (Global Executive Index and working memory/flexibility) and left lobule VI (inhibition/decision‐making), indicating that the relationship between cerebellar connectivity and executive performance differs in OCD relative to controls. These findings support an expanded model of executive circuits in OCD that incorporates the posterior cerebellum as a relevant node.

Article.Title: Protective Role of Netrin‐1 in the Female Nucleus Accumbens Following Amphetamine Exposure in Adolescence
Article.Authors: Teixeira M.; MacGowan D.; Avramescu R.; Zhu A.; Niu Z.; Mahmud A.; Hernandez G.; Flores C.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Adolescence is a period of mesocorticolimbic dopamine remodelling, when exposure to drugs of abuse can alter axon targeting and synaptic maturation. In adolescent male rodents, amphetamine causes dopamine axon mistargeting and long‐term cognitive deficits via downregulation of the Netrin‐1/DCC guidance system. In females, compensatory Netrin‐1 protein upregulation in the nucleus accumbens protects against these effects. How Netrin‐1 expression in the nucleus accumbens is regulated and what role it plays in local synaptic architecture remain unclear. Here, we mapped Netrin‐1 mRNA ( Ntn1 ) across development in nucleus accumbens medium spiny neurons, assessed the role of dopamine D1 and D2 receptor signalling in Netrin‐1 protein expression and examined whether Netrin‐1 maintains medium spiny neuron dendritic spine architecture following adolescent amphetamine exposure. We found that medium spiny neurons, particularly those co‐expressing D1 and D2 receptors, were the principal source of Ntn1 mRNA in the nucleus accumbens in both sexes, with expression declining from early adolescence to adulthood. In adolescent females, systemic blockade of either D1 or D2 receptors reduced nucleus accumbens Netrin‐1 protein levels under both baseline and amphetamine‐exposed conditions. Although amphetamine did not alter Ntn1 mRNA in the nucleus accumbens, it increased its expression in the ventral tegmental area, suggesting a potential contribution from afferent projections. These findings indicate that Netrin‐1 upregulation in adolescent females is dopamine‐dependent and may protect against amphetamine‐induced circuit disruption, possibly involving pre‐ and postsynaptic mechanisms.

Article.Title: Time to Move Upstream? A Framework for Expanding the Focus of Freezing of Gait to Prodromal, Subclinical, and Pre‐FOG Stages
Article.Authors: Hausdorff J.; Ehgoetz Martens K.; Gilat M.; Nonnekes J.; Mancini M.; McKay J.; Ginis P.; Adams J.; Mammen J.; Howe E.; Lewis S.; Horak F.; Nieuwboer A.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Freezing of gait (FOG) is one of the most disabling motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease, yet a fundamental question remains unresolved: why does FOG occur at any given moment? Most research has focused on studying FOG once it is already manifest. The present work aims to synthesize recent observations and propose a conceptual framework in which FOG reflects a dynamic process unfolding across multiple stages and time scales. Subtle changes in gait dynamics and physiology can precede episodes by several seconds (Stage −1), and experimental paradigms show that individuals without clinically recognized freezing may exhibit brief episodes under sufficiently sensitive conditions (Stage −2). At longer time scales, prospective studies indicate that vulnerability to freezing may be detectable years before onset (Stage −3). This framework reflects the idea that FOG emerges from progressive instability across interacting motor, cognitive, autonomic, and environmental systems, rather than as an isolated event. The proposed framework includes a prodromal stage, a subclinical stage, an immediate prefreezing state, and the freezing episode itself (Stage 0). This framework integrates findings from wearable sensing, physiology, and clinical studies and emphasizes that FOG remains latent in Stage −3, may be elicited only under specific conditions in Stage −2, and becomes manifest as instability evolves toward imminent and overt freezing (Stages −1 and 0, respectively). Reframing FOG as a multistage process that includes an upstream phase raises new questions regarding mechanisms, classification, and intervention, and may, ultimately, inform strategies aimed at predicting and preventing freezing rather than simply reacting to it.

Article.Title: Effects of Short‐Term Breathwork on Respiration and Cognitive Performance in a Discrimination Task
Article.Authors: Hehemann L.; Stetza L.; Kayser C.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Respiration is a unique physiological process that can operate automatically but can also be deliberately used to modulate the bodily state. Importantly, respiration is deeply intertwined with neural processes, influencing functions from arousal and attention to executive control. Although structured respiration (breathing practice) has been exploited for centuries, the immediate consequences of short periods of structured respiration for sensation and cognition remain poorly understood. The present explorative study examined how brief, 1‐min episodes of structured respiration affect respiration and performance in a subsequent sensory‐cognitive task. Across two experiments, participants engaged in structured breathing practices that manipulated either respiratory frequency (slow breathing vs. fast breathing) or the inhalation–exhalation ratio (short inspiration–long expiration and long inspiration–short expiration) prior to performing a visual emotion discrimination task. Immediately after breathing practice, participants' respiration deviated from their baseline: Each technique resulted in specific deviations of respiratory frequency, inhalation–exhalation ratio, or the occurrence of atypical respiratory cycles, suggesting technique‐specific returns to regular respiration. During the subsequent discrimination task response accuracy and reaction times did not differ between breathing practices. However, we observed transient changes in reaction times immediately following all practices, suggesting a brief facilitation of attentional or sensorimotor responsiveness following conscious breathing. Our findings indicate that even brief, consciously controlled respiration can transiently influence cognitive performance, highlighting the role of voluntary respiratory modulation in shaping brain function and behavior.

Article.Title: Photoperiodic Regulation of SK Channels in Dorsal Raphe Serotonin Neurons
Article.Authors: Giannoni‐Guzmán M.; Zepeda J.; Kamitakahara A.; Magalong V.; Levitt P.; Grueter B.; McMahon D.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Day length, or seasonal photoperiod, shapes mood and affective behaviors, but the neural mechanisms underlying these effects are still being defined. Serotonin neurons of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) are critical regulators of affective behaviors, and photoperiod modulates their excitability and ongoing activity. Here, we investigated the influence of seasonal photoperiod on the function and expression of small conductance calcium‐activated potassium (SK) channels, which mediate the after‐hyperpolarizing potential (AHP) in dorsal raphe serotonin neurons. Building on previous work demonstrating that long summer‐like photoperiod increases serotonergic neuron excitability and decreases AHP amplitude, we hypothesized that day length influences SK channel activity, thereby contributing to differences in neuronal excitability observed between Long, Equinox, and Short photoperiod conditions. Using multielectrode array recordings from DRN slices, we found a significant, dose‐dependent increase in spike rate upon application of the SK channel inhibitor apamin, indicating that SK channels indeed influence the spike rate of dorsal raphe serotonin neurons. In addition, whole‐cell recordings from DRN neurons in slices demonstrated that SK channel–mediated AHP currents were smaller in amplitude in Long photoperiod mice compared to Short and Equinox photoperiod mice. However, we found no significant differences in mRNA levels of the SK3 subunit ( Kcnn3 ) in DRN serotonin neurons across photoperiod conditions as determined by single‐molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization. Overall, these findings indicate that photoperiod modulates SK channel function in DRN serotonin neurons, possibly through posttranscriptional mechanisms, contributing to the increase in serotonin neuron excitability observed in long summer‐like photoperiods.

Article.Title: Differential NMDA‐Evoked Excitatory and Inhibitory Neuronal Responses Under In Vivo and Ex Vivo Conditions in 5xFAD Mice
Article.Authors: Lee S.; Park T.; Chung S.; Suh M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with profound disturbances in neuronal activity. While spontaneous neuronal hyperactivity is a well‐established feature of AD, how the disease affects stimulus‐evoked responses of excitatory and inhibitory neurons remains unclear. Prior studies examining stimulus‐evoked activity have reported conflicting results, describing both exaggerated and blunted responses, which has hindered a coherent understanding of how neuronal activity is evoked by stimulation in AD. The objective of this study was to determine how experimental context influences stimulus‐evoked neuronal responses in AD and to define cell‐type‐specific alterations in excitatory and inhibitory neurons within the same disease model. We examined N ‐methyl‐D‐aspartate (NMDA)‐evoked calcium responses in the 5xFAD mouse model under ex vivo and in vivo conditions using two‐photon calcium imaging. Excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations were analyzed, enabling assessment of stimulus‐evoked response amplitude and kinetics across experimental contexts. In acute brain slices, NMDA stimulation elicited exaggerated peak responses and altered response kinetics in excitatory neurons from AD mice, whereas inhibitory neurons showed preserved peak amplitude but a significantly delayed time to peak. In contrast, under in vivo conditions, NMDA‐evoked responses were markedly attenuated in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Thus, the same AD model exhibited opposing stimulus‐evoked response profiles depending on experimental context. These findings demonstrate that stimulus‐evoked neuronal dysfunction in AD is context‐dependent and cannot be inferred from a single experimental modality. Our results indicate that AD‐related alterations in neuronal responsiveness reflect changes in how inputs are recruited and transformed, rather than a uniform shift toward hyperexcitability or hypoexcitability, underscoring the need for integrative, multimodal approaches to define neuronal dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.

Article.Title: Structural and EEG Motor Networks Distinguish Level of Motor Impairment After Stroke
Article.Authors: Zhou Z.; Wodeyar A.; Cramer S.; Srinivasan R.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The objective of this study was to determine how structural and EEG‐based functional connectivity jointly distinguish levels of motor impairment after stroke. We estimated patient‐specific (1) structural connectivity using MRI‐derived lesion models and (2) functional connectivity using source‐localized EEG, guided by each patient's structural connectome. Analyses focused on the brainstem and three motor‐related cortical regions bilaterally: primary motor cortex (M1), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), and supplementary motor cortex (SMA). Network analysis metrics (degree centrality, average efficiency, betweenness centrality) were applied to structural and functional data, contrasting motor networks between patients with high (H) and low (L) upper extremity motor function. Structural disconnection of the brainstem from M1 and PMd carried the highest probability of low motor status. All network measures were elevated in the H group compared to the L group across motor‐related regions, indicating a globally strengthened motor network organization associated with better motor function. Functional connectivity revealed convergent but distinct patterns. In the delta band (1–3 Hz), ipsilesional motor regions showed stronger connectivity in the H group. In the beta band (14–29 Hz), contralesional motor regions demonstrated enhanced connectivity in H patients, consistent with prior evidence that contralesional motor regions may contribute to motor function after ipsilesional injury. We also introduced a novel metric, motor betweenness centrality, to quantify the role of nonmotor regions in rerouting motor‐related communication. Almost all new hubs identified structurally were associated with lower motor status, suggesting less efficient network organization in more impaired patients. Thus, preservation of direct motor pathways supports better motor status, while reliance on alternative, less efficient routes correlates with worse outcomes. By contrast, EEG routing revealed that H patients recruited proximal cortical hubs, while L patients relied on distant, inefficient ones, highlighting functional network organization not evident in the structural analysis. These patterns suggest that more local network organization, rather than more distributed rerouting, is associated with better motor status within the motor system. In summary, multimodal network properties reliably identified key motor ROIs predictive of motor status. This concordance suggests that EEG‐based metrics, particularly delta‐ and beta‐band connectivity, are associated with lesion‐derived structural disruption and complementary features of motor‐network organization. Structural connectivity damage within motor circuits defines the extent of network disruption associated with motor impairment, while EEG functional connectivity provides complementary information about network organization measured at the time of assessment. Together, these measures characterize different aspects of motor network integrity after stroke.

Article.Title: Chronic Mild Stress in Male Wistar‐Kyoto Rats Induces Long‐Term Hippocampal Plasticity Impairments Differentially Reversed by Acute and Chronic Ketamine Treatment
Article.Authors: Loizeau V.; Jesic M.; Kuster R.; Hugel S.; Barbelivien A.; Lecourtier L.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Chronic stress induces strong alteration of hippocampal synaptic plasticity, impairing long‐term potentiation and facilitating long‐term depression, processes thought to be involved in the pathophysiology of depression. Ketamine, a noncompetitive antagonist of the N ‐methyl‐D‐aspartate receptor, has emerged as a fast‐acting antidepressant whose action is believed to involve restoring impaired plasticity, though its sustained effects are elusive. Here, we investigated how chronic mild stress and subsequent acute and chronic ketamine treatments modulate synaptic plasticity in the Schaffer collateral pathway in the dorsal hippocampus of stress‐vulnerable Wistar‐Kyoto rats. Adult male rats were subjected to 4 weeks of chronic mild stress and vulnerability was determined through behavioral performance in the forced swim and elevated plus maze tests. Stress‐vulnerable rats received saline or either an acute or chronic subanesthetic dose of ketamine (10 mg/kg), and hippocampal slices were harvested for synaptic plasticity investigation. Conversely to what occurred in nonstressed rats, in stress‐vulnerable rats treated with saline, neither long‐term potentiation (LTP) nor long‐term depression (LTD) could be induced following high‐frequency and low‐frequency stimulation, respectively. Acute ketamine restored normal LTP but not LTD, while chronic ketamine restored LTD but not LTP. These findings highlight complex temporal dynamics in the modulation of hippocampal synaptic plasticity by ketamine following chronic stress and demonstrate that acute and chronic treatment regimens differentially affect the induction of LTP and LTD.

Article.Title: Glycogen Synthase Kinase‐3β as a Central Regulator of Alzheimer's Disease: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Kifayat S.; Kifayat W.; Chauhan S.; Zehra A.; Kaushik R.; Najmi A.; Parvez S.; Ali J.; Akhtar M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurological condition marked by cognitive decline, memory impairment, extracellular amyloid‐β (Aβ) accumulation, and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs). Among the multiple molecular pathways involved in AD pathogenesis, glycogen synthase kinase‐3β (GSK‐3β) has emerged as a crucial signaling regulator due to its extensive contribution to neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, metabolism, and cellular stress responses. Growing evidence suggests that abnormal activation of GSK‐3β contributes not merely to classical AD hallmarks, including tau hyperphosphorylation and amyloidogenesis, but is also linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, autophagic impairment, ferroptosis, insulin resistance, and oxidative stress through modulation of the Nrf2 pathway. These findings place GSK‐3β as a crucial molecular hub linking different pathogenic pathways in AD. This review outlines the structural attributes along with regulatory mechanisms of GSK‐3β and extensively explores its involvement in AD pathophysiology. Specific emphasis is given to evolving mechanisms, such as metabolic dysregulation, ferroptosis, and antioxidant signaling pathways. Additionally, current breakthroughs in therapeutic targeting techniques such as ATP‐competitive inhibitors, non–ATP‐competitive inhibitors, allosteric modulators, natural chemicals, and clinically studied medicines are emphasized. The translational difficulties linked to selectivity, blood–brain barrier permeability, and clinical efficacies are also explored. Collectively, this review reinforces the therapeutic relevance of GSK‐3β and indicates potential opportunities for creating effective disease‐modifying therapies in AD.

Article.Title: Adjunctive Multisensory Passive Immersive Virtual Reality With Synchronized Plantar Tactile Stimulation for Gait and Balance Disorders in Parkinson's Disease: An Exploratory Randomized Controlled Trial
Article.Authors: Shirolapov I.; Natalevich S.; Khivintseva E.; Komarova Y.; Romanchuk N.; Sergeeva M.; Popov N.; Kalinin V.; Zakharov A.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Postural‐locomotor disorders, particularly freezing of gait and postural instability, are among the most disabling symptoms of advanced Parkinson's disease (PD) and respond only partially to dopaminergic therapy. Evidence for virtual reality (VR) approaches in moderate to severe PD remains limited. This prospective randomized controlled open‐label exploratory trial evaluated the addition of multisensory passive immersive VR with synchronized plantar tactile stimulation to conventional rehabilitation for gait, balance, and freezing disorders in moderate‐to‐severe PD (Hoehn and Yahr Stages 2–4). In the study, 80 PD patients were randomized into an experimental group (EXP, n = 40) receiving standard pharmacotherapy and conventional rehabilitation plus 10 sessions of passive immersive VR with synchronized plantar tactile stimulation and a comparison group (COM, n = 40) receiving standard pharmacotherapy and conventional rehabilitation only. Because the VR sessions were added to an otherwise identical program, the trial evaluates the effect of adding this intervention rather than a VR‐ or tactile‐specific effect. Outcomes were assessed at baseline and after 10 days using the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), Berg Balance Scale (BBS), and Freezing of Gait Questionnaire (FoG‐Q). The EXP group showed significant improvements in the UPDRS “Gait” cluster (an eight‐item composite of UPDRS items 2.11, 2.12, 2.13, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13, range 0–32; median from 12.5 to 8.0 points, p < 0.001), BBS (from 38.0 to 43.5 points, p < 0.001), and FoG‐Q (from 9.0 to 6.5 points, p < 0.001). A formal group × time analysis confirmed a differential treatment effect for every outcome. For the main outcome, the UPDRS “Gait” cluster, the baseline‐adjusted between‐group difference was −2.48 points (95% CI −3.37 to −1.59; p < 0.001; Hedges' g = 1.16). Large effects also favored the EXP group for the FoG‐Q (−2.14 points, 95% CI −2.62 to −1.66; g = 1.65), the BBS (+2.20 points, 95% CI 1.31 to 3.10; g = 1.06), the UPDRS freezing subscore (items 2.13 + 3.11; −0.89 points, 95% CI −1.13 to −0.66; g = 1.32), and the UPDRS postural subscore (items 3.12 + 3.13; −0.74 points, 95% CI −1.08 to −0.41; g = 0.93). Secondary outcome p ‐values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg procedures. By contrast, in the COM group, no significant change was observed for freezing of gait ( p = 0.083), and improvements in other outcomes were smaller than in the EXP group. No serious adverse events were recorded. The trial was exploratory, so the effect estimates require confirmation rather than supporting robustness in themselves. Overall, multisensory passive immersive VR with synchronized plantar tactile stimulation was well tolerated and shows preliminary promise as an adjunct to conventional rehabilitation for gait and balance disorders in moderate‐to‐severe PD. Wider clinical implementation requires long‐term multicenter studies with standardized assessment criteria and analysis of long‐term sustainability. These findings support integrating passive VR technologies into personalized neurorehabilitation programs.

Article.Title: Region‐ and Time‐Dependent Gene Expression Responses to Siponimod, Atorvastatin and Methylprednisolone After Spinal Cord Injury
Article.Authors: Bimbova K.; Kisucka A.; Kuruc T.; Ileninova M.; Kucharova K.; Ihnatova L.; Bacova M.; Magurova M.; Lukacova N.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers a secondary injury cascade in which microglia, infiltrating macrophages and astrocytes influence tissue degeneration and repair. These responses are dynamic and region‐dependent, yet the comparative effects of anti‐inflammatory therapies remain unclear. We evaluated siponimod, atorvastatin and methylprednisolone after Th9 compression injury in rats. Gene expression was assessed by quantitative RT‐PCR in rostral, lesion and caudal spinal cord segments at 2 and 6 weeks postinjury. At 2 weeks, all treatments reduced microglia/macrophage‐associated and inflammatory transcripts, particularly rostrally, as shown by reduced Iba1 and iNOS expression. Siponimod and atorvastatin also decreased IL‐1β rostrally, whereas siponimod was associated with region‐specific increases in inflammatory markers at the lesion site and caudally. Siponimod most consistently increased microglia/macrophage‐associated transcripts linked to immunoregulatory and reparative responses caudally, including IL1rn, TGF‐β, SOCS3 and IL4Rα. It also reduced selected inflammatory astrocyte‐associated markers and increased transcripts linked to repair‐related processes, while atorvastatin and methylprednisolone showed mixed effects. At 6 weeks, none of the treatments consistently suppressed pro‐inflammatory microglia/macrophage‐associated markers. Siponimod was associated with elevated transcripts linked to immunoregulatory and repair‐related processes, together with region‐dependent increases in inflammatory markers. Astrocyte‐associated reactivity markers were largely normalised, whereas remodelling‐associated transcripts were altered. Treatments induced modest changes in neuronal/axonal and myelin‐associated transcripts, predominantly rostrally, without significant functional improvement. Overall, these interventions differentially modulated microglia/macrophage‐ and astrocyte‐associated gene expression, with siponimod producing the broadest, but mixed and region‐dependent, gene‐expression pattern. These findings highlight the regional and stage‐dependent complexity of glial and inflammatory gene expression after pharmacological treatment of SCI.

Article.Title: Opioid Modulation of Major Neurotransmitter Systems: Acute, Chronic, and Withdrawal Effects
Article.Authors: Novakova D.; Pritulova E.; Novotny J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Opioids are widely used in clinical practice for the management of moderate‐to‐severe acute and chronic pain. However, their use is associated with the development of tolerance and physical dependence, often followed by a withdrawal syndrome upon discontinuation. The mechanisms underlying opioid dependence and withdrawal are highly complex and remain incompletely understood. These processes involve multiple regions of the central nervous system and are accompanied by widespread alterations in neuronal signaling pathways. Neurotransmitters, which are essential for communication between neurons, play a critical role in opioid addiction and withdrawal. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the major neurotransmitter systems, their involvement, and the changes that occur during acute and chronic opioid exposure. Particular attention is also given to the consequences of opioid discontinuation. Overall, this review summarizes current knowledge of the molecular mechanisms underlying both the acute and long‐term effects of opioids on key neurotransmitter systems in the brain.
