Article.Title: Effect of electrical stimulation of the medial habenula on morphine self-administration in male rats
Article.Authors: Salimi Z.; Khani F.; Erfani S.; Mohamadi M.; Zarei F.
Article.Abstract: Background and purpose: Drug addiction is a major global health concern and an important contributor to morbidity and mortality. Given the central role of the habenula (Hb) in reward processing and addiction-related behaviors, this nucleus has emerged as an important target for investigating the neural consequences of substance abuse. Although the involvement of the lateral habenula (LHb) in addiction has been extensively documented, the contribution of the medial habenula (MHb) remains less clear. Therefore, the present study evaluated the effects of electrical stimulation of the MHb on morphine self-administration in male rats. Materials & methods: In the present study, male Wistar rats were assigned to four experimental groups. During behavioral testing, the first and second groups received an injection of 0.1 mL of vehicle or morphine (5 mg/kg), respectively. In the third and fourth groups, two stimulation groups, the MHb was electrically stimulated at low (25 μA) or high (150 μA) intensity before morphine administration. Morphine self-administration was assessed over 11 consecutive days. Results: The number of active lever presses was significantly higher in the morphine group than in the saline control group. However, electrical stimulation of the MHb combined with morphine administration significantly reduced the number of active lever presses compared with morphine administration alone (p < 0.05). This reduction was particularly pronounced during the last six days of the self-administration protocol (p < 0.05). No significant differences were observed among the groups in inactive lever pressing. Conclusion: These findings suggest that electrical stimulation of the MHb may attenuate morphine self-administration, possibly by modulating reward- and aversion-related neural circuits. The MHb may therefore represent a potential target for further investigation of mechanisms underlying opioid-related behavior.

Article.Title: The basic C-terminal tail of CXCL9/Mig, not its N-terminal chemokine domain, is necessary and sufficient for its neurotrophic activity
Article.Authors: Uwabe K.; Parker S.
Article.Abstract: CXCL9/Mig is unique among the CXCR3 ligands in carrying an extended, basic C-terminal tail that is absent from both CXCL10 and CXCL11. We previously found that CXCL9, but not CXCL10 or CXCL11, promotes neurite outgrowth and survival of PC12 cells and rescues NGF-deprived sympathetic neurons independently of CXCR3. Here, using an eight-member panel of CXCL9-related proteins and peptides that uncouples the N-terminal chemokine core from the C-terminal tail, we show that constructs lacking the C-terminal tail lose all neurotrophic activity and fail to activate ERK1/2 and Akt, whereas the isolated tail - whether expressed as a GST fusion or as a short synthesized peptide - fully reproduces neurite outgrowth, PC12 cell survival, and sympathetic neuron rescue. GST alone was inactive in every assay. These results map CXCL9's neurotrophic activity to its basic C-terminal tail, independent of its canonical N-terminal chemokine domain.

Article.Title: Mechanistic insights into Aβ effects on neural stem cell proliferation and differentiation
Article.Authors: Zhao Y.; Yang Y.; Zhang L.; Hu B.; Yang Z.; Chen Z.
Article.Abstract: Amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation impairs hippocampal neural stem cell (NSC) function, but whether Aβ biases NSC lineage commitment toward the astrocytic lineage remains unclear. In this study, primary hippocampal NSCs from neonatal Sprague-Dawley rats were treated with 60 μM Aβ25-35 fragment, close to the 48-h half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50 ≈ 57.8 μM) determined by a CCK-8 assay. After 48 h, the proportions of Nestin+ and 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU)+ cells were significantly decreased (P < 0.01 and P < 0.001, respectively). After 7 days of differentiation, the proportion of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)+ cells was significantly increased (P < 0.001). GFAP+ cells exhibited an increased number of processes but shortened process length. Western blotting confirmed decreased Nestin and increased GFAP protein levels (both P < 0.01). Network-based bioinformatics screening identified 124 overlapping genes between Aβ-related targets and NSC-associated genes, with the PI3K-Akt pathway most highly enriched; validation showed a reduced p-Akt/Akt ratio (P < 0.01), decreased p-GSK-3β (Ser9) and β-catenin levels (P < 0.001), and upregulated total GSK-3β (P < 0.05). Taken together, these findings indicate that Aβ25-35 inhibits NSC proliferation and promotes astrocytic lineage differentiation, at least partly through suppression of the PI3K/Akt/GSK-3β/β-catenin pathway.

Article.Title: How crocodiles lost a forebrain circuit
Article.Authors: Pritz M.
Article.Abstract: Why do brain circuits differ among species of the same or different classes of vertebrates? Answers to this question are critical in determining brain organization and evolution. Investigations in mammals and in certain model systems have been the main focus of these studies. Among the areas that have commonly been investigated are cell death, synaptic pruning, and synapse organizing proteins. Whether these same or even other factors sculpt similar circuits in other vertebrates such as reptiles is unknown. The present study examined the development of a well defined circuit in crocodiles and compared it with a similar circuit in mammals. In mammals, cortical areas project directly back to the same dorsal thalamic nucleus that provides its input. However, in reptiles, pallial regions in receipt of dorsal thalamic input do not project directly back to dorsal thalamic nuclei. Instead, pallial areas in reptiles project to the basal nuclei, similar, in part, to the striatum of mammals. The basal nuclei then project back to the dorsal thalamus. This suggested the possibility that this circuit might have been lost in reptiles or perhaps added in mammals. To determine which of these two possibilities might be the case, the development of this circuit in Alligator embryos and juvenile crocodiles was investigated. The results indicate that cell death caused the loss of this circuit in crocodiles and is the likely explanation for this difference. However, a distinction between neuronal death and axonal re-modelling could not be determined.

Article.Title: Loss of APOBEC1 disrupts RNA editing homeostasis and accelerates prion disease progression
Article.Authors: Karagianni K.; Kanata E.; Kovatsi E.; Pettas S.; Topouzi M.; Xanthopoulos K.; Sklaviadis T.; Dafou D.
Article.Abstract: Background: RNA editing is an epitranscriptomic mechanism that shapes transcriptome diversity and fine-tunes neuronal function. While adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing by ADAR enzymes has been extensively studied in neurodegenerative disorders, the role of cytidine-to-uridine (C-to-U) editing catalyzed by APOBEC1 remains largely unexplored. Methods: We investigated the impact of APOBEC1 on RNA editing homeostasis and prion disease progression using complementary in vitro and in vivo models. Global RNA editing and gene expression profiles were established in non-infected N2A and prion-infected sc-N2A murine neuroblastoma cells, under control conditions or following APOBEC1 depletion. APOBEC1 was silenced by shRNA-mediated knockdown to assess its regulatory contribution. In vivo disease progression was assessed in Apobec1 knockout mice subjected to RML prion infection to evaluate survival outcomes. Results: Prion infection was associated with a global increase in RNA editing and an expanded repertoire of edited transcripts in sc-N2A cells. APOBEC1 depletion markedly reduced the overall editing levels, affecting both A-to-I and C-to-U editing events, reshaping editing patterns in transcripts associated with RNA and protein transport, cellular stress responses, synaptic signaling, and neuroimmune interactions. Consistently, Apobec1 KO mice exhibited accelerated body weight loss and significantly shortened survival following RML prion challenge. Conclusions: These findings support APOBEC1 as a contributor to RNA editing homeostasis and suggest that APOBEC1 loss reduces resilience to prion-induced neurodegenerative stress. APOBEC1 deficiency was associated with altered editome profiles in prion-infected cells and accelerated disease progression in the RML prion model.

Article.Title: Neuroprotective potential of safinamide against LPS-induced neuroinflammation and cognitive dysfunction in mice
Article.Authors: Kasaraneni R.; Gurram P.; Narne S.; Babiker M.; Salah A.; Narayanarao Alla N/A.; Rebello A.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation, a key pathological hallmark of neurological diseases, contributes to neurodegeneration, synaptic dysfunction, and cognitive decline. Safinamide shows toll-like receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory effects in cellular models; however, it's in vivo neuroprotective and neuroinflammatory effects remain unexplored. In the present investigation, the anti-neuroinflammatory impact of safinamide was evaluated in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced mice using behavioral, biochemical, and histopathological assessments. LPS was administered intraperitoneally from days 8 to 15 to induce neuroinflammation, followed by 15 days of safinamide treatment at 10 mg/kg and 20 mg/kg. Safinamide 20 mg/kg significantly improved spatial and recognition memory, as evidenced by the percentage alternation in the Y-maze and recognition index in the novel object recognition test. Furthermore, safinamide significantly reduced the levels of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), phosphorylated NF-κB (p-NF-κB), NLRP3, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, acetylcholinesterase (AChE), and malondialdehyde (MDA), and increased levels of glutathione (GSH), catalase, and superoxide dismutase (SOD). Histopathological analysis revealed decreased amyloid-β deposition and preservation of neuronal architecture. These findings suggest that safinamide modulates neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress pathways and exhibits promising neuroprotective potential against inflammation-associated cognitive impairment.

Article.Title: Sivelestat sodium improves post-resuscitation brain outcomes possibly by inhibiting cell pyroptosis via inactivating the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway
Article.Authors: Ying P.; Zhou T.; Hu Y.; Luo Y.; Xu J.; Wu X.
Article.Abstract: Sivelestat sodium (SS) is shown to protect vital organs against regional ischemic stimuli. We investigated its effects on brain outcomes after global ischemic stimuli resulted from cardiac arrest (CA) and resuscitation. Adult pigs were randomly divided into sham (S), cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), and CPR + SS groups. The animals were subjected to 9 mins of CA followed by 6 mins of CPR. After resuscitation, a dose of 10 mg/kg of SS was intravenously administered for 60 mins. Post-resuscitation brain injury and neurological function were regularly evaluated. Brain hippocampus tissues were harvested to measure histopathological injury, cell apoptosis, pyroptosis-related proteins and proinflammatory cytokines, and the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway. Consequently, post-resuscitation brain injury and neurological dysfunction were observed in those animals experiencing the CA/CPR procedure. However, they were significantly milder in the CPR + SS group than in the CPR group. Hippocampal histopathological injury and apoptosis were observed after resuscitation in the CPR and CPR + SS groups. Nevertheless, SS treatment significantly decreased both of them compared with the CPR group. Furthermore, pyroptosis-related proteins were upregulated, its-related proinflammatory cytokines were increased, and the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway was activated in post-resuscitation hippocampus in the CPR and CPR + SS groups. Likewise, SS treatment significantly reversed the changes of pyroptosis-related proteins and proinflammatory cytokines, and the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway compared to the CPR group. Thus, SS treatment was effective in improving post-resuscitation brain outcomes, and its protective role was possibly related to the inhibition of cell pyroptosis through the inactivation of the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway.

Article.Title: Endpoint-specific interactions between aerobic exercise and benfotiamine in chronic noise-induced prefrontal cortical dysfunction in mice
Article.Authors: Ziari H.; Shaki F.; Seyedabadi M.; Safarzade A.; Amiri F.
Article.Abstract: Chronic environmental noise can impair brain redox and inflammatory homeostasis, but the effects of combined non-pharmacological and metabolic interventions remain unclear. This study investigated whether aerobic exercise and benfotiamine, separately or combined, attenuate noise-induced behavioral dysfunction and prefrontal cortical injury-related changes. Male Swiss albino mice were assigned to Control, Noise, Noise + aerobic exercise, Noise + benfotiamine (200 mg/kg/day), Noise + aerobic exercise + benfotiamine, or Noise + N-acetylcysteine (500 mg/kg/day) groups (n = 9/group). Noise-exposed mice received broadband industrial noise at 90 dB sound pressure level for 4 h/day for 28 days. Behavioral despair-like phenotypes, cortical redox status, inflammatory gene expression, and histopathology were evaluated. Noise increased immobility in the forced swim and tail suspension tests, elevated reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, malondialdehyde, protein carbonyls, and pro-inflammatory transcripts, and reduced glutathione and antioxidant capacity. Both interventions attenuated multiple abnormalities. Aerobic exercise produced prominent behavioral effects and increased interleukin-10 expression, whereas benfotiamine strongly reduced reactive oxygen species, lipid peroxidation, and interleukin-1β. Significant exercise × benfotiamine interactions occurred for both behavioral tests, reactive oxygen species, tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-10, but not for several other endpoints. The combined intervention frequently produced the most favorable absolute values, although significant interactions were generally subadditive rather than synergistic. Aerobic exercise and benfotiamine therefore provide broad but endpoint-specific protection against chronic noise-associated prefrontal cortical dysfunction.

Article.Title: Repeated ketamine administration induces cross-tolerance to sodium salicylate but not to morphine in male rats
Article.Authors: Moghimian M.; Fathi A.; Ebadi A.; Mansouri S.; Shafaei-Bajestani N.; Abtahi-Evari S.; Gholami M.
Article.Abstract: Cross-tolerance profiles provide critical insights into shared neurobiological substrates among analgesics. This study evaluated whether repeated sub-anesthetic ketamine administration induces cross-tolerance to morphine or sodium salicylate. Thirty-six adult- male Wistar rats (180-200 g, n = 6/group) received either normal saline or ketamine (10 mg/kg, i.p.) once daily for 8 consecutive days. Antinociceptive thresholds were assessed daily using the hot-plate test (52 ± 0.5 °C) at 45 min post-injection and expressed as the percentage of maximum possible effect (MPE%). On day 9, acute cross-tolerance challenges were conducted using morphine (10 mg/kg, i.p.) or sodium salicylate (300 mg/kg, i.p.). Serum malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity were measured on day 8 to evaluate systemic oxidative status. Repeated ketamine administration produced a progressive decline in MPE%, demonstrating marked antinociceptive tolerance by day 8. On day 9, morphine maintained full antinociceptive efficacy in ketamine-pretreated rats, indicating no cross-tolerance. Conversely, sodium salicylate-induced antinociception was significantly blunted, confirming cross-tolerance. Biochemically, ketamine pre-treatment did not elevate serum MDA and preserved SOD activity substantially better than morphine. In conclusion, repeated sub-anesthetic ketamine administration induces antinociceptive tolerance and selective cross-tolerance to sodium salicylate, while sparing morphine responsiveness. These behavioral adaptations parallel a favorable redox balance, highlighting distinct pharmacodynamic mechanisms governing ketamine interactions with opioid versus non-opioid regimens.

Article.Title: Zinc activates autophagy by regulating HDAC6 expression following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Yang N.; Yang X.; Zhao H.; Yan F.; Zhu Y.; Shi W.; Ding M.; Zhao Y.
Article.Abstract: Intracellular zinc accumulation and excessive autophagy have been reported to contribute to neuronal death following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R). Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), which contains a zinc-dependent active site, is closely associated with autophagy. However, the relationship between zinc, HDAC6 and autophagy following cerebral I/R remains unclear. In this study, we aim to investigate whether ischemia-induced zinc accumulation activates autophagy through HDAC6. Rats were treated with zinc chelator, autophagy activator/inhibitor or HDAC6 inhibitor during a 90-minute middle cerebral artery occlusion. Infarct volume, neurological deficits, protein expression, and the colocalization of HDAC6, Beclin1, and zinc in neurons were evaluated. Our results demonstrate that beclin1 expression was significantly increased after cerebral I/R and this elevation was markedly attenuated by zinc chelation. Notably, reactivation of autophagy with rapamycin significantly, though not completely, diminished TPEN-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting that zinc-induced autophagy is an important contributor to neuronal injury following cerebral I/R. Moreover, immunofluorescence revealed that HDAC6 was colocalized with Beclin1 in the penumbra of ischemic rats, and inhibition of HDAC6 reduced Beclin1 expression and alleviated brain injury. Molecular docking analysis suggested a potential interaction between HDAC6 and α-tubulin, which may influence autophagy by regulating microtubule stability and autophagosome transport. Furthermore, chelating zinc decreased HDAC6 expression, while HDAC6 inhibition did not influence zinc levels, demonstrating that zinc acts upstream of HDAC6. In conclusion, our findings identify a novel zinc-HDAC6-autophagy signaling axis underlying neuronal injury following cerebral I/R, suggesting that targeting zinc homeostasis or HDAC6 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy.

Article.Title: RGS6 is a key regulator of itch in female mice
Article.Authors: P. Blount A.; Gavagan S.; Jawhar L.; Sutton L.
Article.Abstract: Pruritus, commonly known as itch, is a protective somatosensory sensation whose dysregulation is a common feature of many pathologic conditions and can severely impact quality of life. Despite its clinical relevance, itch perception is among the least well known of all somatosensory modalities. G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) in pruritic circuits are key modulators of itch, however the intracellular regulators of GPCR signaling in itch circuits remain largely unexplored. Regulators of G protein signaling (RGS) proteins are vital modulators of GPCR signaling and may influence itch processing in histaminergic and non-histaminergic circuits. Here we report that RGS6, a member of the R7 RGS protein family, modulates itch through both histaminergic and non-histaminergic mechanisms in female mice. Using global knockout mouse models, we show that this anti-pruritic phenotype is specific to RGS6, with no comparable effect in RGS7, highlighting functional specificity within the R7 RGS family. This study uncovers a regulatory role of RGS6 in modulating pruritus in females and provides critical insights into mechanisms fundamental to acute and pathological itch.

Article.Title: A drug repurposing-based mechanistic study of ilepcimide against febrile seizures
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Zhao J.; Yang L.; Tian K.; Cheng S.; Cai Z.; Kong D.; Zhang W.
Article.Abstract: Febrile seizures are the most common childhood paroxysmal neurological disorder. Although ilepcimide is used for pediatric epilepsy, its efficacy in febrile seizures remains unknown. Here, we investigated the effects and mechanisms of ilepcimide in a juvenile mouse model of febrile seizures using network pharmacology, molecular docking, brain slice electrophysiology and patch-clamp recordings of transfected cells. Ilepcimide prolonged seizure latency and reduced EEG spike-wave frequency. Network pharmacology linked its targets to glutamatergic synaptic signaling. Molecular docking further predicted that ilepcimide could target two subunits of AMPA receptor. In acute hippocampal slices, ilepcimide suppressed CA1 pyramidal neuron firing, increased rheobase, and prolonged action potential half-width. In HEK293T cells expressing GluA1/GluA2, it prolonged AMPAR deactivation and desensitization time constants. These results suggest that ilepcimide protects against febrile seizures through a multi-faceted mechanism: modulation of glutamatergic transmission, reduction of hippocampal excitability, and altered AMPA receptor gating. This study offers new target predictions and experimental evidence supporting the extended use of ilepcimide in pediatric febrile seizures.

Article.Title: Voltage-sensitive dye imaging reveals chronic peri-infarct hyperexcitability after MCAO in mice
Article.Authors: Kato J.; Dezawa S.; Tominaga T.; Higo N.; Takashima I.
Article.Abstract: Plastic changes in the peri-infarct cortex are thought to play a key role in post-stroke functional recovery, yet the circuit-level mechanisms underlying such reorganization remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated chronic changes in perilesional cortical excitability and synaptic organization using a mouse model of middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO). Evoked cortical activity was assessed by voltage-sensitive dye (VSD) imaging following direct cortical stimulation. The ischemic hemisphere exhibited significantly greater response amplitude and broader spatial spread than the non-ischemic hemisphere, indicating enhanced perilesional cortical excitability. Immunohistochemical analyses focused on superficial cortical layers, the primary source of VSD signals, revealed significant increases in both excitatory (VGLUT1-positive) and inhibitory (VGAT-positive) synaptic markers, with a greater increase in excitatory inputs, resulting in a shift in the excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) balance toward excitation. Reduced NeuN-positive neuronal density was also observed, suggesting concurrent neuronal degeneration. These findings demonstrate chronic peri-infarct hyperexcitability after MCAO and suggest that altered synaptic E/I balance may contribute to persistent changes in cortical network responsiveness. This circuit-level reorganization may represent an important mechanism underlying post-stroke plasticity and a potential target for therapeutic modulation.

Article.Title: Peripheral endotoxemia is associated with microglial activation, neuronal apoptosis, and amyloid precursor protein accumulation
Article.Authors: Niu L.; Yang C.; Li Y.; Qu C.; Guo L.; Wu H.; Zhao L.; Zhang J.; Lu F.; Zhu J.; Liu M.
Article.Abstract: Chronic microglial activation and the resulting neuroinflammatory cascade drive Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression. Systemic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) triggers robust microglial responses and is linked to neurodegenerative disorders, yet the full spectrum of neuroinflammatory and neuronal changes associated with chronic peripheral endotoxemia remains incompletely characterized. We hypothesized that sustained peripheral endotoxemia establishes a neuroinflammatory environment characterized by microglial activation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuronal apoptosis, accompanied by amyloid precursor protein (APP) accumulation. We analyzed public transcriptomic datasets for inflammatory signatures associated with LPS exposure in BV2 microglia (GSE18740) and mouse brain tissue (GSE3253). HT22 neurons were exposed to conditioned medium from LPS-stimulated BV2 cells, and apoptotic markers were measured. Adult rats received repeated systemic LPS injections over six months to model chronic endotoxemia; brain sections were then analyzed by immunohistochemistry for CD68 (microglial activation), cleaved caspase-3 (apoptosis), and APP. Inflammatory-related pathways were consistently upregulated across datasets. Conditioned medium from activated microglia increased neuronal apoptosis. Both LPS-treated microglial cells and HT22 neurons cultured with BV2-conditioned medium exhibited increased reactive oxygen species production and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential. The endotoxemia model exhibited cortico-hippocampal microgliosis, elevated cleaved caspase-3, and APP accumulation. These results support the hypothesis that peripheral endotoxemia probably propagates microglial hyperactivation, which subsequently promotes neuronal apoptosis and APP accumulation. Whether modulation of the inflammation-related pathways identified here can attenuate this microglia-mediated neurodegeneration warrants dedicated investigation.

Article.Title: Nrf2 overexpression ameliorates cognitive deficits and neuronal damage in APP/PS1 mice via attenuation of Aβ deposition and neuronal ferroptosis
Article.Authors: Zhu X.; Bo J.; Qian Y.; Diao F.; Liang H.; Fan L.; Su Y.; Li W.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid-beta (Aβ) deposition, yet the mechanisms underlying Aβ-induced neuronal damage remain elusive. Emerging evidence implicates ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death, in AD pathology. We hypothesized that dysfunction of the Nrf2 pathway critically links Aβ deposition to neuronal ferroptosis and cognitive decline. In this study, AD progression in APP/PS1 mice was associated with progressive cognitive impairment, Aβ accumulation, and neurodegeneration. Aged APP/PS1 mice exhibited marked suppression of the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway, accumulation of reactive oxygen species, and prominent hallmarks of ferroptosis, including elevated DMT1 and TfR expression, accompanied by reduced GPX4 and xCT expression. Remarkably, genetic overexpression of Nrf2 significantly ameliorated cognitive impairment, attenuated neuronal and synaptic loss, and concurrently reduced Aβ deposition, oxidative stress, and neuronal ferroptosis. These findings demonstrate that Aβ accumulation is associated with impaired Nrf2 signaling during AD progression, leading to oxidative stress, neuronal ferroptosis, and cognitive dysfunction. Collectively, these findings suggest that activation of the Nrf2 pathway exerts robust protective effects against AD-like pathology, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic strategy for AD.

Article.Title: Maternal separation reshapes layer-specific PV-PNN architecture in the mouse barrel cortex
Article.Authors: Zhan X.; Miao J.; Chu P.; Tan P.; Chen C.
Article.Abstract: Early-life adversity alters inhibitory circuit maturation across developing brain systems, but most studies have focused on corticolimbic regions involved in emotional and cognitive regulation. Whether early adversity also reshapes inhibitory extracellular matrix architecture in primary sensory cortex remains less clear. Here, we examined the effects of maternal separation on parvalbumin-positive (PV+ ) interneurons and Wisteria floribunda agglutinin-labeled perineuronal nets (PNNs) in the mouse primary somatosensory barrel cortex (S1BF), a highly organized sensory region in which laminar position carries clear developmental and functional significance. Mice underwent daily maternal separation from postnatal day 1 to 14, and PV/PNN anatomical features were analyzed in young adulthood. PV density, PNN density, PV/PNN co-labeled cell density, and PNN-only density were quantified across layers 2/3, 4, and 5/6 of S1BF. Maternal separation did not alter PV+ interneuron density in any cortical layer. Instead, its effects were selective to PNN-related measures in layer 4, where both PNN density and PV/PNN co-labeled cell density were significantly increased. By contrast, PNN structures not associated with PV cells remained unchanged, indicating that the increase in PNN density was predominantly associated with PV-labeled interneurons. These findings show that maternal separation does not produce a generalized loss of PV-PNN architecture in barrel cortex. Rather, early adversity selectively enhances PV-associated PNN organization in the principal thalamorecipient layer of S1BF. This layer-specific pattern suggests that early-life stress may alter the timing or distribution of plasticity and stabilization within primary sensory circuits, with potential consequences for how tactile information is filtered and integrated during cortical maturation.

Article.Title: Single-housed, but not pair-housed, male and female rats demonstrate social conditioned place preference
Article.Authors: Bensing P.; Bowers C.; Moosa I.; Leong K.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the factors that modulate social reward has important implications for conditions characterized by social dysfunction, including autism spectrum disorder and social anxiety disorder. Social isolation is particularly relevant, given rising rates of subjective loneliness and social disconnection in the United States. The present study investigated the impacts of isolation on social reward by testing the effects of single- versus pair-housing on social conditioned place preference (sCPP) in adult male and female Sprague-Dawley rats. Across a ten-day paradigm with eight conditioning days, rats were trained in a two-chamber apparatus in which one chamber was repeatedly paired with a same-sex, weight-matched littermate, while the other chamber served as an unpaired control. Pair-housed rats were co-housed with their conditioning partner for the duration of the study. Single-housed, but not pair-housed, rats of both sexes developed a significant preference for the social-paired chamber. These findings indicate that housing condition modulated sCPP expression in adult male and female rats.

Article.Title: Prior trauma shapes the effects of psilocybin on stress sensitization in mice
Article.Authors: Ottofaro S.; Maltman J.; González-Maeso J.
Article.Abstract: Exposure to traumatic events induces persistent alterations in defensive behavior that extend beyond associative fear memories, including heightened responses to novel stimuli (stress sensitivity) and sustained defensive states in neutral contexts (stress sensitization). While serotonergic psychedelics such as psilocybin have been shown to facilitate fear extinction in associative paradigms, their effects on trauma-induced non-associative stress adaptations remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a behavioral paradigm in mice that dissociates contextual fear recall from stress sensitivity and stress sensitization within the same subjects. Male C57BL/6J mice were exposed to an acute foot-shock stressor, followed by assessment of trauma recall, administration of psilocybin (1 mg/kg) or vehicle, and subsequent evaluation of responses to a novel auditory stimulus and context. Trauma-exposed mice displayed robust associative fear and increased freezing in response to a novel auditory stimulus, consistent with enhanced stress sensitivity. However, psilocybin did not significantly alter this stimulus-evoked response. In contrast, psilocybin produced bidirectional, experience-dependent effects on stress sensitization - it reduced baseline freezing in non-traumatized mice but increased freezing in trauma-exposed animals when re-exposed to a novel context in the absence of a stimulus. Together, these findings demonstrate that psilocybin does not uniformly attenuate trauma-related behaviors, but instead modulates non-associative defensive responses in a manner dependent on prior experience. This work highlights the importance of distinguishing between associative and non-associative components of fear and suggests that psychedelic-induced plasticity may amplify latent trauma-related states under certain conditions.

Article.Title: Left DLPFC activation in the association between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms in college students
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Wu Y.; Yang M.; Xi M.; Si S.; Zhang W.
Article.Abstract: The prevalence of depressive symptoms among college students continues to rise. It has been shown that individuals with higher psychological resilience generally exhibit fewer depressive symptoms. The aim of this study is to examine potential associations between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms in college students and to explore the statistical mediating role of brain activation in this relationship. 140 college students received functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) scans while completing a verbal fluency task (VFT). Psychological scales, oxyhemoglobin (HbO) concentration, partial correlation and mediation analyses were processed. Partial correlation analysis showed that psychological resilience was significantly negatively associated with depressive symptoms. The activation of HbO in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC; CH23), right DLPFC (CH3), and right orbitofrontal cortex (OFC; CH6) were significantly positively correlated with psychological resilience and negatively correlated with depressive symptoms. Further mediation analyses demonstrated a significant indirect association between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms through activation in the left DLPFC (CH23). The findings suggest that the left DLPFC may be involved in the relationship between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms in college students. Future longitudinal or intervention studies are needed to further clarify the causal relationships among these variables.

Article.Title: Efficacy of chitosan-encapsulated carbamazepine on seizures induced by pentylenetetrazole kindling
Article.Authors: Roudini F.; Kohsari I.; Derakhshan M.; Nazemi S.; Azhdari-Zarmehri H.; Mohammad-Zadeh M.
Article.Abstract: Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced kindling is an established model for investigating seizure mechanisms and evaluating the efficacy of antiepileptic drugs. Novel drug delivery systems, such as nanoparticles, offer improved therapeutic outcomes by enhancing brain bioavailability and reducing adverse effects. This study investigated the effects of chitosan-encapsulated carbamazepine nanoparticles on seizure activity in PTZ-kindled mice compared with the free form of the drug. Male BALB/c mice were divided into three groups: PTZ-kindled control, PTZ + free carbamazepine, and PTZ + chitosan-encapsulated carbamazepine. Seizure stage, Stage latencies 1 and 4, seizure duration, and mortality were assessed using a modified Racine scale. The results showed that while free carbamazepine temporarily reduced seizure stage, its effect diminished over time. In contrast, the chitosan-encapsulated formulation significantly reduced seizure stage, seizure duration, prolonged latencies, and completely prevented seizure-induced mortality. Characterization of the optimized nanoparticles revealed a mean particle size of 65 nm, a polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.21, a zeta potential of -34.5 mV, and an entrapment efficiency of 55.35 %, indicating favorable stability and delivery properties. Overall, this study demonstrates that chitosan‑based nanoencapsulation of carbamazepine enhances its antiepileptic efficacy in a PTZ‑kindling model, suggesting its promise as a potential therapeutic strategy for epilepsy.

Article.Title: Varlitinib attenuates neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neurodegeneration in experimental Parkinsonism
Article.Authors: Lim H.; Park J.; Lee W.; Park G.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation mediated by microglial activation plays a critical role in Parkinson's disease (PD), with the NLRP3 inflammasome contributing to dopaminergic neurodegeneration. Varlitinib, a clinically developed pan-human epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor, has been investigated as an anticancer agent; however, its therapeutic potential in PD remains unknown. Here, we evaluated the neuroprotective effects of varlitinib in in vitro and in vivo PD models. BV2 microglial cells were stimulated with α-synuclein and 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium and treated with varlitinib. Varlitinib significantly improved cell viability, reduced lactate dehydrogenase release, and suppressed IL-1β and IL-18 production. Co-treatment with the selective NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 produced no additional anti-inflammatory effects, suggesting that NLRP3 inflammasome signaling contributes, at least in part, to varlitinib's actions. In a 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine-induced mouse model of PD, varlitinib significantly improved motor performance, reduced microglial activation in the substantia nigra and striatum, and preserved tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons. Collectively, these findings support varlitinib as a potential drug-repurposing candidate for PD.

Article.Title: Analysis of the participation and influence of the cerebellum in emotion and emotional memory processing in mice through c-Fos expression
Article.Authors: Prati J.; de Russo T.; Lepesteur Gianlorenço A.
Article.Abstract: The cerebellum's involvement in non-motor functions, such as emotional and cognitive processes, has been gaining attention. The functional topography of the cerebellum remains inconclusive, and both clinical and preclinical studies have aimed to identify it to achieve a better understanding of cerebellar neurophysiology and its influence on other brain structures in different functions. The aim of this study was to analyze activation in cerebellar lobules IV-V, VI and VII under different context and temporal conditions of an inhibitory avoidance (IA) task, and to assess the association between c-Fos expression in these lobules and in other brain regions involved in emotional and memory processing. Thirty-three naïve Swiss Albino mice were exposed to the IA box for 1, 4, and 8 days. After the final exposure of each group to the evaluation apparatus, euthanasia was performed, followed by transcardiac perfusion and brain removal. Immunofluorescence analysis of c-Fos in pre-established structures was performed. Significant c-Fos/DAPI ratio was observed in cerebellar lobules IV-V and VI in animals that performed IA task for 4 days. No significant difference in c-Fos expression was found in the other regions of interest. Spearman's Correlation Coefficient test did not indicate any associations between the c-Fos/DAPI ratios across the regions of interest. These results suggest that cerebellar lobules IV-V and VI may be differentially recruited during the IA task, although their specific involvement in emotional and emotional memory processing remains to be determined.

Article.Title: Anillin functions in distinct glial subtypes to support larval locomotion in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Huynh M.; Dang T.; Thao Dang T.; Yoshida H.
Article.Abstract: Anillin (Ani)/Scraps has a well-characterized function in cytokinesis and has recently been shown to play a role in the nervous system. Ani is expressed in neuroblasts, axons, and neuromuscular junctions in the Drosophila larval nervous system, and pan-neuronal ani knockdown impairs both larval and adult behaviors. However, despite the expression of ani in glial cells, its function in these cells remains unclear. In the present study, we therefore investigated the role of ani in Drosophila glial cells by performing pan-glial ani knockdown and assessing the subsequent effects on larval and adult behaviors. Ani was expressed in a subset of glial cells, including in the central and peripheral nervous systems, and expression levels varied across individual cells. Pan-glial knockdown of ani significantly impaired larval and adult locomotion, larval learning ability, and adult activity; however, it did not affect lifespan. Although ani depletion decreased the number of glial cells in the central nervous system, it did not disrupt neuropil formation. In the peripheral nervous system, ani knockdown increased the total length of neuromuscular junctions. Subtype-specific knockdown analyses suggested that Ani functions in endoreplicating subperineurial and wrapping glia to support larval locomotion. The results also suggested a possible role for Ani in astrocyte-like and ensheathing glia, although the evidence is inconclusive. In contrast, Ani did not appear to have an obvious role in cortex glia or actively proliferating perineurial glia for larval locomotion. Together, these findings indicate that ani exerts both canonical and non-canonical roles in Drosophila glial cells.

Article.Title: Increased CCR2-immunopositive myeloid cells in the putamen and cerebellar white matter with blood–brain barrier disruption in multiple system atrophy
Article.Authors: Okada N.; Togawa N.; Ishimoto T.; Ayaki T.; Maki T.; Matsumoto R.
Article.Abstract: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia, and autonomic dysfunction. Recently, a close relationship of neuroinflammation to MSA pathogenesis was identified. Studies in mouse models of MSA have indicated that peripheral-type myeloid cells and endogenous microglia promote neuroinflammation in MSA. However, their distinct roles in MSA pathogenesis remain unknown. We performed immunohistochemical analyses of brain tissues obtained at autopsy from patients with MSA and age-matched controls to examine the putamen and cerebellar white matter with antibodies against CCR2 (a chemokine receptor expressed by monocyte-lineage cells), TMEM119 for microglia, and fibrinogen for blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage. The CCR2-immunopositive area was significantly increased in both regions in MSA patients compared to controls (putamen, p = 0.0043; cerebellar white matter, p = 0.0438); however, the TMEM119-immunopositive area showed no significant between-group difference (putamen, p = 0.4220; cerebellar white matter, p = 0.8152). The densities of CCR2-immunopositive areas in the putamen and cerebellar white matter were positively correlated (Pearson's r = 0.7325, p = 0.0248). In the putamen, fibrinogen immunoreactivity and perivascular leakage were increased and showed a distribution similar to that of CCR2 immunostaining (p = 0.0398). These findings suggest that CCR2-immunopositive myeloid cell accumulation in regions with BBB dysfunction may involve recruitment of peripheral monocyte-lineage cells.

Article.Title: Neural mobilization combined with a polylactic acid conduit enhances functional and morphological recovery following median nerve repair
Article.Authors: Cardoso F.; Pestana F.; Taboada T.; Silva B.; Campos N.; Souza D.; Oliveira J.; Abreu C.; Mendonça H.; Almeida F.; Blanco Martinez A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Peripheral nerve transection repaired with a poly(lactic acid) (PLA) conduit remains associated with incomplete functional recovery. Neural mobilization (NM) may enhance nerve regeneration, but its optimal timing and effects remain unclear. This study investigated how NM timing affects nerve regeneration and functional recovery after median nerve transection and PLA conduit repair. Methods: Nineteen young adult female Wistar rats underwent median nerve transection and repair using a 10-mm PLA conduit to bridge an 8-mm gap. Animals were assigned to control (no mobilization) or NM groups initiated 1, 5, or 30 days after surgery. Mobilization consisted of scapular depression and forelimb movements for 10 min, three times weekly. Recovery was assessed using von Frey and grip strength tests, electrophysiological, histological, morphometric, and muscle analyses 8 weeks after surgery. Results: NM effects were time-dependent, with mobilization initiated 5 days after surgery producing the most favorable functional and electrophysiological outcomes. This timing improved grip strength, mechanical sensitivity, and CMAP amplitude without affecting latency. NM also enhanced axonal regeneration and increased the proportion of myelinated fibers, but did not significantly affect angiogenesis, myelin thickness, or muscle atrophy. Conclusions: Initiating NM 5 days after nerve repair may represent a favorable therapeutic window following severe peripheral nerve injury. NM at this time point improved functional, electrophysiological, and structural outcomes, although it did not significantly affect muscle atrophy or myelin thickness. These findings support NM as a time-dependent therapeutic approach and provide a basis for further investigation of its translational potential future clinical studies and applications.

Article.Title: Selective vulnerability of the spinal cord in a rat model of asphyxia-induced cardiac arrest
Article.Authors: Lee S.; Shin H.; Kim R.; Lee J.; Sabuj M.; Kim I.; Ahn D.; Tae H.; Kim S.; Yoon J.; Lee J.; Park B.
Article.Abstract: Spinal cord injury after cardiac arrest (CA) can cause devastating neurological deficits, including paraplegia. Although lumbar spinal cord injury is clinically important, regional comparisons remain limited. In this study, we examined region-associated vulnerability of the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord using a rat model of asphyxial CA (ACA). Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent sham surgery or ACA, and thoracic and lumbar spinal cord tissues were collected 24 h after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) from ACA survivors with hindlimb paralysis. Histopathological analysis demonstrated significantly fewer surviving neurons in the lumbar compared with the thoracic spinal cord after ACA. The lumbar spinal cord also showed higher BAX/BCL2 ratios and cleaved caspase-3 expression, together with increased phosphorylation of NF-κB and mitogen-activated protein kinases, including p38, extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK). Exploratory transcriptomic comparison between ACA-L and ACA-T identified 292 upregulated and 187 downregulated DEGs. Enrichment analyses indicated that upregulated DEGs were associated with extracellular matrix-receptor interaction, focal adhesion, integrin signaling, and PI3K-Akt signaling, whereas downregulated DEGs were associated with nervous system development and myelination. Collectively, these findings demonstrate region-dependent molecular and histopathological alterations at 24 h after ROSC, with a more pronounced injury-associated inflammatory and apoptosis-related profile in the lumbar spinal cord of paralyzed ACA survivors.

Article.Title: A neonatal low-dose streptozotocin rat model of a prediabetic phenotype produces metabolic, peripheral nerve, and locomotor alterations
Article.Authors: Alvarado-Cervantes N.; Velasco-Gutiérrez R.; Martínez-Rojas V.; Raya-Tafolla G.; Vidal-Cantu G.; Galindo-Gómez S.; Granados-Soto V.; Delgado-Lezama R.
Article.Abstract: Prediabetes is a state of impaired glucose regulation that precedes diabetes and is increasingly recognized to harbor early metabolic and neuropathic alterations. Because neuronal alterations at this stage may still be reversible, experimental models that reproduce early nerve changes are essential for investigating the mechanisms underlying disease initiation and progression. Here, we characterized a rodent prediabetic phenotype induced by a single low dose of streptozotocin in male and female rats. Treated animals developed a prediabetes-like metabolic profile characterized by moderate fasting hyperglycemia, glucose intolerance, elevated glycated hemoglobin, insulin resistance, lipid alterations, and a partial reduction in pancreatic β-cell islet area and cell density, all while maintaining normal body weight-key features that distinguish this model from diabetic phenotypes in rodents. Importantly, these metabolic alterations were accompanied by early increased expression of activating transcription factor 3 in dorsal root ganglion neurons, indicating neuronal damage. These pathological changes were associated with the progressive development of mechanical hypersensitivity and locomotor adaptations. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that low-dose streptozotocin induces a reproducible prediabetic phenotype in male and female rats that is accompanied by early peripheral nerve damage and functional sensory and locomotor alterations. This prediabetes-like phenotype provides a useful tool for investigating the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving early nerve dysfunction and for evaluating therapeutic strategies aimed at preventing the transition from a prediabetic state to diabetic disease.

Article.Title: SHANK3 drives abnormal neurodevelopment in iPSC-derived 2D and 3D brain models of Phelan-McDermid Syndrome
Article.Authors: Gao M.; Huo M.; Zhang H.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Phelan-McDermid Syndrome (PMDS) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by 22q13.3 deletion involving SHANK3. While SHANK3 is critical for synapses, its role in early human neurodevelopment remains elusive. Here, we generated induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived 2D neuronal cultures and 3D cerebral organoids from two twin Phelan-McDermid syndrome patients with a 1.7 Mb 22q13 deletion encompassing SHANK3 gene. PMDS organoids showed reduced volume due to impaired neural progenitor cells (NPCs) proliferation. PMDS NPCs exhibited biased differentiation with decreased excitatory neurons but increased GFAP+ astroglia and GABAergic neurons. PMDS neurons displayed simplified morphology, reduced synapse density and diminished excitability. Importantly, lentiviral-mediated SHANK3 overexpression largely rescued these defects. Our findings identify SHANK3 as a key regulator of early neurodevelopment and provide mechanistic insights into PMDS pathogenesis.

Article.Title: Choline attenuates lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation in the BV-2 microglial cell line via the α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor/nuclear factor kappa-B signaling pathway
Article.Authors: Xia Z.; Wang D.; Qiu X.; Huang S.; Wen Y.; Huang Y.
Article.Abstract: Objective: This study aimed to investigate the potential mechanisms by which choline (CHO) attenuates lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced neuroinflammatory responses in BV-2 microglial cells through network pharmacology-based prediction and in vitro experiments. These neuroinflammatory responses are implicated in the pathophysiology of sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE). Methods: Putative CHO targets were retrieved from PubChem, the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD), and SwissTargetPrediction, while SAE-associated genes were sourced from OMIM and GeneCards. Overlapping targets from both datasets were subjected to protein-protein interaction (PPI) network construction, along with Gene Ontology (GO) functional annotation and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment, to identify core candidate genes and key signaling cascades. The predicted outcomes were subsequently verified by in vitro experiments, including cell viability assays, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), immunofluorescence, quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), and Western blot. Results: An intersection of 672 SAE-associated genes and 109 CHO-responsive genes yielded 24 common targets. Among them, TNF, IL10, IL6, MMP9, and IL1B were identified as potential hub therapeutic targets. KEGG enrichment analysis revealed the involvement of multiple pathways, with the nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) cascade being particularly notable. In cell-based assays, CHO administration reduced the levels of pro-inflammatory mediators (TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) and concurrently increased those of anti-inflammatory markers (IL-4, IL-10, and CD206). Furthermore, CHO elevated α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR) expression while suppressing IκBα and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation. Treatment with the α7nAChR antagonist methyllycaconitine citrate (MLA) reversed these effects. Conclusions: CHO may inhibit microglial neuroinflammation and promote anti-inflammatory polarization, potentially via the α7nAChR/NF-κB signaling pathway.

Article.Title: Association of midbrain IL-6 with impaired nest-building behavior and therapeutic effect of Ninjin’yoeito in old hindlimb-unloading mice
Article.Authors: Matsubara Y.; Mizuno K.; Yakabe M.; Ogawa S.
Article.Abstract: Psychiatric symptoms can substantially impact rehabilitation outcomes in older patients with disuse syndrome. However, the mechanisms underlying these psychiatric symptoms remain poorly understood, and no established treatment is currently available. This study used hindlimb unloading (HU) as a model of disuse syndrome in old male mice to evaluate the effects of Ninjin'yoeito (NYT), a traditional Japanese herbal medicine. After 2 weeks of HU, old mice underwent the nest building test to evaluate goal-directed behavior, and the open field and elevated plus maze tests to assess anxiety-like behavior. Compared to age-matched sham mice, HU-subjected mice showed declines in nest building and locomotor activity but no appreciable anxiety-like behavior during reloading period. Seven days after HU, IL-6 expression was elevated in the midbrain and was co-expressed with microglia in the ventral tegmental area (VTA). In young mice, intra-VTA injection of IL-6 impaired nest building behavior. In activated primary microglial cultures, NYT reduced IL-6 mRNA expression. During recovery from HU, repeated NYT administration improved nest building and motor function while reducing midbrain IL-6 protein levels in old mice. These findings suggest that elevated IL-6 expression in midbrain/VTA is associated with the impairment of goal-directed behavior after HU and that this impairment can be attenuated by NYT. Collectively, these preclinical findings suggest that pharmacological intervention may provide a therapeutic approach for psychiatric-like behavioral changes associated with disuse syndrome.

Article.Title: Multiscale Neurodynamic Alterations in Major Depressive Disorder Revealed by Lempel–Ziv Complexity of Multi-Paradigm Resting-State EEG
Article.Authors: He Y.; Qi H.; Zhang Z.; Huang J.; Yang J.
Article.Abstract: Background: Electroencephalography (EEG) abnormalities in major depressive disorder (MDD) have predominantly been examined through single-frequency band analyses or single-scale nonlinear measures, and largely within a single resting-state paradigm, which limits the characterization of regulatory interactions across temporal scales. In this study, we investigated dynamic transitions and integrative patterns of multiscale EEG activity in MDD across multiple resting-state paradigms, with a focus on characterizing alterations in multiscale neural dynamic organization. Methods: Based on multiscale Lempel–Ziv Complexity (LZC), we derived two classes of features quantifying the Scale-Dependent Variation Slope and the Cross-Scale Correlation Coefficient. Resting-state EEG from the MDD Patients and Healthy Controls EEG Data (MPHC) was analyzed under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions to compare multiscale regulatory dynamics between patients with MDD and healthy controls. Results: Patients with MDD showed impaired complexity transitions from low to high frequencies and disrupted delta-centered cross-scale integration. Distinct coupling reconfiguration patterns emerged across resting states, indicating a systemic imbalance in multiscale integrative organization. Classification models built from statistically selected features performed consistently across Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbor, and Decision Tree algorithms, reaching a maximum accuracy of 85.71% with a balanced sensitivity–specificity profile. Convergent results across models further suggested the preliminary discriminative value of the proposed features within the present dataset. Conclusions: These findings provide a preliminary multiscale neurodynamic framework for EEG characterization in MDD and suggest that cross-scale integration differences may provide a quantitative basis for characterizing multiscale EEG dynamics in depression.

Article.Title: A Support Vector Machine Method With Correlation-Based Recursive Feature Elimination for the Early Diagnosis of Alzheimer’s Disease
Article.Authors: Zhong H.; Sheng J.; Zhang Q.; Gong Z.; Zhang R.; Sun Z.; Zhu X.; Cheng Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder where early diagnosis is critical. While magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides valuable structural information, most methods rely solely on imaging features, limiting clinical interpretability. Methods: A novel feature selection method using support vector machine with correlation factor-based recursive feature elimination and cross-validation (SVM_CF_RFECV) integrated correlation factors from mini-mental state examination (MMSE) scores into the feature weighting process is proposed for the early identification of Alzheimer’s disease. This approach balances statistical discriminative power with clinical relevance and mitigates the local-optimum issue of traditional recursive feature elimination (RFE). Results: Using the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset, the proposed method achieved a peak accuracy of 87.5% in a single-split experiment and an average accuracy of 0.8489 ± 0.0330 across multiple random partitions, outperforming conventional SVM_RFECV. The selected 74 discriminative brain regions, including the hippocampus and cingulate cortex, align with established AD pathology. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate that SVM_CF_RFECV provides both accuracy and interpretability, supporting its potential as a clinically meaningful tool for early AD diagnosis.

Article.Title: Electroacupuncture in Post-Stroke Cognitive Impairment: A Review From the Perspective of Programmed Cell Death
Article.Authors: Xiang S.; Jin Y.; Liu J.; Chen Y.; An H.
Article.Abstract: Stroke remains a leading cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide, and post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is among its most prevalent and debilitating sequelae. Accumulating evidence suggests that electroacupuncture (EA) modulates dysregulated programmed cell death (PCD) after stroke, including apoptosis, autophagy, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis, which play central roles in neuronal loss, synaptic disruption, and cognitive decline. Specifically, EA may suppress excessive neuronal apoptosis and ferroptosis, modulate autophagic activity, and attenuate pyroptosis-associated neuroinflammation. However, the mechanisms underlying the effects of EA in PSCI remain fragmented, and the lack of standardized treatment protocols limits its clinical translation. In this review we integrate clinical findings with molecular and cellular evidence to propose a unified mechanistic framework in which EA may improve cognitive function and may act through modulation of multiple PCD pathways. We further highlight EA as a potential multi-target and network-oriented intervention with therapeutic potential in stroke rehabilitation, providing a mechanistic basis for future studies and standardized clinical application.

Article.Title: The Role of Drosophila Toll Receptors in the Central Nervous System
Article.Authors: Ma Z.; Xu J.; Yu X.; Wang X.; Gu Q.; Meng H.
Article.Abstract: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are evolutionarily conserved pattern recognition receptors that play pivotal roles in innate immunity by detecting pathogen-associated molecular patterns. While initially characterized for their function in dorsoventral patterning and antifungal defense in Drosophila, the Toll family is now understood to have undergone a functional expansion in the nervous system. This review synthesizes the current understanding of the nine Drosophila Toll receptors (Toll-1 to Toll-9) and their roles in the central nervous system (CNS). We discuss how these receptors, particularly through non-canonical signaling pathways, function as neurotrophin receptors and cell surface recognition molecules. They mediate a wide range of cellular processes, from axon guidance to synaptic partner matching and the regulation of neuronal survival versus apoptosis through the competitive recruitment of adaptor proteins such as dMyD88 and Sarm. We further explore the involvement of Toll signaling in adult brain structural plasticity, sleep homeostasis, and behavioral responses to environmental stressors such as ethanol. Importantly, this article addresses the context-dependent duality of Toll signaling in neuropathology, dysregulation, and aberrant activation, which are closely related to neurodegeneration, lifespan determination, and infection responses. Through this timely summary of current research, this review highlights the molecular switches that govern Toll receptor functional states and their roles in neuro-immune interactions, with implications for understanding neurological diseases in vertebrates.

Article.Title: Rhes as a Potential Modulator of PINK1/Parkin-Dependent Mitophagy in Huntington’s Disease
Article.Authors: Saim M.; Al-Kazzaz H.; Ahmad H.
Article.Abstract: Huntington’s disease (HD) is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by cytosine-adenine-guanine (CAG) repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene, resulting in progressive motor, cognitive, and psychiatric impairment. Despite the widespread expression of mutant huntingtin (mHTT), disease progression is characterized by the selective degeneration of striatal neurons. Mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy have emerged as important contributors to HD pathogenesis; however, the mechanisms underlying defective mitochondrial quality control remain incompletely understood. Ras homolog enriched in the striatum (Rhes), a small striatal-enriched guanosine triphosphatase (GTPase), has been implicated in mitophagy-related signalling. In this study, we examined the potential relationship between Rhes and PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1)/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in HD. We propose that Rhes contributes to selective striatal vulnerability by promoting mitochondrial depolarization through BCL2 interacting protein 3-like (NIX/BNIP3L), facilitating activation of the PINK1/Parkin mitophagy pathway, while enhancing autophagosome biogenesis through Beclin-1 signalling. If validated, our proposed pathway would open new avenues for therapeutic development in HD.

Article.Title: Automated Proofreading of Digitally Reconstructed Neural Morphology Enhances Accuracy, Scalability, and Standardization
Article.Authors: Emissah H.; Tecuatl C.; Ascoli G.
Article.Abstract: Background: The rapid expansion of large-scale neuroscience datasets has increased the need for automated, accurate, and standardized quality control (QC). Manual proofreading of 3-dimensional neural morphology (SWC files) remains labor-intensive, error-prone, and non-scalable. We developed and evaluated a fully automated, machine-learning–driven QC pipeline to standardize neural reconstructions, detect and correct structural anomalies, and rectify dendritic labeling in pyramidal neurons. Methods: We developed an end-to-end, cloud-deployed pipeline for automated QC, correction, and standardization of SWC-formatted neural morphologies. The framework integrates deterministic structural normalization, topology repair, geometric correction, quantitative morphometric analysis, and graph-based dendritic relabeling within a containerized React/Flask architecture deployed on Amazon Web Services. Rule-based algorithms systematically detect, classify, and correct structural irregularities including overlapping nodes, spurious side branches, non-positive radii, disconnected components, and anomalously long parent-child connections. A graph convolutional network, trained on Sholl-derived features from 20,500 pyramidal neurons, performs dendritic relabeling. Model training employed an 80/10/10 train–validation–test split with adaptive learning-rate scheduling and distributed execution across ten runs to evaluate stability and reproducibility. The pipeline generates images of the final product and computes quantitative morphometrics using L-Measure. Results: All neural reconstructions were processed without manual intervention. Automated normalization and topology repair improved structural consistency and standardized neuronal morphologies for quantitative analysis and visualization while preserving topological and morphological continuity throughout the correction process. Dendritic relabeling achieved a test classification accuracy of 99.51%, calculated from 2040 correctly classified neurons out of 2050 test neurons (2040/2050 × 100 = 99.51%). The test dataset comprised a separate 10% partition of the 20,500-neuron dataset, resulting from the 80/10/10 training–validation–test split, with no overlap between the three subsets. The mean validation accuracy across ten training runs also reached 99.51% at the final epoch, with class-weighted precision of 0.978 and recall of 0.977. Validation accuracy increased rapidly during the initial epochs, exhibited a transient decrease at epoch 15 and subsequently recovered and stabilized by epoch 50. Enforcing a single apical dendritic tree per neuron improved anatomical consistency without reducing classification performance. Distributed training completed all runs in approximately 25 hours, demonstrating scalability and reproducibility for large datasets. Conclusions: We present an automated, cloud-scalable open-source pipeline for standardizing neural reconstructions and performing biologically consistent dendritic classification with high accuracy. The automated correction and relabeling procedures do not alter or compromise the size or unaffected morphological detail of the original SWC files, ensuring geometric fidelity and compatibility with downstream analysis tools. This open-access framework provides a robust foundation for high-throughput neural morphology curation and large-scale neuroanatomical analysis.

Article.Title: Resting-State EEG Graph Analysis Reveals Enhanced Alpha-Band Integration in High-IQ Individuals: The MENSA-Connect Project
Article.Authors: Moci M.; Zauli A.; Iacovelli C.; Reale G.; Garbuglia M.; Cacciatore E.; De Grandis M.; Tomaino A.; Rossi S.; Caliandro P.
Article.Abstract: Background: To assess whether resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) connectivity differs between high-intelligence individuals (MENSA members) and controls using graph-theory metrics: clustering coefficient, characteristic path length, and small-worldness. Methods: Resting-state 64-channel EEG data were recorded in 29 MENSA participants and 20 controls. Functional connectivity was estimated using Lagged Linear Coherence across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Graph-theory measures were computed using sLORETA and the Brain Connectivity Toolbox. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test; p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure, and effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Results: Compared with controls, MENSA participants showed significantly lower characteristic path length in the alpha band (Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) critical value = 0.004), indicating greater global network integration. In the beta band, they showed a higher clustering coefficient (BH critical value = 0.008), reflecting greater local specialization; together with a higher characteristic path length (BH critical value = 0.013), suggesting reduced global communication. No significant group differences were observed in small-worldness across frequency bands. Conclusions: High-Intelligence Quotient (IQ) individuals show a frequency-dependent resting-state cortical organization, characterized by enhanced alpha-band integration and increased beta-band local specialization. These findings support a nuanced neural-efficiency model of intelligence without changes in small-world architecture. Given the cross-sectional and observational design, these findings should be regarded as associative rather than causal and require replication in larger, independent samples. These findings indicate frequency-specific differences in functional network organization, although their cognitive implications remain to be established.

Article.Title: Pharmacological modulation of the striatal mGluR5–NR2B association attenuates L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia in 6-OHDA lesioned parkinsonian rats
Article.Authors: Zhao L.; Fu R.; Zhu X.; Qian W.; E Y.; Zheng Z.; Lin J.
Article.Abstract: Objective: The clinical utility of L-DOPA is severely limited by the development of L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). Although metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5) antagonists alleviate LID, the underlying molecular mechanisms, particularly those involving striatal glutamate receptor crosstalk, remain incompletely understood. Methods: Adult female Sprague-Dawley rats with unilateral 6-OHDA lesions were randomized into Sham, PD, LID, MTEP, and MK-801 groups (n=6/group). L-DOPA/benserazide was given twice daily for 14 days, with MTEP or MK-801 30 min before each dose. AIMs, open-field activity, striatal mGluR5-NR2B co-immunoprecipitation, PKC/MEK/ERK phosphorylation, and c-fos/Pdyn mRNA were assessed. Behavioral and molecular data were analyzed by mixed models, ANOVA, or Kruskal-Wallis tests.Results: We observed aberrant elevation of the mGluR5-NR2B interactions in the striatum of 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA)-lesioned parkinsonian rats exhibiting LID. Administration of the mGluR5 antagonist MTEP or the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801 reduced the co-immunoprecipitated association, reduced the synaptic association of mGluR5 with NR2B, and markedly attenuated LID severity. Mechanistically, the decoupling of these receptors was accompanied by decreased ERK1/2 phosphorylation, reduced PKC protein expression, and decreased L-DOPA-induced c-fos and prodynorphin mRNA levels. Furthermore, abnormal involuntary movement (AIM) scores significantly correlated with the extent of NR2B-mGluR5 interaction and downstream signaling activation. These findings suggest that increased mGluR5-NR2B association is associated with LID and may contribute to its expression. Conclusion: The therapeutic efficacy of MTEP or MK-801 is likely mediated by reducing this receptor interaction and downstream signaling, highlighting a potential molecular target for LID treatment.

Article.Title: IL-17 aggravates the neuroinflammatory response in depression by regulating microglial polarization through the JAK1/STAT3 signaling pathway
Article.Authors: Wei Y.; Xiao Y.; Xu Y.; Yuan J.
Article.Abstract: Background: Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation is closely related to the development of depression. As a proinflammatory cytokine, IL-17 plays a key role in various neuroinflammatory diseases. This study aimed to investigate the potential molecular mechanisms through which IL-17 affects neuroinflammation in depression through the regulation of microglial polarization. Methods: A chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced mouse model of depression and an LPS-treated BV2 cell model were used. The depression-like behavior of the mice was evaluated using the sucrose preference test (SPT), tail suspension test (TST), and forced swim test (FST). Neuronal injury was assessed using HE staining. The levels of neurotransmitters and inflammatory cytokines were analyzed using ELISA. Microglial polarization was analyzed by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence, and the expression of IL-17A and JAK1/STAT3 pathway-related proteins was assessed using Western blotting. Results: IL-17 was highly expressed in clinical specimens from patients with depression, mice treated with CUMS and BV2 cells. The inhibition of IL-17 improved depression-like behavior in CUMS-treated mice, reduced neuronal damage, and increased the expression of the neurotransmitters 5-HT, NE, and DA. In addition, IL-17 inhibition inhibited M1 microglial polarization and inflammation. In terms of molecular mechanisms, IL-17 promoted microglial M1 polarization by activating the JAK1/STAT3 signaling pathway and aggravating neuroinflammation related to depression. The use of the JAK/STAT pathway activator RO8191 attenuated the inhibitory effect of IL-17 inhibition on microglial M1 polarization. Conclusion: IL-17 activates JAK1/STAT3 signaling, promotes M1 microglial polarization, and aggravates neuroinflammation related to depression.

Article.Title: Association of metabolic insulin resistance with white matter hyperintensity burden and plasma proteomic signatures in the UK Biobank
Article.Authors: Si X.; Qi X.
Article.Abstract: Background: Metabolic insulin resistance is closely related to cardiometabolic dysfunction and vascular injury. Its association with subclinical cerebral small vessel disease, and the circulating molecular signals that may accompany this association, remain incompletely characterised. Methods: We analysed 59,826 UK Biobank participants with brain magnetic resonance imaging to examine the association between the metabolic score for insulin resistance (METS-IR) and white matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden. Associations were evaluated using multivariable linear regression and restricted cubic spline analysis, with spline models restricted to participants with complete covariate data. Proteomic data were available for 6,790 participants. Protein-wide association analyses, functional annotation and LASSO prioritisation explored circulating protein links between METS-IR and WMH burden, followed by exploratory mediation models in 1,309 participants with complete model data. Results: Higher METS-IR was associated with greater WMH burden after adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle and vascular risk factors. Complete-case spline analysis suggested a nonlinear association, with steeper fitted slopes at higher METS-IR values. Proteomic screening identified 1,266 proteins associated with METS-IR and 122 proteins associated with WMH after false discovery rate correction, yielding 119 overlapping proteins. These proteins were enriched for immune-inflammatory processes and cell adhesion. LASSO prioritisation selected eight candidate proteins, and exploratory mediation models yielded indirect-effect estimates for selected proteins, with GAL showing the largest estimated proportion mediated. Conclusions: METS-IR was associated with WMH burden after adjustment for measured covariates in this large UK Biobank analysis. Integrated plasma proteomic analyses identified immune-inflammatory and cell-adhesion signals that may help characterise molecular correlates of metabolic insulin resistance and cerebral small vessel disease burden.

Article.Title: The diagnostic dilemma of Acute Vestibular Syndrome: why HINTS outperforms diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging?
Article.Authors: Bayar Muluk N.
Article.Abstract: Objectives: To evaluate the diagnostic approaches, specifically the comparative accuracy of bedside clinical examinations versus early neuroimaging, in differentiating central from peripheral causes of Acute Vestibular Syndrome (AVS). Methods: A comprehensive narrative literature review was conducted utilizing established scientific databases, including PubMed/Medline, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase, covering articles published up to 2024. A structured search strategy was applied using keywords such as 'Acute Vestibular Syndrome', 'Central vestibular dysfunction', 'Peripheral vestibular dysfunction', and 'HINTS protocol'. Peer-reviewed clinical trials, mechanistic studies, and authoritative guidelines were included to synthesize the current evidence regarding the diagnosis and management of acute vertigo. Results: The synthesis of the literature reveals that targeted bedside neuro-otological examinations demonstrate superior sensitivity (96.8%) and specificity (98.5%) compared to early 'Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging' in detecting posterior circulation strokes within the initial 48 h. Early neuroimaging frequently yields false-negative results in up to 14.3% of ischemic events. Conclusion: Accurate differentiation of etiologies in continuous vertigo relies heavily on structured bedside clinical assessments rather than immediate neuroimaging. Implementing these clinical protocols prevents severe neurological sequelae from missed posterior fossa strokes while simultaneously avoiding unnecessary healthcare expenditures for benign peripheral conditions.

Article.Title: miR-665 Ameliorates Neuroinflammation After Intracerebral Hemorrhage by Modulating Myeloid Cell Polarization via Targeting STAT3
Article.Authors: Huang Z.; Yang Y.; Sun B.; Luo J.; Yang Y.; Zou D.; Cui Y.; Wang L.; Ma Y.
Article.Abstract: Background Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation contributes to secondary injury after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), but the role of miR-665 remains unclear.Methods An ICH rat model was established. A combination of techniques, including Neurological scoring, brain water content measurement, histology and molecular assays were employed to assess miR-665, the STAT3/NF-κB pathway, myeloid polarization and inflammation. Stereotaxic miR-665 agomir/antagomir delivery verified its function. The targeting relationship between miR-665 and STAT3 was confirmed by a dual-luciferase reporter assay. In vitro experiments were performed in Hemin-stimulated BV2 cells with miR-665 mimics/inhibitor, followed by flow cytometry detection of cell polarization and inflammatory factor analysis. Rescue experiments with STAT3 overexpression were conducted both in vivo and in vitro.Results After ICH, miR-665 was downregulated andinduced excessive activation of the STAT3/NF-κB signaling axis in peri-hematomal tissue, accompanied by M1-like/pro-inflammatory myeloid cell polarization and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines. Upregulation of miR-665 ameliorated neurological function, reduced brain edema, promoted M2-like/repair-associated polarization, and suppressed inflammation, whereas miR-665 downregulation aggravated injury. Dual-luciferase assay confirmed that miR-665 directly targets STAT3. In vitro, miR-665 overexpression inhibited STAT3 phosphorylation and further suppressed the downstream NF-κB signaling, reversing the Hemin-induced M1-like/pro-inflammatory polarization. STAT3 overexpression counteracted the protective effects of miR-665.Conclusion Downregulated miR-665 after ICH exacerbates neuroinflammation by promoting M1-like/pro-inflammatory myeloid cell polarization via disinhibition of STAT3 and subsequent activation of NF-κB signaling. Upregulating miR-665 exerts neuroprotection by inhibiting STAT3 phosphorylation and facilitating M2-like/repair-associated myeloid cell polarization, highlighting the miR-665/STAT3 regulatory cascade as a promising therapeutic target for post-ICH neuroinflammation.
